units.tr: To my most gracious lord.

units.la: QUAM in Cyro, Persarum regni fundatore, uberius Xenophon diduxerat, succinctè in Agesilao boni Principis, & omnium ex honestate animi operationum, ideam Græca fide depinxit.
units.tr: What Xenophon had set out at greater length in Cyrus, the founder of the Persian kingdom, the Greek writer portrayed concisely in Agesilaus, the ideal of a good prince and of all actions that flow from an upright mind.

units.la: Animi magnitudinem in inferendo Persis bello, in perrumpenda militari itinere Macedonia, claustris Thessalia aperiendis; fortitudinem in conflictuum ardore; justitiam & erga deos pietatem in servanda induciarum fide exprompsit. Prompsit æqualitatem in socios, mansuetudinem in victos, munificentiam in gves[?], moderationem in victoriarum cursu. Supra Græca lascivia licentiam, frugalis in victu & laborum tolerans, veneris & jocorum luxuriam compescuit. Quarum e laudum cumulo autoritatem ei vivo, defuncto memoriæ per universum orbem monumenta facundus autor erigit.
units.tr: He displayed greatness of spirit in waging war against the Persians, in forcing a military passage through Macedonia, and in opening the gates of Thessaly; he displayed courage in the heat of battle, and justice and piety toward the gods in keeping faith with a truce. He displayed fairness toward his allies, gentleness toward the conquered, generosity toward the people, and moderation in the course of his victories. Beyond the Greek licence for wantonness, he restrained luxury in pleasure and love by his frugality in diet and his endurance of hardship. From this heap of praises the eloquent author raises a monument to his authority while he lived and to his memory throughout the whole world after his death.

units.la: Nos à Græcorum elegantia Romanæ ad historiæ fidem stylo converso, Taciti candore duce ita virtutes Tiberii in theatrum producimus, ut nec aspersas animo aut fortunæ labes absque censura dimittamus. Quod si Rhodi secessum, si Caprearum latibula, si su-spicacem tristitiam, forensem judiciorum tabem, ut pulchro corpori nævos exemeris: cæteris in rebus nec animi excellentia, nec fortunæ successu Agesilao cesserit. Certe nec injusta ac patriæ exitiosa bella movit, nec Sparta sibi commissa ruinam, tot per ætates inconcussa, vidit.
units.tr: We, having turned the Greek elegance into Roman prose faithful to history, and with the candour of Tacitus as our guide, bring the virtues of Tiberius onto the stage in such a way that we do not let pass without censure the stains cast upon his character or his fortune. But if you remove, as one would remove moles from a fair body, his retreat to Rhodes, his hiding in Capri, his suspicious gloom, and the corruption of the law courts, then in other respects neither the excellence of his mind nor the success of his fortune would have yielded to Agesilaus. Certainly he did not begin unjust wars ruinous to his country, nor did Sparta, which stood unshaken through so many ages, see its ruin entrusted to him.

units.la: Te vero, Serenissimum magnanimæ Cattorum nationis principem, ita virtutum Tiberii participem gaudemus, ut macularum incapacem nobis & universis gratulemur. Quod felicitatis est, partis bellorum messe non interpellatus fructus: quod prudentiæ, bellis non necessarius, futurorum spe deluforia, te non immisces: quod fortitudinis, bella, si ingruant, gerenda non reformidas. Ad pietatis vero in Deum, ad charitatis in cives, ad justitiæ in omnes, ad clementiæ in lapsos contentionem nevoto quidem Tiberius pervenit. Quæ cum sint aliorum plenis tibiis decantata, ad incudem reducere, quasi in curæ aut ingenii certamen, non allaboro. Ad ea, quibus Tiberius[?] nondum corruptum principatum exprimis, minus lu-xuriantem calamum restringo.
units.tr: But we rejoice that you, most serene prince of the magnanimous nation of the Chatti, share in the virtues of Tiberius, so that we congratulate ourselves and all people on your being free of his blemishes. As for good fortune, you reap the fruit of wars without being disturbed by the harvest of battles; as for prudence, you do not involve yourself in wars that are unnecessary, nor are you lured by the illusory hope of the future; as for courage, you do not shrink from waging wars when they break upon you. Tiberius did indeed attain, though not by wish alone, to the striving after piety toward God, love toward citizens, justice toward all, and clemency toward the fallen. Since these things have been sung to the full pipes of others, I do not labour to bring them back to the anvil, as though they were a contest of care or talent. Concerning those matters in which you express a principate not yet corrupted by Tiberius, I restrain a pen that is less extravagant.

units.la: Bellorum formidandos in pace abortus, ne longius incremento proserpant, provida solertia à patriis limitibus amoliris. Nec sumptibus pro pace retinen-da, nec munificentia pro dignitate parcis. Nunquam prudentiam casui, nec judicium temeritati committis. Convenientem imperantis majestati venusta-tem, laboriosò corporis exercitio fovendam, non asper-naris.
units.tr: You remove the dreaded outbreaks of war in time of peace, by provident skill, from the borders of your country, lest they creep further as they grow. You are sparing neither in expenditure for keeping the peace nor in generosity befitting your dignity. You never entrust prudence to chance, nor judgment to rashness. You do not disdain the graceful bearing that suits the majesty of a ruler, which is to be cherished by laborious exercise of the body.

units.la: Imperii tui vires, nec minus vires hostium, & fœ-dera offerentium cum voluntate facultates, maturè metiris. Curarum radios, non uno loci situ concludendos, ad multa simul dispergis. Infecundarum fluxu alteram fortunam, tanquam præsentem, contempla-ris. Luxum, intima reip. viscera corrosurum, legum severitate comprimis. Ærarium inanibus in hi-strionias delusiones erogationibus, & pudendis pota-tionum certaminibus, minus, pro more seculi, exhau-ris. Rebus in aula, in curia, in militia administran-dis capaces rerum viros præficis. Nec paupertatem ignominia, nec opulentiam subditorum incutienda formidine [?]sectaris.
units.tr: You measure in good time the strength of your empire, and no less the strength of your enemies and of those who offer alliances with goodwill. You do not confine the rays of your cares to one place, but spread them over many things at once. You regard the other fortune, the one that is present, as contemptible, because of the flow of unprofitable things. You check luxury, which would gnaw at the inner vitals of the state, by the severity of the laws. You drain the treasury less, as is the custom of the age, through empty expenditures on theatrical trifles and shameful contests of drinking. You put in charge of affairs at court, in the council chamber and in the army men capable of managing things. You pursue neither poverty with contempt nor the wealth of your subjects with frightening terror.

units.la: Fanis religioso cultui dicatis, & honestarum ar-tium officinis lycéis, aperiendis incrementa & sum-ptus porrigis. Inconcussam, domi & foris, pacem bel-li triumpho gloriosiorem ducis. Serenitate vultus & sermonis, opportuna severitate interveniente, cum gravitate venerationem retines. Nec promiscuam religionum colluviem in ditione tua sponte toleras, nec sanguine diversa sententium pasceris. Ut publi-ca tuorum tranquillitati prospicis, ita annonae labo-ranti provida solertia occurris. Humani fastigii modulum excedentes honores, & divinarum occupatio-num appellationes, aversaris. Ut insolentiam in te sermonis non amas, ita adulationes reprimis. Sermo-nes de te vulgi ut non omnino negligis, ita non anxie scrutaris. Minus tibi, quam theatrali plebi, morum licentia permittis. Tuos rumore vano perculsos, contra insultus excubando, confirmas. Nec hosti quidem, quod de te jure conqueratur, integri-tate fidei loco mota, suggeris. Judiciorum sanctimo-niam, utraque parte non propense audienda, confirmas. Nihil hic irae, nihil gratiae, nihil auri cupiditati largiris. Atrocitate poenarum delicta non excedis, nec morbos intempestive saviendo exasperas. Quod potes, poenae gravitatem mitigas: sed nec impunitate scelera proserpere permittis. Nunquam te damnatorum bonis, nunquam hereditatum aucupiis, aut fiscum tuum locupletas. Leges ex usu temporum, non ex rigore apicum, interpretaris. Nec in oblecta-mento solicitudinem, nec in secessu curam reipublicae deponis. In lapsu morum seculi, non temere quod fulgure casurum nequeas attractas. Spem veniae ad sanam mentem rediturus non praecidis. Securitatem civium, pacis armata contubernio, suspendis. Patrum cognitiones & honores, absoluto arbitrii jussu obumbratos, non deprimis. Nec amicos, & in consilii commucommunicationem semel admissos, in horam ut Ver-tumnus mutas. Lenitudine promenda tua injuria offensas, non aliena largiris. Hominem in summa felicitate te esse recordaris: nec tamen claritatem famae negligis. Cujus fomento magnos in eruditione viros alis, & adscribendum donis provocas. Hæc & his plura, quae in Tiberio solertia doctorum hominum miratur, æterna vindicatione possides.
units.tr: You extend growth and expenditure to the opening of temples dedicated to religious worship and of the workshops and lyceums of honourable arts. You regard peace, undisturbed at home and abroad, as more glorious than triumph in war. With serenity of countenance and speech, and with timely severity intervening, you keep respect by dignity. You do not of your own accord tolerate in your dominions a promiscuous mixture of religions, nor do you feed on the blood of those who hold differing opinions. As you look to the public tranquillity of your people, so you meet the distress of the grain supply with provident skill. You avoid honours that exceed the measure of human rank, and titles that belong to divine occupations. As you do not love insolence of speech toward yourself, so you suppress flattery. You do not altogether neglect the talk of the common people about you, yet you do not anxiously search it out. You permit less licence of morals to yourself than to the theatrical crowd. By keeping watch against attacks you strengthen those whom empty rumour has shaken. You do not even bring forward against an enemy, who has no just cause for complaint about you, any pretext that would shake the integrity of your faith. You confirm the sanctity of judgments, which must be heard with neither party favoured. Here you grant nothing to anger, nothing to favour, nothing to the desire for gold. You do not exceed the proper measure of crimes by severity of punishment, nor do you exasperate diseases by cruelty applied at the wrong time. As far as you can, you soften the harshness of punishment, yet you do not permit crimes to creep forward through impunity. You never enrich your treasury with the goods of the condemned, nor with the hunting for inheritances. You interpret the laws according to the needs of the times, not according to the rigour of the letters. You lay aside concern for the state neither in pleasure nor in retirement. Concerning the decline of morals in the age, you do not rashly seize upon what you cannot prevent from falling like lightning. You do not cut off the hope of pardon for one who is about to return to a sound mind. You keep the security of citizens suspended in the company of an armed peace. You do not depress the judgments and honours of the senators, which are overshadowed by the command of unrestrained will. You do not, like Vertumnus, change friends and those once admitted to the sharing of counsel within an hour. You grant pardon for offences by yielding, with gentleness, your own injuries, not those of others. You remember that you are a man, even in the height of happiness, and yet you do not neglect the brightness of fame. By fostering it you nourish great men in learning and you invite them to be enrolled among your gifts. These things, and more besides, which the learned men admire in the skill of Tiberius, you possess by eternal vindication.

units.la: Sed nescio quomodo praesentia invidia, praeterita veneratione prosequimur; & his nos obrui, illis instrui credimus. ut in re simili verbis Paterculi abutar.
units.tr: But somehow we pursue the present with envy and the past with veneration, and we believe that we are crushed by the one and instructed by the other, as I may misuse the words of Paterculus in a similar matter.

units.la: Quae enim in prioris aevi viris admiraculi fastidium stupemus, ea in vita nobiscum fruentibus absque livore, saltem silentio, non intuemur. Sed bene quod te, Principum Celsissime, virtutum con-stantia Tiberius non assequitur; tu illum vitiorum fuga longe superas. Non enim ut in laudum te, sic vi-tuperii cum Tiberio contentionem accersimus. Non tu clarorum in aula tua, aut in militia, virorum magnis progressibus invides; non lege majestatis exa-cerbata, servos in dominorum capita instigas. Non, honorum & familiaritatis decipulis, incautos in perniciem irretis. Non senatusconsulta in alienum sensum, interpretationum novitate, detorques: non illice facultatum, accusatione circumventorum, quadruplatores allicis. Non cavillatione senatores, non simulatione intimos deludis. Non Sejanum aliquem in propinquorum necem, non Macronem illustrium fa-miliarum pestem, evehis. Non Caprearum foedis latebris[?] amorum monstra senex meditaris: nec, quod illis est proximum, clamore accusantis conscientiæ pro-deris.
units.tr: For what we marvel at with weary disdain in the men of an earlier age, we do not look upon in those who live with us, enjoying it without envy, or at least without silence. But it is well that the steadfastness of your virtues, most exalted of princes, does not reach that of Tiberius; you far surpass him in flight from vices. For we do not summon you into a contest with Tiberius in praises, nor in blame. You do not envy the great progress of illustrious men in your court or in your army; you do not, by a harshly applied law of treason, incite slaves against the heads of their masters. You do not ensnare the unwary into ruin with the snares of honours and familiarity. You do not twist decrees of the senate toward an alien meaning by the novelty of interpretations; you do not, by the allurement of wealth, draw in informers who prey on those entangled in prosecutions. You do not mock senators with ridicule, nor deceive your intimates with pretence. You do not raise up some Sejanus for the murder of kinsmen, nor a Macro, the ruin of illustrious families. You, an old man, do not plan the monstrous loves of Capri in its foul hiding-places, nor, what is nearest to these, do you betray yourself by the outcry of an accusing conscience.

units.la: Ista fiducia inducto, non diu dispiciendum fuit, cui principum Germaniæ, cui externorum principum, AULAM Tiberianam ex more temporum nostrorum consecrarem. Non enim verendum erat, ne aut dissimilitudine morum Tiberii, aut nimia in quibusdam similitudine, vitam legenti exprobrarem. Non enim ex eorum te numero, Princeps de tuis & de honesto optimè merite, iudicabam, qui magnitudinem fortunæ suæ delinquendi licentia metiuntur.
units.tr: Led on by this confidence, I did not long need to consider to which of the princes of Germany, or to which of the foreign princes, I should dedicate the AULA Tiberiana, in the manner of our times. For there was no need to fear that I might upbraid the life of the reader either by the dissimilarity of Tiberius's morals, or by too great a likeness in some respects. For I did not judge you, Prince, who have deserved well of your own people and of what is honourable, to be among those who measure the greatness of their fortune by the licence to do wrong.

units.la: Quanquam igitur honestè actæ & agendæ vitæ præ-mia à prædicatione famæ non exspectas, interiori ani-mi plausu beatus: unius tamen loci & seculi unius am-bitu, quantum in me est facultatis, laudum tuarum radios coërceri non patiar. Si quas igitur hæc operis nostri confectio, favore lectorū pronubo, pulsabit nationum fores: si spiritum post fata nostra scriptum hoc producet: sera te gentium posteritas, cum aulæ norma principe collatum, multis antiquorum præferendum mirabitur. Vive, vige, exemplar boni Principis & me tibi cum opere sacratum suscipe.
units.tr: Although, therefore, you do not look for the rewards of an honourably conducted and continuing life from the proclamation of fame, and you are content with the inner applause of your own mind, nevertheless, within the compass of one place and one age, I shall not allow the rays of your praises to be confined, so far as my ability reaches. If this completed work, with the favour of its readers as a go-between, knocks at the doors of nations, and if this writing, produced after our death, keeps its spirit alive, then late posterity of the nations, when it compares you with the standard of the court-prince, will wonder that you are to be preferred to many of the ancients. Live, flourish, be the pattern of a good prince, and receive me together with this work, consecrated to you.

units.la: Sic vovi, voveo, vovebo,
units.tr: So I have vowed, I vow, I shall vow.

units.la: S.T. fide plusquam clientelari devinctus
units.tr: Your most faithful servant, bound to you by a loyalty more than that of a client,

units.la: CYRIACUS LENTULUS.
units.tr: CYRIACUS LENTULUS.

units.la: SECUNDUS ANNALIUM TACITI liber per Aphorismos explicatus.
units.tr: THE SECOND BOOK OF TACITUS'S ANNALS, explained by aphorisms.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: BELLORUM femina, ne incremento proserpant, in primo ortu opprimenda.
units.tr: The seeds of wars are to be crushed at their first rising, lest they grow and spread.

units.la: NON enim quo orta est belli contagio principio subsistit. A simultate prima ad gentium strages, urbium ruinas, agrorum vastationes progressu se effundit. Nec intra populorum, armis pro jure disceptantium, limites pedem infaustum figit: vicinarum, & longè remotarum, nationum clades involvit. Ut aër vento commotus proximum, & hic ulteriorem, propellit; ut unda maris undam fluctu rapit: ita incessu se pascens bellorum rabies, non quo coepit terrarum angulo finitur. Mota, inquit Tacitus, Orientis regna, provinciasque Romanas; initio apud Parthos orta. Quocirca non sine cura esse debent vicinis populis, nonnunquam & remotioribus, mota in alieno regno arma. At si conflictus controversias armis decidentium impediri nequeat: quomodo se gerant finitimi, extra dissidiorum causam, non extra periculi aleam, positi? Acutioris judicii limæ pragmatici præceptum suggerunt, ut se alterutri parti adjungentes turbis immiscent: alioqui prædæ victoribus futuri: causamque armis foveant, in paribus potentia justio-rem, in dubiis potentiorem. Vicinia huic, & nescio an magis politicæ considerationis, suadendi ratio est, quæ apud Dionem Cassium, libro Romanarum historiarum 35, promittur. [illegible, ~55 letters] i. e. naturâ ita comparatum esse, ut omnis victor insatiabilis rerum secundarum desiderio feratur, neque ullum cupiditati finem statuat. Igitur in partes potius maturè veniendum, quam intuto inter efferatos otio desidem, dum decreta belli alea ad se veniatur, commorandum. At quid hoc aliud est, quam certum pro incerto periculum accersere, & inundationi dubiæ clau-stra, diruptis arenarum molibus, laxare. Græci dum se Romanorum ac Carthaginensium furiis ingerunt, vi-ctorem populum ad leges Græciæ scribendas provocant. Nostris ferè moribus vires, occultè aut palàm, inferiori suggeruntur: sufflamen incremento alterius injecturæ. Quod ne quidem barbarus Parthorum Æsymneta Arsaces, arcanum ignoravit, qui, ex utilita-te regni sui, neque Tigranis Armeniorum regis, neque Romanorum, potentiam victoriæ augeri exoptavit. [illegible, ~50 letters] i. e. bellum aquis utrinque viribus geren-dum, summa sibi securitati futurum arbitrabatur. Dio, lib.35.
units.tr: For the contagion of war does not stay where it first arose. From its first quarrel it spreads onward, bringing slaughter of nations, ruin of cities and devastation of fields. Nor does its unlucky foot stay within the borders of peoples who settle their rights by arms: it engulfs the defeats of neighbouring nations and of nations far away. As air stirred by the wind pushes the air beside it, and that in turn pushes the air further off, and as one wave of the sea carries the next with its surge, so the rage of war, feeding as it advances, is not confined to the corner of the earth where it began. "The kingdoms of the East and the Roman provinces were stirred," says Tacitus, "beginning among the Parthians." Therefore neighbouring peoples, and sometimes more distant ones, ought not to be unconcerned by arms stirred up in another's kingdom. But if conflict cannot be prevented from being settled by arms, "how are neighbours to conduct themselves, placed outside the cause of the quarrel but not outside the risk?" The precepts of more discerning, practical writers suggest that they should attach themselves to one side or the other and mix into the troubles; otherwise they will be the spoil of the victors. And they should foster the cause by arms, favouring the more just side where the matter is equal, and the more powerful where it is doubtful. Here the advice to neighbours rests on considerations of neighbourhood and, perhaps more, of political prudence, which is set out in Dio Cassius, book 35 of his Roman History. [illegible] That is, nature has so ordained that every victor is carried off by an insatiable desire for success, and sets no limit to his greed. Therefore one should come to a side early, rather than linger idly in unsafe leisure among the maddened, while the decision of war is left to chance and comes to oneself. But what is this other than to invite a certain danger in place of an uncertain one, and to loosen the barriers against a doubtful flood by breaking the dykes of sand? While the Greeks threw themselves into the furies of the Romans and the Carthaginians, they invited the victorious people to write the laws of Greece. In our customary way, strength is secretly or openly lent to the weaker side, a check placed on the growth of the other. Not even the barbarian Parthian Arsaces, Aesymnetes, was ignorant of this secret: for the advantage of his kingdom he wished the power of neither Tigranes, king of the Armenians, nor of the Romans to be increased by victory. [illegible] That is, he judged that a war waged with forces equal on both sides would be the greatest security for himself. Dio, book 35.

units.la: Tiberius pro rerum occurrentium varietate varius, aliquando fomitem flagranti incendio, dum arbitrum se gessit, occultè summisit. Sic Cheruscos per Drusum filium, ut victo jam Maroboduo usque ad exitium instaretur, illexit. Sæpiùs, ne quid compositi turbaretur, omnes bellorum segetes in primo grami-ne præcidit. Orientes res turbari haud ingrato accidit: ut eâ specie Germanicum suetis legionibus abstraheret, novisque provinciis impositum, dolo simul & ca-sibus objectaret. Tacitus infrà. Crudius est, quod in proditi Mithradatis negocio Romani quidam diffe-runt: rat: Omnescelus externum, cum latitia habendum: femina etiam odiorum jacienda. Annal. 13. ac multorum regum aliis pro excoêto sapientiae me-tallo exceptum.
units.tr: Tiberius, varying with the variety of events as they arose, sometimes secretly put fuel to a blazing fire while acting as arbiter. Thus he enticed the Cherusci through his son Drusus, so that, Maroboduus now defeated, they were pressed on to destruction. More often, so that nothing settled should be disturbed, he cut down all the crops of war while they were still in the first blade. It was not unwelcome that the affairs of the East should be troubled: "so that under that pretext he might draw Germanicus away from his accustomed legions, set him over new provinces, and expose him at once to treachery and chance." Tacitus, below. More cruel is what some Romans said in the affair of the betrayed Mithridates: "Every foreign crime is to be received with joy; women too are to be cast into hatreds." Annals 13. And many kings took up this maxim for other purposes, as a metal refined for wisdom.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Peregrini præ indigenis imperio gerendo non temere admovendi.
units.tr: Foreigners are not to be lightly set over natives in the government of an empire.

units.la: Peregrinitatem ista consideratione non tantum quidam incurrunt; sed & longa absentia, & vita institutis & moribus patriis adversa. Parthi pe-titum Romae acceptumque regem, quamvis gentis Arsacidarum, ut externum aspernabantur. Ex diutur-na cum Romanis, inter quos obses egerat, commoratione arguebant: degeneravisse Parthos, petitum alio ex orbe regem, hostium artibus infectum: jam inter provincias Romanas folium Arsacidarum haberi, darique. Ubi illam gloriam trucidantium Crassum, exturbantium Antonium: si mancipium Cæsaris, tot per annos servitutem perpessum, Parthis imperitet? Quibus verbis, cum peregrinitatis nota, animum in exteros inclinantem, & servitute delibata degenerem, non temere conjiciunt. Quod & Italo, cui genus e Flavio fratre Arminii fuit, apud Cherusos periculum creabat, frementes: adimi veterem Germaniae libertatem, & Romanus opes insurgere. adeo neminem iisdem in terris ortum, qui principii locum impleat: nisi exploratoris Flavii progenies supra cunctos attollatur? &c. infectum alimonia, servitio, cultu, omnibus externum. Nec de nihilo haec Cherusorum querela habebatur, quamvis non paucioribus factione diversa Italum secutus. Hoc enim Cæsaris Claudii de eo fuerat judicium: illum primum Romae ortum, nec obsidem, sed civem, ire externum ad imperium. En Germanorum imperium Italo, Germano patre nato, externum! Quod & in eadem natione patrum memoria Carolo V. Germano quidem patre, sed in Hispana ditione nato, & Hispana in aula educato, amorem & autoritatem imminuit. Alterum quod in Vonone Parthi dedignabantur, erat Vita maiorum institutis adversa. raro venatu, segni equorum cura: quoties per urbes incederet, lectica gestamine, fastuque erga patrias epulas. irridebantur & Graci comites, ac vilissima[?] utensilium anulo clausa, sed promti aditus, obvia comitas, ignota Parthis virtutes, nova vitia: & quia ipsorum moribus aliena, perinde odium pravis & honestis. h. l. Ita non modo molhitiem, parcimoniam, elegantiam Romano-græcanicam: sed ipsas novi principis virtutes, novitatis damnatos, ut vitia horrebant. Plus ita in odio aut amore conciliando familiaritas & vitæ institutio, quam natura & genus & ipse nativitatis locus, valent. Quod cum regni alterius damno, alterius acquisitione, expertus Sigismundus natione Suecus, vita & educatione Sarmata, cujus nunc filius Cafimirus hostilia Suecorum arma, non sine patriæ ruina, finibus Polonorum depellit. Pro iis, qui nativitate aut diuturna absentia peregrinos ad patriæ gubernacula accersunt, militat quidem ista ratio, quod nullis discordiis imbuti, pari in omnes studio agant: uti de Italo Tacitus. Sed nescio quomodo amor ex ea ἀδελφοφιλία ortus, in primo impetu languescit: ad eos qui & genere & vitæ familiaritate, atque eodem patrii cœli haustu, nobis noti, transferendus. quod eleganti versu exprimit in Promethco Tragicorum celsissimus: Τὸ συγγενὲς τε καὶ δεινὸν ὑφ' ὁμιλίας i. e. Cognatio multum potest & crebra conversatio.
units.tr: Not only some men fall into foreignness through this consideration, but also through long absence and a way of life at odds with their ancestral institutions and customs. The Parthians scorned their king, sought and received from Rome, though he was of the Arsacid stock, as a foreigner. From his long stay among the Romans, among whom he had lived as a hostage, they argued that "the Parthians have degenerated, having sought a king from another world, infected by the arts of enemies. Now the throne of the Arsacids is held and given out among the Roman provinces. Where is that glory of slaughtering Crassus and driving out Antony? Shall a slave of Caesar, who endured servitude for so many years, rule the Parthians?" By these words they rightly infer, from the mark of foreignness, a mind inclining to strangers and degenerate, having tasted servitude. This also caused danger for Italus, whose family came from Flavius, brother of Arminius, among the Cherusci, who raged: "The ancient liberty of Germany is being taken away and Roman power rises. Is no one born in these lands fit to fill the place of a beginning, unless the offspring of the spy Flavius is raised above all? etc. Tainted by food, servitude, and culture, foreign in everything." Nor was this complaint of the Cherusci without ground, though many of the opposing faction followed Italus. For this was the judgment of the Emperor Claudius about him: "He, born first at Rome, went not as a hostage but as a citizen, a foreigner to the empire." Behold, Italus, born of a German father, foreign to the German empire! In the same nation, within living memory, the same thing diminished the love and authority of Charles V, German indeed by his father, but born in Spanish dominion and brought up at the Spanish court. The other thing the Parthians disdained in Vonones was a way of life at odds with the institutions of his forefathers: "rarely hunting, careless of horses; whenever he went through the cities he was carried in a litter, and he showed pride toward native feasts. They mocked" his Greek companions, and his cheap utensils closed with a ring, yet his access was easy and his courtesy ready. These were virtues unknown to the Parthians, new vices; "and because they were alien to their customs, they hated the wicked and the honourable alike." Thus they shrank from not only softness, frugality and Romano-Greek refinement, but from the very virtues of the new prince, as if they were vices, condemned for their novelty. So familiarity and way of life count for more in winning hatred or love than nature, birth, and the very place of one's nativity. Sigismund, a Swede by nation but a Sarmatian by life and upbringing, learned this at the cost of one kingdom and the gain of another; his son Casimir now drives the hostile Swedish arms from the borders of Poland, not without ruin to his fatherland. For those who summon foreigners, by birth or long absence, to the helm of their fatherland, this reasoning does have force: being imbued with no discords, such men act with equal zeal toward all, as Tacitus says of Italus. But I know not how love born of that brotherly affection [ἀδελφοφιλία] wanes at the first onset; it must be transferred to those known to us by kinship, by familiarity of life, and by the same breath of our native sky. The most lofty of the tragic poets expresses this in an elegant verse in the Prometheus: "Kinship and close association are a mighty thing" [Τὸ συγγενὲς τε καὶ δεινὸν ὑφ' ὁμιλίας]; that is, kinship and frequent intercourse have great power.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Multa homines ab aula & foro fastidituri ambiunt.
units.tr: Men often pursue what they will later loathe, from court and forum.

units.la: PETITUM Roma acceptumque regem, quamvis gentis Arsacidarum, ut externum ASPERNABANTUR. Quia nimirum aut causa petitionis non satis perpensa præcipites, aut animi levitate mobiles. Sæpè & aliud in ambiendo agentes, id assecuti, aut non assecuti, studio circumferuntur. Pro lege Manilia, & Pompeio ad bellum Mithridaticum cum absoluto imperio mittendo, adversa omni patrum factione, C. Cæsar Tullius Cicero nitebantur. non quod aut publico id profuturum crederent, aut Pompeji incremento studerent. Sed in re ad patrum voluntatem non itura, potentiores populi prae senatu partes Caesar sibi demereri festinabat. nec non in alieno potentiae excessu sibi exemplum, quod imitaretur populus, quaerebat. praeterea Pompejum ex ornamenti mole invidiae obiicere, populum in satietatem favoris conjicere molie-batur. Cicero, in factione civium saepius optimas, quid posset alteri parti momenti adjicere, oftenum[?] iit. simul ad reipublicae gestamen enitens, Pompeji sibi gratiam & popularem auram non aspernandam arbitrabatur. Uti non vana conjectura Dio, libro 36. Postea, quam hic fluctuanti, ille alieno in Pompejum animo fuerit, bellum Civile aperuit.
units.tr: Having been sought from Rome and received as king, though he was of the Arsacid race, they spurned him as a foreigner. This happens because they are either rash, not having weighed the reason for their request, or fickle through lightness of mind. Often, too, while canvassing for something else, they are swept along by their zeal, whether or not they attain what they were after. Caesar and Cicero strove for the Manilian law and for sending Pompey against Mithridates with absolute power, while the whole faction of the senators opposed it. They did not do so because they believed it would profit the state, or because they were eager to advance Pompey. Caesar, in a matter that would not go according to the senate's wishes, was hurrying to win the favour of the more powerful part of the people against the senate. Nor did he look for an example in another's excess of power that the people might imitate. Moreover, he was trying to bring odium on Pompey by the great weight of his honours, and to push the people into satiety of his favour. Cicero, in the faction of the citizens, often the best men, went to add what weight he could to the other side. At the same time, striving for the burden of the commonwealth, he judged that Pompey's favour and popular breeze were not to be spurned. This is no idle conjecture: see Dio, book 36. Afterwards, when the one wavered and the other was turned against Pompey in mind, he opened civil war.

units.la: Tiberius, cujus praecipuè aulam contemplamur, multa Sejano, multa Sejanae factionis hominibus, ornamenta & ultro obtulit & a Senatu cumulare passus est, quae postmodum cum ipsa vita eriperet. Quaedam & Germanico, ut proconsulare imperium, ut triumphos & alia, quae deferendo & petendo aversabatur, praefecti fastidio, sed simulatione tecto, quem fastigio detractum cupiebat, obtinuit. Eadem in Germanici liberos persona usus, quos per Sejanum eversurus erat, per ornamenta feriebat. Cumulandis exemplis, quorum plena est historia Augusta, Tiberiana imprimis, abstineo.
units.tr: Tiberius, whom we are chiefly examining here, both offered many honours of his own accord to Sejanus and to the men of Sejanus's faction, and allowed the Senate to heap them up; these he would afterwards snatch away together with their lives. Some he also gave to Germanicus: proconsular imperium, triumphs and other things, which he refused to offer and to be asked for, through a show of disdain, but concealed by pretence. He obtained them for one whom he wished to be pulled down from the summit. Using the same mask with the children of Germanicus, whom he was going to overthrow through Sejanus, he struck them down through honours. I refrain from piling up examples, of which the history of Augustus is full, and especially that of Tiberius.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Aliud in aula agitur, aliud agi orbi humano persuadetur.
units.tr: Something else is done in the court, and something else is persuaded to the human world.

units.la: Phrahates quamquam depulisset exercitum ducesque Romanos, cuncta venerationis officia ad Augustum verterat: partemque prolis, firmandae amicitiae, misit.
units.tr: Phraates, although he had driven off the Roman army and its generals, turned all the offices of reverence to Augustus, and sent part of his offspring to strengthen the friendship.

units.la: Id fieri Romanorum, quos odio occulto pungebat, veneratione Parthus prae se ferebat. Romana aula formidinem, quia id magnificum Augusto & populo Romano, interpretabatur. Cornelius persona detracta, veram fidei officii causam indagando, in lucem
units.tr: The Parthian displayed as reverence what the Romans did, and he was secretly stung by hatred of them. The Roman court interpreted this as fear, because it was magnificent for Augustus and the Roman people. Cornelius, stripping away the mask and searching out the true cause of the faithful duty, brings it to light

units.la: producit: baud perinde nostri metu, quam fidei popu-larium diffisus. Vanus igitur, aut vana perfuasione de-lusus, Horatius, Carmine Seculari:
units.tr: and produces it: not so much from fear of us as from distrust of the loyalty of his own subjects. Therefore Horace, either a fool or deceived by a vain persuasion, says in the Secular Hymn:

units.la: Jam mari terraque manus potentes
units.tr: Now the mighty hands of the Mede

units.la: Medus, Albanaque timet secures.
units.tr: fear on sea and land the Alban axes.

units.la: & alii in eum sensum pluribus poetae. Singularis in fce-nam oblita facie prodeundi artifex Tiberius, tam mul-ta simulationum exempla genuit, ut copia eligendi fa-cultate laboremus.
units.tr: and other poets say much the same in many places. Tiberius, a singular artist at coming onto the stage with his face concealed, produced so many examples of pretence that we labour under the abundance of choice.

units.la: Ut à Phrahate non abeam: cum eum Pompejus Ponti victor bello non fatis justo premeret, minacefq; ab eo expostulationes percepisset: expendendo Parthorum vires, tum demum simulatam justi reverentiae faciem induit. Non esse sibi à populo Romano provinciam illam demandatam: confectis contentum fe debere esse; neque fortunam aut alienam lacessendam, aut suam periclitandam. Injustam esse rerum alienarum appetentiam; intra modum subsistere debere hominum cupiditatem. Ita praetextam à Philosophis mutuando, metu incertitudinis eventuum cupiditatem repressit.
units.tr: To return to Phraates: when Pompey, victor over Pontus, pressed him with a war not sufficiently just and received threatening complaints from him, he weighed the strength of the Parthians, and only then put on the pretended face of just respect. It was not committed to him by the Roman people to have that province; he ought to be content with what he had won; he should neither provoke another's fortune nor put his own in danger. The desire for other people's possessions is unjust; the appetite of men ought to stop within bounds. Thus, borrowing the pretext from the philosophers, he repressed his desire out of fear of uncertain outcomes.

units.la: Idem Pompejus quantus in dissimulanda honorum gerendorum aviditate fuerit, pleni sunt oratorum & historicorum libri. Quibus amicitiae simulatae crustis ejusdem cum Caesare & Crasso conspiratio obducta fuerit; quo studii in remp. velo eadem dissoluta: plena sunt declamatorum theatra. Neque ab hoc scenae artificio alienus monarchiae Romanae exftructor Augu-ftus, quasi ad tuendam plebem tribunitia potestate af-sumpta, jus & vocabulum omnia suo arbitrio agendi invenit. Sed quid per singulos carptim colligere mo-nimenta juvat: cum totus orbis historiam, ut non illepide olim dictum, agat?
units.tr: How great Pompey was in concealing his eagerness for holding honours, the books of orators and historians are full of. How the conspiracy with Caesar and Crassus was overlaid with the crust of a pretended friendship, and how the same was dissolved under a veil of zeal for the state, the theatres of the declaimers are full of. Nor was Augustus, the builder of the Roman monarchy, a stranger to this art of the stage: as if to protect the plebs, having assumed tribunician power, he found a right and a title for doing everything at his own discretion. But what use is it to gather these monuments one by one, since the whole world is making history, as was once said not unwittily?

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Non in lucri augmento splendor imperii versatur.
units.tr: The splendour of empire does not consist in an increase of profit.

units.la: Lucelli accessu aut decessu publicas actiones, & privatae vitae tranquillitatem, vulgus fere metitur. Non ita in Parthorum legatione audienda & dimitten-da da Tiberius judicavit. venere in urbem legati à primoribus Parthis, qui Vononem vetustissimum liberorum ejus accirent. MAGNIFICUM id sibi credidit Caesar, AUXITQUE opibus. Turpiculam apud Athenienses privatarum litium pro mercede diurna dijudi-cationem dicerem, nisi res judiciaria pauperculorum hominum cognitioni demandata in statu populari fuisset. quo in statu, ad sui conservationem, judiciorum & magistratuum gestioni praemia pecuniaria esse assignanda, inter arcana reip. Aristoteles in Politicis recensuit. Tiberianam fortunam imitatus Claudius, magnificum sibi duxit, fastigium Romanum Parthorum obsequiis (ita vocat majestatem populi Romani comiter agnitam) extolli. Sed ut Tiberius opibus, ita hic praeceptis regem & legatos instructos dimisit. Regem: ut non dominationem & servos, sed rectorem & cives cogitaret, clementiamque ac justitiam, quanto ignara barbaris, tanto tolerantiora, caperet. Legatos: seren-da regum ingenia: neque usui crebras mutationes. Annal. 12. Obiter observandum, legatos à populo non suis juris ad principem Romanum non semel esse mittendos. Quod aut populum defuncto rege suae potestatis esse; aut non omnes legatos pari jure & dignitate censeri, aut vanum esse Politicorum dogma, Nonnisi à pari ad parem legatos mitti, arguit.
units.tr: The crowd mostly measures public actions, and the tranquillity of private life, by the gain or loss of a little money. Tiberius did not judge so in hearing and dismissing the Parthian embassy. Envoys came to the city from the leading Parthians, to summon Vonones, the oldest of his children. Caesar believed this magnificent for himself, and AUGMENTED it with wealth. I might call it a rather shabby judgment of private lawsuits, decided for a daily wage among the Athenians, unless judicial business, entrusted to the cognizance of poor men, were in a popular state; in which state, for its preservation, pecuniary rewards for holding courts and magistracies were to be assigned, as Aristotle reckoned among the secrets of the commonwealth in the Politics. Imitating Tiberius's fortune, Claudius thought it magnificent for himself that the Roman majesty should be exalted by the obsequiousness of the Parthians (thus he calls the majesty of the Roman people, courteously acknowledged). But as Tiberius sent them off with wealth, so he sent off the king and the envoys instructed with precepts. To the king: that he should think not of domination and slaves, but of a ruler and citizens, and should adopt clemency and justice, which are the more tolerable the more they are unknown to barbarians. To the envoys: the dispositions of kings are to be sown; frequent changes are of no use. Annals 12. Incidentally, it should be noted that envoys have more than once had to be sent to the Roman prince by the people, not by their own right. This argues either that the people, once the king is dead, have power over him, or that not all envoys are counted of equal right and dignity, or that the dogma of the Politicians, that envoys are sent only from equal to equal, is vain.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Læta judicii expertibus imperii no-vitas.
units.tr: The novelty of empire is pleasing to those who have not learned judgment.

units.la: Qua degustata, ut pro vetusti vini flore mulsi dul-cedine, ad antiquiora votis recurritur. Et accepere barbari latantes, ut fermè ad nova imperia. Mox subiit pudor. Plura ejusmodi animorum levitatis in Parthica gente monumenta. Nec Romana quanquam gravitatis opinione se commendans, hic immunis. Bellum modò Vitellianum, mira militum in hunc aut illam studia, inhumana populi Romani, publica mutatione laeti, socordia spectatur. Ratio, si quid in vanitate rationis, à spe favoris, à novo & novis laeto principe, ferendi peti queat. Atqui gravissimus Græcanicæ[?] poëseos Æschylus in Prometheo, & Vulcani quidem ore,pronunciat:
units.tr: Once it has been tasted, people turn back with longing to older things, as the sweetness of old wine is preferred for its bouquet. And the barbarians received it with rejoicing, as almost always with new empires. Soon shame followed. Many such monuments of fickle minds survive among the Parthian nation. Nor is the Roman, though he commends himself by a reputation for seriousness, free of this. The recent Vitellian war, with its astonishing zeal of soldiers for this or that candidate, its inhuman cruelty of the Roman people, and their joy at a public change of ruler, shows such heedlessness. The reason, if any can be sought in the folly of reason, is hope of favour, and joy in a new prince and new things.

units.la: Ἄτης δὲ τεχνῆς ὅστις ἂν νέον ἡγῇ[?] i. e. Ductus recentis est acerbum imperii,
units.tr: Yet the most serious poet of Greek verse, Aeschylus, in the Prometheus, says through the mouth of Vulcan: The leadership of a recent rule is bitter [Ἄτης δὲ τεχνῆς ὅστις ἂν νέον ἡγῇ].

units.la: Quod tamen non de quavis imperii, sed imperii ratio-ni reddendæ non obnoxii, novitate capiendum esse, Oceani in eodem dramate persona introducta docuerit:
units.tr: That this, however, is not to be understood of every empire, but of one that is not bound to render an account of its rule, the character of Oceanus introduced in the same drama has taught.

units.la: Πρὸς κέντρα κᾶλον ἐλλεύεις, ὁρᾷ ὅτι[?] [illegible, ~20 letters] i. e. Stimulum ferire calce gestis: scilicet Asper, solutus legibus, rex imperat.
units.tr: You strike the goad with your heel and rejoice; clearly the harsh king, freed from laws, rules [Πρὸς κέντρα κᾶλον ἐλλεύεις, ὁρᾷ ὅτι […]].

units.la: Ejusmodi nimirum Jovem; imò crudelem, humani generis miseria gaudentem, poëtæ fermè inducunt. Hinc præcipui ei regii imperii satellites κράτος[?] & βία, Robur & Violentia. Hinc causa affixi scopulo Promethei, in humanum genus benignitas.
units.tr: Poets commonly portray Jupiter in just this way; indeed as cruel, rejoicing in the misery of the human race. Hence his chief attendants of royal rule are Strength and Violence (κράτος and βία). Hence the cause of Prometheus fastened to the rock: his kindness toward the human race.

units.la: Ὡς ἂν διδάξῃ τὴν Διὸς τυραννίδα[?] σιγῇ, φιλανθρώπως δὲ πειθοῖ[?] i. e. Ut exequi tyrannidem dicat Jovis, Humanitatis lesus[?] ut ponat modum,
units.tr: That he may say the tyranny of Jove is carried out silently, but humanity by persuasion sets a limit [Ὡς ἂν διδάξῃ τὴν Διὸς τυραννίδα σιγῇ, φιλανθρώπως δὲ πειθοῖ…].

units.la: A quo non discrepantia Cornicorum princeps Aristophanes: Plutum divitiarum deum, ne viros probos & sapientes delectu habito adire posset, in prima ætate à Jove excæcatum: cum Epiphonemate: Οὕτως ἀκεῖν ἂν τῶν ἀγαθῶν φρονεῖ[?] i. e. Sic ille mori invidet probi viri.
units.tr: Aristophanes, the prince of the comic poets, is not at odds with this. He says that Plutus, the god of riches, was blinded in his early youth by Jove, so that he could not approach good and wise men when a choice was made; and he adds the epiphonema: Thus he begrudges the death of the upright man [Οὕτως ἀκεῖν ἂν τῶν ἀγαθῶν φρονεῖ…].

units.la: Imò apud Epicorum poëtarum primum, Homerum, hæc & similia convitia Jovi in os aperte ingeruntur: Ζεῦ πάτερ, ἡμῖν ἐς ἀλαστωρῶν[?] i. e. Juppiter, haud divum te vivit acerbior ullus;
units.tr: Indeed among the epic poets, first Homer openly hurls these and similar reproaches at Jove's face: Father Zeus, of all the gods none lives more bitter toward us than you [Ζεῦ πάτερ, ἡμῖν ἐς ἀλαστωρῶν…].

units.la: Missa Jovis tyrannide: sententiam Æschyli de novo principatu hominis, vi ad imperium provecti, aut feroci juventute indomiti, (cujus modi Jovis regnum, pulso per vim & injuriam patre, fuisse fingitur) saepè veram esse pronunciamus. Recenti enim irae fervore, nova libidine, nondum sævitia fatigatâ; magis incon-sulta adolescentia, quam languescentis ætatis jam sa-turata dominatio, extimescenda. Ut autem nullo di-scrimine omnem novi imperii habitum acerbitatis ty-rannicæ damnemus, à modestiæ lege non impetra-mus.
units.tr: Setting aside the tyranny of Jove, we say that the saying of Aeschylus about a new ruler is often true: a man raised to power by force, or untamed by a fierce youth (such as the kingship of Jove is imagined to be, the father having been driven out by violence and wrong). For a new ruler is to be feared more for the fervour of recent anger and the freshness of desire, before his cruelty has grown weary, than for the rule of one whose ageing has already sated him; he is more to be feared for rash youth than for a dominion that has grown languid with age. Yet while we condemn without distinction every new government that bears the marks of tyrannical harshness, we cannot obtain exemption from the law of moderation.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Patriæ consuetudo pro lege, mores pro ratione barbaris observati, temerè principi non infringenda.
units.tr: The custom of the fatherland is to be kept as law, and the customs observed by barbarians are to be kept as reason; a prince must not rashly infringe them.

units.la: De Vonone Tacitus : Accendebat dedignantes & ipse, diversus à majorum institutis. Non quidem ad pestiferos hominum mores, & consuetudinem à recta ratione plane degenerantem, Principi sponte connivendum. In iis tamen quæ meri sunt gentium arbitrii, nec ad vitiorum confinia per se abducunt, patrius mos non temerè immutandus: nec Cynico Diogenis incessu contra maris fluctum,nitendum. Sed in quibus Vononcs[?] animos popularium offenderit, & hicne an illi in culpa fuerint, singula ad lancem æqui judicii expendamus.
units.tr: Of Vonones Tacitus says: He was roused by those who disdained him, and was himself at odds with the institutions of his ancestors. A prince should not, of his own accord, tolerate pernicious human morals or customs that clearly depart from right reason. But in matters that are purely the choice of a people, and do not lead by themselves to the borders of vice, the ancestral custom is not to be changed rashly, nor is one to struggle against it like the Cynic Diogenes against the waves of the sea. But in those matters where Vonones offended the feelings of his subjects, we should weigh each point in the scales of fair judgment, asking whether he or they were at fault.

units.la: Rare venatu. Laudat in Cyro suo venandi studium Xenophon, ut ad alacritatem animi ac corporis conducens, belli meditationes in feris præcipiens, locorum asperitates agili nisu superare exercitato usu docens, varios declinandi & insequendi hostem recessus commonefaciens. Romani id in servilibus operis, indignum senatorio viro, indignum imperatorio, ducebant. Germani his temporibus id fere de suis ductoribus mussitant[?], quod Antiochus, venandi studio mirum in modum captus, à rustico viro coram audivit: Noster quidem rex satis bonus est, eique omnia fausta precamur, sed quia nimium venationi indulget, rerum suarum negligentior habetur. Id igitur inprimis cavendum principi viro, ne remp. sylvis, cives feris postponens, omnes in eo oblectamento vires & cogitationes reponat. deinde ne multitudine canum venaticó- rum & operarum fylveftrium alenda, ærarium exhau- riat: aut paganos ad eum comitatum abreptos, agri- cultura abducat. Ubi verò grata est incolis venatio, ubi intermissio ejus pro desidia aut patriis institutis adversa habetur, quin rex popularium benevolam vo- luntatem ea gratificatione demereri justè queat, non ambigimus. De Zenone,regnum ea venandi assidui- tate adepto, Tacitus infra: favor nationis inclinabat in Zenonem Polemonis regis Ponticifilium, quod ipsa pri-ma ab infantia instituta & cultum Armeniorum æmulatus, VENATU, epulis, & qua alia barbari cela- brant, proceres plebemque juxta devinxerat. Igitur Germanicus in urbe Artaxata, approbantibus, circum- fusa multitudine, insigne regium capiti ejus imposuit. Id laborandum tamen Reip. moderatori, ne afflidua lustrorum & ferarum conversatione fylvefcens, ferè num animum induat. Quanquam vir supra seculi fui mores eruditus, C.Plinius, nescio quid secretæ medi- tationis in ea venatione venatur. Non est quod conte-mnas hoc studendi genus. Mirum est, ut animus agitatione motuque corporis excitetur. Jam undique fylvæ & solitudo, ipsumque illud silentium quod venationi datur, magna cogitationis incitamenta sunt. Sed nihil mirum Plinius ille ad retia SED SED DAT: in proximo erant, NON venabulum & lancea, SED stylus & pugillares. Utipse de se ad C.Tacitum, libri primi epi-stola sexta fatetur. Prolixè pro venatione, libro pecu-liari, Xenophon.
units.tr: Rarely in the hunt. Xenophon praises the zeal for hunting in his Cyropaedia, as conducive to vigour of mind and body; he teaches that the preparations for war are foreshadowed in hunting, that trained practice teaches one to overcome the roughness of the terrain with nimble effort, and he reminds us of the various withdrawals for avoiding and pursuing an enemy. The Romans thought hunting was work for slaves, unworthy of a senator and unworthy of a commander. In these times the Germans grumble about their leaders in much the same way as Antiochus, who was marvellously captivated by hunting, heard it from a country man to his face: Our king is indeed good enough, and we pray that all good things may befall him; but because he indulges too much in hunting, he is regarded as more neglectful of his affairs. A prince above all must therefore beware lest, placing the commonwealth behind the forests and citizens behind the wild beasts, he spends all his strength and thought on that pleasure. Next, he must beware lest, to feed a multitude of hunting dogs and forest workers, he exhausts the treasury, or drags the country folk into that retinue and draws them away from agriculture. But where hunting is pleasing to the inhabitants, and where its discontinuance is regarded as idleness or contrary to ancestral custom, we do not doubt that a king may justly win the goodwill of his people by such a gratification. Of Zeno, who gained the kingdom through such constant hunting, Tacitus says below: The favour of the nation inclined toward Zeno, son of King Polemo of Pontus, because he had from earliest infancy imitated the customs and dress of the Armenians, and by hunting, feasts, and whatever else the barbarians celebrate, had bound nobles and commons alike to himself. Therefore Germanicus, in the city of Artaxata, with the approval of the assembled multitude, placed the royal diadem on his head. Yet the ruler of a commonwealth must take care that he does not, through constant association with dens and wild beasts, grow wild and take on their temper. Although Gaius Pliny, a man learned beyond the manners of his age, hunts in that pursuit something of a secret contemplation: There is no reason to despise this kind of study. It is remarkable how the mind is stirred by the movement and exercise of the body. Everywhere there are woods and solitude, and that very silence which hunting affords, are great incitements to thought. But it is no wonder that Pliny, with his nets, was near at hand; it was not a hunting spear and lance but a stylus and writing tablets that he used. He himself confesses this about himself to Gaius Tacitus in the sixth letter of his first book. Xenophon treats hunting at length in a separate book.

units.la: Segni equorum cura. Romanis etiam priscis militari illa ætate rarior equitii, major peditatus cura. Quam causam Polybius assignat, cur toties campestribus præliis inferiores Hannibale abierint. Mansit tamen apud ingenuorum eminentiores equestris rei studium: donec longa sub Augusto & Tiberio pace, juventute ad theatricas bladitias avocata, omnia nervis virilis roboris incifis soluta. Hæc fuit illa ætas, de qua Horatius: — nescit equo rudis Harere ingenuus puer:
units.tr: The care of horses is a sign of rank. Even in the early Roman times of soldiering, the cavalry was less cultivated, and care for infantry was greater. Polybius gives this as the reason why they so often were defeated by Hannibal in pitched battles on the plains. Yet among the more eminent freeborn youths the study of cavalry continued, until, under the long peace of Augustus and Tiberius, the young men were called away to theatrical frivolity, and everything was loosened, with the sinews of manly strength cut away. This was that age of which Horace speaks: The freeborn boy, untrained, knows not how to stay on a horse:

units.la: VenariVanarique timet: ludere doctior.
units.tr: He fears to hunt, and is more skilled at play.

units.la: Libri IV. Carm. Oda XXIV.
units.tr: Libri IV. Carm. Oda XXIV.

units.la: At apud Parthos omnis ingenuorum ætas in equo, ut Scythis ἱππικοῖς[?] in plaustro, transigebatur. In forum, in comitia, in convivia equis insidentes convenerunt. Hinc altera è discrepanti morum vita in novum regem odii causa. Quam evitare potuisset, tramite vi-tæ a Romana consuetudine ad patrios mores avocato.
units.tr: But among the Parthians the whole life of free men was spent on horseback, as among the Scythians it was spent in the wagon [ἱππικοῖς]. They gathered on horseback in the forum, at the assemblies, and at banquets. Hence came a second cause of hatred toward the new king, arising from a way of life that clashed with the old customs. He could have avoided it by turning his course of life away from Roman custom back to ancestral ways.

units.la: Illud vero de lectica gestamine & mollitiem sapit, & non ferendam superbiam.
units.tr: But that business of the litter as a means of being carried smacks of softness and an intolerable arrogance.

units.la: Fastuque erga patrias epulas.
units.tr: And disdain toward the feasts of his fathers.

units.la: Quibus apud Romanos exquisitioribus insue-verat. Sanè aliquis jam barbarorum regum auste-ritati gentili, cui impar fuerat, se contra prioris vitæ morem tradendo, in morbum & ex eo in mortem in-cidit. At cura valetudinis adesse, fastus & corrugati nasi sannus[?] abesse potuit. Etiam in peregrino non fe-rimus patriæ, ut morum, ita mensæ apertum vilipendium. ne dum in cive, & civium moderatore, etiam hac in parte insolitum quid & insolens feramus. Hæc ter-tia causa, genere cum prioribus conveniens, alienato-rum à rerum patriarum arbitro animorum.
units.tr: These were habits he had grown used to among the more refined Romans. Indeed, one of the barbarian kings, who had given himself up to a way of life contrary to his earlier custom, and who was unequal to the austerity of his native people, fell into illness and from that into death. Yet he could have had care for his health without disdain and a sneering wrinkling of the nose. Even in a foreigner we do not tolerate open contempt for our country's customs, and so too for its table. Much less should we tolerate in a citizen, and in the ruler of citizens, something unusual and arrogant in this respect as well. This is the third cause, agreeing in kind with the earlier ones, for alienating the minds of those who judge the affairs of their own country.

units.la: Irridebantur & Græci comites.
units.tr: The Greek companions were also mocked.

units.la: Jam inde à belli, quod cum Hannibale gestum est, temporibus illustriores Romani Græcos homines, ut Comicorum nonnemo loquitur, ignava opera, Philo-sopha sententia, circumducebant. Alii ad belli & justi-tiæ usum,ut Africanus Minor Polybium, virum ductu Achaicæ militiæ belli peritum. Alii deinceps ad pom-pam & sapientiæ quandam externam speciem: qui mos temporibus Augusti maximè invaluit. Ejusmodi homines à Romanorum civium fæce clandestino, à barbarorum fastu aperto naso suspendebantur. Ac si quidem unum aliquem è Græcis, ut sapientia ita di-gnitate conspicuum, foviset: ut Darius quondam Demaratum, Cyrus antiquioribus temporibus Croe-sum, Croesus ipse Solonem consuluit: minorem subsannandi causam Parthi fortassis habuissent. Nunc in mores Græculorum transiisse visi, præceps ivit auto-
units.tr: From the time of the war waged against Hannibal onward, the more distinguished Romans led about Greek men, as one of the comic writers puts it, of idle work, with philosophical opinions. Some used them for war and justice, as Africanus the Younger used Polybius, a man skilled in war who had led the Achaean forces. Others afterwards used them for display and for a certain outward show of wisdom; this custom grew especially strong in the times of Augustus. Such men were hated in secret by the dregs of the Roman citizens and openly sneered at by the barbarians with their noses in the air. And indeed, if a king had cherished just one of the Greeks who was conspicuous for wisdom and also for rank, as Darius once cherished Demaratus, Cyrus in earlier times Croesus, and Croesus himself consulted Solon, the Parthians perhaps would have had less cause to scoff. But now that he seemed to have passed over into the manners of the little Greeks, his authority fell headlong.

units.la: ritas. Nam fi Scythæ quondam Anacharfin civem suum è Græcia reversum non tulerunt : quomodo Parthorum arrogantia Græcos regis rectores patienti animo tulisset ?
units.tr: For if the Scythians once would not bear Anacharsis, their own countryman, returning from Greece, how would the arrogance of the Parthians have patiently borne Greeks as the governors of their king?

units.la: Ac viliffima utensilium annulo clausa.
units.tr: And the cheapest of utensils, sealed with a ring.

units.la: Istud domesticæ parcimoniæ genus in modico cive ferendum : in rerum Domino, & ut Parthorum reges nuncupari gaudebant, Regum Rege, culpam ignomi-niæ qui effugiat ? Non omnia quæ quis familiari usu homo privatus decenter agit, etiam summæ potefta-tis majestatem decebunt. Invaserit sanè iste mos Au-guftam Romæ familiam , civilis vitæ æquabilitatem præ fe ferentem : in Parthico regno à peregrina illa, & tantum non sordida, novitate abstinendum.
units.tr: That sort of domestic thrift may be tolerated in a modest citizen. But in the master of affairs, and in one who, like the kings of the Parthians, delighted in being called King of Kings, who could escape the blame of disgrace? Not everything that a private man does decently in everyday use will suit the majesty of supreme power. Indeed, that custom may have crept into the Augustan household at Rome, which displayed the evenness of civic life; but in the Parthian kingdom that foreign novelty, which was hardly not squalid, had to be avoided.

units.la: Sed promti aditus , obvia comitas.
units.tr: But ready access and ready courtesy.

units.la: De Maximiliani Cæsaris facilitate Lipfius , Epistola dedicatoria : Admittebantur ad sacros sermones tuos privati cum principibus , pagani cum militibus, viri cum fœminis , senes pœnè dicam cum pueris inter-mixtis. Querelas aut desideria sua promebant , non solum patienter audiente te , sed interdum manu & vultu ipso , fi quos forte insolitus ille splendor percusse-rat,ut auderent,invitante. Et jam audebant : finem sermoni suus cujusque pudor , non fastidium tuum fa-ciebat. De Augusti, Titi Vespasiani , Trajani, Theo-dofii ; de Græcorum principum in regno Macedonico, Syriaco , Asiatico , Ægyptiaco , promptis aditibus ; multi multa. Id est in quaftione positum : Annon ea facilitas autoritatem adimendo , regni fundamenta evertat ? Rem in humaniorem partem ita decidit in Trajano Plinius : Cui nihil ad augendum fastigium fuperefl , hic uno modo crescere potefl , fi fe ipse fubmit-tat, securus magnitudinis suæ. Neque enim ab ullo peri-culo fortuna Principum longiùs abefl , quàm ab humi-litate. Sed nec omnium aures philofophationis hujus sunt capaces : nec apud omnes gentes principatus ac civium libertas in sociétatem coëunt. Serviant levia simul ac tumida Orientis ingenia : regníque majefta-tem E Plinii Trajano subreptum. Quæstio. tm[?] aliena arrogantia, & humili demissione sui, me-tantur.
units.tr: Lipsius, in his dedicatory letter, on the affability of the Emperor Maximilian: "Private persons were admitted to your sacred discourses along with the princes, civilians with soldiers, men with women, old men, I almost say, mixed with children. They put forward their complaints and wishes, not only while you listened patiently, but sometimes, when that unaccustomed splendor had struck some of them, you even encouraged them with your hand and your very face, so that they would dare. And now they did dare; each man's own modesty, not your disdain, set the end to his speech." Of Augustus, Titus Vespasian, Trajan and Theodosius, and of the Greek princes in the kingdoms of Macedonia, Syria, Asia and Egypt, who had ready access, there are many things to say. The question is put this way: Does not such affability, by taking away authority, overturn the foundations of a kingdom? Pliny decided the matter in the kinder sense, in his panegyric on Trajan: "For him to whom nothing remains for increasing his rank, he can increase in only one way, namely by humbling himself, secure in his greatness. For the fortune of princes is no farther from any danger than from humility." But the ears of all men are not capable of this philosophy, nor do the principate and the liberty of citizens unite in fellowship among all nations. The light and puffed-up minds of the East are made for slavery; and the majesty of the kingdom is snatched away from Trajan, as Pliny says, by foreign arrogance and by their own humble submission. [Question.]

units.la: Ignota Parthis virtutes, nova vitia.
units.tr: Unknown to the Parthians, virtues; new vices.

units.la: Naturae quidem interstitio virtus & probrum diri-muntur: sed apud multas nationes non nisi opinionis & recepti usus fine nomina ea terminantur. Justitiae & Pacis nomen antiqui Sarmatae ignorabant. Diem ac noctem potando continuare, apud priscos Germanos nulli probro dabatur. Masculam libidinem pro comitate vetusta Graecia accepit. Sunt inter abditi Orbis populos, qui hostis capti devorationem inter heroica numerent. Parthorum immanis crudelitas, nefaria libido, fastus libero homini non ferendus, in vitiorum censu non reperiebantur. At luxus elegantia, victus & incessus mollities, loquacitatis immoderata jaculatio, tam illis ignorabantur; quam literarum ac sapientiae studium, quam imperantium facilitatem pro monstro ducebant. Qui more receptis vitiis non contentus, nova antiquis rector cumulat: in naturam, in se, in populum suum varie injurius, regno nulla commiseratione excidit.
units.tr: By nature, virtue and disgrace are indeed separated by a clear boundary; but among many nations these names are fixed only by opinion and by accepted custom. The ancient Sarmatians did not know the name of justice and peace. To keep on drinking through day and night was not counted a disgrace among the old Germans. Ancient Greece took male lust for old-fashioned courtesy. Among the peoples of the hidden corners of the world there are some who count devouring a captured enemy among heroic deeds. The monstrous cruelty of the Parthians, their unspeakable lust, and an arrogance intolerable in a free man were not reckoned among vices. But luxury presented as elegance, a soft manner of eating and walking, and an unrestrained flood of talk were as unknown to them as the study of letters and wisdom, and they regarded a ruler's affability as a monstrosity. This ruler, not content with vices received by custom, piles new ones on the old; in various ways he wrongs nature, himself and his own people, and he falls from the kingdom with no one feeling pity.

units.la: Et quia ipsorum moribus aliena, perinde odium pra-vum & honestum. Quia invisum semel principem, seu bona seu mala facta premunt: ut alibi scriptor Annalium loquitur.
units.tr: And because they are foreign to the customs of those people, hatred equally wicked and honorable [arises]. Because they press hard upon a prince once hated, whether he does good or bad deeds, as the writer of the Annals says elsewhere.

units.la: Atque ista quidem morum peregrinitate, ista victus & vitae insolentia, Vonones regnum Orientis potentissimum amisit. Recensendis, qui vitae suae transformatione regna adepti, stabilierint, quia id alibi egi, abstineo. Tiberius, quanquam sui sensus homo, ver-ba & vultum prisci populi moribus congruentem, regno firmando, induit. Cuncta per Consules incipiebat, tanquam vetere Rep. & ambiguum imperandi. Quam artem, antiquitatem in rerum novitate fingendi, ab acri Augusti mente didicerat. Ne edictum quidem, quae patres in curiam vocabat, nisi Tribunitia potestatis praescriptione posuit sub Augusto accepta. 1. Anna-lium. Et quis congerendis aut legendis omnibus, quo-rum plenus est autor, operam impendat?
units.tr: And indeed by this strangeness of customs, by this unusual way of eating and living, Vonones lost the most powerful kingdom of the East. I abstain from reviewing those who, having gained kingdoms by a change in their way of life, established them, since I have treated that elsewhere. Tiberius, although a man of his own mind, put on words and a countenance agreeing with the customs of the old people, in order to strengthen his rule. He began everything through the consuls, as if the commonwealth were still old and the power of ruling uncertain. This art of feigning antiquity amid the novelty of affairs he had learned from the keen mind of Augustus. He did not even issue an edict by which he summoned the senators to the senate-house, except under the form of tribunician power, which he had received under Augustus. Annals, book 1. And who would take the trouble to gather or read all the things of which the author is full?

units.la: VIII. In summis præcipitium, in humilitate ascensus.
units.tr: VIII. At the heights, a fall; in humility, a climb.

units.la: De Artabano apud Dahas adulto, & ab iis ad regnum à popularibus excito, ita Tacitus: primo con-gressu fusus, reparat vires, regnoque potitur. Non potuit rotundius tantarum mutatio rerum contexi. Vi-ctor victi, rex regum exulis locum alterna vice subeut. Discant reges & populi, non una prælii alea omnia de-cerni: nec inde stare semper eventum, unde fortuna primo nisu stetit. Victoris igitur est, victoria modera-te; victi, clade non desperate uti. Laudat Polybius Romanos, à cæteris nationibus bello gerendo multum differentes: in prælio imperterritos, in clade truces & magnanimos, in victoria mites & legum humanarum memores. Quare merito iis, utriusque fortunæ arbitris, orbis succubuit. In cæteris hunc aut similem locum in animo Senecæ habuit, Chorum in Thyeste ita loquentem introducens:
units.tr: Of Artabanus, who was driven out by the Dahae and then raised to the kingship by his own people, Tacitus writes: routed at the first encounter, he recovers his strength and gains the kingdom. No account of such a reversal of fortune could be woven more neatly. The conqueror becomes the conquered, and the exile takes the king's place in turn. Kings and peoples should learn that not everything is settled by a single throw of the dice, and that the outcome does not always remain where fortune first stood. It is the mark of a victor to use victory with moderation, and of the vanquished not to despair over defeat. Polybius praises the Romans, who differ greatly from other nations in waging war: fearless in battle, fierce and high-minded in defeat, gentle in victory and mindful of the laws of humanity. Therefore the world rightly yielded to them, as arbiters of both kinds of fortune. Elsewhere Seneca had this or a similar passage in mind, when he introduces the Chorus in the Thyestes speaking thus:

units.la: Ima permutat brevi hora summis.
units.tr: In a brief hour he exchanges the highest things for the lowest.

units.la: & paucis interjectis:
units.tr: and, after a few lines:

units.la: Quem dies vidit veniens superbum, / Hunc dies vidit fugiens jacentem. / Nemo confidat nimium secundis: / Nemo desperet meliora lapsis.
units.tr: The day that saw him rise proud / That same day saw him fall and lie low. / Let no one trust too much in good fortune; / let no one despair of better things after a fall.

units.la: Igitur
units.tr: Therefore

units.la: Non facundè magis quam sapienter Æschylus de-litiæ nostræ:
units.tr: Aeschylus, our darling, said this no less eloquently than wisely:

units.la: Οἱ [illegible, ~24 letters]
units.tr: Οἱ [Greek line illegible in the scan]

units.la: i. e.
units.tr: that is,

units.la: Qui glorianti temperat linguam, sapit.
units.tr: He is wise who restrains his tongue when he is boasting.

units.la: IX. Casus & fortuna rebus in humanis plurimum possunt.
units.tr: IX. Chance and fortune have the greatest power in human affairs.

units.la: Sed sapientis est, fortunam rectà ansa arripere, & ca-sum in opportunitatem convertere. Vitio Vononi per-fugium Armenia fuit, vacua tunc, interque Partho-
units.tr: But it is the mark of a wise man to seize fortune by the handle that is offered and to turn misfortune to advantage. Through the fault of Vonones, Armenia became his refuge, then empty, and lying between the Parthians

units.la: [illegible, ~1 letter] Greek and Latin notes are not present on this page apart from the marginal references above. rum & Romanas opes infida. Quantum terrarum inter Ciliciam, Syriam, Cappadociam, Parthicam, Ponti & maris Caspii accolas interjacuit, vacuum dominio & libertate nescia solutum, non in perfugium modo Vononcs exul, sed in regnum accepit. Ut clarius theatrum instabilitatis rerum humanarum pateat, tanti regni calamitosas varietates, paucos intra annos, nec totam hominis aetatem, circumactas exigua tabula oculis subjiciam. Reges Armeniae. | Eventus.
units.tr: and the Romans, whose power could not be trusted. However much land lay between Cilicia, Syria, Cappadocia, the Parthian realm, and the neighbours of the Pontic and Caspian seas, it was empty, without a master, and unaccustomed to freedom. Vonones, an exile, received it not merely as a refuge but as a kingdom. So that the stage of human instability may be seen more clearly, I shall set before your eyes, on a small tablet, the troubled changes of this kingdom within a few years, not even over the course of a whole human life. The kings of Armenia. | Outcome.

units.la: 1. Artuasdes. ——— ——— | Catenis illigatus, interfectus.
units.tr: 1. Artuasdes. | Bound in chains and put to death.

units.la: 2. Artaxias filius. ——— ——— | Parthorum cliens, dolo occisus.
units.tr: 2. Artaxias, his son. | A client of the Parthians, killed by treachery.

units.la: 3. Tigranes. ——— ——— | brevi regno defunctus.
units.tr: 3. Tigranes. | Died after a brief reign.

units.la: 4. Artuasdes. ——— ——— | Armis dejectus.
units.tr: 4. Artuasdes. | Thrown down by arms.

units.la: 5. Ariobarzanes — ——— | morte fortuita absumtus. Medus origine.
units.tr: 5. Ariobarzanes. | Carried off by an accidental death. A Mede by origin.

units.la: 6. Erato ——— ——— | regno pulsa. foemina. 7. | Anarchia. 8. Vononcs. ——— | custodia circumdatus, in fuga quasi per iram interfectus.
units.tr: 6. Erato. | Driven from the kingdom. A woman. 7. | Anarchy. 8. Vonones. | Surrounded by guards, and killed in flight, as if in anger.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Corporis pulchritudo tacita ad regnum commendatio.
units.tr: Physical beauty is a silent recommendation for a kingdom.

units.la: Sed major commendatio ingenium, & constans sibi animus. C. Caesar, Agrippae nimirum filius, compo-nendae Armeniae dilectus, Ariobarzanem origine Medum, ob insignem corporis formam, & praeclarum animum, volentibus Armeniis praefecit. Hic unus septem, quos recensui, regum, & is quidem origine adventitia, fato suo regni tenax obiit. Tantum est in forma ad sui commendationem lenocinii. Nec fine causa [illegible, ~10 letters] ab antiquorum non nemine pronunciatum. Etiam barbaris hominibus in corporum majestate veneratio est. Et barbaris quidem saepiculè, animi pulchritudinem lusco oculo intuentibus, aut eam, quod non raro fallit, è corporis lineamento conje-ctantibus.
units.tr: But a greater recommendation is talent and a mind consistent with itself. Gaius Caesar, son of Agrippa, when he was settling Armenia, chose Ariobarzanes, a Mede by origin, for his remarkable bodily form and outstanding spirit, and set him over the Armenians, who were willing. He alone of the seven kings I have listed, and indeed one of foreign origin, died holding fast to his kingdom by his fate. So much does beauty of form serve as a flattering recommendation of oneself. Nor without cause [illegible] has it been pronounced by not a few of the ancients: even among barbarous peoples there is reverence for the majesty of the body. And indeed among barbarians this often happens, when they look at the beauty of the mind with a squinting eye, or infer it, as often they wrongly do, from the features of the body.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Non est in dissolutione imperii, nec in vaga licentia, libertas.
units.tr: Liberty does not consist in the dissolution of government or in wandering licence.

units.la: Armenii pulsis aut interfectis regibus incerti solu-tique, & magis sine domino, quam in libertate, profu-gum Vononem in regnum acceperunt. Libertas enim est populi sub lege, aut justo rege, non servilis conglutina-tio. A quâ in diversum abeunt, qui libertatem in pro-tervia, nobilitatem in disjectione quaerunt.
units.tr: When the kings had been driven out or killed, the Armenians, uncertain and loosed, and more without a master than in freedom, received Vonones, a fugitive, into the kingdom. For liberty is the condition of a people under law or under a just king, not a servile jumble. Those depart from it in the opposite direction who seek liberty in wantonness and nobility in disorder.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Nusquam, nisi in obscuritate, ab offensa potentiorum perfugium.
units.tr: Nowhere, except in obscurity, is there refuge from the offence of the more powerful.

units.la: Receptus quidem in regnum Armeniae Vononès erat. Sed ubi minitari Artabanus, & parum subsidio in Armenia, vel si Romana vi defenderetur, bellum adversus Parthos sumendum erat; rector Syria Creti-cui Sylanus excitum custodia circumdat.
units.tr: Vonones had indeed been received into the kingdom of Armenia. But when Artabanus threatened, and since little help could be had in Armenia, or if he were defended by Roman force, war had to be undertaken against the Parthians; the governor of Syria, Creticus Silanus, placed the stirred-up king under guard.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Ludibrium est victus regius & regium sine autoritate nomen.
units.tr: A royal living and a royal name without authority are a mockery.

units.la: Manente in custodia luxu & regio nomine, quod lu-dibrium ut effugere agitaverit Vonones, in loco reddemus. A quo ludibrio non longe absunt, qui crapulis & otio marcidi, rerum administrationem, & cum ea potentiam, proximis aulae ministris mandant. Cujus-modi reges Galli, senescente Merovingiorum stirpe, vernaculo non magis quam vernili vocabulo, Fai-neants à reappellavere. Ludibrium sibi ipsis accersunt, qui regno nunquam degustato exules, regium sibi nomen imponunt: perinde quasi naturae id nomen esset, non supremi regiminis.
units.tr: While he remained in custody, with luxury and the royal name, which mockery Vonones tried to escape, we shall explain in its place. Not far from this mockery are those who, enfeebled by drunkenness and idleness, hand over the administration of affairs, and with it power, to the nearest servants of the court. The kings of the Gauls, as the Merovingian line was growing old, were called by a name that was no more native than servile, faineants. They bring mockery upon themselves who, having never tasted a kingdom while in exile, impose a royal name on themselves, as if that name were a matter of nature and not of supreme rule.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Honoris offa multis Circeum est po-culum.
units.tr: For many, honour is a Circean cup, a morsel of favour.

units.la: Circe advenas potione oblata in fuces aut feras mu-tatos, incantatione & virga demulsos, in haram compulit.
