Principes, quos metuunt belli administros, ho-norum susurro, aut specie legationis ab aula vel exer-citu ablegant, aut famae incantamento periculis objec-tos, neci exponunt. Tiberio haud ingratum accidit, turbarires[?] Orientis, ut ea specie Germanicum suetis[?] legionibus abstraheret, novisque provinciis impositum, dolo simul & casibus objectaret. Plena est Graeciae antiquitas mandatis Bellerophonti, Jasoni, Herculi, quas exantlarent pro gloria, aerumnis. Eadem gloriae scena Davidi, regum fortissimo, in Hebraeorum populo a Saule socero per praecipitia aperta. Apud Numidas Micipsa, quod erat Jugurtha manu promptus, & appetens gloria[?] militaris, statuit eum objectare periculis, & eo modo fortunam tentare. Sal. Bello Jug. Atque hi quidem pericula feliciter emensi, generosis facinoribus inclaruerunt. Germanicum in Oriente aut casus morbi fortuitus, molliori coelo non affluetum, aut fraus Pisonis per occulta Tiberii mandata oppressit.
units.tr: Circe, offering a drink to strangers, turned them into swine or wild beasts, and soothed them with incantation and a wand, and drove them into a sty. Princes whom they fear as military rivals, they send away from the court or the army by a whisper of honours or the pretext of an embassy, or else, by the enchantment of rumour, they expose them to dangers and hand them over to death. It was not unwelcome to Tiberius that the disturbances of the East should arise, so that under that pretext he might draw Germanicus away from his accustomed legions, place him over new provinces, and expose him at the same time to treachery and chance. Greek antiquity is full of the tasks set for Bellerophon, Jason, and Hercules, which they undertook for glory, and for hardships. The same stage of glory was set for David, the bravest of kings, among the Hebrew people, by Saul his father-in-law, through open dangers. Among the Numidians, Micipsa, because Jugurtha was ready of hand and eager for military glory, decided to expose him to dangers and in this way to test his fortune. Sal. Bello Jug. Yet these men, having passed through dangers happily, became famous for noble deeds. Germanicus in the East was overcome either by a chance illness, having been brought up in a milder sky, or by the treachery of Piso acting on Tiberius's secret orders.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Nosse hostem, nosse suos, prima militaris viri dexteritas.
units.tr: Know your enemy, know your own: this is the first skill of a soldier.

units.la: Etiam jumenta & ferae, quas nec ingenii solertia nec disciplina erudiit, suas & adversarii vires expendunt. In cornua taurus exurgit, ungulas equus expromit, dentem lupus adversum nudat, obliquum ictum aper meditatur. Calcem equi lupus vitando, à latere aut à fronte in eum irruit. Robur suum cum imbecillitate hostium animalia bruta comparant. Nimii igitur aut simplicis aut antiqui animi judicandi, qui victoriae decus quaesitum detrahunt, nisi eodem armorum genere, ac loco quidem & tempore proelii indicio, concur-ratur. Imperatorie Germanicus, arte ad usum advo-cata, tractare praeliorum vias, & quae sibi tertium jam annum belligeranti prospera vel adversa evenissent, fundi Germanos acie & justu loci; juvari sylvis, paludibus, brevi aestate & praematura hyeme: suum militem haud perinde vulneribus, quam spatiis itinerum, damno armorum affici: fessus Gallia ministrandis[?] equis: longum impedimentorum agmen, opportunum ad insidias, defensantibus iniquum. Pari hostium & suorum notitia ante Germanicum Cæsar, suos animo labantes in Ariovistum & Germanos erigit. ἡμεῖς μὲν [illegible, ~25 letters] [illegible, ~45 letters] [illegible, ~40 letters] [illegible, ~35 letters] [illegible, ~6 letters] Nos totum corpus armis tegimus: illi majori fui parte nudi sunt, nos ratione utimur & ordine: illi ad omnia ira incompositi ruunt, ut est apud Dionem libro 38. Cætera quæ sunt artis imperatoriæ, historia duce suis temporibus docebimus.
units.tr: Even beasts of burden and wild animals, whom neither native cleverness nor training has taught, weigh up their own strength and that of their opponents. The bull rears up on its horns, the horse brings its hooves into play, the wolf bares its teeth against the foe, and the boar plans a sideways blow. The wolf, avoiding the horse's kick, attacks it from the side or from the front. Brute animals compare their own strength with the weakness of their enemies. Therefore those who judge too simply or too old-fashionedly, and who take away the glory of a victory that has been won, are mistaken, unless the battle is fought with the same kind of arms, and in the same place and time, as the evidence requires. Germanicus, having taken up the art and made it his practice to handle the ways of battle, and the favourable or adverse things that had happened to him in the third year of his campaigning, observed that the Germans were routed in battle by the lie of the land; that they were helped by forests, marshes, a short summer and an early winter; that his own soldiers were harmed less by wounds than by the lengths of their marches and the loss of their equipment; that Gaul had been worn out by the supply of horses; and that a long baggage train was convenient for ambushes and unfavourable to those defending it. Before Germanicus, Caesar, with equal knowledge of his enemies and of his own men, raised his wavering soldiers against Ariovistus and the Germans. [illegible Greek] We cover our whole bodies with armour; they are for the most part naked. We use reason and order; they rush on everything in disordered anger, as is said in Dio, book 38. The rest of what belongs to the art of command we shall teach, with history as our guide, in its proper times.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Expeditissima militarium copiarum per mare deportatio.
units.tr: The quickest transport of military forces by sea.

units.la: Ac si mare intretur, promtam ipsis possessionem, & hostibus ignotam: simul bellum maturius incipi, legionesque & commeatus pariter vehi: integrum equi-tem equosque per ora & alveos fluminum media in Germaniam fore. Quam tamen non satis tuto ventis & fluctibus, infidis rerum arbitris, tot animarum millia credantur; reditu lacerae classis idem Germanicus do-cuerit. Romani certè quà terrà potuerunt, mari exer-citum vix unquam traduxerunt. Itaque in Græciam aut Asiam ituri, non Hostiæ proximo portu, sed Brun-dysii; in Africam moliturí, Lilybæi, extremo Siciliæ angulo, militem in naves impegerunt. Solertissimus Hispaniarum monarcha legiones, duce Albano, Belgas castigaturas, longo terrarum ambitu, cum mari domi-naretur, felici expeditione circumegit. Qui postmo-dum consilio mutato, annum sæculi 88 insigni naviuum[?] suarum clade insignivit.
units.tr: If the sea is entered, the possession is quick for them and unknown to the enemy; at the same time the war is begun earlier, and the legions and supplies are carried together; the cavalry and horses, whole, would be in Germany through the mouths and channels of the rivers. Yet not so safely can so many thousands of souls be entrusted to winds and waves, unreliable judges of affairs; Germanicus himself taught this by the return of his battered fleet. Certainly the Romans, wherever they could go by land, hardly ever transported an army by sea. And so, when going to Greece or Asia, they embarked their soldiers not at the nearby port of Hostia but at Brundisium; when preparing for Africa, at Lilybaeum, at the far corner of Sicily. The most skilful monarch of Spain, having command of the sea, led his legions, under the Duke of Alba, to punish the Belgians, and carried them round by a long circuit of lands in a successful expedition. Afterwards, changing his plan, he marked the year 1588 by the notable slaughter of his fleet.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Ducis est, in multa simul vigili cura intentum esse.
units.tr: It is the mark of a commander to be attentive to many things at once with watchful care.

units.la: Quod fieri possit sine cogitationum, sine virium di-stractione. Alias una infecutione duas feras captando, utramque è manibus emiseris. Cæsar Germanicus navalem in Cherusços expeditionem meditatus, dum adiguntur naves, Silium legatum cum expedita manu irruptionem in Chattos facere iubet. ipse audito castellum Lupiae flumini appositum obsideri, sex legiones eò duxit. Causa huius belli inferendi maturationis non una 1.Ut nec hosti in se occasionem patefacere, ita nec suam hosti prodere ullo tempore volebat. 2. animi incerto adversario, in istus undique opportunum adiciebatur. audita enim navium conquisitione, sedu-ctiora ab oceano securitate prodebantur. percepta Lupiae & Chattorum regionis invasione, remissius Vi-surgis & Amisiae accolae gerebant. 3 Militem ab armis & ab opere nunquam otiari, tum ad agiliorem belli meditationem, tum ad seditionum femina enecanda interest. De prisca Romanorum sedulitate Salustius: Talibus viris non labos insolitus, non locus ullus asper aut arduus erat, non armatus hostis formidulosus: virtus omnia domuerat. At postquam Italia domita, Siciliæ subacta, Pœnis intra Africæ litora compulsis, quietis blandiente inertia, armatos cominus ferire dedicerant, Hannibali impune insultanti terga praebuere. Quo cum Carthaginensibus devicto, & Græcia cum Asiæ litoribus pacata, post sex septem annorum quietem, belli materiam in Illyrico aperiri patres gavisi sunt: ne, uti censet Polybius, Martius ille vigor Italicæ virtutis, otio & situ detritus, marcesceret.
units.tr: This can be done without dividing thoughts or forces. Otherwise, by pursuing two beasts with one chase, you let both go from your hands. Germanicus, planning a naval expedition against the Cherusci, while the ships were being fitted out, ordered the legate Silius, with a light force, to make an invasion of the Chatti. He himself, having heard that the fort placed on the river Lupia was being besieged, led six legions there. The reason for beginning this war was not single. First, just as he did not wish to reveal to the enemy an opportunity against himself, so at no time did he wish to betray his own to the enemy. Second, the enemy's mind was kept uncertain, and everywhere opportunity was added to it; for on hearing of the requisition of ships, the people, made more careless by their security far from the ocean, were revealed; but once the invasion of the Lupia and the territory of the Chatti was known, the neighbours of the Visurgis and the Amisia acted more carelessly. Third, the soldier should never be idle from arms and work, both for a more agile preparation of war and for smothering the seeds of mutiny. Sallust speaks of the old diligence of the Romans: For such men no unaccustomed toil, no place was rough or steep, no armed enemy fearsome; their courage had mastered everything. But after Italy was subdued, Sicily brought under control, and the Carthaginians driven within the shores of Africa, they unlearned, as quiet and idleness flattered them, to strike armed men at close quarters, and they offered their backs to Hannibal insulting them with impunity. When the Carthaginians had been defeated, and Greece together with the shores of Asia had been pacified, the Fathers rejoiced that after six or seven years of quiet an occasion for war was opened in Illyricum, lest, as Polybius advises, that martial vigour of Italian courage, worn away by leisure and inactivity, should wither.

units.la: Ventus ut amittit vires, nisi robore densa Occurrant sylvæ, spatio diffusus inani: Vtque perit magnus nullis obstantibus ignis:
units.tr: As the wind loses its strength unless dense forests meet it with their oak, spreading out in empty space, and as a great fire perishes when nothing stands in its way:

units.la: Sic hostes mihi deesse nocet. inquit apud Lucanum Julius Cæsar. Malo exemplo, sed exemplo tamen, Catilina si causa peccandi in præsens minus suppetebat, nihilominus insontes, sicuti sontes, circumvenire, jugulare, scilicet, ne per otium torpescerent manus, animus gratuito potius malum atque crudelis erat. itanc ferocia animorum militarium aliquando cicuretur, quà fontium quà insontium sanguis hauritur. Ad Germanicum, temporibus iis bellatorem maximum, redço[?]. Anni superioris principio eadem festinatione, eosdem sibi hostes destinaverat. decernitur Germanico triumphum manente bello; quod quanquam in astatem sum-ma ope parabat, initio veris & repentino in Chattos excursu praecepit. lib.1.Annalium. quod tamen, nisi oc-casione rei bene gerendae monstrata, temere non mo-liendum. quam tum Germanico capillatam fuisse, Cornelius his verbis innuit: nam spes incesserat, diffidere hostem in Arminium ac Segestem, insignem utrumque perfidia in nos aut fide.
units.tr: So the lack of enemies does me harm, says Julius Caesar in Lucan. By a bad example, yet an example nonetheless, Catiline, if the cause for wrongdoing was at present less at hand, nevertheless surrounded, cut the throats of the innocent as of the guilty, lest, through idleness, his hands should grow numb; his mind was rather wicked and cruel for no gain. Will the savage fierceness of military minds ever be tamed, when blood is drawn both from the guilty and the innocent? I come back to Germanicus, at that time the greatest warrior. At the beginning of the previous year he had marked out the same enemies with the same haste. A triumph was voted to Germanicus while the war remained; and although he was preparing it with all his might for the summer, he anticipated it at the beginning of spring with a sudden raid against the Chatti, book 1 of the Annals. Yet this should not be undertaken rashly unless the opportunity for a successful action is shown. How much Germanicus was then hoping for is hinted at by Cornelius in these words: For hope had crept in that the enemy distrusted Arminius and Segestes, both notable, the one for treachery, the other for loyalty toward us.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Nullus imperator consiliorum ratio-nem semper in numerato habet.
units.tr: No commander always has the reasons for his plans in hand.

units.la: In Germanico suo Tacitus aliquid desiderat. Classis Amisia relicta, lavo amne. erratumque in eo, quod non subvexit, transfpofuit militem dextras in terras itu-rum, ita plures dies efficiendis pontibus absumpti. Cyrus Persa, Graecorum annalibus dux inter celebra-tos vetustissimus, vino, callide ab hostibus fugam fi-mulantibus in vacuis castris relicto, se & exercitum in-gurgitans, incædem[?] & in ignominiam foeminae pa-tuit. Alexander, Macedonum suprema gloria, quae-dam fortuna quam consilio felicius expedivit. Hanni-bal tot Romanorum legionibus ad Ticinum, ad Tre-biam, ad Trasimenum cæsis, in Umbriam & Hirpinos victorem exercitum avertendo, Romanis perculsis è trepidatione se recolligendi spatium dedit. Ne post Cannas quidem Romana clade nobilitatas, dignum victoria tanta praemium, Campaniae desidiosis hyber-nis,petiit. Domitor Carthaginis Scipio, tum temporis Hispaniarum victor, uni scaphae & ventorum fidei, & Numidarum regum levissimis ingeniis, suam & Romanorum salutem commisit. quod ei in senatu exprobrans Fabius, Non semper temeritatem felicem esse docuit. Julius Cæsar castris in conspectu Pom[?]ejanorum[?] defertis, piscatoria navi conscensa, inter cœli & aquæ minas Italiam petebat. Idem inconsulta plane temeritate Pompejum, locorum spatiis & copiarum multitudine diffusum, egens commeatu non indigentem, nec sine errati accepta castigatione, ad Dyrrhachium obsedit. Et quorsum plura cumulem? Germanicum tamen, in hoc classis non subvectæ erra-to, erroris propemodum absolverim. Angusto enim inter vicinas ripas flumine, nondum terrarum spatioso traductu absorpto, (Dollart incolæ vocant) & satis violento cursu, navigationem secundam ventis obliquis aut adversis negantibus, illorum maxime temporum navigandi inscitia, velorum usus demebatur. Gravius forte in eo erravit, quod Cheruscos & Arminium infestando, pro Amisia Visurgim non petierit, patulum aperto sinu, & ripas præbentem æstuariis minus incisas. Nisi forte oceanum, iis locis potentiorem, formidans, terræ amore proximis litoribus classem applicuit.
units.tr: Tacitus leaves something to be desired in his Germanicus: The fleet, having left the Amisia with the river on its left. There was an error in this, that he did not carry the soldiers upstream, and he set down those who were about to march into the lands on the right; so many days were spent building bridges. The Persian Cyrus, the most ancient of the famous generals in the Greek annals, left wine in the empty camp for the enemy, who were feigning flight, and when he had overindulged himself and his army, he was exposed to slaughter and to the disgrace of a woman. Alexander, the supreme glory of the Macedonians, got through some matters by luck more happily than by planning. Hannibal, after so many Roman legions had been cut down at the Ticinus, the Trebia and Trasimene, turned his victorious army toward Umbria and the Hirpini. By this he gave the Romans, who were stunned and in panic, room to recover themselves. Even after Cannae, a Roman disaster made famous, he did not seek, as the prize worthy of so great a victory, winter quarters of idleness in Campania. Scipio, conqueror of Carthage and at that time victor in Spain, entrusted his own safety and that of the Romans to a single skiff, to the goodwill of the winds, and to the most fickle minds of the Numidian kings. Fabius, rebuking him for this in the senate, showed that temerity is not always fortunate. Julius Caesar, having abandoned his camp in full view of the Pompeians, boarded a fishing boat and made for Italy between the threats of sky and sea. The same Caesar, with sheer thoughtless rashness, laid siege to Pompey at Dyrrachium, though Pompey was spread out over wide places and a large force, was short of supplies while Pompey was not, and was rebuked for his error. And why should I heap up more examples? Still, I would almost acquit Germanicus of error in this matter of the fleet that was not carried up. For the river, narrow between neighbouring banks, had not yet swallowed up the wide expanse of land (the inhabitants call it the Dollart), and its current was rather violent; the winds were unfavourable or adverse to a fair passage, and, above all, the sailing skill of those times was poor, so the use of sails was taken away. Perhaps he erred more gravely in not making for the Visurgis, rather than the Amisia, in order to attack the Cherusci and Arminius, since the Visurgis has an open mouth and banks that offer less cut-up estuaries. Unless, perhaps, fearing the ocean, which is more powerful in those places, he moored the fleet near the shores out of love for the land.

units.la: XIX. Locorum & temporum peritia ducem bonum insigniat.
units.tr: XIX. Knowledge of places and times marks out a good commander.

units.la: Quæ utraque Germanicum, cætera egregium, decefcit. Humido anni principio per æstuaria Chaucorum, qua litora oceani attingunt palustri solo collu-stantium, exercitum ducens, deleri facili negotio po-terat, nisi hosti in occasionem vigilandi mentem for-tuna admisset[?]. Et eques quidem ac legiones prima æstuaria, nondum accrescente unda, intrepidi transfite-re: postremum auxiliorum agmen, Batavi, in parte eundum[?] insultant aquis, artemque nandi ostentant, turbati, & quidam hausti sunt. Truculentior priori libro aquarum in Vitellium sævitia describitur. In eum usum fortassis expediat, pontes levi materia portatiles, aut ubi latior aquæ campus, naves è viminibus & cratis boum coriis, circumduxisse. Quæ folertia Spi-nolam[?], acerrimum Iberici in Belgio belli ducem, non agit[?].
units.tr: He fell short in these two respects, though otherwise he was an excellent German. Leading his army through the estuaries of the Chauci in the wet beginning of the year, where the shores of the ocean touch marshy ground, he could easily have been destroyed, had fortune not given the enemy an opportunity to be watchful. The cavalry and legions crossed the first estuaries fearlessly, before the water had risen; but the Batavians, the last of the auxiliary column, rushed into the waters at the part to be crossed and showed off their skill at swimming. They were thrown into confusion, and some were drowned. The cruelty of the waters against Vitellius is described more savagely in the earlier book. For that purpose it might perhaps have been useful to carry portable bridges of light material or, where the expanse of water was wider, boats made of wicker and cowhides. Such ingenuity did not occur to Spinola, the most fierce commander of the Spanish war in Belgium.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Maturius in rebelles, & severiùs quàm in arma palàm minantes, vindicandum.
units.tr: Rebels must be punished sooner, and more severely, than those who openly threaten arms.

units.la: Metanti cástra Cafari Angrivariorum defectio à tergo nunciatur. Missus illico Stertinius cum equite & armatura levi, igne & cædibus perfidiam ultus est. Ea antiquissima in bello sæviendi, miseratione seclusa, materia. Hæc bellorum in sacra historia enarrandorum januam aperuit. Genef. 14. Alii cum venia pro libertate ferociré videantur: in fidem recepti firebellent, ut mancipia conditionis admonentur, ut perfidi ultioni simul & exemplo mactantur.
units.tr: While Caesar was pitching camp, news came that the Angrivarii had revolted at his back. Stertinius was sent at once with cavalry and light-armed troops, and avenged the treachery with fire and slaughter. This is the most ancient material for cruelty in war, with pity set aside. It opened the door to the narration of wars in sacred history. Gen. 14. Others, with pardon, seem fierce for liberty; once received into trust they rebel. As slaves are reminded of their condition, the faithless are cut down both for vengeance and as an example.

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Colloquia cum hoste nisi fide perspecta militibus non permittenda.
units.tr: Conversations with the enemy must not be permitted to soldiers unless their faith has been tested.

units.la: Arminius uti liceret cum fratre colloquii oravit, quod, nisi insignem in fe fide Flavium Romani cognoscerent, non impetraret. Cæsar in Hispania Petreium & Afranium exercitu nudasset, nisi propere iussis facessere à colloquio militibus, sermonis commercia diremissent. Plura vel antiqua temporum vel recentior memoria exempla suppeditaverit.
units.tr: Arminius asked that he might have a conference with his brother, which the Romans would not grant unless they recognised a remarkable faith in Flavus. Caesar in Spain would have stripped Petreius and Afranius of their army, had he not promptly ordered the soldiers to leave the conference and broken off the exchange of talk. More examples, both from ancient times and from more recent memory, could be supplied.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Inermem armatis & satellitio stipatis in colloquii fidem se committere, securi quàm cauti ducis est.
units.tr: To entrust oneself unarmed to a conference, surrounded by armed men and bodyguards, is the mark of a commander who is secure rather than cautious.

units.la: Non enim omnium ea fidei æstimatio est, ut eam ultionis explendæ aut victoriæ sperandæ occasioni anteponant. Arminius amotis stipatoribus, ut sagittarii nostra pro ripa dispositi abscederent, postulat: Cavit sibi Arminius fluminis interpositu, cavit sagittariorum à ripa postulato discessu. Cavit sibi, cujus modo mentionem injeci, Cæsar in Ariovisti congressu, planitiei prospectu, & legionis pari intervallo cum equitibus Ariovisi locatione. Nimis pellucida Tiridatis, regis Par-thorum, machinatio in Corbulonem erat. Mille equi-tum praesidium Tiridates affore sibi dicebat: quantum Corbuloni cujusque generis militum assisteret, non stare-tuere; dum positis loricis & galeis in faciem pacis ve-niretur. Cuicunque mortalium, nedum veteri & provido duci barbara astutia patuissent. Ideo artum inde numerum finiri, & hinc majorem afferri, ut dolus pararetur. Nam equitti sagittarum usu exercito si dete-[?]ta corpora objicerentur, nihil profuturam multitudinem. 13. Annalium. Nec desunt historiarum monumenta trucidatorum colloquii specie, aut in vincula conjectorum, belli ducum.
units.tr: For not everyone values trust so highly that he would put it before the chance of exacting vengeance or of hoping for victory. Arminius, with his bodyguards removed, demands that our archers stationed along the bank withdraw: Arminius guarded himself by the interposition of the river, and guarded himself by demanding the archers' withdrawal from the bank. Caesar, whom I have just mentioned, also guarded himself at his meeting with Ariovistus, by the open plain in view and by placing his legion at the same distance from Ariovistus' horsemen. Tiridates, king of the Parthians, devised a scheme against Corbulo that was far too transparent. Tiridates said that a force of a thousand horsemen would be present for him; how many soldiers of each kind would stand by Corbulo, they did not stop to ascertain, since they would come as if for peace with breastplates and helmets laid aside. Such barbarian cunning would have been plain to any mortal, let alone to an old and provident commander. Therefore the number of attendants was fixed small on one side and a larger one brought on the other, so that a trick could be prepared. For if bare bodies were exposed to men trained in the use of arrows, the multitude would be of no help. Tacitus, Annals 13. Nor are there lacking records in histories of commanders who slaughtered men under the guise of a conference, or threw them into chains.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Belli causa, non praemia, non vulnera, magnum ducem coronant.
units.tr: Not rewards, not wounds, but the cause of the war crowns a great commander.

units.la: Catilina nefario ausu senatum trucidaturus, sangui-ne & incendio omnia misturus, patriam ipsam in cinerem conversurus, virtutis & pulcherrimi facinoris vocabulo scelus amicit. Ni virtus, inquit, fidesque vestra fatu spectata mihi foret, &c. eo animum ausus est maximum atque pulcherrimum facinus incipere. Sall. B.C. Qui mos est hodie, Germanorum inprimis, militum; ut vulnera, ut cicatrices, ut diuturnam militiam, etiam contra focos & aras patrias susceptam, crepent: is jam olim Flavio, Germanicae gentis non postremo viro, a fratre exprobratur. Quem ut oris dehonestamento, & mutilatione corporis objecta, in odium peregrinae militiae adducat, unde ea deformitas oris, interrogat. Oculo autem per vulnus non captus modo, sed omnino exutus erat. Flavius damno gloriabundus, more militiae proelium, & rei praeclare gestae locum aeternum testem refert. Sapientior Arminius, qui quanquam bellator egregius non esse temere in acie confligendum noverat, quodnam praemium recepisset, exquirit. Ne hic quidem elinguis Flavius, ut qui [illegible, ~7 letters]larium, non causam, in bello secutus fuisset.
units.tr: Catiline, about to slaughter the senate, to mix everything with blood and fire, and to reduce the fatherland itself to ashes, wrapped his crime in the name of virtue and of a most noble deed. "Unless your virtue and faith had been proved to me by experience," he said, and so on. "Therefore he dared to begin the greatest and most noble deed." Sallust, Bell. Cat. It is the custom today, especially among German soldiers, to boast of wounds, scars and long military service, even when undertaken against the hearths and altars of the fatherland. Long ago this was thrown in the face of Flavius, no minor man of the German race, by his brother. As if to bring him to hatred of foreign service by the disfigurement of his face and the mutilation of his body, Arminius asks whence that disfigurement of the face came. Flavius had lost not only the sight but the whole eye through the wound. Boasting of his loss, in the manner of soldiers, Flavius cites the battle and the eternal witness of that famous deed. Arminius, wiser, who knew that although an excellent warrior one should not rashly engage in battle, asks what reward he had received. Flavius is not at a loss for words even here, since in war he had followed the wages of a hired man, not a cause.

units.la: auſa flīpendia, torquem, & coronam, aliaque militaria dona memorat : irridente Arminio vilia servitii pretia. & merito irridente. quamvis enim torques aut hasta donata, quamvis corona oleagina aut herbida Romanis & Græcis auro præponderabat: ut quæ vir-tutis & pro patria strenuè suscepti periculi monstratus populo index effet : tamen mercenariam militiam professo, & justitiam à nocendi instituto, causam belli à temeritate non discernenti, opprobrio magis quam ornamento fuere. Quanquam non destituitur patro-cinio fui inconsulta ferocia, & quid sequatur vaga mi-litia, magnificè ebullit. magnitudinem Romanam, opes Cæsaris, & victis graves pœnas, in deditionem venienti paratam clementiam. Feré enim aut splendore ducun-tur ejus quem bello sequuntur, aut potentiam ejus formidant, aut comitatem in alto fastigio mirantur, aut, quod crebriùs, præmia sibi largiora pollicentur. Multum etiam ad emolliendos animos & in partem fle&endos facit, in captos, cognatos maximè & genti-les, non inhumana sævitia. quod in postremo perfua-fionis agmine locat Flavius: neque conjugem & filium ejus hostiliter haberi. hæc speciosè ad causam pero-randam militaris orator. Multò apud bonos præpon-derant, quæ à causa militiæ ex adverso adducit Armi-nius: fas patriæ, libertatem avitam, penetrales Germa-nia deos, matrem precum sociam. Patria enim, liber-tas, recepta domi sacra, senes, parentes, liberi armis te-gendi; non arma in illos stringenda. Quod fi præmi-um militiæ spectetur: multò id lautius esse in claritate nominis, meritum in patriam secuta; quam in auto stipendio, aut militarium donorum nugis, cum igno-minia. nè propinquorum & procerum, denique gentis suæ, defertor & proditor, quam imperator esse mallet. Vera audire insolens bellator animus, in jurgia prola-bitur: ut feré promptiores ad facienda, quam ad au-dienda, facinora mortales sunt: & cujus nomen refu-giunt, rem ipsam desertionis, mendacii, rapinæ, prodi-tionis non detestantur.
units.tr: He recounts his splendid pay, a torque, a crown, and other military gifts; Arminius laughs at the paltry prices of slavery, and rightly so. For although a torque or a spear given as a reward, and a crown of olive or of grass, weighed more with Romans and Greeks than gold, as tokens shown to the people of virtue and of bravely undertaken danger for the fatherland, yet to a man who professes mercenary service, who does not separate justice from the practice of harming, and who does not distinguish the cause of war from rashness, they were a reproach rather than an ornament. Yet his ill-considered ferocity does not lack a defender, and he splendidly sets forth what the wandering soldier follows: Roman greatness, the power of Caesar, heavy penalties for the conquered, and the clemency prepared for one who comes to surrender. For men are led either by the splendour of the commander they follow, or they fear his power, or they admire his affability on a lofty height, or, what happens more often, they promise themselves larger rewards. Much also helps to soften minds and to bend them to one side: the not inhuman treatment of captives, especially of kin and countrymen. This is what Flavius places last in his line of persuasion, that his wife and son are not treated as enemies. These things are said speciously by the military orator to plead his cause. Far more weight with good men has what Arminius sets against the cause of soldiering: the right of the fatherland, ancestral liberty, the gods of Germany in their inner shrines, a mother as a companion in prayer. For the fatherland, liberty, the sacred rites of the household, old men, parents and children are to be defended by arms, not to be turned against. If the reward of soldiering is considered, it is far more splendid in the glory of a name won by serving the fatherland than in paltry pay or the trifles of military gifts attended by disgrace, that of being a deserter and traitor to one's kin and nobles, and finally to one's own nation, rather than its commander. The mind of a bellicose man, unused to hearing the truth, will slip into quarrels; mortals are generally more ready to commit wrongs than to hear them spoken of, and while they shun the name, they do not detest the thing itself: desertion, lying, plunder and treachery.

units.la: XXIV. Providi ducis est, ante discrimen de receptu cogitare.
units.tr: XXIV. A wise commander must think about retreat before the crisis.

units.la: Cæsar, nisi pontibus præsidiisque impositis, darent in discrimen legionem haud imperatorium ratus, equitem vado tramittit. Prisci Romani in aciem educturi, tumulum sibi aliquem, aut locum receptui idoneum, si pellerentur, prospexerunt. Captent nonnulli è necessi-tate pugnandi ardorem; naves & cætera refugia ab-ducant; castra ipsi sua incendant; medios se inter ho-stilem urbem & exercitum ponant, latera hinc arena-rum aut montium mole, inde oceani vastitate clau-dant. Quàm ad ferociam desperatio, tam ad torpo-rem animos accendere poterit. Nec vincere tantum ad Neoportum Flandriæ Mauritius Nassovius, sed vinci etiam & deleri ad Thrasimenum exercitus Flaminii potuit.
units.tr: Caesar, having put no bridges or guards in place, and judging it unbecoming for a commander to expose a legion to danger, sends the cavalry across the ford. The ancient Romans, about to lead out their army into battle, looked ahead for some mound or place suitable for retreat should they be driven back. Some men, out of the necessity of fighting, seek to kindle their ardour: they carry off their ships and other means of escape; they burn their own camps; they place themselves between the hostile city and their army, and close their flanks on one side with a mass of sand or mountains, and on the other with the vastness of the ocean. As desperation can rouse minds to ferocity, so the opposite condition can kindle them to torpor. Nor did Maurice of Nassau conquer only at Nieuwpoort in Flanders; the army of Flaminius could be not merely defeated but destroyed at Trasimene.

units.la: XXV. Transfugis nec credendum temerè, nec semper fides abnuenda.
units.tr: XXV. One should neither trust deserters rashly, nor always reject their loyalty.

units.la: Ut caveatur sibi admonentibus paratioribus auribus fides habetur. Cæsar transgressus Visurgim, indicio perfuga cognoscit, dilectum ab Arminio locum pugnæ, convenisse & alias nationes in sylvam Herculi sacram, ausurosque noctur-nam castrorum oppugnationem. habita indicii fides. Omnia vero lætæ afferentibus, & cu-stodiæ solutionem suadentibus, nonnisi explorato cre-dendum. Bello inter Athenienses & Megarenses de Sa-lamine conflato, Coliadem, ubi mulieres Atticæ festum Cereris obibant, Solon navigat. Transfugam in-ter navigandum subornat, qui Megarensibus nunciet, paratam esse ea in insula mulierum choreas ducenti-umprædam. Interea mulieribus emotis, adolescentes imberbes muliebri vestitu amictos, choreām ad litus & tripudia simulantes, pugionibus veste abditis occulte armat. Egressi navibus Megarenses, & tanquam in prædam non dubiam ruentes, micantibus repente gladiis territi laeduntur. Eodem mulierum simulatõ habitu navibus Megarensium in portum hostilem de-vehuntur, obvios & in gratulationem effusos trucidant, Megara sine discrimine potiuntur. Autor post alios Polyænus libro primo Strategematum, quanquam sunt qui Pisistrato hunc dolum adscribunt. Rébus in mediis plurium feré perfugarum indicio statur. quanquam & sic eludi credulorum facilitas poterit: quod Hannibalis, imò & ante eam Samnitium, adversus Romanos astutia docetur. Tutissimum foret, perfugarum indicio speculatorum explorationem, ubi res moram patitur, adjungere, quod hic à Cæsare Germanico factitatum. habita indici fides, & cerne-bantur ignes, suggressique propius speculatores, audiri fremitum equorum, immensique & inconditi agminis murmur, attulere. Ut verò ipse dux castra hostium in-gressus, aut propius suggressus, certiorem fidem exploret, non temerè suadendum. Quod Gedeoni, quod Davidi regi, quod aliis laudi in sacro codice datum; id Claudio Marcello, in insidias præcipitato, & cum co-mitibus trucidato, vituperio dat Polybius. Xenophon tamè non alienum id à boni ducis industria arbitratur.
units.tr: Precaution is taken by giving a ready hearing to those who give warning. Caesar, having crossed the Weser, learns from a deserter's information that Arminius had chosen a place for battle, that other nations had gathered in the forest sacred to Hercules, and that they would dare a night attack on the camp. The information was believed. But whoever brings welcome news and urges that the guard be relaxed must be believed only once the matter has been verified. When war broke out between the Athenians and the Megarians over Salamis, Solon sailed to Coliades, where the Attic women were celebrating the festival of Ceres. On the voyage he suborned a deserter to tell the Megarians that on that island women were leading dances and were ready as prey. Meanwhile he removed the women, and secretly armed beardless youths, dressed in women's clothing, with daggers hidden under their garments, while they pretended to dance and frolic on the shore. The Megarians disembarked and rushed on what they thought was certain booty, but were terrified when swords suddenly flashed and they were wounded. In the same disguise of women, the Athenians were carried in the Megarian ships into the enemy harbour, where they cut down those who came to meet them and poured out in welcome, and seized Megara without resistance. Polyaenus, in the first book of his Stratagems, is the author, though others, Pisistratus among them, are said to have devised this trick. In the midst of affairs one generally stands by the information of deserters, although even so the ready credulity of the gullible can be deceived; this is shown by the cunning of Hannibal against the Romans, and even earlier by that of the Samnites. It would be safest, where the matter admits delay, to add the scouting of spies to the deserter's information, as Germanicus Caesar did here. The information was believed, and fires were seen; when the scouts drew nearer, they reported hearing the neighing of horses and the murmur of a vast and disorderly host. But that the commander himself should enter the enemy camp, or approach it more closely to test the report, is not to be advised rashly. What is praised in the sacred book in Gideon and in King David, and in others, Polybius blames in Claudius Marcellus, who rushed into an ambush and was slaughtered with his companions. Xenophon, however, judges that this is not foreign to the diligence of a good commander.

units.la: XXVI.
units.tr: XXVI.

units.la: Propinquo summæ rei discrimine animos militarium imperator exploret.
units.tr: Before the crisis of a great matter is at hand, a military commander should test the spirits of his soldiers.

units.la: Benè Vegetius in eum sensum monet, ex vultu, ver-bis, incessu, motibus, formidinem vel fiduciam cerni. Non difficulter igitur duci rerum sagaci, quantum iis fidendum, oborietur. Germanicus propinquo summa rei discrimine explorandos militum animos ratus, quanam id modo incorruptum foret, secum agitabat. Ex auditu plerique belli duces judicant: alienis oculis & auribus quam suis plus committunt. Alio Germanicus fertur judicio: Tribunos & centuriones lata sapius, quam comperta, nunciare: libertorum servilia ingenia: amicis inesse adulationem. Si concio vocetur, illic quoque, quæ pauci incipiant, reliquos adstrepere. Penitus noscendas mentes, cum secreti & incussoditi, inter militiamili tares cibos, spem aut metum proferrent. At quo-modo imperator in suis castris fallendo, occultas vo-ces eliciat? quomodo eum non habitus, non lictores & comites, non vultus denique ipse prodat? Nofte coepta, egressus augurali, per occulta & vigilibus igna-ra, comite uno, contectus humeros ferina pelle, adit ca-strorum vias, adfixit tabernaculis, fruiturque fama sui: cum hic nobilitatem ducis, decorem alium, plurimi patientiam comitatem, per feria per jocos eundem ani-mum, laudibus ferrent; reddenda namque gratiam in acie faterentur: simul perfidos & raptores pacis ultio-ni & gloria mactandos.
units.tr: Vegetius rightly advises to the same effect that fear or confidence is discerned from the face, the words, the gait and the movements. It will therefore not be difficult for a commander who is shrewd in affairs to see how far they can be trusted. Germanicus, thinking that the soldiers' spirits must be tested when the crisis of the matter was close at hand, pondered by what means they might be found unfeigned. Most generals judge a war from hearsay, and entrust more to other men's eyes and ears than to their own. Germanicus is reported to have judged otherwise: that tribunes and centurions report what is pleasing more often than what is ascertained; that freedmen have servile natures; and that flattery lurks in friends. If an assembly was called, there too, whatever a few began, the rest would echo. He thought the minds were to be known thoroughly when, in private and unguarded, amid the plain meals of soldiers, they disclosed their hope or fear. But how is a commander to draw out their hidden words, by deceit, in his own camp? How will his rank, his lictors and companions, and finally his very face not betray him? Having begun at night, he went out in the guise of an augur, by hidden ways and unknown to the watchmen, with one companion, his shoulders covered with a wild beast's skin. He approached the paths of the camp, stopped at the tents, and enjoyed the fame of himself: while some praised the nobility of the commander, others his grace, and most his patience and affability, and the same spirit by day and in jest; for they admitted that they would repay his kindness in battle. At the same time they said that treacherous men and robbers of peace must be punished with vengeance and glory.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Ferream cuspidem auro praelinere magno duci non est probrosum.
units.tr: It is no disgrace for a great general to gild an iron spearhead with gold.

units.la: In ea prisca Germaniae simplicitate Arminius, quanquam robori consideret, emercari hostium per fidiam non erubescebat. Inter quas unus hostium Lati-ni linguaeficiens, aito ad vallum equo, voce magna, con-jugis & agros, & stipendii indies, donec bellaretur, sef-tertiis centenos, si quis transfugisset, Arminii nomine pollicetur. Nec tantum id hosti in hostem, sed & civi in suspectos magistratui in populares conjurationis, licet Romani arbitrabantur. Si quis indicaverit de conju-ratione, quae contra remp. facta erat, praemium, servo libertatem & H.S.C. libero impunitatem ejus rei & H.S.C.C. (scrip decrevere) S B C. & non semel pari de li-citatione Livius. Sed non quam emere proditionem licitum, tam eam pretio accepto vendere honestum. Incendit ea contumelia legionum iras, veniret dies, da-retur pugna: sumturum militem Germanorum agros, trasturum conjuges: accipere omen, & matrimonia ac pecunias hostium praeda destinare. Quae autem flagi-tio coercere conventicula, & praemio accepto honeste, & non accepto honestius dissolvuntur.
units.tr: In that ancient simplicity of Germany, Arminius, though he relied on his strength, did not blush to buy off his enemies by treachery. Among them, one of the enemy who spoke Latin rode up to the rampart on horseback and promised in a loud voice, in Arminius' name, wives and fields, and a daily pay of a hundred sesterces each for as long as the war lasted, to anyone who would desert. Nor was this done only from enemy to enemy. A citizen did it against suspected persons, and magistrates did it against the common people in conspiracies, though the Romans considered this lawful. If anyone should inform on a conspiracy formed against the commonwealth, the reward was freedom for a slave and, for a free man, impunity for that matter together with H.S.C.C. (they decreed the writing of it) S.B.C.; and Livy records a similar offer of reward more than once. But although it is lawful to buy treachery, it is not honourable to sell it for a price received. That insult inflamed the anger of the legions: let the day come and battle be given, the soldier would take the fields of the Germans and carry off their wives; he would take the omen, and mark the marriages and money of the enemy as his booty. As for checking such disgraceful gatherings, they are broken up honourably when a reward is received, and more honourably when none is taken.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Contra externum adsultum vallo &
units.tr: Against an external assault the general fortifies himself with a rampart and

units.la: crebris præsidiis imperator se munit.
units.tr: frequent garrisons.

units.la: Tertia fermè vigilia assultatum est castris, fine conjectu tali: post quam crebris pro munimentis cohortes, & nihil remiserunt sensere. Didicit bellicosa seculi nostri ætas, multum in ea cautione momenti poni. Romani quondam non castra modo, vallis claudebant, sed & periculosa bellici nimbi tempestate vigilias in urbe, præsidia in muro, stationes ante urbem locabant. Quod elegantibus verbis Livius memoriæ prodit.
units.tr: About the third watch the camp was attacked, though no such assault had been expected. After that, cohorts were posted at frequent points along the defences, and they noticed no slackening. The warlike age we live in has learned that much weight is placed on this kind of caution. The Romans of old fenced not only their camps with ramparts but, when the storm of war was threatening, also posted watches in the city, guards on the walls and pickets before the city. Livy records this in elegant words.

units.la: XXIX. Somnia & futurorum omina ut non sectabitur, ita non omina contemnet.
units.tr: XXIX. As he will not pursue dreams and omens of the future, so he will not despise omens.

units.la: Nox eadem latam Germanico quietem tulit, viditque se operatum, & sanguine sacro respersa pretextam, pulchriorem aliam manibus avia Augusta accepisse. Auctus omine &c. Sed major hoc duce imperator Pompejus, nocte Pharsalicam cladem antegressa, mirosin theatro Romano, quod nunquam viturus erat, plausus & acclamationes per somnium audivit. Quæ hic divinationis per somnia certitudo? Sed eam quæstionem in Arcanis regnorum excusimus.
units.tr: The same night brought Germanicus a quiet sleep, and he saw himself sacrificing, sprinkled with sacred blood and wearing the purple-bordered robe, and received another, more beautiful one from the hands of his grandmother Augusta. Encouraged by the omen, etc. But a commander greater than this one, Pompey, before the night that preceded the defeat at Pharsalus, strangely heard in a dream applause and acclamations in the Roman theatre, which he was never going to see again. What certainty of divination through dreams is this? But we have examined that question in the Secrets of Kingdoms.

units.la: XXX. Oratione temporibus commoda militum animos erigat.
units.tr: XXX. With a speech suited to the times he lifts the spirits of the soldiers.

units.la: Auctus omine, addicentibus auspiciis, vocat concionem, & quæ sapientia prævisa, aptaque imminenti pugnæ, disserit. Longa præambulorum circumductio-ne, & Tullianis in C. Verrem disgressionibus uti, non est imperatoris hostem vicinum in procinctu intuentis. Quam Cæsari Germanico orationem attribuit Cornelius, in ipsa causæ vicera sine ambagibus irrumpit. Argumentis formidinem dempturis, fiduciam sui genituris, istis insistit. Iab armorum Romanis familiarium ad omnes locos habilitate, Germanicorum ineptitudine. Non campos modo militi Romano, ad prælium
units.tr: Encouraged by the omen, with the auspices favourable, he calls an assembly and sets out the wisdom that foresaw and fits the coming battle. A long circling round of preliminaries, and digressions in the manner of Tully against Gaius Verres, are not for a general who has the enemy close at hand and is drawn up for battle. The speech that Cornelius assigns to Germanicus Caesar rushes without circumlocution straight into the heart of the matter. He relies on arguments that will remove fear and create confidence. Not only plains good for battle are the Roman soldier's, but, if reason is there, woods and thickets.

units.la: lixm ium[?] bonos, sed, si ratio adsit sylvas & saltus. nec enim immensa barbarorum scuta, enormis hastas, inter trans-cursus arborum, & enata humo virgulta, perinde haberi, quam pila & gladios, & harentia corpori tegmina, quam adhortatione rationem munit. densarent ictus, era mucronibus quarerent. 2. à nuditate Germanorum, armorum corpus tegentium inopia adictus patentium. non loricam Germano, nongaleam: ne scuta quidem ferro nervove firmata, sed viminum textus, vel tenues & fucatas colore tabulas. 3. ab armorum hostem ferientium rara tenuitate. primam utcunque aciem hastatam: cateris praufta aut brevia tela. 4. ab aerumnarum & vulnerum impatientia, quod argumentum [illegible, ~6 letters] coloratur. jam corpus, ut visu torvum, & ad brevem impetum validum, sic nulla vulnerum patientia. 5. à fugacitate hostium, & morum inconstantia. sine pudore flagitii, sine cura ducum, abire, fugere: pavidos adversis; inter secunda non divini, non humani juris memores. 6. à spe hoc praelio finiendi belli. Si tadio[?] viarum ac maris finem cupiant; hac acie parari. cui amplificatio à terrae, quam penetraverint, reductiori situ; & clausula exhortatoria accedit. propiorem jam Albim, quam Rhenum: neque bellum ultra. modo se, patris patriqueque vestigia prementem, isdem in terris victorem sisterent. Nec orator Germanicus, quam imperator, melior. Orationem ducis secutum militum ardor: signumque pugna datum. Haec Romana in acie eloquentia: sono Latino Germanicam non minus audiamus. Nec Arminius, aut cateri Germanorum proceres, omittebant suos quisque tesari. Germani ad pugnae ardorem accenduntur. 1. contemptu Romanorum injecto. à Varianae cladis memoria. Hos esse Romanos Variani exercitus fugacissimos. à seditionis flagitio. qui ne bellum tolerarent, seditionem induerint. à praesentium miseriarum cumulo. quorum pars onusta vulneribus tergum, pars fluctibus & procellis fractos artus, infensis rursum hostibus, adversis edita objiciant. ab ominosa, & bonae spei adversa, Oceani navigatione. nulla boni spe: classem quippe & aviam Oceani quasita, ne quis venientibus occurreret, ne pulsos premeret. Fed ubi miscuerint manus, inanes vitiis ventorum remorumve subsidium. 2. imperii Romanorum duritiæ in memoriam vocata. meminissent modò avaritia, crudelitatis, superbiæ. 3. à gravioribus servitutis quàm mortis jugo. aliud sibi reliquum, quàm tenere libertatem, aut mori ante servitium?
units.tr: The arguments are these: (1) from the Romans' familiarity with arms and their adaptability to every kind of ground, against the Germans' clumsiness. Woods and thickets are not to be feared by men who know how to fight in them: the enormous shields and huge spears of the barbarians are of no use among the tree trunks and the brushwood sprouting from the ground, and are not to be rated as highly as javelins, swords, and armour that clings to the body. Reason is strengthened by the Romans' exhortation; they thicken their blows and seek the enemy with their points. (2) From the nakedness of the Germans, whose lack of armour leaves their bodies exposed. No breastplate for the German, no helmet; not even shields strengthened with iron or sinew, but wicker weave or thin boards painted with colour. (3) From the thin scarcity of weapons that strike the enemy: the first line, at least, is armed with spears; the rest have only short or blunt weapons. (4) From their impatience of hardship and wounds, which is shown by their appearance: their body, grim to look at and strong for a short charge, has no patience for wounds. (5) From the fleetingness of the enemy and the inconstancy of their character: without shame for disgrace, without concern for their leaders, they go off and flee; fearful in adversity, and in success mindful neither of divine nor of human law. (6) From the hope that this battle will end the war: if they desire an end to the tedium of roads and sea, it is prepared by this battle. To this is added an amplification drawn from how far back into the land they have penetrated, and an exhortatory close: the Elbe is now nearer than the Rhine, and there is no war beyond. Only let them, treading in the footsteps of their father and their fatherland, show themselves as victors in the same lands. Is there, then, anything more here than the purpose of this speech? Would a Roman soldier have anything left to ask for, except to keep his liberty or die before he submits to slavery?

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Primum, vel in primis, boni ducis officium est ordinata aciei explicatio.
units.tr: First, and above all, it is the duty of a good leader to draw up the battle line in order.

units.la: Incastris, in agmine, in acie ordinis primum autorem ferunt Pana, Dionysii in expeditione indica comitem. inde Cornigeri appellationem, à circumfusis mediæ aciei cornibus, secundum Polyænum traxit. Trojani belli temporibus non multum ordini, plurimum confuso incursui loci fuisse, ex Homeri Iliade deprehenditur. Nisi quod secundo libro Nestor suo Agamemnoni monitum suggerit, ut gentiles, tribules vel curiales junctò incessu misceat: Κεἰν' ἀνδρας κατὰ φῦλα, κατὰ φρήτρας, ἀγάμεμνον. Explicatio paulatim, & curiosior, ordinis increvit ratio: apud Spartanos inprimis bello Messeniaco, Peloponnesiaco; apud Thebanos Leuctrico; apud Athenienses Bœotico; nec non antiquioribus temporibus Dariaco. Ita ut Græci hac in parte omnibus nationibus laudem abstulerint. De qua Æneæ & aliorum scriptis sunt libri Tαχτικῶν. Philippi & Alexandri seculo densa Macedonum acies, Phalanga vocant, ex eventu laudem Græcorum obscuravit. Hanc Romanæ aciei Polybius postponit: præcipuumque victi Philippi secundi & Persei momentum in ea ponit. nec à judicio hoc recedit Livius: addita judicii ratione, quod ista fit distinctior, & ex pluribus partibus constans, facilis partienti quacunque opus fit, facilis jungenti. Lib. 9. Aciei in Hastatos, Principes, Triarios; legionis in cohortes, manipulos, contubernia divisio- nem ex obviis de antiquitate Romana libris, Lipsii in- primis, haurias licet. De ordine aciei Germanici, propinquo summae rei cum Germanis discrimine, his verbis Tacitus: Nester exercitus sic incessit. auxiliares Galli, Germanique in fronte: post quos pedites sagitta-rii: dein quatuor legiones, & cum duabus praetorii cohortibus ac dilecto equite Caesar: exin totidem aliae legiones, & levis armatura cum equite sagittario, caeterAque sociorum cohortes. Pro sagittariis hodie ignia-rii jaculatores, quos bombardarios & sclopetarios appellant; pro auxiliaribus mercenarii e peregrinis gentibus. Caetera non multo morum discrimine in diversum abeunt.
units.tr: Within camps, on the march, and in battle array, the first author of order is said to be Pan, the companion of Dionysus on his Indian expedition. From him, according to Polyaenus, the name "horned" (Cornigeri) came, from the horns of the middle line that surrounded the centre. From Homer's Iliad it is clear that in the time of the Trojan War there was little order and much disorderly rushing about, with no fixed place for each. Yet in the second book Nestor offers Agamemnon advice that he should arrange the men by clans and by brotherhoods, each group moving together in close order: "Set men by tribes, by phratries, Agamemnon" [Κεἰν' ἀνδρας κατὰ φῦλα, κατὰ φρήτρας, ἀγάμεμνον]. Gradually the method of ordering the line grew more elaborate and careful: among the Spartans especially in the Messenian and Peloponnesian wars, among the Thebans at Leuctra, among the Athenians at Boeotia, and also in more ancient times at Darius's battles. So the Greeks in this respect carried off the praise from all nations. Aeneas and others wrote books on this subject, the Tactica. In the age of Philip and Alexander the dense Macedonian battle line, which they call the phalanx, dimmed the glory of the Greeks by its success. Polybius ranks the Roman battle line above this, and he places the chief cause of the defeat of Philip the Second and Perseus in it. Livy does not depart from this judgement, and he adds his reason: the Roman line is more distinct and made up of more parts, easy to divide wherever necessary and easy to join again (Book 9). The division of the line into Hastati, Principes and Triarii, and of the legion into cohorts, maniples and tent-groups, you may learn from the books on Roman antiquity that are everywhere available, especially those of Lipsius. Concerning the order of battle of the Germans, in a matter closely touching the danger of the whole enterprise with the Germans, Tacitus puts it in these words: "Our army advanced in this order: the auxiliary Gauls and Germans in front; after them the foot archers; then four legions, and with two praetorian cohorts and the picked cavalry, Caesar himself; after them as many other legions, and the light-armed troops with the mounted archers, and the remaining cohorts of the allies." Instead of archers, today we have fire-men, javelin-throwers, whom they call bombardiers and musketeers; instead of auxiliaries, mercenaries from foreign nations. In other respects the rest differs little in its customs.

units.la: XXXII. Labentem belli molem periculo suo sustineat.
units.tr: XXXII. He should bear the falling weight of war at his own risk.

units.la: Sintne ducis partes ante primam aciem versari, & manu cum hoste confligere; an satis sit, post principia latitantem inde omnibus signum dare, quod Pyrrhum factitasse Thraso Terentianus commemorat; disquirere in praesens omitto. Illud non ambigitur, re ad fugam aut lapsum inclinata, non consilium modo ducis, exemplum etiam requiri. Talem Cherusci ducem, talem Germani reliqui requirebant. inter quos insignis Arminius, manu, voce, vulnere sustentabat pugnam. Talis infra Inguiomerus: quem tota volitantem acie, fortuna magis quam virtus deserebat. In universum apud eam nationem duces exemplo potius quam imperio, si promti, si conspicui, si ante aciem agant, admiratione praesunt. De Moribus Germ. Arminii factum, & Taciti de eo locum, sine dubio ante oculos habuit Carolus Paschalius, quem Vernulaeus laudat: Is demum dux mihi tanquam fortis & acer probatur, qui inter suos effusè fugientes, ipse insignis manu, voce, vulnere, si forte vulneratus est, sustentat pugnam. Rotundiori elegantia de Julio Caesare, ad Mundam res collapsas erigente, Florus: ablegato equo in primam aciem procurrit: ibi prensare fugientes, confirmare, per totum denique agmen oculis, manibus, clamore volitare. Sed omni spe restituendae rei praecisa, ut cum Paulo ad Cannas, morte nihil reip. profutura, procumbat, non est poscendum. Ad meliora fe reipublicæ tempora, cum Scipione in ea acie tribuno, fervet. & hic Arminius, cum omnia tentanti nihil ad votum fucceffiffet, ni/u tamen corporis, & impetu equi pervasit, oblitus faciem suo cruore, ne nosceretur.
units.tr: Whether a commander's proper place is before the first line, fighting hand to hand with the enemy, or whether it is enough to lurk behind the front and give the signal to all from there, which Terence's Thraso says Pyrrhus used to do, I omit to inquire into for the present. This much is not in doubt: when a battle tilts toward flight or collapse, not only the commander's counsel but his example is required. The Cherusci demanded such a leader, and the rest of the Germans demanded one too. Among them stood out Arminius, who sustained the fight by hand, voice and wound. Below him was Inguiomerus, whom fortune rather than courage deserted, as he flitted about the whole line. In general, among that people, leaders who act by example rather than by command hold their authority through admiration, if they are eager, conspicuous, and fight in front of the line. Carolus Paschalius, whom Vernulaeus praises, doubtless had before his eyes the deed of Arminius and Tacitus's passage about him in the Germania: He alone is approved by me as a brave and keen leader who, when his men are fleeing in disorder, stands out himself by hand, voice and wound, and sustains the fight, even if he happens to be wounded. In a more polished style Florus writes of Julius Caesar, who restored the collapsing battle at Munda: having sent his horse away, he ran forward into the front line; there he seized the fugitives, encouraged them, and at last flew through the whole column with eyes, hands and shouting. But when all hope of restoring the situation has been cut off, a commander should not seek to fall, as Paulus did at Cannae, in a death that will profit the state nothing. He should reserve himself for better times of the republic, as the tribune Scipio did in that same battle. And here Arminius too, when all his efforts had failed to achieve his wish, nevertheless broke through by the strength of his body and the rush of his horse, having smeared his face with his own blood so that he would not be recognized.

units.la: Quod de nisu corporis Tacitus, id in Jugurtha Sallu-ftius, vitabundum per tela elapsum evasisse, referte Quod de facie cruore oblita; ad strategematum exempla referendum.
units.tr: What Tacitus says of the strength of his body, Sallust says of Jugurtha, that he escaped through the weapons, dodging and slipping away. Refer what is said of the face smeared with blood to examples of stratagems.

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: In spe aut cursu fecundarum etiam alteram fortunam ante oculos habeat.
units.tr: Even in the hope or the course of good fortune, one should keep the other fortune before one's eyes.

units.la: Nec cum Germanis de locanda prius quam de paranda victoria cogitet: repertu inter spolia eorum ca-tenu, quas in Romanos, ut non dubio eventu, portave-rant. Simili fiduciae delusione, qui cum Joanne Nafovio Selandiam invasuri naves conscenderant, instrumenta suspendii & carnificinæ, ut non dubia victoria, in Batavorum socios Insulanos adduxerant. Cujus rei detectio gloriosiorem Fr. Henrico Auraico victoriam peperit. Plura, nam fe non parce offerunt, exempla non cumulo.
units.tr: Nor should he think about disposing of the spoils before he thinks about securing the victory. Among the Germans' spoils chains were found, which they had brought to bind the Romans, as if the outcome were certain. By a similar delusion of confidence, those who had boarded ships with John of Nassau to invade Zeeland had brought ropes for hanging and instruments of torture against the Islanders, their allies of the Batavians, as if victory were certain. The discovery of this plot brought Frederick Henry of Orange a more glorious victory. There are more examples, for they offer themselves freely, but I will not heap them up.

units.la: XXXIV.
units.tr: XXXIV.

units.la: Rerum gestarum gloriam ad aufpi-cia præbentem referat.
units.tr: He should refer the glory of deeds accomplished to the auspices that furnish them.

units.la: Gnarus animi Germanici & morum temporis mi-les, in loco proelii Tiberium imperatorem salutavit, struxitque aggerem & in modum tropæorum armaq; subscriptis victarum gentium nominibus, imposuit. De quo mox plutibus.
units.tr: Knowing the Germanic temper and the customs of the age, the soldier saluted Tiberius as imperator on the field of battle, and raised a mound and set upon it, in the manner of trophies, arms with the names of the conquered nations inscribed. On this more will be said shortly.

units.la: XXXV.
units.tr: XXXV.

units.la: Generosos animos ignominia magis cladis quam clades ipsa commovet.
units.tr: Noble spirits are moved more by the shame of a defeat than by the defeat itself.

units.la: Idcoque exprobratione calamitatis, & infultationetropæorum, non nimis irritandi. Haud perinde Germanos
units.tr: Therefore one should not provoke them too much by reproaching their disaster and by insulting them with trophies. The Germans were not so much affected

units.la: manos manu vulnera, lu[?]tus, excidia, quam ea species, dolore & ira adfecit. qui modo abire sedibus, trans Albim concedere parabant, pugnam voluerunt, arma rapiunt. plebes, primores, juventus, senes, agmen Romanum re-tenti incursant, turbant. Quod ad locum de moderanda victoria, non ad modestiae modo laudem, sed ad utilitatem etiam, & quia laetitia victoriae nimii invasio-ni patent, referas.
units.tr: by hands, wounds, grief and slaughter, as by that sight, which filled them with pain and anger. Those who a moment before were preparing to leave their homes and withdraw across the Elbe now wanted battle; they seize their arms. The commons, the nobles, the young men, and the old men rush at the Roman column, which is held back, and throw it into confusion. This passage, on moderating victory, should be cited not only for the praise of moderation but also for its usefulness, since the joy of victory lies open to excessive rashness.

units.la: XXXVI.
units.tr: XXXVI.

units.la: Insidiae nisi probè contestae[?] autoribus in perniciem vertuntur.
units.tr: Ambushes not properly concealed turn to the destruction of their authors.

units.la: Legerant Germani locum, flumine & sylvis clausum, arta intus planicie & humida, sylvas profunda palude ambiente. hic peditem abdiderant. equitem propinquis lucis, ut ingressis sylvam legionibus a tergo foret, texerant. Germanicus, qui censilia[?], locos, prompta, occulta noverat, astus hostiles ipsis in damnum retorquebat. Hac indagandi hostium secreta arte Hannibal sedecim per annos Italiae per viscera, victor plerunque, volitavit. Hac Cicero, contra conjuratorum fraudem, suam & civium salutem est tutatus. Sed circumfusa exemplorum copia, manum a tabula abduco.
units.tr: The Germans had chosen a place enclosed by a river and woods, with a narrow, damp plain within and a deep marsh surrounding the woods. There they hid their infantry, and they had concealed their cavalry in the nearby groves, so that the legions, once they had entered the forest, would be attacked from behind. Germanicus, who knew the plans, the places, and the ready and hidden resources, turned the enemy's tricks back upon themselves to their own harm. By this art of searching out the enemy's secrets Hannibal flitted for sixteen years through the very heart of Italy, mostly victorious. By this art Cicero protected his own life and that of the citizens against the fraud of the conspirators. But the abundance of examples crowds around me, so I withdraw my hand from the tablet.

units.la: XXXVII.
units.tr: XXXVII.

units.la: Necessitas vel timidos ad fortitudinem acuit.
units.tr: Necessity sharpens even the timid to courage.

units.la: Hostem a tergo palus Romanos flumen aut montes claudebant, utrisque necessitas in loco, spes in virtute, salus ex victoria. Sed quam non semper tutum sit, in eam pugnandi aut moriendi necessitatem militem conjici, supra a nobis monitum.
units.tr: The enemy blocked the Romans from behind with a marsh, a river or mountains; for both sides, necessity was in the place, hope in courage, safety in victory. But how little it is always safe to drive a soldier into such a necessity of fighting or dying, I have warned above.

units.la: XXXVIII.
units.tr: XXXVIII.

units.la: Non omnia in belli eventibus audacia & animi promptitudo sibi deposcit.
units.tr: Boldness and readiness of spirit do not claim everything in the outcomes of war.

units.la: Nec minor Germanis animus: sed genere pugnae & armorum superabantur. De quo in Arcanis[?] regno-rum explicatius egi.
units.tr: The Germans' spirit was no less, but they were overcome by the kind of fighting and the arms. I have treated this more fully in the Arcana regnorum.

units.la: XXXIX.
units.tr: XXXIX.

units.la: Nec ira victorem populum nec habendi cupido regat. Ad honestatem & reip. salutem omnia referat. cujus intuitu ne misericordiæ quidem miserorum semper locum dabit. de hac, & habendi cupiditate frenanda, capias licet, & mitiùs interpreteris illud Germanici: nil opus captivis, solam internecionem gentis finem bello fore. Huc & Hebræorum duce Jofua acerbitatem, in exscindendis Cananæ populis, mitigatione à Deo ipso increpita, per me trahas.
units.tr: Let a victorious people be ruled neither by anger nor by the desire to possess. Let it refer everything to honour and the safety of the commonwealth. With that aim in view, it will not always leave room even for pity toward the wretched. On restraining this desire for possession you may take what I have said, and you may interpret more mildly that saying of Germanicus: there is no need for captives, and the destruction of the nation alone will be the end of the war. To this you may also draw, through my argument, the severity of Joshua, leader of the Hebrews, in destroying the peoples of Canaan, which God himself rebuked with a softening correction.

units.la: XL.
units.tr: XL.

units.la: Dux belli victor in sua parcus, in mi-litum benignus, in principis laude effu-sus esse cogitet. Germanici omnia hæc complexi exemplo. Lau-datis pro concione victoribus Cæsar, congeriem armo-rum struxit, superbo cum titulo: Debellatis inter Rhe-num Albimque nationibus exercitum Tiberii Cæsaris ea monimenta Marti & Jovi & Augusto sacravit, de se nihil addidit, metu invidiae, an ratus conscientiam factis esse. Quod si non ficta hæc tantæ Ro-manorum victoriæ monumenta: crediderim non illis temporibus natum esse rhythmum nationi huic vernaculum: Wer in dem Krieg wil vnglück han/ Der fang es mit den Teutschen an: i. e. Vulnera quisquis amas & acerbi funera belli, Teutonicas crudo Marte lacesse manus.
units.tr: Let a general who is victorious in war be sparing with his own men, generous toward his soldiers, and lavish in praise of his prince. Germanicus embraced all of this in his conduct. Caesar praised the victorious soldiers before the assembly and raised a heap of arms with a proud inscription: "With the nations between the Rhine and the Elbe subdued, the army of Tiberius Caesar dedicated these monuments to Mars, Jupiter and Augustus." He added nothing about himself, either from fear of envy or because he thought his conscience was clear. But if these monuments of so great a Roman victory are not fabricated, I would believe that a rhyme native to this nation was already current in those times: "Whoever wants misfortune in war, let him begin with the Germans." That is: "Whoever loves wounds and the bitter deaths of war, let him provoke the Teutonic hands with savage Mars."

units.la: Sed de hoc antiquarii rerum Germanicarum viderint: & nos in arcanis regnorum fidei vacillantis conjecturas ex ipso Tacito deduximus. Quod est præ manibus, agamus. Laudati pro concione milites victores, ad præclara in postèrum facinora eriguntur. Monumentorum autem superbæ inscriptiones, triumphi supplicationes duci petiti aut decreti, libero magis populo, quam servienti regibus, conveniunt. Maxime ubi militaris gloriae cupido ingrata temporibus, quibus finitima erga eminentes interpretatio, nec minus periculum ex magna fama quam ex mala, in Julii Agricolae Vita. Sapiunt, qui cum eodem Agricola nec unquam in suam famam gestis exultant; ad autorem & imperatorem, ut ministri, fortunam referunt, ita virtute in obsequendo, verecundia in praedicando, extra invidiam, nec extra gloriam degunt.
units.tr: But the antiquaries of German affairs may see to that. We have drawn our guesses about the secrets of kingdoms with faltering loyalty from Tacitus himself. Let us deal with what lies before us. Soldiers who are praised as victors before the assembly are roused to notable deeds in the future. Proud inscriptions on monuments, and triumphal thanksgivings requested for or decreed to the general, suit a free people better than a people serving kings, especially where the desire for military glory is unwelcome in times when the neighbour's interpretation of eminent men is hostile, and the danger from great fame is no less than from bad fame, as in Agricola's Life. Those are wise who, like Agricola himself, never exult in their deeds for their own reputation. As ministers, they refer their fortune to the author and commander; thus they live with virtue in obedience, with modesty in proclaiming, outside envy, and not outside glory.

units.la: XLI.
units.tr: XLI.

units.la: In pervicaces acerbum, in supplices & deditios mansuetum se gerat.
units.tr: Let him be harsh toward the obstinate, and gentle toward suppliants and those who surrender.

units.la: Mox bellum in Angrivarios Stertinio mandat, ni deditionem properavissent, atque illi supplices, nihil ab-nuendo, veniam omnium accepere. Quae si constanter abnegetur, aut fluctuanti fide promittatur, verendum est, ne extremam desperationem accendant querelae: Nihil profici patientia, nisi ut graviora tanquam ex facili tolerantibus imperentur. Verba sunt Britannis deicisscentibus[?] adscripta, in vita Agricolae. aut quod in ejusdem insulae recessu de Romanis Calydones: quorum superbiam frustra per obsequium & modestiam effugeris, raptores orbis, postquam cuncta vastantibus defuere terra, & mare scrutantur. Si locuples hostis est avari; si pauper, ambitiosi. & mox: auferre, trucidare, rapere falsis nominibus imperium: atque ubi solitudinem faciunt, pacem appellant.
units.tr: Soon he entrusts war against the Angrivarii to Stertinius, unless they hasten to surrender; and when they came as suppliants, refusing nothing, they received pardon for all. If this is refused steadfastly, or promised with a wavering faith, we must fear that complaints will kindle final despair: Patience accomplishes nothing, except that heavier burdens are imposed on those who bear them as if they were easy. These are the words placed in the mouths of the Britons who were revolting, in the Life of Agricola. Or there is what the Caledonians say of the Romans in the remote part of the same island: Those plunderers of the world, when the land fails them as they lay everything waste, search the sea too. If the enemy is rich, they are greedy; if poor, they are ambitious. And soon after: they seize, slaughter and plunder under false names, and where they make a desert, they call it peace. Your pride, you cannot escape by obedience and moderation.

units.la: XLII.
units.tr: XLII.

units.la: Non omnem, etiam fortuitorum casuum, culpam praestabit.
units.tr: He will not answer for every fault, even for accidents of chance.

units.la: Classe cum parte militum remissa, atro nubium globo effusa grandō: simul variis undique procellis in certi fluctus profligatum adimere, regimen impedire. &c. pars navium hausta sunt plures apud insulas lon-gius ejecta: milesque nullo illic hominum cultu fame absumptus. Nulla hic Germanici, qui solus cum[?]
units.tr: When part of the soldiers had been sent back with the fleet, a dark cloud of hail poured down; at the same time, from all sides, the storms wrested the fleet, shattered by uncertain waves, from his command and hindered its steering, etc. Many of the ships were swallowed up, and others were driven far off among the islands, and the soldiers were consumed by hunger, with no sign of human habitation there. Here there is no fault of Germanicus, who alone with

units.la: Note: the scan shows only part of the final line; the last word is partly hidden at the page edge. triremi evasit, culpa. aut, si qua, in eo deliquit, quod homines navigandi imperitos fluctibus & vadis occa-ni commisit. Jocularium in re non jocosa est, quod Polyaenus de Croesi consilio, & Biantis ab eo dehorta-tione narrat. Croesus adversus maris Aegaei insulas bel-lum parabat. A quo ut eum deterreret Bias Prienensis, sermonem subjecit, insulanos magnam equorum vim in eum conducere. Ille risum non tenens: Utinam, inquit, insulanos in continenti deprehendam. Et te igitur, inquit Bias, maris expertem ut in mari corri-piant, annon optabunt Insulani?
units.tr: a trireme escaped. Or if he sinned in anything, it was in that he entrusted men unskilled in sailing to the waves and shallows of the ocean. Polyaenus tells a joke, not a joking matter, about the plan of Croesus and the dissuasion of Bias from it. Croesus was preparing war against the islands of the Aegean Sea. To deter him, Bias of Priene offered the remark that the islanders would hire a great number of horses against him. He could not keep from laughing and said: "I wish I could catch the islanders on the mainland." And so, said Bias, if they catch you, who know nothing of the sea, at sea, will not the islanders desire it?

units.la: XLIII.
units.tr: XLIII.

units.la: Animum in adversis intrepidum gerat.
units.tr: In adversity let him keep a fearless spirit.

units.la: Sin minus, vultu & verbis dolorem animo concep-tum premat. In quorum alterutro hic a Germanico peccatum, quem per omnes illos dies noctesque apud scopulos & prominentes oras, cum se tanti exitii reum clamitaret, vix cohibuere amici, quo minus eodem mari oppeteret. Eheu Germanice, adversis & secundis eru-dite, ita nunc de statu mentis dejiceris, ut iidem fluctus, qui socias[?] naves, animum tuum absorbeant? Sin personatus iste dolor, ut in ficto propinquorum luctu: audi quid Seneca consulat. Duces rebus afflictis hilaritatem de industria simulare, & adversas res adumbrata laetitia abscondere, ne militum animi, si stractam ducis sui mentem viderint, & ipsi collabantur. Sed bene, quod non diuturna ista simulatio, aut dolor cito abstersus fuit: dum terribilior in hostes afflictione tua ketos[?] insurgis.
units.tr: If not, let him suppress the grief conceived in his mind by his face and words. In either of these, Germanicus here sinned: over all those days and nights, among the rocks and jutting shores, while he kept calling himself guilty of so great a disaster, his friends could scarcely restrain him from seeking death in the same sea. Alas, Germanicus, you who were trained in both adversity and prosperity, are you now so cast down in the state of your mind that the same waves which swallowed the allied ships are swallowing your spirit? But if that grief is a mask, like a feigned mourning for relatives, hear what Seneca advises: leaders in afflicted circumstances should deliberately feign cheerfulness and hide adverse events under a shadow of joy, lest the minds of the soldiers, if they see the mind of their leader shaken, collapse as well. But it is well that this pretence did not last long, and that the grief was soon wiped away, while your affliction rises more terrible against the enemy as a sea-monster [κῆτος].

units.la: XLIV.
units.tr: XLIV.

units.la: Viribus & animo auctior accepto damno resurgat.
units.tr: Having suffered a loss, he rises again with greater strength and spirit.

units.la: Ut humi stratus attacta terra Antaeus: ut post Can-nensem stragem Romani. Fama classis amissa ut Germanos ad spem belli, ita Cafarem ad coercendum erexit, &c. Ex qua invicti animi constantia id assecuti sunt duce Germanico Romani, ut invictos & nullis casibus superabiles eos Germani praedicarent. Pari majores eorum laude Hannibal, caeso post tot clades Asdrubale, mactavit. Duris ut ilex tonsa bipennibus Nigra feraci frondis in Algido, Per damna, per clades, ab ipso Ducit opes animumque ferro. Non hydra secto corpore firmior Vinci dolentem crevit in Herculem: Monstrumve submisisse Colchi Majus, Echionaeve Thebae. Merses profundo: pulchrior evenit. Luctere: multa proruet integrum Cum laude victorem: geretque Prælia conjugibus loquenda. Horat. lib. 4. Carm. od. 4.
units.tr: Just as Antaeus, thrown to the ground, grew stronger when he touched the earth, and as the Romans did after the slaughter at Cannae. When the fleet was lost, the report of it roused the Germans to hope of war and roused Caesar to restrain them.
