By the steadfastness of this unconquered spirit, under their leader Germanicus, the Romans achieved that the Germans called them unconquered and not to be overcome by any reverses. Hannibal, after Hasdrubal had been slain following so many disasters, achieved the same praise for his own side. Like a holm-oak, dark with leafy growth on fertile Algidus, cut by hard axes, it draws its strength and spirit from its own wounds, from losses and slaughter, from the iron. Not the Hydra, its body cut, grew stronger against Hercules, grieving at Vincus; nor did Colchis or Thebes of Echion send forth a greater monster. Sink it in the deep: it comes up more beautiful. Wrestle with it: it will break down many a victor, with honour intact, and it will fight battles that wives will speak of. Horat. lib. 4. Carm. od. 4.

units.la: XLV.
units.tr: XLV.

units.la: Spinosa est, sub anxio aliena belli gloria principe, successuum progressio.
units.tr: It is a thorny matter: under an anxious prince, the progress of successes won by another man's military glory.

units.la: Bello parrando Germanicum intentum crebris epistolis Tiberius monebat, rediret. Bellica quippe ejus gloria, ut primo Annalium libro vidimus, angebatur. Tum populi in eum favor, militum legionariorum studium, Galliarum in eum propensio, provinciarum inclinatio, quorsum evaderent verebatur. Nec quod Gallias in verba Tiberii adegit, fausta militum in se imperaturum omina sprevit, monumenta Germanicae victoriae principis, non suo, nomine extruxit, satis magnum perpetuae modestiae argumentum ducebat. ἐπὶ ... i. e. non idem aut sentiunt aut agunt, rei alicui imminentes, & eam assecuti. uti apud Dionem lib. 41. plebecula Romana judicat. Nec tamen aperto mandato, sed precibus & suasione (quae vim imperii in imperante obtinent) abstrahendum a suetis legionibus aggreditur. inescare honorum & belli praemiorum dulcedine incautum conatur. rediret ad decre-
units.tr: Tiberius kept sending Germanicus, who was intent on finishing the war, frequent letters urging him to return. For his military glory, as we saw in the first book of the Annals, was a source of distress to him. He feared where the people's favour towards Germanicus, the zeal of the legionary soldiers, the goodwill of the Gauls towards him, and the inclination of the provinces might lead. Nor did Germanicus think it a sufficiently great proof of lasting moderation that he had brought the Gauls to swear to Tiberius, that he spurned the soldiers' auspicious omens that they would make him emperor, and that he raised monuments to the prince's German victory in the prince's name, not his own. i.e. they neither think nor act alike, bearing down on some matter and having attained it, as the Roman rabble judges in Dio, book 41. Yet he did not use an open command but entreaties and persuasion (which carry the force of command in one who commands), and he set about drawing Germanicus away from his accustomed legions. He tried to lure the unwary man with the sweetness of honours and the rewards of war. should return to the decree-

units.la: Invidia tenda artes. tum triumphum, quasi vero Germanicus non plus in factorum gloria, & conscientia generis humani, quam in evanitura brevis temporis pompa reponeret. tum quasi miseratione periculorum ejus & reipublicae, porro profatur, fatis jam eventuum, fatis casuum. unius horae momentum posse & parata decora abolere, & magnum ignominiae dedecus familiae aspergere. maxime cum jam fortuna vultus novercantis documenta, laetis intervenientia, dedisset. prospera illi & magna praelia. quod per prolepsin concedit. eorum quoque meminisset, quae venti & fluctus, nulla ducis culpa, gravia tamen & fava damna intulissent. inde juvenilem belligerendi ardorem, tacita moderandi impetus commonefactione, redarguit. fenovies a divo Augusto in Germaniam missum, plura consilio quam vi perfecisse rerum testimonia verborum probationem repellere, sic Sugambros in deditionem acceptos, sic Suevos, regemque Marobodiuum pace objiciatum. nec esse felicis consilii exemplum spernendum. posse & Cherusicos, caeterasque rebellium gentes, quando Romana ultione confultum est, interna discordia relinqui. Tutius esse, & nomini Romano gloriosius, expleta jam Varianae ignominiae ultione, abductis legionibus, gentes feroces mutuo excidio furere, quas nunc commune periculum conjungit. quando urgentibus imperii fatis nihil jam praestare fortuna majus potest, quam hostium desordiam.
units.tr: He employed the arts of envy. Then he spoke of a triumph, as if Germanicus did not place more in the glory of his deeds and in the consciousness of mankind than in a pageant that would pass away in a moment. Then, as if out of pity for his own danger and the state's, he went on to speak of the fates of events and the fates of chance: that the moment of a single hour could wipe out prepared honours and cast a great stain of disgrace upon the family, especially since fortune, showing a stepmother's face, had already given examples of reverses coming in the midst of success. He had had prosperous and great battles, which he concedes by prolepsis. He should also remember those losses which winds and waves, through no fault of the commander, had nonetheless inflicted, grievous and foul. Thence he rebukes the youthful ardour for war, with a quiet reminder to curb its rush. He reminds him that he had been sent into Germany nine times by the deified Augustus and had accomplished more by counsel than by force; the evidence of facts refutes the proof of words. So the Sugambri were received into surrender, so the Suevi and King Maroboduus were brought to peace. Nor was the example of a fortunate plan to be scorned. The Cherusci and the other rebellious tribes could likewise be left to their internal discord, since Roman vengeance had been provided for. It was safer, and more glorious for the Roman name, once vengeance for the disgrace of Varus was complete, to withdraw the legions and let the fierce tribes rage in mutual slaughter, whom a common danger now unites; for, with the fates of empire pressing, fortune can now offer nothing greater than the discord of enemies.

units.la: Ut de Domitiani temporibus Cornelius, tractatu De Moribus Germanorum.
units.tr: As Cornelius (Tacitus) says of the times of Domitian, in his treatise On the Manners of the Germans.

units.la: Intelligebantur artes, sed pars obsequii in eo, ne deprehenderentur. Corn. IV. Histor. Tiberius gravi-ri tum blandimentorum illice, tum necessitatis ariete admoto, quod imperare poterat extorquet. Confer cum Tiberio Domitianum, cum Germanico Julium Agricolam: & amplissimam pro assertione roborandam segetem prehendes.
units.tr: The arts were understood, but part of compliance lay in this, that they were not detected. Tacitus, Histories IV: Tiberius, with the lure of flattery on one side and the battering-ram of necessity on the other, extorts what he could command. Compare Domitian with Tiberius, and Julius Agricola with Germanicus, and you will grasp an ample harvest to strengthen the assertion.

units.la: XLVI.
units.tr: XLVI.

units.la: Immanis gloria belua, a sanguinis humani pastu ad incrementum grassatur.
units.tr: A monstrous beast of glory advances to its growth by feeding on human blood.

units.la: Quanquam simulatè Tiberius, ex gentium tamen opinione verè: relinqueret materiem Drusi fratris glo-ria: quì nullo tum alio hoste, nonnisi apud Germanias[?] assequi nomen imperatorium, & deportare lauream posset. Adeò rem rediisse, ut propter inane nomen, inaniorem lauream, gentes humanæ patere injuriæ, patere excidio debeant! Sed benè Tiberius conditione positâ: Si foret adhuc bellandum. Calidiores animi ruptis conditionum repagulis, per alienam & suam stragem ad vanæ gloriæ umbram ruunt.
units.tr: Although Tiberius pretended otherwise, by general opinion he truly left to his brother Drusus the material for glory, since Drusus, with no other enemy at that time, could win the title of imperator only in Germany and bring home the laurel. So the matter had come to this: for an empty name and an emptier laurel, the nations of men must suffer wrong and must suffer destruction! But Tiberius wisely stated the condition: If there were still war to be waged. Hotter spirits, breaking through the barriers of such conditions, rush through the slaughter of others and of themselves toward the shadow of vain glory.

units.la: XLVII.
units.tr: XLVII.

units.la: Imperii & aulæ minister est, premere quæ intelligas, & potentiori parere.
units.tr: A minister of the empire and the court must suppress what he understands and obey the more powerful.

units.la: Haud contentus est ultrà Germanicus, quanquam fingi ea, sequeque per invidiam parto jam decori abstrahi intelligeret.
units.tr: Germanicus was not content to go further, though he understood that these things were feigned, and that through envy he was being drawn away from the honour already won.

units.la: XLVIII.
units.tr: XLVIII.

units.la: Anceps est, avido rumorum & suspi-cace sub principe, civium conversatio.
units.tr: Dangerous is the conversation of citizens under a prince who is greedy for rumours and full of suspicion.

units.la: Plena fuit aula Tiberiana delationum strepitu. Nec ulla aut crebrior aut periculosior, quam majestatis & rerum novarum molitionis, insimulatio. Vix à metu Germanici, octo legionum cum sociis cohortibus du-ctoris[?], suspicax Tiberii animus conquieverat: Sub idem tempus, è familia Scriboniorum Libo Drusus deseritur moliri res novas. Nobilissimum quenque, & aut divitiis & factione aut sapientia conspicuum, rumor delator arripit. Viliores aut curiosa inquisitio præterit, aut cura principis negligit. Nobilitas, opes, omissique gestique honores pro crimine: & ob virtutes certissimum exitium. Nec minus præmia delatorum invisa quam scelera: cum alii sacerdotia & consulatus ut-spolia adepti, procurationes alii & interiorem potentiam, agerent ferrent cuncta. Odio & terrore corrupti in dominos servi, in patronos liberti: & quibus deerat inimicus, per amicos oppressi. lib.i.[?] Historiarum.
units.tr: The court of Tiberius was full of the clamour of informers. Nor was any accusation more frequent or more perilous than that of treason and of plotting revolution. Scarcely had the suspicious mind of Tiberius been calmed by fear of Germanicus and of the eight legions with their allied cohorts under that commander, when at about the same time, Libo Drusus of the family of the Scribonii was reported to be plotting revolution. Rumour, the informer, seizes upon every man of high rank who is conspicuous for wealth, for faction, or for wisdom. The humbler sort either escape a close inquiry or are overlooked by the prince's care. Nobility, wealth, and honours either laid aside or held were counted as crimes, and virtue meant certain ruin. The rewards of informers were no less hateful than their crimes: while some obtained priesthoods and consulships as spoils, others procurations and a power behind the throne, they managed and bore everything. Servants were corrupted by hatred and terror against their masters, freedmen against their patrons, and whoever had no enemy was crushed by his friends. Histories, book 1.

units.la: Quæ in Domitiano ad culmen educta, quia sub Tiberio, in Libonis Drufi inprimis tristi casu, fundamenta videtunt: ejus negotii initium, ordinem, finem curatius differam. IN IT IO [?] luctuosæ tragœdiæ continentur. 1. proditoria amicorum perfidia. 2. stolida mentis cla-tæ vanitas. 3. curiosa somniorum & divinationum ob-servatio. 4. tumida generis jactantia. 5. profligata luxus & opum ostentatio. 6. servorum conscientia. MED IO five ordine: 1. intermedius ad Principem aditus. 2. Honorum & victus communicatio. 3. profunda intellectus dissimulatio. 4. irae arcana repressio; 5. dictorum & factorum exploratio. 6. sævum accusatorum indicium. 7. atrox patrum cognitio. 8. delata causæ dictio. 9. servorum per tormenta interrogatio. FINIS: 1. extremæ rei præjudicio damnati preces; 2. deluforia ad senatum rejectio. 3. armatæ septæ domus custodia. 4. cædis inter novissimas epulas roga-tio. 5. violentæ manus adactio. 6. perseverata post mortem accusatio. 7. gratuita principis post sævitiam expletam clementia. 8. Bonorum inter accusatores divisio. 9. honorum in vultures collatio. 10. memoriæ Libonis damnatio. 11. supplicationum & dierum festorum consecratio. 12. Magorum exilia, & quorundam supplicia. Vano principio per medium dolosum ad luctuosum finem ducitur. Qui vitare vult calamitatis extrema, ingressum & vestigia ad finem ducentia fugiat. Singula nos, aliquid ad politicam considera-tionem momenti habitura, eductius per aphorismos efferemus.
units.tr: What was carried to its height under Domitian, but which laid its foundations under Tiberius, especially in the sad fall of Libo Drusus, I shall treat more carefully: its beginning, its course, and its end. The beginning of this mournful tragedy consists of: (1) the treacherous faithlessness of friends; (2) the foolish vanity of a boastful mind; (3) the curious observation of dreams and divinations; (4) the swollen boasting of family; (5) the reckless display of luxury and wealth; (6) the complicity of slaves. The middle, in order: (1) the intermediate access to the Prince; (2) the sharing of honours and of food; (3) the deep concealment of understanding; (4) the hiding of anger; (5) the spying upon words and deeds; (6) the cruel information of accusers; (7) the savage inquiry of the senators; (8) the hearing of the accused case; (9) the questioning of slaves under torture. The end: (1) the condemnation of a man prejudged in his last extremity, and his prayers; (2) the deceitful referral to the senate; (3) the custody of a house surrounded by armed men; (4) the request for death during the last banquet; (5) the forced violence of the hand; (6) accusation persisted in after death; (7) the prince's gratuitous clemency after his cruelty was sated; (8) the division of goods among the accusers; (9) the bestowing of honours upon vultures; (10) the condemnation of the memory of Libo; (11) the consecration of thanksgivings and festal days; (12) the exile of magicians and the punishment of some. From a vain beginning, through a deceitful middle, the course leads to a mournful end. Whoever wishes to avoid the utmost calamity should flee the entrance and the footsteps that lead to that end. I shall set out the individual points, which will carry some weight for political reflection, more fully, by way of aphorisms.

units.la: XLIX.
units.tr: XLIX.

units.la: Cavenda in aulis proditoria amicorum perfidia.
units.tr: In courts, the treacherous faithlessness of friends must be guarded against.

units.la: Sunt qui nocendi studio, quo promptius incautos opprimant, vultum amici induunt. Ita Sejani clandestini satellites Agrippinam, & posthumos Germanici amicos, per blandimenta conculcabant. Sunt qui honorum aditus delatoria proditione emercantur. Ut hic Firmius Catus Senator, ex intima Libonis amicis sus: autor luxus & spei rerum novarum. idem sociis libidinum & necessitatum, quò pluribus indiciis inli-garet. Nec alia magis frequentata in aula Tiberiana ad emergendum via. Natura mortalium avida im-perii, & præceps ad explendam animi cupidinem, dum voti suprem compos evadat, nec fidei in rebus huma-nis, nec affectuum amicitiæ, natura aut multo familia-ritatis usu inditorum, recordatur. Sunt qui non pravo illi ingenio, sed inani & futili, quidvis apud quosvis ef-furiunt: quod à delatoribus exceptum, aut vulgi ser-monibus jactatum, ad aures suspicacis principis defer-tur. Hi non minus quam priores illi, deliberatè mali, fugiendi; nec in interiorem amicitiæ sinum admitten-di. Alii, cæteris in rebus amicitiæ tenaces, occasionem rei bene pro patria gerendæ, indicio sibi facto arri-piunt. Cleo Abydenis Sestum acquisivit (Verba sunt Poliæni lib. 1. Stratag.) non aperto prælio, sed tecto dolo. Theodorus Sesto præfectus, in amicis Cleonis, adulterii usu cognita quadam in suburbio muliere, a-quæducțu per muros angusto ferente, lapidem unum sub noctem eximens exibat: & intrans lapidem repo-nebat. Ita cum diu fefellisset, Cleoni rem per jocum aperuit, qui arcanum Abydenis enuncians, noctemque illunem observans, per aquæductum cum lapidem Theodorus exemisset, & amicæ operam daret, milites clam introduxit. qui custodibus interfectis, & portis intus reseratis, omnibus copiis receptis, facili opera Sesto poriebantur. Hæc Polyænus. Malum detectum vidimus: quod adversus illud remedium? Tutissimum est, nihil fovere animo, quod divulgatum damno sit aut pudori. proximum, quid sis acturus, tecum ipso deliberare, nec aspernanda amicorum ante communicationem consilii exploratio, quæ fallax perspæpè, & expectationi non respondens. Ridicula est, quam idem Polyænus de Alcibiade, amicos ante interiorem admissionem tentante, profert. Simulacrum hominis in tenebricoso domus angulo conclusit, quod amicorum cuilibet introducto ostendit, tanquam hominem occisum. Rogabatque eorum operam, quò tutius lateret. Reliqui piaculi communionem refugerunt. Callias
units.tr: Some, eager to harm so that they may more readily crush the unwary, put on the face of a friend. Thus the secret henchmen of Sejanus trampled Agrippina and the surviving friends of Germanicus by flattery. Some buy their way to honours by informing treacherously. So did Firmius Catus, a senator, once an intimate friend of Libo, the author of his luxury and of his hopes of revolution; he also made partners of his lusts and needs, so that he might bind Libo with more evidence. No other way was more often trodden in the court of Tiberius to rise. The nature of mortals is greedy for empire and headlong in satisfying the desire of the mind, so that, once it has attained its wish, it remembers neither faith in human affairs nor the bonds of friendship, formed by nature or by long familiarity. Some, not from a wicked disposition but from an empty and foolish one, blurt out anything before anyone; what is caught by informers, or spread by the chatter of the crowd, is carried to the ears of the suspicious prince. These men, no less than the former, are deliberately harmful and must be shunned; they must not be admitted into the inner bosom of friendship. Others, steadfast in all other matters of friendship, seize the opportunity to do a good service for their country when a betrayal has been made known to them. Cleo of Abydos acquired Sestos (these are the words of Polyaenus, book 1 of the Stratagems), not by open battle but by a hidden trick. Theodorus, the prefect of Sestos, among the friends of Cleo, having become acquainted with a certain woman in a suburb through adultery, would take out one stone at night from the narrow aqueduct that carried water through the walls, enter, and put the stone back. When he had long gone undetected in this way, he revealed the matter to Cleo in jest; Cleo, announcing the secret to the Abydenes and watching for a moonless night, when Theodorus had removed the stone through the aqueduct and was helping his mistress, secretly brought in soldiers. These killed the guards, opened the gates from within, received all the forces, and with little effort took Sestos. So says Polyaenus. We have seen the evil uncovered; what is the remedy against it? The safest course is to harbour in the mind nothing that would bring harm or shame if it were divulged. Next, to deliberate with yourself about what you are going to do; and the testing of friends before you share your counsel should not be scorned, though it is often deceptive and does not match expectation. The trick which the same Polyaenus relates of Alcibiades, testing his friends before admitting them to his inner circle, is absurd. He shut up a dummy of a man in a dark corner of the house, and showed it to whichever friend was brought in, as though it were a man who had been killed, and asked for their help so that he might hide more safely. The rest shrank from sharing in the guilt.

units.la: D autem Hipponici filius libenter simulacrum admisit, quod explorandis amicis factum erat. Itaque fidelem amicum ducebat Calliam, & deinceps in intimis habebat Calliam.
units.tr: Callias, son of Hipponicus, gladly admitted the dummy, which had been made for testing friends. So he took Callias as a faithful friend, and afterwards held Callias among his intimates.

units.la: L.
units.tr: L.

units.la: Pestis est animorum, saepe & vitae ac fortunarum, vana de se & virtute sua persuasio.
units.tr: Vain self-persuasion, about oneself and one's own worth, is a plague of the mind, and often of life and fortunes.

units.la: Hac porta exitii reserata Catus juvenem improvi-dum, & facilem inanibus, praecipitem ad luxum, & in-de in perniciem propellit. Ista Bironius Gallorum principatum affectans, Burgundionis carnificis in ma-nus incidit. Levius est, sed ob existimationem famae non spernendum, quod in persona Thrasonis Comici in theatro traducunt. Cujusmodi hominibus, opum aliqua facultate instructis, nunquam defuturi sunt Gnathones, qui eos comedendos & deridendos aliis propinent.
units.tr: Through this open gate of ruin, Catus drives the young man, heedless and easily taken in by empty things, headlong into extravagance and from there into destruction. By these means Bironius, aspiring to the principality of the French, fell into the hands of the Burgundian executioner. It is a lesser matter, but one not to be scorned for the sake of reputation, that they mock such men on the stage in the person of the comic braggart Thrasos. Men of this sort, provided with some means, will never lack parasites who serve them up to others to be devoured and derided.

units.la: LI.
units.tr: LI.

units.la: Illusio mentis est Magorum & aruspicum & somniorum observatio.
units.tr: Observation of magicians, soothsayers and dreams is an illusion of the mind.

units.la: Quae si floccifecisset Libo Drusus, quem perfidus amicus ad Chaldaeorum promissa, Magorum sacra, somniorum etiam interpretes impulit, ad maturam necem praecipitio non pervenisset. qui dum infernas umbras carminibus elici curat, ad infernas ipse umbras citis quadrigis devehitur. dum consultat, an habiturus foret opes, quis viam Appiam Brundisium usque pecunia operiret, quas habuit, opibus, una cum vita, & honesta vitae memoria, exuitur. Simili vecordia Lentulus, e nobilissima Corneliorum gente. ex libris Sibyllinis, regnum tribus Cornelii[?] portendi: Cinnam atque Sullam antea; se tertium esse, cui fatum foret urbis potiri, vaticinabatur. cui fatum fuit, sed non e libris Sibyllinis, iu Tulliano vindici rerum capitalium gulam praebere. Ab inani mentis delusione abeat, qui amicis dolori, inimicis gaudio, sibi probro esse & da-mno abominatur.
units.tr: Had Libo Drusus cared nothing for these things, the faithless friend who drove him to the promises of the Chaldeans, the rites of the magi, and even the interpreters of dreams would not have brought him to an early death. While he takes care to have the shades of the dead summoned by incantations, he is himself carried down to the shades below in swift chariots. While he consults whether he will have wealth, and who would cover the Appian Way all the way to Brundisium with money, he is stripped of the riches he had, together with his life and the honourable memory of his life. With like madness Lentulus, of the most noble family of the Cornelii, prophesied, from the Sibylline books, that the kingdom was portended for the three Cornelii: that Cinna and Sulla had gone before, and that he himself was the third to whom it was fated to hold the city. It was fated for him, but not by the Sibylline books, to offer his throat to Tullianum, the avenger of capital crimes. Let him keep away from this empty delusion of the mind, who sees that it brings grief to his friends, joy to his enemies, and shame and loss to himself.

units.la: LII.
units.tr: LII.

units.la: Contemptor aliorum, & sui admirator, nobilitatis spiritus, in malum saepe incidit.
units.tr: One who despises others and admires himself, with the spirit of nobility, often falls into evil.

units.la: Hinc luxus & paternarum facultatum profusio, hinc rapinarum tantum non justa excusatio, hinc regni factum[?]. & principatus affectatio, hinc non raro tragica vitae catastrophe. Hic Liboni non postremus ad lapsum gradus, dum insidiator vitae proavum Pompejum, amitam Scriboniam, quae quondam Augusti conjux fuerat, consobrinos Caesares, plenam imaginibus domum ostentat[?]. Haec generis jactantia, inter multos alios, etiam Hiempsalem, Masanissae nepotem, maturo exitio affecit. natura ferox, etiam ante ignobilitatem Jugurtha, quia materno genere impar erat, despiciens &c. qui praecepti potius paterni memor cum fratre esse debuit: imitamini virtutem: & enitimini, ne ego meliores liberos sumpsisse videar, quam genuisse. S.B.J.
units.tr: From this come extravagance and the squandering of paternal property, from this a not quite just excuse for plunder, from this an attempt at kingship and principate, and from this, not rarely, a tragic end to life. Here is no small step in Libo's fall, while he plots against life, and displays to the world his great-grandfather Pompey, his aunt Scribonia, who once had been the wife of Augustus, and his cousins the Caesars, with a house full of their portraits. This boasting of birth, among many others, also brought Hiempsal, the grandson of Masinissa, to an early ruin. Fierce by nature, and despising Jugurtha even before his low birth, because he was unequal to him on his mother's side, and so on. He ought rather to have been mindful of his father's precept, and to have been at one with his brother: Imitate virtue, and strive that I may not seem to have adopted better children than I begot. S.B.J.

units.la: LIII.
units.tr: LIII.

units.la: Patrimonii & famae illuvies, luxurio-sa vita, profligetur.
units.tr: The squalor of one's patrimony and reputation, a life of luxury, is ruined.

units.la: Maxime si cum aere alieno conjuncta. Haec jam vi-cinus plenae ruinae Druso gradus, ad luxum & as alie-num converso. ob quem dum in oculis civium esse la-borat, nimium in se oculos malignè observantium convertit. Campus hic exemplorum consimilium ape-nitur[?]: quem propter copiae fastidium praetereo.
units.tr: Especially when it is joined with debt. Drusus was already a step away from complete ruin, with his life turned to luxury and debt. Because of this, while he labours to be in the eyes of the citizens, he draws to himself the eyes of those who watch him with ill will. A field of similar examples lies open here, but I pass it by because of its abundance.

units.la: LIV.
units.tr: LIV.

units.la: Quot servi, tot fermè proditores he-ri, tot hostes domestici.
units.tr: As many slaves, almost as many traitors in the household; as many enemies within the house.

units.la: Nam & ob libertatem ademptam cupiunt, & ob fe-cretorum participationem possunt domino nocere. Ut satius tuissent[?], & qui servi eadem noscerent, reperit. In laborante nimirum publicè civium libertate ; & principe servorum audacia contra heros abutentes. Quod tyrannis in more esse, Aristoteles V. Politicorum docet. Pallanti, quamvis arrogantiæ insimulato, profuit, nunquam sermonem cum servulis communicasse ; omnia nutu, aut in re ardua scripto, significavit. 13. Annal. Si qui aut silentio constanti, aut morte fortiter obita, dominorum vitam redemerunt : axioma, ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ [?] [illegible, ~8 letters] haud infringunt.
units.tr: For they both desire liberty, once it has been taken away, and because they share in secrets they can harm their master. So that it would have been better, and he found slaves who knew the same things. Clearly this happens when the liberty of the citizens is failing in public, and when the leader of the slaves abuses his audacity against his masters. Aristotle, in the fifth book of the Politics, teaches that this is the custom of tyrants. It benefited Pallas, although he was accused of arrogance, never to have communicated speech with his little slaves; he signified everything by a nod, or in writing when the matter was weighty (Annals 13). If some have bought their masters' lives by constant silence, or by dying bravely, these are exceptions that [illegible] do not break the rule, ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολύ [as a rule].

units.la: LV.
units.tr: LV.

units.la: Ut omnia cernentem, & audientem omnia, absentem principem verere.
units.tr: That one should fear the absent prince, who sees all things and hears all things.

units.la: Multi sunt principis non somnolenti oculi, multæ aures. Quo fit, ut in arcanorum abdita, & clausa secretorum penetralia, facillimo negotio penetret. Sunt nuncii, sunt interhuncii, sunt oculati & auriti testes plurimi. Firmius Catus, libidinum & necessitatum socius, aditum ad principem postulat, demonstrato crimine & reo per Flaccum Vescularium equitem Romanum, cui propior cum Tiberio usus erat. Cæsar indicium haut aspernatus, congressus abnuit. Posse enim, eodem Flacco internuncio, sermones commeare. Congressus ideo abnuit, nec aliquid subodoratus Libo, aut à consuetudine sua Cætum removeat, aut à prioris vitæ vanitate & luxu remittat. Ita in conjuratione Catilinaria detegenda indicio Curii Fulvia quæ suspecta non erat interprete, Cicero confulsi plurimum utebatur.
units.tr: Many are the prince's eyes, which do not drowse, and many his ears. Hence it comes about that he penetrates with the greatest ease into the hidden recesses of secrets and the closed sanctuaries of confidences. There are messengers, there are go-betweens, and there are very many eyewitnesses and earwitnesses. Firmius Catus, the companion of Libo's lusts and needs, demanded access to the prince, having laid out the crime and the accused, through Flaccus Vescularius, a Roman knight with whom Tiberius had a closer acquaintance. Caesar did not disdain the information, but refused the meeting, since words could pass between them through the same Flaccus as intermediary. He refused the meeting for this reason, and Libo, suspecting nothing, neither removed Catus from his company nor gave up his vanity and luxury of former life. So in uncovering the Catilinarian conspiracy, Cicero made great use of the information of Fulvia, through Curius, who was not suspected as an intermediary.

units.la: LVI.
units.tr: LVI.

units.la: Tiberianum est, incautos honorum incremento & familiaritatis usu fe-rire.
units.tr: It is Tiberian to strike the incautious with the increase of honours and the familiar use of friendship.

units.la: Jam inter occultè reos, jam inter tacitè damnatos Libo erat. atque interim Libonem ornat pratura, con-victibus adhibet. Si id ab Augusto factum fuisset, beneficiorum magnitudine eum à facinore concepto detordetorquere voluisse crederes. Sed non is Tiberio erga labantes animus, non ea morum via.
units.tr: Already Libo was among those secretly accused, already among those silently condemned. And meanwhile the praetorship adorns Libo, and he is admitted to the banquets. If this had been done by Augustus, you would believe that he wished by the greatness of his favours to turn Libo from the crime he had conceived. But Tiberius did not have this disposition towards those who were wavering, nor this way of behaving.

units.la: LVII.
units.tr: LVII.

units.la: Tiberii est, alta verborum & vultus constantia conceptam iram condere.
units.tr: It is the mark of Tiberius to hide a wrath he has conceived behind a deep constancy of words and countenance.

units.la: Non vultu alienatus, non verbis commotior: adeo iram condiderat. Gemella his quae primo Annalium libro leguntur: Accendebat haec onerabatque Sejanus, peritia morum Tiberii, odia in longum jaciens, quae reconderet, auctaque promeret.
units.tr: He was not estranged in face, nor more agitated in speech: so thoroughly had he hidden his anger. This is similar to what is read in the first book of the Annals: Sejanus, knowing Tiberius's character, fanned and loaded this anger, throwing out hatreds to be stored up and brought forth when they had grown.

units.la: LVIII.
units.tr: LVIII.

units.la: Ante sententiam ferendam cogno-scę, ante cognitionem investiga.
units.tr: Before pronouncing sentence, find out; before judgment, investigate.

units.la: Hoc vel mediocris Principis: ut Tiberii, qui in causa Libonis, cuncta ejus dicta factaque cum prohi-bere posset, scire maluit. Ad absolute imperantem illud Medeae refertur:
units.tr: This is the practice even of a moderate prince, as Tiberius, who in the case of Libo preferred to know all his words and deeds, though he could have forbidden them. To an absolute ruler that line of Medea is applied: If you judge, hear the case; if you rule, command.

units.la: Si judicas, cognosce; si regnas, jube.
units.tr: If you judge, hear the case; if you rule, command.

units.la: At quanto humanius fuerat, errantem stolidae vanita-tis admonere, aut vanam ejus spem contemnere; quam labi & ruere sinere, ut puniendi causam habeas.
units.tr: But how much more humane it would have been to admonish one who was wandering in foolish vanity, or to despise his empty hope, than to let him slip and fall so that you would have a cause for punishing him.

units.la: Ut enim mediocris ingenii principes nonnisi explora-to judicio condemnant: ita optimae notae rectores pu-niendi necessitatem tempestiva licentiae se effusurae coercitione praeveniunt. Non fine salis mica quondam Silanus censuit: ne quiu[?] vita probrosa & opertum infamia provinciam sortiretur: idque princeps dijudi-caret. nam a legibus delicta puniri, quanto fore mitius in ipsos, melius in socios, providere ne peccaretur. Cui foro judicii, quam humanitatis legi, convenientius Tiberius respondet. ideo leges infacta[?] constitui, quia futura in incerto sint. sic a majoribus institutum, ut si antissent delicta, poena sequerentur. ne verterent sa-pienter reperta, & semper placita. 3. Annal.
units.tr: For as princes of mediocre ability condemn only after a tested judgment, so rulers of the best reputation anticipate the need to punish by timely restraint of licence that is about to spill over. Not without some wit, Silanus once proposed: lest a shameful life and one hidden in infamy should obtain a province, and the prince should judge this. For if crimes are punished by the laws, it would be milder for the offenders themselves and better for their associates to take care that no wrong is done. To this proposal, more fitting to the law of courts than to the law of humanity, Tiberius replies: therefore laws are made for things not yet done, because future things are uncertain. So it was instituted by our ancestors, that punishments should follow if offences had been committed. Let them not overturn what was wisely discovered and always approved. Book 3 of the Annals.

units.la: LIX.
units.tr: LIX.

units.la: Accusatores publici honestae reip. purgamenta.
units.tr: Public accusers: the cleansing of an honourable commonwealth.

units.la: Non de quovis in sua aut aliena causa accusante, sed de iis quos publica reorum miseria pascit, pronuncia-tum cape. Quorum e numero Neronis saevitiam alens Eprius Marcellus, Tiberii obscuritati ingenii commodus Fulcinius Trio fuit. celebre inter accusatores Trio-nis ingenium erat, avidumque fama mala. Statim cor-ripit reum, adit consules, senatus cognitionem poscit. Hæc fori judiciarii lues a Romano Hifpone, paulatim fe explicante a trepidis initiis audacia, serpere primitus coepit, qui formam vitæ iniit, quam postea celebrem miseria temporum, & audaciæ hominum fecerunt; nam egens, ignotus, inquies, dum occultis libellis saevitiæ principis adrepit, mox clarissimo cuique periculum facessit, potentiam apud unum, odium apud omnes adeptus, dedit exemplum, quod secuti ex paupe-ribus divites, ex contemtis metuendi, perniciem aliis ac postremum sibi invenere. uti noster lib. 1. Annal. Boni principis non aliud initium majorem senatus applausum meruit, quam horum hominum aut dejectio, aut in solas infulas cum ramentis & cum libellis deportatio. Hinc bene de Vespasiano sperandi, quamvis Muciano pro accusatoribus censente, patres conscripti omen capiunt. Hinc laudis paginas in Trajano suo, cum Domitiani temporum accusatoria saevitia, comparato, Pliniusimplevit. Quantæ Atheniensium populo execrationi fuerint οἱ ῥήτορες [?] & sycophantæ, non uno in loco Ariftophanes in Pluto suo, & aliis comœdiis commonefacit. Demosthenes autem, & fi quis alius oratorio nomine populum fascinavit, non tam accusando, quam aut orationibus de republica habendis, aut miserorum patrocinio laudem & populi favorem invenit.
units.tr: Take what is said not of any accuser pleading in his own or another's cause, but of those whom the public misery of the accused feeds. Among them, Eprius Marcellus, who fostered the cruelty of Nero, and Fulcinius Trio, suited to the obscure character of Tiberius, were of this kind. The talent of Trio was famous among accusers, and greedy for ill fame. At once he seizes the accused, approaches the consuls, and demands a hearing before the senate. This plague of the courts, creeping in from the Roman Hispo, gradually unfolding itself from timid beginnings, first began to spread; it took on the form of life that later the misery of the times and the audacity of men made famous. For being needy, unknown, and restless, while he slipped into the prince's cruelty through secret pamphlets, he soon brought danger to every most distinguished man. Having gained power with one man and hatred with all, he set an example which, followed by paupers who became rich, by the despised who became feared, they found a ruin for others and at last for themselves, as our author says in Book 1 of the Annals. The first act of a good prince earned the senate's greatest applause: the removal of such men, or their deportation to the bare islands with their scraps and their pamphlets. Hence there was good hope of Vespasian, although Mucianus advised against the accusers, and the conscript fathers took it as an omen. Hence Pliny filled pages with praise of his Trajan, when he compared him with the accusing cruelty of Domitian's times. How much hatred the Athenian people held for the orators [οἱ ῥήτορες] and sycophants, Aristophanes reminds us in his Plutus and other comedies. Demosthenes, however, and whoever else captivated the people with the name of orator, won praise and popular favour not so much by accusing as by delivering speeches on public affairs or by defending the wretched.

units.la: LX. Saevo sub principe saeva patrum cognitio.
units.tr: LX. Under a cruel prince, a cruel inquiry by the fathers.

units.la: Adit consules, senatus cognitionem poscit: & vocantur patres, addito, consulandum [?] super re magna & atroci, nec in mitiorem sententiam patres decreto abiisse,
units.tr: He approaches the consuls and demands a hearing before the senate: and the fathers are summoned, with the addition that they must deliberate upon a great and atrocious matter, and that the fathers did not depart in a milder opinion once the decree was passed.

units.la: Apoc. 12. vid. abiisse, miseri damnata etiam post violentam neccem memoria docuit.
units.tr: Revelation 12. Look at "departed": the memory of the condemned, even after a violent death, teaches the wretched.

units.la: LXI.
units.tr: LXI.

units.la: Offenso principe nutantibus vocem patronam nemo largitur.
units.tr: When the prince is offended, no one lends a voice in defence to those who waver.

units.la: Ut in triviis jacens bidental, ut fulminis afflatu quasi Jovis ira perculsos, omnes ne contractu contaminentur refugiunt: sic maiestatis causam dicentes qua proximi qua remoti repellunt. Libo interim veste mutata cum prioribus fœminis, circumire domos, orare affines, vocem adversum pericula poscere: abnuentibus cunctis, cum diversa prætenderent, eadem formidine.
units.tr: As a struck-by-lightning place lying at the crossroads, which people shun for fear of contamination, as if struck by Jupiter's anger, so those who plead a charge of treason repel both the near and the distant. Meanwhile Libo, changing his clothes and going about with the earlier women, begged his relatives to go round the houses and demand a voice against the dangers; yet all refused, offering different excuses but with the same fear.

units.la: LXII.
units.tr: LXII.

units.la: Leges & Senatus consulta callidorum principum arbitrio torquentur.
units.tr: Laws and decrees of the senate are twisted at the will of shrewd princes.

units.la: Iniqua sanè, moribus tamen recepta, judicii forma Romam invaserat, ut servi, ad exsculpendam pro do-mino veritatem, in quæstionem & tormenta dederen-tur. quæstio tamen in caput domini veteri senatus consulto prohibebatur. Negat Libo Drusus crimina objecta. servi ejus in tormenta poscuntur. Senatusconsultum huic atrocitati repugnat. Ut salvo jure interrogari possint, callidius & novi juris repertor Tiberius, mancipari singulos actori publico jubet. Quid est leges & jura specie juris perfringere, si hoc non est? Sic veteratoria juris interpretatione, quia triumvirali supplicio affici virginem inauditum habebatur, Sejani filiam à carnifice laqueum juxta comprimi voluit.
units.tr: Admittedly unjust, yet received by custom, a form of judgment had invaded Rome: slaves were handed over to questioning and torture to extract the truth for their master. Yet questioning against the head of the household had been forbidden by an old decree of the senate. Libo Drusus denies the charges made. His slaves are demanded for torture. A decree of the senate opposes this cruelty. So that questioning might still be possible without violating the law, Tiberius, the more cunning inventor of new law, ordered each slave to be handed over to the public prosecutor. What is it to break laws and rights under the appearance of law, if this is not it? Thus by a crafty interpretation of law, since it was unheard of for a virgin to suffer the triumviral punishment, he wished the executioner to tighten a noose beside the daughter of Sejanus.

units.la: V.Annal.
units.tr: Annals 5.

units.la: LXIII.
units.tr: LXIII.

units.la: Captata clementiæ fama, cognitorum invidia sævitur.
units.tr: A reputation for clemency is sought, yet cruelty is vented through the envy of those already known.

units.la: Reus ab omni patronorum ope, à spe mitigandi per se principis depulsus, extremas preces per propinquos ad placandam principis offensi iram movit. responsum si,ut[?] senatum rogaret. quem imperatoris metu per-[?]culsum, ideoque suam iudicandi acerbitatem sævitiæ principis gratificaturum noverat. cumque domo mi-litum strepente globo cincta, necessitate moriendi adacta, Libo ferales sibi manus intulisset: juravit Ti-berius, petiturum se vitam, quamvis nocenti, nisi vo-luntariam mortem properavisset. Quamvis tenuitate pellucida facile simulatio se ipsam detexit. Tam clemens, tam benignus, cur eadem adseveratione in jam defunctum accusationem peragi permisit? cur bona ejus inter accusatores dividit? cur ignominia nomen extincti affecit? cur adulationes non repressit? Nimirum ut Julius Cæsar extincto Pompejo, jam tutum putavit pium esse socerum[?]: sic Tiberius vitam adver-sario, nunquam à dante accepturo, donabat. Quan-quam Julius nec in memoriam generi sæviebat, nec percussores præmiis affecit, & majorem evertendi Pompejum Magnum, quam hic Libonem puerilitèr ineptum, causam habebat.
units.tr: The accused, cut off from all help from his advocates and from any hope of softening the prince by his own efforts, sent his last pleas through his relatives to appease the anger of the offended prince. The answer was that he should ask the senate, which, as Tiberius knew, was terrified of the emperor and would therefore gratify the prince's savagery by the harshness of its own judgment. Then Libo, surrounded by a crowd of soldiers making a din in his house and driven by the necessity of dying, turned the deadly blow upon himself. Tiberius swore that he would have spared his life, guilty though he was, had he not hastened into a voluntary death. Yet the pretence was easily exposed, for it was transparently thin. So merciful, so kind, why did he allow the same accusation to be pursued with the same vehemence against a man already dead? Why did he divide his goods among the accusers? Why did he load the name of the dead man with disgrace? Why did he not check the flatterers? Clearly, just as Julius Caesar, once Pompey was dead, thought it safe to be dutiful toward his father-in-law, so Tiberius granted his enemy a life that the giver would never receive back. And yet Julius did not rage against Pompey's kin, nor did he reward his assassins, and he had a greater reason to overthrow Pompey the Great than this man had to overthrow Libo, who was childishly foolish.

units.la: LXIV.
units.tr: LXIV.

units.la: Bonis damnatorum dividendis, & honorum ornatu gerendo; quadrupla-tores allici non placet.
units.tr: On dividing the goods of the condemned and on bearing the trappings of office; it is not pleasing that the quadruplators be enticed.

units.la: Sic enim ad opulentissimum quenque arripiendum rapaces vultures confugient: & ambitio sitim[?] ut ex-pleat, honorum caeca aviditate ruens, per clarissima quaeque civium honestorum capita grassabitur. Non omnia quae scripsit, cum assensu & approbatione facti scripsit Tacitus. Ut nec hanc executionem: Bona inter accusatores dividuntur: & pratura extra ordi-nem data, his[?] qui senatorii ordinis erant.
units.tr: For in this way the rapacious vultures will flock to seize upon the wealthiest man of all, and ambition, blindly rushing on in its greed for office, will rage through the most distinguished heads of honourable citizens, to quench its thirst. Tacitus did not write everything he recorded with approval and endorsement of the deed. The same is true of this execution: the goods are divided among the accusers, and the praetorship is given outside the ordinary course to those who were of senatorial rank.

units.la: LXV.
units.tr: LXV.

units.la: Nominis damnatorum expun&tio-nem non prorsus ratio omnis fugit.
units.tr: Nor does every consideration altogether shun the erasure of the names of the condemned.

units.la: Jure nimirum, nec eo interverso damnatorum nec id co sensu, quasi recordationi hominum & libris scri-ptis ptis evelli nomen debeat. Exemplo enim ad deterren-dum non modò præsentes, sed diutius hæsuro etiam posteros docere queunt. Itaque si merito ad necem adactus, non injuria Cotta Mesallinus, ne imago Libo-nis exequiis posterorum comitaretur, censuit. nimirum quia majorum imagines ad similitudinem virtutis posteros excitant, causa cur nepotes hunc Libonem imitarentur, & facta ejus in funebribus exequiis recen-serent, nulla erat. Tum ne ad ultionem aliquando, aut odium Cæsareæ domus, hæredes incenderentur; abolendum è familia nomen invisum erat. Tam tenera etiam hic est principum perceptio, ut morti nonnullos adjudicaverint, qui Brutorum & Cassiorum, adversa Augusto castra secutorum, imagines coluerint: damnatusque fit Cremutius Cordus, quod libro edito Brutum ultimum Romanorum appellaverit. Supplicationum autem dies, & festorum eo nomine celebritates, ineptiarum & fædæ adulationis labecula non vacant.
units.tr: Rightly, of course, and not with the opposite intent, as if the name of the condemned ought to be torn away from the memory of men and from written books. For by example they can teach not only the present but also posterity, whose lesson lasts longer, to be deterred. Therefore, if he was rightly condemned to death, it was not unjustly that Cotta Messalinus advised that the image of Libo should not accompany the funerals of his descendants. Of course, since the images of ancestors stir up their descendants to imitate their virtue, there was no reason why his grandsons should imitate this Libo and recount his deeds at funeral rites. Then, lest the heirs should at some time be inflamed to vengeance or hatred against the house of Caesar, the hated name had to be wiped out of the family. Such is the tenderness of the princes' perception that some were adjudged to death for honouring the images of the Bruti and Cassii, who had followed the camp hostile to Augustus; and Cremutius Cordus was condemned because in a published book he had called Brutus the last of the Romans. Moreover, the days of thanksgiving and the festivals celebrated on that account are not free from the blemish of folly and foul flattery.

units.la: LXVI. De Mathematicis & Magis Italia pellendis accedo patrum decreto.
units.tr: LXVI. On the expulsion of mathematicians and magicians from Italy, I agree with the decree of the Fathers.

units.la: Non tantum ob vanitatem scientiæ, aut, quod in sacris vetatur, characterum & nominis divini profanam abusionem: sed, quod politicæ inprimis est considerationis, ne magnificis promissis incautos ad res novas, ad spes nimis elatas, ad luxum & ad sumptuosum otium propellant. Sed si pro magnitudine materiæ dicere velim: dies me citius quam res deficiat. Salomonem autem incantationes morbis pellendis invenisse, cur Josepho credam, causam non video.
units.tr: Not only because of the vanity of their science, or because of the profane misuse of characters and the divine name, which is forbidden in sacred matters, but chiefly for a political reason: they drive the unwary, with magnificent promises, to revolution, to hopes raised too high, and to luxury and expensive idleness. If I wished to speak as fully as the magnitude of the subject allows, the day would run out before the material did. Yet I see no reason why I should believe Josephus that Solomon discovered incantations for driving out diseases.

units.la: LXVII. Excedere relationem, & reip. necessitates loco sententiæ promere, nihil absurdum.
units.tr: LXVII. To go beyond the report and put the needs of the state forward in place of an opinion is not absurd.

units.la: Plerisque populis, libertate plena gaudentibus, more receptum fuit,ut nonnisi de qua consuleretur re sententiam senator ferret. alibi etiam nonlicuit nisi de re, propter quam conventus indi&tus fuerit, referre quod de gentis more Achaei Romanis, fi&té an veré, oggerunt. Nos ita aut mori patrio subscribimus, aut modestiam senatoris laudamus: ut necessitates reip. ab hac necessitate eximamus. Idque priscis Romanis in more positum fuisse hic Tacitus testatur. Erat quip-pe adhuc frequens senatoribus, fi quid é Rep. crederent, loco sententia promere. Sic Cato priscus aliis de rebus confultus, pro sententia semper pronunciavit, Cart ha-ginem non esse. Ut veró quis neglecta reip. cura, de suis utilitatibus in senatu differat, non est aut temere admittendum, aut in exemplum trahendum. nec sanè[?] ideò à majoribus concessum est egredi aliquando relationem, & quod in commune conducat loco sententia proferre, ut privata negotia, res familiares nostras hic augeamus. uti Hortensium Tiberius repellit. An & Consiliarius non confultus, non ad arcana conferenda vocatus, Principi salutaria imperii ultro suggeret? censeo, vel cum periculo offensionis, nec nautam, imo & vectorem rei nauticæ peritum, fi non à nauclero in consilium advocetur, silentium, nave in scopulum impingenda, excusat.
units.tr: In most peoples that enjoy full liberty, the custom has been received that a senator gives his opinion only on the matter about which he is being consulted. Elsewhere too it was permitted to speak only on the business for which the assembly had been convened. The Achaeans, according to their national custom, reported this to the Romans, whether truthfully or not. We either subscribe to this as the custom of our fathers, or we praise the moderation of the senator, provided that we exempt the needs of the state from this requirement. That this was the established practice among the early Romans is attested here by Tacitus. For it was still common for senators, whenever they believed something concerned the commonwealth, to put it forward in place of an opinion. So Cato the Elder, when consulted on other matters, always gave his opinion with the words that Carthage must not be (destroyed). But if anyone, neglecting the care of the commonwealth, speaks in the Senate about his own advantages, this is neither to be admitted lightly nor to be taken as a precedent. Nor, for that reason, did our ancestors grant that one may ever go beyond the report and put forward, in place of an opinion, what serves the common good, so that we may here increase our private affairs and family fortunes. Tiberius rebuffs Hortensius for doing this. Or is a counsellor who has not been consulted, and who has not been called in to share state secrets, to offer unasked to the Prince what is salutary for the empire? I judge that he should, even at the risk of giving offence. Nor does a sailor's silence excuse him, nor does a passenger skilled in seamanship, if he is not called into council by the pilot, when the ship is about to be driven onto a rock.

units.la: LXVIII.
units.tr: LXVIII.

units.la: Luxus, ut vermis intima corrodens, è Republica tollendus.
units.tr: Luxury, gnawing at the vitals like a worm, must be removed from the commonwealth.

units.la: Suaserat id Q. Haterius consularis,tra&to in sententiam senatu : à quo non adversante principe decretum, ne vasa auro [solida] ministrandis cibus fierent, ne vestis serica viros fædaret. Sed non aut omnibus patribus, aut inprimis Tiberio, O&avius Fronto praetura functus persuasit, in ar&um esse contrahendam ar-genti fa&i & infe&i, vasorum Corinthiacorum & quic-quid pretiosæ fupelle&ilis, famulitii & fervorum am-plam possessionem. Obortus enim, & cum consensu auditus, luxuriæ patronus Gallus Afinius. quem ne in-auditum damnemus, pro fe loquentem audiamus.
units.tr: Q. Haterius, a former consul, had urged this when the Senate's opinions were being taken. By decree, with the Prince not opposing, it was ordered that food should not be served in solid gold vessels, and that silk clothing should not defile men. But Octavius Fronto, who had held the praetorship, persuaded not all the fathers, nor above all Tiberius, that the possession of wrought and unwrought silver, Corinthian vessels, and whatever costly furniture, and the large holdings of household slaves and servants, should be restricted. Then Gallus Asinius, the patron of luxury, rose and was heard with agreement. Lest we condemn him unheard, let us hear him speaking on his own behalf.

units.la: Augustus ait imperii adolevisse etiam privatas opes: idque non novum, sed a veteribus moribus. Aliam apud Fabricios, aliam apud Scipiones pecuniam: & cuncta ad Remp. referri. Qua tenui, angustas civium domos, postquam eo magnificentia venerit, glisc̃ere singulos, neque in familia & argento, quaque ad usum parentur, nimium aliquid, aut modicum, nisi ex fortuna pessidentis, distinctos senatus & equitum census: non quia diversi natura, sed ut locis, ordinibus, dignationibus antistent, &c. nisi forte clarissimo cuique plures curae, majora pericula subeunda, delinimentis curarum & periculorum carendum esse. Non adeo acerbi rerum & morum censores fumus, ut non plus elegantiae in cultu, non plus magnificentiae, auctae splendore & majestate imperii Romae, quam Ulubris largiamur, nec sua patribus & equitibus prae forensi plebe ornamenta, & censum legibus etiam quaesitum, eripimus. Sed modum in iis omnibus, memoremque non civilitatis modo sed & humanitatis vitam, postulamus. Duas enim ex una civitates facit, & maximum reip. vinculum e Repub. tollit, concordiam & libertatis exaequationem, nimia morum & census diversitas. Praeterea ad plus habendi cupiditatem, praesentem reip. & honestatis pestem, luxuria impellit. Mutuo enim sibi pabulo sunt, quamvis natura diversissima, luxuria & avaritia. Bene de Metello Numidico Sallustius: in Numidiam proficisci tur, magna sive civium, cum propter artes bonas, tum maxime quod adversus divitias invictum animum gerebat: & avaritia magistratuum ante id tempus in Numidia nostra opes contusa, hostiumque auctae erant. Unde autem ea magistratuum avaritia, nisi ex luxu, Romam victa Carthagine, Achaja, Macedonia, Asia, adorto? unde in Metello invictus adversus divitias animus, nisi ex continentia & prisci moris in domestico cultu sobrietate? Quid quod nervos exolvit, & quicquid est ferociae militaris deterit, laxa mollioris vitae licentia. nec in urbe se continet morum contagio: in castra & in pelles militum proserpit. de quo nostrer iterum Sallustius audiatur. exercitus ei traditur à Sp. Albino proconsule, iners, imbellis, neque periculi neque laborum patiens, lingua quam manu promptior, prædator ex sociis, & ipse prada bostium, sine imperio & modestia habitus, ita imperatori novo plus ex malis moribus folicitudi-nis, quam ex copia militum auxilii, aut bona sbei[?], acce-debat. causam, &c, ut philosophi loquuntur, formam depravati exercitus in luxuria, ignaviae matre, Crispus reponit. postremò quaecunque dici aut fingi queunt, ignavia luxuriaque probra, in illo exercitu cuncta fuere. Jactet Romani regni post libertatem funda-tor, Julius Cæsar: milites suos etiam unguento deli-butos benè pugnare. Magis nos movet, quod de Phi-lopoemene cum elogio scribit Polybius, Achaeorum luxum in vestibus & conviviis utiliter in armorum splendorem vertisse. Magis, quod de Spartana Lycurgi disciplina, expulsis urbe patria delitiis, post alios Plu-tarchus recenset. Mitte luxuriam, vicinam conver-tendæ, aut plane evertendæ, reipublicæ causam esse, & ab Ariftotele V. Politicorum doceri, & plurimis im-mutatarum, aut funditus prostratarum, rerump. exemplis commonstrari.
units.tr: Augustus says that private wealth too has grown with the empire, and that this is not new but comes from ancient customs. Under the Fabricii the money was one kind, under the Scipios another, and everything was referred to the commonwealth. With such slender means the houses of citizens were narrow; since magnificence has come to this point, individuals are growing in their household, their silver, and whatever is procured for use, and nothing in excess, or only a modest amount, is distinguished except according to the fortune of the possessor. The censuses of the senators and the knights are distinct, not because they differ in nature, but so that they stand out by place, rank and dignity, etc. Unless perhaps the most distinguished men have more cares, and must undergo greater dangers, so that they need solace for their cares and dangers. We are not so harsh censors of affairs and morals that we would not grant more elegance in dress, more magnificence, increased by the splendour and majesty of the empire at Rome, than at Ulubrae; nor do we take from the senators and knights their own distinctions, set apart from the common people of the forum, and the wealth acquired even by law. But we require moderation in all these things, and a life mindful not only of civility but also of humanity. For excessive difference in manners and property makes two states out of one city, and removes from the commonwealth its greatest bond, concord and equality of freedom. Moreover, luxury drives on the desire to have more, which is the present plague of the commonwealth and of honesty. For luxury and avarice, though by nature most unlike, feed each other. Sallust speaks well of Metellus Numidicus: He set out for Numidia, great in the esteem of citizens, both for his good arts and especially because he bore an unconquered spirit against riches; and before that time the avarice of magistrates had crushed our power in Numidia and increased that of the enemy. But whence came that avarice of magistrates, unless from luxury, which rose up once Carthage, Achaia, Macedonia and Asia had been conquered and brought to Rome? Whence in Metellus an unconquered spirit against riches, unless from self-restraint and the sobriety of ancient custom in domestic life? Moreover, lax licence of a softer life loosens the sinews and wears away whatever is military ferocity. Nor does the contagion of morals stay within the city; it creeps into the camp and into the tents of the soldiers. Concerning this, let our own Sallust be heard again: An army was handed over to him by the proconsul Sp. Albinus, idle, unwarlike, enduring neither danger nor toil, more ready with the tongue than with the hand, a plunderer of allies and himself plunder of the enemy, held without command or discipline; so that for the new general there was added more anxiety from bad morals than help from the abundance of soldiers or good hope. Crispus assigns the cause, as the philosophers say, the form of a corrupted army: luxury, the mother of idleness. Finally, whatever can be said or invented as disgrace of idleness and luxury, all of it was present in that army. Let Julius Caesar, the founder of the Roman monarchy after liberty, boast that his soldiers fight well even when anointed with perfume. What moves us more is what Polybius writes in praise of Philopoemen, that he usefully turned the luxury of the Achaeans in clothing and feasts into splendour of arms. Still more, what Plutarch, after others, recounts concerning the Spartan discipline of Lycurgus, when the pleasures of the city had been expelled. Set aside that luxury is the cause of the overthrow, or complete ruin, of a commonwealth, which Aristotle teaches in the fifth book of the Politics, and which is shown by very many examples of states changed or utterly overthrown.

units.la: LXIX.
units.tr: LXIX.

units.la: Morum inveterata consuetudo corruptioni ferme patrocinatur.
units.tr: The long-established custom of living often lends its support to corruption.

units.la: Nemo in valetudinario decumbere erubescit, nec in popina comessari. Facilem assensum Gallo, sub no-minibus honestis, confessio vitiorum & similitudo au-dientium dedit. Quaeres res cum sit à sapientibus, & in-primis à Seneca, jactata: tempus in ea dilatanda non tero.
units.tr: No one blushes to lie down in a sickbed, or to revel in a tavern. The confession of vices, and the likeness of the hearers, gave the Gaul an easy assent under honourable names. Since this saying is much tossed about by the wise, and above all by Seneca, I will not waste time in expanding on it.

units.la: LXX.
units.tr: LXX.

units.la: Privato fastigio altiùs coràm impe-ratore neque enitaris.
units.tr: Do not strive higher than your private station in the presence of the emperor.

units.la: Honestam de luxu civium castigando vocem, sed cura sua altiorem, Fronto ediderat, quem obliquè Ti-berius reprimendo, monet, non id tempus censura: net, si quid in moribus labaret, defuturum corrigendi auctorem. Censoria quondam potestas, ut libertati nimia, primum a Mamerco temporis angustia coercita, postmodum a Clodio sublata penitus fuit. quam quia alio nomine senatus prope invadit: Tiberius imminui fastigium suum occulte arbitratus, morum censuram sibi reservat. Plus enim de pleno imperio decerpit vitae civium, ex auctoritate jubendi, informatio; quam aut causarum cognitio, aut cognitarum dijudicatio. Ac mirum est, eos qui jura Majestatis & Reservata principum tam anxie conquirunt, hunc locum praeterire voluisse. Tiberius certe qui aliis in rebus speciem antiquitatis, & senatoriae in curia censendi libertatis, praebuit: frenum in hac sententia, extra relationem prompta, adduxit. Atqui Tiberio ipso arbitro majus aliquid & excelsius a principe postulatur.
units.tr: Fronto had published an honest protest against the luxury of citizens, but it touched on matters above his own concern. Tiberius rebuked him obliquely and warned that this was not the time for censure: if anything in morals should slip, there will be no lack of someone to correct it. The censorial power, once too great for liberty, was first restrained by Mamercus for a short time and afterwards was utterly abolished by Clodius. Because the senate was almost usurping it under another name, Tiberius, secretly thinking his own dignity would be diminished, reserved the censorship of morals for himself. For from the full power of the empire he takes more by shaping the lives of citizens through the authority of command than by hearing cases or judging those already heard. It is remarkable that those who so anxiously search out the laws of majesty and the reserved rights of princes wished to pass over this point. Tiberius certainly, who in other matters gave the appearance of antiquity and of the freedom to vote in the senate house, brought a curb to bear in this proposal, which he put forward outside the formal relation. Yet from Tiberius himself, as judge, something greater and loftier is demanded of a prince.

units.la: §. Annal. & mox: quantulum istud est, de quo aediles admonent! quam, si catera respicias, in levi habendum. Resp. Tiberiana simulatione rem pro levicula, quae non sit, haberi, interiori animi sententia idem quod hic proferri: non defuturum, nimirum principem, corrigendi autorem, quod arcanorum capaci satis illa verba aperiunt, exonerari laborum meorum partem fateor. Non est in levibus, & cura principis minoribus, habenda morum & facultatum, & incolumitatis civium inspectio.
units.tr: Annals, and soon after: how small is this matter about which the aediles give warning! How, if you look at the rest, it should be held as trifling. Reply: by Tiberian pretence the matter is held to be a trifle when it is not one, while in his inner judgment the same thing is put forward here: that there would be no lack of a prince as author of correction. Those words, intelligible to those who know the secrets, reveal it: I confess that a part of my labours is lifted from me. The oversight of morals, property and the safety of citizens is not to be counted among trivial matters, nor is it a minor concern of the prince.

units.la: LXXI.
units.tr: LXXI.

units.la: Dicendi & agendi sub principe libertas plus admirationis ad posteros, quam securitatis in praesens autori suo confert.
units.tr: Freedom of speech and action under a prince brings more admiration to posterity than security to its author in the present.

units.la: Magis ad aulam facit ad nutum fortunae & principis, utilitate duce, circumacta loquendi & vivendi ra-tio. Ejusmodi omnium temporum, omnium horarum hominem, beatum Chorus Comicus deprae-dicat.
units.tr: A way of speaking and living that is shaped by the nod of fortune and of the prince, with advantage as its guide, suits the court better. The comic chorus pronounces a man of this kind happy at all times and in every hour:

units.tr: These things, as of a man [?] in [?]

units.tr: From us, but of the most magnificently grown

units.la: Πρὸς τὸ μεγαλοψυχώτερον;

That is:

units.la: Hoc viri graves habentis Pectoris versutias
units.tr: Such are the wiles of a man of grave bearing,

units.la: Antra perlati maris, Semper ad beatiorem Parietem fe commovere;
units.tr: The caves of the stormy sea, always turning to a more fortunate wall;

units.la: More quam fi imaginis Unica perfiet figura.
units.tr: In the manner of a figure that is one single image.

units.la: Persequi nam molliora Mobili vita via,
units.tr: For to pursue softer things by a changeable path

units.la: Est viri nafutioris quales est Theramenes:
units.tr: Is the way of a more crafty man, such as Theramenes was.

units.la: Qualem fe minimè Tiberio præbuit L. Piso ; modò ambitum fori, corrupta iudicia, sævitiam oratorum; accusationes minitantium increpans: modò liberi doloris documentum edens, vocata in suis Urgulania, quam supra leges amicitia Augusta extulerat. Quod quidem auctoritatem aliquam vivo, defuncto modò annalium; sed & recondita principis irarum creavit, cui nisi matura morte ereptus fuisset, commune multis supplicium non effugisset: quod ille non tam improvido animo incurrifle, quam animi magnitudine & fati perceptâ neceflitate sprevisse videri queat.
units.tr: Not at all the kind of man that Lucius Piso showed himself to be to Tiberius. Now he rebuked the ambition of the forum, corrupt judgments, and the savagery of orators, and those threatening accusations; now he gave proof of free grief when Urgulania was summoned in his own house, whom Augustan friendship had raised above the laws. This indeed gained him some authority while he lived, and now that he is dead a memory in the annals. But it also stirred up the hidden anger of the prince, from which, had he not been snatched away by a timely death, he would not have escaped the punishment common to many. One may think he did not rush into this with a careless mind, but rather scorned it, out of greatness of spirit and a perceived necessity of fate.

units.la: Τὸ μὲν [?] ὡς [?] ἀπὸ [?] μὲν
units.tr: [?] as [?] from [?] indeed

units.la: Καὶ τὰ ἀπὸ [?] τὰ [?] Περὶ τῶν [?]
units.tr: And the things from [?] the [?] Concerning the [?]
That is:

units.la: Fatalis aquè liberum dies manet; Et servitutis invido pressum jugo.
units.tr: The fated day remains equally free, and the man pressed by the envious yoke of servitude.

units.la: LXXII.
units.tr: LXXII.

units.la: Splendida est aulae & fori, sed incruento dolore splendida, miseria.
units.tr: The splendour of the court and of the forum is splendid, but it is a misery splendid with a bloodless pain.

units.la: Vidit hoc cum multis, aulicam & judiciariam vitam detestatis, & portum liberae tranquillitatis saltem in extrema senecta optantibus, L. Piso, qui rupto tandem silentio, & gratia Tiberii veritati posthabita, abire vitae ambi- fe, & cedere urbe, vi&urum in aliquo abdito & longinquo rure testabatur. simul curiam relinquebat. Et quae, per Deum immortalem, gravi viro vitae jucunditas, inter strepitum concursantis absque judicio populi; inter honorum empta aut gratia emendicata suffragia; inter justitiae in ipso tribunali pecuniariam corruptionem; inter causidicorum & rabularum caninam saevitiam? quae, quod libertati molestissimum, in servili vultus & verborum schemate, in mutuo arridentium, & per arrisum prodentium, metu beatitudo? Vivere tum demum se incepisse, cum ex hac aulae tenebricosa luce in solitudinem se contulit, nonnemo judicavit.
units.tr: Lucius Piso saw this, along with many others who detested court and judicial life and who wished, at least in extreme old age, for a harbour of free tranquillity. Having at last broken his silence, and placing truth above the favour of Tiberius, he declared that he would withdraw from the ambition of life, and yield the city, and live in some hidden and distant countryside. At the same time he was leaving the senate house. And what joy of life, by the immortal God, can a serious man have amid the din of a crowd rushing about without the judgment of the people; amid votes bought with office or begged by favour; amid the corruption of justice by money in the very tribunal; amid the dog-like savagery of advocates and wranglers? What, most hostile to liberty, is happiness in the servile countenance and manner of speech, in mutual smiling, and in fear betrayed through a smile? Someone judged that he then at last began to live, when he withdrew from this gloomy light of the court into solitude.

units.la: LXXIII.
units.tr: LXXIII.

units.la: Periculosa est sub unius dominio legum cum omnibus exaequatio.
units.tr: To place everyone on a level with the laws under the rule of one man is dangerous.

units.la: Nec temporum satis Piso meminerat, vocata in jus urgulania, quasi in veteri Romae libertate, & prisca senatus dignitate, quod si non ignoratione status pergit, arcana procul dubio imperii Tiberiani tentavit. Quae quamquam Tiberius dissimulatione abscondit, Augusta fe violari & imminui conquesta est: & propinqui Pisonem frustra coercuerunt.
units.tr: Piso did not bear the times sufficiently in mind when he summoned Urgulania to court, as if Rome still enjoyed its old liberty and the senate its ancient dignity. If he did not act out of ignorance of the state of affairs, he undoubtedly tested the secrets of Tiberius's rule. Although Tiberius concealed this by pretence, Augusta complained that she had been violated and diminished, and her relatives tried in vain to restrain Piso.

units.la: LXXIV.
units.tr: LXXIV.

units.la: Princeps astutus dominatui firmando personam servientis induet.
units.tr: A crafty prince, to strengthen his dominion, assumes the role of a servant.

units.la: Laborabant ex una parte potentia Liviae, matris Tiberii, per Urgulaniam punitam infringenda; ex altera judicia & senatorum confessus, per eandem Ulrgulaniam non judicandam, spretus. Tiberius bastenus indulgere matri civile ratus, ut se iturum ad praetoris tribunal, adfuturum Urgulania diceret. Itane prin-cipis autoritatem Tiberius abjecit, ut advocati & cau-tela fidici demissionem affumeret? pracessit palatio, procul sequi jussis militibus, quamvis procul, sequebantur ta-men armati: nec ea in ordinem se redigentis histrionia terrorem principis detersit. [?]pectabatur occursantes populo compositus ore, & sermonibus variis tempus atque iter ducens. gloriam ex aura popularis susurro, poenitentiam Pisonis ex itineris & sermonum produ-ctione captabat. donec propinquus Pisonem frustra coercentibus, deferri Augusta pecuniam qua petebatur juberet. Leviorem enim pecuniolae jacturam, quam dignitatis domus Augustae vilipendium, demisso ad praetoris tribunal principe, ducebat. praesertim cum ea nihil Urgulaniam laesura foret, pleno ex Augustae aera-rio haurienda, & aliunde è civium, ac ipsorum quidem senatorum, sanguine & facultatibus resarcienda. Isque finis rei, ex qua neque Piso inglorius, & Caesar majore fama fuit. Majore fama, quam siterrore & minis Pisonem deterruisset, vel matris dolorem non leniendum judicasset. Receptum enim civium Ro-manorum judicio erat, judicem quidem non posse li-mites veri & aequi honeste transilire: advocato autem ignorantia judicis, aut pravo judicandi affectu, in ami-corum patrocinio abuti licere. Quod arcanorum ci-vilium penetralia propius pulsat: nunquam in eum diem concesso jure regiam potestatem vel Augustus vel Tiberius exercuerant, aliis nominibus, & civilis vitae simulata exaequatione, jus principis promebant. Pisone livorem cicatricis autoritate [?]enatoria tangen-te, temporibus inserviendum potius, quam jus Ro-manae civitatis publicum disceptatione periculosè traducendum fuerat.
units.tr: On one side, the power of Livia, Tiberius's mother, had to be checked by punishing Urgulania. On the other, the judgments and the confession of the senators were scorned, because Urgulania was not to be judged by them. Tiberius, thinking it civil enough to indulge his mother, said that he would go to the praetor's tribunal and be present for Urgulania. Did Tiberius cast off the authority of the prince so completely that he took on the humility of an advocate and a surety? He went ahead of the palace, and the soldiers, ordered to follow at a distance, still followed armed. Nor did this theatrical lowering of himself to the ranks remove the terror of the prince. He was watched as he met the crowd, with a composed face, and he occupied the time and the journey with varied conversation. He sought glory from the breath of popular murmur, and Piso's repentance from the lengthening of the journey and the talk. Finally, while his relatives vainly restrained Piso, he ordered the money that was being sought to be paid over to Augusta. For he judged the loss of a little money lighter than the contempt shown to the dignity of the Augustan house, with the prince lowered to the praetor's tribunal. This was especially so since it would not harm Urgulania at all, being drawn from the full treasury of Augusta and made good elsewhere from the blood and property of the citizens, indeed of the senators themselves. This was the outcome of the affair, from which Piso was not without glory and Caesar had greater fame. He had greater fame than if he had deterred Piso by terror and threats, or had judged his mother's grief not to be softened. For it was accepted in the judgment of Roman citizens that a judge could not honourably cross the bounds of right and fairness, but an advocate might, in defending friends, take advantage of a judge's ignorance or a perverse inclination to judge. This touches more closely the inner sanctum of civil secrets: up to that day neither Augustus nor Tiberius had exercised royal power by a conceded right. Under other names, and by a feigned levelling with civil life, they put forward the right of the prince. With Piso touching the spiteful scar with senatorial authority, it had been better to serve the times than to expose the public law of the Roman state to dangerous debate.

units.la: LXXV. A testimonio ante tribunal dicendo forum Romanum paucos liberat.
units.tr: LXXV. The Roman forum frees a few from giving testimony before the tribunal.

units.la: Egregias personas (quas vocat) eosque qui valetudine impediuntur, ad quos domum mitti oportet, Paulus J. C. ista necessitate solvit. De Urgulania indignabunde Tacitus: Urgulania potentia adeo nimia civitati erat, ut testis in causa quadam, quae apud senatum tractabatur, venire dedignaretur. missus est praetor, qui domi interrogaret, cum virgines Vestales in foro et iudicio audiri, quoties testimonium dicerent, vetus mos fuerit. Tanta Vestalium virginum Romae existimatio fuit, ut iis Consules fortuito occurrentibus decederent; & ad supplicium extra Metiam portam ducti, illarum temerario occursu liberarentur. Nihilominus ab hac, dicendae publice pro testimonio sententiae, necessitudine immunes non erant. Alia illorum causa erat, quos a proferendo testimonio aut imbecillitas aetatis, aut judicii perpetua labes, aut vitae turpitudo arcebat. Hos intestabiles Romani fori frequens locutio vocabat. De Turpilio, Vaccae apud Numidas praefecto, Sallustius: quia illi in tanto malo turpis vi-ta integra fama potior fuit, improbus intestabilisque videtur. Ex quo, & pluribus aliis locis apparet, etiam extra judiciorum consuetudinem, intestabiles & infames eodem indignitatis gradu stetisse. ad quem morem Plautus, joco ex ambiguitate capto, allusit. apud quem filium pater inter castitatis praecepta ita hortatur:
units.tr: The jurist Paulus releases from this necessity distinguished persons (as they are called) and those hindered by ill health, to whom it is proper to send for the testimony at home. Tacitus is indignant about Urgulania: Urgulania's power was so excessive for the state that she disdained to come as a witness in a certain case that was being heard before the senate. A praetor was sent to question her at home, although it had been the old custom for the Vestal virgins to be heard in the forum and in court whenever they gave testimony. So great was the esteem of the Vestal virgins at Rome that consuls gave way to them when they met them by chance, and those led to execution outside the Metian gate were freed by their rash encounter with them. Nevertheless they were not exempt from the necessity of giving public opinion as testimony. Others were kept from giving testimony by the weakness of age, a perpetual defect of judgment, or the disgrace of their life. The common phrase of the Roman forum called these men intestable. Sallust, speaking of Turpilius, prefect of Vacca among the Numidians, says: Because in so great an evil a dishonourable life was preferred to an unblemished reputation, he seems wicked and intestable. From this, and from several other passages, it appears that even outside the customs of the courts, the intestable and the infamous stood on the same level of disgrace. Plautus, taking a joke from the ambiguity, alluded to this custom, in whom a father, among the precepts of chastity, exhorts his son thus:

units.la: Semper videto, ne sis intestabilis: Quod amas, amato testibus praesentibus.
units.tr: Always take care that you are not intestable: what you love, love with witnesses present.

units.la: LXXVI.
units.tr: LXXVI.

units.la: Major à praesentia principis patrum consessui splendor accedit.
units.tr: The presence of the prince adds greater splendour to the assembly of the fathers.
