units.la: At major ex absentia libertas, & majestatis non aliunde fulgentis opinio. Circa hos cardines diversae Cn. Pisonis & Asinii Galli, dissentientium illo negotio, sententiae versabantur. Piso, quanquam abfuturum se dixerat Caesar, ob id magis agendum censebat, ut absente principe, senatus & equites possent sua munia [?]fungi, ac. Non ab uno homine pendere Rei publicae fore.
units.tr: But greater freedom comes from absence, and from an opinion of majesty that does not shine from elsewhere. Around these hinges turned the differing opinions of Gnaeus Piso and Asinius Gallus, who disagreed in that business. Piso, although Caesar had said he would be absent, thought that for this very reason more should be done, so that with the prince absent the senate and the knights could perform their duties. The Republic would not depend on one man.

units.la: E dere vel salutem vel dignitatem senatus populique Ro-mani. Fuisse id quondam patribus, fuisse populo dé-corum, per fe munia publicæ rei sustinere. posse & nunc priscæ reipub. imaginem, saltem absente princi-pe, reduci. Gallus, quia speciem libertatis Piso prace-[?]perat, nihil fatis inlustre, aut ex dignitate populi Ro-mani, nisi coram & sub oculis Cæsaris: eoque conven-tum Italiæ, & adfluentes provincias, præsentiæ ejus fer-vanda dicebat. Pisonem quidem, ut in Fabriciorum aut Curiorum republica, verba facere. At jamdudum rem eo rediisse, ut moles aucti[?] imperii nonnisi ab uno, hominum summo, & deorum generi proximo, fusti-neri queat, ab hoc splendorem negotiis, ab hoc digni-tatem senatui accedere, ab hoc populum Romanum fastigii tanti radios mutuari. nec capere proceres Ita-liæ, & affluentes provinciarum legatos, majestatem imperii, nisi prefente rerum moderatore decorati. Consulendum esse existimationi Romanæ, quæ jam dudum laboret, nisi tanti principis autoritate & prae-fentibus excubiis fulciatur. Audiente hac Tiberio ac silente, magnis utrinque contentionibus acta. Et tem-pestivè quidem silente: ne aut pro fastigio suo decer-nendo, in moderationis famam impingeret; aut de-trahendo de majestate sua, præjudicio fe ipsum ac po-fteros imminueret. sed res dilata, quod fieri amat in ejusmodi honorum contentionibus: ne res decisa ce-lerem pœnitentiam adduceret.
units.tr: It had once been fitting for the fathers, fitting for the people, to sustain the duties of public affairs by themselves, and to risk either the safety or the dignity of the senate and the Roman people. Even now they could restore, at least with the prince absent, the image of the old republic. Gallus, because Piso had presented the appearance of liberty, said that nothing was sufficiently illustrious or worthy of the Roman people except before and under the eyes of Caesar. Therefore, he said, the assembly of Italy and the provinces flowing in should keep to his presence. Piso, he said, spoke as if in the republic of the Fabricii or the Curii. But for some time the matter had come to this: the weight of the enlarged empire can be borne only by one man, the highest of men and nearest to the race of the gods. From him splendour comes to affairs, from him dignity comes to the senate, and from him the Roman people borrow the rays of so great a height. Nor do the nobles of Italy and the envoys of the flowing provinces grasp the majesty of empire unless it is adorned by the presence of the ruler of affairs. Care must be taken for the Roman reputation, which has long been wavering, unless it is propped up by the authority of so great a prince and by his present guards. This was argued with great contention on both sides while Tiberius heard it and kept silent. He kept silent, and rightly so: lest by decreeing honours for his own greatness he should fall into a reputation for moderation, or by detracting from his majesty he should diminish himself and his successors by a precedent. But the matter was deferred, as is usual in such contests over honours, lest a decided question bring quick repentance.

units.la: LXXVII.
units.tr: LXXVII.

units.la: Pupillum principis, magistratuum demandandorum curam, senator ne attingat.
units.tr: The prince's ward: a senator should not meddle with the appointment of magistrates.

units.la: Afinius Gallus quasi pro incremento Cæsaris ni-tendo, potestatem ejus occulte imminuere conaba-tur,censendo, in quinquennium magistratuum comi-tia habenda: utque legionum legati, qui ante pratu-ram ea militia fungebantur, jam tum prætores defi-gnentur[?]: princeps duodecim candidatos in annos sin-gulos. [?]ulis nominaret. Quod à Julio Cæsare inceptum, ab Antonio & Augusto ferme frequentatum, Tiberius non omnino infregerat, ut quinquennales essent magistratus: id ut optimo jure liceret, senatus auctoritatem Tiberio accedere censebat, idem de legatis prætoriis, vel etiam consularibus, judicium esse debere voluit. Nec non quasi pro jure principis confirmando, de duodecim candidatis prætura, à Tiberio in annos singulos (an quinos?) nominandis, pari modo disseruit. Comitiorum autem rationem omnem, aut in momento præponderantem, in manus principis deferri, nonne magnificum Tiberio ducendum? Haud ita vel ipse, vel pro eo Cornelius Tacitus judicabat. Haut dubium erat, eam sententiam altius penetrare, & arcana imperii tenturi. Nam quod arbitrii prin-cipum erat, si legis & necessitatis aut beneficii patrum decreti fieret: nulla in eo principum auctoritas, nulla designatorum gratia. Deinde quinquennii comitia partim Tiberio facultatem plures beneficio demerendi demebant, partim diuturnitate publicæ dignitatis principi quodammodo eos exæquabant. Illud verò de legionum legatis, ipso militiæ jure prætoribus futuris, parum occultè Tiberio machinas admovebat. Neç aliter de duodecim principis candidatis judicandum: quod in arbitrio principis positum, opes ejus adauget; decreto publico introductum, multorum honoris communicatione eadem debilitat.
units.tr: Asinius Gallus, pretending to promote the advancement of Caesar, was secretly trying to diminish his power when he proposed that the elections of magistrates be held for five years at a time, and that the legates of the legions, who had previously served in that military post before the praetorship, should now be designated praetors. The prince should nominate twelve candidates each year [?]. Julius Caesar had begun this practice, and Antony and Augustus had mostly kept it up. Tiberius had not entirely abolished it, so that the magistracies could be held for five years; he proposed that the Senate's approval should be added to Tiberius's, so that this would be permitted under the best law. He also wished the same judgement to apply to the praetorian, or even consular, legates. Likewise, as if to confirm the prince's right, he argued in the same way about the twelve candidates for the praetorship whom Tiberius was to nominate each year (or five years?). But should it not be considered a great thing for Tiberius that the whole management of the elections, which carried the weight at every moment, was placed in the hands of the prince? Neither Tiberius himself nor Cornelius Tacitus on his behalf judged it so. There was no doubt that this proposal reached deeper, and aimed at the secrets of empire. For what depended on the prince's discretion, if it were done by law and necessity or by the decree of the fathers, would leave the prince no authority and the designated candidates no favour. Next, the five-year elections partly took from Tiberius the opportunity of winning favour by many benefits, and partly made the prince in some way equal to those men through the length of public office. Moreover, that point about the legates of the legions, who would be praetors by the very law of military service, plainly brought engines to bear against Tiberius. Nor is the matter to be judged otherwise about the twelve candidates of the prince: what is placed at the prince's discretion increases his resources, and what is introduced by public decree weakens them by sharing the honour among many.

units.la: LXXVIII.
units.tr: LXXVIII.

units.la: Astus astu, simulatio simulatione retunditur.
units.tr: Craft is blunted by craft, pretence by pretence.

units.la: Ἀλωπεκίζειν ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀλώπηξ, Græcorum proverbio, καὶ [illegible, ~10 letters]. Tiberius dissimulato verborum Asinii intellectu, quasi declinaturus invidiosum potestatis augmentum, ita disseruit. Non convenire moderationi suæ, nec animi tranquillitati, tantum designatorum numerum, & tot annorum odiosam rejectionem. quis enim spe in quinquennium semper dilata, tacitam præteritorum offensam non metuat? quantum deinde periculi fore ex diuturno magistratu, moribus, factione, domestico subsidio non ante satis perspecto, aut in horas mutabili! quantum in remp. ex arrogantia magistratuum discriminis! nam si annuam imperii gerendi felicitatem impotens hominum animus concoquere non potest: quonam diuturnitate honorum & imperandi consuetudine elatus, nescius modi & æquabilitatis incapax feretur? quintuplicem pro uno magistratum cives gesturos; vim legibus antiquis allaturos. sapienter à majoribus institutum, & magno reip. commodo semper placitum, ut annuæ honorum vicissitudines aliorum celsi-tudinem refringerent, aliorum impatientes nimiæ morae spes consolarentur. Quin & alendæ civium industriæ annuas vices fomentum adferre. alioqui illi desidia, aut magistratuum tædio torpescerent; hi desperatione languidi marcescerent. Hunc in sensum philosophatus; Tiberius, favorabili in speciem oratione vim imperii tenuit.
units.tr: To play the fox [Ἀλωπεκίζειν] instead of "to be a fox" [ἀλώπηξ], as the Greek proverb has it, and [illegible]. Tiberius, pretending not to understand the words of Asinius, as if about to turn aside the hateful increase of power, argued as follows. It did not suit his moderation nor the tranquillity of his mind to have so many designated candidates and the hateful rejection of so many years. For who, with hope always deferred for five years, would not fear the silent resentment of those passed over? How great, moreover, would be the danger from a long magistracy, whose character, party and domestic support had not been sufficiently tested beforehand, and which could change from hour to hour! How great the peril to the state from the arrogance of magistrates! For if an unrestrained human mind cannot digest the happy conduct of power for a single year, what will it do when puffed up by a long tenure of office and the habit of command, ignorant of moderation and incapable of evenness? Citizens would hold five magistracies in place of one and would bring violence against the ancient laws. Our ancestors wisely instituted, and it has always pleased the state for its great advantage, that the yearly rotation of offices should check the eminence of some and console others, impatient of excessive delay, with hope. Indeed, the yearly turns also bring a stimulus to foster the industry of citizens; otherwise the one would grow torpid from idleness or weariness of office, and the others would wither, languid with despair. Philosophising to this effect, Tiberius, with a speech favourable in appearance, kept hold of the power of empire.

units.la: Not printed on this page.
units.tr: Not printed on this page.

units.la: LXXIX.
units.tr: LXXIX.

units.la: Magnum beneficii publici incenta-mentum familiæ claritas.
units.tr: Family renown is a great incentive to public benefit.

units.la: Pro temporum, & locorum varietate ambiguæ probationis assertio. M. Hortalus, nepos oratoris Hortensii, [?]inlectus à divo Augusto liberalitate decies sestertium ducere uxorem, suscipere liberos, ne clarissi-ma familia extingueretur: cum auctus liberis, ad claritudinem generis provocando, suppetias à principe & senatu petiisset; à Tiberio aspera oratione rejectus est. Est aliqua, quæ Augustum moverit, in Hortalo prae aliis juvando ratio. Clarorum enim hominum, & de rep. benè meritorum, memoriam in stirpe conser-vari; nec eam aut dedecore affricari, aut internecione extingui; gratorum civium & non iniquæ patriæ est. Tum eâ spe ad præclara facinora, æternitate memoriæ in posteris victuræ, cum animæ præ gloria vilipendio adeunda, generosi animi eriguntur. Interest & ad splendorem & decus reipublicæ, cives habere prosapiæ vetustate, & majorum quos imitentur antiqua gloria conspicuos. Sed hic mihi aliquis Mariano, vel quod propius est, Sallustiano ore novus homo obstrepat: hominem veteris prosapiæ, ac multarum imaginum, sed nullius stipendii, non esse viro sua virtute inclarescenti præferendum. Levius esse, fortunam, quam probra objectari. naturam unam & communem omnium: fortissimum quemque generosissimum esse. non esse res natura diversissimas, ignaviæ voluptatem, & præmia virtutis, eidem exspectandas, majorum gloriam posteris lumen esse: bene & male facta detegere. veram nobilitatem non hæreditate relinqui; laboribus & periculis quæri. virtutem animi, veram nobilitatis radicem, dono nec dari nec accipi. Quæ ut magna ex parte vera esse non diffitemur: ita omnem virtutem in posteris nobilium extingui, periculosæ est assertionis. Quod si qui à paterna indole degenerant, suo periculo, non alieno, labis attractæ pœnam ferant.
units.tr: An assertion of doubtful proof, depending on the variety of times and places. Marcus Hortalus, grandson of the orator Hortensius, lured by the generosity of the deified Augustus into marrying a wife worth a million sesterces and having children, so that the most illustrious family would not be extinguished, sought help from the prince and the Senate, appealing to the renown of his line, now that his family had grown with children; but he was rejected by Tiberius in a harsh speech. There is some reason why Augustus was moved to help Hortalus above others. For it is the duty of a grateful citizen and of a fair country that the memory of famous men who have deserved well of the state be preserved in their stock, and that it be neither tarnished by disgrace nor destroyed by extinction. Then, with the hope of noble deeds whose memory will live eternally among posterity, generous spirits are roused to despise their lives for the sake of glory. It also matters for the splendour and dignity of the commonwealth to have citizens conspicuous for the antiquity of their lineage and for the ancient glory of the ancestors whom they may imitate. But here someone, a new man speaking in the manner of Marius, or, what is closer, of Sallust, may cry out against me: that a man of ancient lineage and many images, but of no service, should not be preferred to a man who grows famous by his own virtue. It is a lighter thing to be cast in one's teeth with fortune than with disgrace. Nature is one and common to all; the bravest of each is the most noble. Things are not so utterly diverse by nature that the pleasure of idleness and the rewards of virtue should be expected by the same person; the glory of ancestors is a light for posterity, revealing good and bad deeds. True nobility is not left by inheritance but is sought through labours and dangers; the virtue of the mind, the true root of nobility, is neither given nor received as a gift. We do not deny that these things are largely true; but to say that all virtue is extinguished among the descendants of the noble is a dangerous assertion. And if some degenerate from their father's character, let them bear the punishment of the stain they have contracted at their own risk, not at another's.

units.la: LXXX.
units.tr: LXXX.

units.la: Alia in libertate, alia sub umbra principis, etiam domestica vivendi ratio.
units.tr: Different ways of living in freedom and under the shadow of a prince, even in private life.

units.la: In civium omnium ἰσηγορία animi ad belli gloriam, ad facundiam in foro exercendam, ad populi auram captandam, unde & pecuniæ sæpè emolumentum, eriguntur. Sub principe, Tiberianæ præsertim farinæ, militare civium decus comprimitur, studium eloquentiæ conteritur, populi factiones inhibentur. Etiam pecuniæ aut acquisitio non æquè in promptu, aut ostentatio pro crimine. De se & familia sua Hortalus: nam ego, qui non pecuniam, non studia populi, neque eloquentiam gentile domus nostra bonum varietate temporum accipere vel parare potuissem.
units.tr: In a free state, the minds of all citizens are raised to the glory of war, to the practice of eloquence in the forum, and to catching the breeze of popular favour, from which money often follows as well. [Isēgoria] Under a prince, especially one of the Tiberian stamp, the military honour of citizens is suppressed, zeal for eloquence is worn down, and popular factions are checked. Even the acquisition of money is not so readily within reach, and display of wealth is counted as a crime. Hortalus speaks of himself and his family: For I, who could neither receive nor acquire money, popular favour, or eloquence, which were the hereditary good of our house, owing to the changing of the times.

units.la: Et hæc præcipuè ratio Ciceronem, linguæ acumine potentiam inter populares adeptum, moverit; cur tantoperè Julii Cæsaris monarchiam, & postmodùm Antonii molitiones, ut incremento suo adversas, oderit. Causam quidem extinctæ apud Romanos facundiæ, mutatam temporum & publici regiminis rationem, non obscuré autor Dialogi asserit. Hinc leges af- fidua, populare nomen, hinc conciones magistratuum panè pernoctantium in rostris, hinc accusationes poten- tiam reorum, & assignata etiam domibus inimicitia, hinc procerum factiones & assidua senatus adversus plebem certamina. Qua singula etsi distrahebant Rem- publicam, exercebant tamen illorum temporum elo- quentiam, & magnis cumulare pramiis videbantur. Quia quanto quisque plus dicendo poterat, tanto faci- lius honores assequebatur, &c. Caeterain Arcanis Re- gnorum, nec non tractatu De Republica, diduxi.
units.tr: This is chiefly the reason that moved Cicero, who had gained power among the popular party through the sharpness of his tongue, to hate so bitterly the monarchy of Julius Caesar and afterwards the schemes of Antony, as hostile to his own advancement. The author of the Dialogue plainly asserts the cause of the extinction of eloquence among the Romans: the change of the times and of the system of public government. Hence came the laws, the popular name, the speeches of magistrates who almost spent the night on the rostra, the accusations, the power of the defendants, and enmity passed down even between households; hence the factions of the nobles and the constant struggles of the senate against the plebs. Although each of these was tearing the commonwealth apart, they nonetheless gave exercise to the eloquence of those times and seemed to heap great rewards upon it, for the more a man could accomplish by speaking, the more easily he attained honours, and so on. The rest I have set out in the Arcana Regnorum and in the treatise On the Commonwealth.

units.la: LXXXI.
units.tr: LXXXI.

units.la: Non est clari viri &inopis, uxoriæ rei & liberis operam dare.
units.tr: It is not the part of a distinguished man, when he is poor, to concern himself with his wife's affairs and his children.

units.la: Nulla res magnos animos, & in publico confpi- cuos, magis quam paupertatis ignominia, deterit. Quam fi quis magno animo supergreditur, ne in libe- ris, ad injuriam & ad mendicitatem natis, hic dolor re- crudescat, cavendum. Agnovit hoc, sed propè ferò agnovit M. Hortalus. Fatis habebam, fi tenues res mea nec mihi pudori, nec cuiquam oneri forent, jussus ab imperatore, uxorem duxi. En stirps & progenies tot consulum, tot dictatorum, nec adinvidiam istam, sed concilianda misericordia refero. At nunc, mi Hor- tale, affictæ res tuæ & tibi pudori, & senatui nequic- quam oneri sunt. Omnes enim miseriæ tuæ fortassis ignoscunt, nemo subvenit. Aspera quin etiam prin- cipis oratione increpitus, malles domesticam mife- riam tacitè devoravisse, neque miseratus est possibas Tiberius, quamvis domus Hortensii pudendam ad in- ö piam dilaberetur. Quas contra movere rationes vel Medici vel Theologi queant, ut non Politici fori ma- chinationes, transeo.
units.tr: Nothing wears down great spirits, those conspicuous in public life, more than the disgrace of poverty. If a man rises above it with a great spirit, he must take care that this pain does not break out again in his children, who are born to injury and beggary. Marcus Hortalus recognised this, but only almost too late. I thought it enough if my modest means were neither a shame to me nor a burden to anyone, and so, ordered by the emperor, I married. Behold the stock and progeny of so many consuls and dictators; I bring this up not to provoke envy but to win pity. But now, my Hortalus, your ruined fortunes are a shame to you and a useless burden to the senate. For perhaps all your miseries are pardoned, yet no one comes to help. Indeed, rebuked by the harsh speech of the prince, you would rather have silently swallowed your domestic misery; and Tiberius, though able, did not pity you, though the house of Hortensius was collapsing into shameful poverty. What counter-arguments physicians or theologians might bring, I pass over, as I do the machinations of the political forum.

units.la: LXXXII.
units.tr: LXXXII.

units.la: Suspicax Principis animus nulla ar- gutia vellicandus.
units.tr: A suspicious prince's mind must not be provoked by any subtlety.

units.la: Incredibilis ingenii Tiberiani altitudo, ut fui animi fecresecreta vultu & verbis abdidit, ita suspicaci rerum indagatione aliorum operta & aperta rimabatur. Jecerat inter alia Hortalus temporum varietatem, ut incremento suo per eloquentiam gentile domus bonum adversam. Id Tiberium, qui nihil in Rep. mutatum videri voluit, aut tempora sua non esse prioribus infeliciora; aut saltem haec in publicum proferri noluit, interiori tactu pupugit. Cumque orationem Hortali cum assensu a Patribus audiri percepit, graviori irae æ-stu imperorantem Hortalum effervescebat. Inclinatio senatus incitamentum Tiberio fuit, quo promptius ad-versaretur. Desinat igitur mirari Cornelius, cur cum censum quorundam senatorum Tiberius ultro juve-rit, preces M. Hortali, nobilis juvenis, in paupertate manifesta, superbius acceperit.
units.tr: Tiberius had an incredible depth of mind. As he hid his secret feelings behind his face and words, so with a suspicious probing of affairs he searched out what was hidden and what was open in others. Among other things, Hortalus had remarked on the changeable times, saying that by his eloquence he would restore the family's ancient good fortune. This touched Tiberius inwardly, since he wanted it seen that nothing in the commonwealth had changed, that his own times were no worse than former ones, or at least he did not want such things brought before the public. When he perceived that the Fathers heard Hortalus's speech with approval, he flared up with a heavier heat of anger against the speaker. The senate's inclination was an incitement to Tiberius, by which he opposed more readily. Let Cornelius therefore cease to wonder why Tiberius, who had freely granted money to some senators, received the petition of Marcus Hortalus, a noble young man in plain poverty, so haughtily.

units.la: LXXXIII. Providi rerum suarum principis non est, ærarium per erogationes exhaurire.
units.tr: LXXXIII. A provident prince does not drain the treasury through gifts.

units.la: Quanquam acerbius in M. Hortalum non fuacul-pa egentem, prodigentibus tamen moribus accom-modatè Tiberius: Si quantum pauperum est, venire huc, & liberis suis petere pecunias coeperint: singuli nunquam exsatiabuntur, Resp. deficiet. Fœdius erat: si quantum histrioniæ vanitatis, quantum artis pyro-bolicæ, quantum adulatoriæ levitatis, quantum hominum aulica ostentatione inanium. Nec sane ideo a majoribus concessum est egredi aliquando relationem, & quod in commune conducat loco sententiæ proferre, ut privata negotia, res familiares nostras hic augea-mus. Providendum vel inprimis erat, ne de republica sententiæ singulorum utilitati, gratiæ, simultatibus prætexantur; ne domi pecuniæ senatores aut amicorum precibus, in curia factionibus studeant. Non tantum, ne quis patrum, ad inopiam miseria temporum collapsus, ærumnarum suarum sensum promat, & modicum calamitatis allevamentum petat. cum invidia senatus & principum, sive indulserint largitionem, sive abnuerint. Si enim indulserint; compilato-
units.tr: Yet Tiberius, not too harshly toward Marcus Hortalus, who was in need through no fault of his own, but suitably to the prodigal habits of the time, said: If as many poor people as there are come here and begin to ask their children's money from us, individuals will never be satisfied, and the commonwealth will fail. It would have been more shameful if so much of theatrical vanity, so much of fireworks art, so much of flattering levity, and so much of men empty in courtly display [had been paid for]. Nor indeed was it therefore conceded by our ancestors that a report should ever go out, and that one should express an opinion for the common good, so that we might increase our private affairs and family property here. Above all it had to be provided that opinions on the commonwealth should not be put forward as pleasing to individuals' advantage, favour or private quarrels; that senators should not strive for money at home through the petitions of friends, or for factions in the senate house. Nor should any of the fathers, fallen into want through the misery of the times, display the sense of his distresses and seek a modest relief from calamity, with the envy of the senate and of the princes, whether they grant the largesse or refuse it. For if they grant it, the

units.la: res aerarii, boni publici dilapidatores, à pravo rerum judice vulgo audient. Sin abnuerint: ut immites, cla-riffimarum familiarum negligentes, commodo tantùm suo viventes, eodem rumore vulgi vapulabunt. non enim preces sunt istuc, sed efflagitatio intempestiva quidem & improvisa. Cogendi enim vim habent cla-rorum virorum à collegis, & à benigno principe, miseriae domesticae sublevandae efflagitationes. cum aliis de rebus convenerint patres, consurgere, & numero atque aetate liberûm suorum, urgere modestiam senatus. Publicae enim curae hic locus est, non domesticae rei studii, eandem vim in me transmittere, ac velut perfringere aerarium. quid enim refert, qua machinatione id exhaurias? cuniculisne manuariis admotis, an modestia principis per vim, & similes vi preces, expugna-ta. quod si ambitione exhauserimus, per scelera supplendum erit. Verè, quamvis aliud agente à principe, dictum. Qui enim largitione amicos parant, qui te-merè publica profundunt magis quam donant: ad ra-pinas, ad iniquas exactiones, ad subornatas opulento-rum accusationes, ad similia scelera reficiendo aerario convertentur. dedit tibi Hortale divus Augustus pe-cuniam, sed non compellatus, nec ea lege ut semper daretur. At nescio quomodo ii qui semel beneficio affecti sunt, ad idem quasi debitum, quod meri arbitrii fuerat, recurrunt. languescet alioqui industria, intendetur se-cordia, si nullus ex se metus, aut spes: & securi omnes aliena subsidia exspectabunt, sibi ignavi, nobis graves. Gravissimè acerba principis oratio obsignata. quod di-ctum quomodo adversus Platonicam bonorum com-munionem applicaverimus, vide nostram de Republi-ca tractationem.
units.tr: plunderers of the treasury and squanderers of public goods will be heard by the common people, who are a crude judge of affairs. But if they refuse, they will be beaten by the same rumour of the crowd as cruel men, neglectful of distinguished families, living only for their own convenience. For these are not petitions but an untimely and unexpected demand. For distinguished men have power to compel, from their colleagues and from a kindly prince, pleas for relief from domestic misery. When the fathers have agreed on other matters, they rise and, by the number and age of their children, press the modesty of the senate. For this is a place for public concerns, not for zeal about domestic affairs. To transmit the same force against me, as if to break open the treasury. For what does it matter by what contrivance you drain it: by hand-dug tunnels, or by overpowering the prince's modesty with force and petitions extorted by violence. But if we have drained it through ambition, it will have to be made up by crimes. Truly, though the prince was speaking of something else, it was rightly said. For those who buy friends with largesse, who rashly pour out public funds rather than give them, will turn to robberies, unjust exactions, suborned accusations of the wealthy, and similar crimes to refill the treasury. Divus Augustus gave you money, Hortalus, but he was not appealed to, nor on the condition that it should always be given. But I know not how, those who have once been favoured with a benefaction run back to it as if it were a debt, when it had been a matter of free discretion. Otherwise industry will languish and sloth will be stretched, if there is no fear or hope arising from oneself, and all, feeling secure, will wait for other people's help, idle for themselves and burdensome to us. The prince's bitter speech was sealed most gravely. How we have applied what was said against Plato's community of goods, see our treatise on the Commonwealth.

units.la: LXXXIV.
units.tr: LXXXIV.

units.la: Æqua iniqua principis oraculorum vicem obtinent.
units.tr: The just and unjust decisions of a prince take the place of oracles.

units.la: Non desunt tamen, qui animo erectiori, & aut su-perstitione altiori, aut adulationis vitore, rem magis quam autorem intuentur. Hac atque talia, quanquam cum assensu audita ab his, quibus omnia principum bonesta atque inhonesta laudare mos est, plures per silentium aut occultum murmur excepere. Si quos autem praesens vel metus & principis veneratio, vel placendi studium aut praemii expectatio, à vero judi-cio detorquet: his aut illo defunctis, clarior fidei & veri existimatio erumpit.
units.tr: Yet there are not lacking those who, with a more lofty spirit and either a higher superstition or the victory of flattery, look at the matter rather than at its author. These and such things, though heard with assent by those who are accustomed to praise all the honourable and dishonourable acts of princes, were received by most in silence or with a hidden murmur. If, however, fear and veneration of the prince, or the desire to please, or the expectation of reward, turns certain people from true judgment, then once these have either died or departed, a clearer estimate of faith and truth breaks forth.

units.la: LXXXV.
units.tr: LXXXV.

units.la: Odio est magnis animis canina beneficii objectio.
units.tr: A benefit thrown in one's face like a bone to a dog is hateful to great minds.

units.la: Imò & canes nonnunquam & jumenta offam, post recusationem deluforiam, aut cum increpatione ob-latam, adversantur nedum generosum animal, Homo, gloriæ ac ignominiæ capacus, non irritetur. Tiberius murmure patrum aut ingrato silentio percepto, increpationem Hortali oblato liberis ejus, qui sexus virilis essent, ducenorum sestertiorum beneficio convertit. Ægre alii grates: fluit Hortalus, pavore, an avita no-bilitatis etiam inter angustias fortuna retinens. qua de re in Arcanis Regnorum, primi libri Annalium politi-co commentario, prolixius egimus.
units.tr: Even dogs and beasts of burden sometimes turn against a morsel offered after a mocking refusal or with a rebuke. How much more, then, should a noble creature like man, capable of glory and disgrace, not be provoked? When Tiberius perceived the murmur of the fathers or their ungrateful silence, he turned the rebuke given to Hortalus into a benefaction of two hundred thousand sesterces for his sons. Others gave thanks grudgingly; Hortalus hesitated, whether from fear, or because his ancestral nobility kept its dignity even amid straitened fortune. On this matter we have treated at greater length in the Arcana Regnorum, in the political commentary on the first book of the Annals.

units.la: LXXXVI.
units.tr: LXXXVI.

units.la: Ad componendas pauci, ad turbandas res compositas nemo non satis idoneus.
units.tr: Few are fit to settle matters, but almost anyone is fit to disturb settled matters.

units.la: Præsertim si alienato à pœnæ exspectatione animo, contumeliæ opinione ad vindictam præceps fertur. [?]ὅτι γὰρ ἐπὶ ἀνθρώπῳ ἀδικήσεως[?], ἢ νομίζῃ ἀδικεῖσθαι[?]. inquit apud Dionem Tullius Cicero. i. e. terribile quid est homo injuria affectus, aut qui se ea affectum putat. lib. 44. Tiberio quiete imperante, mancipii unius audacia, nisi maturè subventum foret, discordiis armisque civilibus Remp. perculisset. Julio Cæsare in Curia Pompeii à conjuratis occiso, sapien-tia Ciceronis, malorum [illegible, ~2 letters] suadentis, præsentia vix constituebantur. Antonii vero ἀλογίαι[?], cadavere in forum illato in laudem Cæsaris intempestivè perorantis, tanta tumultuantis populi tempestas exarsit, quantam ipse autoritate consularì ægrè compescuit: & quam pro dominandi occasione postmodum arripuit. Cujusvis est homunculi, imò & contemptissimæ bestiolæ, nocere valetudini; non nisi artificis in medica arte egregii, turbatam sanitatem restituere.
units.tr: This is especially so if, with his mind turned away from fear of punishment, a man is rushed headlong into vengeance by the belief that he has been insulted. For Cicero says, as Dio reports: "It is a terrible thing for a man to be wronged, or to think himself wronged" [ὅτι γὰρ ἐπὶ ἀνθρώπῳ ἀδικήσεως ἢ νομίζῃ ἀδικεῖσθαι], that is, a man who has been injured, or who thinks he has been injured, is a dreadful thing. Book 44. When Tiberius was quietly ruling, the audacity of one slave, unless help had come promptly, would have shaken the commonwealth with discord and civil arms. When Julius Caesar was killed by the conspirators in Pompey's Curia, things were scarcely settled by the wisdom of Cicero, who recommended remedies for the evils. But when Antony, in a madness of reasoning [ἀλογίαι], carried the corpse into the forum and gave an ill-timed speech in praise of Caesar, such a storm of the stirred-up people blazed up that he himself could hardly quell it with his consular authority, and afterwards he seized it as an opportunity for domination. It is within the power of any little man, indeed of the most despised little creature, to harm health; only a skilled artist, eminent in the medical art, can restore a disturbed health.

units.la: LXXXVII.
units.tr: LXXXVII.

units.la: Servitutem & regnum audacia aut fortuna, non natura aut meritum, distinguit.
units.tr: Audacity or fortune, not nature or merit, distinguishes slavery from kingship.

units.la: Nulla quidem regnandi spe aut cupiditate, sed fide in dominum & amore, Clemens Agrippæ Poftumi servus res novas principio moliebatur. comperto fine, Augusti pergere in infulam Planafiam, & fraude aut vi raptum Agrippam ferre ad exercitus Germanicos non servili animo concepit. ausa ejus impedivit tardias oneraria navis. Grata res legionibus Germanicis, ob ferociam ingenii, & Agrippæ generi Augusti moriam, & ob spem prædæ fuiflet. Nec plebeculæ Romanæ, mobili & tum Tiberium exosæ, ingrata accidisset. Patrata mandatu Tiberii cæde Agrippæ, ad magis præcipitia conversus, five ardore vindictæ, five etiam regnandi quadam spe & cupidine, fe pro Agrippa venditavit. quam adrem ut non audaciæ, ita nec astus egebat. ignoti loci sese abdit, donec crinem barbamque promitteret. nam atate & forma haut dissimili in dominum erat. capilli & barbæ promissio vel ad tegenda faciei lineamenta, vel ad exilii arguendum squalorem, & diuturnæ solitudinis indicium, affumes batur. tum per idoneos & secreti ejus conscios crebescit, vivere Agrippam: occultè primum sermonibus, ut vetita solent: mox vago rumore apud imperitiffimos cujusque promptas aures, aut rursum apud turbidos, eóque nova cupientes. initium, progressum, & incrementum ficti in præcipitibus rumoris intuere, quem frustra dispersisset servulus, nisi astu eum & dolo alere fcivif. scivisset, atque ipse adire municipia obscuro diei, neque propalam aspici, neque aiutim iisdem locis, commorari.
units.tr: Clemens, the slave of Agrippa Postumus, began to stir up revolution, not from any hope or desire of ruling, but from loyalty and affection for his master. Having learned that Augustus was going to Planasia island, he conceived, without a servile spirit, the plan of seizing Agrippa by fraud or force and carrying him to the German armies. His attempt was foiled by a slow transport ship. The scheme would have pleased the German legions, because of their fierce temper, their admiration for Augustus's son-in-law, and their hope of plunder. Nor would it have been unwelcome to the Roman common people, who were fickle and at that time hated Tiberius. Agrippa was killed on Tiberius's orders, and Clemens, driven to still more desperate courses, whether from a passion for revenge or from some hope and desire of ruling, passed himself off as Agrippa. For this he needed no more boldness than cunning. He hid himself in a place no one knew, until he could let his hair and beard grow; for he was of much the same age and appearance as his master. Letting the hair and beard grow would serve either to hide the features of his face or to show the squalor of exile and the marks of a long solitude. Then, through trusted men who were privy to his secret, the report grew that Agrippa was alive: at first secretly, by whispers, as forbidden things usually are; then by a wandering rumour, taken up by the most ignorant and by the restless who were eager for change. Observe the beginning, progress and growth of this invented rumour, which the slave would have spread in vain had he not known how to nourish it by cunning and deceit. He himself went to the towns at night, not showing himself openly, and stayed in the same places only briefly.

units.la: Causam vagabundae trepidationis, quamvis oculato lectori non ambiguam, ista sententia Cornelius detexit: quia veritas visu & mora falsa festinatione & incertis valescunt, nimirum relinquebat famam, aut praveniebat. Alia bellicoso Numidiae regi trepidandi, & incertis locis vagandi, ex metu nimirum & amicorum diffidentia, causa erat. de quo ita Historicus: neque postea ullo in loco amplius uno die, aut una nocte moratus; simulabat sese negotii gratia properare: caeterum proditionem timebat, quam vitare posse celeritate putabat: nam talia consilia per otium & ex opportunitate capi. Haec de Jugurtha Sallustius. Nos ad Clementem, & increbescentem de Agrippa rumorem, revertamur. Vulgabatur interim per Italiam, servatum munere deum Agrippam, credebatur Roma. jamque Hostia invectum multitudo ingens, jam in urbe clandestini coetus celebrabant. Quantum igitur aut a regno capiendo, aut a permiscenda civilibus armis Italia, verna abfuit? Similis audaciae, & nonnunquam ad regni fastigium evectae, exempla, ob copiam dilectu difficilia, omnium temporum historia suppeditat. Noti sunt Andrisci, quem Pseudo-Philippum vocabant, adversus Romanos in Macedonia progressus: noti Alexandri, terrae filii, in Syria adversus Demetrium. Nota in Germania Friderici, in Flandria Baldui-ni, ficta regnandi causa nomina. Quas vero Pseudo-Demetrii turbas in Moscorum amplissima regione, Polonorum artificio, seculi hujus initio concitaverint, barbarorum gentium annales docent. Ut Tyri heris interfectis, vernae imperium splendidissimum arripuerint, vel historiae primae tyronibus e Justino innocuit. Ita dignis & indignis fraus & audacia, modo fortuna comitatum non abnegaverit, saepe viam ad regnum aperit.
units.tr: The reason for this restless alarm, though it is not hard for the attentive reader to see, Cornelius reveals in that saying: "because truth gains strength from sight and delay, and falsehood from haste and uncertainty"; clearly he left a rumour behind him, or he got ahead of it. The Numidian king Jugurtha had another reason for fear and for wandering from place to place: naturally, fear and distrust of his friends. Of him the historian says thus: "Nor did he afterwards stay in any one place for more than a day or a night; he pretended he was hurrying on business; but he feared betrayal, which he thought he could avoid by speed, since such plans are made at leisure and as opportunity offers." Sallust says this of Jugurtha. But let us return to Clemens and the rumour about Agrippa that was growing. Meanwhile it was spread throughout Italy that Agrippa had been saved by the gods' favour, and it was believed at Rome. Already a great crowd had been brought in from Ostia, and already secret gatherings were being held in the city. How far, then, was Italy from being taken over by the aim of seizing the throne, or thrown into confusion by civil war? Examples of similar audacity, which sometimes rose to the summit of kingship, though difficult to find in abundance, are supplied by the history of every age. Known are Andriscus, who called himself Pseudo-Philip, and who advanced against the Romans in Macedonia; known is Alexander, the son of a tanner, in Syria against Demetrius. Known in Germany is Frederick, and in Flanders Baldwin, names assumed for the sake of reigning. But the annals of the barbarian nations tell what disturbances the Pseudo-Demetrius stirred up at the beginning of this century in the vast region of the Muscovites, by Polish craft. That slaves, after their masters were killed at Tyre, seized the most splendid empire, is told even to beginners in history from Justin. Thus fraud and audacity, whether deserved or not, often open the way to the throne, provided fortune has not refused them her company.

units.la: LXXXVIII.
units.tr: LXXXVIII.

units.la: Solertis principis est, exorientem
units.tr: It is the mark of a skilful prince to suppress a rising

units.la: tumultum sine tumultu compescere.
units.tr: tumult without tumult.

units.la: Serpentem de Agrippa vivo famam, famae auto- rem Clementem & ejus assleclas, vine armorum coer- ceret, an contemptu languescere cum vano rumore vanum tumultum sineret, ambiguus animi Tiberius distrahebatur. Si arma objiceret: parem se pari face- ret, & metu suo dignum declararet. tum quasi bello indicto, vires adversariorum ad audendum, & ad sui defensionem cogeret. Si connivendo conquiesceret; verendum erat, ne modestia in conscientiam & metus confessionem duceretur; & ne serpendo, nullo impe- dimento objecto, pabulum seditio inveniret. cum Ti-berium anceps cura distrahere, vine militum servum suum coerceret, an inanem credulitatem tempore ipso evanescere sineret. modo nihil spernendum, modo non omnia metuenda, ambiguum pudoris ac metus reputa- bat. Inventa est media via, in talibus tutissima, ut nec metum armis coactis fateretur, nec, dum pudori con- sulitur, salutem posthaberet. dileċti[?] sunt, qui simulata conscientia adeant, offerant pecuniam, sidem atque pericula polliceantur. En stratagema rebus commotis ποικιλωτάτων[?]! quo & arcana adversariorum indagan- tur, & omnes illorum aditus ac tempora patescunt. ita per fidem, cujus pignus pecunia communicata, fide labefactanda everruntur. Ulsus fuerat hoc astu antea, in conjuratione Catilinaria detegenda, Cicero. Lega- tis Allobrogum praecepit, uti studium conjurationis vehementer simulent, caeteros adeant, bene pollicean- tur, dentque operam, ut eos quam maxime manife- stos habeant. Ulsi fuerunt & alii, magno suo & reip. commodo, sine strepitu a conversione confervandae. Sed caetera Tiberiani astus, contra dolum novi Agrip- pae, persequamur, qui conjurationem & partium stu- dium pecunia oblata, & fide interposita, simulaverant, speculati nocte in custoditam, accepta idonea manu, vinctum claso ore in palatium traxere. Agendi mo- dum, & fidem simulatam improbaremus, nisi major sides, principi debita, & publicae tranquillitatis studium praeponderaret. nec vitio datur reip. custodibus, aliorum ficta opera, ad comprimendas in herba malorum publicorum segetes, abuti.
units.tr: Tiberius, uncertain of mind, was torn between two courses: whether to restrain by armed force the living rumour about Agrippa, its author Clemens and his followers, or to let the empty tumult die away through contempt, and so let the vain rumour fade. If he set arms against it, he would make himself equal to his enemy and show that he feared him; then, as if war had been declared, he would force his opponents to dare more and to defend themselves. If he quietly connived and kept still, there was reason to fear that his moderation would be taken as a consciousness of guilt and a confession of fear, and that the sedition, creeping on with no obstacle set in its way, would find fuel. Anxious care drew Tiberius in two directions: whether to restrain his slave by the force of the soldiers, or to let his empty credulity wither away in time. Now he thought nothing should be despised, now not everything should be feared; he weighed these doubts about his dignity and his fear. A middle way was found, the safest in such cases: he would confess neither fear by armed force nor, while looking to his dignity, neglect his safety. Men were chosen who would approach them under a pretended complicity, offer money, and promise faith and dangers. Here is a most cunning stratagem [ποικιλωτάτων] for stirring up affairs! By it the secrets of the enemies are searched out, and all their approaches and times are laid open. So, through a faith whose pledge is money shared, their trust is undermined and they are swept away. Cicero had used this trick earlier, in uncovering the Catilinarian conspiracy. He instructed the envoys of the Allobroges to pretend a keen interest in the conspiracy, to approach the others, to promise them much, and to take pains that they should have them as clearly as possible in their power. Others too have used it, to their great advantage and that of the state, to restrain a conversion without noise. But let us follow the rest of Tiberius's craft against the trick of the new Agrippa, who, having been offered money and having pledged their faith, pretended to share the conspiracy and the zeal of the faction; they watched by night, took a suitable band, and dragged him bound and gagged into the palace. We might disapprove of the manner of acting and of the feigned faith, were it not that the greater faith owed to the prince and the concern for public tranquillity outweigh it. Nor is it a fault that the guardians of the state should misuse the feigned work of others to crush the harvests of public evils in the blade.

units.la: LXXXIX.
units.tr: LXXXIX.

units.la: In manifesto crimine tempora Reip. non semper processum juris requirunt.
units.tr: In a manifest crime, the needs of the commonwealth do not always require the ordinary course of law.

units.la: Ut quis indicta publice causa jure puniatur, hæc tria postulamus. 1. ut de commisso aut cogitato facinore non ambigatur. 2. ut è mora periculum metuendum esse videatur. 3. ut fine distractione reip. ad causæ dictionem pervenire non queat. Quibus positis, si quis etiamnum ordinarios judices, actores, testes, juris habendi formulas exposcat: næ ille formulis & legum apicibus nimis quam pueriliter addictus est. Tiberius ut criminis, jam rumore vulgi exagitati, coram se rerum convinceret, percontabatur, Quomodo Agrippa factum esset? qui si modum confiteretur, rem ipsam non negaret. Ille ita susceptum facinus admisit, ut interrogantem criminis paritate involveret. Quomodo tu Cæsar. Ut tu senili adoptione & ambitu uxorio in familiam Cæsarum irrepsisti; ut tu occiso clam Agrippa, regnum alienum invasisti: ita ego irrependo in po-men[?] & familiam Agrippæ, regnum non jure mihi debitum invadere sum conatus. Ad quæstionem facti, & cognoscendæ causæ imaginem, ipsæ[?] etiam sociorum inquisitio. Sed ille, fidei in populares conjurationis pertinax, ut ederet socios, subigi non potuit. Causæ in foro aut curia dicendæ locum futurum non fuisse, clandestina supplicii exactio fatetur, nec Tiberium poenam ejus palam ausus, in secreta palatii parte interfici jussit, corpusque clam auferri. quæ eadem & moræ periculum, & factionis jam dilatatæ exstimatione, colligunt. Multa, similitudine detegendæ con-jurationis & puniendæ affinia, congeri huc poterant. Sed ne lectorem taedio obruam, unum, non omnibus forte vulgatum, duntaxat depromam. Spartanæ reip. Ephori indicio cognoverant, Cinadonem insidias vitæ ipsorum struere. corripere eum in urbe non ausi, equi-
units.tr: To have someone punished by law without a public hearing of the case, we require three things: (1) that there be no doubt about the crime committed or contemplated; (2) that delay appear to be dangerous; (3) that the matter cannot come to a hearing without the distraction of the commonwealth. Once these are granted, if anyone still demands ordinary judges, accusers, witnesses and the formalities of law, he is far too childishly bound to legal forms and the letter of the law. When Tiberius wished to convict Agrippa face to face of a crime already stirred up by public rumour, he asked him, "How was the deed done?" Agrippa, if he admitted the manner, would not deny the thing itself. He confessed the deed in such a way as to entangle his questioner in the same crime: "How did you, Caesar, creep into the family of the Caesars by a senile adoption and a marriage intrigue; how did you, having secretly killed Agrippa, seize another's kingdom? In the same way I, creeping into the power and household of Agrippa, have tried to seize a kingdom not rightly owed to me." For the examination of the fact, and as an image of inquiring into the cause, there was also the questioning of accomplices. But Agrippa, stubborn in his loyalty to the conspiracy of his fellow citizens, could not be compelled to name his accomplices. That there would be no place for a hearing in the forum or the senate-house, the secret execution itself confesses: Tiberius did not dare to punish him openly, but ordered him killed in a secret part of the palace and the body carried off in secret. These same facts together show both the danger of delay and the estimate of a faction already spread abroad. Many examples similar to uncovering and punishing a conspiracy could be heaped up here, but lest I overwhelm the reader with tedium, I will bring forward just one, perhaps not known to everyone. The Ephors of the Spartan commonwealth had learned from information that Cinadon was plotting against their lives. Not daring to seize him in the city, they

units.la: tibus quibusdam operam dant, in convalle Lacónicæ regionis clam delitescant. hanc ipsam in vallem Cina-donem cum gemino milite; quasi ad arcanum aliquod negotium, ablegant. quem comprehensum equites, cruciatu torquentes, socios conjurationis eliciunt: quos cum ephori litetarum indicio cognovissent, sub-lato jam Cinadone; nullo tumultus metu jugulave-runt. Autor post Xenophontem Polyænus libro 2, Stratagematum.
units.tr: assigned some horsemen the task of lying hidden in a valley of the Laconian region. They sent Cinadon, with two soldiers, into this very valley, as if on some secret errand. When he was seized by the horsemen and tortured, they drew out his fellow conspirators; and when the ephors had learned their names from written information, Cinadon having now been removed, they cut the men's throats without any fear of tumult. The author, after Xenophon, is Polyaenus, book 2 of the Stratagems.

units.la: XC.
units.tr: XC.

units.la: Non irritandi severitate inquisitio-nis crabrones.
units.tr: Not to stir up the hornets by the severity of an inquiry.

units.la: Quædam quæ sciveris, nescire; quam quæ nescie-ris, proruere; tum ad modestiæ laudem, tum ad fecu-ritatem tutius est. Multi enim dum fe latere putant, quiescunt; ad pœnam luendam protrahendi, audent & aut amoliri perniciem omnia turbando, aut non in-ulti perire satagunt. Sapienter Tiberio, quanquam multi è dómo principis, equitesque ac senatores, fuf-ten-taffe opibus, juvisse consilii diverentur, haud qua-situm; Quæ moderatio locum maximè invenit, autoribus tumultuum jam sublatis, nec caussam inquirendi ne-ceffitate suggerente. Supra modum placabilis Julius Cæsar, victoria potitus, omnes litteras in secretis Sci-pionis scriniis inventas; ne inspectas quidem, combuf-fit. Dio lib. 43. Quam benignitatem præcipuè Anto-nius exaggerans, invidiam apud populum interfecto-ribus ejus movit. lib. 44. Pari mansuetudine, & litera-rum Sertorii aut ad Sertorium abolitione; eodem Dione autore, usus antea fuerat Pompejus; multisque necessitatem belli Sertoriani reliquias renovandi adeò. Inerat. Quafe moderationis laude ineptè amicire vo-luit, qui libellos civium supplices aut æceufatorios, ut fe fastidio alios metu eximeret, omnes in subjectum amnem projecit. qua negligentiæ culpa iram & arma, subditorum in fe concitavit. Factum Constantini Ma-gni, querelas episcoporum ecclesiæ ad fe delatas abo-lentis, ut nec plenè absolverim, ita à culpa fecordiæ remoremoverim. Ecclesiastici enim ordinis veneratione, & pacis inter eos studio, sepelire eorum lites, quam judi-ciaria sententia decidere maluit.
units.tr: Some things you have known you should pretend not to know, and what you do not know it is safer not to press into; this is safer both for the praise of moderation and for security. For many, while they think they are hidden, keep quiet; but those who are dragged out to pay the penalty dare either to avert destruction by throwing everything into confusion, or strive not to perish unavenged. Wisely, with Tiberius, although many from the prince's household, knights and senators were said to have supported the tumults with resources and aided them with counsel, this was not investigated. This moderation found its place most of all when the instigators of the tumults had already been removed and necessity did not call for an inquiry into the cause. Julius Caesar, once he had gained the victory, was excessively merciful: he burned all the letters found in the secret chests of Scipio without even reading them. Dio, book 43. Antony, magnifying this kindness especially, stirred up hatred among the people against Caesar's murderers. Book 44. With the same mildness, and by the abolition of letters from or to Sertorius, Pompey had used earlier, by the same Dio's account; and many were so inclined that the need to renew the remnants of the Sertorian war was all the greater. He foolishly wished to clothe himself in the praise of moderation who, to free himself from anxiety by his own disgust, threw all the supplicating or accusing pamphlets of his citizens into the river below him. By this fault of negligence he stirred up anger and arms against himself among his subjects. The deed of Constantine the Great, who abolished the complaints of the bishops brought before him against the Church, I can neither fully absolve nor so entirely free from the fault of folly. For out of reverence for the ecclesiastical order and a zeal for peace among them, he preferred to bury their lawsuits rather than settle them by a judicial sentence.

units.la: XCI.
units.tr: XCI.

units.la: Clarior à ferocioribus gentibus triumphus.
units.tr: A more illustrious triumph over fiercer nations.

units.la: Macedonia domita Paulus Æmylius, Asia subacta Scipio Asiaticus, plus in aerarium aeris intulerunt: Julius Cæsar à Gallis, Germanicus à Transrhenanis pacatis, plus gloriæ intulerunt. Quatuor totidem diebus triumphos, Gallicum, Ægyptiacum, Ponticum Pharnacis, Africum Jubæ victi, Cæsar triumphos egit. Cæteris vero conspectior Gallicanus, à gentis ferocia, non ab opulentia claritatem adeptus. Celebrior prope, etsi non magnificentior, Germanici de nationibus inter Albim & Rhenum triumphus. Vesta scholia, capti-vi, simulacra montium, fluminum, prœliorum. Major celebritatis tantæ gratia fuisset, si non triumphatæ prius, quam domitæ, hæ nationes fuissent. at nunc bellum quia conficere prohibitus erat, pro confecto accipiebatur. ut mollius in gratiam Germanici Tacitus interpretabatur. ut vero singulari De moribus Germanorum libro: non Samnis, non Poeni, non Hispania, Galliæ: ne Parthi quidem sapius admonuere: nimirum inconstantiæ & fragilitatis rerum humanarum.
units.tr: When Macedonia was subdued, Paulus Aemilius, and when Asia was conquered, Scipio Asiaticus, brought more money into the treasury; Julius Caesar, from the Gauls, and Germanicus, from the peoples beyond the Rhine once they were pacified, brought more glory. Caesar celebrated four triumphs in as many days: the Gallic, the Egyptian, the Pontic over Pharnaces, and the African over Juba defeated. But among them the Gallic triumph was the most conspicuous, gaining its distinction from the fierceness of the nation rather than from its wealth. Nearly as celebrated, though not as magnificent, was Germanicus's triumph over the nations between the Elbe and the Rhine: spoils, captives, and images of mountains, rivers and battles. The celebration would have had greater grace if these nations had been triumphed over only after they were subdued, not before. But now, because he was forbidden to finish the war, it was accepted as finished, as Tacitus interpreted it more gently in Germanicus's favour. Yet in his singular book On the Manners of the Germans he writes: "Neither the Samnites, nor the Carthaginians, nor Spain and Gaul, not even the Parthians, have warned us more often": no doubt of the inconstancy and fragility of human affairs.

units.la: Decretus tamen Germanico triumphus; & ante triumphum arcus ob recepta signa cum Varo amissa; nec non ædes Fortunæ, sacrarium genti Juliæ, effigies divo Augusto dicata. Nam quæ inanis pompæ aut jactantiæ fuere, sacrorum nomen & cultus deorum honestiori titulo induerunt.
units.tr: Still, a triumph was decreed to Germanicus; and before the triumph an arch for the standards recovered after the loss with Varus; likewise a temple of Fortune, a shrine to the Julian family, and an effigy dedicated to the deified Augustus. For what had been empty display or boasting took on the name of sacred rites and the worship of the gods under a more honourable title.

units.la: XCII.
units.tr: XCII.

units.la: Gaudium mœror, triumphum luctus excipit.
units.tr: Joy is followed by grief, triumph by mourning.

units.la: Furius Camillus curru quatuor albis equis in Ca-pitolium tractus, invidiam civium, & mox exilium meruit. Paulus Æmylius intra quos dies de Perseo triumphavit, domestica clade filiorum gaudium moe-rore interpunxit. quantò vix ullus anteà vulgo acce-ptus Germanicus,curru quinque liberis onusto trium-phavit. sed suberat occulta formido reputantibus, haud prosperum in Drufo patre ejus favorem vulgi: avunculum ejusdem Marcellum flagrantibus plebis studiis intra juventam ereptum. breves & infaufios populi Romani amores. nec fefellit ominatores augurium. Germanicus enim specie honoris in Orientem ablega-tus,miserum vitæ exitum brevi invenit. liberis ejus & uxori Tiberius per Sejanum calamitates varié moli-tus,crudeli tandem eos exitio absumpsit. praeter Ca-jum Caligulam, & Agrippinam Domitii Neronis ma-trem. quos ob detestationem infamis vitæ nunquam natos,aut ante rationis usum extinctos, melius fuisset. Sapienter prisci Romani instituerunt, ut triumphan-tem minister publicus, eodem curru vectus, admone-ret, respiceret, id est, reliquum vitæ cursum contem-plaretur. Eodem signo appensum currui tintinnabu-lum & flagellum : lacerandi flagris tergi & ultimi fup-plicii admonitoria signa. Ita effusa lætitia & ingrata auribus admonitio, supremus honor & ultima igno-minia eodem curru vehebantur.
units.tr: Furius Camillus, drawn up to the Capitol in a chariot with four white horses, earned the envy of his fellow citizens and soon after exile. Aemilius Paulus, within the very days in which he triumphed over Perseus, mixed his joy with grief through the domestic disaster of his sons. How much more so Germanicus, who was hardly welcomed by the common people, triumphed in a chariot laden with five children. But a hidden dread lay beneath, for those who considered that the people's favour had not been fortunate for his father Drusus, nor for his uncle Marcellus, snatched away in youth while the people's affections were blazing. Brief and unlucky were the loves of the Roman people. Nor did the omen fail those who foretold it. For Germanicus, sent away to the East under the appearance of honour, quickly found a wretched end to his life. Tiberius, through Sejanus, variously plotted calamities against his wife and children, and at last destroyed them by a cruel death, except Gaius Caligula and Agrippina, the mother of Domitius Nero; it would have been better had these, on account of the detestable infamy of their lives, never been born, or had died before they reached the use of reason. The ancient Romans wisely instituted that a public servant riding in the same chariot as the triumphant man should admonish him and bid him look back, that is, consider the remaining course of his life. With the same design a little bell and a whip were hung from the chariot: signs warning of the lashing of the back and of the final punishment. Thus unrestrained joy and admonition unwelcome to the ears, the highest honour and the ultimate disgrace, rode in the same chariot.

units.la: XCIII.
units.tr: XCIII.

units.la: Occultos fallacis aulæ scopulos, amicitiæ simulacra & honorum imitamenta, vir magnus vix effugiet.
units.tr: A great man will hardly escape the hidden reefs of a deceitful court, the counterfeits of friendship and the imitations of honours.

units.la: Nimiæ potentiæ suspicaci principi fufpe&us, nuf-quam terrarum fatis tuto latebit. Domus ei procar-cere, peregrinatio exilium, omnis locus pro laqueo. Retracto in urbem à copiis Germanico, quasi deside-rium absentis ferre Tiberius non potuisset, testandæ amicitiæ trecenos plebi sestertios viritim dedit, feque-collegam consulatui ejus destinavit. sestertios eos fi-ftulam aucupariam, consulatum viscum Germanicus judicavit, & ipse Tiberius præfentem Germanici ho-norem, in urbe ad omnia mobili, & inclinatione non dubia, ut leonem ovili inclusum, suspectum habebat. nec idèo sincerâ caritatis fidem adsecutus, amoliri ju-venem specie honoris statuit. Hæc sunt quæ aphorismo expressi honorum imitamina, quibus ut infulis redimitus quis ad aram statuitur. hic est scopulorum alter, generoso viro vix enavigabilis. Est aliqua quæ Tiberium & simulationes edoctam aulam, ratio in able-gando Germanico moverit. Aut enim non est alendus in civitate converso facili vir magnæ fiduciæ, aut interiorem potentiam admissi moribus obsecundandum.
units.tr: Suspected by a prince wary of excessive power, he will hide nowhere on earth that is safe enough. His home is no protection to him, travel is exile, every place is a snare. When Germanicus was recalled to the city from his armies, Tiberius, as if he could not bear to feel the longing for one who was absent, gave three hundred sesterces apiece to the common people as a pledge of friendship, and designated him as his colleague in the consulship. Germanicus judged those sesterces to be a bird-catcher's pipe and the consulship a birdlime. Tiberius himself, too, regarded Germanicus's present honour with suspicion, since in the city he was ready for everything and his inclination was beyond doubt, like a lion shut up in a sheepfold. Yet, not having won the trust of sincere affection on that account, he resolved to remove the young man under the appearance of honour. These are the imitations of honours which I have expressed in this aphorism, by which a man is set up at the altar garlanded with fillets as a victim. This is the second reef, scarcely navigable for a noble man. There is some reason which may have moved Tiberius, a court taught in pretences, to send Germanicus away. For either a man of great trust is not to be kept in a state that has been turned to easy ways, or his greater power, once admitted, must be yielded to in accordance with the court's habits.

units.la: quod Æschyli persona Ariftophanes in Ranis graviter hisce versiculis expressit:
units.tr: This is what Aristophanes expressed with grave little verses in the Frogs, in the character of Aeschylus:

units.la: Οὐ χρὴ λέοντος σκύμνον ἐν πόλει τρέφειν, [?]
units.tr: Οὐ χρὴ λέοντος σκύμνον ἐν πόλει τρέφειν, [one must not rear a lion's whelp in the city]

units.la: Μάλιστα μὲν λέοντος μὲν ἐν πόλει τρέφειν. [?]
units.tr: Μάλιστα μὲν λέοντος μὲν ἐν πόλει τρέφειν, [best of all, not to rear a lion in the city]

units.la: Ἢ δ' ἐκτρεφῆ τὰς τοῖς τροφοῖς ὑπηρέτην. [?]
units.tr: Ἢ δ' ἐκτρεφῆ τὰς τοῖς τροφοῖς ὑπηρέτην. [but if one has reared it, one must serve its ways]

units.la: i. e.
units.tr: That is:

units.la: Non est alendus in foro leunculus;
units.tr: A little lion must not be reared in the forum;

units.la: Non educandus est in oppido leo:
units.tr: A lion must not be brought up in a town:

units.la: Sed educatæ mos gerendus est feræ.
units.tr: But once it is reared, its nature must be humoured.

units.la: Tyrannum Sparta profugum Alexandréa, juvene Pto-lomæo & animis juvenili, receperat. Brevi factionem & opes in aula assecutus, vires ad recuperandum Spartæ regnum, pecuniam, naves, viros petiit. Ptolomæus qui se rebus Græciæ immiscere nollet, tergiversari primum, deinde ex aulicorum suggestione abnuere. Inanem opum missionem Lacon, tanquam per se Spartam receptturus, petebat. Aula Ægyptiaca, nec fraudis nec consilii egens, non aspernanda regi monita suggerebat. Spartanum [illegible, ~8 letters] & cætera belli-cosum, ex rerum successu negotium Ptolomæo, si emittatur, moturum. Rursus Alexandreæ si liber vagetur, urbe Græcis hominibus repleta, & rerum fem-pernovarum studiosa, præsentius Ptolomæo periculum. Placuit libera eum custodia, deinde turri inclusum, nec sine cædis cogitatione, cohibere. Cætera Polybius in Historia Romana. Poterat de Germanico Tiberius proloqui, quod de Sulla Æmilius: eò processit, uti nihil gloriosum, nisi tutum, & omnia retinenda dominationi honesta existumet. Sall. lib. 1. Histor. Poterat,inquam,si quam suspectus Tiberio Germanicus fuit,tam avidus potentiæ fuisset. Sæpè enim fulmen illud invidiæ,& Capitolini Jovis vibratio, nihil merentes percellit. Urficinus magister equitum,factis & fama sub imperatore Byzantino clarus, fraudes Eusebio struente,ab aula in confinia Persiæ,tanquam regni custodiæ, ablegabatur. Quem cum absentem aula, ad nutrum[?] Eusebii eunuchi conversa, timeret, aut per opportunitatem extinctum cuperet: successorem illi Sabinianum, alia omnia quam belli negotia edoctum, dedit. Occasione arrepta Persiæ Romano imperio, tanquam armis & eorum peritia vacuo futuro, immi-nebant. Veritus ex commutatione rerum invidiam Eusebius, dedit operam, ut fine imperio Urficinus ibidem subsistere juberetur. Ita cladis fortean à Persis acceptæ,per ignaviam aut occultam proditionem,autor habendus erat Urficinus, & proditæ Reip. causam dicturus. Profligatorum barbarorum,aut ejus metu digressorum, nulla ad eum confecti belli gloria reditura erat. Ita pilæ percussæ & datatim acceptæ ritu, quod hic Germanico acciderat, modò remissus in aulam, modò ab aula ablegatus. Nec impossuit Nemesi æquè ac imperatori Eusebius,in Cyprum postmodum, non occultato exilii nomine, rejectus. Non omni prorsus culpa liber Histiæus, opum apud Jonas fundamento nimius, à Satrapia in aulam Darii, tanquam consilio ejus indigentis, avocabatur. Quæ olim apud Medos, Romanos,Thracas; eadem nostris moribus apud Europæos interiores, mutatis Theatri personis, fabula agitur.
units.tr: Sparta, a tyrant in exile, had received him at Alexandria, where young Ptolemy and his youthful spirit were. Having soon gained a faction and resources at court, he sought forces to recover the kingdom of Sparta, money, ships and men. Ptolemy, who did not wish to meddle in the affairs of Greece, first evaded him and then, at the suggestion of his courtiers, refused. The Laconian kept asking for the empty sending of money, as though he would recover Sparta by his own power. The Egyptian court, lacking neither cunning nor counsel, offered the king advice that should not be scorned: that the Spartan, and the rest of his warlike people, if let go, would by the success of events set the business in motion against Ptolemy. Again, if he wandered free at Alexandria, a city full of Greeks and eager for ever new things, the danger to Ptolemy would be more immediate. It was resolved to restrain him under free custody, then shut up in a tower, and not without a thought of murder. The rest is in Polybius's Roman History. Tiberius could have said of Germanicus what Aemilius said of Sulla: he went so far that he thought nothing glorious unless it was safe, and that all things were honourable to keep for his dominion. Sallust, Histories, book 1. He could have said this, I mean, if Germanicus had been as greedy for power as he was suspected by Tiberius. For that thunderbolt of envy, and the hurling of the Capitoline Jupiter, often strikes down those who deserve nothing. Urficinus, master of the horse, famous for his deeds and reputation under the Byzantine emperor, was sent away from the court to the frontiers of Persia, as a guardian of the kingdom, while Eusebius was contriving treachery. When the court, turned to the nod of the eunuch Eusebius, feared him while he was absent, or wished him dead at the first opportunity, it gave him a successor, Sabinianus, trained in everything except the business of war. Seizing the occasion, the Persians threatened the Roman empire as though it would be empty of arms and of men skilled in them. Eusebius, fearing envy from the change of affairs, took care that Urficinus should be ordered to remain there without command. Thus, if a defeat was suffered at the hands of the Persians through cowardice or secret treachery, Urficinus was to be held responsible and was to answer for the cause of the betrayed state. No glory from a war completed against routed barbarians, or against those who had withdrawn for fear of him, was going to come back to him. Thus, like a ball struck and caught in turn, what happened to Germanicus here happened to him: now recalled to the court, now sent away from it. Eusebius did not spare Nemesis any more than the emperor, and afterwards was thrown out to Cyprus, under the name of exile, not disguised. Histiaeus, not entirely free from blame, who had too much wealth as the foundation of his power among the Ionians, was called from his satrapy to the court of Darius, as though he were needy of Darius's counsel. What was once played among the Medes, the Romans and the Thracians is now performed, with the actors of the theatre changed, among the inner Europeans, in our own manners.

units.la: XCIV. Publica rerum convulsio domesticis cicatricibus obtentui.
units.tr: XCIV. A public upheaval in affairs as a screen for domestic wounds.

units.la: Tiberius ut invisum sibi Germanicum ab urbe, & à plaudentis populi occursu, amoliretur, aliquid ægri in imperio Romano esse voluit,struxitque causas, aut forte oblatas arripuit. Sunt qui bellum non necessa-rium moliuntur: ut tributorum à populo exigendotum honesta ratio occurrat, aut ut liberos in armis exercendi occasionem nancisceantur, aut ut famam sibi & ad posteros memoriam e clade populorum emendicent. Et quis omnia humani cerebri portenta, in fraudem generis humani nata, recenseat? In statu po-pulari opifices, & id genus hominum, pacem lucelli causa morantur. Quod magis detestabile: belli civilis incendio domesticam ruinam nonnulli abscondunt. flagrantes inopia & cupidinibus, scelerum conscientia exagitati: quibus quies in seditionibus, in pace turbæ sunt: hi tumultum ex tumultu, bellum ex bello ferunt. S.H. lib.1. Hoc genus hominum, publico exitio na-tum, in solas insulas deportari, aut in primo ortu ex-tingui, illorum & reip. interesset.
units.tr: Tiberius, wanting to remove Germanicus from the city and from the cheering crowds that met him, wished there to be some trouble in the Roman empire, and he devised causes or seized upon those that chance offered. There are those who stir up an unnecessary war: so that a respectable pretext for exacting tributes from the people presents itself, or so that they may find an opportunity to train their children in arms, or so that they may beg from the slaughter of peoples fame and remembrance for posterity. And who could enumerate all the monstrosities of the human brain, born for the defrauding of the human race? In a popular state, craftsmen and that sort of people delay peace for the sake of gain. More detestable still, some men conceal their domestic ruin under the fire of civil war. Burning with want and desire, tormented by the consciousness of their crimes, for whom rest lies in sedition and who are a disturbance in peace, these men bring tumult out of tumult and war out of war. S.H. book 1. It would be in the interest of these men and of the commonwealth that this kind of men, born for public destruction, be deported to islands alone, or be extinguished at their first birth.

units.la: XCV.
units.tr: XCV.

units.la: Levi fermento ira offensi principis turgescens, longo vix tempore defervescit.
units.tr: A slight anger of an offended prince, swelling from a small leaven, scarcely cools down over a long time.

units.la: Quare non modo regnantes, sed & regnaturos aut offensa prius cultu officii devinci, aut offensa irritatos ne provocacipium re-. Tiberius Augusto regnante privatus, secreto recessu Rhodum coluerat. Archelaus Cappadociæ rex amicorum Romani nominis non in postremis, officii ab eo necessitudines averterat. quodnec Romani fastigii contemptu, ac ne quidem ignorantia Romani moris ab eo factitatum, in detrimentum ipsi vertit. quod sagaci pro temporum ratione consilio commisit, id imprudenter factum eventus evicit. Colere Tiberium paene exulem neglexerat, ab intimis Augusti monitis, quia florente C. Caesare, missoque ad res Orientis, intuta Tiberii amicitia credebatur. Factionibus aula sæpè discinditur, aliis alium regni hæredem occulte aut palam destinantibus. nec ea semper ex affectu aut voto discessio: sed ut sibi quisque gratiam aut offensam fingit; imo ut fortuna velum, cum omni aura transfe-rendum, expandit. quæ res multos consilii prioris pœ-nitere, circumacta fortunæ aut favoris rota, cogiti quod tum Archelao, quinquagesimum jam annum Cappadocia potito, accidit. Tiberius enim otii Asiatici nimium memor, elicit Archelaum matris literis, qua non dissimulatis filii offensionibus clementiam afferebat, si ad precandum veniret. Sibene noverat Tiberium Archelaus, offensam ejus pro certissimo mortis indicio accipere poterat. Ille tamen, innocentia doli quam fiducia animi purgatior, ignarus doli, vel si in-telligere crederetur vim metuens, in urbem properat.
units.tr: Hence not only those who reign, but also those who are to reign, ought either to be bound by prior attentions of duty, or, once offended, be kept from provoking further. Tiberius, while still a private man under the reign of Augustus, had lived in a secluded retreat at Rhodes. Archelaus, king of Cappadocia, one of the not least friends of the Roman name, had turned away from the duties of respect owed to him. This did not turn to his detriment, nor even through contempt for Roman dignity or ignorance of Roman custom practised by him; what he had entrusted to a shrewd counsel suited to the circumstances, the outcome proved to have been done imprudently. He had neglected to cultivate Tiberius, who was almost an exile, since, following the closest warnings of Augustus, while Gaius Caesar was flourishing and had been sent to the affairs of the East, Tiberius's friendship was believed to be unsafe. Courts are often split by factions, some secretly or openly designating one man, another, as heir to the kingdom; nor is that division always from feeling or wish, but as each one feigns favour or offence for himself; indeed, as fortune spreads its sail to be carried with every breeze. This matter makes many regret an earlier counsel once the wheel of fortune or favour has turned, as then happened to Archelaus, who had held Cappadocia now for fifty years. For Tiberius, too mindful of his leisure in Asia, summons Archelaus by his mother's letters, which, without disguising the son's offences, offered clemency if he came to beg. Yet did Archelaus know Tiberius so well that he could take his offence as a most certain sign of death? He nonetheless, more cleansed by the innocence of his intent than by confidence of spirit, ignorant of the trickery, or fearing violence if he were thought to understand it, hastens to the city.

units.la: Non praestabat Livia, quam promiserat, clementiae fi-dem. quam palatio suo extrema in senecta debebat, Romae in adversatrice regibus urbe, & nunc accusa-tionibus infesta, animam efflat. vel angore victus & debilitate aetatis, vel ignominiam non ferens causae dicendae, qui dare jura assueverat: quia regibus aquae nedum infima insolita sunt. Discant, si quid ex incerti-tudine eventuum certi disci potest, qui circa potentio-rum aulas versantur, non ita fe uni addicere, ut non & apud alterum aliquid speis, si res in diversum nutet, re-linquant.
units.tr: Livia did not keep the faith of clemency she had promised. To her he owed his palace in extreme old age; at Rome, a city hostile to kings and now hostile with accusations, she breathes out her life, either overcome by anguish and the frailty of age, or not bearing the disgrace of having to plead a case, she who had been accustomed to give laws; for even the lowest waters are unusual to kings. Let those learn, if anything certain can be learnt from the uncertainty of events, who move about the courts of the powerful, not to commit themselves so entirely to one man that they leave no hope with another, should the affair tip in the opposite direction.

units.la: XCVI.
units.tr: XCVI.

units.la: Sanctum publici boni nomen mul-tis sceleribus obtenditur.
units.tr: The sacred name of the public good is held out to cover many crimes.

units.la: Sive offensionem Tiberius finxit, ut rege damna-to regnum publicare posset; five invidiam circum-venti regis hac offa populo objecta placare voluit: ultra honestum veterum mortalium morem hanc fraudem perpetravit. Regnum in provinciam redactum est, fraudibusque ejus levari posse centesima ve-tigal professus Caesar, ducentesimam in posterum flatuit. Cypri regnum Ptolomaeo regi, citra ullam culpam aut offensae suspicionem, cum facultatibus aulae, armorum vi ademptum, non referrem: nisi Catone sceleris nefarii ministro turpissimus hominum Clodi-us abusus fuisset. Atque illud quidem facinus Cato ille, sanctitate vitae pro numine, imo supra numen, Se-necae & Lucano habitus, contra Ciceronem defendit; feque in quadam causa factioni Clodianae contra eum adjunadjunxit. Tanta persuasio nominis Reipublicæ: quasi omnia pro eâ perpetrata, ex ipso incremento, aut voluntate civium remp. augere properantium, sacratissimi juris laudem accipiant. Societati ejusmodi homi-num non nimis confidant, qui ad vicinos opprimendos, aut civitatem suam[?] tutandam, fœdere cum iis coierunt. Remotis enim quos obstare progressibus opinabatur, & potentia flammæ in morem proserpente, si quid alicui fui[?] juris in aliquo prædiorum angulo restat; quo jure qua injuria domini rerum deglutient.
units.tr: Either Tiberius invented an offence so that he could confiscate the kingdom once the king was condemned, or, wishing to appease the hatred aimed at the circumvented king, he threw this morsel to the people. He committed this fraud beyond the honourable custom of the ancient mortals. The kingdom was reduced to a province, and Caesar, professing that the hundredth tax could be lightened by his frauds, set the two-hundredth for the future. The kingdom of Cyprus was taken from King Ptolemy, with the resources of his court, by force of arms, without any fault or suspicion of offence. I would not have mentioned it, had not the most disgraceful of men, Clodius, used Cato as the minister of an abominable crime.
