Cato himself, held in the place of a divinity, indeed above a divinity, by Seneca and Lucan on account of the holiness of his life, defended that deed against Cicero; and in a certain case he joined himself to the Clodian faction against him. Such is the power of the name of the Republic: as if all things done on its behalf receive the praise of the most sacred right, from the very growth of the state or the will of citizens hastening to enlarge the commonwealth. Those men should not place too much trust in an alliance of this kind who have joined with others by treaty to oppress their neighbours or to protect their own state. For, having removed those whom he thought stood in the way of his advances, and his power spreading like a flame, if anything of his own right remains in some corner of his estates, the masters of things will swallow it up, by whatever right or wrong.

units.la: XCVII.
units.tr: XCVII.

units.la: Imperii mutationem inexperti cupiunt, experti horrent.
units.tr: Those who have not experienced a change of empire desire it; those who have experienced it dread it.

units.la: Soli inter Gades & Euphratem Cilices, & Comagena Syrorum natio, regibus suis parebant: omnibus circumcircà Romani imperii incendio correptis. Fato functis Antiocho & Philopatore, hoc Cilicum, illo Comagenorum, regibus: multi seu novitatis cupidi-tate, seu potentiæ admiratione, rem ad Romanos trahebant: alii, quibus vetera satis placebant, nihil è patrio more immutatum volebant. quo ipso tempore provincia Syria atque Judæa, fessa oneribus, diminu-tionem tributi orabant. In tanta rerum circumfluen-tium abundantia, multi illustrium Romanorum rem familiarem luxu, alii & fidem consumpserant. alendæ erant, pacato etiam tempore, supra quadraginta legiones, imperii Romani custodiæ, gemina mari supero & infero custodiendæ Italiæ classis, prætoriæ in urbe cohortes. Exornanda erat Roma tectorum, præ sub-jectis nationibus, magnificentia. Ærarium in incerta casuum, & subitos rerum tumultus, præterea ad largitiones & necessitates, & expromendam in legatos gentium magnificentiam, replendum. Ista onera à civibus in provincias, & provincias maximè extremi loci, devolvebantur. Artis quidem Romanæ fuit, ut nationes rerum mutatione gauderent, levare tributum regibus pendi solitum. Sed nec diu illa subleva-tione gaudebant, & pecuniæ ad exteros delatæ damnum, ut fastum dominantium praeteream, defeti-scentes inopia fero lamentabantur.
units.tr: From Cadiz to the Euphrates the Cilicians and the Comagenian nation of the Syrians obeyed their own kings, while all around them the Roman empire was caught in fire. With Antiochus and Philopator dead, the Cilicians had this king and the Comagenians that one. Many, whether out of a desire for novelty or admiration of power, dragged the matter over to the Romans; others, for whom the old ways pleased well enough, wanted nothing changed from the ancestral custom. At this very time the province of Syria and Judaea, worn out by burdens, was begging for a reduction of tribute. Amid such an overflowing abundance of things, many illustrious Romans had consumed their private fortunes through luxury, and others even their credit. Even in peacetime more than forty legions had to be maintained to guard the Roman empire, a fleet to guard Italy in both the upper and the lower seas, and the praetorian cohorts in the city. Rome had to be adorned with buildings, in a magnificence surpassing the subject nations. The treasury had to be filled for uncertain chances and sudden upheavals of affairs, and besides for largesse and necessities, and for displaying magnificence before the envoys of the nations. These burdens were rolled down from the citizens onto the provinces, and most of all onto the provinces in the remotest places. It was indeed the art of Rome that the nations rejoiced in a change of rule, with the tax paid to their kings lifted. But they did not rejoice long in that relief, and, to say nothing of the arrogance of their masters, they groaned in their poverty and lamented, growing faint, the money carried off to foreigners.

units.la: XCVIII. Media hominis aetas rebus gerendis aptissima.
units.tr: XCVIII. The middle age of a man is most suited to affairs.

units.la: De Romani imperii post interfectum Julium statu Dio Cassius: τὰ τῆς ἐλευθερίας ἐργα ἰφωνῶ, καὶ τὰ τῆς δυναστείας ἔργα ἐπίγγελ. libertatem imagine quadam praeferebant, revera dominatio truebatur. lib. 4 §. De Tiberii in senatu actione nos: aliud specioso sermone proferebat, aliud animo volvebat. Animo agitabat, uti supra vidimus, Germanicum uti ante suetis legionibus abstraxerat, ita nunc oculis populi subdu-cere. oratione ferebat: nee posse motum Orientem nisi Germanici sapientia componi. Nam suam aetatem vergere, Drufi nondum satis adolevisse. Subjecerit quis, cur igitur publicum bonum morare? quid nos deludis inani aut mortis tuae, aut Drusi adultae aetatis, expe-ctatione? cur te imperante modo legiones Pannonicae & Germanicae seditione non ferenda turgescunt, modo Germaniae spreta Romani imperii majestate armis insurgunt, modo res Orientis turbato rerum fluctu moventur? Cur senex decrepita aetate non deponte ultro decedis, recepto ad gubernaculum vegetiori junio-ris vigore? Respon. Non eadem quae gerendis, & consultandis rebus aetas requiritur. De geredis bello inprimis rebus non insulse Sulmonensis poeta: Turpe senex miles. De consultandis vero vetus est Graecorum proverbium: hastas juvenibus, consilia senibus convenire. Sedeat Tiberius ad imperii gubernacula, clavum mo-derata sapientia torqueat, futuras coeli tempestates prospiciat: velorum expansionem aut contractionem, sententiae evacuationem, anchorae expeditionem, fca-phae attractionem ministris mandet. Tum quod Mu-cianus Domitiano fidta adulatione, id vere Tiberio suggeri poterat. Si statu imperii, aut falsus Galliarum in discrimine verteretur, debuisse Caesarem in acie sta-re. Caninefates Batavosque minoribus ducibus dele-gandos gandos[?]. lib.iv. Histor. Pro Galliis Orientem, pro Cani-nefatibus Batavisque Cilices & Comagenos ponamus: ratio utrobique eadem militabit. nisi quod minus etiam decore Tiberius, quam Domitianus nondum Augustus, rebus minoribus se immiscebit. Denique sibi Tiberius voce vergendi, filio particula Satis immi-sta cavit. Non enim quae ad praecipitium vergunt, jam sunt in praecipitio; & quae nondum satis adoleve-re, vicinum adultioris germinis fructum promittunt.
units.tr: On the state of the Roman empire after the death of Julius, Dio Cassius writes: "I name the works of liberty, and I conceal the works of dominion" [τὰ τῆς ἐλευθερίας ἔργα ἐπονομάζων, τὰ τῆς δυναστείας ἔργα ἐπικρύπτων]. They displayed liberty as a kind of image, while in truth domination was practised. Book 4, on Tiberius' conduct in the Senate, says: he said one thing in his fine speech and thought another in his mind. In his mind he was turning over, as we saw above, how to withdraw Germanicus from the legions he was used to, and now how to remove him from the eyes of the people. In his speech he claimed that the unrest in the East could be settled only by the wisdom of Germanicus, for his own age was declining and Drusus had not yet grown up sufficiently. Someone might reply: why then do you delay the public good? Why do you mock us with the empty expectation either of your death or of Drusus reaching adult age? Why, under your rule, do the Pannonian and German legions now swell with a mutiny that cannot be tolerated, now the Germans, scorning the majesty of the Roman empire, rise up in arms, and now the affairs of the East are stirred by a storm of troubles? Why, old man, do you not voluntarily step down from your decrepit age and hand the helm to the fresher vigour of a younger man? The answer is that affairs of war and affairs of counsel do not require the same age. As for conducting war, the poet of Sulmo rightly says: "An old soldier is a shameful thing." As for giving counsel, there is an old Greek proverb: spears suit the young, counsel suits the old. Let Tiberius sit at the helm of empire, let him steer the rudder with measured wisdom, let him foresee the coming storms of heaven; let him leave to his ministers the spreading or furling of the sails, the release of the sentence, the lowering of the anchor and the hauling in of the boat. Then what Mucianus, with feigned flattery, said to Domitian could truly be suggested to Tiberius: if the state of the empire, or the safety of Gaul, were at stake, Caesar ought to stand in the battle line; the Caninefates and the Batavians should be entrusted to lesser leaders. Book 4 of the Histories. Let us put the East in place of Gaul and the Cilicians and Commagenians in place of the Caninefates and Batavians: the reasoning will hold good in both cases, except that Tiberius would involve himself in lesser matters with less dignity than Domitian, who was not yet Augustus. Finally, Tiberius guarded himself against the word "decline" by inserting the particle "enough" for his son. For those things that are sliding toward a precipice are not yet in the precipice, and those that have not yet grown up sufficiently promise the near fruit of a riper sprout.

units.la: XCIX.
units.tr: XCIX.

units.la: Moderanda provinciarum & imperii in unum collatio.
units.tr: The gathering of provinces and of empire into one hand must be moderated.

units.la: De Cn. Pompejo M. Lepidus tr. pl. ad plebem: quem ipsum ubi pertimuere, sublatum in cervices suas, mox demto metu laceravant. Sall. lib. 3. Histor. Hujus postea in immensum potentiam auxerunt bello piratico, dato quocunque adisset in provincias imperio. quod primum libertatis naufragium. neque enim ab eo tempore Pompejus aut privatus esse, aut mediocri potentia contentus esse poterat. Qua re non anim- adversa, decreto patrum permissa Germanico provin-cia, quae mari dividuntur, majusque imperium quoque adisset, quam his qui forte aut missu principis obtinerent. Resp. 1. Parum de libertate soliciti patres hic erant, ut quae jam conclamata fuerit. 2. Manebat pene unum rerum gubernaculum, quem superiorem Germanicus agnosceret: cum supra se magistratum alium Pompejus non viderit. 3. Si quid Germanicus in Tiberium movisset, non invita Roma moturus videbatur. Attamen e re Tiberii non fuit ea imperii non circumscripta licentia: cur igitur, quia antea de matre Livia censuerat, moderandos esse foeminarum honores, nunc non sententiam profert, frenandas esse juvenum cupiditates? Non est quod cautionis admonea-tur Tiberius, in cavendo sibi & suis satis vigil. S E D Tiberius demoverat Syria Creticum Silanum per ad-finitatem connexum Germanico &c. praefeceratque Cn. Pisonem ingenio violentum, & obsequii ignarum.
units.tr: On Gnaeus Pompey, Marcus Lepidus, tribune of the plebs, said to the people: "When they had feared him, they lifted him onto their shoulders, but soon, once the fear was removed, they tore him apart." Sallust, Histories book 3. Afterwards they greatly increased his power by the piratical war, giving him whatever province he wished to enter, with unlimited command. This was the first shipwreck of liberty; for from that time Pompey could be neither a private citizen nor content with moderate power. For this reason, it is not an unfavourable thing that by the decree of the fathers the provinces divided by the sea were granted to Germanicus, and that he received a greater command than those who held them by chance or by the sending of the prince. Answer: (1) the fathers here were not very anxious about liberty, since it had already been given up for lost; (2) almost one single control of affairs remained, which Germanicus would acknowledge as superior, since Pompey had not seen any other magistrate above himself; (3) if Germanicus had moved against Tiberius, he would seem to be about to move with Rome not opposed. Nevertheless, it was not in Tiberius' interest that such unbounded licence of command should exist. Why then, when earlier he had given his opinion about his mother Livia that the honours of women ought to be restrained, does he now not put forward the view that the desires of young men should be curbed? There is no need for Tiberius to be warned to be cautious, since he was watchful enough in guarding himself and his own. BUT Tiberius had removed Creticus Silanus from Syria, bound to Germanicus by kinship, and had put in charge Gnaeus Piso, a man violent in temper and ignorant of obedience.

units.la: Vim tanti imperii Germanico infregit, amovendo qui ipsi usui futuri erant; præficiendo, qui magno impe- dimento. quæ omnia ante decretum patrum matura- ta; ne quid in fraudem ejus fieri oboleret. Sed unde Tiberio indomitum Pisonis ingenium innotuerat? insita ferocia à patre Pisone, qui civili bello refurgen- tes in Africa partes acerrimo ministério adversus Ca- farem juvit. Et alioqui Pisones etiam sub Tiberio & Nerone nimium libertatis memores fuere. Ita alieno odio in aliorum perniciem uti noverunt aulici, & ve- nenum serpentium pro jaculo arripere. sed prater pa- ternos spiritus, uxoris quoque Plancina nobilitate ope- ribus accendebatur, vix Tiberio concedere, liberos ejus ut multum infra despectare. Quod de Tullia, Tar- quinii ad scelus inftigatrice, Titus Livius; Sed initium turbandi omnia à fœmina ortum; id in pervertendo Germanico de Plancina non incommodé dixeris. Sic ingens ipse animi ac ferociæ, à spiritus elatioris fœmi- na accendebatur. maximé quia voluntatis Tiberii fe- sum aut conjectura persentisceret, aut occulto man- dato calleret. nec dubium habebat, fe dilectum, qui Sy- ria imponeretur, ad spes Germanici coercendas, credi- dere quidam data & à Tiberio occulta mandata. Un- de ea aut fufpicatio, aut studiorum in aula æmulatio? divisa namque & discors aula erat, tacitus in Drufum aut Germanicum studiis. de qua divisione suprà mo- nui. nec quo propenderet Tiberius, dubium cuiquam esse poterat. De Livia cur aut Germanicum odisset, aut Tiberii filium, nepotem æquè nepoti, præferret; obscura conjectandi ratio, nisi quod muliebri æmula- tione Agrippinam, ferocioris ingenii mulierem, & tum fœcunditate sua tum rebus gestis mariti tumentem, non ferret. Ita rerum humanarum suprema momen- ta, aut à frigida alicujus suspicione, aut à mulierçula- rum obscurâ altercatione, suspenduntur.
units.tr: He broke the force of so great a command for Germanicus, by removing those who would have been of use to him and by putting in charge those who would be a great hindrance to him. All these things were arranged before the decree of the fathers, so that nothing could be done to his injury without his noticing. But how had Tiberius come to know of Piso's unbroken temper? The fierceness was inborn from his father Piso, who, when the parties rose again in Africa, helped their side with the most zealous service against Caesar. Moreover, the Pisos, even under Tiberius and Nero, were too mindful of liberty. Thus courtiers know how to use another's hatred for the destruction of others, and to snatch up a serpent's poison in place of a javelin. But apart from his father's spirit, his wife Plancina also inflamed him by her nobility and resources, scarcely yielding to Tiberius and looking down on his children as much beneath her. Of Tullia, the instigator of Tarquinius' crime, Titus Livy says: "but the beginning of all the disturbance came from a woman"; this may fairly be said of Plancina in the ruin of Germanicus. So he himself, of great spirit and ferocity, was inflamed by the wife of a more haughty spirit, chiefly because she either perceived the will of Tiberius by a sign or guess, or knew it from a secret command. Nor did she doubt that she was chosen, when Syria was given to him, to check the hopes of Germanicus; some even believed that secret commands were given by Tiberius. Whence then came that suspicion, or that rivalry of parties in the court? For the court was divided and discordant, with quiet partisanship for Drusus or for Germanicus, a division of which I have already warned above. Nor could there be any doubt to anyone toward which side Tiberius leaned. As for why he should hate Germanicus, or prefer his own son Drusus, nephew equally to nephew, to Livia: the reason is obscure to guess, except that by a womanish rivalry Livia could not bear Agrippina, a woman of fiercer temper, swelling both with her fertility and with her husband's achievements. Thus the highest turning points of human affairs hang either on a cold suspicion of someone or on the obscure quarrel of little women.

units.la: C.
units.tr: C.

units.la: Iis qui ad imperium destinantur castra,non tabernæ lusoriæ,pro rudimen-to esse debent.
units.tr: Those destined for empire should regard the camp, not the gaming-house, as their training ground.

units.la: Quatuor de causis Tiberius filium ab aulæ deliciis in Illyricum, locum minus præ Italiæ blandimentis amœnum, ablegavit. 1. ut suesceret militiæ, ne penes cum aliquando adultum nomen imperatoris, penes alios res ipsa resideret. 2. studiaque exercitus para-ret. qui cum ut commilitonem, lætaque & adversa cum ipsis tolerantem, studio amplesterctur[?].quo pacto Germanicum,quo filium ejus in castris natum,parique cum militibus habitu caligatum , ferventi desiderio Germanicæ legiones fovebant. 3. simul juvenem urbane luxu lascivientem melius in castris haberi[?]. hic enim ignorantia urbanarum voluptatum, & laborum corporis ac animi tyrocinio,ad masculum virilis ætatis robur juventus exercetur. Hac eadem de causa imperator Antoninus filium disparem Commodum eandem in regionem in castra misit. quem tamen absentis Romæ memoria mox ab iis avellit. autor Herodia-nus. 4. Tiberium se tutiorem rebatur, utraque filio legiones obtinente. Ne aut à carie ignaviæ aula, aut ab externis insidiis imperium laboraret. quo consilio Augustus non uni omnes legiones mandaverit, in arcanis regnorum aperui. cur autem domesticis potiùs,quam alienis ea pars imperii credita fit,causæ non in occulto latent. Quod si Galliarum reges aut ipsi, aut ipsorum liberi, exercitus ductassent, quos Majoribus domus commiserant, non tam facili momento nomen simul regni cum re amissuri fuissent. Hæc quidem de causis Tiberium moventibus, cur adolescentem Drufum legionibus & bello gerendo præficeret. Sed nulla ne justitiæ in demandando bello mentio? Suevi prætendebantur, auxilium adversus Cheruscos orantes. Nunquam deest belligerendi cupidis causæ prætendendæ inventio. Sed,si vera Mithridates regno deje-ctus judicat, Romanis cum nationibus, populis, regi-bus cunctis, una & ea vetus causa bellandi est, cupido profunda imperii & divitiarum. idem Parthorum regi, quem ad belli communicationem impulit: An ignoras Romanos, postquam ad occidentem pergentibus fi-nem Oceanus fecit, arma huc convertisse ? neque quicquam a principio nisi raptum habere, domum, conjuges, agros, imperium? convenas, olim fine patria, fine parentibus, peste códitos orbis terrarum. &c. Romani in omnes arma habent, acerrima in eos, quibus victis spolia maxima sunt. audendo & fallendo, & bella ex bellis ferendo, magni facti. per hunc morem exstinguent omnia, aut occident. Haec de Romanis Mithridates apud Crispum Salluftium lib. IV. Hiftor. Utinam aut soli Romani, aut ultimi, hunc morem bella ex bellis ferendi invenissent!
units.tr: For four reasons Tiberius sent his son away from the pleasures of the court to Illyricum, a place less pleasant than the charms of Italy. (1) That he might become accustomed to military service, so that the name of commander should not one day rest with him while the reality of power rested with others. (2) That he might prepare the army's loyalty, since the soldiers would embrace him as a fellow soldier who shared their joys and hardships; in this way the legions of Germany cherished Germanicus, and his son born in the camp, clad in the same caligae and dress as the soldiers, with ardent longing. (3) That the young man, wantonly luxuriating in urban pleasures, might be kept better in the camp; for in ignorance of urban pleasures and in the apprenticeship of bodily and mental toil, youth is trained to the manly strength of mature age. For this same reason the emperor Antoninus sent his son Commodus, unlike himself, to the same region and the camp; yet soon the memory of Rome, from which he was absent, drew him away from them. The authority is Herodian. (4) Tiberius reckoned himself the safer, with both legions held by his son, so that the empire should not suffer either from the rot of courtly idleness or from foreign plots. By this plan Augustus did not entrust all the legions to one man; this I have explained in the secrets of kingdoms. But why that part of the empire was entrusted to domestic rather than foreign hands is not hidden. For if the kings of Gaul had themselves, or their own children, led the armies which they had entrusted to the Mayors of the palace, they would not so easily have lost the name of kingship together with its reality. These are the reasons that moved Tiberius to place the young Drusus over the legions and the conduct of war. But is there no mention of justice in entrusting the war? "The Suevi were put forward, asking for help against the Cherusci." There is never a lack of a pretext for those eager to make war. But if Mithridates, deposed from his kingdom, is right, the one and ancient cause of war for the Romans against all nations, peoples and kings is the deep desire for empire and riches. The same he said to the king of the Parthians, whom he urged to join the war: Do you not know that the Romans, after the Ocean put an end to those advancing toward the west, turned their arms here, and that from the beginning they have had nothing but plunder: homes, wives, fields, empire; they, once the strangers without country, without parents, founded by pestilence on the whole world, and so on? The Romans have arms against all; they are most fierce against those whose defeat brings the greatest spoils. By daring and deceit, and by carrying wars out of wars, they grew great. By this custom they will extinguish or destroy all things. These are Mithridates' words about the Romans, as reported by Sallust in the fourth book of the Histories. Would that either the Romans alone, or the last of mankind, had invented this custom of carrying wars out of wars!

units.la: CI.
units.tr: CI.

units.la: Barbaris bellandi consuetudo pro jure, armorum gloria pro lege est.
units.tr: Among barbarians, custom of making war serves as law, and the glory of arms as right.

units.la: Romani saltem causam aliquam belli movendi specioso titulo captabant, & orbis rapinae juris aliquod velamentum imponebant. Graeci etiam, quanquam mutuo fe latrocinio lacerantes, arma in quenquam injuria movisse videri nolebant. At Germani, barbarorum ferocia bellica nobilissimi, causa belli gerendi posthabita, fatis gloriae inipfa armorum expeditione ponebant. discessu Romanorum, &c vacui externo metu, gentis assuetudine, & tum aemulatione gloriae, arma in fe verterant. Quod ne Scythis quidem & Getis, raptu viventibus, nec Sarmatis, pacis & belli difcrimi-na ignorantibus, in more fuit, ut publicae cædis & prædandi licentiae, idque è populo cognato, gloriae vexillum praefigerent. Multum ex antiquo etiamnum Germani, quanquam post Caroli Magni tempora in mi-tiorem vivendi consuetudinem coacti, Martia saltem inter eos ingenia trahunt.
units.tr: The Romans at least sought some specious pretext for starting a war, and put a veil of justice over their plunder of the world. The Greeks too, although they tore one another apart in mutual brigandage, were unwilling to appear to have taken up arms unjustly against anyone. But the Germans, most noble in the warlike fierceness of the barbarians, set aside any cause for waging war and placed their destiny in the glory of an armed expedition itself. After the Romans withdrew, free from external fear, and by the custom of their people, and then from a rivalry for glory, they turned their arms against one another. This was not the practice even among the Scythians and Getae, who live by plunder, nor among the Sarmatians, who know nothing of the difference between peace and war, that they should set up the banner of glory in public slaughter and the licence to plunder, and that against a kindred people. Germans still keep much of the old character, although after the time of Charlemagne they were forced into a milder way of life; among them, at least, warlike dispositions remain.

units.la: CII.
units.tr: CII.

units.la: Aureum libertatis tuendae vexillum speciosissima belli gerendi materia.
units.tr: The golden banner of defending liberty is the most splendid subject for waging war.

units.la: Priscum id Graecis, nonignoratum Romanis, proceleufceleusima[?], etiam Arminio apud Germanos pro ansa arreptum est. vis nationum, virtus ducum in aquo: sed Maroboduum regis nomen invisum apud populares: Arminium pro libertate bellantem favor habebat. Qui ipse postea pulso Maraboduo, regnum affectans, libertatem popularium adversam habuit, uti de eo Cornelius ad calcem hujus libri. Adeo splendida libertatis praetentio illis ipsis, qui nihil minus quam populi libertatem quaerunt, pro pallio struendae sibi potentiae arripitur. Caesare adversus Pompejanas partes armis fulminante, uterque vindicationem reip. ab alterius dominatione passim crepabat. victoriae ratio victis non reddebatur.
units.tr: This practice was ancient among the Greeks and was not unknown to the Romans, and it was seized upon by Arminius among the Germans as a pretext. The strength of the nations and the valour of the leaders were equal; but the name of king was hated among the people; Arminius, fighting for liberty, had their favour. Later, after Maroboduus had been driven out, he himself aimed at kingship and came to have the liberty of his own people against him, as Cornelius says at the end of this book. So splendid is the pretence of liberty that it is seized, as a cloak for building up their own power, by those very men who seek nothing less than the liberty of the people. When Caesar thundered in arms against the Pompeian party, each side everywhere cried out that it was vindicating the commonwealth from the domination of the other. The reason for victory was not rendered to the vanquished.

units.la: CIII.
units.tr: CIII.

units.la: Gloriae aemulatio etiam necessitudine junctissimos disjungit.
units.tr: Rivalry for glory separates even those joined by the closest ties.

units.la: Maxime si nobilior natalibus obscuro, opulentior tenuiori, aetate major minori subesse debeat. Inguio-merus Arminio contra communes hostes, Romanos, aequato imperii jure, strenuam operam navaverat. At nunc summa rerum ad Arminium, ut belli peritio-rem, vergente; a patruele, & modo armorum socio, ad externum desciscit. non aliam ob causam, quam quia fratris filio juveni patruus senex patere dedignabatur.
units.tr: This is especially so when the nobler by birth should be subject to the lowlier, the richer to the poorer, the elder to the younger. Inguiomerus had served vigorously with Arminius against the common enemy, the Romans, with equal authority in command. But now, when supreme power was passing to Arminius as the more skilled in war, he deserted from his paternal cousin and recent comrade in arms to the foreigner. For no other reason than that the old uncle disdained to submit to the young son of his brother.

units.la: CIV.
units.tr: CIV.

units.la: Diuturna belli attritio militarem peritiam acuit.
units.tr: Long wearing war sharpens military skill.

units.la: Habet aliquid ex optato omnis belli calamitas, ut non modo fortiores indurando, sed & peritiores fa-ciat. Germani impetu magis, quam bellandi ratione, & vagis incursibus aut disjectas per catervas, quam ordinata acie, bellum inferre sueti; longa adversus Romanos militia insueverant sequi signa, subsidiis firmari, dictaque imperatorum accipere. Forte & Poloni his annis quam Suecis tyrocinii gratiam referant, habe-bunt. Inter caetera militiae arcana Spartanos Lycurgus monuit, ne adversus eosdem diuturna militiae exerci-tatione uterentur. Quod Meffeniaco bello negle-ctum, vires Laconicas multum attrivit: Thebano verò prorsus afflixit. Qua tempestate Turcarum, ferocia formidanda nationibus erat, idem Ottomannica consuetudine pro instituto observatum. Minerval magi-sterii non fatis placiturum rependunt, qui vel invicti militiam ordinatam sequi docentur.
units.tr: Every calamity of war has something of good in it, in that it not only hardens the stronger but also makes them more skilled. The Germans were accustomed to make war by assault rather than by method, and by roving raids or by scattered bands rather than in a drawn-up line of battle; but in their long campaign against the Romans they learned to follow the standards, to be strengthened by reserves, and to receive the orders of their commanders. Perhaps the Poles, in these years, will have the advantage of the training they have given the Swedes in return. Among the other secrets of military science, Lycurgus warned the Spartans not to wage war against the same enemies in a long-continued exercise of arms. This was neglected in the Messenian war and greatly wore down Laconian strength; in the Theban war it utterly broke it. At the time when the fierceness of the Turks was a thing to be feared by the nations, the same thing was observed by the Ottomans as a settled custom. Those who are taught to follow an ordered military life repay the teacher's fee in a way that will not please the one who gave it.

units.la: CV.
units.tr: CV.

units.la: Patriam prodit, qui felaboranti subducit.
units.tr: He betrays his country who withdraws from a struggling fellow citizen.

units.la: Multò etiam magis, qui seorfim fœdus & pacem cum hoste init. Maroboduum Arminius increpat, per dona & legationes petivisse fœdus, proditorem patriæ tria, satellitem Cæsaris. Ac de unius quidem reip. ci-vibus minus res habet dubii. de quibus apud Athe-nienses Lex extitit Solonis: Privatim nemo fœdus aut admicitiam, fine civitatis consensu ineat. quem morem fere in jus gentium transfiiffe observatum. Cæterùm qui inter Belgas fœdere conjunctos habitantes, pa-cem sibi seorsim ab Hispaniarum rege, propter agro-rum in Artesia aut Hannonia jacentium securos redi-tus, impetraverint, populo Belgarum non contradi-cente, ipsi novimus, quod vitam privatam agentibus facilius, quam se rei militaris aut publicæ immiscenti-bus, concesseris. Ab eodem etiam Hispaniarum rege, vel potius à provinciæ ejus præfectis, belli exemptio ad iter securè faciendum, aut à vastatione militari, tributi concessa exactione, emebatur. idem sibi juris Fœ-derati in regi subjectos Belgas sumebant. Prisco Græ-corum & Romanorum ævo, in proelii concursu ma-nus mutuò abstinebant, qui privato hospitii fœdere innectebantur[?]. Unde illa Diomedéa apud Homerum cum Glauco armorum permutatio:
units.tr: Much more so does he who makes a separate covenant and peace with the enemy. Arminius reproached Maroboduus for having sought a covenant through gifts and embassies, calling him a traitor to his country and a satellite of Caesar. Indeed, regarding the citizens of a single commonwealth, there is less room for doubt; among the Athenians there was a law of Solon: no one may enter into a covenant or friendship privately, without the consent of the state. This custom has been carried over almost into the law of nations. Moreover, that those living among the Belgians, who were joined by a covenant, secured a peace for themselves separately from the king of Spain, for the sake of safe returns from their fields lying in Artois or Hainault, while the Belgian people did not object—this we know, since you permitted it to those who lead a private life more easily than to those who mix themselves in military or public affairs. From the same king of Spain, or rather from the governors of his provinces, exemption from war was bought, in return for a tax paid, to travel safely or to be free from military devastation. The same covenant right, as federated people, they claimed for themselves over the Belgians subject to the king. In the early age of the Greeks and Romans, men who were bound together by a private covenant of hospitality refrained from touching one another's hands in the clash of battle. Hence that exchange of armour between Diomedes and Glaucus in Homer:

units.la: Χρύσεα χαλκέων[?], ἑκατόμβοι εἰκοσιβοίων[?]
units.tr: Χρύσεα χαλκέων, ἑκατόμβοι εἰκοσιβοίων [Golden for bronze, a hundred oxen's worth for twenty oxen's worth]

units.la: i. e.
units.tr: i.e.

units.la: Aurea mutantur cypriis, pretiosa[?] minutis.
units.tr: Golden armour is exchanged for bronze, costly things for trifles.

units.la: An vero jure Maroboduum proditionis Arminius, ob opem aduersus Romanos non latam, & fœdus cum Cæsare percussum, insimulet; sine inquisitione non dimittendum. Constat varias Germanici nominis fuisse gentes, linguæ quidem communione connexas, non uno tamen reip. complexu glutinatas. Communis quidem patriæ amor, & sanguinis cognatio postula-bat, ut, contra universi Germanorum nominis odium professos, arma communi nomine promerentur. Sed si quis suo nomine iram alienigenarum provocaverit; si ultrò potentem hostem lacessierit; si vindicta exte-rorum non sit ultra injuriæ cancellos proreptura: extra culpam belli positi, ut securi spectatores, extra periculum belli se continere queunt. Vejentes cum suo nomine Romanis bellum intulissent, ac præter eventus expectationem ab iis premerentur: auxilium a consanguineis Hetruriæ populis petebant. Responsum est, quod bellum sine communi gentis consilio movissent, sine communi gentis commotione exan-tlarent. Magistigi ur ad causam accommodatè, quam ad rei veritatem exacte, si de Romanorum moderatione constaret, Arminius Maroboduum traduxit.
units.tr: But whether Arminius rightly accuses Maroboduus of treason, for not bringing aid against the Romans and for striking a covenant with Caesar, must not be let pass without inquiry. It is agreed that the peoples bearing the German name were various, joined indeed by a common language, yet not bound together in one political union. Certainly love of the common fatherland and kinship of blood demanded that they should take up arms under the common name against all who professed hatred of the whole German name. But if anyone has provoked the anger of foreigners in his own name, if he has voluntarily attacked a powerful enemy, if the vengeance of outsiders is not going to go beyond the bounds of the injury, he stands outside the fault of the war and can keep himself, like safe spectators, outside the danger of war. The Veientes, when they had waged war on the Romans in their own name, and were hard pressed by them beyond what they expected, sought help from the kindred peoples of Etruria. The answer was that they had begun the war without the common counsel of the nation, and must endure it without the common stirring of the nation. Arminius, in making his case, was more fitting in his argument than exact about the truth of the matter, if the moderation of the Romans was established, when he betrayed Maroboduus.

units.la: CVI. Illibata potentiæ formidandæ gloria jactatâ belli aleâ & speratâ victoriâ potiot.
units.tr: CVI. The unimpaired glory of a power to be feared: the dice of war being cast and victory hoped for, he gains the upper hand.

units.la: Cujus de viribus & fortitudine animi non dubita-tur, si se intra modestiæ limites contineat; & viri magni nomen facile tuetur, & ab insultu hostili quieta cum moderatione tutus est. Non de nihilo Maroboduus hic gloriatur: se duodecim legionibus petitum duce Tiberio, illibatam Germanorum gloriam servavisse. nosque conditionibus æquis discessum. neque pœnitere, quod ipsorum in manu sit, integrum adversus Romanos bellum, an pacem incruentam malint. Similitudine quadam temporum horum, & moti magna cum virium fiducia belli, circumfundor. Sed dubio etiamnum jactæ aleæ eventu, judicium reprimo.
units.tr: Of his strength and courage of spirit there is no doubt, provided he keeps himself within the bounds of moderation; he easily maintains the name of a great man, and with calm moderation he is safe from hostile attack. Maroboduus does not boast without reason here: that, though assailed by twelve legions under the leadership of Tiberius, he preserved the unimpaired glory of the Germans, and that we parted on fair terms. Nor should they regret that it lies in their own hands whether they prefer to keep war against the Romans open and whole, or a bloodless peace. Struck by a certain resemblance to these times, and moved by great confidence in my strength, I am swept up in thoughts of war. But since the outcome of the dice that have been cast is still uncertain, I hold back my judgement.

units.la: CVII. Reducta ab aliorum negotiis vitā jū-cundior quam fecurior.
units.tr: CVII. Life withdrawn from the affairs of others is more pleasant than it is safer.

units.la: Si quid enim in eos bellici nimbi ingruat; si quā praeter spem fors exierit: quos adversarum socios aut invocent aut sperent, non temere invenient. Maro-boduus ab Arminio pulsus, rogatum auxilia legatos ad Tiberium misit. Responsum est, non jure eum adversus Cheruscos arma Romana invocare, qui pu-gnantes in eundem hostem Romanos nulla ope juviﬀet. Quanquam Tiberius veteratorie hic egit, qui fractus Marobodui opes, regnumque ejus extinctum voluerit. Plus enim Romano fastigio a junctu unius viri poten-tia, quam a disjuncta Cheruscorum libertate, metue-bat. Quod autem Drufus missus pacis firmator, non voluntatem Tiberii erga Maroboduum arguit, sed versutiarum Romanae aulae suspectas artes reddit. Tantum enim Drufus a concilianda pace absuit, ut contra hostes illiceret, ut Maroboduo usque in exi-tium insisteretur. quod Romae ut praeclarum Drufi facinus acceptum. Pulso quidem Germania Marobo-duo tutam in Italia sedem concessit: caterum apud senatum disseruit, non Philippum Atheniensibus, nec Pyrrhum, aut Antiochum, populo Romano perinde metuendos fuisse. Extat oratio, quā magnitudinem viri, violentiam subjectarum et gentium, & quam propinquus Italiae hostis, suaque in destruendo eo consilia extulit, ut noster infra disserit.
units.tr: If a storm of war should break upon them, or if fortune should turn out beyond expectation, they will not easily find allies whom they can call on or hope for in their adversity. Marobodus, driven out by Arminius, sent envoys to Tiberius to ask for help. The reply was that he had no right to invoke Roman arms against the Cherusci, since he had given no aid to the Romans when they were fighting against that same enemy. Yet Tiberius was acting craftily here, because he wanted Marobodus's power broken and his kingdom destroyed. For he feared the power of one man, if joined together and raised to Roman heights, more than the divided liberty of the Cherusci. That Drusus was sent as a guarantor of peace does not show Tiberius's goodwill toward Marobodus; rather, it makes the arts of the Roman court's cunning appear suspect. For Drusus was so far from securing peace that he enticed the enemies to press on against Marobodus, even to his destruction, which at Rome was received as a splendid exploit of Drusus. Driven from Germany, Marobodus did indeed settle in a secure seat in Italy; but he argued before the senate that Philip was not to be feared by the Athenians, nor Pyrrhus or Antiochus by the Roman people, to the same degree that he himself was. A speech survives in which he set forth the greatness of the man, the violence of the peoples subject to him, how near an enemy he was to Italy, and his own plans for destroying him, as our author discusses below.

units.la: CVIII. Publica gentium calamitas in laudis occasionem vertatur.
units.tr: CVIII. A public calamity of the nations should be turned into an occasion for praise.

units.la: Non quidem exoptanda sunt bella, incendia, ruinae, inundationes, terrae commotiones: sed ingruentia in laudem & virtutem torquenda. Duodecim Asiae urbes noctūrno motu terrae collapsae, occasionem Tibe-rio exerendae cum applausu gentium munificentiae de-derunt. Asperrima in Sardianos luses, plurimum in eosdem misericordia traxit. nam centies sestertium policitus Cæsar: & quantum ærario aut fisco pendebant, in quinquennium remisit. Plus masculi fulgoris virtus habet, ubi ipsi qui pernicie æternuntur, ex ipsis mi- seriæ ruderibus in æternitatem famæ exurgunt. Cujus illustriæ præ cæteris exemplum in Sagunthinorum fide, & fidem secuto excidio Historici, poëtæ, oratores celebrant. Sallustius de iis, laudante eum Hieronymo: Saguntini fide atque armis incliti, per mortalium studium majores quam opibus: quippe quis etiam tum seminruta mœnia, domus intectæ, parietesque templorum ambusti manus Punicas ostentabant. Historiam petite e Livio, lib. xxi. & Silio Italico lib. 2. ubi versu 656 in hoc Epiphonema exurgit:
units.tr: Wars, fires, collapses, floods and earthquakes are not, to be sure, to be wished for; but when they befall us, they should be turned to praise and virtue. When twelve cities of Asia collapsed in a nocturnal earthquake, they gave Tiberius an occasion to display his generosity, to the applause of the nations. Caesar, who had been very harsh towards the Sardians in the matter of their debts, was moved above all by pity for the same people: he promised a hundred million sesterces, and remitted for five years whatever they had been paying into the treasury or the privy purse. The courage of misery has a more manly splendour when those who are destroyed by ruin rise, from the very rubble of their misfortune, into an immortal fame. The most famous example of this is the loyalty of the Saguntines, which historians, poets and orators celebrate, and the destruction that followed their fidelity. Sallust speaks of them, as Jerome praises him: the Saguntines, renowned for their loyalty and arms, were greater through the zeal of mortals than through their wealth; for even then, their half-ruined walls, their roofless houses and the burnt walls of their temples showed the hands of the Carthaginians. Look up the history in Livy, book 21, and in Silius Italicus, book 2, where at verse 656 the following exclamation rises up:

units.la: Quis diros urbis casus, laudandaque monstra, Et fidei poenas, & tristia facta piorum, Temperet evolvens lacrymis? &c.
units.tr: Who could restrain his tears as he unrolls the dreadful fall of the city, the monstrous deeds worthy of praise, the punishments of loyalty, and the sad deeds of the pious? etc.

units.la: Ite decus terrarum animæ, venerabile vulgus, Elysium, & castas sedes decorate piorum.
units.tr: Go, glory of the lands, souls, venerable crowd; adorn the Elysian and chaste abodes of the pious.

units.la: Queis vero non æqua dedit victoria nomen, Audite o gentes, neu rumpite fœdera pacis, Neu regnis postferte fidem.
units.tr: But you, nations, to whom victory has not given an equal name, hear, and do not break the covenants of peace, nor set faith behind your kingdoms.

units.la: CIX.
units.tr: CIX.

units.la: Pares cum paribus non facile jun-guntur.
units.tr: Equals are not easily yoked with equals.

units.la: In eadem nimirum provincia, munere dispari. Ad inspectandam provinciæ cladem refovendamque dilectus est M. Aletus à prætorius, ne consulari obtinenti Asiam æmulatio inter pares, & ex eo impedimentum oriretur. Prætorius enim, gradu dignitatis minor, æquiori animo cessurus videbatur, quam consularis consulari. nec superiori cura æmulationis erga minorem eadem, quæ erga parem. Inter genere nobiles, maxime ubi gradus nobilitatis ignorantur, ut in Polonia & Dania, illud ex æqualitate malum, quod nec in militia ordo ac imperium facile observatur, nec in regem ex indigenis legendum fine tumultu consentitur. Ideo Dani ad Holsatos & Oldenburgios; Poloni ad Lituanos, Gallos, Auftriacos, Tranfylvanos, postremò Suecos confugerunt. Curlandiæ Ducis Ketleri, è nos bilitate Veftphalica oriundi, pares nobilitate, Noldii inprimis, imperium detre&averunt. quæ listamen fi- ne tumultu, necfine damno Noldiorum, composita est. Sæpius eximparitate, figenere & opibus minori contra decus parendum est, dissensio oritur. Non enim aut novæ virtuti fortunâ tempore radicata facilè con- cedit, aut voluntati eligentium opinio & alti spiritus acquiescunt. Quæ disceptatio Hispaniam præ cæteris attingit: magnatibus regni ducem aliquem exercitus infra fastigium suum æstimantibus, inque eo autori- tatem regiam spernentibus. Quod & in Germania Fridlandio, nuper ad ducalem dignitatem evecto, & severo alias pœnarum exactori, necfui contemptori, contigerat.
units.tr: Certainly in the same province, but with unequal offices. Marcus Aletus, a praetorian, was chosen to survey the province's disaster and to restore it, so that rivalry between equals, and the hindrance that would arise from it, might not occur with the consular who held Asia. For a praetorian, lower in rank of dignity, seemed likely to yield with a more even mind than a consular would to a consular; nor does a superior feel the same care about rivalry towards a lesser man as towards an equal. Among nobles of the same kind, especially where the degrees of nobility are unknown, as in Poland and Denmark, the evil arising from equality is this: neither is the order and command in the army easily observed, nor can a king be chosen from among the natives without tumult. Hence the Danes fled to the Holsteiners and Oldenburgers, and the Poles to the Lithuanians, the French, the Austrians, the Transylvanians and, finally, the Swedes. Among the nobles of Courland, Duke Ketler, who came from a Westphalian nobility, and his equals in nobility, above all the Noldes, refused to submit to his rule; yet this was settled without tumult and without loss to the Noldes. Quite often, when someone of lesser rank, birth and wealth must yield to what is held honourable, a dissension arises. For neither a new virtue, which has not yet taken root in fortune over time, readily yields, nor does the opinion of those who choose, nor a proud spirit, acquiesce. This dispute touches Spain above all others: the magnates of the kingdom judge some leader of the army to be beneath their own rank, and in doing so despise royal authority. This also happened in Germany to Friedland, recently raised to ducal dignity, a man otherwise a severe exactor of penalties, and no contemptor of fidelity.

units.la: CX. Hæreditates captare non est ex ma- gnitudine principis.
units.tr: CX. To seek inheritances is not in keeping with the greatness of a prince.

units.la: Obrepserat mos Augustorum ævo, partim adula- tione, partim metu, à paucis amicitia, principem hæ- redem scribendi. Cui spernendo fatis forti animo Ti. berius, bona Æmiliæ Musæ, & Patulci, divitum, justis hæredibus tradidit. Neque hæreditatem cujufquam aduit, nisi cum amicitia meruisset. Ignotes & aliis in- sensos, eoque principem nuncupantes, procul arcebat. Non pari continentia agebat Claudius, non Nero, non Domitianus. hic fe in partem hæreditatis testamento vocari, velut id honori ipsorum datum effet, lætabatur. tam caca & corrupta mens, assiduis adulationibus erat, ut nesciret à bono patre non scribi hæredem, nisi malum principem. ut noster in Vita Julii Agricolæ.
units.tr: In the age of the Augusti a custom had crept in, partly from flattery, partly from fear, by which a few friends wrote the prince as their heir. Tiberius, who with a brave spirit scorned this, handed over the goods of Aemilia Musa and of Patulcus, rich men, to their rightful heirs. Nor did he accept anyone's inheritance unless he had earned it through friendship. He kept away those who were strangers and hostile to others, and who named the prince for that reason. Claudius did not act with the same restraint, nor Nero, nor Domitian. The last rejoiced that he was called into a share of an inheritance by a will, as if this had been granted as an honour to them. So blind and corrupt was the mind, through constant flattery, that it did not know that a good father does not make a prince his heir, but only a bad one. So our author says in the Life of Julius Agricola.

units.la: CXI.
units.tr: CXI.

units.la: Non paupertas, sed ex flagitiis pau- pertas, virgulâ censori notatur.
units.tr: Not poverty, but poverty arising from disgraceful conduct, is marked with the censor's rod.

units.la: Bene hoc discriminis & accurato judicio observavit Tiberius, qui ut bonefam innocentium paupertatem levavit,
units.tr: Tiberius observed this distinction well and with a careful judgment: as he relieved the poverty of innocent men of good family,

units.la: Sine probro & cum pro- bro pauper- tas. levavit, ita prodigos & ob flagitia egentes movit senatu, aut sponte cedere passus est.
units.tr: poverty without disgrace and with disgrace. so he moved the prodigal and those who were needy through their crimes out of the senate, or allowed them to withdraw of their own accord.

units.la: Claudius media quadam via incedens, motos senatu & excusatos simul proposuit: ut judicium censorum ac pudor sponte cedentium permixti, ignominiam moliren-t. XI.Annal. quanquam postea fui dissimilis, ob solam paupertatem quoldam senatu movit. quae res aliquam probationem admitteret, si non nisi ex opum splendore senatoria dignitas arcessenda foret. Lace-daemonii pauperes, Atheniensibus divitiarum studium objectabant. quos argute apud Thucydidem Pericles defendit, ut quibus spontanea & ex ignavia paupertas probro sit, innoxia & ex fortunae injuria excusationi. Cui Periclis judicio Tiberius, nec sine nostro calculo, modo & in re & in studio moderamen accedat, sub-scribit.
units.tr: Claudius, walking a middle way, proposed that those who were moved from the senate and excused at the same time should be disgraced by a mingling of the censors' judgment and the shame of those who gave way of their own accord. Book 11 of the Annals. Yet afterwards he was unlike himself, and for poverty alone removed certain men from the senate. This act would admit some justification, if senatorial dignity were to be sought only from the splendour of wealth. The Lacedaemonians, who were poor, objected to the Athenians their zeal for riches; Pericles defends them shrewdly in Thucydides, since poverty that is voluntary and arises from idleness is a disgrace, while poverty that is harmless and arises from the injustice of fortune is an excuse. To Pericles' judgment Tiberius subscribes, and not without my own reckoning: moderation should be added both in the matter and in the zeal, that is, in measure.

units.la: CXII.
units.tr: CXII.

units.la: Magnifica templorum structura, aut collapsorum instauratio, auctoritate principem circumfundit.
units.tr: The magnificent construction of temples, or the restoration of ruined ones, wins the prince authority.

units.la: Ipsa per se tectorum magnificentia, non ex aerumnis civium quasita, magnos viros commendat. quae gratior, si sumptibus opulenta, publico usui sacretur. Hinc theatrum Pompeji, hinc Curia ejusdem, & vivo gratiam, & mortuo diuturnam memoriam paravit.
units.tr: The very splendour of buildings, when it is not gained at the expense of the citizens' hardships, commends great men. Such magnificence is more welcome if, rich in its expense, it is dedicated to public use. Hence Pompey's theatre and his Curia won him favour while he lived and a lasting memory when he was dead.

units.la: Quae vero in sacras aedes, quae in gymnasia & templa impenduntur, praeter magnificentiae amorem, ex opinione pietatis & erga coelestes numen curae, benevolentiam principi conciliant. Noverat id Tiberius, imperandi egregius artifex. Deum aedes vetustate aut igni abolitas, captasque ab Augusto, dedicavit. &c. No-verat idem temporibus Germanicus, imperandi proximus. Spei aedes a Germanico sacratur; hanc Ati-lium voverat eodem bello. bello nimirum Punico, quod Siciliae ademptione finitum. In more enim Romanis imperatoribus, prisca populi libertate, positum, ut bel-li prospere finiendi causa aedes numinibus suis, aut virtutibus, quas numinum loco colebant, aut fortunæ, aut etiam pallori & tremori voverent. Ita ut posteros opum luxuriosa ostentatio, ita priscos placandi deos opinio, ad fanorum dedicationem impulit. An verò & à populo sibi dicato Unus ille & æternus Deus, nul- lo temporum & locorum spatio definitus, istam tem- plorum opulentam structuram exigat, an eâ capiatur, cœlestem sapientiam professis expendendum relin-quo. Illud obfervatu forte non indignum ante Mo- fes faicorum temporum instituta nullam tabernaculi, ne- dum templi, Deo sacrati, fieri mentionem. Aras mo- dò, holocaustorum & oblationum gratia, viri pietate insignes erigebant. Tabernaculo duce Jofua in regio- nem Cananæam illato, & Silunti diu locato, supra qua- dringentos annos nullum struendi templi præceptum, nulla cujufquam religio. Primus David, & regia opum potentia, & prophetico sapientiæ inftin&tu excellens, in animum eam cogitationem, non fine repulía à Deo, admisit. Hunc regno Salomon excipiens, opulentia verò & varia rerum scientia excedens, templum stru- &ura superbum, cultu dicato religiosum, erexit. Sednec præter hoc vel Hierosolymis, vel tota in Hebræo- rum regione, aliud exactum; & piaculum fuisset, aliud præterea extruere. cum nunc una in urbe trecenta, etsi non pari omnia elegantia, conventicula & templa re- periantur. Quàm verò apud ipsos Judæos, carnali sacrorum cultui magis addictos, & in religionis cogni- tione ephebos, Deus templo fe alligaverit, ipse per Prophetarum principem admonuit. Cælum folium meum, & terra scabellum pedum meorum: ubinam ea domus, quam ædificaretis mihi? & ubinam locus quie- ti mea? Atqui omnia ista fecit manus mea, &c. sed in hunc intuor, in pauperem & contritum spiritu, ac trepidantem ad verbum meum. Sed ea, uti dixi, Theo- logis enucleanda transmitto. Illud ex hoc Taciti loco annotandum, sacrarum ædium dedicationem adim- perantium curam fpectaffe, qua de re pleniùs in Ar- canis regnorum egi.
units.tr: Whatever is spent on sacred buildings, on gymnasia and temples, wins the prince goodwill, apart from the love of splendour, through the reputation for piety and for concern for the heavenly power. Tiberius, an outstanding master of ruling, knew this: He dedicated the temples of the gods that had been destroyed by age or fire, and that Augustus had taken over, etc. Germanicus, who was next in line to rule in his time, knew the same: The temple of Hope was dedicated by Germanicus; Atilius had vowed it in the same war. Clearly this was the First Punic War, which ended with the loss of Sicily. For it was an old custom among the Roman generals, from the ancient liberty of the people, to vow temples, after a successful end to a war, to their own deities, or to virtues which they worshipped in place of deities, or to Fortune, or even to Pallor and Trembling. Just as the boastful display of wealth prompted the later dedications of shrines, so the older belief that the gods had to be appeased prompted the earlier ones. Whether the one eternal God, who is bound by no span of time or place, demands such rich construction of temples from the people dedicated to him, or is won over by it, I leave for those who profess heavenly wisdom to weigh. It is perhaps not unworthy of notice that before Moses, in the times of the patriarchs, no tabernacle, let alone a temple, consecrated to God, is mentioned. Men distinguished for piety only erected altars for burnt offerings and oblations. When Joshua, with the tabernacle as his guide, had brought it into the land of Canaan and it had long been placed at Shiloh, for more than four hundred years there was no command to build a temple, and no one felt such an obligation. David first, excelling both in the power of royal wealth and in a prophetic instinct for wisdom, admitted that thought into his mind, not without rebuke from God. Solomon, succeeding him in the kingdom and surpassing him in wealth and in varied knowledge of affairs, erected a proud temple, sumptuous in its ritual and dedicated to worship. Yet beyond this one, neither at Jerusalem nor in the whole region of the Hebrews was another required; indeed it would have been an offence to build another besides. Now, in a single city, three hundred meeting-houses and temples are found, though not all of equal elegance. How God bound himself to the temple among the Jews themselves, who were more attached to carnal worship and were novices in the knowledge of religion, he himself admonished through the chief of the prophets: Heaven is my throne, and earth is my footstool: where is the house that you would build for me? And where is the place of my rest? For all these things my hand has made, etc. But on this man will I look, on the poor and contrite in spirit, who trembles at my word. But these matters, as I have said, I leave to the theologians to work out. From this passage of Tacitus it is to be noted that the dedication of sacred buildings was a concern of rulers aiming at power; I have discussed this more fully in the Arcana of Kingdoms.

units.la: CXIII. Nihil in simulatæ pietatis principe sincerum.
units.tr: CXIII. Nothing sincere in a prince of feigned piety.

units.la: Tiberius censum quorundam senatorum juverat; terræmotu afflictorum opes recreaverat; hæreditates alienas à se removerat; ædes sacras vetustate collapsas restituerat, aut novas dedicaverat. Sed quid hæc ad sinceram civium sine metu quietem? Adolescebat interea lex majestatis. Significanter adolescendi voce usus, tacitum pestiferæ rei incrementum producit. Primo monstri ortu prætentata crimina in modicis æquitibus. Nunc in progressu adolescentiæ illustriores personæ, non sine aliqua principis moderatione, arreptæ. Jam corroborata statura, passim in omne genus hominum lues hæc sine miseratione proferpsit. Non est equidem sermonis lascivi in principes licentia laxanda. Sed nec à bono principio, compescendi proter-viæ petulantiam, sævitiæ & immodicæ dominationis claustra patefacienda. Omnia mala exempla ex bonis initiis orta sunt, inquit apud Sallustium Cæsar: sed ubi imperium adipiscares[?] aut minus bonos pervenit, novum illud exemplum ab dignis & idoneis, ad indignos & non idoneos transfertur. Addendum etiam, ubi se mores imperantium convertunt, aut simulatione exuta deteguntur, quod in Tiberio deprehensum.
units.tr: Tiberius had relieved the financial burdens of certain senators; he had restored the fortunes of those ruined by earthquake; he had kept other men's inheritances away from himself; he had restored sacred buildings collapsed with age, or dedicated new ones. But what do these things matter to the sincere quiet of citizens who live without fear? Meanwhile the law of majesty was growing. Using the word growing with purpose, he presents the silent increase of a pestilential thing. At its birth the monster first tested its charges against minor knights. Then, as it advanced in growth, persons of higher rank were seized, though not without some restraint on the prince's part. Now that its stature is strengthened, this plague creeps everywhere, among every kind of man, without pity. Certainly the license of wanton speech against princes should not be relaxed. But neither should the bars of cruelty and immoderate domination be thrown open, under the pretext of checking insolent wantonness, from a good beginning. All bad examples have arisen from good beginnings, says Caesar in Sallust: but when those who gain power are less good, that new example is transferred from the worthy and fit to the unworthy and unfit. It should also be added that this happens when the morals of rulers change, or when their pretence is stripped away and they are exposed, as was discovered in Tiberius.

units.la: CXIV. Leges corruptis moribus ludibrio sunt.
units.tr: CXIV. Laws are mocked when morals are corrupted.

units.la: Et gratia prævalente contemptui. De prætore in locum Vipsanii Galli, quem mors abstulerat, subro-gando, certamen patrum incessit. Liberi Tiberii, Drusus & Germanicus, propinquum aliquem fovebant; alii, ne leges hac de re latæ infringerentur, numerum liberorum in candidatis urgebant. Iætus[?] disce-ptationem inter leges & liberos, nec quorsum certa-men evaderet dubius, Tiberius audivit. Vitia est sin[?] dubio lex: sed neque statim, & paucis suffragiis: quo-modo, etiam cum valerent, leges vincebantur.
units.tr: Favour also prevails over respect. When a praetor was to be appointed in the place of Vipsanius Gallus, whom death had taken away, a contest arose among the senators. Tiberius's sons, Drusus and Germanicus, were supporting some kinsman, while others, lest the laws passed on this matter be broken, pressed the number of children among the candidates. Tiberius heard the dispute between the laws and the children, and it was uncertain where the contest would end. The law was undoubtedly corrupted, but not immediately, and by only a few votes. In this way laws were overcome even when they still held force.

units.la: CXV.
units.tr: CXV.

units.la: Principio exorientium tumultuum occurrendum.
units.tr: Uprisings must be confronted at their beginning.

units.la: Saepe in principio neglecta, progressu vires acce-pere, vix ullo robore compescendas. Tacfarinas na-tione Numida, Romanae militiae defertor, vagos pri-mum, & latrociniis suetos, ad praedam & raptus congregare, dein more militia per vexilla & turmas com-ponere. postremo non incondita turba, sed Mufulano-rum dux haberi valida ea gens, & solitudinibus Afri-ca propinqua, nullo etiam tum urbium cultu, cepit: arma, Mauroque accolas in bellum traxit. &c. Quem etsi Furius Camillus primo congressu fudit, longum tamen, & ob fugae similitudinem pene inexplicabile, bellum successo-ribus reliquit. Quod fi Romani di-fpofitos locis suspectis equites, more Turcarum im-perii,aluissent; minus facile turba pastorum & latro-num coalescere in tantum agmen potuisset. quae con-venarum turba, ducem ingenio violentum nacta, quam non fit contemnenda imperantibus, ut alios plures omittam, hi ipsi Turcae regni fui primordio commonefaciunt.
units.tr: Often neglected at the start, they gain strength as they progress, and can scarcely be checked by any force. Tacfarinas, a Numidian by birth and a deserter from Roman service, first gathered wandering men accustomed to brigandage for plunder and raids, and then arranged them in military fashion by companies and squadrons. At last he became leader, not of a disorderly mob, but of the Mufulani, a strong people close to the African wilderness and still without any settled towns. He took up arms and drew the neighbouring Moors into the war, etc. Although Furius Camillus routed him at the first encounter, he left a long war to his successors, one almost impossible to pin down because of his habit of fleeing. But if the Romans had stationed cavalry at suspicious places, in the manner of the Turkish empire, a crowd of shepherds and robbers would have found it less easy to coalesce into so large a host. This crowd of outsiders, finding a leader of violent temper, is not to be despised by rulers. To say nothing of many others, the Turks themselves remind us of this at the beginning of their own kingdom.

units.la: CXVI.
units.tr: CXVI.

units.la: Nulla victoriae civilis monumenta fine eriftitiae morsu laeta.
units.tr: No monuments of civil victory are joyful without the bite of sadness.

units.la: Germanicus lustrato Hadriatici maris recessu, & sinu Actiaca victoria inclyto, factas ab Augusto ma-nubias, castraque Antonii cum recordatione majorum suorum adiit. &c. magnaque illic imago tristium latorum-rumque. Imago laetorum, ex avunculi Augusti victo-riae monumentis; tristium, ex Antonii avi suprema clade. Et hoc quidem decimo poftillam pugnam lu-ftro. Recenti clade & victoria, quotus quisque à luctu propinquorum, in eo conflictu aut proimminenti do-mino caesorum, aut fugae ignominia & proscriptionis notanotatorum, immunis fuit? quotusquisque, non extre-mæ de patriæ cura negligentiæ, non libertatem ad exequias trahendum luxit?
units.tr: Germanicus, having surveyed the receding Adriatic and the gulf made famous by the victory at Actium, visited the works Augustus had built and the camp of Antony, with memories of his forebears. &c. There a great image of sorrows and joys met him. The joys came from the victory monuments of his uncle Augustus; the sorrows from the final disaster of his grandfather Antony. And this was fifty years after that battle. In the immediate aftermath of the victory and defeat, who was free from mourning for relatives killed in that conflict, either slain alongside their lord, or marked by the shame of flight and proscription? Who did not, out of no small neglect of the country's final fate, mourn and drag liberty into the funeral?

units.la: CXVII.
units.tr: CXVII.

units.la: Lictorum apparitio terroris & imperii, non libertatis, indicium.
units.tr: The lictors' attendance is a sign of terror and dominion, not of liberty.

units.la: Summovere itaque in sui juris populo, aut suis re-gibus parente, non est aut jura publica callentis, aut imperium moderatè ferentis. Quod cum observare Julius Cæsar neglexisset, Pompejo victo fascibus præ-latis Ægyptum ingressus, tumultu coorto, populum universum in se concivit. Moderatius Germanico, quanquam non pari tumultuandi periculo, sine strepitu Athenas invisit, fœderique socii & vetustæ urbis datum, ut uno libere uteretur. Erat enim urbs Athe-narum ut situ, ita & libertatis aut servitii jure, inter Achaiam & Macedoniam provincias media. Quamvis enim Romani non semper priscæ societatis meminis-sent, fuere tamen nonnulli duces æquitatis hactenus memores, ut inter socias urbes & belli jure subactas, aliqua suæ majestatis imminutione, distinguerent.
units.tr: Therefore to keep the lictors at a distance among a people under its own law, or a people ruled by its own kings, is the mark neither of one skilled in public law nor of one who bears rule with moderation. When Julius Caesar neglected to observe this, having entered Egypt after Pompey's defeat with the fasces carried before him, a tumult arose and he drew the whole people against himself. More moderately, Germanicus, though not at the same risk of tumult, visited Athens without fuss, as was granted to the ally of the treaty and the ancient city, that it might enjoy one thing freely. For the city of Athens was, both in its position and in its right of liberty or servitude, midway between the provinces of Achaia and Macedonia. Although the Romans did not always remember the old alliance, there were nonetheless some leaders mindful of fairness, who distinguished between allied cities and those subdued by right of war, with some diminution of their majesty.

units.la: CXVIII.
units.tr: CXVIII.

units.la: Major honoris æstimatio à magnitudine honorantium accedit.
units.tr: Greater esteem for honour comes from the greatness of those who honour.

units.la: Qui enim subjectione nimii sunt, natura servi aut adulatores habentur. qui verò in honore exhibendo dignitatem suam non celant; splendori exceptorum, non animi sui abjectioni, tribuere videntur. Germanicum excepere Græci quæsitissimis honoribus, vetera suorum facta dictaque præferentes, quo plus dignationis adulatio haberet. Mancipiorum ritu se abjicere, quo alteri honos accedat, nec hominum est libertatis memorum, & dominantibus etiam aliquando fastidio est. Quamvis jam serva Roma, quamvis fastigii cupi-dissimus Tiberius, cum adulationes patrum nimiæ ipsi viderentur, proditur, quoties curia egrederetur, Græcis verbis in hunc modum elocutus, O homines ad serviautem paratos! scilicet etiam illum, qui libertatem publicam nollet, tam projecta servientium patientia tædebat. 3. Annal.
units.tr: Those who are excessively submissive are regarded by nature as slaves or flatterers. Those who do not hide their dignity in paying honour seem to attribute the splendour to the recipients, not to any abjection of their own spirit. The Greeks received Germanicus with the most elaborate honours, recalling the old deeds and sayings of his ancestors, so that the flattery might carry more weight. To cast oneself down like slaves so that honour may accrue to another is not the mark of men mindful of liberty, and it is sometimes distasteful even to rulers. Although Rome was already enslaved, and although Tiberius was most eager for preeminence, when the excessive flattery of the senators seemed too much even to him, it is recorded that whenever he left the senate-house he spoke in Greek words to this effect: O men ready for slavery! Clearly even he, who did not want public liberty, was wearied by such abject patience of the servile. 3. Annal.

units.la: CXIX. & CXX. Magna morbi concussio magno Chirone indiget.
units.tr: CXIX. & CXX. A great shaking of disease needs a great Chiron.

units.la: In corpore humano dum suavi inter fe concentu membra, spiritus, humores conspirant; nil opus est externo medici magisterio. In reip. corpore dum cives cum civibus, magistratus cum subditis consentiunt; alieni imperii autoritati minus loci patescit. Ast ubi nec civibus inter fe convenit, & magistratus libidinem dominandi pro regiminis cynosura habent; validior adversus utrosque crescens insurgit. De Seleucenfibus Cornelius: quoties concordes agunt, spernitur Parthus: ubi dissensere, dum sibi quisque contra æmulos subsidium vocant, accitus in partes, adversus omnes valescit. v1. Annal. non enim omnes, quibus secanda vena praebetur, molliori in medendo manu tuntur. ut Germanicus, qui provincias internis certaminibus aut magistratuum injuriis fessas refovebat. Immitior eadem in loca Æsculapius vocatus, saeva Turcarum dominatio, internis quidem certaminibus & magistratuum in injuriis locum omnem eripit; sed nec vestigium ullum libertatis, aut civilis denique vitæ, relinquit. Quod fi Thraces & Græci moderatè fecundas res tulissent; fi minus flagitiis & sceleribus corruptâ aula Byzantina fuisset; tergum lacerandum tam superbi domini flagello non præbuisset.
units.tr: In the human body, while the limbs, spirits and humours agree in sweet harmony among themselves, there is no need for the external guidance of a physician. In the body politic, while citizens agree with citizens and magistrates with subjects, there is less room for the authority of a foreign rule to gain a foothold. But when citizens do not agree among themselves, and magistrates regard the lust to dominate as the guiding star of government, a stronger power, growing against both, rises up. Cornelius, on the Seleucenses: whenever they act in concord the Parthian is despised; when they disagree, each calls in support against rivals, and the one summoned into their factions grows strong against all. 6. Annal. For not all who are offered a vein to be opened handle the healing with a gentle hand, as Germanicus did, who restored provinces worn out by internal strife or the injustices of magistrates. A harsher Aesculapius, called into the same places, the cruel dominion of the Turks, takes away all room for internal strife and for the injustices of magistrates; but it leaves no trace of liberty, or of civil life at all. But if the Thracians and Greeks had borne their prosperity with moderation, and if the Byzantine court had not been corrupted by shameful and criminal conduct, it would not have offered its back to be lashed by the whip of so proud a master.

units.la: CXXI. Sanctius est & reverentius de mysteriis divinis credere quam scire.
units.tr: CXXI. It is holier and more reverent to believe the divine mysteries than to know them.

units.la: Hæc fuit gentilium mystarum perfuafio. Germanicum sacra Samothracum visere nitentem, obvii Aquilones depulere. & Drufo ultra limites veterum itinere obstitit oceanus in fe & in sacra Herculis inquirere, ut noster alibi. Sed ne Judæis quidem olim, & nunc ChriChristiano populo, concessum sine reverentia in sacra inquirere; nec prophetis ipsis absque tremore faciem Dei ([illegible, ~12 letters]) accipias) intueri.
units.tr: This was the persuasion of the Gentile initiates. Germanicus, striving to visit the sacred rites of the Samothracians, was turned back by the northern winds that met him. Drusus too was checked by the ocean beyond the limits of the ancients when he tried to inquire into the sacred rites of Hercules, as our author says elsewhere. But not even to the Jews of old, nor now to the Christian people, is it permitted to inquire into sacred things without reverence; nor could the prophets themselves look upon the face of God without trembling ([illegible, ~12 letters]).

units.la: CXXII.
units.tr: CXXII.

units.la: Nunquam deest locutuleiis obtrectandi materia.
units.tr: There is never any lack of matter for a chatterer to disparage.

units.la: Multò minùs malevolo animo rabiosè insectantibus. Moderatione imperii in urbe socia, laudanda magis quam reprehendenda, Germanicus usus fuerat. Laudem pro crimine arripiens Pisò, civitatem Athenien-sium turbido incessu territam oratione sua inerepat: obliquè Germanicum perstringens, quod contra decus Romani nominis non Atheniensis tot cladibus extinctos, sed colluviem illam nationum comitate nimia coluisset. At idem Pisò infrà magnificentiam convivii, & coronam Germanico acceptam, modò humilitatem modò superbiam, increpat. Ita detractandi furor rabiosae linguae venenum ex omni occasione colligit. Quid Germanico contra haec remedii? diffi- mulatio[?], patientia, beneficentia. noverat enim, qua autoritate occulti mandati nixus Pisò, tantae se audaciae accingeret: aut insita naturae bonitate malitiam alienam vincere conabatur. Solatium capere Germanicus ex illo Salluftii, aut cujuscunque denique, poterat: vives interdum fortuna, sape invidia, fatigat: ubi anima natura cessit, demptis obtrectatoribus ipsa se virtute magis magisque extollit. Orat.2.ad Caesarem De Republica Ordinanda.
units.tr: Much less for those who attack with a malevolent and rabid mind. Germanicus had used a moderate rule in an allied city, a rule to be praised rather than blamed. Piso, seizing on this praise as a crime, reproached the Athenian state, frightened by its disordered gait, in his speech: obliquely censuring Germanicus, because he had cultivated that dregs of nations with excessive courtesy, rather than the Athenians, who had been wiped out by so many disasters, against the honour of the Roman name. Yet this same Piso, below the magnificence of the banquet and the crown accepted by Germanicus, rebukes now his humility, now his pride. Thus the frenzy of detraction gathers the poison of a rabid tongue from every occasion. What remedy had Germanicus against these things? Dissimulation, patience, beneficence. For he knew by what authority of a secret command Piso was supported, and so armed himself with such audacity; or he tried by his innate goodness of nature to overcome another's malice. Germanicus could take comfort from that saying of Sallust, or of whoever it was: life is sometimes worn down by fortune, often by envy; when the soul has yielded to nature, and the detractors are removed, virtue itself raises itself more and more. Oration 2 to Caesar, On the Ordering of the Republic.

units.la: CXXIII.
units.tr: CXXIII.

units.la: Seipsam plerumque contradicendo redarguit convitiatio.
units.tr: Backbiting often refutes itself by contradicting itself.

units.la: Quos modò colluviem nationum pro Atheniensibus Pisò vocaverat, iis vetera objectabat, quae in Ma-cedones improsperi[?], violenter in suos fecissent. Si non sunt Athenienses, tot cladibus extincti, quid iis clades aut a Philippo, aut a Demetrio accepta; quid ingratus in Miltiadem, Themistoclem, Phocionem, alios benè de republica meritos, animus objicitur? Quod fi, qui in civitatem, ii in jus civium succedunt; cur non me-liori jure recentioris memoriæ arctiffima Atheniensi-um cum Romanis societas, & libertatis illibatæ gloria, valebunt? quod verò Theophilum quendam, Aréo judicio falsi damnatum, precibus Pisonis non concef-fiffent; id gloriæ Atheniensibus, non ignominiæ, dat-tur. Non enim judicia aut venalia pretio, aut precibus pervia esse debent.
units.tr: Those whom Piso had just called the dregs of nations in place of the Athenians, he charged with old wrongs which they had done violently against the Macedonians, to their own people. If they are not Athenians, wiped out by so many disasters, what does it matter to them that they received disasters from Philip or from Demetrius? Why is ingratitude toward Miltiades, Themistocles, Phocion, and others who deserved well of the state laid against them? But if those who come into a city succeed to the rights of citizens, why will the very close alliance of the Athenians with the Romans in more recent memory, and the glory of their unimpaired liberty, not count for more? But that they did not grant to a certain Theophilus, condemned by the judgment of the Areopagus for forgery, at the entreaty of Piso, that is given to the Athenians as glory, not disgrace. For judgments ought not to be for sale for a price, nor open to entreaties.

units.la: CXXIV. Largitio, ambitus, conniventia, perniciosi quidem Reip. sed gratiæ militum turbæ, artes.
units.tr: CXXIV. Largess, electioneering and connivance: these are harmful to the commonwealth, but are arts for winning the favour of the soldiery.

units.la: Quibus eò usque provectus est Cn. Piso; severos tribunos removendo, deterrimum quemque promovendo, desidiam in castris & licentiam in urbibus per-mittendo; ut sermone vulgi parens legionum habere-tur. Quæ si instinctu aut permissu Tiberii patravit, dubium non est, quin alienandis à Germanico legio-num animis corruptio castrensis, ab homine acerbi alias ingenii, sumpta fuerit. nam utipfe largitione & ambitu, quæque alia corrumpendæ militum disciplinæ faciunt, regnum speraverit; non facile est in animum inducendum. Est cum, via inter severitatem & ambitionem media, fine probro quis gratiam militarium hominum captet. Ita Mauritius Naffovius, libertatis Batavicæ post fundatorem patrem extructor, blandè milites appellando, periculis non temerè objectando, castigationis modum non excedendo, stipendia non decurtando; parens militum non modo apud suos, verum etiam in hostium castris audivit. Inde rara ad Hifpanienfes, crebra ab illis transfugia; & sæpè qui-dem integrarum legionum aut cohortium: Italici in-primis aut Teutonici generis. Hinc tanta militum in-eum obsequia, ut etiam contra eum à Barneveldii af-feclis conscriptæ copiæ, nomini fe Mauritiano sub-mitterent. Nec alia proniori, ad tumultus compefcen-dos, dos. & Auriacos in altius fastigium locandos, progressio.
units.tr: By these means Gnaeus Piso advanced so far: by removing severe tribunes, promoting the worst men of every kind, and allowing sloth in the camps and licence in the cities, so that by common talk he was called the parent of the legions. If he did these things at the instigation or with the permission of Tiberius, there is no doubt that the corruption of the camp, taken up by a man of otherwise harsh temper, was meant to alienate the minds of the legions from Germanicus. That he himself hoped for kingship through largess and ambition, and through the other means that corrupt military discipline, is not easy to believe. There is a middle way between severity and ambition, by which a man may win the favour of soldiers without disgrace. Thus Maurice of Nassau, builder of Batavian liberty after its founding father, won the title parent of the soldiers not only among his own men but even in the camps of the enemy: he addressed the soldiers kindly, did not expose them rashly to dangers, did not exceed the measure of punishment, and did not cut short their pay. Hence there were rare desertions to the Spaniards and frequent desertions from them, and often whole legions or cohorts, chiefly of Italian or German stock. Hence such great obedience of the soldiers to him that even against him, troops raised by the partisans of Barneveld submitted themselves to Maurice's name. Nor was there any other easier advance toward suppressing tumults and raising the Orangists to a higher pinnacle.
