units.la: CXXV.
units.tr: CXXV.

units.la: Fœminæ domus custodia, non cura castrorum, decora.
units.tr: A woman's proper concern is the keeping of the household, not the care of the camps.

units.la: De Fulvia, virilis animi muliere. Dio lib. 48. Suet.in Augusto. De Aggripina, curas fœminarum egressa, alibi Cornelius. De Plancina, Agrippinæ indecore æmulatricæ, hoc in loco: Nec Plancina se intra decora fœminis tenebat: sed exercitio equitum, decursibus cohortium interesse. Quæ vero sequuntur, magis familiaria sequiori sexui, sed cum vitio familiaria. in Agrippinam, in Germanicum contumelias jacere. hoc mulicbris armaturæ telum tam validæ aliquando læ-sionis est, ut viros etiam, & viros quidem non pessimæ notæ, transfigas. quibusdam etiam bonorum militum ad mala obsequia promptis. non tantum quod impu-dentiæ munimine tuta calumnia, audacter & cum se-curitate eventus in alios jactatur: sed etiam quod ta-cita hominum suspicio multa sibi, vera an mania[?], permittit. quod haud invito imperatore ea fieri occul-tum rumor incedebat. I nunc, convitiorum in viros bonos spicula audacter sparge, linguæ viperinæ sibulos impune vibra: aut lætorum te gloria, aut saltem virulentiæ impunitas sequetur.
units.tr: Of Fulvia, a woman of manly spirit: Dio, book 48; Suetonius, in Augustus. Of Agrippina, who went beyond the cares of women: Cornelius, elsewhere. Of Plancina, an indecorous rival of Agrippina, in this place: Nor did Plancina keep herself within what befits women, but took part in the cavalry exercises and the drills of the cohorts. What follows is more familiar to the weaker sex, though familiar with fault: she hurled insults at Agrippina and at Germanicus. This is the weapon of a woman's armour, which at times wounds so strongly that it pierces men, and men not of the worst repute: with some good soldiers also ready for wicked services. Not only because calumny, sheltered under the shield of impudence, is hurled boldly and with security of outcome at others, but also because the silent suspicion of men allows itself many things, whether true or invented. That these things were done with the commander not unwilling, the rumour went about in secret. Go now, boldly scatter the darts of insults against good men, and shoot with impunity the venomous hisses of a viper's tongue: the glory of the wicked, or at least the impunity of virulence, will follow you.

units.la: CXXVI.
units.tr: CXXVI.

units.la: Verba, generosi animi virum, à factis non morantur.
units.tr: Words do not hold a man of noble spirit back from deeds.

units.la: More magnæ feræ, minorum canum latratus securè transit: ut Seneca noster. maculas inuri sibi ab iis, qui suos clucre nunquam possunt, minimè judicat. Nota hæc Germanico: sed præverti ad Armenios instantior cura fuit. Nec omnes omnium de se sermonēs vir magnus magni pendit; nec omnes negligit. A compescenda aliorum maledicentia sæpe cum animi magnitudo, conscientiæ munimento tuta, sæpè sordes a luto attrahendi fuga, alias vindictæ abscem[?] opportunitas, nonnunquam instantium negotiorum moles reducitur. Non quid alios pati, sed quid ipsum facere dignum fit, & quid rumor hominum admittat, secum perpendit. plerique, mortales postrema memine-re; & in hominibus impiis, sceleris eorum obliti, de-pœna differunt, fi ea paulo sævior fuerit. uti facundè in bello Catilinario Salluftii Cæsar. Atqui moderatior castigatio hominem asperum, vi non adempta, magis irritaffet. Atque ut idem in eadem oratione Cæsar: qui demissi in obscuro vitam agunt, fi quid iracundia deliquere, pauci sciunt; fama atque fortuna eorum pares sunt: qui magno imperio præditi, in excelso ætatem agunt, eorum facta cunćti mortales novere. ita in maxima fortuna minima licentia est. neque studere, neque odisse, sed minimè irasci decet. quæ apud alios iracundia dicitur, ea in imperio superbia atque crude-litas appellatur. quæ Cæsaris admonitio tanto plus vi-rium habet, quanto propius ad veritatem accedunt, quæ senior Micipfa fidenti ætati & Romanorum fa-vori Jugurthæ occinit: in omni certamine, qui opulen-tior est, etiam fi accipit injuriam, tamen quia plus po-teft facere videtur. S. B. J. Hæc & similia Germani-cum ad mansuetudinis recordationem impellere, & ab ultionis cogitatione, abstrahere potuerint. Quan-quam interdum & Publii Mimi versus cum applausu auditur; nec theatri modo, sed & vitæ humani ap-plausu:
units.tr: Like a great wild beast, he passes calmly by the barking of smaller dogs, as our Seneca says. He does not think that stains are burned into him by those who can never clear their own. Germanicus was aware of this, but he was more eager to hasten to the Armenians. Nor does a great man weigh all the talk about himself, nor does he ignore all of it. Often his greatness of spirit, protected by the defence of a clear conscience, restrains him from silencing the slander of others. Often he avoids dragging himself through the mud. At other times the chance of revenge is lost, and sometimes the weight of pressing business holds him back. He weighs with himself not what others have suffered, but what it is worthy for him to do, and what the rumour of men will allow. Most mortals remember the last thing, and forget the wickedness of impious men, and put off punishment if it is a little too severe. Caesar speaks eloquently of this in Sallust's Catilinarian War. Yet a milder punishment would have angered a harsh man more, without taking away his power. And as Caesar says in the same speech: those who live humbly in obscurity, if they commit some offence in anger, few know of it; their reputation and fortune are equal. But those who live high, endowed with great power, have all mortals know their deeds. Thus in the greatest fortune there is the least licence. One should neither be eager nor hateful, but above all should not be angry. What among others is called anger, in a position of command is called pride and cruelty. This warning of Caesar has all the more force, the more closely it approaches the truth, which the elder Micipsa sang to Jugurtha, who trusted in his age and the favour of the Romans: in every contest, the more powerful man, even if he receives an injury, seems nevertheless to be able to do more. These and similar things, Germanicus could have urged to a remembrance of gentleness, and could have drawn away from the thought of vengeance. Yet sometimes the verse of Publius Mimus is also heard with applause, not only in the theatre but also in the applause of human life:

units.la: Veterem ferendo injuriam in vitas novam.
units.tr: By bearing an old injury, one invites a new one.

units.la: Quem non inaniter pronunciatum esse, Germanicus ab Armenia reversus, nihil jam profutura lamentatio-ne, didicit.
units.tr: That this was not said in vain, Germanicus learned on returning from Armenia, when lamentation would no longer help at all.

units.la: CXXVII. Vicinitas invidiam, peregrinitas odi-um conflare nata est.
units.tr: CXXVII. Nearness breeds envy, distance breeds hatred.

units.la: Linguæ enim, morum, vestitus diversitas efficacius animos, quam vicinorum æmulatio, distrahit. Arme-nii maximis imperiis interjecti, & sapius discordes sunt, adversus Romanos odio, & in Parthum invidia, Quam-vis vis Græcorū civitates de principatu Græciæ discordes, acriori odio in Carbanos (ita non uno in loco apud Æschylum barbarae nationes vocantur) stimulabantur. Italiæ populi cum Romanis de gloria, Galli de vita, (utri esslent, non utri imperarent) certabant. Moschos Poloni, linguæ & vestium similitudine conjunctos, ob potentiæ æmulationem, Germanos interiori animi aversione, non facile tolerant. Scotos Angli contemptu ob tenuitatem, Gallos & Hispanos ob vitæ dissimilitudinem odio graviori notant. Prudentis reip. moderatoris est, affectus animorum populi cognitos habere, secundumque eos aut recto aut obliquo ventorum cursu navigare. Sæpè nec amor nec ira, sed spes aut metus incrementi vel damni, bello vel pace nationes & principes collidit. quod vix ullis temporibus luculentius, quam nutante, post cædem Julii, incertitudine dominorum Romano imperio, patefactum est. Eosdem enim modo amicos, modo inimicos, pro flatu fortunæ immutato, Cæsar & Antonius habebant.
units.tr: For the difference of language, customs and dress divides minds more effectively than the rivalry of neighbours. The Armenians, placed between great empires, are often at odds: they hate the Romans and envy the Parthians, although the states of Greece, quarrelling over the leadership of Greece, were stirred to a sharper hatred against the Carbani (for so the barbarian nations are called in more than one place by Aeschylus). The peoples of Italy contended with the Romans for glory, the Gauls for their lives (whether they should be, not whether they should rule). The Poles, bound to the Muscovites by a similarity of language and dress, but moved by rivalry for power, do not easily tolerate them, and with an inner aversion they regard the Germans. The English mark the Scots with contempt for their poverty, and the Gauls and Spaniards with a heavier hatred for their unlike way of life. It is the mark of a prudent ruler of the commonwealth to know the moods of the people, and to sail according to them, with a straight or slanting course of the winds. Often it is not love nor anger, but hope or fear of gain or loss, that sets nations and princes against one another in war or peace. This was shown more clearly than in almost any age, after the murder of Julius, when the uncertainty of the masters of the Roman empire was in flux. For Caesar and Antony had the same men now as friends, now as enemies, as the wind of fortune changed.

units.la: Dio lib. 48. A quo non multum dissentanea Machiavellus.
units.tr: Dio, book 48. Machiavelli, not much at odds with him, says the same.

units.la: CXXVIII. Peregrinitatis odium moderata imperia mitigant.
units.tr: CXXVIII. Moderate government softens hatred of foreigners.

units.la: Tributorum inprimis remissio aut levatio, donec assuefactione morum jugum patientius feratur. Romanis id imperii arcanum non ignorabatur. Cappadoces in formam provinciæ redacti, & Veranium legatum accepere, & quaedam ex regiis tributis deminuta, quo mitius Romanum imperium speraretur. Significanter SPERARETUR: quanquam ipse postea delusi, se irretitos sero sensuri essent. Eadem spe illusione Illy-riis, Macedonibus, aliis impositam, cum interim, ne communicare vires & consilia possent, in plures po-pulos dissectis, matrimonia & commercia plerisque interdicta. Haud satis commodè Albanus, domitis ut arbitrabatur Belgis, inveterato Hispani nominis odio exactionum gravitatem, decimam rerum venalium, adjunxit, quæ causa ultima, & cum effectu, Belgarum defectionis.
units.tr: First of all, taxes are remitted or lightened, so that the yoke is borne more patiently until people grow accustomed to it. The Romans did not fail to know this secret of empire. The Cappadocians, reduced to the form of a province, received Veranius as their governor, and some of the royal tributes were cut, so that Roman rule might be hoped for as milder. Mark the word HOPED: they themselves were afterwards deceived, and too late did they realise that they had been ensnared. By the same hope and deception the Illyrians and Macedonians were burdened, while meanwhile, so that they could not combine their strength and plans, their people were split into several peoples, and marriages and trade were forbidden to most. Alba, having, as he thought, subdued the Belgians, imposed with little prudence, out of his long-standing hatred of the Spanish name, the heavy exaction of a tenth on saleable goods. This was the last cause, and the actual one, of the Belgians' revolt.

units.la: CXXIX.
units.tr: CXXIX.

units.la: Acriori morsu domestica quam externa imperii detractatio imperantis animum vellicat.
units.tr: Domestic disparagement of a ruler tears at the ruler's mind more sharply than foreign enmity does.

units.la: Germanicus turbidis rebus Armeniam, dubiis Cappadocas, Comagenos, Cilicas exemerat. Cunctaq; socialia prosperè composita, non ideò latum Germani-cum habebant ob superbiam Pisonis, qui jussu partem legionum ipse, aut per filium in Armeniam ducere, utrumque neglexerat. Vide cætera de conventu Pisonis & Germanici, illius obfirmato animo, & precum contumacia, sermonum dissensione, luxus obliqua exprobratione apud autorem.
units.tr: Germanicus had, by his efforts, rescued Armenia from troubled affairs, and Cappadocia and Commagene and Cilicia from doubtful ones. Although all the allied matters had been settled prosperously, they did not regard Germanicus with favour, because of the arrogance of Piso, who, by command, had neglected to lead part of the legions into Armenia either in person or through his son, and had neglected both. See the rest about the meeting of Piso and Germanicus: the author describes Piso's obstinate mind, his stubborn refusal to yield to entreaties, his disagreement in conversation, and his indirect reproach of luxury.

units.la: CXXX.
units.tr: CXXX.

units.la: Faces offensionum susurrones amici.
units.tr: Whispering friends are the torches of quarrels.

units.la: Non Tiberius tantùm, senilis ætatis vitio suspicax, sed & Germanicus, juventæ calore erectior, patulas criminantibus aures præbebat. Amici accendendis offensionibus callidi, intendere vera, adgerere falsa, ipsumque & Plancinam, & filios variis modis criminari. quibus contra demenda rumoris inania, extenuanda quæ levia viderentur, erant. Acuminis est veram rationem apud sapientes non inventuri, morbo pec-cantem humorem, incendio pabulum adjicere. Sed dum sibi quisque gratiæ augmentum captat, nec amici tranquillitati, nec publicis rebus consulitur.
units.tr: Not only Tiberius, suspicious through the failings of old age, but also Germanicus, more heated by the fervour of youth, offered open ears to accusers. Friends, skilled at kindling quarrels, stretched the truth and heaped up falsehoods, and accused both Plancina and the sons in various ways. Against these things one had to remove the empty rumours and play down what seemed trivial. It takes shrewdness not to find the true method among the wise: to add fuel to the fire, or to feed with humours a sin that is a sickness. But while each man seeks an increase of favour for himself, the peace of the friend and the public affairs are alike neglected.

units.la: CXXXI.
units.tr: CXXXI.

units.la: Multum precibus in aula, plus alio-rum contumeliæ damus.
units.tr: At court we give much to entreaties, and more to the insults of others.

units.la: Igitur amicitia alicujus non est palam habenda,qui apud imperantem, vel potentiorem aulae scissae factio invisus est. Saepe enim qui per se staturus erat, cum pariete cui innitebatur ruit, & alienae invidiae maactatur. Artabani regis Parthorum legati, inter alias pacis & societatis leges petierant, ut VononES a Syria removeretur. Statim VononDES ab amoenissima Syriae regione, & illiciendis Armeniae proceribus propinquua, in solitudinem Ciliciae, Pompeiopolim rejicitur. Datum id non modo precibus Artabani,sed contumelia Pisonis, cui gratissimus erat ob plurima officia & dona, quibus Plancinam devinxerat. M. Marcellus Noviocomenses quosdam in contumeliam Caesaris, qui Gallos civitate donaverat, virgis in foro proscindi jussit. Tiberius alios ob necessitudinem Germanici & Agrippinae; favoris rota conversa, alios ob amicitiam Sejani, palam vel occulte mactabat. In aula Neronis, qui sub Claudio regnaverant liberti, Pallas[?],Narcissus, Callistus, quod hanc aut illam in matrimonio Claudiano foverant, variis nominibus, eodem exitio omnes protumbunt. Et quis exempla, quae paene sunt innumera, cuncta recenseat?
units.tr: Therefore one should not openly display friendship with anyone who is hated at court by the ruler, or by a more powerful faction of the divided court. For often the man who was going to stand by himself falls together with the wall on which he leaned, and is slaughtered by another's hatred. The ambassadors of Artabanus, king of the Parthians, among other terms of peace and alliance, had asked that Vonones be removed from Syria. At once Vonones was thrown out of the pleasant region of Syria, which lay near to the enticing of the Armenian nobles, into the desolate Cilicia, to Pompeiopolis. This was granted not only to the entreaties of Artabanus, but to the insult of Piso, to whom Vonones was most pleasing on account of the many services and gifts by which he had bound Plancina to himself. Marcus Marcellus ordered certain men of Novum Comum to be flogged with rods in the forum, as an insult to Caesar, who had granted citizenship to the Gauls. Tiberius, as the wheel of favour turned, struck down some, openly or secretly, because of their connection with Germanicus and Agrippina, and others because of their friendship with Sejanus. At the court of Nero, the freedmen who had held power under Claudius, Pallas, Narcissus, Callistus, all perished by the same destruction under various pretexts, because they had favoured this or that woman in Claudius's marriage. And who could list all the examples, which are almost innumerable?

units.la: CXXXII. Non est viro agendis rebus nato vita peregrinando transeunda.
units.tr: CXXXII. A man born to conduct public affairs must not spend his life in travel.

units.la: Multo minus inertia & somno, & mergentibus animam corporeis voluptatibus. Ne quidem honesta rerum contemplatio, & cognoscendae antiquitatis terrarum & maris lustratio, virum principem ab imperii cura remorabitur. Germanicus Ægyptum proficisci-tur, cognoscenda antiquitatis. sed cura provinciae prae-tendebatur. Tempus aliquod suffurabatur publicis negotiis: quod ipsum publicis negotiis impendi comminiscebatur. Contemplando terrarum situi, astrorum ordinato cursui, antiquitatis recognitioni, naturae ob-scuritati, quibus otium vitae privatae conditio largitur, indulgeant. Princeps pro grege sibi vigilandum, pro disjectis excubadum, pro subditorum quiete sibi laborandum noverit. Ut verò quis aurigationi & cythara cantui in publico cum Nerone, gladiatoriæ arti cum Commodo, epulationibus cum Heliogabalo, aut a-liis imperii dehonestamentis, operam det; non est in viro, autoritatem publicæ rei gerente, toleran[?]dum,
units.tr: Much less should he give himself over to idleness and sleep, or to bodily pleasures that drown the soul. Nor will even the honourable contemplation of things, or the study of ancient history and the exploration of lands and seas, hold back a prince from the care of empire. Germanicus set out for Egypt to study antiquities, but the care of the province was put forward as the pretext. He would steal some time from public business, and pretended that this very time was spent on public business. Let those who are at leisure in private life indulge in contemplating the lie of the lands, the ordered course of the stars, the recovery of antiquity, and the obscurity of nature. A prince should know that he must keep watch over his flock, be on guard for those who have gone astray, and labour for the quiet of his subjects. But when a man devotes himself to chariot-driving and to singing to the lyre in public, as Nero did, to the gladiatorial art, as Commodus did, to feasting, as Heliogabalus did, or to other disgraces of empire, this is not to be tolerated in a man who holds the authority of public affairs;

units.la: CXXXIII.
units.tr: CXXXIII.

units.la: Displicent imperantibus nimis civilia præsidum ingenia.
units.tr: Rulers are too displeased by the civil dispositions of governors.

units.la: Alii imperii autoritatem deteri illa fubmiffione, & conversandi facilitate, interpretantur. Plures gratiam vulgi captari, studia popularium aut provincialium, & per ea vastis animis, & immoderata cupientibus, pe-riculofas imperio opes quæri suspicantur. Germani-cus in Ægypto pretia frugum apertis horreis levavit; multaque in vulgus grata usurpavit; sine milite in-cedere, pedibus intectis, & pari cum Gracis amicitiâ. Quæ quam accepta provincialibus, tam imperatori Tiberio dolentia fuere. Nec, quanquam animi secreta abdere multo usu edoctus, à perstringendo ejus cultu abstinuit. Ne Augustus quidem, Tiberio altior & à suspicione erectior, vel in Marcello sororis filio populi amorem, vel in privigno Druso civilem animum amplexabatur. Et hunc ipsum Augustum, etiamnum puerum ephebum, Julius Cæsar adoptasse, quod mi-jestate vultum & sermonem dignum in eo conspice-ret, traditur. Crediturque Philippus rex Hispania-rum Ferdinandum Toletanum, Albæ famosum du-cem, ob perspectam in eo ingenii truculentiam, Cami-panis primo & Apulis, deinde Belgarum provinciis, postremò Lusitaniæ præfecisse. Quod verò Germa-nicus in eam se comitatem demisit, P. Scipionis æmu-lationes, quem eadem factitavisse apud Siciliam acce-perat; temporum non observata diversitate lapsus est. Quanquam ne ipse quidem Scipio, tanto rerum belli-carum apparatu, vel accusationem Fabii, vel patrum ante rem satis inspectam censuram effugit.
units.tr: Others interpret the weakening of imperial authority as the result of that condescension and easy manner of dealing with people. More suspect that he is courting popular favour, the goodwill of the common people or of the provincials, and that through this, with vast and immoderate ambitions, he is seeking wealth dangerous to the empire. Germanicus in Egypt lowered the price of grain by opening the granaries; he took up many things pleasing to the common people: he walked without a military escort, with his feet uncovered, and on terms of equal friendship with the Greeks. These things were as welcome to the provincials as they were painful to the emperor Tiberius. Nor, although he had learned from long experience to hide the secrets of his mind, did he refrain from disparaging Germanicus's manner of life. Not even Augustus, who was higher than Tiberius and more elevated above suspicion, embraced the people's love in Marcellus, his sister's son, or a civic spirit in his stepson Drusus. And it is said that Julius Caesar adopted this same Augustus when he was still a boy, a youth, because he saw in him a dignified countenance and speech. And it is believed that Philip, king of the Spains, placed Ferdinand of Toledo, the notorious Duke of Alba, first over the Campanians and Apulians, then over the provinces of the Low Countries, and finally over Lusitania, because of the savage temper of his character that he had observed. As for Germanicus lowering himself to such affability, he slipped by ignoring the difference of the times, in imitation of P. Scipio's rivalries, whom he had heard did the same thing near Sicily. Yet not even Scipio himself, with all his warlike preparation, escaped the accusation of Fabius, or the censure of the senators who judged the matter before they had looked into it closely.

units.la: CXXXIV. Vel umbram strenui viri potentiae retinendae anxii reges formidant.
units.tr: CXXXIV. Kings anxious to keep their power fear even the shadow of a vigorous man.

units.la: Nam regibus boni quam mali suspectiores sunt: semperque his aliena virtus formidulosa est. S. B. C. Eurystheus Herculem, quem debellandi monstra praeceptis onerabat, adeò extimuit, ut conspectum ejus non ferens, contra decus regium, post vasa abditus delitesceret. Tiberius Germanicum apud legiones, in urbe, in Syria & Armenia metuendo, nunc acerrimè increpuit, quòd contra instituta Augusti, non sponte principis, Alexandriam introisset[?]. Est quidem aliqua vel timendi vel irascendi ratio: sed in Germanico non locum habitura. Nam is Tiberio, cujus saluti vitam suam dicabat, imperium ereptum non ibat. Quae si cupiditas eum intrasset, facilius vel apud legiones, rebellioni promptas, vel Romae, tanto civium studio, voti compos fuisset. Nec erat ea ingenii lentitudine Germanicus, ut spe armorum abjecta, in claustris Ægypti, & civibus fame premendis, fiduciam locaret. Concedatur id Vespasiani frigidae aetati, & per eam lentori; ut armis in Vitellium motis, fauces Ægypti premat. Primo Antonio, & Muciano, & pari horum Germanici fervori, terror magis armorum, & rapti obviam exercitus, quam lenta consilia, conveniunt.
units.tr: For kings are more suspicious of good men than of bad ones, and another's virtue is always frightening to them. S. B. C. Eurystheus was so afraid of Hercules, whom he burdened with orders to subdue monsters, that he could not bear the sight of him and, contrary to royal dignity, hid himself behind the jars. Tiberius, who feared Germanicus among the legions, in the city, in Syria and in Armenia, now rebuked him most sharply, because he had entered Alexandria contrary to the institutions of Augustus, without the prince's bidding[?]. There is indeed some ground for fear or anger, but it would have no place in Germanicus's case. For he did not go after the empire that had been snatched from Tiberius, to whose safety he was devoting his life. If that desire had entered him, he could more easily have fulfilled it, either among the legions, which were ready for rebellion, or at Rome, with such zeal of the citizens. Nor was Germanicus of such sluggish temperament that, having cast aside hope of arms, he would put his trust in the closed-off Egypt and in starving the citizens. Let this be conceded to Vespasian's cold old age, and to the sluggishness that came with it: that when arms were raised against Vitellius, he squeezed the throat of Egypt. For Antonius Primus and Mucianus, and for the equal ardour of these men as of Germanicus, terror of arms and an army seized in their path suit better than slow plans.

units.la: CXXXV. Nec unus omnium locorum genius, nec eadem apud omnes imperii ratio.
units.tr: CXXXV. No single genius belongs to all places, nor is the same method of rule suited to every people.

units.la: Non erat de nihilo Tiberii solicitudo, si inter indolem Germanici, & quemvis alium, distinguere didicisset. nam Augustus, inter alia dominationis arcana, vetitu, nisi permissu, ingredi senatoribus aut equitibus Romanis illustribus, se posuit Ægyptum: ne fame urgeret Italiam, quisquis eam provinciam, claustraque terra ac maris, quamvis levi praesidio adversum ingentes exercitus insedisset. Alias rationes, & quidem argutius, alibi, Vespasiano Ægyptum insidente, commemorat : quas in Arcanis regnorum expendimus; Nunc verò ipsam Augusti rationem, & Tiberii ex eâ timorem, Vespasiani fiduciam, expendamus: Tem- poribus Augusti, Italia incolis deserta, provinciis belli calamitate praeter Ægyptum prostratis; Urbe anno- næ penuria sæpissimè laborante; quin justa metuendi causa fuerit, minùs ambigimus. At verò tot anno- rum alta pace, refecto provinciarum robore, annonæ præfectorum & ipsius Tiberii sedulitate, prospici ali- unde, extra belli incendium, poterat. Sardinia Italiæ vicina, Sicilia Romani imperii horreum, Africa, fege- tum ad miraculi portentum fœcunda, & copia fru- gum & vecturæ celeritate laboranti fame urbi fuccur- rere nata erat. Remotior quidem, Ægypto tamen propinquior, Asia, decuriis & scripturis, nonin pecu- niam & publicanorum quaestum vertendis, vel solá ingentem civium multitudinem alere potuisset. Quid Italia? quae belli Punici primi temporibus, quibus co- piarum multitudine & navium Augustorum seculum Roma excessit, non suffecit modo tot alendis terrâ marique exercitibus, verùm, Polybio teste, & aliis na- tionibus impertiri frugum & porcorum altilium co- piam valuit. Causa commutatarum rerum in homi- num, non in locorum, vitio quaerenda. Dilapsi è mu- nicipiis & agris oppidani & rustici, urbem ignavo nü- mero, Italiam vacuitate impleverunt. Deserta agri- cultura, civitatis Romanæ & forensis otii amore, va- ftitas Italiæ, urbi inediâ importabatur. Tum Asia de- victa, luxuriosi multi cives Romani, quot fatis agro- rum & pecorum pastui dandum erat spatii, hortorum amoenitate & sumptuosarum villarum amplitudine oc- cupabant, ut taceam, à Lucullo, Pompejo, aliis montes subversos, maria cœftrata, lacus in planitiem inductos, & alia publicæ & privatæ luxuriæ prodigia. Ad hæc fo- ciali Italiæ bello, Pompejano tumultu, triumvirorum rapinis, enervatæ Italorum superstitum facultates; Quas ægrè refectas coloniis militaribus, & pellendis antiquæ possessionis incolis, Augustus pater ille patriæ prostravit. Longa deinde Italiæ sub Augusto & Tiberio, nec non insequentium imperatorum, quies. Sed quod Cornelius in Vita Agricolæ de ingeniis se-mel oppressis pronunciat, natura tamen infirmitatis humanæ, tardiora sunt remedia quam mala, non ineptè huc applicaveris. Nam ne quidem nono Tiberiani imperii anno remedium esse quæsitum, aut quærendo inventum, hæc principis in senatu verba declarant. nemo refert, quod Italia externa opis indiget, quod vita populi Romani per incerta maris & tempestatum quotidie volvitur. ac nisi provinciarum copia & dominis, & servitiis, & agris, subvenerint: nostra nos scilicet nemora, nostraque villa tuebuntur? 3. Annal. Ubi suo more Tiberius, id est obscurè, causam indigentis provinciarum ope Romæ tangit; nemorum & villarum infinita spatia, servorumque, frumenti curculionum, domibus ingestas, nationes.
units.tr: Tiberius's anxiety was not without cause, if he had learned to distinguish the character of Germanicus from that of any other man. For Augustus, among his other secrets of rule, forbade senators or illustrious Roman knights to enter Egypt without permission, lest whoever held that province, the bolt on the gates of land and sea, should press famine upon Italy, even with a small garrison against vast armies. Elsewhere, when Vespasian held Egypt, the author records other reasons, and more subtle ones; we weighed those in the Arcana of Kingdoms. Now let us weigh Augustus's own reasoning, Tiberius's fear arising from it, and Vespasian's confidence. In Augustus's time Italy was emptied of its inhabitants, the provinces were prostrate from the calamity of war apart from Egypt, and the city was very often short of grain. We have little doubt that there was just cause for fear. But after so many years of deep peace, with the strength of the provinces restored and through the diligence of the prefects of the grain supply and of Tiberius himself, supplies could be obtained from elsewhere, outside the fire of war. Sardinia lies near Italy; Sicily is the granary of the Roman empire; Africa is fertile beyond belief, and was born to succour the city when it labours under hunger, with its abundance of crops and speed of transport. Asia, more distant but nearer to Egypt, could have fed a huge multitude of citizens by itself, if its tithes and records had been turned not into money and the profit of the tax-farmers. And what of Italy? In the time of the First Punic War, when Rome, with its multitude of troops and the fleets of Augustus, had outgrown its age, Italy was not only sufficient to feed so many armies by land and sea, but, as Polybius attests and others too, it could supply other nations with grain and fattened pigs. The cause of the change must be sought in men's vice, not in the places. Townsmen and farmers, having slipped away from the country towns and fields, filled the city with their idle numbers and Italy with emptiness. With agriculture abandoned, through love of Roman civic and forensic leisure, the vast emptiness of Italy was carried to the city as starvation. Then Asia was conquered, and many luxurious Roman citizens occupied with the charm of gardens and the grandeur of sumptuous villas the space that should have been given over to the pasture of fields and flocks. I say nothing of how Lucullus, Pompey and others levelled mountains, paved over seas, led lakes into the plain, and of the other prodigies of public and private luxury. Besides these, the Social War in Italy, the Pompeian uprising and the plunder of the triumvirs enfeebled the resources of the surviving Italians. These, scarcely restored by military colonies and by driving out the occupants of old estates, Augustus, that father of his country, laid low. Then followed a long quiet for Italy under Augustus and Tiberius, and under the emperors who came after. But what Cornelius says in the Life of Agricola about talents once crushed, yet by the nature of human weakness, remedies are slower than evils, may not be inappropriately applied here. For not even in the ninth year of Tiberius's reign was a remedy sought, or found by searching, as the emperor's words in the senate declare: no one reports that Italy needs foreign help, that the life of the Roman people turns daily on the uncertain sea and its storms; unless the abundance of the provinces, both masters, slaves and fields, comes to our aid, shall our groves and villas alone protect us? Annals 3. Here Tiberius, in his usual manner, that is obscurely, touches on the cause of Rome's need for help from the provinces: the endless spaces of groves and villas, the slaves, the grain-weevils, and the nations heaped into households.

units.la: CXXXVI.
units.tr: CXXXVI.

units.la: Temporis vetustas priscarū gentium facta oblivione tumulat vel obscurat.
units.tr: The antiquity of time buries or obscures the deeds of ancient peoples through forgetfulness.

units.la: Vel etiam, cum Terentiano Thrafone, Labore alieno magno partam gloriam Verbis sæpè in se tranf-movet. Stupenda de antiquæ Ægypti gloria Diodo- rus Siculus, antiquitatis gentium ingeniosus scrutator. A quibus non longè abeunt, quæ hic Cornelius de Hercule apud Ægyptios partu edito, & reliquis in cognomentum ejus adscitis; de dirutarum Thebarum vestigiis, veterum opulentia; de regis Rhamsis potentia, indicto gentibus tributo, Romanorum magnifico ornatu non minoribus. Quorum certitudinem adeo memoria temporum induxit, ut à plerisque inter anides fabulas ferantur. Profectò fortuna in omni re dominatur: ea res cunctas, ex libidine magis, quàm ex vero, celebrat obscuratque. uti ad hanc rem appositè Crispus Bello Catilinario.
units.tr: Or, as the Terentian Thraso, one often transfers to oneself, by mere words, the glory won by another's great labour. Diodorus Siculus, the ingenious investigator of the antiquity of nations, says astonishing things about the glory of ancient Egypt. Not far from these are the things Cornelius says here: that Hercules was born among the Egyptians and that the rest were adopted in his name; the ruins of destroyed Thebes and the wealth of the ancients; the power of King Rhamsis, who imposed tribute on the nations, no less magnificent in its display than the Romans'. Memory of the times has so persuaded many of these things that they are reported among the fables of ancient times. Truly fortune rules in every matter: it celebrates and obscures things more by desire than by truth, as Crispus aptly says in the Catilinarian War.

units.la: CXXXVII.
units.tr: CXXXVII.

units.la: Insanæ opulentorum regum moles profundi otii indicium.
units.tr: Insane piles built by wealthy kings are a sign of deep leisure.

units.la: Ferri potest saxea Memnonis effigies, ubi radiis so-lis icta est vocalem sonum reddens. nec culpanda, es-fossa lacus humo, superfluentis Nili receptacula. Sed quem in usum, aut quam in delectationem, inter dif-jectas, & vix itineri hominum pervias, arenas, instar montium eduƈa [?] Pyramides? quid reges adhanc tem-poris, opulentiæ, laborum profusionem impulerit? causam unam in aphorismo expressimus, otii profun-ditatem. alteram Cornelius indigitat, opum jactatio-nem: certamine & opibus regum. Magis politicæ considerationis est, multitudinis, ad res novandas mo-bilis, in exstruendis molibus occupatio; & tum otii, decisio, tum animorum per æruumnas depressio. Nec incommode fortassis pro quarta causa Salluftianum illud militaverit: namque animus impurus, diis bomi-nibufque infestus, neque vigilis, neque quietibus sedari poterat: ita conscientia mentem excitam vastabat.
units.tr: The stone figure of Memnon, which gives a vocal sound when struck by the rays of the sun, may be borne; nor is the lake dug out of the earth, a receptacle for the overflowing Nile, to be blamed. But for what use, or what delight, were the pyramids raised like mountains among scattered sands, scarcely passable for men's journeys? What drove the kings of that time to such prodigal expenditure of wealth and labour? We expressed one cause in the aphorism: profound leisure. Cornelius points to another: the boasting of wealth, the rivalry of kings and their resources. It belongs more to political consideration: the occupation of a restless multitude, prone to revolution, in building huge structures; and both the removal of leisure and the depression of spirits through hardship. Perhaps not inappropriately, that saying of Sallust may serve as a fourth cause: an impure mind, hostile to gods and men, could be calmed neither by waking nor by rest, so conscience tormented the troubled mind.

units.la: CXXXVIII.
units.tr: CXXXVIII.

units.la: Sine sanguine victoria est, hostium inter fe collisio.
units.tr: Victory without blood is the collision of enemies among themselves.

units.la: Stultitia hostium pro armis uti, non vetitarum bel-li artium est. Quos enim vi nequeas, astu & arte de-bellare, licitum censetur. Sibi quippe imputent, quod credulitate delusi, consilio hostium utuntur. haut leve decus Drufus quæsivit, inliciens Germanos ad discor-dias, utque fracto jam Marobodvo [?] usque in exitium insisteretur. Quanquam candorem Romanain gente hic requiro, & priscos in adolescente Drufo mores. In auxilium enim Marobodui, cum quo pacem Tiberius icerat, vocatus; pacis autem firmatorem utrisque professus, hostilia agere non debebat. minime autem omnium causam adversus eum dicere, cui advocatus aderat. Igitur, ut verba Taciti invertam, haut leve de-cus Drufus quæsivit, illiciens Germanos ad discor-dias. Timoris quippe hæc & imbecillitatis professio erat, cupere Germanorum gentem extinctam; suam vero manum, sua arma præbere non audere. Animi porrò priscæ ingenuitatis obliti erat, pacis interpretem partes, belli & pacis dubias, exitioso bello commi- scere. Nostra & patrum memoria Galli in Belgio, Hi- fpani in Gallia, Galli iterum in Catalonia, turbarum ansam suppeditare, aut turbantibus favere. quod dum quisque ab altero patitur, contra jus gentium esse, cla- mitat; dum agit contra alterum, sibi ignoscit, & ini- quitatis reum se judice se absolvit.
units.tr: To use the folly of enemies in place of arms is not a forbidden art of war. For those whom you cannot subdue by force, it is considered lawful to conquer by cunning and craft. They have only themselves to blame if, deluded by their credulity, they follow the counsel of their enemies. Drusus sought no small glory by enticing the Germans to discord, so that, with Marobodus now broken, they might press on to his destruction. Yet here I look for Roman candour in the nation, and for the old morals in the young Drusus. For he had been called to the aid of Marobodus, with whom Tiberius had made peace; professing himself the guarantor of peace to both, he ought not to have acted hostilely, and least of all to argue a cause against the man for whom he was present as advocate. So, to turn Tacitus's words around: Drusus sought no small glory, enticing the Germans to discord. For this was a profession of fear and weakness: to wish the German nation destroyed, yet not to dare to offer his own hand or his own arms. Moreover, he had forgotten the old frankness of spirit, mixing the role of peace's interpreter with the doubtful parts of war and peace, in a ruinous war. In our own and our fathers' memory, the Gauls in Belgium, the Spaniards in Gaul, and the Gauls again in Catalonia have supplied the occasion of disturbances, or favoured those who disturbed. While each complains that what he suffers from another is against the law of nations, he pardons himself for what he does against another, and, judging himself, absolves himself as guilty of injustice.

units.la: CXXXIX.
units.tr: CXXXIX.

units.la: Magnorum regum magna in thea- tro humano tragœdia.
units.tr: The great tragedy of great kings in the human theatre.

units.la: Terror ille Germaniæ, formido Romani imperii, Maroboduus, à profugo Catualda victus, regno exu- tus, extorris, hostium opes & tutam apud eos sedem implorat. Maroboduo undique deserto, qui modo tot validissimarum nationum agminibus stipatus erat, non aliud subsidium quam misericordia Cæsaris fuit. Cæsaris, qui ipsi novi belli causa, qui cladis autor, qui exitii ansa occultis dolis fuerat. Idem post paulo Ca- tualdam casus excipiens, idem perfugium præbuit. Liber in re tragica tragicorum principis gnomis uti.
units.tr: That terror of Germany, the dread of the Roman empire, Maroboduus, was defeated by the fugitive Catualda, stripped of his kingdom and driven into exile, and he sought the resources of his enemies and a safe seat among them. With Maroboduus deserted on all sides, he who a little while before had been surrounded by the armies of so many very powerful nations, his only help was the mercy of Caesar. Caesar, who had himself been the cause of the new war, the author of the disaster, and who by hidden tricks had been the occasion of ruin. The same Caesar, after a short time, received Catualda in his misfortune and likewise offered him refuge. I am free in a tragic matter to use a maxim of the prince of tragedians.

units.la: {Greek: Ἀπαντῶν ἐπὶ ἀξαμ... ἑλαύνειν ... τοῦ ἑαυτοῦ ... }
units.tr: {Greek: Ἀπαντῶν ἐπὶ ἀξαμ... ἑλαύνειν ... τοῦ ἑαυτοῦ ...} [Ἀπαντῶν ἐπὶ ἀξαμ... ἑλαύνειν ... τοῦ ἑαυτοῦ ...]

units.la: i. e.
units.tr: That is:

units.la: Nil est negatum, præter imperium Dei.
units.tr: Nothing is denied, except the rule of God.

units.la: Nam nemo, nisi Jupiter, liber eluet.
units.tr: For no one, except Jupiter, emerges free.

units.la: Quo dicto monemur, neminem mortalium ita abso- luti juris esse, ut non fortunæ vi succumbat. nisi id ita se haberet, hominii in Deum, non Dei in hominem im- perium foret.
units.tr: By this saying we are reminded that no mortal is of so absolute a right that he does not succumb to the force of fortune. Unless this were so, it would be the command of man over God, not of God over man.

units.la: CXL.
units.tr: CXL.

units.la: Vultus & verba scænæ, habitus præ- senti fortunæ conveniat.
units.tr: The countenance and words of the stage should suit present fortune.

units.la: Quamvis magno in re adversa animo, verbis arro- gantibus ergà majores abstineas. Cujus præcepti Ma- roboduus immemor, scripsit Tiberio, non ut profugus aut supplex, sed ex memoria prioris fortunæ. Multorum sibi benevolentiam, de Romanorum amicitia certus,
units.tr: However great your spirit in adversity, abstain from arrogant words towards your betters. Maroboduus forgot this rule: he wrote to Tiberius not as a fugitive or suppliant, but in the manner of his former fortune. Certain of the friendship of the Romans, he promised himself the goodwill of many.

units.la: pollicebatur. nam multis nationibus clarissimum quondam regem ad fe vocantibus Romanam amicitiam praetulisse. Poterat fiduciam suam tutari regis Argorum sententia:
units.tr: promised. For he had said that many nations, calling the once most famous king to themselves, he had preferred Roman friendship. The saying of the Argive king could support his confidence:

units.la: Τοῖς γὰρ σοφοῖς οὐ πάντες ἐμισοῦσι Φύσει.
units.tr: For not all men hate the wise by nature. [Τοῖς γὰρ σοφοῖς οὐ πάντες ἐμισοῦσι Φύσει.]

units.la: i.e. Nam clade fracti nemo non forti favet. Ita est, fi supplicem fe, fi minorem, fi submissum gerat. Si contra: verius in eum legati, in eodem poëtae dramate, sententia quadrabit:
units.tr: That is: for no one fails to favour a man broken by defeat, with some strength. So it is, if he presents himself as a suppliant, as lesser, as submissive. If on the contrary, the saying from the same drama of the poet will fit him more truly, the words of the envoys:

units.la: Θεσμοῖσι μὲν ἢ ἀγ' ἐπεὶ τὸς ἢ ὁσσοῖς.
units.tr: Given to the laws, or ... [Θεσμοῖσι μὲν ἢ ἀγ' ἐπεὶ τὸς ἢ ὁσσοῖς.]

units.la: i.e. Os grande fortuna minores non decet.
units.tr: That is: A great mouth does not befit those lesser in fortune.

units.la: Supplex Francifco II. Galliarum regi, sed minacitet supplex, Colignius, libello 15000 hominum fubfcri- ptuors protestatus, indignationem prometu, excanf defcentiam pro miseratione movit. Nec fatis intra supplicum limites, quod hic liceat, steterunt; qui duci- bus Brederodio, Naffovio, Culeburgio, Bergio, Marit garitae Parmenfi libellum nobilitatis nomine porrexe- runt.
units.tr: [Δεῖ ξένον ἀρχαῖον Φιλίας, ἔτι ἀξιῶ, δὲ τύχης.] The leaders of the Phaeacians in Homer's Odyssey say so. And so Caesar rightly and wisely answered Maroboduus that he would have a safe and honoured seat in Italy, and that if he chose to stay, but if his affairs led him to choose otherwise, he would depart under the same good faith with which he had come. Tiberius did not change his promise, knowing that nothing diminishes a prince's authority more than the violation of his good faith. It is reported that a saying of a great German prince (Philip, Landgrave of Hesse) was that the dignity of a ruler is known from three things: the integrity of his coinage, the safety of travel, and the keeping of his promises. Though this does not exhaust all the duties of a prince, it does touch not the least of them.

units.la: CXLI. Hospitem fede receptum nec abigas, necinvitum retineas.
units.tr: Egre-

units.la: Δεῖ ξένον ἀρχαῖον Φιλίας, ἔτι ἀξιῶ, δὲ τύχης.
units.tr: CXLII. A remarkable opportunity to stir up trouble abroad, and the restoration of one driven from his homeland.

units.la: Ajunt in Odyfféa Homeri Phaeacum proceres. Et jure igitur & erudite Marobodio responsum à Cafare, tu- tam ei honoratamque sedem in Italia fore, fi manere, sin rebus suis aliud conduceret, abiturum fide quâ ve- niffet. nec fidem promissi Tiberius mutavit: gnarus, nulla re magis autoritatem principis, quàm fidei reli- gione violanda, concidere. Fertur magni alicujus Germaniæ Principis (Philippi Landgravii Hassiae) di- ctum: tribus ex rebus dignationem imperantis cognos- sci; monetæ integritate, itinerum securitate, & pro- miforum fide. Quod ut non omne Principis officium exhaurit, ita non postremas ejus partes attingit.
units.tr: The Phaeacian nobles say this in Homer's Odyssey. And so, rightly and skilfully, Caesar gave Marobodus this answer: that a safe and honoured seat would be his in Italy if he stayed, but if he judged otherwise for his own affairs, he would be free to leave with the good faith with which he had come. Nor did Tiberius change his promise, knowing that nothing brings down the authority of a prince more than violating the sanctity of faith. There is a saying reported of a great prince of Germany (Philip, Landgrave of Hesse): that the dignity of a ruler is known from three things: the integrity of the coinage, the safety of travel, and the keeping of promises. As this does not exhaust all the duties of a prince, so it does not touch its last part either.

units.la: Egre-
units.tr: Egre-

units.la: CXLII. Egregia res externas turbandi occasio, patria elapsi restitutio.
units.tr: CXLII. A remarkable occasion for disturbing foreign affairs; the restoration of one driven from his homeland.

units.la: Ista quidem spe Maroboduus Romanis Ravennæ fovebatur: si quando infelescerent Suevi, quasi redi-turus in regnum ostentabatur. Et ista quidem minarum ostentatio, segni sub Principe, segnior fuit. Ala-criores isto ævo Suevones & Galli, reducendis in patriam, qui aut Cæsareo fulmine proscripti erant, aut triftiorem sententiam fuga prævenerant, ingentes in Germania fluctus concitarunt. Nec nuper inventæ aliena invadendi artes, nec hac ætate desituræ!
units.tr: With this hope Marobodus was kept by the Romans at Ravenna: if the Suevi ever became unhappy, he was held out as one about to return to his kingdom. And indeed this display of threats, under a sluggish prince, was itself more sluggish. In that age the Suevi and the Gauls were more eager to bring back to their homeland those who had either been outlawed by Caesar's thunderbolt or had anticipated a harsher sentence by flight, and they stirred up great waves in Germany. Nor are the arts of attacking others newly discovered, nor will they cease in this age!

units.la: CXLIII. Vitæ dulcedo & magnos viros in vitæ squalore detinet.
units.tr: CXLIII. The sweetness of life keeps great men in the squalor of life.

units.la: Libertatem quidem aut regnum nonnisi cum ani-ma simul amittere, elatioris animi est; sed vitæ habitum ad præsentem fortunæ vultum convertere, manfuetioris. Maroboduus regnandi incertæ spei certam vivendi facultatem præponens, in Italia consenuit, multum imminuta claritate, ob nimiam vivendi cupidinem. Huic tragicus aliquis impunè occinere potuisset:
units.tr: To lose liberty or a kingdom only together with life is the mark of a more lofty spirit; but to turn one's way of life to the present face of fortune is that of a gentler one. Marobodus, preferring a certain means of living to the uncertain hope of reigning, grew old in Italy, with his renown greatly diminished, on account of his excessive desire to live. To him some tragic poet might have sung with impunity:

units.la: — — [illegible, ~12 letters] [illegible, ~14 letters] i. e. — — vel semel præstat mori, Quam ferre cunctas asperam fortem dies.
units.tr: — — [illegible, about 12 letters] [illegible, about 14 letters] That is: — — it is better to die once than to bear all the harsh days of fate.

units.la: Æschyl. Prometh.
units.tr: Aeschylus, Prometheus.

units.la: CXLIV. Gloriosior triumpho belli compres-si ovatio.
units.tr: CXLIV. A triumph more glorious than a triumph: the ovation for a suppressed war.

units.la: Fraudo occultis Tiberii consiliis Maroboduo, atque ita violentarum gentium viribus elisis; composito Germanici opera Oriente, ac novi belli formidine depulsa: senatus ovationem, pleno triumpho minorem, decreverat: latiore Tiberio, quia pacem sapientia fir- maverat, quàm si bellum per acies confecisset. Ferventis ætatis est, gloriam è temerario conflictu quaerere, necessitatis, ingruentem belli molem armorum vi depellere: Sapientiæ simul ac felicitatis, belli in primo ortu fauces elidere. Romanorum armis ab occasu solis ad Euphratem, Syenen, & Mæotidem paludem, omnia domita erant. quod defuit imperio gentium ferocia efferarum, magis extra claustra imperii cohibendum, quam belli temeritate lacessendum erat. In ipso autem Romani juris diftri&tu res quietas movere, & belli incendium suis ædibus injicere, extremæ dementiæ fuisset. Nam ut acutum videatur, quod apud Tragicum Oedipus Creonti oggerit;
units.tr: Marobodus was deceived by Tiberius' secret counsels, and so the strength of the violent peoples was broken; through Germanicus' work the East was settled, and the fear of a new war was driven off: the Senate decreed an ovation, less than a full triumph, since Tiberius had secured the peace by wisdom, which was a greater thing than if he had finished the war by battle lines. It belongs to a hot age to seek glory from a rash clash; to repel the advancing mass of war by force of arms belongs to necessity. To strangle war at the very first birth of its jaws belongs to wisdom and good fortune at once. By Roman arms all things had been subdued from the setting of the sun to the Euphrates, to Syene and the Maeotic marsh. What was lacking to the empire, the fierceness of savage peoples, was to be restrained beyond the barriers of the empire rather than provoked by the rashness of war. But to stir up quiet affairs within the very jurisdiction of Roman law, and to set fire to war in one's own house, would have been the height of madness. For though the words of Oedipus in the tragedian to Creon may seem sharp:

units.la: Tuò movetur, quicquid extremo in loco est: fanior est, & ad Tiberii mentem accommodatior, Creontis ad Oedipum oratio:
units.tr: Whatever is in the furthest place is moved by you: more sane, and better suited to the mind of Tiberius, is the speech of Creon to Oedipus:

units.la: Non expedit concutere felicem fatum.
units.tr: It is not expedient to shake a fortunate fate.

units.la: Seneca Oedipo.
units.tr: Seneca, Oedipus.

units.la: Sic apud Persas Artaxerxes, sic quicunque sanam cum magna potentia mentem conjunxerunt, felicitati suæ modum imponendo, ad pacem otio & legibus fir- mandam fe converterunt.
units.tr: Thus among the Persians Artaxerxes, and thus whoever have joined a sound mind with great power, by setting a limit to their good fortune, turned themselves to establishing peace and laws in leisure.

units.la: CXLV.
units.tr: CXLV.

units.la: Adversus violatorem fidei non fuit degeneres insidiæ.
units.tr: Against a violator of faith, the ambushes were not unworthy.

units.la: Livius, & ex eo recentiores nonnulli, morum apud Romanos cum tempore mutationem observant. Quorum majores Pyrrhum, ut sibi à veneno medici caveret, monuerant, ii Prufiæ Bithyniæ regi Hanniba- lis, violato hospitii & societatis jure, occidendi auctores fuere. Ego, quanquam remisse Romanos à priscæ morum sanctitate, non nego, majorem in reipfa, quam in temporibus & genio civium, mutationem reperio. Cum Pyrrho, gloriæ causa honesta arma quatiente, intra receptas belli leges steterunt. Perfidum Hannibalem, & ruinæ imperii Romani hostili animo immi- nentem, quovis modo perimere, extra fidei tamen datæ violationem, moliti sunt. Tiberius, qui Adgan-destrio Cattorum principi responderat, non fraude, neque occultis, sed palàm & armatum populum Ro-manum hostes suos ulcisci: nunc Rhefcuporim Thra-cie regem astu aggreditur. per Pomponium Flaccum, amicitiæ regiæ nomine fraudi struendæ aptiorem, illi-cio blanditiarum intra præsidia Romana pertractum, & specie honoris valida manu circundatum, Romam ad dicendam causam eduxit. Non ab ingenio suo Ti-berius abiit: sed res & homines agendi modum varia-verunt. Arminius,justus Romani nominis hostis, nec odium gentium sceleribus promeritus,aperta via ster-nendus erat. Rhefcuporis, fidei erga suos & alienos transgressor, occulte domari poterat. Nec si veneni submissi crimen, ad hostem interimendum, honestos viros dedecet ; etiam simulatio actionum,& ad dicen-dam causam pertractio, turpitudine involvetur. Ita rerum & hominum mutatio, colorem actionibus di-versum induunt. Nec finis contemplatio, in agendis aut omittendis rebus,nullius ponderis habenda. Thra-cie res, & pereas Romanum statum, nisi amoto tur-batore, quietas imperator tenere non poterat. Ger-maniamne, extra imperii limites positam, Arminius turbaret,extra Romanorum curam fuit. Imo ne quidem extra curam : cum Maroboduum ab Arminio frangi, tranquillitatis Romanæ interesset. Quod au-tem insidiis, non aperta armorum vi, Rhefcuporin amovendum duceret: Tiberianis id moribus conve-nientius erat. Nihil quippe aquè Tiberium anxium habebat, quàm ne composita turbarentur. quod quia præcedenti monito diduxi, à crambe recoquenda ab-stineo.
units.tr: Livy, and some more recent writers after him, observe a change of morals among the Romans over time. Those who were their elders had warned Pyrrhus to beware of poison from his physicians; these men, in violation of the right of hospitality and alliance, were the instigators of the killing of Hannibal by Prusias, king of Bithynia. I do not deny that the Romans had relaxed from the sanctity of their ancient morals, but I find the greater change in the thing itself than in the times and the temper of the citizens. With Pyrrhus, who brandished arms for the sake of honourable glory, they kept within the accepted laws of war. They undertook to destroy the treacherous Hannibal, who threatened the ruin of the Roman empire with hostile purpose, by any means, yet outside the violation of a given faith. Tiberius, who had answered Adgandestrius, prince of the Catti, that the Roman people would avenge its enemies not by fraud or secrecy, but openly and under arms, now attacks Rhescuporis, king of Thrace, by craft. Through Pomponius Flaccus, more suited to contriving deceit under the name of royal friendship, he drew him by enticing flatteries within the Roman garrisons, surrounded him with a strong band under the appearance of honour, and led him to Rome to plead his case. Tiberius did not depart from his own nature; but circumstances and men changed the manner of acting. Arminius, the just enemy of the Roman name, who had deserved hatred of the nations by no crimes, was to be laid low by open way. Rhescuporis, a breaker of faith towards his own and others, could be subdued secretly. Nor is the charge of a poison sent in to kill an enemy unbecoming to honourable men; even the pretence of actions, and the luring of a man to plead his cause, is not stained with baseness. Thus the change of circumstances and of men puts on actions a different colour. Nor is the consideration of the end, in doing or omitting things, to be held of no weight. The affairs of Thrace, and the Roman state itself, could not be kept quiet by an emperor unless the disturber were removed. Whether Arminius would disturb Germany, which lay beyond the limits of the empire, was outside the Romans' concern. Indeed, it was not even outside their concern, since it concerned Roman tranquillity that Marobodus be broken by Arminius. But that he judged Rhescuporis should be removed by ambush rather than by open force of arms was more suited to Tiberian ways. For nothing equally troubled Tiberius, than that settled matters should be disturbed. Because I have digressed by the preceding admonition, I refrain from warming up the cabbage again.

units.la: CXLVI.
units.tr: CXLVI.

units.la: Acri unius mente, quàm fluctuante multorum consilio, imperii res felicius geruntur.
units.tr: Affairs of state are carried on more happily by the sharp mind of one man than by the wavering counsel of many.

units.la: Tiberius Thraciæ motum compositurus, non ex-
units.tr: Tiberius, about to quell the rising in Thrace,

units.la: peͤtat, quid hic autille aulicorum fuggerat; nec mul- torum confcientia opportunitatem rei gerendæ cor- rumpit. fed fuo animi motu, fuo confilio diligit cen- turionem, qui nunciaret regibus, ne armis difceptarent, cæteraque per fe, non ex amicorum fuggeftione, ex- pedit. Diverfus à Tiberii ingenio Claudius, ne quidem in domefticis rebus judicio fuo utebatur. modò huc, modò illuc, ut quemque fuadentium audierat, præm- ptus. 12. Annal. Quanquam autem difcordantes in concilium vocat, ac promere fententiam, & adjicere rationes jubet: voluntate magis trahentium, quàm confulentium rationibus torquetur. Claudio non multò felicior Sergius Galba, quanquam prudentiam multo rerum ufu collegiffe vifus, inter T. Vinii, Corn. Laconis, & Iceli liberti, difcordium confiliorum fua- fiones, animo diftrahebatur. 1. Hift. Ut quemque impetus animi, aut propriæ rei metus ac fpes duce- bat, ita rei adminiftrandæ fententiam non fui juris principi fuggerebat. Diu multorum lite difceptatum eft, uniͤfne principis confilio, an confiliariorum con- junêta fagacitate, refpublica felicius adminiftretur. Egodiftinctionem expedio: mentis acrimoniam in principe requirens. Nec tamen nullos omninò, quaf- cunque ad res deliberandas, quod de Ludovico X I. Galliarum rege ferunt, in confilium advocabit. In mul- titudine enim confiliariorum falus reipublicæ, fecun- dum Hebræorum fapientiffimi oraculum. Quorfum autem confiliariorum multitudo, fiis nemo utatur? Nec fperno Agamemnonis pronunciatum malle fe decem Neftoras ad Trojam expugnandam, quam to- tidem Ajaces. Quamquam fi pares futuri funt confi- lio Neftores, quid opus eft decem, eandem fententiam promputuris? fi difpares: nifi judicio imperator pol- leat, obruetur magis diftractione confilii, quàm extri- cabitur. Sed nec Agamemnon acrimonia judicii ad Tiberium noftrum comparandus eft; & ftultos inter reges à Lyrico poëta recenfetur. Stultorum regum & populorum continet effus. Horat, lib. 1. Epift. 2. Quam ob rem alieno magis consilio regendus, quam suo rapiendus, magnarum in rerum decisione, videba-tur. Voti igitur summa est, regem sua ipsum sapientia pollere, nec tamen sapientium virorum monita, si è re-publica esse evideritm, aspernari.
units.tr: does not ask what this or that courtier suggests, nor does the conscience of many spoil the opportunity for acting. Instead, by his own impulse and his own counsel, he chooses a centurion to tell the kings not to settle their dispute by arms, and he arranges the rest by himself, not at the suggestion of his friends. Claudius, unlike Tiberius in temper, did not even use his own judgment in domestic matters, but was swayed now this way, now that, as he had heard each adviser. (Tacitus, Annals 12.) Although he calls the disagreeing men into council, and bids them state their opinions and add their reasons, he is turned more by the wishes of those who pull him than by the reasons of those who advise. Not much happier than Claudius was Sergius Galba, although he seemed to have gathered prudence through long experience of affairs; he was distracted in mind between the conflicting counsels of T. Vinius, Cornelius Laco and the freedman Icelus. (Tacitus, Histories 1.) As the impulse of each man's mind, or his own fear and hope for his affairs, led him, so he did not offer the prince the plan for managing affairs, which was not his right. For a long time it has been disputed whether the commonwealth is better administered by the counsel of a single prince or by the united shrewdness of his counsellors. Here I draw the distinction, requiring sharpness of mind in the prince. Yet I do not, as they report of Louis XI, king of France, call in no counsellors at all to deliberate on any matter. For in a multitude of counsellors lies the safety of the commonwealth, according to the oracle of the wisest of the Hebrews. But what is the use of a multitude of counsellors if no one uses them? Nor do I scorn Agamemnon's saying that he would rather have ten Nestors to storm Troy than as many Ajaxes. Yet if the Nestors are to be equal in counsel, what need is there for ten, who would only utter the same opinion? If they are unequal, then unless the commander excels in judgment he will be overwhelmed by the distraction of counsel rather than extricated from it. But Agamemnon is not to be compared in sharpness of judgment with our Tiberius, and the Lyric poet counts him among foolish kings: "He holds back the outpourings of foolish kings and peoples." (Horace, Epistles 1.2.) For this reason, in deciding great affairs, a king seemed to be ruled by the counsel of others rather than hurried by his own. The sum of the wish, then, is that the king excel in his own wisdom, yet not reject the admonitions of wise men when these are clearly for the good of the commonwealth.

units.la: CXLVII.
units.tr: CXLVII.

units.la: Nimia concedendi facilitas, in homine ferocis ingenii, suspecta.
units.tr: Excessive readiness to grant is suspect in a man of fierce temper.

units.la: Per quam natura faciles, & fraudis ut rectendae ita cavendae ignari, in casses temere incidunt. Rhescupo-ris decidendis, quas cum fratre habebat, controversiis colloquio diem postulavit. nec diu dubitatum de tempore, loco, dein conditionibus: cum alter facilitate, alter fraude, cuncta inter se concederent, acciperentque. Quo pacto violentiae fratris obnoxius Cotys, catenis injectis libertate, ac mox vita, privatus est. Quod facile factu fuit, credulo Cotye, & doli nihil suspicato. At cum hominibus acrioris ingenii aliter agitur: multum disceptationibus obnitendo, postremo quasi rationibus victi, manus damus, rei gerendae consilium altiori animo premen-tes. Quod in re non illicita non indecorum: in fraude & perniciae struenda, nollem a me doceri.
units.tr: Those who are easy by nature, and as ignorant of how to guard against fraud as of how to practise it, rashly fall into snares. Rhescuporis, to settle the disputes he had with his brother, asked for a day to meet and confer. There was little doubt about the time and place, and then about the terms; while the one, with his easy temper, and the other, with his fraud, conceded and accepted everything between them. By this method Cotys, exposed to his brother's violence, was deprived of his liberty by chains thrown on him, and soon of his life. This was easy to bring about with the credulous Cotys, who suspected no trick. But men of sharper temper are dealt with otherwise: by resisting much in the debates, and finally, as if overcome by reasons, we give our hand, while secretly pressing on with the plan of action in a higher spirit. Which in a matter not unlawful is not unbecoming; but in contriving fraud and destruction, I would not wish to be taught this by myself.

units.la: CXLVIII.
units.tr: CXLVIII.

units.la: Bona causa patrono non indiget.
units.tr: A good cause needs no advocate.

units.la: Mala nullo patrono absolvitur. In ficta Thracis innocentia, à Tiberio molliter rescriptum, si fraus abesset, posse eum innocentia fidere: caterum neque se, neque senatum, nisi cognita causa, jus & injuriam discretu-ros. Quod à Tiberio, simulationes edocto, refcri-ptum, syncere omnium judiciorum vestibulis, & mul-to magis animis, inscribi optandum.
units.tr: A bad cause is cleared by no advocate. When the Thracian pleaded his feigned innocence, Tiberius replied mildly that if there was no fraud he could trust his innocence; but that neither he nor the senate would separate right from wrong unless the case had first been examined. It is to be wished that this reply, written by Tiberius, who had learned of pretences, were inscribed on the vestibules of all honest judgments, and far more on men's minds.

units.la: CXLIX.
units.tr: CXLIX.

units.la: Audacis est, improbitatem modo nullo metiri.
units.tr: It is the mark of a bold man to measure wickedness by no standard at all.

units.la: Rhescuporis de capto fratre in judicium vocatus,
units.tr: Rhescuporis, called to judgment over his captured brother,

units.la: inter metum & iram contatus, maluit patrati quàm incepti facinoris vetus esse: occidi Cotyn jubet. Confer Jugurthini facinoris historiam: vix aliam magis gestam reperies. Ita non virtutum modò, aut mediarum actionum, sed sceleram etiam eadem sæpe in ore-be fabula luditur. Quod autem Macchiavellus, Ari-stotelis loco V. politic. non bene intellecto, docet; homines non temere reperiri plenè improbos: id ex hoc loco, & huic similibus aliis vefellitur. Coercenda magis, quam verbis extenuanda, improborum audacia.
units.tr: caught between fear and anger, preferred that his crime be finished rather than merely begun: he orders Cotys killed. Compare the history of the Jugurthine deed; you will hardly find another more notorious. Thus not only virtues and ordinary actions, but even crimes, are often staged again and again on the same stage of the world. As for Machiavelli's teaching, which misreads Aristotle, Politics V, that men are not readily found to be wholly wicked: this is refuted by this passage and others like it. The audacity of the wicked must be restrained rather than softened with words.

units.la: CL.
units.tr: CL.

units.la: Aptissimum fallendi instrumentum amicus.
units.tr: A friend is the most suitable instrument for deceiving.

units.la: Nam quod minus ab eo cavetur, quod secretorum particeps est, quod tempora & exitus omnes indagat; laqueis ejus obnoxii patemus. Latinium Pandum, Rhescuporis, quem sibi infensum arguebat, vitaverat, at non vitavit Pomponium Flaccum, arta sibi amicitia conjunctum, eoque accommodatiorem ad fallendum. Ita Jugurtham Metellus, per Bomilcarem, amicorum regi fidissimum, ideoque ad fallendum accommodatissimum, aggreditur. Sed exemplorum tanta abundantia imminet, ut nihil frequentius ævo suo fuisse poëta Sulmonensis testetur.
units.tr: For the one who is least guarded against is the friend who shares in our secrets and investigates all our times and departures; we lie open to his snares. Latinius Pandus avoided Rhescuporis, whom he argued was hostile to him, but he did not avoid Pomponius Flaccus, joined to him by close friendship, and therefore all the more suitable for deceiving him. So Metellus approaches Jugurtha through Bomilcar, the king's most faithful friend, and therefore most suitable for deception. But such an abundance of examples presses upon us that the poet of Sulmo testifies nothing was more frequent in his age.

units.la: Tuta frequenfq, via est, per amici fallere nomen:
units.tr: Safe and frequent is the way, to deceive under the name of friend;

units.la: Tuta frequenfq, licet sit via, crimen habet.
units.tr: though the way be safe and frequent, it carries a crime.

units.la: Anigitur nec Pomponium Flaccum, specie amicitiæ nocentem, absolvimus? Refp. Plus erat principi, plus patriæ, plus publicæ rerum tranquillitati, quàm privatae alicujus, & quidem facinorosi, amicitiæ devinctus. De Bomilcare nonidem est judicium, nam, si absque vitii contaminatione Metellus perfidia aliena abuti poterat; tuit; non iccirco Bomilcar regem suum, & regem quidem amicissimum, circumveniendi per dolum jus habebat. Si enim justum bellum gerebant Romani, Jugurtha injustum; primo armorum crepitu ad juvenem fiorem causam desciscendi facultatem habuit, quantum patriæ tantus est amor, tanta in cives potentia, ut nec in causa iniquiori fe deferendi fatis apertum jus alicui conferat. Sin libido dominandi causa bel-landi Romanis fuit, aut fi ad eos, quid in Numidia ge-rerētur[?], nihil spectabat: ne quidem Romano judice crimen perfidiæ Bomilcar effugit. Nobis in vita pri-vata & publica, quantum & cui fidamus, in tanta sal-lendi facilitate, præcavendum.
units.tr: Shall we then not absolve even Pomponius Flaccus, harmful under the appearance of friendship? I answer: the prince had more claim, the fatherland more, and public tranquillity more, than the friendship of any private person, and a criminal one at that, could bind him. Of Bomilcar the judgment is not the same. For if Metellus could abuse another's treachery without stain of vice, that did not give Bomilcar the right to circumvent his own king, and indeed a very dear friend, by guile. For if the Romans waged a just war and Jugurtha an unjust one, then at the first clash of arms the young man had the chance to desert to the better cause; so great is love of country and so great its power over citizens that it confers on no one a clearly lawful right to desert, even from a less just cause. But if the lust for domination was the reason for his war against the Romans, or if he looked to them only for what was happening in Numidia, then nothing could excuse him: not even by a Roman judge does Bomilcar escape the charge of treachery. For us, in private and public life, we must take care how far and in whom we trust, given how easily we can be deceived.

units.la: CLI.
units.tr: CLI.

units.la: Honoris exhibendi species multis pro offendiculo.
units.tr: The appearance of showing honour as a stumbling block for many.

units.la: Clarum in hoc Thrace exemplum. circundata hinc regi specie honoris valida manus, tribunique & centu-riones, monendo, suadendo, & quanto longius abscedebat, apertiore custodia. postremo gnarum necessitatis in urbem traxere. Nonnemo ad genua inimici potentioris procidendo, impulsis cruribus eum prostravit. quod initium cædis Neronianæ faciendum, cohorti Pisonianæ conjurationis placuerat. quod facinus in Q.Haterio suspicati milites, à cæde ejus parum abstinuerunt. Constat Haterium, cum deprecandi causa palatium intrõisset[?], ambulantisque Tiberii genua advol-vererur, propè à militibus interfectum, quia Tiberius easu, an manibus ejus impeditus, prociderat. 1. Annal. Alius abditis æduum penetralibus monstrandis, quasi id honori alicujus detur, arĉtiori custodia comprehen-sum alligavit. Et quis omnium fraudis itinerum do-cumentis cumulandis sufficiat?
units.tr: A clear example in this Thracian case: a strong hand of soldiers surrounded the king on all sides under the pretence of honour, and the tribunes and centurions, by warning and persuading, and the further he withdrew, the more open the guard became; at last, knowing he was in need, they brought him into the city. Someone threw himself at the knees of the more powerful enemy and, by knocking his legs from under him, brought him down. This was the beginning of the slaughter under Nero, which the cohort of the Pisonian conspiracy had resolved to carry out. The soldiers, suspecting this deed in the case of Q. Haterius, scarcely refrained from killing him. It is agreed that Haterius, when he had entered the palace to beg for mercy and was clasping the knees of Tiberius as he walked, was almost killed by the soldiers, because Tiberius, either by stumbling or by his hands being entangled, had fallen. 1. Annals. Another, pretending to show the hidden inner shrines of the temple, as if this were granted as an honour to someone, seized him and bound him under closer guard. And who among all could suffice to pile up the proofs of all the frauds of such journeys?

units.la: CLII.
units.tr: CLII.

units.la: In judicando nemo omnium libidi-ni simul & usui paret.
units.tr: In judging, no one serves at once the lust and the advantage of all.

units.la: Convictus in senatu cædis fraternæ Rhefcuporis, à regno procul amovetur. Romanis invadendi va-cuam possessionem, & provinciali onere premendi, occasio patebat. Vicit libidinem æquitas. Thracia in Rhœmetalcen[?] filium, quem paternis consiliis adversa-tum constabat, inque liberos Cotyis dividitur. Hinc quæri potest, utrum proditionis, majestatis, rebellio-
units.tr: Convicted in the senate of the fraternal murder, Rhescuporis is removed far from the kingdom. The Romans had an opportunity to invade the empty possession and to burden it with provincial taxes. Fairness overcame desire. Thrace is divided between Rhoemetalces, the son, who was known to have opposed his father's counsels, and the children of Cotys.

units.la: nis, perduellionis damnatorum liberis jure paterna-rum facultatum hæreditas, & ditionum regendarum successio adimatur? Quocunque Juris publici Con-sulti propendeant: saltem hoc Romanorum facto mi-tiorem in omnibus sententiam tutari nequeunt. Rhefcuporis nullo Romanorum beneficio regnum paternum possidebat, at qui feudo, ut his temporibus loquuntur, districtum aliquem possident, alia in conditione censentur. Nisi expressis verbis in lege fœderis cautum sit, ipsi & liberis distrinctum regendum permitti. Par est conditio alicujus regni, in quo successio non hæreditate paterna, sed antiqua populi lege, unde successio legitima devolvitur. Hic si, justa populi offensa, rex patriæ legibus inimicus pellatur: succedendi jus liberorum maximo, aut proximo ex agnatis, non adimitur. 2. Filius Thracii regis in facinus patris non modò non consenserat, sed paternis consiliis adversatum consultabat. Quare præmium, non pœnam, merebatur. Hoc nomine Piso, majestatis moto in Cilicia bello reus, filium M. Pisonem, repetere Syriam dehortatum, culpæ eximendum precatur. 3. Annal. 3. Romani multa de jure suo decedendo, multa victis, plura victorum liberis largiebantur. quæ in imitationem laudis, non in exempli necessitatem, trahantur. 4. Romani tamen ipsi, quod una manu largiebantur, altera ereptum ibant. nondum adultis Trebellienus Rufus pratura functus datur, qui regnum interim tractaret. Qui regna arbitrio suo dividunt; qui tutorem regnaturis imponunt: quid nisi summum regni jus, populo Thraciæ ereptum, sibi deinceps vindicant? Et alioqui sociis ita regna & gentes assignavere, ut illorum usum & fructum, suam possessionem esse judicaretur. quod apud Salluftium Atherbal agnovit, Romano in senatu ita locutus: Micipsa pater meus moriens mihi præcepit, uti regni Numidiæ tantummodo procurationem exi-stimarem meam: caterum jus & imperium penes vos esse. quo jure non diu quieti, utilitates regnorum cum imperii jure paulatim invasere. Igitur ejusmodi im-perii Romani exemplis, in re multum dissimili, parce u-tendum.Manife-
units.tr: Hence it may be asked whether the inheritance of paternal property and the succession to rule over territories are taken away by right from the children of those condemned for treason, majesty, rebellion or enmity to the state? Whatever the jurists of public law may incline to, they cannot at least defend a milder judgment in all cases by this Roman action. Rhescuporis possessed the paternal kingdom by no benefit of the Romans, but those who hold some territory by fief, as they say in these times, are reckoned in another condition. Unless it is expressly provided in the law of the covenant that the holder and his children are permitted to rule it in a separate way. The case is the same for a kingdom in which succession is not by paternal inheritance but by the ancient law of the people, from which lawful succession devolves. Here, if the king is driven out as an enemy of the laws of his country by a just offence of the people, the right of succession of the children is not taken away, either to the greatest or to the nearest of the agnates. 2. The son of the Thracian king had not only not consented to his father's crime, but had opposed his father's counsels and was known to have done so. Therefore he deserved a reward, not a punishment. On this ground Piso, accused of majesty for the war in Cilicia, begged that his son Marcus Piso, who had been dissuaded from returning to Syria, be exempted from blame. 3. Annals 3. The Romans granted many things by giving up their own rights, many to the conquered, and more to the children of the victors. These things should be drawn into imitation of praise, not into a necessity of precedent. 4. Yet the Romans themselves took back with the other hand what they gave with one. Trebellienus Rufus, who had held the praetorship, was given to the children, who were not yet grown, to manage the kingdom in the meantime. Those who divide kingdoms at their own pleasure, who impose a guardian on those who are to reign, what else do they claim for themselves afterwards but the supreme right of the kingdom, taken from the people of Thrace? And moreover they assigned kingdoms and nations to allies in such a way that their use and fruit were judged to be their own possession. This Adherbal acknowledged before Sallust, speaking thus in the Roman senate: "My father Micipsa, when dying, instructed me that I should consider my charge of the kingdom of Numidia only as a stewardship, but that the right and rule rested with you." By this right, the advantages of the kingdoms gradually, with the right of rule, encroached upon the quiet of others, which did not last long. Therefore the examples of such Roman rule, in a matter much different, are to be used sparingly. Manife-

units.la: {B.J} ita locutus: Micipsa pater meus moriens mihi præcepit.
units.tr: ...spoke thus: "Micipsa my father, when dying, instructed me..."

units.la: CLIII. Manifesti rerum capitalium suppli-cium ne fugiendo quidem effugiunt.
units.tr: CLIII. Those who are manifestly guilty of capital crimes do not escape punishment even by flight.

units.la: Romani cujus apertè poenam, regii nominis verecundia, non audent; occulto ministerio, aut intentato fugæ crimine, veniam eripiunt. Rhescuporis Alexan-driam devectus, atque illic fugam tentans, an ficto crimine, interficitur. Nec expedire Romanis visum, re-gem damnatione offensum vivere; nec iræ divinæ ultio tutum usquam perfugium permittebat. Similis vitæ exitus Vononem, non eadem scelere promeritum, excepit. nisi quod corrumpere custodes, bellum novum per Albanos Heniochosque & Scytharum regem movere, tumultuosius judicabatur. specie quidem venandi elabebatur, & equi pernicitate evaserat, nisi amnis Pyrami pontes ab accolis ruptos offendisset. Eum Remmius Evocatus, prioris custodiæ regis appositus, quasiper iram gladio transfigit. nimirum ne ad indicium consentientis in fugam servaretur. Sic illum sceleris magnitudo, hunc casus, utrumque fugæ conatus perdidit.
units.tr: Out of respect for the royal name, the Romans do not dare to punish him openly; by secret agency, or by a pretended charge of attempted flight, they snatch away his pardon.
