Rhescuporis, having been brought to Alexandria and there attempting flight, is put to death, whether on a fabricated charge or not. Nor did it seem expedient to the Romans to let a king who had been offended by condemnation live, and the vengeance of divine wrath allowed no refuge safe anywhere. A similar end overtook Vonones, who had not deserved it by the same crime, except that bribing his guards and stirring up a new war through the Albani, the Heniochi and the king of the Scythians was judged a more tumultuous matter. He was slipping away under the pretext of hunting and had escaped by the speed of his horse, had he not found the bridges over the river Pyramus broken by the local inhabitants. Remmius, a veteran (Evocatus) set over his earlier guard, runs him through with a sword as if in anger. Doubtless this was so that he would not be kept alive to inform against his accomplice in the flight. Thus the magnitude of his crime destroyed the one, chance the other, and the attempt at flight destroyed both.

units.la: CLIV. Venenum & incantamenta carminum, degenerum animorum occulta nocendi tela habentur.
units.tr: CLIV. Poison and the incantations of verses are regarded as the hidden weapons of degenerate minds for doing harm.

units.la: De veneno his verbis Cornelius: sævam vim morbi augebat persuasio veneni à Pisone accepti. de incantatione pluribus: & reperiebantur sola ac parietibus trita[?] humanorum corporum reliquiæ, carmina, & devotiones, & nomen Germanici plumbeis tabulis insculptum, feminifi[?] cineres, ac tabe obliti, aliaque maleficia, quis creditur animas numinibus infernis sacrari. Venenum quin interimendi vim habeat, nec intra viscera modò esu aut potu receptum, sed si paulo subtilius fuerit, chartæ libri aut epistolæ illitum, ardenti-um tædarum fumigatione cerebro attractum, chirothecis aut interiori toge aspersum, à paucis ambigitur. Quo loco sint habenda, & cujus efficacia, dirarum devotionum carmina, nec inter theologos video, nec inter medicos convenire. Sane quid characteres, aut quid verborum susurrationes, roboris habeant, non facile est indagatu. nisi imaginationis vehementia, aut occulta mali genii inspiratio accedat, vanitate qui-dem sunt vaniora. Poena tamen ejusmodi malefico-rum genus coercendum, etiamsi ad nocendi effectum forte non perveniat.
units.tr: Concerning poison, Cornelius says in these words: the belief that the poison received from Piso had been given to him increased the savage force of the disease. On incantation he says more: there were found buried in the ground and in the walls the remains of human bodies, spells and curses, and the name of Germanicus inscribed on leaden tablets, the ashes of a woman smeared with decay, and other charms by which souls are believed to be consecrated to the infernal gods. That poison has the power to kill, not only when it is taken into the body by eating or drinking, but also, if it is made more subtle, when it is smeared on the pages of a book or a letter, drawn into the brain by the smoke of burning torches, or sprinkled on gloves or the inner toga, few doubt. But where the verses of dire curses should be placed, and what their efficacy is, I see that neither the theologians nor the physicians agree. Indeed, what characters or whispered words have strength is not easy to investigate. Unless the vehemence of the imagination or the secret inspiration of an evil spirit is present, they are emptier than vanity itself. Nevertheless this kind of wicked sorcery must be punished, even if it perhaps does not reach its effect of harming.

units.la: CLV.
units.tr: CLV.

units.la: Aperté irasci quàm occulté odisse, nihil metuentis viri est.
units.tr: To be openly angry rather than secretly to hate is the mark of a man who fears nothing.

units.la: Romani, quos justis de causis aversabantur, iis ami-citiam renuntiabant: ne, fi quid in posterum damni accipiffent, violationem amicitiæ, cujus nomen inte-f omnes sanctum ac inviolabile, incusarent. Hoc exmo-re Germanicus, componit epistolas, quis amicitiam et renuntiabat. Laudi Agricolæ, in vita ejus, datur aperi-tum offensæ indicium. ut boni comis, ita adversus malos injucundus, caterum ex iracundia nihil supere-rat. secretum & silentium ejus non timeres. bonefti putabat offendere, quam odisse. quæ parum ad aulæ Tiberianæ occultos mores faciunt.
units.tr: The Romans, whom they shunned for just causes, they renounced friendship with, lest, if they suffered any loss afterwards, they could accuse them of violating a friendship whose name everyone holds sacred and inviolable. In this manner Germanicus composed letters in which he renounced friendship. In the Life of Agricola, an open sign of offence is praised: as he was kind to the good, so he was unpleasant to the bad, and there was nothing hidden in his anger. You would not fear his secrecy or silence. He thought it more honourable to offend than to hate. These things have little in common with the hidden manners of the court of Tiberius.

units.la: CLVI.
units.tr: CLVI.

units.la: Magnorum belli ducum vita æru-mnofa, exitus vitæ lamentabilis.
units.tr: The lives of great commanders in war were full of hardship, and their ends were lamentable.

units.la: Fortunatum tantorum exercituum ductu, tot ex-peditionum triumphis ac plausibus vulgus Germani-cum ducebat. Aliter ipse, morti vicinus, de vita sua & vitæ catastropha judicabat. referatu [?] patri ac fratri, quibus acerbitatibus dilaceratus, quibus insidiis cir-cumventus, miserrimam vitam pessima morte finie-rim. Miserrimam certè vitam, inter hostiles clamores, mutuas civium & barbarorum clades; inter seditio-nes militares, ad cædis minas progressas; inter occul-tas parentum iras & insidias, aulæ non obscura æmu-latio[?]lationum studia! Pessimam mortem, non tolerando cruciatu inimicorum votis, ac penè oculis, pascendis, quorum ipsi autores jactentur! Lubet in annales Grae-corum & Romanorum exspatiari, indeque funera non funera eximiorum belli ducum decerpere. nam de vi-tae aerumnis, nimis fastidiosum foret differere. Cyrus, Persarum imperii fundator, Tamyris foeminae ferro truncatus, avulso cervice capite, inque utrem sanguine repletum conjecto, cum exprobratione sanguino-lentae sitis, miserrimum in modum interiit. Alexander Macedo, à rerum gestarum magnitudine Magni cognomen adeptus, ipso quietis à tot laboribus primor-dio, poculi haustu, sive immodico sive pharmacis in-secto, excruciatus, infelicem animam efflavit. Roma-nis celebrati hostes externi Pyrrhus & Annibal. Quo-rum ille lapidis, manu mulieb̄ri rotati, ictu concidit. hic miseriarum finem, & majoris metus remedium, à veneno in fauces injecto petiit. Romanorum ante urbem à Gallis dirutam bellicosissimus, Martius Co-riolanus, hostili in exilio, post tristem patriae à fe-stae[?] memoriam, concursu hominum lapides jaculan-tium fœdissimè obrutus occubuit. Florente imperio celeritate victoriarum priores omnes & posteros antegressus, C. Julius Caesar, strictis in curia gladiis, plus-quam triginta ictibus confossus jacuit. Graeciae uni-versae decus, flos Athenarum, Themistocles, patria profugus, apud infensos hostes exul, desperabundus haustu taurini cruoris mortem quaesivit. Felicior eo Epaminondas, Boeotarum extra dubium vir bello praestantissimus, hostium saltem telo mortem invenit. Spartana in republica Pausanias, Persarum ad Plataeas debellator, Ephororum consensu ignominiosa morte deletus obiit. Achaeorum fortissimus Philopoemen, casu ab hostibus circumventus, in squalorem carceris conjectus, crudeli tandem nece exspiravit. Mitto vi-cinis in regionibus Bajazethem à Tamerlano (sive Timero) in cavea circumductum; mitto ipsius Time-ri cruentum interitum. mitto apud Romanos Marii, Suillae, aliorum potentia nimiorum, extrema. Europae universæ terror Attila, ubi sævitia bellorum fatigatus, quieti se ac epulis mancipavit, frusto carnis in fauces injecto, suffocatus, cum esculentis crudis sanguinem ejaculatus, animam crudelem exspuit magis quam efflavit. Nostra memoria Suecorum primum & su-premum ornamentum, Gustavus Adolphus, ita lace-ratis in pugna membris distractus fertur, ut in hunc diem de corpore ejus invento, & non fictis exequiarum honoribus terræ mandato, multi dubitant. Sic quam quæsivere per strages gentium nominis memoriam, caro ærumnarum & tandem miserabilis fati au-ctoramento redemerunt.
units.tr: Germanicus was led by the common people, who saw him as fortunate in commanding such great armies and in the triumphs and applause of so many campaigns. Otherwise he himself, near death, judged his own life and its catastrophe differently: I shall tell my father and brother by what bitterness I was torn, by what snares I was surrounded, and how I ended a most wretched life by a most wretched death. Indeed a most wretched life: amid the cries of enemies, the mutual slaughter of citizens and barbarians; amid military mutinies that advanced to threats of murder; amid the hidden anger and plots of parents, and the no-less-obvious zeal of rivalry at court! A most wretched death: not enduring the torment that the wishes of enemies, and nearly the eyes of those whose very authors are boasted of, fed upon! It is pleasant to range through the annals of the Greeks and Romans and to pluck from them the deaths, not the deaths, of eminent commanders in war; for to dwell at length on the troubles of life would be too tedious. Cyrus, founder of the Persian empire, was beheaded by Tomyris, a woman, who cut off his head and threw it into a skin filled with blood, with the taunt of bloodthirsty thirst, and so he died most miserably. Alexander the Macedonian, who gained the name of Great from the greatness of his deeds, at the very beginning of his rest from so many labours, was tortured by a draught from a cup, whether it was immoderate or infused with drugs, and breathed out his unhappy soul. Among the Romans, the foreign enemies most celebrated were Pyrrhus and Hannibal. Of these, the one fell to a blow from a stone hurled by a woman's hand; the other sought an end to his miseries, and a remedy for greater fear, by putting poison into his throat. Marcius Coriolanus, the most warlike of the Romans before the city was razed by the Gauls, after sad memories of his country, in hostile exile, was most foully overwhelmed and died by a crowd of men throwing stones. While the empire was flourishing, Gaius Julius Caesar, who outstripped all earlier and later men in the speed of his victories, lay pierced by more than thirty blows of drawn swords in the senate house. Themistocles, the glory of all Greece and flower of Athens, fleeing his country and an exile among hostile enemies, in despair sought death by drinking bull's blood. Happier than he was Epaminondas, beyond doubt the most outstanding man of war among the Boeotians, who at least found death by an enemy's weapon. In the Spartan state, Pausanias, who defeated the Persians at Plataea, died in an ignominious death, destroyed by the consent of the Ephors. Philopoemen, the bravest of the Achaeans, was surrounded by enemies by chance, thrown into the squalor of a prison, and at last expired by a cruel death. I pass over Bajazet, led about in a cage by Tamerlane (or Timur) in neighbouring regions; I pass over the bloody death of Timur himself. I pass over the downfall of Marius, of Sulla, and of others among the Romans whose power was excessive. Attila, the terror of all Europe, when he was worn out by the cruelty of wars, gave himself over to rest and feasts; a piece of meat thrust into his throat choked him, and with raw food he spewed out blood, and breathed out his cruel soul rather than breathing it out. In our own memory, Gustavus Adolphus, the first and last ornament of the Swedes, is said to have been so torn in battle that many still doubt, to this day, whether a body found and committed to the earth with unfeigned funeral honours was indeed his. Thus what they sought through slaughter of nations, the memory of their name, they bought at the price of troubles and at last a wretched fate.

units.la: CLVII.
units.tr: CLVII.

units.la: * Plures fortunam principis quam principem adorant.
units.tr: Many worship the prince's fortune rather than the prince himself.

units.la: Quem ut viventem mimica persona colebant, ita vivis ereptum histrionio fletu deplorant. Qualem fui memoriam Germanicus, extremum amicos affatus, deprecatur. Non hoc præcipuum amicorum munus est, prosequi defunctum ignavo questu : sed qua volueris, meminisse, quæ mandaverit exequi. flebunt Germani-cum etiam ignoti : vindicabitis vos, si me potiùs quàm fortunam meam fovebatis. Sensit hoc monitum Ser-gius Galba, eoque Pisonem, adoptione filium, instru-xit. Etiam ego ac tu simplicissimè inter nos bodie lo-quimur ; cæteri libentiùs cum fortuna nostra, quam nobiscum. Etiam in sincerè amicis, alii regem inho-mine, alii hominem in rege ampleCtuntur. Exhac di-stinctionum origine Alexander Macedo, amicorum alium φιλοβασιλεὺς[?], alium φιλαλέξανδρος[?] appellavit. Sic vice versa reges alium ut potentiæ suæ studiosum, consiliorum suggestione, alium venustatis gratia & oblectamento otii, diligunt.
units.tr: They worshipped him while he lived as one worships a mask on the stage, and now that he has been snatched from the living they mourn him with theatrical weeping. This is the kind of memory of himself that Germanicus, speaking to his friends at the end, asks for. It is not the chief duty of friends to attend the dead with idle lamentation, but to remember what he wished and to carry out what he commanded. Even strangers will weep for Germanicus; you will vindicate yourselves if you cherished me rather than my fortune. Sergius Galba perceived this warning, and therefore prepared Piso, whom he had adopted as his son, accordingly. Even you and I speak most candidly with each other today; others gladly speak more with our fortune than with us. Even among sincere friends, some embrace the king in the man, others the man in the king. From this origin of the distinction, Alexander of Macedon called some of his friends "lovers of the king" [φιλοβασιλεύς] and others "lovers of Alexander" [φιλαλέξανδρος]. So, conversely, kings love one man as devoted to their power, for the counsel he offers, and another for the charm and delight he brings to their leisure.

units.la: CLVIII.
units.tr: CLVIII.

units.la: Splendor natalium & conjugii commiserationis incitamentum.
units.tr: The splendour of birth, and a spur to pity for a wife.

units.la: Utitur hoc sperandae ultionis argumento Germanicus: Ostendite populo Romano divi Augusti neptem, vandemque conjugem meam. Quod aliquando in con-trarium vergit. Certe huius ipsius Agrippinae filia, matri cognominis, novo Neronis principatu principium saeviendi a Junio Silano cepit, viro nobili, & quod tunc spectaretur, à Caesarum posteris. quippe & Silanus D. Augusti abnepos erat. hac causa necis. Ipsa quam hic misericordiae accendendae proponit, uxor Germanici, divi Augusti nepos, iis nominibus odium apud Tiberium & Sejanum, & cum numerosa prole exidium meruit. quod in sequentibus docebitur.
units.tr: Germanicus uses this as an argument for hoped-for vengeance: Show the Roman people the granddaughter of the divine Augustus, and my wife. Yet this sometimes turns to the opposite effect. Indeed, the daughter of this very Agrippina, who shared her mother's name, began her savagery under Nero's new principate with Junius Silanus, a noble man, and what was then looked at among the posterity of the Caesars. For Silanus was also a great-grandson of the divine Augustus. This was the cause of his death. The same woman whom he here puts forward to kindle pity, the wife of Germanicus and granddaughter of the divine Augustus, earned hatred from Tiberius and Sejanus by these very titles, and exile for herself and her numerous offspring. This will be shown in what follows.

units.la: CLIX.
units.tr: CLIX.

units.la: Columna domus paternae liberi.
units.tr: Children are the pillars of a father's house.

units.la: Est ex antiquo Graecorum senario depromptum axioma, ab iis, & per eos a judicibus, ultionem sperat Germanicus: numerate sex liberos. Antiqui apud Romanos moris, liberorum productione misericordiam rei, aut actoris iniqua passi, apud judices movere. Sed jam Augustorum tempore alia flectendi ratio a foecunditate accessit, honoris lege praescripti expectatio. Exhausta enim caedibus Italia, caelibatu ob desperationem temporum frequentato, Augustus ferendis de matrimonio legibus, praemia foecunditati, poenas caelibatui irrogaverat. Quam in spem erectus Germanicus, numerum liberorum, & conjugis fertilitatem, profecerat, ut aequos judices adipiscantur, interpretatur. Quod in civili quidem ordine non dubitandum erat, at eminenti principum conditione, numerus liberorum, privatae vitae nescio-rum, oneri civitati aut distractioni futurus videbatur. Jam tum ab excessu Augusti, aula inter duos tantum, Drusum minorem & Germanicum, suspensa populi Romani forensis factio quaerebatur: serviendum feminae, duobusque inter super adolescentibus, qui tempus interim praemant, quandoque distrahant. Non equidem vanitatis arguo illud I. Titi ad patrem Vespasianum monituri: Non exercitus, non classes, perinde firma imperii munimenta sunt, quam numerum liberorum. sed nec illud pro levi hâs bendum, quod non nemo (13.Annal.) in animum re- vocat antiquas fratrum discordias, & insociabile regnum. Thebanum regnum duo fratres, & illi quidem eodem partu editi, propemodum everterunt: quid à multitudine aliquando non sperandum?
units.tr: Germanicus hopes for vengeance from the judges by an old axiom taken from a Greek senarius, which the Greeks, and through them the judges, adopted: Count six children. It was an old custom among the Romans that by producing children they moved judges to pity, whether the defendant or the party wronged had suffered unjustly. But already in the time of the Augusti another way of swaying them had been added to fertility: the expectation of reward prescribed by the law of honour. For Italy had been drained by slaughter, and celibacy had become common through despair of the times; Augustus, in bringing in laws concerning marriage, had attached rewards to fertility and penalties to celibacy. Raised up by this hope, Germanicus interpreted his number of children and his wife's fertility as a means of obtaining fair judges. In the civic order this was beyond doubt, but in the eminent condition of princes, a number of children, unknown in private life, seemed likely to become a burden on the state or a cause of division. Already from the death of Augustus, a faction in the Roman forum was sought between the only two in the court, Drusus the younger and Germanicus, held in suspense: One must serve a woman, and two young men above her, who meanwhile seize the time and at some point tear everything apart. I do not indeed charge with vanity that saying of Titus when he was about to advise his father Vespasian: Not armies, not fleets, are as firm a defence of empire as the number of children. But nor should that be set aside lightly, which someone (Annals 13) recalls: the ancient discords of brothers and a kingdom that cannot be shared. Two brothers, and indeed brothers born of the same birth, nearly overturned the kingdom of Thebes. What might not sometimes be feared from a multitude?

units.la: CLX. Ficulneum gratiæ scelere quæsitæ præsidium.
units.tr: CLX. A fig-leaf defence of favour sought by crime.

units.la: Piso & Plancina è simultate cum Germanico & Agrippina, aut etiam clandestinis Tiberii & Augustæ mandatis, placabilem sibi judicem sperabant. Germanicus causæ cognitione ad plures judices, non creditu-ros ejusmodi à Tiberio suggestiones, aut iis non subscripturos, devoluta spem reis conceptam intervertit. Misericordia cum accusantibus erit: fingentibusque scelesta mandata, aut non credent homines, aut non ignoscent. Quid enim tacita Tiberii & Liviæ conscientia, quid gratia quam profiteri non auderent, profutura præjudicio oppressis erat: Est tibi Augusta conscientia, est Cafaris favor, sed in occulto: & periisse Germanicum nulli factantius mærent, quàm qui maximè lætantur: sapienter Pisonem patrem filius infrà monebit. Nonnunquam aperte autoritatem defugiunt scelesti mandati autores. Hic ipse Tiberius, qui cædem Agrippæ Postumi per Sallustium Crispum mandaverat, nunciantì centurioni, ut mos militiæ, factum esse quod imperasset: neque imperasse sese, & rationem factı reddendam apud senatum, respondit. 1.Annal. aut sinistris oculis nequitiæ ministros aspiciunt: quod Aniceti apud Neronem parricidam præmium.
units.tr: Piso and Plancina, out of enmity towards Germanicus and Agrippina, or even on the secret orders of Tiberius and Augusta, hoped to find a judge who would be lenient to them. Germanicus, by referring the case to several judges, who would either not believe such insinuations from Tiberius or would not put their names to them, cut short the hope the accused had conceived. There will be mercy for the accusers: but men will either not believe those who invent wicked orders, or will not forgive them. For what good to the oppressed would the silent complicity of Tiberius and Livia be, or the favour which they dared not openly profess? Augusta has your conscience on your side, and Caesar's favour, but in secret: and those who rejoice most keenly at Germanicus's death are the first to mourn it in public, as the son will wisely warn Piso the father below. Sometimes the authors of wicked orders shrink from openly owning their authority. Tiberius himself, who had ordered the killing of Agrippa Postumus through Sallustius Crispus, when the centurion reported to him, as is the custom of the army, that what he had commanded was done, replied that he had given no such order, and that an account of the deed would have to be rendered before the senate. 1 Annals. Or they look askance at the agents of their wickedness, as Anicetus was rewarded by Nero the parricide.

units.la: CLXI. Viri constantis est, anima ante quam fide data emigrare.
units.tr: CLXI. It is the mark of a steadfast man to lose his life before he breaks faith once it has been pledged.

units.la: Maximè fi ea fides jurejurando fancita, & bonitate causæ stabilita perstat. Juravere amici, dextram morientis continges, spiritum ante quàm ultionem amissuros. In militie vel absque causae intuitu pugnae constantia laudi dabatur. De Catilinae collectitio exercitu Sallustius: nam fere, quem quisque vivus pugnando locum ceperat, cum amissa anima, corpore tegebat.
units.tr: This holds especially when the pledge is confirmed by an oath and kept firm by the justice of the cause. They swore as friends that they would lose their lives before they lost their grip on the dying man's hand, before they had avenged him. Even in a war, or regardless of the justice of the cause, steadfastness in battle was praised. Sallust writes of Catiline's ragged army: for nearly every man, having taken his place in the fight while alive, covered that place with his body after his life had gone.

units.la: De Telebois, Thebani populi hostibus, in Amphitruo-ne M. Plautus: Crebri hostes cadunt, nostri contra ingruunt. Sed fugam in se tamen nemo convertitur: Nec recedit loco, quin statim rem gerat. Animam amittunt, priusquam loco demigrent.
units.tr: Of the Teleboans, enemies of the Theban people, Plautus says in the Amphitryo: "Many enemies fall, while ours press forward." But no one turns his back in flight, nor gives up his ground without fighting on the spot. They lose their lives before they leave their post.

units.la: CLXII.
units.tr: CLXII.

units.la: Non est tuta adversus potentiores ferocia.
units.tr: Ferocity is not safe against the more powerful.

units.la: Nam nec illis nocueris, & tibi exitii maturitatem accersiveris. Germanicus ad uxorem versus, per memoriam sui, per communes liberos oravit, exueret ferociam, savienti fortunae submitteret animum, neu regressa in urbem, aemulatione potentia validiores irrita-ret. Cujus praecepti non satis Agrippina memor, aut minus in exequendo fortunata, vita, sermone, silentio lentorem animi Tiberiani pupugit. Multa in aulica servitute incommoda mussitanda, multae injuriae silentio devorandae. Imo necimperantibus in ultionem, aut apertum contumeliae acceptae sensum, sine freni morsu omni occasione prorumpendum. Sæpè iis à necessitate temporum, sæpè à personae quam gerunt gravitate, dissimulatio imperatur. Hannibale fauces Italiae premente, cum cladis Gallicanae rumor patres ad ultionem stimularet: Consul in senatu disseruit, cum ab Hannibale jugulum Reip. foderetur, illic scuta objicienda esse; reliqua vulnera interim dissimulatione tegenda. perituros Romanos, si tantum audeant, quantum dolor & ira suadeant. uti facunda oratione, tertia Historiae Romanae decade, T. Livius. Idem Romani nefaria petulantia, quam Dionysius Halicarnassensis in Excerptis legationibus describit, in suis legatis violati, ab animi sui altitudine id imperarunt, ut contumeliae pudendae vindicta, circumfusis hostium[?] nationibus, in commodiorem temporum opportuni- tatem prolataretur. De nonnemine apud Corneliurn. xi.Annal. ira magis quam ex usu prafenti accenfua, qui non meminerat, viro sapienti saluti ante quam vin- dictae consulendum. Haec irae moderatio necessitate rerum imperarut: alia ab imperantium, quos minima tela non laedunt nec attingunt, altitudine in qua re multus est Seneca. In universum illud Ludovici XI. ad Carolum filium, nominis ejus inter reges Galliae octavum, praeceptum, Qui nescit dissimulare, nescit regnare, fano sensu non diffplicet. Ergo multo ad fco- pum nostrum accommodatius, Qui nescit dissimula- re, nescit potentioribus parere.
units.tr: For you will neither harm them, and you will bring on your own ruin sooner. Germanicus turned to his wife and, by the memory of himself and by their common children, begged her to lay aside her ferocity, to submit her spirit to a savage fortune, and not to return to the city and provoke the more powerful by rivalry. Agrippina, not sufficiently mindful of this advice, or less fortunate in carrying it out, by her life, her speech and her silence, stung the sluggish spirit of Tiberius. In the servitude of the court many grievances must be muttered under the breath, many wrongs swallowed in silence. Indeed, when one cannot take revenge, or openly show the sense of an insult received, one must not let slip at every opportunity the bite of an unbridled tongue. Often dissimulation is demanded by the necessity of the times, often by the weight of the person one represents. When Hannibal was pressing on the jaws of Italy, and the rumour of the defeat in Gaul was urging the senators to vengeance, the consul argued in the Senate that while Hannibal was digging into the throat of the commonwealth, shields must be held up in front of it, and the other wounds meanwhile concealed by dissimulation; the Romans would perish if they dared as much as their grief and anger urged them to. So Livy, in the third decade of his Roman History, with eloquent speech. The same Romans, with the wicked insolence which Dionysius of Halicarnassus describes in his Excerpts from the Embassies, when their envoys were wronged, from the depth of their spirit ordered that the vengeance for a shameful insult be postponed to a more convenient moment of opportunity, while the hostile nations were thrown around them. Concerning a certain man, Cornelius, Annals 11: "kindled more by anger than by the advantage of the present moment"; he had forgotten that a wise man must look to his safety before his vengeance. This moderation of anger was imposed by the necessity of circumstances; another kind comes from the height in which the rulers stand, whom the smallest weapons do not wound or reach, a matter on which Seneca has much to say. In general, that precept of Louis XI to his son Charles, the eighth of that name among the kings of France, "He who does not know how to dissemble does not know how to reign," does not displease in a sound sense. Therefore, far more fittingly for our purpose: He who does not know how to dissemble does not know how to obey the more powerful.

units.la: CLXIII. Summae fortunae altitudinem fere- nitas vultus non deprimit.
units.tr: CLXIII. A calm countenance does not lower the height of the highest fortune.

units.la: Extremum Germanici elogium, paucis cum summa elegantia verbis expressum: cum magnitudinem & gravitatem summâ fortunâ retinuerit, invidiam & arrogantiam effugerat, at quibus rebus eam effugerat? comitate in socios, mansuetudine in hostes, vul- tus & verborum venerabile amoenitate, quae mire grata populis, nec in vitiorum limites deflectunt, ut illa Itali regis Cherufcorum facilitas. modo comitatem & temperantiam nulli invisam, fapius vinolentiam ac libidines, grata barbaris, usurpans. x 1. Annal. Non enim aut honesta, aut fatis firma, à vitiorum similitudine vivacis gratiae aucupatio. Propius ad Germanicos mores Julius Agricola accedit: cui tempora cura- rum remissionumque divisa, ubi conventus ac judicia poscerent, gravis, intentus, severus, & saepius miseri- cors, ubi officio satisfactum, nulla ultra potestatis per- sona. tristitiam & arrogantiam & avaritiam exuerat; nec illi, quod est rarissimum, aut facilitas autoritatem, aut severitas amorem deminuit, uti facundè Cornelius in Vita Agricolae.
units.tr: The final eulogy of Germanicus, expressed in a few words with the greatest elegance: though he kept his greatness and dignity at the height of his fortune, he escaped envy and arrogance. But by what means did he escape them? By courtesy towards his allies, mildness towards his enemies, and a venerable pleasantness of face and speech, which is wonderfully pleasing to the peoples and does not bend towards the limits of vice, like the affability of the Cheruscan king Italicus, who, while using courtesy and temperance, which were hated by no one, often used drunkenness and lusts, which are pleasing to barbarians. Indeed, a pursuit of favour that copies the likeness of vices is neither honourable nor secure enough. Julius Agricola comes closer to the manners of Germanicus: his times were divided between the cares of office and times of relaxation; when assemblies and courts demanded it he was serious, attentive, strict, and more often merciful; when his duty was done, he did not carry on the character of his power at all. He had laid aside sullenness, arrogance and avarice; and neither did his affability lessen his authority, nor his strictness his being loved, which is very rare, as Cornelius eloquently says in the Life of Agricola.

units.la: CLXIV. Virtutum memoria omni exequiarum funebri pompa fulgentior.
units.tr: CLXIV. The memory of virtues shines brighter than any funeral pomp.

units.la: Hæc & supplicia turpitudine vitæ promeritis, illa nonnisi bonis contingit. Nec quicquam Germanici laudi detcritur, cui funus sine imaginibus & pompa, per laudes & memoriam virtutum ejus celebre fuit, quia.
units.tr: These punishments fall only on those who have earned them by a shameful life; the other honours come only to good men. Nor is anything taken from Germanicus's praise, since his funeral was without ancestral masks or pageantry, and was famous for the praises and remembrance of his virtues, because.

units.la: Animosè Ennius poëta:
units.tr: The poet Ennius boldly says:

units.la: Nemo me lacrymis decoret, neque funera fletu, Faxo: cur? volito vivus per ora virum.
units.tr: Let no one adorn me with tears, nor honour my funeral with weeping. I will tell you why: I fly alive through the mouths of men.

units.la: Animosius Lyrici carminis princeps:
units.tr: The prince of lyric poetry says more boldly still:

units.la: Absint inani funere næniæ, Luctusque turpes & querimoniæ, Compescè clamorem, ac sepulcri Mitte supervacuos honores.
units.tr: Let dirges be absent from the empty funeral, and base lamentations and complaints. Check the clamour, and omit the superfluous honours of the tomb.

units.la: Oda xx. libri secundi Carminum.
units.tr: Ode 20 of the second book of the Odes.

units.la: Molliter, qui tanto opere sumptuosos funerum honores in extremis requirunt. A cujusmodi ineptiis Homerici heroës, ut à poëtis non abeam, haud alieni sunt; & Solon, sapientum Græciæ non postremus, carmine emissò cupiditatem eam non diffitetur. Si quid datur mœstitiæ animi nostri, si quid honori defuncti; sine pomposis publicæ tristitiæ imitamentis, dolorem animo concoquamus, memoriam vivis erepti jucunda virtutum laude celebremus. Non male prisci Germaniæ incolæ; apud quos funerum nulla ambitio: & qui monumentorum arduum & operosum honorem, uti gravem defunctis, aspernantur. Lamenta ac lacrymas cito, dolorem & tristitiam tardè ponunt. Fœminis lugere honestum est, viris meminisse. Si quid è sacro etiam penu promendum: felicissimum exequiarum genus est, quo defunctos, ærumnarum beatam requiem nactos, opera sequuntur. de quâ exequiarum sempiterna pompa autor Apocalypseos, cap. 14. v.13. Sed ad Germanicum, & caducam virtutum civilium memoriam, revertor.
units.tr: Softly, those who so eagerly seek lavish funeral honours at the end of life. The Homeric heroes, not to depart from the poets, are not unlike such follies, and Solon, not the least of Greece's wise men, does not deny this desire in a poem he published. If anything is given to the sadness of our mind, and anything to the honour of the dead, let us digest our grief without the showy imitations of public mourning, and celebrate the memory of the one snatched from us with the pleasing praise of his virtues. The ancient inhabitants of Germany were not wrong; among them there is no ambition in funerals, and they scorn the lofty and laborious honour of monuments, as a burden to the dead. They are quick to put aside laments and tears, and slow to lay down grief and sadness. It is fitting for women to mourn, for men to remember. If anything is to be drawn even from the sacred storehouse, the happiest kind of funeral is that in which the dead, having won the blessed rest from their toils, are followed by their works. The author of the Apocalypse speaks of this eternal pomp of funerals in chapter 14, verse 13. But I return to Germanicus and to the fleeting memory of civic virtues.

units.la: Magno cum Alexandro, è vulgi tamen magis, quam vel Cornelii vel meo, sensu, comparaverunt. ætatu non abnuo,genere mortis non repugno; de propinqua-tate locorum in quibus interiit, litem non moveo. Sed magnitudine rerum gestarum, & felicitatis bellici non interrupto cursu, immane quantum distant! nam externorum, quae res & actiones circumstant, contentione vel stultissimus sapientissimo, ignavus viro[?] fortissimo comparetur. Temeritatem in Alexandro, qua & Seneca eum aspergit, non per omnia deprehendo. Noverat Persas, nondum in eam corporum ac animo-rum mollitiem fractos, non semel in Graecia terra ma-rique cecidisse. Non eum fugerat, Xenophontem militiae rudem tantillas copias, per immensum terra-rum spatium, invitis Persis reduxisse: Agesilaum nu-per exigua manu Asiam propinquam concussisse. Phalangas in promptu habebat, & genere armorum ac ordinis, & exercitio bellico Graecis praestantiores. Se vero ducem quot millibus anteferat? Virtutem au-tem militum, non hominum numerum, in acie vince-re, vel cum mediocriter eruditis callebat. Suam igitur laudem Germanico non invidentes, abiis quae invi-diam magis, quam laudis cumulum motura suint[?], ab-stinemus.
units.tr: They have compared him with Alexander the Great, though by the judgment of the crowd more than by that of Cornelius or of myself. I do not deny the age, I do not resist the manner of death, and about the nearness of the places where he died I do not stir up a dispute. But in the greatness of the deeds done and the uninterrupted course of military success, how immensely they differ! For when external things and circumstances are set side by side, even the most foolish man might be compared with the wisest, and the coward with the bravest. I do not wholly detect the rashness in Alexander with which Seneca also taints him. He knew that the Persians, not yet broken into that softness of body and mind, had more than once fallen in the land and sea of Greece. Nor had it escaped him that Xenophon, unskilled in war, led a tiny force back across an immense stretch of land despite the Persians; and that Agesilaus only recently shook nearby Asia with a small band. He had phalanxes at hand, superior to the Greeks in kind of arms, in order, and in military training. But how many thousands does he set himself above as a leader? Even men moderately learned knew that battles are won by the courage of soldiers rather than by the number of men. Therefore, not begrudging Germanicus his praise, we refrain from those things which would stir up envy rather than add to his glory.

units.la: CLXV.
units.tr: CLXV.

units.la: Affectuum & praejudicii nebulas ve-ri judicii radii ægre perrumpunt.
units.tr: The clouds of emotion and prejudice are hardly pierced by the rays of true judgment.

units.la: Non tantum furore correptus Ajax Telamonius pecora pro Atridis mactat, aut pro Ulysse verberat: veiùm[?] etiàm mente & oculis non capti, falsum pro vero arripiunt. In tanta judicii de obitu Germanici di-sceptatione, corpore in foro celebris urbis nudato, pratulerint venefici signa, parum constitit. nam uti quis mi-sericordia in Germanicum, & praesumpta suspi-cione, aut favore in Pisonem pronior, diversi interpre-tabantur[?]. In re oculis subjecta caecutiebant: quid eos in ambiguo jure facturos arbitrere? Quamobrem aut ad judicandum vocandi non sunt, qui his aut illis amore vel odio implicantur, aut omni affectuum im-perio superiores evadant oportet. Ex hac scaturigine orta judicium apud Romanos rejectio, donec ab utra- que litigantium parte consentiretur: quanquam ne sic quidem veri judicii finem assecuta. Quod judici, non minus historiam scripturo imperamus: ut aures praejudicio vacuas, inclinationi partium aut aversationi clausas, circumgerat. qua de re alio in loco fusius.
units.tr: Ajax son of Telamon was not only seized by fury when he slaughtered the cattle for the Atreidae or beat them for Ulysses; men with minds and eyes not blinded also snatch the false for the true. In so great a dispute over the death of Germanicus, with the body laid bare in the forum of the famous city, the signs of poisoning hardly agreed. For as each man was more inclined to pity for Germanicus, with suspicion already presumed, or to favour for Piso, they interpreted the same things differently. In a matter laid before their eyes they grew blind; what do you suppose they would do in a doubtful case of law? Therefore, either those who are entangled by love or hatred for one side or the other must not be called to judge, or they must rise above all the dominion of the passions. From this source arose the Roman practice of rejecting judges, until agreement was given by each of the litigating parties; yet even so they did not attain the end of true judgment. We require of a judge no less than of one who will write history that he go round with his ears free of prejudice, and closed to leaning towards one party or aversion to the other. On this matter more fully in another place.

units.la: CLXVI.
units.tr: CLXVI.

units.la: Ultionis cupiditas omni affectu flagrantior.
units.tr: The desire for vengeance burns more fiercely than any other passion.

units.la: Luctu mariti, metu imperantis Tiberii, miseratione parvulorum Agrippina rapiebatur. Quibus omnibus vindictae posthabitis, quamquam defessa luctu, & corpore agro, omnium tamen quae ultionem morarentur intolerans, ascendit classem cum cineribus Germanici. ne hybernae quidem navigationis ancipiti casu formidato: ut in sequentis hbri[?] exordio docetur. Ratio tamen, & constantior natura, hujus perturbationis stimulum, consilio vel mora, retundit. Sexus & aetas imbecillior, aut viri impetu abrepti, isto monstro facilius vincuntur.
units.tr: Agrippina was carried away by grief for her husband, by fear of the emperor Tiberius, and by pity for her little children. With all of these set aside, although weary with grief and worn in body, she was nonetheless intolerant of everything that delayed vengeance, and she boarded the fleet with the ashes of Germanicus, not fearing even the perilous chance of winter sailing, as is taught at the beginning of the following book. Reason, however, and a steadier nature, blunt the goad of this disturbance by counsel or by delay. Weaker sex and age, or men seized by sudden impulse, are more easily overcome by this monster.

units.la: At vindicta bonum, vita jucundius ipsa.
units.tr: But vengeance is a good thing, dearer than life itself.

units.la: Nempe hoc indocti, quorum praecordia nullis interdum, aut levibus videas flagrantia causis, ut erudite Juvenalis.
units.tr: Surely this is said by the unlearned, whose hearts you may sometimes see burning for no cause or for trivial ones, as the learned Juvenal observes.

units.la: CLXVII.
units.tr: CLXVII.

units.la: Res adversae consilium adimunt.
units.tr: Adverse circumstances take away counsel.

units.la: Etiam constantis animi judicia in adversis hebescunt: nedum foemina, incerta ultionis, anxia fui, & infelici fecunditate fortuna toties obnoxia, nihil laba-scat. Pergit tamen, & dilationem aspernata, omnibus rebus, securitati etiam suae & suorum ultionis executionem anteponit. Quod consilium ut prima fronte ad votum, ita in exitu ipsi non satis respondit.
units.tr: Even the judgment of a steadfast mind grows dull in adversity, much more a woman's, uncertain of revenge, anxious, and so often exposed to fortune through her unhappy fertility, who wavers at nothing. Yet she persists, and, rejecting delay, she puts the execution of her vengeance before every other consideration, even her own safety and that of her family. This plan, which at first sight matched her wish, in the outcome did not altogether answer to it.

units.la: CLXVIII.
units.tr: CLXVIII.

units.la: In re ancipiti praeceps consilium tu-tissimum videtur.
units.tr: In a doubtful matter, a headlong counsel seems the safest.

units.la: Quanquam non fempe[r] felix est temeritas: ut ait apud T. Livium Fabius Maximus. Sæpius, quod est apud eundem Livium, consilia calida & audacia prima fronte læta sunt, tractatu dura, eventu tristia. Motus à provincia Syria Piso erat, eique Cn. Sentius præfectus, Piso audita Germanici morte, gaudio non moderatus, victimas cædit, templa adit. uxor ejus Plancina luctum amissæ sororis tum primùm læto cultu mutat. Jam in eo non mediocriter peccatum: sed ad magis præ- cipitia feruntur. Repetatne provinciam, quam non jure ablatam putabat, promptis centurionum & le- gionum studiis, Piso deliberat. Filius ejus M. Piso, ad tutiora inclinans, properandum in urbem censebat. argumentum fuafioni à spe impunitatis adjicit, nihil adhuc inexpiabile admissum, neque [fuf]piciones imbe- cillas aut inania fama pertime[scenda]. premi aliquem suspicione posse, convinci non posse. nec famæ, ubi senuerit evanituræ, serviendum. nam quod de simul- tate erga defunctum : discordiam erga Germanicum odio fortasse dignam, non paena: & ademptione provin- cia [satisfactum] inimicis, non permittendum, ut vindi- &tæ ansam quærentibus, graviori lapsu gladius & cri- minandi mucro in manum porrigatur. Quod fi regre- detur, obsistente Sentio, civile bellum incipi. quo su- fcepto, nihil inter dominationem sperandam, & cau- fam læsæ majestatis dicendam, medium futurum. dominationem, tanta Cæsareæ domus potentia, non esse inani spe in animum inducendam. vix obtinendæ Syriæ fiduciam vano conceptu alendam. nec duratu- ros in partibus centuriones militesque, apud quos re- cens imperatoris fui memoria, & penitus in fixus in Cæsares amor prævaleret. Hæc faniori adolescentis consilio, ituro in præceps parenti suadebantur. Contrà, ut ferme qui exintima amicitia creduntur, placitura audienti suggerunt, Domitius Celer auribus ejus ejusmodi monita non monita instillat: Utendum eventu. militum impetus acres cunctatione langue- fcere, aut in contrarium mutari. itaque urgendam, quæ fe offerat, fortunam. prompto militum animo pro munimento dubiorum utendum. addit aliquam juris & æqui micam : Pisonem, non sentium, Suria praepositum. Huic fasces & jus praetoris, huic legiones datas, nec posse autoritate principis mandata paucorum factiosorum audacia rescindi. Ratiunculam praeterea ab incerto pacis & belli casu accumulat. si quid hostile ingruat, quem justius arma oppositurum, quam qui legati autoritatem, & propria mandata acceperit? nutare socios onerum defatigatione, erectos in occasionem Parthos, dubiae fidei ut situ terrarum ita animis ambiguos Armenios pendere. qui si abesse legatum, deesse provinciae praetorem audiverint, rebus novis alacriter operam daturos. Ab his ad magis urgentem metum, & e rumoribus periculum accedit. Relinquendum etiam rumoribus tempus, quo senescant, plerumque innocentes, recenti invidia impares. quod argumentum validum fortassis fuisset, nisi aliquod inter belli civilis audaciam & adventus in urbem praecipitantiam, medium sperari quivisset. Potuisset enim Piso in aliquo Asiae angulo subsistere; inde Tiberium litteris adire, aperiret utri provinciam decerneret. si nihil impetraret; commeandis ultro citroque maddatis, moram qua fama veneficii senescere lucraretur. Sed ille ad calidiora promptior, urget ruentem. At si tenea exercitum, augeat vires, multa quae provideri non possint, fortuito in melius casura. metuendum se magis quam metuentem efficiat, quem arma tegant, fore intermi tutiorem. nec posse divinari, quid gaudens novandis rebus fortuna spondeat. Hinc ad metum, praecipuum dissuadendi reditus in urbem robur, relabitur. An festinamus cum Germanici cineribus appellere, ut te inauditum & indefensum plantus Agrippina, ac vulgus imperitum, primo rumore rapiant? Impetu enim, non ratione, vulgus duci: & judicum ipsorum oculos misericordiae ac odii glaucomate obduci. Quam vero ex Augustae, quam ex Tiberii occulto favore defensionem sperret, nullam fore. Est tibi Augusta conscientia, est Caesaris favor, sed in occulto: & perniffe Germanicum, nulli jactantius morrent, quam qui maximè latantur. Tam abstrusi esse Tiberium anî‑mi, tam secreta condentem, ut quid velit nec verbis nec fronte aperiat. Nec eum latere, quantæ invidiæ fit fatum Germanici, quibus rumoribus occultè diffe‑ratur. Tantum igitur abfore, ut quicquam ab eo pa‑trocinii sperandum fit, ut contra omnia adversa sint extimescenda. Utendum igitur fortuna,& casu obla‑tain sapientiam vertenda. Quid ad hæc Piso? quo ar‑gumentorum pondere abducitur? Haut magna mole Piso promptus ferocibus in sententiam trahitur. Infi‑tam animi ferociam facilè tumida verba propellunt, quam non bene sibi consuluisse, insipientium doctor eventus aperiet.
units.tr: Yet rashness is not always fortunate, as Fabius Maximus says in Titus Livius. More often, as the same Livy has it, bold and hasty plans look cheerful at the start, are hard to manage, and end sadly. Piso had been moved from the province of Syria, and Gnaeus Sentius, the prefect, was set over him. When Piso heard of Germanicus' death, he could not restrain his joy: he offered sacrifices and visited the temples. His wife Plancina now, for the first time, changed her mourning for festive dress, to mark the loss of her sister. In this there was already no small fault, but they were carried on to still greater rashness. Piso deliberated whether to seek back the province, which he thought had been taken from him unjustly, given the ready zeal of the centurions and legions. His son Marcus Piso, leaning towards safer courses, argued that they must hurry to the city, and added an argument for this advice from the hope of impunity: nothing inexpiable had yet been committed, and they should not dread weak suspicions or empty rumours. A man might be under suspicion, but could not be convicted; and they must not be enslaved to reputation, which would fade once it grew old. As for the hostility he had shown towards the dead man: the quarrel with Germanicus, perhaps deserving hatred but not punishment, and the removal from his province, which satisfied his enemies, must not be permitted, lest a sword and the point of accusation be put into the hands of those seeking an occasion for vengeance, by a graver fall. If he returned, and Sentius opposed him, civil war would begin. Once that was undertaken, there would be nothing in between: it would be either domination or a trial for treason. Domination was not to be hoped for in empty expectation, given the great power of the house of Caesar; nor should confidence of holding Syria be nursed by a vain notion. Nor would the centurions and soldiers hold out on his side, among whom the recent memory of their general, and a love deeply fixed in the Caesars, would prevail. These were the counsels offered to the young man, for the sake of his father, who was rushing headlong. On the other side, as is usual with those thought to be on intimate terms, they offered advice that would please the listener. Domitius Celer dripped into his ears such admonitions, which were no admonitions: One must make use of the event. The fierce impulse of the soldiers would weaken through delay, or be turned the other way; therefore the fortune that offered itself must be pressed. The soldiers' ready spirit must be used as a bulwark against doubts. He added a little of the language of right and justice: Piso was set over Syria, not Sentius. To him were given the fasces and the authority of a praetor, to him the legions, and the commands of a few factious men could not be annulled by the audacity of such men, when the authority of the emperor stood. Besides, he piled on a small argument from the uncertain chance of peace and war: If any hostile attack should come, who would more justly oppose it with arms than he who had received the authority of a legate and his own commission? The allies were wavering from the weariness of their burdens, the Parthians were raised up for the opportunity, and the Armenians, of doubtful loyalty as much in their minds as in their position, hung in suspense. If they heard that the legate was away and the province lacked a praetor, they would eagerly set to work on revolution. From these arguments he moved to a fear that pressed harder, and danger arose from rumours: There must also be left time for rumours, in which the innocent, as a rule, grow old and are unequal to fresh hatred. This argument might have been strong, had there not been some middle course to hope for between the boldness of civil war and the headlong rush to the city. For Piso could have stayed in some corner of Asia, from which he might have written to Tiberius and asked him to decide which of the two should have the province. If he got nothing, he could gain time by sending messages back and forth, during which the rumour of poisoning would grow old. But he, readier for hotter courses, pressed on the rushing man: But if he held the army, and increased its strength, many things that cannot be foreseen would turn out for the better by chance. He would make himself more feared than fearing, for he would be safer when protected by arms, and it could not be divined what fortune, rejoicing in revolution, might promise. From here he slid back again to fear, which was the chief strength of the argument against returning to the city: Are we hastening to arrive with the ashes of Germanicus, so that Agrippina, with her lamentations, and the ignorant mob, may snatch you, unheard and undefended, at the first rumour? For the mob is led by impulse, not by reason, and the eyes of the judges themselves are clouded by the mist of pity and hatred. As for the defence he might hope for from Augusta's secret favour, or Tiberius' hidden goodwill, he thought there would be none. You have the conscience of Augusta, you have the favour of Caesar, but it is in secret; and those who most loudly mourn Germanicus are the ones who most loudly rejoice. Tiberius, he said, was so reserved in spirit, so close in hiding his purposes, that he revealed what he wanted neither in words nor in his face. Nor was it hidden from him how great the hatred for Germanicus' fate was, and how it was being secretly fanned by rumours. Therefore it was so far from being the case that any protection could be hoped for from him, that everything adverse was to be feared. One must therefore make use of fortune, and turn the wisdom offered by chance to account. How did Piso answer these arguments? By what weight of reasoning was he drawn away? Piso, ready and fierce, was drawn into their opinion with no great effort. Words swollen with pride easily drive out a spirit that is already fierce by nature; that he had not consulted his own good well, the outcome, the teacher of fools, will reveal.

units.la: CLXIX.
units.tr: CLXIX.

units.la: Fœcunda apud infensos calumnian‑diseges.
units.tr: Occasions for slander abound among enemies.

units.la: Piso nisi Germanicum odio Tiberio fuisse olfecit set, tam frivola ad eum scribere, detrahendæ defunͤi famæ,ausus non fuisset.ad quem missis epistolis,incu‑lumniarum. sat Germanicum luxus & luperbia. quæ fi maximè ve‑ra fuissent,nec apud Pisonem inimicitias,nec apud Ti‑berium suspicionem affectati regni merebantur. ideo‑que ad urgentiora, & fufpicationi propiora, vergit, feque pulsum, ut locus rebus novis patefieret. feunum consiliis Germanici obstitisse: promptiores ingenio suo eum sibi legisse,sic benevolentia ex adversariorum odio quæsita, ad ea quæ recentioris invidiæ erant pal‑landa labitur. curam exercitus,eadem fide qua tenue‑rit,repetitiuiffe, Maximum in Tiberii favore prætidium, innocentia vitæ validius,ducebat. poteratque non mi‑nus commode de eo jactari, quod de Felice Judæa præfecto scribitur: Cunctamalefacta sibi impune ra‑tus,tanta potentia subnixo. x 11. Annal.
units.tr: Piso would never have dared to write such trivial things to him, to detract from the dead man's reputation, unless he had sensed that Germanicus was hateful to Tiberius. He sent letters to him full of accusations: that Germanicus was too fond of luxury and pride. Even if these charges had been wholly true, they deserved neither enmity from Piso nor suspicion of aiming at kingship from Tiberius. So he turns to more pressing charges, closer to suspicion, and says that he himself was driven out so that a place for revolution might open. He says that Germanicus had obstructed his plans, and that he had read him as too quick-witted for his own good. Having won goodwill by playing on his enemies' hatred, he slides on to matters of more recent envy that needed covering up. He claimed to have restored the army's care with the same loyalty with which he had held it. He reckoned his greatest protection to be Tiberius' favour, and his innocence of life to be the stronger safeguard. And what is written of Felix, prefect of Judaea, could be said of him no less fittingly: thinking that all his evil deeds would go unpunished, he relied on such great power. x 11. Annal.

units.la: CLXX.
units.tr: CLXX.

units.la: Mutua formido sæviti prorumpen‑tis retinaculum.
units.tr: Mutual fear, the restraint on one who would break out in fury.

units.la: Pifonianis Agrippinenfi classi occurrentibus, arma utrinque infestis animis expedita. dein mutua formi-dine,non ultra jurgium protessum est. offendendi cu-pidine mentes ardebant, dolorem recipiendi formidi-ne retinebantur. Non in singulis tantum, aut pauco-rum factionibus,verum & magnis nationum imperiis, vindictæ aut proserpenti potentiæ,ii ponuntur obices. De Sarmatarum & Germanorum limitibus Tacitus: Germania à Sarmatis Dacisq; mutuo metu ,aut mon-tibus separatur. singulari De Germania libello. Ro-manos,ab occasu Solis in orientem grassantes,Parthi; Parthos in occidentem tendentes Romani, Euphrate interjecto, & mutua formidine stiterunt. Nec ausus est Pompejus , Orientis post Lucullum domitor, quamvis cupidine arderet, Parthos lacessere; nec Par-thus Mithridati & Tigrani implorantibus opem con-tra Romanos ferre. Crassus tribunis obstrepentibus, obnunciante augure,arma parum felicia ultra Euphra-tem movit. nec Pacorus, quanquam depulso Crasso, victoriam persequebatur. Conversis deinde in se Ro-manorum armis, Parthi quidem Syriam depopulati, ad Hellespontum progressi sunt; sed ægrè à Labieno, Julianis partibus adverso, industi. Hos à Ventidio, Antonii legato, bis rejectos; non satis feliciter ipse Antonius suis eos in finibus perculit. Quies deinde, & mutuæ formidinis beneficio pacati imperii sereni-tas. donec amborum senescente imperio, Persarum vires, nomini Romano & Byzantino graves, resurge-rent. Obiter hic observandum , non posse propri-o sensu jactari, Romanos, aut ullam denique nationem, totius orbis imperium habuisse. Nam, ut mittam na-tiones jure suo fruentes, & Romanæ potentiæ no-men ne fando quidem audientes, qua tempestate ma-ximè formidandi Romani erant, pari poretia in orien-te Parthi obsistebant. Quod, præter historiæ indici-um, Taciti confessione arguitur. Ægyptiorum anti-quam dominationem, vel inanem summi imperii ja-ctationem,recensendo,detributis orbi victo imperatis addit: haud minus magnifica ,quàm nunc vi Parthorum, aut potentia Romana jubentur. Supra hoc ipso Annalium libro. Ecce Parthos Romanis imperandi vi pares; & ordine recensendi Romanis præpositos! Verùm sententiam, vulgi palato non acceptam, & commodiori loco deducendam, istic non urgeo.
units.tr: When the Pisonians met the Agrippinensian fleet, both sides took up arms with hostile spirits. Then, through mutual fear, the quarrel went no further. Their minds burned with desire to do harm, but they were held back by fear of suffering it in return. This restraint is set not only between single individuals or factions of a few, but also between great nations and empires, against revenge or against a growing power. Tacitus, on the frontiers of the Sarmatians and the Germans: Germany is separated from the Sarmatians and Dacians by mutual fear, or by mountains, in his separate book On Germany. The Parthians held back the Romans, who were advancing from the setting of the sun towards the east, and the Romans held back the Parthians, who were reaching towards the west; with the Euphrates lying between them, they stood still through mutual fear. Pompey, conqueror of the East after Lucullus, did not dare to provoke the Parthians, although he burned with desire to do so; nor did the Parthians bring aid against the Romans to Mithridates and Tigranes, though they begged for it. Crassus, with the tribunes shouting against him and the augur announcing ill omens, moved his arms beyond the Euphrates with little success. Nor did Pacorus pursue victory, although Crassus had been defeated. Then, when the Roman armies turned against themselves, the Parthians indeed laid waste Syria and advanced as far as the Hellespont, but Labienus, who was hostile to the Julian party, drove them back only with difficulty. They were twice repulsed by Ventidius, legate of Antony, and Antony himself did not strike them down in their own territory with much success. Then came a pause, and the calm of the empire was kept in peace by the benefit of mutual fear, until, as both empires grew old, the forces of the Persians, grievous to the Roman and Byzantine name, rose again. Here, by the way, it should be noted that the Romans, or indeed any nation at all, cannot justly boast in their own sense that they possessed dominion over the whole world. For, to pass over nations enjoying their own right, and not even hearing the name of Roman power spoken of in fable, at the very time when the Romans were most to be feared, the Parthians resisted them in the East with equal strength. This is shown, apart from the evidence of history, by Tacitus' own admission. Recounting the old dominion of the Egyptians, or their empty boast of supreme power, and adding the commanders assigned to the conquered world, he says: no less splendid than now they are ordered by the power of the Parthians or the might of Rome. This is in the same book of the Annals, above. See, the Parthians are equal to the Romans in strength to rule, and are listed in order of rank alongside them! But I do not press this opinion here, since it is not welcome to the common taste and should be brought forward in a more suitable place.

units.la: CLXXI. Aleajacta fortunæ instandum.
units.tr: CLXXI. The dice of fortune must be pressed on with.

units.la: Et sæpè adverso ejus flatu[?] obnitendum: maximè ubi nec tutus datur, nec honestus recessus. Nec Piso, quanquam cœpta secus cadebant, omisit tutissima præsentibus. Ita vita est hominum, quasi cùm ludas tesseris: Si illud, quod maximè opus est jactu, non cadit: Illud, quod cecidit forte, id arte ut corrigas: in-quit apud Terentium Mitio. Notum est illud Julii Cæsaris, Rubiconem cum exercitu contra patrios mores transgressi, Jacta est alea. Quæ si Pisoni æquè prosperè cecidisset, minùs eum incepti tæduisset. Hæc non eo animo scribo, quod pervicaciæ improbè ceptorum patrocinari velim. Sed in re laudis & vituperii media, laudatur [illegible, ~6 letters] minùs [illegible, ~8 letters] decretum.
units.tr: And often one must struggle against its adverse blast, especially where no safe or honourable retreat is offered. Nor did Piso, although his undertakings were falling out otherwise, neglect the safest course open to him in the circumstances. So is human life, as when you play at dice: if the throw that matters most does not fall, you must correct by skill the one that fell by chance, says Mitio in Terence. The saying of Julius Caesar is well known, when he crossed the Rubicon with his army against the customs of his country: The die is cast. Had that throw fallen as favourably for Piso, he would have been less weary of his undertaking. I do not write this in order to plead for the stubborn obstinacy of wicked undertakings. But in a matter that lies between praise and blame, [illegible] is praised less than [illegible] decided.

units.la: CLXXII. Honestæ causæ pannus, minùs honestæ affluendus.
units.tr: CLXXII. A cloak of an honourable cause, to be thrown over a less honourable one.

units.la: Nec hoc more præcepti, sed seculi consuetudine detecta, scribo. Quod Piso, majoribus etiam usurpatum, imitabatur, Cæsarisque se legatum testabatur. Nusquam lusciniolæ sua deest cantio, inquit Comicorum locupletissimus: nec turbare pacem cupientibus belli prætextus. E multis unum, reliquis ex eo facilè judicandis, eligam. Belli inter Antonium & Octavianum Cæsarem, quod decretum uni principatum haud dubiè adjudicaturum erat, hæ causæ jactabantur. Cæsari Antonius Lepidum imperio detrusum, cujus potentiam ipse eversam cupiverat, objecit. provincia-rum ejus & copiarum dimidium non quasi obtentu-rus, sed belli causam, postulavit. Cæsar Antonio mul-to acerbiora, & veri majorem speciem habitura, ex-probravit: Ægyptum extra sortem invasam, Artuafdam Armeniae regem per fraudem in vincula conjectum, manubiarum omnem facultatem inversam, Cleopatram scortum Niliacum uxoris in loco habitam, exque ea liberos quasi justo matrimonio suscep-tos, provincias Romani imperii iis donatus. Nec Sext. Pompejum ab eo occisum, cujus tamen cæde audita supra modum gavisus erat, reticuit. Verioribus ad bellum causis, profunda imperandi remoto arbitro cupidine, stimulabantur. Nam quod uterque orbis Romani imperium ad se trahebat, non poterat non in-visus esse, qui eadem cupiditatis flagrantia ruebat.
units.tr: I write this not as a precept but as an observation of the customs of the age. Piso, following a practice even his ancestors had used, kept insisting that he was Caesar's legate. "Nowhere is the little nightingale's song absent," says the richest of the comic poets, and those who want to disturb the peace never lack a pretext for war. I shall choose one case out of many, the rest being easily judged from it. In the war between Antony and Octavian Caesar, which the decree was certain to settle in favour of one ruler, these were the grounds put forward. Antony charged Caesar that Lepidus had been thrown out of power, whose strength Caesar himself had wanted destroyed. Antony demanded half of Lepidus's provinces and forces, not as a mere pretext but as a real cause of war. Caesar threw back at Antony charges far harsher, and more likely to carry the appearance of truth: that Egypt had been seized beyond his lot; that Artavasdes, king of Armenia, had been treacherously thrown into chains; that all the wealth from the spoils had been squandered; that Cleopatra, a Nile harlot, had been kept in the place of a wife, and children born of her acknowledged as though from a lawful marriage, and provinces of the Roman empire given to them. Nor did he pass over in silence that Sextus Pompey had been killed by Antony, though Antony had rejoiced beyond measure at hearing of his slaughter. The truer causes of the war were the deep desire to rule, with no judge to restrain it. For since each was drawing the Roman empire of both worlds towards himself, the one rushing on with the same burning lust could not but be hateful to the other.

units.la: CLXXIII. Causa bene sperandi injuris & armorum connubio.
units.tr: CLXXIII. Grounds for good hope in wrongs and in the marriage of arms.

units.la: Eorundem elementorum voces, JUS & VIS, im-mane quantum in re discrepare dicuntur. Ego verò, si Vis pro non inani armorum motu capiatur, à socie-tate juris eam non excludo. Hæc enim duo bonum imperatorem, imò & bonum militem, absolvunt; Jus belli inferendi, & armorum perita copia, qualem se bellatorem, quamvis falsis nominibus, Piso gloriatur: si jure ageretur potiorem ; si armis, non invalidum. De jure belli abunde post Alb. Gentilem Grotium: de armis explicandis plures. quibus non nudum armorum apparatum, sed animum gerendis armis idoneum, simul accipimus. fortem nimirum in periculis, & in promendis consiliis acutum. quæ in paucis hominibus pari consortio habitant. propterea quod, ut ait belli Jugurthini scriptor, alterum ex providentia timorem, alterum ex audacia temeritatem adferre plerumque solet.
units.tr: The words of these same elements, JUS and VIS, are said to differ hugely in meaning. For my part, if Force is taken not as an empty display of arms, I do not exclude it from partnership with Right. For these two make a good commander, and indeed a good soldier: the right to wage war, and a skilled supply of arms, the sort of warrior Piso boasts himself to be, though under false names. If it were conducted by right, he would be the stronger; if by arms, not the weaker. On the right of war there is plenty after Alberico Gentili and Grotius; on arms, many have explained it. By arms we understand not a bare apparatus of weapons, but a mind fit for bearing arms: brave in dangers and keen in putting forward counsels. These qualities seldom dwell together in the same men, because, as the writer of the Jugurthine War says, the one generally brings fear from foresight, and the other rashness from boldness.

units.la: CLXXIV. Desertionis militaris præsens remedium, manuum consertio.
units.tr: CLXXIV. A ready remedy for military desertion: hand-to-hand fighting.

units.la: Sæpe id, Græcis inprimis, observatum; in tempore Sentius usurpat. Piso seditionem in castris ejus, & ad se transitionem, pollicitandis præmiis, & sua in eos indulgentia[?] commemoranda, movebat. Jamque signifer signum legionis; defectionis initium, transtulerat; Tum Sentius occanere cornua tubaque, & peti agge-rem, erigi scalas jussit, ac promtissimum quenque succe-dere; alios tormentis bastis, saxa, & faces ingerere; Namque transeundi pacta, aut ardorem in pugna re-mittendi, quod [illegible, ~8 letters] Graecis, mora & delibera-tione indigent.
units.tr: This has often been observed, especially among the Greeks, and Sentius employs it at the right moment. Piso was stirring up sedition in his camp and defection to himself, by promising rewards and by reminding them of his own indulgence towards them. And now the standard-bearer had carried the legion's standard over, the beginning of the defection. Then Sentius ordered the horns and trumpet to sound, the rampart to be attacked, the ladders to be raised, and each of the most willing men to advance; others he ordered to hurl spears, stones and torches with the engines. For terms of changing sides, or any slackening of ardour in battle, need delay and deliberation, not such haste.

units.la: CLXXV.
units.tr: CLXXV.

units.la: Secreta animorum claustra fama perrumpit.
units.tr: Fame breaks through the secret locks of minds.

units.la: Satis occulta sua, de opprimendo Germanico, con-filia Tiberius arbitrabatur. Rimando ea populus pe-nettrat, & in aperto traducit: Ideo nimirum in extre- ma terras relegatum: ideo Pisoni permissam provin-ciam: hoc egisse secretos Augusti cum Plancina sermo-nes. Acumine deinde popularæ judicium superante; causam tam infesti in Germanicum odii venando pro-munt: vera prorsus de Drufo seniores locutos, dissiliceré regnantibus civilia filiorum ingenia. i. e: comitatem; facilitatem, ac animum populi ac publicæ libertatis himis amantem, neque ob aliud interceptos, quam quia populum Romanum æquo jure complecti reddita liberae tale agitaverint: quo tamen eos judicio labi potuisse, in Arcanis regnorum monstravi.
units.tr: Tiberius believed his plans for crushing Germanicus were hidden well enough. The people, by probing, penetrate them and bring them into the open. This is why, they say, he was relegated to the farthest lands; why the province was granted to Piso; why Augustus's secret conversations with Plancina had this aim. Then, as popular judgment outstrips cunning, they hunt out the cause of such hostile hatred against Germanicus: the elders spoke truly about Drusus, that the civil natures of sons are a trouble to those who reign. That is: their courtesy, affability, and spirit, most fond of the people and of public liberty; and that they were removed for no other reason than because they had conceived such plans, that the Roman people should be embraced with equal right, restored to freedom. Yet I have shown in the Arcana of Kingdoms that they could have fallen into this judgment.

units.la: CLXXVI.
units.tr: CLXXVI.

units.la: Sine autore rumor, vanus præsertim, brevi mora vanescit.
units.tr: A rumour without an author, especially an empty one, vanishes after a short delay.

units.la: Ideo sapienti civium moderatori sæpe sperhendus. Reviviscere Germanicum, & ad pristinæ valetudinis robur rediisse, incertus rumor ferebat. Non se prae-gaudio continet plebecula: templorum fores noctu molitur, gratias diis immolando actura. Nec obstitit fatis Tiberius, donec tempore ac spatio vanescerent. Rebus etiam aperte malis, nec intra vanum rumorem conclusis, tempus aliquando medetur. Inde illud amor-eorum Galbae: daret malorum poenitentia, daret bono-rum rath[?] consensui spatium. scelera impetu, bona consilia mera valescere. 1. Histor.
units.tr: Therefore it is often to be disregarded by a wise governor of citizens. The uncertain rumour reported that Germanicus was reviving and had returned to the strength of his former health. The common crowd could not contain its joy: at night they forced open the doors of the temples, intending to offer thanks to the gods with sacrifices. Tiberius did not oppose the fates, but waited until with time and space the rumour would vanish. Even with things openly bad, not confined within an empty rumour, time sometimes heals. Hence that saying of Galba: let time be given for the repentance of wrongs, let time be given for the agreement of good men; crimes grow strong by impulse, good counsels only by delay. Histories, Book 1.

units.la: CLXXVII. Honores alicui decreti non sunt certum summae potestatis indicium.
units.tr: CLXXVII. Honours decreed to someone are not a certain sign of supreme power.

units.la: Nam sic & Germanico, qui alienis auspiciis exercitum duxaverat, jam mortuo summa potestas delata diceretur. Honores, ut quis amore in Germanicum aut ingenio validus, reperti decretique. En honores, non metu aut vi extortos, ut qui Julio, Antonio, Octavio, patriae domitoribus, à trepidante senatu deferebantur; sed amore, & vero animi affectu oblatos! Nec eos vulgaris commatis, verum divinitatis famam praeferentis. ut nomen ejus Saliari carmine aneretur. quod vix antiquis Romae regibus concessum. sedes curules sacerdotum Augustalium locis, superque eas quercea corona statuerentur. & quae alia in domum Juliam & Augustam adulationis vanitas invenit. Ne à divini quidem cultus communicatione abstinebatur. Statuarum locorumve in quis COLERETVR, haud facile quis numerum inierit. Ad quam divinitatis celebrationem ne Romulus quidem, ille Romanae urbis conditor, pervenerat. Nam reges insequentes, religionis cultu insignis Pompilius, bellicis artibus Hostilius, probitate vitae Ancus, insignium splendore Tarquinius, legum & aequitatis conditor Servius; ne quidem inter deos relati leguntur. Non extremi loci in Jure Publico quaestio est: Quo jure quave injuria Julium Cajar, & post eum Octavium, in imperii sedem irrepserint? Fuisse eis imperii summam potestatem à S. P. Q.R. oblatam, inter prima argumentorum monumenta Honorum decretorum cumulus militat. Julio, hostibus undique debellatis imperii jam securo, senatus autoritate datum: ut triumphali veste semper & omni in loco uterentur; ut, ludis exceptis, curuli sede semper sederet; &c. & quae plura Dio recenset, lib. 44. Quibus honorum accumulationibus Octavium, Antonio oppresso jam terris omnibus Romanam majestatem trementibus absque controversia leges dattu-rum [?], ornaverint; idem Dio libro 51. describit. qui, fi non vano Graeci scriptoris commento finguntur; praeterquam quod metu autore conscripti, quod militiae regendae fastigium non egresso communicati: summa potestas penes eos manfitaffe videbitur, qui honorum mensuram & modum, è suo arbitrio deprompsum, imperaturo praescripserunt. Certè non Romulo à Senatu adulatione, ut lictoribus ad terrorem populi ureretur, impetrandum fuit. ipse sibi eos; munimini simul & terrori circumdedit. Non Priscus Tarquinius, ut insignibus Hetruscæ gentis Romæ prælatis fulgeret, à senatu emendicavit. Regio jure ad regium splendorem, & majestatis popularem indicem, grassatur [?]. Non igitur regia potestas Julio & Augusto deLata, ex honorum decreto arguitur: sed ea, fi tyrannicæ imperii invasionis purgari velint, aliunde accersenda.
units.tr: For in this way it would also be said that supreme power was conferred on Germanicus, who had led the army under another's auspices, even after he was dead. Honours, such as were found and decreed for someone through love of Germanicus or through his strength of character. Behold honours not extorted by fear or force, such as were offered to Julius, Antony and Octavian, the subduers of the fatherland, by a trembling senate; but offered out of love and from a true affection of the mind! Nor were they honours of the common sort, but ones bearing the reputation of divinity: so that his name should be sung in the Salian hymn, which was hardly granted even to the ancient kings of Rome. Curule seats were set up for the Augustal priests in their places, and above them a crown of oak. And whatever other vanity of flattery was devised for the house of Julius and Augustus. Nor was he kept from sharing in divine worship. Of statues and places in which he is WORSHIPPED, one could hardly count the number. Not even Romulus, the founder of the city of Rome, attained to such a celebration of divinity. For the kings who followed, Pompilius, distinguished for religious worship, Hostilius for warlike arts, Ancus for uprightness of life, Tarquinius for the splendour of his insignia, and Servius, the founder of laws and equity, are not even read of as having been placed among the gods. The question is not of the least importance in public law: By what right, or by what wrong, did Julius Caesar, and after him Octavian, creep into the seat of empire? That supreme power was offered to them by the Senate and People of Rome is shown by the heap of honorary decrees, which stand as the first monuments of the argument. For Julius, when the enemies had been beaten down on every side and the empire was now secure, was granted by senatorial authority that he should always wear triumphal dress in every place; that, except at the games, he should always sit in a curule chair; and so on, and the many other things Dio lists, book 44. With such accumulations of honours the senate adorned Octavian, when Antony was crushed and all lands were trembling at Roman majesty, and he would without dispute give laws; Dio describes the same in book 51. If these are not invented by the vain fiction of a Greek writer, then apart from the fact that they were written under the influence of fear, and were shared only up to the height of commanding the army, it will seem that supreme power remained in the hands of those who, by their own judgment, prescribed to the future emperor the measure and limit of his honours. Certainly Romulus did not have to obtain from the Senate, by flattery, that lictors should attend him to strike terror into the people; he himself surrounded himself with them, as both a guard and a terror. Tarquinius Priscus did not beg from the senate that he might shine with the insignia of the Etruscan people set above him at Rome. By royal right he advanced to royal splendour and to the popular sign of majesty. Therefore royal power conferred on Julius and Augustus is not proved from the decree of honours; but if they wish to be cleared of the charge of tyrannical usurpation of empire, it must be sought from elsewhere.

units.la: CLXXVIII.
units.tr: CLXXVIII.

units.la: Pari celebritatis laude imperatoria facultas & oratoria ambulant.
units.tr: Skill in war and skill in oratory walk together in equal praise of fame.

units.la: Cultiorum quidem nationum judicio: non bar-barum gentium: à quibus rectum rerum judicium non est petendum. Germanico, imperatorum bellicæ rei eâ tempestate primo, & rerum potitis neceffitudis ne proximo, cum cenfaretur clypeus, auro & magnitudine in signis, inter autores eloquentia, Tiberius, tanquam id infra magnitudinem imperatoriam eflet, non prohibuit; sed eminendi praeceteris oratoribus cupiditatem repressit. neque enim eloquentiam fortunae discerni: & fatis illustre, fi veteres inter scriptores ba-[?]beretur. O dignam imperatore Romano sententiam! At nunc angusti alicujus terrae anguli aulae mancipis um eruditorum nomen, nisi aulae fe mancipet, aut inter cras-fos centuriones militet, summo despectui du-cit. Nec novum id in Germanico populique & principi-cipis de celebritate oratoriae laudis judicio. jam ante eum Scipiones, Cornelius Sulla, Pompejus, Lucullus, Julius Cæsar, Augustus, qui cæterorum ducum nomen bellicis rebus obscuraverant, eruditionem cum militari arte miscuerant. Apud Graecos Pericles magnus bello gerendo imperator, major ducendo populo orator. quod idem de Phocione, Demosthenis aequali, sentiendum. qui Demosthenes forensi oratione laudes imperatorum suae aetatis, praeter hunc Phocionem, absorpsit. Nam de Isocrate, docendis tantum privatos intra parietes adolescentulis claro, nihil hic refero. Thebanorum prima & summa gloria Epaminondas, Philosophiae an belli studio clarior fuerit, inter multos ambigitur. Cujus domesticis praeceptis eruditus Philippus, nomen Macedonum, obscurum antea, & vel vicinis barbaris contemptum, in eam claritatem evexit, quae facilem domitu terrarum orbem Alexandro, & ipsi non levi doctrina imbuto, traderet.
units.tr: This is by the judgment of the more cultivated nations, not of barbarous peoples, from whom a right judgment of things is not to be sought. Germanicus, in that age the first of the emperors in the art of war and the nearest to the highest rank of affairs, when his shield was valued for its gold and size among the ensigns, was counted among the authors of eloquence.
