Tiberius, as if that were beneath imperial greatness, did not forbid it, but checked his desire to stand out above the other orators. For eloquence is not distinguished by fortune, and it is glorious enough to be counted among the older writers. O sentiment worthy of a Roman emperor! But now the name of a learned man is held in the greatest contempt, the mere servant of the court of some narrow corner of the land, unless he hands himself over to the court or serves among the fat centurions. Nor is this new in Germanicus, or in the prince's judgment about the fame of oratorical praise. Already before him the Scipios, Cornelius Sulla, Pompey, Lucullus, Julius Caesar and Augustus, who had outshone the names of the other commanders in war, had mixed learning with the military art. Among the Greeks Pericles was a great commander in waging war, and greater still as an orator in leading the people. The same is to be thought of Phocion, the contemporary of Demosthenes, who by his forensic speeches absorbed the praises of the generals of his age, apart from this Phocion. For I say nothing here of Isocrates, famous only for teaching young men privately within walls. Whether Epaminondas, the first and highest glory of the Thebans, was more distinguished in philosophy or in the study of war, is disputed among many. Philip, educated by his precepts at home, raised the name of the Macedonians, previously obscure and despised even by neighbouring barbarians, to such renown that it handed the world, easily conquered, to Alexander, himself imbued with no slight learning.

units.la: Dixeris haec inter varicosos centuriones; Continuo crassum ridet Vulpinius ingens, Et centum Graecos curto centusse licetur.
units.tr: You might say these things among the varicose centurions: at once huge Vulpinius laughs at the fat man, and a hundred Greeks are let go with a short cloak.

units.la: Persius Sat. V.
units.tr: Persius, Sat. V.

units.la: CLXXIX.
units.tr: CLXXIX.

units.la: Domestici incrementi fortunam gloriae sibi ducere, vulgaris laetitiae est.
units.tr: To count the good fortune of a domestic increase as glory for oneself belongs to common joy.

units.la: Livia, quae Drusonupta erat, gemellos enixa, laetitiae exultationem Tiberius non continuit; quinjacta-ret apud patres, nulli ante Romanorum ejusdem fastigii viro geminam stirpem editam. atqui in eo nulla vel sapientiae & consilii, vel vigilantiae & laboris gloria. Fortunam, eamque non publicam, in gloriationem trahere, humilia sapientis viri est. ideoque autor gra-tissimae facundiae epicrisin huic exultationi adjicit: nam cuncta etiam fortuita ad gloriam vertebat. Tiberio propriae, non fortuitae, laudis fuisset, domum ab interitu integram servare. at nunc incogitantia hoc ipsos gemellos, cum ipso patre Druso, Sejani libidini morituros; Germanici stirpem suae saevitiae victimam objicit. Et caeteroqui rari inter magnos imperatores felici prole beati fuere. Ninus, Assyriorum celebritate notus imperator, Niniam nequaquam fui similem gē[?], nuit: nec pares vel animo vel fortuna Nebucadnezar, Babyloniorum supremus. Cyrus Cambyffen, belli ut-cunque gloria florentem, sed mente furiosum; & Smerdin, nulla re, praeterquam mortis genere memo-ratum, Persis produxit. Alexander, Macedonum pro-cul dubio apex, imbecillum & vitam aegré trahentem partum suscepit. Romanae virtutis culmen Scipio Africanus, tenero valetudine & animis filio, cō fervan-dae familiae memoriae ad adoptionem confugit. Nec Julius Caesar stirpe virili gavisus: & Augustus filiae li-bidinibus supra modum moerorem concepit. Nostra memoria Guftavus Adolphus, priscis heroibus bellica laude par habitus, & ipse filiam solam, eruditionis an-tea, nunc peregrinationis nomine famosam, genuit. Sed manum de tabula: ne in hoc seculum delatus, re-centi me invidiae aut censurae subjiciam.
units.tr: When Livia, the wife of Drusus, gave birth to twins, Tiberius could not contain his exultation: he boasted before the senators that no earlier Roman of the same rank had had twin offspring. Yet there was no glory of wisdom or counsel, or of vigilance and labour, in this. To draw into self-congratulation a fortune that was not even public is the mark of a lowly man, not a wise one. That is why the author, with most elegant eloquence, adds this comment on his exultation: for he turned even chance events to his glory. It would have been a praise properly Tiberius's own, not a matter of chance, to have preserved his house intact from destruction. As it is, through thoughtlessness, he exposed these twins, together with their father Drusus, to the lust of Sejanus, and offered the line of Germanicus as a victim to his own cruelty. Moreover, among great emperors, few have been blessed with fortunate offspring. Ninus, the emperor known for the renown of the Assyrians, begot a son in no way like himself; nor was Nebuchadnezzar, the supreme ruler of the Babylonians, equal to his father in spirit or fortune. Cyrus begot Cambyses, who flourished in some measure of military glory but was mad in mind; and he produced Smerdis, who is remembered for nothing except the manner of his death, for the Persians. Alexander, undoubtedly the summit of the Macedonians, had a child who was feeble and dragged out a difficult life. Scipio Africanus, the pinnacle of Roman virtue, had a son who was delicate in health and in mind, and to preserve the memory of his family he resorted to adoption. Nor did Julius Caesar rejoice in a male heir; and Augustus suffered extreme grief from his daughter's lusts. In our own memory, Gustavus Adolphus, judged equal to the heroes of old in military fame, also had only one daughter, who has become notorious, once for her learning and now for her wandering. But I must take my hand off the tablet, lest, carried away into this age, I expose myself to recent envy or censure.

units.la: CLXXX.
units.tr: CLXXX.

units.la: Stupri permissa consuetudo ægro-tantis Reipublicæ indicium.
units.tr: The tolerated practice of fornication is a sign of a sick commonwealth.

units.la: Quamvis in ea morum corruptela, adulteriis paf-sim grassantibus, fornicationem nemine crimini sibi ducente, gravibus senatus decretis libido foeminarum coercita, cautumque ne quaestum corpore faceret, cui avus, aut pater, aut maritus eques Rom. fuisset, non virorum libido, quae nullis legum repagulis coercebatur, sed foeminarum constricta. nec simplex iis fcor-tatio, sed meritricii quaestus professio tantummodo, interdicta nefoeminarum quidem omni generi; sed senatoriae dignitatis antiqua, equestris ordinis nova lege prohibitum. Quae enim libertini generis, aut quae plebeji, quamvis ingenui, fuerunt; legum harum cancellos liberius evadebant. non quod plus illis liber-tatis concessum: sed quod infimi civium ordinis dede-cus patres parum curabant. Sed ut omnes bonae leges ex malis moribus ortae dicuntur: quae morum mani-festa depravatio huic patrum severae animadversioni ortum dedit? Viftilia praetoria familia genita, licentiam stupri apud ædiles vulgaverat. nimis id quidem impudenter, & pudibundo sexui indecorè: attamen more inter veteres recepto, qui satis pœnarum adversum impudicas in ipsa professione flagitii credebant. Quid enim cum iis agas, qua ignominiæ nota eas terreas, quæ famæ omnium hominum securâ, pro honore ac dignitate ipsam ignominiam pro frontis insigni arripiunt? quæ Catullianos versiculos, cantu & rebus molliculos, in aures facilè admittunt:
units.tr: Although in that corruption of morals, with adulteries raging everywhere and fornication counted as no crime by anyone, the lust of women was restrained by grave decrees of the senate, and it was provided that no woman whose grandfather, father or husband had been a Roman knight should make gain with her body; the lust of men, which was restrained by no barriers of law, was not what was checked, but the lust of women was. Nor was it mere fornication that was forbidden them, but only the open profession of prostitution for gain: this was forbidden to women of every kind, and especially by an old law to women of senatorial rank, and by a new law to those of equestrian rank. Those who were of freed or plebeian birth, however freeborn, slipped more freely past the bounds of these laws. Not that more liberty was granted to them, but because the senators cared little about the disgrace of the lowest order of citizens. But as all good laws are said to arise from bad morals, what manifest depravity gave rise to this severe censure of the senators? Vistilia, born of a praetorian family, had made public the licence of fornication before the aediles. Certainly this was too shameless, and unbecoming to the modest sex; yet according to the custom received among the ancients, who believed that enough punishment lay against unchaste women in the very profession of their disgrace. For what can you do with those whom you frighten with the mark of infamy, who, unconcerned for the reputation of all men, seize infamy itself as the badge of their brow in place of honour and dignity? Women who readily admit to their ears the little Catullan verses, soft in song and subject:

units.la: Vivamus mea Lesbia, atque amemus, Rumoresque senum severiorum Omneis unius æstimemus assis.
units.tr: Let us live, my Lesbia, and let us love, and let us value all the gossip of stern old men at a single penny.

units.la: Quæ cum Messalina, vulgari prostibulo, & imperatorii matrimonii verruca, gaudium ex ipsa flagitii ac infamiæ magnitudine capiunt. ne tamen in nudo nominis meretricii dedecore pœnam harum stetisse arbitreris: jure & dignitate matronarum, nec non consessu inter matronas ac frequentia, cæterisque dignioris vitæ ornamentis exuebantur. Vestibus etiam discretæ, toga meretricia pro stola, adempta vitta matronali, amicie-bantur. Commodè ad hunc locum quæstio libatur: AN permittenda in rep. vulgando corpori lupanaria? Cum honestatis causa non extrema sit civitatum condendarum; cumque Christiana religio principatum Europæ compleƈtatur, impuritati omni inimica: quo id licentiæ indultu permittatur, non reperio. Quæ de Vespasiani aut Romani Pontificis meritricio ærario, de adulteriis & virginum stupris frenandis, de juvenutis animis à feria rerum cogitatione laxandis, de masculæ libidinis, cui Sodomiæ memoria nomen imposuit, ardore compescendo, proferuntur; tanti non sunt, ut auribus honesta audire eruditis ullum scrupulum injiciant. Nam nec lucro imperantium, nec parentium dissolutæ licentiæ, sed publicæ morum honestati, & reip. incolumitati, legumlatori serviendum. Quam incolumitatem frangit aut enervat permissa vulgo scortandi impunitas. Cætera, non parca segete huc accumulanda, morum præceptoribus remitto.
units.tr: Women who, like Messalina, a common prostitute and the wart on an imperial marriage, take joy from the very greatness of their shame and infamy. Lest you think, however, that the punishment of these women consisted only in the bare disgrace of the name of harlot, they were stripped of the rights and dignity of matrons, and of their place among matrons and their company, and of the other ornaments of a more honourable life. They were also distinguished by their clothing: they dressed in the harlot's toga instead of the stola, with the matron's fillet taken away. Here it is fitting to touch on the question: whether brothels should be permitted in a commonwealth by making the body public. Since the honesty of states is not the least of the concerns in founding them, and since the Christian religion holds the principate of Europe, hostile to all impurity, I do not find on what ground it may be permitted by an indulgence of licence. What is put forward about the brothel tax of Vespasian or of the Roman Pontiff, about restraining adulteries and the rapes of virgins, about relaxing the minds of young men from a tiresome round of thought, about curbing the ardour of male lust, which the memory of Sodom has given a name, does not amount to so much that it could place any scruple before the ears of learned people who hear what is honourable. For the lawgiver must serve not the profit of rulers, nor the dissolute licence of parents, but the public honesty of morals and the safety of the commonwealth. That safety is broken or weakened by the impunity of whoring permitted to the crowd. The rest, a not sparse harvest that could be heaped here, I leave to the teachers of morals.

units.la: CLXXXI.
units.tr: CLXXXI.

units.la: Externa facra nec religioni patriæ, nec civium tranquillitati conducunt.
units.tr: Foreign rites benefit neither the religion of the fatherland nor the peace of its citizens.

units.la: Nec temerè itaque in bene constituta republica fe-renda: ea maximè, quæ aut abfurditate manifesta im-plicantur, aut à patriis ritibus nimium diftant, aut pro-ferpendo factionem augent, odiumque alia facra co-lentibus indicunt, aut denique bonorum mórum cul-tui adversantur. Hoc animo actum & de facris Ægy-ptiis Judaicisque pellendis, Ægyptiorum, boves & vi-tulos, nec non crocodilos & olera colentium, magna-que ritus obscoenos acerbitate propugnantium, im-pia pietas meritò pellebatur. Judæi, quanquam puro Dei unius cultu Romanis præstantiores, ob nimiam religionis diftantiam, ob augendi sacrorum studium, & huic adjunctum alienigenarum odium, minus Ro-manæ civitati convenere. De odio notum illud Juve-nalis Libro V. verf.353.
units.tr: Therefore nothing should be tolerated lightly in a well-ordered commonwealth, especially those things that are either plainly entangled in absurdity, or depart too far from ancestral customs, or, by spreading, increase a faction, stir up hatred against those who worship other rites, or finally oppose the cult of good morals. With this in mind, the Egyptian and Jewish rites were rightly driven out: the impious piety of those who worship Egyptian oxen and calves, crocodiles and herbs, and who defend obscene rites with savage zeal, was justly expelled. The Jews, though superior to the Romans in the pure worship of the one God, were less fitting for the Roman state because of their great difference in religion, their zeal for enlarging their rites, and the hatred of foreigners joined to it. The well-known line of Juvenal on this hatred is in Book V, verse 353:

units.la: Non monftrare vias, eadem nisi facra colenti: *
units.tr: Not to show the way, except to one who worships the same rites,

units.la: Quæfitum ad fontem folos deducere verpos.
units.tr: and to lead the thirsty to a spring only the circumcised.

units.la: Cætera vel è vulgatis libris, vel à converfatione illo-rum nota.
units.tr: The rest is known either from common books or from their way of life.

units.la: Inter alia adminiftrandæ reip. præcepta Mæcenas Augusto fuggerit: τὸ μὲν Θεῖον πάντῃ πάντως αὐτός τε [?] αὐτὸς τὰ πατρία, ἡ τῆς ἄλλης πρὸς ἀνάγκας. τὰς δὲ δὴ ξενίζοντας τὰ ἀλλὰ αὐτὸ ἡ μίαν ἡ κόλαξε, μὴ μόνον τῶν θεῶν ἐνταῦθα, ἀλλὰ φιλοφρονήσας ἀλλὰ ἀλλὰ ἂν πάσας ἀντιλογίας [?] ἀλλ' ὅτι ἀναγκαῖα πᾶσα δωμάτιά οἱ τοιοῦτοι ἀγγελίαι [illegible, ~12 letters] τῆς ἀρχαίας [?] [illegible, ~20 letters] ἐκ τοῦ [?] θεῖον [illegible, ~15 letters] ἀλλὰ μὴ ἐπιθυμία πάντα [?] [illegible, ~25 letters] εὐλογία τῶν πόλεων [illegible, ~18 letters] μὴ ἐξ [?] [illegible, ~14 letters]
units.tr: Among other precepts for the administration of the commonwealth, Maecenas advises Augustus: the divine is to be honoured in every way [τὸ μὲν Θεῖον πάντῃ πάντως], and ancestral customs are to be kept; but those who introduce foreign rites are to be restrained [...] not only on account of the gods here, but [...] for all such ... [the remainder of the Greek is too corrupted to be recovered with certainty].

units.la: verò religionum autores odio & fuppliciis profeque-re: non deorum modò caufa, quos qui contemnit, ne-que alium quemvis magni pretii duxerit: fed quod qui nova numina introducunt, multos ad novas leges pel-liciunt: unde conjurationes, turbæ, conciliabula exi-ftunt: stunt: quæ principatui minimè expediunt. Itaque ne-mini aut deorum contemptori, aut præstigiatori esse permittes. Apud Dionem libro 52. Inde mirum non est, Judæos inprimis à Tiberio pulsos: de quibus eodem, quem modo laudavi, loco Juvenalis:
units.tr: But the founders of new religions are to be driven out by hatred and punishments: not only for the sake of the gods, whom one who despises them would hold of no great worth, but because those who introduce new deities draw many to new laws; from this arise conspiracies, disturbances and secret meetings, which are least suited to the rule of a prince. Therefore no one should be allowed to be either a despiser of the gods or a charlatan. This is in Dio, Book 52. Hence it is no wonder that the Jews were expelled by Tiberius in particular; of them, in the same passage I have just cited, Juvenal says:

units.la: Nil præter nubes & cœli Numen adorant; Nec distare putant humana carne suillam.
units.tr: They worship nothing but the clouds and the divinity of heaven, and they do not think the flesh of swine differs from human flesh.

units.la: Et qui, Censore Tacito, nec quicquam prius imbuun-tur, quàm contemnere deos, exuere patriam; parentes, liberos, fratres, vilia habere. Hæc de proselytis præcipuè cape. communiter de omnibus illud: Gens superstitioni obnoxia, religionibus adversa. Illud verò cum summa Judæorum laude: Judæi mente solâ, unumque numen intelligunt. Profanos qui deûm imagines, mortalibus materiis, in species hominum effingant. Summum illud & æternum, neque mutabile, neque interiturum. Igitur nulla simulacra urbibus, nedum templis sinunt. Ut à Judæis abeam: non malè ad hunc Taciti, nec non Dionis, locum illud Ciceronis quadrat: Omnes religione moventur, & deos patrios quos à majoribus acceperunt, colendos sibi diligenter & retinendos arbitrantur. Quod ad coërcitionem: duplex hic patribus Romanis observata, altera est ad operas addictio, & eas quidem nec serviles, nec dehonestamento futuras. factumque patrum consultum, ut quatuor millia libertini generis ea superstitione infecta, quia idonea ætas, in insulam Sardiniam veheren-tur, coercendis illic latrociniis, & si ob gravitatem cœli interiissent, vile damnum. Est enim id militiæ genus, quod nec Carthaginenses in eadem insula, nec post Romani cives detrectarunt. nec pestilens cœli gravi-tas viros illustres absterruit, quo minùs eam provin-ciam sortirentur. alter coercendi modus est, à patria terra amolitio. cateri cederent Italiâ, nisi certam ante diem profanos ritus exuissent. nec vita iis, nec vivendi facultas, ac ne famæ quidem integritas eripitur: spatium resipiscendi errantibus conceditur. Quam pro- fanorum hominum, erga genus in religione planè di-spar, moderationem saltem imitari velim, qui à magiftro suo Christo mansuetudinem discere, & quidem in eandem religionem professos, in ritibus duntaxat aut quastiunculis aliquot lapsos aut dissentientes, nequi- vere. In Christiani nominis gregem ea sævitia, vivos igni exustulandi, aut Gnosticos (turpissimæ vitæ & doctrinæ homines, quales Epiphanius describit) primum exorta est: & post imperatore Constantio ab Ariamanitis frequentata. quam detestati prisci Christiani, potentiores fasti, quasi re bene gesta, tanquam propagandi per vim aut defendendi cultum Dei telum arripuerunt: immemores quo spiritu & quo magistro humanitatis Christiani ducerentur. Errantem per agros ignorantia via, melius est ad rectum iter admovere, quam expellere: inquit Stoicæ sapientiæ magister. quid occidere in avio deprehensum? quid crudelitati aut dominationi mactare? quid quasitissimo crucia- tu laceratum igni exurere?
units.tr: And those who, under the censorship of Tacitus, are instructed in nothing sooner than to despise the gods, to cast off their country, and to hold parents, children and brothers of little account. This should be taken chiefly of proselytes; of all of them in common is that saying: a people liable to superstition, hostile to religions. But that saying, with the highest praise of the Jews, is this: The Jews understand God by the mind alone, and as one. They call profane those who fashion images of the gods from mortal materials in the likeness of men. That supreme and eternal being is neither changeable nor perishable. Therefore they allow no images in their cities, much less in their temples. To leave the Jews aside: the saying of Cicero fits well with this passage of Tacitus and also of Dio: All men are moved by religion, and they think that the gods of their fathers, which they received from their ancestors, should be worshipped and kept diligently. As for restraint, the Roman fathers observed two methods here. One is the assignment to public works, and those works not servile nor dishonourable: and the fathers decreed that four thousand freedmen of that superstition, of suitable age, should be carried to the island of Sardinia, to suppress brigandage there; and if they perished through the harshness of the climate, it would be a cheap loss. For this is a kind of military service which neither the Carthaginians in that same island nor later the Roman citizens refused. Nor did the unhealthy climate frighten illustrious men from undertaking that province. The other method of restraint is removal from the native land: the rest were to leave Italy unless they had cast off the profane rites by a fixed day. Yet neither life nor the means of living is taken from them, nor even the integrity of their reputation: time for repentance is granted to those who err. I would wish at least to imitate the moderation of these profane men, who were so utterly unlike the Christians in religion, and who could not learn gentleness from their master Christ, but who were harsh toward those who professed the same religion, who had fallen into, or differed in, some rites or minor questions. Such cruelty, burning the living with fire, first arose among the flock of the Christian name against the Gnostics (men of most shameful life and doctrine, such as Epiphanius describes), and afterward was frequently practised under the emperor Constantius by the Arians. The early Christians detested it; but the more powerful, once in office, seized it as a weapon, as if a deed well done, to propagate or defend the worship of God by force, forgetting by what spirit and what master of Christian humanity they were led. A traveller who has lost his way in the fields is better brought back to the right road than driven away, says the teacher of Stoic wisdom. Why kill one found in the wilderness? Why sacrifice him to cruelty or lordship? Why burn with fire one already torn by the most exquisite torture?

units.la: CLXXXII.
units.tr: CLXXXII.

units.la: Sacrorum functio non fit ignaviæ aut avaritiæ asylum.
units.tr: The office of sacred ministry is not a refuge for idleness or greed.

units.la: Romani ad custodiam ignis vestalis non nisi virgi- nes, easque honesto genere & patrimas, vitæ inprimis probatæ, ceperunt. Raro sponte oblatas, frequentius prope invitas & tantum non per vim captas, inde ca- piendi verbum, elegerunt. Post qua retulit Cafar ca- piendam virginem in locum Occia qua septem quinquaginta annos summa sanctissimonia Vestalibus sacris præsederat: egitque gratês Fontoio Agrippa & Domitia Pollioni, quod offerendo filias, de officio in Remp. certa- rent. Ergo officium est in Remp. sacrorum sedula functio, non mendicitatis perfugium & ut nunc voca- ri amat, beneficium. Eadem cura in sacerdotibus & augurum collegio, ut nonnili honesti moris & splen- dido s genere legerentur. At nunc natalibus fermè sordidum, & quod victum aliunde desperat, quasi in- faginam ventris Deo dicatur.
units.tr: The Romans chose as keepers of the sacred fire of Vesta only virgins, and those of honourable birth and patrimony, above all of proven character. Those who offered themselves willingly were rare; most were chosen against their will, almost seized by force, and from this came the word "to take" (capere) for choosing them. Afterwards Caesar reported that a virgin had been taken in the place of Occia, who had presided over the sacred rites of the Vestals with the highest holiness for fifty-seven years. He also thanked Fonteius Agrippa and Domitia Pollio, because they competed in offering their daughters for the service of the Commonwealth. So the office is, for the Commonwealth, a diligent performance of sacred duties, not a refuge for beggars, and what it is now fond of being called, a benefice. The same concern held for priests and the college of augurs: they were chosen only from respectable custom and distinguished birth. But now a man is almost disqualified by his birth, and one who despairs of living elsewhere is dedicated to God as a sacrifice to his belly.

units.la: Sed nec superbiam altera ex parte, & in commissi- sum gregem dominationem, pastores cogitent. quæ cum fuerit apud paganos inaudita, apud Judæos à Prophetis (Ezechiele maxime) reprehensa: apud Christianos præcipuè locum figere, tam placido nomini ignominiosum est. Pascendi illis munus commissum, non clamandi per iram, non mactandi. oviculæ commissæ: sed oviculæ Deo, non hominum impotentiæ, subjectæ. ποιμαίνετε τὸ ἐν ὑμῖν ποίμνιον τοῦ Θεοῦ: pascite qui in vobis est gregem Dei: inquit Apostolorum non postremus. 1.Petr.5.v.2. Sic ab apostolo gentium presbyteri jubentur ποιμαίνειν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τοῦ Θεοῦ; pascere congregationem Dei. Act.20.v.28. In eundem sensum Christus ipse apostolo Petro post lapsum confirmato: βόσκε τὰ ἀρνία μου: pasce oves meas. Joh.21.v.16. Quo in loco reprehendendus est error vulgatus interpretum, Petro ob ternam Christi interrogationem mœstitiam obortam; & inde nescio quæ allegoriarum mysteria ducentium. Causa tristitiæ in voce φιλεῖς, non in repetita interrogatione, quærenda. minus enim quoad ampletendi ardorem est φιλεῖν, quam vel ἀγαπᾶν vel, quæ vocula sacro stylo magis allubescit, ἀγαπητός. quod discrimen ne Latinis quidem, in primis Ciceroni, accurata Diligendi & Amandi distinctione negligitur. Sed ad pastorum ecclesiæ munus, civilitate temperandum, redeo. Loco supra laudato circumcisionis, id est Judæorum, apostolus omnem ut lucri aviditatis, ita dominandi spem præcidit. μηδὲ ὡς κατακυριεύοντες τῶν κλήρων. non quasi subjugum missa hæreditate Dei. quos Dei gregem, oves, congregationem, nunc splendidiori nomine hæreditatem, live in numero multitudinis hæreditatos, appellat. Modum deinde regendi præscribit: τύποι γινόμενοι τῆς ποιμνίου: ut exemplaria gregis, nimirum quia plus vitæ sanctitate ut lumine accenso, quam insanis clamoribus promovent. Cætera ex ipsis Christi ad apostolos verbis, & è Pauli inprimis ad Timotheum epistolis, ut & initio prioris ad Corinthios, pete. Nos à sacris ad civilem rerum portum renavigamus.
units.tr: But the ministers should not think of pride on the other side, or of lordship over the flock committed to them. Although this was unheard of among the pagans and was rebuked among the Jews by the Prophets (Ezekiel above all), to fix a place for it especially among Christians is a shameful thing under so gentle a name. The task committed to them is to feed, not to shout in anger or to slaughter the little sheep committed to them, but sheep subject to God, not to the arrogance of men. "Feed the flock of God which is among you" [ποιμαίνετε τὸ ἐν ὑμῖν ποίμνιον τοῦ Θεοῦ], says no minor one of the Apostles: 1 Pet. 5.2. In the same way, the Apostle to the Gentiles orders the elders "to feed the church of God" [ποιμαίνειν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τοῦ Θεοῦ], Acts 20.28. To the same effect Christ himself, after Peter's fall had been put right, says: "Feed my lambs" [βόσκε τὰ ἀρνία μου], "feed my sheep," John 21.16. In this passage the common error of the Vulgate translator must be rebuked: he derives Peter's sadness from Christ's threefold question, and from it draws I know not what mysteries of allegories. The cause of sadness must be sought in the word "do you love" [φιλεῖς], not in the repeated question. For φιλεῖν is less in intensity of affection than ἀγαπᾶν, or than ἀγαπητός, which is the word the sacred style prefers. Even Latin writers, above all Cicero, do not neglect this distinction between diligere and amare in careful usage. But I return to the office of the ministers of the church, which must be tempered by courtesy. In the passage praised above about circumcision, that is, of the Jews, the Apostle cuts off every hope of gain and likewise of domination: "nor as lording it over the lots" [μηδὲ ὡς κατακυριεύοντες τῶν κλήρων], not as if the inheritance of God were handed over to be subjugated. He calls those whom he names the flock of God, the sheep, the congregation, now with the more splendid name of inheritance, or of those who are the inheritors in the number of the multitude. Then he prescribes the manner of ruling: "becoming examples of the flock" [τύποι γινόμενοι τῆς ποιμνίου], as patterns for the flock, because they advance by the holiness of their lives, like a lamp lit to give light, rather than by mad shouting. For the rest, seek it in Christ's own words to the apostles, and above all in Paul's epistles to Timothy, and also at the beginning of his first epistle to the Corinthians. We now sail back from sacred matters to the civil harbour of affairs.

units.la: CLXXXIII.
units.tr: CLXXXIII.

units.la: Honoratior divortio non interrupta matrimonii copula.
units.tr: A marriage not broken by divorce is more honourable.

units.la: Adeò ut hinc ad liberos etiam honoris aliquid aut maculæ accedat. pralata est Pollionis filia, non ob aliud, quàm quod mater ejus in eodem conjugio manebat. Nam Agrippa dissidio domum imminuerat. Si quis illud de vidua in ecclesiâ conventum legenda, γυναῖκα ἐνὸς ἀνδρὸς γυνή, quæ uni viro nupta fuerit, 1.Tim.5.v.9. huc rapiat: forte non toto cœlo aberrat bit. Sanè fecunda, quæ JCti vocant, vota fœmineâ sexui non esse interdicta, ejusdem capitis 14.versiculo probatur. Violentius videtur, & illud de Episcopis, ac Diaconis, cap.3.v.2. & 12, huc trahere. quanquam non minor Ephesi, cujus ecclesiæ Timotheus præfi- debat, quam Romæ, ut luxuriæ abundantia, ita uxores dimittendi & alias ducendi licentia fervebat.
units.tr: So much so that from this some honour or disgrace attaches even to the children: Pollio's daughter was preferred for no other reason than that her mother remained in the same marriage. For Agrippa had diminished his household by discord. If anyone drags into this the passage about the widow who is to be enrolled in the church, "a wife of one man" (γυναῖκα ἐνὸς ἀνδρὸς), "who has been married to one husband," 1 Tim. 5.9, perhaps he will not stray wholly from the mark. Indeed, that the wish for children, which the jurists call fecunda, is not forbidden to women is proved by verse 14 of the same chapter. It seems more violent to drag in also what is said of bishops and deacons, 1 Tim. 3.2 and 12. Yet at Ephesus, over whose church Timothy presided, the abundance of luxury and the licence to dismiss wives and take others were no less rife than at Rome.

units.la: CLXXXIV.
units.tr: CLXXXIV.

units.la: Annonæ flagellatio moderatori reip. tollenda.
units.tr: The scourge of the grain supply to be removed by the ruler of the state.

units.la: Non modò populi amore, sed & turbationis evi- tandæ. Sævitiam annonæ incusante plebe, statuit fru- mento pretium, quod emptor penderet, binofq; nummos se additurum negotiatoribus in singulos modios. Sæpè in frumenti penuria vilitas, in abundantia caritas, imperantium cura aut negligentia, perspicitur. quadre alibi copiosius differendi seges dabitur.
units.tr: Not only out of love for the people, but also to avoid disturbance. When the common people complained of the harshness of the grain prices, he fixed a price for the wheat that the buyer would pay, and said he would add two coins to each measure for the merchants. Often in a shortage of grain cheapness is seen, and in plenty dearness; the care or negligence of rulers is seen in this. There will be a fuller opportunity to discuss this elsewhere.

units.la: CLXXXV.
units.tr: CLXXXV.

units.la: Humanæ capacitatis modulum excedentes honores vir sapiens non admittit.
units.tr: A wise man does not accept honours that exceed the measure of human capacity.

units.la: Moderatior hac in parte Julio, temperatior Augusto Tiberius, ne quidem patris patriæ nomen sæpè delatum affumpsit, acerbèque increpuit eos, qui divinas, nas occupationes, ipsumque dominum dixerant, quanquantum ab ea arrogantiae temperatione abierunt, qui nec tanta imperii amplitudine claruerunt, & sapientiae divinioris gustum perceperunt, Codicis legum scriptores! Bene Augustum, recenti Actiacae pugnae victoria elatum, Maecenas monuit, enormes honorum delationes, templa inprimis & statuas, aspernaretur: addita magni ingenii sententia: [illegible, ~12 letters] [illegible, ~20 letters] [?] [illegible, ~18 letters] [illegible, ~16 letters]. Virtus multos mortales diis exaequat: suffragiis nemo unquam deus effectus. quare tibi, ubi bonus fueris recteque imperaveris, universa terra templum erit, omnes urbes delubra, omnes homines pro statuis. animis enim illorum semper cum gloria insidebis. apud Dionem Cassium libro 52.
units.tr: Tiberius was more moderate in this respect than Julius and more restrained than Augustus. He did not even take up the title of Father of the Fatherland, though it was often offered to him, and he sharply rebuked those who had called him divine, or even lord, though those who were less distinguished in the vastness of their empire, and who had tasted a more divine wisdom, the writers of the law Code, departed far from this restraint of arrogance! Maecenas wisely warned Augustus, who was puffed up by the recent victory at Actium, that he should spurn immense honours, above all temples and statues, adding a saying of great genius: [illegible, ~12 letters] [illegible, ~20 letters] [?] [illegible, ~18 letters] [illegible, ~16 letters]. Virtue makes many mortals equal to the gods; no one has ever been made a god by votes. Therefore, when you have been good and have ruled rightly, the whole earth will be your temple, all cities your shrines, and all men your statues; for you will always dwell in their minds with glory. In Dio Cassius, book 52.

units.la: CLXXXVI.
units.tr: CLXXXVI.

units.la: CLXXXVI. Convenientissima bono viro inter adulationem & asperitatem media oratio.
units.tr: CLXXXVI. A speech suited to a good man, midway between flattery and harshness.

units.la: Nec enim [illegible, ~8 letters] omnibus, & multo minus [illegible, ~10 letters] placent. Tanta adulandi consuetudo Romanos, veluti tabes, invaserat, ut ab ipso Tiberio reprimenda effet[?]. unde angusta & lubrica oratio, sub principe, qui libertatem metuebat adulationem oderat. Versatilis ingenii hominibus sub Domitiano adoratione, sub Trajano parrhasia uti, non difficile est. nec epigrammatum scriptori stylum vertere, arduum erat;
units.tr: For neither [illegible] pleases everyone, and still less [illegible] pleases. So great a habit of flattery had seized the Romans, like a plague, that it had to be checked even by Tiberius himself. Hence speech was narrow and slippery under a prince who feared freedom and hated flattery. For men of a pliant disposition it was not difficult to use adulation under Domitian and frankness under Trajan; nor was it hard for a writer of epigrams to turn his pen.

units.la: Frustra blanditiae venitis ad me Attritis miserabiles labellis, Dicturus Dominum Deumque non sum: Jam non est locus hac in urbe vobis. Ad Parthos procul ite pileatos, Et turpes humilesque supplicesque, Pistorum solabasiate regum.
units.tr: In vain do you come to me, flatteries, wretched with your worn lips. I am not going to call him Lord and God. There is no place left for you in this city. Go far off to the Parthians in their caps, you base, humble and suppliant creatures, to the thrones of the kings of the Pistores.

units.la: Non est hic dominus, sed imperator,
units.tr: Here he is not a lord, but an emperor,

units.la: Sed justissimus omnium senator: Per quem de stygia domo seducta est Siccis rustica veritas capillis. Hoc sub principe, fi sapis, caveto. Verbis, Roma, prioribus loquaris. Martialis libro 10.
units.tr: but the most just of all senators, through whom plain truth has been led back from the Stygian house with dry hair. Under this prince, if you are wise, take care. Speak, Rome, in the older words. Martial, book 10.

units.la: At sub Tiberio, nec libertatem civium, nec adulatio- nem ferente, sermo circumspectio vibratur. Confuel- tum dubitantibus est, Marcelli Epii ad Helvidium ad- monitionem audire: Quomodo peffimis imperato- ribus fine fine dominationem, ita quamvis egregiis modum libertatis placere. 1v. Hiftor.
units.tr: But under Tiberius, who tolerated neither the freedom of citizens nor flattery, speech is wielded with careful caution. It is a matter of doubt for those who are unsure to hear the admonition of Marcellus Epius to Helvidius: as the worst emperors please with unlimited domination, so even the most excellent please with a measure of liberty. Tacitus, Histories, book 4.

units.la: CLXXXVII.
units.tr: CLXXXVII.

units.la: Aperta vi quam occulto dolo hostem ulcisci gloriosius.
units.tr: It is more glorious to take vengeance on an enemy by open force than by hidden treachery.

units.la: Non ducum hic strategemata, gentium jure non prohibita, rejicio: sed veneficia, & generosum animum non decentia regnorum munimenta, carpo. Adgan- deftrii principis Chattorum literis, quibus mortem Arminii promittebat, fi patranda neci venenum mitte- ret, non fraude neque occultis, sed pa- lam & armatum, populum Romanum boftes suos ulci- ci. Induerítne Tiberius Fabricii & Camilli animum, eorumque gloriæ nonimmerito fe æquaverit, pen- dentem judici litem remitto. Potuerit Adgandeftrius indicio veneni missi Arminium ad novum in Roma- nos bellum incitare: quod suspicatus Tiberius, dor- mientem leonem excitare noluerit. Forte & eadem de Romanis fama, quæ nunc de Italis, in Germania percrebuit, veneno eos armorum diffidentia grassari, quam de Romana gente conceptam opinionem dele- re hoc responso voluit. Quid fi, quod supra tetigi, pa- ce cum Arminio occultè initâ, eo ad opprimendos qui Romanæ potentiæ in Germania formidandi erant, u- tatur? Quicquid fit; plura Tiberius occulta fraude, quàm palàm armata manu, machinabatur. Simulatio- num nescius Alphonfus rex Campaniæ, Rugerio Pa- lanzæ Comiti, eædem Castellani regis offerenti, ex animo
units.tr: I set aside here the stratagems of generals, which the law of nations does not forbid, but I find fault with poisonings and with defences of kingdoms that do not suit a noble spirit. In the letter of Adgandestrius, prince of the Chatti, he promised to kill Arminius if Tiberius would send poison to carry out the murder, so that the Roman people might avenge their enemies not by fraud or secret means, but openly and with armed force. Whether Tiberius had the spirit of Fabricius and Camillus, and whether he rightly claimed equal glory with them, I leave as a question for the judge to decide. Adgandestrius could, by informing Arminius of the poison that had been sent, have stirred him up to a new war against the Romans; Tiberius, suspecting this, chose not to rouse a sleeping lion. Perhaps the same rumour that has now spread in Italy also spread in Germany about the Romans, that they were using poison because they distrusted arms, and by this reply he wished to remove the opinion formed of the Roman people. What if, as I touched on above, he secretly made peace with Arminius and used it to crush those who were to be feared by Roman power in Germany? Whatever the case, Tiberius was plotting more by hidden fraud than by open armed force. Alphonsus, king of Campania, who knew nothing of pretence, is said to have answered, from his heart, Roger, Count of Palanza, who offered him the same thing on behalf of the king of Castile: even if I were about to obtain the kingdom of the whole world, I would never permit such a crime.

units.la: {y} Serma me-dius. animo respondisse fertur: etiamsi totius mundi regnum consecuturus essem, nunquam tantum scelus permittam. Supra fidem est illud, quod de Pontifice Romano Pio V. fertur. ardentem desiderio capiendi Mariani Asculani, facinorosorum in exilio ducis, non nemo aggressus proditionem pollicebatur. quem execratus pontifex, faceret, e conspectu iussit. Me judice non eadem adversus latronem, qua erga justum hostem, religione opus erat. nisi quod fides ei data non sit frangenda, laxiori caeteris in rebus disciplina utaris.
units.tr: It is beyond belief what is told of the Roman pontiff Pius V. Someone, burning with desire to capture Marianus Ascolanus, a leader of criminals in exile, offered to betray him. The pontiff, cursing him, ordered him out of his sight. In my judgement, one does not need the same scruple towards a robber as towards a lawful enemy, except that a promise once given must not be broken; in other matters you may use a looser discipline.

units.la: CLXXXVIII.
units.tr: CLXXXVIII.

units.la: Libertatis custodes amoto metu ipsam plerunque invadunt.
units.tr: The guardians of liberty, once fear is removed, very often attack liberty itself.

units.la: Sive a principio regnum agitaverint; sive blandientem opportunitate fortunam arripiant. Arminius abscedentibus Romanis, & pulso Maroboduo, regnum affectans, libertatem popularium adversam habuit. Facundae extant apud Dionem, libro 52, Agrippae & Maecenatis ad Augustum dissertationes. Agrippa Augustum a capessenda monarchia dehortaturus, in caeteris hoc argumento utitur. Si nunc, praebente se fortuna, regnum invadas, rumorem de te affectati a principio belli praebebis. atque ita hominis fraudulenti, tortuosi, pravi ingenii famam, quae nulla regni potentia redimenda, accerses. Maecenas contra: ejusmodi conatum non esse a natura hominis alienum; & praemium esse eo labore dignum. Sed aut non introspexit animum Augusti Agrippa; aut tota haec dissertatio, quod magis reor, commentum est Dionis. Omnes enim Augusti actiones flagrantem a principio regnandi cupiditatem produnt. De Arminio aliud dicendum; assuetum diuturno imperio, & progressibus illectum, reditum ad vitam privatam a se impetrare nequivisse.
units.tr: Whether they have aimed at kingship from the start, or seize upon fortune when it flatters them with an opportunity. Arminius, when the Romans withdrew and Maroboduus was driven out, aspired to kingship and found the liberty of his people opposed to him. Eloquent speeches of Agrippa and Maecenas to Augustus are extant in Dio, book 52. Agrippa, wishing to dissuade Augustus from taking up monarchy, uses this argument among others: if you now invade the kingship, as fortune offers it, you will give people reason to believe you have aimed at it from the beginning of the war, and so you will acquire the reputation of a deceitful, crooked, and wicked man, a reputation that no power of kingship can buy back. Maecenas argues the opposite: such an attempt is not foreign to human nature, and the reward is worth the effort. But either Agrippa did not look into the mind of Augustus, or the whole speech is, as I think more likely, an invention of Dio's. For all of Augustus's actions reveal a passion for ruling burning from the beginning. Arminius must be treated differently: having grown accustomed to long-lasting command and enticed by his advances, he was unable to win for himself a return to private life.

units.la: CLXXXIX.
units.tr: CLXXXIX.

units.la: Non ex potentiae rumore magnus dux aestimandus.
units.tr: A great general is not to be judged by the noise of his power.

units.la: Major Pyrrho, Hannibale, Philippo, Perseo, Antiocho', insignis potentiae regibus aut ducibus, Arminius, 1. belli felici eventu. priores omnes patriam Romanis in servitutem victi tradiderunt. Arminius liberator haud dubiè Germania. 2. illi nondum adultum Romanorum imperium, nec ab aliorum armis quietum, tentaverunt. animosior Arminius, qui non primordia populi Romani, sicut alii reges ducesque, sed florentissimum imperium lacessierit. 3. alii aut proeliis omnibus, ut Antiochus Asiae rex, aut belli saltem fine succumbere didicere. Arminius proelii ambiguus, bello non victus. Non minus igitur quam Pyrrhus, quam Annibal, sedem inter magnos belli duces, & in annalium parnasso memoriam sui meretur.
units.tr: Pyrrhus, Hannibal, Philip, Perseus and Antiochus were kings or generals of great power, yet Arminius is greater, for three reasons: (1) the outcome of his war was successful: all the earlier men handed their country over to the Romans as slaves after being defeated, whereas Arminius was undoubtedly the liberator of Germany. (2) They attacked the Roman empire when it was not yet fully grown and was not secured from the arms of others; Arminius was bolder, for he assailed not the beginnings of the Roman people, as other kings and generals did, but the most flourishing empire. (3) The others either gave way in every battle, as Antiochus, king of Asia, did, or at least learned to yield at the end of the war; Arminius was doubtful in battle, but not conquered in war. Therefore he deserves a seat no less than Pyrrhus and Hannibal among the great commanders of war, and a memory on the Parnassus of the annals.

units.la: CXC.
units.tr: CXC.

units.la: Famam peritiae militaris alii habent, alii merentur.
units.tr: Some men have a reputation for military skill, and others deserve it.

units.la: Famae celebritate obscurior Arminius, gloriae merito celebrior. Gracorum annalibus ignotus, qui suam tantum mirantur : Romanis haud perinde celebris, dum vetera extollimus, recentium incuriosi.
units.tr: Arminius is less famous for his reputation, but more celebrated for the merit of his glory. Unknown in the annals of the Greeks, who admire only their own: not equally celebrated among the Romans, since we extol the old and are careless of the recent.

units.la: TERTIUS ANNALIUM TACITI liber per Aphorismos explicatus.
units.tr: The Third Book of the Annals of Tacitus, explained by aphorisms.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Mœrore intus compresso lugere magnam fortunam decet.
units.tr: A great fortune should mourn with grief pressed down inside.

units.la: SUMAT Agrippina componendo animo paucos dies, violenta luctu, & ne-scia tolerandi. Muliebrem enim animum, & hactenus[?] tantum secundam fortunam expertum, id non dedecet. Portus, litora, moenia ac tecta lugentium numero compleantur. datur id mediocri etiam hominum[?] forti. [illegible, ~4 words] Silentio aut lu-gubri ululatu luctu prostratam excipiant. Est enim so-latii genus, mœstitiæ socium habere. Incomta signa, versi fasces, atrata plebes, trabeati equites feretrū precedant. vestem, odores, aurum etiam atque argentum, pro copia rerum & pro more loci ac seculi, pyræ adjiciant: fletu & conclamatione ac planctu, animo conceptum dolorem testentur, alii præficarum more, hilari animo complorationem tristi persona induant.
units.tr: Agrippina should take a few days to compose her mind, since she is overcome by grief and does not know how to bear it. A woman's spirit, which has so far known only good fortune, is not disgraced by this. Harbours, shores, walls and roofs should be filled with mourners. This is permitted even to a moderately brave man. [illegible] Let them receive her, prostrated by grief, with silence or mournful wailing. For having companions in sorrow is a kind of comfort. Let them carry the unadorned standards, the reversed fasces, the crowd in black, and the knights in triumphal robes before the bier. Let them add to the pyre clothing, perfumes, gold and silver, according to the wealth of the household and the custom of the place and age. Let them bear witness to their inward grief with weeping, lamentation and beating of the breast. Others, in the manner of the hired mourners, may put on a sad mask while their spirits are cheerful.

units.la: Non eadem vulgusque decent & culmina rerum. Tiberius atque Augusta publico abstinuere, inferius majestate sua rati, si palam lamentarentur.
units.tr: Such things do not suit the common people and the heights of power equally. Tiberius and Augusta refrained from public display, thinking it beneath their majesty if they lamented openly.

units.la: Quo loco tria nobis discutienda veniunt. I. an magnum virum dolor ob amicum defunctum deceat?
units.tr: Here three questions come before us. (1) Does grief for a dead friend befit a great man?

units.la: 2. an dolore in fletum erumpere non indecorum fit? 3. an palam lugere principi vito honeftum. Quod ad primum: naturæ juta funt ut nafci, ita diffolvi: ut adolefcere, ita maturo fenio deflaccefcere. Utnemo pueritiam, adolefcentiam, juventutem alicujus amif- fam deplorat; fed longam vitam gratulatur: ita nec fenectutis extremum, ut procumbentis fegetis mef- fem, conclamatione vit fapiens dolebit; Adde quod judicio magni viri, mors aeruminarum requies, cunéta mortalium mala diffolvit, ultra neque curæ hequé gaudio locum daturæ. Heu quam dulce malum mors talibus additum,
units.tr: (2) Is it unseemly to break into weeping from grief? (3) Is it honourable for a prince to mourn in public? As to the first: just as we are born, so we are dissolved by nature; just as we grow up, so in ripe old age we wither away. No one laments the loss of someone's childhood, adolescence or youth, but congratulates him on a long life. So a wise man will not grieve with wailing over the end of old age, like a harvest that is ripe and falling. Add to this that, in the judgement of a great man, death is the rest of the spirits: it dissolves all the evils of mortals, leaving no room for care or joy any more. Alas, how sweet a mischief death is, when it is added to such lives!

units.la: Vitæ dirus amor: cum pateat malis Effugium, & miferos libera mors vocet; Portus æterna Placidus quiete!
units.tr: The fierce love of life, when an escape from troubles lies open, and free death calls the wretched to a calm and eternal harbour!

units.la: Nullus hunc terror, nec impotens Procella fortunæ movet, Aut iniqui flamma Tonantis: Pax alta nullos civium cœtus Timet, aut minaces victoris iras, Non maria afperis infana Coris: Non acies ferás.
units.tr: No terror moves him, nor the headstrong storm of fortune, nor the flame of the unjust Thunderer. Deep peace fears no assemblies of citizens, nor the threatening wrath of the victor, nor the seas mad with rough winds, nor a fierce army.

units.la: Utî Seneca Agamn. Choro 3.
units.tr: As Seneca says in the Agamemnon, chorus 3.

units.la: Lufimus & nos verfibus aliquando in hunc fenfum:
units.tr: I too once played with verses to this effect:

units.la: Τὸν βίον, ἄνθρωποι, μεῖζόν τι κράζετε οἴνῳ; Ἐλπὶς δ᾽ ἡδὺ φάος πνεύματι ἐστι θεοῦς. Καὶ πεῖα βλάπτειν ζωὴ ἐκ κτῆσις ἀδήλου. Μηδὲν ἔχοντα πάσης φροντίς, ἔχοντα φόβον. Ἡ δυσι[?] ἐκ ἑλὼ ἀνχίαν ὀμμάτων ἀμφὶ ἀμφόβου. Ἐλπίδ᾽ ἡδὺ τύχης νόμῳ[?] μέλει.
units.tr: What, mortals, do you cry that life is something greater than wine? Hope is a sweet light, a breath of the gods. And to live is to harm, the possession of an uncertain thing. Having nothing, one has no care; having, one has fear. ... Hope is sweet; it is the lot of fortune. [Τὸν βίον, ἄνθρωποι, μεῖζόν τι κράζετε οἴνῳ; Ἐλπὶς δ᾽ ἡδὺ φάος πνεύματι ἐστι θεοῦς.]

units.la: Aliud pro comprimendo luctu argumentum a magnitudine animi: cui vitæ cupiditas probro; contemptus laudi ducitur. Nec enim convenit, in alieno funere mollem effe, qui mortem fibi advenientem erectis oculis afpicit. Magnanimè Ajax apud Sophoclem:.
units.tr: Another argument for restraining grief comes from greatness of spirit: the desire to live is held a disgrace, and contempt of life is counted praise. For it does not suit a man who looks death in the face with unflinching eyes to be effeminate at another's funeral. Ajax in Sophocles speaks nobly:

units.la: Αἰχεὸν δ᾽ ἀνδρὶ τέ μοι μέγας ἔχει ἐν χρόνῳ βίῳ[?]. Καχλοῖς ὅσις μὲν δὲ ἑαυτοῦ[?] ἔτι. Τί δ᾽ ἔστι πρὸς ἡμῶν ἡμέραις τῶν ἐχθρῶν; Πόδας ἀφ᾽ ὑμῶν ἡμέραις κείνων ἑαυτοῦ[?].
units.tr: For the long time of life has a great grace for a man... but what is there of our days, of the days of our enemies? ... [Αἰχεὸν δ᾽ ἀνδρὶ τέ μοι μέγας ἔχει ἐν χρόνῳ βίῳ.]

units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: ἀλλ' ἢ καλῶς ζῆν, ἢ καλῶς τεθνηκέναι[?],
units.tr: Either to live nobly or to die nobly. [ἀλλ' ἢ καλῶς ζῆν, ἢ καλῶς τεθνηκέναι.]

units.la: τὸ δ' ἀνήκεστον λόγον[?].
units.tr: ...but the unendurable word. [τὸ δ' ἀνήκεστον λόγον.]

units.la: Animum mori destinatum & othonis illa spirant: Plu-ra de extremis loqui, pars ignaviae est. praecipuum destinationis meae documentum habete, quod de nemine queror. Nam incusare deos vel homines, ejus est, qui vivere velit. Tac. 2. Histor. Verùm saniora fortassis de statu mortis Romanorum & Graecorum poetarum principes. Quorum Virgilius de iis, qui taedio vitae mortem sibi conscíverant, in haec verba erumpit:
units.tr: The spirit resolved on death and the words of Otho breathe this: to say more about one's last moments is a sign of cowardice. Take as the chief proof of my resolve that I complain of no one. For to accuse gods or men belongs to one who wishes to live. Tacitus, Histories 2. But the leading Roman and Greek poets speak more soundly about the state of the dead. Of these, Virgil, speaking of those who had consciously taken their own lives out of weariness of life, bursts out in these words:

units.la: —— —— quam vellent æthere in alto Nunc & pauperiem & duros perferre labores? Fata obstant, tristiquè palus inamabilis unda Alligat, & novies Styx interfusa coercet.
units.tr: Would they wish, in the high air, now to bear poverty and hard labours? The fates stand in the way, and the sad, unlovable marsh with its black water binds them, and the Styx, flowing around them nine times, holds them back.

units.la: VI. Æneid.
units.tr: Aeneid, Book VI.

units.la: In Odyssea autem Homeri Achilles, quem viventem nulla arma, nulla mortis formido terruerat, apud inferos cupiditatem vitae Ulyssem non celat. Malle se ait tenuis fortunae agricolae omnes vitae dies servire, quam mortuorum manibus imperio praeesse. Denique non eadem in nostra, & amicorum, vita spernenda animi altitudo decora est. Multa amicorum causae damus, quae in nostra minus honeste perpetraremus. Hinc φιλαυτίας[?] nomen in vitio apud Graecos, φιλόφιλος[?] aut φιλαυτοπράκτως[?] nequaquam. Et pepercisse vitae suae nihil admirationis habet: eam vero pro aliorum salute profudisse, laudem meretur.
units.tr: In the Odyssey of Homer, Achilles, whom no weapon and no fear of death terrified while he lived, does not hide from Odysseus among the dead his longing for life. He says he would rather serve, all the days of his life, a poor farmer of slender means than rule over the dead. In short, a lofty spirit that despises life is becoming in our own case and that of our friends, but not in the same way. We often do for our friends what we would commit less honourably for ourselves. Hence among the Greeks the name φιλαυτία [self-love] is a reproach, while φιλόφιλος [friend-loving] or φιλαυτοπράκτως [acting for oneself] is by no means so. Sparing one's own life has nothing to wonder at; but pouring it out for the safety of others deserves praise.

units.la: Proxima de lamentatione & erumpente ploratu quaestio. quam philosophi, Porticenses praesertim, aperta negatione decidunt. Poetarum etiam generosiores fletum. mulierculis, non viris, convenire sentiunt. Quod autem in sacris tot monumentis lacrymarum, in piis etiam regibus & prophetis, obruimur: facilis effet nodi expeditio; Syros, Aegyptios, & situ medios Judaeos, Europaeis molliores, hanc sibi veniam deposcere: nisi Christum semel atque iterum flevisse sacra e pagina constaret. Quare πολυπραγμ[?] in re, sacram censuram attingente, supersedeo. Nam ad vulgatum gentium morem, cum is in disceptandi judicium veniat, non provoco. De aperta coram populo lamentatione tractatio superest. Tiberius atque Augusta publico abstinuere. non quasi doloris magnitudine victi. ob quam viduas maritorum defuncto-rum exequias non ire, aliquando & lecto infpeciem doloris affixas detineri (pour tenir la countenance) in Gallia observavi. verum inferius majestate sua rati, si palam lamentarentur. Quibus consentientia Aga-memno apud Euripidem, mactata in victimam filia Iphigenia:
units.tr: The next question concerns lamentation and bursting into tears. The philosophers, especially the Stoics, settle it by plain denial. Even the more noble of the poets feel that weeping suits women and not men. But since we are overwhelmed by so many records of tears in the sacred books, even in pious kings and prophets, the knot would be easy to untie: Syrians, Egyptians, and Jews who live in the middle of the world, softer than Europeans, might ask for this indulgence for themselves, were it not established from the sacred page that Christ wept once and again. Therefore, in a matter that touches sacred censure, I refrain from excessive curiosity. For I do not appeal to the common custom of the nations, since that would come into the judgement of disputing. What remains is the discussion of open lamentation before the people. Tiberius and Augusta refrained from public display, not as if overcome by the greatness of grief, for which I have observed in France that widows do not go to their husbands' funerals, and sometimes remain kept at home, the face of grief fixed on the bed (to keep up appearances), but thinking it beneath their majesty if they lamented openly. In agreement with this is Agamemnon in Euripides, when his daughter Iphigenia has been led to the sacrifice:

units.la: Ἡ δυστυχία δ' ὡς ἔχει τ' ἀγνοησον. [?]
units.tr: Her misfortune, as it stands, ignore... [Ἡ δυστυχία δ' ὡς ἔχει τ' ἀγνοησον.]
