units.tr: Since such a mysterious misfortune has come... [Εἰς ὥς μυστηρίως συμφορας ἀφιγμένης.]

units.la: Quibus verbis privatae vitae fortem regiae, lacrymandi concessa potestate, praefert. Hoc regum Romanorum & Grajorum de fletu judicium: dispar Hebraeorum, etiam pientissimorum, nec rebus bello gestis contemnendorum, quos inter princeps David, Saulis & Abneris, non amicissimorum aliquandiu hominum, coram populo funera, fletu & lamentabili vocifera-tione, prosecutus dicitur. Ut taceam liberorum obi-tus molliter ab eo & luctuose latos.
units.tr: By these words he prefers the fortune of a private life to that of a king, which is allowed the liberty of weeping. This is the judgement of the Roman and Greek kings on weeping. The Hebrews differ, even the most pious of them, nor were they to be despised in warlike deeds; among them the prince David is said to have followed the funerals of Saul and Abner, men not very friendly to him for a time, before the people, with weeping and a mournful outcry. Not to mention that he bore the deaths of his children gently and with sorrow.

units.la: Hactenus quasi nihil astute Tiberio agente, quae-stiones excussimus: nunc suspicacem Taciti conjectu-ram, de simulandi gnaro principe, promamus. Publico cum matre abstinuisse auguratur, ne omnium oculis vultus eorum [scrutantibus, falsi intelligerentur]. i.e. ne omnium oculis in eos conjectis, larva simulati lu-ctus, & compressum sinu gaudium, revelaretur. Quo spectat mater Antonia die exequiarum domi detenta, ut par maeror, & matris exemplo avia quoque & patruus attineri viderentur. Quod ut à moribus Tiberii non alienum, nec tamen certa demonstratione perspicuum, in medium relinquo. Quibus à sinistra suspicione Tiberium purgare animus est, invictum ejus animum luctu unici filii afferant. Nam per omnes va-letudinis ejus dies, nullo metu, an ut firmitudinem animi ostentaret, etiam defuncto nec dum sepulto, curiam ingressus est. consulesque fede vulgari per speciem moestitiae sedentes, honoris locique admonuit: & effusum in lacrymas senatum, victo gemitu, simul oratione continua erexit. 1 v. Annalium. Quae animi firmitudo non omnem Tiberio sinistrae famae maculam abstergeret. Vultu enim aequè obfirmato exequias Germanico ire, atque hic curiam intrare, potuit. nisi quod ibi compressas lacrymas non aequè tacita hominum suspicio ignovisset, aut profluentes aestimasset, atque hic in obitu Drusi, aemulationis causa amota, ignovit.
units.tr: Hitherto we have examined these questions, as if Tiberius was doing nothing cunningly. Now let us bring forward Tacitus's suspicious conjecture, that the prince was skilled at pretence. He is said to have refrained from public display with his mother, so that the faces of those looking at them would reveal what was false, that is, lest, with all eyes turned upon them, the mask of feigned grief and the joy hidden in the breast would be exposed. To this purpose the mother Antonia was kept at home on the day of the funeral, so that equal grief, and by the example of the mother, the grandmother and the uncle also seemed to be restrained. Whether this was in keeping with Tiberius's character, but not clearly shown by any certain demonstration, I leave open. I wish to clear Tiberius of this sinister suspicion by pointing to the unconquered spirit that he showed in the grief for his only son. For through all the days of his sickness, with no fear, perhaps to show firmness of spirit, he even entered the senate-house while the dead man was not yet buried, and he reminded the consuls, sitting in ordinary dress as a sign of sorrow, of their rank and place; and when the senate dissolved into tears, he raised it again by a continuous speech, his grief overcome. Annals, Book 1. This firmness of spirit would not have wiped away every stain of ill repute from Tiberius. For he could have gone to Germanicus's funeral with a face equally steadfast, as he entered the senate-house here; except that the silent suspicion of men would have pardoned tears held back there no more than it would have judged them flowing freely; just as here, at the death of Drusus, with rivalry removed, he pardoned.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Studia in vivos magis, quàm desiderium mortuorum, aemulatione accensum principem mordent.
units.tr: The prince is stung more by those who are inflamed with rivalry toward the living than by longing for the dead.

units.la: Hi enim, quamvis tacito voto praeferantur, obesse amplius Principi non possunt. At illi praeter affectum subditorum, & spem imperii deferendi non abjecerint. Magno animorum magis quam facum ardore funus Germanici Romani celebrantes, cecidisse remp. nihil spei reliquum conclamaverunt. Nihil tamen Tiberium magis penetravit, quam studia hominum accensa in Agrippinam. haec enim virum paris ingenii, sanguinis, studii popularis nacta, devolvere solio Tiberium poterat. quare nec nubere eam unquam permisit, nec metuere eam, donec è medio tolleretur, desiit. praecipuè cum voces populi ac de ea judicia perciperet: cum decus patria, solum Augusti sanguinem, unicum antiquitatis specimen appellarent. se in ea laudata despici: se labem patriae, surreptitiam adoptione Augusti sobolem, morum reip. novatorem interpretabatur. Parcant laudi alicujus propinquorum princi-pis,qui quo animo in eum feratur,ignorant. Caveant nimium laudari, qui suspicaci principi proximi voto destinantur. Marcellum sub Augusto, & eo extincto Agrippam, deinde Cajum ac Lucium liberos ejus, in oculis & ore populus ferebat : pars & officium in principem rati, plures aliorum judicio rapti, quod illis à Livia,vel ab ipso Augusto,exitio fuisse perhibetur.
units.tr: These men, though they are preferred in a silent wish, cannot harm the prince any further. But those others, beyond the affection of their subjects, did not give up hope of passing on the empire. Celebrating the funeral of Germanicus the Roman with a fervour of spirit greater than that of their torches, they cried out together that the commonwealth had fallen and no hope was left. Yet nothing pierced Tiberius more than the zeal of men kindled toward Agrippina. For she, having a husband of equal talent, blood and popular zeal, could hurl Tiberius from the throne. Therefore he never allowed her to marry, and he ceased to fear her only when she was removed from the midst. This was especially so when he heard the voices of the people and their judgments about her: when they called her the glory of the fatherland, the sole blood of Augustus, the unique specimen of antiquity. He interpreted this praise as contempt for himself: she was the stain on the fatherland, a child secretly brought into the family by Augustus' adoption, an innovator in the morals of the state. Let those who do not know the spirit in which the prince regards them spare praise of a kinsman of the prince. Let those beware of being praised too much who are marked out by the wish of a suspicious prince as his successors. The people bore Marcellus on their lips and before their eyes under Augustus, and after his death Agrippa, then Gaius and Lucius, his sons. Some did so from duty toward the prince, thinking it right; many were carried away by the judgment of others. It is said that this was their ruin, brought about by Livia or by Augustus himself.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Ne sibi nimium plebecula judicii in principis acta permittat.
units.tr: The common crowd should not take too much upon itself to judge the acts of the prince.

units.la: Si sumptuosus funere Germanici Tiberius fuisset, prodigum ærarii publici, de alieno largum vociferati fuissent. Nunc more suo parcimonia gaudente Tiberio, fuere qui publici funeris pompam requirerent, ita invisum semel principem seu bene seu male acta premunt : ut alibi Cornelius. qua tamen judicandi protervia nihil fermè lucratur vulgus, nisi ut afperio-rem sibi reddat, quem placabiliorem habere poterat. Et alioqui non est magnarum animarum, de funebri pompa nimis esse folicitum. Sicuti Julius Cæsar, qui rerum gestarum gloriam pulcherrima ad posteros & mansura manumenta credebat, irrisisse Cyri soler-tiam, formam sepulturæ suæ præscribentis, traditur. Quid hic egisset, fi in acta morientis Philippi Hispania-rum regis, Carolo V. geniti, incidisset. quæ à tempo-rum illorum scriptoribus nec non à nobis in nondum edito Historiæ Belgicæ opere, pertexuntur.
units.tr: If Tiberius had been lavish at Germanicus' funeral, they would have cried out that he was wasteful of the public treasury and generous with another's money. As it was, Tiberius rejoicing in his usual thrift, "there were those who demanded the pomp of a public funeral." So they press upon the prince, once he is hated, whether he has acted well or badly, as Cornelius says elsewhere. Yet by this obstinacy in judging the crowd gains almost nothing, except to make him harsher toward itself, when it could have had him more placable. Besides, it is not the mark of great spirits to be overly anxious about the pomp of a funeral. Julius Caesar, who believed that the glory of his deeds would be the most beautiful and lasting monument for posterity, is said to have laughed at the cleverness of Cyrus, who prescribed the form of his own burial. What would Caesar have done had he come upon the acts of the dying Philip, king of Spain, son of Charles V? These are recounted by the writers of those times and by us in the work on the Belgian History that is not yet published.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Omnes de fe sermones vulgi scire, non omnes poena coërcere, imperato-ris est.
units.tr: It belongs to the emperor to know all the talk of the common people about himself, but not to punish all of it.

units.la: Paucorum de fe dicta contemptu, multorum edicto reprimet. Magnificentiam in funerando Germanico garrula plebs desideraverat. Gnarum id Tiberio fuit, utque premeret vulgi sermones, monuit edicto. Nec omnes populi sermones in animum admittendos esse, nec omnes contemnendos, olim a Platone monitum, quod tanto acrius principi servandum, quanto ejus fama pluribus procellis jactatur. Omnium autem si rimari sermones velit, & eorum notitiam prae se ferre: si poena grassabitur, odium attrahet; si praeter iram non procedet, contemptum. Quare & hic, ut in aliis reip. gubernandi scopulis, inter Charybdin & Scyllam media via navim torquebit. qui scopulo principem assimulant, infultus omnes constanti quiete frangenti, nec nihil, nec omnia proferunt.
units.tr: He will check the disparaging words of a few by an edict aimed at many. The chattering crowd had wanted magnificence in Germanicus' funeral. Tiberius knew this and, to suppress the talk of the crowd, gave warning by an edict. That not all the talk of the people is to be taken to heart, nor all of it despised, was advised long ago by Plato. The prince must observe this the more carefully, the more his reputation is tossed about by many storms. But if he wishes to search out all the talk and show that he knows it, then if he punishes it he will draw hatred; if he goes no further than anger, he will draw contempt. Wherefore here too, as among the other rocks of governing the state, the middle way will steer the ship between Charybdis and Scylla. Those who liken the prince to a rock, which breaks every assault with constant calm, say neither nothing nor everything.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Minus principibus quam plebi licentiae permissum.
units.tr: Less licence is permitted to princes than to the common people.

units.la: Vulgus potentiam imperantium licentia, & soluto magis quam remisso animo, metitur. ad vulgi sensum, quam ad gravitatem historiae accommodatius, Dio Cassius illud Ἀλλ᾽ ἐλευθέω τῶν νόμων[?] solvi legibus,libro 53. interpretatur. Permissam enim Augusto a senatu quid libet faciendi & omittendi potestatem ait. quod si de impunitate accipias; ferendum: si de condendarum & abolendarum legum arbitrio; nimium, in republica recentis libertatis adhuc memori. de iis vero, quae hic Tiberius pronunciat, non eadem decora principibus viris & imperatori populoque, non poterat naturam rerum senatus immutare. Est autem Tiberius capiendus primo de affectuum laxato freno; deinde & de virtutum & vitiorum licentia aut cohibitione. Tristitiae, luctus, timoris, iracundiae, gaudii, & exultationis capistra solutiora habere plebeculam non plane decet. At principis, gravitatis personam induti, in vultu & sermone nihil ut abjectum, ita gesticulatione exultabundum apparere debet. deluctu sic Tiberius: modicis domibus, aut civitatibus, convenisse recenti dolore luctum, & ex moerore solatia. At urbem rerum dominam, & principes in ea viros, unius hominis, quem mortalem non ignoraverint, obitu prosterni, non decere. referendum jam animum ad firmitudinem, non immoderato moerore solvendum. ut quon- dam divus Julius amissa unica filia,ut divus Augustus ereptis nepotibus, abstruserint tristitiam, quorum hic tanto labore partum imperium privigno, ille adoptio- ne irreptitiis externis reliquerit. quanto magis nunc compescendum esse dolorem, superstitibus vel Tibe- rio,vel ipsi Germanico, liberis, qui reip. curam capef- fant. denique, ut populi Romani, qui olim fuit, & qui nunc est, diversitas deprehendatur: quoties populus Romanus clades exercituum, interitum ducum, fun- ditus amissas nobiles familias constanter tulerit. ut de- letam ad Cremeram Fabiorum gentem, ut fusos ab Annibale tot exercitus. Poftcladem illos animofiores & hosti terribiliores resurrexisse, at nunc in oculis gentium animos civium Romanorum, quasi a&tum de salute imperii effet, concidere! De injiciendo cæ- teris affectibus freno, neclaxando in perturbationes imperantium animo, pari fuso filum sermonis duci possit, fitemporinon esse & lectoris otio parcendum judicaremus. Vitiorum autem (namque is alter erat locus licentiæ nemini quidem mortalium, sed mini- mè omnium imperantibus, permissa effusio.
units.tr: The crowd measures the power of rulers by licence, and by a loosened rather than a relaxed mind. Dio Cassius, in book 53, interprets the saying "But he is free from the laws," solvi legibus, in a way better suited to the understanding of the crowd than to the gravity of history. For he says that the senate granted Augustus the power to do or omit whatever he pleased. If this is taken to mean impunity, it may be borne; if it means the power to make and abolish laws, it is too much in a commonwealth still mindful of its recent liberty. As for what Tiberius here pronounces, that "the same things are not becoming to princely men and to the emperor and people," the senate could not change the nature of things. Tiberius is to be understood first of the loosened rein of the passions, and then of the licence or restraint of virtues and vices. For the common crowd it is not altogether fitting to have looser bridles on sadness, grief, fear, anger, joy and exultation. But the prince, having put on the person of gravity, ought to show in countenance and speech nothing abject, and in gesture nothing exultant. Tiberius speaks thus about mourning: "It is fitting for modest households or cities to gather in fresh grief and to seek consolation in sorrow. But for the city, mistress of affairs, and the men in it to be laid low by the death of one man, whom they knew to be mortal, is not fitting. The mind must now be turned back to firmness, not dissolved in immoderate grief." Just as the deified Julius hid his sadness when he lost his only daughter, and the deified Augustus when his grandsons were snatched away, the one leaving the empire won by such labour to his stepson, the other leaving it by adoption to outsiders who had crept in. How much more, then, must grief be restrained now, since Tiberius and Germanicus himself survive as children to take up the care of the commonwealth. Finally, let the difference be noted between the Roman people who once were and those who now are: how often the Roman people steadfastly bore the destruction of armies, the death of commanders, and the utter loss of noble families. Think of the Fabian clan destroyed at the Cremera, of so many armies routed by Hannibal. After those defeats they rose up more spirited and more terrible to the enemy. But now, in the eyes of the nations, the spirits of Roman citizens sink as if the safety of the empire were at stake! Whether a bridle should be placed on the other passions, or the mind of rulers should be loosened to disturbance, could be drawn out at equal length in discourse, were it not that the time and leisure of the reader must be spared. But the unbridled outpouring of vices, which was the second place of licence, is permitted to no mortal, and least of all to rulers.

units.la: Fidem datam solvisse, privatæ conditionis homini in probris dicitur: de principe verò, quanquam con- fuetudine jam pervagatum, in portentis. Justitiæ li- mites tranfiliiffe, privato turpe est: principi, cui ea cu- ftodienda permissa, fœdissimum. Labi,errare, decipi, privato irridendum: principi,qui oculus esse reipubli- cæ providendo debebat, ignominiosum. Abjectis ar- mis fugere, privato dedecorum: principi ne timoris quidem confessionem prodere, permissum. Ventrem popinæ fagina explere, privato famosum: principem cura corporis alto folio indignum esse, res ipsa clami- tat. Quod vero plus in aulis alicubi,quàm in taberna mercatoria aut casa rusticana, libidinis, violatæ fidei, legum conculcatarum, juris venundati, crassæ rerum ignorantiæ,& similium monstrorum reperiatur,fecu- li depravationi, non dato aulæ juri, accendum.
units.tr: Breaking a given pledge is said to be a disgrace in a man of private condition, but in a prince, though already common by custom, it is a portent. To overstep the limits of justice is shameful for a private man; for a prince, to whom the keeping of those limits was entrusted, it is most foul. To slip, to err, to be deceived is laughable in a private man; for a prince, who ought to be the eye of the commonwealth in foresight, it is disgraceful. To throw away one's arms and flee is dishonourable for a private man; for a prince, not even to confess fear is permitted. To fill the belly with feasting is infamous in a private man; the thing itself proclaims that care for the body is unworthy of a lofty throne for a prince. But that more lust, broken faith, trampled laws, sold justice, gross ignorance of affairs, and similar monsters are found in some courts than in a merchant's shop or a rustic cottage, is to be imputed to the depravity of the age, not to the right of the court.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Orbe Reip. inconcusso principes nascuntur & intercidunt.
units.tr: Princes rise and fall while the commonwealth stands unshaken.

units.la: Tiberii effatum est, Principes mortales, Remp. aeternam esse. quo dicto quanquam principum nomine viri, in civitate præ cæteris genere & opibus insignes, more priscæ consuetudinis, aut imperantibus cognatione proximi, capiuntur: nihilominus illud vulgari sensu, de summis imperii potestatibus, interpretari nihil vetat. Nec mortales tantum principes: sed & moribus ac fortuna mobiles, aut enim bonis deteriores, vel contra, succedunt: aut ipsi a priori vitæ consuetudine degenerantes, ad deteriora inclinant. Nonnunquam & orbe in dexteriorem partem circumacto, a pravis ad rectiora, a detortis ad æqua, fit inclinatio. Vitia erunt, donec homines, sed neque hac continua: & meliorum interventu pensantur: inquit apud Cornelium Cerialis, iv. Histor. Qua re se politeia, quam democratiam vulgo vocant, magis etiam aristocratia, præ monarchia jactitat. Semel enim bene constituta ac legibus firmata, cum immortale imperantium corpus permaneat; non nisi lento gradu ad immutatio-nem fit depressio.
units.tr: Tiberius's saying is recorded: Princes are mortal, but the commonwealth is eternal. Although by "princes" are meant men who, in the state, are distinguished above others by birth and wealth, according to the custom of earlier times, or those closely related to the rulers, nothing forbids us also to take the saying in the common sense, of the supreme powers of empire. Not only are princes mortal, but they are also changeable in character and fortune: they succeed either worse than their predecessors or the reverse, or themselves degenerate from their earlier way of life and incline to worse things. Sometimes, too, when the wheel has turned the other way, there is a shift from wicked to better things, from distorted to fair. There will be vices as long as men are men, but not continuously, and they are balanced by the intervention of better men, says Cerialis in Cornelius Tacitus, Histories book iv. For this reason the polity that people commonly call democracy boasts even more of aristocracy than of monarchy. For once well constituted and confirmed by laws, since the immortal body of rulers endures, decline into change comes only by a slow step.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Mœrore deterso ad firmitudinem, justitio omisso ad munia revertendum.
units.tr: Grief being wiped away, one must return with firmness to one's duties, the suspension of public business laid aside.

units.la: Constantis quidem ut viri, sic civitatis est, nulla calamitate ab officio deduci. At si quid humano sen-sui, si quid publicis moribus permittendum: proxi-mum est, lamentationes æternas non esse. jure igitur a Tiberio Romani moniti, repeterent folennia: & quia ludorum Megalensium spectaculum suberat, etiam solvendum. voluptates resumerent. Voluptatum nomine, locutione iis moribus familiari, ludos & theatrorum spectacula hic accipe. Similis locutio primo libro Annalium: neque ipse abhorrebat talibus studiis, & civile rebatur misceri voluptatibus vulgi. quem locum in-
units.tr: Just as it is the mark of a steadfast man, so it is of a state, not to be turned aside from its duty by any calamity. But if anything must be allowed to human feeling and to public custom, the nearest thing is that grief should not be eternal. Rightly, then, Tiberius admonished the Romans to resume the festivals; and because the Megalesian games were at hand, they should also be held, and they should resume their pleasures. By "pleasures," a usage familiar in that age, understand the games and the theatrical shows here. A similar phrasing occurs in the first book of the Annals: nor did he himself shrink from such pursuits, and he thought it civil to mix with the pleasures of the crowd. That passage

units.la: epte,& in Augustum ignominiose, de voluptate amo-ris, quo Mæcenas Bathyllum complexus erat, acci-piunt. Eadem phrafi & illud accipiendum, plus volu-ptatibus quam armis Romanos adversus subjectos valuisse. plures locos in re clara congerere non libet. Quem autem usum habuerint apud Romanos, hoc-dieque apud nos habere queant, theatrorum ludicra in Arcanis regnorum reclusi.
units.tr: foolishly, and to the discredit of Augustus, people take as referring to the pleasure of love, with which Maecenas embraced Bathyllus. In the same idiom, the saying that the Romans prevailed over their subjects more by pleasures than by arms must also be understood. I do not wish to heap up more passages on a matter so clear. What use they made of these among the Romans, they could make among us today; the theatrical diversions are the secrets of kingdoms laid open.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Non ex rumore, necinaudita causa judicandum.
units.tr: Judgment must not be made on rumour, nor without hearing the cause.

units.la: Accedimus ad celebre Pifoniani judicii tribunal: quo Cn.Piso provinciæ bello petitæ, & interfecti be-neficiis Germanici reus peragebatur. Prior accusatio plus ad gravandum reum ponderis, posterior plus po-pularis invidiæ gerebat. Actores in hac multum mo-menti, reus in gratia principis, & emolliendo per fili-um præmissum Drufo ponebat. Tiberius quo inte-grum judicium ostentaret, exceptum comiter juvenem, suetum erga filios familiarium nobilis liberalitate au-get. Recte ac ordine Tiberius nec ante causam cogni-tam judicat, nec immerentes pœna onerat, nec in al-terutram partem fe inclinare ostendit. Juri enim, non affectui; causæ, non personæ servire; integri nec præ-judicio corrupti judicis est.
units.tr: We now come to the famous court of the trial of Piso, in which Gnaeus Piso was prosecuted as a defendant for the war he had waged in the province and for the death of Germanicus, whom he was accused of having killed by his arts. The first accusation carried more weight in bringing charges against the defendant, the second more popular hatred. In this trial the prosecutors had great influence, while the defendant placed his hopes in the favour of the prince and in softening him through the son whom he had sent ahead to Drusus. To show that the trial was fair, Tiberius received the young man courteously and enlarged his generous kindness, as was customary towards the sons of friends. Tiberius rightly and in good order neither judged before the cause was heard, nor burdened the undeserving with punishment, nor showed himself leaning to either side. For it is the mark of an upright judge, not uninfluenced by prejudice, to serve the law and not feeling, and the cause and not the person.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Nihil in causa cognoscenda iræ, nihil largiundum gratiæ.
units.tr: Nothing should be allowed to influence the investigation of a case: neither anger nor favour.

units.la: Iræ enim & gratia, peffimis consultoribus, veri ju-dicium obfuscatur. Drufus non ille quidem judex, at-tamen futuro judici intimus, è præscripto Tiberii, Pi-soni favorem ambienti: fi vera forent quæ jacerentur, præcipuum in dolore suum locum respondit: sed malle falsa & inania, nec cuiquam mortem Germanici exi-tio fam esse. Candidè dolorem interfecti Germanici fatetur, aut honestatis causa subdolè fingit, sed ficta rei, aut perquam humana, commiseratione, nullum vindictae & judicii severitatis locum exoptat. Quae hic, fugge-stione fenis, facilis juventa Drusus respondet; judicum animo infixa esse debebant: ut nec dolori causam, nec rursus misericordiae largiantur; nec ad sanguinariam sententiam nimis prompti ferantur. sed accusationem, quae supplicium cujusquam petat, confictam esse optent; aut, quod proximum est, inviti damnatoriam sententiam pronuntient. quod longe a moribus illorum abest, qui, nisi damnato reorum cumulo, judicii diem se perdidisse autumant.
units.tr: For anger and favour, the worst of advisers, obscure the judgement of truth. Drusus, though not himself the judge, was nevertheless close to the future judge, and acting on Tiberius's instructions he courted favour for Piso. If the things said were true, he replied, Piso's own grief would have the chief place; but he preferred them to be false and empty, and he held that Germanicus's death had been fatal to no one. Either he frankly admits grief for the murdered Germanicus, or he pretends it dishonestly for the sake of appearances; but in either case, through a feeling that is either pretended or very human, he wishes for no place for vengeance or for the strictness of justice. Drusus, a young man easily swayed by the old man's suggestion, gives this answer. The minds of judges should have been fixed on this: they should neither yield to grief nor, on the other hand, to pity, nor be too ready to be carried towards a bloodthirsty sentence. They should rather wish that an accusation seeking the punishment of anyone was made up; or, which is the next best thing, they should pronounce a condemning sentence reluctantly. This is far from the habits of those who, unless the number of the accused has been heaped up with condemnations, think they have wasted the day of judgement.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Reorum alacritas infensos ira accendit.
units.tr: The eagerness of the accused kindles the anger of those who are hostile.

units.la: Miseria enim illorum, & animi demissione ante supplicium pascuntur. Piso Narnia, vitandae suspicionis, an quia pavidis consilia in incerto sunt, Nare [?] ac mox Tiberii devehitur. Vultu deinde alacres, ipse & Plancina, per ora hominum incedentes, convivium Romae celebri in loco adornant. quod inter irrita-menta invidia fuit. Quod illi ad fiduciam causae, quasi nihil sibi conscii, egerunt, vulgus ad premendam arripuit. Graviter, & ad hanc quæstionem accommodate, Hebræorum sapientissimus: odium plumbo quidem esse gravius; invidiam vero & æmulationem ferri non posse.
units.tr: For they feed on the wretchedness of the accused and on their dejection before punishment. Piso, either to avoid suspicion, or because the plans of frightened men are uncertain, withdrew to Narnia and soon was carried back by Tiberius. Then, cheerful in countenance, he and Plancina walked about on the lips of men and prepared a banquet in a well-known place in Rome. This was one of the provocations of envy. What they did to keep up confidence in their cause, as if they were conscious of nothing, the common people seized upon to suppress them. A very wise man of the Hebrews, and one well suited to this question, said gravely: hatred is indeed heavier than lead, but envy and rivalry cannot be borne.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Ab æquitate veri cognitio, non judicantium numero, dependet.
units.tr: Knowledge of the truth depends on fairness, not on the number of judges.

units.la: Jactat quidem Cn. Piso: vera, aut in deterius credita, judice ab uno facilius discerni: odium & invidiam apud multos valere. Sed, si penitius rem intro-spiciamus; judex non incorruptus Piso, de incorrupto judice pronunciat. Recte quidem, hac in causa, multi-tudinem odii erga se & invidiae accusat. sed nec sententia ea generalis est, nec unus judex per omnia iis ab-solvitur. Multo certe plures unius iniqua sententia, quam populi aut senatorum fortuita discordia, suppli-cio addixit. Multitudinem enim ruentem aut legis cancelli cohibent, aut pars diversum suadens frangit, aut denique animi mobilitas celerem ad pœnitentiam adducit. In uno forte offenso & ardentior est gravitate, & diuturnitate constantior, iracundia. Tum nec ab obstrepente multitudine, nec à legis auctoritate, repa-gulum formidat. Sanè si judex semper sedeat, veteri Græcorum verbo, [illegible, ~20 letters], [illegible, ~20 letters], qui nulla vi à re-&to[?] deducatur, qui pari in omnes animi affectione fe-ratur, qui nullam in partem favore aut odio propen-deat; non est de eo admodum laborandum. Sed ubi judex unus animi sui cupiditati, non causæ, cognitioni sedet: parum ab unitate auxilii sperandum. Jam quotusquisque tanta est sapientia, ut non cum aliis, judice sæpe non melioribus, causam communicet? Itá & unitatis, & multitudinis vitio, reus miserrimè obructur. Sed hæc occasione largiori fusius.
units.tr: Gnaeus Piso indeed boasts: that the truth, or things believed to be worse than they are, can more easily be discerned by one judge; hatred and envy prevail among many. But if we look more closely into the matter, Piso, who was not an impartial judge, pronounces about an impartial judge. In this case he rightly accuses the great number of those who hate and envy him. But this opinion is neither general, nor is a single judge free from fault in every respect. Certainly the unjust sentence of one man has condemned far more people to punishment than the chance disagreement of the people or the senators. For the rushing crowd is held back either by the barriers of the law, or a part of it, urging the opposite, breaks its force; or finally the fickleness of mind brings it quickly to repentance. In one man, if he is offended by chance, anger is both more fiery in its severity and more constant in its duration. Then he fears no bar, neither from the clamouring crowd nor from the authority of the law. Indeed, if a judge were always seated, as the old Greek saying has it, [illegible], [illegible], who cannot be turned aside from what is right by any force, who is carried with an equal disposition of mind towards all, who leans to no side by favour or hatred, there would be no great cause for anxiety about him. But where a single judge sits in judgement, giving way to the desire of his own mind rather than to the examination of the case, little help is to be hoped for from his being one. Now how few are so wise that they do not share the case with others, often no better judges than themselves? Thus, through the fault both of unity and of multitude, the accused is most wretchedly overwhelmed. But these matters I shall discuss more fully on a more suitable occasion.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Moles cognoscendæ culpæ judici, quaipse premitur, incumbit.
units.tr: The burden of investigating guilt falls on the judge himself, who is under pressure.

units.la: Quo enim ore eum judicet, cui societate criminis connexus, reus ore populi traducitur, aut interiori animi indicio arguitur? Haud fallebat Tiberium moles cognitionis, quaque ipse fama distraberetur. Alii hic perfricta fronte condemnato reo, crimini suo impu-dentiam adjiciunt. Ut M. Scaurus, qui legatus Bestiæ & Jugurthinæ participes fuerat, cum ex Mamiliana rogatione tres quæsitores rogarentur, efficerat, ut ipse in eo numero crearetur. Quæstionem-que asperè violenterque, ex rumore & libidine plebis, contra nobilitatem exercuit. S.B.J. Ut Fenius Rufus, Pisonianæ in Neronem conjurationis popularis, reos violenter urgebat, quò fidem incitiæ pararet, atrox adversus socios. T. xv. Annal. Alii pudori quidem suo, sed non justitiæ, consulentes, in alieno crimine suum absolvunt. Ut Augustus, crebro adulterio pol-lutus, lutus, adolescentem adulterii reum culpae insontem pronunciavit. Et saepe videas in pari crimine animadvertendo lenes esse, qui eadem culpa tenentur. Quod lenitatem animi vulgus interpretatur, culpae societas aut conscientia habenda. Non ita Sallustianus Cato: qui, cum animo suo nullius unquam delicti gratiam fecisset, haut facile alterius libidini malefacta condonabat. cui vitae integritas, & ex ea severitas, di-gnitatem addiderat; nihil largiundo gloriam adepto, qui non divitiis cum divite, neque factione cum fa-ctioso, sed cum strenuo virtute, cum modesto pudore, cum innocente abstinentia certabat: esse, quam videri, bonus malebat. B. C. Alii inter frontem urbanam & causae prostitutionem medii, integram causam a cognitione sua amoliti, mole se judicandi, sed nec su-spicione semper, exolvunt. Horum in classe Tiberius, paucis familiarium adhibitis, minas accusantium, & hinc preces audit, integramque causam ad senatum remittit. Veritus nimirum, ne audiret illud Satyrici: Loripedem rectus derideat, Aethiopem albus: Quis tulerit Gracchos de seditione querentes?
units.tr: For with what face can he judge a man to whom he is bound by a share in the crime, who is dragged before the people as accused, or is convicted by the inner evidence of his own mind? Tiberius was not unaware of the burden of the investigation, and of how he himself was being torn apart by rumour. Others, with brazen face, add shamelessness to their crime after the accused has been condemned. Thus Marcus Scaurus, who had been legate to Bestia and a partner of Jugurtha, when three investigators were to be chosen under the Mamilian law, brought it about that he himself was appointed among that number. He then conducted the inquiry harshly and violently against the nobility, driven by the rumour and lust of the common people. S.B.J. Thus Fenius Rufus, a popular participant in the conspiracy of Piso against Nero, pressed the accused violently, so that he might win credit for his own loyalty, and was savage against his associates. T. xv. Annal. Others, consulting their own reputation but not justice, clear themselves by the crime of another. Thus Augustus, defiled by frequent adultery, pronounced a young man accused of adultery innocent of the guilt. And you will often see that those who are caught in the same fault are lenient in punishing the same crime. The common people interpret this leniency of mind as an association in guilt or a consciousness of it. Not so Sallust's Cato: since he had never granted pardon to any fault of his own mind, he was not easily willing to pardon the wrongdoing of another's lust. The integrity of his life, and the severity that came from it, had given him dignity; he gained glory without favouring anyone, since he did not compete for wealth with the rich, nor for faction with the factious, but with the energetic in virtue, with the modest in decency, with the innocent in self-restraint; he preferred to be good rather than to seem so. Others, midway between an urban brow and the prostitution of a cause, remove the case, which is whole, from their own examination, and free themselves from the burden of judging, though not always from suspicion. Among these is Tiberius, who, having called in a few of his friends, hears the threats of the accusers and their prayers from that quarter, and sends the whole case back to the senate. No doubt he feared that he would hear that saying of the satirist: the straight-legged man mocks the crooked-footed, the white man the Ethiopian. Who could endure the Gracchi complaining of sedition?

units.la: Juvenal. lib.1. v.194.
units.tr: Juvenal, book 1, verse 194.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Occulta hominum judicia suspectus judex aegre cohibeat.
units.tr: A judge who is under suspicion can hardly restrain people's hidden judgments.

units.la: Sic is qui judicio promendo assidet, a circumstantibus ipse judicatur. Haut aliàs intentior populus, plus sibi in principe occulta vocis, aut suspicacis silentii per-misit. Falluntur, qui omnia in omnes principem posse, nemini quicquam in eum juris esse aut licentiae, pronunciant. Nec imperium in animos quisquam mortalium promere, nec animorum in se occultum impe-rium cohibere potest.
units.tr: So the man who sits to pronounce judgment is himself judged by those standing around him. Never at any other time was the people more attentive, or did it allow itself more hidden meaning in the prince's voice, or in his suspicious silence. They are mistaken who declare that the prince can do everything to everyone and that no one has any right or licence against him. No one among mortals can bring the power of rule over minds into the open, nor can anyone restrain the hidden power that minds exercise over him.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Suspensum rerum incertitudine judicem suspensa oratio decet.
units.tr: A judge held in suspense by the uncertainty of affairs ought to speak in a suspended manner.

units.la: Ut & judicii de se varietate distractum. Die senatus Cafar orationem habuit meditato temperamento. Modò enim Pisoni praejudicii onus demere, comme-morata paterna amicitia & senatus autoritate, labo-rat. modò objecta crimina nec molliendo, nec exag-gerando, animorum integritati reservat. Nunc dolo-rem in facinore detegendo suum testatus, judices ad severitatem cohortatur. nunc culpam non gravando, accusatorum nimio studio fuccenfet. Iterum addo-loris ex obitu filii teftificationem delapsus, ad æquita-tem erga reum refle&itur. Æquum deinde fe partibus ostentans, ad fidem & perorandi diligentiam omnes exstimulat. Postremò absentiæ suæ causam & Drufi filii, lacrymas & moestitiam, prætexit. Ita versipelli oratione, ne usquam judicio vulgi teneatur, elabitur.
units.tr: Torn between varying opinions about himself, and on the day of the Senate Caesar delivered a speech with deliberately measured moderation. Now he tries to remove from Piso the burden of prejudgment, recalling their paternal friendship and the authority of the Senate; now, neither softening nor magnifying the crimes charged, he leaves them to the integrity of the judges' minds. Now, declaring his own grief at uncovering the crime, he exhorts the judges to severity; now, by not weighing down the guilt, he rebukes the accusers for their excessive zeal. Again, slipping into a testimony of grief at his son's death, he turns back to fairness toward the accused. Then, showing himself impartial to both sides, he spurs everyone on to good faith and diligence in pleading. Finally he puts forward as the excuse for his absence the tears and sorrow of his son Drusus. Thus with a shifty speech, so as not to be held anywhere by the judgment of the crowd, he slips away.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Privatæ simultatis executio non est judicii in locum inferenda.
units.tr: The execution of private enmity is not to be carried into the place of judgment.

units.la: Non semel admirabundus voces ejusmodi audivis adducatur modò iste vel illein judicium; opprobrium nostrum, aut non solutum salarium, egregiè ulcifce-mur. Et Romano in judicum consessu, favorem aut odium primas sibi partes in reum sumpsisse, ne in tur-pibus quidem habebatur. Animosius Tiberius, aut integri judicii fimulantiùs: odero, seponamque à domo mea, & privatas inimicitias non Principis ulciscar. Perfectæ quidem Christi legi conveniret, inimicitias omnes humanitati donare, nec incujufquam ultionem exardescere. Sed quoniam vivitur cum hominibus non perfectè sapientibus, aut omnia ad coelestis per-sectionis normam exigentibus: proximum est in civili hominum honestate, privatas injurias privata ultione persequi, publicis domestica negotia non immiscere. Non enim hic nostrarum rerum judices, sed alienarum arbitri sedemus: nec cui bene vel male velimus, sed uter justiorem causam foveat, spectandum.
units.tr: I have more than once, to my astonishment, heard words of this kind: "Let this man or that one be brought to trial now, and we shall avenge our insult or our unpaid wages handsomely." Yet in a Roman court of judges, to have taken up favour or hatred as the leading part against the accused was not even counted as disgraceful. Tiberius put it more boldly, or with a show of impartial judgment: "I shall hate, and I shall keep such feelings out of my house, and avenge my private enmities, not the Prince's." Indeed, it would befit the perfect law of Christ to forgive all enmities for the sake of humanity and not to flare up in anyone's revenge. But since we live among men who are not perfectly wise, or who do not measure everything by the rule of heavenly perfection, the nearest course, within the civil decency of men, is to pursue private wrongs by private vengeance and not to mix domestic affairs with public ones. For we do not sit here as judges of our own affairs but as arbiters of other people's; we must look not at whom we wish well or ill, but at which side supports the juster cause.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Quid, non cūi judices, cognosce.
units.tr: Know what, and before whom, you are not to judge.

units.la: Nota Non enim nostro tantum dolori aut commodo, sed nec amicorum gratiæ aut potentioris libidini, gra-tificari debemus. Rotundè Tiberius : oro,ne,quia dolori meo causa connexa est, objecta crimina pro approbatis accipiatis[?]. Sed nec Tiberius ipse sanctè per omnia in ea judicandi integritate perstitit. Unde falsum illud cujusdam senatoris: Quo loco censebis, Cæsar! si primo; habebo quod sequar: si post omnes; vereor ne imprudens dissentiam. Et Augustus, ille tam sacer, ille cœlo receptus, vapulante aliquando sinistro judi-cio Mæcenate, ob causam improborum patrocinio crebro defensam, prætoris tribunali assidens, vetito ne quis propinquos ipsius aut necessarios lacesseret, se ira commotior proripuit: ut est in Dionis historia. Adeò minus operosum est, præcepta aliis præscribere, quàm à ratione præscripta sequi.
units.tr: Note: we ought to gratify not only our own grief or advantage, but neither the favour of friends nor the lust of the more powerful. Tiberius bluntly said: I beg you, lest, because the charges are bound up with my grief, you accept the objected crimes as proven. Yet Tiberius himself did not remain in complete and holy integrity in judging such cases. Hence the saying of a certain senator is false: "Where will you vote, Caesar? If first, I shall have something to follow; if last, I fear I may dissent without meaning to." And Augustus, so sacred, received into heaven, once rushed out more moved by anger when Maecenas was being lashed by an unfavourable judgement, because the cause of wicked men was often defended by his patronage, and though he himself sat on the praetor's tribunal, he had forbidden anyone to harass his relatives or dependants; as is related in Dio's history. So much less laborious is it to prescribe precepts for others than to follow the precepts prescribed by reason.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Machinæ, flectendo[?] à vero judici ad-hiberi solitæ, absint.
units.tr: Devices customarily brought in to bend the judge from the truth should be absent.

units.la: Ut sunt compositæ ad fallendum orationes, amicorum atrata turba, preces & lacrymę propinquorum, quas his verbis tangit Tiberius: nemo Drusi lacrymas, nemo mœstitiam meam spretet[?]. qua judiciorum labe Romanos licentius hallucinatos, alibi à nobis obser-vatum.
units.tr: Such are speeches composed for deceiving: a crowd of friends in mourning dress, the prayers and tears of relatives, which Tiberius touches with these words: let no one scorn Drusus's tears, let no one scorn my sadness. By this blemish of judgments the Romans went astray more freely, as we have observed elsewhere.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Spatium reo ad diluenda crimina non arte contrahendum.
units.tr: The accused's time to refute the charges must not be cut short by artifice.

units.la: Quod vulgò in judiciis jactatur, favorabiliorem Rei causam esse, id ferri hactenus potest, ne aut pre-mente iracundiæ vultu, aut præcisa defendendi sui mora, aut interrogandi asperitate reus obruatur. Triduum criminibus objiciendi[?] statuitur, utque sex dierum spatio interjecto, reus per triduum defendere-tur. Definito enim horarum & dierum spatio, plusculum reo ad defensionem sui, quàm accusatori ad ar-guendum tribui solet. Humanitatis enim est, in molliorem potiùs partem, quàm in rigidiorem propende-re; nec ad damnationem quamvis nocentis nimis præ-cipitato calculo prorumpere.
units.tr: What is commonly bandied about in courts, that the cause of the defendant is more favourable, may be allowed so far, so that the accused is not overwhelmed either by a face darkened with anger, or by a cut-short time for self-defence, or by harshness in questioning. A three-day period is fixed for objecting the charges, and after an interval of six days the accused is to defend himself for three days. For when a definite span of hours and days is set, a somewhat longer time is usually allowed the accused for his defence than the accuser has for his charge. It is a mark of humanity to lean towards the gentler side rather than the harsher, and not to rush to condemnation, however guilty a man may be, with an overly hasty vote.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Superflua in accusando amputanda.
units.tr: Superfluous matter is to be cut out in accusing.

units.la: Non enim audiendis rei convitiis judices, verum causæ dijudicationi convocantur. Argutè Tacitus: Tum Fulcinius vetera & inania orditur, ambitiosè avaréque habitam Hispaniam, quod neque convictum noxa reo, si recentia purgaret: neque defensum absolutioni erat, si teneretur majoribus flagitiis. Si qua in[?] ea re culpa hæsit, eorum fuit, qui avaritiæ compertum, auctoritate sua novæ provinciæ præfecerunt. Verùm ita mos in judicio perorandi fuit, ita consuetudo in forum Romanum irrupit: quæ ferri poterat, si more Persarum vita accusati anteacta in compensationem recentis facti veniret. Nunc cum leges Romanæ in singulas actiones, non in totam civium vitam, conscriptæ sint: a vanitate abundantiæ forensis ista consuetudo satis purgari nequit.
units.tr: For judges are summoned not to hear the insults of the accused, but to decide the case. Tacitus writes acutely: Then Fulcinius began with old and empty matters, that Spain had been held ambitiously and greedily, which neither would convict the accused of guilt, if he cleared himself of recent charges, nor would be a defence to absolution, if he were held for greater crimes. If any blame attached in that matter, it belonged to those who, having learned of his greed, placed him in charge of the new province by their own authority. But such was the custom of pleading in court, and such the habit that broke into the Roman forum; it might be tolerated if the past life of the accused were brought in to offset a recent deed, as among the Persians. Now, since Roman laws are framed for individual actions, not for the whole life of the citizens, this habit of forensic excess cannot be sufficiently cleansed of its vanity.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Non eadem est agniti peccati & non commissi defensionis firmitas.
units.tr: The firmness of defence against an admitted sin is not the same as that against a sin not committed.

units.la: Pisoni Vitellius objecerat, ambitionem militarem, provinciam pessimo cuique obnoxiam, in imperatorem contumelias, tentatam armis reip. utque reus agi posset, acie victum. Quodque caput criminis, devotionibus & veneno Germanicum peremptum. Defensio in cæteris trepidavit. Nam quod Terentianus Antipho, id de se Pisoni affirmare poterat: Egomet-me novi, & peccatum meum. Veneni autem crimen, quod anili devotionum conjectura nitebatur, aut infirma convivii suspicione stabat, constantius diluit. Ex conscientia justa metuentem, maximè ubi rerum testimonia adsunt, nulla facundia eripuerit: nullius absurdi sibi conscius animus nullam facundiam metuerit.
units.tr: Vitellius had charged Piso with military ambition, with a province exposed to every worst man, with insults against the emperor, with an attempt on the republic by arms, and, so that he could be tried, with having been defeated in battle. And as the chief charge, that Germanicus had been destroyed by curses and poison. Piso's defence faltered on the rest, for he could say about himself what Antipho the Terentian says: I know myself, and my own fault. But the charge of poison, which rested on the old woman's guess about curses, or stood on a weak suspicion of a banquet, he refuted more steadily. Where fear arises from a just conscience, especially where testimony of the facts is present, no eloquence will snatch it away; a mind conscious of no absurdity will fear no eloquence.

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Male sub offenso judice praejudicata causa agitur.
units.tr: A case is badly pleaded before a judge who is already prejudiced.

units.la: Piso id,cui judices per diversa implacabiles erant, perniciesua didicit. Non enim eadem omnibus, amore aut odio, ira aut lenitate prosecutis, aut saltem non ejusdem omnibus momenti, videntur. Quod Aristo-teles 2. Rhetoric cap.1. his verbis extulit: Οὐ γὰρ τοῖς [?] φιλίαν καὶ μισοῦσι[?], ἀλλ' ὀργιζομένοις καὶ ἀπλῶς[?] [illegible, ~12 letters] ἢ κατὰ τὸ μέγεθος ἕτερα. Subest tamen in hoc Pisonis judicio aliqua ratio, cur forum horum judicum declinare nequiverit. quandoquidem ira & implacabilis animus, non alia, quam objecti criminis magnitudine, ex causa nascebatur.
units.tr: Piso learned to his ruin that the judges were implacable towards him in different ways. For they do not seem the same to all, when some are moved by love or hatred, anger or mildness, or at least not all of equal weight. Aristotle expressed this in the second book of the Rhetoric, chapter 1, in these words: "For not to those who love and hate, but to those who are angry and simply [illegible] or differently according to magnitude" [Οὐ γὰρ τοῖς φιλίαν καὶ μισοῦσι, ἀλλ' ὀργιζομένοις καὶ ἀπλῶς [?] ἢ κατὰ τὸ μέγεθος ἕτερα]. Yet in this trial of Piso there is some reason why he could not avoid the crowd of these judges, since their anger and implacable spirit arose from no other cause than the magnitude of the crime laid against him.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Offensa multitudo, caeca judicii belua.
units.tr: The hostile crowd, the blind beast of judgment.

units.la: Nam & judicium sibi non delatum, & cui judicando ob praecipitantiam impar est, temere arripit; & executioni ante sententiae pro locutionem manum injicit. Satis infestis Pisoni patribus, nec mitiori ob bellum provinciae illatum Caesare, tamen populi ante curiam voces audiebantur, non temperaturos manibus, si patrum sententias evasisset. effigiesque Pisonis traxerat in Gemonias, ac divellebat, ni jussu principis protecta repositaque forent. Sed bene quod uno rerum potito ira ea citra effectum effervescit: quae pari omnium libertate intra fremitum fortassis non stetisset.
units.tr: For a crowd both snatches up a judgment not committed to it, and one to which it is unequal in judging because of its haste, and lays hands on execution before the sentence is pronounced. The senators were hostile enough to Piso, and Caesar, not milder on account of the war waged on the province, yet voices of the people were heard before the senate-house, that they would not keep their hands off him if he escaped the senators' sentence; and they had dragged Piso's effigy to the Gemonian steps and were tearing it apart, unless it had been protected and put back by the emperor's order. But it is well that, with one man in possession of affairs, this rage fizzled out without effect; with the equal freedom of all it perhaps would not have stayed within murmuring.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Causae divisio in favoris inaequalitate alteri damnosa.
units.tr: The division of a cause is harmful to the other party when the favour shown to one of them is unequal.

units.la: Ubi tanta praevales alterius gratia, ut eum absolutum iri satis appareat, separari defensionem socio causae non conducit. Plancina donec media Pisoni spes, sociam fecujusque fortunae, & si ita ferret, comitem exitii promittebat. Ut secretis Augustae precibus veniam obtinuit, paulatim segregari à marito, diuidere defensionem cœpit. Quod rëus exitiabiale sibi intelligens, an omitteret defensionem, non fine causa secum disceptavit. Extra quæstionem obseruandum, rarain esse mulierum ad extrema fidem, etiamsi principio fe- rociter locutæ sint. Sic uxor Ovidii exulatum ituri, hæc quidem verba, plena in maritum pietatis,effudit:
units.tr: Where the favour shown to one party is so great that he clearly appears certain to be acquitted, it is not advantageous to separate one's defence from one's co-defendant. Plancina, while Piso still held out hope in her, promised to share his fortune and, if it came to that, his ruin. As soon as she had obtained pardon through secret prayers to Augusta, she gradually began to separate herself from her husband and to divide the defence. The defendant, realising that this was fatal to him, debated with himself, not without reason, whether he should abandon the defence. Apart from the question, it should be observed that women rarely keep faith to the end, even if at first they have spoken fiercely. Thus the wife of Ovid, about to go into exile, poured out these words, full of devotion to her husband:

units.la: Non potes avelli : simul hinc simul ibimus ambo : Te sequar, & conjux exulis exul ero. Et mihi facta via est, & me capit ultima tellus : Accedam profugæ sarcina parva rati. Te jubet à patria discedere Cæsaris ira : Me pietas : pietas hæc mihi Cæsar erit. Verum magnificè locuta, domi subsistit, patriamque exilio prætulit : Vixque dedit victas utilitate manus.
units.tr: "You cannot be torn away: from here we shall go together, both of us. I shall follow you, and as the wife of an exile I shall be an exile too. The way is open to me as well, and the farthest land will receive me; I shall go as a small burden on the fleeing raft. Caesar's anger bids you leave your country; my devotion bids me go. This devotion will be my Caesar." But she spoke grandly, and then stayed at home, preferring her country to exile, and scarcely gave her hands, won over by self-interest.

units.la: Ov.l.1. Trift. Eleg.3.
units.tr: Ov. l. 1. Trist. Eleg. 3.

units.la: Constantior Senecæ uxor Pompeja Paullina, sibi quoque destinatam mortem afleverans, manum percusso- ris poposcit. quæ tamen ipsa hortatu militum obligari sibi brachia, premi[?] sanguinem, blandimentis vitæ evicta, passa est. T.xv. Annal. Porcia Bruto fecundum nupta, supra cæterarum exempla est : conjurationis in Cæsarem, & sponte sumtæ mortis gloriosè particeps. Gloriosè inquam, veterum Romanorum, nec non Stoicæ disciplinæ suffragio.
units.tr: The wife of Seneca, Pompeia Paulina, was more constant. Declaring that death was destined for her too, she demanded the hand of the executioner; yet she herself, persuaded by the soldiers, allowed her arms to be bound and the blood to be staunched, and, overcome by the allurements of life, submitted. T. xv. Annal. Porcia, married second to Brutus, surpasses the examples of the others: she shared gloriously in the conspiracy against Caesar and in a death she chose of her own accord. Gloriously, I say, and with the approval of the ancient Romans and of the Stoic discipline as well.

units.la: XXIV.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: Spes nec in extremis deferenda.
units.tr: Hope is not to be abandoned even at the last.

units.la: Nec omittendum fui, quamvis adverso judice, pa- trocinium.
units.tr: Nor, though the judge is hostile, should the defence be given up.

units.la: Nec mihi nauta placet, qui tempestate coorta Prosilit in medias interiturus aquas : Nec probo bellantem, raptis qui fortiter armis, Abjecta parvo vulnere mente cadit. Dum regit hos artus animus, dum dextra movetur, Non nihil in nobis esse putremus[?] opis.
units.tr: I do not approve of the sailor who, when a storm arises, leaps into the middle of the waves, destined to perish; nor do I approve of the warrior who, having seized arms bravely, falls with his spirit cast down by a small wound. While the mind rules these limbs, while the right hand moves, we should think there is some help in us.

units.la: ut nos quondam adolescentiori ætate lusimus.
units.tr: As we once played in our younger years.

units.la: Piso, an adhuc defensionem fui experiretur dubius, hortantibus filiis durat mentem, senatumque rursus ingreditur. Aliud Thrasæ amici nonnulli autores fuere, defensionis inanæ ludibrium spontanea morte præveniret: subtraheret aures convitiis & probris. quorum ille suasum secutus, tædia incertæ vitæ abrupit. Sed haud scio, annon animosius, & humanitati convenientius, alii subjecerint: segnes & pavidos supremis suis secretum circumdare. Aspiceret populus virum morti obvium, audiret senatus voces quasi ex aliquo numine supra humanas: posse ipso miraculo etiam Neronem permoveri. sin crudeliter persisteret, distingui certe apud posteros memoriam honesti exitus ab ignavia per silentium pereuntium. T.xvi.Ann.
units.tr: Piso, still uncertain whether to try the defence further, while his sons urged him, hardened his resolve and re-entered the senate. Some friends of Thrasea were the authors of a different course: he should forestall the mockery of a vain defence by a voluntary death, and shut his ears to abuse and insults. He followed this advice and cut short the weariness of an uncertain life. But I do not know whether others did not suggest something more spirited and more fitting to humanity: that the cowardly and fearful should surround their last moments with secrecy. Let the people see a man facing death, let the senate hear words as if from some divinity above the human: by that very wonder even Nero might be moved. But if he persisted in cruelty, the memory of an honourable end would surely be distinguished, among posterity, from the cowardice of those who perish in silence. T. xvi. Ann.

units.la: Sic illi pro suæ sapientiæ modo. Christianæ doctrinæ mysteria suggererent: culpæ sibi conscio culpam fatendam, delicto crimine, pœnam a judice infligam sponte subeundam: criminis vero objecti puro, ne causa sibi necis feratur, defensionem ad extremum non deferendam.
units.tr: Thus they spoke according to the measure of their own wisdom. Had they been suggesting the mysteries of Christian doctrine, they would have said this: that one who is conscious of fault should confess the fault, and, the crime being admitted, should willingly undergo the punishment inflicted by the judge; but that one charged with a crime he has not committed should not abandon his defence to the end, lest the cause of his death be laid at his own door.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Clausas affectui, apertas veritati, aures judex immotus habeat.
units.tr: Let the judge, unmoved, keep his ears shut to feeling and open to truth.

units.la: Obsidant animum ejus preces, dona, ambitus, gratia, odium.
units.tr: Prayers, gifts, canvassing, favour and hatred beset his mind.

units.la: Ille, velut pelagi rupes immota, resistit: Ut pelagi rupes, magno veniente fragore, Quæ se[?]se, multis circumlatrantibus undis, Mole tenet.
units.tr: He, like an immovable rock in the sea, resists: as a sea-rock, when the great roar comes, holds itself firm by its mass, while many waves bark round it. As Virgil says of the Latins, Aeneid VII.

units.la: Ut de Latino Virgilius. VII Æneid. Piso infensas patrum voces, odia vulgi expertus, nullo magis exterri-tus est, quàm quòd Tiberium fine miseratione, fine ira, obstinatum clausumque vidit, ne quo affectu perrum-peretur. Huc illuc pelli & inflecti potest, qui se prius à constantiæ sede dimovit. qui vero in rationis & æquitatis centro se continet, ad extrema non temere cir-cumducitur.
units.tr: Piso, having experienced the hostile voices of the fathers and the hatred of the crowd, was terrified by nothing so much as that he saw Tiberius obstinate and closed, showing neither pity nor anger, so that no emotion could break through to him. A man who has first moved himself from the seat of constancy can be pushed and bent this way and that; but he who keeps himself at the centre of reason and fairness is not easily carried off to extremes.

units.la: XXVI. Poena delicti gravitatem non excedat.
units.tr: XXVI. The punishment should not exceed the gravity of the offence.

units.la: Cujus mitigationem quàm acerbitatem promptius excusaveris. Romanis mitigandæ pœnæ genus fuit, arbitrium mortis permittere: &, si ipsi sibi manum admoverent, carnificis minisserium abducere. Ita Piso solita curanúo corpori exsequitur. dein multam postea noctem, egressa cubiculo uxore, operiri fores jussit: capta luce, perfosso jugulo, jacente humi gladio, reperti sunt. Ita Libo Drusus, Annalium fecundo, ita plures alii, mortem suo manuum ministerio invenere. quod nostris moribus improbatur. Non praetereunda est, in tanta suppliciorum diversitate, priscorum Germanorum consuetudo. Distinctio poenarum ex delictis. proditores transfugas arboribus suffendunt, ignavos imbelles corpore infames, caeno ac palude, injecta in super crate, mergunt. Diversitas supplicii illuc recipit, tanquam scelerà officii oportet dum puniuntur flagitia abscondi. Tac. libro Germanorum moribus dicato, ubi & levioribus delictis leviores poenas, equorum pecorumque multam, applicatas recenset. Quod illi multò sapientius, quam Atheniensium legislator Draco, qui delictis vel minimis ultimum supplicium addixit. Nec tamen, Draconem cum impro-bamus, τῷ ἀντιπέρᾳ, jus talionis, pari mensura exigi-mus: ut par debeat esse periculum nocentis & innocentis, par poena deliberate & fortuito peccantis. Ratio ac aequitas, non facti nuda contemplatio, infligendae poenae norma accedat.
units.tr: It is easier to excuse a mitigation of punishment than its harshness. The Romans had one way of softening a penalty: they allowed the condemned to choose their own death, and if they laid hands on themselves, they spared the executioner's service. So Piso carried out the usual care for his body. Then, after spending a long night with his wife dismissed from the room, he ordered the doors to be kept shut. When daylight came, he was found with his throat pierced and the sword lying on the ground. So too Libo Drusus, in the second book of the Annals, and many others found death by their own hands, which our customs disapprove. In such a variety of punishments, the custom of the ancient Germans must not be passed over. They hang traitors and deserters from trees, and sink cowards, the unwarlike and the infamous, in mire and bog, with a hurdle laid over them. That difference in punishment, Tacitus says, serves the principle that the crimes of cowardice should be hidden while they are being punished. In his book devoted to the customs of the Germans, Tacitus also lists the lighter penalties applied to lighter offences, such as fines of horses and cattle. The Germans did this far more wisely than Draco, the lawgiver of the Athenians, who condemned even the smallest offences to the final penalty. Yet when we disapprove of Draco, we do not thereby demand the law of retaliation [τῷ ἀντιπέρᾳ], an exact measure, so that the danger to the guilty and the innocent should be equal, and the punishment for deliberate and accidental wrongdoing the same. Reason and equity, not the bare consideration of the deed, should be added as the rule for inflicting punishment.

units.la: XXVII. Justitia judex, non executione justi-tiae, laetetur.
units.tr: XXVII. The judge of justice should rejoice not in the execution of justice.

units.la: Non ut hanc, fine qua illa esse nequit, omittat: sed ut, humanitatis non oblitus, istam invitus pronunciet, spectet, audiat, praesertim si causa rei dolori judicis connexa sit. Cafar flexo in mafititiam ore, suam invi-diam diam tali morte quaesitam apud senatum, crebrisque interrogationibus exquirit, qualem Piso diem supremum noctemque exegisset. Quanquam ad Tiberianum simulandi artificium non male hanc scenam, ut alibi docui, referre queas. Sicut hostis aperta populatur, abdita autem & defossa aut ignorantur, aut eo ipso fallunt quod quaerenda sunt: ita vultum & verba Tiberii populus rimabatur; interiorem animi sensum non temere ex sermone penetrabat.
units.tr: Not that he should omit it, since justice cannot exist without it, but that, mindful of humanity, he should pronounce it reluctantly, look on it, and hear it, especially if the cause is connected with the judge's own grief. Caesar, his face turned to malice, asked the senate, with repeated questions, about the envy he had sought through such a death, and what kind of last day and night Piso had spent. Although, as I have shown elsewhere, one may fairly refer this scene to Tiberius's art of dissimulation. As an enemy lays waste open places, while hidden and buried things are either overlooked or deceive by the very fact that they must be sought; so the people scrutinised Tiberius's face and words, and did not easily penetrate his inner feeling from his speech.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Suprema morientium verba pro vaticinio.
units.tr: The last words of the dying taken as prophecy.

units.la: Hinc fabulam cygneae cantionis ortum traxisse attributis. Poetae sane, & inprimis poetarum principes, obeuntium proelio heroum praedictiones, ut Patrocli de vicina morte Hectoris, hujus de Achille propediem morituro, non semel referunt. Vaticinandi vim proxime accedunt verba, sincero animo prolata credita: qualia haec Pisonis: quatenus veritati & innocentiae mea nusquam locus est, deos immortales testor, &c. Nec obstruendi fauces, & sermones extremos prohibendi, immanitas probanda. Athenienses ad necem damnatis tria verba loqui permiserunt: inde obvoluto capite ad supplicii locum trahebant: immanitatis & affectuum humanorum medii.
units.tr: Hence the fable of the swan's song is said to have arisen. The poets, certainly, and above all the princes of poets, have more than once related the predictions of heroes dying in battle: Patroclus on Hector's approaching death, and Hector on Achilles, who was soon to die. Words spoken with a sincere mind and believed come closest to the power of prophecy, such as these of Piso: since there is no place for truth and innocence in my case, I call the immortal gods to witness, etc. Nor should the cruelty be approved which stops the throat and forbids final speech. The Athenians allowed those condemned to death to speak three words; then they dragged them with covered head to the place of punishment: a mean between cruelty and human feeling.

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: Poena culpae autorem ne transeat.
units.tr: Punishment should not pass over from the guilty author.

units.la: Cum caeteris in criminibus filius parentum peccata non luat: cur in laesae majestatis delicto peculiare jus usurpetur, non apparet. In stabilimento quidem regni aliquid rationis, nihil in jure reperitur. Piso multis modis majestatem & principis & populi Romani violaverat. nihilominus Tiberius non modo alterum filiorum, qui in urbe agendo qualicunque patris fortunae non fuerat adjunctus, silentio tramisit; verum etiam alterum, qui patri strenue operam navaverat, crimine civilis belli purgavit: patriis quippe jussa nec potuisse filium detractare. Obsequiúmne patris eò uf-que aliquem devinciat, ut patriam & majestatem po-puli ci postponat, nunc non excutio. Quod verò Ti-berius juvenes ne quidem purgandos culpa paterna, nec poenam deprecandam judicavit, id fatis argumenti est, poenam læsæ majestatis iis temporibus ad libe-ros extensam non fuisse. Blasphemiam in Deum com-missam, negatam Dei providentiam, & alia delicta di-recte in Deum tendentia, in liberis non punimus. Et terreni imperii caducum principem immensæ Dei glo-riæ præferemus? Si quando Deus peccata parentum in posteris, in tertia & quarta generatione, requirit: id absoluta juris potestate, qua omne genus hominum, cum orbe universo, momento delere potuit, facit, quod jus in subditos nulli regum permissum. Non igi-tur aut securitatem suam, aut regni tutelam, metuen-da parentum in liberis vindicta, aut paterni affectus fi-militudine, sævitiæ suæ in quæstione juris prætexere poterit. Quid fine securitati quidem semper, auto terrore hominum & ex formidine odio, consulitur?
units.tr: Since in other crimes a son does not bear the sins of his parents, it is not clear why a peculiar right should be claimed in the crime of treason. In the establishment of a kingdom there is perhaps some reason, but in law there is none. Piso had violated the majesty both of the prince and of the Roman people in many ways. Nevertheless Tiberius not only passed over in silence the one son, who had not been associated with his father's fortunes in any way at all in the city; but he also cleared the other, who had strenuously served his father, of the charge of civil war, on the ground that a son could not have refused his father's commands. How far the obedience of a father binds someone so as to make him set aside his country and the majesty of the people, I do not now examine. But that Tiberius judged the young men were not even to be cleared of their father's guilt, nor to plead for their punishment, is sufficient evidence that the penalty for treason was not extended to children in those times. We do not punish in children blasphemy committed against God, the denial of God's providence, and other offences aimed directly at God. Shall we set a fleeting earthly prince above the immeasurable glory of God? If at any time God requires the sins of parents of their posterity, in the third and fourth generation, he does so by his absolute power of law, by which he could destroy in a moment every kind of men together with the whole world; a right not granted to any king over his subjects. Therefore he cannot pretend, in a question of law, either his own security or the protection of his kingdom, nor a vengeance against children that is to be feared, nor the likeness of paternal affection, as a cover for his cruelty. What end is served for security, or for terror of men, and from fear, hatred?

units.la: Ut arbores quaedam recisæ pullulant, ita regia crudeli-tas auget inimicorum numerum, tollendo: inquit Se-neca noster I. de Clementia. Augustus, ut est apud Dionem Cassium libro LV, anxium de adversariorum numero, suppliciis ex ipsis incrementum capiente, Livia uxor oratione sævitiæ dissuasoria aggreditur.
units.tr: As some trees, when cut down, sprout again, so royal cruelty, by removing enemies, increases their number: says our Seneca, in the first book On Clemency. Augustus, as is recorded in Dio Cassius, book 55, being anxious about the number of his opponents, which grew through the executions themselves, was approached by his wife Livia with a speech dissuading him from cruelty.

units.la: Qua inter alia clementiam his verbis commendat: [illegible, ~30 letters]
units.tr: Among other things, she commends clemency in these words: [illegible, ~30 letters]

units.la: [illegible, ~30 letters] Meo judicio longe plus humanitate quam sævitia proficitur. Ad veniam enim promptos non modo quibus delicti gratia facta est, amore am-plectuntur, ut etiam de referenda gratia laborent: sed reliqui etiam omnes venerantur ac colunt, ut nec lædendi animum capiant. Deinde multis in eum sensum interjectis pergit: [illegible, ~20 letters] &c. Non omnia gladius conficit. &c. Consilium Li-viæ secutus Augustus, omnibus qui vitæ ejus insidiati fuerant ignovit: Cornelium etiam Cinnam ad consu-latum evexit. Et ex eo tempore civibus multò tran-quillioquillioribus[?] usus, maturam pacato imperio fenedam[?] attigit. Augustus, toties convitiis in publico, toties insidiis impetitus, iniuriae autoribus condonavit. Christianam mansuetudinem edocti principes, ne quidem in autore culpae puniendo subsistet? Priscos apud Germanos suscipere tam inimicitias patris aut propinqui, quam amicitias necesse erat. nec implacabili tamen odio simultas tradebatur. Iuendo enim mulcta pecuaria homicidio, satisfactionem universa domus recepit. utiliter in publicum: inquit gravis autor. Quidni igitur & princeps utiliter in publicum, utiliter domui suae, aculeum severitatis contrahat? Plurium se copia offerebat: sed ab aliorum industria occupata, nolim in messem meam vertere.
units.tr: [illegible, ~30 letters] In my judgment far more is achieved by humanity than by cruelty. For those who are quick to forgive are embraced with love not only by those to whom a pardon has been granted, so that they even labour to repay the favour, but all the rest also venerate and honour them, so that they do not form any intention of harming. Then, after many things to that effect have been inserted, she goes on: [illegible, ~20 letters] etc. The sword does not accomplish everything. etc. Augustus followed Livia's counsel and pardoned all who had plotted against his life; he even raised Cornelius Cinna to the consulship. And from that time, enjoying citizens far more tranquil, he reached a ripe old age with the empire at peace. Augustus, attacked so often with insults in public and so often with plots, forgave the authors of the injuries. Shall princes, taught Christian gentleness, not stop short even of punishing the author of a fault? Among the ancient Germans it was as necessary to take up the enmities of a father or kinsman as to take up friendships; yet the feud was not handed down with implacable hatred. For by the payment of a fixed number of cattle as compensation for homicide, the whole household received satisfaction: usefully for the public, says the serious author. Why then should not a prince also, usefully for the public, usefully for his own house, draw back the sting of severity? Many examples offered themselves, but since they have been harvested by the diligence of others, I would not wish to turn them into my own harvest.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: Sed nec culpae autorem flagitiose praetereat.
units.tr: But let him not pass over the author of the fault in silence.

units.la: Si quid veri crimen veneni habuit, maximam ejus partem Plancina traxit. Si insectatio Germanici, ambitio militaris ac domestica, Agrippinae apertum odium, victima de morte imperatoris caesa, supplicium merebatur: Plancina immunitatem sperare non debuit. Attamen bonus ille imperator Tiberius, pro Plancina cum pudore & flagitio disseruit, matris preces obtendens: in quam optimi cujusque secreti quaestus magis ardescebant. Primum imperatoris flagitium in precibus pro insolenti foemina erat: alterum in causa precum: tertium in civium judicii negligentia. quas praeterea occulte judicandi voces, cum Plancina Tiberium solere, hoc patrocinio moverit; nolo nimia conjectandi solertia rimari. Liviam potius matrem, Augusto olim salutaria suggerentem, & hic audire debuisset. Οὐ λέγω τοῦτο, ὅ τι δεῖ πάντων ἁπλῶς τῶν ἀλλήλων φιλεῖν, ἀλλ' ὅτι τὸν μὲν
units.tr: If the charge of poisoning had any truth, Plancina took by far the largest share of it. If Germanicus' harassment, her ambition in the army and at home, Agrippina's open hatred, and a victim slain over the emperor's death deserved punishment, Plancina ought not to have hoped for immunity. Yet that good emperor Tiberius pleaded for Plancina with shame and disgrace, holding forward his mother's prayers, and the secret gains of every good man burned all the more against him. The emperor's first disgrace lay in begging for an insolent woman; the second lay in the reason for his pleading; the third in the negligence of the citizens' judgment. As for the secret words of judging which, since Plancina was in the habit of moving Tiberius by such patronage, I do not wish to search out with excessive cleverness of conjecture. He ought rather to have listened to his mother Livia, who once gave wholesome counsel to Augustus. Οὐ λέγω τοῦτο, ὅ τι δεῖ πάντων ἁπλῶς τῶν ἀλλήλων φιλεῖν, ἀλλ' ὅτι τὸν μὲν [I do not say this, that one must simply love all men one another, but that the one...]
