units.la: Non hoc dico, omnibus injuste agentibus nullo discri-mine parcendum esse: sed hominem audacem & in-quietum, pravum ac sinistri consilii, sanari nescie & perpetuae malitiae obsequentem, exscindendum, ut medicinam respuentia corporum membra: reliquos, qui adolescentia, imperitia, ignorantia, aut alio quodam casu, sponte vel inviti peccant, verbis castigandos, minis admonendos, aliave ratione in ordinem redigendos. Haec Livia, sanis dementiae praeceptis: à quibus lentitudo, mollities, flagitium nimiae tolerantiae, longissime recedunt.
units.tr: I do not say that all who act unjustly should be spared without any distinction. But a man who is bold and restless, perverse and of sinister purpose, who cannot be cured and submits to unceasing malice, must be cut off, like the limbs of a body that reject medicine. The rest, who sin from youth, inexperience, ignorance, or some other chance, whether willingly or unwillingly, are to be chastised with words, warned with threats, and brought back into line by some other means. This is Livia's advice, healthy precepts against madness, from which sluggishness, softness, and the disgrace of excessive tolerance stand far apart.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Jus aut imago juris orbem gubernant.
units.tr: Law, or the image of law, governs the world.

units.la: Imagine juris Tiberius in innocentes saeviit: ima[?]-bine juris & nocentes absolvit. Plancinae criminibus percepto, biduum super imagine cognitionis absumptum, nec patrocinii nomen inanes ubi in juris locum ascendit, omissum: gente Tiberio liberos Pisonis, matrem uti tuerentur. Leviori quidem delicto nocens absolvitur, quam innocens damnatur: juris tamen rescripta, & innocentiae candor, pari utrobique à recto aberratione violantur.
units.tr: By the image of law Tiberius raged against the innocent; by the image of law he also acquitted the guilty. When the charges against Plancina had been received, two days were spent on the image of an inquiry, and the name of patronage, which in an empty show was dropped once the matter reached the place of law, was not dropped at all: Tiberius, by his own authority, ordered the children of Piso to protect their mother. The guilty is indeed acquitted for a lighter offence than the innocent is condemned for; yet the written rulings of law and the purity of innocence are violated on both sides by an equal deviation from what is right.

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Nimia miseria in miserationem vertit.
units.tr: Extreme misery turns into pity.

units.la: Infestis Plancinae judicibus, infestiore plebe, cum
units.tr: Though her judges were hostile to Plancina, and the common people even more hostile, pity for her grew greater than envy,

units.la: nullo, miseratio quam invidia augebatur. Huic fini[?] squalor & atratus color vestium rei ex consuetudine sumebatur, ut quamvis bene sibi consci effent, non causae magis quam judicium misericordiae siderent.
units.tr: with no one to lead it. In this cause, by custom, the accused put on squalor and dark clothing, so that, however conscious they were of their own innocence, they sought the pity of the court rather than the merits of the case.

units.la: Ita Jugurtha, fide publica Romam venire jussus, con-tra tra decus regium, cultu quam maximè miserabili, apparuit. Ita Cleopatra, post cladem Actiacam Augusti in potestatem redasta, cultu quam maximè abjecto, qui tamen mirè eam decuit, humili in sella Cæsari, in altiori collocato, assedit. Est & cum nimia cultus & frontis abjectio, in altæ nimirum fortunæ hominibus, omnem miserationem adimit. Sic Perseo, demisso vultu se ad pedes victoris abjicienti, victor Æmylius succensuit. Vitellius pudebunda latebra semet occultans, ab Julio Placido tribuno cohortis protrahitur. Vinctæ ponè tergum manus. laniata veste, soedum spectaculum ducebatur, multis increpantibus, nullo illacrymante. deformitas exitus misericordiam abstulerat. T.iii.Histor. Contrà Caractacus, è Britannorum rege captivus, non vultu demisso, aut verbis misericordiam requirens, Claudii tribunali astitit. cui Cæsar veniam, conjugique & fratribus, triumpho remisso, tribuit. xii. Annal. Degeneris enim victoriæ ipsos victores puduit.
units.tr: So Jugurtha, summoned to Rome under a public guarantee, appeared in a manner most pitiful, against his royal dignity. So Cleopatra, after the defeat at Actium, when she had been brought back into the power of Augustus, sat down before Caesar in a low chair, while he was seated higher, dressed in the most abject manner, which nevertheless suited her wonderfully. An excessive humbling of dress and countenance also takes away all pity from men of high fortune. Thus Aemilius Paulus was angered at Perseus, who lowered his face and threw himself at the feet of the victor. Vitellius, hiding himself in a shameful hiding place, was dragged out by the tribune Julius Placidus of a cohort; his hands were bound behind his back, his garment was torn, and he was led along as a foul spectacle, many reviling him, no one weeping. The wretchedness of his end had taken away pity. T. iii. Histor. On the contrary, Caratacus, a captive king of the Britons, did not lower his face or beg for mercy with words, but stood before the tribunal of Claudius. Caesar granted him pardon, and to his wife and brothers, remitting the triumph. xii. Annal. For the victors themselves were ashamed of such a degenerate victory.

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Ultra damnati sanguinem non sævire, placabilis ingenii est.
units.tr: Not to rage against the blood of one condemned is the mark of a merciful disposition.

units.la: Solent alicubi bona suppliciis affectorum fisco adjudicari, nomen fastis aut honestæ hominum memoriæ radi, liberi superstites aliqua ignominia notari. Tiberius hæc omnia in executione Pisoniana, ut sæpè aliis in reis, mitigavit. ne nomen Pisonis fastis eximeretur, quando M. Antonii qui bellum patriæ fecisset, Julii Antonii qui domum Augusti violasset, manerent. & M. Pisonem ignominia exemit, concessitque ei paterna bona. Non displicet Hassiæ principum abstinentia, nihil è damnatorum bonis in fiscum rapientium. Alii locupletiores è judicio discedant: hæc animi firmitudo, adversus avaritiam munita, plus gloriæ meretur.
units.tr: In some places the goods of those put to death are commonly awarded to the treasury, their names are erased from the calendars or from the honourable memory of men, and surviving children are marked with some disgrace. Tiberius softened all these things in the execution of Piso, as he often did with other accused men: he did not allow the name of Piso to be removed from the calendars, since the names of Marcus Antonius, who had waged war on his country, and Julius Antonius, who had violated the house of Augustus, remained. He also freed Marcus Piso from disgrace and granted him his father's goods. The abstinence of the princes of Hesse, who snatched nothing of the condemned men's goods into the treasury, is not displeasing. Other men may leave a trial richer; but this firmness of spirit, fortified against avarice, deserves more glory.

units.la: XXXIV.
units.tr: XXXIV.

units.la: De hoste, non de cive subacto, trium-phatur.
units.tr: One triumphs over a foreign enemy, not over a subdued fellow citizen.

units.la: Sanctè id Romanorum antiquo mori observatum, ut civilis belli victoriam luctuoso silentio, intra sinum gaudentes, involverent. Unde illa Lucani exclamatio:
units.tr: The ancient custom of the Romans was religiously kept, that they should wrap the victory in a civil war in mournful silence, rejoicing within their own breast. Hence that exclamation of Lucan:

units.la: Bella geri placuit nullos habitura triumphos!
units.tr: It has pleased them to wage wars that shall bring no triumphs!

units.la: Cæsar victis luculenta victoria in Macedonia, & deinde Africa, qui arma contra tulerant Romanis civibus; nullum de iis, quatuor de externis, Gallia, Ægypto, Pharnace, Juba, triumphos egit. Suetonius in Julio: Dio Cassius libro 43. Minori in victoria, Pisone judi-ciariis armis post Sentiana debellato, Tiberius pari moderatione usus: cum Valerius Mesallinus signum aureum in æde Martis ultoris, Cacina Severus aram ultioni statuendam censuissent, prohibuit: ob externas ea victorias sacrari dicitans, domestica mala tristitia operienda. Quod ad privatæ vitæ conditionem referens vir sapiens, aut jurgio inter necessarios abstinebit, aut de victoria non gloriabitur.
units.tr: Caesar, after his brilliant victory over those who had taken up arms against Roman citizens in Macedonia and then in Africa, celebrated no triumph over them, but four over foreigners: Gaul, Egypt, Pharnaces, and Juba. Suetonius in Julius; Dio Cassius, book 43. In a lesser victory, when Piso had been subdued by the judicial arms after the Sentian affair, Tiberius used the same moderation: when Valerius Messalinus proposed that a golden statue be placed in the temple of Mars the Avenger, and Caecina Severus proposed that an altar be set up to Vengeance, he forbade it, saying that such things were consecrated for foreign victories, and that domestic misfortunes should be covered with sorrow. Referring this to the condition of private life, a wise man will either abstain from quarrelling with his kinsmen, or will not glory in his victory over them.

units.la: XXXV.
units.tr: XXXV.

units.la: Fato, non dignitate apiscentis, impe-ria conferuntur.
units.tr: Empires are conferred by fate, not by the merit of those who obtain them.

units.la: Claudius, qui tredecim per annos orbi Romano leges daturus erat, tanta obscuritate, vel contemptu potiùs, in aula Tiberiana latuit, ut fratrem eum Ger-manici, cujus de vindicta gratulandum erat, index imprudens præteriret. Idem Claudius Cajo imperanti non despicatui modo, qui eum sævitiæ furentis principis eripuit, verum irrisui etiam ob tarditatem ingenii, & aulico ludibrio fuit. Nō immerito igitur Cornelius in hæc ingeniosæ admirationis verba erumpit: Mihi quanto plura recentium, seu veterum revolvo, tanto magis ludibria rerum mortalium cum-ctis in negotiis obversantur. quippe fama, spe, venera-tione potiùs omnes destinabantur imperio, quàm quem futurum principem fortuna in occulto tenebat. Quod-que mirandum magis est; illo sub caudice, illo sub stipite principe nec quicquam res Romana adversi con-cepit, & accessu Britanniæ adaucta est. Nec veri modum in laudatione funebri Nero excessit: nihil regen-[?] tt eo Reip.triste ab externis accidisse. Nimirum fortunæ imperio multa, ut verius dicam, divinæ providentiæ nutu omnia, pauca humana sapientia geruntur. Viri etiam gerendis aliàs rebus intenti, & in suscipiendis inductrii, plura felicitate quam ingenio confecere. nec omnibus, quod de Cornelio Sulla dictum, nunquam super inductriam fortuna fuit. Marius, Romanorum Jucum inter primos, correcta casu non semel temeritate, gloriam ex culpa invenit. sic ex eventu omnia non bene consulta in virtutem trahebantur.
units.tr: Claudius, who was to give laws to the Roman world for thirteen years, lay so hidden in the Tiberian court, or rather so despised, that an informer, unaware of who he was, passed him over as the brother of Germanicus, for whose vengeance he ought to have been congratulated. This same Claudius, under the emperor Caligula, was not only held in contempt, though he had rescued him from the cruelty of that raging prince, but was even laughed at for his slowness of mind and was a figure of mockery at court. Not undeservedly, therefore, Cornelius breaks out into these words of admiring wonder: The more I turn over the recent and the ancient examples, the more the mockeries of mortal affairs present themselves in every undertaking. For all were destined for empire by reputation, hope and veneration, rather than by the one whom fortune was keeping hidden as the future prince. And what is still more to be wondered at: under that stump, under that log of a prince, Roman affairs conceived nothing adverse, and by the advance into Britain they were enlarged. Nor did Nero go beyond the bounds of truth in his funeral oration: nothing sad had happened to the Republic from abroad while he ruled. Plainly, much is done by the command of fortune, or, to speak more truly, everything by the nod of divine providence, and little by human wisdom. Men, too, who were otherwise intent on conducting affairs and bold in taking them up, accomplished more by good fortune than by talent; and, as was said of Cornelius Sulla, fortune was never lacking to the industry of all. Marius, among the first of the Roman commanders, who more than once had his rashness set right by chance, found glory out of his fault. Thus, by the outcome, every ill-considered action was turned into a mark of virtue.

units.la: Unde fama de eo spargebatur, illi aut mentem divinam esse, aut deorum nutu cuncta portendi. nimirum quia rationem, cur ita res succederet, non ceperunt; nec dari ulla poterat. Scipio etiam, qui Africani nomen Carthagine pacata invenit, pauca ratione, plurima occulto numinis favore, patravisse Romanis credebatur. qua eum opinione liberare Polybius annititur. Alexandrum vero, supra captum ætatis gloria rerum evectum, temerarium adolescentem pronunciare Seneca non veretur. Hinc illud Ciceronis pro lege Manilia judicium: Maximo, Marcello, Scipioni, Mario, & cæteris magnis imperatoribus, non solum propter virtutem, sed etiam propter fortunam, sæpius imperia mandata, atque exercitus esse commissos. Rationem aliquam felicitatis humanæ, ex alto hominis etiam fatui ingenio, & cum cœlestibus consensu, Aristoteles in Eudemiis moralibus reddere conatur. Sed vereor, ut ea non subtilior, quam ad firmitatem solidior, dicatur.
units.tr: Hence a rumour spread about him that he had a divine mind, or that all things were foreshadowed by the nod of the gods. This was surely because people did not grasp the reason why things turned out as they did, and no such reason could be given. Scipio, too, who won the name Africanus when Carthage was pacified, was believed to have accomplished things for the Romans with little reasoning and much by the hidden favour of the divine power. Polybius labours to free him from this opinion. Seneca does not hesitate to call Alexander, raised by the glory of his deeds beyond the measure of his age, a rash youth. Hence Cicero's judgment in the speech for the Manilian law: "To Maximus, Marcellus, Scipio, Marius and the other great commanders, commands and armies have been entrusted more often, not only on account of their virtue but also on account of their fortune." Aristotle, in the Eudemian Ethics, tries to give an account of human good fortune, drawn from the hidden nature of even a foolish man and from his agreement with the heavenly bodies. But I fear it will be said to be less subtle than it is sound in its firmness.

units.la: XXXVI. Clarorum virorum clara, sed sæpe incerta, monumenta.
units.tr: XXXVI. The famous but often uncertain records of famous men.

units.la: Nihil Germanici nomine iis temporibus celebrius, nihil obitu ejus luctuosius, nihil quod hominum sermone magis jactaretur. Nec tamen idem apud omnes, de ulciscenda ejus morte, rumor percrebuit. adeò ma-rum in pu-xima quæque ambigua sunt: dum alii quoquomodo te[?]. audita pro tempore habent, alii vera in contrarium vertunt : & gliscit utrumque pofleritate.Livius etiam de corruptis veterum annalium fastis, &nominibus triumphorum per ambitionem irrepentibus, conque-ritur. Sed multò etiam magis Dio de Auguftani tem-poris rerum obscuritate : perquam, consilio princi-pum non,ut anteain populi libertate, divulgato, ma-gis ardua fit suscipiendarum rerum penetratio. Alia ambiguæ scriptorum fidei causa, ex metu & adulatio-ne,aut rursus odio,imperantium. Utramque Tacitus paucis verbis eleganter compleƈitur: Simul veritas pluribus modis infratta. primum inscitia Reip. ut alie-na; mox libidine assentandi, aut rur[us odio adversus dominantes. Ita neutris cura pofleritatis, inter infen-fos vel obnoxios. Quæ principi obnoxiorum affenta-tio,præcepta præmiorum gloria, erecta ingenia à fcri-bendo deterruit, de quo iterum noster: temporibuf-que Augusti dicendis non defuere decora ingenia, donec gliscente adulatione deterrerentur, Nòn enim ut cum Lipfio legamus deterrerentur, ulla necessitate adigi-mur. Aliud est apud Horatium laudes Cæsaris & A-grippæ Culpa deterere ingeni, quod non adulando, sed ingenii tenuitate committitur. nec, fi ferocia mi-litaris popinis & comessationibus deteritur, ingeni-um ex adulatione detrimentum capit. Sed missis cri-ticis,ad id quod præ manu est pergamus.
units.tr: Nothing was more talked of in those times than the name of Germanicus, nothing more mournful than his death, and nothing was more widely repeated in people's conversation. Yet the report about avenging his death did not spread in the same way among everyone. So in recent events everything is uncertain: while some take what they have heard in whatever way suits the moment, others turn the truth into its opposite; and both versions grow stronger with posterity. Livy also complains about the corrupted records of the ancient annals and about triumphs that crept into the lists through ambition. But Dio complains even more about the obscurity of affairs in the age of Augustus, when, since the counsels of the rulers were no longer published as they had been in the earlier days of popular liberty, it became much harder to penetrate and bring to light the things that were to be undertaken. Another cause of doubtful writers' credibility lay in the fear and flattery, or again the hatred, of those who ruled. Tacitus sums up both in a few words with elegance: "At the same time truth was broken in many ways: first by ignorance of the state, as of something foreign to oneself; then by a fondness for flattery, or again by hatred toward those who dominated." Thus neither kind of writer cared for posterity, being caught between those who were hostile and those who were obliged to them. The flattery of those obliged to the prince, and the glory of rewards set before them, turned fine talents away from writing; on this point our author says again: "Talents of distinction were not wanting to describe the times of Augustus, until, as flattery grew, they were deterred." We are not forced by any necessity to read "deterrerentur" with Lipsius. It is a different matter in Horace, where he speaks of the praises of Caesar and Agrippa; the loss of talent that comes not through flattery but through the slightness of a man's gift is a fault of its own. Nor, if military fierceness is worn down by taverns and drinking parties, does the talent suffer loss from flattery. But, setting aside the critics, let us proceed to what lies at hand.

units.la: XXXVII.
units.tr: XXXVII.

units.la: Quosdam fortuna ex humili loco in altum læsura allevat.
units.tr: Fortune raises some from a humble place only to strike them down from a height.

units.la: Alter Augustus,potentia,opibus, rerum gestarum gloria, Agrippa, quanquam obscuro patre natus, æ-quabili apud principem & cives gratia, quod paucisadmodum contigit, decessit. Cui vivo pepercerat, in liberis vultu mutato fortuna non pepercit. Vipfania vita excessit, una omnium Agrippa liberorum miti obitu. Nam cateros manifestum ferro, vel creditum est, veneno aut fame extinctos. Nullum tamen in Agrippa manifestum, quod in posteritate puniretur, scelus. Cujus encomium, cum paucis in magna for-tuna. tuna viris commune, apud Dionem libro 54 vide. Quod ideo refero, ne quis ex eventu de hominum vita ac moribus, ut mos est fere mortalium, semper judicet. Magnae Britanniae primum regem Jacobum, ex humili ac tenebricoso Scotiae regno ad amplum Angliae evectum, sapientiae, pietatis, felicitatis ideam plerique judicabant. Sed nunc liberorum ejus alios e regno profugos, alios gladio ultore percussos, conspicati: mutato judicio, nescio quod scelus aut flagitium in Jacobo, aut genitrice ejus, quaerunt. qui occultum potius Dei, vitam & regna pro arbitrio dantis & adimentis, judicium suspicere debebant.
units.tr: Another Augustus in power, wealth and the glory of his deeds, Agrippa, though born of an obscure father, died with the favour of the prince and the citizens alike, which has happened to very few. Fortune did not spare his children after he had been spared by her while he lived, and their countenance changed. Vipsania died, the only one of Agrippa's children to die a gentle death. For the others were killed, as is plainly known or believed, by the sword, by poison or by starvation. Yet no crime of Agrippa's is plainly known for which he was punished by posterity. His encomium, which is shared by few men in great fortune, may be seen in Dio, book 54. I mention this so that no one judges of a man's life and character from the outcome, as most mortals usually do. Many people once thought that James, the first king of Great Britain, raised from the humble and gloomy kingdom of Scotland to the great realm of England, was the very image of wisdom, piety and happiness. But now, having seen some of his children driven into exile from the kingdom and others struck down by the avenging sword, they have changed their judgement and seek some crime or disgrace in James or in his mother. They ought rather to revere the hidden judgement of God, who gives and takes away life and kingdoms at his own pleasure.

units.la: Est aliqua in toleranda obsidione timoris aut imbecillitatis confessio.
units.tr: There is some confession of fear or weakness in enduring a siege.

units.la: Judiciario ac aulico negotio armorum strepitum, filum Cornelii secuti, interponimus. Romanorum non fuit, in castris, quamvis a multitudine, circumsederi. Tacfarinas, latro Numida, a vagis populationibus ad obsidendam in castello Romanam cohortem audacia pervenit. Decrius, impiger manu, illam obsidionem flagitii ratus. Is cohortatus milites, ut copiam pugnae in aperto facerent, aciem pro castris instruit. Dignum id quidem Romano nomine generoso animo dignum. caeterum quod normam omni gentium militiae, & omni tempori, non praescribat. Praestitisset quippe, obsidionem aliquandiu tolerare, & commodo suo eruptione facta hostem profligare, quam aciem ausos, postea terga fugiendo dare. Bello cum Hispanis Belgico inter arcana militiae fuit, obsidionis patientia hostium nervos elidere, agendi tempora frangere, robur suum augere: postremo viribus frustra exhaustis, obsidionem solvere. Sic obice castelli alicujus, aut oppidi opera vel natura muniti, objecto primus copiarum impetus retardabatur. Hoc astu Mauritius, cum opem citius ferre obsessis[?] potuisset, in tempus autumnale saepe produxit. Quae productio non sem-per suadenda est: si procrastinatione munimenta hoftium augeamus, nostris animum aut commeatum adimamus, bene gerendae rei occasionem hosti proda- mus. In his, & aliis quam plurimis, verum est illud Thucydidis : [illegible, ~25 letters]. Bello administrando non possunt domi regulae praescribi.
units.tr: Turning from the business of the courts and the court, I interpose the clash of arms, following the example of Cornelius. It was not a Roman practice to be besieged in camp, however great the numbers of the enemy. Tacfarinas, the Numidian brigand, grew bold enough to pass from roving raids to besieging a Roman cohort in a fort. Decrius, vigorous in hand, thought that siege a disgrace. He urged his soldiers to give the enemy a chance of battle in the open, and drew up his line in front of the camp. This was indeed worthy of the noble name of Rome and of a generous spirit, but it does not set a rule for every kind of warfare and every occasion. It would have been better to endure the siege for a while and, by making a sortie when it suited them, to rout the enemy, than to dare a battle and afterwards turn their backs in flight. In the war with the Spaniards in Belgium it was among the secrets of soldiering to wear down the enemy's strength by patience under siege, to waste the time of his operations, to increase one's own strength, and finally, when his forces were spent in vain, to lift the siege. Thus, with some fort or town protected by its works or by nature standing in the way, the first onslaught of the troops was delayed by the obstacle. By this artifice Maurice, although he could have brought help to the besieged more quickly, often put it off until the autumn. Such delay is not always to be recommended: if by procrastination we strengthen the enemy's defences, deprive our own men of spirit or supplies, we give the enemy the chance to do well. In these and very many other cases that saying of Thucydides holds true: [illegible, ~25 letters]. The rules of conducting a war cannot be prescribed from home.

units.la: XXXIX.
units.tr: XXXIX.

units.la: Pugnando cadere, quàm fugiendo servari, praestantius.
units.tr: To fall fighting is more excellent than to be saved by fleeing.

units.la: Quod ad generosi animi laudem; non semper quod ad utilitatem publicam. Prius decretum secutus Decius, quanquam transfosso oculo, adversum os in hostem intendit, neque prælium omisit, donec desertus suis caderet. Pari animo Callicratides, dispari temeritatis damno, classem quam recedendo servare patriae debuisset, potentiori hosti & navibus instructiori objecit: classe ea amissa Spartanos aliam parare posse, se sine dedecore suo fugere non posse, dictitans.
units.tr: This is so for the praise of a generous spirit, though not always for the public advantage. Following an earlier decree, Decius, although with an eye pierced through, still turned his face towards the enemy and did not give up the battle until, abandoned by his men, he fell. With equal spirit, but with a different loss from rashness, Callicratidas threw himself and his fleet, which by withdrawing he ought to have preserved for his country, against a more powerful enemy with better-equipped ships. When that fleet was lost, he kept saying that the Spartans could build another, but that he could not flee without dishonour to himself.

units.la: XL.
units.tr: XL.

units.la: Severitas disciplinae remissione salubrior.
units.tr: Strict discipline is more wholesome than remissness.

units.la: L. Aponius ignominiosa suorum fuga comperta, magis dedecore suorum, quàm gloria hostis anxius, revocato è veteri disciplina more, decimando cohortem ignominiosam virtutis admonuit. Tantumque severitate profectum, ut vexillum veteranorum nom[?] amplius quingenti numero, easdem Tacfarinatis copias, praesidium, cui Thala nomen, aggressus fuerint. Aponii felix imitator sub Claudio Corbulo, copias veterem ad morem reduxit. Feruntque militem, quia vallum non accinctus, atque alium, quia pugione tantum accinctus, foderet, morte punitos. Qui terror usu salutaris, virtutem Romanam augendo, hostium ferociam infregit. T. xi. Annal. Medius inter eam severitatem & indulgentiam Julius Agricola, & ante eum Metellus Numidicus, ante utrumque Scipio Africanus, prohibendo à delictis magis quàm vindicando, exercitum confirmavere.
units.tr: When Lucius Aponius learned of the disgraceful flight of his men, anxious more for the disgrace of his own men than for the glory of the enemy, he recalled the old custom of discipline and by decimation admonished the disgraced cohort to virtue. So much was achieved by severity that the veterans, no more than five hundred in number, attacked the same forces of Tacfarinas, the garrison called Thala. Corbulo, a happy imitator of Aponius under Claudius, restored the old discipline. They report that one soldier was put to death because he dug the rampart without his belt, and another because he was girded only with a dagger. This terror, salutary in practice, increased Roman valour and broke the ferocity of the enemy. Tacitus, Annals, book 11. Between that severity and indulgence stood Julius Agricola, and before him Metellus Numidicus, and before both Scipio Africanus, who strengthened their armies more by preventing offences than by punishing them.

units.la: XLI.
units.tr: XLI.

units.la: Alterum militaris virtutis calcar, praemia.
units.tr: The second spur to military valour: rewards.

units.la: Non enim cogi tantum & metu impelli vult, erigi vult & laude excitari. Eodem praemii quo severitatis autore, Rufus Helfius gregarius miles servati civis decus retulit, donatusque est ab Apronio torquibus & hasta Casar[?] addidit civicam coronam. Nostris mori-bus milites magis auri & argenti pondere, quam herbida aut oleastri corona, delectantur. Caeterum poe-nae & praemiorum gravitate non alius magis, isto quidem aevo, Wallesteinio exercitum diversi hominum generis continuisse memoratur, quanquam major de saevitia ejus, quam largitione militari, rumor orbem pervasit.
units.tr: For he does not wish soldiers merely to be driven and impelled by fear; he wishes them to be raised up and roused by praise. In the same way that he was the author of severity, Rufus Helfius, a common soldier, was honoured for saving a citizen, and was presented by Apronius with a torque and a spear; Caesar added the civic crown. Our soldiers take more delight in the weight of gold and silver than in a crown of grass or of wild olive. Yet in the severity of punishments and the weight of rewards, no one in that age is recorded to have held an army of such mixed peoples together more than Wallenstein, although the rumour of his cruelty, rather than of his generosity to the soldiers, spread throughout the world.

units.la: XLII.
units.tr: XLII.

units.la: Spargere bellum, est aut causae aut viribus diffidentis.
units.tr: To spread a war out is the mark of a man who is either short of cause or short of strength.

units.la: Causae: dum praedae magis cogendae, quam debellando certamini, incumbas. Viribus: dum percul-sos in aciem producere non audeas. Utrumque de Tacfarinate memoratur, qui praedae intentus, pugnam velocitate devitans, ea ratione irritum fessumque Romanum impune ludificabatur. Quod genus militiae, si cum gravis armaturae hoste tibi mobili res fuerit, non est omnino aspernandum. Sic ante in eadem Numidia Jugurtha duces Romanos diu ludificabatur. Sic Parthi equestres Romanis, Sueonum agminibus Poloni, damno aut taedio fuerunt.
units.tr: It is a matter of cause when you devote yourself more to gathering plunder than to decisive fighting. It is a matter of strength when you dare not bring the beaten enemy into battle. Both are recorded of Tacfarinas, who, intent on plunder and avoiding battle by his speed, mocked the Roman, worn out and frustrated, with impunity. This kind of warfare should not be altogether despised if you have to deal with an enemy of heavy armour while you yourself are mobile. So earlier, in the same Numidia, Jugurtha long mocked the Roman generals. So the Parthian horsemen were a loss and a vexation to the Romans, and the Polish columns to the Swedes.

units.la: XLIII.
units.tr: XLIII.

units.la: Plurimae lites ex habendi cupidi-tate.
units.tr: Most quarrels arise from the desire to possess.

units.la: Quae bellorum frequentissima, eadem & litium in foro creberrima materies.
units.tr: The most frequent material of wars is also the most frequent material of lawsuits in the forum.

units.la: [illegible, ~28 letters] inquit Phocylides. i. e.
units.tr: [illegible in the scan] says Phocylides, that is:

units.la: Omne genus culpæ nummi generatur amore. Cum quo convenit illud Apostoli Pauli: ῥίζα γὰρ πάν-τῶν τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία[?]. radix omnium malorum est amor argenti. 1. Timoth. 6. v. 10. Romæ plu-rimarum imaginum fœmina,Lepida defertur simulatiue visse partum ex P. Quirinio divite atque orbo. cujus hæreditatem partu fictitio captabat.
units.tr: Every kind of wrong is produced by love of money. With this agrees that saying of the Apostle Paul: the root of all evils is the love of money [ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία]. 1 Timothy 6:10. At Rome Lepida, a woman of many images, was reported to have pretended to have given birth from the rich and childless P. Quirinius, by which fictitious childbirth she sought to catch his inheritance.

units.la: Frequens id genus captionis fuisse, titulus de Ventre inspiciendo docuerit. Præter hanc hæreditatis aucupii, & aliæ possunt esse simulati partus causæ. aut enim regno, ducatu, feudo quod vocant, imperio militari successio in eadem familia, & ex ea lucrum & dignitas matronæ viduæ quæritur. aut præmia honorum & ut apud Judæos olim, fœcunditatis gloria petitur, sterilitatis ignominia vitatur. aut alimonium ab amasio, vel ejusdem conjugii copula speratur. De alimonio: Philocomasium a glorioso milite pecuniam apud Plautum extorquet: missura puerum, ubi voti nummarii compos facta fuerit. de conjugio sperato: Glycerium in Andria Terentii ejusdem culpæ insimulata, præsenti arbitrio aliquot ingenuarum fœmina-rum per ancillam se defendit.
units.tr: That this kind of deception was common the title on examining the womb teaches. Besides this hunting for inheritances, there can be other causes of a feigned birth. For either succession in the same family to a kingdom, a dukedom, what they call a fief, or a military command is sought, and with it the gain and dignity of a widowed matron; or the rewards of honours are sought, or, as once among the Jews, the glory of fruitfulness, and the disgrace of barrenness is avoided; or maintenance is hoped for from a lover, or from the bond of the same marriage. As to maintenance: in Plautus Philocomasium extorts money from the boastful soldier, promising to send the child once she has got what she wanted in money. As to the hoped-for marriage: Glycerium in Terence's Andria, accused of the same fault, defends herself through a maidservant before the present judgement of several freeborn women.

units.la: Quémne ego heri vidi ad vos afferri vesperi? inquit Davus,& mox:
units.tr: Whom did I see brought to you yesterday evening? says Davus, and soon after:

units.la: verum vidi Cantharam suffarcinatam.
units.tr: But I did see Cantharus loaded up with bundles.

units.la: cui Myfis, quæ animum Davi non introspiciebat: dis pol habeo gratias,
units.tr: To which Mysis, who did not look into Davus's mind, replied: By Pollux, I thank the gods,

units.la: Cum in pariundo aliquot affuerunt libera.
units.tr: since several free women were present at the birth.

units.la: fiquæ præterea sunt fictionis causæ,ad scrutinium no-ftrum non pertinent. Id non præterundum: vitium unum sine connubio aliorum raro in uno commorari. adjiciebantur adulteria, venena: quasitumque per Chaldæos in domum Cafaris. Exigua enim pudicitiæ cura animo avaritiæ mancipato. nec magiæ incantationes & veneficia exhorrescet, quæ se totam auri cupidini sacravit. Ita veritas dicti Paulini &, quod ve-stibulo[?] præfixi, Phocyllidéi comprobatur.
units.tr: Whatever other causes there are for pretence do not belong to our inquiry. This must not be passed over: one vice rarely dwells alone without the marriage of others. Adulteries were added, poisons; and it was sought through the Chaldeans in the house of Caesar. For there is little care for chastity in a mind enslaved to greed, and it does not shrink from magic incantations and poisonings, since it has consecrated itself wholly to the lust for gold. Thus the truth of the Pauline saying, and of what is fixed on the vestibule, is confirmed by Phocylides.

units.la: Nulla
units.tr: None

units.la: XLIV.
units.tr: XLIV.

units.la: Nulla commiseratio, commiserationi proxima.
units.tr: No pity is close to pity.

units.la: Quod paradoxon auribus, aliquo sensu verum detegitur. Quirinius post dictum repudium adhuc in-sensus, quamvis infami ac nocenti miserationem addiderat. Vide Aphorismum XXXII. ad illa verba: cum accusatores ac testes certatim perorarent, respondente nullo, miseratio quam invidia augebatur.
units.tr: This paradox is shown to be true in a certain sense. Quirinius, still unmoved after the divorce spoken of, had added pity to a man infamous and guilty. See Aphorism XXXII on those words: when the accusers and witnesses pleaded eagerly, no one answering, pity was increased more than envy.

units.la: XLV.
units.tr: XLV.

units.la: Praesides judicii animum in fronte ne gerat.
units.tr: Let the presidents of a court not wear their feelings on their face.

units.la: Ne scilicet judices, accusatores, advocati, testes, mente ejus introspecta, gratiae captatione quid sequantur habeant. Haud facile quis dispexerit illa in cognitione mentem principis: adeo vertit ac miscuit ira & clementia signa. Quanquam illa Tiberiani vultus ac sermonis perplexitas, non est in omnibus pro regula judici sequenda: & pro irae ac clementiae mistis indiciis, serena vultus constantia magis probatur.
units.tr: That is, so that judges, accusers, advocates and witnesses, having looked into his mind, may not know what they should follow in seeking his favour. One could hardly discern the mind of the prince in such an examination: so much do anger and clemency turn and mix their signs. Still, that perplexity of Tiberius's look and speech is not to be followed as a rule by every judge; and, given signs mixed of anger and clemency, a calm constancy of countenance is more to be approved.

units.la: XLVI.
units.tr: XLVI.

units.la: Nec gravitate personae judicii libertatem opprimat.
units.tr: Let the dignity of the person not crush the freedom of judgement.

units.la: Tiberius praeter occultata favoris ac irae indicia, exemit etiam Drusum consulem designatum dicenda primo loco sententia. ne caeteri ad sentiendi necessitate abrepti, judicium non ex animi sententia proferrent. Non absurde alicubi observatur, ut aut promiscue, aut ab inferioribus facto initio sententiae rogentur. Quod ad potentiae vitandam gratificationem commodum, ad sententiae decisionem, numero magis quam judicio valituram, non usque quaque integrum.
units.tr: Tiberius, besides his hidden signs of favour and anger, also excused Drusus, consul designate, from giving his opinion first, so that the others, not hurried by the necessity of agreeing, would not pronounce judgement against their own minds. It is not absurd that somewhere it is noted that votes be asked either in a mixed order, or starting from the lower ranks. This is useful for avoiding the flattery of power, but for deciding the opinion it has more force by number than by judgement, and is not altogether sound.

units.la: XLVII.
units.tr: XLVII.

units.la: Domi nonnunquam miseri, qui publice felices.
units.tr: Sometimes wretched at home, though happy in public.

units.la: Felices principes, infelices iidem patres aut mariti. Ut valida divo Augusto in Remp. fortuna, ita domi im-proffera fuit, ob impudicitiam filiae at neptis, quas urbe depulit. Juliae filiae lascivam, eo progressam, ut in ipso foro & rostris noëturnas comesationes ageret, Dio libro 55 describit. Cujus proterviam cum diu ignoraret Augustus, compertâ tandem ita exarsit, ut infula Pandateria eam claudeeret, nec ullis populi precibus ad eam reducendam flecteretur.
units.tr: Princes are happy, and the same men are unhappy as fathers or husbands. As the fortune of the deified Augustus was strong in the state, so at home it was ill-starred, because of the shamelessness of his daughter and granddaughter, whom he drove from the city. Dio in book 55 describes the wantonness of his daughter Julia, which went so far that she held nocturnal revels in the very forum and on the rostra. When Augustus had long been ignorant of her shamelessness, once it was discovered he flared up so that he shut her up on the island of Pandateria, and he could not be moved by any prayers of the people to bring her back.

units.la: i. e. Principes enim omnia faciliùs quàm sua cognoscunt: ac neque clàm suos quicquam agunt; neque eorum actiones curiosè scrutantur: inquit ibi-dem Dio. Miserior Augusto, sed ingenii culpa mife-rior, Claudius: cum publicè non infelicem principem ageret. Hic Meffalinæ primùm protervia, & infami adulteriorum nomine, nec non potentiæ immoderata libidine, diu ignoratis flagitiis, infamiæ maculam at-traxit. deinde Agrippinæ impotenti dominio, nec non Domitii adoptione, fe & domum suam pessundedit. Alii republica victoriis aucta, cladem & funera indo-mum intulerunt: gloriamque clari triumphi & exe-quiarum luctum, eodem prope temporum momento susceperunt. Nota Æmylii, Perfeum cùm libetis ini triumpho ducentis, liberos suos ad rogum efferentis, historia. Quid fi & Davidem iis, regem gloria magni-ficum, patrem luctu & infamia liberorum miferri-mum; accenseam? Raro per omnia fe blandientem præbet, ut non aliquid aliunde largiundo abradat, hu-mana felicitas.
units.tr: That is, princes know everything more easily than their own affairs, and they do nothing secretly from their own people, nor do they closely scrutinise their actions, says Dio in the same place. Claudius was more wretched than Augustus, but wretched through his own nature, since he was unhappy as a prince in public. First the shamelessness of Messalina, and the infamous name of her adultery, and also the immoderate lust for power, while his crimes were long unknown, drew on him the stain of infamy. Then, under the uncontrolled rule of Agrippina, and by the adoption of Domitius, he ruined himself and his house. Others, while the state was increased by victories, brought defeat and death into their own household, and at almost the same moment received the glory of a famous triumph and the mourning of funerals. Note the story of Aemilius, when Perseus was led in his triumph in chains, and he carried his own children out to the funeral pyre. What if we also reckon David, magnificent in glory as a king, most wretched as a father through the grief and disgrace of his children? Human happiness rarely shows itself flattering in all respects without taking something away from elsewhere by its gifts.

units.la: XLVIII. Exilium non loci, sed ignominiosæ fugæ nomen.
units.tr: XLVIII. Exile is the name of a disgraceful flight, not of a place.

units.la: D. Silanus, ob adulterium cum nepte Augusti, admi-citia Cæsaris prohibitus, exilium sibi indici interpreta-tus, exulatum ultrò iit. De impetrato ejus reditu gra-tias agenti fratri Silano, Tiberius respondit, se quoque lætaris latari, quod frater ejus e peregrinatione longinqua re-vertisset. idque jure licitum, quia non senatusconsulto, non lege pulsus foret. peregrinationem vocat non lege aliqua fancitam absentiam. Audaciori interpretatione, Stoice nimirum paradoxa, Cicero in exilio fe exulem fuisse negat; Clodium in media Romae urbe exulare aflerit. profugam a patria absentiam eo nomine exilii nota eximit, quod latronum illa congregata unum in locum multitudo, quam fugerat; non civitas fuerit: utpote in qua leges & judicia jacebant, mos patrius occiderat, magistratuum & senatus nomen delectum fuerat. Clodium autem, exilii fui autorem, decentius Romae exulare speciosis verbis contendit.
units.tr: D. Silanus, forbidden the emperor's friendship because of his adultery with Augustus' granddaughter, interpreted the sentence as an exile declared against himself, and went into exile of his own accord. When his brother Silanus thanked Tiberius for obtaining his return, Tiberius replied that he too was glad his brother had returned from a long journey, and that this was lawful, since he had not been driven out by a decree of the senate or by a law. He calls a voluntary absence without any legal sanction a "journey." With a bolder interpretation, in the manner of the Stoic paradoxes, Cicero denies that he was an exile while in exile, and asserts that Clodius was in exile in the middle of Rome itself. He frees the fugitive's absence from his country from the stigma of exile on the ground that the crowd of brigands gathered into one place, which he had fled, was not a commonwealth, since laws and courts lay prostrate there, the ancestral custom had perished, and the name of the magistrates and senate had been abolished. But Clodius, the author of his own exile, claimed with more propriety, in fine words, that he was exiled at Rome.

units.la: An tu civem ab hoste natura ac loco, non animo fa-ctijque, distinguis? &c. non igitur ubi quisque erit, ejus loci jus tenebit, fi ibi eum legibus esse non oportebit. Lege quidem, vel privilegio potius, Cicero solum mutare jubebatur: sed eam legem non intelligit, quae non a fano populo, vera ad sanciendum ratione inducto, rogetur. Qua in re profugus ab exule, & hic a relegato differat, alio in loco aperui.
units.tr: Do you distinguish the citizen from the enemy by nature and place, not by mind and deeds? etc. Therefore, wherever someone is, he will not hold the right of that place if he ought not to be there by the laws. By law, or rather by a privilege, Cicero was ordered only to change his country; but he does not recognise that law, which was not proposed by a sound people, moved to sanction it by true reason. In this respect I have set out elsewhere how the fugitive differs from the exile, and the exile from the relegated man.

units.la: XLIX.
units.tr: XLIX.

units.la: Officii nomen & in offensione quaeritur.
units.tr: The name of duty is also sought in offence.

units.la: Laetatum fe reduce Silano, Tiberius pronunciaverat. at nunc quasi alio vultu induto: sibi tamen adversus eum integras parentis fui offensiones; neque reditu Silani dissoluta, quae Augustus voluisset, quasi ex abdito oraculum depromit. quom do laetari ejusdem reditu, & praefentia offendi poterat? nisi personata utrisque rei, gratulationis nimirum & offensionis, aflimulatione. Alii domi fumus, alii in publico: nec iidem quidem semper, ut hic Tiberius, in publico: sed ad colorem rerum figura circumaefi. Amicitiae tamen, ne- minem laesurae, tolerabilior est, quam simulatis affectatio. Ad mutua enim officia nos humanitas, non ad distractionem, impellit. Atque utinam in Tiberii falcem fi&a offensione subsisteretur, neque ad ultionem juris opinione prorumperetur! Tiberius hominum tacito judicio, de non abjecto Augusti dolore, contentus; nullam a Silano poenam vel satisfactionem exegit: nisi quod ab honorum aditu, forte nec ambientem, tacita praeteritione exclusit. Noftrates homines, Galli in primis, & horum morem stulte secuti, ob vericbum audacius prolatum, saepe nulla intus ira suscepta, aut ad amicorum ostentandam vindictae promptitudinem, gladiatorio ausu, morituri aut vitam fccio admpturi, concurrunt. Superior vestis exuitur (mettre le pourpoint bas) Galli appellant) ante pugnam decretoriam mutuum in amplexum ruunt, honori fe ideo- rum quod armati appareant, non irae, dare, testantur; veniam eripiendae vitae aut laesionis membri dant & accipiunt. Hac ceremonia amicitiae, saepe & affectu, praemisso, Gallina Thrax & Syrus in mutuam aut alter- utrius perniciem strictis gladiis concurrunt: nisi, quod non semper in promptu, arbitrorum interventu, pari officii simulatione, dirimantur. Quanto rectius fue- ratiram humanitati, quam irae humanitatem succum- bere; & aut nihil personate agere, aut amicitiae pa- tius quam offensae larvam induere!
units.tr: Tiberius had declared that he rejoiced at Silanus's return. But now, as if he had put on a different face, he brings forth, as if from some hidden place, an oracle: that he had nonetheless kept his parent's resentments against Silanus intact, and that Silanus's return had not dissolved what Augustus had wished. How could he rejoice at Silanus's return and yet be offended by his presence? Unless both feelings, that of congratulation and that of offence, were a pretence, each put on like a mask. Some men are one thing at home and another in public; and not always the same men in public, as Tiberius is here, but they put on a figure to suit the colour of affairs. Yet a pretended friendliness, which harms no one, is more bearable than a feigned hostility. For humanity impels us to mutual duties, not to estrangement. Would that the feigned offence had stopped at Tiberius's sickle, and had not burst out into revenge under the appearance of law! Tiberius, content with men's silent judgement and with Augustus's unabated grief, exacted no punishment or satisfaction from Silanus, except that he excluded him, by a silent passing over, from access to offices, though perhaps Silanus was not even seeking them. Our own people, the Gauls above all, foolishly following their custom, often take up arms over a word spoken too boldly, though no anger is harboured within, either to display readiness to avenge their friends. With gladiatorial daring, about to die or about to risk their lives, they rush together. They strip off the upper garment (the Gauls call this "stripping down the doublet") and, before the decisive fight, they rush into mutual embrace, testifying that they give honour to each other by appearing armed, not that they give way to anger; they give and receive pardon in advance for taking a life or injuring a limb. In this ceremony of friendship, often preceded by a show of affection, the Gaul, the Thracian and the Syrian run together with drawn swords for the mutual or one-sided destruction of each; unless, which is not always at hand, they are parted by the intervention of arbiters, with an equal pretence of duty. How much more rightly would humanity have given way to humanity than to anger; and either done nothing in pretence, or put on the mask of friendship rather than that of offence!

units.la: L.
units.tr: L.

units.la: Leges ex usu temporum nonnunquam mitigandae.
units.tr: Laws should sometimes be softened to suit the times.

units.la: Aliquando & plane abrogandae, fi id utilitas populi non adversante honestate, postulet. Relatum deinde de moderanda Papia Poppaea, quam [senior Augustus post Julias rogationes incitandis caelibum poenis, & augendo aerario, sanxerat. Augusto rerum potiente, fo- litudo Italiam, infrequentia ingenuorum, post tot bel- lorum civilium nimbos, Romam invaserat. Aerarium praeterea largitionibus, & innumera legionum ac claff- ium multitudine, exhauriebatur. Calcari ad augendam prolem, illice ad complendum aerarium, opus fuerat. At nunc alta pace frequentata liberorum edu- catione, Romae aucto aerarii reditu, numero legionum imminuto; cauta rigoris Papia-Poppaeani praecidebatur. batur. Sæpe quas bellum jusserat leges, firmata pacé abrogantur: & paci quam armis convenientiores, bellum in potestatem suam redigit.
units.tr: Sometimes they should even be wholly repealed, if the advantage of the people demands it and honour does not stand in the way. Next came a proposal to moderate the Papian law of Poppaea, which the elder Augustus had enacted after the Julian statutes, to increase the penalties on the unmarried and to swell the treasury. When Augustus held power, desolation had invaded Italy, and the scarcity of freeborn citizens had invaded Rome after the storms of so many civil wars. Besides, the treasury was being drained by largesse and by the countless multitude of legions and fleets. Spurs were needed to increase offspring, and lures to fill the treasury. But now, with deep peace, the rearing of children flourishing, the revenue of the treasury increased at Rome, and the number of legions reduced, the strictness of the Papian-Poppaean law is being cut back. Laws that war had ordered are often repealed once peace is secured; and what is better suited to peace than to arms, war brings back under its own power.

units.la: LI. Coelibatus pœnam natura sua non meretur.
units.tr: LI. Celibacy does not by its nature deserve punishment.

units.la: Præcedenti aphorismo [illegible, ~12 letters] dedi, legem coelibatus prohibitoriam temporibus Augusti non inutilem fuisse. nunc id ipsum quod dedi, reposco; & Penelopea textura [illegible, ~10 letters] Autor mihi refcissionis Tacitus, non aliud agente animo intuendus. Primum argumentum (ut referendi & moderandi voces, fontem probationis adversæ & ipsas porrigentes, præteream) ab ætate Augusti sumitur. quasenior. M. Pappio Mutilo nimirum & Q. Poppæo Secundo Cos. id est quadragesimo potentiæ, septuagesimo vitæ Augusti, qua ætate & parum animo eum valuisse, & seneƈtutis vitio tum ad rem attentiorem, tum etiam morosiorem fuisse, non aspernanda sunt indicia. morositas illa, vel potius in cives acerbitas, inde clarescit, quod ne quidem Juliis rogationibus contentus, acerbiorem multo legem tulit. idque eo ipso momento, quo equites magno studio legem de cœlibum pœnis antiquandam flagitarunt. quod [illegible, ~8 letters] certius signum: Consulum, qui ipsi in cœlibatu vivebant, hominibus legem de maritandis ordinibus, quam Cos. tacito suffragio resciderunt, promulgavit nec non oratione, herilem objurgationem, non legislatoris suasionem sapientis, quæ omnia apud Dionem, quanquam summa laude Augusti, fusius lib. 56. Alterum argumentum a duplici fine, incitan-dis cœlibum pœnis, & augendo ærario, petitur. Non pœnam civium augendam, sed morum emendationem lex pro scopo habere debet, nec pecuniæ attrahendæ, sed honestati muniendæ serviat. Tertium ab effectu primum inani, deinde & incommodo. Inani: quia nec ideo conjugia & educationes liberorum frequentabantur. Incommodo: dum multitudo periculitantum gliscebat, cum omnes domus delatorum intra pretationibus subverterentur, utque antebac flagitiis, ita tunc legibus laborabatur. Hoc Taciti de sanctione Poppæa, Dionis quanquam id non agentis affenst munitum, judicium. Copiosus esse queam, si altitudinem coelestis animæ, libidini dominantis, Deo aut gravibus vioribus orbis negotiis se mancipantis; si sacri codicis in hanc hominum partem favorem, novi inprimis instrumenti, referam. Possem tranquillitatem animi, curarum sepulturam, philosophorum consensum commemorando recitare. Sed quia non de commendatione dationeque solitariæ vitæ, sed de pœna & objurgatione agitur; supervacaneis non insisto. Unum Creontis, in Sophoclis Antigona, judicium ob antiquitatem non prætereundum censeo. Gravissimæ orationis & hæc emblemata visuntur.
units.tr: In the preceding aphorism I gave [illegible, ~12 letters], that the law prohibiting celibacy was not useless in the times of Augustus. Now I demand back what I gave, and the Penelopean web [illegible, ~10 letters]. Tacitus is my authority for the retraction, and he is to be read without any other purpose in view. The first argument (I pass over the words of reference and moderation, which supply the source of the opposing proof and themselves offer it) is taken from the age of Augustus, as an old man. Namely, in the consulship of M. Papius Mutilus and Q. Poppaeus Secundus, that is, in the fortieth year of his power and the seventieth of his life. At that age, indications not to be scorned show that he was somewhat weak in mind and, through the infirmity of old age, both more attentive to business and more peevish. That peevishness, or rather harshness towards the citizens, becomes clear from this: not content even with the Julian laws, he passed a much harsher law, and did so at the very moment when the knights were eagerly demanding that the law on the penalties for celibates be repealed. A more certain sign of this is that [illegible, ~8 letters] the consuls, who themselves lived in celibacy, were given a law on marrying the orders, which they rescinded by silent vote. He promulgated it with a speech that was a master's rebuke rather than a wise lawgiver's persuasion. All of this is set out more fully in Dio, book 56, although with the highest praise for Augustus. The second argument is taken from the twofold aim of spurring celibates with penalties and increasing the treasury. A law ought to have as its aim not the punishment of citizens but the correction of morals, and it should serve not to attract money but to fortify honour. The third is taken from the effect: first that it was empty, then that it was harmful. It was empty, because marriages and the rearing of children were not thereby more frequent. It was harmful, because the danger of informers grew only more, while all households were overturned by the accusations of informers, and as formerly men suffered from vices, so then they suffered from laws. This is Tacitus's judgement on the Poppaean sanction, supported by Dio, though he does not treat of this. I could be copious, if I were to cite the loftiness of the heavenly soul, which is ruled by lust, or which gives itself over to God or to the heavy business of the world, or the favour of Sacred Scripture, especially of the New Testament, toward this part of mankind. I could recite the tranquillity of mind, the burial of cares, and the agreement of the philosophers. But since the matter is not commendation or advice about a solitary life, but punishment and rebuke, I do not dwell on superfluous things. I think the judgement of Creon in Sophocles's Antigone, on account of its antiquity, is not to be passed over. These emblems too are seen in a most weighty speech.

units.la: Quod majus ulcus est, amicus quam malus? Sed his, ut dixi, missis, quam vim obiurgatoria argumenta habeant, examinemus. Augustus conjugibus & cœlibibus, qui multo plures fuerant, feorsim positis; orationem ad utrosque, si fides Dioni, habuit: illos in honesto proposito confirmavit, hos à pervicacia deterruit. Commendationem matrimonii pertexit: à mortalitate naturæ humanæ corrigenda; à sexuum distincta notione, etiam diis cum hominibus commu- nis; à suavitate prolis & conjugis; à spe successionis labore partorum; à reipub. emolumento. Quæ ut omnia nullo falsitatis vitio laborent; libertatem commodis illis carendi, uni & alteri non admunt, nec quidQuidquid reip. usui esse poterit, ab universis legis coactione jure exigitur. multum enim officium a necessitate, promptitudo ab imperio herili differt. Cœlibatum vituperat: a generis humani abolitione; a maximorum scelerum consortio; a Romuli morum contemptu; a raptu Sabinarum; a vitæ solitariæ impuritate; a molestiarum conjugii tenuitate. Quorum primum & secundum argumentum procederet, si in paucorum cœlibatu totum genus humanum verteretur. Tertium & quartum nihil, quod ajunt, stringit. Quintum de Romanis civibus fortasse vere: de omnibus hominibus concipiendo, alios ex ingenio suo judicare, impuri & sacrilegi hominis est. Ultimum suadendi forte vim aliquam habet; cogendi nullam obtinet. Noftrates a benedictionis cumulo, qui matrimonio junctos sequatur, communem feminam fugientes deserat, rationem ducere solent. quibus accederem, nisi plures in matrimonio quam in cœlibatu depauperrate querulos audirem. Deum vero cœlibes aversando punire; nollem a Brentio & ejus farinæ theologis prolatum.
units.tr: What is a greater sore than a friend who is bad? But, as I said, these things being set aside, let us examine what force the arguments of rebuke have. Augustus, with the married and the celibates, who were far more numerous, placed apart, gave an address to each, if Dio is to be trusted. He confirmed the first in their honourable purpose and deterred the second from their obstinacy. He wove together his commendation of marriage: from the need to correct the mortality of human nature; from the distinct notion of the sexes, which is common to gods with men; from the sweetness of offspring and spouse; from the hope of succession, and the toil of childbirth; and from the advantage of the commonwealth. But even if all these are free from any fault of falsehood, the freedom to go without those advantages is not granted to one or another, and whatever can be of use to the commonwealth is demanded by law of all by compulsion. For duty differs much from necessity, and readiness from the command of a master. He disparaged celibacy: from the abolition of the human race; from association with the greatest crimes; from contempt for the morals of Romulus; from the rape of the Sabine women; from the impurity of a solitary life; and from the slightness of the troubles of marriage. Of these, the first and second argument would hold if the whole human race were turned over to the celibacy of a few. The third and fourth touch nothing of what they say. The fifth, about Roman citizens, is perhaps true; but to judge all men by one's own disposition in conceiving them is the mark of an impure and sacrilegious man. The last may perhaps have some force in urging, but it has none in compelling. Our countrymen are accustomed to argue from the abundance of blessing that follows those joined in marriage, and that those who flee a common woman abandon her. I would agree with them, were I not hearing more complaints of poverty from those in marriage than from those in celibacy. But that God punishes celibates by turning away from them, I would not wish to have been brought forward by Brenz and theologians of his kind.

units.la: LII. Sanctior sine legum imperio innocentia.
units.tr: LII. Innocence more holy without the authority of laws.

units.la: De Germanis, leges & plebiscita ignorantibus, Tacitus: Nemo enim illic vitia ridet: nec corrumpere & corrumpi seculum vocatur. Vitæ integritatis hanc apud eos causam asserit: plusque ibi boni mores valent, quam alibi bonæ leges. De Scythis Trogi Epitome: fuisse in iis ignorationem magis vitiorum quam cognitionem virtutis. De priscis omnium generum hominibus iterum hoc loco Tacitus: Vetustissimi mor-talium, nulla adhuc mala libidine, sine probro, scelere, eoque sine pœna aut coercitionibus agebant, neque præmiis opus erat, cum honesta suopte ingenio peterentur, & ubi nihil contra morem cuperent, nihil per metum vetabantur. Nota est aurei sæculi apud poetas celebrata beatitudo. Qui aut de primorum hominum in paradiso felici libertate aliquid fando audiverunt; aut lectores blanda ingenii licentia paverunt. Atque ut hi detorto sacrorum oraculo abusi videri queunt; ita Hugo Grotius, magnæ vir eruditionis, ex horum commentis oracula sacra non bene interpretatur. De jure belli ac pacis. cap. 2. libri 2.
units.tr: Of the Germans, who knew no laws or plebiscites, Tacitus says: For no one there laughs at vices, nor is it called "the age" to corrupt and be corrupted. He asserts this as the cause of their integrity of life: and good customs prevail there more than good laws do elsewhere. Of the Scythians, the Epitome of Trogus says that among them there was ignorance of vices rather than knowledge of virtue. Tacitus again, speaking of the earliest men of all races: The most ancient of mortals, while no base desire yet existed, lived without disgrace, without crime, and therefore without punishment or restraints. Neither rewards were needed, since what is honourable was sought of its own accord, and when they desired nothing contrary to custom, nothing was forbidden them by fear. The blessedness of the golden age, celebrated by the poets, is well known. Those who heard something about the free state of the first men in the happy paradise either spoke of it from hearsay, or fed their readers with the pleasing license of their wit. And just as these seem to have twisted the sacred oracle and abused it, so Hugo Grotius, a man of great learning, does not interpret the sacred oracles well from their fictions. On the Law of War and Peace, ch. 2, book 2.

units.la: Quoloco, blandiente verborum elegantia, quia facile incautum lectorem in assensum raperet: phylacteria quædam fanatici interpretationis, è sensu literarum rarum, adhibenda[?].
units.tr: In this passage, with its smooth elegance of words, since it would easily snatch an unwary reader into assent, certain phylacteries of fanatical interpretation, rare from the sense of the letters, are to be applied[?].

units.la: Simplicitatis in qua primi homines sunt conditi argumentum prabuit nuditas. atqui nuditas hæc non puerilis fuit stuporis, aut cynicæ impudentiæ, verum integri moris & innocentiæ, quod contra Socinum à viris doctis observatum.
units.tr: Nakedness provided the proof of the simplicity in which the first men were created. But this nakedness was not that of childish stupidity or Cynic shamelessness, but of upright morals and innocence, as learned men have observed against Socinus.

units.la: Erat in illis ignoratio magis vitiorum quàm cognitio virtutis. Perfectissima ergo imago Dei, ad quam typus humani generis Adam conditus fuit, in stupore, ruditate, bruta ignorantia, potebatur? quod vel cogitatu absurdum. Si vero ignorationem vitiorum pro nondum cognito experimento capias; non admodum repugno. Sed quid de negata virtutis cognitione fiet?
units.tr: There was in them an ignorance of vices rather than a knowledge of virtue. Was the most perfect image of God, to which Adam, the type of the human race, was made, then possessed in stupor, rudeness and brute ignorance? That is absurd even to think. If, however, you take the ignorance of vices to mean an experience not yet tried, I do not greatly object. But what will become of the denied knowledge of virtue?

units.la: Hæc simplicitas videtur dici sapienti Hebræi at mihi non videtur, eam esse sapientis Hebræi mentem. quod enim mortis conditioni opponitur, quod divinæ naturæ imaginem affirmulat, pro incorrupto potius vitæ statu, vel ipso vocis sono exprimente, quam pro simplicitate animi accipiendum erat. Vide lib. Sapientiæ, cap. 2. v. 23. corrigendus enim numerus, margini libri Grotiani appositus. Nec firmior in annotatis Grotii ex epistolis Paulinis probatio. Verba Ephes. 6. v. 24. sunt. Ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων τῶν ἀγαπώντων τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ. quæ vel ita vertas: Gratia cum omnibus dominum nostrum sincero animo amantibus. Velit: gratia incorruptibilis cum omnibus dominum nostrum Iesum Christum amantibus; vel ita, ut Beza vertit: ad incorruptionem bilitatem. Alter locus parallelus extat Tit. 2. v. 7. Περὶ πάντα σεαυτὸν παρέχων τύπον καλῶν ἔργων ἐν τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ ἀφθαρσίαν, σεμνότητα[?]. τῆς διδασκαλίας ἀδιαφθορίαν, σεμνότητα. in omnibus te-ipsum praebens exemplar bonorum operum, in doctrina sinceram incorruptionem, gravitatem. quid haec ad simplicitatem ignorantiae? qua ad docendum nihil minus idoneum. Nec ejusdem Apostoli [?] quam [?] τῆς [?] καλλιτεχνίας, [?] vafrae calliditati, opponit, Grotianae interpretationi favet. Locus est 2. ad Corinth. cap. 11. v. 3. Φοβοῦμαι δὲ μήπως ὡς ὁ ὄφις Εὔαν ἐξηπάτησεν ἐν τῇ πανουργίᾳ αὐτοῦ, οὕτω φθαρῇ τὰ νοήματα ὑμῶν, ἀπὸ τῆς ἁπλότητος τῆς εἰς τὸν Χριστόν. Verear autem ne quemadmodum serpens Evam vafritie sua decepit, ita cogitationes vestrae corrumpantur (seducta) a simplicitate quae est in Christo. simplicitatem cape non ignorantiae: in Christo enim omnes thesauri sapientiae: sed integrae notitiae, veteratoriam detorsionem excludentis. Pergit Grotius:
units.tr: This simplicity seems to be spoken of by the Hebrew sage, but it does not seem to me to be the sage's meaning. For what is opposed to the condition of death, what expresses the image of the divine nature, must be understood as an incorrupt state of life, or as the very sound of the word itself expresses it, rather than as simplicity of mind. See the Book of Wisdom, ch. 2, v. 23; the number needs correcting, as noted in the margin of the Grotian book. Nor is Grotius's proof from the Pauline epistles stronger in his annotations. The words of Ephesians 6, v. 24 are: Ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων τῶν ἀγαπώντων τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ [grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption]. You may translate this either: "Grace with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with a sincere heart", or: "Incorruptible grace with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ", or as Beza translates it: "to incorruptibility". Another parallel passage is Titus 2, v. 7: Περὶ πάντα σεαυτὸν παρέχων τύπον καλῶν ἔργων, ἐν τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ ἀφθαρσίαν, σεμνότητα [in all things showing yourself a pattern of good works, in your teaching incorruption, gravity]. What has this to do with the simplicity of ignorance, which is least of all suited to teaching? Nor does the same Apostle's opposition of the ... to crafty cunning favour the Grotian interpretation. The passage is 2 Corinthians 11, v. 3: Φοβοῦμαι δὲ μήπως ὡς ὁ ὄφις Εὔαν ἐξηπάτησεν ἐν τῇ πανουργίᾳ αὐτοῦ, οὕτω φθαρῇ τὰ νοήματα ὑμῶν ἀπὸ τῆς ἁπλότητος τῆς εἰς τὸν Χριστόν [But I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ]. Take this simplicity not as ignorance: for in Christ are all the treasures of wisdom; take it as integral knowledge, which excludes crafty distortion. Grotius goes on:

units.la: Negotium erat illis unicum Dei cultus, cujus symbolum arbor vitae, ut Hebraei veteres explicant, assentiente Apocalypsi.] nec negotium illis hoc unicum, ad colendum hortum & custodiendum collocatis, Gen. 2. v. 15. & arbor illa vitae magis producendae aut symbolum aut remedium erat, quam Dei colendi sacramentum. alioqui Deus hominum a cultu sui abegisset. Gen. 3. v. 22. quid Hebraei nonnulli contra scripturae sensum statuerint, parum moror. Locus Apocalypseos, quem assignavit, nihil de terrestri paradiso, nihil de primorum hominum innocentiae statu, promit. quin, si de paradisi arbore interpretationem admittamus, adversus hic locus Grotio est. Gentium enim sanationi, non cultui Dei, destinata scribitur.
units.tr: The one business for them was the worship of God, whose symbol, as the ancient Hebrews explain, with the Apocalypse agreeing, was the tree of life. Nor was this their one business, since they were placed to cultivate and guard the garden (Gen. 2, v. 15), and that tree of life was a symbol or remedy for prolonging life rather than a sacrament of the worship of God; otherwise God would have turned men away from his worship (Gen. 3, v. 22). What some Hebrews have laid down against the sense of Scripture I care little about. The passage of the Apocalypse which he cites says nothing about the earthly paradise or the state of innocence of the first men. Indeed, if we admit an interpretation about the tree of paradise, this passage is against Grotius. For it is written as destined for the healing of the nations, not for the worship of God.

units.la: Animum applicuerunt ad artes varias, quarum symbolum erat arbor scientiae boni & mali, id est, earum scientia rerum, quibus tum bene tum male uti licet.] Ævi Saturnini ad Jovianum detorsionem dixeris: artibus variis & terrae cultu, ad situm otii pellendum, Jovis consiliis introducto. at ego in arboris ejus, vel potius praecepti divini, violatione, totius decalogi transgressionem fuisse, facile probaverim. sed campum eum theologi, metendum relinquo. Huc respiciens Salomo ; Deus, inquit, creavit hominem rectum, id est simplicem, sed ipsi sibi quaesiverunt cogitationes multas : inanes variarum artium subtilitates, nihil ad vitam profuturas, hoc loco redargui non nego. Nec male inde probaveris, Deum non creavisse hominem cum naturæ infirmitate & depravatione in-genii, qui verò quæsita multa ratiocinia de lapsu Adæ, mi & Evæ theologi accipiunt, quid Grotio reponant ipsi viderint.
units.tr: They applied themselves to various arts, whose symbol was the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, that is, the knowledge of those things which may be used either well or badly. You might call this a distortion of the age of Saturn into that of Jupiter: various arts and the cultivation of the earth, introduced by the counsels of Jupiter, to drive away the state of idleness. But I could easily prove that in the violation of that tree, or rather of the divine precept, there was a transgression of the whole decalogue. But that field I leave for the theologians to mow. Looking to this, Solomon says: God made man upright, that is, simple, but they sought out many devices; the empty subtleties of various arts, which will profit nothing for life. I do not deny that this is refuted in this place. Nor would you badly prove from this that God did not create man with a weakness of nature and a depravity of disposition. As for the many arguments sought out about the fall of Adam and Eve, the theologians will see for themselves what they reply to Grotius.

units.la: Ex studiorum diversitate æmulatio] & contra Aris-totelis doctrinam, & contra communis vitæ experientiam, mentum, denique præter sacræ scripturæ sensum hæc affertatio. Notum illud :
units.tr: From diversity of studies, emulation: this is contrary both to Aristotle's teaching and to common experience, and, apart from the sense of Holy Scripture, this is an empty assertion. That saying is well known:

units.la: Καὶ [illegible, ~6 letters] λόγος.
units.tr: And [illegible, about six letters] word. [Καὶ ... λόγος]

units.la: Vitæ quædam ob studii & morum diversitatem distra-ctio : nonautem disparis vitæ æmulatio, quæ inter pares, & eandem artem professos, citiùs oboritur. Fratrum igitur æmulatio, & inde ortæ cædes, ob im-molationis disparem à Deo acceptationem. Cain ut natu major, vitæ genere nobilior, moribus ferociorr erat : ita & coram Deo præstantiorem se esse, & priores mitiùs oblatis acceptiorem, debere arbitrabatur. Hinc ex reje&tione, præsato fratre, indignatio.
units.tr: There is a certain distraction of life due to diversity of study and character, but not an emulation of unequal lives, which arises more quickly among equals who profess the same art. So the emulation of the brothers, and the murders that arose from it, came from the unequal acceptance of their sacrifices by God. Cain, as the elder by birth, nobler in his way of life and fiercer in character, believed that he ought to be more distinguished before God and more acceptable than his brother, whose offerings were milder. Hence came indignation at his brother's rejection.

units.la: Mundo per diluvium purgato, pro ferina illa vita successit cupido voluptatis, cui inserviit vinum : unde & illicitè amores.] Suavis & hæc de prisco hominum statu somniatio. Cur voluptatis cupidinem à proto-plastorum primo peccato secludit ? cur in extremum Noachi jam senioris, jam contra voluptates munitis, seculum rejicit ? Vini vero plantationem à Noacho fuisse inventam, receptior est quàm mihi probatior sententia. Et cœpit Noa vir terra ( nimirum colendas deditus) & plantavit vineam. Quemadmodum pa-ce post diuturnum bellum restituta, agricolæ admu-nia obeunda redeuntes, sicut scipere dicuntur : ita Noa animo post diluvium recolle&to, plantare vineam in-cepit : inundatione nimirum obliteratam, palmitibus disje&sis. Unde, si autor fuit vineæ, si idem Noachus : qui Jacchus aut Bacchus, vites & palmites accepit ? cœlocœlóne delapsa sinu excepit, an ipse Deum imitatus jussu creavit? Vero similius est, cum aliis arboribus, fruticibus, herbis, & vitem à Deo primordio mundi producìam; nec usum ejus vetustissimis mortalium ignoratum. Verùm de iis ex ingenio suo quisque de-mat vel addat assensum. Illiciti vero amores ante di-luvium catervatim orbem universum, ferinæ vitæ & giganteæ causa, irruperunt. Gen. 6. v. 4. Lothi vero cum filiabus incestus, in quem quinto post diluvium seculo non sponte lapsus memoratur, peculiarem Notam hominum moribus non imprimit. curis & senio confectus facile vino avidius hausto in profundum somnum collapsus, à filiabus, non tam libidine quam simplicitate (en simplicitatis Grotianæ fructum!) ruentibus irretitus, patris & avi, filiorum & nepotum in iisdem appellationem confudit.
units.tr: After the world was purged by the flood, the desire for pleasure succeeded that wild life, and wine served it; whence also illicit loves. This is a pleasant fancy about the early state of men. Why does he exclude the desire for pleasure from the first sin of the protoplasts? Why does he throw it back into the age of Noah, already old, and by then fortified against pleasures? That the planting of the vine was invented by Noah is a more received opinion than one I find more probable. "And Noah, a man of the earth (namely, one devoted to cultivation), began and planted a vineyard." Just as, when peace is restored after a long war, farmers returning to their duties are said to scrape off the rust, so Noah, with his mind recollected after the flood, began to plant a vineyard, the earlier vines having been obliterated by the inundation and the shoots broken off. Hence, if he was the author of the vineyard, if he was the same Noah, who then received the vine and its shoots, as Jacchus or Bacchus? Did he catch them fallen from heaven in his lap, or did he create them by command, imitating God himself? It is more likely that the vine, along with other trees, shrubs and herbs, was produced by God at the beginning of the world, and that its use was not unknown to the most ancient mortals. However, let each person add or withhold assent according to his own judgement. Illicit loves rushed in crowds over the whole world before the flood, the cause of a wild and gigantic life (Gen. 6, v. 4). But the incest of Lot with his daughters, into which he is recorded to have fallen, not willingly, in the fifth century after the flood, does not impress a peculiar mark on men's morals. Worn down by cares and old age, having drunk wine too greedily, he collapsed into deep sleep, and was ensnared by his daughters, who rushed on him not so much from lust as from simplicity (behold the fruit of Grotian simplicity!). And he confused the names of father and grandfather, of sons and grandsons, in the same persons.

units.la: Præcipuè verò concordiam rupit generosius vitium, ambitio, cujus signum turris Babylonica.] imò contraxit concordes vitii consensus: quos pœna superbiæ dispersit. quid verò sibi vult signum turris Babylonica? Pro fabulane tota Geneseos historia, quod nec in su-perioribus obscurè tulit, accipienda videatur? an turris Babylonica sacramentum ambitionis; ut arbor sci-entiæ boni & mali symbolum variarum artium, ut arbor vitæ Dei colendi? an verò homines illi turrim tanto studio laboris, mnemosynam superbiæ suæ po-steris futuram, erigere festinarunt?
units.tr: Above all, however, ambition, a more noble vice, broke concord. Indeed it rather drew the vices into a harmonious agreement, which the punishment of pride then scattered. But what does the sign of the Tower of Babel mean? Should the whole history of Genesis be taken as a fable, as the author did not conceal in the earlier chapters? Or is the Tower of Babel a sacrament of ambition, just as the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is a symbol of the various arts, and the tree of life a symbol of the worship of God? Or did those men hasten to build the tower with such eagerness and labour, so that it would be a memorial of their pride for posterity?

units.la: Postea quoque inter homines vicinos mansit non pe-corum[?] sed terrarum pascuarum communio.] Abraha-mum, & ejus filium ac nepotem pascua in Cananitide variè mutasse, observatur. Sed & Jacobum à Sichemi-tis agrum emisse, agrum nimirum pascuum, depre-hendítur. ne urgeam speluncam à terræ ejusdem in-colis, quam & ipsi pretio paraverant, ad sepulturam fuisse emptam[?]. Unde[?] igitur & occupatione, promis-sionis divinæ jure freti, an incolarum conniventia, an pretii interventu pascua invaserint, ut rem antiquitate obrutam, non eruo. Nec poëtas, quibus ne signare quidem aut partiri limite campum placuit, nunc re-darguo. Ad Tacitum, & ejus ingeniosam folertiam redeo: cui Caini fratricidium, & scelera, ob quæ priscis mortalibus inundatio immissa, ignoranti, promptius, quam tot in sacra commentariorum autori, ignosco. Inconcussa nihilominus assertio nostra perstabit, sanctiorem esse fine legibus vitæ innocentiam, quam legum multitudine laborantem inertiam, aut vi ac minis extortum obsequium.
units.tr: Afterwards too, among neighbouring men, the sharing of grazing land, not of flocks, remained. It is observed that Abraham, and his son and grandson, moved their pastures about in the land of Canaan. It is also found that Jacob bought a field from the Shechemites, namely a pasture field. I will not press the cave, which they too had acquired for a price from the inhabitants of that land, to serve as a burial place. Whether they seized the pastures by occupation, relying on the right of the divine promise, or by the connivance of the inhabitants, or through the intervention of a price, I do not dig up, since the matter is buried in antiquity.
