Nor do I now refute the poets, to whom it did not seem fit to mark or divide the field with a boundary. I return to Tacitus and his clever ingenuity. I forgive his ignorance more readily than I forgive the many authors of sacred commentaries, for the fratricide of Cain and for the crimes on account of which the flood was sent upon the men of old. Nevertheless our assertion will stand unshaken: the innocence of life without laws is holier than idleness weighed down by a multitude of laws, or obedience extorted by force and threats.

units.la: LIII.
units.tr: LIII.

units.la: Primum concordiæ civilis turbamentum ambitio.
units.tr: The first disturbance of civil concord is ambition.

units.la: Quoad sua cuique fatis placent, aut ultra civilem vicinorum æmulationem non proceditur, statumine suo salva Refp. libratur. At ubi magna est civium in eminendi studio inæqualitas, libertas omnium aut quies labefactatur, poffquam exui æqualitas, & pro modestia ac pudore ambitio & vis incedebat: provene- re dominationes. aut dominatione deterior belli civi-lis fluctuatio, vel inter dominum ac libertatem nutans incertitudo. Unus aliquis corruptis reip. moribus prorumpat, imperandi cupidinem palàm gerat: non defuturi sunt, qui servitium suum dominationis in re-liquos cives pignus dent; & utriusque conditionis medii esse malint, quam optimo jure liberi agere. Ergo civitatis prima perturbatio, æqualitatis depofi-tio. Quod fi etiamnum peregrina auribus hæc positio videatur; à civitate in orbem universum aciem mentis circumferat. Primam angelorum labem, primam humani generis, superbiam, cumque ea primam solutæ pacis luem deprehendet.
units.tr: As long as each man is content with his own lot, or rivalry between neighbours does not go beyond civil bounds, the commonwealth is kept in balance and its state is safe. But when citizens differ greatly in their eagerness to rise, the liberty or quiet of all is shaken. Once equality was stripped away, and ambition and violence advanced in place of modesty and shame, dominations arose. Worse than domination comes the wavering of civil war, or an uncertainty swaying between a master and liberty. Let some one man, with the morals of the commonwealth corrupted, break forth and openly show his desire to rule. There will not be lacking those who would pledge their servitude as a guarantee of his domination over the remaining citizens, and who would rather belong to either middle condition than live free by the best right. Therefore the first disturbance of the state is the loss of equality. But if this statement still seems strange to the ear, let the mind turn its gaze from the state to the whole world. There it will discover the first fall of the angels, the first pride of the human race, and with it the first plague of dissolved peace.

units.la: LIV.
units.tr: LIV.

units.la: Optimus interpres legum, Simplicitas.
units.tr: Simplicity, the best interpreter of laws.

units.la: Pro populo enim ad obsequentiam flectendo, & in libertate à populo feruntur. Hæ[?] primò rudibus homi-num animis simplices erant, maximèque fama celebravit Cretenfium, quas[?] Minos: Spartanorum, quas LycurLycurgus; ac mox Atheniensibus quasitiores jam & plures Solon perscripsit. Non sola simplicitatis legum causa, ruditas hominum; sed legislatorum integritas, quæ ubi præter civium salutem, honestatem, tranquil-litatem nihil quaerunt: satis exactæ creduntur: de sub-tilitate minus laborandum. Hoc Lycurgus apud Spartanos, hoc Minos, antiquissimi legumlatores, hoc post Draconem mitior Solon spectavit. Ubi vero leges in captiones, æqualitas in dominationem transierunt; mirum non est, si populus nullas nisi à se latas leges perferre potuit. Qua in re quanquam, ut ait apud Sallustium Philippus, quæ pessimi & stultissimi decre-vere, ea bonis & sapientibus facienda sunt: libertati tamen publicæ, & omnium securitati, sic melius consulitur. Ab hac populi in ferendis legibus auctoritate lex apud Platonem definitur: [illegible, ~20 letters] ἐς τινα χρόνον ἀφωρισμένον[?]; civile multitudinis decretum, nullo spatio temporis definitum. In qua definitione posteriora verba, legis à psephismate distinguendæ causa adduntur. Eidem enim Platoni ψήφισμα μὲν ἐστὶ [illegible, ~10 letters] ἐς τινα χρόνον ἀφωρισμένον, ci-vile decretum, in tempus aliquod definitum. Unde apparet, non idem per omnia esse psephisma Atheniensium, quod apud Romanos plebiscitum.
units.tr: For laws are proposed to the people to bend them to obedience, and they are carried by the people in freedom. At first these laws were simple, because of the rough minds of men. The fame of the laws of the Cretans, given by Minos, and of the Spartans, given by Lycurgus, was most widely celebrated; and soon afterwards Solon wrote out laws for the Athenians which were now more subtle and more numerous. The simplicity of laws is due not only to the rudeness of men, but also to the integrity of the lawgivers. When they seek nothing beyond the safety, honesty and tranquillity of the citizens, their laws are believed to be sufficiently exact, and there is less need to labour over subtlety. Lycurgus among the Spartans, Minos, the most ancient of lawgivers, and Solon, milder than Draco, after him, kept this aim in view. But when laws passed into quibbling and equality into domination, it is no wonder that the people could bear no laws but those they had proposed themselves. In this matter, although, as Philip says in Sallust, "the things decreed by the worst and most foolish are to be done by the good and wise," public liberty and the security of all are better served in this way. Plato defines law by this authority of the people in enacting laws: [illegible] for a certain fixed time [ἐς τινα χρόνον ἀφωρισμένον]; a civil decree of the multitude, not limited by any span of time. In this definition the latter words are added to distinguish law from a psephisma. For in the same Plato a psephisma is [illegible] for a certain fixed time, a civil decree defined for some period. Hence it appears that the psephisma of the Athenians is not the same in every respect as the plebiscitum among the Romans.

units.la: LV.
units.tr: LV.

units.la: Libertati magis quàm regno leges conveniunt.
units.tr: Laws suit liberty more than kingship.

units.la: Vinculo aliquo ad continendam à dissolutione rem̃ opus est: aut unius arbitrio, aut legum conventione. Optima quin etiam regni forma est, ubi legum præscripto imperatur. Nam quod à Tacito ponitur, nobis Romulus, ut libitum, imperitaverat, nec appro-bationis ab eo indicium ponitur; & contrarium à Dio-nysio ac Livio, Romulum leges rogatu populi tulisse, asseritur. Nihilominus quia idem Livius ejectis regibus imperia legum potentiora quam hominum, libro 2, nuncupat; & quia Aristotelis non uno in loco hæc sententia jactatur; dictum nostrum consensu stabilinus, libertati[?] magis quam regno supremam legum autoritatem convenire.
units.tr: Some bond is needed to keep the commonwealth from dissolving, either the will of one man or an agreement of laws. Indeed the best form even of kingship is that in which rule is exercised by the prescription of laws. For what Tacitus states, "Romulus had ruled us as he pleased," is no sign of his approval, and the opposite is asserted by Dionysius and Livy, that Romulus enacted laws at the request of the people. Nevertheless, since the same Livy, in book 2, calls the authority of laws more powerful than that of men after the kings were expelled, and since this opinion is repeated by Aristotle in more than one place, let us establish our statement by consensus: the supreme authority of laws is more fitting for liberty than for kingship.

units.la: LVI.
units.tr: LVI.

units.la: Reges obtemperare legibus, majestatis non derogat.
units.tr: That kings obey the laws does not detract from majesty.

units.la: Quicquid de Romulo, quicquid de exterarum na-tionum regibus neges aut adstruas: non levis momen-ti sunt hæc verba habenda; præcipuum Servius Tullius sanctor legum fuit, quis etiam reges obtemperarent. Sed quia alio in loco hanc quæstionem excussimus, nunc abrumpendam esse aliis, quibus prævertendum monemur.
units.tr: Whatever you deny or affirm about Romulus, or about the kings of foreign nations, these words must not be regarded as of slight importance. Above all, Servius Tullius was a most devoted keeper of the laws, and kings also submitted to them. But since we have examined this question in another place, it must now be left for others, to whom we are urged to turn.

units.la: LVII.
units.tr: LVII.

units.la: Legis nomine & juris publici con-ventio censetur.
units.tr: The name of law is taken to mean a compact of public right.

units.la: Colligo ex his Taciti verbis: adversum patrum factiones multa populus paravit tuenda libertatis, & firmanda concordia. imo quæ à T. Livio recensentur, leges & senatusconsulta, quæ nec re contemnenda sunt nec pauca numero, plurimum in jure publico vertuntur. In iisdem Platonis νόμων libri, in eadem materie Ariftoteles ipse multus est[?]. Quam rem tractatu de Republica curatius diduxi.
units.tr: I gather this from the words of Tacitus: against the factions of the fathers, the people secured many means to protect liberty and to strengthen concord. Indeed the laws and senatorial decrees that T. Livy recounts, which are neither trivial in substance nor few in number, for the most part concern public right. Plato's books of Laws [νόμων] deal with the same matters, and Aristotle himself is full of them on the same subject. I have set this out more fully in my treatise on the Commonwealth.

units.la: LVIII.
units.tr: LVIII.

units.la: Antiquissimæ quæque leges tutif-simæ.
units.tr: The most ancient laws are the safest.

units.la: Non quod à tempore robur accipiant, sed quia mutatio legum aut accumulatio raro non fit indete-rius[?]. creatis decemviris, & accitis quæ usquam egre-gia, composita duodecim tabulæ, finis æquijuris. Causa æquitatis duodecim tabularum prima in fine legum & populi flagitatione, ut summi cum infimis pari jure exæquarentur. Altera in optimarum legum conqui-sitione, & spatii ac sumptus ad eam rem largitione. Tertia in omnium finiendi populi & patrum certamini-bus cupiditate. Quarta in decemvirorum æquabilitate. Quinta in publica ad examinandum promulgatione, Nam quę secutæ sunt leges, quanta festinatione, quanto partium studio, depravatione, æmulatione latæ sint, gnaris Romanæ antiquitatis inculcare piget.
units.tr: Not because they gain strength from time, but because a change or an accumulation of laws is rarely not for the worse. Decemvirs were created and the most excellent laws from wherever they could be found were brought in, and the Twelve Tables were composed, the end of equal right. The first cause of fairness in the Twelve Tables was the people's demand at the end of the laws, that the highest should be made equal in right with the lowest. The second was the search for the best laws, and the grant of time and expense for that purpose. The third was the desire to end the strife between the people and the fathers in all disputes. The fourth was the even-handedness of the decemvirs. The fifth was the public promulgation of the laws for examination. As for the laws that followed, with what haste, what partisan zeal, what corruption and rivalry they were passed, it is a shame to recount to those who know Roman antiquity.

units.la: LIX. Morbus judiciarius è Rep. tollen-dus.
units.tr: LIX. The judicial disease must be removed from the Commonwealth.

units.la: Laboratur hic acrimonia legum & calumnia. de qua supra: utque an ehac flagitius[?], ita tunc legibus la-borabatur. laboratur & legum multitudine, corrupti a Rep plurima leges. laboratur corrigendi feve-ritate, morum in becillitati[?] non accommodata. graviora remedia quàm dilecta[?] erant. Laboratur varietate, continuadictione, inconstantia legum. suarumque legum autor idem ac subverfor. Laboratur legum perplexitate, multisque aliis, quae hic commemorare nihil attinet, vitiis. Saepe non in legibus, verum in legum in-sano usu proterve laboratur. Cum judices, causidicos, cives, nescio quae dulcedo causas dijudicandi, agendi, litigandi, ceu fori quaedam tabes invasit. Quo vitio supra modum Athenienses insaniisse, ab hostibus exagitandis in fe togata militia conversos, Ariftopha-nes, poëta in Comoedia Satyricus, tum alibi tum maxime in Vespis commonstrat. Senem, fi&o nomine Philodeonem, a judicandi assiduitate ad otium domesticum traducere, filius Bdelydeon conatur. Ille nullis delitiis postponendum judicandi regnum, ut arbitratur, exfistimat. Hic nihil forensi situ esse laboriosius, contemptius, generoso animo indignius, contendit. Postremo ita inter utrumque convenit, ut domi judex ancillarum & canum domesticorum lites dirimat. Quae quamvis ridicula, vitae judiciariae phrenesin, nullam nisi in judiciis vitae jucunditatem agnoscentem, non male exprimunt. Causidicorum, praeter lucri avidi-tatem, strepitus forensis epulisque jucundior oblectatio ab eodem poeta in Pluto notatur. apud quem magni-fice συκοφάντ[?] jactat:
units.tr: Here the state suffers from the sharpness of its laws and from chicanery, of which I spoke above: and just as in that case the shameful practices, so then the state was suffering from its laws. It suffers also from the multitude of laws, very many laws having been corrupted by the Commonwealth. It suffers from a severity of correction ill suited to the weakness of morals: the remedies were harsher than the diseases. It suffers from the variety, contradiction and inconstancy of its laws, and the same man was both the author and the destroyer of his own laws. It suffers from the obscurity of its laws and from many other faults, which it is pointless to recount here. Often the trouble lies not in the laws themselves but in the insane and wanton use of them. Judges, advocates and citizens alike were seized, as by some sickness of the forum, with a certain sweet passion for judging, pleading and litigating. Aristophanes, the satirical poet, shows in his comedies, and above all in the Wasps, how far the Athenians had gone mad with this vice, so that they turned from the military service of the citizen-soldier to harassing their enemies in court. His son Bdelycleon tries to draw the old man, whose fictitious name is Philocleon, from his constant judging to domestic leisure. The old man thinks the rule of judging is to be preferred to every pleasure. The son argues that nothing is more laborious, more contemptible, or more unworthy of a noble spirit than the squalor of the courts. In the end they came to this agreement: at home the old man should settle the quarrels of the maidservants and the household dogs. Although these scenes are ridiculous, they express well the frenzy of a judicial life, which recognises no pleasure except in the courts. The same poet, in the Plutus, censures the advocates for a delight in the noise of the forum and in feasting, beyond their greed for gain. There the sycophant magnificently boasts:

units.la: Τῶν τῆς πόλεως ἐμὲ ἐπιμελητὴς ἀπαγγέλλοντες[?] Καὶ τῶν ἰδίων πάντων. i. e.[?]
units.tr: Announcing that I am the guardian of the city's affairs and of all my own affairs. [Τῶν τῆς πόλεως ἐμὲ ἐπιμελητὴς ἀπαγγέλλοντες Καὶ τῶν ἰδίων πάντων.] That is:

units.la: Urbana res & cuncta me domestica Tutore perstat.
units.tr: Public affairs and all my domestic concerns persist under my guardianship.

units.la: neque se omni opulentia vel Batti Silphio hanc vitam permutare velle testatur. Qua tempestate Sarmatica Warsaviae aulam, cognoscendi linguam & mores Polonorum causa, terebam; causidicorum nonnemo mihi monstrabatur senio fermè decrepitus, qui à rege Uladislao, quasi commiserato fortem ejus, interrogatus: ecquando se ab aula ad otium conferat, nihil aliud, nisi se non posse, respondessat. Alius in Gallia, judiciorum valetudinario magis afflicta, multitudine causarum susceptarum, ut videbatur, oneratus, cum rex eum ob senectutem necessitate patrocinandi & accusandi, praemio laborum non adempto, exolvisset; supplex, ut saltem decem reorum causae, obleftamentur futurae, concederentur, rogavit. Sordibus hominis rex commotus, gratiae an poenae loco, omnes eum susceptas retinere jussit. Civium temere, & quasi consuetudine, litigantium eadem Gallia, & regio inprimis Pictonum, gymnasium est. nec non in Anglia, extremis pacifici Caroli temporibus, querelas honestorum virorum percepi, multas honestas domos judiciorum licentia subverti; gravioremque bello pacem felici alias gentium incumbere. Quam misera sub Tiberio alia pace Roma fuerit, quam se cives Romani mutua traditione, accusatione, laesae majestatis infimulatione prostraverint, sequentibus Tacitilibris docebitur.
units.tr: He declares that he would not exchange this life for all the wealth of the world, or even for the silphium of Battus. At the time when I was spending time at the court in Warsaw, in Sarmatia, for the sake of learning the language and customs of the Poles, I was shown one of the advocates, an old man nearly decrepit with age. When King Ladislaus, moved, as it were, by pity for his toil, asked him when he would retire from the court to leisure, he answered only that he could not. Another, in France, which is more afflicted by a sickly state of its courts, was weighed down by a multitude of cases he had taken on, as it seemed. When the king, because of his old age, had released him from the necessity of pleading and prosecuting, without taking away the reward for his labours, he humbly begged that at least ten cases of defendants, which were about to be brought, might be granted to him. The king, moved by the man's squalor, ordered that he keep all the cases he had taken on, as a grace or as a punishment. France, and especially the region of the Poitevins, is a school for citizens who litigate rashly and as a matter of habit. Likewise in England, in the last years of the peaceable Charles, I heard complaints from honourable men that many honourable households were overthrown by the licence of the courts, and that a peace, otherwise happy for the nations, weighed more heavily than war. How wretched Rome was under Tiberius, in another kind of peace, and how the Roman citizens ruined one another by mutual betrayal, accusation and the charge of treason, will be taught by the following books of Tacitus.

units.la: LX.
units.tr: LX.

units.la: Anarchia pestis civitati nocentior.
units.tr: Anarchy is a more harmful plague for a state.

units.la: Judiciorum excessus phrenesi, haec furori similli-ma. quae in civilem discordiam, aut grassandi per sce-lera licentiam, collapsa, remp. exagitat. Exin continua per viginti annos discordia: non mos, non jus, deterri-ma quaeque impune: ac multa honesta exitio fuere[?]. Tempus illud, quod inter Julii Caesaris caedem & Au-gusti secuti securam potentiam intercessit, fine dubio notat. quo non aliud magis Romanam civitatem fortunis, bonis moribus, civibus exhausit. Anarchiæ, quod ad flagitiorum conniventiam, nimium laxata imperantis indulgentia proximè accedit. Notum est illud non nemini s de Nervæ soluto imperio judicium: tolerabi- liorem esse principem, sub quo nihil, quam sub quo omnia liceant. nec dubitatur, quin fi diutius Nerva vi- xiffet, pejus Domitiano remp. afflictur us fuisset, quàm temperata imperandi facilitate Trajanus conservavit.
units.tr: An excess of judicial proceedings is very like a frenzy, which, falling into civil discord or a licence to rage through crimes, tears the Commonwealth apart. Thence came twenty years of continual discord: no custom, no law, and all the worst things went unpunished, and many honourable men perished. That period which intervened between the murder of Julius Caesar and the secure power that followed under Augustus certainly marks this. Nothing else drained the Roman state more of its fortunes, good morals and citizens. Anarchy is closest to that connivance at crimes which comes from an overly lax indulgence of the ruler. It is well known that the judgement of a certain man on the loosened rule of Nerva was that the prince under whom nothing is allowed is more tolerable than the one under whom everything is. And there is no doubt that if Nerva had lived longer, he would have afflicted the state worse than Domitian did, whereas Trajan preserved it by a moderate ease in ruling.

units.la: LXI.
units.tr: LXI.

units.la: Leges annariæ in libera rep. non te- mere solvantur.
units.tr: Annual laws in a free commonwealth should not be lightly repealed.

units.la: Non temere inquam: quia ingenium annos præ- currens non est civilis necessitatis vinculo semper a- stringendum. In regno autem & adducto unius prin- cipatu omnia ad eum morem velle reformare, tem- porum commutatorum ignorantis est. Tiberius Ne- renem è liberis Germanici jam ingressum juventam, commendavit patribus, utque munere capessendi vi- ginti viratus fuveretur, & quinquennio maturius quam per leges Quæsituram peteret, non fine irrisu au- dientium postulavit. quasi vero non alia quàm per quæsturam via extollere, & proximo etiam sibi loco, quem vellet, collocare Augusti exemplo liceret. Sic libertati jam oppressæ, jam conclamatæ, illudeba- tur. Veteris Reip. mores prætendebantur; novæ dominationis facta exercebantur.
units.tr: I say "not lightly," because a talent that outruns its years is not always to be bound by the chains of civil necessity. But in a kingdom, and where sole rule has been established, to wish to remodel everything after that old custom belongs to someone who does not understand how times have changed. Tiberius recommended Nero, one of Germanicus's sons, who had now entered young manhood, to the senators, and asked, not without the laughter of his hearers, that he be excused from the office of the twenty-men-commission and be allowed to seek the quaestorship five years earlier than the laws permitted. As if there were no other way to raise him to honour and to place him in whatever position he wished, the next one to himself, as Augustus had done! In this way liberty, already crushed and already proclaimed dead, was mocked. The customs of the old commonwealth were held up as a pretence, while the deeds of a new domination were carried out.

units.la: LXII.
units.tr: LXII.

units.la: Celsior honorum gradibus potentia.
units.tr: Power raised higher by the steps of honours.

units.la: Quanto ambitu Romani senatoriam dignitatem, & ex ea amplissimos honores petierint, Historiæ veteris monumenta perhibeant. Fervorem eum vanitatis in libera republica, nisi quis Epicuræam securitatem præ publicarum rerum strepitu amaverit, aut Stoica animi altitudine suo se regno metiatur, non arguo. Uno vero rerum potito, quid præter titulorum tu- fumus.
units.tr: Ancient history records how eagerly the Romans sought senatorial rank and, through it, the highest honours. I do not condemn that fervour for vanity in a free commonwealth, unless someone prefers Epicurean security to the noise of public affairs, or measures himself by Stoic loftiness of spirit. But once one man has gained control of affairs, it is clear that the praetorships and consulships, with their burdens of empty expense, bring nothing beyond the smoke of titles to a mind capable of greatness.

units.la: thumus aut inanium sumptuum oneră, praeturæ & cōs: fulatūs tulerint, capaci verĕ, celsitudinis animo nos apparet. Sapienter itaque in eo rerum statu egerunt, qui si privatæ obscuritatis tædeat, gratia apud princi- pem, & aut consili ministerio, aut rerum bellicarum promptitudine, pœtentiam à principe secusidam, nec minorem in vulgi animis autoritatem, quæsiverunt. Eorum é numero apud Augustum Mæcenas, apud Claudium Pallas & cæteri liberti, apud Tiberium Sal- lustius Crispus fuit, qui quàm prompto ad bono- res capessendos aditu, Macenatem simulatiùs, sine di- snitate senatoria, multos triumphalium consulariumque potentia antè fuit. Quàm five militari in re, five aulicâ, potentiàm non insolenter ferre, nec famam extorque- re magis quàm véniéntem amplexari, secundæ mode- stationis est. Militaris gloriæ capacem, non ja&abun- dum, pro exemplari habemus Julium Agricolam. Nec Agricola prosperitate rerum in vanitatem usus expeditionem aut vitoriam vocabat; vitios continuis- fe ne laureatu quidem gerta prosecutus est, sed ipsa dif- simulatione fama famam auxit, astissantibus quantâ futuri spetâm magna tacuisset. Idem Britannia paca- ta redux, ut militare nomen, grave inter otiosos, aliis virtutibus temperaret, tranquillitatem atque otium auxit, cultu modicus, sermone facilis, uno aut altero amicorum comitatu: adeo ut plerique, quibus ma- gnos viros per ambitionem æstimare mos est, viso aspeāoque Agricola quærerent famam, pauci inter- pretarentur. T.in Vita Agricolæ. Moderationis in au- senaliquid clarius Mæcenate, quem modò nomina- vimus, exemplar. Ei tantum Augustus detulerat, ut ad senatum, aut quosvis alios, literas non mitteret, nif à Mæcenate & Agrippa prius legendas. Dio lib. 5t: ab eo régende reip. præcepta acceperat. lib.52. Ei si occultissimis rebus, ut Agrippa aut vita tollendo aut ad consulatum provehendo, aurem prebuerat. lib.5 4. ab eo, ut abacerbo patruo admonitiones graviores absque exacerbatione admiserat, ei urbis custodiam primo commiserat; neminem tamen vel arrogantia morum[?] offendit, vel acerbitate in odium sui provocavit. [illegible, ~40 letters]. i. e. Maximum vero virtutis Mæcenatis indicium fuit, quod & Augusto, cujus tamen cupiditatibus restitit, familiaris fuit, & omnibus aliis acceptus. cumque plurimum apud eum posset, adeo ut multis honores & magistratus conferret, animo tamen nihil elatus, in ordine equestri vitam exegit. idem Dio, lib. 55.
units.tr: Those who acted in that situation acted wisely. Weary of private obscurity, they sought favour with the prince, either through service in counsel or through readiness in war, and they won a power second only to the prince's and no less authority in the minds of the crowd. Among these, under Augustus there was Maecenas, under Claudius Pallas and the other freedmen, and under Tiberius Sallustius Crispus. Crispus, with how ready an access he gained to honours, far surpassed in influence many men of triumphal and consular rank, though he did so in a feigned way, without senatorial dignity, as Maecenas did. To bear power without arrogance, whether in military or in courtly affairs, and to embrace fame as it comes rather than to wrest it, is the mark of a modest and well-ordered mind. We have Julius Agricola as the model of one capable of military glory without boasting. Agricola, using his successes for no vanity, did not call his expedition or his victory by grand names. He did not even make a show of his continual victories with a laurelled triumphal display, but his very concealment increased his fame, and those who were present thought how much great things he would have left unsaid. The same Agricola, returning from a pacified Britain, tempered his military reputation, which weighs heavily on idle men, with other virtues. He increased his tranquillity and leisure, being modest in dress, easy in speech, and attended by only one or two friends. So much so that most people, who are accustomed to judge great men by their ambition, looked on Agricola and sought his fame, and few understood it. Tacitus, in the Life of Agricola. Scarcely anything is a clearer example of moderation in a private man than Maecenas, whom we have just named. Augustus had granted him so much that he sent no letters to the senate or to anyone else before they had first been read by Maecenas and Agrippa. Dio, book 51. He had received from him precepts for governing the commonwealth. Book 52. Maecenas lent an ear to Augustus in his most secret affairs, as he did to Agrippa concerning either removing or advancing him to the consulship. Book 54. He had admitted from him more severe admonitions, without exasperating his harsh uncle. Augustus had first entrusted him with the guardianship of the city, yet he offended no one by arrogance of manner, nor provoked hatred against himself by harshness. [illegible, ~40 letters]. That is, the greatest proof of Maecenas' virtue was that he was a friend of Augustus, though he resisted his desires, and was welcome to everyone else. And although he could do very much with him, so that he conferred many honours and magistracies on many men, he lived in the equestrian order, not elated in spirit at all. The same Dio, book 55.

units.la: LXIII.
units.tr: LXIII.

units.la: Aulicæ servitutis autoramentum splendor.
units.tr: Splendour, the pledge of courtly servitude.

units.la: Non sunt ad gustum dominantium Catones, non prisca gravitate Thrasæ ac Helvidii. Etiam Senecæ odium Neronis conciliavit abjecta vitæ mollities, majusque opum quam luxuriæ studium. Etiam Socrati, quanquam fortuna tenui, vultus gravitas & mollioris vitæ contemptus, apud triginta tyrannos, exitio fuit. Minus enim ut potentiæ avidos, negligentes famæ suæ viros, domini rerum suspiciunt, & servitutis æternæ pignus habent servientem luxui animum. Hac forte ratione Crispus, diversa a veterum instituto, per cultum & munditias: copiaque & affluentia, luxu proprio mollitiem tamen vestitu magis & epulis, quam animo voluptatibus fracto gerere, magis ad aulicam rationem accedit. Sibi enim & dominantibus inutiles vivunt, qui blandimentis in animum admissis, Circæa potione enervantur. Suberat tamen vigor animi, ingentibus negotiis par: eo acrior, quo somnum & inertiam magis ostentabat. Ex hoc luxuriæ & vigoris temperamento, ad agendum magis, quoties res agilem animum poscebat, quam ostentandum nato, incolumi Mæcenate proximus, mox præcipuus cui secreta imperatorum inniterentur. Crispo non dissimilis C. Petronius, luxu superior, exitu etiam vitæ infausior. Huic dies perfomnum, nox officiis & obleCtamentis vitæ transigebatur. Vltque alios industria, ita hunc ignavia ad famam protulerat, &c. Proconsul tamen Bithyniæ, & mox consul, vigentem fe ac parem negotiis ostendit: dein revolutus ad vitia, seu vitiorum imitationem. T.xvi. Annal. Quartum, fi placet, in hoc censu Othonem adjungamus: cætera Mæcenati & Crispo parem, gloriæ moderatione disparem. Otho puericiam incuriosè, adolescentiam petulanter egerat, gratis Neroni æmulatione luxus. i. Histor. At quam magnanima hujus oratio: Mortem omnibus ex natura æqualem, oblivione apud posteros vel gloria diftin-gui. Adeo ut epicrifin adjicere non veteatur Cornelius: Non erat Othonis mollis & corpori similis animus. Ut tamen alii virtutes, temporum injuria, ita hic vitia, cupidine imperii, dissimulando texit. Otho interim, contra spem omnium, non deliciis, neque desidia torpere, fcere. dilata voluptates, dissimulata luxuria, & cuncta ad decorem imperii composita. Eoque plus formidinis afferebant falsa virtutes, & vitia reditura. ibid. Nequior his omnibus Tigellinus, fœda pueritia, impudica senecta [?]; præfecturam vigilum & prætorii, alia præmia virtutum, quia velocius erat vitiis adeptus; crudelitatem mox, deinde avaritiam, & virilia scelera exercuit: corrupto ad omne facinus Nerone, quædam ignaro ausus. ibid. Paucioribus [?] de eodem, xiv. Annal. Validior Tigellinus in animo principis, ex intimis libi-dinibus affumptus, Altioris animi viros, & exitus ob scelera magis tragici, Sejanum apud Tiberium, Plautianum in aula Severi, in commodiorem differendi occasionem reservo: Illud de somni ac inertiæ simulatione non prætereundum, interdum locum habere id, quod Creonti Oedipus objicit: Certissima est regnare cupienti via,
units.tr: Cato-like severity is not to the taste of masters, nor the ancient gravity of Thrasea and Helvidius. The soft living that had been despised even by Seneca won him Nero's hatred, and a greater zeal for wealth than for luxury. Socrates too, though of slender fortune, was done to death by the Thirty Tyrants because of the seriousness of his face and his contempt for a softer life. For masters of affairs regard as less dangerous men who are greedy for power, careless of their reputation, and who keep a spirit given over to luxury as a pledge of endless servitude. Perhaps for this reason Crispus, differing from the custom of the ancients, through refinement and neatness, and abundance and affluence, in his own luxury, nevertheless carried his softness more in dress and feasts than in a spirit broken by pleasures, and so came closer to the courtly way. For those who, having admitted flattery into their minds, are enervated by a Circean draught, live uselessly both for themselves and for their masters. Yet vigour of spirit lay beneath, equal to great affairs; it was all the keener, the more he displayed sleep and sloth. From this blend of luxury and vigour, he was born more for acting, whenever affairs demanded an agile mind, than for display, close to Maecenas while he was safe, and soon the chief man on whom the emperors' secrets rested. Not unlike Crispus was C. Petronius, superior in luxury and more unfortunate in the end of his life. For him the day was spent in sleep, and the night in duties and the pleasures of life. And just as industry advanced others, so idleness advanced him to fame, etc. Yet as proconsul of Bithynia, and afterwards consul, he showed himself vigorous and equal to affairs; then he turned back to vices, or to the imitation of vices. Tacitus, Annals 16. If you like, let us add Otho as a fourth in this rank: in other respects he was equal to Maecenas and Crispus, but unequal in moderation of glory. Otho had spent his boyhood carelessly and his youth wantonly, emulating Nero's luxury in a bid for favour. Tacitus, Histories 1. Yet how magnanimous his speech is: that death is equal for all by nature, and is distinguished only by oblivion or glory among posterity. So much so that Cornelius does not hesitate to add his judgement: The spirit of Otho was not soft and like his body. Yet as the injustice of the times concealed other virtues, so by dissimulation he hid his vices, out of desire for power. Meanwhile Otho, contrary to everyone's expectation, did not grow torpid with delights or idleness. He postponed pleasures, concealed his luxury, and arranged everything to the dignity of empire. And for that reason false virtues caused more fear, and vices that would return. Ibid. More wicked than all these was Tigellinus, foul in boyhood and shameless in old age. He obtained the prefecture of the watch and of the praetorian guard, and other rewards of virtue, because he had reached them more quickly by vices. Then he practised cruelty, and afterwards avarice and manly crimes, Nero being corrupted to every wickedness and some things being done without his knowledge. Ibid. Tacitus, Annals 14, says a little more about the same man. Tigellinus, taken up from the innermost lusts, was more powerful in the mind of the prince. I reserve for a more convenient occasion men of loftier spirit, and those whose ends were more tragic because of their crimes: Sejanus with Tiberius, and Plautianus in the court of Severus. This must not be passed over: the pretence of sleep and inertia sometimes has a place, as Oedipus objects to Creon: The most certain way for one who desires to reign,

units.la: Laudare modica, & ocium ac somnum sequi,
units.tr: is to praise moderation, and to pursue leisure and sleep,

units.la: Ab inquieto sæpe simulatur quies.
units.tr: Often quiet is feigned by the restless man.

units.la: Seneca Oedipo. Act. 3.
units.tr: Seneca, Oedipus, Act 3.

units.la: LXIV.
units.tr: LXIV.

units.la: Prodigium in aulâ perpetua principis amicitia.
units.tr: A marvel in the court: a prince's lasting friendship.

units.la: Ne congeram exempla mutati in apertum odium favoris: multi qui principis intimi creduntur, occulto ejus odio aut per neglectum contemptu pulsantur. Crispus ille secretorum omnium Tiberii unice participeps, corculum illud imperatoris, cui arcana domus inniterentur, state provecta speciem magis in amicitia principis, quàm vim tenuit. Graviori Plancina lapsu, pro qua cum pudore & flagitio Tiberius disseruerat, quam ut superstites liberi tuerentur urgendo impulerat, Agrippina vivis erepta, trucidari jubebatur. quia, ut inquit Tacitus, ubi odium & gratia desiere, jus valuit, lib.v. Annal. ut Dio lib.58, viva Agrippina occidere eam, ne hæc solatium è morte ejus caperet, noluit.
units.tr: I will not pile up examples of favour turned into open hatred. Many who are thought to be the prince's closest intimates are in fact struck down by his secret hatred, or by neglect that amounts to contempt. That Crispus, the one man who shared all of Tiberius's secrets, the darling of the emperor on whom the household's hidden affairs rested, kept the appearance of the prince's friendship for longer than its power. Plancina fell more heavily. Tiberius had argued for her, with shame and disgrace, and had pressed the case only so far as to spare her surviving children. Agrippina was taken from the living and ordered to be put to death. As Tacitus says, when hatred and favour have ceased, the law prevails (Annals 5). As Dio says (book 58), Tiberius would not have her killed while she was alive, lest she gain some comfort from her death.

units.la: Sed hæc de Tiberio minus admirationis habent, versipelle homine, nec iram nec amorem in fronte gerente: qui φύσει ἰδιώτης ἐκ ... peculiaris ingenii homo, neque præ se ferebat quæ cuperet, & sermone ab animi sui sententia diversissimo utebatur, negando quæcunque desiderarét, annuendo iis quæ odio haberet. irâtum se, cum minimè succensèret, æquo animo esse, cum maximè indignari etur, præ se ferebat. ut idem Dio, principio libri 57. Cujusmodi homini quis aut amicus ex animi sententia esse posset, aut de amicitia ejus ad horæ momentum securus degere? Magis de Augusto quod admirere audias. idque & Macenati accideràt. nec Mæcenati tantum, sed & Agrippæ, victoriarum omnium socio aut autori, quem in gratiam Marcelli in Syriam, honesta relegatione, seposuerat. & Marcellus lo. Augusti & populi delitiis, nec non Drusus, Germaniarum terrori, ob nimis apertum populi in eos favorem. & huic ipsi Tiberio: quem genere adoptionis filium, collegam imperii, confortem tribunitiae potestatis po-testatis, non ad extremum dilexit. Unde ea potentia in aula, unde gratiae mutatio? Invenerit aliquid Au-gustus offensione in Tiberio dignum, tetricam nimirum morum arrogantiam: offenderit cum Agrippae cum Marcello simultas: cum Graecorum proverbio, μία λόγῳ δύο ἐξ ἰσότητος [?] Non tulerit civilia Marcelli & Drusi ingenia, populique in utrumque ocu-los conversos. Causam mobilis potentiae generalio-rem, & omnibus ubique adaptandam, Cornelius ex-primit: Fato potentia raro sempiternae. nam quae ab opum distributione adjunguntur, an fatis capit, autem illos cum omnia tribuerunt, aut hos, cum jam nihil re-liquum est quod cupiant, nimis pro rerum amplitudine ne sunt angustae. Alios aetas, & cum aetate mores im-mutant: alios irrepentium adulatorum susurratio: alios facti alicujus occulta exprobratio. sic quia Te-rentiam Maecenatis uxorem Augustus adulterio co-gnovit, eamque rem aegre Maecenas tulit, multum de gratia imminutum, quia Poppaeam solus ductare Ne-ro desideravit, Orbonem ab aula removit. Haec in praecepta ac in ordinem cogere idem effet, ac fi quis ipsas hominum cupiditates, modi ac spatii refcias, & mobiles omnium voluntates, lege & modo circum-feribat.
units.tr: But these things are less astonishing in Tiberius, a shifty man who showed neither anger nor affection on his face. He was by nature a private man of an odd disposition, who never showed what he wanted, and who used speech utterly at odds with his inner thoughts, denying whatever he desired and assenting to whatever he hated. He made a show of being calm when he was not at all angry, and of being indignant when he was most at ease, as Dio says again at the start of book 57. Who could be a true friend to such a man, or live at ease about his friendship for even a single hour? You may hear of something more to be wondered at in Augustus. The same thing happened to Maecenas. It happened not only to Maecenas but also to Agrippa, the partner and author of all his victories, whom Augustus sent away to Syria under the pretext of an honourable exile, to placate Marcellus. Marcellus, the delight of Augustus and the people, fell out of favour, and so did Drusus, the terror of the Germans, because of the people's too open goodwill towards them. The same happened to Tiberius himself, whom Augustus loved by adoption as a son, made his colleague in empire, and sharer of the tribunician power, and loved to the very end. Whence this power at court, and whence the change of favour? Augustus may have found something in Tiberius that deserved offence, namely his gloomy arrogance of manner. He may have been offended by the rivalry of Agrippa and Marcellus, and, as the Greek proverb has it, one word, two from equality [?]. He may not have tolerated the civic gifts of Marcellus and Drusus, and the people's eyes turned upon both of them. Cornelius states the general cause of this fickle power, one that fits everyone everywhere: power rarely lasts for ever by fate. For those things that come with the distribution of wealth are not so narrow that they fail to match the greatness of the matter, whether fate takes them away, or whether the princes give everything to these men, or the men have nothing left that they might desire. Some men are changed by age, and with age their manners change. Others are changed by the whispering of flatterers who creep in, and others by the secret reproach of some deed. So when Augustus discovered that Terentia, Maecenas's wife, had committed adultery, and Maecenas took this hard, his favour was much diminished. Nero, who wished to have Poppaea to himself alone, removed Orbo from the court. To try to bring these matters under precepts and rules would be the same as if someone were to mark out, by law and measure, the very desires of men, which have no limit or bounds, and the wills of all men, which are changeable.

units.la: In qua cupidinum humanarum infinitate, cautio-num monita finita aut facilia dari non possunt. E mul-tis tamen pauca, in aulicorum usum, delibabo.
units.tr: Given this endless variety of human desires, warnings about caution cannot be given in a finite or easy form. Nevertheless, I will gather a few from many for the use of courtiers.

units.la: 1. Nunquam ita blandienti serenitati credas, ut non in irruentes imbres penulam paratam geras. sic fiet, ut aut depellas pluviam molestiam, aut praevisam aequi animo feras.
units.tr: 1. Never trust a sky so smiling that you do not carry a cloak ready against the rains that are coming on. In this way you will either ward off the troublesome shower, or bear it calmly once foreseen.

units.la: 2. Diffidentis animi indicia abscondas; monitu Euripidis:
units.tr: 2. Hide the signs of a distrustful mind, following the advice of Euripides:

units.la: σωφρονῶ δ' ἀνδρὸς ἀπέλεσεν [?]
units.tr: ...I am prudent, but the man has lost... [?]

units.la: Οὐκ ἔστιν ἄλλο γένος βροτοῖς [?]
units.tr: There is no other race among mortals... [?]

units.la: Nam fronte cauta tecta diffidentia;
units.tr: For diffidence, covered by a cautious brow,

units.la: Immane quanto commodo gentes juvat.
units.tr: is a monstrous thing; how greatly it serves nations' advantage.

units.la: 3. Speciem amicitiæ pro vi amplexus, aut deceptæ hominum opinioni imponęs, aut umbram in corpus aliquando, ubi se mobilis affectus circumegit, commutabis.
units.tr: 3. Either impose a semblance of friendship in place of real embrace, deceiving men's opinion, or, when a shifting feeling has turned you about, change the shadow into the substance.

units.la: 4. Omnia ferendo, & ad omnia gratias agendo, ulteriorem indignationem declinabis.
units.tr: 4. By bearing everything and giving thanks for everything, you will turn aside a greater indignation.

units.la: 5. Ulyssis personam, non Ajacis, induces.
units.tr: 5. Put on the character of Ulysses, not of Ajax.

units.la: 6. Invidiæ te & infidiatrici aulæ subduces. Quod extremum remedium; & sæpe portus quieti exoptatissimus. Notum veterani, in palatio Adriani imperatoris, aulici monumentum: Hic jacet Similis, cujus quidem ætas multorum annorum fuit, caterum septem tantum annos vixit. Nimirum septennium illud, quod extra aulam extrema in senectute fui potestatis degit, vitæ tantum adscripsit. Hic quidem recessus moderato sub principe folicitudinum effugium fuerit. at sub tyrannis crudelitatis famam non erubescentibus, & lux exitio, & tenebræ infragilis futuræ munimenti.
units.tr: 6. Withdraw yourself from envy and from the court that lays snares for you. This is the last remedy, and often the most desired harbour of rest. There is a well-known monument of a veteran courtier in the palace of the emperor Hadrian: Here lies Similis, whose age was of many years, but who lived only seven years. Clearly that seven-year period, which he spent outside the court in the last part of his old age, free of power, was the only part he counted as life. Such a retreat under a moderate prince might be an escape from anxieties. But under tyrants, who do not blush at a reputation for cruelty, the light is for destruction, and the darkness is a shelter that will not be safe.

units.la: LXV. Nec imperantibus aulæ semper stre-pitus perplacet.
units.tr: LXV. Rulers of the court do not always enjoy its constant noise.

units.la: Quem tanto ambitu quæsiverunt principatum, solitudine libenter commutant. Tiberius tædio curarum, & fallaci splendoris vultu, defatigatus, quasi firmanda valetudini, in Campaniam concessit: longam & continuam absentiam paulatim meditans. quo discessu diuturnis Capreārum latebris prælusit. nam quam annectit Tacitus conjecturam, ut amoto patre, Drusus munia consulatus solus impleret, infirmior censetur.
units.tr: Those whom they sought with such great ambition to rule, they willingly exchange for solitude. Tiberius, worn out by the weariness of cares and by the deceptive look of splendour, went off to Campania, as if for the sake of strengthening his health, gradually planning a long and continuous absence. By this departure he previewed the long hiding-place of Capreae. For the conjecture that Tacitus adds, that with the father removed, Drusus alone should discharge the duties of the consulship, is considered rather weak.

units.la: LXVI. Conciliatio decreto favorabilior.
units.tr: LXVI. A conciliatory approach is more favourable than a decree.

units.la: Sontem quidem damnare, quam alienam injuriam condonare, magis officio judicis convenit. At ubi, satisfactione intervenientè, judex temperandis animis idonea disserit, mitigatio sententiam præcedit. Lucius Sulla ætate junior seniori, & prætura functo, Domitio
units.tr: It is more fitting for a judge to condemn a guilty man than to pardon a wrong done to another. But when, with satisfaction intervening, the judge speaks in ways suited to calming minds, mitigation comes before the sentence. Lucius Sulla, younger in years, did not give up his place to the older Domitius Corbulo, who had already held the praetorship.

units.la: Corbuloni, loco non decesserat. Id apud senatum Corbulo questus, ad morem Romanorum & dignitas tem suam provocabat. pro Corbulone atas, patrius mos studia seniorum erant. ad majorum exempla, qui juventutis oblitam reverentiæ proterviam ignominiâ notaverant, animi revocabantur.
units.tr: Corbulo complained of this before the senate and appealed to Roman custom and to his own dignity. On Corbulo's side were his age and the ancestral custom that the young should defer to their elders. Following the examples of our ancestors, who had branded with disgrace the insolence of youth that forgot reverence, minds were called back.

units.la: Improbitas illo fuit admirabilis ævo. Credebant hoc grande nefas, & morte piandum, Si juvenis vetulo non assurrexerit.
units.tr: Wickedness was remarkable in that age. They believed it a great crime, to be expiated by death, if a young man did not rise for an old man.

units.la: Uti Juvenalis.
units.tr: As Juvenal says.

units.la: Contra oratores, ea ætate uberrimi, imprudentiam ætatis, & theatrorum libertatem excusabant. donec Drufus apta temperandas animis disseruit, & fatisfa- ctum Corbuloni per Mamercum. qua animorum di- stractorum compositione plus favoris Drufus invenit, quàm si rigore judicis alteram partem offendisset, apud neutros stabilem fortassis gratiam initurus.
units.tr: On the other side, the orators, very rich in that age, excused the thoughtlessness of youth and the freedom of the theatres. Then Drusus, with apt words, argued for calming minds, and satisfaction was made to Corbulo through Mamercus. By this composing of divided minds Drusus gained more favour than he would have if, by the severity of a judge, he had offended one party, and perhaps he would have won no lasting goodwill from either side.

units.la: LXVII. Temporis serviens conniventia juris rigore salutarior.
units.tr: LXVII. Forbearance that serves the times is more wholesome than the rigour of law.

units.la: Summum jus veterum alii summam injuriam , alii summam crucem appellaverunt. Ejusrei in eodem Corbulone, gravius modo recensito, exemplum habes mus. plurima per Italiam itinera , fraude mancipum & incuria magistratuum , interruptâ & imperviâ clamitando , executioñem ejus rei libens suscepit. Quis non aut mancipum res invertas indignaretur, aut Corbulonis amantem juris animum laudaret? eventus, plurimarum retum censor, arguit. quod bau& perinde publicè usui habitum; quàm exitiosum multis, quorum in pecuniam atque famam damnationibus & bafta favieba.
units.tr: The ancients called the strictest law by different names: some called it the greatest injury, others the greatest cross. You have an example of this in the same Corbulo, in a more serious matter, recounted above. Since many roads throughout Italy were broken and impassable through the fraud of contractors and the negligence of magistrates, he willingly undertook the execution of this business, crying out against it. Who would not be indignant at the contractors, or praise Corbulo's love of justice? The outcome, the censor of most things, proves it: this measure was equally useful to the public, but deadly to many whose fortunes and reputations were being ruined by such condemnations.

units.la: LXVIII. Princeps ne in otio quidem negotium.
units.tr: LXVIII. A prince is not idle even in leisure.

units.la: necin secessu curam reip. deponat. Tiberius Campaniâ in peregrinatione Romano se- natu vigilantior, prævidendo pro urbe & providendo excubaexcubabat. Prævidendo : motam rursum Africam incursu Tacfarinatis docuit. Providendo : diligendum proconsulem, gnarum militia, corpore validum, & bello suffecturum. De priori membro quæritur: Unde id quod Italiam, quod Romam, quod patres latuit, Tiberius resciverit. Astrorum non vulgari notitiæ, & conjectandi futura ac præsentia scientiæ, cujus eum peritissimum fuisse Dio ac Tacitus tradidere, id ad-scripseris.
units.tr: Nor does he lay down the care of the state even in retreat. Tiberius, while travelling in Campania, was more watchful than the Roman senate, keeping guard both by foreseeing and by providing for the city. By foreseeing, he showed that Africa was stirred again by the incursion of Tacfarinas. By providing, he chose a proconsul to be picked out: one skilled in soldiering, strong in body, and equal to the war. On the first point a question arises: how Tiberius learned what escaped Italy, Rome and the senators. You would ascribe it to his not ordinary knowledge of the stars and his skill in conjecturing future and present things, in which Dio and Tacitus report that he was most expert.

units.la: Atqui si Ennium audias:
units.tr: But if you listen to Ennius:

units.la: Non vicanos aruspices, non de circo astrologos, Non Iliacos conjectores, non interpretes somnium. (sc. consulemus.) Non enim sunt ii aut scientia aut arte divini, Sed superstitiosi vates, impudentesque harioli, Aut inertes, aut insani, aut quibus egestas imperat: Qui sibi semitam non sapiunt, alteri monstrat viam, Quibus divitias pollicentur, ab iis drachmam ipsi petunt.
units.tr: "We shall not consult village soothsayers, nor circus astrologers, nor Trojan conjecturers, nor interpreters of dreams. For these are not men of divine knowledge or skill, but superstitious seers and shameless fortune-tellers, either idle, or mad, or those whom want commands; they do not know the path for themselves, yet show the way to another; they promise others riches, and from them they themselves seek a drachma."

units.la: Hæc Ennius Thyeste.
units.tr: Thus Ennius in the Thyestes.

units.la: Quibus consentientia pluribus Cicero de divinatione, Calvinus contra Astrologicam prædictionem. &c.
units.tr: Cicero's book On Divination agrees with many of these points, and so does Calvin against astrological prediction, and so on.

units.la: De Thrasyllo si vera sunt, quæ historiæ memorant: aut conjecturæ, aut casui, aut peculiari afflatui tribueris. Ad Tiberium autem, principem rerum omnium, & principem vigilantia solertem[?], magis quam ad senatum, primos bellorum motus perscriptos[?] fuisse, nihil est admirandum. De providentia, laudo proconsulem gnarum militia, non genere tantum natalium aut favore provectum; laudo corpore validum, qui asperitates Numidici soli pervadat, nec cœli insolentia lætatur; laudo bello sufficiturum, nec ante profligatum hostem copias in amoeniora Africæ loca abducturum, aut triumphi honores ante confectum bellum petiturum, quia in re sæpe a Romanis erratum.
units.tr: As for Thrasyllus: if the things history reports about him are true, they must be attributed either to conjecture, to chance, or to some peculiar inspiration. That the first movements of war were reported to Tiberius, the prince of all things and most vigilant, rather than to the senate, is nothing to wonder at. As for foresight, I commend a proconsul skilled in soldiering, promoted not merely by birth or favour; I commend one strong in body, who can cross the rough places of the Numidian land and is not unsettled by the harshness of the climate; I commend one who will be equal to the war, and who will not lead his forces into the pleasanter parts of Africa before the enemy is crushed, or seek triumphal honours before the war is finished, since the Romans have often erred in this matter.

units.la: LXIX.
units.tr: LXIX.

units.la: Fortuna opes hominum, non ingenium mutat.
units.tr: Fortune changes men's wealth, not their character.

units.la: Quarenemini bono paupertas, non sua culpa com-tracta, exprobranda est. Bene igitur, cum Sex. Pompe-jus M. Lepidum secordem, inopem, & majoribus suis dedecorum clamaret; senatus mitem magis quam ignavum, paternas ei angustias & nobilitatem sine probro actam, bonori quàm ignominia habendam du-cebat. Male enim de virtute, malè de viris agetur, si ad divitiarum lancem & hi & illa pendantur.
units.tr: Poverty not brought on by one's own fault ought not to be reproached. Rightly, then, when Sextus Pompeius called Marcus Lepidus a fool, a pauper, and a disgrace to his ancestors, the senate thought him rather mild than lazy, and judged that his ancestral straitened circumstances and his nobility, lived without disgrace, should be held in honour rather than shame. For virtue will be ill-used, and men ill-used, if both they and it are weighed on the scales of riches.

units.la: LXX.
units.tr: LXX.

units.la: Animus principis è sensu verborum, non è verbis rimandus.
units.tr: The prince's mind is to be sought from the sense of his words, not from the words themselves.

units.la: Missis ad senatum literis Tiberius monuerat, judi-cio patrum legendum belli ducem gnarum militiae, &c. Senatus haec ut erant magis quam ut scribeban-tur intelligens, de Africa decrevit, ut Cafar legeret, cui [?] mandanda foret.
units.tr: Having sent letters to the senate, Tiberius had advised that a commander skilled in soldiering should be chosen by the judgement of the fathers, and so on. The senate, understanding these things as they were meant rather than as they were written, decreed about Africa that Caesar should choose to whom it was to be entrusted.

units.la: Sic & culpam ducis non bene lecti vitavit, nec jus Tiberio in provincias ulteriores & exercitum ademit.
units.tr: In this way it avoided the fault of a poorly chosen commander, and it did not take from Tiberius his right over the outer provinces and the army.

units.la: Quanquam enim Numidia inter provincias erat, se-natus ac populi administrationi decretas: (Dio libro 53) tamen armis turbatam in Cafaris districtum cecidisse, ex interiori Augusti animo, & nunc Tiberii cupiditate, quia arma senatum tractare nolebat, facilè perspiciebatur. Itaque avidi imperantium, gratiae volun-tatem eorum, non apices verborum, adorabuntur.
units.tr: For although Numidia was among the provinces assigned to the administration of the senate and people (Dio, book 53), it was easily seen that it had fallen, disturbed by arms, into Caesar's control, from the inner mind of Augustus and now from the desire of Tiberius, because the senate did not want to handle arms. Thus the eager courtiers of rulers will worship the will of those who grant favour, not the niceties of their words.

units.la: LXXI.
units.tr: LXXI.

units.la: Virile opus militia foeminarum adi-tum repellit.
units.tr: Military service, a man's business, shuts out women's approach.

units.la: An vero nec magistratum, cui provincia milis-taris (aut etiam pacata) obveniflet, uxor comitare-tur, olim Romano in senatu controvertebatur. Verus Caecina, foemineo comitatui adversus, dis-suasoria argumenta promebat: 1. à prisca Romano-rum consuetudine: Haec enim frustra placitum olim, ne foemina in socios aut gentes externas traherentur. Nec verterent igitur sapientes provisa, & feminaeo-cita. 2. ab incommodo simul & indecoro: inesse mu-lieres[?]. lierum comitatui, quae pacem luxu, bellum formidine morentur, & Romanum agmen ad similitudinem barbari incessus convertant. viris enim quid lucrosum, non quid in commune expediat, suggerere. nec Pompejum ancipiti contra Sertorium bello cum alacribus saltu, cum velocibus cursu, cum validis vecte certaturum fuisse, si lateri emollitura virum mulier adhaesisset, quinetiam pudendum quid, & contemnendum hosti, in discinito agmine, & fluitante vestitu, conspici. 3. à vitiis mulierem sexum prementibus. non imbecillum tantum & imparem laboribus sexum, sed si licentia adsit, savum, ambitiosum, potestatis avidum. priora ut in confesso posita non urget. posteriora tacito Plancinae in Syria vel Cilicia, aut etiam Agrippinae apud pontem Rheni, exemplo commonstrat. incedere inter milites, habere ad manum centuriones: praefidisse nupe foeminam exercitio cohortium, decursu legionum. 4. à peculiari avaritiae, sordium, peculatus, repetundarum crimine. cogitarent ipsi, quoties repetundarum aliqui arguerentur, plura uxoribus objectari. 5. ab ambitu provincialium, & turbatis per cum publicae rei negotiis. his statim adhaerescere determinum quemque provincialium: ab his negotia suscipi, transfigi: duorum egressus coli, duo esse pratoria, pervicacibus magis & impotentibus mulierum jussis. 6. à legis Oppiae auctoritate, qua foeminis omni in viros regimine adempto, ne ornatus quidem arbitrium permittebatur. qua Oppiis quondam, aliisque legibus constricta, nunc vincla exsolutis, domos fora, jam & exercitus regerent. quod futurum M. Porcius Cato, abrogationem legis Oppiae dissuadens praedixerat.
units.tr: Whether a magistrate to whom a province, whether at war or already pacified, had fallen should be accompanied by his wife was once debated in the Roman senate. Caecina, opposing the women's retinue, put forward arguments against it: (1) from the ancient custom of the Romans. For it was once decreed, to no effect, that women should not be dragged along to allies or foreign peoples. The wise, therefore, should not overturn what the ancestors provided and decreed. (2) from the inconvenience and at the same time the indecency: the women's retinue, which delays peace with luxury and war with fear, and turns the Roman column into the likeness of a barbarian march. For it suggests to men what is profitable for themselves, not what is expedient for the common good. Nor would Pompey, fighting a doubtful war against Sertorius, have contested with nimble men in leaping, with swift men in running, with strong men at the lever, if a woman, destined to soften her husband, had clung to his side. Moreover, something shameful and contemptible to the enemy would be seen: a disordered column and fluttering dress. (3) from the vices that beset the female sex: not only a sex weak and unequal to labours, but, if licence is at hand, savage, ambitious and greedy for power. He does not press the former points, as being admitted; the latter he illustrates by the silent example of Plancina in Syria or Cilicia, or even Agrippina at the bridge over the Rhine. To walk among the soldiers, to have centurions at hand: a woman has lately presided over the drill of cohorts and the marching of legions. (4) from the peculiar crime of avarice, meanness, peculation and extortion. Let them consider, whenever someone is accused of extortion, how many charges are laid against wives. (5) from the canvassing of provincials and the public business thrown into confusion through them. Immediately each provincial clings to them: business is taken up and carried through by them; the exits of two are cultivated; there are two praetoria, for the stubborn and domineering orders of women. (6) from the authority of the Oppian law, by which, with all control over husbands taken from women, not even the choice of their dress was permitted them. Once constrained by the Oppian and other laws, now with their chains loosed, they would rule homes, forums, and now armies. This, Marcus Porcius Cato had foretold when, dissuading the repeal of the Oppian law, he said it would come to pass.

units.la: Paucis Cæcinae assentientibus, autor tam rigidae sententiae rejiciebatur: neque relatum de negotio, neque Cacinam dignum tantae rei censorem, more judicii humani, quo non quid, sed a quo dicatur attenditur.
units.tr: Though a few assented to Caecina, the author of so rigid an opinion was rejected: the matter was neither put to a vote, nor was Caecina deemed a worthy judge of so great a question, according to the manner of human judgement, which attends not to what is said but to who says it.

units.la: Gravius Valerius Messalinus, & senatorio ordine dignius, sententia ac rationibus agit, tum adversarii argumenta refellendo, tum sua promendo. Ad primum Cæcinae argumentum, ab antiquitate & consuetudine petitum ; respondet : Multa duritie veterum melius & latiùs mutata. multa enim apud priscos horridae rusticitatis yeftigia, casas & rura Sabina sapere: quae emendati seculi elegantior usus correxerit. attamen necessitate temporum illam veterum duritiem excusare: qua remota necessitate in eo rigore morum velle perstare ; quid esse, nisi frumentum pro glande, uvas pro Acheloo rejicere? neque enim, ut olim, obsideri urbem bellis, aut provincias hostiles esse. Sed ne omnia, non eosdem nervos habitura, expendam; ad belli alacritatem, foeminarum comitatu remorandam, regeritur bella plane accinctis obeunda: sed revertentibus post laborem, quod boneftius quàm uxorium levamentum? Honestius enim Agamemno cum Clytemneftra sua, quam domi reliquerat, quàm cum captiva aliqua, post proelii laborem consuevisset. Decentius Achilles uxorem in castris Myrmidonum, quàm captam Bryfeidem fovisset. Avaritiam verò & arrogantiam muliebrem, pari virorum in provincias missorum libidine, excusat. corruptos sape pravitatibus uxorum maritos: num ergo omnes caelibes integros? atque ita, quod damnat poetalyricus, litem lite resolvit. ad Oppiae legis acer-bitatem, temporum diversa ratione, respondet: remis-sum aliquid postea, & mitigatum, quia expedierit, non enim reip. utilitas adleges civiles : sed hae ad illam expendendae. Generatim ad foeminarum in provin-ciis culpam respondet : frustra nofiram ignaviam alia advocabula transferri. nam viriin eo culpam, fi foemina modum excedat. Virienim est regere uxorem, non ab uxore frenum accipere. Retusis Caecinae mif-filibus, jam sua argumentorum tela spargit. 1. à per-mittendo vitae solatio. male eripi mariti consortia re-rum fecundarum adversarumque. five jugum est con-jugium, non deberi periculosis temporibus resolvi: fi-ve solatium, tum maximè eo opus esse, cum maximè adversa intonant. 2. à pudicitiae in defertis periclita-tione. sexum naturam invalidum deseri, & exponi sua luxu, cupidinibus alienis. labilem naturae imbecillita-te mulierem, custodia mariti amota, stimulante flam-ma malibidinum, nec defuturis pudicitiæ insidiatoribus, ad deteriora pronam pendere. nec defore[?] Clytemnestræ, decennii moram non ferenti, Ægysthum, nec Helenæ vel abducturum Paridem. Sic obviam irent iis quas alibi peccarent, ut flagitiorum urbis meminissent. Non enim æquum esse, ut dum saluti provincialium prospicitur, Roma, caput gentium & compendium orbis, ut flagitiorum quædam sententia deferatur. Messalinæ sententiæ Drusus accedens, Augusti & suo exemplo concludit.
units.tr: Valerius Messalinus, more weighty and more worthy of the senatorial order, argues the case with greater force of opinion and reasons, both by refuting his opponent's arguments and by setting out his own. To Caecina's first argument, drawn from antiquity and custom, he replies: many things have been changed for the better and more thoroughly by the harshness of the ancients. For among the old people there were traces of rough rusticity; huts and Sabine farms smacked of it, and the more refined usage of a corrected age has amended these. Yet the necessity of the times excuses that old hardness; if that necessity is removed, to persist in that rigour of morals would be nothing but to reject wheat for acorns and grapes for Achelous. For the city is no longer besieged by wars as once, nor are the provinces hostile. But, lest I weigh everything as though it had not the same sinews: it is objected that for readiness in war the women's retinue must be held back, since wars must be undertaken with men fully girded; but on returning after labour, what is more honourable than a wife's comfort? For Agamemnon would have behaved more honourably with his Clytemnestra, whom he had left at home, than with some captive woman after the toil of battle. Achilles would more becomingly have cherished his wife in the camp of the Myrmidons than the captive Briseis. Yet he excuses the avarice and arrogance of women by the equal lust of men sent into the provinces: husbands are often corrupted by their wives' wickedness; are then all unmarried men blameless? And so he answers the charge with a charge, as the lyric poet does with what he condemns. To the harshness of the Oppian law he replies that, with a different reckoning of the times, something was afterwards relaxed and softened because it was expedient; for the welfare of the commonwealth is not to be measured by civil laws, but civil laws by it. To the general fault of women in the provinces he replies that our own cowardice is in vain transferred to other names; the fault lies with men if a woman exceeds due measure, for it is the man's part to rule his wife, not to take the bridle from her. With Caecina's missiles blunted, he now hurls his own arguments: (1) from allowing the solace of life: it is wrong to rob a husband of his wife's companionship in prosperous and adverse fortune; if marriage is a yoke, it should not be loosed in perilous times; if it is a solace, then it is most needed when adversity thunders most. (2) from the danger to chastity when wives are left behind: the weaker nature of the sex, deserted and exposed to its own luxury and to others' desires, with the guard of the husband removed and the flame of lust goading her, and with seducers of chastity not wanting, inclines to worse things. Nor would there lack a Clytemnestra, unable to bear a ten years' delay, to take up with Aegisthus, or a Paris to carry off Helen. Thus they would meet head-on those whom they might sin with elsewhere, so that they remembered the disgraces of the city. For it is not right that, while the safety of the provincials is looked to, Rome, the head of the nations and the treasury of the world, should have its disgraceful examples brought forward. Drusus, joining his opinion to Messalina's, concludes with the example of Augustus and his own.

units.la: Decisio.
units.tr: Decision.

units.la: Aptiorem quidem militiæ ac habiliorem cælibatum, ut & administrationi publicæ, censemus. Potius tamen quam aut castitas virorum, aut pudicitia mulierum periclitetur, conjugii consortium negetur. Ne urgeam, quasdam gentes præsentia mulierum incitatas acriùs pugnasse. De Britannis Galgacus in Vita[?] Agricolæ: Omnia victoria incitamenta pro nobis sunt: nulla Romanos conjuges accendunt[?]. Brigantes.Britanniæ citerioris populus, fœmina duce, colonia Romanorum exusta, castra expugnaverunt; ac nisi felicitas in fœcordiam vertisset, jugum Romanum exuere. Sed hoc quidem apud Britannos, qui ne in imperio quidem sexum discernunt. Apud Germanos memoriæ proditur, quasdam acies inclinatas jam & labantes à fœminis restitutas, constantia precum, & objectu pectorum, monstrata cominus captivitate.
units.tr: We judge celibacy to be the more suitable and more useful state for military service and for public administration. Yet rather than let either the chastity of men or the purity of women be put in danger, we would deny them the partnership of marriage. I need not press the point, but some nations are known to have fought more fiercely when stirred by the presence of their women. Galgacus, in the Life of Agricola, says of the Britons: Every incentive to victory is on our side: no Roman wives inflame them. The Brigantes, a people of Britain on this side, under a woman's leadership, stormed the Roman colony and its camps; and had not good fortune turned into sloth, they would have thrown off the Roman yoke. But that is among the Britons, who do not even distinguish the sexes in ruling. Among the Germans it is recorded that some lines already bending and wavering were restored by women, through the steadfastness of their prayers and by throwing their breasts before the men, showing them the captivity that was close at hand. The older writers report the same of the women of Persia, as well as of the Germans in their customs.

units.la: T[?]De moribus Germanorum. quod & de Persarum mulieribus antiquiores produnt. Non ita visum est, iis, qui ordines militares, Teutonicum, Templarium, Rhodium & ex eo Melitensem, cum cælibatu creaverunt. Promptiores procul dubio, & arcendis barbaris alacriores, nisi Templarios luxus & infandæ libidines, postremò proditoriæ cum Saracenis conspirationes pessundedisset. nisi Teutonicos raptus puellarum, adulteria, sævitia, immanis avaritia, possessione Prussorum depulisset. Nam de Melitensibus fictum esse rumorem credere, quàm temere judicare, malim.
units.tr: It did not seem so to those who founded the military orders of the Teutonic Knights, the Templars, the Knights of Rhodes, and from them the Maltese, with celibacy. They would doubtless have been readier and more eager to keep off the barbarians, had not the luxury and unspeakable lusts of the Templars, and finally their treacherous conspiracies with the Saracens, ruined them; and had not the Teutonic Knights, by their abductions of girls, their adulteries, cruelty and monstrous greed, been driven out of possession of Prussia. As for the Maltese, I would rather believe that the rumour about them was invented than rashly judge it.

units.la: LXXII.
units.tr: LXXII.

units.la: Recusando arripere Tiberianorum morum est.
units.tr: To refuse and then seize is the manner of Tiberius.

units.la: Quanti Tiberium nominare proconsulem Africæ interesset, nec in manu patrum ac populi arbitrium arripere morum effet, suprà monstravi. Hic tamen Tiberius obliquè patres castigavit, quod cuncta curarum ad principem rejicerent. Sed exactione magis quam sermone Tiberius judicandus, M. Lepidum & Junium Blæsum nominavit, ex quis proconsul Africa legeretur. Nimirum quæ in suscipiendo fuerat, eadem instabiliendo imperio fuit, simulata curarum detrectatio. Tiberii [illegible, ~7 letters] imitatus Blæsus, specie recusantis, sed neque eadem adseverations recusantis, proconsulare imperium admisit. Acco mulier versutos apud Græcos ludibrio fuerat, quod quæ maxime concupiverat spernere se præ se ferret. At viros principes, & Romanæ quidem gravitatis principes, eadem simulatione patres ludos facere, decorum habetur.
units.tr: I have shown above how much it mattered that Tiberius nominate the proconsul of Africa, and that it would not be the manner of seizing power to put the decision into the hands of the senate and people. Yet here Tiberius obliquely rebuked the senators, because they threw all cares back upon the prince. But Tiberius should be judged more by his conduct than by his words: he named Marcus Lepidus and Junius Blaesus, from whom the proconsul of Africa was to be chosen. Clearly, what he had shown in taking up power, he showed in securing it: a feigned reluctance to bear the burdens. Blaesus imitated Tiberius, under the appearance of refusing, yet with none of the same protests of one who refuses, and he accepted the proconsular command. Among the Greeks a clever woman was a laughing-stock for professing to despise in front of everyone what she desired most. Yet for leading men, and indeed for princes of Roman dignity, to make sport of the senators with the same pretence is regarded as fitting.

units.la: LXXIII.
units.tr: LXXIII.

units.la: Asylorum cohibenda licentia.
units.tr: The licence of asylums must be restrained.

units.la: Non quæritur hoc loco, utrum patria ob tyrannidem, aut grave æs alienum, profugos, asylo aperto, recipere liceat: quanquam & hic modum poni, nec passim Romuli imitationem fieri, magis ex usu gentium: sed an ejusdem civitatis improbos cives, adversus nas & servos, ad locum, sanctione hominum muni-tum, confugientes in jus abripi nefas ducatur. Vetere republica aræ miserorum refugia erant: servorum in-primis contra herorum iracundiam, quos, uti deorum supplices, ad supplicium abduci impium ac intestabile credebatur. Converso rerum statu, imperatorum statuis honos dabatur. Cæsaris enim imagine arrepta, servi dominos, patronos liberti, malefici injuria affecti, eos ludibrio habebant, cujus licentiæ dolor multorum intimis quæstibus tegebatur. donec C. Cestius auc-toritate sua in senatu sententiam promere, juris & legum patrocinia suscepit. Principes quidem instar deorum esse: sed neque a diis nisi justas supplicum preces audiri.
units.tr: The question here is not whether it is lawful for a country to receive fugitives under an open refuge because of tyranny or heavy debt, although here too a limit must be set, and the imitation of Romulus should not be practised everywhere, going more by the custom of nations. The question is whether it is thought wrong to drag from the place, protected by the sanction of men, the wicked citizens of the same state who flee to it from their own people and their slaves. In the old republic, altars were refuges for the wretched, and especially slaves against the anger of their masters; it was believed impious and abominable to drag them off to punishment, since they were suppliants of the gods. When the state of affairs changed, honour was given to the statues of emperors. For slaves, seizing the image of Caesar, mocked their masters; freedmen mocked their patrons; and wrongdoers who had been punished mocked those who had punished them. The distress of many at this licence was hidden in their inmost complaints, until Gaius Cestius, by his authority, took up in the senate the cause of the law and the protection of the laws. Princes indeed are like gods; but the gods hear only the just prayers of suppliants.

units.la: Quemadmodum igitur vota in cœlum fundendo nemo à pœna liberatur, ita statuarum Cæsaris amplexu non debere conferri {a}celerum immunitatem. neque quenquam in Capitolium, aliáve urbis templa perfugere, ut eo subsidio ad flagitia utatur. supplicibus enim, & nulla culpa miseris, ea subsidia, non scelerum luto immersis, patere. Certi sermone a nobis comprobato, quæstio superest. Annon Christianorum templis ea non abripiendi supplices immunitas largienda? Nisi gravitas criminum, supplicandi modus, & ignoscendi libertas perpendatur: vagam impunitatis licentiam & istinc amovemus. Nec obstat sanctitas templorum, cui nulla vis, nulla violentia inferenda. Non enim defendendo justitiam, sed eam conculcando, sacrorum religio violatur. Nonne Deus ipse facinorosum ab altari ad pœnam abripi præcepit? nonne Salomon Joabum adipsum altare interfici, exoleti sceleris vindex, mandavit? Nec etiam asyla Hebræorum, Dei mandatu aperta, obstant. Nam & numero angusto finita fuerunt, nec templorum sanctimonia alligata: quodque caput est, non nisi infortunatè reis, reclusa. Quod vero Chrysostomus Eutropium, e fastus impotentia supplicum in sedem collapsum, recepit: non jure ille, sed commiseratione, sed precibus imperatori offerendis nitebatur. Quanquam nec omnia oratoris ecclesiastici dicta aut facta defendenda, tanquam hominis labi nescii, suscipimus. Jam leges civiles Honorii, Theodosii, Leonis, Gundemiri, ad rationem, ad jus naturæ & æquum; non hoc ad illas examinandum judicamus. Neque meretur beneficio legis uti, qui contra autorem legis committit. uti JCtus definit. Nec Pactyæ Cumanum in templum profugi, apud Herodotum, & adyti voce defensi, exemplum movet. Nam nec inter scelestos Pactyas, & multum gentilium fanorum impuritas à puritate sacrarum ædium discrepat. Nec repudianda fortassis media Gallorum via: apud quos delinquens sacris ex ædibus abstractus, examini subjicitur, an immunitate ecclesiæ dignus reperiatur. Lapsis quidem & erroris pœnitentibus ecclesia misericordiæ sinum pandit: jus autem suum judiciis civilibus non eripit, nec vexillum impunè peccandi sustollit.
units.tr: Therefore, just as no one is freed from punishment by pouring out vows to heaven, so the immunity of the guilty should not be conferred by embracing the statue of Caesar. Nor should anyone flee to the Capitol or to other temples of the city, so as to use that refuge for crimes. For such refuges lie open to suppliants, and to the wretched who are guiltless, not to those sunk in the mire of their crimes. Having approved this point, a question remains: should not the same immunity, of not dragging off suppliants, be granted to the temples of the Christians? Unless the gravity of the crimes, the manner of supplication, and the freedom to pardon are weighed, we also remove that wandering licence of impunity. Nor does the sanctity of the temples stand in the way, since no force or violence is to be used there. For the religion of holy things is violated not by defending justice but by trampling it underfoot. Did not God himself command that a wrongdoer be dragged from the altar to punishment? Did not Solomon order Joab to be slain at the very altar, as the avenger of his unpardonable crime? Nor do the asylums of the Hebrews, opened by God's command, stand in the way. For they were limited to a narrow number, and were not bound to the sanctity of the temples; and, what is the chief point, they were opened only to the unfortunate accused. As for Chrysostom receiving Eutropius, who had fallen into the sanctuary from the arrogance of his pride, he did not rest on law but on pity and on the prayers offered to the emperor. Yet we do not undertake to defend all the words and deeds of that ecclesiastical orator, as if he were a man free from error. Now, as for the civil laws of Honorius, Theodosius, Leo and Gundemir, we judge that they are not to be examined against these by reason, by the law of nature and by equity.
