Nor does he deserve to enjoy the benefit of a law who acts against its author, as the jurists define it. Nor does the example of the Pactyans who fled into the temple at Cyme, as told by Herodotus, and were defended by the voice of the inner sanctuary, move us. For the Pactyans were wicked men, and the impurity of many pagan shrines differs greatly from the purity of sacred buildings. Nor perhaps should the middle course of the Gauls be rejected: among them, a wrongdoer dragged from the sacred building is brought to examination, to see whether he is found worthy of the immunity of the church. To the fallen, and to those who repent of their error, the Church indeed opens the bosom of mercy; but it does not take away its right in civil judgements, nor does it raise the banner of sinning with impunity.

units.la: LXXIV.
units.tr: LXXIV.

units.la: Coërcenda pœnis accusandi protervia.
units.tr: The insolence of accusers must be restrained by punishments.

units.la: Quæ vel inani invisi otii oblectamento, & facunditate ostentatione, vel placendi sævis judicibus animo, lucrive improba cupiditate, vel denique nocendi aliis, negotiumque facessendi, & se formidabilem efficiendi studio, multis molesta fuit. Jure unus & alter equitum Rom. quod fictis majestatis criminibus Magnum Cæcilianum prætorem petivissent, autore principe, ac decreto senatus punitit, quod gratum vulgo, Drufo in laudem cedebat. Agrippina quoque, Germanici filia, apud Neronem mater accusata, ultionem in delatores & præmia amicis obtinuit. XIII. Annal. Raro Tiberius, rarius Nero ea ad æquitatem promptitudine: frequentius præmiis illecti accusatores; vel sæviendi libidine, & bona damnatorum fisco addicendi, vel rare imperii muniendi præpostero artificio.
units.tr: Such men, whether from the empty pleasure of idle leisure and the display of eloquence, or from a wish to please cruel judges, or from wicked greed for gain, or finally from a desire to harm others, to make trouble, and to make themselves feared, were a burden to many. Rightly, one or two Roman knights who had sought to prosecute Magnus Caecilianus the praetor on fabricated charges of treason were punished by the emperor's authority and a decree of the senate. This pleased the common people and redounded to Drusus's praise. Agrippina too, daughter of Germanicus, when accused by her mother before Nero, obtained vengeance against the informers and rewards for her friends. Annals, book 13. Rarely did Tiberius, and more rarely Nero, show such readiness to do justice. More often accusers were enticed by rewards, either from lust for cruelty and for handing the goods of the condemned over to the treasury, or through the perverse device of securing a shaky empire.

units.la: LXXV.
units.tr: LXXV.

units.la: Principi altiorum virtutum non capaci voluptas permittenda.
units.tr: Pleasure is to be allowed to a prince incapable of higher virtues.

units.la: Voluptatem theatri, honesti convivii, venationis; non fornicandi licentiæ, non saltandi cum Cajo, nom cum Nerone in publico aurigandi aut cythara canendi, capio. Huc potius trahere volentem Drufum populus Romanus studebat, quàm solus & nullis voluptatibus avocatus, mœstam vigilantiam & malas curas exerceret, per quas judicii sævitiam, & damnandi fontes insontes acerbitatem intelligebant. Sequitur enim, non enim Tiberius, non accusatores fatiscebant. Ita Neronem Burrhus & Seneca, si virtutem aspernaretur, leviorum vitiorum concessione retinebant. Magnum super maximæ insularum regem censores pro fugge-ftu traducebant, ut saltationum & comœdiarum festi-vitate nimium. quibus ille voluptatibus dejectus, in sæviendi contra ipsos buccinatores asperitatem, & mox in arma civilia, convertebatur. Quàm præstitisset conversionem à satietate, ab ætate graviori, à placidis informatoribus opperiri, quam feram dormientem contra se excitare!
units.tr: I do not approve of the pleasures of the theatre, of a decent banquet, or of hunting; nor of the licence of fornication, of dancing with Gaius, or of driving a chariot or singing to the lyre in public with Nero. The Roman people were eager to draw Drusus toward such pursuits rather than see him, alone and undistracted by any pleasures, exercise a gloomy vigilance and troubled cares, through which they understood the cruelty of the judgement and the springs of condemnation, bitter to the innocent. For it follows that neither Tiberius nor the accusers grew weary. So Burrhus and Seneca, if Nero scorned virtue, kept him by allowing lighter vices. Censors, to make the great king's shame public, dragged him from the platform, and he was carried away by the excessive festivity of dances and comedies. Once he was cast down from those pleasures, he turned to savage cruelty against the very flatterers who had cheered him on, and soon to civil war. How much better it would have been to wait for his turn from satiety, from advancing age, from calm tutors, than to rouse against oneself a beast that was asleep!

units.la: LXXVI. Majestatis crimen omnium accusa-tionum complementum.
units.tr: LXXVI. The crime of majesty, the completion of all accusations.

units.la: Sub sævo nimirum aut suspicace principe. [?]᾿Ασεβείας Dio vertit, quasi quo in principem tanquam in Deum sint injurii. Antharius Prifcu Casium Cordum, pro-consulem Creta, postulaverat repetundis, addito majestatis crimine: quod tum omnium accusationum complementum erat. Et crimen unicum eorum, qui sine crimine erant: ut alibi Tacitus. crimen quod in magnos inprimis viros, proconsules & consulares, intendebatur: contraque eos cupidissime recipiebatur. Infimos vero e plebe, vita proletaria tutos, raro majestatis fulmen afflavit. Cajus ille, deterior Tiberio fuc-cessor, qui nec vocem nec incessum liberum in senatore ferebat, sutorem natione Gallum se irridentem, & magnum deliramentum appellantem, non indignatur. [illegible, ~40 letters] adeo facilius vulgarium hominum, quàm dignitate conspicuorum, dicendi libertatem, ejusmodi ingenia tolerant, inquit Dio libro 59. Unde ea in proceres odii, unde sævitiæ materia. Eam libro eodem idem Cajus, quanquam mente motus, exprimit. Sic enim Tiberium se exin-feris alloquentem introducit: μήτε φιλήσης τινὰ αὐτῶν, μήτε φιλήσῃ τινος [?]. &c. neque diligas quenquam illorum, neque ulli parcas. omnes enim te oderunt, omnes mortem tuam in votis habent. neque à cæde tui, si poterunt, abstinebunt. Non igitur, quid illis gratum facias, cogita; neque eorum de te sermones cura. sed voluptatem modò ac securitatem tuam, tanquam rem omnium iustissimam, prospice.sic enim nec mali quicquam patieris, & omni voluptatis desiderio perfrueris: & præterea ab illis, volentibus vel invitis, honorabere. Alio modo te gerens, nihil reipsa consequeris, verbo inanem gloriam adeptus ; præter frustra insumptam operam, insidiis circumventus, inglorius peribis. Ἀδεὶς γὰρ (addit) ἀνθρώπων ἐκὼν ἀρχέτω, ἀλλ' εἰ δ' ὄντως ἀρχὴν ἔχει, ἀλλ' ἀπὸ Φοβέτω, Ἀεὶ γὰρ ἀλλ' ἡ πλεῖον, ἑτέρου ὅτι δὲ ἡ Δημοκρατία, πρὸς ἀρχὴν τὴν ἀδικίαν. Nemo enim hominum spon- te imperio se submittit : sed metu auctore potentiorem colit: ubi vero audere incipit, infirmiorem vindicta deprimit. Hæc apud Dionem Caligula : nequaquam sæviora factis locutus. Quanquam spes eum diutur- nioris imperii sefellit, ad quartum anni metam potentiæ non adductus.
units.tr: Surely under a cruel or suspicious prince. Dio renders it as impiety [ἀσέβεια], as if they had wronged the prince as though he were God. Antharius had accused Casius Cordus, proconsul of Crete, of extortion, adding the charge of treason, which at that time was the completion of all accusations. And it was the one crime of those who had no crime, as Tacitus says elsewhere. The charge was aimed above all at great men, proconsuls and consulars, and it was received against them most eagerly. But the lowest of the common people, safe in their humble station, were rarely struck by the thunderbolt of treason. That Gaius, a worse successor than Tiberius, who could not endure a free voice or gait in a senator, did not take offence when a Gallic cobbler mocked him and called him a great madman. [illegible] So much more easily do such men tolerate freedom of speech from common people than from the distinguished in rank, as Dio says in book 59. Hence that hatred of the nobles, hence the material for cruelty. Gaius himself, though moved in mind, expresses this in the same book. For he introduces Tiberius addressing the informers thus: neither love any of them [μήτε φιλήσης τινὰ αὐτῶν], nor be loved by any [μήτε φιλήσῃ τινος], etc.: neither love any of them, nor spare any. For all of them hate you, all have your death in their prayers, and if they are able, they will not refrain from slaying you. Therefore do not consider what would please them, nor care about their talk about you, but look out only for your pleasure and your safety, as the most just of all things. For thus you will suffer no harm and enjoy every desire of pleasure; and besides, you will be honoured by them, whether they wish it or not. If you conduct yourself otherwise, you will achieve nothing in reality, having gained only an empty glory in word; besides the labour expended in vain, you will be surrounded by plots and perish without glory. For (he adds) no man willingly submits to rule [Ἀδεὶς γὰρ ἀνθρώπων ἑκὼν ἀρχέτω]; but if he truly holds power, let him fear the one stronger; for it is always the case that one who is weaker is ruled by another, and democracy is unjust toward authority. For no one of men submits to rule of his own accord; but he worships the more powerful out of fear, and when he begins to dare, he crushes the weaker by vengeance. These are the words of Dio's Caligula, not at all harsher than his deeds. Yet hope of a longer reign deceived him, since he was not brought to the fourth year of his power.

units.la: LXXVII.
units.tr: LXXVII.

units.la: Non eadem lupo quæ leoni pugnæ constantia.
units.tr: Not the same steadfastness in fighting for the wolf as for the lion.

units.la: Nec eandem belli gerendi pervicaciam à generoso & degenere duce expectes. Thracię quædam natio- nes arma coepere ; ducibus diversis, & paribus inter se per ignobilitatem : quæ causa fuit, ne in bellum atrox coalescerent. Sed major in ignavia, imperitia, metu causa non diuturni belli, quàm causam turbarum citò inter Orthonem & Vitellium comipositarum Tacitus lib. 2. Histor. assignat. Eadem causa primo impetu à Flavianis debellati Vitelli. Tangit hanc perseverantiæ & remissionis causam Horatius, Sat. 7 lib. 1.
units.tr: Nor should you expect the same stubbornness in waging war from a noble leader and a degenerate one. Certain Thracian nations took up arms under different leaders who were equal to each other in their obscurity, and this was the reason they did not coalesce into a fierce war. But the cause of a war that does not last long lies more in cowardice, inexperience and fear, as Tacitus assigns in Histories book 2 to the cause of the disturbances quickly settled between Otho and Vitellius. For the same reason Vitellius, defeated at the first onslaught by the Flavians, was crushed. Horace touches on this cause of perseverance and of slackening in Satire 7 of book 1.

units.la: hoc etenim sunt omnes iure molesti, Quo fortes, quibus adversum bellum incidit intet Hectora Priamiden, animo surmque inter Achilleum Ita fuit capitalis, ut ultima divideret mors: Non aliam ob causam, nisi quòd virtus ut utroque summa fuit, duo si discordia vestat intertes: Aut si disparibus bellum incidat, ut Diomedi Cum Lycio Glauco : discedet pigrior ultro Muneribus missis. Alia belli cito profligari causa est, omnium virium in unum aleae jactum collatio. Qui mos fuit, servatis etiam nunc ejus moris vestigiis, Orientis regibus, Contra Graeci, Romani, & caeterae fere Europaei transfus nationes, difspensant vires, differunt impetus, fortunam inter dubia, virtutem inter certa numerant: semel aut iterum prostrati cladem tegunt, & in acriorem iram resurgunt.
units.tr: For all men are rightly troublesome in this way, those brave men upon whom war has fallen, between Hector son of Priam and high-spirited Achilles, so that death alone divided them; and for no other reason than that their courage was equally great. If discord between two equal men has stirred up war, or if the war falls between unequal men, as between Diomedes and the Lycian Glaucus, the weaker one withdraws of his own accord once gifts have been sent. Another cause of a war being quickly crushed is the gathering of all forces into one throw of the dice. This was the custom of the kings of the East, and traces of that custom survive even now. The Greeks, Romans and nearly all the other European nations, on the contrary, divide their forces, delay their attacks, count fortune among the uncertain and valour among the certain. Once or twice struck down, they conceal the disaster and rise again in fiercer anger.

units.la: LXXVIII.
units.tr: LXXVIII.

units.la: Pax exigendi modestia firmanda.
units.tr: Peace is to be secured by moderation in exacting (taxes).

units.la: Multos enim ad bellum quieturos rapinarum licentia, & tributorum infaturabilis exactio compulit. Tiberio imperante Galliarum civitates ob magnitudinem aeris alieni rebellionem coeptavere. Eodem aeris alieni flabello parum abfuit quin Umbrenus, Catilinariae factionis conscius, Allobrogas ad bellum Romanis inferendum concitaret. Ob gravitatem exactionum, & ob aes alienum, Britannia imperante Nerone commota est. Avertendis, aut minuendis, exactionibus proceres Galliae bellum quod Boni publici vocabatur (le bien commun) Ludovico XI. intulerunt. Quo nullum Europa vidit diuturnius, belli inter Au-raicos [?] in Belgio & Hispaniarum regem exorti, ansa propinqua fuit decimae rerum venalium ab Albano exactio. Quare tributorum, vectigalium, donorum gratuitorum (le don gratuit) injuncta onera ad aequitatis modum jurisque revocanda. Quod ut ab aulae moderatoribus impetretur, cohibenda aulae & proximorum aulae civium luxuria, insatiabilis cupiditatis mater. Prodigendi enim voragine, in rapiendi barathrum plerique demerguntur. Sumptuum igitur profusio demenda est, qui rapinarum licentiam cohibitus est quodni fiat, animus ferox, prava via ingressus, ubi consueta non suppetunt, fertur accensus in socios modo, modo in cives; movet composita, & res novae veteribus acquirit.
units.tr: For the licence of plunder and the insatiable exaction of taxes drove many to war who would otherwise have kept quiet. In the reign of Tiberius the cities of Gaul began a rebellion on account of the great size of their debt. By the same spur of debt, Umbrenus, an accomplice of Catiline's conspiracy, came close to stirring up the Allobroges to make war on the Romans. Because of the severity of the exactions and because of debt, Britain was thrown into turmoil under the emperor Nero. In order to turn away or lessen the exactions, the nobles of Gaul waged against Louis XI the war called (le bien commun). No war that Europe ever saw lasted longer than the one that broke out between the Auraici [?] in Belgium and the king of Spain; its immediate occasion was the tithe on saleable goods imposed by Alva. Therefore the burdens laid on by taxes, duties and (le don gratuit) must be recalled to the measure of fairness and of law. So that this may be obtained from the rulers of the court, the luxury of the court and of the citizens close to it, the mother of insatiable greed, must be restrained. For most men are plunged, by the whirlpool of squandering, into the abyss of plunder. The profusion of expenses must therefore be removed, which restrains the licence of plunder, lest it happen that a fierce spirit, having entered a wrong path, where customary resources fail, is carried off, inflamed now against allies, now against citizens; it stirs up settled affairs and seeks new things at the cost of the old.

units.la: Sall. de Rep. ordinanda.
units.tr: Sallust, on ordering the commonwealth.

units.la: LXXIX.
units.tr: LXXIX.

units.la: Nonnisi magnae curae magna merces.
units.tr: Great reward comes only from great care.

units.la: Major in Republica merces generosis viris non est honoribus: ad quos, nondum corrupto rerum statu, nonnisi per virtutem & merita devenitur. Honorum pars non infima est, Civitatis communicatio: per quam Romani altiora provincialium ingenia allexe-runt. De Julio Floro & Julio Sacroviro Tacitus: bilitas ambobus, & majorum bona facta, eóque Romae nā civitas olim data, cum id rarum, nec nisi virtute pretium eflet. Proximus honor externis communicatio- ri solitus, est amicitia ac fœderis conjunctio. Senatus & populus R. beneficii & injuria memor esse solet: terum Boccho, quoniam poenitet, delicti gratiam facit: fœdus & amicitia dabuntur, cum meruerit. S. B. J. Alius alliciendi per honores fiderites Romanis fuit, regis appellatio. quam nisi ob summa merita conferri; Cæsar Ariovisto exprobrat. Quanquam ejusmodi reges fere instrumentum servitutis, & injecti externis compedes, fuere. Quartus devinciendi modus fuit, in societatem allectio. quæ, quanquam ex usu civitas- tis Romanæ fuisset, polt devictum Antiochum Asiæ regem, beneficii loco haberi coepit. Quam magno ambitu, spretam antea, quamvis conjunctis contra Philippum opibus, Rhodios, fracto jam armis Perfeos, frustra desideravisse, autor est in excerptis legationibus Polybius. Hæc meritorum ingentium, hæc vitæ tutum ingentia præmia, totidem libatæ libertatis pe-dicæ, totidem splendidæ servitutis auctoramenta Ro-manis fuere. Quare etiam atque etiam libero populo videndum, ne fe beneficio honorum potentioribus tè-merè illiget. quod & de nobilitatis insignibus, ab ex-terno rege vel populo impetrandis, in Arcanis regno-rum monui.
units.tr: Among free peoples, the greatest reward for noble men is not honours. While the state of affairs was not yet corrupted, these were reached only through virtue and merit. The grant of citizenship was no small part of the honours. By it the Romans won over the more gifted spirits of the provincials. Tacitus says of Julius Florus and Julius Sacrovir that both had nobility and their ancestors' good deeds, and so Roman citizenship was once given to them, since it was rare and was a prize won only by virtue. The next honour customarily given to foreigners was friendship and the bond of alliance. The Senate and people of Rome are wont to remember both benefits and injuries. To Bocchus, because he repented, they granted pardon for his offence, and alliance and friendship would be given when he had earned them (S. B. J.). Another means of attracting and binding foreign peoples to the Romans through honours was the title of king, which Caesar reproaches Ariovistus for having received, since it was conferred only for the greatest merits. Yet such kings were generally an instrument of slavery and fetters placed upon foreigners. A fourth means of binding was the invitation into alliance. Although this had been customary for the Roman state, after Antiochus, king of Asia, was defeated it began to be regarded as a favour. Polybius, in the Excerpta from the Embassies, is the authority that the Rhodians, though they had earlier scorned it and had sought it in vain with great ambition, even though they had joined forces against Philip, now that Perseus was broken in arms, desired it without success. These were the great prizes for great merits, these the lures of life, as many snares of lightly tasted liberty, as many splendid badges of servitude for the Romans. Therefore a free people must consider again and again that it does not rashly bind the more powerful with the benefit of honours. I have also warned of this in the Arcana regnorum, concerning the noble insignia to be obtained from a foreign king or people.

units.la: Inter ipsos cives honorum collatio præcipua, spectatur in magistratuum & imperiorum demandatio-ne. de qua apud Salluftium in bello Jugurthino Ma-tius: nam illi falsi sunt, qui diversi imas res pariter exa-spectant, ignavia voluptatem, & pramia virtutis. Verum corruptis civium moribus, nimis quam saepe haec inter fe miscentur. Proxima est militaria præ-miorum, miorum,
units.tr: Among the citizens themselves, the chief conferral of honours is seen in the granting of magistracies and commands. Marius speaks of this in Sallust's Jugurthine War: those men are indeed mistaken who expect at the same time things that are opposed, idleness and pleasure together with the rewards of virtue. But when the morals of the citizens are corrupted, these are mixed together all too often.

units.la: [illegible, ~12 letters] miorum, laudis, coronatum, donariorum distributio, quibus, quod alio loco de iis actum, chartam non illino.
units.tr: Next is the distribution of military rewards: ... praises, crowns and gifts. Since this has been discussed elsewhere, I will not spoil paper with it.

units.la: LXXX. Comprimenda bellorum in ortu femina.
units.tr: LXXX. Stifling the seeds of wars at their birth.

units.la: Quorum opprimendorum, cum in occulto geran-tur, non semper datur copia. Agitur enim fere secretis colloquiis: ut hic a Gallicani motus auctoribus: aut in abdicis aedium penetralibus; ut Catilinariae coniurà-tionis populares, ut Romani adolescentes de reducen-do Tarquinio consilia miscentes: aut in sylvarum in-teriora concione advocata; ut a Claudio civili Batavo: aut secreto procerum in solitudine aliqua conventu; ut fuit quondam Germaniae dynastarum, de bello His-panis inferendo, in seminuta[?] quadam Nassoviae[?] arce, non procul a Sigenae oppido: aut flexo in vesperam die, & delapsis melioribus: ut Vibulenius & Percennius, Germanicae seditionis autores, nec re cum omnibus primo ausu communicata: verum ferocissimo quoque adsumpto, aut quibus ob egestatem, ac metum ex flagitiis, maxima peccandi necessitudo. hi enim innovan-dis rebus aptissimi, vel ob vanitatem ingenii, vel ob tranquillitatis odium. Ab his initiis paulatim se pan-dente audacia, per conciliabula & coetus injiciendo turbandis rebus formiti idonea differuntur. nec desu-turae sunt subditorum de imperantium oneribus que-relae: de continuatione tributorum gravitate faenoris, saevitia ac superbia praesidentium. tradi se praefectis centurionibusque: quos ubi spoliis & sanguine explevE-rint, mutari, exquirique novos sinus, & varia prae-dandi vocabula. Instare dilectum, quo liberi a parentibus, fratres a fratribus, velut suprema dividantur: quo rebellionis flabello Claudius Civiles tumidos Batavorum animos inflabat. iv.Histor. Nihil profici patientia, nisi ut graviora tanquam ex facili tolerantibus imperentur. nihil jam cupiditati, nihil libidini excep-tum. jam ipsos, quod difficillimum fuerit, deliberare,
units.tr: Since these things are carried on in secret, it is not always possible to suppress them. They are usually conducted in private conversations: as here, by the instigators of the Gallic uprisings; or in the inner recesses of a private house, as with the followers of Catiline's conspiracy, or Roman young men plotting the return of Tarquin; or in the remote interior of the forests, with an assembly called, as by Claudius Civilis the Batavian; or in a secret meeting of nobles in some solitary place, as once happened among the lords of Germany when they planned war against the Spaniards, in some half-ruined fortress of Nassau, not far from the town of Siegen; or when the day is turned towards evening and the better men have withdrawn, as Vibulenus and Percennius, the authors of the German mutiny, did, not having shared the matter with everyone at first, but having taken on the most fierce, or those who, from poverty and fear of their crimes, had the greatest necessity for wrongdoing. Such men are most fit for upheaval, either from the vanity of their character or from hatred of peace. From these beginnings, as their boldness gradually spreads, they spread the seeds of disorder through private meetings and gatherings, suited to throwing affairs into turmoil. Nor are complaints of subjects about the burdens of their rulers lacking: about the continual imposition of taxes, the severity of usury, the cruelty and arrogance of those in command. They say they are handed over to prefects and centurions, who, once they have filled themselves with plunder and blood, are replaced, and new pockets are sought, and various names for plundering are devised. A levy is about to be imposed, by which children are divided from their parents and brothers from brothers, as if for their last parting; with this bellows of rebellion Claudius Civilis inflamed the swollen spirits of the Batavians (Tacitus, Histories 4). Patience achieves nothing except that heavier burdens are imposed on those who endure as if they were easy to bear. Nothing is any longer withheld from desire or lust. Now, what is most difficult, they themselves begin to deliberate,

units.la: porrò in ejusmodi consiliis periculosius esse depre- hendi, quam audere, & quæ fuit aliis inflammandis ad bellum fumendum animis incitamentra. Spes ab oc- cafione rei benè gerendæ, à virium nostrarum appara- tu, imbecillitate hostium accenditur. discordare mili- tem, audito Germanici exitio. egregium resumenda libertati tempus, fi ipsi florentes, quàm inopes Italiæ, quàm imbellis urbana plebes, nihil validum in exerci- tibus, nisi quod externum cogitarent. Pari fiduciæ ftli- mulo Civilis: Nunquam magis affiictum rem Romanam, nec aliud in hibernis quam prædam & senes, at- tollerent tantum oculos, & inania legionum nomina ne pavescerent. esse sibi robur peditum equitumque, consanguineos Germanos; Gallias idem cupientes. ne Romanis quidem ingratum id bellum: cujus âm- biguam fortunam Vespasiano imputaturos: victoria rationem non reddi. 1v. Hiftor. His & similibus ver- borum flatibus, vicina secum & ulteriora rapientibus; belli contagio progrediatur. Haud fermè ulla civitas intacta feminibus ejus motus fuit. à feminibus ad fe- getem, à segete ad malorum messem, eruptione alii- cunde facta, proserpitur. sed erupere primi Andecavi &c Turonii. malo quidem suo, nondum adultæ messe, eruperunt, à legionario milite coercit. Astu- tiùs Galliarum alii primores, qui auxilium Romanis nis tulere, quo dissimulârent defectionem, magisque in tempore efferrent. Astutè & ipse belli concitator. Sacrovir, inteëto capite pugnam pro Romanis cien- ftentandi, ut ferebat, virtutis : sed captivi, neinceffe- retur telis, agnoscendum se præbuisse, arguebant. Non ex aphorismi nostri præscripto Tiberius eo de motu confultus, aspernatus est indicium, aluitque dubitatio- ne bellum. Ineptior Tiberio Vitellius, fraudis apud Cremonam rebus, nuncios cladis occultans, stulta dis- simulatione, remedia potius malorum quàm mala differebat. Quippe confitenti consultantique super- erant spes viresque: cum è contrario læta omnia sin- geret, falsis ingravescebat. Mirum apud ipsum de bel- lo silentium. prohibiti per civitatem sermones; eóque plu-
units.tr: and moreover, in such plots it is more dangerous to be caught than to dare. This was also an incitement to inflame the minds of others to take up war. Hope is kindled by the opportunity for waging war successfully, by the preparation of our forces, and by the weakness of the enemy. The soldiers are at odds, now that the destruction of Germanicus has been heard of. It is a splendid time to resume liberty, if they themselves are flourishing while Italy is poor, the urban populace is unwarlike, and nothing in the armies is strong, except that they are thinking of foreigners. Civilis, with the same goad of confidence, said: "Never was the Roman state more afflicted, and in winter quarters there is nothing but plunder and old men. Let them only lift their eyes and not be afraid of the empty names of legions. We have the strength of infantry and cavalry, Germans who are our kinsmen, and the Gauls wish the same. That war is not unwelcome even to the Romans, whose uncertain fortune they will impute to Vespasian; victory gives no account of itself." (Tacitus, Histories 4.) By such gusts of words, carrying along neighbours and those farther away, the contagion of war spreads. Almost no state was untouched by the seeds of that movement. From the seeds to the crop, from the crop to the harvest of evils, it creeps forth, the outbreak having been started from every side. But the Andecavi and Turonians first broke out, to their own harm, before the harvest was ripe, and were checked by the legionary soldiers. More craftily, other leading men of the Gauls, who brought help to the Romans, so that they might conceal their revolt and bring it forth more opportunely. Sacrovir, the chief instigator of the war, also acted craftily: with bared head he fought on the Roman side, as he claimed, of courage; but the captives, complaining that he had not been wounded by any weapon, argued that he had shown himself to be in on it. Not following the precept of our aphorism, Tiberius, when consulted about the uprising, scorned the information, and by hesitation he nourished the war. Vitellius was more foolish than Tiberius: at Cremona, by his fraud, concealing the messengers of the disaster, by foolish pretence he postponed the remedies for evils rather than the evils themselves. For to one who confessed and sought advice, hopes and strength remained; but while he falsely reported everything as cheerful, the evils grew worse. There was a strange silence from him about the war; conversations were forbidden throughout the state, and so

units.la: Vanum tu- multuum remedium. plures: ac si liceret, vera narraturi, quia vet abantur, atrociora vulgaverant. Verba sunt de Vitellio Taciti: iii. Histor. Ac Tiberium aliqua fortassis ratio moverit: vel quod modicas conjuratorum vires nosset, vel quod occulta in iis frangendis consilia, occultas machinas moveret. Sed non iccirco hostici bellorum duces quietiora consilia captabant. Nam Florus insisterè destinatus pellicere alam equitum, quæque alia bellò mature erupturo. quamvis nec Andecavis cautior, pro exercitato milite vulgus obstratorum aut clientium in arma rapiens, exercitatiori Romano trucidandum objecit. & ipse spe manuum conferendi abjecta, incertis latebris victores frustratus, postremo visis militibus qui effugia insederant, sua manu cecidit. Hunc vitæ simul & belli Treverici finem habuit dux, qui cupidius quam providentius arma contra Romanos induerat.
units.tr: A vain remedy for tumults. Many more: and if they were allowed to tell the truth, since they were forbidden, they had spread more atrocious reports. These are the words of Tacitus about Vitellius (Histories 3). Perhaps some reason moved Tiberius as well: either because he knew the forces of the conspirators to be small, or because he was moving secret machinations to crush them with secret plans. But the enemy leaders did not for this reason pursue calmer counsels. For Florus, determined to persuade a wing of cavalry and whatever else was to break out early in the war, although not more cautious than the Andecavi, seizing the common mass of debtors or clients for arms, threw them against the Roman troops, more experienced, to be slaughtered. And he himself, his hope of coming to hand-to-hand combat cast aside, deceiving the victors by uncertain hiding-places, at last, when he saw the soldiers who had occupied the escape routes, fell by his own hand. This was the end of the life and of the Treveran war of this leader, who had taken up arms against the Romans more eagerly than prudently.

units.la: LXXXI. Non ostentandum ante quàm gerendum bellum.
units.tr: LXXXI. That a war should not be displayed before it is waged.

units.la: Quod monitum quia Andecavi, Turonii, Treviri neglexerant, propero cladis damno mulctati fuerunt.
units.tr: Because the Andecavi, the Turonii and the Treviri had neglected this warning, they were punished with a swift loss in defeat.

units.la: Apud Æduos major moles exorta. primò quia iram non ante contractas vires effuderunt. deinde quia opibus magis pollebant. quanto civitas opulentior. Viros enim, arma, stipendium, commeatum bellum contra potentes requirit. Tertio quia erumpendi opportunitatem exspectabant. comprimendi procul praesidium. Quarto quia aptam gerendo aut trahendo bello sedem legunt. Augustodunum, caput gentis, armatis cohortibus Sacrovir occupaverat. copias quà vi quà arte augent. nobilissimam Galliarum sobolem, liberalibus studiis ibi operatam, ut eo pignore parentes propinquosque eorum adjungeret, detinuit. 5. arma antequam pugnam adornant. simul arma occultè fabricata juventuti dispertit. 6. nec servilis conditionis gladiatores aspernantur. adduntur è servitiis gladiatura destinati, quibus moregentico continuum ferri tegumen. 7. vicinorum studia & opes allicíunt. augê- bantur ha copia, vicinarum civitatum, ut nondum aperta consensione,ita viritim promptis studiis. 8. ho- ftium errorem in sapientiam sibi convertunt. certa- mine ducum Romanorum, quos inter ambigebatur, utroque bellum sibi poscentes.
units.tr: Among the Aedui a greater upheaval arose. (1) First, because they poured out their anger before their forces had been gathered. (2) Second, because they were more powerful in resources, the wealthier the state, since war against the powerful demands men, arms, pay and supplies. (3) Third, because they were waiting for an opportunity to break out, a garrison stationed far off to hold them down. (4) Fourth, because they chose a seat suited to waging or prolonging the war, Sacrovir had seized Augustodunum, the capital of the tribe, with armed cohorts; they increased their troops by force or by craft, and he held back the noblest offspring of Gaul, who were being educated there in the liberal arts, so that with that pledge he might bind their parents and kinsmen to himself. (5) They prepared their arms before the battle: he secretly distributed among the young men weapons that had been made in secret. (6) They did not scorn gladiators of servile condition: gladiators destined for the arena were added from the slaves, to whom a continuous covering of iron was given. (7) They attracted the goodwill and resources of their neighbours; these forces were increased by the neighbouring states, not yet by open agreement, but with ready zeal, man by man. (8) They turned the enemy's error to their own advantage, since the Roman commanders were disputing with one another, each demanding the war for himself.

units.la: LXXXII.
units.tr: LXXXII.

units.la: Altitudine animi septus vano rumore non movetur.
units.tr: A mind of high courage, sheltered, is not moved by empty rumour.

units.la: Levium animorum est, ut & popularis Euripi, rumor Famatimori morum incônstantia jactari. Si quid adversæ tempestatis ingruat, fi quid pertinam fatiscentem unde irrepserit, de tota navi actum clamitabunt. Si quis provinciae angulus in motu esse coeperit, omnia ad commotionem nutare fulpicabuntur. cuncta (ut mos fama) in majus credita.
units.tr: Light-minded men, like the popular Euripus, are tossed about by rumour fed by fear and by their own inconstancy. If some storm of adversity rises, or if a plank in the ship begins to give way anywhere, they cry out that the whole ship is lost. If some corner of the province begins to stir, they suspect that everything is tottering towards upheaval. Everything is believed to be larger than it is, as is the custom of rumour.

units.la: Quaerunt in scirpo (soliti quod dicere) nodum. ut ait Ennius, xvi. Annal.
units.tr: They look for a knot in a bulrush, as the saying goes, as Ennius puts it, Annals book 16.

units.la: Nec uno omnes vultu, tristi vel laeto, adversum rumor excipiunt. optimus quisque Reip. causa morere bat. Horum, ut de publico folicitorum, lenius inter pretanda trepidatio, plures privatae tantum rei jactura damnum communi metiuntur. multi odio prefentium, & cupidine mutationis, suis quoque periculis labantur. peffimi cohortatis cives, qui non tantum publicae ruinae expectatione non moerent, sed laetari tur. Sic motu Catilinario, incendio urbi parato, pleri-que Catilinae inceptum, animi levitate & inconsulto motu, probabant. Sic post Galbae in urbe caedem, post Othoniam ruinam, post Vitellianam stragem, Flavianis in ipso foro savientibus, populares Romae balneis, epulis, scortis, applausu insaniebant. Tam in humana publicae simul & privatae rei securitas ple-rosque invalerat, ut eandem urbem & futuram credere res & laetari, nec probris in imperantes, commotis fe-mel animis, abstinetur. clausa secreto animorum, & concepta adversus rectores odia, trumpunt. increpa-bantque Tiberium, quod in tanto rerum motu, libelli accusatorum insumeret operam. priscum rerum in libertate statum, quo domi tranquillis rebus, nullo liberorum nisi ad summovendum usu, ferrum in hostium cervicem stringebatur. miseram pacem vel bello bene mutari. Tiberius constans animi contra hostilem motum, firmus adversus populi rumores, tanto impensius in securitatem compositus, neque loco, neque vultu mutato, sed, ut solitum, per illos dies egit. non enim concursatione, loci mutatione, vultus incerta trepidatione, hostem ferire poterat. Et petulantiae popularis insultum non alio modo commodipori frangere, quam non curando, aut non ulterius irritando, noverat.
units.tr: Not all men receive the rumour with the same face, whether sad or cheerful. Every good citizen was grieving for the commonwealth's sake. Among these, the anxiety of those concerned for public affairs is the more moderate, and they reckon the loss of private property alone as a harm to the common good. Many, from hatred of the present and a longing for change, are carried away even at the cost of their own dangers. The worst citizens rejoice, not only not grieving at the expectation of the public ruin, but exulting in it. So in the Catilinarian commotion, with fire prepared for the city, most approved Catiline's enterprise out of levity of mind and rash agitation. So after the slaughter of Galba in the city, after the ruin of Otho, after the massacre of the Vitellians, while the Flavians raged in the very forum, the common people of Rome went mad over baths, feasts and prostitutes, and applause. So widely had a certain carelessness about public and private affairs taken hold of most men, that they both believed the city would fall and rejoiced in it; nor did they refrain from insults against those in power once their minds had been stirred. They kept their hatreds hidden in their hearts and nursed them against the rulers. They inveighed against Tiberius because, in so great an upheaval, he spent his effort on the libels of accusers. They praised the old state of things in freedom, when in peaceful times at home iron was drawn against an enemy's neck and used for nothing but driving off the enemy. They said that a wretched peace was better exchanged even for war. Tiberius, steady of mind against the hostile agitation, firm against the rumours of the people, set himself all the more earnestly to keep things secure; he changed neither his place nor his expression, but spent those days as was his custom. For he could not strike the enemy by running about, by changing places, or by a wavering agitation of the face. And he knew that the assault of popular wantonness could be broken in no other way than by not heeding it, or by not provoking it further.

units.la: Bacchae bacchanti si velis adversarier, Ex insana insaniorem facies; feriet saepius: Si obsequare, una resolvas plaga, apud Plautum monetur Amphytr. Act.2.Sc.2.
units.tr: If you wish to oppose a raving Bacchante, you will make her more mad than before, and she will strike more often; if you comply, you will loosen her with a single blow. Plautus gives this warning in the Amphitryon, Act 2, Scene 2.

units.la: Hac vulgi trepidatione sive altitudine animi superior fuit, sive quod Gallorum belli momenta comperat modica esse, et vulgatis leviora; vel constantis in adversis animi, vel providentiae. Tiberius laudem meretur.
units.tr: In the face of this popular alarm Tiberius was superior, either through the height of his spirit, or because he learned that the dangers of the Gallic war were slight and less than rumour made them; he deserves praise either for steadfastness of mind in adversity or for foresight.

units.la: LXXXIII.
units.tr: LXXXIII.

units.la: Militem fiducia, ducem solertia commendat.
units.tr: Confidence commends the soldier, skill the general.

units.la: Egregie Otho imperator: Vobis arma et animus sit; mihi consilium, et virtutis vestrae regimen relinquite. lib.1.Histor. non quod strepitus et fiduciae sui gloriatio, nondum experimento hostis capto, bellum profligaret. contra, ut idem Otho monet, fortissimus in ipso discrimine exercitus est, qui ante discrimen quietissimus. Datur haec venia Germanicis legionibus, urgendo spatia itinerum frementibus: viderent modo ad-versos et adspicerentur, id satis ad victoriam. Nove-rant enim Gallos ea tempestate mollitie diuturnae pa-cis fractos, et armorum juxta cum ignarissimis peritos. Quare fiduciam eam Silius hortando etiam auget: pudendum ipsis, quod Germaniarum victores, adver-
units.tr: Otho the emperor spoke admirably: "Let the arms and the spirit be yours; leave me the counsel and the direction of your valour." Not that noise and boasting of one's own confidence, before the enemy has been tested by experience, will bring a war to an end. On the contrary, as the same Otho warns, the army is most brave in the very crisis which was most quiet before the crisis. This indulgence is granted to the German legions, who, in marching, rage at the length of the journeys; they need only see the enemy and be seen by them, and that is enough for victory. For they knew that the Gauls at that time had been broken by the softness of long peace, and were skilled in arms only in the way that the most inexperienced men are. Therefore Silius, in exhorting them, even increases that confidence: it would be a disgrace for them, the conquerors of the Germans, to be led against the Gauls as though against an enemy. This na-

units.la: sum Gallos tanquam in hostem ducerentur. Hæc nam-
units.tr: tion of the Gauls, once to be feared by the Romans, had so fallen away from itself that under the emperor Trajan it was regarded as a por-

units.la: tio Gallorum, Romanis olim formidanda, tantum à
units.tr: The nation of the Gauls, once feared by the Romans, had so far degenerated from itself that under the emperor Trajan it was regarded as a portent.

units.la: fe ipsa degeneraverat, ut Trajano sub imperatore por-
units.tr: had itself so degenerated that under the emperor Trajan it was regarded as a portent.

units.la: tentiloco haberetur, Gallos olim belli gloria floruisse,
units.tr: ...was held in the place of a tent-dweller, though the Gauls of old had flourished in the glory of war,

units.la: nam Gallos quoque in bello floruisse accepimus. mox:
units.tr: For we have also heard that the Gauls flourished in war. Soon:

units.la: segnitia cum otio intravit, amissa virtute pariter ac li-
units.tr: Sloth came in along with idleness, and virtue was lost together with liberty.

units.la: bertate. in Vita Julii Agricolæ. De Gallis, quod de
units.tr: What was said of the Ionians, Campanians and Milesians could be said of the Gauls.

units.tr: It could be thrown at them, as at the Ionians, Campanians and Milesians: [illegible, ~12 letters]. There were once vigorous men

units.la: Milefii. Cæterum glorioso militi, quàm provido duci,
units.tr: The Milesians. But for a glorious soldier, rather than for a provident commander,

units.la: convenientius fuerit illud Spartani imperatoris, non,
units.tr: it would have been more fitting for that saying of the Spartan commander, which runs: not

units.tr: (continued from the previous unit)

units.tr: as if victory were already in hand, the outcome of the war beyond doubt, however strong the enemy may be.

units.la: gloriationem dedocere Spartanum Thebanus impe-
units.tr: The Theban commander, outstanding in both courage and skill, could have taught the Spartan to unlearn that boasting.

units.la: rator, virtute simul & solertia eximius poterat.
units.tr: (continued from the previous unit)

units.la: LXXXIV.
units.tr: LXXXIV.

units.la: Opulentia prædæ quam bello gerendo aptior.
units.tr: Wealth is more suited to plunder than to waging war.

units.la: Opulentia nimirum voluptatibus enervata, & ar-moru[?] intermisso usu fluxa. de qua hoc loco Silius: quanto pecunia dites, & voluptatibus opulentos, tanto magis imbellis Æduos[?], evincite, & fugientibus confilite. Nec insulsè, quicunque ille ad Cesarem De Ordinanda Republica Declamator: Sapè jam audivi, qui reges quæ civitates & nationes per opulentiam magna im-peria amiserint, quæ per virtutem inopes ceperant, quam dicti assertationem per nationes & imperia, per imperandi & serviendi vicissitudines, exemplis in Augusto nostro diduximus. Quare Mæcenas Augustum dissertiffima oratione, quæ extat apud Dionem Cassium libro 52, monet; perpetuum, ex inopi maximè hominum genere, militem conscribat, alat, procul ab urbe habeat; cæteris ad sua, ut in pace, negotia dila-suris. Solertiffimi nimirum ingenii homo videbat, non posse jam à censu, ut rudi Tullii & tenuis opulen-tiæ ætate, militem legi. alios amplexu divitiarum, plures delitiarum solvente nervos somite, à bello ge-rendo. rendo[?] abhorrere. Aeropum & Damasippum tribunos, quod psaltriam è lupanari mercede conductam in ca-stra adduxerant, è regni sui finibus Philippus ejecit.
units.tr: Wealth, indeed, enervates men with pleasures and loosens them through disuse of arms. Silius speaks of this place: "The richer a people is in money and the more luxurious in pleasures, the more unfit it is for war; conquer them, and make a stand against those who flee." Nor unwisely does that declaimer to Caesar, in his work On Ordering the Commonwealth, say: "I have often heard of kings, cities and nations who lost great empires through wealth, having held them when poor through virtue." We have drawn out this assertion, through nations and empires and the alternation of ruling and serving, with examples from our Augustus. Hence Maecenas, in a most eloquent speech found in Dio Cassius, book 52, advises Augustus to enroll a standing army chiefly from the poorest class of men, to feed them, and to keep them far from the city, while the others attend to their own affairs as in peacetime. That man of most subtle genius saw that soldiers could no longer be levied by the census, as in the days of Tullius, when wealth was rude and slight. Others, embraced by riches, and most by pleasures which, like fuel, loosen the sinews of the spirit, shrink from waging war. Philip expelled from his kingdom the tribunes Aeropus and Damasippus, because they had brought into camp a harpist hired for money from a brothel.

units.la: Idem Tarentinum quendam, magnæ in castris existi-mationis hominem, tribunatu militiæ dimovit, quod calidis balneis usus fuisset: nescire mihi videris, inquiens, Macedonum mores, apud quos ne mulier quidem puerpera calido lavacro utitur. At Romæ, Augusti quidem ætate, minimum ex opulentia vitiorum fuit, Bajis & balneis assidere. Quam vero divitiæ homines immutent, ut non cognoscas eundem esse, non alii magis, quam illi ipsi Macedones, bello Alexandri ditati, documento fuerint. Cum præda Bactriana pigri, militiam apud Indos detrectarent, Alexander omnium plaustra spoliis onusta, orsus à suo, concremavit. Exeo promptos ad militiam, & strenuos ut ante, milites habebat. Nondum voluptas viros militares, nondum otium ab armis, jam opulentiæ con-spectus fregerat. Ejusdem Alexandri, qui jam naturæ concesserat, virtute quondam nunc argenteis clypeis conspicui milites, Argyraspides, ab Eumene in novam militiam allecti, à jejunis Macedonum tyronibus, ut gloriæ Asiatici belli ita prædæ nescii, victi, clypeis & arrogantia simul exuebantur. Non vano igitur hor-tamento Silius legionarios, ut nuper Sueonas Gusta-vus, à divitiis hostium in spem victoriæ adducit.
units.tr: Philip also removed from the tribunate of the soldiers a certain Tarentine, a man of great esteem in the camp, because he had used hot baths. "You seem not to know," he said, "the customs of the Macedonians, among whom not even a woman who has just given birth uses a hot bath." But at Rome, in the age of Augustus indeed, there was least of vice arising from wealth, in sitting at Baiae and the baths. How much riches change men, so that you would not recognise the same man, no one shows more clearly than those very Macedonians, enriched by Alexander's war. When the lazy men, having the Bactrian booty, refused military service among the Indians, Alexander set fire to all the wagons laden with spoils, beginning with his own. Thus he had soldiers ready for service and as vigorous as before. Not yet had pleasure weakened the military men, not yet had leisure drawn them from arms; now the sight of wealth had broken them. Of that same Alexander, who had already gone to nature, the soldiers once renowned for virtue, now conspicuous for their silver shields, the Argyraspides, enlisted by Eumenes into a new service, were defeated by the hungry Macedonian recruits. These, as ignorant of plunder as they were of the glory of the Asiatic war, stripped them of their shields and their arrogance together. Not in vain, therefore, does Silius lead the legionaries into hope of victory from the riches of the enemy, as lately Gustavus led the Swedes.

units.la: LXXXV.
units.tr: LXXXV.

units.la: Continua ferrearum laminarum moles operosior, quàm militiæ utilior.
units.tr: A continuous mass of iron plates is more laborious to make than it is useful to soldiers.

units.la: Ut accipiendis ictibus impenetrabilis, ita inferendis inhabilis. Paulum mora attulere ferrati, restantibus laminis adversum pila & gladios. Sed miles correptis securibus & dolabris, ut si murum perrumperet, cadere tegmina & corpora. Quidam trudibus aut furcis, inertem molem prosternere, jacentesque nullo ad resur-gendum[?] nisi, quasi exanimes linquebantur. Præstabat per futuras[?] & compages complicatilem armaturam, ut Trojanis temporibus, gerere, aut, ut Romanorum militia, galeam capiti, loricam pectori, ocreas cruris, clypeum manui sinistrae aptare ac demere. Quam ad panopliam Apostolus in militia Christiana, Ephes. 6. [illegible, ~12 letters] v.13. respexit. Aliis levior aut nulla [illegible, ~10 letters] armatura, ut fere olim Germanis placuit. Medius inter hos & illos Alexander, Macedonibus loco tho- racum assignavit, ut pectora tegi, terga vero nudari, pugnae magis quam fugae memores, vel salutis absque gloriae intuitu, resisterent. Equiti fortassis quam apud Gallos Crupellario pediti, id genus tegminum melius conveniret, quod Sarmatis in usu fuisse, sed non magno adversus Romanos expeditiores usu, primo Hi-storiarum traditur. cataphractarum pondere (id princi-pibus & nobilissimo cuique tegmen, ferreis lamin-is, aut praduro corio confertum:) ut adversus illum impetum hostium provolutis inhabile ad resurgendum. Quod equestris militiae genus, habili-tate quadam discrepans, cum Mauritius Auraicus Bel-gica militia inter primos reduxisset, mirum non est, fi equos robore & altitudine ad certam mensuram equi-bus praescriberet.
units.tr: It is impenetrable to blows received, but unfit for striking them. The armoured men caused a little delay, since the plates held against javelins and swords. But the soldier, seizing axes and mattocks, cut through the coverings and bodies as if he were breaking through a wall. Some, with cudgels or forks, overthrew the inert mass, and those who lay down were left as if lifeless, with no means of rising again. It was better to wear armour fitted together with joints and seams, as in the days of the Trojans, or, as in the Roman army, to put on and take off a helmet for the head, a breastplate for the chest, greaves for the legs and a shield for the left hand. The Apostle had this panoply in view in the Christian warfare, Eph. 6. [...] v. 13. Others wore lighter armour or none, as the Germans once preferred. Alexander, midway between these and those, assigned to the Macedonians the thorax, so that the chest was covered and the back left bare, mindful of fighting rather than fleeing, or of safety without regard to glory, they might stand their ground. For the horseman, perhaps, that kind of covering would suit better than for the heavily armoured Gallic foot-soldier. The Sarmatians used it, but as the first Histories record, it was not much used against the Romans, who were more mobile. The weight of the cataphracts (a covering for princes and every noble, made of iron plates or of hardened leather) left them, against that onslaught of the enemy, unable to rise once thrown down. Since this kind of cavalry service differs in its suitability, it is no wonder that Maurice of Orange, when he first restored it among the foremost of the Belgian army, prescribed to the horses a fixed measure of strength and height.

units.la: LXXXVI.
units.tr: LXXXVI.

units.la: Media virum principem oratio, nec addens vero nec demens, addecet.
units.tr: A moderate manner of speech suits a leading man: neither adding to the truth nor going out of his mind.

units.la: [illegible, ~20 letters] enim laudi suæ detrahendo, irrisum, [illegible, ~8 letters] aliena facta in suam gloriam vertendo, occul-tum odium meretur. [illegible, ~24 letters] quam Dionysius Halicarnaffæus vocat, vacare omni tempore agré po-terit. ad hanc mensuram Tiberius ortum patratumque bellum [?] senatui scripsit: neque dempsit aut addidit, vero: [?] sed fide ac virtute legatos, fe consiliis superfuisse. Benè de legatis Tiberius: qui non peralios gesta avi-dus intercepit; aut, quod in Corbulonem Claudius factitavit, à militiæ gloria invidus retraxit.
units.tr: [...] for by detracting from his own praise he deserves ridicule, and by turning the deeds of others to his own glory he deserves hidden hatred. [...] which Dionysius of Halicarnassus calls ... will be able to be free at every time. By this measure Tiberius wrote to the senate about the war that was begun and carried through: he neither subtracted nor added to the truth, but wrote that his legates had surpassed him in faithfulness and courage, and that he had surpassed them in counsel. Tiberius spoke well of his legates: he did not greedily seize the deeds of others, nor, as Claudius habitually did against Corbulo, did he begrudgingly withdraw them from the glory of war.

units.la: LXXXVII.
units.tr: LXXXVII.

units.la: Minora belli negotia regis præfen-tiam non requiruntur.
units.tr: Minor matters of war do not require the presence of the prince.

units.la: Quod enim salvo rerum statu per legatos confici potest, graviorum rerum curam principi non extor-quear. Ilto velamine absentiam suam & Drufi, pro-fundamque commota Gallia securitatem, fingere an fiće, Tiberius tegebat: magnitudinem imperii extol-lens, neque decorum principibus, si una alteraye[?] civi-tas turbet, omissa urbe, unde in omnia regimen. Pri-mum igitur excusationis pondus à magnitudine im-perii, quod distractionem curarum ad unum vulnus non admittat, certè non exigat alterum ab indecoro: si rerum supremus arbiter in omni acie versetur. Ter-tium à necessitudine Italiæ & urbis, cui laboraturæ ante omnia subcurrendum. Plura quæ huc pertinent, &[?] primi libri annalium, ad ea verba non omittere caput rerum, neque se remque publicam in casum dare. Sed quid sibi volunt sequentia: nunc quia non metu duca-tur, iturum, an igitur tantus Romanorum imperator, toties ante adeptum principatum triumphalis, bellum & carma Gallorum formidaverat. non hic legitimus verborum sensus: verum urbi, quæ sua præsentia foven-da erat, ne quid absente concussi paterentur metuerat. nunc eo metu sublato, iturum se in Galliam pollicetur; si polliceri est, verbis, quod nunquam sis facturus, præste ferre.
units.tr: For what can be carried out through legates, with the state of affairs unharmed, the prince should not be dragged into caring for the more serious matters. Tiberius concealed behind this veil both his own absence and that of Drusus, and pretended that the deep alarm in Gaul was security: extolling the greatness of the empire, and saying it was unbecoming for princes, if one or another city were disturbed, to leave the city from which the government of everything is directed. First, then, the weight of his excuse rested on the greatness of the empire, which does not admit the distraction of cares to a single point, and certainly does not demand a second from the disgrace of inaction, if the supreme arbiter of affairs is to be present in every battle line. Third, it rested on the need of Italy and the city, which had to be run to before all else. More that bears on this is found in the first book of the Annals, at the words not to leave the head of affairs, nor to put himself and the commonwealth at risk. But what do the following words mean: now that he is not led by fear, he will go? Was so great a Roman emperor, so often triumphant before he gained the principate, afraid of the war and the arms of the Gauls? This is not the legitimate sense of the words. Rather, he had feared for the city, which was to be cherished by his presence, lest it suffer any shaking in his absence. Now that this fear is removed, he promises to go into Gaul. If to promise is to say in words what one will never do, then he has carried it out.

units.la: LXXXVIII.
units.tr: LXXXVIII.

units.la: Inter potentiæ æmulos amborum gratiam captare, raro nocebit.
units.tr: To seek the favour of both of two rivals for power will rarely do harm.

units.la: Dum id fiat sine obtrectatione alterius: id enim tum sordidum est, tum, si emanet, minus tutum. Ar-chelai, Cappadocum regis, acerbum in fenestute ca-sum, qui Caji offensione vitata Tiberium Rhodi agen-tem neglexerat, superiori libro percepimus. Quirinius, qui rectore C. Cæsar Armeniam obtinenti datus, Tiberium quoque Rhodi agentem coluerat, perpetua apud imperantes gratia, publicis exequiis, petente à senatu principe, quod rarum, frequentabatur. Tu, si me au-dis, captanda omnium gratia benignus, contrahenda vel unius offensa astrictus esto.
units.tr: This holds provided it is done without disparaging the other, for that is then base and, if it comes out, less safe. We related in the previous book the bitter fall of Archelaus, king of the Cappadocians, who, having avoided the offence of Gaius, had neglected Tiberius while he was staying at Rhodes. Quirinius, who had been given to Gaius Caesar as adviser while he held Armenia, had also cultivated Tiberius while he was staying at Rhodes, and enjoyed a lasting favour with those in power; when the emperor asked it of the senate, he was given a public funeral, a rare honour that was frequently granted. You, if you will listen to me, should be kindly in seeking the favour of all, and should keep yourself bound not to incur the offence of even one person.

units.la: LXXXIX.
units.tr: LXXXIX.

units.la: Délatorem interpretetem nemo fatis vitabit.
units.tr: No one will sufficiently avoid the informer who twists meanings.

units.la: Quid enim evites, ubi & honori data, & praemio coronata, à circumstantia aliqua facti, in crimen tra-huntur? C. Lutorium Priscum equitem Romanum, post celebre carmen, quo Germanici supremâ defleverat, pecunia donatum à Cafare, corripuit delator: objectans agro Drufo composuisse, quod fi exfinctus foret, majore pramio vulgaretur. Oderat quidem Tiberius Germanici affectatores, verum occulte oderat, ubi vero nimium defuncti studium, cum aemuli offensione aut neglectu, arguitur: sycophanta interprete justus irae pannus affuitur, quasi in atroci delicto, indicium reo ultimum supplicium. Circumspiciant, qui per vanilo-quentiam pangendis panegyricis, laude aut vituperatione nimii sunt, quid, perquem, cui, quo rerum statu efferant.
units.tr: For what can you avoid when even things given as honours and crowned with rewards are twisted into a charge by some circumstance of the deed? The informer seized Gaius Lutorius Priscus, a Roman knight, who after the famous poem in which he mourned Germanicus at his death had been rewarded with money by Caesar. He accused him of having composed it for the estate of Drusus, and said that if Drusus had died, it would have been published for a greater reward. Tiberius indeed hated those who aspired to Germanicus, but he hated them in secret; yet when the excessive zeal for the dead man is charged as an offence to, or neglect of, a rival, the informer's interpretation adds a cloak of anger, as if for an atrocious crime, the accusation brings the ultimate punishment on the accused. Let those who, through extravagant speech in composing panegyrics, go too far in praise or blame consider well what they are extolling, about whom, to whom, and in what state of affairs.

units.la: XC.
units.tr: XC.

units.la: Non omnia ad vivum judici resecanda sunt.
units.tr: Not everything is to be cut back to the quick by a judge.

units.la: Infestis judicibus capitis causam Lutorius, ob car-minis vanitatem, dicebat. Caeteris ad ultimi supplicii calculum, captandae Tiberii gratiae, properantibus; M. Lepidus non ille quidem patrocinium rei, sed miti-gationem sententiae suscepit. Ejus orationem quod gravitate monitorum plena est, examinabimus. Si P.C. unum id spectamus, quàm nefaria voce Lutorius Pri-fcus mentem suam & aures hominum polluerit. Viam ingreditur severitate dicti, quò plus autoritatis in sen-tentia dicenda expectetur. monemur interim, vanilo-quentia ac obtrectatione mentem linguamque dicen-tium, & aures audientium pollui. Neque carcer, neque laqueus, ne serviles quidem cruciatus in eum suffece-rint. [illegible, ~8 letters] potius, quàm quod ita sentiret, largitur. subjicit enim: vana à scelestis, dicta à malefi-cus differunt. praemittit tamen: sin flagitia, & faci-nora nora sine modo sunt : supplicius ac remediis principis moderatio, majorumque & vestra exempla, tempe-rant.
units.tr: Lutorius faced a capital charge before hostile judges, for the vanity of a poem. While the others hurried to the final verdict of execution, seeking to win Tiberius's favour, M. Lepidus undertook not indeed the defence of the accused but the softening of the sentence. Since his speech is full of weighty warnings, we shall examine it. If, Conscript Fathers, we look only at this one point, how wickedly Lutorius Priscus has polluted his own mind and the ears of men with his voice. He enters on a path of severity in his words, so that more authority may be expected in the sentence to be pronounced. Meanwhile we are reminded that the minds and tongues of speakers, and the ears of listeners, are polluted by idle talk and detraction. Neither prison, nor noose, nor even slavish tortures would have been enough against him [illegible, about eight letters] rather than concede that he thought so. For he adds that idle words differ from wicked deeds, and sayings from crimes. He premises, however, but if crimes and deeds are without measure, the moderation of punishments and the remedies of the prince, and the examples of our ancestors and of you, temper them.

units.la: Ab infinita scelerum graffatione ad majorum,sup-pliciis irrogandis in mitiorem partem propendenti-um, exempla impellit. Quod iis observari velim, qui sententiae rigidioris autores,illud in ore semper ferunt: Crescentibus delictis crescunt poena. Sic audientia sibi praeparata,illud in quo maxima vis est, proponit: & vana a scelestis, dicta a maleficiis differunt. non enim pari supplicio garrule loquax & parricida, sermone ac ingenio vanus & sceleribus coopertus, premendus. Locum in scholarum umbra habeat Stoicorum effatum: delicta esse aequalia : a tribunalium severitate, & a recepto vitae usu exulet. Caetera orationis Lepidi mediocria sunt: quare ad magis urgentia abimus.
units.tr: From the endless rage of crimes he turns to the examples of our ancestors, who leaned towards milder measures in inflicting punishments. I would have this observed by those who are the authors of the harsher opinion and always carry on their lips the saying: As offences grow, so do punishments grow. Thus, having prepared his audience, he sets forth the point in which the greatest force lies: idle words differ from wicked deeds, and sayings from crimes. For a chattering talker and a parricide, a man empty in speech and talent and a man covered in crimes, are not to be punished with the same penalty. Let the Stoic maxim that all offences are equal have its place in the shade of the schools; let it be banished from the severity of the courts and from the accepted practice of life. The rest of Lepidus's speech is ordinary, so we pass on to matters that press more urgently.

units.la: XCI.
units.tr: XCI.

units.la: Ad ampliandum promptior quam ad damnandum judex esto.
units.tr: The judge should be readier to acquit than to condemn.

units.la: Damnati enim iniquo judicio ad supplicium non est in integrum restitutio, nec damni compensatio, quin & inter sententiam, & executionem supplicii, temporis aliqua mora intercedat. quemadmodum laudando patrum exemplo factum S.C.ne decreta patrum, ante diem decimum, ad aerarium deferrentur, idque vitae spatium damnatis prorogaretur. quanquam fronte speciosius, quam usu efficacius, decretum hoc reperiebatur. quia non senatui libertas adpœ-nitendum erat, neque Tiberius interjectu temporis mitigabatur. vanum igitur judicum decretum, vana mitigationis ostentatio. nec vana tantum, sed & productione[?] miseriae crudelis. Quosdam enim Tiberius, quod se nondum in gratiam cum iis rediisse affirmaret, diuturna supplicii expestatione cruciatos, ut autor est Dio Cassius, in carcere detinuit. Beneficium enim judicabat, promptam supplicii irrogationem. Atrea fortassis imitatus, quem ita loquentem Seneca in Thyeste introducit:
units.tr: For there is no restoration to the condemned who have been put to death by an unjust judgment, nor any compensation for the loss, and moreover some interval of time intervenes between the sentence and the execution of the punishment. Following the example of the Fathers, the Senate in its praiseworthy decree ordered that the decrees of the Fathers should be carried to the treasury before the tenth day, and that the span of life should thereby be extended for the condemned. Yet this decree, though fairer in appearance than effective in practice, was found to be so, because the Senate had no freedom to repent, and Tiberius was not softened by the lapse of time. The decree of the judges was therefore empty, and the display of mitigation empty too; and not only empty, but cruel in its prolonging of misery. For Tiberius, because he affirmed that he had not yet returned to favour with some men, kept them in prison, tormenting them with a lengthy expectation of punishment, as Dio Cassius reports. For he judged that a prompt infliction of punishment was a kindness. Perhaps he imitated Atreus, whom Seneca introduces speaking thus in the Thyestes:

units.la: De fine pœnæ loqueris, ego pœnam volo: Perimat tyrannus lenis: in regno meo Mors impetretur.
units.tr: You speak of the end of punishment; I want punishment: let the gentle tyrant destroy; in my kingdom let death be begged for.

units.la: XCII.
units.tr: XCII.

units.la: Non attrectandum quod obtinere nequeas.
units.tr: What you cannot obtain, do not meddle with.

units.la: Non modò de vitiorum coërcitione, verùm etiam de coërcendi facultate sapienti reip. moderatori cogitandum. Ne remedium intempestivè susceptum vel perseverando corpus reip. concutiat, vel omittendo pudorem medenti afferat. Cum de luxu, qui civitatem pervaserat, coërcendo sermones in senatu jacerentur; Tiberius ea de reconsultus, maturè pensitavit, an[?] coërcere tam profusa cupidines possent; num coërcitio, plus damni in Remp. ferret; quàm indecorum attrectare quod non obtinere tur, vel retentum ignominiam & infamiam virorum illustrium posceret. Populum aliquem grassandi per omnia scelera licentia invasit, leges intermortuæ quiescunt, regi, à nobilitate aut plurium factione dependenti, nulla ad comprimendum facultas. Quis hic remedio locus, aut quid emendandi errorem spei? Concionatorum aliquis, aut antiquorum morum civis, clamabit: non permittendam sceleribus impunitatem, resecanda malorum facinorum ulcera, Deum & naturæ communis vocem flagitio-rum coërcitionem flagitare. Vir prudens, & seculi morum peritus, an coërcere sit in potestate nostra, an fine reip. eversione agitari queat, in animum advocabit. Nimis crudum illud: Fiat justitia, & pereat mundus: nisi, Salutem populi supremam esse legem, inepte Romani legumlatores in prima lege monuerunt. Prior ut corpus integrum permaneat, quam ut nociturum parti corporis ulcus rescindatur, cura legislatorem capiat.
units.tr: The wise ruler of the state must consider not only the restraint of vices but also his ability to restrain them. Lest an untimely remedy, by persevering, shake the body of the commonwealth, or, by being dropped, bring shame upon the healer. When in the Senate, while deliberating on restraining the luxury that had pervaded the city, remarks were made, Tiberius, having consulted on these matters, weighed in good time whether he could restrain such lavish desires at all; whether restraint would do more harm to the state than it would be unseemly to meddle with what could not be obtained, or than the retention of it would demand the disgrace and infamy of illustrious men. A people has been seized by a licence to rage through every kind of crime, the laws lie dead and quiet, the king depends on the nobility or on the faction of the many, and there is no means of checking them. What place is there here for a remedy, or what hope of correcting the error? Some preacher, or a citizen of the old morals, will cry out that impunity must not be granted to crimes, that the ulcers of evil deeds must be cut away, and that God and the common voice of nature demand the punishment of wickedness. The prudent man, skilled in the morals of his age, will consider whether restraint is within our power, or whether it may be pursued at the cost of the overthrow of the state. That saying, Let justice be done though the world perish, is too harsh; the Romans, lawgivers though they were, wisely warned in their first law that the safety of the people is the supreme law. Let the lawgiver take care that the body remain whole first, rather than that a sore which would harm one part of the body be cut away.

units.la: XCIII.
units.tr: XCIII.

units.la: Primus prudentiæ, alter justitiæ locus debetur.
units.tr: The first place belongs to prudence, the second to justice.

units.la: Primus enim officii fons est veri perspicientia, & communis utilitatis investigatio. Hac imperandi facie Tiberius consilium ex adyto profundae mentis eruit: omittere potius prævalida & adulta vitia, quam hoc adsequi, ut palam fieret, quibus flagitiis impares essemus. Verum hic aphorismus nec a praecedente discedit, & in Augusto nostro, pagina editionis primae 35[?], deductius excusus est. Actum igitur, quod veteri proverbio monemur, ne agamus.
units.tr: For the first source of duty is the perception of truth and the investigation of the common good. With this kind of rule Tiberius drew his counsel out of the sanctuary of a deep mind: rather to pass over strong and grown vices than to bring about that it should become plain how unequal we were to such crimes. But this aphorism does not depart from the preceding one, and it is set out more fully in our Augustus, on page 35 of the first edition. Thus what was done is what the old proverb warns us not to do.

units.la: XCIV.
units.tr: XCIV.

units.la: Unius invidia ab omnibus peccatur.
units.tr: Everyone sins through the envy of one man.

units.la: Quod praemittit Cornelius ore Tiberii axioma: Majus aliquid & excelsius a principe postulatur, excussu non satis dignum judico. Quod enim officii censura diversum genus in civitate majus, quod principe dignius, mo-rum correctione? Quod prae manu est, ita a Tacito formatur: cum recti factorum sibi quisque gratiam trahant, unius invidia ab omnibus peccatur. Nam si invidia licentiae morum frenum laxet: publica morum corruptela illi, ut nimis lento ad castigationem, ut scelerum conniventia autori, impingitur. Sin ad vindicandum severitate prorumpat; alperum eum, saevum, Phalariden, humanitatis legum nescium omnes clamabunt. Quid hic suadendum principi? illud nimirum Senecae, saniori sensu perceptum: Ars prima regni est, posse te invidiam pati.
units.tr: I do not think much of the maxim that Cornelius puts in the mouth of Tiberius: something greater and loftier is demanded of the prince. What kind of office is greater in the state, and more worthy of the prince, than the correction of morals? Tacitus puts into words what lies to hand: since each man claims for himself the credit for good deeds, through the envy of one man all sin. For if envy loosens the bridle of licence, the public corruption of morals is charged against him as too slack in punishing, and the tolerance of crimes as their author. But if he breaks out into severity in punishing, everyone will cry that he is harsh, cruel, a second Phalaris, ignorant of the laws of humanity. What, then, should be urged on the prince here? Surely that saying of Seneca, understood in a sounder sense: the first art of kingship is to be able to endure envy.

units.la: Nam qui ad omnium palatum se circumferret, qui popularis invidia nimium movebitur: hoc certo uspiam gradu consistet, ac ne sis quidem omnium gratiam colliget. Si populi rumorem saluti Fabius ante posuisset, obstrepentem Fabium Scipio moratus fuisset; nec ille victoris Poeni currentem impetum fregisset; nec hic Hannibalem faucibus Italiae abduxisset.
units.tr: For the man who turned himself to suit everyone's palate, and who was too easily moved by popular envy, would never stand firm at any point, and would not gather the goodwill of all, not even of a few. If Fabius had put the people's talk before the safety of the state, Scipio would have been held back by the Fabius who was clamouring; nor would Fabius have checked the onrushing attack of the victorious Carthaginian; nor would Scipio have drawn Hannibal away from the throat of Italy.

units.la: XCV.
units.tr: XCV.

units.la: Legem non ferri, quam contemptu aboleri, consultius.
units.tr: It is more advisable that a law not be enacted than that it be abolished by contempt.

units.la: Rationem pro me reddat Tiberius: nam si velit quod nondum vetitum est: timeas, ne vetere, at si pro-bibita impunè transcenderis, neque metus ultrà, neque pudor est. A legibus ad alias in vita civili conventiones transfer.
units.tr: Let Tiberius give me the reason. For if he wishes to do what has not yet been forbidden, you should fear that the thing may be forbidden later; but once you have transgressed a forbidden thing with impunity, there is neither fear nor shame left. Turn from laws to other agreements in civil life.

units.la: nes transfer. Metu potentioris fœderis, quod fit in-certum, feliciùs vicinum ab inferendo bello absterruis, ris, quàm inito fœmel, & rupto aut contempto fœdere: Expectatione futuri concilii pacatiùs opinionum li-centiam domueris, quàm decreto scissa ecclesiæ concordia, quàa asperaveris faciliùs, quàm in viam reduxeris luxuriantia ingenia.
units.tr: Through fear of a more powerful alliance, whose outcome is uncertain, you will more happily deter a neighbour from waging war than by making and then breaking or scorning a treaty once it is made. By the expectation of a future council you will more calmly tame the licence of opinions, than by a decree that splits the Church's harmony, which will more easily roughen luxuriant minds than bring them back to the right path.

units.la: XCVI.
units.tr: XCVI.

units.la: Fideliorterrã quàm maris excolenti di fundus.
units.tr: Better to cultivate the land than the sea.

units.la: Longissimè à civitatis metà, publica srvgesu, absunt, qui incertis imperii aut negotiationis reditibus fidentes, fundum familiarem deserunt. Tanquam in re sociétati periculosa Tiberius: at Herculè nemo rè-fert, quòd Italia externa opis indiget, quòd vita populi Romani per incerta maris & tempestatum quotidie volvitur. Sed hac de re & in Politicis, & hoc ipso tra-ctatu supra, egimus.
units.tr: Those are far from the middle of the state, and far from the public welfare, who, trusting in the uncertain returns of empire or trade, abandon the family estate. Tiberius speaks as though this were a dangerous matter for the commonwealth. But by Hercules, no one objects that Italy needs foreign help, or that the life of the Roman people is every day tossed about by the uncertainties of the sea and of storms. However, we have treated this matter both in the Politics and earlier in this very treatise.

units.la: XCVII.
units.tr: XCVII.

units.la: Acerrimum necessitatis frenum.
units.tr: The sharpest bridle is necessity.

units.la: At pudoris præstantius. Nobilissimum omnium, quòd voluptatum contemptu, generosi animi capi-tro, à luxu retinet: qui verò satietate tantum & copiæ fastidio mutantur, eos, qui rerum inopia conistringuntur, facultate rerum, non laude virtutum superant.
units.tr: But shame is the more excellent. It is the noblest of all, since it restrains from luxury by the contempt of pleasures, as the bridle of a generous spirit; whereas those who change only from satiety and disgust at plenty surpass, not in the praise of virtue but in the means of obtaining things, those who are held back by lack of resources.

units.la: Probo interim, quòd pudorem imperantibus, non lu-xum, convenire Tiberius docet. Nos pudor s paupertes necessitas; divites satiàs in melius mutet. Malè enim principatus luxuria, malè voluptatum effusa licentia mensuratur.
units.tr: I approve, meanwhile, of Tiberius' teaching that shame, not luxury, befits those who rule. Necessity and poverty bring shame to us; let the rich change for the better by satiety. For the principate is badly measured by luxury, and badly by the unrestrained licence of pleasures.

units.la: XCVIII.
units.tr: XCVIII.

units.la: Morum emendatio nobile supremi principis opus. Fatetur sui oblitus Tiberius: exonerari laborum meorum partem fateor. Inter arcana imperii, sublatum a principibus censorium munus, fuisse, alibi locorum docui.
units.tr: The correction of morals is the noble work of the supreme prince. Tiberius, forgetting himself, confesses: I admit that a part of my labours is being lifted from me. I have shown elsewhere that among the secrets of empire the office of censor was removed by the princes.

units.la: XCIX.
units.tr: XCIX.

units.la: Censores, ut & judices, multorum simultates ægre evitant.
units.tr: Censors, like judges, scarcely avoid the enmities of many.

units.la: Sponte autem, qui simultates colligunt, temere quosvis censura offendendo, aut arrogantes sunt, aut judicii expertes. Tiberius hos scopulos agnovit: credite P.C. me quoque non esse offensionum avidum. quas cum graves, & plerunque iniquas [?], pro Rep. suscipiam, inanes & irritas, neque mihi aut vobis usui futuras, jure deprecor. Hunc locum a Sallustio mutuatus Cornelius, verbis nonnihil dilatatum, videtur. apud quem Cotta Consul ita ad populum: avidissimus privata gratia, maximas inimicitias pro republica suscepi.
units.tr: Those who of their own accord gather enmities, rashly offending everyone by censure, are either arrogant or lack judgement. Tiberius recognised these rocks: Believe me, Conscript Fathers, I too am not greedy for offences. Since I undertake them for the state, though they are grave and for the most part unjust, I rightly protest against them as empty and vain, neither useful to me nor to you. Cornelius seems to have borrowed this passage from Sallust and somewhat expanded it in his words; in whose work the consul Cotta speaks thus to the people: most eager for private favour, I have undertaken very great enmities for the commonwealth.

units.la: Fragmentis.
units.tr: Fragments.

units.la: C.
units.tr: C.

units.la: Exiguum inter magnificentiam & luxuriam interstitium.
