units.tr: A small gap between magnificence and luxury.

units.la: De viris claritudine insignibus Tacitus: studio magnificentia prolabebantur in luxum nimirum & inanem profusionem. Μεγαλοπρέπεια [?] Philosophus appellat: τὸ σεμνὸν [?] præcipuum in ea virtute momentum faciens, quam generosa Stoicorum familia inter virtutes recipere dedignaretur. Virtus enim, ex illorum edicto, & omnibus colenda est; & ultro se facilem omni venanti exponit. Magnificentiæ vero studium nec omnes decet, & nonnisi potentia felicibus contingit. Sit quoddam alti animi, nummorum non tenacis, indicium; serviat civili decoro sumptuosa ædificandi ostentatio; sit rarae beatitudinis fortune munere gloriantis, præclarum signum: inter virtutes omni hominum generi præceptas, & veram animi tranquillitatem generantes, pari consortio non recipitur.
units.tr: Tacitus says of men notable for their renown that they slid, through their zeal for magnificence, into luxury and empty extravagance. The philosopher calls it magnificence [μεγαλοπρέπεια], making dignity [τὸ σεμνὸν] the chief element in that virtue, which the noble family of the Stoics disdained to admit among the virtues. For virtue, by their decree, is to be cultivated by all, and offers itself readily to anyone who seeks it. But the pursuit of magnificence does not befit everyone, and comes only to the favoured of power. Let it be a sign of a lofty spirit that is not tight-fisted with money; let showy building serve a civil decorum; let it be a distinguished sign of a man who boasts of the gift of rare happiness from fortune: yet among the virtues prescribed to every kind of man, and producing true tranquillity of mind, it is not received on equal terms.

units.la: CI.
units.tr: CI.

units.la: Lex viva vita imperantis.
units.tr: The living law is the life of the ruler.

units.la: Vita Principis censura est : ad hanc dirigimur, ad hanc convertimur : nec tam imperio nobis opus est, quàm exemplo. Plinius in Panegyrico de speculo parcimoniae Vespasiano Tacitus : praecipuus affectus morum auctor Vespasianus fuit, antiquo ipse cultu victuque, obsequium inde in principem, et aemulandi amor, validior quàm poena ex legibus et metus. Memorabile est, quòd de Agesilao rege Spartanorum fertur : qui per hyemem solo pallio amictus cum ambularet, cau-sam rogatus : ut, inquit, adolescentiores hanc senioris principis vitam intuiti, quid imitentur habeant. Non igitur abs re Patterculus : Facere recte cives suos Principes optimus faciendo docet. Et post eum Claudianus : componitur orbis Regis ad exemplum : nec sic inflectere sensus Humanos edicta valent, quàm vita regentis. Mobile mutatur semper cum principe vulgus.
units.tr: A prince's life is the standard by which we are guided and turned. We need his example more than his command. Pliny, in the Panegyric, speaks of the mirror of thrift set before us by Vespasian, and Tacitus says: "Vespasian was the chief author of good morals. Living himself in the old fashion, both in dress and diet, he won obedience to the prince and a love of imitating him, which were stronger than punishment under the laws or fear." It is worth remembering what is told of Agesilaus, king of the Spartans: when he walked in winter wearing only a cloak, and was asked why, he said: "So that the young men, seeing the life of an older prince, may have something to imitate." Not without reason, then, Velleius Paterculus says: "The best prince teaches his citizens to act rightly by his own doing." And after him Claudian: "The world is shaped after the king's example; edicts have no power to bend human minds as much as the life of the ruler does. The fickle crowd always changes with the prince."

units.la: De quarto Consulatu Honorii. v. 300.
units.tr: On the Fourth Consulship of Honorius, v. 300.

units.la: Sed unde, inquiés, nota domestica vitae Principis ratio? aperit idem Claudianus : v. 273.Nam lux altissima fatiOccultum nihil esse finit, latebraque per omnesIntrat, et obtrusos explorat fama recessus.
units.tr: "But," you will say, "how can the private life of a prince become known?" Claudian himself explains: v. 273. "For the highest light of fate allows nothing to remain hidden; fame enters every hiding place and searches out even the most secluded recesses."

units.la: Quanquam ut, quid sentiam, recludam, vitia saepius Principum, quàm virtutes aulici, et ab his vulgus imitatur, nec à Tiberio parcimonia, Vespasiani virtutem, sed simulandi artificium, et accurato oriam fori tabernam, cives Romani discebant. Ut ab antibus cognitionem facilius, quàm sanitatem attrahas, ita foeditas contagione fiunt malorum quam bonorum morum exempla. Nimirum perceptu facilior et arte ptu proniores labes, omnium se oculis, omniumque mani-bus ingerit. Honesta ad fui apprehensionem spatio indigent, labore et meditatione firmanda. Quare nil nisi liberali est illud Senecae :
units.tr: Yet, to tell what I think, the vices of princes are more often imitated than the virtues of courtiers, and the common people copy them. From Tiberius the Roman citizens learned not Vespasian's thrift but the art of pretence, and the polished manners of the forum's shops. As you catch sickness from the sick more easily than you gain health, so the examples of bad morals spread by contagion more readily than those of good. Doubtless vice, being easier to grasp and more inclined to take hold, forces itself upon everyone's eyes and into everyone's hands. Honourable things need time to be grasped, and must be strengthened by labour and reflection. Hence that saying of Seneca is quite right:

units.la: Rex velit honesta, nemo non eadem volet.
units.tr: "If the king wills what is honourable, no one will not will the same."

units.la: Thyeste, act. 2. quod & Cornelius dubio procul agnovit: sententiam suam ita corrigens: nisi forte rebus cunctis inest quidam velut orbis. &c.
units.tr: Seneca, Thyestes, act 2; which Cornelius also undoubtedly recognised, correcting his own sentence thus: "unless perhaps there is in all things a certain circle, as it were," etc.

units.la: CII.
units.tr: CII.

units.la: Orbis rerum & morum in se circum-actus revolvitur.
units.tr: The world of things and morals turns round upon itself and revolves.

units.la: Nihil in uno rerum statu permanere, vel ipsum Orbis nomen indicat. Variae sunt ut temporum, ita morum & voluntatum humanarum vicissitudines. Belli taedio ad pacem, pacis fastidio ad bellum prorumpi-tur. Quos modo regum pertaesum erat, circumacta turbarum civilium rota, nonnisi Caesares rerum omnium arbitri delectant. In morum conversione eadem facilitas, eadem levitatis constantia. Non fortu-nam igitur magis, quam vitam ipsi suam, homines le-vitatis insimulent. rebus cunctis inest quidam velut orbis, ut quemadmodum temporum vices, ita morum vertantur. nec, ut querela omnium temporum auditur, semper in deterius fit immutatio: quod circumactioni rotae minus convenit. nec omnia apud priores meliora, sed nostra quoque aetas multa laudis & artium imitanda posteris tulit.
units.tr: That nothing remains in one state among things is shown even by the very name of the world. The changes of the times are matched by changes in morals and human wills. From weariness of war men break out into peace; from distaste for peace, into war. Those who a little while ago were tired of kings, once the wheel of civil disturbances has turned, delight in nothing but Caesars as the arbiters of all things. In the shifting of morals there is the same readiness and the same steady fickleness. Men should therefore blame their own levity of life rather than fortune. There is in all things a certain orbit, so that just as the vicissitudes of the times turn, so do the manners of men. Nor, although a complaint about every age is heard, does change always go for the worse, which agrees less with the turning of a wheel. Nor were all things better among the men of old, but our own age too has produced many things worthy of praise and of imitation by posterity in the arts.

units.la: Fuerit verum illud Horatii:
units.tr: That saying of Horace may be true:

units.la: Damnosa quid non imminuit dies? Aetas parentum pejor avis, tulit Nos nequiores, mox daturos Progeniem vitiosiorem.
units.tr: What does the ruinous day not diminish? Our parents' age was worse than that of our forefathers; it bore us, more worthless, who soon will bring forth an even more vicious offspring.

units.la: Fuerit verum de militiae desuetudine, luxu irrepente, oratorio studio languescente: pace per omnes pro-vincias reducta, repetundis & peculatu, nec non am-bitu & avaritia magistratuum sublata; ingeniorum cultura, tempora Horatiana prioribus feliciora censemus. Et illam ipsam luxuriae & ἀσωτείας[?] dissolutio-nem, Galbæ, Flavii, Trajani aetas dispunxit.
units.tr: It may be true of the neglect of military service, of luxury creeping in, and of oratory languishing; with peace restored throughout all the provinces, and extortion and embezzlement, as well as bribery and avarice in magistrates, removed; yet in the cultivation of talent we judge the times of Horace to be happier than earlier ones. And the age of Galba, the Flavians and Trajan dispelled that very dissolution of luxury and profligacy [ἀσωτείας].

units.la: CIII.
units.tr: CIII.

units.la: Summi imperii potestatem Augu-
units.tr: Augustus and his successors received the power of supreme rule

units.la: ftus & successores ejus nulla expressa lege acceperunt.
units.tr: without any express law.

units.la: De Augusto, quem Lege Regia supra omnes legitimè evectum plerique JCtorum contendunt, prius agendum. quo lege hac depulso, minùs de successoribus laborabitur. Cum tyranni nomen Augustus perhorresceret,& tamen nec populi jussu, nec plena sena-tus autoritate orbi Romano leges præscriberet, tribuniciam potestatem, ut Medulæ caput, objecit. Id summi fastigii vocabulum Augustus reperit, ne regis aut dictatoris nomen assumeret,ac tamen appellatione aliqua cætera imperia præmineret. Quo vocabulo summi fastigii concessio, populi consensu expressa, neutiquam evincitur. Nam nec tribunis plebis unquam jus supra consules concessum: & proximo loco post principem collocatis eadem potestas communi cata. Sed & Tiberius, cum se pro privato gereret, principatus dignitate nondum senatu extorta, pote-statis hujus titulum edictis præscripsit. ambiguus im-peratoris toritas, se-perandi: ne editum quidem, quo patres in curiam natui maje-vocabat, nisi Tribunitia potestatis præscriptione posuit stas: &c. sub Augusto accepta. 1.Annal. Nam & tribuni vetere rep. senatum aliquando cogebant: quanquam prima origine nihil, præter auxilii lationem, iis concessum. revocata. Sic plebi Augustus elusit, quasi contra potentiorum de imperio fastum hoc scuto desendæ. Nec novum hoc Au-gusto; sed receptum priscis Græciæ tyrannis, ut ἄνομ. ἔχω, ἄρχοντος, aut defensorum populi nominibus remp.invaderent. Nec Julius Cæsar, cujus hic se hæ-redem gessit, aliam viam institit. Marianarum enim se partium professus, Pompejum, & Sullanæ factionis reliquias, cervicibus civium se depulsurum præ se tu-lit. Multaque Romam reversus, Pompejanis devictis, gratain populum suscepit. Sed luculentiora è Tacito, legis Regiæ fastigium deje&ura, proferamus. Princi-pio annalium ἀναγεραθων veteris Reip. facta, ita de Monarchiæ primordio concludit: Lepidi atque Antonii arma in Augustum cessere, qui cunctia discordiis civili[illegible, ~8 letters] nomine principis sub imperium accepit. Arma Augustum, & vis patriae illata, non jus, non lex evexit. Principis vero nomen non summi imperii po-tentiam, sed primae in senatu sessionis praerogativam involvit. [illegible, ~40 letters: Greek] Princeps Senatus appellatus est, more in acerrima libertate in consuetudinem admisso. Dio lib. 53. Paulo deinde Tacitus di-gressus, Caesaream emergendi viam multis rationum momentis pandit. Consulem se ferens. Id nomen li-bertatis praesidio, non regni tutelae, inventum. Quod & acri in monarchia, tanquam principali dignitate altius, principes aliquoties, quanquam simulata humilitate, acceptum gessere, collegam ejus sastigii admiserunt: quodque mirere magis, stantes sedenti consuli juraverunt. Autor cum aliis Plinius in Trajani Panegyrico. ad tuendam plebem tribunitio jure contentum. de qua regnandi calliditate modo dictum.
units.tr: Concerning Augustus, whom most of the jurists (JCti) maintain was raised lawfully above all others by the Lex Regia, I must speak first. If that law is overthrown, there will be less trouble over his successors. Augustus dreaded the name of tyrant, yet without the command of the people or the full authority of the senate he prescribed laws to the Roman world. So he put forward the tribunician power, like the head of Medusa. Augustus devised this title of highest rank so that he would not assume the name of king or dictator, and yet still excel the other magistracies by some appellation. That the grant of the highest rank was made by this word, with the consent of the people, is by no means proven. The tribunes of the plebs never had a right granted above the consuls, and the same power was shared with those placed next after the prince. Tiberius too, while still acting as a private citizen, before the dignity of the principate had been wrung from the senate, prescribed the title of this power in his edicts. The ambiguous authority of the commander, and not even the edict by which he summoned the fathers into the senate did he issue except under the heading of tribunician power, received under Augustus (Tacitus, Annals 1). For the tribunes also sometimes convened the senate in the old republic, although at its first origin nothing had been granted to them beyond the bringing of aid. So Augustus deceived the plebs, as it were, by holding up this shield of defence against the pride of the more powerful. Nor was this new with Augustus. It was a practice taken over from the early tyrants of Greece, who, under the names of defenders of the people, invaded the state [ἄνομος ἔχω, ἄρχοντος]. Nor did Julius Caesar, whose heir Augustus made himself, follow another path. Professing to be of the Marian party, he declared that he would strike down Pompey and the remnants of Sulla's faction under the necks of the citizens. Returning to Rome after many exploits, and having defeated the Pompeians, he received the favour of the people. But let us bring forward, from Tacitus, more striking evidence that would pull down the height of the Lex Regia. At the beginning of his Annals, after recounting the deeds of the old commonwealth, he concludes thus about the beginning of the monarchy: the arms of Lepidus and Antony yielded to Augustus, who, when all things were disordered by discords, took the government under the name of prince. Arms, and the force of the fatherland, raised Augustus; not right, not law. The name of prince did not wrap up the power of supreme rule, but the prerogative of the first seat in the senate. [illegible Greek] He was called Princeps Senatus, a custom admitted into use in a most fierce liberty. (Dio, book 53.) Then Tacitus, digressing a little, lays open the Caesarean way of rising by many considerations. Presenting himself as consul. That title was invented as a safeguard of liberty, not as a protection of kingship. Princes, too, in a harsh monarchy, though with feigned humility, sometimes accepted and carried it, as something loftier than a princely dignity; they admitted a colleague in this rank, and, what is more remarkable, swore to the standing consul while they themselves sat. The author, along with Pliny in his Panegyric of Trajan, is content with tribunician right for protecting the plebs. Of this cunning of ruling I have already spoken.

units.la: Ubi militem donis. armis quaesitum regnum, armis tutandum erat. Nec unquam, profundissima licet pace, legiones, auxilia, classes Augustus exarmavit. Atque hinc alterum summi fastigii vocabulum, Imperator, inventum. Idque ipsum, e prisco libertatis more, regnandi ad libidinem detortum.
units.tr: Where he won the kingdom by gifts to the soldiers: a kingdom won by arms had to be defended by arms. Nor did Augustus ever disarm the legions, auxiliaries, or fleets, even in the deepest peace. And from this came the second title of highest rank, Imperator, which was invented, and which itself, from the old custom of liberty, was twisted to the lust of ruling.

units.la: Populum annona. non enim tribunitiae defensionis parmae satis sidebat: potentiori lenocinio plebecula irretienda, ventre ducenda erat, quae solis auribus non trahebatur.
units.tr: He kept the people by the corn supply: for the shield of tribunician protection was not enough; the little people had to be ensnared by a more powerful allurement, and led by the belly, since they were not drawn by ears alone.

units.la: Cunctos dulcedine otii pellexit. ut armis nimirum positis, & plenae libertatis [illegible, ~6 letters: Greek] abjecta, lene capistrum ferrent. Atqui hoc fuisse tempus dixeris, quo omni se jure populus Romanus exuit, in Augustum lege regia delato. Minime vero gentium, sequitur enim insurgere paulatim. quod non est uno ictu impe-rii plenam potestatem acceptantis.
units.tr: He drew everyone in by the sweetness of leisure: so that, of course, with arms laid down and full liberty cast off, they might bear a gentle bridle. Yet you would say this was the time when the Roman people stripped itself of every right, once power was conferred on Augustus by the Lex Regia. By no means, for it follows that the sovereignty grew gradually, since full power was not received by a single blow.

units.la: Munia Senatus, magistratuum, legum in se trahere. manebant splendida patrum, praetorum, legum nomina: vim vero omnium princeps in se trahebat.
units.tr: He drew to himself the functions of the senate, of the magistrates, and of the laws: the splendid names of the fathers, praetors and laws remained, but the prince drew the power of all of them into himself.

units.la: Nullo adversante, quod ad legis autoritatem fâſ ćiendam non sufficit: nam quibus aut metus silentium imponit, aut ferum mutatio spem ostentat, quieti quie dem quam turbis aptiores : non tamen ad legis latæ certitudinem, ut infallibile testimonium, adducendi.
units.tr: No one opposed, but that does not suffice to make the authority of a law: for those whom fear imposes silence on, or whom the change of the times holds out hope to, are more fitted for quiet than for disturbance; yet they cannot be adduced as an infallible witness to the certainty of a law passed.

units.la: Neque provincie illum rerum statum abnuebant. Quale jus imperii Augusto à provinciâm prompta voluntate accessit; tale & à nobilium & quorundam se populo connivebat. Plus enim virium habere vide- retur mutati status desiderium, quam nuda rerum transeuntium tolerantia. Jam vero provinciis nihil in civitatem Romanam potentiæ, nullus ad capessendos honores aditus, multo minus jus ullum transferendi honoris. Desinant igitur nonnulli à promptiorum servitio quicte summam potestatem Augusto stabili- re: nisi pari rationis ludibrio à provinciarum consensu argumentum arcessant. Nec leve contralegem giam adferunt mostentum subsidia dominatione tot hæredes provisi, & maturis honoribus evecti. Ut & honores juvenum à senatu petendi: quos pro iis specie vecu[antiu flagrantissime cupiverat, arbitrum igitur honorum conferendorum senatum agnosce- bat. Huc refer Germanicum osto apud Rhenum le- gionibus impositum, & peradoptionem asciri à Ti- berio jussum; quò pluribus munimentis insisteret. Quorsum hæc dominationis munimenta, si volente populo, silege deimperio lata, imperium obtinuit?
units.tr: Nor did the provinces refuse that state of affairs. The right of rule that came to Augustus from the provinces with ready will, the same came to him from the nobles, and from some of the people, who gave way to him. For the desire for change seemed to have more strength than the bare endurance of passing circumstances. But the provinces had no power over the Roman state, no access to seeking offices, much less any right of transferring an office. Let some, then, cease to establish supreme power for Augustus from the willing servitude of the more ready; unless with equal mockery of reason they derive their proof from the consent of the provinces. Nor do they bring forward a slight proof for the same contention: so many heirs provided for the rule, and raised to early honours. As also the young men's honours to be sought from the senate, which he had most eagerly desired for them in the appearance of an annual office; so he acknowledged the senate as the judge of conferring honours. Refer here Germanicus, placed over the legions on the Rhine, and ordered by Tiberius to be adopted, so that he might stand on more defences. To what end these defences of domination, if, the people being willing, the power that was not conferred by law obtained the rule?

units.la: quam legem & sequentia infringunt, eadem magi- stratum vocabula juniores post Actiacam victoriam etiam senes plerique inter bella civium nati, quotus- quisque reliquus, qui vemp. vidisset? antiquitatis quæ- dam specie glaucoma oculis, remp. ignorantium, obse- jecit. Igitur verso civitatis statu, nihil usquam pri- sci & integri moris: omnis exuta, qualitate jussa prin- cipis aspectare. à morum priscorum in servilem con- versione, à singulorum immutatione, non à lege ali- qua aut consensus momento, status conversionem
units.tr: The subsequent events also break that law. The same names of magistracies: the younger men, and after the Actian victory, even the old, most of whom were born during civil wars, how many of them remained who had seen the state of the commonwealth? A certain appearance of antiquity cast a mist over the eyes of those who did not know the commonwealth. So, the condition of the state having been turned round, nothing anywhere remained of the old and untouched custom: every trace of the old quality was stripped away, and they looked only to the commanded will of the prince. The conversion of the old morals into servitude, and the change of individuals, not any law or moment of consent, brought about the conversion of the state.

units.la: accersit. Nec tu sub fine Augusti spes novas, & bona libertatis sermone jactata, spreveris. Quid? quod, iure imperandi seposito[?], ne exilii quidem suis irrogan-di integram potestatem sibi Augustus sumpserit. Multa de Postumo Agrippa questus, ut exilium ejus sena-tus consulto sanciretur, perfecerat. Jam quorsum se-niorum civium irrisus pertinebat, nunc senem princi-pem longa potentia, provisis etiam haeredum in remp. epibus, auxilio scilicet militari tuendum, ut sepultura ejus quieta foret, si res ridicula non videretur, pro domino sepeliri, qui nullam dominandi potestatem habuerit? Potestatem enim a potentia, quam ei non detrahunt, semper distinguo. illi vero senem tyrannum, quod rarum etiam in mediocri civitate, longa potentia mirantur. Cur etiam numerum consulatu-um, tribunitiae potestatis annos alii admirantur; si uno principis nomine culmen honorum adaequari potuit? Quid sibi volunt prudentiorum de regimine ejus fa-ventes interpretationes? Non regno tamen, neque di-ctatura, sed Principis nomine constitutam Remp. ecce constitutam, non inversam, remp. & regni ab ea omen amotum! Haec quidem favitorum judicia, plures prudentiorum, quorum sermones intentius Tacitus refert, ita ortum, & ex parte administrationem, impe-rii Augustani recensent, ut illum a tyrannica reip. invasione nihilum purgare videantur. Dicebatur contra. &c. Plura Taciti prudentia suggerere nobis potuisset, si ille res Augusti accuratius describere aggressus fuisset. Ad Dionem Cassium me verto: quem plerique legis Regiae, & legitimae Augusti potestatis patronum allegant.
units.tr: Nor, at the end of Augustus' reign, should you disregard the new hopes and the talk of good liberty that was boasted. What of this: that, setting aside the right of ruling, Augustus did not even take to himself the full power of inflicting exile on his own people? He complained much about Postumus Agrippa, and had brought it about that his exile was sanctioned by a decree of the senate. Now, to what end was the mockery of the aged citizens, that now an old prince, by long power, with heirs provided even into the commonwealth, must be protected by military aid, so that his burial might be quiet, and, if the thing did not seem ridiculous, that he should be buried as master, who had no power of dominating? For I always distinguish power from potency, which they do not take away from him. But they marvel at an old tyrant, which is rare even in a moderate state, by long potency. Why do others also admire the number of consulships and the years of tribunician power, if by the single name of prince the summit of honours could be equalled? What do the interpretations of the more prudent, favouring his government, mean? Yet the commonwealth was established not under a kingdom, nor a dictatorship, but under the name of Prince. Behold, established, not overturned; and the name of king was removed from it! These are indeed the judgments of his favourers, and the opinions of several prudent men, whose talk Tacitus reports more closely; they so review, in part, the administration of Augustan rule, and so arranged, that they seem to purge him not at all of the tyrannical invasion of the state. It was said on the other side, etc. Tacitus' prudence could have suggested more to us, if he had set out to describe the affairs of Augustus more accurately. I turn to Dio Cassius, whom most people cite as the advocate of the Lex Regia and of Augustus' lawful power.

units.la: Duo sunt tempora, quibus principatum legitime adeptus Augustus videri queat: prius, ante pugnam ad Actium debellatam; alterum, post defunctos Antonium & Cleopatram, nemine armis de imperio cum Augusto decertante. Prioris temporis molitiones ad haec fermè capita rediguntur: corruptos largitione veteranos; paratum ab adolescente privato exerci-tum; corruptas consulis legiones; simulatam Pom-pejanarum partium gratiam; victorum consulum, sed morte praereptorum, arreptas copias; minis extortum patribus consulatum; arma pro republicâ accepta, contra remp. versa, conjunctione cum hostibus patriæ facta; patriam armis & cæde occupatam; proscriptionem innocentium civium crudelissimè exercitam; Italiam militaribus coloniis & divisionibus adflictam; grorum vastatam; urbem fuga & cædibus & rapinis exhaustam; imperii Romani cum Antonio Lepidoque distributionem. Ut fraudes in Sex. Pompejum, nec non in Lepidum collegam, ut civile cum Fulvia bellum prætereám. Quæ omnia legitimum eiimperium de-tulisse, nemo sani judicii dixerit. Supererat illud tempus, quo solus rerum arbiter, disjecta reip. rudera colligit, quo rerum summam adunum, & quidem vi-torem, deferri pacis interfuisse, non inficias eo. Sed am id plena potestatis abrogatione, & in Augustum translatione, lege quam vocant Regia, à populo Romano factum; id verò controvertitur. Facto igitur ab Actiaca victoria initio, quid Dio in utràmque partem momenti adferat, examinis ad lancem appendamus.
units.tr: There are two times in which Augustus could seem to have lawfully obtained the principate: the first, before the battle at Actium was fought; the second, after Antony and Cleopatra were dead, no one contending with Augustus in arms for the rule. The schemes of the former time may be reduced more or less to these heads: veterans corrupted by largesse; an army readied by a young private man; the legions of the consul corrupted; a feigned favour towards the Pompeian party; the forces of the consuls who had been victorious, but snatched away by death, seized; the consulship extorted from the fathers by threats; arms received for the commonwealth, turned against the commonwealth; a conjunction with the enemies of the fatherland made; the fatherland occupied by arms and slaughter; the proscription of innocent citizens carried out most cruelly; Italy afflicted by military colonies and distributions of land; the provinces laid waste; the city exhausted by flight, slaughter and plunder; the distribution of the Roman empire with Antony and Lepidus. I pass over the frauds against Sextus Pompey, and also against his colleague Lepidus, and the civil war with Fulvia. No one of sound judgment will say that all these things conferred on him a lawful empire. There remained that time when, as sole arbiter of affairs, he gathered up the scattered ruins of the commonwealth; I do not deny that it was in the interest of peace that the sum of affairs should be entrusted to one man, and that man the victor. But that this was done by the Roman people through an abrogation of full power and a transfer to Augustus, by the law they call the Lex Regia, that is what is disputed. Therefore, with the beginning taken from the Actian victory, let us weigh in the balance of examination what weight Dio brings on either side.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Reverso ab Ægypto ad decretos triumphos Augusto, immensus honorum cumulus patrum adulatione delatus. fornix, ludi, feriæ, vota, imagines, primus in consessu locus. adde Antonii ornamenta dejecta, & natalem ejus diem inter nefastos judicatu, Dio, lib. 51. Hæc ut magnifica, & modum propè egressa, ita si-ne certo regni delatiindicio. nec opus fuisset primi in consessu loci decreto, si privati hominis fastigio altiorem esse constaret.
units.tr: When Augustus returned from Egypt, the decreed triumphs were followed by a huge heap of honours, offered by the flattery of the senators: an arch, games, holidays, vows, statues, and the first place in the assembly. Add that the ornaments of Antony were torn down and his birthday was judged an unlucky day (Dio, book 51). These honours were magnificent and nearly excessive, yet they were not a clear sign of a kingdom being offered. Nor would there have been any need for a decree giving him the first place in the assembly, if it were established that he stood above the rank of a private man.

units.la: Tribunitia per omnem vitam potestas, & ad eum provocationes, patrum judicio decreti tribunitia verò potestas multò prisci tribunis amplior: ut ei liceret intra & extra pomœrium, usque ad x. passus, implo-ranti auxilium ferre.
units.tr: He received tribunician power for life, and appeals were made to him by a decree of the senators. Yet the tribunician power was much broader in earlier times, so that it was lawful for the tribune, within and beyond the pomerium, up to a thousand paces, to bring aid to anyone who called for help.

units.la: Refp.1. Vitiosa est Xylandri de provocatione ver-sio. Græca habent [illegible, ~12 letters] quod non de provocatione, tanquam ad superiorem, intelligen-dum. dum, alii loci docebunt. 2. Tribunorum vis quæ-dam fuit, oppressos à factiosis defendendi; nulla au-tem nobilioris loci dignitas, nulla in cives universos potestas. de jure loquor, non de usurpata tribunorum potentia. non ergo magis regnum hac appellatione Augusto delatum, quam primis potestatis ejus auto-ribus.
units.tr: Answer. 1. Xylander's rendering of "provocatio" is faulty. The Greek does not mean an appeal, as to a superior; this will be shown by other passages. 2. The tribunes had a certain power of defending the oppressed against factious men, but no dignity of higher rank and no power over all citizens. I speak of right, not of the usurped power of the tribunes. Therefore the title did not offer Augustus a kingdom any more than the first grants of his power did.

units.la: Juramento omnia ejus acta confirmata sunt.
units.tr: By oath all his acts were confirmed.

units.la: Resp. Et Sullæ, cujus acta non probaverant, pacis tamen & concordiæ causa decreta rata esse patres juf-ferant. Et Julii Cæsaris, quem jure cæsum judicave-rant, acta non rescinderunt. Augustique cum Antonio & Lepido sæva facinora, quorum memoriam ipse postmodum Augustus abolevit, decreto confirmave-rant. Quin & Philippi quondam Barberii, è servo prae-toris, in præitura gesta populus Romanus non revoca-vit: quem tamen & præitura & civitate indignum, in-dicio facto, censuerunt.
units.tr: Answer. The senators also ordered that the acts of Sulla, which they had not approved, be ratified for the sake of peace and concord. And they did not rescind the acts of Julius Caesar, whom they had judged rightly slain. They also confirmed by decree the cruel deeds of Augustus with Antony and Lepidus, whose memory Augustus himself later abolished. Indeed the Roman people did not revoke the deeds of Philippus Barbarius, once a slave of a praetor, done during his praetorship; yet after an information was laid, they judged him unworthy both of the praetorship and of citizenship.

units.la: Sacraria (ἱερὰ) & divini honores Augusto tributi.
units.tr: Shrines and divine honours were paid to Augustus.

units.la: Resp. Nimiam fuisse ea tempestate, qua omnis ex animis Dei metus exciderat, consecrandi facilitatem, non invitus concessero. Sed nullum ex eo delati regni argumentum. Nam & Germanico Drusi filio, nun-quam rerum potito, post fatum pares honores decreti. Honoris ut quis amore in Germanicum aut ingenio validus, reperti decretique. ut nomen ejus Saliari car-mine canerentur &c. Statuarum locorum ve in quis co-lerentur, haut facile quis numerum inierit. Tacit. 2. Annalium.
units.tr: Answer. I will readily grant that in that age, when all fear of God had vanished from men's minds, the facility of deifying was excessive. But this is no proof of a kingdom offered. For equal honours were also decreed after his death to Germanicus, son of Drusus, who never held power. As each was strong in love for Germanicus or in ability, so honours were found and decreed: that his name be sung in the Salian hymn, and so on. As for statues, and the places where they would be worshipped, one would not easily count them. Tacitus, Annals 2.

units.la: Sed quid congerendis & examinandis probatio-num momentis invitum calamum fatigo? Monarchiæ Augustanæ initium post ea tempora, ab anno Urbis conditæ 1CCCXXV, accersendum esse, autore Dione flamus. Cujus hæc sunt, principio libri 52, verba.
units.tr: But why do I weary my pen, against my will, with gathering and weighing the arguments of proof? I follow Dio in saying that the Augustan monarchy must be dated from the year 725 after the founding of the city. His words, at the beginning of book 52, are these.

units.la: Ταῦτα γὰρ ἐπὶ τῇ βασιλείᾳ, καὶ ἐν τῇ δημοκρατίᾳ, τῆς τε δυναστείας, πάντε καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν ἐπιγνωμόνων ἐπὶ, καὶ
units.tr: For these things were done both under kingship and in democracy, of the rule of the few and of the many, and were undergone by all [Ταῦτα γὰρ ἐπὶ τῇ βασιλείᾳ, καὶ ἐν τῇ δημοκρατίᾳ, τῆς τε δυναστείας, πάντε καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν ἐπιγνωμόνων ἐπὶ, καὶ]

units.la: [illegible, ~60 letters] Hæc itaque Romani sub regibus, inque populari Reip. administratione, & violenta paucorum dominatione, & operati & passi sunt. ex eo autem tempore iterum ab uno imperari absque controversia coeperunt. quanquam armorum depo-nendorum, resque omnes senatus populique potestati tradendi consilium Cæsar agitavit. Hæc Dio. Exeo igitur tempore Monarchiæ imperialis jus, & delatam à populo Romano potestatem, ductum Dionis Cassii secuti, contemplemur.
units.tr: Thus the Romans, under kings and in the popular government of the commonwealth, and under the violent domination of a few, both did and suffered these things. But from that time onward they began, without dispute, to be ruled by one man again, although Caesar considered laying down arms and handing all affairs over to the power of the senate and people. These are Dio's words. From this time, then, let us consider the right of the imperial monarchy and the power conferred by the Roman people, following Dio Cassius.

units.la: Deponendi imperii deliberationem Octavius infti-tuit, adhibitis in consilium Agrippa & Mæcenate, ar-canorum omnium intimis. [illegible, ~30 letters] Non aliud igitur imperii jus, quam violentum, ar-mis oppressæ patriæ extortum, Augustus habuit. nec potuit Agrippæ aut Mæcenatis assensus, hominum in rep. Romana novorum, aut nullo honore functorum, Remp. quasi in sinu suo locatam, transferre. Quid? quod unum tantum Mæcenatis Cæsar suffragium tu-lit. nam Agrippa consiliis monarchicis aperte refi-stebat.
units.tr: Octavius set up the deliberation on laying down power, taking into counsel Agrippa and Maecenas, the most intimate of all his confidants. Augustus therefore had no right of empire other than a violent one, wrested by arms from an oppressed fatherland. Nor could the assent of Agrippa or Maecenas, men new to the Roman commonwealth or who had held no office, transfer the commonwealth as though it lay in their bosom. What is more, Caesar took only the single vote of Maecenas, for Agrippa openly opposed monarchical counsels.

units.la: Vis igitur deliberandi in eo posita fuerit: egregiam nunc esse occasionem remp. armis defatigatam, inva-dendi: sublatis æmulis, ægro reip. inermis corpore, quid igitur in ea rerum opportunitate autores effent? Speciosa Agrippa & magnis nominibus honesta: uti-lia Mæcenas & blandientia Augusto suggessit. procul dubio in sententiam tracturus, quem cupido regnandi ad arma civilia impulerat. Hæc Monarchiæ Romanæ auspicia, examussim cum Cornelii dictis consentientia.
units.tr: The power of deliberating therefore lay in this: that it was now an excellent opportunity to seize the commonwealth, worn out by arms, with its rivals removed and its sick body defenceless. What, then, did the authors advise in that favourable situation? Agrippa suggested showy measures, honourable through great names; Maecenas suggested useful measures and things that flattered Augustus, no doubt to draw him to their opinion, since desire for rule had driven him to civil arms. These are the auspices of the Roman monarchy, agreeing exactly with the words of Cornelius.

units.la: Aliud argumentum cunctatio Augusti, & res imperii fle&endi trepidatio, suppeditat. [illegible, ~20 letters] ἀνθρώπων ἐξελάσαι[?] [illegible, ~12 letters] μετασχηματισμόν τὰς ἀνθρώπους ἐξελαύνειν, ἀλλὰ τὰ ἀρχαῖα μετασχηματίσαι, τὰ δ' ὑστερον καὶ νῦν καὶ τῆς μὴ πάντα ἀξιῶσαι ποιῆσαι κατέλιπεν, ὡς καὶ κοινὸν[?] [illegible, ~10 letters] ἐξηλλαγμένα.non tamen omnia statim quæ suaserat (Mæcenas) agere instituit: veritus ne parum succederet, si subito homines in alium statum traducere conaretur. Sed alia quidem confestim, alia postea temporis immutavit: nonnulla etiam sequentibus imperatoribus perficienda tradidit, ut quæ ex opportunitate rerum commodius constitui queant. Eodem libro 52. Quid his verbis clarius; quid explicandis Cornelianis insurgere paulatim magis perspicuum?
units.tr: Augustus's hesitation, and his trepidation at bending the affairs of empire, supplies another argument. He did not at once carry out everything Maecenas had advised, fearing that it would succeed less well if he tried to lead men suddenly into another state. Some things he changed at once, others later; some he left to be completed by succeeding emperors, so that they might be arranged more conveniently as the circumstances allowed. Dio, book 52. What is clearer than these words? What is more evident for explaining Cornelius's phrase "to rise up gradually"?

units.la: Levius videri queat, non tamen silentio prætereundum, quod Agrippa, in exequendo Monarchiæ arripiendæ decreto, adjutore usus deinde memoratur. καὶ αὐτῆς ὁ Ἀγρίππας [?] πάντα καὶ τὴν ἀνωτέρω[?] [illegible, ~8 letters] Suæ igitur cupiditati, Mæcenatis consilio, Agrippæ auxiliationi, imperium Romanum Augustus acceptum ferat.
units.tr: It may seem a lighter matter, yet it should not be passed over in silence, that Agrippa is afterwards mentioned as his helper in carrying out the decree to seize monarchy. Let Augustus therefore credit the Roman empire to his own desire, to Maecenas's counsel, and to Agrippa's assistance.

units.la: Nec illa anno, nec deinceps unquam in plenam summi imperii potestatem consensum esse, docet ma-gistratuum non sine collega adjuncto functio. Non regi Galliarum, non Hispaniarum, ac ne Poloniæ quidem ac Daniæ minus laxioris potestatis regibus, annui honoris aut oneris functionem imponas, collegam è civibus ad latus adjungas. καὶ μετὰ τῶν τῶν πρώτων[?] [illegible, ~6 letters] ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀγρίππα. Deinde censor, collega Agrippa, fuit. Sed quis numerum consulatuum Augusti, Tiberii, insequentium imperatorum subducat? quibus etsi collegarum splendorem obscuraverunt, id tamen inconcussum manet, veteris reip. imaginem illa honorum communicatione retentam fuisse, nec jus imperii, plena servitutis confessione, è manibus populi dimissum.
units.tr: That neither in that year nor ever afterwards was there consent to the full power of the supreme rule, the discharge of magistracies not shared with a colleague shows. You do not impose an annual honour or burden on the king of France, nor of Spain, nor even on the kings of Poland and Denmark, who have less extensive power, nor attach a colleague from among the citizens at their side. [Greek fragment]. Then Agrippa, his colleague, became censor. But who would count the consulships of Augustus, of Tiberius, and of the later emperors? Although they overshadowed the splendour of their colleagues, this remains unshaken: the image of the old commonwealth was kept by that sharing of honours, and the right of empire was not released from the hands of the people with a full confession of servitude.

units.la: Arma Augustum, arma ad imperii splendorem pro-texere. num justæ causæ arma; num moderato fine gesta aut deposita? minimè; quorum memoriam ipse abolendo damnavit. [illegible, ~40 letters] [illegible, ~45 letters] [illegible, ~50 letters] [illegible, ~35 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] quoniam multa omnino in seditionibus & bellis, præ-fertim in triumviratu, injustè & iniquè constituerat, omnia ea uno edicto antiquavit. libro 53. Hæc ille quidem gratiæ populi captandæ, & viæ ad regnum muniendæ: cæterum quibus causam ipse suam, & progressum ad dominationem, iniquitatis damnavit.
units.tr: Arms protected Augustus; arms protected the splendour of his empire. Were they arms for a just cause? Were they waged or laid down with a moderate end? By no means: he himself condemned their memory by abolishing it. Since in seditions and wars, especially in the triumvirate, he had established many things unjustly and wrongly, he cancelled all of them by a single edict (book 53). These were his measures for winning popular favour and paving the way to kingship; but by them he himself condemned his cause and his advance to domination as iniquitous.

units.la: 10. Pauci per vim aut fraudem imperio fe ingerentium adeò negligentes judicii hominum, & ad posteritatem famæ sunt, ut non aliquam arti suæ speciem juris imponi quærant. Quare & Augustus, ut volentibus imperii depositione, perare videretur, simulata imperii depositione, de-mandationem ejusdem captavit. Forte & ad intro-spiciendas procerum voluntates, quod de Tiberio Cornelius tradit, dubitatio ab eo induta. Sed quot in ea propositione, quot in adeptione voti vitia la-teant, mecum lector perpende.
units.tr: 10. Few who force or defraud their way into empire are so careless of men's judgement and of their fame with posterity that they do not seek to give their enterprise some appearance of right. Wherefore Augustus too, so that he might seem to be willing to lay down power, sought the commission to rule again through a pretended laying down of it. Perhaps also, as Cornelius relates of Tiberius, he put on a show of hesitation in order to probe the wishes of the nobles. But, reader, weigh with me how many faults lie hidden in that proposal, and how many in the attainment of the wish.

units.la: 1. Imperium, quod nullum jure habuit, molestia-rum pertæsum fe reddiderum pollicetur. Cur non fa&to,quod timulavit, præstitit? cur non prætoritorum veniam rogando, legiones exarmavit, aut patrum pulique inmanus resignavit?
units.tr: 1. He declared that he was weary of an empire which he had no right to hold. Why did he not do what he pretended? Why, by asking pardon for his past acts, did he not disarm the legions or return the power into the hands of the senate and people?

units.la: 2. Per senatorum idoneos, quod sibi respondere-tur, præparavit. [illegible, ~30 letters]
units.tr: 2. Through suitable senators he prepared what answer would be given to him. [illegible]

units.la: 3. Eas legum æquabilitatis, concordiæ, provincia-rum cum æquitate administrandarum, pacis confer-vandæ difficultates movet; ut fatis appareret, fuaden-do eum communem libertatem dissuadere.
units.tr: 3. He raises the difficulties of laws of equity and concord, of administering the provinces with fairness, and of keeping the peace; so that it was clear enough that in advising this he was dissuading common liberty.

units.la: 4. Multis quidem eum verbis precati sunt, ut solus imperii summam gereret, patres nimirum conscriptis, qui populo non jubente rempublicam transferre non poterant; sed alii donis aut necessitudine illecti, alii metu aut pluribus assentientes, pauci veterum præ-[?] rebus odio. §. Nec alienatio sine consensu, nec deditio sine acceptatione perficitur. Cum itaque Caesar, modestiae simulatione an syncere parum interest, donationem imperii non acceptaverit, pro nulla apud posteros habenda. Temporis angustiae & loci, imperii summam anstrinxit: quam plena monarchia, limitibus nullis interclusa, non agnoscit. paucas gubernationi suae provincias, decennii tempore definitas, assignando; plures senatui ac populo remisit. Non me latet, provincias belliciosas legendo, armorum sibi tractationem integram servasse; & decennio aliud deinceps tempus adjectum, finem imperio non praefixisse. Verum hic non quid arcanae subtilitatis fuerit, verum quid juris ad imperium firmandum acceperit, in quaestione ventilatur.
units.tr: 4. Many indeed begged him, in many words, to take up the whole sum of power alone. These were the conscript fathers, who could not transfer the commonwealth without the people commanding it. Some were enticed by gifts or family ties, some by fear or by going along with the majority, and a few of the old men out of hatred for the public affairs. §. Neither alienation nor surrender is completed without consent and acceptance. Therefore, whether Caesar refused the gift of empire out of feigned modesty or in sincerity matters little; it is to be regarded as nothing before posterity. Because of the narrowness of time and place, he confined the sum of power, which full monarchy, shut in by no limits, does not acknowledge. He assigned to his own government a few provinces, fixed for a period of ten years, and he returned the rest to the senate and people. I am not unaware that, by choosing warlike provinces, he kept the handling of arms entirely to himself, and that another period was added afterwards to the decade, so that he did not fix an end to his empire. But the question here is not what secret subtlety there was, but what right he received to confirm the empire.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Nomen Augusti, quod postmodum accessit, a venerationis amplitudine, imperii vim non exprimere, ipse sensit, qui mirum in modum Romulus dici desideravit. [illegible, ~20 letters] i. e. cum sentiret, hinc se suspectum affectati regni fieri, cupidinem ejus celavit. Hoc Dio. ergo imperii vim non sentiente populi in se retraxit: nomen, & cum eo jus, regni quamvis invitus remisit.
units.tr: The name Augustus, which was added afterwards, did not express the force of empire but the greatness of veneration; he himself perceived this, for he wonderfully wished to be called Romulus. [illegible, ~20 letters] that is, since he perceived that by this he would be suspected of aiming at kingship, he concealed his desire for it. Dio therefore, when the people did not perceive the force of empire, drew it back onto himself: though unwillingly, he gave up the name and with it the right of a king.

units.la: Ὡς ἀγαθὸν ἐς ἐπωνυμίας πολλὰς ἔχειν.
units.tr: It is good to have many names [Ὡς ἀγαθὸν ἐς ἐπωνυμίας πολλὰς ἔχειν.]

units.la: Res utilis, valere nominum penu: inquit Cario in Pluto Aristophanis.
units.tr: A useful thing, to have a good stock of names, says Carion in the Plutus of Aristophanes.

units.la: Ficulneam perpetuitatis imperii basin (de jure imperii loquor, non de armata potentia) Augustus cernens, plures magistratuum titulos, per subornatos ambiendo accepit. Principis & imperatoris nomina, quae sola apud posteros haeserunt, non repeto. Consulis, Proconsulis, Censoris, Sacerdotis, Tribuni quoad potestatem, Legibus solutus, Patris patriae appellationes Augusto non inanes accesserunt. Consulis atque proconsulis nomine provincias administrabat, militem conscribebat, pecuniam conficiendo fisco consulcbat,&c. Censoria viin vitam & mores civium inqui-rebat, census agebat, in equestrem ac senatorium or-dinem legebat, aut pro arbitrio locis movebat. Ponti-ficis nuncupatione, religiones & sacra in manu habe-bat. Tribunitia potestate aliorum sibi adversantium, placitis obstabat, à violatione sacrosanctus erat, plebis contra potentiores defensione suam potentiam com-muniebat. De legum solutione mox dicetur. Patris autem patriæ, non nisi honorifica primitus, mox & profutura appellatione jus patrium in cives, & pater-nam ab iis observantiam, exigebat. Ita regis omissio nomine, vim regiam, occupato magistratuum jure, in fe trahebat. Securus de nominatione, dum fatis fir-ma frueretur dominatione.
units.tr: Augustus, seeing that the fig-tree was the base of the empire's perpetuity (I speak of the right of empire, not of armed power), took up several magistracies' titles, by having men put forward to request them for him. I do not go back to the names of Prince and Emperor, which alone stuck with posterity. The titles of Consul, Proconsul, Censor, Priest, and Tribune, as far as their power went, and free of the laws, and Father of the Fatherland, came to Augustus not as empty names. In the name of consul and proconsul he administered the provinces, enrolled soldiers, and looked after the treasury by collecting money, and so on. By the censorial power he inquired into the life and morals of citizens, conducted the census, enrolled men in the equestrian and senatorial orders, or moved them between places at his pleasure. By the title of Pontiff he held religions and sacred rites in his hand. By tribunician power he blocked the decrees of those who opposed him; he was sacrosanct against violation, and by defending the plebs against the more powerful he strengthened his own power. Concerning release from the laws, I shall speak shortly. But the title of Father of the Fatherland, at first only honorary and soon also useful, claimed for him a paternal right over the citizens and their paternal observance. Thus, by omitting the name of king, he drew to himself the royal power, having seized the right of the magistracies. Secure about the name, he enjoyed a dominion firm enough by the fates.

units.la: 13. Legibus in vetere Romanorum Republica nonnul-li solvebantur; ut Fulvius, ut Scipio, ut Pompejus, & fiqui alii communi legum vinculo eximebantur. V.gr, ut ante annos lege præscriptos ædilitatem, prætura consulatum petere liceret: ut proconsul urbem in-gressus cum imperio maneret: ut provinciæ admini-stratio non mora annua, sed rei gerendæ spatio finire-tur. Horum ad exemplum Senatus Romanus legibus Augustum solvebat: quanquam modum nonnihil in eo prisci moris excedebat. ἰλαῦ ἔχεις ... liberi ab omni legum necessitate, nulla scriptarum te-nentur. Mos ab antiquitate liberæ Reip deductus, ni-hil nisi in modi exceflu novum habuit. Cui explicatio-ni non refragaturus Dio, huic ipsi de legum solutione loco subjungit: ... ἐνομοθέτων, πῶς ... τῶν ... i.e. atque ita popularium nominum ratione, omnem reip. vim induit sunt. Imperitè itaque antiquitatis Romanæ, & contra Dionis mentem faciunt, qui ex hoc loco juris regii originem vel stabilimentum statuant. Contrà, quia senatus erat, qui Augustum lege solvebat, penes senatum ac populum Romanum majestatem residere intelligendum. Non enim sol-vere Legibus vere nexu, quo ipse quis ligatur, alium potest; nec su-perioris est, immunitatem legum accipere. An vero regum nota sit, legibus imperare, alibi locorum excussimus.
units.tr: 13. In the old Roman commonwealth some were released from the laws, such as Fulvius, Scipio, Pompey, and any others who were exempted from the common bond of the laws: for example, to seek the aedileship or praetorship before the years prescribed by law, or the consulship; that a proconsul entering the city should remain with his command; that the administration of a province should end not at a fixed yearly term but when the business was finished. Following these examples, the Roman senate released Augustus from the laws, although in this it went somewhat beyond the ancient custom. [ἰλαῦ ἔχεις ...] Free from every necessity of the laws, you are bound by none of the written ones. This custom, derived from the antiquity of the free commonwealth, had nothing new except in its excess of measure. Dio, who does not oppose this explanation, adds right after it, on the release from the laws: [ἐνομοθέτων, πῶς ... τῶν ...] that is, and so by the reckoning of popular names, they put on the whole force of the commonwealth. Therefore those who, from this passage, set down the origin or foundation of royal right act unskilfully in Roman antiquity and against the mind of Dio. On the contrary, since it was the senate that released Augustus from the laws, it must be understood that the majesty resided with the senate and the Roman people. For one cannot release another from the laws, since he is not bound by the same bond by which he himself is bound; nor does it belong to a superior to receive immunity from the laws. Whether it is the mark of kings to command the laws, we have examined elsewhere.

units.la: Inter alia Senatus Romanus Augusto extra ordi-nem largiebatur, ut quibuscunque de rebus, etiamsi consulatum non gereret, referre posset: ut proconsulare imperium urbem intrando non deponeret, neque auspiciis repetendis opus esset: ut major ipsi in provinciis, quam praefectis earum, semper potestas esset. apud eundem Dionem, libro 53. Quae omnia & legum solutionem exemplis illustrant, & regnum Augusto nunquam delatum fuisse arguunt. Quorsum enim his paucarum legum exemptionibus gratiam imperatoris quaesivissent: si absque ejusmodi senatus consulto omnia in omnes ei licerent. Nullum igitur in hunc usque locum regiae legis vestigium, nulla vola apparet.
units.tr: Among other things, the Roman senate granted Augustus beyond the ordinary, that he could make a proposal on whatever matters, even if he did not hold the consulship; that he would not lay down proconsular command on entering the city, nor would it be necessary to take the auspices again; that he would always have greater power in the provinces than their prefects. This is in the same Dio, book 53. All these things both illustrate the release from the laws by examples and prove that kingship was never offered to Augustus. For why would they have sought the emperor's favour by these few exemptions from the laws, if by no senatorial decree of this kind everything had been permitted to him against everyone? There is therefore no trace of a royal law in this passage, and no will appears.

units.la: Romani cum lue simul coeli & annonae penuria premerentur, iram id Deorum ob neglectum Augu-stum interpretati, obsepta curia patres, ut Augustum dictatorem & annonae procuratorem dicerent, compulerunt. Annonae procurationem cum non asperna-retur Augustus, dictaturam ut acciperet, nulla ratione adduci potuit: quin vestem etiam urgente populo, ut Dio libro 54, dilcidit. Tergiversandi, cum simulate hic non ageret, quae ratio? Dixeris: animi magnitudi-ne, sua se celsitudine, non honorum enormi fastigio metientis. regnum ergo acciperet, qui temporariam supra omnes dignitatem supra modestiam suam judi-caret? Dubium non est, quin nominis invidiam, ex odio Sullae & non nullo C.Caesaris, & ex ea periculum aversaretur. atqui regis nomen, & quicquid regiae appellationis, ut Lex Regia, Romanis odiosius. Altiorem ego curam, velamentis animi detectis, in penetra-libus Augusti peripicio. Cum dictatura ex lege longius semestri, aut summum annua, mora non gerere-tur; cumque sub ea caeteri omnes magistratus quie-
units.tr: When the Romans were oppressed at once by a plague, by the unclearness of the sky, and by a scarcity of grain, they interpreted it as the anger of the gods for the neglect of Augustus, and the fathers, with the senate house surrounded, compelled him to be named dictator and overseer of the grain supply. Augustus did not spurn the charge of the grain supply, but he could in no way be brought to accept the dictatorship, not even when the people pressed him, as Dio explains in book 54. What reason was there for his shirking, if he was not acting in pretence? You might say: by the greatness of his spirit, measuring himself by his own loftiness and not by the lofty height of honours. Would he then accept a kingship, he who judged a temporary dignity above all others beneath his modesty? There is no doubt that he was averting the odium of the name, arising from the hatred of Sulla and somewhat of Gaius Caesar, and the danger that came with it. Yet the name of king, and whatever is of royal appellation, such as the Royal Law, was more odious to the Romans. I, with the veils of his mind removed, look at a deeper concern in Augustus's inner parts. Since the dictatorship was not held by law for longer than six months, or at most a year, and since under it all the other magistrates went on in office,

units.la: fcerent: Augustus tempore aut necessitate dictatur finita, ea deposita privatam ad vitam rediturus crede- batur. quam ille viperino odio refugit. non enim qui dictatura fe abdicabant, alium eo anno magistratum gerebant. Magistrum equitum dictatori adjungen- dum non urgeo: quando & in censura, & in confula- tu, collegam Principes admitterent. Forte & ex cir- cumscripta dictaturæ dignitate, aliqua Augusto fasti- gii ejus aversatio. non enim tempore tantùm, sed & loco includebatur. Dictatori enim Italiam egredi, nè procul ab oculis civium facilius res innovaret; non permissum. Equum etiam, nisi ad bellum iturus, ascen- dere vetabatur. Quicquid fit: cum plebes Romana aliquid principatu Augusti altius judicaret, non potest eadem regiæ dignitatis & legis regiæ autor, aut saltem conscia, censeri:
units.tr: Augustus, once the dictatorship ended at the appointed time or the need was past, was believed to be going to lay it down and return to private life. This he avoided with a viperish hatred. For those who gave up the dictatorship did not hold any other magistracy that year. I do not press the point that a master of the horse must be joined to the dictator, since princes also admitted a colleague both in the censorship and in the consulship. Perhaps also, from the restricted dignity of the dictatorship, there was some aversion of Augustus from that rank: for he was confined not only in time but also in place. For a dictator was not permitted to leave Italy, lest he more easily bring about revolution far from the citizens' eyes; nor was he allowed to ride a horse unless he was going to war. Whatever the case, since the Roman plebs judged something higher in the principate of Augustus, the author of the royal dignity and of the Royal Law cannot be counted the same person, or at least one who knew of it.

units.la: 16. Aliam ex eodem Dionis libro, contra confensuit regiæ in Augusto potestatis, demonstrationem eruo. M. cuidam Primo dies erat dicta; quòd Macedoniæ præfectus, bellum Odrysis intulisset, is cum modò Augusti, modò Marcelli ex sententia id se fecisse præ se ferret, Augustus nemine vocante ad tribunal venit. interrogatusque à prætore; mandassétne id bellum Primo, inficiatus est, tum Licinio Murenæ, qui cau- sam Primi agebat, multis eum maledictis incesserit; ac percontanti quid hic in foro ageret, aut à quo voca- tus adesset; unum hoc modò respondit: A te publica: Ob hoc ab amicè affectis laudabatur; adeò ut sena- tum, quoties vellet, convocandi licentiam ei permit- terent. ab aliis autem in contemptum addu&us est: inventique non modò qui Primum suis suffragiis libe- rarent, sed etiam qui in Augusti perniciem conspira- rent. Quot in hac historiola, quam valida contra opi- nionem regiam argumenta! 1. Majestate læsi, non prætoris; fuisset de bello fine publica autoritate gesto cognoscere. 2. Nec tribunalis aditus, neminè vocante, summo rerum moderatori vitio daretur: nec prætor eum ex alto loco interrogare auderet.
units.tr: 16. From the same book of Dio I draw out another demonstration, against the consensus concerning royal power in Augustus. A certain Primus had a day set for trial, because, as prefect of Macedonia, he had made war on the Odrysians. When he declared that he had done this now in accordance with the wishes of Augustus, now of Marcellus, Augustus came to the tribunal without anyone summoning him. Questioned by the praetor whether he had entrusted that war to Primus, he denied it; then he attacked Licinius Murena, who was pleading Primus's case, with many abuses. And when Murena asked what he was doing in the forum, or by whom he had been summoned to be present, he answered only this: "By you, the public." For this he was praised by those well disposed toward him, so much so that they allowed him the licence to convene the senate whenever he wished. But others he brought to contempt, and men were found not only to free Primus with their votes, but also to conspire for Augustus's destruction. How many strong arguments against the royal opinion are in this little story! First: he was injured in his majesty, not the praetor's; the matter of a war waged without public authority should have been investigated. Second: the approach to the tribunal without anyone summoning him would have been counted a fault in the supreme manager of affairs, nor would the praetor have dared to question him from a high place.

units.la: 3. Causidici convitia, vel populo censore, non sic impune abiissent.
units.tr: Verbal abuse of an advocate would not have gone unpunished so easily, even with the people acting as censor.

units.la: 4. Nec ad munus suum Augustus, nec ad legem de potestate sua latam provocavit.
units.tr: Augustus appealed neither to his office nor to the law passed concerning his power.

units.la: 5. Nihil a benevolis novi autoritati ejus adjectum fuisset. regi enim senatum quovis tempore convocare concessum.
units.tr: Nothing new would have been added to his authority by his well-wishers, for it was lawful for the king to convene the senate at any time.

units.la: 6. Quorsum in eum conspiratio quorundam; nisi responsio a republica, quasi in eum publicae rei negotia, recumberent, arrogantior visa multis fuisset?
units.tr: Why would a conspiracy of certain men have arisen against him, unless the answer "from the commonwealth", as if the business of the public state rested upon him, had seemed too arrogant to many?

units.la: Haec, nisi fallor, evidentis probationis argumenta sunt, in Augusto, quamvis magnae in animis hominum autoritatis viro, inviolabilem regiae dignitatis majestatem agnitam non fuisse.
units.tr: These, unless I am mistaken, are arguments of clear proof that in Augustus, though a man of great authority in people's minds, the inviolable majesty of royal dignity was not acknowledged.

units.la: Ex hac argumentorum nube, quantum praesidii in Dione sit legis regiae patronis, perceptu non difficile fuerit. Qui si, abrogata historicis autoritate, ad nescio cujus lapidis rudera, principum secreta archiva, JCtorum multitudinem confugerint; inaniori opera inanem laterem lavabunt.
units.tr: From this cloud of arguments it is not hard to see how little help Dio gives to the defenders of the royal law. If, with the authority of the historians set aside, they flee to the rubble of I know not what stone, to the secret archives of the princes, or to the multitude of jurists, they will wash an empty brick with empty labour.

units.la: Nam nec Limnaei vel fidei, vel judicio, in antiquitatis palaestra, nimium tribuo: & JCti, ad causam dicendam vocati, pro se contra antiquitatem historiae testes, aut judices, minus idonei sunt habendi, ut taceam, gravissimos ex eo numero viros pro nobis non obscure stare. quorum labores compilare nolui. Omnes autem historiarum scriptores ofcitantiae vel ignorantiae arguere velle, ad scrinia principum confugientem, aut ineptiarum est aut argutiarum & vafritici nimiae. Qui enim res vel minimas, & saepe quisquilias rerum, argute stylo persecuti sunt; illi a maximi momenti rebus animum aversum gererent? Qui consulares, ut Dio, remp. Romanam penitus cognitam habuerunt; quique militari simul & aulica assiduitate, ut Tacitus, cum non vulgari eruditione claruerunt: eorum cognitionem pars aliqua reip. fugiat? Quod si ex rumore duntaxat vulgi historiam consarcinarent, tamen tantae celebritatis decretum eos neutiquam lateret. Nec
units.tr: For I do not put too much trust in Limnaeus, either in his good faith or in his judgment, in the arena of antiquity. Jurists, when called to plead a case, are to be regarded as less fit witnesses or judges against the testimony of antiquity in history. Not to mention that the most serious men from their ranks stand, not obscurely, on our side; I did not wish to compile their labours. But to want to charge all the writers of history with drowsiness or ignorance, while fleeing to the cabinets of the princes, is either silliness or excessive cleverness and trickery. For those who have pursued even the smallest matters, and often the trifles of affairs, with a subtle pen, would they have turned their minds away from the most important matters? Those who were consuls, like Dio, had a thorough knowledge of the Roman commonwealth; and those who shone with no common learning through their military and court attendance, like Tacitus: could some part of the affairs of the state escape their knowledge? But even if they had patched together their history from the mere rumour of the crowd, still such a decree of great fame would by no means have escaped them. Nor

units.la: JCti. Archivi. Historici.
units.tr: Jurists. Archives. Historians.

units.la: Οὐ γὰρ ἐ- ὡς πα ἐνδ- ἕα ὅτω καὶ [?] πρὸς πολλὴν [?]
units.tr: (Greek fragment, not legible in the scan.)

units.la: Sed & eodem tempore populus suam Democratiæ non abjecit imaginem. multoque rectius de eo dici potuerat, quod apud Thucydidem de Periclea Athe- nienfium tempestate jactatur: ἐξηγεῖτο τε λόγῳ μὲν, ἔργῳ δὲ, ὁ τῶν πρώτων ἀνὴρ. Verbo quidem, status popularis; re autem vera, pes nes vitum in civitate principem imperium erat. lib. 2. Hiftor. Vix enim priscæ libertatis umbram, nomi- nibus & ritum speciebus delusi, rerum domini Ro- mani tenebant. Quia tamen à Dionis patrocinio exs clusos, ad Strabonis protectionem confugere audio, quantum fit in illo perfugii recludam. Principio hos- mini ne quidem Græci generis, nedum Itali aut Ros mani, inter Armenios & Cappadocas barbaro, & non semel vanitatis aut ofcitantiæ etiam in leviori- bus con- vincendo, quique interiora reip. Romanæ arcana nuntiant quam penetraverit, tantum vel fidei vel autoritatis non tribuo, ut contra rerum Romanarum conflictus testis idoneus fit audiendus. Quod proximum, & nostræ sententiæ faventius, verba ejus mitiorem interpretationem non aspernantur. Sedulò quid contra nos machinamenti adferret scrutatus, in locum incidi, sexto Geographiæ libro, ambiguum. χαλεπὸν δὲ ἄλλως [?] οἰκεῖν τὴν Πλιχαωτῶν ἡγεμονίαν [?], ἢ ἐν ἐπιτροπεύεσθαι ὡς πατρί [?]. Quod & nos de commoda magni imperii administratione largimur. De pleno jure, legis aliqua sanctione delato, & populo eadem adempto, quæritur. Sed nimirum fulmina verborum insequentium nos feriunt: ἀφ' ἑ πτερίλαβες [illegible, ~6 letters] ἀντπλὴ [?]. Ferirent, si aut modum accipiendi, Corneliano contrarium, aperuisset, aut omnis ratione reddendâ soluta potestas regiam vim Græcis autoribus designaret. Alter, quem deprehenderim, locus exstat sub calcem operis, libro videlicet XVII. ἐπεὶ τοῖς ἡ πατρὶς ἐπιτρε- [illegible, ~12 letters] ἀπὸ τῆς ἡγεμονίας, ἡ τὸ ἐμὸν ἐγέννησε [?] κατὰ τὴν χύσιν [?] ἀλλὰ βίᾳ [?] Turbulenta rerum domi & foris tempestate, arbitrium eì pacis firmandæ aut belli expediendi, ut quond.m dictatori aut decemviris, simul imperii protectionem, temporum finitione circumscriptam, patria, id est necessitas temporum permisit. Majore nuper apud Britannos jubendi potestate, protectoris arrepto nomine, Cronvellus quidam emicuit, in quem jus omne populi delatum esse, extincto Reipublicæ inter cunabula prima nomine, Anglorum natio non dabit. Ἐπιτροπία igitur a pleno regno, βασιλεία manente populi ἡγεμονία a supremo arbitrio, pacis & belli dispensatio ab altiori imperandi culmine, accurata loquendi religione distinguenda. Est & genus quoddam summi imperii, publico patriæ libertatis bono, fraude vel vi arreptum, quod abignaris Pittaco vitio, ab eventu & rerum gnaris laudi dabatur, de quo XIII libro Geographus. Πιττακὸς δ' εἰς μὲν τὸ [illegible, ~10 letters] τὴν πόλιν [?] c. Pittacus nit dominationes quorundam dissolveret, summum imperium ipse usurpavit: re confecta, libertatem civium restituit. Quod & Augusti animo volvisse, invalis imperii capitis, aut aru simulandi, aut generosi animi laudi dedermus. R
units.tr: But at the same time the people did not cast off the image of its democracy. And something much more correct could have been said of him than what is said in Thucydides of Pericles, the leading man of the Athenians' age: "he led the city in word, but in deed he was the first man" [ἐξηγεῖτο τε λόγῳ μὲν, ἔργῳ δὲ, ὁ τῶν πρώτων ἀνὴρ]. In word indeed it was a popular state; in truth, however, it was the rule of one leading man in the state (Book 2 of the History). For the Roman masters, deceived by names and outward forms, scarcely held a shadow of the old liberty. Yet since, I hear, they have been shut out of Dio's patronage and flee to the protection of Strabo, I will show how much refuge there is in him. To begin with, I do not grant so much faith or authority to a man who was not even of Greek stock, let alone Italian or Roman, a barbarian among the Armenians and Cappadocians, who has been convicted more than once of vanity or carelessness even in minor matters, and who reports the innermost secrets of the Roman state, however far he penetrated into them, that he should be heard as a fit witness against the conflicts of Roman affairs. As for the passage nearest to us and more favourable to our view, his words do not reject a milder interpretation. Searching carefully for what machinery he brought against us, I came upon a passage in the sixth book of the Geography which is ambiguous: [χαλεπὸν δὲ ἄλλως οἰκεῖν τὴν Πλιχαωτῶν ἡγεμονίαν, ἢ ἐν ἐπιτροπεύεσθαι ὡς πατρί]. This too we grant concerning the convenient administration of a great empire. What is asked is about full right, given by some sanction of law and taken away from the people. But surely the thunderbolts of the words that follow strike us: [ἀφ' ἑ πτερίλαβες ἀντπλὴ]. They would strike if either he had opened a way of receiving contrary to Cornelius, or if power released from any rendering of account designated regal force in Greek authors. Another passage which I have found stands at the end of the work, namely in book XVII: [ἐπεὶ τοῖς ἡ πατρὶς ἐπιτρε… ἀπὸ τῆς ἡγεμονίας, ἡ τὸ ἐμὸν ἐγέννησε κατὰ τὴν χύσιν ἀλλὰ βίᾳ]. In the turbulent storm of affairs at home and abroad, the power to establish peace or to conduct war was granted, as once to a dictator or to the decemvirs, together with the protection of the empire, limited by a term of time; the fatherland, that is the necessity of the times, permitted it. Recently among the British, with greater power of commanding, a certain Cromwell has come forward, having seized the title of protector, to whom all right of the people has been transferred, the name of the commonwealth having been extinguished at its very cradle; the English nation will not deny it. Therefore epitropia must be distinguished from full kingship, and basileia, which remains with the people's leadership, from supreme authority, and the dispensing of peace and war from the higher summit of command, with careful scrupulosity of speech. There is also a kind of supreme power, seized by fraud or force for the public good of the country's liberty, which, though the ignorant counted it a fault in Pittacus, was praised by the outcome and by those who knew the facts, as the Geographer tells in book XIII. [Pittacus, when he dissolved the dominations of certain men, usurped supreme power himself; the business done, he restored the liberty of the citizens.] Which, too, we may attribute to Augustus' intention, either to the pretence of a feeble head of empire, or to the praise of a generous spirit.

units.la: CIV. Non leve principatus invidi fulcrum successor destinatus.
units.tr: CIV. A successor designated as no small prop for an envied principate.

units.la: Aliquando & in partem societatis imperii assume ptus. Sic apud Germanos Carolus V, Hispanica edu-catione non omnibus æquè acceptus, Ferdinandum fratrem sibi imperio proximum, & tantùm non foci-um,adjunxit. Sic, nascente Romanorum monarchia, Augustus Vipsanium Agrippam sociium tribunitiæ potestatis, quo defuncto Tiberium Neronem delegit, ne successor in incerto foret. Sed quæ ratio aphorismi no-stri, & quæ Augustum impulerit? aperit eam Cornelius: sic cohiberi pravas aliorum spei rebatur, minus vitæ imperantis, minus imperio insidiantur, qui eo sublato successorem, & manus illatæ ultorem confpi-cantur. Sic & famæ invitis imperantis, ac ad posteros memoriæ,consulitur. Reducto enim ad populum orbe imperii, memoria ejus ut tyranni damnatur. Hæc rede autem habenas regni excipiente, inter divos re-fertur. Julii Cæsaris cædes, antequam ultor extaret, pulcherrimum facinus populi ore ferebatur. Eminentè triumvirorum,& mox Augusti solius,potentia; divi appellatione consecratus, locum inter sidera accepit. Nonnunquam & successor alienus, à dominante non provisus, nec cum necessitudine aliqua attingens, volente populo memoriam sublati prosternit. Quod Neroni à Galba & Vespasiano, Domitiano à Nerva & Trajano obtigit. Sed annon ab ipso successore designato, & militari manu armato, periculum metuendum, ne habere imperium,quàm exspectari malit? Est persæpè: nec à successore filio satis latera regnantis munita, Sed Augustus integritati Agrippæ, & eo defuncto mo-destia Neronis, & sua magnitudini sidebat. Necitaque ambitionis nimiæ hominem, aut popularibus gratio-rem,proxima sibi fede locare,tutum. nec ita quisquam evehendus,ut non plus virium, plus autoritatis penes imperantem resideat. Augusti, quem in plerisque actionibus imitabatur, exemplo Tiberius Drusum sum-m& [?] admovet: cum incolumi Germanico, integrum inter duos judicium tenuisset. Populi magis quàm suum judicium. Germanicum enim ipse & vivo sibi insidiatorem, & mortuo successorem, judici anxius, timuerat. Plura de successore diligendo, & circa eam curam cautionibus, pete ex Arcanis regnorum, pagina primæ editionis 159.
units.tr: Sometimes a ruler also takes a man into partnership in the empire. Thus among the Germans Charles V, who was not equally acceptable to everyone because of his Spanish upbringing, joined to himself in the empire his brother Ferdinand, who stood next to him and was almost a partner. Thus too, when the Roman monarchy was coming into being, Augustus took Vipsanius Agrippa as partner in tribunician power and, when Agrippa died, chose Tiberius Nero, so that the succession would not be left uncertain. But what is the reason for our aphorism, and what moved Augustus? Cornelius explains it: he thought that in this way the wicked hopes of others were restrained. Men plot less against the life of a ruler, and less against his empire, when they see that if he is removed there is a successor, and an avenger of the violence done to him. Thus too the good name of the ruler, against his unwilling critics, and his memory among posterity, are secured. For if the empire is handed back to the people, his memory is condemned as that of a tyrant; but when the reins of the kingdom are taken up by a successor, he is counted among the gods. Caesar's murder, before an avenger existed, was spoken of by the people as a most glorious deed. Once the power of the triumvirs, and soon of Augustus alone, had become eminent, Caesar was consecrated with the title of god and received a place among the stars. Sometimes a successor from outside, not provided by the ruler and not connected to him by any kinship, overthrows the memory of the one removed, when the people wish it. This happened to Nero at the hands of Galba and Vespasian, and to Domitian at the hands of Nerva and Trajan. But is there not danger to be feared from the designated successor himself, armed with a military force, lest he prefer to seize the empire rather than wait for it? It happens very often. Nor is the ruler's flank sufficiently protected by a successor who is his son. But Augustus trusted in the integrity of Agrippa, after his death in the modesty of Nero, and in his own greatness. Nor is it safe to place next to oneself, in the nearest seat, a man of excessive ambition or one more popular with the people. Nor should anyone be raised so high that more strength and more authority do not remain with the ruler. Following the example of Augustus, whom he imitated in most of his actions, Tiberius advanced Drusus to a high place, and while Germanicus was alive he had kept the judgement between the two undecided. It was the judgement of the people rather than his own. For he himself, anxious in his judgement, had feared Germanicus, as a plotter against him while alive and as a successor once he was dead. More on choosing a successor and on the precautions to be taken in that care, seek in the Arcana regnorum, page 159 of the first edition.

units.la: CV. Successor non à natalium tantum genere, sed inprimis à moribus & actionum felicitate commendatur.
units.tr: CV. A successor is recommended not only by the rank of his birth, but above all by his character and the success of his actions.

units.la: Si adoptione successor quærendus, non probatissimæ vitæ principes sæpè deteriores sibi surrogant, quare securitati suæ consulti, & mortuorum memoriam desiderari, arbitrantur. Augustus multorum sermone arguitur, quoniam arrogantiam sævitiamque Tiberii introspexerit, comparatione deterrima sibi gloriam quæsivisse, primo libro Annalium. Sic Tiberius unum Germanici liberorum Cajum Caligulam non interemit; imperiumque ei non illibenter fertur tradidisse, ut & ipsius facinora gravioribus Caji flagitiis occultarentur, & quod in senatu nobilitatis reliquum, post mortem suam trucidaretur. Dio Cassius libro 58. Qui vero recip. incolumitatem sibi propositam habent, aut qui victuram in liberis gloriam quærunt; longè aliam in formando successore viam insistunt. Primò in Dei nutum, & in veram imperiorum metam, oculis defixis, Deum venerantur, ut consilia sua reip. prosperè evenire velint. Deinde mores imperaturi scrutantur: ut imperaturus omnibus omnes virtutum excellentia præstet. Quantum enim homo natura omnibus animantibus antecellit, tantum, si fieri per imbecillitatem humanam potest, qui regit cæteros virtute sublimiorem esse, optandum. Sed quoniam toto genere nemo a mortalium renuitate differt, & rari sunt heroum fœtus, satis est, si a communi hominum natura principes non degenerant, naturam non depravata confuetudine corruptam , sed integram , nec àftatú suo sponte deficientem,capio. Prima igitur pudicitiæ, cum omni genere temperantiæ , cura moderatori reip. habenda.
