Cum luxum adolescentiæ , nimis apud Romanos tum receptum , amoliri Tiberius non audebat: pudicitiam Drufi à fœcundo conjugio commonstrat. esse illi con-jugem & tres liberos. non enim verisimile iis tempori-bus credebatur , esse quenquam ea continentia vitæ, ut castum degere cœlibatum posset. Hinc ea Augusti ad cœlibem vitam agentes objurgatio: [illegible, ~20 letters] solitudo vos vivendi capit,ut abíque mulieribus dega-tis: nec est quisquam vestrûm, qui non & mensæ & lecti sociam habeat: sed licentiam libidini aclasciviæ vestræ quæritis. apud Dionem, libro 56. præcipua vero principis ab autoritate, prudentia experimento quæsita, fortitudine in periculis, exantlandorum feli-citate, commendatio. quas artes in Drufo Tiberius coacervando, dignum suscipiendo regimine ostentat. Neque nunc properè, sed per octo annos capto experi-mento, compressis seditionibus, compositis bellis, triumpha-lem c[?] bis consulem, noti laboris participem sumni. At de justitia, clementia, mansuetudine, æquitate, non postremo virtutum principum choro,cur verbum non mutit? nimirum rectorem universi palàm Tiberius proponere non ausus, tanquam militiæ imperatorem commendans, nota modestiæ imitatione, quæ coràm in senatu tot per annos justè aut clementer décreverit, tacitis patrum judiciis relinquit. A Tiberio, quamvis fictam sæpè personam induente, saltem Christianam pieratem professi reges discant, quales imperio gubernatores futuros obtrudant.
units.tr: If a successor is to be sought by adoption, princes of the most blameless life often choose worse men for themselves. Therefore those who look to their own security, and think the memory of the dead should be lamented, do otherwise. Augustus is accused by many people's talk of having looked into the arrogance and cruelty of Tiberius and of having sought glory for himself by the worst possible comparison, in the first book of the Annals. Thus Tiberius did not kill Gaius Caligula, one of Germanicus's children; and he is said to have handed the empire to him not unwillingly, so that Gaius's own crimes would be hidden behind his more serious disgraces, and so that whatever remained of the nobility in the senate would be butchered after Tiberius's own death. Dio Cassius, book 58. Those, however, who keep the safety of the commonwealth before them, or who seek glory that will live on in their children, take a very different course in forming a successor. First, with their eyes fixed on the will of God and on the true goal of empires, they worship God, that they may wish their counsels for the commonwealth to turn out prosperously. Then they examine the characters of those about to rule, so that the one who is to rule excels all others in the eminence of his virtues. For as man surpasses all living creatures by nature, so it is to be wished, if human weakness allows it, that the one who governs others should be higher than them in virtue. But since no one among mortals differs from the common run of the species, and offspring of heroes are rare, it is enough if princes do not fall away from the common nature of man, understanding that nature not as depraved and corrupted by bad custom, but as whole, and not spontaneously failing with age. The first care of the ruler of the commonwealth, then, must be for chastity, together with every kind of self-restraint. Since Tiberius did not dare to check the luxury of young men, which was then too widely accepted among the Romans, he pointed to the chastity of Drusus in his fruitful marriage: that he had a wife and three children. For it was not thought probable in those times that anyone could live with such self-restraint as to be able to live chastely unmarried. Hence Augustus's rebuke to those living a single life: [illegible] "Solitude captures you for living, so that you pass your lives without women; yet there is not one of you who does not have a companion at his table and in his bed; but you seek licence for lust and wantonness." In Dio, book 56. The chief commendation of a prince, however, comes from his authority, from prudence proved by experience, from courage in dangers, and from success in carrying out hard tasks. Tiberius displays these arts gathered together in Drusus, to show that he is worthy to take up government. And this was not done hastily, but after a trial of eight years: seditions were quelled, wars settled, and he had been made a partner in the great labours of the one who had triumphed and been consul twice. But why does he not change the word about justice, clemency, gentleness, and fairness, which are not the least of the chorus of princely virtues? Surely because Tiberius did not dare to set forth openly a ruler of the universe, and so, commending him as a commander of the army, he leaves to the silent judgements of the Fathers those things which he had decided so justly or mercifully in the senate for so many years, with a show of modest imitation. Let Christian kings, who profess true piety, learn from Tiberius, though he often put on a feigned mask, what kind of governors they should impose on their realms as future rulers.

units.la: CVI.
units.tr: CVI.

units.la: Vilium animorum est nimia in prin-cipem adulatio.
units.tr: Excessive flattery of the prince is a sign of base minds.

units.la: Nam & servientis animi indicium, & sæpè deridi[?]eulo est,ipsique principi aut tædio aut morum corruptioni. Omnium sub Tiberio senatorum animos quæsitior adulatio invaserat. Non tantum petitioni ejus, id quod necessum erat, subscribebant: sed, &c. quod non perebatur, effigies principum, aras deum, templa & arcus, prompto consuetudine obsequio, censebant. Hæc more non inusitata videbantur. Excessit modum M. Silanus: dixitque pro sententia, ut publicis privatisve monimentis, ad memoriam temporum, non consulum nomina præscriberentur, sed eorum qui tribunitiam potestatem gererent. id erat uno momento remp. evertere; quæ veteris in libertate dignitatis umbram vel præcipuam in consulum designatione, & fastorum ab iis inscriptione, conservabat. Sed nec memoriæ temporum versa inscriptio consulebat: perpetua Cæsareæ domus tribunitia potestate. Sed hæc sententia paucorum assensu, aut levi admurmuratione, dimissa. Haterius vero cum ejus diei, senatusconsulta aureis literis figenda in curia censuisset, deridiculo fuit, senex fœdissima adulationis tantum infamia usurus. Quam quidem sententiæ adulatoriæ insolentiam Tiberius ipse, per literas arguendo, repressit. Sic nec Tiberio gratus Haterius, & sibi apud patres ludibrio fuit. Quàm vero corrumpendis principum moribus exitiosa sit effusa in adulationem levitas, in Arcanis re-gnorum detexi. Nunc quemadmodum & in libera republica perniciosa sit, paucis consideremus.
units.tr: For it is both a mark of a servile spirit and often an object of ridicule, and it is either a weariness to the prince himself or a corruption of his morals. Under Tiberius a more exquisite flattery had seized the minds of all the senators. They not only subscribed to his petition, which was necessary, but also, what was not sought, they voted, by a readiness made habitual by custom, statues of the princes, altars to the god, temples and arches. These proposals seemed not unusual in their manner. But M. Silanus went beyond the measure: and he gave his opinion that in public or private monuments, for the memory of the times, the names not of the consuls should be written, but of those who held tribunician power. That would have overturned the commonwealth in a single moment; the consuls' designation and the inscription of the fasti with their names preserved the shadow of ancient dignity in liberty, and above all that dignity. But the reversed inscription would not have served the memory of the times either, since the house of Caesar would hold tribunician power in perpetuity. However, this opinion was dropped with the assent of a few, or with slight murmuring. Haterius, indeed, when he proposed that the decrees of the senate of that day should be fixed in the Curia in golden letters, became a laughing-stock, an old man who would reap only the disgrace of the most shameful flattery. Tiberius himself checked the arrogance of this flattering proposal by writing to the senate in rebuke. So Haterius was neither pleasing to Tiberius nor a figure of ridicule before the Fathers. How ruinous to the corruption of princes' morals is the lightness that pours itself out into flattery, I have shown in the Arcana of Kingdoms. Now let us briefly consider how it is also ruinous in a free commonwealth.

units.la: Periclem quidem, gravitate imperatorii viri servata, populum in officio continuisse: at qui secuti sunt populi ductores, omnia ad voluptatem ac gratiam loquentes, ac facientes, navim reip. Atticæ gravissimè impegisse Thucydides libro secundo commemorat. Cui ætate proximè conjunctus Aristophanes antiquæ Comœdiæ luculentus, quanquam verborum spurcitie sæpè lutulentus, autor, ventosam oratorum vanitatem, & credulam populi Attici levitatem, non uno in loco traducit. Præ cæteris insignis locus est in Equi-tibus: populi senio delirantis persona in theatrum introducta. Quo in dramate, quam falsè Cleo, popuIi sectator, traducatur à farciminum venditore, reme-dium[?] malorum pollicito, ex ipso poëta, cui tanti est, decerpat.
units.tr: Pericles, indeed, keeping the dignity of an imperial man, held the people in duty; but the leaders of the people who followed him, speaking and acting entirely for pleasure and favour, Thucydides records in book two as having struck the ship of the Attic commonwealth very heavily. Aristophanes, closely connected in age to him and a brilliant writer of Old Comedy, though often muddied by the filth of his words, portrays in more than one place the windy vanity of the orators and the credulous fickleness of the Attic people. Most notable among these is the passage in the Knights, where the figure of the people, raving in old age, is brought onto the stage. In that play, see how falsely Cleon, a follower of the people, is portrayed by the sausage-seller, who promises a remedy for the ills, from the poet himself, to whom it matters so much.

units.la: CVII.
units.tr: CVII.

units.la: Minus est summa unius potestate ær-mulationi & ferræ contentionum loci.
units.tr: Less is there room for rivalry and bitter contention where the supreme power rests in one man.

units.la: Quanquam apta ad causam suam oratione, nonta-men rejicienda ratione, Maluginensis : Privatis olim simultatibus effectum, ut à pontificibus maximis in-provinciis prohiberentur. nunc deinde munere sum-mum Pontificum etiam summum hominum esse non amulatione, non odio, aut privatis affectionibus obno-xium. non quod humanis affectuum perturbatio-nibus purgatiores principes: sed quod inter conditione vitæ dispares æmulatio honorum, ac simultates ex re-pulsa non æque accenduntur. Cæterum vindicandus hic locus à pravo sensus intelle&u. Non hoc vel au-toritate Taciti, vel sententia Maluginensis, asseritur: summum Pontificem supra omnes homines imperio vel dignitate, esse: sed contigisse, ut idem Tiberius, quem fortuna imperii supra omnes homines evexit, etiam congesto in ipsum Pontificatus honore, utraque dignitate præfulgeret. Si quis verò à Tiberio ad Pa-pam Romanum argumentetur, paganos Romano-rum mores cum Christiana simplicitate ineptè consu-derit.
units.tr: Although Maluginensis argues aptly for his cause, his reasoning should not be rejected outright. He says: In former times it was brought about by private rivalries that the greatest pontiffs were forbidden to hold provinces. Now, by the office of the highest Pontiff, the highest of men is exposed to no rivalry, no hatred, and no private affections. This is not because princes are purer than human passions, but because rivalry over honours is not kindled as fiercely between people of unequal conditions, and rivalries arising from rejection do not burn as hotly. Yet this passage must be defended against a perverse reading. It is not asserted, on the authority of Tacitus or the opinion of Maluginensis, that the highest Pontiff is above all men in power or dignity. Rather, it happened that the same Tiberius, whom fortune raised above all men to the empire, also shone with both dignities once the honour of the Pontificate had been heaped upon him. If anyone argues from Tiberius to the Roman Pope, he has most clumsily combined pagan Roman customs with Christian simplicity.

units.la: CVIII.
units.tr: CVIII.

units.la: Nihil superba modestia morofius.
units.tr: Nothing is more troublesome than a proud modesty.

units.la: Ex alio enim fastigii sui sensu, & humilitatis alie-rum contemptu, arrogantiæ moderationem ut sui di-millionem imputat. Drufus, quinovos honores ad-eptus, adire urbem, coràm gratias agere patribus de-bebat, epistolis duntaxat senatum aggreditur. quæ quanquam ad modestiam flexa, pro superbissimis acci-piebantur. Similis de Tiberio locutio libro primo Annalium. Cum patres, adulatione alius alium vin-centes, ut corpus defuncti Augusti senatorum bume-ris. ris ad rogum ferretur, conclamarent: Remisit Cæsar adroganti moderationem.
units.tr: For from one sense of his own eminence, and from contempt for the humility of others, such a man ascribes the moderation of his arrogance to his own condescension. When Drusus had obtained his honours, he ought to have come to the city and thanked the fathers in person; he approached the senate only by letters. Although these were framed with modesty, they were taken as most arrogant. A similar expression is used of Tiberius in the first book of the Annals: when the fathers, each outdoing the others in flattery, were shouting that the body of the dead Augustus should be carried to the pyre on the shoulders of senators, they cried out: Caesar has remitted his arrogant moderation.

units.la: CIX.
units.tr: CIX.

units.la: Imagine antiquitatis novitas, pictura libertatis dominatio stabilitur.
units.tr: Novelty dressed in the image of antiquity, and domination dressed in the picture of liberty, are made secure.

units.la: In quibus est patrum de levioribus rebus permissa à principe cognitio. Tiberius vim principatus sibi fir-mans, imaginem antiquitatis senatui præbebat, postulata provinciarum ad disquisitionem patrum mittendo. Sic primo Annalium libro inter patres altercatio de histrionum coërcenda licentia incessit, silente Tiberio, qui ea simulacra libertatis senatui præbebat. Ejusdem libri fine de candidatorum edendis nominibus: speciosa verbis, vana aut subdola: quanto majore libertatis imagine tegebantur, tanto eruptura ad infensius servitium. Plura de his ex Arcanis regnorum hauri.
units.tr: Among these is the permission the prince granted the fathers to hear minor matters. Tiberius, establishing the power of the principate for himself, offered the senate an image of antiquity, by sending the demands of the provinces to the fathers for investigation. So in the first book of the Annals, a dispute arose among the fathers about restraining the license of actors, while Tiberius was silent, he who offered the senate those images of liberty. At the end of the same book, concerning the publishing of the names of candidates: They were speciously worded, empty or deceitful; the more they were covered with the image of liberty, the more they were bound to break out into a more hostile slavery. More on these matters I have drawn from the Secret Arts of Kingdoms.

units.la: CX.
units.tr: CX.

units.la: Supplicibus asyla, non insultantibus, perfugia præbent.
units.tr: Sanctuaries offer refuge to suppliants, not to those who insult.

units.la: Nec populi seditionibus, flagitia hominum ut care-monias deum protegentis. Sed de asylis peculiari aphorismo supra egimus: illinc assumes, quæ ad hunc locum pertinebunt. Pauca modo addenda: honestissi-mam perfugii causam videri, injusta patientium pro-tectionem. Honestati autem utilitatem adjungi, si rebellantes vires ad societatem conferant. Hoc argumento magis, quam supplicum veneratione, Mityle-næi ab Atheniensibus deficientes, Lacedæmonios commoverunt. [?]ἦν δ᾽ ἱκετεύοντες φαίνωνται[?], τῇ κρατοῦντι τῇ πόλει [?]βεβαιότερον ἔσται[?]. ἀλλ᾽ ὠφελουμένης [?]ἐπὶ τοῦ Ὀλυμπίου[?], ἐν ᾗ τῇ [?]ἱερῷ[?] ἐκτίσθη ... i. e. Sin vos liberatores ostenderitis, vires belli firmiores habebitis. Græcorum igitur spes de vobis, & Jovem Olympium veniti[?], cujus in templo prope ut supplices adsumus, Mityl-enæos inita soci-ætate protegite. Thucyd. libro 3. Instructam autem classem in procinctu habebant, praecipuum societatis non aspernandae momentum.
units.tr: Nor do they protect the crimes of men who are in revolt against the commonwealth, the wicked deeds of men who shelter behind the ceremonies of God. But I have already treated sanctuaries in a special aphorism above; take from there what pertains to this place. Only a few things need adding: the most honourable cause of refuge seems to be the protection of those suffering injustice. Usefulness, moreover, is joined to honour if those who rebel bring their strength into alliance. The Mytileneans, revolting from the Athenians, moved the Lacedaemonians more by this argument than by the reverence due to suppliants: [ἦν δ᾽ ἱκετεύοντες φαίνωνται, τῇ κρατοῦντι τῇ πόλει βεβαιότερον ἔσται. ἀλλ᾽ ὠφελουμένης ἐπὶ τοῦ Ὀλυμπίου, ἐν ᾗ τῇ ἱερῷ ἐκτίσθη ...] that is, if you show yourselves to be liberators, you will have firmer forces for the war. Therefore the hopes of the Greeks rest on you, and we are present as suppliants, as it were, at the temple of Olympian Jove; protect the Mytileneans, with whom an alliance has been entered. Thucydides, book 3. They also kept their fleet equipped and ready for battle, a principal weight in the alliance that should not be scorned.

units.la: CXI. Immoderati honoris avidissimum animal fœmina.
units.tr: CXI. A woman is the most greedy creature for immoderate honour.

units.la: Non pessima mulierum Romanarum Livia, Marcelli effigie divo Augusto dicata, Tiberii nomen suo postscripserat. ὅτι καὶ αὐτὴ τὴν [?] σεβασμῶν, ὡς καὶ αὐτὴ [illegible, ~12 letters] ἀντεπιτάσσειν. nam & ipsa rebus administrandis, quasi imperatrix, se ingessit. Dio libro 56. imo se filio rebus gerendis, & imperii autoritate, praetulit: ut ex hoc Taciti, & alio Dionis, loco perspicitur. ἐπὶ τε τοῦ Αὐγούστου μέγιστον ἡδυνήν [?], καὶ τὸν Τιβέριον αὐτὴν αὐτῷ [?] ... ἐξ ὧν ὅσον ἐξ ὧν οἱ ἀρχὴν, ἀλλὰ ἐθέλειν αὐτοῦ ἠξίωσεν [?]. i. e. etenim Augusto rerum potito plurimum potuerat, Tiberioque se imperium dedisse jactitabat. ideoque non exaequata modo potestate cum eo imperare, sed ipso priores ferre voluit. lib. 57. Nota Agrippinae, matris ac filiae, nota Medicearum in Gallia impotentia. Quapropter Tiberius muliebre fastigium in diminutionem sui accipiens, non absque ratione, Moderandos esse fœminarum honores, rescripsit. lib.1.Annal.
units.tr: Livia, not the least of Roman women, had added the name of Tiberius beneath the image of Marcellus that was dedicated to the deified Augustus. [ὅτι καὶ αὐτὴ τὴν ... σεβασμῶν, ὡς καὶ αὐτὴ ... ἀντεπιτάσσειν.] For she too thrust herself into the conduct of affairs, as if she were an empress. Dio, book 56, says that she even placed herself above her son in managing affairs and in the authority of empire, as is clear from this passage of Tacitus and another of Dio's. [ἐπὶ τε τοῦ Αὐγούστου μέγιστον ἡδυνήν, καὶ τὸν Τιβέριον αὐτὴν αὐτῷ ... ἐξ ὧν ὅσον ἐξ ὧν οἱ ἀρχὴν, ἀλλὰ ἐθέλειν αὐτοῦ ἠξίωσεν.] That is: for while Augustus held the reins of affairs she had very great power, and she boasted that she had handed the empire over to Tiberius. Therefore she wished not merely to share power with him on equal terms, but to take precedence over him. Book 57. Notorious is the arrogance of Agrippina, mother and daughter, and notorious the overbearing of the Medici women in France. Therefore Tiberius, taking the women's elevation as a diminution of himself, not without reason wrote back that the honours of women must be moderated. Book 1 of the Annals.

units.la: CXII. Magnum historiae scribendae pretium in vitae actae testimonio.
units.tr: CXII. The great reward of writing history lies in the testimony of a life lived.

units.la: Quod non vano de scriptis suis elogio Cornelius pronunciat. Exequi sententias haud instituti, nisi insignes per honestum, aut notabili dedecore. quod praecipuum munus annalium reor, ne virtutes sileantur, atque pravis dictis factisque ex posteritate & infamia metus sit. Nec tamen solus hic annalium edendorum fructus: plures ab aliis in historiae commendatione congesti; & oculis omnium expositi non occultantur.
units.tr: Cornelius (Tacitus) does not make this claim about his writings out of vain boasting. It is not my purpose to set out the opinions of those who were not notable for honour or for some notable disgrace. This is, I think, the chief office of annals: that virtues should not be passed over in silence, and that bad words and deeds should bring fear of posterity and infamy. Nor is this the only fruit of publishing annals. Several others, gathered by different writers in praise of history and set before the eyes of all, are not hidden.

units.la: CXIII. Cupido lucri aut vitæ, adulationis fomentum.
units.tr: CXIII. Desire for gain or for life, the fuel of flattery.

units.la: Cupidinem a cupiditate ita Cajus Lucilius distinguit: Cupiditas ex homine, cupido ex stulto nunquam tollitur: quod cupiditas pars quædam fit temperatior defluens ex cupiditne. lib.23. Satyr. Eaplerunque libidinum est, & intemperati amoris. Sed instituto nostro servientes, lucri eam aut vitæ fecimus. De lucri avidi- tate, propria adulationis matre, affatim Aristoteles & discipulus ejus Theophrastus. De cupidine vitæ, & ei oppositomortis metu, hoc loco Cornelius: non modo primores civitatis quibus claritudo sua obsequiis pro- legenda erat. Ergo obsequium, quod honestius adulationi nomen imponitur, claris viris pro umbone fæ-vitiæ. quam ut effugerent, mellita semper & placentia tyranno verba stillabant. Sed an placentia semper, & voti finem assecuta? Negat de Tiberiano more Cornelius. Memoria prodidit, Tiberium, quoties curia egrederetur, Græcis verbis in hunc modum eloqui solitum, O homines ad servitutem paratos! scilicet etiam illum, qui libertatem publicam nollet, tam projecta servientium patientia tædebat, nec plerique eorum, ad obsequium principum affabre factorum, sub Tiberio ac mox Caligula crudelem necem effugerunt. [?]φύκε[?] [?]ἀνθρώπων καὶ [?]ὅλως [?]τὸ μὲν [?]τὸ δὲ [?] μὴ [?]ὑπερ[?]ζῆν[?] i.e. Natura ita comparatum est, ut colentes quemque contemnat, nulla in re cedentes admiretur. Thucyd.lib.3.
units.tr: Cajus Lucilius distinguishes cupido from cupiditas as follows: cupiditas is never removed from a man, cupido from a fool, because cupiditas becomes a somewhat more moderate part of cupido as it flows away from it. (Lucilius, Satires, book 23.) Usually it concerns lusts and intemperate love. But, following our plan, we have made it a matter of gain or of life. Concerning the greed for gain, the proper mother of flattery, Aristotle and his disciple Theophrastus speak at length. Concerning the desire for life, and the fear of death opposed to it, Cornelius speaks here: not only the leading men of the state, whose renown had to be preserved by compliance. Therefore obsequium, which is more honourably called by the name of flattery, was used by distinguished men as a shield against danger, and in order to escape it they always dripped honeyed and pleasing words to the tyrant. But were these words always pleasing, and did they attain the end they wished for? Cornelius denies it, in the case of Tiberius' manner: Records tell that Tiberius, whenever he came out of the senate house, used to say in Greek words, "O men ready for slavery!" Evidently even he, who did not want public liberty, was disgusted by such abject patience in servants; nor did many of those who had skilfully made themselves compliant to the princes escape a cruel death under Tiberius and soon under Caligula. (The Greek is garbled in the scan; the sense is that nature is so constituted that men despise those who court them and admire those who yield in nothing. Thucydides, book 3.) [φύσει ἀνθρώπων ... ]

units.la: CXIV. Lentus ad honorem adipiscendum gradus, præceps ad ignominiam.
units.tr: CXIV. Slow steps to win honour, headlong fall into disgrace.

units.la: De multis dici potest, quod de Brutidio Cornelius: si rectum iter pergeret, ad clarissima quæque iturum, festinatio exstimulabat, dum æquales, dein superiores, postremo suas ipse spes anteire parat. quod multos etiam bonos pessundedit, qui pretium quæ tarda cum jucuritate, pramatura vel cum exitio properant. Nam jam urgemus, honores, virtutum umbras, fugientem sequi, frequentem fugere. Adsit cupiditati modus, ambitioni patrum. Raro praecipitati honores, ut porma praecocia, in diuturnitatem maturescunt. Nec a mendicitate ad opulentiam, a servitute ad regnum, ni-per mediaitinera, ordinariadatur transgressio.
units.tr: What Cornelius said of Brutidius can be said of many: if he were pursuing the straight road, he would go toward all the most distinguished things; haste spurred him on, while he prepared to outstrip first his equals, then his superiors, and finally his own hopes. This has also ruined many good men, who hurry to a reward before its time: what comes slowly comes with youth, what comes too early comes with ruin. For now we press on: we chase honours, the shadows of virtues, as they flee from us, and we flee from them as they pursue us. Let desire have its limit, and ambition likewise. Rarely do hasty honours, like precocious fruit, ripen into lasting ones. Nor is there any passage from beggary to wealth, or from servitude to kingship, except through the middle stages, by the ordinary way.

units.la: CXV.
units.tr: CXV.

units.la: Elinguis est offenso auditore elo-quentia.
units.tr: Eloquence is struck dumb when the hearer is offended.

units.la: Et trepida infesto judice causae dictio praesertim quis patrocinio destitutus, adversus gratiam & facundiam respondeat; erandi nescius, proprio in metu, quae exercitam quoque eloquentiam debilitat.
units.tr: A trembling speech is made when the judge is hostile, especially when the speaker, who lacks a patron, must answer against favour and skill: unskilled at speaking, in his own fear, which weakens even practised eloquence.

units.la: Quod si ipse princeps accusando vel creberrime interrogando urgeat: & refellendo & reticendo cau-fam tuam everteris. Argui enim & convinci aegre fe-runt, qui verba sua pro oraculis accipi volunt. Nec semper simulatio Vitellii, furioso principe, nec M. Terentii libertas loquendi, astute suspicace, proderit. Vitellius a Cajo Caligula ut interficeretur accersitus, cum necis causam virtutum suarum invidiam esse non ignoraret, ignaviae simulatione periculum effugit, in humilitatem habitus deje&tus & divinitatis gloriam insano principi adscribens, non modo veniam consecutus, verum & amicorum primus habitus est. Pari astutia, vel ad hanc quaestionem accommodatiori, Domitius Afer, oratorum sub eodem Caligula primus, praesentem mortis terrorem evasit. Prolixam defcri-pto oratione contra eum, jactandae per vanitatem eloquentiae, Caligula habuit. Qua fe obstupefactum simulans Domitius, orationis proffluentis vim mira-tum, nihil tanquam dicendo superatus respondit. Vi-ctoriae laetitia perfusus Cajus, irae finem posuit. Ita Domitius amissae eloquentiae damnatus, poenae eripie-batur. Dio lib. 59. M. Terentius contra, Sejani ami-ciriam fatendo, & principem Tiberium culpae inne-ctendo, constantia orationis, non modo iram princi-pis. pis mitigavit, verum accusatores suos exilio aut mor-ti objecit. Orationem ejus, constantiae & gravitatis plenam, Tacitus libro vi. Annalium describit.
units.tr: But if the prince himself presses you, by accusing you or questioning you very often, you will ruin your case both by refuting and by keeping silent. For those who want their own words taken as oracles bear being argued against and convicted with difficulty. Nor did the pretence of Vitellius help against a raving prince, nor did the frankness of speech of M. Terentius help before a shrewd and suspicious one. When Gaius Caligula summoned Vitellius to have him killed, Vitellius knew that the cause of his death was the envy his virtues aroused. He escaped the danger by feigning cowardice: he put himself in a humble state and ascribed the glory of divinity to the insane prince. He not only obtained pardon but was made first among the prince's friends. With equal cunning, or with a cunning better suited to this question, Domitius Afer, first of the orators under the same Caligula, escaped the immediate terror of death. Caligula delivered against him a long speech, written out in advance, to show off his eloquence through vanity. Domitius pretended to be stunned and, marvelling at the force of the flowing speech, answered as one overcome, saying nothing. Gaius, flooded with the joy of victory, put an end to his anger. So Domitius, condemned for having lost his eloquence, was snatched from punishment. Dio, book 59. M. Terentius, on the other hand, confessed his friendship with Sejanus and laid the blame on the prince Tiberius. By the constancy of his speech he not only softened the prince's anger but sent his accusers into exile or to death. Tacitus, in book vi of the Annals, describes his speech, which is full of constancy and dignity.

units.la: CXVI. Inevitabile miseris majestatis fulmen
units.tr: CXVI. The unavoidable thunderbolt of majesty against the wretched

units.la: Nam & in quemvis torqueri potest, & vox patrona reo abscinditur. ne quis necessariorum juvaret periclitantem, majestatu crimina subdebantur, vinculum & necessitas silendi. Sed quia de majestatis crimine alio loco liberalius egimus, vela hic contrahenda censemus.
units.tr: For a person may be tortured on anyone at all, and the voice of the patron is cut off from the accused. Lest any of his close relations help the one in peril, charges of treason were imposed as a bond and a necessity of silence. But since we have treated the crime of majesty more fully elsewhere, we judge that sails should be furled here.

units.la: CXVII. Delicta prohiberi, quàm puniri, civilius.
units.tr: CXVII. Offences are more civilly prevented than punished.

units.la: Prohibentur delicta. 1. severa educatione. 2. legum terrore promulgato. 3. delinquendi occasione praecidenda. Non igitur ad imperia, ad honores, ad praefecturas promovendi, quos peccaturos morum licentia arguit. Nec absurde Cornelius Dolobella censuit: ne quis vita probrosus, & opertus infamia, provinciam sortiretur. Sed unde ea vitae probrosae judicatio? unde luxus, avaritia, crudelitas, quae domesticae in vitae latebris delituit, protrahenda? nam ut judicium hoc principi deferatur, cum onere dijudicandi incertitudini subjacet. Recte quidem Dolobella subjungit, a legibus delicta puniri. quanto fore mitius in ipsos, minus[?] infocios, provideri nec peccaretur. Melius hominum saluti medici consulunt, qui antidotis, diaeta praescripta futuro morbo occurrunt, quam qui principiis negligenter habitis, ustione & sectione in corpora saeviunt. Nec multum provincialesjuvat, repetundarum aliquem damnari, qui non spoliari maluerant. Haec in consilio dando faciliùs: sed non in exequendo aeque prompta. Semper enim difficultas de incertitudine judicii & vitae la-tebroso probroso[?] lapsu[?], de futuri incerta exspectatione, de legum[?] non aspernanda autoritate remanet. Igitur juxta Dea- lobellam Tiberii etiam sententia audienda, nec ante causam plenè cognitam de tantæ rei momento pro- nunciandum.
units.tr: Offences are prevented: (1) by a strict upbringing; (2) by publishing the terror of the laws; (3) by cutting off the occasion for offending. So those whom the licence of their morals shows will sin should not be promoted to commands, honours or prefectures. Cornelius Dolabella not unreasonably judged that no one whose life is disgraceful and who is wrapped in infamy should receive a province by lot. But whence is that judgment of a disgraceful life to come? Whence are luxury, avarice and cruelty, which lurk in the hidden corners of private life, to be dragged out? For if this judgment is left to the prince, it is subject to the burden of deciding under uncertainty. Dolabella rightly adds: offences should be punished by the laws; how much milder it would be, and how much better for the less guilty, to make provision so that no sin is committed. Physicians serve the health of men better when they meet a future disease with antidotes and a prescribed diet, than when, having neglected the first beginnings, they rage against the body with cautery and the knife. Nor does it much help the provincials that someone is condemned for extortion, when they would rather not have been plundered at all. These things are easier to give as advice than to carry out with equal readiness. For difficulty always remains, arising from the uncertainty of the judgment and the hidden slips of life, from the uncertain expectation of the future, and from the authority of the laws, which is not to be scorned. Therefore, following Dolabella, the opinion of Tiberius too should be heard, and no one should pronounce on a matter of such weight before the case has been fully known.

units.la: Non ex rumore statuendum. Multa rumorem vel ex invidia in hominibus, vel ex garrula loquacitate, vel ignorantia rerum fingere, præterea non eosdem homines in publica & privata vita, in otio & negotio, esse neminem, antequam hostem & castra viderit, militiæ ineptum judicari. ficnec imperio indignos, qui nunquam imperii partem degustarunt, æstumandos. mul- tos in provinciis, contra quam spes aut metus de illis fuerit, egisse. nam aut latentia vitia specie probitatis imposuisse, aut delitescentem virtutis scintillam flabello negotiorum in flammam prorupisse. excitari quosdam ad meliora, magnitudine rerum, bebescere alios multorum generosos animi impetus minora negotia, aut privatæ vitæ humilitatem, negligenter habere: exsurrecturos, ubi ingenio suo par pabulum invenerint. Leonem ad latrátum minorum canum præterire; consistere ubi molossum aut leopardum conspexerit. Alios in parvis rebus negotiosos, admaguitudinem graviorum rerum torpescere. nec ipsum tumescentis oceani aspectum ferre, qui in Garumnæ aut Ligeris angustia se jactitaverit. In tanta autem in- geniorum diversitate neque posse principem sua scientia cuncta complecti: neque expedire, ut ambitione aliena trahatur. Non vacare ei in singulorum civium mo- res inquirere, cui universi cura est commissa. Ut verò ex aliorum commendatione, vel ambitione potiùs, circumferatur; nec ipsi principi decorum, nec reip. utile. ideò leges in facta constituit, quia futura in in- certo sint. qui verò legum vel reverentia vel terrore à delicto non absterreatur, eum frustra arcano princi- pis examini subjeceris. sic à majoribus institutum, ut si anteiffent delicta, pœna sequerentur. ne verterent sapientes reperta, & semper placita. nec posse vel ma- jorum sapientiam ineptitudinis, vel omnium seculo- rum consensum inscitiæ coargui. ne novitatis invidiam[?], cum curarum immenso onere, principis humeris injicerent. satis onerum principibus, satis etiam potentia. Nec censurae gravitatem, & in singulorum vitas inquisitionem, libertati civium exoptandam esse. Nec utendum imperio, ubi legibus agi possit esse aliquam in exaequationem legum antiquae libertatis imaginem: quam novitatis, & placendi imperanti, studio ne ultro amitterent. Hunc esse sensum postremae Tiberii orationis, judicio scriptoris evincitur. Quanto rarior apud Tiberium popularitas, tanto laetioribus animis accepta. Est enim popularitas oratio & gestus, populi libertati accommodatio. Sed ne obstrepere aphorismo videar: mitius omnino est, praecidere quam punire delicta. Sed ob incertitudinem judicii, & ne potentiam dominantis immensum augeamus, recepta legum consuetudine frequenter stamus.
units.tr: One should not decide on the basis of rumour. Rumour may be invented either from envy of men, or from garrulous chatter, or from ignorance of affairs. Besides, the same men are not the same in public and in private life, in leisure and in business; and no one should be judged unfit for soldiering before he has seen the enemy and the camp. Nor should those unworthy of command be esteemed who have never tasted any part of command. Many men in the provinces have behaved contrary to the hopes or fears that were held about them: for either hidden vices have deceived by a show of probity, or a smouldering spark of virtue has burst into flame when fanned by the bellows of business. Some are roused to better things by the greatness of affairs; others grow sluggish, and many generous impulses of mind are neglected in smaller business or in the humility of private life. These will rise up when they find fodder suited to their talent. A lion passes by the barking of small dogs, but halts when he sees a mastiff or a leopard. Others who are busy in small matters grow torpid in the face of weightier affairs, and cannot bear the sight of the swelling ocean, having boasted of themselves in the narrowness of the Garonne or the Loire. Given such diversity of talents, the prince cannot embrace everything by his own knowledge, nor is it expedient that he be swayed by the ambition of others. It is not his business to inquire into the morals of individual citizens, since the care of all has been committed to him. But if he is carried about by the recommendation of others, or rather by their ambition, it is neither seemly for the prince himself nor useful to the commonwealth. Therefore laws are laid down for deeds, because future things are uncertain. But whoever is not deterred from crime by reverence for the laws or by fear of them, you subject in vain to the secret scrutiny of the prince. It was so instituted by our ancestors: that if offences had gone before, punishment should follow; lest wise men overturn what has been discovered and always approved. Nor can the wisdom of our ancestors be convicted of incompetence, or the consensus of all the ages of ignorance. Lest they lay the odium of novelty, together with the immense burden of cares, on the shoulders of the prince; there are enough burdens for princes, and enough power too. Nor should the severity of censure and the inquisition into the lives of individuals be desired as a thing good for the liberty of citizens. Nor should power be used where the matter can be managed by the laws. There is in this equal application of the laws some image of ancient liberty, which they should not willingly give up through eagerness for novelty and for pleasing the ruler. That this is the sense of Tiberius's last speech is proved by the judgment of the writer: the rarer popularity was with Tiberius, the more gladly it was received. For popularity is speech and bearing adapted to the liberty of the people. But lest I seem to drone on in aphorisms: it is altogether milder to cut off offences than to punish them. Yet, on account of the uncertainty of judgment, and lest we greatly increase the power of the ruler, we often keep to the accepted custom of the laws.

units.la: CXVIII.
units.tr: CXVIII.

units.la: Major in viro erudito turpitudinis infamia.
units.tr: A greater infamy for a learned man who disgraces himself.

units.la: Alios enim aut ignorantia recti, aut degener vitae professio, excusat. Qui vero supra vulgus quid sapere prae se ferunt, minus excusate vel in minoribus offendunt. L. Ennius eques R. majestatis postulabatur, quod effigiem principis promiscuum ad usum argenti vertisset. Quasi vero interiorem argenti naturam cum externa forma amiserit, aut in vivam Tiberii faciem ex officina argentarii prodierit; aut denique moneta, insculptam Cæsaris effigiem gerens, non sit promiscui negotiorum & fori usus. Quare sapientior, aut certe mitior, accusatoribus Tiberius, Ennium recipi inter reos vetuit. Palam aspernante Ateio Capitone, quasi per libertatem. Stultitiam hominis, & foedam servitutis adulatoriae notam, cui tamen libertatis nomen imponit, mirare. Non enim debere eripi patribus vim statuendi, neque tantum maleficium impune habendum. Sane lentum in suo dolore esset: Reip. injurias ne-largiretur. Quasi vero, aut maleficium in argenti usu, aut Reip. injuria verteretur. Plures adulatoriae libertatis maculas in Arcanis regnorum congessimus, & fœditatem monstri ridendam exposuimus. nec prin- cipem gratia dicti permulsit, pellucidam simulatio- nem facile penetrantem. Intellexit hac Tiberius ut erant magis, quàm ut dicebantur: perflitiitque inter- cedere. vi nimirum Tribunitiæ potestatis : quam, ubi commodum visum, exprompsit; ubi incommodum, recondidit. Quo artificio detecto eum Scaurus in fe- natu tetigerat: fbem esse ex eo,non irritas fore Senatus preces, quòd relationi consulum jure Tribunitia pote- statis non intercesserit. Sed ad Ateium Capitonem re- deo, quem Tacitus ejusmodi elogio, aphorismo no- ftro consentiente,ferit: Capito insignior infamia fuit quòd humani divinique juris [ciens, egregium publi- cum, & bonas domi artes, dehoneftavifet. Non tan- tum è juris egregia scientia, verum etiam ex vita pro- bè anteacta, adulationis dedecori infamia accessit. Quod acumen Cornelii non alio magis quam simili Thucydidis loco illustrem. Cujus in Tertio belli Pe- loponnefiaci, Thebani Platæenfes ita redarguunt: ἀ ἀξυδεσης ... ὅτι ... ἀμφοτέρων ... ἐπὶ ... ἀγαθὰ ... ἐκ ... ἀλλ' ... i.e. Quas (virtutes antiquas) injuriam quidem patientibus prænfidio esse oportet; iis verò qui aliquid turpitudinis admiserunt, duplici pœnæ: eò quod à virtute sua degenerant. apud eundem autorem de Atheniensibus Sthenelaidas, Lacedæmoniorum epho- rus: ἐι ... ... ... ... ... ... Si contra Medos tunc boni fuerunt, nunc autem erga nos mali sunt, duplici sunt digni fup- plicio, quòd mali ex bonis effecti sunt. libro primo Bel- li Peloponn. Verùm quia de famæ damno, non judi- ciario supplicio hic agimus, dictum sapientissimi He- braorum audiamus: Muscarum mortuarum una effi- cit ut fœtorem eructet unguentem pigmentari: pre- tiofum sapientia & gloria virum fœtidum efficit ftoli- ditatis parum. Ecclef.10. v.3.
units.tr: Others are excused by ignorance of what is right or by a base manner of life. But those who claim to know more than the common people are less excusable when they offend, even in small matters. Lucius Ennius, a Roman knight, was prosecuted for treason because he had turned the image of the prince to common use as silver. As if he had lost the inner nature of the silver along with its outward form, or as if the living face of Tiberius had come out of the silversmith's workshop, or, finally, as if a coin bearing the carved likeness of Caesar were not for everyday use in business and the marketplace. Therefore Tiberius, wiser or at least milder than his accusers, forbade Ennius to be admitted among the accused. Atteius Capito openly disapproved, as if it were a matter of liberty. Marvel at the folly of the man, and at the foul mark of servile flattery, which he nevertheless calls by the name of liberty. For, he said, the senators ought not to be deprived of the power of deciding, nor should so great a wrong go unpunished. Indeed, it would be a sluggish man who did not, in his own grief, refuse to pass over injuries to the state. As if the wrong lay in the use of silver, or in an injury to the state. We have heaped up more stains of flattering liberty in the Arcana imperii, and have exposed the foulness of this monster to ridicule. Nor did the prince's saying soothe him with its grace, since the transparent pretence easily shows through. Tiberius understood that these things were more as they were than as they were said, and he persisted in interceding, by the power of the tribunate, no doubt, which he brought out when it seemed convenient and put away when it was inconvenient. By this trick Scaurus had touched him in the matter of the senate's resolution: that the senate's prayers would not be in vain, since he had not interceded, by the right of tribunician power, against the consuls' proposal. But I return to Atteius Capito, whom Tacitus, agreeing with our aphorism, marks with such a judgment: Capito was more notorious for infamy, because he had disgraced his knowledge of divine and human law, his distinguished public reputation and his good arts at home. Infamy came to him not only from his distinguished knowledge of law but also from an honourable former life, as a stain on his flattery. Cornelius's sharpness is made more famous by a passage like that of Thucydides. In the third book of the Peloponnesian War, the Thebans of Plataea rebuke them in this way: [ἀξυδεσης ... ὅτι ... ἀμφοτέρων ... ἐπὶ ... ἀγαθὰ ... ἐκ ... ἀλλ' ...] That is: those ancient virtues ought indeed to be a protection to those who suffer wrong, but for those who have committed some disgrace a double punishment follows, because they have fallen away from their own virtue. In the same author, Sthenelaidas, ephor of the Lacedaemonians, says of the Athenians: [εἰ ... ... ... ... ... ...] If the Medes were good then, but now are bad towards us, they deserve a double punishment, because they have been made bad from good. In the first book of the Peloponnesian War. But since we are here concerned with the loss of reputation and not with judicial punishment, let us hear the saying of the wisest of the Hebrews: Dead flies make the perfumer's ointment give off a stinking smell; a man precious for wisdom and glory is made foolish by a little folly. Eccles. 10.1.

units.la: CXIX. Et sacra juri imperii cedunt.
units.tr: CXIX. Even sacred things yield to the authority of empire.

units.la: Saltem iudicio Romanorum: a quo gentium usus non discrepat. Cunctas caeremonias Italicis in oppidis, templisque, & numinum effigies, juris atque imperii Romani esse. inde deditione alicujus populi facta, sacra simul cum profanis dedebantur. Quae vero extra jus imperii erant, ea ne sacra quidem judicabant: nec violatione eorum ulla religione commovebantur.
units.tr: At least by the judgement of the Romans, from which the practice of the nations does not differ. All the ceremonies in the Italian towns and temples, and the images of the gods, belong to the law and authority of Rome. Hence, when some people surrendered, their sacred things were surrendered along with their profane ones. But things that lay outside the authority of the empire they did not even regard as sacred, and they were not moved by any religious scruple at violating them.

units.la: Τῆς ἀμφὶ Νεῖλον δεισιδαιμονίας σπιζόμενοι[?]
units.tr: [Τῆς ἀμφὶ Νεῖλον δεισιδαιμονίας σπιζόμενοι[?]] Taking offence at the superstition about the Nile.

units.la: Nili colentes ambitum colo deos: inquit Aegyptiorum nuncius, abstractione supplicum, templum Graecorum violaturus. Nec Persae subvertendis Graecorum fanis, proruendis imaginibus, ullo deorum metu tangebantur. Nec Germanicus evertendo Tanfanae apud Germanos templo, nec ante eum duces Romani spoliandis victarum gentium templis, pollui se ullo modo arbitrabantur. Plura cogniturus adi Hugonem Grotium De jure belli ac pacis.
units.tr: "Those who dwell along the Nile, I worship the gods of the border," says the Egyptian envoy, about to violate the temple of the Greeks by carrying off its suppliants. Nor were the Persians restrained by any fear of the gods from overthrowing the Greek shrines and tearing down their images. Nor did Germanicus, in destroying the temple of Tanfana among the Germans, nor the Roman commanders before him, in plundering the temples of conquered nations, think that they were defiled in any way. If you wish to learn more, consult Hugo Grotius, De jure belli ac pacis.

units.la: CXX. Provinciarum administratio Dialibus interdicta.
units.tr: CXX. The administration of provinces forbidden to the Flamen Dialis.

units.la: Servius Maluginensis Flamen Dialis, provinciae cupidus, nec absentiam annuam nec provinciae administrationem cum sacro officio pugnare, frustra contenderat. Huic ex decreto Pontificum Tiberius adversantem promsit sententiam: annuam absentiam & provinciarum administrationem dialibus non concedi. nec enim praesentiam tantum sacrorum cura requirit: sed & res sunt toto coelo distantes, sacrorum ritus & forensium rerum strepitus. Quod si haec religio Romanos intravit, ultra caeremonias quasdam nihil divinis in rebus sapientes: quanto magis Christiana pietas, & excellentiori fine beata, ei docendi munere assidua, rerum sacrarum episcopos a terrenarum cura avocabit?
units.tr: Servius Maluginensis, the Flamen Dialis, was eager for a province and argued in vain that an annual absence and the administration of a province did not conflict with his sacred office. Tiberius opposed him and, following the decree of the Pontiffs, pronounced the sentence that an annual absence and the administration of provinces were not to be granted to the Flamen Dialis. For the care of sacred things requires more than bodily presence: the two things are worlds apart, the rites of worship and the din of public affairs. If the Romans, who were wise in divine matters only up to a point, held this scruple, how much more will Christian piety, blessed with a more excellent end and wholly devoted to the office of teaching, call the bishops of sacred things away from the care of earthly affairs?

units.tr: Entangled in the affairs of this life, says the Apostle of the Gentiles (2 Tim. 2:4). Those enrolled in the Roman army were not drawn away either to act as guardians or to give testimony in the forum. Will those set over the Christian army be so free from their duty that they sit in the law courts, or direct and order military affairs by command? If ... they delight ..., let them inquire with their predecessor Paul. Let them not fortify the way to heaven and eternal blessedness among heavenly things with civil secrets and court sophistries, though these are sometimes permitted, nor even with writings published on civil matters. Or let them believe the Pythoness, who was not always a liar in everything, crying out: "These men are servants of the Most High God, who announce to you the way of salvation" (Acts 16:17). Of course this is the salvation of eternal life, to be obtained through a pious life, by faith and by the merciful compassion of God who gives freely; it is not the salvation of citizens, to be introduced by Aristotelian or Machiavellian ... . Indeed it is entirely to be wished that Politics should not shrink from piety, that is, from knowing God and worshipping him holily. But for that reason the office of feeding the sheep with the pasture of the heavenly Word must not be abandoned for the office of the shepherd ... . It is not acceptable (namely to the Holy Spirit) that we, leaving the word of God, should cling to the serving of tables (Acts 6:2). Yet that care of widows nevertheless pertained in some measure to the ecclesiastical ministry. What was said generally to all the pious, but especially to the predecessors in sacred teaching: ... For here we have no abiding city, but we seek the one to come (Heb. 13:14). That city is to be sought by all who long for the heavenly life; but some seek it in such a way that they also apply themselves to civil business, while others seek it so that they know nothing but it, in their life, speech and all their conduct. If anyone, holding up Melchizedek as a shield, a figure going before Christ's priestly and royal office, ... confesses that he does not know how to distinguish those matters which lie outside the ordinary order from the usual ones.

units.la: CXXI.
units.tr: CXXI.

units.la: Ne publica quidem magnificentia passim privatis concessa.
units.tr: That even public magnificence is not granted to private persons everywhere.

units.la: Privatum in luxum multi, non sine populi suffragio, invecti leguntur. Nec defuit aliquando patronus luxu-riae; nihil nimium aut modicum afferens, nisi ex fortuna possidentis. Quae vero in populi oblectationem, aut publicum civitatis ornatum effunduntur, applau-sum fere omnium ferunt. Oblectationi spectaculum, visceratio, & id genus erogationes inserviunt. Ornatui theatrorum, ambulacrorum, fanorum exstructiones faciunt. Laudem propius accedit, quod ornatui, quam quod brevi oblectamento datur. At ne hanc quidem magnificentiam omnibus concessam, antiquitas Ro-manae historiae docebit. Lepidus a senatu petivit, ut basilicam Pauli Æmilia monumenta propria pecunia firmaret ornaretque. Quod a senatu petendum erat, non erat proprii arbitrii, multo minus per se in laude positum. Nam quod laudis est, quod virtutis, veniae impetratione non indiget. Inde colligere facile est, quo virtutum in genere collocetur magnificentia. Et haec quidem Lepidi profusio alienae memoriae, non propriae, cedebat. Ut vero sibi ipsi statuas, ut quis epi-taphiorum sibi splendida monumenta, quasi in urbis aut templorum ornatum, nullo in publicum merito, erigat; nec priscus Romanorum usus, nec nostri aevi consuetudo perfert. Et hanc ipsam, aliena monumenta firmandi, licentiam Trajani temporibus exolevisse, sequentia Taciti verba testantur: erat etiam tum in more publica munificentia. Principum enim est, aut proximo principibus loco positorum, ut Agrippae, ut Sejani, sua pecunia oculis civium publice studere. Qua-re Augustus non arguerat magis, quam laude erexerat, Taurum, Philippum, Balbum, hostiles exuvias, aut τῷ βίῳ[?] πραγματείαις[?] gotiis implicatur[?]: inquit Apostolus gentium[?], 2.Tim. 2.v.4. Nemo qui militat, civilibus negotiis implicatur: inquit Apostolus gentium, 2.Tim. 2.v.4. Militiæ Romanæ adscripti nec adtutelam, nec ad testimonium in foro dicendum abstrahebantur. Et militiæ Christianæ præfecti adeò ab officio suo vacabunt, ut etiam judiciis forensibus assideant, res militares ducta aut imperio ordinent? Si πολιτεία[?], εἰ πολιτεύματα[?] cos deleãt: ἐν τῷ ἐγκλήματι[?] cum antecessore suo Paulo, inquiant. Viam ad coelum, & æternam in coelestibus beatitudinem, non ad arcana civilia & aulæ, quamvis concessa interdum, so- phismata etiam scriptis de re civili edendis muniant. units.tr: Many private persons are read of as having been carried into luxury, and not without the approval of the people. Nor has a defender of luxury ever been lacking, one who allows nothing excessive or modest except in proportion to the possessor's means. But the things that are poured out for the people's pleasure or for the public ornament of the city almost always win applause from everyone. Shows, public feasts and expenditure of that kind serve pleasure. Building theatres, promenades and temples serves ornament. Praise comes more readily to what adorns than to what gives brief delight. But the antiquity of Roman history will show that even this magnificence was not granted to everyone. Lepidus asked the senate to secure and adorn, at his own expense, the basilica and the monuments of Paulus Aemilius. What had to be asked of the senate was not a matter of one's own discretion, much less something that lays claim to praise in itself. For what belongs to praise and to virtue does not need to obtain pardon. From this it is easy to gather where magnificence is placed among the kinds of virtue. Indeed, this lavishness of Lepidus was yielded to the memory of another, not his own. But that someone should set up statues to himself, or splendid epitaph monuments, as if for the ornament of the city or the temples, with no merit to the public, neither the old Roman custom nor the practice of our age tolerates. The following words of Tacitus bear witness that even this licence, of securing the monuments of others, had fallen out of use in the times of Trajan: there was still then a custom of public munificence. For it belongs to princes, or to those placed next to princes, such as Agrippa or Sejanus, to labour publicly before the eyes of the citizens with their own money. Therefore Augustus did not so much rebuke Taurus, Philippus and Balbus, with their hostile spoils or (...) as he raised them with praise. Those enlisted in the Roman army were not drawn away either into guardianship or to give testimony in the forum. Will those enlisted in the Christian army be so far absent from their duty that they sit in lawcourts, or direct military affairs by command? If they wipe out the citizenship and its arrangements (…), let them say so with their predecessor Paul, who in his accusation (…). The way to heaven and eternal blessedness in heavenly things is not fortified by hidden civil matters and court sophisms, though these are sometimes permitted, even in writings published on civil affairs. Or let them believe the Python, not always a liar in everything, who cries out: "These men are servants of the most high God, who show unto you the way of salvation." Acts 16.v.17 [Οὔτοι οἱ ἄνθρωποι, δοῦλοι τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ὑψίστου εἰσίν, οἵτινες καταγγέλλουσιν ὑμῖν ὁδὸν σωτηρίας]. Clearly this is the salvation of eternity, to be obtained by a godly life through faith and by the merciful gift of God, not the salvation of citizens, nor a civic polity of Aristotelian good breeding or Machiavellian kind to be introduced. It is wholly to be wished that politics not be divorced from piety, that is, from knowing God and worshipping him holily. But it does not follow that the office of feeding the sheep with the pasture of the heavenly word should be abandoned for the cares of this age, which I do not now touch so happily, as if the pastoral office were to be passed over. It is not right (namely, for the Holy Spirit) that we, leaving the word of God, should attend to the serving of tables. Acts 6.v.2 [Οὐκ ἀρεστόν ἐστιν ἡμᾶς καταλιπόντας τὸν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ διακονεῖν τραπέζαις]. Yet that care of widows in some measure pertained to the ministry of the Church. It was said generally to all the godly, but especially to the leaders of sound doctrine: "For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one to come." The author to the Hebrews, 13.v.14 [Οὐ γὰρ ἔχομεν ὧδε μένουσαν πόλιν, ἀλλὰ τὴν μέλλουσαν ἐπιζητοῦμεν]. To all who long for the heavenly life that city is to be sought; but the others in such a way that they also apply themselves to civil business, while those others breathe nothing but it, in life, speech and all conduct, (...) if someone should hold up Melchizedek, the figure going before Christ's priestly and kingly office, as a shield, (...) he confesses that he does not know how to distinguish those things which lie outside the ordinary from the customary.
