units.tr: Many men are read of as having been carried into private luxury, and not without the people's vote. Nor has there ever been lacking a patron of luxury, who brings forward nothing excessive or moderate except what the owner's fortune allows. But those things which are poured out for the people's delight, or for the public adornment of the state, usually win applause from almost everyone. Spectacles, public feasts and that kind of expenditure serve delight. The construction of theatres, promenades and temples serves adornment. Praise comes closer to what is given to adornment than to what is given to brief delight. But that even this magnificence was not granted to everyone, the antiquity of Roman history will teach. Lepidus asked the senate that he might shore up and adorn the basilica of Paulus and the Aemilian monuments at his own expense. What had to be sought from the senate was not a matter of private discretion, much less something in itself deserving praise. For what is truly praiseworthy and virtuous does not need to obtain pardon. From this it is easy to infer under which kind of virtue magnificence is to be placed. And indeed this lavishness of Lepidus was for the memory of another, not his own. But that someone should erect statues to himself, or splendid epitaph monuments to himself, as if for the adornment of the city or the temples, with no merit toward the public, neither the ancient Roman custom nor the custom of our own age tolerates. And that this very license of restoring the monuments of others had fallen into disuse in the times of Trajan, the following words of Tacitus bear witness: there was still then a custom of public munificence. For it belongs to princes, or to those placed next to princes in rank, such as Agrippa or Sejanus, to strive publicly before the eyes of citizens with their own money. Hence Augustus did not so much censure as commend Taurus, Philippus and Balbus, who contributed hostile spoils and overflowing wealth to the adornment of the city and the glory of posterity.

units.la: § exundantes opes, ornatum ad urbis, & posterûm glo-riam, conferentes. Quod verò in templorum, in gy-mnasiorum , in murorum & pontium decus & firmi-tatem pecuniæ spargitur,an[?] non fine controversia laus dem meretur? A laude quam à vituperatione propiùs absunt, qui in hæc sponte aurum conferunt. non tamen men suo nomine hæc exstruendi omnibus licentia per-mittitur. Hebræos , tabulatis in domibus habitantes, ad conferendum autem struendo templo pigros,Deus Chaggai ore increpat. Chagg.1. v. 4. 9. Non tamen uni alicui , ne duci quidem aut pontifici, gloria & in-fcriptio exstructi templi data est. Templum ut in co-lonia Tarraconensi strueretur Augusto , perentibus Hispanis permissum : datumque in omnes provincias exemplum. 1. Annal.à Tiberio verò ne temere quidem id ipsum permissum : quanquam publico populorum magnificentiæ studio. Pontium autem & murorum, & quæ sunt generis ejusdem , fabricationes juris pu-blici esse , nec privatis quanquam studio ferventibus permissum,non operosæ foret probationis. Statigitur inconcussa nostra assertio : Ne publicam quidem ma-gnificentiam , id est, in publicum erogatam , passim omnibus concedi.
units.tr: But as for the fact that money is spread for the honour and solidity of temples, gymnasia, walls and bridges, does this not deserve praise, though not without controversy? Those who of their own accord contribute gold to these things are far closer to praise than to blame. Yet even so, the license to build these things is not granted to all in their own name. God rebukes the Hebrews, who dwelt in panelled houses but were sluggish in contributing to the building of the temple, by the mouth of Haggai: Chagg. 1. v. 4. 9. Yet the glory and the inscription of the temple built were given to no single person, not even a leader or a high priest. A temple to Augustus was allowed to be built in the colony of Tarraco when the Spaniards asked for it, and an example was given to all the provinces. 1. Annal. But by Tiberius even this was not permitted lightly, though the peoples eagerly pursued public magnificence. That the building of bridges and walls, and things of that kind, belongs to public right, and was not permitted even to private persons burning with zeal, would not be a laborious proof. Therefore our assertion stands unshaken: that not even public magnificence, that is, expenditure devoted to the public, is granted to all indiscriminately.

units.la: CXXII. Pacis redemptio majestati non parum derogat.
units.tr: CXXII. Buying peace does not a little detract from majesty.

units.la: Fit ea redemptio aut agrorum concessione, aut pe-cuniæ collatione. Quæ eò fœdior, quo aut necessitas concedendi minor, aut is, cui ceditur , contemptior. Ideoque sua populique Romani contumelia Tiberius indoluit,quod defertor & prædo[?],hostium more agerent. i. e. quasi belli jure legatos ad principem imperii Ro-mani mitteret; aut tanquam bello victor , sedem sibi atque exercitui suo poftulaseret, aut bellum inexplicabi-le minitaretur. idque non necessitate Rempublicam urgente : ut quondam, Sertoriani & Mithridatici belli illuvie, Spartacus Italiam cladibus, immota populi Romani constantia , vastavit. Sed pulcherrimo populi Romani fastigio: ne Parthis quidem aut Germanis pacem lacessere audentibus.
units.tr: Such a ransom is paid either by the cession of lands or by the contribution of money. It is the more shameful the less necessity there is for granting it, or the more contemptible the party to whom it is granted. Hence Tiberius was grieved at the insult to himself and to the Roman people, that deserters and robbers should act like enemies, that is, should send envoys to the prince of the Roman empire as though by the law of war; or, as if they were conquerors, should demand a seat for themselves and their army, or threaten an endless war. And this was not because necessity pressed upon the Republic, as once when Spartacus laid waste Italy with disasters, in the aftermath of the Sertorian and Mithridatic wars, while the Roman people stood unshaken. But at the most glorious height of the Roman people, not even the Parthians or the Germans dared to provoke peace.

units.la: Multum quidem splendoris pacis redemptio detulerit [?]: ultima tamen temporum necessitate extorta veniam meretur. Ut quondam Galliae reges Neustriam Normannis, Galliam impune urentibus, tranquillitatis pactione concesserunt. At posteri eorum Anglis, quamquam ruente cladium torrente fracti, donec finibus pellerentur, non cesserunt. Nollem Germaniam Alsatiae ac Pomeraniae cessione, pecuniae praeterea collatione, pacem ab exteris mercatos. Verum dissidiis interminis, & tot bellorum tempestatibus fracti, nimbo proterrentis calamitatis honestiori lege cedere nequivere. Ne veteres quidem invicti roboris Romani, & illa militaris disciplinae severitate, nimio semper rigore perstitere. Ligures enim, vexandis Italiae agris indomitos, montibus deractos fertili Campaniae agro, idque publico itinerum sumptu collocarunt. Ut taceam multa Gallis Cisalpinis antiquiori tempore, multa Celtiberis & Cantabris concessa. Urbem ipsam a Senonibus Gallis redemptam, ne quidem interneccione deleti Senones memoriae hominum & fastis exemere. Imo ne potentissimi quidem rerum arbitri tranquillitatem publicam, objecta munusculi offa, ab inaccessis [?] latronibus redimere, pudore sibi duxerunt. Quod Xenophon de Babylonis & Persis, nostrorum temporum annales de Turcis commemorant. Tacfarinas mitiores Frisii & Ansibarii, sine belli comminatione, vacua Romanorum militum pascua, possessioni olim petebant. Sed rejecti, morem Romanum didicerunt, nihil per speciem minarum extorquendi. At iidem Romani Sugambros, sedibus extractos, Galliae in ripa collocarunt. Nimirum quasi captivos a patria abduxerunt, quasi ripae custodes immanitati barbarorum objecerunt.
units.tr: Buying peace certainly brings a good deal of splendour, yet when it is extorted by the final necessity of the times it deserves pardon. Thus once the kings of Gaul ceded Neustria to the Normans, who were burning Gaul with impunity, by a treaty for the sake of tranquillity. But their successors did not yield to the English, though broken by the torrent of disasters, until they were driven from their lands. I would rather Germany had not bought peace from outsiders by the cession of Alsace and Pomerania, and by the further contribution of money. Yet broken by internal discords and by so many storms of wars, they could not yield by a more honourable law than the cloud of terrifying calamity. Nor did the old Romans of unconquered strength, with their severe military discipline, always persist in unbending rigour. For the Ligurians, who were harassing the fields of Italy and could not be subdued, were driven down from the mountains and settled on the fertile land of Campania, and this at public expense for the road journey. To say nothing of the many concessions made to the Cisalpine Gauls in earlier times, and to the Celtiberians and Cantabrians. The Senones, though destroyed by slaughter, did not erase from the memory of men and from the annals the fact that the city itself had been ransomed from the Gallic Senones. Nor did even the most powerful arbiters of affairs think it shameful to buy public tranquillity from unapproachable robbers by throwing them a little bribe of food. This is what Xenophon records of Babylon and Persia, and the annals of our own times record of the Turks. Tacfarinas, and the gentler Frisians and Ansibarii, without any threat of war, once sought to possess the unoccupied pastures of the Roman soldiers. But when they were rejected, they learned the Roman custom of extorting nothing by the appearance of threats. Yet the same Romans settled the Sugambri, when they had been torn from their seats, on the bank of Gaul. Clearly they led them away from their homeland as captives, and as guardians of the bank they exposed them to the savagery of the barbarians.

units.la: CXXIII. Venia terrore potentior.
units.tr: CXXIII. Favour is more powerful than terror.

units.la: Non modo ad constringendos benevolentia dubiotum animos, sed aliquando ad hostium acies diffipan das. Quod non ignorans Tiberius, bello in Africa a latrone Tacfarinate coorto, dat negotium Blafo, cæte-ros quidem ad spem proliceret arma sine noxa ponendi, ipsius autem ducis quoquo modo potiretur. Quod du-cem latrocinii spe veniæ eximii, ad moderationem cle-mentiæ spectat. Ne soluta nimium, & omnibus ob-via, in lentorem imperante indignum degeneret. Se-ditionum & tumultuum ducibus, ferocientibus præ-sertim & majestatem arroganter carpentibus, deli&ti gratia non temere impertienda. In cæteris dictum Pli-nii Secundi moderator populorum imbibat: Male ter-rore veneratio acquiritur: longeque valentior amor ad obtinendum quod velis, quàm timor.
units.tr: Not only to bind the hearts of the wavering by goodwill, but sometimes to scatter the battle lines of enemies. Tiberius, not unaware of this, when war broke out in Africa under the robber Tacfarinas, gave Blaesus the task of enticing the rest with hope of laying down arms without harm, but of getting hold of the leader himself by whatever means. This, that the leader of the robbery should be spared by the hope of pardon, looks to the moderation of clemency, lest, relaxed too much and open to all, it degenerate into a sloth unworthy of one who rules. Pardon should not be lightly bestowed on the leaders of seditions and tumults, especially when they are fierce and arrogantly assail majesty. In other matters the saying of Pliny the Younger, the moderator of peoples, may be taken to heart: Veneration is won badly by terror; love is far more powerful than fear for obtaining what you wish.

units.la: CXXIV. Belli gerendi facies temporibus aptanda.
units.tr: CXXIV. The manner of waging war must be adapted to the times.

units.la: Romani stabilem per aciem bellare sueti, militemq; æstivis expeditionibus exercitatum in hibernacula re-ducere. Tacfarinate per vagos incursus quietem nun-quam concedente, utramque belli gerendi rationem, duce Blæso, in Africa mutaruht. pars aliqua militiæ Romani in ore, in latere, & sape à tergo erat. multique eo modo cæsi aut circumventi. mox additur: net, ut-mos fuerat, acta assate retrahit copias, aut in hiberna-culis veteris provincia componit: sed ut in limine belli, dispositis castellis, per expeditos & solitudinum gnaros, mutantem mapalia Tacfarinatem protur-bat. Maris trastandi olim rudes Romani, ad Punici belli consue-tudinem se circumegerunt. Quod & Spartani, bello contra Athenienses iuscepto, fa&itaverant. Idem, quorum in historia versantur, Romani, arma pleraque à Samnitibus, elephantos ab Antiocho devicto, furta belli ab Hannibale, alia ab aliis hostibus desumpta, suum in usum converterant.
units.tr: The Romans were accustomed to fight in a stable battle line, and to lead their soldiers, trained in summer campaigns, back into winter quarters. When Tacfarinas never allowed quiet through his roving raids, they changed both methods of waging war under Blaesus in Africa. Some part of the Roman army was in front, on the flank, and often at the rear, and many were cut down or surrounded in this way. Then it is added: nor, as had been the custom, did he withdraw the troops once the summer campaign was over, or station them in winter quarters in the old province; but, as at the very threshold of the war, with castles set up, he harassed Tacfarinas, who was moving his huts, through light-armed men familiar with the wastes. The Romans, once inexperienced in crossing the sea, turned themselves to the custom of the Punic war. The Spartans too had done this when they undertook war against the Athenians. The same Romans whose history we are reading likewise converted to their own use many things: arms taken mostly from the Samnites, elephants from Antiochus when he was defeated, stratagems of war from Hannibal, and other things taken from other enemies.

units.la: CXXV. Animi libertas famæ, obsequium aulæ accommodatius.
units.tr: CXXV. Freedom of mind suits fame better; servility suits the court.

units.la: Duo pacis decora, Labeo Antistius & Capito Ateius, gloriam civilibus studiis assecuti, non pari honorum dignatione floruerunt. Labeo incorrupta libertate, & ob id famâ celebratior: Capitonis obsequium dominantibus magis probabatur. Illi, quod praturam intra stetit, commendatio ex injuria: huic, quod consulatum adeptus est, odium ex invidia oriebatur. Hic quaedam ad mores hominum, & ad usum vitæ, observanda. 1. Magnam integritatis famam, & dominorum gratiam, haud facile una fede recipi. 2. Vultus & sermones libertatem spirantes, dominantibus ingrata; submissionem & obsequium acceptiora esse. 3. Libertatem ab incorrupto judice pluris, quàm obsequium & placendi domino studium, æstimari. 4. Illam famæ ad posteros parandæ; istud captandæ imperantium gratiæ convenire. 5. Altum de aliquo judicium, consulatus insignibus, & cæteris honorum civilium titulis, quod ad famæ judicium, præferendum. 6. Ex injuria repulsæ iniquæ commendationem nasci. 7. honorum indignè acceptorum invidiam in odium populi transfire. Singula monitorum exemplis collustrari poterant: si molis præscriptæ capacitas, & vitandum lectoris fastidium, copiam admitteret.
units.tr: Two glories of peace, Labeo Antistius and Capito Ateius, won renown through their civil studies, yet they did not flourish with equal recognition of their honours. Labeo, by his incorruptible liberty, was the more celebrated for his reputation. Capito's servility was more approved by those in power. For the former, because he stopped short of the praetorship, commendation arose from injustice; for the latter, because he attained the consulship, hatred arose from envy. Here are certain points to be observed for the conduct of men and the conduct of life: (1) a great reputation for integrity and the favour of masters are not easily held together; (2) a countenance and speech breathing liberty are ungrateful to those in power, while submission and obedience are more welcome; (3) liberty is valued more highly by an incorruptible judge than obsequiousness and the desire to please one's master; (4) the former befits the winning of fame for posterity, the latter the seeking of the favour of rulers; (5) a high judgment about someone, with the insignia of the consulship and other titles of civil honours, is to be preferred to the judgment of fame; (6) undeserved commendation arises from an unjust rejection; (7) the envy aroused by honours unworthily received passes over into the hatred of the people. Each of these precepts could be illustrated by examples, if the capacity of the planned work and the need to spare the reader's weariness allowed such abundance.

units.la: CXXVI. Magnanimo Principi non convenit nomen hæredipetæ.
units.tr: CXXVI. A magnanimous prince does not fit the name of a fortune-hunter.

units.la: Junia die obita, cum Cæsarem testamento præteriisset, offensum eum non habuit: neque Tiberius pro- hibuit, quo minus laudatione pro rostris, caterisque solennibus funus cohonestaretur. Plura moderationis ejusmodi de Tiberio monumenta: sed nullum, quam secundo Annalium, illustrius. Neque hæreditatem cujusquam adiit, nisi cum amicitia meruisset. Ignotos & alios infensos, eóque principem nuncupantes, procul arcebat.
units.tr: When Junia died and had passed over Caesar in her will, he did not take offence at her. Nor did Tiberius prevent her funeral from being honoured with a eulogy from the Rostra and the other solemn rites. There are many monuments of this kind of moderation in Tiberius, but none more striking than in the second book of the Annals. He never entered upon anyone's inheritance unless he had earned it through friendship. Strangers and those hostile to him, who would name him prince, he kept far away.

units.la: CXXVII. Non in splendore splendor famæ.
units.tr: CXXVII. Not in the splendour of the splendour of fame.

units.la: In gratiosa hominum recte sentientium memo-ria, non in fumosarum imaginum numerosa pompa, claritas bonorum virorum fundatur. Funus Juniæ vi-ginti clarissimarum familiarum imagines antelatę co-mitabantur. Cassii & Bruti ingrata dominantibus, vivens in civium animis imago, negligebatur. sed praefulgebant Cassius atque Brutus, eo ipso, quod effigies eorum non visebantur. Gratam igitur sui memoriam, & autoritatem post fata mansuram, paret[?]; de imaginum pompa securior; qui vivere adempta vita, qui clarescere in secutura secula desiderat.
units.tr: The renown of good men rests not on a long procession of smoky images but on the kindly memory of those who think rightly. At the funeral of Junia, the images of twenty most illustrious families went before her. The images of Cassius and Brutus, unwelcome to those in power, were passed over, and the living image kept in the minds of citizens was disregarded. But Cassius and Brutus shone all the more brightly for the very reason that their effigies were not on view. Therefore let him who wants a grateful memory of himself, and an authority that will outlive his death, be less anxious about the pomp of images; let him who wishes to live when his life is taken away, and to shine in ages to come, look elsewhere.

units.la: QUARTUS ANNALIUM TACITI liber per Aphorismos explicatus.
units.tr: The Fourth Book of the Annals of Tacitus, explained by aphorisms.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Uni summam rerum committere, perniciosum principi.
units.tr: To entrust the highest affairs of state to one man is harmful to a prince.

units.la: QUOD Thraso in Eunucho Terentia-no jactar, regem Persarum sibi credere omnem exercitum, consilia: id Ælio Sejano apud Tiberium imperatorem contigit. Quamvis enim non omnibus legionibus, cohortibus tamen prætoriis, quod unum robur erat urbanæ militiæ, præfecit. In consiliis vero communicandis adeo sibi devinctum imperatorem Sejanus habuit, ut obscurum adversum alios sibi uni incautum intellectumque efficeret. Quod magis in Tiberio mirere: socium laborum, non modo in sermonibus domesticis, verum in curia apud patres, in foro apud populum jactavit. quin & effigies ejus per theatra & fora, inter principia legionum coli permisit. Inde major in eum popularium, fictè an sincerè colentium, inclinatio. Qua in re varie à Tiberio, cæteris in rebus imperandi gnaro, er-ratum. 1. Omnia invadere, deturbato sede Principe, moliuntur, quibus tanta regnandi occasio. Quod Drusus Tiberii filius non vano augurio cognovit: Primas dominandi spes in arduo: ubi sis ingressus, adesse studia
units.tr: When Thraso in Terence's Eunuchus boasts that the king of the Persians entrusts to him every army and every plan, this is what happened to Aelius Sejanus with the emperor Tiberius. Although he did not command all the legions, he was placed in charge of the praetorian cohorts, which were the only real strength of the city garrison. In sharing counsels, Sejanus so bound the emperor to himself that he made himself the only one who was unseen by others, unsuspected, and understood. This is more remarkable in Tiberius: Sejanus boasted of being his partner in labours, not only in private conversation but in the senate among the fathers and in the forum before the people. Tiberius even allowed his image to be honoured in theatres, in forums and among the standards of the legions. From this came a greater inclination of the common people to him, whether they honoured him feignedly or sincerely. In this matter Tiberius, otherwise skilled in ruling, erred in several ways. 1. Those for whom such a great opportunity of ruling existed set about attacking everything, planning to overthrow the prince from his seat. Drusus, the son of Tiberius, recognised this, and not in vain, from the omen: The first hopes of ruling lie in a steep place; once you have entered, the eager ministers are there.

units.la: ¶ minisstros. Necideò minorem vel animis vel potentiâ Sejanum duxeris, quod municipio oriundus, patrem equitem Romanum habuit. Nam & Augustus non altioribus à principiis, majores difficultates elu-ctatus, ad regnum pervenit. Et Agrippa obscuriori loco natus, tantum apud legiones, tantum in animis civium valuit, ut à regno arripiendo sola modestia depelleretur. Hinc illud Mæcenatis dictum: [illegible, ~25 letters] suum se suo[?] ... sed [?] ...
units.tr: ¶ Therefore you should not think Sejanus was lesser in spirit or power because he was born in a provincial town and had a father who was a Roman knight. For Augustus too, starting from no higher beginnings and struggling against greater difficulties, came to the kingship. And Agrippa, born in an humbler place, held so much power with the legions and so much in the hearts of the citizens that only his moderation kept him from seizing the kingdom. Hence that saying of Maecenas: [illegible, about 25 letters] ... [?] ...

units.la: Tantum eum fecisti, ut vel in generum tuum assumendus, vel occidendus sit. Dio. lib.54.
units.tr: You have made him so great that he must either be taken as your son-in-law or be killed. Dio, book 54.

units.la: 2. Si nihil ab invasione regni periculi, saltem oculis hominum in ministrum conjectis, autoritati principis decedit. Quod in Lysandro Spartano Agefilaus expertus, detractum militari dignitate, ad vilia civilium rerum ministeria detrusit.
units.tr: 2. If there is no danger to the kingdom from an attempt at usurpation, still, when a minister is exposed to the eyes of men, the authority of the prince declines. Agesilaus of Sparta learned this in the case of Lysander: he stripped him of his military rank and thrust him down into the humble duties of civil affairs.

units.la: 3. Cum multis aufertur, quod uni tribuitur, ex usu nius amore & aliorum aversatione odium nasci necesse est. Verba sunt è Plutarcho deprompta. Quæ vera esse, turbatæ Galliæ status edoceat. Inter arcana quidem aulæ regiæ est, non claros genere natalium & militari peritia viros, ut olim Majores Domus & quos vocabant Comites Stabuli, sed ab ecclesiastica digni-tate Cardinales, ut sceptrorum non capaces, proxima sibi sede collocare. Sed invidiam exeo principum, & ex invidia turbas non effugiunt.
units.tr: 3. When something is taken from many and given to one, hatred must arise from the use of the one and from the aversion of the others. These are words taken from Plutarch. The disturbed state of France teaches that they are true. Among the secrets of the royal court, it is not men of noble birth and military skill, as the Mayors of the Palace and the so-called Counts of the Stable once were, but men raised to the rank of Cardinals by ecclesiastical dignity, who, being unfit to bear the sceptre, are placed in the nearest seat to him. But they do not escape the hatred of princes, and from that hatred they do not escape disturbances.

units.la: 4. Dedecus est regis & regni, omnibus imperantem ab unius consilio vel nutu pendere. Hinc in regem contemptus, & à contemptu commotio, vel in regem ludibria. Venustum est quod Nicolaus Vernulæus, Eloquentiæ apud Lovanienses Professor, de Duce Ler-mæo memorat. Repertæ, inquit, aliquando in mensa Regia ficta literæ, cum hac epigraphe, Philippo III. Regi Hispaniæ, nunc in servitio Ducis Lermæ.
units.tr: 4. It is a disgrace to the king and the kingdom that, while ruling over all, he depends on the counsel or nod of one man. Hence come contempt for the king, from contempt agitation, and mockery of the king. Nicolaus Vernulaeus, professor of eloquence at Louvain, tells a witty story about the Duke of Lerma. Once, he says, forged letters were found on the royal table, with this inscription: To Philip III, King of Spain, now in the service of the Duke of Lerma.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Non una regnum ansa arripitur.
units.tr: A kingdom is not seized by one handle.

units.la: Tria ferè in hoc negotio occurrunt. 1. occasio rei gerendæ. 2. mores & aptitudo hominis. 3. Gradus potenpotentiæ struendæ, & audaciæ facinora.
units.tr: Three things usually come up in this business. 1. The opportunity for carrying out the deed. 2. The character and aptitude of the man. 3. The steps for building up power, and the crimes of daring.

units.la: Occasio Sejano dabatur, Tiberii facilitas, &, quam describimus, virium ac consilii communicatio. Mores & aptitudo ad audendum:
units.tr: The opportunity was given to Sejanus by Tiberius' easiness and by that sharing of power and counsel which we have described. His character and aptitude for daring were these:

units.la: 1. Corpus laborum tolerans. nam teneri illi, & deli-tiis marcentes, non sunt tam altæ curæ capaces. Quan-quam plus animo, quam corpori, hæc in parte tribuitur. ideoque sequitur
units.tr: 1. Enduring of labours of body. For the soft and those who wither in pleasures are not capable of such deep cares. Yet this is attributed more to the spirit than to the body. Therefore there follows

units.la: 2. Animus audax. audaciæ nihil impervium: quæ vel servos ad spem regnandi, aut regna evertendi, protrudit. manciptii unius audacia, ni mature subventum foret, discordiis armisque civilibus Remp. perculisset[?], a Annal, De Tacfarinate latrone, & per occasionem de Spartaco servorum duce, nuper vidimus. De Viriatho Lusitano, cui etiam exercitus Romani cesserunt, præter variorum historiam, Cicero 2. de officiis agit. De Timero, quem Tamerlanem vulgo vocant, e pastore & fure ad gloriosissimum Orientis regnum audacia evecto, Chalcocondylas, & annales Arabici.
units.tr: 2. Bold spirit. Nothing is impervious to daring, which thrusts even slaves toward the hope of ruling or of overthrowing kingdoms. The daring of a single slave, unless help had come in time, would have shaken the commonwealth with discord and civil arms. We have recently seen this in Tacfarinas the brigand, in the Annals, and incidentally in Spartacus, leader of the slaves. Concerning Viriathus the Lusitanian, before whom even Roman armies gave way, Cicero treats in book 2 of On Duties, apart from the histories of various writers. Concerning Timur, whom the common people call Tamerlane, raised by daring from a shepherd and thief to the most glorious kingdom of the East, see Chalcocondylas and the Arabic annals.

units.la: 3. Sui obtegens. Sola enim audacia, nisi vires abundè suffecerint, ad quærendam potentiam non sufficit. Comes ei, ut in Catilina, dissimulator animus accedat.
units.tr: 3. Concealing oneself. For daring alone, unless strength suffices abundantly, is not enough to seek power. A dissembling spirit must accompany it, as it did in Catiline.

units.la: 4. In alios criminator. Sic enim & fidem sibi apud su'picacem[?] Principem astruxit; & alios ab eadem regnandi spe dimovit.
units.tr: 4. Accusing others. For in this way he also gained trust with a prince who was suspicious, and drew others away from the same hope of ruling.

units.la: 5. Juxta adulatio & superbia. Quanto erga dominantem summissior, tanto erga pares & inferiores arrogantior. Qui feré mos est aulicæ servientium jactantiæ.
units.tr: 5. Flattery and pride together. The more humble one is toward the ruler, the more arrogant one is toward equals and inferiors. This is almost the custom of courtly boasting among servants.

units.la: 6. Palam compositus pudor, intus summa apiscendi libido. Hypocritam uno nomine diceret, qui sacri styli verbis assuevit.
units.tr: 6. Outwardly composed modesty, inwardly the highest lust for attaining. One might call such a man a hypocrite in a single word, one accustomed to the words of sacred style.

units.la: 7. Modo largitio & luxus, sapius industria ac vigilantia. Largitio conciliandis hominum animis; luxus ostentandæ magnificentiæ, & dissimulandæ aviditati sumebatur. Sed ne luxu, ut fit, animi vigor remittere-tur, plus operæ industriæ ac vigilantiæ seposuit.
units.tr: 7. Now generosity and luxury, more often diligence and vigilance. Generosity was used to win the minds of men; luxury to display magnificence and to hide greed. But so that the vigour of his spirit might not relax through luxury, as usually happens, he set aside more effort for industry and vigilance.

units.la: Hæc a se Ælius, regno parando munimenta, attulit. adde his, quæ de Catilina Sallustius, cujus facundiam sibi imitandam Tacitus proposuit, profatus est. Cor-pus paticns inediæ, algoris, vigiliæ, suprà quàm credibile est. animus audax, subdolus, varius, cuiuslibet rerfimulator ac dissimulator, alieni appetens, fui profusus; ardens in cupiditatibus, fatis elo-quentiæ, sapientiæ parum. vastus animus immodera-tà, incredibilia, nimis altafemper cupiebat.
units.tr: These were the defences Aelius brought to himself for preparing his kingdom. Add to these what Sallust said of Catiline, whose eloquence Tacitus proposed for imitation. A body able to endure hunger, cold and sleeplessness beyond what is credible; a bold, sly, changeable spirit, a pretender and dissembler of whatever kind; desirous of others' goods, prodigal of his own; burning in desires, sufficient in eloquence, little in wisdom; a vast spirit that always desired immoderate, incredible, and overly lofty things.

units.la: Gradus, quibus ad regnum nitebatur. 1. Dispersa-rum cohortium unum in locum congregatio. 2. Favor castrorum & studia militum quæsita. 3. Senatorum & magistratuum clientelæ. 4. Liviæ per adulterium corruptio. 5. Drufi veneno sublati remotio. 6. Liberorum Germanici per Tiberium, structis criminibus, depressio. 7. Machina cædis in Tiberium deprompta, quæ antequam detorqueretur, Sejanum, supremo gradui jam vicinum, casu præcipitem dedit.
units.tr: Steps by which he strove toward the kingdom. 1. The gathering of the scattered cohorts into one place. 2. Winning the favour of the camps and the goodwill of the soldiers. 3. Clienteles of senators and magistrates. 4. Corruption of Livia through adultery. 5. Removal of Drusus by poison. 6. Oppression of the children of Germanicus by Tiberius, through contrived charges. 7. A machine of murder devised against Tiberius, which, before it could be turned, threw Sejanus headlong by chance when he was already close to the highest step.

units.la: Hæc omnia Sejano, cui cum vigilante principe, ac populi Romani potentia, negotium erat, emetienda fue-runt. Prisci paratioribus itineribus, aut satellitum obtentu, aut arcis munitione, ad regnum sunt enisi.
units.tr: All these things had to be measured out by Sejanus, who had to deal with a watchful prince and the power of the Roman people. The ancients strove for the kingdom by more prepared routes: either under the pretext of bodyguards, or by fortifying a citadel.

units.la: Memoratu inprimis dignum est, quod de Phalari-de, Agrigentinorum tyranno, Polyaenus commemo-rat. Agrigentini Jovis gubernatoris templum in arce struere decreverant. Phalaris, qui tum publicanus erat, promisit fe operi curando præfuturum. Populus ob genus vitæ locationibus fabrorum, & conducendæ materiæ, aptum arbitratus, rem e itotam commisit.
units.tr: Especially worth remembering is what Polyaenus records about Phalaris, tyrant of Agrigentum. The Agrigentines had decided to build a temple of Jupiter the Governor on the citadel. Phalaris, who was then a tax-farmer, promised that he would take charge of the work. The people, judging him suitable because of his way of life for hiring workmen and procuring materials, entrusted the whole business to him.

units.la: Publica igitur pecunia accepta, magnum mercenario-rum numerum conducit, captivos multos mercatur, lapidum, lignorum, ferri non parvam copiam in arcem comportat. Rumorem deinde, cum fundamenta jam exurgerent, peridoneos homines subjicit, lapides ac ferrum furto ex arce subduci. Indignante sacrilegio populo, potestatem impetrat, quasi excludendis aditu furibus, arcem communiendi. Qua communita, pro fede dominationis utitur. Ac ne vis irruentium civium formidetur, captivos vinculis exsolutos, lapidibus, bi-pennibus ac securibus armat. Eorum agmine eduço, cum Cereris festum celebraretur, cives nec opinato ador-
units.tr: Therefore, having received public money, he hired a large number of mercenaries, bought many captives, and carried a considerable quantity of stones, timber and iron into the citadel. Then, when the foundations were already rising, he placed men well suited to the task to spread a rumour that stones and iron were being secretly taken out of the citadel. When the people were angry at the sacrilege, he obtained the power to fortify the citadel, as if to keep thieves from access. Once it was fortified, he used it as the seat of his domination. And so that the force of the citizens rushing in should not be feared, he freed the captives from their chains and armed them with stones, double axes and hatchets. Leading them out in a column, while the festival of Ceres was being celebrated, he attacked the citizens who did not expect it, and made a great slaughter of them.

units.la: { } adortus, magnam eorum stragem edit. Alii, inter quos Dionysius, quasi vim factionis potentiorum metuentes, armatorum circa se custodiam a populo obtinentes, armis regnum tutati sunt. Utramque, & arcis invadendae & armatorum custodiae, viam Pisistratus insistendo, diu Atheniensium collis invisus dominus insultavit.
units.tr: Others, among them Dionysius, fearing as it were the force of the more powerful factions, kept an armed guard around themselves gained from the people, and defended their rule by arms. Pisistratus, by following both ways, the seizing of the citadel and the guarding by armed men, long ruled as an unwelcome master over the hill of the Athenians.

units.la: Sunt qui pretia frugum apertis horreis levando, nexos e vinculis liberando, lege agraria promulganda; sunt qui comitate, alioquio, pari cum infimis amictu; sunt qui aedificandi & vestium nitore, ampla cum regibus externis affinitate, vel in gratiam vulgi irrepunt, vel conspiciendos populo se praebent. ac ita paulatim privatorum subselliis exempti, ad altiora fastigia ascendunt. De quibus nunc non est ubertim differen-di locus. Quare ad Sejanum, & quaesitas obscure emergendi vias, reve[?]tor.
units.tr: There are those who creep into the favour of the common people, some by lowering the prices of grain by opening the granaries, others by freeing debtors from bonds, others by proposing an agrarian law; some by courtesy and by dressing like the lowest; others by the splendour of their buildings and clothing, or by a wide marriage alliance with foreign kings; and they present themselves to be looked upon by the people. And thus, gradually removed from the benches of private men, they climb to higher heights. Of these there is now no place to discuss at length. Therefore I return to Sejanus and to the hidden ways of rising that he sought.

units.la: 1. Vim praefecturae modicam antea intendit, dispersas per urbem cohortes una in castra conducendo. quid hinc utilitatis? quid ad potentiam roboris? ut simul imperia acciperent, numeroque & robore, & visu inter se fiducia ipsis, in cateros metus crederetur. Minus enim formidanda vis in multas cohortes, loco divisas, dissoluta. Sed an non Tiberio suboluit[?], fraudem ab eo strui, si nullam novitati rationem praetexeret? Nunquam desunt speciosae astutis ratiunculae, quas dissito[?] sermone praeferant. Praetendebat lascivire militem ductum: si quid subitum ingruat, majore auxilio pariter subveniri. & saevius astutiores[?], si vallum statuatur procul urbis illecebris. Ergo disciplinae severitas, necessitatis ingruentis provisio, urbanae mollitiei fuga, dolo velum invenit.
units.tr: 1. He first enlarged the power of the prefecture modestly, by bringing the cohorts scattered through the city together into one camp. What was the advantage of this? What strength did it add to his power? It let the soldiers receive orders together, and their numbers, their strength and their sight of one another gave them confidence, while fear was felt by everyone else. A force split among many cohorts, quartered in different places, is less frightening because it is divided. But did it not occur to Tiberius that a trap was being laid for him, if Sejanus gave no reason for the novelty? There are always plausible little reasons that the crafty put forward in their talk. He pretended that the soldiers were growing soft through idleness; that if anything sudden threatened, help could be brought at once with a larger force; and that the more cunning would be kept in check if the rampart were set up far from the allurements of the city. So the strictness of discipline, provision against an impending emergency, and flight from urban luxury gave his deceit a veil.

units.la: 2. Ut perfecta sunt castra, irrepere paulatim militares animos, adeundo, appellando: simul centuriones ac tribunos ipse diligere. & indulgentia sive comi sermone rudes militum animos flectit, & praemiorum ordinumque arbitrio alios sibi devincit, alios potius ad obsequendum erigit. Amat enim miles licentiae autores duces: truces & asperos animo, si non[?] sermone,avertfatur. Recenti exemplo sunt in Germa-nia Mansfeldius,in Belgio Auraicus,usitatæ in militem comitatis. Quorum tamen iste nec disciplinam remi-fit,& stipendio tempestive soluto compositum mode-stia exercitum habuit. ille vero & disciplina soluta, & stipendii solvendi inops, promptissimum fere militem & benevolentissimum, hostium ac sociorum rapinis, aluit. nec defuit facultas Auraico,prono quocunque duceret exercitu,regnum sibi apud Batavos ad poste-ros firmandi. De voluntate honestè, & defunctorum Principum memoria digne,dissentitur. In eadem vero, Belgii regione Joanni Austriaco ne voluntatem qui-dem defuisse, provincias in suum obsequium à rege abstrahendi, nisi maturè obiisset, Philippus suspicatus, fertur. Nec apud Fœderatos Leicestrius Anglus,non-dum adulto Mauritio, culpæ suspicione purgatur.
units.tr: 2. As soon as the camp was complete, he gradually crept into the soldiers' minds, by approaching and addressing them. At the same time he himself chose the centurions and tribunes. By indulgence and affable speech he bent the rough minds of the soldiers, and by his control of rewards and ranks he bound some to himself and raised others to obedience. For the soldier loves leaders who grant licence; he turns away from those who are harsh and rough in temper, even if they are good speakers. Recent examples are Mansfeld in Germany and Orange in Belgium, both of whom practised affability towards their soldiers. Yet the former did not relax discipline, and by paying wages on time he kept his army orderly and well behaved. The latter, with discipline loosened and unable to pay wages, fed his most ready and well-disposed soldiers on the plunder of enemies and allies. Nor did Orange lack the means, whichever way his army turned, to establish a kingdom for himself and his descendants among the Batavians. Opinions differ, and rightly so, about his intention and about the memory of the dead princes. In the same region of Belgium it is said that Philip suspected John of Austria of not even lacking the will to draw the provinces away from the king's obedience to his own, had he not died in time. Nor among the Federated Provinces is the Englishman Leicester cleared of suspicion of guilt, while Maurice was not yet grown.

units.la: 3. Neque senatorio ambitu abstinebat, clientes suos honoribus aut provinciis ornando. Novas res molitu-ro non militum tantùm benevolentia captanda, sed ad togatum etiam ordinem,& ad provinciarum regimina solicitudo extendenda. Cleo ab Aristophane in Equi-tibus traducitur, pedem unum in foro alterum in Pylo, insula habuisse. Rectiùs hic Sejanus dicetur, oculum & brachium unum in castris,alterum in senatu defixise. Firmato enim militum studio, patres & regionum præsides in partes suas traxit. Quos sibi prompté ob-sequentes, aut necessitudine aliqua conjunctos con-spexit; consulatibus aut præfecturæ evexit. Quos verò obstrepentes, variis criminibus circumventos, in odi-um Cæsaris adduxit, atque ita miserrimè irretitos,aut honoribus inanes dimisit, aut plane fortunis & vita exutos afflixit. Quod conspicati senatores, certatim in obsequium ejus ruebant. adeò ut jam nonnullorum aditum, ut conspectum quorundam fastidiret. Quod palàm proferre M Terentius, post necem Sejani, co-ram Tiberio non erubuit. Illius propinqui & affines honoribus augebantur: ut quisque Sejano intimus, ita ad Cæsaris amicitiam validus, contrà quibus infensus effet, metu ac sordibus conslictabantur. VI. Annalium, 4. Cate-
units.tr: 3. Nor did he refrain from senatorial ambition, adorning his clients with honours and provinces. One who is about to attempt a revolution must seek the goodwill not only of the soldiers, but must also extend his concern to the civil order and the governance of the provinces. Aristophanes, in the Knights, portrays Cleon as having one foot in the forum and the other on the island of Pylos. Sejanus could more rightly be said to have fixed one eye and one arm in the camp and the other in the senate. For, having secured the zeal of the soldiers, he drew the senators and the governors of the provinces to his side. Those whom he found ready to obey him, or bound to him by some tie of kinship, he raised to the consulships or the prefecture. Those who grumbled he entangled in various charges and brought into Caesar's hatred. So most wretchedly ensnared, they were either dismissed empty of honours, or utterly stripped of fortune and life and destroyed. Seeing this, the senators rushed eagerly to his service, so that he now scorned the approach of some and the sight of others. Marcus Terentius openly said this after the death of Sejanus, and was not ashamed to say it in Tiberius's presence. His relatives and kinsmen were advanced in honours: each man was as powerful in Caesar's friendship as he was close to Sejanus, while those against whom he was hostile were tormented by fear and degradation. Tacitus, Annals, book 6, [chapter] 4. Cate-

units.la: 4. Caeterum plena Caesarum domus, juvenis filius, Scelerum nepotes adulti, moram cupitis adferebant. & quia vi tot simul corripere intutum, dolus intervalla scelerum poscebat. placuit tamen occultior via, & a Drufo in-ripere, in quem recenti ira ferebatur. Largitionem fundo carere, veteri proverbio dictum refertur. nobis nec cupiditates fundum, nec scelera modum habere, in dominandi inprimis aviditate, aptius dicetur.
units.tr: 4. Otherwise the house of the Caesars was full: a young son and grown grandsons stood in the way of his desires. And since it was unsafe to seize so many at once by force, cunning required intervals between the crimes. Yet a more covert way was chosen, and he resolved to strike at Drusus, against whom anger was then fresh. There is an old proverb that generosity lacks a farm; it can more aptly be said of us that our desires have no bounds, nor our crimes any measure, especially in the greed for domination.

units.la: Jam rerum novarum studio Sejanus morem urbanae militiae mutaverat; jam ambitioso sermone & cultu in animos militum irrepserat, ordines & munia militaria sui arbitrii fecerat; jam curiam, jam provincias clientela sua impleverat: tanquam parum impudentia peccatum sit, ad Caesareae domus caedem, ad ruinam imperatoriae stirpis vastum aviditate animum applicat. Quam ipsam scelerum lernam, per flagitia, per matrimonii corruptelam, per adulteria auspicatur.
units.tr: Now, with a passion for revolution, Sejanus had altered the custom of the city garrison; now, by ambitious speech and dress, he had crept into the minds of the soldiers; he had made the ranks and military duties subject to his own will; now he had filled the senate, now the provinces, with his clients. As if it were too little to sin in impudence, he turns his mind, vast in its greed, to the slaughter of Caesar's house and the ruin of the imperial line. This very Lernaean hydra of crimes he begins with shameful acts, through the corruption of marriage and through adultery.

units.la: Cuncta tentanti potissimum visum, ad uxorem ejus (Drusi) Liviam convertere. Inter arcana munimenta regnorum stupra quoque & adulteria, sed plerunque infelici eventu, allumi, in Augusti descriptione docui.
units.tr: Trying every means, he chose above all to turn to Drusus's wife, Livia. Among the secret fortifications of kingdoms, illicit unions and adulteries are also kindled, but usually with an unhappy outcome, as I showed in the account of Augustus.

units.la: Hanc, ut amore incensus, adulterio pellexit. Facili ad lubricitatem sexu, ubi pulchritudinem suam adorari, vanitate sibi placentis ingenii, persuadetur. & postquam primi flagitii potitus est, neque foemina amissa pudicitia alia abnuerit: ad conjugii spem, consortium regni, & necem mariti impulit. neque enim tam improvidus animi, tam artium suarum oblitus Sejanus fuit; ut primo flagitii tentamine a caede mariti suadenda inciperet. Scelus animo conceptum, qui mos est infernorum spirituum, per gradus evomendum promit. Amor, blanditiae, formae laudatio praecedunt: his pronubis ad vulgandum corpus venitur. ejecta animo honestatis cura, nullum nequitiae genus imprimere arduum erat.
units.tr: He enticed her into adultery, as if inflamed with love. A sex easily led into wantonness, when persuaded by the vanity of a self-pleased mind that its beauty is adored, is won over. Once he had obtained the first shameful act, the woman, having lost her chastity, refuses nothing else: he drove her on to hopes of marriage, to a share in the kingdom, and to the murder of her husband. For Sejanus was not so reckless of mind, so forgetful of his arts, that he would begin by urging the husband's murder at the first attempt at adultery. A crime conceived in the mind is brought forth by degrees, as is the way of infernal spirits. Love, flattery and praise of beauty go before; with these as bridesmaids one comes to the defiling of the body. Once concern for honour has been cast out of the mind, it is no hard task to bring it to every kind of wickedness.

units.la: Atque illa tum avunculus Augustus, socer Tiberius, ex Drufo liberi, feque ac majores & posteros municipali adultero foedabat: ut pro honestis & praesentibus, flagitiosa & incerta exspectaret. Ignorantia Socratem, insania Stoicos, delictorum gravitatem metitos, mirari desinamus. Non modò ignoran-tia rerum, & errore judicii, honesta commodis & blan-dientibus non præferentis, erratur. in ipsa fortuito-rum, & splendore ac utilitate se commendantium, elec-tione mens humana catspitat. Sed ad textuam sceleri-rum introspiciendam redimus.
units.tr: And so, with the emperor Augustus as her uncle, Tiberius as her father-in-law, and children by Drusus, he defiled herself, her ancestors and her descendants with a common adulterer, so that instead of honourable and present things she looked for shameful and uncertain ones. Let us cease to wonder at Socrates' ignorance, or at the madness of the Stoics, who measured the gravity of crimes by their own standard. Men err not only through ignorance of things and a mistaken judgement, which does not put honourable things before advantage and flattery; the human mind also stumbles in its choice among chance things that commend themselves by their splendour and usefulness. But let us return to looking into the web of crimes.

units.la: tiam Eudemus amicus ac medicus Livia, sprecie artis frequens secretis. Multa infidæ medicorum operæ exempla, si brevitas abductionem pateretur, adduci poterant. sed magis urgentibus prævertamur. pellit domo Sejanus uxorem Apicatam, ex quâ tres liberos genuerat, ne pellici suppletaretur. Mitius inter tanta facinora peccatum, divortium: nimis tamen Romanis illo sæculo frequentatum. Sed magnitudo facinoris mutuum, prolationes, diversa interdum consilia adferebat. Vix quisquam est tam projectæ ad delinquendum audaciæ, ut non interdum honestioris cogitationis occursu pungatur. Vide apud poetas Medeæ, de proden-do Jasoni patre, de sequendo incesto amore, de jugu-landis liberis, reciprocas animi deliberantis fluctuatio-nes. Verùm nos Æliana tragœdiæ theatro nonnihil sepositio, in lætiorem civilium sine flagitio rerum cam-pum animi oculos circumferamus.
units.tr: Eudemus, Livia's friend and physician, came often in secret under the pretext of his art. Many examples of the faithless service of physicians could be brought forward, if brevity allowed a digression; but let us hurry on to what presses us. Sejanus drives his wife Apicata, by whom he had three children, from his house, lest the mistress be supplanted. Among such great crimes the wrong is milder: it is divorce, though in that age divorce was too frequent among the Romans. But the magnitude of the deed brought hesitation, delays and, at times, differing plans. Hardly anyone is so far projected into daring to sin that he is not sometimes pricked by the approach of a more honourable thought. See among the poets Medea's wavering: betraying her father for Jason, following an incestuous love, slaying her children, the back-and-forth tossing of a deliberating mind. But let us set aside for a little the theatre of Aelian tragedy, and turn the eyes of the mind to the happier field of civil affairs, where there is no shame in the deeds.

units.la: III. Rata inter propinquos in domo re-gnatrice concordia.
units.tr: III. Concord among kinsmen remains secure in a ruling house.

units.la: Quod nisi ita effet, non tantâ cum laudis mole Ti-berius pietatem filii sui, quòd patriâ benevolentiâ in fratris liberos foret, extulisset. Nec Tacitus quasi admirabundus judicium suum adjecisset. Nam Drusi (quanquam arduum fit, eodem loci potentiam & cordiam esse) æquus adolescentibus, aut certè non adversus habebatur. Satis de animo Drusi, suspensi habebatur: nam interiora, sermonum & oculorum velo obducta, quis dijudicet? Boni tamen illa externa faciei benevolentia, præ sciendi difficulta licentia, consulentes da Absint à moderata aula, absint à civitate, illi Corcyræ mores: de quibus tertio libro Thucydides. πλ[illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~60 letters] [illegible, ~60 letters] [illegible, ~55 letters] [illegible, ~50 letters] i.e. Temeritas enim, studiosa amicorum fortitudo vocabatur: consideràta cunctatio, decora formido, modestia, ignaviae velamentum. in omnibus solertia, in omnibus segnities. praeceps indignatio virilitati adscribebatur. tuto consulrare, excusata tergiversatio erat. &c. [illegible, ~60 letters] [illegible, ~60 letters] [illegible, ~55 letters] i.e. In summa, qui nocendo alterum praevenisset, laudabatur, & qui ad hoc no.i cogitantem exhortatus esset. Quin & propinqui externis infestiores erant, eo quod ad audendum sine excusatione paratiores essent.
units.tr: Were this not so, Tiberius would not have extolled with such great praise the piety of his son, in that he showed a fatherly goodwill toward his brother's children, and Tacitus would not have added his judgment as though in wonder. For Drusus (although it is hard for power and goodwill to dwell in the same place) was regarded as fair to the young men, or at least not hostile to them. Enough about Drusus's disposition: it was regarded as uncertain, for who can judge inner feelings veiled by words and looks? Nevertheless that outward kindness of countenance, together with the license that foreknowledge makes difficult, was consulted... Let them be absent from a moderate court, absent from the state: those are the manners of Corcyra, of which Thucydides speaks in book three. (illegible in the scan) (illegible in the scan) (illegible in the scan) (illegible in the scan) That is: rashness was called the zealous courage of friends; considered delay was called graceful fear; modesty was a cover for cowardice. In everything, cleverness; in everything, sloth. Headstrong indignation was ascribed to manliness; to consult safely was excused as evasion, and so on. (illegible in the scan) (illegible in the scan) (illegible in the scan) That is: in sum, whoever had harmed another first was praised, and whoever had urged a man who was thinking of this... Indeed, kinsmen were more hostile to outsiders, because they were readier to dare without excuse.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Militia ex delectu, quam fortuito ignotorum hominum confluxu, ornatior.
units.tr: A militia raised by levy is more splendid than one gathered from a chance crowd of unknown men.

units.la: Rationem hujus aphorismi tangit Romanus imperator: voluntarium militem non eadem virtute ac modestia agere: quia plerunque inopes ac vagi, sponte militiam sumant. Sed quia Lipsius accurate de hoc praecepto egit, nolo alieni laboris gloriam in penum meum convertere.
units.tr: The Roman emperor touches on the reason for this aphorism: a volunteer soldier does not act with the same courage and discipline, because for the most part it is poor and wandering men who take up soldiering of their own accord. But since Lipsius has treated this precept carefully, I do not wish to turn the glory of another's labour into my own larder.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Pax armata securitate valentior.
units.tr: An armed peace is stronger through security.

units.la: Alta per orbem Romanum pace Augustus, alta Tiberius agebat. Nihilominus ut in belli formidine, terras conscriptae legiones, maria classes procinctae consternebant. Italiam utroque mari duae classes, Misenum apud & Ravennam, proximumque Galliae litus rostra navis praesidebant. nec naves duntaxat in speciem & ornatum litorum, nulla hominum manu, compositæ, sed valido cum remige. Hæc Italiæ à subito extétˆs norum incursu, (nam cætera Alpes claudebant) hæc à piratarum insolentia custodia. Sed præcipuum ro- burimperii in terrestri militia, & legionum aptapet provincias connexione, collocabatur. Quarum fituit & numerum ob oculos, quasi in brevitabella, pone- thus.
units.tr: Under deep peace throughout the Roman world, Augustus and then Tiberius held sway. Nevertheless, as though in fear of war, legions enrolled on land and fleets ready for action at sea were stationed to strike dismay. "Italy was guarded on both seas by two fleets, one at Misenum and one at Ravenna, and the nearby coast of Gaul was held by a fleet with beaked ships." Nor were these ships merely for show and ornament of the shores, with no crew, but they were manned with a strong complement of rowers. These guarded Italy against sudden incursions of foreigners (for the Alps closed off the rest of the frontier) and against the insolence of pirates. But the chief strength of the empire was placed in the land forces and in the legions' deployment across the provinces. Setting out their stations and numbers before the eyes, as it were in a brief table, I place them thus.

units.la: Legiones
units.tr: Legions

units.la: Urbem verò tres urbanæ, novem prætoriæ cohortes, insidebant. Auxiliares cohortes, & socias provin- ciarum triremes, numero comprehendere, fupervaˆ cuum autori visum. Unde colligitur, ingentes in ar- mâ expensas Remp. Romanam, pacifico licet gen- tium seculo, toleravisse. Quas cum concidere By- zantini imperatores, militemque & ætma undique dimittere, in animum induxerunt, non sumptu im- perium Romanum, sed securitate pacis levaverunt; Barbaris enim in pacatas, armis nudatas, longo otio florentes, regionesalle&is, virtute veterum parta uno momento everterunt. Alendæ igitur in pace copiæ militum, repentinum subitæ formidini auxilium, & spei barbaræ invasionis impedimentum.
units.tr: In the city itself, three urban and nine praetorian cohorts were stationed. I judged it superfluous to count the auxiliary cohorts and the allied provincial triremes. From this it is gathered that the Roman commonwealth bore enormous expenses on its army, even in a peaceful age of the nations. When the Byzantine emperors resolved to cut these back and to dismiss soldiers and arms everywhere, they lightened the Roman empire not in expense but in security. For barbarians, falling upon pacified regions stripped of arms and flourishing in long idleness, overturned in a single moment what had been won by the courage of the ancients. Therefore, keeping troops in peacetime is both a help against sudden fear and an obstacle to the hope of a barbarian invasion.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Urbana negotia militaribus, præstan- tia aut curæ necessitate, non cedunt.
units.tr: Urban affairs do not give way to military matters, whether of superior importance or of pressing need.

units.la: Minus enim est hostem armis repellere, quàm ci- vem in officio continere. Illud fortunæ sæpè est aut alicujus animorum impetus, hoc confidenti animi folertiæ. Arma quis Alexandrum imitatus per omnes gentes circumferat, fortunam etiam fecundis proeliis obsequentem habeat: nisi pacis leges ornandæ reip. ferre possit; tantum a boni principis officio recedit, quantum gladiatoriæ temeritati propinquior esse voluit. Quod Alexandro Macedoni Augustum Tiberi-us apud Dionem præfert, non tam facile de proeliorum felicitate concedo, quam de universo principis quæsiti munere largior. Quam primum enim qui-escere Augusto, compositā a turbis Republica, licuit; bonis beatæ pacis artibus urbem, Italiam, gentes composuit. Qua ratione etiam ipsum Tiberium Alexan-dro, vel quicunque alius omnem ætatem bellis non necessariis trivit, antefero. Tiberium intellige nondum Germanici obitu, Drusi nece, Sejani stimulatione depravatum. Sub quo Tiberio qui status urbis, quis imperii fuerit, Taciti vestigia secuti contemplabimur. Jam primum publica negotia, & privatorum ma-ximā, apud patres tractabantur. Non se negotiorum omnium solum judicem, clausis intra unam domum judicibus & reis, exhibuit. Nihil in penatibus suis venale, aut ambitioni pervium habuit: discreta domus & respublica. Tenuit antiqua munia senatus. Consu-lum tribunalibus Italiæ & publicæ provinciæ astiterunt. Ut verba Neronis, Tiberio accommodata, re-feram.
units.tr: It is less work to repel an enemy by arms than to keep a citizen in his duty. The former often depends on fortune or on the impulse of some spirit; the latter depends on the careful skill of a mind that is steady. Let someone who imitates Alexander carry his arms through all the nations and have fortune obeying him in many successful battles: unless he can bring the laws of peace to adorn the commonwealth, he departs as far from the duty of a good prince as he chose to come close to gladiatorial recklessness. I do not grant as readily as Dio does, who sets Augustus above Alexander the Macedonian, the point about the success of battles; I concede rather the whole office of the principate that was sought. For as soon as Augustus was able to rest, with the Republic settled after the upheavals, he settled the city, Italy and the nations by the good arts of a happy peace. For this reason I also put Tiberius before Alexander, or before anyone else who spent his whole life in unnecessary wars. Understand Tiberius as he was before he was corrupted by the death of Germanicus, the murder of Drusus and the incitement of Sejanus. Under this Tiberius we shall consider, following the traces of Tacitus, what the condition of the city was and what the state of the empire was. First, public business and the most important private business were handled before the senate. He did not show himself the sole judge of all affairs, with judges and defendants shut up within one house. Nothing in his household was for sale or open to ambition: the house and the commonwealth were kept separate. He maintained the ancient duties of the senate. The consuls' tribunals were attended in Italy and in the public provinces. To report the words of Nero, applied to Tiberius:

units.la: Dabaturque primoribus differere. nec vox eorum compressa, quorum præsentiam ferebat.
units.tr: And the leading men were allowed to speak at length. Nor was the voice of those suppressed whose presence he endured.

units.la: Et in adulationem lapsos cohibebat ipse. adeo ut gravissime increparet, qui divinas occupationes, ipsumque dominum appellarent.
units.tr: And he himself restrained those who had slipped into flattery. So much so that he very severely rebuked those who called his occupations divine, and himself lord.

units.la: Mandabatque honores, nobilitatem majorum, claritudinem militiæ, illustres domi artes spectando. Tria honorum mandandorum argumenta, ambitui, favori, emptioni munerum opposita, observa.
units.tr: And he entrusted honours by looking to nobility of ancestors, distinction in military service, and arts that shone at home. Notice the three grounds for entrusting offices, set against ambition, favour and the purchase of posts.

units.la: Ut facta constaret, non alios potiores fuisse. at moribus corruptis faventiores quæruntur, aut opulentiores.
units.tr: So that it might be clear that no others were preferred. But with corrupt morals, the more favoured or the wealthier are sought.

units.la: Sua consulibus, sua prætoribus species. Significanter dictum species : nam potestas magna ex parte exóle-verat.
units.tr: He gave consuls one kind of appearance, praetors another. The word "appearance" is significant, for power had for the most part faded away.

units.la: Minorum quoque magistratuum exercita potestas, quae nimirum majestatem summi imperii nō carpebat: Legesque, si majestatis quaestio eximeretur, bono in usum. nam istæc aut frequentia aut rigore modum excessit. At frumenta & pecunias vectigales &c. in his nihil à prisco reip. more recedebatur.
units.tr: The power of the lesser magistrates was also exercised, which indeed did not diminish the majesty of the supreme power; and the laws were applied for the good, if the question of treason were set aside. For these things had exceeded their measure either by frequency or by severity. But in grain, tax revenues and the like, nothing departed from the ancient custom of the commonwealth.

units.la: Res suas Cafar spectatissimo cuique, quibusdam igno-tis ex fama mandabat. nihil in his laudē non dignum. Semelque affumpti tenebantur, cujus rei æstimatio-nem in Arcanis perpendi.
units.tr: Caesar entrusted his own affairs to the most distinguished man of each kind, and to some unknown men on the strength of their reputation. Nothing in these matters is unworthy of praise. And once they were taken on, they were held to account, the assessment of each matter being weighed in the secret archives.

units.la: Plebes acri quidem annona fatigabatur: sed nulla in eo culpa ex principe, major ex ignavia colentium & ex agrorum desertione.
units.tr: The common people were indeed burdened by the harsh price of grain, but no blame for this lay with the prince; the greater cause was the idleness of the farmers and the desertion of the fields.

units.la: Ne provincia novis oneribus turbarentur, utque ve-tera sine avaritia aut crudelitate magistratuum tole-rarent, providebat. O dignam magno principe, ô ra-tione seculis continentiam, assiduitatem, providentiam! Corporum verbera, ademtiones bonorum aberant, quas nunc honesto Executionis nomine palliant.
units.tr: He took care that the provinces should not be disturbed by new burdens, and that they might bear the old ones without the greed or cruelty of magistrates. O restraint worthy of a great prince, O constancy, diligence and foresight worthy of the ages! Beatings of bodies and confiscations of goods were absent, which they now cover with the honourable name of execution.

units.la: Rari per Italiam Cafaris agri &c. ne civibus, ne fo-cius victus quaerendi ratio praerepta videretur.
units.tr: Caesar's estates in Italy were few, lest the means of earning a living should seem to be snatched from citizens and from allies.

units.la: Si quando cum privatis disceptaret, forum & jus, quo extremo regiae laudis cumulo Germania etiam, aliquando & Gallia, beatam se praedicat.
units.tr: If ever he disputed with private persons, he gave them a fair hearing and justice, a supreme crown of royal praise, by which Germany too, and at times Gaul, call themselves blessed.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Imperii majestas consortii impa-tiens.
units.tr: The majesty of empire is impatient of a partner.

units.la: Non levi errore Tiberius erravit, qui Sejano cohortes, munia senatorum, consilia imperandi commisit; in omnibus quae eum, incolumi filio, adjutorem im-perii affumpsit. Nam Augustum, imperii inter initia dominationis incertum, temporum necessitas excusavit. Ac neis ipse quidem ita externos, Agrippam & Mæcenatem, evexit; cum filio careret; ut non alteri quodammodo opponeret. At Tiberius, imperio servientium consuetudine jam roboraro, filio annis animis & autoritate adulto, jamque tribunitia potestate ornato, non ex necessitate municipali Sejanum sibi, quasi collegam, adjunxit. Quare ita se princeps beni-gnum honorum communicatione gerat, ut modestiae limites non a solo ministri potentioris animo imperetur. quod in Sejano Drusus non sine causa suspicatur: precandam posthac Modestiam, ut contentus esset.
units.tr: Tiberius erred, and not in a small way, when he committed to Sejanus the cohorts, the duties of senators and the counsels of ruling; in all these things he took him as a helper in the empire while his son was still alive. For the necessity of the times excused Augustus, whose sovereignty was uncertain in the early stages of his rule. Indeed Augustus himself raised outsiders in such a way, Agrippa and Maecenas, since he lacked a son, that he did not in a sense set them against another. But Tiberius, with his empire already strengthened by the custom of obedience, his son now grown in years, spirit and authority, and already invested with tribunician power, joined Sejanus to himself as if a colleague, not from the necessity of a municipal figure. Therefore a prince should so conduct himself in bestowing honours, in sharing them, that the limits of moderation are not dictated by the mind of a minister who is too powerful. Drusus rightly suspected this in Sejanus: Modesty must henceforth be prayed for, that he might be content.

units.la: Imitandus principi sapientissimus Hebraeorum Salomo: qui freno adductiori Israelitis imperans, munia administrationum non in unum congessit. Alium praesidem, alios scribas, alium a memoria designavit. Hunc militiae, illum sacris praefecit. Alium annonae curandae, alium consiliis participandis allexit. Hic domui praefectus, ille delectui praepositus erat. De rege autem solo dicebatur: Salomo erat dominans in omnia regna. 1.Regum.4. v.1.2.3.4.5.6.7.21. Aureis literis frontispicio aulae illud Aristotelis inscribendum: Κοινὴ φύσις ... v.Politic.
units.tr: The wisest of the Hebrews, Solomon, is to be imitated by a prince; he, ruling the Israelites with a tighter rein, did not gather the offices of administration into one man. He appointed one as governor, others as scribes, another as recorder. He set one over the military, another over sacred matters. He engaged one to look after the grain supply, another to share in counsels. This man was placed over the household, that one was put in charge of levies. But of the king alone it was said: Solomon was ruling over all kingdoms. 1 Kings 4:1–7, 21. And let this saying of Aristotle be inscribed in gold letters on the frontispiece of the court: Κοινὴ φύσις [Common nature ...] Politics, book 5.

units.la: VIII. Non apud quosvis secretus animi dolore effundendus.
units.tr: VIII. Not to be poured out in secret grief before just anyone.

units.la: Maxime ubi de magnatum & potentiorum injuria queraris. Quod quia Druso negligebatur, maturum sibi exitium accersivit. Neque raro, neque apud paucos talia jaciebat: & secreta quoque ejus, corrupta uxore, prodebantur. Cautius in causa Pisoniana idem Druso egit: si vera forent, quae jacerentur, praecipuum in dolore suum locum respondit. sed malle falsa & inania, nec cuiquam mortem Germanici exitiosam esse. Hac palam, & vitato omni secreto. Sed nimirum illa sermonum ἀφίξεις a Tiberio praescribebatur: cujus tum similibus artibus utebatur. Nunc ira & dolore facilis, in ipsum Tiberium, non minus quam Sejanum, quaestus effundit. Sed quo doloris levamento? Igitur Sejanus maturandum ratus, diligit venenum, quo paulatim irrepente, fortuitus morbus assimularetur. Hic cum Thyeste exclamet licet.
units.tr: Above all when you complain of an injury done by great and powerful men. Because Drusus neglected this, he brought an early ruin upon himself. He did not speak such things rarely or before a few people, and even his secrets were betrayed through his corrupted wife. In the case of Piso he acted more cautiously against Drusus: if what was being said were true, he replied, his own grief held the first place; but he preferred to think the reports false and empty, and that no one's death was fatal to Germanicus. He said this openly and avoided all secrecy. But clearly this was the sort of reporting that Tiberius prescribed, and he himself used such tricks at that time. Now, quick to anger and grief, he pours out complaints against Tiberius himself, no less than against Sejanus. But what relief does this bring to his grief? So Sejanus, judging that the matter must be hurried, chose poison, by which, creeping on slowly, a chance illness could be feigned. Here he may cry out with Thyestes:

units.la: ó quantum bonum est,
units.tr: O how great a good it is,

units.la: Obstare nulli, capere securas dapes!
units.tr: to stand against no one, and to take a safe meal!

units.la: Humi jacentem scelera non intrant casam,
units.tr: The man lying low on the ground, crime does not enter his hut,

units.la: Tutusque mensa capitur angusta cibus:
units.tr: and food is taken safely at a narrow table;

units.la: Venenum in auto bibitur.
units.tr: poison is drunk from a golden cup.

units.la: Seneca Thyeste, Act. 3. Sc. 1.
units.tr: Seneca, Thyestes, Act 3, Sc. 1.

units.la: Quid tutum in aula, si herilis filius, à jurisconsultissimo [?] perantis ministro, ab uxore, à Spadone, à medicis veneno tollitur. Non enim desunt flagitii ministri, ubi de voluntate propinquorum constat. Id Drufo datum per Lygdum Spadonem, ut octo post annos cognitum est. Tam diu scelera in occulto latent: mala sæterno silentio tacita fæcinoroforum conscientia sepelit. Sic compescendi nescius dolor, & libera injuria querela, Drufo imperatoris unico filio nocuit: nocuit & Germanici libertis, nocuit Agrippinæ, nō- cuit Quiritibus lamentantibus, eodem sub Tiberio. Dies quo reliquiæ (Germanici) tumulo Augusti infe- rebantur, modo per silentium vastas, modo ploratibus inquiés: plena urbs itinera, colluentes per campum Martii faces, illic miles cum armis, sine insignibus ma- gistratus, populus per tribus, concidisse remp. nihil sibi reliquum clamitabant: promptius apertiusque, quam ut meminisse imperantium crederes. Itane, Tiberio annis vigente, filio Drufo superstite, concidit Respu- blica; & nihil spei reliquum? Is dolor altius animum Tiberii penetravit: inde apertius in liberos Germani- ci fuerè, in Agrippinam sævire, in Quiritesefferri, Sex- jano ministro, cœpit. Nec tam fortissis animi firmi- tudine, aut simulatione firmitudinis, quam suspicioso in filium odio, querelis improvidis accenso, perOmnes valetudinis ejus dies, etiam defuncto nec dum sepulto, suriam ingressus est, consule sque sede vulgaris per spe- ciem mostitia sedentes, bonoris locique admonuit: effusum in lacrymas senatum, sicto gemitu, simul orationem continua erexit. Nam & Tiberium, unicum è Drufo nepotem, neglexit: & aut nullum, aut pessimum mortalium, successorem optavit. Quam voti summam impio dicto, nec acuminis vacuo, præ se ferebat:
units.tr: What is safe at court, if the son of the master is removed by poison, by the minister of the ruling power, by the wife, by the eunuch, by the physicians? For there is no lack of wicked ministers when the will of the relatives is known. This was given to Drusus through the eunuch Lygdus, as was learned eight years later. So long do crimes lie hidden in secret; the conscience of the criminals buries evil things in eternal silence. Thus a grief that knew not how to restrain itself, and a complaint that free injury made, harmed Drusus, the emperor's only son; it harmed the freedmen of Germanicus, it harmed Agrippina, it harmed the Romans lamenting under the same Tiberius. On the day when the remains of Germanicus were carried to the tomb of Augustus, the city was now vast in silence, now loud with weeping; the roads were full, torches blazed across the Campus Martius, the soldiers were there in arms, the magistrates without their insignia, the people by tribes, and they kept crying out that the state had fallen and nothing was left to them, more openly and plainly than you would believe anyone could remember under rulers. Is it so, that while Tiberius was still vigorous in years and his son Drusus was still alive, the commonwealth has fallen and no hope remains? That grief pierced the mind of Tiberius more deeply; from then on he raged more openly against the children of Germanicus and against Agrippina, and began to rage against the Romans, with Sejanus as his minister. Not by the firmness of a very brave spirit, nor by a pretence of firmness, but by a suspicious hatred of his son, kindled by rash complaints, he entered upon every day of his illness, even when the dead man was not yet buried; he reminded the consuls and the common senators, sitting in the seats of their rank, of their honour and place, under a show of mourning; the senate, dissolved in tears, he roused with feigned groaning and a continuous speech. For he neglected Tiberius, the only grandson of Drusus, and wished for either no successor or the worst of mortals; the sum of this wish he expressed in an impious word, not without a sharp edge:

units.la: Eus
units.tr: Eus

units.la: [illegible, ~30 letters]
units.tr: [illegible, ~30 letters]

units.la: Me miscceatur igne terra mortuo.
units.tr: May the earth be mingled with fire when I am dead.

units.la: Dio libro 58.
units.tr: Dio, book 58.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Patris personam aut mariti exuat, qui principis suscepit.
units.tr: One who has undertaken the person of a prince must not strip off the person of a father or husband.

units.la: Publicam enim vitam, non domesticam, agens pu-blico bono aut damno afficitur. Quo argumento lu-ctum domesticae cladis compressum, Tiberius in senatu excusat: se fortiora solatia e complexu Reip. petivisse.
units.tr: For one who lives a public life, not a domestic one, is affected for good or ill by the public. By this argument Tiberius, in the senate, excused the restraint of his grief over a domestic disaster: he had sought stronger consolations from the embrace of the commonwealth.

units.la: De dolore ex offensa idem Tiberius in Junio Silano: quem cum patriae incolumem reddidisset: orationem annexuit, sibi tamen adversus eum integras parentis sui offensiones, publice nec senatus consulto damnatum, nec lege pulsum, publice punire non dignatus privatas hereditarias offensionis injurias privatae simultati sepo-nebat. Clarius idem Tiberius, eodem Annalium libro, odero, seponamque a domo mea & privatas inimicitias non principis ulciscar. Quae a Tiberio, simulationum plenissimo, prolata, non tantum laudis merentur, quantum illud Germanorum imperatoris, qui ex humili comitatu ad imperatoriam dignitatem evectus, instigatus a susurronibus aulicis, ut veteres injurias facultatem nactus ultione persequeretur, generose re-spondit: non esse imperatoris fastigii, ut is Comitis in-jurias in animum admitteret. Nec minus paradoxae ad hanc mentem rei est, quod Carolus Austriacus ipse sibi, aliam personam gerenti, per edictum imperavit: Nos, Carolus V. Romanorum Imperator, tibi Carolo Comiti Tirolii injungimus. Animi altitudine consuetudinem mortalium, non rationem humanam, excedit; quod Romanorum alii se pro republica in praesens exitium devoverunt, alii sibi & domui suae eadem, a publico avertendam, imprecati leguntur. Ex eo imperantium cum imperio connexu causa deduci potest, punitorum, vel a Deo vel ab hominibus, in subditorum sensu principum. Hinc ea Davidis Hebraeorum regis publica in lue ejulatio; & damni publici in fe quod ad preces, detorsio: fit quaeso, manus tua con-tra me [?] contra domum paternam meam. 2.Sam.24.
units.tr: Tiberius showed the same kind of grief over an offence in the case of Junius Silanus. When he had restored him safe to his country, he added a speech saying that he still bore against him the unbroken offences of his own father, which had been publicly condemned neither by a decree of the senate nor by a law; he did not think it worthy of a prince to punish them publicly, and so he set aside the private injuries of hereditary offence for private enmity. More clearly, the same Tiberius, in the same book of the Annals: I shall hate, and keep my private enmities far from my house, and I shall not avenge them as prince. These words, uttered by Tiberius, most full of pretence, deserve not as much praise as that saying of the German emperor, who, raised from a humble retinue to imperial dignity, was urged by courtly whisperers to seize the chance and avenge old injuries; he answered nobly that it did not befit the height of an emperor to admit the injuries of a count into his mind. Nor is it less paradoxical in this matter that Charles of Austria, when bearing another person, commanded himself by edict: We, Charles V, Emperor of the Romans, enjoin you, Charles, Count of Tyrol. In the loftiness of his spirit he goes beyond the custom of mortals, not human reason; for some Romans devoted themselves to present destruction for the commonwealth, and others are read to have prayed that the same destruction be turned from the public upon themselves and their house. From this connection of rulers with their rule the cause can be drawn of the punishment of the punished, whether by God or by men, in the feeling of the subjects of princes. Hence came David's public lamentation, king of the Hebrews, in the public plague, and the turning of the public harm upon himself in his prayer: Let thy hand, I pray thee, be against me and against my father's house. 2 Sam. 24.
