units.la: v.17. Apud poetas Tragicos Oedipus, parricidii & incestus occulto Dei foro reus, magno dolentis animi sensu, coacervatis civium Thebanorum funeribus punitur. Cumque se tantæ stragis autorem ex oraculo, cognosceret, non ad preces Davidicas, sed ad desperationem & odium vitæ conversus, oculos ipse sibi eruit, indignos qui lucem à se pollutam aspicerent. vixque concessit filiæ, ut, ne in præcipitia irrueret, manu ejus circumduceretur. Momentum trahentia verba sunt, quæ à Seneca illi tribuuntur:
units.tr: Verse 17. Among the tragic poets, Oedipus, guilty of parricide and incest before the hidden court of God, is punished with great feeling of grief, the funerals of the citizens of Thebes having piled up. When he learned from the oracle that he was the author of so great a slaughter, he turned, not to Davidic prayers, but to despair and hatred of life, and tore out his own eyes, thinking himself unworthy to look upon the light he had polluted; and he scarcely yielded to his daughter, that she might lead him by the hand, lest he rush over the precipices. The words that Seneca gives to him are weighty:

units.la: eculi crimen vagor,
units.tr: The crime of my wandering,

units.la: Odium deorum, juris exitium facit.
units.tr: the hatred of the gods, makes the destruction of justice.

units.la: Oed.Act.4.Sc.3.
units.tr: Oedipus, Act 4, Sc. 3.

units.la: Nondum quid sit principem gerere, didicere, quidos meflicæ ruinæ populum ruiturum objiciunt.
units.tr: They have not yet learned what it is to govern as a prince; they object to the people, about to fall, the ruin of a calamity that is coming.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Principum fortuna momento Reip. stat vel cadit.
units.tr: The fortune of princes stands or falls together with the commonwealth in a moment.

units.la: Principium appellatio prisca reip. natione in cives fa-ctione & opibus excellentes cadit: recentiori significatione non modo imperantibus, verum etiam impe-rantes proxima spe attingentibus, tribuitur. Sic de Germanico Tiberius: Principes mortales, Remp. [?]-nam esse. 3. Annal. de Germanici liberis h.l. ita nati
units.tr: In the old usage, "principes" was the name for those who excelled the citizens in birth, faction and wealth; in the more recent sense it is applied not only to those who rule but also to those who are close to ruling by the hope of succession. So Tiberius said of Germanicus' sons: "Princes are mortal, the commonwealth ... ; you are born so that ..."

units.la: estis, ut bona malaque vestra ad Remp. pertineant. Surgere enim vel cadere, sine incremento vel convul-sione rerum, magnarum domuum fortuna ægrè po-test.
units.tr: You were born in such a way that your good and bad fortunes pertain to the commonwealth. For to rise or fall, without an increase or an upheaval of great affairs, can hardly happen to the fortune of great houses.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Modi nescia simulatio pellucet.
units.tr: Simulation that knows no measure shows through.

units.la: Candidi viri est, sæpiùs aperta quàm simulata ora-tione uti: caute simulantis, modum figmentis ponere.
units.tr: It is the mark of an honest man to speak openly more often than to speak with pretence; it is for one who dissembles with caution to keep his fictions within bounds.

units.la: De Tiberio Cornelius: ac si modum orationi posuisset, misericordia sui gloriaque animos audientium [?] verat. ad vana & tenues irritamenta revolumus, de redden-
units.tr: Of Tiberius, Cornelius (Tacitus) writes: as if he had set a limit to his speech, he would have ... [the hearers' minds were turned away from pity for himself and from glory]; we return to vain and slight incitements, ... to restore the Republic, so that the consuls or someone else might draw up the government.

units.la: da Rep.utque consules seu quis alius regimen fuscriperet, vero quoque & honesto fidem dempsit. Plura de excessu Tiberianæ simulationis pete ex Arcanis regnorum: pag. 183.
units.tr: He also took away trust in what is true and honourable. For more on the excess of Tiberian dissimulation, see the Arcana regnorum, p. 183.

units.la: XII. Fœcunda adulationum vanitas.
units.tr: XII. The fertile vanity of flattery.

units.la: Priores enim superare honorum cumulatione sequentes conantur, ut fermè amat posterior adulatio. Quo titulorum congestæ vanitates in Germania excreverint, ut jam & magnitudine & multitudine sua laborent, viri sapientioris animi vident, ridént, aut ingemiscunt.
units.tr: For those who come later try to outdo their predecessors by piling up honours, as later flattery generally loves to do. How far the heaped-up vanities of titles have grown in Germany, so that they now labour under their own size and number, men of wiser mind see, laugh at, or groan over.

units.la: XIII. Corrupta in miraculum historia prudenti examine arguitur.
units.tr: XIII. A history corrupted into a miracle is refuted by prudent examination.

units.la: Multos non vera, sed fabulosa in legenda historia juvant. Hinc Vera Luciani, nihil minus quam vera, Historia; hinc qui inscribitur liber Die wahrhaftige Lügen/hinc qui Gallis dicuntur Les Romans & Amadis de Gaule tenacius lectorem, quam res nudè descriptæ attinent. Ex hac prodigiosæ novitatis aviditate in historiam Romanam irrepsit fabulosa de ortu Romuli & Remi narratio: nec plus fidei apud me repertura, toties bos in Campanis locuta. Similibus historiæ portentis Tacitus accensèt, quæ de Drusi interitu spargebantur, monitum Tiberium, vitaret potionem, quæ prima ei apud filium epulanti offerretur, ea fraude tum senem, postquam convivium inierat, exceptum poculum Druso tradidisse. atq; illo ignaro & juveniliter hauriente, auctam suspicionem, tanquam metu & pudore sibimet irrogaret mortem, quam patri struxerat. Quod ubi recensuit, hoc argumento Cornelius refutat.
units.tr: Many people are charmed not by true history but by fabulous stories. Hence Lucian's True History, which is nothing less than true; hence the book called Die wahrhaftige Lügen; hence the French Les Romans & Amadis de Gaule, which hold the reader more tenaciously than plainly described facts. From this same eagerness for prodigious novelty, the fabulous account of the birth of Romulus and Remus crept into Roman history. It will find no more credit with me, since the ox spoke so often in Campania. Tacitus counts among such portents of history the rumours spread about the death of Drusus: that Tiberius, having been warned, avoided the drink that was first offered to him at dinner with his son; and that the old man, after he had entered the dining room, handed the cup he had been given to Drusus by that trick. Then, while the young man drank it unaware and eagerly, the suspicion grew that he was inflicting on himself, out of fear and shame, the death he had prepared for his father. After Tacitus has recounted this, Cornelius refutes it with the following argument.

units.la: Quis enim mediocri prudentia, nedum Tiberius, tantis rebus exercitus, inaudito filio exitium offerret, idque sua manu, & nullo adpœnitendum regressu? Quin potius ministrum veneni excruciaret, auctorem exquireret, insita denique etiam in extraneos contatione[?] & mora, adversum unicum & nullius ante flagitii com- pertum uteretur. Quae Tiberium factum fuisse Ta- citus innuit, ea viro prudenti pari in casu facienda sunt. Alias non deest similitudo, alias apud gentes & aulas, historiae.
units.tr: For who of moderate prudence, let alone Tiberius, who was occupied with such great affairs, would offer death to his son, a thing unheard of, and that with his own hand, with no way of returning from it? Rather he would torture the servant who prepared the poison, seek out the author of it, and finally use delay and caution even toward outsiders, against the one person whose crime had not yet been established. What Tacitus hints was done by Tiberius is what a prudent man ought to do in a like case. Other times a comparison is not lacking; other nations and courts have their histories.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Veneni genus est criminatio.
units.tr: Slander is a kind of poison.

units.la: Serpentes & afflatu sibili aliquid lethiferi halitus aspergunt: & serpentina criminatoris lingua, quos manu non audet, deferendo interficit. Drufo pharmacis vita erepto, Agrippina, & liberi Germanici, quorum non dubia post Drusum successio, Sejano ad regnum grassanti removendi erant. neque spargi venenum intra poterat, egregia custodum fide, & pudicitia Agrippina impenetrabili. Igitur à pharmaco ad pestiferum linguae sibilum Sejanus confugiens, primam Agrippinam arripit. Quia enim tenerae puerorum aetati favetur magis quàm invidetur; & materexcuba- trix pro iis aut ultrix metuebatur; placuit ab ea tra- goedia stamen ordiri. Prima criminandi seges à con- tumacia Agrippinae: spes in Augustae odio, & Liviae conscientia: progressus in superbię ob foecunditatem interpretatione: culmen in dominationis affectatione. Igitur contumaciam ejus infestari, vetus Augusta odii recentem Livia conscientiam exagitare, ut superbiam foecunditate subnixam, popularibus studiis in- biare dominationi apud Cafarem arguerent. Gradus hos lapsus procurandi adverte.
units.tr: Serpents spread something deadly with the hiss of their breath, and the serpent-like tongue of an accuser kills by informing against those whom he dares not touch with his hand. When Drusus had been carried off by poison, Agrippina and the children of Germanicus had to be removed, since their succession after Drusus was not in doubt, and Sejanus was aiming at the kingdom. Yet poison could not be spread among them, given the excellent loyalty of the guards and Agrippina's impenetrable chastity. So Sejanus, fleeing from poison to the deadly hiss of the tongue, first seized upon Agrippina. For tender childhood is pitied more than it is envied, and a mother who stood guard over her children was feared as their avenger. So it pleased him to begin the tragedy's warp with her. The first crop of accusations came from Agrippina's stubbornness; their hope lay in the Augusta's hatred and Livia's guilty conscience; their progress lay in interpreting her pride from her fertility; their climax lay in the charge of aspiring to domination. So they would attack her obstinacy, the Augusta's old hatred would stir up Livia's recent guilty conscience, and they would accuse her pride, supported by her fertility, of plotting for domination with Caesar's own people. Mark these steps of a contrived fall.

units.la: 1. Contumaciam. quae prima odii Tiberiani in eam fax, & Sejani occasio. Hanc in uxore & agnovit, & ut deponeret, ultimis precibus Germanicus oravit, exuere ferociam, fœvienti fortunae submitteret animum, neu regressa in urbem, æmulatione potentiae validio- res irritaret. 2. Annal. cujus præcepti non fatis mentor Agrippina, & nunc Drusfo defunc̃to in spem nimis aperte erecta, præcipitem sibi & liberis ruinam addu- xit. Agrippina quoque proximi illiciebantur, pravis sermonibus tumidos spiritus perflimulare, nec Agrippinam pinam ex eo fœminarum genere exemeris, quas tertio Annalium libro Cæcina depingit, non imbecillum tantum, & imparem laboribus sexum, sed si licentia adsit, fauum[?], ambitiosum, potestatis avidum, incedere inter milites, habere ad manum centuriones: praesedisse nuper fœminam exercitio cohortium, decursu legionis[?]. Ergo prima aculei criminatorii hebetatio, criminis, & contumaciae inprimis, fuga.
units.tr: 1. Stubbornness: this was the first torch of Tiberius's hatred against her and Sejanus's opportunity. Germanicus acknowledged this in his wife, and in his last prayers begged her to lay aside her ferocity, to submit her spirit to a raging fortune, and not, once she had returned to the city, to provoke those more powerful by rivalry for power. 2. Annals. Agrippina, not sufficiently mindful of this precept, and now that Drusus was dead and she was raised too openly into hope, brought headlong ruin upon herself and her children. Neighbours too were enticed to puff up her swollen spirit with wicked talk. Nor should Agrippina be excluded from that class of women whom Caecina depicts in the third book of the Annals: not only weak and unequal to labours, but, if licence is given, fierce, ambitious, greedy for power, walking among the soldiers and keeping centurions at hand; a woman who had lately presided over the training of cohorts and the drill of a legion. Therefore the first blunting of the accusing sting lies in avoiding the charge of stubbornness above all.

units.la: 2. Affectus in aliorum animis rimationem. Augu-sta apud filium, Livia apud soceerum[?], multum laudando aut obtrectando poterant. Harum occultos animi motus in Agrippinam Sejanus exstimulat. Augusta odium. erat enim ei vetus cum Agrippina ex aemulatione potentiae simultas,recentem Liviae conscientiam; veneni nimirum in Drusum parati & ex eo regni cupiditatis.
units.tr: 2. The stirring up of feelings in the minds of others. Augusta could work on her son, and Livia on her father-in-law, by praising or disparaging. Sejanus goaded their hidden movements of mind against Agrippina. Augusta's hatred. For she had an old feud with Agrippina arising from rivalry for power. Livia's recent guilty conscience; namely over the poison prepared against Drusus, and from that, her desire for the kingdom.

units.la: Ægre odium placaveris: quod quo injustius, eo fae-pe acrius, animi tamen & vultus demissione, lenitate sermonis & ingenii, culpae quamvis fictae deprecatione, prompto ministerii obsequio, magnam ejus partem fregeris. At spem ex lapsu tuo commodi, & alienam cupiditatem aegerrime vitaveris. Satis est latroni ad caedem humanam stimuli, satis militi ad invadendam opulentam urbem calcaris, praedae & rapinarum praesentatio. Frequentissima haec in aulis criminandi & evertendi proximos ubertas, commodi pro se aut suis ex alieno casu adeptio.
units.tr: Hatred is hard to appease: the more unjust it is, the more often it is sharp. Yet by lowering your spirit and countenance, by gentleness of speech and manner, by pleading guilt even if it is feigned, and by ready obedience in service, you may break a large part of it. But the hope of gain from your fall, and another's greed, you will very hardly avoid. A robber needs only a stimulus to human slaughter, and a soldier only a spur to seize a rich city: the display of plunder and booty. This is the most frequent yield of courts: accusing and overthrowing one's neighbours, and gaining advantage for oneself or one's own from another's downfall.

units.la: 3. Invidiae ex aliqua praestantia commotionem. Etiam qui bonis alienis non inhiant, ab alio tamen se superari non satis aequo animo ferunt. Igitur aut im-minutio eminentis, aut praecipitatio quaeritur. Foecunditatem Agrippinae, & ex ea superbiam, criminatores arguunt. Augustae extremam fenestram[?], unico tantum filio Tiberio, eoque aetate vergente, subnixam; & ipsum Tiberium amisso filio infelicem, satis hoc stimulo fodicare poterant. Nam & dii, vana gentilium perfuasione, alienae foecunditatis flamma, noto Apollinis & Dianae in Nioben odio, urebantur. Frequentior tamen ex opum, dignitatum, opulentiae, studii popu-
units.tr: 3. The stirring of envy because of some eminence. Even those who do not covet other people's goods still bear it ill when they are surpassed by another. So either the eminent man's standing is to be lessened or his headlong fall is sought. Accusers charge Agrippina with fertility, and from it with pride. They could easily prick Augusta, who leaned on her last hope in her extreme age, and on her only son Tiberius, now growing old; and Tiberius himself, unhappy after losing his son, could be goaded enough by this sting. For the gods too, by the vain persuasion of the Gentiles, were burning with the flame of another's fertility, through the known hatred of Apollo and Diana against Niobe. More frequent, however, is the envy that comes from the influx of wealth, dignities, opulence, and popular favour.

units.la: laris affluxu, invidiæ materiei, Cui etiam criminatio- nis potentiæ primas delator tribuit. & ab ea ad extre- mum, & veré mortiferum iɛtum (4) dominationis inhiationem transgreditur. quo telo nullum in animis dominantium, adversus cives potentiores, validius.
units.tr: This is the matter of envy, to which the informer also assigns the first charge of power. From there he passes on at last to the truly deadly blow: the craving for domination. No weapon is more potent in the minds of rulers against more powerful citizens (4).

units.la: Hæc suspicione, hoc metu in animis imperantium ra- dicato, nihil fatis vel quietis amantissimis tutum su- perit. Hæc Tiberium. Hæc Neronem sævitiæ area exercuit. Inde Tigellino in aula Neroniana incremen- tum, rimando metus ejus, & suspectos regni cupidita- tis, aut nimiæ potentiæ, criminatione flagellando. Hanc aliquando effugeris, vitæ ad humilitatem tradu- ctione, opulentiæ quoque in fiscum delatione. quod securitatis munimentum Seneca, apud Neronem ten- tavit. cum opes meas ultrà fuffinere non possim, prafi- dium peto. Jube eas per procuratores tuos administrari, in tuam fortunam recipi. mox inflitæ prioris poten- tiæ commutat: prohibet cœtus salutantium : vitæ comitantes : rarus per urbem, quasi valetudine infen- fa, aut sapientiæ studio domi attineretur. xiv. Annal. Quanquam ne sic quidem metum ignavi Principis, & ultimam sævitiam effugit. Significanter de C. Graccho infrà Cornelius : nec tamen effugit magna fortuna pericula.
units.tr: When this suspicion and this fear have taken root in the minds of rulers, nothing is safe enough, not even for the most peaceable. This fear tormented Tiberius; this fear, Nero, as a field for his cruelty. Hence Tigellinus grew in influence at Nero's court, by searching out his fears and his suspected lust for the kingdom or excessive power, and by beating them with accusations. Sometimes one may escape this by reducing one's life to humility and by handing one's wealth over to the treasury. Seneca tried this as a bulwark of security with Nero: "Since I can no longer bear my wealth, I seek protection. Order that it be administered through your procurators and taken into your own fortune." Soon afterwards he changed his former power: he forbade gatherings of those greeting him and his life-long companions; he was rarely seen in the city, as if kept at home by poor health or by the study of wisdom. Annals 14. Yet even so he did not escape the fear of a cowardly prince and his final cruelty. Cornelius says significantly of Gaius Gracchus below: "Nor yet did great fortune escape dangers."

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Animus à luctu ad negotia avocan- dus.
units.tr: The mind must be turned from grief to business.

units.la: Luctu, & quacunque factura mœstitia, non afflicit, minùs humanum est; obrui, minùs virile. nec com- moda est, præter animi mollis pudorem, animi in tri- stitiam demerso, & anxius vellicantis cogitationis morsus. Quare de remedio ejus mali tum prisci eru- ditæ Græciæ philosophi, cum recentiores cultiorum nationum doctores cogitaverunt. Quorum argu- menta è libris Consolationum pete. Tiberius nihil intermisit rerum curæ, negotia pro solatiis accipiens, quia civium præces sociorum tractabat. Ergo remedium Tiberii, animi à luctu avocatio. quam & Stoicorum nonnulli, qui omnem mali sedem in opinione locarunt, instillaverunt. Sed cum animi cogitatio avocari, nisi ad aliud traducatur, aegrè possit, aliqua vaganti meta statuenda. Prisci sapientes in contemplatione rerum sublimium, aut virtutum suarum jucunda memoria, metam hanc fixerunt. Quæ ut hominę dignissima, ita non est quibusvis obvia. Celsiores Græcis Christiani, & inter eos nondum corrupti ignavia aut superstitione monachi, ad delictorum tristem memoriam, & ab hac ad placandum Deum confugerunt. Sublimis animi dictum est Thomæ à Kempis: in omnibus se quæsivisse requiem, sed nusquam invenisse, nisi in angello cum libello. Belgico idiomate sonat, <bl>in een hoecken met een boecken</bl>[?]. Alii longè diverso itinere, ad voluptates mergedum iis animum, ad ebriosam mali oblivionem, sevocant. Qui, præter turpitudinem vitæ inurendam, sæpè in tristiorem quam deflexerunt morsum, somno voluptatum excitati, incidunt, nec est omninò in hoc remedii genere animus terendus. Minus culpandi qui pro solatiis negotia arripiunt: aut bellica, ut Julius Agricola: modo non sæviendi libido, aut justitiæ inter arma oblivio, pro solatio subrepat: aut forensia: ut sunt Tiberio nostro Jus civium, & preces sociorum audiendæ. Hoc solatii campo, homo civili vitæ addictior, se gloriosè exercebit. Hic damnum nulli, spem afflictis, negotioso solatium præbebit. Quos non ingenii inclinatio, aut fortuna obsequentior, ad primam & secundam classem vocavit: voluptatum saltem scopulis vitatis, in hoc salo, portui vicino, se jactitent.
units.tr: Grief, and any sadness that brings it on, does not trouble a man, though it is less than human to be overwhelmed by it and less than manly. Nor is it of any good, except that it causes a soft shame in the mind, a mind sunk in sorrow, and an anxious gnawing of thought that plucks at it. So it was that the ancient philosophers of learned Greece, and later the teachers of the more cultivated nations, considered a remedy for this evil. Seek their arguments in the books of Consolations. Tiberius never let up on the care of affairs, taking business in place of comfort, because he handled the prayers of citizens and allies. So Tiberius's remedy was the diversion of the mind from grief, which some of the Stoics also recommended, who placed the whole seat of evil in opinion. But since the mind's thought can hardly be diverted unless it is led to something else, a goal must be set for the wandering mind. The ancient sages fixed this goal in the contemplation of sublime things, or in the pleasant memory of their own virtues. Since this is most worthy of a man, it is not open to just anyone. The Christians, loftier than the Greeks, and among them the monks, not yet corrupted by idleness or superstition, took refuge from the sad memory of their sins, and from this to appeasing God. The saying of Thomas à Kempis is of a lofty mind: he had sought rest in all things, but found it nowhere except in a little corner with a little book. In the Dutch idiom it sounds like "in a corner with a book" [?]. Others, by a very different road, lead the mind off into pleasures, into a drunken forgetting of evil. Besides the shame that such a life brands on a man, these often fall, once roused from the sleep of pleasures, into a bitterer gnawing than the one they turned away from, and in this kind of remedy the mind is by no means to be worn out. Less to be blamed are those who take up business as comfort: either warlike, as Julius Agricola did, provided that the lust for cruelty or forgetting of justice amid arms does not creep in as comfort; or legal business, as Tiberius had for his own part in the rights of citizens and the hearing of the prayers of allies. On this field of comfort a man more devoted to civic life will exercise himself with glory. Here he will bring harm to no one, and will offer comfort to the afflicted, hope to the troubled, and business to the idle. Those whom no bent of mind or more compliant fortune has called to the first and second class, let them at least, with the rocks of pleasure avoided, cast themselves into this sea, near the harbour.

units.la: XVI. Histrionia cum morum gravitate non bene copulatur.
units.tr: XVI. Stage-playing does not agree well with gravity of character.

units.la: Ludo & joco uti quidem illis licere, sed sicut somno, & quietibus cæteris, tum, cum gravibus seriisque rebus satisfecerimus: Cicero libro primo Officiorum commentatur. Inde licere quidem operam theatro dare, sed tempore gravibus negotiis vacuo, quis argumentetur. Sed nec eadem est ludi ac joci, quæ famni, & laborum remissionis, à natura præscriptio: & datur aliud jocandi & ludendi, præter conductitiam semper- feriantium hominum operam, genus. Novimus nec Socratem apud Athenienses, Catonem apud Romanos, nos,à spectaculis publicis abhoruiffe; Senecam etiam ad ejusmodi animorum, statis diebus, laxationem cò- hortatum. Sed non quicquid illi homines vita aut scri- pto probaverunt, nobis pro regula sequendum. Nec, fi ipsi blando naturæ stimulo illuc pellamur, jus & hos- neftum inde stabilimus. Quæ Tiberium rationes mo- verint, cur pellendos Italia histriones censeret, vide- mus. Multa abiis in publicum seditiosè, fœda per do- mos tentari. Distrahebatur in factiones populus, li- centia theatralis in rixas, clamores, manuum confer- tionem excrescebat. domus civium Romanorum, spurcitiæ morum, lascivia, stupris complebantur. Quæ. fi flagitia minus nostris moribus timenda sunt: saltem, turbas hominum licenter circumvagari, magno-sum- ptu alendorum, qui fictis fabulis, jocis, commeffatio- nibus vitam omnem terendo, pietati nuncium remit- tant, nunquam feria cum cultu Christianorum gratia, coalescit. Si quis ampliora à nobis de theatrorum hi- ftrionia lascivia, deprifco ejus apud Romanos usu & abusu, defiderat, Commentarium nostrum in primum Taciti librum consulat.
units.tr: It is indeed permitted to use play and jest, but as sleep and other kinds of rest are permitted, once we have attended to serious and weighty matters. Cicero makes this point in the first book of the Offices. From this, who would argue that one may attend the theatre at a time free from serious business? But the play and jest that nature prescribes are not the same as sleep and relief from labour, and there is another kind of jesting and playing, apart from the paid labour of idle men who are always on holiday. We know that Socrates among the Athenians and Cato among the Romans kept away from public spectacles, and Seneca urged that minds be relaxed in this way on set days. But we must not take as our rule everything those men approved in their life or writing. Nor, if we are driven there by the gentle goad of nature, do we thereby establish that it is right and honourable. We see what reasons moved Tiberius to judge that actors should be driven out of Italy. Many things were attempted from them in public in a seditious manner, and shameful things in private homes. The people were split into factions, and theatrical licence grew into brawls, shouting and hand-to-hand fighting. The homes of Roman citizens were filled with corruption of morals, wantonness and debauchery. Even if these disgraces are less to be feared in our morals, at least the wandering about of crowds of men, at great expense to feed them, who waste their whole lives on invented tales, jokes and buffoonery and so send away the message of piety, never fits with the grace of Christian worship. If anyone wants a fuller account of the stage-acting of the theatres, of its use and abuse among the Romans, let him consult our commentary on the first book of Tacitus.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Longa apud principes constantis amicitiae memoria.
units.tr: The long-standing memory of constant friendship among princes.

units.la: Tenacior quidem injuriarum, contemptus, negli- gentiæ memoria: quod in Archelao Cappadociæ re- ge, in Afinio Gallo, Pisone, aliis Tiberius docuerit. Sed nec diuturni obsequii, & tristium lætorum parti- cipationis, apud mediocris ingenii viros gratia vacil- lat. Lucillius Longus amici locum, ad mortis diem apud Tiberium tenuit, omnium illi tristium lætorum sociis, unusque è senatoribus Rhodii secessus comes. Quemadmodum autem multi apud reges speciem magis, quàm vim, amicitiæ postremò ferant; & nec ipsi semper speciei fidendum sit, alibi docuimus. Quid ex amicitia Tiberii commodi, quid gloriæ lucratus est Lucillius? quanquam novo homini, censorium funus, effigiem apud forum Augusti publica pecunia patres decrevere. More enim id patrum receptum fuit, ut ad favorem & odium principis pari nutu circumferrentur. Quod in re passim obvia docere, supervacanei operis foret.
units.tr: Indeed the memory of injuries, contempt and neglect is more tenacious, as Tiberius showed in the cases of Archelaus, king of Cappadocia, Asinius Gallus, Piso and others. But among men of moderate talent, the favour due to long service and to sharing sorrows and joys does not waver. Lucius Longus held the place of friend with Tiberius up to the day of his death, being the sharer of all his sorrows and joys, and the only one of the senators who accompanied him into retirement at Rhodes. But just as many men at courts generally put up with the appearance of friendship rather than its reality, and as we have shown elsewhere, one must not always trust appearances. What advantage or glory did Longus gain from Tiberius's friendship? Although for a new man, the fathers decreed a censor's funeral and a statue at the Forum of Augustus at public expense. For it was the established custom of the fathers that such honours were voted up or down with a single nod, according to the favour or hatred of the prince. To show this from a matter found everywhere would be a superfluous labour.

units.la: XVIII. Procuratori mandati officii limites non excedendi.
units.tr: XVIII. The procurator must not exceed the limits of his commission.

units.la: Procuratori a principe in provinciam missio, jus in servitia & pecunias familiares principis datur: jurisdictio & merum imperium non communicatur. Si quis hos fines egressus, arma, praesidia, forum judiciarium tractaverit: nomine se principis, cujus mandatis non sletit, tueri non potest. Ita Tiberius contra procuratorem suum, Lucillium Capitonem, pronunciavit: quod si vim praetorii[?] usurpasset, manibusque militum usus foret: spreta in eo mandata sua: audirent socios.
units.tr: A procurator sent by the prince into a province is given authority over the prince's slaves and private funds, but jurisdiction and the power of the sword are not shared with him. If anyone, going beyond these limits, takes up arms, garrisons and the judicial court, he cannot shelter himself under the name of the prince, whose commands he has not kept. So Tiberius pronounced against his procurator, Lucilius Capito: "But if he had usurped the power of the praetorium and made use of the soldiers' hands, his commands were spurned in that matter; let the allies be heard."

units.la: Nec procurator tantum, sed & magistratus provinciales, judices, praesides militiae, mandata principum sperneře intelliguntur, dum locis & collegiis immunitatem privilegio assecutis injuriam, quasi principis jura tuentes, inferunt. Quod ab iis caute observari velim, qui academiarum aedificiis, aut vivis membris, nullum non contumeliae genus inturunt: detrectando, jura imminuendo, manus in subjectos eorum immittendo, salaria curtando, quietem eorum perturbant.
units.tr: It is understood that not only procurators but also provincial magistrates, judges and commanders of the forces spurn the princes' commands when they inflict injury on places and colleges that have obtained immunity by privilege, as though they were defending the prince's rights. I would wish this to be carefully observed by those who inflict every kind of insult on the buildings of the universities or on their living members: by disparaging them, diminishing their rights, laying hands on their subjects, cutting short their salaries, and disturbing their quiet.

units.la: XIX. Multis pericula pro commendatione.
units.tr: XIX. Many dangers as a recommendation.

units.la: Detracta enim per commiserationem invidia, quod adest in forma, sermone, moribus gratiae, sinceris animis dijudicatur. Nero, è Germanici liberis, gratias avo & patribus, de Capitone justa sententia damnato,
units.tr: For when envy is removed by pity, the graces that are present in appearance, speech and manners are judged by sincere minds. Nero, one of the children of Germanicus, gave thanks to his grandfather and to the fathers for the just sentence by which Capito had been condemned.

units.la: agendo ; favorem quidem ex memoria parentis tulit; Sed quae erat in juvente modestia ac forma, principes viro digna, notis in eum Sejani odiis ob periculum gra- tiora. Sed & parenti ejus Germanico favorem popu- li,& post fata desiderium, non obscura in eum Tiberii & Augustae odia lenocinabantur. Hac fere de causa omnes in proelio occisos; aut gravi vulnere affectos; laude; integros, quamvis virtute non posteriores, vi- tuperio aut silentio, non raro & invidia, prosequimur. Quasi vero sagitta, ait Spartanus ille, strenuum virum ab ignavo seligeret. Hugoni Grotio ; viro inter erudi- tos minime postremo, magnum applausus popularis accessum carcer, periculosa evasio, foli mutatio, & in- exilio emerfio confecit. In hunc illud Ennii poetae di- &tum torseris:
units.tr: In giving thanks he gained favour from his father's memory. But the modesty and bearing in the young man, worthy of a prince, were more pleasing because of the marks of Sejanus' hatred against him, which put him in danger. Also, the people's goodwill towards his father Germanicus, and their longing for him after his death, together with the hatred of Tiberius and Augusta that was not hidden, fed the feeling against him. For this reason we commonly praise with commendation those who were killed in battle or grievously wounded, but blame or ignore the unhurt, though they were no less brave, and not rarely regard them with envy. As if, said that Spartan, an arrow would choose the brave man over the coward. For Hugo Grotius, by no means the least among the learned, great popular applause brought imprisonment, a dangerous escape, a change of climate, and an end to his exile. To him may be applied that saying of the poet Ennius:

units.la: Multi suam rem bene gessere & publicam
units.tr: Many have managed their own affairs well and the public's,

units.la: Patria procul: multi qui domi aetatem agerent.
units.tr: Far from the fatherland; many who spent their lives at home

units.la: Propterea sunt improbati.
units.tr: for that very reason have been disapproved.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Non omnia meliùs vidit antiquitas:
units.tr: Antiquity did not see everything better:

units.la: Ideo quaedam non optima ratione nitetia; vel obtoga- ta lege rollere; vel intermisso usu negligere, non est ho- neftis moribus adversum. Ficut Augufus quaedam ex horrida illa antiquitate ad prafentem usum flexisset; Exemplo est cofarreationis ritus: cujus oribiffa Tiberii aevo; aut inter paucos retenta, conjuetudo. De triplici matrimonii cotrahendi more; Usu, Farre, Coemptio- ne; Lipfius & Antiquarii, nec non legum interpretes; consulendi.
units.tr: Therefore it is not contrary to honest morals to abolish by law certain customs that rest on no very good reason, or to let them lapse once their use has ceased. Thus Augustus bent some things from that rough antiquity to present use. An example is the rite of confarreation, whose custom had fallen into oblivion in the age of Tiberius, or was kept up by only a few. On the threefold manner of contracting marriage, by use, by the spelt-cake, and by purchase, consult Lipsius and the antiquaries, as well as the interpreters of the laws.

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Parit & adulatio offensionem.
units.tr: Flattery also breeds offence.

units.la: Vel quod nimia, vel quod nimis aperta, vel quod in alteri offensos: Postremo lapsu Pontificees Romani; & eorum exemplo caeteri sacerdotes, impegerunt. cum pro incolumitate principis vota susciperent, Ne- ronem quoque & Drufum iisdem diis commendavere: non tam caritate juvenum, quam adulatione: qua meritus corruptis, perinde anceps, fi nulla, & ubi nimia est, §7. Boni illi viri, sacrorum quàm morum aulæ peritio-res, magnam à Tiberio gratiam se inituros arbitrabantur, vota pro juvenibus nuncupando; cum odium & increpationem principis incurrerent. Nam Tiberius haud nunquam domus Germanici mitis, tum verò aliquanti adolescentes sene&a sua impatienter indoluit. Nota è sacro codice Saulis offensio, ex honoribus in Davidem collatis, & votis in pontifice pro eo nuncupatis, officium in regem id esse arbitrato, quod genero tribueret. Sunt & qui filios ex se genitos secundo populi plausu efferri indignantur. De Philippi Macedonis in Demetrium filium animo, ob populi favorem iniquo, multis Livius libro 35. More quidem suo Tiberius iniquam iram sententia velat, ne quis mobiles adolescentium animos, præmaturis honoribus, ad superbiam extolleret, sed non tam de modestia illorum, quàm fastigii sui depressione, honore cum iis communicato, angebatur. Idem cum nimia in matrem Liviam senatus censeret, muliebri honore anxius, moderandos esse fœminarum honores, respondit. Et cum nonnemo senatorum, captandæ adulatione principis gratiæ, sententiam diceret, ut prætoriani milites in quatuordecim sederent; gravissimè commotus eum increpuit; quid illi cum militibus? statimque curia, mox Italia, adulatorinte mpestivus ejectus, erudite artem Gnathonicam tractandam esse, exemplo suo docuit. Multis amicitia Agrippinæ exitio fuit, inter quos C. Silio & Titio Sabino, incusante Sejano, diductam civitatem, ut civili bello esse qui se partium Agrippinæ vocent: ac ni resistatur, fore plures. neque aliud glis-centis discordiæ remedium, quàm si unus alterve maximè promti subverterentur. Sub Domitiano, Poetus Thrasea Aruleno Rustico, Priscus Helvidius Herennio Senecioni laudato, capitale fuit: neque in ipsos modò autores, sed in libros quoque eorum sævitum. in Vita Agricolæ. Lurorii Prisci, Germanicum defunctum carmine adulatorio celebrantis, calum tertio Annalium libro vidimus. Quot illustrium familiarum viros adulatio in Sejanum, ac ipso principe cultum. afflixerit, sequenti libro intuebimur. Quam nimiz, aut perlucentis, adulationis Tiberium tæduerit, mul-tis exemplis, jam anteà excussis, docemur. Unde lu-brica oratio, sub principe, qui libertatem publicam nollet, adulationem aspernaretur. Astuta L.Vitellii adulatio: qui à C. Caligula interrogatus, vidisset nefe cum dea (luna) congredi, terram quasi attonito vultu intuens: Solis, inquit, vobis diis licet invicem videre, narrat præter Suetonium Dio, lib.59.
units.tr: Either because it is excessive, or because it is too open, or because it is offensive to someone else. Finally the Roman pontiffs stumbled in this way, and the other priests followed their example. When they undertook vows for the safety of the prince, they also commended Nero and Drusus to the same gods. They did this less out of affection for the young men than out of flattery, which is equally hazardous when it is absent and when it is excessive. Those good men, more skilled in the ways of the court than in sacred matters, thought they would win great favour from Tiberius by offering vows for the young men, but they incurred the prince's hatred and rebuke. For Tiberius was not always gentle toward the house of Germanicus, and then indeed he was impatiently grieved by some of the young men, because of his own old age. We note from the sacred book the offence of Saul, who was angered by the honours heaped on David and by the vows the priest made for him. He judged it a duty owed to the king to give such honours to his own son-in-law. There are also those who are indignant when the sons they begot are extolled by the second applause of the people. Livy, in book 35, tells at length of Philip of Macedon's unjust feeling toward his son Demetrius, because of the people's favour. In his usual manner Tiberius veils his unjust anger with a pretext: lest anyone lift the fickle spirits of young men to pride with premature honours. But he was troubled not so much by their modesty as by the lowering of his own eminence, since honour was shared with them. When the senate proposed excessive honours for his mother Livia, Tiberius, anxious about the honour owed to women, replied that the honours of women must be moderated. And when one of the senators, seeking the prince's favour by flattery, proposed that the Praetorian soldiers should sit in the fourteenth row, Tiberius rebuked him very severely: what business had he with soldiers? At once the senator was ejected from the senate, and soon from Italy. By his own example, Tiberius taught that the art of the parasite must be practised with skill, and that a flatterer who comes at the wrong time is thrown out. Friendship with Agrippina was fatal to many, among them Gaius Silius and Titius Sabinus, with Sejanus as accuser: the state is divided, so that there are men who call themselves partisans of Agrippina, as in civil war; and unless this is resisted, there will be more. Nor is there any other remedy for the spreading discord than that one or two of the most eager be overthrown. Under Domitian, Paetus Thrasea and Arulenus Rusticus, and Priscus Helvidius, for praising Herennius Senecio, faced a capital charge. Cruelty was directed not only against the authors themselves but against their books as well. (See the Life of Agricola.) We saw in the third book of the Annals the fate of Lurius Priscus, who celebrated the dead Germanicus in a flattering poem. How many men of illustrious families were afflicted by the flattery paid to Sejanus, and to the prince himself, we shall see in the following book. How excessive or too transparent flattery wearied Tiberius is shown by many examples, already set out earlier. Hence a slippery speech is dangerous under a prince who did not want public liberty and scorned flattery. The clever flattery of Lucius Vitellius is well known: when Gaius Caligula asked him whether he had seen the goddess (the moon) lie with a man, he looked at the ground with a dazed face and said: "It is permitted for you gods to see one another in turn." Dio relates this, in book 59, besides Suetonius.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Beneficii accepti commemoratione reges erubescunt.
units.tr: Kings blush to recall the benefits they have received.

units.la: Præsertim fi tantum fit, quod exolvi levi gratiæ de-functione non possit. Nam obligari beneficio minoris est: devincire majoris. &, ut ait apud Salluftium Bocchum (?), flagitiosum. In C.Silium, quem Agrippinæ & Germanici amicitia præcipitem dederat, auctam Tiberii of-fenfionem plerique credebant linguæ intemperantia; non mansurum Tiberio imperium fuisse, fi legiones sibi commissæ in obsequio ejus non perstitissent. Destrui per hac [?] fortunam suam Cafar, imparemque tanto merito rebatur. Nam beneficia eò usque lata sunt, dum videntur exolvi posse: ubi multum antevenere, pro gratia odium redditur. Vera erant, quæ Antonius Primus jactabat, Sc Pannonicas legiones in arma egifle, suis stimulis excitos Moefiæ duces, sua constantia perruptas alpes, occupatam Italiam, interfepta Germanorum Rhætorumque auxilia, non fe nunciis, neque epistolis, sed manu & armis imperatori suo mili-tare. Sed cecidisse in irritum labores, fi præmia pericu-lorum foli assequantur, qui periculis non affuerint. 3. Hiftor. Sed quæ commemorandi meriti gratia? Unde paulatim levior viliorque haberi, manente tamen in speciem amicitia: 1Y. Hiftor. In promptu erat recens duarum in Pruffia civitatum: quarum altera prompte collum Suecorum regi præbuit, altera vires hosti & arma opposuit, quarum illa in gratiam recepta, culpam confessa placabiliorem regem habuit; ista ja-ctantius beneficium commemorando, offensam non vitavit. Sed nolo me recentium rerum arbitrum, præ-fertim facie rerum denuo mutata, interponere.
units.tr: Especially when the benefit is so great that it cannot be repaid by a slight discharge of gratitude. For to be obliged by a benefit is a lesser thing; to be bound fast by it is a greater. And, as Sallust says in the case of Bocchus (?), it is shameful. In the case of Gaius Silius, whom friendship with Agrippina and Germanicus had hurled headlong, most people believed that Tiberius's offence was increased by the intemperance of Silius's tongue. The empire would not have remained with Tiberius had the legions committed to him not persisted in obedience to him. Caesar thought his own fortune was being ruined by this, and that he was unequal to so great a service. For benefits extend only so far as they seem able to be repaid; when they far outrun that, gratitude is returned as hatred. What Antonius Primus boasted was true: the Pannonian legions had taken up arms, the generals of Moesia, roused by their own goads, had broken through the Alps by their steadfastness, Italy had been occupied, and the auxiliaries of the Germans and Rhaetians had been slain; and they had served their emperor not by messages or letters but by hand and arms. But labours come to nothing if only those who were absent from the dangers obtain the rewards of the dangers. (3. Histor.) But why should I recall merit? From this, he is gradually held lighter and cheaper, although the friendship remains in appearance. (IV. Histor.) There was at hand the recent case of two states in Prussia. One of them readily offered its neck to the king of the Swedes; the other opposed its strength and arms to the enemy. The former, received back into favour, confessed its fault and so had the king more placable. The latter, boasting too loudly of its benefit in recalling it, did not avoid offence. But I do not wish to set myself up as judge of recent events, especially since the face of affairs has been changed anew.

units.la: XXIII. Sævitiam juris velamento ornare, Tiberiani moris est.
units.tr: XXIII. To cloak cruelty under the veil of law is the custom of Tiberius.

units.la: Varro consul ad accusandum Silium, Sejano gratificaturus, se accingebat. Reus brevem moram, dum Varro consulatu abiret, petebat. Nam accusantis gravitas, & ex auctoritate momentum, reum desertum premeret. Petitioni Cæsar adversabatur: solitum quip-pe magistratibus, diem privatis dicere. nec infringendum consulis jus, cujus vigiliis[?] niteretur, ne quod resp. detrimentum caperet. Quasi vero aut salus imperii in morte innocentis civis verteretur, aut quicquam consularis potestas antiqui juris contineret. Proprium id Tiberio fuit, scelera nuper reperta priscis verbis obtegere. De mancipatis publico actori servis, ut liceret salvo senatusconsulto in caput domini quæstionem instituere; de compressa ad laqueum à lictore puella, ut supplicium de ea sumendi facultas esset; alio loco egimus & agemus.
units.tr: Consul Varro was preparing to accuse Silius, to gratify Sejanus. The defendant asked for a short delay, until Varro should have left the consulship. For the weight of an accuser and the influence of his office would crush a defendant left without support. Caesar opposed the request: it is customary, of course, for magistrates to appoint a day for private persons. Nor should the consul's right be infringed, since the safety of the state rests on his vigilance, lest the commonwealth suffer harm. As if the safety of the empire turned on the death of an innocent citizen, or the power of a consul contained anything of ancient law. This was peculiar to Tiberius: to cover recently devised crimes with old words. Concerning slaves handed over to the public prosecutor, so that an inquiry might be opened into the life of their master, the senatus consultum being saved; and concerning the girl forced into a noose by the lictor, so that there might be power to exact punishment from her: we have dealt with these elsewhere, and will do so again.

units.la: Quod ad accusatoris in agendo autoritatem timendam: lepidum est, quod Polyænus libro v. Strategematum recenset. Timoleon,inquit,oppugnabat Mylartum tyrannum, qui multos dolo circumvenerat, & neglecta juris jurandi religione trucidaverat. Tyrannus judicium apud Syracusanos se subiturum, si Timoleon non accusaret, profitebatur. Ille juravit, se non accusaturum. Hac conditione Milarcus Syracusas pervenit. Timoleon cum eum in concionem protra-xisset, nequaquam, inquit, eum accusabo: hoc enim pactus sum: verum interfici celerrime jubeo. Nam æquum est, cum qui multis imposuit, semel pari ratione circumveniri.
units.tr: As for fearing the accuser's authority in conducting a case, there is a witty story which Polyaenus records in book 5 of his Stratagems. Timoleon, he says, was attacking the tyrant Mylartus, who had deceived many by treachery and, disregarding the sanctity of an oath, had butchered them. The tyrant declared that he would submit to judgment before the Syracusans, provided Timoleon did not accuse him. Timoleon swore that he would not accuse him. On this condition Milarchus came to Syracuse. When Timoleon had dragged him before the assembly, "I will by no means accuse him," he said, "for that is what I agreed. But I order him to be killed very quickly. For it is only fair that one who has deceived many should be caught once in the same way."

units.la: XXIV.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: Artis est, interaffentationem & exâ- ctam justitiam clavum torquere.
units.tr: It is a skill to steer the helm between servile assent and strict justice.

units.la: Si enim portum tenere nequeas, in statione con- quiescere, quam frustrá cum ventis colluctari præstat. Talis sententiæ sub doloso principe moderator M.Le- pidus fuit. Hunc ego Lepidum, temporibus illis gravem & sapientem virum fuisse comperio. Gravem, adula- tione contemptá; sapientem, offensa principis vitata. Nam pleraque ab sævis adulationibus aliorum in men- tem [?]lius deflexit. Neque tamen temperamenti egebat, cum æquabili auctoritate & gratia apud Tiberium viguerit, auctoritatem illi adulationis fuga, gratiam sententiæ obliqua moderatio contraxit.
units.tr: For if you cannot hold the harbour, it is better to rest at anchor than to struggle in vain against the winds. Marcus Lepidus was a guide to this kind of judgment under a treacherous prince. I find that Lepidus was a grave and wise man in those times: grave, because he scorned flattery; wise, because he avoided offending the prince. For he turned his mind away from most of the cruel flatteries of others. Nor did he lack moderation, since he flourished with steady authority and favour with Tiberius. His authority came from avoiding flattery, and his favour from the indirect moderation of his opinions.

units.la: Lepido morum & fati consors L. Piso Pontifex adjungatur, qui, rarum in tanta claritudine, fato obiit? nullius servilis sententia sponte auctor, & quoties necef- sitas ingrueret, sapienter moderans. VI. Annal. At non necessitati temporum, pari temperamento, alter Piso cessit. Qui ambitum fori, corrupta judicia, sævitiam o- ratorum, accusationes minitantium, increpans, abiré fe & cedere urbe, victurum in aliquo abdito & longin- quo rure testabatur. Simul curiam relinquebat. 2. Annal. Et sané viro gravi, & virtutem splendoribus fori præferenti, satius in aliquo angulo delitescere, quam vocem, aut saltem præsentiam, corruptis judiciis præ- bere. Sed qui dignitates, qui securitatem ex principis gratia captandam, serenitati conscientiæ præferunt, medio saltem, quod aphorismus monuit, itinere inces- dent. Quod ne ipsum quidem semper & omnibus, versicolore sub principe, securum. Unde dubitare co- gor, fato & fortenafcendi, ut catera, ita principum in- clinatio in hos, offensio in illos: an fit aliquid in nostris consiliis, liceatque inter abruptam contumaciam, & deforme obsequium, pergere iter ambitione ac periculis vacuum. Nam quod de Agricola, Domitiani sævam dominationem vitante, autor scribit: Sciant, quibus moris illicita mirari, posse etiam sub malis principibus magnos
units.tr: Let L. Piso the Pontiff be joined to Lepidus as a companion in character and fate: rare amid such distinction, he died a natural death. He was never the author of any servile opinion of his own accord, and whenever necessity pressed, he wisely moderated himself. Annals VI. But another Piso, not with equal moderation, yielded to the necessity of the times. Complaining of the ambition of the forum, corrupt judgments, the cruelty of orators and accusers threatening, he declared that he would leave and withdraw from the city, and would live in some hidden and distant country estate. At the same time he quit the senate house. Annals II. And indeed, for a serious man who prefers the glory of virtue to the glitter of the forum, it is better to hide in some corner than to lend his voice, or at least his presence, to corrupt judgments. But those who prefer rank and security, to be won from the prince's favour, over a serene conscience, will at least walk, as the aphorism advises, the middle road. Yet even that road was not always safe for everyone under a many-coloured prince. Whence I am compelled to doubt whether, as with other things, so the leaning of princes toward some men and their offence toward others depends on fate and the fortune of birth; and whether there is anything in our plans, and whether it is permitted, between abrupt obstinacy and shameful servility, to pursue a path free of ambition and danger. For as the author writes of Agricola, who avoided the savage domination of Domitian: let those who are accustomed to marvel at what is forbidden know that great men can exist even under bad princes; and that obedience and moderation, if industry and vigour are present, win as much praise as those who, by an abrupt death, though without any later use, gained fame through ambition. That does not overturn the verdict. For Domitian is not cleared of all blame, though Agricola was removed by poison.

units.la: Lucrufta-mentum mor sus animi. magnos viros esse; obsequiumque ac modestiam, si industria ac vigor adsint, eo laudis excedere, quo plerique per abruptam, sed in nullum rei post usum, ambi-tiosa morte inclaruerunt: sententiam non evertit. Si-quidem Domitianus omni culpa, Agricolae veneno sublati, non purgatur.
units.tr: The profit of fortune, the character of the mind. Great men, that is; and obedience and moderation, if industry and vigour are present, win as much praise as those who, by an abrupt death, though without any later use, gained fame through ambition. That does not overturn the verdict. For Domitian is not cleared of all blame, though Agricola was removed by poison.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Culpa domesticorum provinciæ re-ctori præstanda.
units.tr: The fault of household members must be answered for by the governor of the province.

units.la: Nimirum si vel ingenium eorum perspectum habuerit, vel carere eorum opera in provinciæ administratione potuerit. Hoc spectans Messalinus Cotta censuit cavendum senatusconsulto, ut quanquam insontes magistratus, & culpa aliena nescii, provincialibus uxorum criminibus, perinde quam suis, plecteren-tur. Liberum enim illis erat, imo plausibile, sortiendo provinciam, uxorem domi relinquere. Idque Severus Cæcina approbante Taciti judicio censuerat, ne quem magistratum, cui provincia obvenisset, uxor comitaretur. Cui si cum Valerio Messalino objicias, sexum na-tura invalidum deseri, & exponi suo luxu, cupidinibus[?] alienis. vix præsenti custodia manere illæsa conjugia? quid fore si per plures annos in modum dissidii oblitterentur? Sic obviam irent ii, quæ alibi peccarentur, ut flagitiorum urbis meminissent. aderat in promptu remedium Romanis, dimissa uxore aliam ex animi sententia ducendi. Sin & amor conjugalis, & lex naturæ Romana consuetudine antiquior, hunc morem dissuaderet, beneficium excusationis, provinciam sortito, nemini denegabatur. Ita omnibus ad amussim vocatis, nihil iniqui sententia Cottæ promere videatur.
units.tr: Certainly, if he had come to know their character, or could not do without their help in administering the province. With this in view, Messalinus Cotta proposed that a senatus consultum be drawn up so that magistrates, though innocent and unaware of another's fault, should be punished for their wives' crimes in the provinces just as for their own. For it was open to them, indeed commendable, when drawing lots for a province, to leave their wives at home. Severus Caecina, with the approval of Tacitus's judgment, had proposed the same so that no magistrate to whom a province fell should be accompanied by his wife. If you object to this with Valerius Messalinus, that the female sex is weak by nature, and is abandoned and exposed to its own lust and to others' desires; that marriages can scarcely remain unharmed even under present guard; what would happen if for several years they were dissolved as by a separation? Thus they would meet in advance the things that were done elsewhere, as if mindful of the city's disgraces. There was at hand a remedy for the Romans: to dismiss the wife and take another as they pleased. But if both conjugal love and the law of nature, older than Roman custom, dissuaded this custom, the benefit of excuse was denied to no one who had drawn a province by lot. Thus, with everything brought to strict measure, nothing unfair seems to be pressed by Cotta's opinion.

units.la: XXVI.
units.tr: XXVI.

units.la: Raro aculeus offensi principis he-bescit.
units.tr: Rarely does the sting of an offended prince grow blunt.

units.la: Initium igitur ei cavendum, qui finem devitare cu-pit. Calpurnius Piso, quem abitum ab urbe minitatum, ob factiones accusatorum, corrupta ob judicia, diximus, id adjecit, laedendi Tiberii securus, ut spreta Augustae potentia, Urgulaniam e domo principis in jus exciret. Qua inpræsens Tiberius civiliter habuit. Sed in animo revolvente iras, etiamsi impetus offensio-nis languerat, memoria valebat. Victa igitur patientia, Pisonem secreti sermonis adversus majestatem habiti, aliorumque facinorum, incusatum inter reos, id est, more Tiberiano, damnandos, recepit. Quem sola mortis opportunitas judicio exemit. Non igitur verbis, non vultui, placati principis credendum. prin-cipis inprimis Tiberio similis, qui [illegible, ~6 letters] [illegible, ~5 letters] πεφυ-[illegible, ~6 letters] lutum sanguine maceratum: ut de eo magister ejus, inspecto ingenio, judicaverat.
units.tr: Therefore one who wishes to avoid the end must guard against the beginning. Calpurnius Piso, whom we said had threatened to leave the city because of the factions of accusers and judgments corrupted by bribery, added this, heedless of harming Tiberius: scorning the power of Augusta, he summoned Urgulania from the prince's house to court. Tiberius treated her courteously at the time. But as he turned his anger over in his mind, though the impulse of offence had faded, his memory remained strong. Patience overcome, he admitted Piso among the accused on charges of secret speech against majesty and other crimes, that is, to be condemned in the Tiberian manner. Death alone, at its opportune moment, removed him from judgment. Therefore one must not trust the words or face of a placated prince, especially one like Tiberius, who [illegible] ... was like clay steeped in blood, as his tutor had judged after inspecting his nature.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Multorum etiam inimicitiæ caveñ-dæ.
units.tr: The enmities of many must also be guarded against.

units.la: Et propter eas accusandi studium: quod odia-ho-minum, adversum rumorem, tandem vitæ periculum concinnat. Cassius Severus, sordida originis, malefica vitæ, sed orandi validus, per immodicas inimicitias, ut judicio juratisenatus Cretam amoveretur, effecerat. atque illic eadem actitando, recentia veteraque odia advertit: bonisque exutus, interdicto igni atque aqua, saxo Seriphio consenuit. Etiam qui judicandi frequen-tia oratoris atrocitate abutebantur, hominem e con-spectu Reipublicæ amovebant. Nec simplici tantum judicio, (sed juratisenatus: i. e. Senatu deum testem invocante, se censiturum, quod e fide sua reque publica videretur. Ulti[?] non male Lipsius e Livio, Appiano, Plinio, Xenophonte, Tacito ipso explicat. Quare in-ter alia conciliandæ hominum gratiæ præcepta, & hoc monitum Cicero, libro secundo officiorum, inculcat, accusandi frequentem usurpationem vitandam.
units.tr: Both for these reasons and because of the zeal for accusing, which by hatred of men, against public opinion, at last brings about danger to life. Cassius Severus, of base origin and wicked life but strong in pleading, through immoderate enmities brought it about that by a judgment of the senate, sworn in, he was removed to Crete. And there, by continuing the same practices, he drew upon himself both recent and old hatreds; stripped of his goods, banned from fire and water, he grew old on the Seriphian rock. Even those who abused the frequent judgments by the savagery of their oratory removed the man from the sight of the commonwealth. Nor was it by a simple judgment only, but by the senate sworn in, that is, with the senate calling God to witness that it would judge what seemed consistent with its faith and with the commonwealth. Lipsius explains this not badly from Livy, Appian, Pliny, Xenophon and Tacitus himself. Wherefore, among other precepts for winning men's favour, Cicero also inculcates this warning in the second book of De Officiis: that the frequent use of accusing must be avoided.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Veritas judici certis indiciis inda-ganda.
units.tr: Truth must be investigated by certain indications.

units.la: Sermo quidem index animi, & latentis veritatis character, à natura datus est. Sed quia sæpè character ille mendacio adulteratur, ad alia indicia sagaci judici recurrendum. Plautius Sylvanus prætor, incertis causis Aproniam conjugem in præceps jecerat. à propinquis Aproniæ in judicium tractus, turbata mente respondit, tanquam ipse somno gravi, atque eò ignarus, & uxor sponte mortem sumpsisset. Quid hic Tiberius? an neganti, & somnum fingenti crederet? an rem non judicatam relinqueret? minimè gentium. non enim boni judicis officium tantùm est ex auditu, & ut vulgo aiunt, ex actis & probatis, dijudicare. Certa rerum indagine veritas è latebris protrahenda, & ex obscuro in lucem proferenda. Non cunctanter Tiberius pergit in domum, visit cubiculum: in quo reluctantis & impulsæ vestigia cernebantur. Argutè facti indicium è signis & vestigiis sumebatur. De præcipitio constabat: de scelere mariti nondum constabat. non enim insolitum ea tempestate erat, aliquem sponte in mortem ruere. Scelus mariti vestigia reluctantis uxoris & impulsæ prodebant. Aliquis veneno interemptus creditur: suspicio in hæredem aut inimicum cadit. Corpus defuncti inspicitur, lividæ maculæ, aut siqua sunt alia veneficii signa, investigantur. Sic multis in judiciis, ubi sermoni confitentis aut diffitentis non creditur, à signis argumentamur. Creberrimè ab animi perturbationibus; gaudio, mœrore, metu, spe exultante, trepidatione, ira, commiseratione veritas eruitur. Astyanax, Hectoris occisi unicus, ad mortem Græcis, misso Ulysse, quærebatur. Negat mater Andromache, & se juramento obstringit inficiando, in vivis esse. Ulysses indicia veri aut falsi sermonis à gestibus, & proditis animi affectibus, venatur.
units.tr: Speech is indeed the index of the mind and the mark of hidden truth, given by nature. But because that mark is often adulterated by lying, the shrewd judge must have recourse to other indications. Plautius Silvanus, the praetor, having on uncertain grounds thrown his wife Apronia headlong, was dragged to trial by Apronia's relatives. In a disturbed state of mind he replied, as if he himself had been in deep sleep and so ignorant, that his wife had of her own accord taken her own death. What did Tiberius do here? Would he believe the denying man who feigned sleep? Or would he leave the matter unjudged? By no means. For it is not the duty of a good judge to decide merely from hearsay, and, as people commonly say, from the proceedings and approved evidence. By careful investigation of things, truth must be dragged out of its hiding places and brought from obscurity into the light. Without hesitation Tiberius goes into the house and visits the bedroom, in which traces of a struggling and pushed woman could be seen. The evidence of the deed was cleverly taken from signs and traces. The fall was certain; the husband's crime was not yet certain, for it was not unusual in that age for someone to rush to death of his own accord. The traces of a struggling and pushed wife revealed the husband's crime. When someone is thought to have been poisoned, suspicion falls on the heir or an enemy. The corpse is inspected, and livid spots or any other signs of poisoning are sought. So in many trials, where the speech of the confessing or denying party is not believed, we reason from signs. Very often the truth is drawn out from disturbances of the mind: from joy, grief, fear, hope exulting, trembling, anger, pity. Astyanax, the only son of the slain Hector, was sought by the Greeks for death, Ulysses having been sent. His mother Andromache denies it and binds herself by oath that he is alive. Ulysses hunts out the signs of true or false speech from gestures and from the betrayed emotions of the mind.

units.la: Scrutare matrem: mœret, illacrymat, gemit. Et huc & illuc anxios gressus refert, Missaque voces aure sollicita excipit. Magis hæc timet, quàm mœret.
units.tr: Examine the mother: she grieves, weeps, groans. And she moves anxious steps here and there, and with a troubled ear she catches the voices sent. She fears these things more than she grieves.

units.la: Troade Senecæ: Actu 3. Sc. 1. A metu matris, vivere puerum; quo defuncto mœrere magis debuit, aut ob supplicium evitatum lætari, colligit. A fuga post recentem eædem, à trepidatione, à lactebris, à confusis incerti vultus notis, nón raró judici ad veritatis cognitionem pervenitur. A somno, à cra-pula, ab exultatione, varie ad pervestigationem facti, prout illa sunt vera aut ficta, ducimur. Aliquos, quos constantia sermonis & vultus protexerat, repentinum gaudium protraxit. In has animi latentis, aut fe pro-dentis, notas judici, non perfunctorie sententiam latu-ro, est descendendum. A commiseratione, à mater-no affectu, magna cum hominum ea ætate simplicium, admiratione, Salomon addecifionem obscuri judicii pervenit. 1.Reg.3.v.24. Quo exemplo, ut omnium celeberrimo, quiesco.
units.tr: Seneca's Trojan Women, Act 3, Scene 1. From the mother's fear one gathers that the boy is alive; if he were dead she ought rather to grieve, or to rejoice at a punishment avoided. From flight after a recent ..., from trembling, from hiding places, from the confused marks of an uncertain face, the judge often arrives at knowledge of the truth. From sleep, from drunkenness, from exultation, we are led in various ways to the investigation of the deed, according as those things are true or feigned. Sudden joy has drawn out some whom constancy of speech and face had protected. Into these marks of a hidden mind, or of one betraying itself, the judge who is about to pronounce sentence must not descend perfunctorily. From pity and from maternal affection, to the great admiration of men who were so simple in that age, Solomon arrived at a decision in an obscure judgment: 1.Reg.3.v.24. With this example, as the most famous of all, I rest.

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: Nullus ante victoriam triumphus.
units.tr: No triumph before victory.

units.la: Romani quidem eò stoliditatis pervenerant, ut ma[?] nente bello, sæpè vix inchoato, triumphos, triumpha-lia insignia, statuas, arcus duci per vanitatem adulandi decernerent. Sed hæc, præter ludibrium inanis arro-gantiæ, rebus gerendis obfuere. Sæpè enim duces, ubi impetrando triumphalium insigni sufficere res suas crederant, hostem omittebant. Quod in Tacfarinate nondum debellato eò magis pudendum, quò minus justo bello, latrociniis tantùm, vagis & sparsis, provin-ciam Africam raptabat. Aut illibatus verè virtuti & felicitati honos est fervandus, aut communicatione indignis vulgata, non magni ab ea progressus exfpe-ctandi.
units.tr: The Romans had indeed reached such a pitch of foolishness that, while the war was still going on, and often barely begun, they voted triumphs, triumphal insignia, statues and arches to their generals out of vain flattery. But apart from being a mockery of empty arrogance, these things hindered the conduct of affairs. Often generals, once they believed their achievements were enough to win the triumphal insignia, let the enemy go. This was all the more shameful in the case of Tacfarinas, who had not yet been subdued and who, since there was no proper war, kept plundering the province of Africa with mere scattered and roving bands of brigands. Either the honour must be kept untouched for true virtue and good fortune, or, once it has been made common and bestowed on the unworthy, we should not expect great progress from it.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: Classicum belli non necessarii à for-tuna & moribus.
units.tr: The signal for a war not needed, from fortune and morals.

units.la: Fortuna quidem varie aut opulentia luxuriante, aut inopiâ ad bellum propellit. Mores animi inquietudi-ne, favitia, avidi tate Bellonæ obstetricantur. Ut quis fortuna inops, moribus turpibus, promptus ruebant, Nulla Nulla justitiae in armis capiendis mentio? Nulla, in mercenario quidem milite, aut ad rapinas confluente. Reges, & avidi bellorum duces, speciem aliquam juris unde mutuati, ne latrocinari praedonum more videantur, vexillo suo praefigunt. Sed si, quod res est, dicedum: nos veri juris, germanaque justitia solidam & expres-sam effigiem nullam tenemus : umbra & imaginibus utimur : easque ipsas utinam sequeremur. Cicero iii. offic.
units.tr: Fortune drives men to war in various ways: sometimes through luxuriant wealth, sometimes through poverty. The disposition of the mind, through restlessness, savagery and greed for Bellona, acts as midwife. Since men who are poor in fortune, base in character, and ready are rushing into war, where is any mention of justice in taking up arms? There is none, least of all among mercenary soldiers, who flock together for plunder. Kings and generals greedy for wars borrow some semblance of right and raise it as their banner, so that they may not seem to act as pirates do, like robbers. But if we must say what is the case: we hold no solid and express image of true right or genuine justice; we make use of shadows and likenesses, and would that we at least followed those very things. Cicero, On Duties, book 3.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Non est in multitudine hominum, aut inconsulta ferocia, belli victoria.
units.tr: Victory in war does not lie in the number of men or in reckless ferocity.

units.la: Alia sunt quae bellum motum profligant : densa vi- rorum acies, ordo & disciplina militaris, providum duc-cis consilium, arma & commeatus affluentes : & supra omnia virtus ac ardor militaris, ducum solertia gubernatus. Ab Romanis confertis pedes, disposita turma, cuncta praelio provisa : hostibus contra omnium nescius, non arma, non ordo, non consilium : sed pecorum modo trahi, occidi, capi.
units.tr: There are other things which bring a war to a successful end: a dense battle line of men, order and military discipline, the prudent counsel of the commander, weapons and abundant supplies, and above all courage and military ardour, steered by the skill of the generals. The Romans had their infantry in close ranks, their cavalry squadrons deployed, everything provided for the battle; the enemy, on the other hand, was ignorant of everything: no weapons, no order, no plan, but was dragged, slaughtered and captured like a herd of cattle.

units.la: Quantum autem peritia armorum, & vita usu castrorum trita, contra tirones & belli nescios, momenti adferat, non est multis docendum. Ædui duce Julio Sacroviro a Romanis defecerant : omnia illis, praeter belli peritiam, affatim aderant. Itaque victi prius, ita dixerim, quàm proelio concursum est. etenim propinquabat legionum acies, inconditique ac militia nescii oppidani, neque oculis neque auribus satis competebant. 3. Annal. Haec in militia campestri belli peritia plurimum valet : plusculum etiam in navali, qua sola freti Athenienses, quamvis magnam Spartanorum classem, in alto deprehensam, saepe spernebant. Ergo ut actionum civilium, ita belli quaedam praescripta ratio est. à quà temerè recedendo, ferocì hominum multitudinem parum profecceris.
units.tr: How much weight skill in arms and a life hardened by camp experience carry against raw recruits who know nothing of war, there is no need to teach to many. The Aedui, under the leader Julius Sacrovir, had revolted from the Romans; they had everything in abundance except skill in war. And so they were beaten, so to speak, before the battle was joined. For the battle line of the legions was approaching, and the townsmen, untrained and ignorant of soldiering, could not keep up with it either with their eyes or with their ears. Tacitus, Annals, book 3. In the field, skill in war counts for very much in this kind of soldiering, and somewhat more still at sea, the sea on which alone the Athenians relied, and often despised the great fleet of the Spartans when it was caught on the open sea. Therefore, just as there is a fixed method for civil affairs, so too there is a set method of war, and if one departs from it rashly, one will gain little from the fierce multitude of men.

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: In factis, non in laureatis statuis, mansura gloria.
units.tr: Glory that will last rests on deeds, not on laurelled statues.

units.la: Possunt enim hæ & indignis conferri, & meritis ne- gari. Blæso ob affinitatem Sejani triumphalia Tibe- rius largitus, Dolabellæ qui bellum inexplicabile con- fecerat, petenti negavit. Sed neque Blæsus ideo illu- strior, & huic negatus honor gloriam intendit. Confer quæ de Capitone Ateio, & Labeone Antistio, tertio Annalium libro memorata sunt. Illi, quod præturam intra stetit, commendatio ex injuria: huic, quod con- sulatum adeptus est, odium ex invidia oriebatur. Si lubet, adde quæ de liberatoribus patriæ, quamvis eventu infelicibus, eundem Annalium librum obsi- gnant: Sed præfulgebant Cassius atque Brutus, eo ipso quòd effigies eorum non visebantur.
units.tr: For such honours may be conferred on the unworthy and withheld from the deserving. Tiberius, out of regard for his kinship with Sejanus, granted triumphal honours to Blaesus, but refused them to Dolabella, who had brought to an end a war that was hard to resolve, when he asked for them. Yet Blaesus did not become more famous for this, and the honour denied to Dolabella did not diminish his glory. Compare what is recorded in the third book of the Annals about Capito Ateius and Labeo Antistius. The former's commendation arose from injustice, because he stopped short of the praetorship; the latter's hatred arose from envy, because he obtained the consulship. If you wish, add what the same book of the Annals records about the liberators of their country, though unfortunate in the outcome: "Yet Cassius and Brutus stood out all the more because their images were not to be seen."

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Sociorum laboris non est confecto bello obliviscendum.
units.tr: The labour of allies must not be forgotten when the war is over.

units.la: Primùm ipsa naturæ humanæ dignitas eò impellit, ut non ingrati erga benè meritos reperiamur; & ne adversarum rerum socios, participatione fecundarum, excludamus. Deinde socios ea humanitate in officio, & pari amici animi affectione retinemus. Romanis id, quoties antiquo more agebant, non intermissum. In mediocri societatis studio, repetitum ex vetesto mos, missusque senatoribus, qui Scipionem eburnum, togam pictam, antiqua patrum munera daret, regemque & socium atque amicum appellaret. Ardentiori belli jun- gendi opera, socios reges & populos, urbium, agro- rum, regnorum accessu augebant. Sic quondam Rho- dios, Eumenem ac Attalum, Mafanissam, fide eorum bellicis laboribus perspecta, è mediocri aut dubia po- tentia ad ampliorem evexerunt. Nec eos grati in a- micos animi, vel nominis auctæ claritudine, vel incre- mento imperio prolato, poenituit.
units.tr: First, the very dignity of human nature drives us not to be found ungrateful towards those who have deserved well of us, and not to shut out from the fruits of success those who shared our hardships. Second, by such kindness we keep our allies in their duty and bound by the same affection of friendship. The Romans did this whenever they acted in the old manner, and it was never discontinued. In the ordinary cultivation of fellowship, the custom was renewed from ancient times: senators were sent to give Scipio an ivory chair, a painted toga, and the ancient gifts of the fathers, and to call him king, ally and friend. In the more eager work of forming alliances, they increased their allies by adding kings and peoples, cities, lands and kingdoms. Thus they once raised the Rhodians, Eumenes and Attalus, and Masinissa, whose loyalty had been proven in warlike labours, from a middling or doubtful power to a greater one. Nor did they ever regret their grateful feeling towards their friends, whether from the increased fame of their name or from the enlargement of their empire.

units.la: XXXIV.
units.tr: XXXIV.

units.la: Magna fortunæ in omnem partem potentia.
units.tr: The great power of fortune in every direction.

units.la: Sine aliquid præter inane nomen fortuna, nunc non inquiro. Satis est, quædam casu, quam provisò hominum consilio, facilius expediri. Mota per Italiam servilis belli feminafors oppressit. Multa in omni historia monumenta sunt, tumultuum fortuito exortorum, fortuito compressorum; multa fortuiti incrementi aut decrementi exempla. Unde occasionem Macchiavellus sumpsit, discurso in Livium, quæstionem movendi, Plúsne fortuna, an virtus, ad amplitudinem Romani imperii contulerit.
units.tr: Whether fortune is anything more than an empty name, I do not now inquire. It is enough that some things are settled more easily by chance than by human plan foreseen. A servile war stirred up across Italy was crushed by a woman, by chance. Every history contains many records of disturbances that arose by chance and were put down by chance, and many examples of growth or decline that came by chance. From these Machiavelli took his occasion, in his Discourses on Livy, to raise the question whether fortune or virtue contributed more to the greatness of the Roman empire.

units.la: XXXV.
units.tr: XXXV.

units.la: Servitiorum crescens numerus ingenuo civi formidandus.
units.tr: The growing number of slaves is a danger to the free citizen.

units.la: Cum sæpè alias Romana civitas aut in periculo, aut in metu periculi, ob conjurationem servilem, fuit; tum sub Tiberio, servili tumultu per Italiam coorto, trepidavit, ob multitudinem familiarum, quæ glisceabat immensum, minore in dies plebe ingenua. Quoties, quot civitatibus, periculum a servorum adortu extremum imminuerit, docere; non capit hujus chartæ angustia. Quantum privata clade heris mācipia nocere queant, Liv aphorismo libri secundi Annalium monuimus.
units.tr: Although the Roman state was often in danger, or in fear of danger, because of a conspiracy of slaves, yet under Tiberius, when a servile uprising broke out across Italy, it trembled on account of the multitude of households, which grew immensely, while the free plebs diminished day by day. To show how often, and in how many cities, the danger from an attack by slaves has brought things to the brink would take more room than this page allows. How much harm slaves can do to their masters through a private disaster, we have noted in the aphorism of Livy's second book of the Annals.

units.la: XXXVI.
units.tr: XXXVI.

units.la: Extremum miseriarum forensium, patris a filio accusatio.
units.tr: The utmost of forensic miseries: a son's accusation of his father.

units.la: Corrupti erant servi in dominos, uxores in maritos: id restabat, ut & filii coram præclaro imperatore contra parentes perorarent. Præparatur adolescens multis munditiis, alacri vultu. nimirum quia sævo principi gratas ejusmodi delationes esse noverat, præmium non dubio animo captabat. deferebat enim in judicium, structas principi insidias.
