Quod falsum fuisse indicium, testium defectus, rei constantia, causæ ob actore implicatio, adversa accusatori è servis quæstio convinceret. Sed ponamus, patrem non insontem criminis fuisse. Num excusanda, num laudanda filii in patrem accusatio? Similem quæstionem movet, & paucis verbis nervose decidit, Cicero 3. offic. Quid si pater fana expilet, cuniculos agat ad erarium, indicet ne id magistratibus filius? nefas id quidem est; quis etiam defendat patrem, si arguatur. Non igitur patria praeflat omnibus officiis? immo vero: sed ipsi patria conducit, pios habere cives in parentes. Haec quidem contra filium accusatorem: sed quae sequuntur, pro eo facere videntur. Quid? si tyrannidem occupare, si patriam prodere conabitur pater, silebitne filius? immo vero obsecrabit patrem, ne id faciat: si nihil proficiet, accusabit, minabitur etiam: ad extremum, si ad perniciem patriae res spectabit, patria salutem anteponet, salutis patriae. Quod de patria antiqui, id de principe, in quem transierit maiestatis in eo caesu violatio, recentiores celebrant. Tum quia principis caedes ad perniciem patriae spectare videtur, quandoquidem non postea fine publica ruina princeps convelli: recte delatio ad magistratus a filio fieri censebitur.
units.tr: Slaves had been corrupted against their masters, and wives against their husbands. What remained was for sons also to plead against their parents before a distinguished emperor. The young man is prepared with much finery and a cheerful face. Clearly he knew that accusations of this kind were welcome to a savage prince, so he sought the reward without hesitation. He brought the matter into court, laying traps for the prince. That the information was false could be shown by the lack of witnesses, the steadfastness of the accused, the entanglement of the accuser's own case, and the examination of the accuser's slaves, which went against him. But let us suppose the father was not innocent of the crime. Is the son's accusation of his father to be excused, or to be praised? Cicero raises a similar question and settles it briefly and forcefully in book 3 of his De officiis: What if a father were to plunder temples, or dig tunnels to the treasury; would a son be wrong to report it to the magistrates? That would indeed be wrong; who would even defend the father if he were accused? Does not the fatherland then take precedence over all duties? Indeed it does; but it is also in the fatherland's interest to have citizens who are dutiful to their parents. So much for a son who accuses. But what follows seems to point the other way. What if a father should try to seize tyranny, or to betray his country? Would the son keep silent? Indeed he would not; he would beg his father not to do it; if that achieved nothing, he would accuse him, and even threaten him; and in the end, if the matter concerned the destruction of the fatherland, he would place the safety of the fatherland before the safety of his father. What the ancients said of the fatherland, more recent writers apply to the prince, against whom the violation of majesty is committed in an assassination. Since the killing of a prince seems to aim at the ruin of the fatherland, since the state cannot be torn from its prince without public ruin, a report made to the magistrates by a son will rightly be judged lawful.

units.la: Anceps est ob temporum nostrorum statum, & ob Jctorum autoritatem, decisio. Ex mente vero Ciceronis non idem esse, patriae ac Tiberio insidias struere, nemo non videt. Si enim illi Julius Caesar jure caesus videtur, multo minus Tiberium haeredem Caesarum, animi vero magnitudine inferiorem, defendendum fuisse. Nec est, quod Ciceronem, & illam libertatis dulcedinem contra filium indicem eundem & ceftem, adducamus. Ipso servientium civium judicio, & animi scelus convincentis terrore, non absolvitur. Fcelere vetoes, finul vulgi rumore territus, robur & saxum, aut parricidarum poenas minitantium, cessit urbes.
units.tr: The decision is doubtful, both because of the condition of our times and because of the authority of the jurists. Yet, according to Cicero's mind, that plotting against the fatherland and plotting against Tiberius are not the same thing, everyone can see. For if Julius Caesar seems to have been justly killed, much less should Tiberius, the heir of the Caesars but inferior in greatness of spirit, have been defended. Nor should we bring forward Cicero, and that sweetness of liberty, against a son who was both informer and witness. Not even by the judgment of enslaved citizens, nor by the terror of a man convicted of wickedness, is he absolved. Though forbidden the crime, and at once frightened by the rumour of the crowd, he yielded, a man of oak and stone, though threatened with the punishments of parricides.

units.la: Quinipfe Tiberius, ut invidiam atrocis judicii, retra&to ad executionem actionis juvene, leniret, sæviori sententiæ intercessit. Nam cum alii more majorum puniendum, alii Gyaro aut Donufa infula claudendum censerent, dandos vita usus cui vita concederetur, profatus, Amorgum deportandum curavit. Haec tragoedia a filio accusati patris, nec ob id ad extremum laeti filii, cataftrophe. Sitne pietatis, ob domesticam injuriam opinionem patrem a filio in jus vocari, alii meditationi integrum reiervo.
units.tr: Indeed Tiberius himself, in order to soften the odium of the atrocious trial, when the young man had been drawn back from carrying out the action, interposed a sentence that was harsher still. For when some advised that he be punished in the manner of the ancestors, and others that he be shut up on the island of Gyaros or Donusa, he declared that life should be given for use to the one to whom life had been granted, and he arranged for him to be deported to Amorgos. This tragedy, with the son accusing his father, ended in a catastrophe that brought no joy to the son in the end. Whether it is a dutiful act for a son to summon his father to court on account of a private wrong, I leave for further reflection.

units.la: Delator
units.tr: The informer

units.la: XXXVII. Delatores publice & privatim invisi.
units.tr: XXXVII. Informers, hated both publicly and privately.

units.la: Est aliqua medii generis, ut non sine crimine, ita sine publica ignominia, delatio, vel potius obtrectatio. de qua Athenagoras Syracusarum praetor: Διαβολὰς ἐφ᾽ ᾧ σωφρονῶν τὴν λέγειν πνὰς εἰς ἀλλήλους, ἐπὶ τὰς ἀκροάσεις, ἐπιδέχεσθαι [?]. Obtrectationes alios aliis dicere, vel audientes admittere, non est moderati ingenii. apud Thucydidem libro sexto Hist. Alia est, quae in judicio, vel auribus principis irrependo, pernicie civibus strumenda pascitur. Haec Tiberiano aevo, vel tabe fori, vel lucri aviditate, immensum excreverat. Cui indies proserpenti ut limes figeretur, in senatu actum de praemiis accusatorum abolendis, si quis majestatis postulatus, ante perfectum judicium se ipse vita privavisset. Quod genus absolutionis quia frequens iis temporibus erat, imminuta lucri spe, accusatorum fervor mi-nuendus videbatur. Nec plane novitatis insimulanda ea patrum sententia erat: siquidem receptum jam erat, ut si quis de se ipso statuisset, in fiscum bona ejus non reciperentur. Igitur in eam sententiam ibatur, ni Caesar contra, Irritas leges, Remp. in praecipiti conque-stus effet. subverterent potius jura, quam custodes eorum amoverent. Honesto custodum juris encomio ornantur, qui non obscuro hominum rumore vapulabant. Et quos publica gentium infamia notabat, sine iis Resp. in praecipiti esse principis voce praedicabatur. Sic delatores, genus hominum publico exitio repertum, & poenis quidem nunquam satis coercitum, per praemia elicitabantur. Cui Taciti, de exstimatione delatorum, suffragio plurimi autores subscribunt. Nec publico tantum, sed & principum aliquando, & tandem suo, exitio aluntur. Edoardus II. Albionis rex, cum delatorum instigatione 25 è proceribus regni supplicio dedisset, conjugemque cum filio solum vertere coegisset; cardine rerum converso regno nudatus, delatores vero exquisitissimis cruciatibus laceratis supplicis affecti sunt. Plura sunt in eo, nec non vicina. Galliarum, plura in Asiatico regno exempla: quæ bre- vitatis studio non scrutor.
units.tr: There is a kind of informing, or rather slander, of a middling sort, which carries no public disgrace though it is not without fault. Of it Athenagoras, praetor of Syracuse, said: To speak slanders against one another, and to admit them to the hearing, is not the mark of a prudent man [Διαβολὰς ἐφ᾽ ᾧ σωφρονῶν τὴν λέγειν πνὰς εἰς ἀλλήλους, ἐπὶ τὰς ἀκροάσεις, ἐπιδέχεσθαι [?]]. To tell one another's disparagements, or to lend an ear to them, is not the mark of a moderate character. See Thucydides, book six of the History. There is another kind of informing, which is nourished for the ruin of citizens, creeping into the courts or into the ear of the prince. In the age of Tiberius this grew immensely, through the corruption of the forum or the greed for gain. To set a limit to it as it crept forward day by day, a motion was brought in the senate concerning the abolition of the rewards for accusers, if anyone who had been charged with treason had taken his own life before the trial was completed. Because this kind of escape was frequent in those times, the zeal of the accusers seemed to need checking by reducing the hope of gain. Nor can that opinion of the fathers be charged with being wholly novel: indeed it was already established that if someone had decided upon his own death, his goods would not pass to the treasury. So the senate was inclined toward that opinion, had not Caesar objected: the laws would be void and the state would be in peril; they would overturn the rights rather than remove their guardians. The guardians of the law are honoured with a worthy praise, though they were being beaten by no faint rumour of men. And those whom public infamy among the nations marked, the emperor's voice declared that without them the state would be in peril. Thus informers, a class of men devised for public destruction, and never sufficiently restrained by punishments, were drawn out by rewards. To this opinion of Tacitus on the reputation of informers most authors subscribe. They are fed not only to the public's destruction, but sometimes to that of princes, and at last to their own. Edward II, king of Albion, when at the instigation of informers he had handed over to execution twenty-five of the nobles of the realm, and forced his wife and son to go into exile, the pivot of affairs turned, and the kingdom was stripped of him; but the informers were torn with the most exquisite tortures and put to death. There are many examples of this, and also nearby: in France, and many in the Asiatic kingdom; these, for the sake of brevity, I do not search out.

units.la: Nulli ne ergo principi (peculatores, delatores, accu- satores fovendi? Temporum necessitas, ut multa ad quæ connivendum, ita & eahominum portenta alii-quando admittit. Quibus quatenus aures præben- dæ, Mæcenas Augustum, 52 libro Dionis, edocet.
units.tr: Should no prince, then, cherish embezzlers, informers and accusers? The necessity of the times, as it requires that many things be tolerated, so also at times admits these monsters of men. How far ears should be lent to them, Maecenas teaches Augustus in book 52 of Dio.

units.la: [illegible, ~120 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: Non omnia statim quæ ab his referun- tur, credenda: sed diligens adhibenda consideratio est.
units.tr: Not everything that is reported by these men is to be believed at once; a careful consideration must be applied.

units.la: Permultienim velodio aliorum, vel facultatum eo- rum appetentia, velin aliorum gratiam, vel irati ob- postulatam ab aliis, ac non acceptam, pecuniam; eos novarum rerum crimine, aut alicujus contra impera- torem absurde concepti aut dicti facinoris, evertunt. Ideo non temere animus iis est advertendus, sed o- mnia accurate indaganda. Quæ indagatio quibus artibus apte fieri possit, nos in Arcanis regnorum re- clusimus.
units.tr: For very many, either from hatred of others, or from a desire for their property, or to win the favour of others, or angry because money demanded from others was not received, overthrow them with the charge of revolutionary plans, or of some crime absurdly conceived or spoken against the emperor. Therefore one should not give them a hasty hearing, but investigate everything carefully. By what arts such an investigation can be aptly made, we have unlocked in the Secrets of Kingdoms.

units.la: XXXVIII.
units.tr: XXXVIII.

units.la: De suo clementia, non dealieno largitur.
units.tr: Of his own, he gives clemency; not of another's.

units.la: Quemadmodum liberalitas non est, quæ fundum alienum exhaurit; ita clementiæ nomen non mere- tur, quæ aliorum injuriis condonandis largum finum effundit. Tiberius in suo dolore largæ, in alieno astri- ctæ lenitudinis exempla, multis sævitiæ exemplis in- terlucentia, præbuit. 1. C. Cominium equitem Romanum probrosi in fe carminis convictum, Cafar precibus fratris qui senator erat, concessit. Errant qui delicta in principem commissa venia aboleri posse, ne fide qui- dem publica interposita, negant. Aliud Tiberius, aliud depredeprecator, aliud senatus indulgentia laetatus judicavit. 2. P. Suilium quaestorem quondam Germanici, cum Italia arceretur, convictus pecuniam ob remjudicandam accepisse, amovendum in insulam censuit, tanta contentione animi, ut & jurejurando obstringeret, è Rep. id esse. Hic locum habeat illud Davidis: Singulis matutinis exscindam omnes improbos terrae, ad rescindendum a civitate Jehovae omnes qui operam dant iniquitati. Psalmo apud Hebraeos c.1. ubi non lenitudine in delinquentes, sed poenae severitate officium regium celebrat.
units.tr: As liberality is not liberality when it drains another's estate, so the name of clemency is not deserved by one who pours out a lavish largesse by forgiving the injuries of others. Tiberius, in his own grief, showed examples of generous mildness, shining through many examples of cruelty. 1. Caesar granted to Gaius Cominius, a Roman knight convicted of a shameful poem against himself, the prayers of his brother, who was a senator. Those who deny that offences committed against the prince can be cancelled by pardon, even without public faith being pledged, are mistaken. Tiberius judged one thing, the suppliant another, the senate another, rejoicing in its indulgence. 2. Publius Suilius, once quaestor of Germanicus, when he was banished from Italy, having been convicted of accepting money for a judicial decision, Tiberius thought should be removed to an island, with such intensity of mind that he also bound himself by oath that this was for the good of the state. Here let that saying of David have its place: Every morning I will destroy all the wicked of the land, to cut off from the city of Jehovah all who work iniquity. Psalm 101 [101] among the Hebrews, where the royal office is performed not by gentleness toward offenders but by the severity of punishment.

units.la: XXXIX.
units.tr: XXXIX.

units.la: Severitas indulgentia salubrior.
units.tr: Severity is more wholesome than indulgence.

units.la: Sibi enim probro, aliis ad peccandum incitamento, bonis terrori vivunt, qui connivente ad facinora judicio impune dimittuntur. Suilium, quod pecuniam ob rem judicandam acceperat, (quod leve crimen hodie habebatur) in insulam Tiberius amoverat. Quod aspere acceptum ad praesens, mox in laudem vertit, regresso Suilio: quem vidit sequens atas prapotentem, venalem, & Claudii principis amicitia diu prosperè, nunquam bene usum.
units.tr: For they live as a disgrace to themselves, an incitement to others to sin, and a terror to the good, who are dismissed unpunished when judgment is winked at for their crimes. Tiberius had sent Suilius to an island because he had accepted money for a judicial decision (a slight crime, as it was then regarded). This was harshly received at the time, but soon turned to praise when Suilius returned; the following age saw him as overbearing, venal, and one who, though he enjoyed the friendship of the emperor Claudius for a long time with success, never used it well.

units.la: XL.
units.tr: XL.

units.la: Minus florida forensium negotiorum quam historiae bellicae conscriptio.
units.tr: Less florid than the writing of forensic affairs is the writing of military history.

units.la: Quod de labore suo Tacitus agnoscit. nemo Annales nostros cum scriptura eorum contenderit, qui veteres populi Romani res composuere. Inter quos principem locum T. Livius obtinet, ad cujus lectionem facile tum antiquitatis cognitio, tum varietates rerum bellicarum alliciunt. Nobis in arto & inglorius labor, nec tamen vitae humanae inutilis. Rerum enim bellicarum monumenta ut plus oblectationis pariunt: ita parum ad vitae civilis prudentiam momenti adferunt.
units.tr: Tacitus acknowledges this about his own labour: "No one will compare our Annals with the writings of those who in earlier times recorded the affairs of the Roman people." Among these, Titus Livy holds the chief place, and reading him easily attracts one both to knowledge of antiquity and to the variety of military events. "Our labour is narrow and without glory," yet it is not useless for human life. For just as the records of military affairs give more delight, so they contribute little weight to the prudence of civil life.

units.la: Nec semper aut omnibus bella gerenda, exercitus regendi: at semper in publica & privata vita norma recte, ne in erraticos fluctus abripiamur, utendum. Ad quam non omnes nuda exemplorum ratio, plurës alienorum eventuum informatio deducit.
units.tr: Wars are not always, nor for everyone, to be waged, nor armies to be commanded; but in public and private life one must always use a rule of right conduct, so that we are not swept away into aimless waves. To this rule a bare account of examples does not lead everyone; rather, a fuller acquaintance with the fortunes of others does.

units.la: XLI. Noscenda imperantium natura.
units.tr: XLI. The nature of rulers must be known.

units.la: Nihil magis in ore est omnium, qui aliquid de Politica doctrina deguftarunt, quam tres esse imperii formas : Monarchiam, Ariftocratiam, Democratiam; Quod Tacitus his verbis pronunciat: Cunctas nationes urbes populus, aut primores, aut singuli regunt; Quod ad temperatam ex his omnibus, quam Mixtam vulgo nuncupant, eam diserte autor tollit. dilecta ex his et constituta Reip. forma laudari facilius, quàm evenire, vel fi evenit, haud diuturna esse potest.
units.tr: Nothing is more often on the lips of anyone who has tasted political doctrine than that there are three forms of government: monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy. Tacitus states this in these words: all nations and cities are ruled by the people, or by the nobles, or by single men. The same author expressly sets aside the temperate form made from all of these, which is commonly called mixed. A commonwealth chosen and established from these forms is more easily praised than realised, and even if it is realised, it cannot last long.

units.la: Verùm quid inde ad vitam civilem commodi? quid generalia Politicorum præcepta terentibus emolumenti restat? Nostra in usu versatur, & in fructus perceptione commentatio. Igitur ut olim plebe valida, vel cum patres pollerent, nostenda vulgi natura, quibus temperanter haberetur, senatusque & optima-tium ingenia qui maxime perdiderant, callidi temporum & sapientes credebantur: sic converso statu, neque alia re Rom. quàm si unus imperitet, hac conquiri tradique in rem fuerit. Minimè otiosa indagatio est, qua imperii forma populus quis gubernetur: fi non in ea contemplatione, qui mos est vulgariter erudito-rum, substiteris. Cognito imperii statu, & perceptâ imperantium natura; vir sapie is ad tempora & ad mores, nullo honestatis dispendio, fe applicat. In Demo-cratia, five Ariftotelica phrafi Politeia, populum regum dominium agnoscens, ad ejus nutum fe conver-tet. In paucorum moderata potentia, paucos magis quam universos colet. Read unum delata, unum in oculis, animo, cultu gerét; & ab offendendis, qui lateri ejus proximi sunt, abstiset. Cætera usus fori; curiæ aulæ expediet.
units.tr: But what advantage does this bring to civil life? What benefit remains for those who wear themselves out with the general precepts of the political writers? Our discussion is concerned with practice and with gathering its fruit. So, as formerly, when the plebs was strong, or when the fathers held power, knowing the nature of the common people, by which one might be treated with moderation, and the character of the senate and of the best men, especially of those who had lost the most, was thought to be the mark of the shrewd and wise who understood the times. In the same way, now that the state has changed and Rome is ruled by no one but a single man, these things must be sought out and handed down as useful. The inquiry into the form of government under which a people is ruled is by no means idle, provided you do not stop at that mere contemplation which is the habit of learned men in general. Once the state of government is known and the nature of the rulers perceived, the wise man adapts himself to the times and the manners of the age, with no loss of honour. In a democracy, or in Aristotle's term polity, acknowledging the people as lord of the kings, he turns himself to their nod. Under the moderate power of a few, he courts the few rather than the many. Where rule is handed to one man, he keeps that one before his eyes, in his mind and in his attentions, and he refrains from offending those who stand nearest to his side. The rest the practice of the forum and of the court will settle.

units.la: XLII. Inamoena Annalium Taciti tritura. Gaufas,
units.tr: XLII. The Tedious Grinding of Tacitus's Annals.

units.la: Causas, quae nos in prima juventute a lectione Taciti, praeter stylum minus florentem, abstulerunt, auctor hic ferme colligit. nos savajussa, continuus accusationes fallaces amicitias, perniciem innocentum, & eadem exitu causas conjungimus: obvia rerum similitudine, & satietate. Nimirum quae animum sublimia captantem raperent, aut rerum amoena varietate perfunderent, quaerebamus. Nunc gravium virorum autoritatem secuti, nec a lectione Cornelii animum alienum gerimus; & fructus ex hoc campo non poterunt nitendos carpimus.
units.tr: The author here gathers roughly the reasons that, in our early youth, kept us from reading Tacitus, apart from his style, which is less polished. We join together cruelties, continual false accusations, false friendships, the ruin of the innocent, and the same outcome for cases, because of the ready similarity of events and the satiety it breeds. Of course, we were looking for things that would carry off a mind bent on lofty matters, or would refresh it with a pleasing variety of events. Now, following the authority of serious men, we do not feel averse to reading Cornelius, and from this field we gather fruit worth striving for.

units.la: 1. Aulici splendoris contemptum. Qui vestem detracta, tam foeda tristis vitae monstra interiori forma exhibet.
units.tr: 1. Contempt for courtly splendour. He strips away the clothing and shows, in its inner form, such foul monsters of a sad life.

units.la: 2. Aliquam civilis vitae prudentiam. nam quomodo haec monstra evitanda, debellanda aut lenienda sint, praesens imaginum inspectio commonstrat.
units.tr: 2. Some measure of civil prudence. For the present survey of these images shows how such monsters are to be avoided, combated, or softened.

units.la: 3. Vitae, si quis in simili imperio similis casus, ad duriora praeparationem. Non enim tantum minus laedunt, sed etiam laesum minori dolore animi afficiunt, quae tela praevidentur. Spectatu juvenis, & omnia quidem dii prohibeant: caeterum in ea tempora nati estis, quibus firmare animum expedit constantibus exemplis. inquit magnanimi in cursu & exitu vitae exempli Thrasea. xvi. Annal. Quae Tacitus de raro antiquis scriptoribus obtrectatores, de offensa eorum, qui ob similitudinem morum aliena malefacta sibi objectari putent; de gloria ac virtute dissimiles animos offendente, praeterea accumulat: ad scribendi magis Annales, quam legendi taedium spectabunt. Nos, quod hic generatim autor declaravit, rerum gestarum monumentis intueri pergimus.
units.tr: 3. Preparation for harder things, should anyone in a similar empire meet a similar fate. For blows that are foreseen wound less, and they strike the one hurt with less pain of mind. Young man, having witnessed these things (may the gods forbid anything of the kind), but you were born in times when it is useful to strengthen the mind with steadfast examples. So says Thrasea, the example of a great-souled man in the course and end of his life (Annals, book 16). What Tacitus further piles up about the rarity of ancient writers, about the detractors who take offence, who, because of the likeness of morals, think others' misdeeds are imputed to them, and about glory and virtue offending minds unlike their own: all this will attract attention to writing Annals rather than to the tedium of reading them. We, as this author has declared in general, continue to look at the records of deeds done.

units.la: XLIII. Nihil factionibus accusatorum impervium.
units.tr: XLIII. Nothing is proof against the factions of accusers.

units.la: Factorum innocentes, ob verba onerantur: linguae & verbis temperantes, ob scripto emissam liberiorem vocem accusantur. Cremutius Cordus postulatur, novo ac tunc primùm audito crimine , quòd editis an- nalibus ,laudatoque M.Bruto,C.Cassium Romanorum ultimum dixisset.. Visarguendi rei in eo,quod sub Au- gusto & Tiberio, qui maximè stabilivisse Rem Roma- nam videri volebant, exolevisse virtus & nomen Ro- manorum,imperantibus invidiosum , ita sentientibus factiosum videbatur. Ac tamen Philopœmenes quon- dam Græcorum ultimus dictus , quod cum eo mafcu- lum Græcorum robur & libertatis amor extinctus ef- set ,nullam hoc proloquenti perniciem attulit. Apud ipsos Romanos theatrum Pompeji in oculis civium erat, collapsumque Tiberii sumptibus reponebatur. Nec scriptoribus rerum ante eum diem noxæ fuit, Pompeji vel Catonis, vel ullius partibus Julianis ad- versi,cum laude meminisse. Unde igitur illa scripti Cremutiani infimulatio , nisi à suspicaci principis len- tore,& accusatorum omnia penetrantium,omnia fini- ftre interpretantium, perversa diligentia? Interim hi- storiæ scribendi opus aggressi, ne frenos dictioni la- xent,lyricos Horatii versus in animum advocent:
units.tr: The innocent are burdened for their deeds, and for their words. Those who have restrained their tongue and speech are accused for a freer voice let out in writing. Cremutius Cordus was prosecuted on a charge that was new and then heard of for the first time: in his published Annals he had praised Marcus Brutus and called Gaius Cassius the last of the Romans. He was thought to deserve punishment for this, because under Augustus and Tiberius, who especially wished to be seen as having firmly established the Roman state, virtue and the name of Roman had faded. To those in power such talk seemed offensive, and to those who thought this way it seemed factious. Yet Philopoemen was once called the last of the Greeks, because with him the manly strength and love of liberty of the Greeks had been extinguished, and this brought no harm to the man who said it. Among the Romans themselves, the theatre of Pompey stood in the sight of the citizens, and after it had collapsed it was rebuilt at Tiberius's expense. Before that day, no writer of history was harmed for recalling Pompey or Cato with praise, even though he was opposed to the Julian party. Where, then, did the charge against Cremutius's writing come from, except from the suspicious lenience of a prince and from the perverse diligence of accusers who pry into everything and interpret everything in the worst sense? Meanwhile, those who undertake the task of writing history should, lest they loosen the reins of their style, call to mind the lyric verses of Horace:

units.la: Periculosæ plenum opus alcæ
units.tr: You are handling a work full of dangerous

units.la: Tractas, & incedis perignes
units.tr: game, and you walk through fire

units.la: Suppositos cineri doloto.
units.tr: hidden under deceptive ash.

units.la: XLIV.
units.tr: XLIV.

units.la: Verborum strepitu viri non permo- ventur.
units.tr: Men are not moved by the noise of words.

units.la: Non deterrore tantum minarum, verùm etiam de insolentis linguæ aut calami garrulitate accipias. quà multi autin ægritudinem animi,aut in ardorem ultio- nisimpelluntur. sed ipse divus Julius , ipse divus Au- gustus,& tulere istà, & reliquère, baut facile dixerim, moderatione magis an sapientia. Moderatione : quià altum, & supra nubes evectum ,animum nulla linguæ petulantia lædere , nulla loquacitas cesso mentis quie- tæ statu dejicere , nulla garrulorum protervia ad fæ- viendi furorem adducere potest. Sapientia: quia dif- simulatione aggniti doloris & sermo vulgi opprimitur, & gaudium lædentis infuscando deterruit. namque spreta spreta exolescunt: si irascare[?], agnita videntur. quod dictum, alta radice cogitationi infigant, qui sibi rem cum convitiatoribus esse noverint. Est aliquis qui te proterve insultando laesit? aut vince animi magnitu-dine dolorem, aut sensum doloris taciturnitate tege. In judicium provocas? rumorem vulgi pasces. contra-rio convitiandi scripto insectabere? audaciae flammam & causam subjicies, clamore indignabere? va-nam viribus iram vicini ridebunt. Manu & ferro in ul-tionem surges? Virile hoc quidem videtur: sed gravius leviori vulneri remedium. Denique superior læ-dente, existimationi; inferior, tuae saluti nocebis.
units.tr: You should take this not only as a warning against terror of threats, but also against the chattering of an insolent tongue or pen. By these many men are driven either into grief of mind or into the heat of revenge. But the deified Julius himself and the deified Augustus both bore such things and left them alone, which I could hardly say was more from moderation or from wisdom. Moderation: because no pertness of tongue can wound a mind raised high and lifted above the clouds, no chatter can throw down the state of a quiet mind, and no insolence of babblers can drive it into the frenzy of cruelty. Wisdom: because by feigning that one does not feel the injury, the talk of the crowd is suppressed, and by darkening the joy of the one who wounds, it is deterred. For "things despised fade away; if you show anger, they seem acknowledged." Those who know they have a quarrel with men who revile them should fix this saying deep in their thoughts. Has someone insolently insulted you? Either overcome the pain with greatness of spirit, or hide the feeling of pain by silence. Do you summon him to court? You will feed the rumour of the crowd. If, on the other hand, you attack him in writing with abuse, you will add fuel and cause to his boldness. If you grow indignant with shouting, the neighbours will laugh at your futile anger. Will you rise to vengeance with hand and sword? That seems manly indeed, but a remedy more grievous than the lighter wound. In short, by striking at a superior you harm your reputation; by striking at an inferior, your own safety.

units.la: XLV.
units.tr: XLV.

units.la: Vita ingeniorum à violento inte-ritu.
units.tr: The violent destruction of talents does not spare life.

units.la: Quo solamine Cremutius vitam sibi ereptam mitigat. suum cuique decus posteritas rependit. nec deerunt, si damnatio ingruit, qui non modo Cassii & Bruti, sed etiam mei meminerint. Quare prudenter agunt moderatores rerum, nisi modum petulantiae excreverit, si dissimulata offensione, ultione palam igni & ferro jussa, curiosos hominum animos ad inquisitionem talium librorum non accendant. libros per aedilis cremandos censuere patres: sed manserunt occultati, & editi, negligentia fortasse tumulandi, nisi illa flammae luce orbi monstrati fuissent. Quo magis secordiam eorum irridere libet, qui praesenti potentia credunt exstingui posse etiam sequentis aevi memoriam. Nam contrà, pu-nitis ingeniis, glisecit[?] auctoritas. neque aliud externi re-ges, aut qui eadem saevitia usi sunt, nisi dedecus sibi, atque illi gloriam peperere. Rectius rogum & cinerem Fabricii Veientonis probrosa scripta, in patres & sacerdotes, merebantur. Et tamen quo exustionis eventu? libros exuri jussit, conquisitos lectitatosque donec cum periculo parabantur: mox licentia habendi, oblivionem attulit. xiv.Annal. Optimum vindictæ[?] genus est, vitae integritate scripta in se refutare; inimicos autem scripto laudatos virtute superare.
units.tr: With this consolation Cremutius softens the life that was snatched from him: Posterity repays to each man his due honour. Nor, if condemnation rushes upon me, will there be lacking those who will remember not only Cassius and Brutus but me as well. Therefore the rulers of affairs act wisely, unless the wantonness of a man has grown beyond measure, if, while concealing their offence, they do not stir the curious minds of men to search out such books, which were ordered to be burned openly with fire and sword. The senators decreed that the books be burned by the aediles, but they remained hidden, and were published, perhaps neglected in the burial, had they not been shown to the world by the light of that flame. Therefore it is all the more pleasant to laugh at the folly of those who believe that by present power the memory of even a following age can be extinguished. For on the contrary, when talents are punished, authority grows brighter. Foreign kings, or those who used the same cruelty, have brought nothing but disgrace upon themselves and glory upon those they punished. More rightly did the shameful writings against the senators and priests deserve the pyre and ashes of Fabricius Veiento. And yet, with what result of the burning? He ordered the books burned; they were sought out and read the more, and were copied at the risk of those who copied them. Soon the freedom to possess them brought oblivion. Tacitus, Annals 14. The best kind of vengeance is to refute in writing a man's attacks by the integrity of one's life; and to surpass enemies who have been praised in writing by virtue.

units.la: xiv.Annal.
units.tr: Annals 14.

units.la: XLVI.
units.tr: XLVI.

units.la: Leviorum vindicem ad graviora cōns-nivere minime convenit.
units.tr: It is by no means fitting for an avenger of lesser matters to connive at greater ones.

units.la: Qui convenit in minore negotio legem observare, cum eam in majore neglexeris? inquit apud belli Catilinarii scriptorem Julius Cæsar.
units.tr: How is it fitting to observe the law in a minor matter when you have neglected it in a greater? So says Julius Caesar, in the writer on the Catilinarian war.

units.la: Quo objurgationis nexu se Tiberius obstrinxit, Importunitate accusandi Calpurnius Salvianus peccaverat, qui ne feriarum quidem Latinarum dies exemptas negotio habuit: sed praefectum urbis Drusum, auspicandi gratia tribunal ingressum, contra Sextium Marium adiit. quod a Cæsare palam increpitum, causa exilii Salviano fuit. Minus poenarum meriti, vel potius nihil poenarum meriti, incuria caeremoniarum divi Augusti, amissere libertatem, quam bello Mithridatico meruerant circumfusi. At Vibium Seneca num, qui ficto crimine Fonteium Capitonem procul fulem Asiæ pulsaverat, censura praeteriit. quem nimium odium publicum tutiorem faciebat: nam ut quisque districtior accusator, velut sacrosanctus erat, leves, ignobiles, poenis afficiebantur. Ita delatores genus hominum publico exitio repertum, non modo praemiis, verum etiam falsae accusationis impunitate, eliciebantur. Quae ubi lues civitatem opprimit, nihil adeo rabulârum audaciam honestate fatis munitum, nihil auctoritate tutum est. Haec non postrema pars miseriarum aevi Tiberiani.
units.tr: By this rebuke Tiberius bound himself. Calpurnius Salvianus had sinned by the importunity of his accusing, for he did not keep even the days of the Latin holidays free from business. But he approached Sextius Marius against the prefect of the city, Drusus, who had entered the tribunal to take the auspices. Because Caesar openly rebuked him for this, it became the cause of Salvianus's exile. Those who had gathered around him, deserving fewer punishments, or rather no punishment at all, lost their liberty through their carelessness about the ceremonies of the deified Augustus, which they had earned by the Mithridatic war. But the censure passed over Vibius Seneca, who by a feigned charge had driven Fonteius Capito, a man of Asia, into exile. Public hatred of him made him all the safer; for the more harsh an accuser, the more he was regarded as sacrosanct, while the light, the obscure, were punished. Thus informers, a race of men invented for public ruin, were enticed not only by rewards but by impunity for false accusation. When such a plague grips a state, nothing is safe: neither the audacity of the rabble-rousers, which is not sufficiently fortified by honesty, nor anything protected by authority. This was not the least part of the miseries of the age of Tiberius.

units.la: XLVII.
units.tr: XLVII.

units.la: Supra hominem, non supra homines imperator ascendat.
units.tr: Let the emperor rise above man, not above men.

units.la: Qua moderationis laude Tiberius antegressis Julio & Augusto, secutis Cajo, Claudio, Neronē superior fuit. Hispania ulterior delubrum Tiberio matrique ejus, exemplo Asiae, exstruendi licentiam petebat. Tiberius excusata prioris admissionis conniveнтia, divini honoris in posterum ambitionem egregia ora-tione repellit. Ego me P.G. mortalem esse, & hominum officia fungi, satisq; habere, si locum principem impleam, & vos restor, & meminisse posteros volo. Hoc monstro Hercules, qui omnia monstra domuit, victus; aram sibi ut Deo poni, cupidissime admisit. Hoc Alexander ille Magnus monstrum, in Dario & Poro victo, non vicit. Vere dictum est, etiam sapienti ultimam tunicam superbiam exui: Sed non iccirco cuiquam mortalium, ut se mortalem esse oblivisceatur, conceditur.
units.tr: By this praise for moderation Tiberius surpassed Julius and Augustus, who went before him, and Gaius, Claudius and Nero, who came after. Hispania Ulterior asked for permission to build a temple to Tiberius and his mother, following the example of Asia. Tiberius, excusing his earlier tolerance of the first request, rejected the ambition of divine honour for the future in an outstanding speech: "I, Conscript Fathers, am a mortal man and perform the duties of a man. I am content if I fill the leading place, and I wish you and posterity to remember me." Hercules, who tamed all monsters, was overcome by this monster: he most eagerly allowed an altar to be set up to himself as to a god. Alexander the Great did not overcome this monster when he had defeated Darius and Porus. It is rightly said that even the wise man must cast off the last tunic of pride. But this is not granted to any mortal so that he may forget that he is mortal.

units.la: qui satis superque memoriae meae tribuunt, ut majoribus meis dignum, rerum vestrarum providum, constantem in periculis, offensionum pro utilitate publica non pa-vidum, credant. Divinos honores ita amolitur, ut cadentem in principem virum famam non repellat. Primum se a majorum claritudine non degenerantem auxisse imperatorio fastigio nomen familiae agnoscit. Providentiam deinde constantiam, offensionum tolerantiam sibi tribuendo, nec veri modum excedit, & quae sint munia principum describit. Hac mihi in animis vestris templa, hae pulcherrimae effigies & mansurae.
units.tr: "who give my memory more than enough, so that they believe me worthy of my ancestors, provident in your affairs, steadfast in dangers, and not fearful of offences for the sake of the public good." He drives away divine honours in such a way that he does not repel the fame of a prince who is falling. First he acknowledges that he has not degenerated from the glory of his ancestors and has increased the name of his family to the height of imperial dignity. Then, by ascribing to himself foresight, steadfastness and endurance of offences, he neither exceeds the measure of truth and describes what the duties of princes are. "These are the temples in your minds, these the most beautiful and enduring images."

units.la: Si non immolandi, quod superbum, sed memoriae causa templa principum nominibus, arae & statuae ponuntur: certiora sunt & diuturniora, quae animis infixa, posterorum sermone celebrantur. Nam quae saxo struuntur, si judicium posterorum in odium vertit, pro sepulcris sternuntur. ab hominum igitur aestimantium judicio, non a structura fabrorum, honoris per manfu-ra dignatio. Proinde socios, cives, & deos & deas ipsas precor; hos, ut mihi ad finem usque vitae, quietam & intelligentem humani divinique juris mentem duint[?]: illos, ut quandocunque concessero[?], cum laude & bonis recordationibus, facta atque famam nominis mei prosequantur. Digna sapiente viro precatio? quid enim majus a Deo, quam solertiam, acumen, judicandi prudentiam petas? quid gloriosius ab hominibus, quam vitae cum laude peractae recordationem impetres?
units.tr: If temples and altars and statues are set up in the names of princes not for sacrifice, which is proud, but for the sake of remembrance, then those things are more certain and more lasting which are fixed in minds and celebrated in the talk of posterity. "For what is built of stone is thrown down as a tomb if the judgement of posterity turns to hatred." Therefore the worth of honour that endures comes from the judgement of men who weigh it, not from the craftsmanship of builders. "Accordingly I pray to my companions, my fellow citizens, and to the gods and goddesses themselves: to the former, that they grant me to the end of my life a quiet mind that understands human and divine law; to the latter, that whenever I depart, they may follow my deeds and the fame of my name with praise and good remembrance." Is this prayer worthy of a wise man? For what greater thing could you seek from God than skill, keen insight and prudence in judging? What more glorious thing could you obtain from men than the remembrance of a life lived with praise?

units.la: At non effugit vulgi, omnia arrodentis, modestia vituperium. multi quia dissideret, quidam ut degeneris animi interpretabantur. at quo sinistrae interpretationis argumento? Optumos quippe mortalium al
units.tr: But the modesty of the crowd, which gnaws at everything, did not escape blame. "Many thought it was because he disagreed, some as a sign of a degenerate spirit." But on what evidence of an unfavourable interpretation? "For indeed the best of mortals ..."

units.la: XLVI.
units.tr: XLVI.

units.la: Leviorum vindicem ad graviora cōs-nivere minimè convenit.
units.tr: It is by no means fitting that an avenger of lesser offences should wink at greater ones.

units.la: Qui convenit in minore negotio legem observare, cum eam in majore neglexeris? inquit apud belli Ca-tilinarii scriptorem Julius Cæsar.
units.tr: How does it fit to observe the law in a minor matter when you have neglected it in a greater? So Julius Caesar says, in the writer of the Catilinarian war.

units.la: Quo objurgationis nexu se Tiberius obstrinxit, Importunitate accusandi Calpurnius Salvianus pec-caverat, qui ne feriarum quidem Latinarum dies exemptas negotio habuit: sed præfectum urbis Drusum, auspicandi gratia tribunali ingressum, contra Sex. Marium adiit. quod a Cassare palam increpitum, causa exilii Salviano fuit. Minus poenarum meriti Cyzicenī, vel potius nihil poenarum meriti, incuria cæremoniarum divi Augusti, amisere libertatem, quam bello Mithridatis meruerant circumscripti. At Vibium Serenum, qui fictō crimine Fonteium Capitonem procon-sulem Africæ pulsaverat, censura prætereriit. quem nimirum odium publicum tutiorem faciebat: nam ut quisque diffricitior accusator, velut sacrosanctus erat, levis, ignobiles, pœnis afficiebantur. Ita delatores, genus hominum publico exitio repertum, non modo præ-miis, verum etiam falsæ accusationis impunitate, elicientur. Quæ ubi lues civitatem opprimit, nihil ad-versus rabularum audaciam honestate fatis munitum, nihil autoritate tutum est. Hæc non postrema pars miseriarum æVI Tiberiani.
units.tr: By what bond of rebuke Tiberius bound himself: Calpurnius Salvianus had offended by the importunity of his accusations, for he did not even spare the days of the Latin holidays from his business. When he approached Sextus Marius, after the prefect of the city Drusus had entered the tribunal to take the auspices, this was openly rebuked by Caesar, and it was the cause of Salvianus's exile. The people of Cyzicus, who had less deserved punishment, or rather had deserved no punishment at all, lost their freedom through their neglect of the ceremonies of the deified Augustus, a freedom they had earned by their service in the war against Mithridates. But Vibius Serenus, who by a false charge had brought down the proconsul of Africa, Fonteius Capito, was passed over by the censors. Public hatred, indeed, made him safer; for the more shameless an accuser was, the more sacrosanct he seemed, while the light and the obscure were punished. Thus informers, a race of men devised for public ruin, were enticed not only by rewards but also by impunity for false accusation. When such a plague overwhelms a state, nothing is sufficiently protected by honesty against the audacity of these hirelings, nothing is safe by authority. This was not the least of the miseries of the age of Tiberius.

units.la: XLVII.
units.tr: XLVII.

units.la: Supra homines, non supra hominem, imperator ascendat.
units.tr: Let the emperor rise above men, not above man.

units.la: At non effugit vulgi, omnia arrodentis, modestia vituperium. multi quia dissideret, quidam ut degenerans animi interpretabantur. at quo sinistrae interpretationis argumento? Optimos quippe mortalium altiffima cupere. Atqui mortalem in deum fe tranfmit= tare velle, & id voto expetere, insipientiæ est; mortali= tatis conscium, divinos honores affectare, impiæ inii= quitatis. Est quidem innatus generosæ menti gloriæ consequendæ ardor, nec ut diligentiæ stimulus vitu- perandus. Pueris inprimis, & adolescentiori ætati, quam nondum proprii sillecebris virtus attrahit, hæc inter pares æmulatio permittitur. Mihi detur ille puer, inquit Quintilianus, quem laus excitet, quem gloria juvet, qui vitius fleat. Hic erit alendus ambitu, hunc mordebit objurgatio, hunc honor excitabit, in hoc defi- ciam nunquam vérebor. Sed nec quicquid puero, & sapienti viro concessum: nec quisquam puto ludima- gifter, spe divinitatis proposita, ad declamationem, aut ad prima litterarum elementa, ephebum excitabit. Sed ratione, vel opinionis potius imaginatione, à popu- lo ad exemplar itur. Sic Herculem & Liberum apud Gracos, Quirinum apud nos, dum numero additos. Sed magno cum illorum temporum irrisu, nostrorum indignatione. Obiter cultioris literatûræ candidati observent, quo loco apud Romanos divinitas Hercu- lis & similium hominum fuerit. eo nimirum, quo sint dii factitii, siti, & hominum calculo fastis deorum ad- scripti. Melius Augustum, qui speraverit. Immo me- liùs Tiberium, qui humana fapuerit. Sed jam oracu- lum Delphico clarius, pronunciatum audiamus. Cæte- ra principibus flatim nde[ffe]: unum infatiabiliter pa- randum, prosperam fuit memoriam. Nihil humanarum rerum infatiabiliter parandum. limites non minus ambitioni, quam avaritiæ, quam crudelitati, figendi: nec sapientes insatiabilem Alexandri, domandi orbis humanum cupiditatem, & per eam frages & funera gentium, collaudant. necin eo divinitatis affectationem, & Persicam regum adorationem ipsi Macedones coquere potuerunt. nam contemtu fama, contemni virtutes hoc non magis ad principem, quàm ad quem- vis è media plebe, dictum quadrabit quanto Porticen- fis philosophorum familia genero, virtutem fe ipsa contentam, externarum rerum fumo ad fplendo- rem.
units.tr: But the modesty of the crowd, which gnaws at everything, did not escape blame. "Many thought it was because he disagreed, some as a sign of a degenerate spirit." But on what evidence of an unfavourable interpretation? "For indeed the best of mortals desire the highest things." Yet to wish to transform oneself into a god, and to pray for it, is folly; to affect divine honours while knowing one is mortal is the height of impious injustice. Indeed the ardour to win glory is innate in a noble mind, and it is not to be condemned as a spur to diligence. This rivalry among equals is allowed especially to boys and to younger age, which virtue does not yet draw by its own allurements. "Let me have that boy," says Quintilian, "whom praise stirs up, whom glory helps, who weeps at being beaten. He will be nourished by ambition, rebuke will bite him, honour will rouse him; I shall never fear for him." But this is not granted to a boy and a wise man alike, nor do I think any schoolmaster, holding out the hope of divinity, would rouse a youth to declamation or to the first elements of letters. Rather, by reason, or rather by the imagination of opinion, men proceed from the people to the model: thus they added Hercules and Liber among the Greeks, and Quirinus among us, to the number of the gods. But this was to the great derision of those times and to the indignation of ours. In passing, let the candidates of more cultivated literature observe at what point among the Romans the divinity of Hercules and of such men arose: namely, at the point where they became made-up gods, placed among the gods by the reckoning of men and enrolled in the calendar of the gods. It is better to have hoped as Augustus did; better still as Tiberius, who had the wisdom of a man. But let us now hear the oracle pronounced more clearly than the Delphic one. "Other things for princes are to be taken immediately; one thing is to be acquired without limit: a good memory." Nothing in human affairs is to be acquired without limit. Limits must be set for ambition no less than for avarice and cruelty; nor do the wise praise the insatiable desire of Alexander to conquer the world, and through it the ruin and deaths of nations. Nor could the Macedonians themselves bring themselves to that point of seeking divinity and the Persian adoration of kings. For the saying that fame is despised, and that virtues are despised along with it, will fit a prince no more than any man from the common people, however much the Porch's family of philosophers exalted virtue, contented in itself, above the smoke and splendour of external things. Fame is a desire; the thing does not need... But we are not those who teach that fame should be neglected, provided we do not give ourselves over entirely to the talk of the crowd, nor place our hope of reward in fleeting rumour, much less in that which is the hinge of the question, the thirst for fame...

units.la: Fama cupiditas. rem non indigere. Sed non fumus[?] ii, qui famam negli-gendam doceamus. modo non sermonibus vulgi to-tos nos dederimus : nec in praemiis caduci rumoris spem posuerimus rerum nostrarum, multo minus, in quo quaestionis cardo versatur, famae sitim ad divinae gloriae aviditatem extendamus. Homines nos esse, tum corporis in dies fluentis fragilitas, tum adhaerentes animo maculae, & in multis actionibus miser infelicitatis lapsus, docebit.
units.tr: The desire for fame. The matter needs no lengthy treatment. But we are not those who teach that fame is to be disregarded, provided we do not give ourselves wholly over to the talk of the crowd, nor place the hope of our affairs in the rewards of a fleeting rumour. Much less should we extend our thirst for fame into an eagerness for God's glory, which is where the hinge of the question lies. That we are men will be taught both by the frailty of a body that wastes away day by day, and by the stain that clings to the mind, and by the wretched slips of unhappy error in many of our actions.

units.la: XLVIII.
units.tr: XLVIII.

units.la: Sermonem non vulgare, non est in principe arrogantia.
units.tr: A speech not commonplace is not arrogance in a prince.

units.la: Sejanus morum Tiberii gnarus, quamvis amicitiae consideret, matrimonium Liviae, compositis ad Caesarem codicillis, petebat. moris quippe tum erat, quan-quam praesentem, scripto adire. quod tanquam de more abolito loquitur Cornelius, de Ulpiani temporis facilitate capias. Non decet principem in publico, nisi rara, nisi gravis, nisi astricta oratio. nec omnibus pro-miscue aures praebere, quod citra justitiae aut publicarum rerum dispendium fiat, semper a principe exigitur. Qui vero facili aditu, sermone, comitate, salva autoritatis reverentia, se civibus communicant, non sunt ob id vituperandi. Modestiae famam neque summis mortalibus aspernandam, & a diis aestimari: monet non nemo apud nostrum autorem, xv. Annal. Cujus modestiae magna pars est facilitas, & sobria cum cive sermonis communicatio. Ut vero quis libertini generis homo, praeter meritum ad potentiae aliquem gradum evectus, cum Pallante, splendido aulae Claudianae mancipio, domesticis nutu aut scripto mandata praescribat, ne vocem homo, cum hominibus consociet, non est ferendae arrogantiae.
units.tr: Sejanus, who knew Tiberius's habits well, although he was considering friendship, sought the marriage of Livia by writing codicils to Caesar. For it was then the custom to approach someone in writing, even when he was present. Cornelius speaks of this as a custom now abolished, and you may take it as the easy manners of Ulpian's time. A prince ought to speak in public only rarely, only gravely, and only in concise speech. It is always required of a prince that he not lend his ears indiscriminately to everyone, when this could be done without loss to justice or to public affairs. Those, however, who share themselves with their fellow citizens through easy access, conversation and courtesy, while the reverence due to authority is preserved, are not on that account to be blamed. Our author, in book xv of the Annals, warns that the reputation for modesty is not to be scorned even by the greatest mortals, and is valued by the gods. A large part of this modesty is affability and a sober sharing of speech with the citizen. But when a man of freed origin, raised beyond his merit to some degree of power, like Pallas, the splendid servant of Claudius's court, lays down orders to his household by a nod or in writing, and does not deign to share his voice with other men, this is arrogance that cannot be tolerated.

units.la: XLIX.
units.tr: XLIX.

units.la: Astuti animi versipellis oratio.
units.tr: The speech of a crafty and shifty mind.

units.la: Ardua erat Sejani petitio, Liviam in matrimonium flagitantis. nam quod de Julio Agricola traditur, Domitiam Decidianam splendidis natalibus ortam, s- bi junxit; idq; matrimonium ad majora nitenti, decus ac robur fuit: id Sejano dici poterat, & à Tiberio non occultabatur: Falleris enim Sejane, si te mansurum in eodem ordine putas, & Liviam quæ C. Cæsari, mox Drufo nupta fuerat, ea mente aćturam [?], ut cum equite Romano senescat [?]. Scala enim ad regnum per ejusmodi connubium tendebatur, Iccirco oratione varia varius animus, & plura quàm promeret occultans, utebatur. Benevolentia patris Augusti, & mox plurimis [?] Tiberii judicis ita infuevile, ut spes votaque sua non prius ad deos, quàm ad principum aures conferret. Principum in se beneficia commemorando, & diis eos votorum nuncupatione conferendo, immò ratione quadam præferendo, benevolum animum captat. Paulatim ad meritafua. sed occultiori via, & ad anteactæ vitæ modestiam, progreditur. Neq; fulgorem honorum un- quam præcatum: excubias ac labores, ut unum à mili- tibus, pro incolumitate imperatoris malle. Altius deinde oratione exsurgens, familiarem cum imperatore vitam extollit. Attamen quod pulcherrimum, ade- ptum, ut conjunctione Cæsaris dignus crederetur, hinc initium sui. Propositionem, ut auribus peregrinam, non ita nudè molitur: sed duplici argumento, exempli Augusti, & suæ modestiæ, conte&tum inserit. Et quo- niam audiverit, Augustum, in collocanda filia, nonnihil etiam de equitibus Romanis consultavit: ita si marito Liviæ quæreretur, haberet in animo amicum, sola necessitudinis gloria usurum. non enim exuere imposita munia. huic tam novæ, tam suspectæ petitioni argu- mentum adjungit, in animo Tiberii efficax: fatis assi- mare, firmari domum adversum iniquas Agrippina offensiones. Idque liberorum causa. ultimum ab adu- latione argumentum, aculeum, quod est boni orato- ris, postremo loco defigit. nam sibi multum superque vita sore, quod tali cum principe explevit. Hæc sermonis, sed non & voti, Sejaniam summa.
units.tr: Sejanus's petition, in which he asked for Livia's hand in marriage, was a difficult one. For what is related of Julius Agricola, that he joined Domitia Decidiana to himself, though she was of noble birth, and that this marriage was an ornament and a support to him as he aimed at greater things, could have been said to Sejanus too, and Tiberius did not hide it from him: "You are mistaken, Sejanus, if you think you will remain in the same rank, and that Livia, who was once married to Gaius Caesar and afterwards to Drusus, will mean to grow old with a Roman knight. For a ladder to the throne was being built through such a union." Therefore, with a varied speech, his mind also varied, and he used a speech that concealed more than it revealed. He had been accustomed to the goodwill of the elder Augustus and then of many of Tiberius's judges, so that he did not bring his hopes and vows to the gods before he had brought them to the ears of the princes. By recalling the princes' benefits to himself, and by commending them to the gods in the utterance of his vows, or rather by placing them before the gods with a certain method, he courts their goodwill. Gradually he advances to his services, by a less conspicuous road, and to a modesty of life such as he had shown before. He never asked for the glitter of honours; he preferred, like one of the soldiers, to keep watch and labour for the safety of the emperor. Then, rising higher in his speech, he extols his familiar life with the emperor. Yet what is most beautiful he sets forth at the start, namely that he might be thought worthy of the emperor's marriage connection. He does not push this proposal, strange to the ears, too baldly. Instead he wraps it in a twofold argument: the example of Augustus and his own modesty. And since he had heard that Augustus, in arranging his daughter's marriage, had also consulted somewhat about Roman knights, he says that if a husband were being sought for Livia, he would have in mind a friend who would enjoy only the glory of the connection, for he would not put off the duties laid upon him. To this so new and so suspect a request he adds an argument that is effective in Tiberius's mind: that by such a match the house would be strengthened against the unjust offences of Agrippina, and that this would be for the sake of the children. Last of all, from flattery, he drives home the final argument, the sting, as is the mark of a good orator: that the chief joy of his life will be that he has fulfilled such a union with such a prince. This is the sum of Sejanus's speech, but not of his wish.

units.la: Inter[?]
units.tr: Inter[?]

units.la: L.
units.tr: L.

units.la: Inter negationis odium, & promissi periculum, media responsi dilatio.
units.tr: Between the hatred of a refusal and the danger of a promise, a middle course of deferring the answer.

units.la: Non quæ fiat perpetuo silentio: quod, nisi distractionum multiplici labore excusetur, in ministro præsertim aulæ, a rusticana fastidii arrogantia parum distabit. Sed quæ responso neutram in partem inclinante, spem expectanti non adimat, promittentem non obliget. Ita Tiberius, Laudata pietate Sejani, fuiss[?] in eum beneficiis modice percursis, cum tempus tanquam ad integram consultationem petivisset, adjunxit, suspensam nimirum inter spem & metum, quæ sequitur, orationem.
units.tr: Not a reply given in unbroken silence, which, unless excused by the heavy labour of many distractions, will differ little from rustic disdain and haughtiness, especially in a minister of the court. Rather, a reply that inclines neither way, that does not take hope from the one who waits, and does not bind the one who promises. So Tiberius, after praising the loyalty of Sejanus and touching only lightly on the benefits conferred on him, when he had asked for time as though for a full consultation, added the speech that follows, one suspended between hope and fear.

units.la: LI.
units.tr: LI.

units.la: Fama non negligenda principi.
units.tr: Reputation is not to be neglected by a prince.

units.la: Nec ad eam omnes actiones sunt dirigendæ. Cum grano salis accipiendum illud Tiberii: Cateris[?] morta-libus in eo stare consilia, quid sibi conducere putent, principum diversam esse fortem, quibus præcipua rerum ad famam dirigenda. Nam & primum pronunciati membrum & secundum laborat. Primum: quandoquidem intra commoda terminos omnes deliberationes claudi, minus est hominum vita dignum.
units.tr: Nor should all actions be directed toward it. That saying of Tiberius must be taken with a grain of salt: "For other mortals, their plans rest on what they think advantageous to themselves; the lot of princes is different, for whom the chief matters must be directed toward reputation." For both the first part of the statement and the second are faulty. First: since it is less worthy of human life for all deliberations to be confined within the limits of personal advantage.

units.la: Secundum: quia ad salutem civium potius, quam ad rumorem vulgi, præcipua imperantium opera du-cenda. Auro inculpenda Fabii Maximi ad Paulum consulem monita: quibus ipse antea rem populi col-lapsam, spreto sermone hominum, restituit. Accommodata tamen ad causam Tiberii oratio, absurditate sententiæ liberatur. Cæteri enim mortales in ducendis & locandis uxoribus, quid sibi conducat, aut quo voluptas trahat, fere spectant: principes viri etiam quid publice decorum sit, in animum advocant.
units.tr: Second: because the chief efforts of rulers must be directed to the safety of citizens rather than to the rumour of the crowd. The admonitions of Fabius Maximus to the consul Paullus are worth their weight in gold, by which he himself earlier restored the collapsed state of the Roman people, disregarding people's talk. Yet the saying, when applied to Tiberius's cause, is rescued from absurdity. For other mortals, in leading and giving away wives in marriage, mostly look to what benefits themselves or where pleasure draws them; but princely men also take into account what is becoming to the public good.

units.la: LII.
units.tr: LII.

units.la: Inter artes aulæ commemoratur, dextre negare posse.
units.tr: Among the arts of the court, it is recorded that one can refuse skilfully.

units.la: Non enim hic semper, utin peripatetica schola, lo-cum habet categorica enunciatio. Tiberius cum pe-titi Liviæ matrimonii concessionem inconvenientem innuisset; quod fama principis adversaretur, quod ini-micitias Agrippinæ invidia furentis accenderet, quod privati hominis conditionem emineret; cumq; exem-plum Augusti rerum & temporum dissimilitudine re-futasset: ad extremum spem non per omnia tollendo, & asperitatem blandiloquentia leniendo, repulsam edulcorat. Cæterum neq; tuis, neq; Livia destinatis ad-versabor. Ipse quid intra animum volutaverim, qui-bus adhuc necessitudinibus immiscere te mihi parem: omittam ad præsens referre. id tantum aperiam, nihil esse tam excelsum, quod non virtutes ista, tuumq; in meo animus mereantur. Atque ut petitionem repellentis, ita & repulsam timentis, ejus in abnuendo, hujus in procando, artificia adhiberi solent. Inter quæ non postremum est, internunciis uti, non tanquam mandato instructis, sed tanquam suo instinctu rem gerentibus. Præsentissimum autem repulsæ antidotum est, nihil petere, quod tibi jure denegetur. In iis autem, quæ juri nihil derogant, perspectam habere interiorem ani-mi cogitationem, a quo petiturus es, vel conjectura vel certis indiciis deprehensam, multum juvabit. De-nique ita petitio instituenda, ut aut ejus depulsio pau-cis mortalibus innotescat, aut percrebescens non in suborem depulso cedat.
units.tr: For here a categorical statement does not always hold, as it does in the Peripatetic school. When Tiberius had hinted that the proposed marriage with Livia was unsuitable, he gave several reasons: it would damage the prince's reputation, it would stir up enmity with Agrippina, who raged with envy, and it would raise a private citizen above his station. He also rejected the example of Augustus on the ground that the circumstances and times were different. In the end, without destroying all hope and softening the harshness with flattering words, he sweetened the refusal. For my part, I shall not oppose your plans or Livia's. What I have turned over in my own mind, and by what ties I might yet make you my equal, I will leave unsaid for now. I will only make this plain: nothing is so lofty that your virtues and your character do not deserve it in my eyes. Just as with one who refuses a request and one who fears a refusal, so the arts of the first are used in declining and those of the second in pressing. Among these, not the least is to use go-betweens, not as men sent with a commission, but as men acting on their own impulse. The most effective antidote to a refusal is to ask for nothing that may rightly be denied you. In matters that take nothing from anyone's right, it will greatly help to have a clear sense of the inner thoughts of the one you are going to ask, grasped by conjecture or by certain signs. Finally, the request must be made in such a way that either its rejection is known to few mortals, or, if it spreads, it does not fall upon the one who was refused.

units.la: LIII.
units.tr: LIII.

units.la: Longa principis absentia potentiam ministrorum auget.
units.tr: A prince's long absence increases the power of his ministers.

units.la: Quod sentiens Ælius Sejanus, ne assiduos in do-mum cœtus arcendo, infringeret potentiam, aut rece-ptando, facultatem criminantibus præberet; huc fe-xit, ut Tiberium ad vitam procul Roma, amœnis locis degendam impelleret. Quid ex abscessu eo spei Sejano, quid bonæ frugis? hoc etiam aperit Cornelius. Multa quippe providebat, sua in manu aditus, literarumque magna ex parte se arbitrium fore, cum per milites commeavent; mox Cafarem vergente tam fenettâ, fecre-toq; loci mollitum, munia imperii facilius tramiffu-rum : & minui sibi invidiam, adempta salutantum turba : fublatisfq; inanibus, vera potentia augere. Principem agit, non qui Principis nomen inani appel-latione gerit, cura negotiorum ad alios tramiffa: sed cujus domus aditu civium, otium suscepta de bono publico cura, secretum ipsum literarum commercio frequentatur. Hanc ad fe principatus vim Sejanus tracturus, paulatim negotia urbis, populi accursus, multitudinem adfluentium increpat: extollens laudi-bus quite em & solitudinem: quis abesse tadia & offensiones : ac pracipua rerum maximi agitari. Negari non potest, homini quietis amanti non esse gratum fori ac aulae strepitum, sordere dissonas populi querelas & acclamationes, taedium movere offensas dijudicandis litigiis ortas. Sed qui praeesse imperio multis cogitat,epulis haec debent esse jucundiora. Nec simul commorari possunt gloriae amplitudo,& curarum solutum laxamentum. Haec causa secessus Tiberiani, Sejani nimirum vafrities. Alia Tiberium causa impulerit conspectum honestorum virorum fugere, animi ex conscientia pudor. audivit Tiberius probra, quis per occulta lacerabatur. Sed non fuga hominum, verum vitae emendatae integritate adversus rumor corrigitur. Pejor secessus arrepta ansa, libidinum secreto promendarum occultatio. quam infra Cornelius, & libri sexti vestibulo, promit.
units.tr: Ælius Sejanus perceived this. Lest by keeping the crowds of visitors away from the house he should weaken his power, or by admitting them should give his accusers an opportunity, he set himself to persuade Tiberius to live far from Rome, in pleasant places. What hope and what good result Sejanus gained from that withdrawal Cornelius also reveals. Indeed, he foresaw many advantages: access would be in his own hands, and he would largely control correspondence, since it passed through the soldiers; then, as the Caesar grew old and sluggish in his seclusion, he would more easily hand over the duties of empire to him; and the envy directed at him would lessen, with the crowd of greeters removed, and with empty show gone, he would increase his true power. He acts as prince, not one who bears the name of prince in empty title, having handed over the care of affairs to others, but one whose house is frequented by citizens' access, who has taken up leisure with the care of the public good, and whose very secrecy is thronged by the traffic of letters. Sejanus, about to draw this power of the principate to himself, gradually disparages the business of the city, the rush of the people, and the crowd flowing in; he extols solitude and quiet, saying that the tedium and offences of the court are absent and that the greatest affairs are handled there. It cannot be denied that for a man who loves quiet, the noise of the forum and the court is not pleasant, that the discordant complaints and shouts of the people are distasteful, and that the disputes arising from judging lawsuits cause weariness. But for one who thinks about ruling a great empire, these things ought to be more agreeable than feasts. The magnitude of glory and the free relaxation from cares cannot dwell together. This was the reason for Tiberius's retreat: the cunning of Sejanus, no doubt. Another cause may have driven Tiberius to avoid the sight of honourable men: a shame arising from his conscience. He heard the reproaches by which he was torn apart in secret. But the reputation is not corrected by fleeing from men, but by the integrity of a reformed life. The retreat was worse, since, seizing the occasion, he could bring out his lusts in secret and hide them. Cornelius, below, and at the threshold of the sixth book, sets this forth.

units.la: LIV. Nullum in paupertate flagitium.
units.tr: LIV. No Disgrace in Poverty.

units.la: Sed fi quod est, in ignavia & luxu, paupertatis nutricibus; in mollitie animi, paupertatem tolerare nescientis, flagitium. Flagitium in divitiis aut injuste & avare partis, aut sordide retentis, aut superbe vel luxuriose profusis. Lentulo super consulatum & triumphalia de Getulis, gloria fuerat bene tolerata paupertas, dein magna opes innocenter parta, & modeste habita. En paupertas bene tolerata, Taciti & civium Romanorum judicio, Lentulo gloriae data? Ubi sunt, quae Christi, paupertatis vita ac doctrina magistri nomine induti, paupertatem viro honesto, ut ignominiae extre- mum objiciunt? Angustam, amici, pauperiem pati. Robustus acri militia puer Condiscat. monet Horatius, paupertatem & cipfe prima aetate expertus.
units.tr: But if there is any disgrace, it lies in idleness and luxury, which are the nurses of poverty, and in a softness of mind that cannot bear poverty. Disgrace lies in riches that are gained unjustly and greedily, or hoarded meanly, or squandered arrogantly or luxuriously. For Lentulus, besides his consulship and his triumph over the Getulians, poverty borne well was a glory, and then great wealth, innocently gained and modestly kept. Was poverty borne well given to Lentulus as glory by the judgment of Tacitus and the citizens of Rome? Where are those who, wearing the name of Christ, the master of a poor life and teaching, throw poverty at an honest man as the last word in shame? "To endure narrow poverty, my friends, let the sturdy boy learn in hard soldiering." Horace gives this advice, having himself known poverty in his early years.

units.la: LV.
units.tr: LV.

units.la: Honestum literatura ignominiae pallium.
units.tr: The cloak of disgrace on respectable literature.

units.la: Nunquam quidem fatis laudari philosophia potest: cui qui parceat, omne tempus aetatis fine molestia possit degere: utloquitur in Catone Majore Cicero.
units.tr: Philosophy can never be praised enough. Whoever devotes himself to it can spend his whole life without trouble, as Cicero says in the Cato Maior.

units.la: Sed saepe philosophiae studium pudori velamentum affumitur: pudori velignave vitae, quo segne otium decoro nomine veletur: vel faedae voluptatis, ut quondam dam philosophi barba promissa latentia sub crasso pallio flagitia abscondebant: vel interdicte patriae. Sic L. Antonium adolescentulum Augustus Maffiliam seposuit, ubi studiorum nomen exilii tegeretur. De Agrippa in Syriam, Tiberio in infulam Rhodum, specie peregrinationis sub Augusto amotis, supra modo nuil. De multis illustrium familiarum utrisque sexus liberis monasterio includis, ubi pietatis speciosus praetextus vel ignominiam poenae, vel avaritiam familiae texit, aptior dicendi locus alibi dabitur.
units.tr: Yet the pursuit of philosophy is often taken up as a veil for shame: a veil for shameful conduct or a idle life, under which slothful leisure is covered with a respectable name; or for disgraceful pleasure, as once the promised beards of philosophers hid vices beneath thick cloaks; or for a homeland from which one is banished. Thus Augustus sent the young L. Antonius to Massilia, where the name of study concealed his exile. Agrippa was sent to Syria, and Tiberius to the island of Rhodes, both removed under Augustus under the appearance of travel, as I have said above. Concerning the many children of illustrious families, of both sexes, shut up in monasteries, where the specious pretext of piety covered either the disgrace of a punishment or the greed of a family, a more suitable place for discussion will be given elsewhere.

units.la: LVI.
units.tr: LVI.

units.la: Nulla autoritate contra desperatam audaciam munimur.
units.tr: We are protected by no authority against desperate boldness.

units.la: Contempsit omnes ille, vitam quiprius: inquit Tragoediarum scriptor Seneca, Cujus dicti exemplum in L. Pisone, citerioris Hispaniae praetore, a quodam agreste nationis Termeftinae interfecto, praebetur. Agrestis ille praetorem Romanum, majestate praetoria non fatis protectum, pace incuriosum ex improviso in itinere adortus, uno vulnere in mortem affecit. Cujus fasti non magis ferocia admirationi est, quam tor-mentorum perferendorum constantia. cum tormentis edere conscios adigeretur: voce magna, sermone pa-trio, frustra je interrogari clamitavit. adsisterent foci, ac spectarent: nullam vim tantam doloris fore, ut veritatem eliceret. Nec fidiculatum fortior, quam mortis contemptor, quod ignominiosum iis temporibus non habebatur, fuit. cum posterò ad quaestionem traheretur, eo nisu proripuit fe custodibus, faxoq; caput afflixit, ut statim exanimaretur. Firmius igitur imperii munimentum in benevolentia subditorum, quam in terrore armorum, contra ejusmodi projectae audaciae firmitatem, quaerendum, quod a Pisone neglectum: qui pecuniis e publico interceptas, acrius, quam ut tolerarent barbari, cogebat. Nec desunt nostro aut patrum proximo aevo improvisae magnatum caedis, ne veteria semper scrutemur, exempla Buccingamus, potentiae & apud regem Britannorum gratiae nimius, cum quasi male gestae a rege rei autor vulgo traduce-retur: inventus est ex infimo capite censorum genere homuncio, qui cum in aula regia, interdiu obtruncaret. Arreptus Ficarius, facinoris manifestus, nihil aliud voce edidit, nisi non potuisse alio modo infelici patriae, nisi malorum omnium autore sublato, subveniri. Reges Galliarum, Henricum III. in suis castris, Hen-ricum IV. in urbe & in carpento suo, a fanaticis hominibus, aut falsa pietatis opinione delusis, ferro in pe-stus demisso trucidatos, vel in toustrinis decantata hi-storia celebratur.
units.tr: He who has despised his life has despised everything, says the tragic writer Seneca. An example of this saying is given in L. Piso, praetor of Hispania Citerior, who was killed by a certain rustic of the Termestine nation. The countryman, finding the Roman praetor not sufficiently guarded by his praetorian dignity and off his guard in peacetime, attacked him unexpectedly on the road and struck him dead with a single blow. His deed was no less remarkable for its ferocity than for his steadiness in enduring torture. When he was forced under torture to name his accomplices, he cried out in a loud voice, in his native tongue, that they were asking him in vain. Let the torturers stand by and watch: no degree of pain would be great enough to draw the truth from him. Nor was he braver under the lash than in contempt of death, which at that time was not regarded as shameful. When he was dragged to the examination the next day, he broke free from his guards with a sudden lunge, struck his head against a stone, and died at once. A firmer bulwark of empire, therefore, is to be sought in the goodwill of subjects rather than in the terror of arms, against the steadiness of such reckless audacity; this is what Piso neglected, who was exacting the money seized from the public treasury more harshly than the barbarians could bear. Nor, to avoid always searching through old times, are examples lacking from our own age or the age immediately before ours of unforeseen murders of great men. Let us pass over Buckingham, who was too powerful and too favoured by the king of the Britons, when he was commonly represented as the author of a policy that had gone badly for the king. A little fellow of the lowest rank of the common people was found, who, in the royal court itself, in broad daylight, cut him down. Ficarius, seized and manifestly guilty of the deed, said nothing but that his unhappy country could not otherwise be relieved than by removing the author of all its evils. The kings of France, Henry III in his camp and Henry IV in the city and in his carriage, were butchered by fanatics, or men deceived by a false opinion of piety, who plunged steel into their breasts; and this story is celebrated, sung in barbers' shops.

units.la: LVII. Armorum peritia ruentem ferocia ruditatem superat.
units.tr: LVII. Skill in arms overcomes the rash ferocity of an untrained foe.

units.la: Incultas nationes, montium accolas, ruricolas, & in Aquilonem versos populos elegantia eruditis, plana colentibus, urbanis, & Austro obversis bellicosiores esse, vulgo jactatur sententia. Notum illud Senecae: Fortior miles e confragoso venit; segnior est urbanus
units.tr: It is commonly said that uncultivated peoples, dwellers in the mountains, country folk, and the peoples who face the north are more warlike than those who are refined by learning, live on the plains, belong to cities, and face the south. That saying of Seneca is well known: the soldier who comes from rough country is braver; the townsman and the slave-born is softer.

units.la: & verna. Verùm fi ex unà parte ferocia virium cum̄, inscitia, exaltera usus militaris in contentionem ve-niat: sæpiùs his illos inferiores exitu bellorum depre-hendemus. Nelongè abeamus: Poppæus Sabinus, milite fermè Italici generis è cœli plaga molliori, Thracum populos contuderat, qui montium editis, inculti, atq; eo ferociùs agitabant. Nota Græcis & Ro-manis scriptoribus effera Thracum, ipso vocabuli fo-no terribilium, ferocia. Accessit sueta nationi & diu-turna libertas, non levis masculæ virtuti flamma. ne. regibus quidem parere nisi ex libidine soliti, aut si mit-terent auxilia, suos ductores præficere.
