Hac ingenita animi nobilitate freti, ne causa quidem belli Romanis cedere volebant: quæ sæpè vel imbellem in proelio, strenuum, in concurlu victorem efficit. antequam ar-ma inciperent, misere legatos, amicitiam, obsequium q. memoraturos: & mansura hac, fi nullo novo onere tentarentur. sin ut vitiis servitium indiceretur; esse sibi ferrum, & juventutem, & promptum libertati aut ad mortem animum. Accessit ad audaciam loci fiducia, charorum pignorum ut ad rem desperati faci-noris femotio. Simul castella rupibus indita, collatos illuc parentes & conjuges ostentabant, bellum q; impe-ditum, arduum, cruentum minitabantur. Victi ta-men: nec hoc tantum conflictu, sed omnibus ferè proeliis Romano milite Thraces inferiores fuere.
units.tr: But if, on the one side, the fierce strength of untrained men comes into conflict with the practised discipline of war on the other, we shall more often find the former worsted in the outcome of the wars. Let us not go far afield. Poppaeus Sabinus, with a soldier mostly of Italian stock from a milder part of the sky, crushed the peoples of Thrace, who lived in the high mountains, were untaught, and therefore fought more fiercely. The ferocity of the Thracians is noted by Greek and Roman writers, and the very sound of the name is frightening. To this was added the long-standing liberty of the nation, no small spark of manly courage. They were accustomed to obey their kings only when they pleased, or, if they sent auxiliaries, to appoint their own leaders over them. Relying on this native nobility of spirit, they would not yield even on the ground of the war's cause to the Romans. Such confidence often makes a man who is unwarlike in battle a stout fighter and a conqueror in a clash. Before they began to fight, they sent envoys to declare friendship and obedience, and said these would last if they were not burdened with some new load; but if slavery were imposed on them as a vice, they had iron, young men, and a spirit ready for liberty or death. Confidence in the place added to their boldness, as did the removal of their dear pledges, so that they were desperate in their deed. At the same time they showed their parents and wives gathered in the castles set on the cliffs, and threatened a war hindered, hard, and bloody. Yet they were defeated; and not only in this one clash, but in almost all the battles, the Thracians proved inferior to the Roman soldier.

units.la: Quid Thraces, quid rudes montium accolas com-memoro? quasi non clarum habueremus in ipsis Ro-manis exemplum. Longè versus meridiem reductio-res Afri & Numidæ, ardore solis ad periculà belli mi-nus ardentes, Romanos quatuor proeliis pene ad in-ternecionem, duce Hannibale Hamilcaris filio, contu-derunt, Italiam impune multos per annos raptaverunt. Nimirum quia perito sub duce exercitatus armis mi-les, diuturnæ pacis otio fojutum Romanum aggredie-batur. Iidem Romani, jam cladibus ipsis exercitati, eundem Hannibalem sustinuerunt, in Brutios Italiæ angulum compulerunt, Italia post decimum sextum belli annum expulerunt, ignominiosas ad pacis condi-tiones. [?]nes adegerunt. Quid Romanos Gallorum, Celtiberorum, Britannorum, (sæpe etiam Germanorum vi-ctores (cœli enim mollitie solutos, & luxu enervatos, Græcos & Syros & Ægyptios omitto) præter disciplinam, ordinem, & armorum peritiam effecit. Naturæ pro septentrione ferocia, pro Romanis exercitatio. Vicit ferociam exercitatio. Quid patrum memoria paucis Hispanorum legionibus Belgium universum, libertatis improspere repetiti clarum exemplum, subjecit? quid postea Mauritio duce Batavos, & Batavorum socios, erexit? Vicit illic exercitatio, istic accedens promptitudini naturæ exercitatio. Quid est quod Scythas & Sarmatas, ferocia ingenii indomitos, Gef[?]-mani, si in unum consentiant, non exhorrescant? Eadem, quæ Romanos quondam ad mundi imperium judice Vegetio evexit, armorum dextera tractatio. Concludo igitur verbis, quem modo laudavi, Vegetii: In omni proelio, non tam multitudo & virtus indocta, quam ars & exercitium solent præstare victoriam.
units.tr: Why do I mention the Thracians, the rough dwellers of the mountains? As if we did not have a clear example among the Romans themselves. Far to the south, the Africans and Numidians, more restrained, less burning in the heat of the sun for the dangers of war, under the leadership of Hannibal, son of Hamilcar, crushed the Romans in four battles almost to annihilation, and for many years plundered Italy with impunity. Surely this was because the soldier, trained in arms under a skilled leader, attacked a Roman who had grown soft in the idleness of long peace. The same Romans, now trained by their own defeats, withstood the same Hannibal, drove him into the Bruttian corner of Italy, expelled him from Italy after the sixteenth year of the war, and forced him to accept shameful terms of peace. What made the Romans victors over the Gauls, Celtiberians and Britons (and often over the Germans)? I say nothing of the Greeks, Syrians and Egyptians, who were loosened by the softness of their climate and enervated by luxury. It was discipline, order and skill in arms. Nature gave ferocity to the north; exercise gave it to the Romans. Exercise overcame ferocity. What of the memory of our fathers, when a few Spanish legions subdued the whole of Belgium, a clear example of an unsuccessful attempt to win back liberty? What later, under the leadership of Maurice, raised up the Batavians and their allies? There exercise conquered, and here exercise, added to the readiness of nature, prevailed. What is there that the Scythians and Sarmatians, untamed in the ferocity of their character, would not dread, if the Germans came together in one? The same thing that once raised the Romans to rule the world, according to Vegetius: the skilled handling of arms. I therefore conclude with the words of Vegetius, whom I have just praised: In every battle, it is not so much numbers and untaught courage as art and practice that usually secure victory.

units.la: LVIII.
units.tr: LVIII.

units.la: Non est minus antequam armis bellum gerendum.
units.tr: Waging war before resorting to arms is no less needful.

units.la: Nec majestati principis populi derogat, cedere tempo-ribus, dum vires contrahantur. Sabinum, donec exercitus in unum conduceret, datis mutuis responsis, dum Pomponius Labeo è Moesia cum legione, rex Rhoe-metalces cum auxiliis popularium, qui fidem non mutaverant, venire: addita præsenti copia, ad hostem pergit. Non est imperatoribus pudori, blanditiis prius quam armis motis indomitum hostem debellare. Pu-gnam in diem detractantem, mite responsum reddere, victoriæ ex cunctatione certum, latius est; quam inu[?]-tili pudore insultationes non ferentem, pugnandi in-tempestivo ardore, hosti victoriam tradere. Nihil vel a natura, vel a civili ratione, momento ad perfectionem ducitur. In terræ cultu arationem præcedit stercoratio, sequitur arationem frumenti satio, sationem occatio, culmo fovente terræ matrice in aristam spitato, & ad maturitatem perducto; prius theretidis, percipiendis, deinde condendis, tandem fruendis frui- tibus agricolae dies impendunt. Sic in civili, sic in bel-li negotio, nemo victoriam ab exitu, omnes qui sapiunt à principio, armorum apparatu, auspicantur.
units.tr: It does not detract from the majesty of a prince to yield to circumstances while his forces are being gathered. Sabinus, while the army was being brought together, gave mutual replies, until Pomponius Labeo came from Moesia with a legion and King Rhoemetalces with auxiliaries from his own people, who had not changed their loyalty; then, with the added strength at hand, he set out against the enemy. It is no shame for commanders to subdue an unbroken enemy by soft words before moving to arms. To put off a battle and return a mild answer, sure of victory through delay, is more honourable than, out of a useless sense of shame, not bearing insults and handing victory to the enemy through an ill-timed zeal for fighting. Nothing, whether by nature or by civil reason, is brought to perfection in a moment. In the cultivation of the land, ploughing is preceded by manuring, and sowing of grain follows the ploughing, and harrowing follows the sowing; when the earth as mother nurtures the stalk so that it shoots up into an ear and is brought to ripeness, the farmer spends his days first on reaping, then on gathering, then on storing, and finally on enjoying the fruits. So in civil affairs and in the business of war, no one who has sense looks for victory from the outcome; all who are wise begin from the beginning, with the preparation of arms.

units.la: LIX.
units.tr: LIX.

units.la: Confusioni nox obnoxia.
units.tr: Night exposes one to confusion.

units.la: Ideoque nisi desperatis in rebus, aut omnibus tutò provisis, nullâ aggressiò, excursatio, ac ne populatio quidem, noctu tentandâ. Thracibus auxiliaribus à Sa-bino permissum vastare, urere, trahere praedas, dum po-pulatio lucem intra sisteretur, noctemq, in castris tutam vigilem capessèrent. à proeliis vero multò magis bonus dux noctu abstinebit, qui quidem disciplina moderatum agmen ducet. Qui vero vagas cohortes, ordine & jussu regi nescias ductabit, qui locorum pe-ritiæ confidet, is noctem pro fe arbitrabitur. Ultimam etiam necessitatem, aut summam rei gerendæ occa-fionem, fionem, excipio. Sic Platæenfes à Thebanis obsessi, noctúrna castrorum hostilium adortione, plerique perrumpentes evaserunt. Sic Turefis Thrax contra huncipfum Sabinum, ad erumpendum noctem operi-zar. Sic L. Marcius binâ Carthaginiensium in Hifpa-nia castra, geminâ contra Scipiones victoriâ secura, noctu adortus, rem Romanam restituit. Noctem pro fe Pompejus contra Mithridatem, Primus Antonius contra Vitellianos arripuit: quibus Luna pro muni-mento umbras corporum majores efficiendo, irritá hostium tela, umbras pro corporibus petentia, effecit; Sed extra has necessitatis aut opportunitatis exceptio-nes, noctis arbitrio non temere res belli committendæ: Miserabile nocturnæ cladis Atheniensium, Syracusas obsidentium, theatrum Thucydides libro VII. expan-dit.
units.tr: Therefore, unless affairs are desperate or everything has been safely provided for, no attack, sortie, or even raid should be attempted by night. Sabinus allowed his Thracian auxiliaries to lay waste, burn, and carry off booty, provided the raiding was confined to daylight, and that they spent the night safe and watchful in camp. A good commander will abstain from battles at night far more, especially one who leads a well-ordered force under discipline. But he who leads wandering cohorts that do not know how to be governed by order and the commander's command, and who trusts in his knowledge of the terrain, will regard the night as his own. I make an exception for final necessity, or for the supreme opportunity of the action. Thus the Plataeans, besieged by the Thebans, escaped by a night assault on the enemy camp, most of them breaking through. Thus the Thracian Turesis, against this same Sabinus, awaited the night in order to break out. Thus Lucius Marcius, after a double victory against the Carthaginian camps in Spain, attacked by night with confidence against the Scipios and restored the Roman cause. Pompey seized the night for himself against Mithridates, and Primus Antonius against the Vitellians; for the moon, by making the shadows of bodies larger as a protection, rendered the enemy's weapons ineffective, since they aimed at shadows instead of bodies. But apart from these exceptions of necessity or opportunity, the matters of war should not be rashly entrusted to the judgement of night. Thucydides, in book VII, lays out the pitiable spectacle of the nocturnal disaster of the Athenians who were besieging Syracuse.

units.la: LX.
units.tr: LX.

units.la: Comessationes à castris præcidenda.
units.tr: Drinking parties must be cut off from the camp.

units.la: Nox. Non modo quod vires & animos militares enervant, obsequium erga duces & tribunos exuunt; sed etiam hosti occasionem invadendi patefaciunt. Quod a Thracum maniplulis, qui Romanis in castris mercabant, non observatum versi in luxum, & rapti opulentia, omittere stationes, lascivia epularum, aut somno & vino procumbere. Igitur hostes incuria eorum tomperta, duo agmina parant. &c. Quibusdam pro strategemate fuit, vini ingentem apparatum hosti urgenti objicere, & praeda se injurgitantem pecorum in modum interimere. Vino abstinendum esse Plato secundo de Legibus docet, militi tempore militiae, servo, magistratui, navis gubernatori, judici, consiliario, liberis operam daturo. De militiae abstinentia verba sunt Platonis: Πρεσβεύμενον ἐν τῇ Καρχηδονίων πόλει, μὴ πίνειν μηδὲν ἐπὶ ῥεῖθρον μεταξὺ ταῦτα. ἀλλ᾽ ὑδροποσίᾳ συνεχῶς τὸν χρόνον ἀπολαύειν. Legi Carthaginiensium subscriberem, neminem unquam in castris hanc potionem gustare, sed omne militiae tempus omnes aquam potare. Quod Platonis judicium nō de vino tantum, sed omni potu inebriante, & quicquid militem incuria resolvit, accipi velim. Germanos prisco aevo vini potum ignoravisse, consessu traditur. At apud eos diem noctemque potando continuare, nulli probro dabatur. Quae animorum soluție non raro eos hosti, temporibus insidiantibus oppor-tunos fecit. De Germanico Drusi filio: ventum ad vicos Marsorum, & circumdata stationes, stratis etiam tum per cubilia, propterque mensas, nullo metu, non antepositis vigiliis. adeo cuncta incuria disjecta erant neq; belli timor: ac ne pax quidem nisi languida & soluta inter temulentos. Quae commessandi licentia magnae Germanis cladis, Romano victoriae initium dedit.
units.tr: Night. Not only do they weaken soldiers' strength and spirit and strip away their obedience to commanders and tribunes, but they also open the way for the enemy to attack. The Thracian maniples, who were trading with the Romans inside the camp, did not notice this: turning to luxury and carried away by wealth, they abandoned their posts through the wantonness of feasting, and collapsed in sleep and wine. Therefore the enemy, discovering their carelessness, prepare two columns, etc. Some commanders have used as a stratagem the offering of a huge supply of wine to an advancing enemy, and then cut down the foe as he rushes in greedily, like cattle. Plato, in the second book of the Laws, teaches that wine must be avoided by the soldier during his service, and by the slave, the magistrate, the ship's helmsman, the judge, the councillor, and anyone engaged in public business. Plato's words about abstinence in the field are these: Πρεσβεύμενον ἐν τῇ Καρχηδονίων πόλει, μὴ πίνειν μηδὲν ἐπὶ ῥεῖθρον μεταξὺ ταῦτα. ἀλλ᾽ ὑδροποσίᾳ συνεχῶς τὸν χρόνον ἀπολαύειν. [Carthaginian law (as I would put it): that no one should ever drink this drink in camp, but that all should drink only water through the whole time of service.] I wish Plato's judgment to be understood not only of wine but of every intoxicating drink, and of whatever relaxes a soldier through carelessness. It is recorded by writers that the Germans of old were ignorant of drinking wine. Yet among them to drink continuously day and night was no disgrace. This loosening of their spirits often made them easy targets for an enemy who lay in wait for the right moment. Of Germanicus, the son of Drusus: They came to the villages of the Marsi, and the outposts were surrounded while they were still stretched out in their beds and beside their tables, with no fear and no sentries set before them. So completely had all things been thrown into disorder by carelessness, and by no fear of war; even peace was lax and loose among the drunkards. This license for drinking bouts gave the Romans the beginning of victory and the Germans a great slaughter.

units.la: LXI. Extremum civilium malorum discordia.
units.tr: LXI. The final evil of civil strife is discord.

units.la: Nec civilium tantum, id est, togatarum, sed & caftrenfium. Thraces ab hoste obsidente, ab aquartâ inopia, pabuli armentorum egestate, odore pereun- tium premebantur. Sed nullare magis, quàm fenten- tiarum dissensione, fatigabantur. Rebusque turbatis malum extremum discordia accessit: bis deditionem, aliis mortem, & mutuos interfe itus parantibus. & erant quinon inultum exitium, sed eruptionem suade- rent. Igitur aut hosti discordiam callidè injiciunt, aut inventam in opportunitatem vertunt, qui temporum sunt periti duces. Contra à civibus, à castris hoc venè- num omni ope, qui sapiunt, amoliuntur.
units.tr: Not only civil matters, that is, those of the gown, but also military ones. The Thracians were pressed by the besieging enemy, by lack of water, by a shortage of fodder for their herds, and by the stench of the dying. Yet they were worn down by nothing so much as by disagreement over opinions. With affairs already in confusion, the final evil of discord was added: some were arranging a surrender, others death, and others mutual slaughter. And there were those who urged not a destruction without vengeance but a sally. Therefore either the enemy cunningly sows discord, or skilled leaders, who know the times, turn whatever discord they find to their advantage. On the other hand, wise men by every means drive this poison away from both the citizens and the camp.

units.la: LXII. Tiberianæ aulæ est, immolando oc- cidere.
units.tr: LXII. It is characteristic of Tiberius' court to kill by way of sacrifice.

units.la: Augusti, cujus mortem ægrè exspectaverat, poste- ros, Germanicum, Agrippinam, communes utriusque liberos, necnon clientes & amicos, Tiberius infecta- batur. Nihilominus victimas illi, tanquam Deo, cæ- debatur, aras & templa statuebat. Quod ei Agrippina, inter sacrificandum deprehenso, exprobrat. Non ejus- dem ait esse maftare divo Augusto victimas, & posteros ejus insectari. non in effigies mutas divinum spiritum transfusum: sed imaginem veram cœlesti sanguine ortâm intelligere discrimen, suscipere sordes. Interim inmentem aphorismus revocetur, Multum in aulâ gratiæ, plus aliorum contumeliæ dari, quod quin in- telligeret, non adeò obesæ naris fuit Agrippina. Fraftra Pulchram prascribi, cui sola exitii causa fit, quòd Agrippinam stulte prorsus ad cultum dilegerit, oblita Sofia ob eadem affli&a. Quod di&tum adeò pupugit Tiberium, ut raram occulti pectoris vocem elicuerit: ideo ladi, quia non regnaret. Nam regni quædam imaæ go est, multum in aulâ gratiâ & autoritate posse, alios in tutelam suam recipere. Quo regno Agrippina excidebat, sobrinâ ejus ad capitis causam dicendam in jus vocâ catâ.
units.tr: Tiberius was troubled by Augustus' descendants: Germanicus, Agrippina, their common children, and also their clients and friends, whose deaths he had reluctantly awaited. Nevertheless, victims were sacrificed to him as to a god, and he set up altars and temples. Agrippina caught him at the sacrifice and rebuked him for it. It is not the same thing, she said, to slaughter victims for the deified Augustus and to harass his descendants. The divine spirit was not poured into mute effigies. To recognise the true image, born of heavenly blood, is to undergo a distinction; it is to take on filth. Meanwhile, let the aphorism be recalled: at court there is much favour, but more insult is given to others. Agrippina was not so dull-nosed as not to understand this. In vain is Pulchra proscribed, whose only cause of ruin is that she foolishly chose Agrippina for her devotion, forgetting that Sosia had been afflicted for the same things. This saying stung Tiberius so deeply that it drew from him a rare utterance of his hidden heart: she was hurt because she was not reigning. For there is a certain image of kingship: to have great favour and authority at court, and to take others under one's protection. Agrippina fell from this kingdom, and her niece was summoned before the court to answer a capital charge.

units.la: Est
units.tr: There is

units.la: LXIII.
units.tr: LXIII.

units.la: Est & bonarum artium abusus.
units.tr: There is also an abuse of the liberal arts.

units.la: Qui vel in prava applicatione, vel in diuturna retentione perspicitur. De eloquentia in Domitio Afro ad res minus honestas applicatione: tapeffendis[?] arcu-sationibus, aut reos tutando, prosperiore eloquentia quàm morum fama fuit. crudele enim est, miserorum accusandorum suppliciis pasci: & rursus facinorosos lingua venali defendere, iniquum. De fera ad extremam aetatem usurpatione: nisi quod aetas extrema multum etiam eloquentia demsit, dum fessa mente retinet silentii impatientiam. Non meminerat ille Versus Horatiani:
units.tr: This is seen both in their perverse application and in their long retention. On the application of eloquence to less honourable ends in Domitius Afer: by hurling accusations, or by defending the guilty, his eloquence was more successful than his reputation for character. For it is cruel to feed on the punishment of wretches one has accused, and equally unjust to defend criminals with a hireling tongue. On the use of an old age that persists too long: except that his extreme age has also taken away much of his eloquence, since his weary mind keeps an impatience of silence. He did not remember that verse of Horace:

units.la: Solve senescentem maturè sanus[?] equum, ne Peccet ad extremum ridendus, & illa ducat.
units.tr: Unharness the horse while it is still sound and growing old, lest at the end it stumble, a laughing-stock, and drag its flanks.

units.la: Cicero tamen, non pravus oratoriae facultatis judex, vel apud eum Cato Major, in diversum sensum[?] abit. Orator, metuo, ne languescat senectute. est enim mu-nus ejus non ingenii solùm, sed laterum etiam & viri-um. omninò canorum illud in voce splendescit etiam nescio quo pacto in senectute: quod equidem adhuc non amisi: & videtis annos meos. sed tamen est decorus senis sermo quietus, & remissus; facitque persaepè ipsa sibi audientiam diserti senis compta & mitis oratio.
units.tr: Yet Cicero, no poor judge of oratorical ability, or Cato the Elder with him, takes a different view. "An orator, I fear, may grow languid with age; for his office depends not only on talent but also on lungs and strength. Indeed, that musical quality in the voice somehow grows more brilliant in old age, which I have not yet lost, as you see from my years. Still, a quiet and restrained manner of speech becomes an old man, and a mild and measured delivery often wins him a hearing for itself."

units.la: LXIV.
units.tr: LXIV.

units.la: Silentium pro denegatione.
units.tr: Silence as a refusal.

units.la: Quod Germani, aulicae consuetudinis non impe-riti, his verbis efferunt: Keine Antwort ist auch ein Antwort. Agrippina, corporis morbo implicata, cum viseret eam Caesar, in preces, ut videbatur, non iniquas effundebatur: subveniret solitudini, daret maritum habilem adhuc juventam sibi: neque aliud probiis, quàm ex matrimonio solatium. Quod illa non tam fortassis domesticae solitudinis taedio, quàm domi-nandi aviditate, petiit. Vidua enim, virili ope desolata, nullas in rep. partes factura erat. Maritum vero non degeneris animi nacta, violento ipsa ingenio, & ex Augusti domo, imperio non indigna videretur. Sed Cafar non ignarus quantum ex Rep. peteretur: ne tamen offensionis aut metus manifestus foret, fine responso, quanquam infi antem, reliquit. Plura, de hac illustris matrimonii cautione, in Arcanis Regnorum reperies.
units.tr: The Germans, who are not inexperienced in court custom, express this in the words: No answer is also an answer. Agrippina, caught up in a bodily illness, when Caesar came to visit her, poured out what seemed to be not unreasonable requests: he should relieve her loneliness and give her a husband, since her youth was still fit, and that for good men there is no comfort other than marriage. She sought this perhaps less from weariness of her domestic solitude than from a greed for power. For a widow, bereft of male support, would have no part in public affairs. But finding a husband of no mean spirit, and herself of a violent temper and from the house of Augustus, she might seem not unworthy of empire. Caesar, however, was not unaware of how much was being sought from the state. So that no clear sign of offence or fear might appear, he left the matter without an answer, though not without suspicion. You will find more about this distinguished caution in marriage in the Secrets of Kingdoms.

units.la: LXV.
units.tr: LXV.

units.la: Suspicio metus & odii genetrix.
units.tr: Suspicion, the mother of fear and hatred.

units.la: Pravum inimicorum genus, qui specie amicitiæ suspiciones, qui odia animis imprimunt. Præterquam enim quod in angorem eos frustra conjiciunt, aliorum in eos odia non obscura conciant. Qui enim fe alteri suspectum esse novit, non poterit eum amicis oculis ex animo intueri. Hoc ad deprimendam Agrippinam compendio, cum nimis iracundia lentus Tiberius videretur, Sejanus grassabatur. Mœrentem dam altius perculit, immissis qui per speciem amicitiæ monerent, paratum ei venenum, vitandas soceri epulas. Qui diffidendum esse suadent; & hos esse prudentiæ nervos: non malè omninò præcipere videntur: dum ipsi diffidentiæ modus adhibeatur, ad quem modum hoc etiam spectabit, ut quibus fidendum fit aut diffidendum, dicernamus. Inter quos ii primi aliquando sunt, qui metum nobis, qui suspicionem ingenerant. Si autores cum re Agrippina examinaffet, non tam faciles inimici satellitibus aures præbuisset, aut metum epularum Tiberianarum saltem aliqua dissimulatione texisset. Atque illa simulationum ne-scia, cum propter discumberet, non vultu aut sermone flecti, nullos attingere cibos. Quæ cibi omnis abstentio, quin ab occulto animi affectu proficisceretur, diu latere Tiberium non potuit, quo acrius experiretur, poma ut erant apposita laudans, nurui suæ manu tradi-dit. quo hic fe verteret Agrippina? quo vel ore formidatos cibos attingeret, vel velamento metum tegeret? ausa ex eo suspicio Agrippina, & intacta ores,[?] feruis tramifit. mortem, ut arbitrabatur, effugit: in acrius principis iracundi odium, id quod Sejanus vo-lebat, incidit, qui ad matrem obversus, non mirum, [?]t, si quid severius in eam statuisset, à qua veneficii insimularetur. Cui enim non tantum ut inimici formidamur, sed ut deterrimi mortalium venefici suspectamur, non potest erga eum integra amicitia perstare.
units.tr: There is a wicked kind of enemy who, under the appearance of friendship, plants suspicions and hatreds in men's minds. For apart from the fact that they cast their victims into anxiety for no reason, they stir up no small hatred of others against them. For one who knows that he is suspected by another cannot regard him with friendly eyes. Sejanus was busy with this shortcut to crush Agrippina, since Tiberius seemed too slow in anger. He struck her deeply in her grief, sending people who, under the guise of friendship, warned her that poison was prepared for her, and that she should avoid her father-in-law's banquets. They advise her to distrust, and they seem to give fine advice in saying that this is the sinew of prudence, provided a measure of distrust is applied; and this measure too will look to this, that we discern whom we should trust or distrust. Among these, those are first who sometimes instil fear and suspicion in us. Had Agrippina examined these informers closely, she would not have lent such ready ears to the emperor's henchmen, or at least she would have covered her fear of the Tiberian banquets with some pretence. But she, ignorant of dissimulation, when she reclined beside him, neither softened her face nor her speech, and touched no food. Since this total abstinence from food came from a hidden feeling of her mind, Tiberius could not long remain ignorant of it. To test her more sharply, while praising the fruit as it had been set out, he handed it to his daughter-in-law with his own hand. What could Agrippina do here? How could she either touch the dreaded food with her lips or hide her fear with a veil? Thus Agrippina, having dared to refuse it and leaving it untouched, escaped death, as she supposed, but fell into the more bitter hatred of the angry prince, which was what Sejanus wanted. He, turning against her mother, said it was no wonder if he had decided on something harsher against her, by whom he was being accused of poisoning. For when a man is feared not merely as an enemy but suspected as the most vile poisoner of mortals, an unbroken friendship cannot persist with him.

units.la: Inde rumor, parari exitium: neq; id imperatorem palam audere, secretum ad perpetrandum quæri. Præter aphorismum frontispicio præscriptum, quàm lubrica sit inter corvos, columbino colore nitentes, quàm in senticeto, quàm in præcipiti[?] posita vita, homini præsertim non satis cauto & antiquorum morum, monemur.
units.tr: Hence a rumour that destruction was being prepared: that the emperor did not dare to do it openly, and that a secret means was sought to carry it out. Apart from the aphorism prefixed to the frontispiece, we are warned how slippery life is among crows that shine with a dove-like colour, how it lies among briars and on a precipice, especially for a man who is not cautious enough and who keeps to the old ways.

units.la: LXVI.
units.tr: LXVI.

units.la: Merita tempore, non facti magnitudine, æstimantur.
units.tr: Merits are judged by the time, not by the size of the deed.

units.la: Vera quidem beneficiorum æstimatio ex animo sumitur: sed animus ipse temporum necessitate dijudicatur. Inter undecim Asiæ civitates de templi statuendi impetrando privilegio, arbitro Tiberio, certabatur. Quædam vetustate generis, aut terrarum fertili vel firmo situ; aliæ, quod hic præponderabat, studio in populum Romanum nitebantur. Ex his, temporum ratione consider ata, Smyrnæi cæteris præferebantur. Duplex eorum studii, factis declarati genus: unum honoris & cultus, alterum auxilii & munificentiæ. De cultu urbis Romanæ à Smyrnæis iactabatur: primos templum urbi Roma statuisse, M. Porcio consule, magnis quidem jam Romani populi rebus, nondum tamen ad summum elatis, stante adhuc Punica urbe, & validis per Asiam regibus. Romana potentia modum vulgarem egressa, crebra ea adulatio: sed quæ fortunæ, non loco, non ex animo dabatur. Smyrnæi seu affectu, seu divinatione futuræ magnitudinis vincebant. Auxilium navali copia, non modo externa ad bella, sed quæ in Italia tolerabantur, mensurabatur. Quorum pretium necessitate temporum, populo Romano domi laborante, venibat. Sed simul tempore si-mul materia præfulgebat, quod Sullano exercitu, aspe-ritate hyemis & penuria vestium, laborante, & à Smyr[?]ñzis prompte adjuto, adferebatur: cum id Smyrnæis in concionem nunciatum foret, omnes qui aflabant detraxisse corporis tegmina, Romani[?] legionibus mi-ffe. Premebatur respublica Romana ab occidente Sertoriano per Hispaniam belli incendio, ab oriente Mithridatica armorum (ex vitia), & sociorum defectio-ne, domi penuria nummorum, & civilis belli nondum sedato ulcere. Tempora veros amicos a fictis, hostes à sociis discernebant. Ita rogati sententiam patres, Smyrnæos pratulerunt.
units.tr: A true estimate of benefits is indeed taken from the intention, but the intention itself is judged by the needs of the time. When eleven cities of Asia were competing for the privilege of erecting a temple, with Tiberius as arbiter, some relied on the antiquity of their stock, or on their fertile land or secure position, and others, which was the decisive factor, on their zeal for the Roman people. Of these, when the circumstances of the time were considered, the Smyrnaeans were preferred to the rest. Their zeal showed itself in two kinds of deeds: one of honour and worship, the other of help and generosity. As to worship of the city of Rome, the Smyrnaeans boasted that they had been the first to set up a temple to the city of Rome, in the consulship of Marcus Porcius, when the affairs of the Roman people were already great, though not yet raised to the highest point, while the city of Carthage still stood and kings powerful in Asia were still in existence. Roman power had long since passed the ordinary measure, so such flattery was common; but it was given to fortune, not to the place, and not from the heart. The Smyrnaeans surpassed the rest either through affection or through foresight of the future greatness of Rome. As to help, it was measured by naval strength, not only for foreign wars but for those waged in Italy itself. Their aid was valued according to the needs of the time, when the Roman people were struggling at home. At the same moment the matter also shone out, because when the army of Sulla was suffering from the harshness of winter and a lack of clothing, and was promptly helped by the Smyrnaeans, it was reported to them in an assembly that all those who breathed had stripped off their own coverings and sent them to the Roman legions. The Roman commonwealth was pressed on the west by the fire of Sertorius's war in Spain, on the east by the armed power of Mithridates, by the defection of allies, by a shortage of money at home, and by the civil war, whose sore was not yet healed. The times distinguished true friends from false, and enemies from allies. So when the fathers were asked for their opinion, they preferred the Smyrnaeans.

units.la: Quæcunque homines homini tribuunt, ad eum aut benevolentiæ gra-gendum, atque honestandum: aut benevolentiæ gra-tia faciunt, cum aliqua de causa quempiam diligunt; aut honoris, fi cujus virtutem suspiciunt, & fi quem dignum fortuna quam amplissima putant; aut cui fi-dem habent, & bene rebus suis consulere arbitrantur: aut cujus opes metuunt; aut contra à quibus aliquid exspectant, ut cum reges, populares ve homines largi-tiones aliquas proponunt: aut postremo pretio, aut mercede ducuntur. Verba sunt Ciceronis 2. offic. Smyrnæi & benevolentia ducti videbantur, & honori populi Romani id tribuisse, nec non fidem Romani nominis adoravisse. Digni igitur, qui factis ex animo pensitatis, inter amicos amicissimi, in sociorum gregè honoratissimi haberentur.
units.tr: Whatever benefits men bestow on another man, they bestow either to win his goodwill and to do him honour, because they love someone for some reason; or out of respect, when they admire someone's virtue, or think someone worthy of the greatest possible fortune; or to someone whom they trust and believe will look well after their interests; or they fear his power; or, on the other hand, they expect something from those to whom they give, as when kings or popular leaders offer some largesses; or, finally, they are led by reward or payment. These are the words of Cicero, De Officiis 2. The Smyrnaeans seemed to have been moved both by goodwill, and to have granted this to the honour of the Roman people, and also to have venerated the good faith of the Roman name. They were therefore worthy, since their deeds had been weighed by their intention, to be held the dearest of friends among friends and the most honoured in the company of allies.

units.la: LXVII. Majestati principis à corporis gratia commendatio accedit.
units.tr: LXVII. Commendation to the majesty of the prince is added from the grace of the body.

units.la: Et à deformitate, contemptus, odium, detrimen-tum. Quare oculis hominum fe subducunt, qui vitium formæ in fe deprehendunt. Inter diuturnæ Titerii absentiæ causas, qui undecim vitæ postremis annis nunquam Romam rediit, & hanc commemorant: Erant qui crederent, in senectute quoq; corporis habitu pudori fuisse, quippe illi præ gravitate incurva proceritas, nudus capillo vertex, ulcerosa faciei, ac pleni rumq; medicaminibus interflua. Galbæ quoque fe-nilis macilento corpore tenuitas vilipendium, & ex eo
units.tr: From deformity come contempt, hatred and loss. That is why those who find a bodily defect in themselves withdraw from people's eyes. Among the reasons for Tiberius's long absence, which lasted through the last eleven years of his life, during which he never returned to Rome, some also cite this: there were those who believed that even in old age his bodily appearance was a source of shame, since he had a stooped, bent tallness, a head bare of hair, and a face covered with sores and oozing with medicated plasters. In Galba's case too, the thinness of an aged, emaciated body brought him contempt, and from that contempt his ruin came quickly.

units.la: exitium, maturavit. Neronem contra quamvis mori-bus foedissimum, juventus & procera corporis erectio, gratum plebi Romanae, gratum militibus effecerat.
units.tr: Nero, on the other hand, though most foul in his morals, had won the favour of the Roman plebs and the soldiers through his youth and his tall, upright bearing.

units.la: LXVIII.
units.tr: LXVIII.

units.la: Altera à comitatu commendatio.
units.tr: Another commendation is from the retinue.

units.la: Comitatus non a numero, sed dignitate imperatori legendus. Profectio arto comitatu fuit. Dignitas ab honorum functione, legum peritia, ordine, genere, eruditione quaerenda. Unus senator consulatu functus, Coccejus Nerva, cui legum peritia, eques Romanus, frater Sejanum, ex illustribus Curtius Atticus, cateri liberalibus studiis praditi, fermè Graeci, quorum sermonibus levaretur. Supra omnia fortunae ac animi munera mores, proprium hominis bonum, in comitatu spectandi.
units.tr: The retinue of the emperor is to be chosen not by number but by dignity. The departure was with a small retinue. Dignity is to be sought from the discharge of offices, from skill in law, from rank, from birth, and from learning. One senator who had held the consulship, Coccejus Nerva, skilled in law; a Roman knight, the brother of Sejanus; from the illustrious, Curtius Atticus; and others endowed with liberal studies, mostly Greeks, by whose conversation he might be relieved. Above all things, in the retinue one must look for the gifts of fortune and of mind, and for character, which is man's proper good.

units.la: Nimis aulico gregi scholasticus, aut sacerdotalis, M. Aurelius videtur, qui viris tantum eruditione & vita probatis in consortium adhibitis, blasphemos, gulosos, libidinosos, avaros, iracundos, invidos, arrogantes ab aula sua removit. Quam vellem hunc gentilem, caeterā in superstitione sua virum pium, Christiani imperatores imitarentur! Saltem, si virtutem ipsi non magnificiunt, autoritati imperii melius consulerent.
units.tr: M. Aurelius seems too much a schoolman, or priest-like, for a court company; he admitted to his fellowship only men approved for learning and life, and removed from his court the blasphemers, the gluttons, the lecherous, the greedy, the wrathful, the envious and the arrogant. How I wish that Christian emperors would imitate this heathen man, a pious man in his own superstition! At least, if they do not esteem virtue itself, they would better look after the authority of the empire.

units.la: Superbia enim tumetes imperio accipiendo, & promptè jussis exequendis, non sunt idonei. Invidi dissensionibus, & mutuis obtrectationibus, nec non impedimentis objiciendis, aulae negotia perturbant. Iracundi vel verberum & caedis promptitudine maculam aulae aspergunt, vel subditos a principe ob saevitiam ministrorum alienant. Avari aut aerarium peculatu perfringunt, aut tributorum gravitate odium civium irritant. Libidinosi, tanquam è sociis princeps nosca-tur, ignominia domum imperatoriam traducunt. Gulosi ventri servientes, consiliis dandis & omni ministerio, quod dexteritatem requirat, sunt inhabiles. Blasphemi, qui Dei majestatem non verentur, ne de rege quidem suo magnificè sentient. Vides igitur, ut morū probitas non honestati tantum & aulæ decoro, veríum & utilitati serviat?
units.tr: For men puffed up with pride are not fit to receive power or to carry out orders promptly. The envious, by quarrels, mutual disparagement, and the throwing up of obstacles, disturb the business of the court. The wrathful, either by their readiness to beat and kill, stain the court's reputation, or they alienate the subjects from the prince because of the cruelty of his ministers. The greedy either break open the treasury by embezzlement, or by the heaviness of taxes they stir up hatred among the citizens. The lecherous, since the prince is known by his companions, bring disgrace upon the imperial household. The gluttonous, slaves to their belly, are unfit for giving counsel and for every service that requires dexterity. The blasphemers, who do not fear the majesty of God, will not think well even of their own king. Do you see, then, how the uprightness of morals serves not only honour and the dignity of the court, but also truth and usefulness?

units.la: LXIX.
units.tr: LXIX.

units.la: Vatum prædictio multis ambagibus involvitur.
units.tr: The prediction of seers is wrapped in many ambiguities.

units.la: Genus hoc divinationúm, positum incredulorum perfuafione, plus admirationis ex aliquo fortuito eventu, quàm certitudinis à ratione habet. Vaticiniis, auguriis, oraculis prædictionem ex astrorum motu & positu non pauci inter eruditos vanitate adjungunt. A quorum sententia nec Tacitus noster abhorret.
units.tr: This kind of divination, resting on the persuasion of unbelievers, draws more wonder from some chance event than certainty from reason. Not a few learned men add to oracles, auguries and prophecies a prediction drawn from the motion and position of the stars, and they do so with vanity. Our Tacitus does not dissent from their opinion.

units.la: Ferebant periti cœlestium, ius motibus fiderum excessisse Romá Tiberium, ut reditus illi negaretur. unde exitii causa multis fuit, properum finem vitæ conjectantibus, vulgàtibus, neq; enim tam incredibilem causam providebant, ut undecim per annos libens patria careret. Mox patuit brevé confinium artis & falsi, verāq; quàm obscuris tegerentur. nam in urbem non refrefurum, haut forté dictum: caterorum nescii egére. Periti illi fiderum nec longam Tiberii absentiam prævidebant, & instantem vitæ finem falsò augurabantur. Inde quis forté collegerit, & idquod de reditu ei negato veri prodiderunt, magis vatum more instinctu, aut fortui-ta eventione, quam scientiæ certa ratione divinaffe, Antiquiores, nisi Chaldæos forté & Ægyptios exci-pias, astrorum non ita periti, ad raptus animi, ad ora-culorum obscuros nexus, ad cæca vaticinia converte-bantur. Quibus quantum veri aut falsi infit, Athe-nienfes omnium maxima Sicula clade didicerunt. Qua non uno nuncio, præter omnium exspectationem, au-dita, ... inquit gravissimus autor Thucidides, principio libri Octavi i.e. irascebantur ariolis atque vaticinis, deni-que omnibus qui fanatico furore in ipsum capien-dæ Siciliæ ipsos conjecerant.
units.tr: Astrologers reported that by the motions of the stars it had been decreed at Rome that Tiberius should not return. This became the cause of death for many, who guessed that his end of life was near and spread the rumour; for they did not foresee so incredible a cause, that he would gladly do without his fatherland for eleven years. Soon it became plain how narrow the border is between art and falsehood, and how truth is hidden under obscure things. For the words that he would not return to the city were not spoken by chance; they were said by men ignorant of the rest. Those star-gazers foresaw neither Tiberius' long absence, and falsely predicted the imminent end of his life. Hence someone might gather that what they truly declared about the denial of his return was spoken more in the manner of seers, by impulse or chance event, than divined by the sure reasoning of knowledge. The older people, unless perhaps you except the Chaldeans and Egyptians, who were not so skilled in the stars, turned to ecstasies of the mind, to the obscure links of oracles and to blind prophecies. How much truth or falsehood these contain, the Athenians learned from their greatest disaster, the Sicilian one. When that news was heard, not from a single messenger, beyond all expectation, says the most weighty author Thucydides at the beginning of the eighth book, they raged against the soothsayers and the prophets, and finally against all who, with frantic fury, had urged them to seize Sicily itself.

units.la: Obscu-
units.tr: Obscu-

units.la: LXX.
units.tr: LXX.

units.la: Obscuro limite vera amicitia a simulata separatur.
units.tr: True friendship is separated from feigned friendship by an obscure boundary.

units.la: Nam,si sermonis blanditias in lancem accersas; plus vero amico adulator pollet. Si facta quaedam consulas: & hic personatus amicus posteriora non feret.
units.tr: For if you weigh the flatteries of speech in the scales, the flatterer carries more weight than a friend. If you consider deeds, this friend in a mask will not hold out to the end.

units.la: Oblatum Cæsari anceps periculum, auxit vana rumoris: prabuitq; ipsi materiem, cur amicitia constantiaq; Sejani magis sideret. Sed nec vanus populi de amicitia Sejani tumor, nec opinio de ea Cæsaris, nec factum Sejani liberare eum interiori animi sensu, amicitiæ non sincerè cū domo Cæsariana cultæ, poterat. Sed quodnam illud Cæsaris periculum? quod factum Sejani? Vescebantur in villa cui vocabulum Spelunca, mare Amuclanum inter Fundanosque mōtes, nativo in specu. ejus os lapsis repente saxis, obruit quosdam ministros. hinc metus in omnes, & fuga eorum qui convivium celebrabant. Ingens Tiberii discrimen: quod amicitiæ & constantiæ Sejani specimen? Sejanus genu, vultuque & manibus super Cæsarem suspensus, oppositit sese incidentibus, atque habitu tali repertus est a militibus qui subsidio venerant. Verum non Cæsarem, sed se & suam magnitudinem, illo gestu quaerebat. Major ex eo, & quanquam exitio suaderet, ut non sui anxius, cum fide audiebatur. Nihil ab eo tempore tam absurdum cogitatu, tam saevum facto, auribus Tiberii insusurrare poterat, quin id fidem mereri videretur. Sed cur non proxima ad dominationem via, perire imperatorem sivit? cur non rudera spelunca ipse in caput ejus injecit? Absens a praetoriis cohortibus, absens a senatu & fidei suae clientibus, nondum ad invadendum imperium omnia parata habuit. Nec dum stirps Germanici, haereditate regni proxima, e medio remota erat. Adversus hanc judicis partes latro sumebat, subditis qui accusatorum nomina sustinerent, maximeque infesta-rentur Neronem proximum successioni, & quanquam modestia juventa, plerunque tamen quid in praesentiarum conduceret oblitum, quodin sequenti aphorismo com-modiùs explicabitur.
units.tr: Caesar was faced with a doubtful danger, which the empty rumour magnified, and it gave him reason to think that the friendship and steadfastness of Sejanus rested more firmly on him. But neither the empty boasting of the people about Sejanus' friendship, nor the opinion Caesar held of it, nor Sejanus' own act could free him from the inward feeling that his friendship, not sincerely cultivated with the house of Caesar, was not genuine. But what was that danger to Caesar? What was Sejanus' deed? They were dining in a villa called Spelunca, between the Amyclaean sea and the Fundan hills, in a natural cave. Its mouth, suddenly collapsing with rocks, crushed some of the attendants. Hence fear seized everyone, and those who were holding the banquet fled. A great peril for Tiberius: what proof was there here of Sejanus' friendship and steadfastness? Sejanus, bending over Caesar with his knees, face and hands, took the falling stones upon himself, and was found in that posture by the soldiers who had come to help. Yet by that gesture he was seeking not Caesar's safety but his own greatness and that of his position. From that time he was heard with greater trust, even when he advised the deed with cruelty, as though he were not anxious for himself. From that time nothing so absurd to think of, nothing so cruel to do, could he whisper into Tiberius' ears without seeming to deserve belief. But why did he not, by the nearest route to dominion, let the emperor perish? Why did he not himself throw the ruins of the cave upon his head? He was absent from the praetorian cohorts, absent from the senate and from those bound to him by loyalty, and he did not yet have everything ready for seizing the empire. Nor had the stock of Germanicus, next in line to the kingdom by inheritance, yet been removed from the midst. Against this stock the robber assumed the role of judge, by subordinating men who would bear the names of accusers, and by harassing above all Nero, next in succession, who, though young and modest, had forgotten for the moment what was to his advantage, as will be explained more conveniently in the following aphorism.

units.la: LXXI.
units.tr: LXXI.

units.la: Nec sincere suadentes amici semper audiendi.
units.tr: Nor are friends who advise insincerely always to be heard.

units.la: Nec omnes cum domesticis, quanquam fidei non suspectis, sermones communicandi. Solatium quidem rerum adversarum, & fecundarum fructus non minus est, in amici mutua benevolentia conquiescere; habere quocum audeas, ut tecum, sermones conferre. Sed non semper id tutum est: cum multi non malevolentia, sed imprudentia delinquant. Multi erga nos non male animati, in consiliis de re ardua dandis affectus in nos, aut fortunae suae per nos incrementum speratum consulunt. Nero, cui modestum silentium imperante Tiberio conveniebat, à libertis & clientibus suis, bus apiscenda potentia properes exfimulatur, ut ereum fidentem animi offenderet: velle id populum Romanum: cupere exercitus, neq; ausurum contra Senatum, qui nunc patientiam fenis, & segnitiam juvenis iuxta insultet. Ingenuae naturae adolescens, cum cupiditati suae fecundas voces audiret, in libertatem, temporibus inutilem, vultu & voce prorumpebat, & quanquam nihil in principem insidiarum, nihil tumultus concitandi, animo conciperet: tamen interdum voces procedebant contumaces, & inconsulta, quas ap-positi custodes exceptas auctaf, cum deferrent, neq; Neroni defendere daretur, diversa insuper folicitudinum forma oriebantur. Nunquam fatis monemur,
units.tr: Nor should we share all our conversations with our household, though they be not under suspicion of loyalty. Indeed, it is no small comfort in adversity, and a fruit of prosperity, to rest in the mutual goodwill of a friend, to have someone with whom you may dare to talk as with yourself. But this is not always safe, since many offend not from malice but from imprudence. Many who are not ill-disposed towards us, when asked for advice on a difficult matter, consult in a way that favours themselves or hopes for an increase of their own fortune through us. Nero, to whom a modest silence was fitting while Tiberius reigned, was hurried by his freedmen and clients, who pretended that he must hasten to seize power, so that he would offend the man who trusted him: that the Roman people wished it, that the armies desired it, and that he would not dare to act against the Senate, which now insulted the patience of the old man and the sluggishness of the young. The young man, of a generous nature, when he heard these flattering words that fed his ambition, burst out with his face and voice into a freedom that was unfitting for the times. Although he conceived no plot against the prince and no plan to stir up tumult, yet at times contumacious and ill-considered words escaped him. The guards placed beside him caught them and magnified them, and when they reported them, and Nero was not permitted to defend himself, anxieties of a different kind arose. We are never warned enough

units.la: potentioribus linguam. Nam fi custodes clam appo-siti desunt, ipsa januæ limina quasi lo-quacia suspectemus. Aut nihil igitur de imperantibus, quod quidem securitati proximum, aut nonnisi magnificè loquamur. Egregie enim nobiscum agitur, fi non sermones detorti, fi non ipsæ laudationes in convitia conversæ deferantur. Hoc ubi fit, absentes abin-secto judice judicamur, absentes damnamur, nec de-fendenfendendi nobis copia, plerumque delationis ignoran-tibus, ut hic Neroni ante causam auditam damnato, conceditur.
units.tr: to keep a tight rein on our tongues before the powerful. For if hidden guards are not present, we should suspect even the very threshold of our door, as though it were talkative. Therefore let us say nothing about the rulers that is not at least safe, or else speak only in the most exalted terms. For we are dealt with admirably if our words are not twisted, if even our praises are not turned into insults and reported. When this happens, we are judged absent before an unseen judge, we are condemned in our absence, and we are not given the chance to defend ourselves, since usually the informers are unknown, just as was granted to Nero here, who was condemned before his case had been heard.

units.la: LXXII.
units.tr: LXXII.

units.la: Rara in principi invisos amicorum fides.
units.tr: Rare is the loyalty of friends toward a prince's hated favourites.

units.la: Alii ut fulmine afflatum, ut triste in agris bidental, fuga arrepta deferunt. alium occursum ejus vitare, quidam salutatione reddita statim averti, pleriq; ince-ptum sermonem abrumpere. alii commiserationem simulantes, quod ad iratum principem deferant sermone eliciunt. insistentibus contra irridentibusque (i.e. arridentibus) qui Sejano fautores aderant. ita mi-sereo[?] calamitatis recidit, ut amicis refugientibus, ini-micissimis ut amicis vitam suam committat. Nec in se quicquam, ad placandum imperatorem, spei. Enim-verò Tiberius torvus, aut falsum renidens, vultu, seu loqueretur, seu taceret juvenis: crimen ex silentio, ex voce. Ne secreto quidem diei tempori, cubili, vitæ consortio fidendum. ne nox quidem secura, cum uxor vigilias somnos, suspiria matri Livia, atq; illa Sejano patefaceret. Fratrum verò gratiam raram esse, etiam poëtis in adagium abiit. Fratrem quoq; Neronis Drufum traxit in partes, spe objecta principis loci, si prio-rem ætate[?] & jam labefactum demovisset. qui non raro domesticæ perfidiæ, domo per discordiam soluta, pœnas luunt: neq; tamen Sejanus ita Drufum fove-bat, ut non in eum quoq; femina futuri excidii medi-taretur: gravius[?] præferocem, & insidiis magis opportunum. Ita non modo simulatio favoris conjunctionem benevolentiæ mendaci vultu imitatur; sed etiam natura junctissimorum consensum æmulatio, cupido potentiæ, incogitantia dissolvit.
units.tr: Others, as if struck by lightning, or as if a sad bidental stood in the fields, take to flight and avoid him. Some avoid meeting him at all; some, returning his greeting, at once turn away; most break off the conversation they have begun. Others, feigning pity, draw out of him words they can carry to the angry prince. Those who were supporters of Sejanus stood by, pressing in on him and smiling. So the misery of his fall grows, since his friends flee and he must entrust his life to his bitterest enemies as if they were friends. He has no hope of anything in himself by which to appease the emperor. Indeed Tiberius, with a grim look or a forced smile, whether the young man spoke or kept silent: his silence became a charge, and his voice likewise. Not even in secret can he trust the time of day, his bed, or the company of his life. Not even the night is safe, since his wife would report his wakefulness, his sleep and his sighs to his mother Livia, and she to Sejanus. That a brother's favour is rare has passed into a proverb even among the poets. He also drew Nero's brother Drusus into his party, with the hope of the prince's place offered to him, if he could remove the elder, already weakened by age. Those who do this often pay the penalty for domestic treachery, once the household is broken up by discord. Yet Sejanus did not so favour Drusus that he did not also plot against him, a woman of the future ruin, more fierce in front and more suitable for ambush. Thus not only does the pretence of favour imitate the bond of goodwill with a lying face, but also nature's closest partnerships are dissolved by rivalry, the lust for power and thoughtlessness.

units.la: LXXIII.
units.tr: LXXIII.

units.la: Elaborata facilitate ruentibus viva-ciora.
units.tr: Things hastily polished are livelier than things laboured over.

units.la: In eloquentiæ applausu id inprimis perspicuum, Sunt qui canora voce, aut rapiente auditorem sermo-nis impetu, nomen sibi differorum acquirunt: quorum cum ipsis labor & fama extinguitur. Alii minus in aures caveæ irrepunt, quorum post mortem scripta cele-brantur. Qu. Haterius, eloquentia quoad vixit ce-lebrata, monimenti ingenii ejus baud perinde retinen-tur. Scilicet impetu magis, quàm cura vigebat, utq. aliorum meditatio & labor in posterum valescit: sic Haterii canorum illud & profluens, cum ipso fimulex-tinctum est. Nec in viva modò dictione, sed in fcri-bendi quoque dispari successu, discrimen hoc reperias. Est qui fcribédi impetu, & ruente verborum torrente, quidvis calamo imperat. Alius cum cura limatior, ut poma serotina, tardè ad maturitatem, sed annos latu-ram, perducitur. Exempla in promptu erant: sed parco amicorum manibus.
units.tr: In the applause given to eloquence this is especially clear: some men win for themselves a name among the orators by a ringing voice, or by sweeping the listener along with the rush of their speech; with these, their labour and reputation are extinguished together. Others creep less conspicuously into the ears of the audience, and their writings are celebrated after their death. Quintus Haterius was famous for his eloquence while he lived, but the monuments of his talent are not preserved in the same way. Clearly his talent flourished more by impulse than by care, and as the meditation and labour of others gain strength for posterity, so that resonant and flowing quality of Haterius was extinguished together with the man himself. This difference can be found not only in spoken delivery but also in the unequal success of writing. Some men, by the rush of their pen and the torrent of words pouring forth, command whatever they please with the quill. Another, more polished by care, is brought slowly to maturity like late-ripening apples, but will last for years. Examples were at hand, but I spare the shades of my friends.

units.la: LXXIV.
units.tr: LXXIV.

units.la: Negligentiæ non est eadem quæ doli commissi poena.
units.tr: The punishment for negligence is not the same as that for a deliberate wrong.

units.la: Non enim ex non præviso eventu æquè, ac animo lædendi, culpa arguitur. Atilius quidam libertini generis, quo spectaculum gladiatorum celebraret, neque fundamenta per solidum subdidit, neq; firmis nexibus ligneam compagem superstruxit: ut qui non abundan-tia pecunia, nec municipali ambitione, sed in sordida mercede id negotium quaesivit. En culpam negligen-tiæ! sed majorem in turba hominum, ad specta-culum avidè ruentium. Convulsa enim mole, & cum onere insidentium offusa, ingens hominum multitudo, in præceps tracta affligitur, velut ruente opere operitur. Quinquaginta hominum millia eo casu debilitata, vel abrita sunt. Si effectum spectemus: quinquaginta mortes Atilio infligendæ, ad expiandam plagam, non sufficerent. Nihil tamen in eum durius, quàm ut in exilium pellatur, patres decernunt. Ne vero in poste-rum simili modo peccetur, Senatusconsulto cavetur, ne quis gladiatorum munus ederet, cui minor quàm [?]ducentorum millium numerus sese in amphitheatrum im-ponereponeretur, nisi solo firmitatis spectata. Praestat enim futuro malo providentia legum occurrere, quam errato commissum nihil profutura saevitia corrigere. Si quis hoc publicae moestitiae spectaculum contra spectacu-lorum ludicram lasciviam adducere in animo habebit, facere id ei me non invito licebit.
units.tr: For fault is not charged on the same footing for an unforeseen outcome as for an intention to harm. A certain Atilius, of freedman stock, who was putting on a show of gladiators, neither laid foundations through the whole site nor built the wooden framework with firm joints. He sought this business not from abundant money or civic ambition, but for a sordid fee. There is the fault of negligence! But the greater harm lay in the crowd of men rushing eagerly to the spectacle. For when the structure collapsed and fell on the people sitting on it, a huge multitude was thrown headlong and crushed, as if the building fell on them. Fifty thousand men were maimed or killed in that accident. If we look at the outcome, fifty deaths inflicted on Atilius would not be enough to expiate the disaster. Yet the Fathers decreed nothing harsher against him than that he be driven into exile. And lest a similar fault be committed in future, a decree of the Senate provided that no one should give a gladiatorial show in which fewer than two hundred thousand could be seated in the amphitheatre, unless only its firmness had been examined. For it is better to meet a future evil with the foresight of laws than to correct a wrong already done with a cruelty that profits nothing. If anyone intends to bring this public spectacle of mourning against the playful wantonness of the shows, I shall allow him to do so.

units.la: LXXV. Fortuita vulgus in omen aut in culpam trahit.
units.tr: LXXV. Chance events the crowd turns into an omen or into a fault.

units.la: Quo anno Tiberius Roma secessit, clades alia post aliam civus & Italiam conterruit. Amphitheatri ruinam secuta ignis violentia, montem Coelium deussit.
units.tr: In the year when Tiberius withdrew from Rome, one disaster after another terrified the city and Italy. After the collapse of the amphitheatre, a violent fire burned the Caelian Hill.

units.la: Id Romani interpretatione expendentes, feralem annum ferebant, & omnibus adversis susceptum principi consilium absentia, qui mos vulgo, fortuita ad culpam trahentes. Anno V. C. 732. Tiberis inundatione Roma navibus vehebatur, statuae fulminibus ictae cernebantur, pestis per Italiam grassata agros cultoribus vastavit. Romani prodigiis, lue, fame domiti; non aliam malorum causam reperiebant; quam quod Augustum non eo etiam anno consulem haberent. Memoriae prodit Dio Cassius, libro 54. Quasi vero aut rerum natura consulatum Augusti curaret, aut iratus Augustus imperium in naturam coeli & terrae exercerret. Plebe Romana fortasse non peritiores, qui ad ec-clipsin aut terrae motum praecedentem omnia proximorum annorum mala reducunt: quae etiam sine iis futura erant. Sin alta pax nationes, agros fertilitas, urbes corporum salubritas inviserit: cur non & haec ad illas causas, vel futurorum indices, appendunt? Sapientiores, qui fortuita in occasionem virtutis exercendæ vertunt; aut beneficentiae; ut hic Tiberius, qui pestis ignis obviam, & rumori vulgi, ivit, tribuendo pecuniis ex modo detrimenti, quam benignitatem gratiorem omnibus fecit, quod sine ambitione, aut proximorum precibus, ignotos etiam & ultro accitos munificentia juverat. aut in occasionem seditionis comprimendae: ut Drusus Tiberii filius, cum miles lunae defa[?]ctionem in triste praesentium omen verteret, utendum inclinatione ea, & quae casus obiulerat in sapientiam vertenda ratus, conjuratorum factionem disjicit. 1. Annal. aut in hostem forti animo ruendi: ut Graecorum non pauci, terriculamentorum sinistram interpretationem in hostem torquentes, animum suis & spem victoriae indiderunt. aut modestiae vitae & morum sobrietatis reducendae: quasi coelestia sidera publicam lasciviam intueri erubescentia, objecto velo lumina tegant, aut terra imminentis hominum poenae metu contremiscat. In bello praesertim magni duces illud Hectoris, contra Polydamantem augurium terrentem, in animo habebunt:
units.tr: The Romans, interpreting this, reckoned it a deadly year and said that the emperor's counsel, undertaken in adversity, was the cause of his absence. This is the custom of the crowd, which drags chance events into blame. In the year of the city 732 the Tiber flooded, and Rome was carried about by boats; statues were seen struck by lightning; a plague spreading through Italy laid waste the fields and their cultivators. The Romans, overcome by portents, pestilence and famine, found no other cause of their evils than that they did not have Augustus as consul that year. Dio Cassius records this in book 54. As if nature cared about Augustus' consulship, or as if an angry Augustus exercised his power over the nature of heaven and earth! The Roman populace were perhaps no more skilled in these matters, who attribute all the evils of the preceding years to an eclipse or an earthquake, though these would have come even without such signs. But if deep peace, fertile fields and healthy bodies in the cities have looked on the nations, why do they not also hang these blessings on those same causes, or on signs of future things? More wise are those who turn chance events into an occasion for exercising virtue or beneficence, as Tiberius did, who went to meet the fire's damage and the rumour of the crowd, by granting money in proportion to each loss, a kindness which made him more pleasing to all, because without ambition or the entreaties of his intimates, he helped even strangers and those who had come to him unasked, by his generosity. Or they turn it into an occasion for checking sedition, as Drusus, son of Tiberius, did, when the soldiers turned the eclipse of the moon into a gloomy omen for the present. He judged that this inclination and what chance had offered should be turned to wisdom, and he broke up the faction of the conspirators (Annals 1). Or they turn it into an occasion for bold courage against the enemy, as not a few of the Greeks did, twisting the ominous interpretation of their terrors against the enemy and putting courage and hope of victory into their own men. Or they use it to restore modesty of life and sobriety of manners: as if the heavenly stars, blushing to look upon the public wantonness, hid their light behind a veil, or as if the earth trembled at the fear of the punishment hanging over men. Especially in war, great leaders will keep in mind that saying of Hector against Polydamas, who tried to frighten him with an augury:

units.la: Εἷς οἰωνὸς ἄριστος ἀμύνεσθαι περὶ πάτρης[?]
units.tr: One omen is best: to fight for one's fatherland. [Εἷς οἰωνὸς ἄριστος ἀμύνεσθαι περὶ πάτρης]

units.la: Auspicii culmen, patriam defendere ferro.
units.tr: The highest augury is to defend the fatherland with the sword.

units.la: LXXVI.
units.tr: LXXVI.

units.la: Solitudo & quies foedæ lasciviæ ma-gistra.
units.tr: Solitude and quiet, the teachers of foul lasciviousness.

units.la: Non enim cujusvis est, solitudine ac otio, quae lan-guorem plerisque afferunt, ad altiores de Rep. cogitationes cum Africano acui; aut ad contemplationem Dei, animique a corporeo luto revocationem cum Platone erigi. plures depositae verecundiae lasciviunt. Capreas Tiberius, quo se taedio frequentiae abdiderat, duodecim villarum molibus insedit: quanto intentius olim publicas ad curas, tanto occultior in luxus, & ma-lum otium resolutus. Non homines tantum singuli, sed & praepotentia imperia, ut ait Valerius Maximus, agitatione rerum ad virtutem capessendam excitantur, nimia quiete in desidiam resolvuntur. Quare quietis languorem fugiat, qui vitae rubiginem, desidiam & luxuriam, effugere tentabit. Non male lasci-vus poëta, erroris causa intellecta, Catullus:
units.tr: It is not for just anyone to have his thoughts about the Commonwealth sharpened to higher levels, with Africanus, by solitude and leisure, which bring languor to most people, or to be raised with Plato to the contemplation of God and to the recall of the soul from its bodily mire. Many, once they have laid aside shame, grow wanton. Tiberius, when he had withdrawn to Capri out of weariness of crowds, settled himself in the massive structures of twelve villas. As he had once been more intent on public affairs, so much more secretly did he sink into luxury, dissolved in idle leisure.

units.la: Otium, Catulle, tibi molestum est: Otio exultas, nimiumque gaudes, Otium reges prius & beatas Perdidit urbes, Sed quid severiori poetæ Horatio, otium tantopere commendanti, quid Senecæ Otium Sapientis laudanti, regerimus? Non est cujusvis, otium recte ferre posse: ut nec benigniorem fortunam: quæ tamen votis nulli fugatur. Otium cum Sapientia exoptandum: qua re-strice[?], ne in lasciviæ scopulos detrudatur, non est exti-mescendum. Otium autem Horatius intelligit vacationem a navigatione lucri causa, a belli gerendi necessitate, ab immoderata honorum ambitione, a cumulandi aurum studio, a peregrinandi inquieto tumultu, a curæ edaci tortura. Negotium quod aut fortunæ necessitas, aut animi inquietudo impo[?]suit, hoc otio dispungitur.
units.tr: "Leisure, Catullus, is troublesome to you; you exult in leisure and rejoice too much. Leisure has destroyed kings before now, and prosperous cities." But what shall we answer to the more serious poet Horace, who commends leisure so highly, or to Seneca, who praises the leisure of the wise man? Not everyone can bear leisure rightly, just as not everyone can bear a more favourable fortune; yet no one prays to be rid of that. Leisure is to be desired together with wisdom; provided it is held in check, so that it is not thrown onto the rocks of wantonness, there is no need to dread it. Horace, however, understands by leisure a release from sailing for the sake of gain, from the necessity of waging war, from immoderate ambition for office, from the zeal for piling up gold, from the restless tumult of travel, and from the gnawing torment of care. Business that either the necessity of fortune or the restlessness of the mind has imposed is set aside by this leisure.

units.la: Non enim gazæ, neque consularis Summovet lictor miseros tumultus Mentis, & curas laqueata circum Tecta volantes.
units.tr: "For neither riches nor the consular lictor drives away the wretched tumults of the mind, nor the cares that flutter round panelled ceilings."

units.la: Vivitur parvo bene, cui paternum Splendet in mensa tenui salinum, Nec leves somnos timor aut cupido Sordidus aufert.
units.tr: "He lives well on little, for whom the ancestral salt-cellar shines on a modest table, and whom neither fear nor sordid desire takes away from light sleep."

units.la: Hoc otium à curâ mentis, & jucunda rerum sublimium contemplatione, non abducit; sed ad eam compendiosa via adducit. Hoc otium ubi nacti fuerimus, non opus erit illo Severi symbolo, Laboremus; aut illo Pertinacis Militemus. Datur enim homini ad altiora nato, præter militiæ durum laborem, honesta vitæ occupatio.
units.tr: This leisure does not draw us away from care of the mind and from the pleasant contemplation of lofty things; rather it leads us to them by a short road. Once we have gained this leisure, there will be no need for that motto of Severus, "Let us labour", or that of Pertinax, "Let us serve as soldiers". For, apart from the hard labour of military service, a man born for higher things is given an honourable occupation in life.

units.la: LXXVII.
units.tr: LXXVII.

units.la: Pestiferi nomine amicitiæ interimentium morsus.
units.tr: The deadly bites of those who destroy under the name of friendship.

units.la: Nec ulla ratione homine ingenuo digni, aperte enim vel odisse, magis ingenuum est, quam frontem occultare sententiam: ait ille, quid fronte amici afflum-pta interimere? Hæc tamen emergendi via Sejano placuit, hæc illis qui Sejano existimationem suam gratificabantur. Neroni & Agrippinæ additus milites, nuncios, introitus, aperta, secreta, velut in annales referebat, fruebantur qui monerent perfugere ad Ger-manią exercitus. salutem in eorum protectione in-venturi. at quid hoc aliud erat, quam tentati civilium armorum subsidii crimen & laqueum injicere? vel ce-leberrimo fori effigiem divi Augusti amplecti. quo & Tiberius capiendæ sævitiæ admoneretur, ut paventem aut conscium; & populus ab ea, jam manifeste rea; studia abduceret. populumq; ac senatum auxilio vo-care. quod animum Tiberii exulceratum, ad factionis poenam fumendam incitaret.
units.tr: Such conduct is by no means worthy of a free-born man. It is more gentlemanly to hate openly than to hide one's opinion behind a face. As that man put it: why destroy someone with the face of a friend put on? Yet this was the route to advancement that pleased Sejanus, and it was the route taken by those who sought to win his favour. Soldiers were attached to Nero and Agrippina, to report messages, visits, and open and secret matters, as if writing them into the annals. Those who advised fleeing to the German armies were indulged, on the expectation of finding safety under their protection. But what was this, other than setting a trap and laying on a charge of seeking civil war support? Or of embracing the statue of the deified Augustus in the most crowded part of the forum. By this Tiberius would be prompted to seize upon cruelty against her, as against a fearful or guilty woman, and the people would withdraw their sympathy from her, now plainly a defendant. They would also summon the people and the senate to help. All this would inflame Tiberius's embittered mind and urge him to exact punishment on the faction.

units.la: Sed intuere calumniandi impudentiam! Ea spretâ ab illis, velut pararent, objiciebantur.
units.tr: Though they rejected this, they were charged with it as if they had been preparing it. But look at the shamelessness of the slander!

units.la: Omnem vero in amicitia simulata nequitiam fupe-rat, quod de circumvento Titio Sabino adjicitur. Hunc Latiaris cum perfidiæ sociis aggreditur: cupidine con- fulatus, ad quem non nisi per Sejanum aditus. neque Sejani voluntas, nisi scelere, quarebatur. O maculatum honorum splendorem, qui turpitudine emitur! Latia-ris jacere fortuitos primum sermones, mox laudare con-stantiam, quod non, ut cateri, florentis domus amicus, adfliftam deferuisset. O cacodæmonis humana spe-cie versutiam! nos abinfidiatoribus ejusmodi & fer-monum satoribus, compreffaintra fauces voce, ca-veamus. Et pallquam Sabinus, ut sunt molles in tala-mitate mortalium animi, effudit lacrymas, junxit questus : audentius jam onerat Sejanum, favitiam, su-perbiam, spes ejus ne in Tiberium quidem convitio ab-ftinet. quid fi Sabinus delationem hic occupaffet? fi doli sentiens, perniciem amoliendo prævenisset? non erat ejus commatis Sabinus. & quod fine teste locu-tus erat Latiaris, fine teste prolatum rejiceretur. Iig sermones, tanquam vetita miscuissent, speciem artæ mi-citiæ facere. Sabinum ante oculos habeant, qui ad omnia annuere, politicæ artis arcanum non moven-dum ducunt.
units.tr: Yet what is added about Titius Sabinus, who was ensnared, surpasses all the wickedness of feigned friendship. Latiaris attacks him together with his accomplices in treachery. Driven by desire for the consulship, to which there was no access except through Sejanus, and since Sejanus's favour could be sought only by crime. O the stained splendour of honours bought with baseness! Latiaris first let fall casual remarks, then praised his steadfastness, because he, unlike the others, a friend of a prosperous house, had not deserted the afflicted one. O the cunning of a demon in human form! Let us beware of such ambushers and sowers of talk, with our voice choked in our throat. And when Sabinus, as human hearts are soft in the misfortunes of mortals, shed tears and joined in complaints, Latiaris now more boldly burdened Sejanus with charges of cruelty and pride, and his hopes did not even refrain from abusing Tiberius. What if Sabinus had anticipated the denunciation here? What if, perceiving the trap, he had forestalled the ruin by averting it? Sabinus was not that sort of man. And what Latiaris had said without a witness would be dismissed if reported without a witness. These remarks, as if they had mingled forbidden things, make a show of close friendship. Let them keep Sabinus before their eyes, those who think it a secret of political art to nod assent to everything and never to be moved.

units.la: At jam ultro Sabinus quærere Latiarem, ventitare domum, dolores suos quasi ad fidiffimum deferre. Hic ad delationem nihil præter testes, qui eadem audive-rint, defuit: nam nec fine teste Sabinū Latiaris, omnia neganegaturum, arguerit: & coram pluribus dolori liberè proferendo Sabinus pepercerit. Tectum inter & quaestoria, tres senatores, haud minus turpi latebra quàm detestanda fraude, sese abstrudunt, foraminibus & rimis aurem admovent. Hoc ad eum diem dolosæ indagationis genus decerat: nisi quod in Pausania deprehendendo eandem fraudem Spartani ephori invenerant. qui tamen patriæ laborantis periculo excusabantur. Interea Latiaris repertum in publico Sabinum, velut recens cognita narraturus, domum & in cubiculum trahit: prætéritaq; & instantia, quorum affatim copia, ac novos terrores cumulat. Eadem ille, & diutius: quando mœsta, ubi semel prorupere, difficilius reticentur. Ad hunc locum Dio (lib. 58.) commentatur: Hic enim Sycophantis mos est, ut convitiis proscindere aliquem, & arcani quippiam efferre ipsi incipiant, ut audiens alter, ipse quoque simile aliquid enuntiando, crimini obnoxius fiat. nam illis quidem nulli periculo est dicendi libertas, ut qui ex compacto id faciant: non quod ita sentiant, sed ut aliorum sententiam expiscentur. at hi si vel minimum, præter quàm licitum est, verbulum emittant, puniuntur. Properata inde accusatio, missique ad Cæsarem litteris, ordinem fraudis, suum quoque ipsi dedecus narravere. An tantum in deferendo dedecus? Non: si quis insidias principi structas detegat: crimen silentio laturus. Sed ut quis amico simulato, aliquem ad liberiorem sermonem eliciat, domi ipsum suæ circumveniat, voces dolore extortas ut crimen majestatis accusetur: non potest sine dedecorosa deterrimi quadruplatoris nota concipi.
units.tr: But now Sabinus himself seeks out Latiaris, frequents his house, and brings his griefs as if to his most trusted friend. For the denunciation nothing was lacking except witnesses who had heard the same things. Latiaris would not accuse Sabinus of denying everything without a witness, and Sabinus would not spare himself in speaking freely of his grief before several people. Between the ceiling and the coffered roof, three senators hid themselves, in a hiding place no less shameful than the fraud was detestable, and put their ears to holes and cracks. Until that day this kind of deceitful spying had been unheard of, except that the Spartan ephors had found the same trick when catching Pausanias; yet even they were excused by the peril of their country in distress. Meanwhile Latiaris, having found Sabinus in public, as if about to tell news just learned, drags him home into a bedroom; and piling up past and impending matters, of which there is no lack, and new terrors, he went over the same things again and at greater length, since sorrowful complaints, once they have burst forth, are harder to hold back. On this point Dio comments (book 58): "This is the custom of sycophants: they begin to tear someone apart with reproaches and to let out some secret themselves, so that the other, hearing this and saying something similar in turn, becomes liable to the charge. For these men have no danger in speaking freely, since they do it by agreement, not because they think so, but to fish out the opinions of others. But if the others utter the least word beyond what is permitted, they are punished." The accusation was then hurried on, and letters were sent to Caesar, relating the order of the fraud and their own disgrace. Is there disgrace only in informing? No: if someone uncovers plots laid against the prince, he would bear the crime by keeping silent. But if someone, under the guise of a friend, draws another into freer speech, meets him at home, and then accuses the words wrung from him by grief as treason, this cannot be done without the disgraceful mark of the most vile informer.

units.la: Non aliàs magis anxia & pavens civitas, etiam adversus proximos, congressus, colloquia, nota ignotaque aures vitari: etiam muta atque inanima, tectum atque parietes circumspectabantur. Sabinus eodem die in carcerem conjectus. deinde indicta causa supplicio affectus: corpus in Gemonias projectum, ac post in fluvium missum.
