Casus atrocitatem commiseratione auxit canis Sabini: qui carcerem cum eo ingressus, morienti assistens, denique cum eo in flumen te præ-
units.tr: At no other time was the city more anxious and afraid, avoiding meetings and conversations even with its nearest neighbours, and guarding against every known and unknown ear; even dumb and lifeless things, the roof and the walls, were watched. Sabinus was thrown into prison the same day, and then, without a hearing of his case, was put to death. His body was cast onto the Gemoniae and afterwards thrown into the river. The atrocity of the event was heightened by the pity shown for Sabinus's dog, which entered the prison with him, stood by him as he died, and at last threw itself headlong with him into the river

units.la: cipitavit : autore Dione,lib.s8. Plúsne sensus, ut sic dis cam, humani in cane, plus fidei in bestia, quàm in hos minibus,in senatoribus,domum amicorum specie fre- quentantibus , fuisse! Sed quorsum indignationes, quasi mores humani generis hoc demum Latiaris exemplo discamus. Nostrum erit,nisi ludibrio multis, hostibus gaudio esse velimus, non omnes èfermone quasi certo animi pignore, aut ex ingenio nostro judi- cate,
units.tr: Dio is the authority for this, book 58. Was there more feeling, so to speak, in a dog, more fidelity in a beast, than in men, senators, who frequented a friend's house under the appearance of friendship! But why these indignations, as if from this example of Latiaris we were learning the ways of mankind? Our task, unless we wish to be a laughing-stock to many and a joy to our enemies, is not to judge everyone by speech alone, as if it were a sure pledge of the mind, nor by our own disposition.

units.la: LXXVIII.
units.tr: LXXVIII.

units.la: Quadruplatores etiam iis qui eorum opera utuntur invisi.
units.tr: Informers are also hateful to those who make use of their services.

units.la: Sive quod iis tanquam venenatis animantibus, ad lædendum, non ad ludendum, utuntur; five quod iis fidere diu nequeunt,qui sociorum,qui tribulium pro- ditione vivunt; five quod iis in victimam mactandis, gratiam subditorum aucupantur. Aliquando & vete- rum satietas,recens oblatorum gratia,illos afflixit,hos in illorum locum evexit. Tiberius scelerum ministros, ut perverti ab aliis nolebat, ita plerumque satiatus, & oblatis in eandem operam recentibus, veteres & pra- graves afflixit. Forte & jam notis, ideoque in sermo- nes hominum minus occultè irrepentibus, uti diutius per commoditatem non potuit: aut praegraves opu- lentia, ad munus quadruplatorium tardiores erant, aut opulentia ipsa incitamentum, ad perniciem cum evertentis lucto,fuit. Quocunque praetextu autcau- fa, veritatem illius de Romano Hifpone dicti com- probavit: potentiam apud unum, odium apud omnes adeptus, dedit exemplum, quod secuti ex pauperibus divites, ex contemptu metuendi, perniciem alii, ac po- stremum sibi invenere. 1.Annal.
units.tr: Either because they use them as venomous creatures, to harm and not to amuse themselves; or because they cannot long trust men who live by betraying their associates and fellow-countrymen; or because by handing over victims to be destroyed they court the favour of the subjects. Sometimes the surfeit with the old informers and the favour shown to newly offered ones ruined the former and raised these in their place. Tiberius, who did not want the instruments of his crimes corrupted by others, was often sated, and when fresh men were offered for the same work he crushed the old and over-burdensome ones. Perhaps, too, because they were already known and therefore crept less secretly into people's talk, he could not keep using them for long for his convenience; or the over-burdensome wealth of some made them slower to take up the informer's office, or their wealth itself was an incitement to their ruin, since it was the gain of the one who overthrew them. Whatever the pretext or cause, he confirmed the truth of that saying about the Roman Hispo: having gained power with one man and hatred with all, he gave an example which those who followed, rising from poverty to riches and from contempt to fear, found to be ruin for others and at last for themselves. 1.Annal.

units.la: LXXIX.
units.tr: LXXIX.

units.la: Principum, qui metui quàm amari malunt, vita metu miserrima.
units.tr: The life of princes who would rather be feared than loved is most wretched through fear.

units.la: Aut qui suspicione, & in omnes diffidentia,trahun- tur. Afinius Gallus pro non dubio hoc axioma cepit, dum censuit, petendum a principe, ut metus suos senatui fateretur, amoveriqueque sineret. i.e. ut aperiret, quos nam potissimum civium vel peregrinorum, domesticorum vel externorum, metueret; eosque senatui trucidandos, aut insula aliqua claudendos, traderet. Huic sententiae Tiberius ipse ansam dederat, ad senatum scribendo, trepidam sibi vitam, suspectas inimicorum insidias.
units.tr: Or of those who are carried away by suspicion and distrust of everyone. Asinius Gallus took this as an indisputable axiom when he proposed that the prince should be asked to confess his fears to the senate and allow them to be removed, that is, that he should disclose which of his citizens or foreigners, household members or outsiders, he feared most, and hand them over to the senate to be slaughtered or shut up on some island. Tiberius himself had given occasion for this opinion when he wrote to the senate that his life was anxious and his enemies' plots were suspected.

units.la: Quae trepidatio non minima causa tam diuturnae a principe urbe absentiae, & foedissimarum in deserta insula latebrarum, fuerit. Nota Ludovici XI. Galliarum regis, diffidentia & suspicione alterius Tiberii, solitaria vita, arca potius quam arce per formidinem inclusi.
units.tr: This anxiety was no small cause of such a long absence of the prince from the city, and of his most shameful hiding on a deserted island. Note the distrust and suspicion of Louis XI, king of France, another Tiberius: a solitary life, shut up out of fear in a chest rather than a fortress.

units.la: Alii cubiculum in dies, aut mensae locum, alii vestitum & caesariem in horas: metu insidiarum, mutant. Minus futuri miseri, si semel cadendo solicitudine liberentur, quam nunc sunt inter praecipitium & saxi apprehensionem aegerrime pendentes. Haec vita est eorum, quibus nulla est fides, nulla charitas, nulla stabilis benevolentiae fiducia. quis enim aut eum diligat, quem metuit, aut eum, a quo se metui putat? inquit apud Ciceronem, De Amicitia, Laelius.
units.tr: Some change their bedroom or their place at table every day, others change their clothes and hairstyle every hour, from fear of plots. They would be less wretched in future if once they fell and were freed from anxiety, than they are now, hanging most painfully between a precipice and a rock they barely grasp. This is the life of those who have no faith, no love, no firm confidence in goodwill. For who loves the one he fears, or whom does he think fears him? So says Laelius in Cicero's De Amicitia.

units.la: LXXX.
units.tr: LXXX.

units.la: Prima Tiberianarum virtutum Dissimulatio.
units.tr: The first of Tiberius' virtues: dissimulation.

units.la: Non tantum nostro & plurimorum, sed ipsius etiam iudicio. Nullam aeque Tiberius, ut rebatur, ex virtutibus suis quam dissimulationem diligebat. An non adulterino iudicio? & an virum gravem Simulatio & Dissimulatio deceat, ardua est inter eruditos disceptatio. Nos ut candorem in communi vita medullitus amplectimur, ita pectus & sermonem omnibus, in hoc veteratorum colluvie, apertum ut suadeamus, aegre adducimur. Multis simulationum involucris tegitur, & quasi velis quibusdam obtenditur, uniuscujusque natura. Frons, oculi, vultus persaepe mentiuntur, oratio vero saepissime: inquit Romanus orator. Quinimo multae singulis, plurimae imperantibus, tendiculae,
units.tr: Not only by our judgment and that of most people, but by his own as well. Tiberius, as he thought, valued no virtue of his own more than dissimulation. Is this not a counterfeit judgment? Whether simulation and dissimulation befit a serious man is a difficult dispute among the learned. We embrace frankness of heart in common life, yet we are hardly persuaded to advise an open heart and open speech toward everyone in this crowd of crafty men. Each person's nature is covered by many veils of pretence and held out as if behind curtains. The brow, the eyes and the face often lie, but speech lies most often, says the Roman orator. Indeed, many snares are set for individuals, and very many for those who rule,

units.la: eorum flatui evertendo, struuntur. Quas ad effeEtum ... eo facilius perducent, quo magis animus & consilia patebunt. Contra ejusmodi dolos animus dissimula- tione, frons tegumento, lingua loquendi opportunita- te munienda. Non faciunt ad hanc imperandi scenam, qui nihil obsignatum silentio, omnia fronte depicta gerunt. Nonnemo, eruditorum Belgii non postremus, certas promendæ aut condendæ dissimulationis claf- fes tradere ausus est. Juxta eum primus dissimulatio- nilocus est, ubi defectus virium absconduntur. Simi- litudinem ab occultandis corporis nævis petit, mo- nente Amorum magistro: Rara tamen menda facies caret: occule mendas, Quodque potes vitium corporis abde tui.
units.tr: to overturn their plans. They will lead men to their goal all the more easily the more open their minds and counsels are. Against such deceits the mind must be fortified by dissimulation, the brow by a covering, the tongue by a readiness of speech. Those who carry everything painted on their face, with nothing sealed by silence, are not suited to this stage of ruling. One of the Belgian scholars, no small one, has dared to lay down fixed classes of dissimulation, to be brought forward or stored away. According to him, the first place for dissimulation is where weaknesses of strength are hidden. He takes his comparison from concealing blemishes on the body, following the warning of the master of Love: "Yet a rare blemish spares no face: hide the blemishes, and hide whatever fault of your body you can."

units.la: Alter dissimulationi locus datur, in administrandæ Reip. sinuoso labyrintho. In quo tanquam in dramate fcenico, persona rebus gerendis apta fumi, & mutato actu deponi debeat. Adducitur in hanc scenam L.Syl- la, cui ad simulanda negotia altitudo ingenii incredi- bilis fuit. Nec non M.Cato: qui adeo versatilis erat ingenii, ut quocunque loco natus effet, fortunam sibi ipse factus videretur. Quod tamen Livii de Porcio Catone elogium, magis ad ingenii ad res diversas promptitudinem, quam ad dissimulandi artificium, refertur. Huic rerum argumento illud Senecæ, lau- dante Firmio Lactantio, dictum adaptatur: Faciet fa- piens etiam quæ non probabit, ut ad majora transi- tum inveniat: nec relinquet bonos mores, sed tem- pori aptabit; & quibus alii utuntur in gloriam aut voluptatem, utatur agendæ rei causa.
units.tr: The second place for dissimulation is given in the winding labyrinth of administering the commonwealth. There, as in a stage drama, one must take up the role suited to the business at hand and, when the act changes, lay it down. Lucius Sulla is brought onto this stage, whose depth of mind for feigning affairs was incredible. So too Marcus Cato, whose mind was so versatile that wherever he was born he seemed to have made his own fortune. Yet this eulogy of Livy on Porcius Cato refers more to readiness of mind for diverse affairs than to the art of dissimulation. To this subject the saying of Seneca, praised by Firmianus Lactantius, applies: "The wise man will even do things he does not approve, so as to find a passage to greater things; nor will he abandon good morals, but will fit them to the time; and what others use for glory or pleasure, he will use for the sake of getting the business done."

units.la: Tertius locus est in obtegendo offensionis sensu, & ulciscendi ante paratas vires animo. Securitati consu- lendum, antequam vindictæ. & Professa perdunt odia vindictæ locum.
units.tr: The third place is in concealing the sense of an offence, and in taking vengeance only once one's forces are ready in mind. Safety must be considered before revenge, and openly declared hatreds lose the chance of vengeance.

units.la: Quartus locus, qui tamen ad tertium commodè re- ducitur, est in conjurationum dissimulato intellectu, ubi cum Tiberio, cum Augusto, cum aliis imperandi peritis, non in omnes facinoris conscios inquirendum: ne spe latendi sublata, audaciam provoces. Quintus locus est in spernendis loquacis populi de principe rumoribus.
units.tr: The fourth place, which however is conveniently reduced to the third, is in dissembling knowledge of conspiracies, where, like Tiberius, Augustus and other experts in ruling, one must not inquire into all the accomplices of a crime, lest by removing the hope of hiding you provoke boldness. The fifth place is in despising the rumours about the prince that a chattering populace spreads.

units.la: Sextus in obtegendis adversis: quæ nec producta remedium invenient, & protracta auctoritatem minuent. Sic nautæ in adversa tempestate, sic belli duces periculorum nimbo, frontem obducto animo explicant.
units.tr: The sixth is in concealing adversity: which, if brought out, finds no remedy, and if prolonged diminishes authority. Thus sailors in a raging storm, and leaders in war amid a cloud of dangers, unfold a calm brow over a troubled mind.

units.la: His addo Septimum in licitis belli furtis, quæ Stratagemata vocant: quorum vis maxima in Simulatione consistit.
units.tr: To these I add a seventh: the lawful stratagems of war, as they call them, whose greatest power consists in simulation.

units.la: Infiniti laboris esset, omnia quæ huc faciunt describere: unum e multis deligam. Thrasybulus Milesio tyrannus, cum Halyattes Miletum oppugnaret, eamque fame adacturus esset, missoque legato induciasq; condendo Arsiæ Minervæ templo peteret; civibus mandavit, ut pro se quisque frumentum omne quod haberet in forum comportarent, ibique discumbentes convivium agitarent. Hæc conspicatus legatus Haliatti renunciavit, qui affatim ciborum Milesiis esse existimans, oppugnationem solvit. narrat Polyænus lib. vi. Rerum vero quæ non admittant Dissimulationem, tres Classes vir eruditus assignat. 1. in religionis negotio: quod nihil fidi admittat. 2. in contradictibus: qui claudicare non debeant. 3. in malorum conniventia: quia autore Seneca:
units.tr: It would be an endless labour to describe all that bears on this; I will choose one from many. Thrasybulus, tyrant of Miletus, when Alyattes was besieging Miletus and was about to force it by famine, sent an envoy and asked for a truce to be made at the temple of Athena at Arsia. He ordered the citizens that each should bring to the forum all the grain he had, and there hold a banquet reclining at table. The envoy, observing this, reported to Alyattes, who, thinking the Milesians had food in plenty, abandoned the siege. Polyaenus relates this in book 6. Of things that do not admit dissimulation, the learned writer assigns three classes: (1) in matters of religion, since nothing faithful admits it; (2) in contradictions, which ought not to limp; (3) in connivance at evils, because, on the authority of Seneca:

units.la: Qui non vetat peccare, cum possit, jubet.
units.tr: He who does not forbid sin, when he can, commands it.

units.la: Quibus ego pro jure meo addo. 4. interiorem amicitiæ conjunctionem, in rebus quæ nec perniciem amico de teʒ & dolorem adferant, nec aliquid de reip. emolumento deradant. 5. in fœderibus: quæ non simulate iniri, sine fuco servari par est. 6. in judiciis & proferendis publice restimoniis. 7. virtutum in vitioso, vitiorum in probo animo simulationem.
units.tr: To these I add, by my own right, (4) a closer intimacy of friendship, in matters that bring neither ruin nor grief to a friend and detract nothing from the advantage of the commonwealth; (5) covenants, which ought to be entered without pretence and kept without guile; (6) judgments and the public giving of testimony; (7) the simulation of virtues in a vicious mind, and of vices in an upright one.

units.la: 1. In religionis negotio merito rejicimus Libertinorum errorem: quem erudito scripto J. Calvinus profert & refutat.
units.tr: (1) In matters of religion we rightly reject the error of the Libertines, which J. Calvin sets forth and refutes in a learned work.

units.la: 2. In Contradictibus nullum admittimus fucum, nullas in verbis aut in actione fallacias. Illustrandæ rei, quod de Pythio Syracusano Cicero 3. off. recenset fecerit.
units.tr: (2) In contradictions we admit no pretence, no deceit in words or in action. To illustrate this, Cicero in De Officiis book 3 records what Pythius of Syracuse did.

units.la: Improborum conatus non esse conniventia alien- dos omnes boni agnoscunt. In levioribus tamen peccatis, ubi spes est animi ad fe redituri, conniventiae ali- quando locus datur. Est & dilationi supplicii aut ob- jurgationis locus, ubi magnæ potentiæ homo, aut cu- jus præfenti ductu salus reip. carere nequeat, periculo- sè offenderetur.
units.tr: All good people acknowledge that the attempts of the wicked are not to be tolerated through connivance. Yet in lighter sins, where there is hope that the mind will return to itself, room is sometimes given to connivance. There is also room for postponing punishment or rebuke where a man of great power, or one whose present leadership the safety of the commonwealth cannot do without, would be dangerously offended.

units.la: Cum amico aliud agere, aliud simulare, non est amicum sincera fide & non fucata benevolentia complectentis. Duos tamen casus admittendæ dissimulationis excepi. 1. ne quid quod dolorem amico frustra pariat, intempestivè aperias. 2. ne arcana Reip. persona publica privato reclùdat. addi potest & ter- tius: ubi cavetur, ne quod tibi pudori aut damno futu- rum fit, per amici conscientiam emanet.
units.tr: To act one way with a friend while pretending another is not the mark of one who embraces a friend with sincere faith and unfeigned goodwill. Yet I have made exceptions for two cases where dissimulation is admissible: (1) that you do not unseasonably disclose something that would cause your friend pain to no purpose; (2) that a public person does not disclose the secrets of the commonwealth to a private one. A third may be added: where care is taken that nothing which will bring you shame or loss leaks out through a friend's conscience.

units.la: Fœdera nulla virium simulatione, aut cæterarum rerum, fine quibus fœdus non coiturum erat, coalescere æquum est: non minus opulentiæ aut generis excellentia amatorem, matrimonii & liberorum causa, allicere. Pisci Spartani & Athenienses, ad societatem aut defensionem vocati, quid navium effet in portu, quantum in ærario argenti, invituros mittebant. Quod cum ab Atheniensibus, ad Siculum bellum spe ineicatis, fieret; Egeftani magnam auri & argeti vim, vicinis ab urbibus commodato acceptam, fanis ornandis deponebant. Legati divitias conspicatæ domum reversi, cives ad bellum Siculum impulerunt. Egeftani auro confestim urbibus reddito, claf- fem Atheniensium pro auro ventis alebant.
units.tr: It is fair that covenants be formed without simulated strength, or without the other things without which the covenant would not have been made. Likewise, it is no less usual to attract a suitor for marriage and for the sake of children by wealth or distinction of family. When the Spartans and Athenians were called to alliance or defence, they would send to inquire what ships were in the harbour and how much silver was in the treasury. When the Athenians did this, lured by hope of the Sicilian war, the Egestans, who had received a great quantity of gold and silver lent by neighbouring cities, displayed it to adorn their temples. The envoys, seeing the riches, returned home and drove the citizens into the Sicilian war. The Egestans, having at once returned the gold to the cities, kept the Athenian fleet supplied, paying for it with that gold.

units.la: In iudicio nisi iuratum testem, iudicem, reum veritatem dissimulare, non esse improbandi moris, multis persuasum est. Ego iudices loco Dei sedentes, actores & testes quasi in conspectu Dei agentes, nihil nisi ex animo, quod salva veritate dirimendæ ocyffime liti faciat, proferre debere, nec quicquam veri abfconere, cum pie eruditis censeo.
units.tr: Many are persuaded that in a court of law it is not a reprehensible custom for a sworn witness, a judge or an accused person to conceal the truth. I hold that judges, who sit in God's place, and plaintiffs and witnesses, who act as if in God's sight, ought to bring forward nothing but what comes from the heart, something that, while preserving the truth, will bring the dispute to an end as quickly as possible. I think pious and learned people should conceal no truth at all.

units.la: Multi sub oviculæ pelle vulpinam nocendi vim suam abscondunt: idque ex aulæ moribus esse, sibi & aliis persuasum eunt. Verum totius injustitiæ nul- la causa [illegible, ~4 letters] la capitalior est, quàm eorum, qui tum, cum maximè fallunt, id tamen agunt, ut viri boni esse videantur. Sunt alii qui vitium animo detestati, ululandum esse cum lupis, ut ajunt, & Romæ Romano more viven-dum, crepant. His, præter dicta sacræ scripturæ, Psal. 50,v.18.Rom.12.v.2. 1.Thess.5.v.22.
units.tr: Many hide their power to harm under a sheep's skin, and they persuade themselves and others that this is the way of the court. But of all injustice there is no more deadly cause than the conduct of those who, at the very moment they are most deceiving, nonetheless take pains to seem good men. There are others who, loudly condemning vice, cry out that one must howl with the wolves, as they say, and live in Rome in the Roman manner. Against these people stand the words of Holy Scripture: Psal. 50, v. 18; Rom. 12, v. 2; 1 Thess. 5, v. 22.

units.la: In animum advocari velim: è socio, actione, mala præsertim, sermone animum ab hominibus judicari: nec posse sine vitii periculo, vitii imitationem addisci. Sit illud suo loco verum:
units.tr: I would have this brought to mind: that from a companion, from one's actions, and especially from bad ones, and from one's speech, people judge a man's mind; and that one cannot learn to imitate vice without danger to one's character. Let this be true in its proper place:

units.la: Stultitiam simulare loco, prudentia summa est.
units.tr: To feign folly at the right moment is the height of prudence.

units.la: Laudetur L.Brutus, qui sub Tarquinio Superbo habitum Stulti assumpserit, ut majori cum ubertate suo tempore sapientiam promeret. Excusentur, qui sub fœvis tyrannis, vitæ amore, inertiam ac crapulam pa-lam induerint. Nobis ea pravorum morum imitatio necessitate temporum ægrè excusatur: nulla necessitate, placendi studio, arrepta, ad scelerum propinquos limites ablegatur.
units.tr: Let L. Brutus be praised, who under Tarquin the Proud put on the guise of a fool, so that at a better time he might bring forth his wisdom with greater abundance. Let those be excused who, under savage tyrants, from love of life, openly took on sloth and drunkenness. For us, such imitation of wicked manners is hardly excused by the necessity of the times; when taken up from a desire to please, with no necessity at all, it is driven toward the neighbouring borders of crime.

units.la: LXXXI.
units.tr: LXXXI.

units.la: Præposteræ beneficentiæ est juvando opprimere.
units.tr: It is a perverse beneficence to crush by helping.

units.la: Est hoc quibusdam in more positum, mulierculis inprimis, ab iis quorum florentem fortunam ferre non possunt, speciem ac famam misericordiæ captare. Julia neptis Augusti viginti annis in exilio, ad finem vitæ degerat, pro novercæ Liviæ ope sustentata: quà florentes privignos cum per occultum subvertisset, miseri-cordiam erga afflictos palàm ostentabat. Stultè amantium genus amicorum est, miseriam quorundam optare, operiri, aut occultè producere, ut postea majori beneficentiæ splendore subveniant: Odio quàm gratia digniores. Hi cum Livia illud fortasse Corinthiorum ad Athenienses dictum, perverso sensu intelleCtum, in animo habuerint: [illegible, ~40 letters] Posterius namque beneficium opportunè collatum, etiamsi minus fuerit, majus crimen diluere potest. Thucyd. lib.1. Ejusmodi benefactores aut amicos similes iisjus[?]-dico, qui ut extrahere quenquam aqua possint, totum aqua demergunt; aut qui miserè per speciem amicitiæ alendos carceri impingunt. in his posterius benefi-cium veniam fortassis delicti[?], gratiam nullam meretur, Juvando opprimentium ordini & fœneratores, modum præsertim excedentes, accenseri possunt. Possunt huc etiam referri lenocinia agentes; possunt qui sumptus in flagitia suppeditant, qui ad nequitiam, ad corrumpendam honestatem, aut vivendi facultates, consilio vel suasu suppetias ferunt; aut qui, cum coercendi potestatem habeant, per indulgentiam im-providam ætatem ruere sinunt. Tiberiani moris fuit, quos ad supplicium rapturus erat, epulis adhibere, ho-noribus exornare, & aliis modis dementiam alere po-tius, quàm tempestivè opprimere. Ejusdem fuit, im-pari matrimonio animos & eminendi spem præcidere. Et quis omnia callidè nocentis, benignitatis monstra in classem compegerit?
units.tr: Among some people this is a settled habit, especially among women, to seek the appearance and reputation of compassion from those whose flourishing fortune they cannot bear. Julia, the granddaughter of Augustus, spent twenty years in exile until the end of her life, sustained with the help of her stepmother Livia. By this means Livia secretly undermined her flourishing stepsons, while she openly displayed compassion for the afflicted. Foolish is the kind of friend who wishes for someone's misery, waits for it, or secretly brings it about, so that afterwards they may come to the rescue with a greater show of kindness; such people deserve hatred rather than thanks. Perhaps these people, with Livia in mind, have taken to heart that saying of the Corinthians to the Athenians, understood in a perverse sense: [illegible]. For a later benefit, timely bestowed, even if it is smaller, can wash away a greater crime. Thucyd. book 1. Benefactors or friends of this sort are like those who, in order to pull someone out of the water, plunge him entirely under it; or who, under the appearance of friendship, thrust into prison those they wretchedly pretend to nourish. For such people a later benefit perhaps pardons the offence, but earns no thanks at all. Those who help the oppressors of others can be counted among them, especially usurers who exceed all measure. Here too may be referred those who act as pimps; those who supply the means for shameful deeds, who give aid by counsel or persuasion toward wickedness and the corruption of honour or of the means of living; and those who, though they have the power to restrain, allow a life to rush headlong through an unseasonable indulgence. It was the custom of Tiberius to invite to feasts those whom he was about to drag off to punishment, to adorn them with honours, and to nourish their madness by other means, rather than to crush them in good time. It was also his habit to cut off the hopes of those whose minds were unequally matched in marriage and of rising to eminence. And who, having gathered all these things together cunningly, would bring the monsters of kindness into one fleet of harm?

units.la: LXXXII.
units.tr: LXXXII.

units.la: Belli gerendi cupidis causæ belli non decerunt.
units.tr: Causes of war never fail those who are eager to wage war.

units.la: Alios inquietudo animi aut acquirendi fiducia, alios necessitas & lacessentium injuriæ ad bellum exstimu-lant. In posteriori ordine nostra memoria Belgæ; & in eodem regionum tractu olim Frisii, de quibus Tacitus ingenuè: pacem exuere, nostra magis avaritia, quàm obsequii impatientes. De causis belli, & suscipiendi promptitudine aut prolongatione, egregiæ ex- stant apud Thucydidem libro primo Historiarum, dif-fertationes. Corinthi, dolore consiliario, omnibus votis ad bellum ruentes, Lacedæmonios tarditatis accusant. Athenienses, majorum bellica gloria elati, ad jus tamen & æquum provocant. Archidamus belli difficultatem, adversus homines audacia & opulentia valentes, remoram objicit. Cui contradicens ephorus, nomine Sthenela dasy[?], nec socios Atheniensibus pro-dendos, nec crescentem eorum potentiam negligen-dam. dam, proloquens, Lacedæmonios in belli inferendi sententiam trahit. Qui si molestias diuturni belli, &c tandem communem Græciæ ruinam prævidissent, tardiores ad gratificandum aut cupiditati suæ, aut Corinthiorum voluntati fuissent.
units.tr: Some are stirred to war by restlessness of mind or confidence in acquiring more, others by necessity and by the injuries of those who provoke them. In the latter class, within our own memory, are the Belgians; and in the same region once the Frisians, of whom Tacitus honestly writes: they cast off peace, impatient more from our greed than from unwillingness to obey. Outstanding discourses on the causes of war, and on readiness or delay in undertaking it, exist in Thucydides, book 1 of his Histories. The Corinthians, driven by grief as their counsellor, rush to war with every wish and accuse the Lacedaemonians of sluggishness. The Athenians, elated by the military glory of their ancestors, nonetheless appeal to justice and fairness. Archidamus objects as a hindrance the difficulty of war against men strong in boldness and wealth. Sthenelaidas, the ephor, contradicting him, declares that allies must not be betrayed to the Athenians, nor their growing power neglected, and draws the Lacedaemonians into the decision to wage war. If they had foreseen the troubles of a long war and the common ruin of Greece at last, they would have been slower to gratify either their own desire or the wishes of the Corinthians.

units.la: LXXXIII. Bello decreto modus gerendi expendendus.
units.tr: LXXXIII. The manner of conducting a war once it has been decided upon.

units.la: Qui vel particularis, prælii committendi est; vel generalis, universi nimirum belli. In manu conferen-da inter alia quæritur: Uno ictu de summa rerum de-certandum, an per subsidia reservata hostium impetus fatigandus. Prius Persis & barbaris, posterius Græcis & Romanis in usu, & rerum tamen & ducum varieta-te mobili, fuit. Attamen, quod non simul omnibus vi-ribus impressio in hostem facta, cladis accipiendæ pri-mordium fuit. Tres leves cohortes, ac rursum dua, dein tempore interjecto, acrius sequentes immissus. satis validi, si simul incubuissent: per intervallum adventantes, neque constantiam addiderant turbatu, & pavore su-gientium auferebantur. De belli in universum gerendi ratione, quædam Corinthii, altera apud Thucydidem oratione, tangunt. De ducum solertia: [illegible, ~25 letters] τὰ ἰδία ἐξ ἴσου νέμοντας[?] [illegible, ~20 letters] Debent enim ii qui præsunt, res privatas æquabiliter distribuentes, in commune prospicere. De consilii maturitate: ἐνθυμεῖσθαι γὰρ [illegible, ~30 letters] ἀλλὰ μετ᾽ ἀσφαλείας μὴ [?] ἐν τῷ ἔργῳ ἐμπεσεῖν. Nemo tali opere rem exequitur, quali fiducia[?] deliberat: sed cum securitate sententias ferimus, cum timore autem in actione deficimus. De militum numero, peritia, alacritate: [illegible, ~40 letters] πολλὰ δὲ ἡμῖν [illegible, ~20 letters] Victores nos fore, multis de causis credibile est: primum quod hominum numero, & rei militaris peritia præcellimus: deinde quod omnes pæneque ad ea quæ sunt imperata pro-
units.tr: This concerns either a particular engagement to be joined or the war as a whole. In hand-to-hand fighting, among other questions, it is asked whether the matter should be decided at a single blow, or whether the enemy's attack should be worn down by reserves held back. The former was the practice of the Persians and barbarians, the latter of the Greeks and Romans, though with a changeable variety of circumstances and commanders. Yet the beginning of the disaster lay in this: the attack on the enemy was not made with all forces at once. Three light cohorts, and then two again, and after an interval a sharper pursuit sent in against them: strong enough had they attacked together, but arriving piecemeal they neither added steadiness to the disordered, nor were they carried off by the panic of those fleeing. On the general conduct of war, the Corinthians touch on certain points, and another passage in Thucydides's speech does so as well. On the skill of commanders: [illegible] [τὰ ἰδία ἐξ ἴσου νέμοντας] [illegible]. For those who preside ought to distribute private concerns evenly and look to the common good. On the maturity of counsel: [ἐνθυμεῖσθαι γὰρ] [illegible] [ἀλλὰ μετ᾽ ἀσφαλείας μὴ ἐν τῷ ἔργῳ ἐμπεσεῖν], that is, one must consider beforehand, but with safety, and not rush headlong into the deed. No one carries out such an undertaking with the confidence with which he deliberates: we pronounce our opinions in security, but we falter in action through fear. On the number, skill and eagerness of the soldiers: [illegible] [πολλὰ δὲ ἡμῖν] [illegible]. That we shall be victors is credible for many reasons: first, because we surpass them in the number of men and in military skill; then, because almost all of us are quick to carry out what is commanded.

units.la: peramus, De milite domestico : ... [illegible, ~40 letters]
units.tr: On the domestic soldier: ... [illegible]

units.la: cenariæ enim magis quàm vernaculæ sunt Athenien- fium copiæ : quod minùs in nobis contingit ; qui plus corporibus quàm pecuniis pollemus. De nautico exercitio : ... [illegible, ~30 letters] Dnos in tempore rem nauticam meditabimur.
units.tr: For the Athenian forces are mercenary rather than native; this is less the case with us, who are stronger in our bodies than in our money. On naval exercise: ... [illegible] We shall take up naval affairs in due time.

units.la: De conjungenda audentiæ perīa: ... [illegible, ~50 letters] Cum æqualem illis peritiam consecuti sueri- mus, animi nimirum generoso superabimus. Depe- cunia conferenda : ... [illegible, ~30 letters] Pecuniás, quæ huic rei suppetant, conferemus.
units.tr: On joining boldness with skill: ... [illegible] Once we have attained skill equal to theirs, we shall surpass them by the nobility of our spirit. On contributing money: ... [illegible] We shall contribute the money that is available for this purpose.

units.la: De hostium imbecillitate tendanda : ... [illegible, ~60 letters] ... [illegible, ~40 letters]
units.tr: On weakening the enemy: ... [illegible] ... [illegible]

units.la: Adsunt nobis & aliæ belli gerendi viæ, & in primis ciorum abductio, quæ illis adimat proventum redi- tuum, quibus pollent ; tum caftelliin eorum regionem inædificatio, & alia quæ nondum quis prospiciat. De bello seipsum explicante : ... [illegible, ~40 letters] Minimè enim bellum præscripta ra- tione geritur : ipsum autem à fe ad rerum circum- stantias multa invenit.
units.tr: There are also other ways of conducting war open to us, and above all the removal of their cities' revenues, which would deprive them of the income on which they rely; then the building of fortresses in their territory, and other measures that no one has yet foreseen. On war as it unfolds itself: ... [illegible] For war is by no means conducted according to a prescribed plan; rather, it discovers many things of its own accord, according to the circumstances of affairs.

units.la: LXXXIV.
units.tr: LXXXIV.

units.la: Non quævis belli causa regem adar- macon citabit. ...
units.tr: No cause of war whatever will summon a king to arms. ...

units.la: Sed ut privatæ injuriæ optimum remedium oblivio, ita publicæ sæpè dissimulatio. Frifii, ob tributorum iniquitatem rebellantes, bis in fugam Romanum exercitum compulerant, duplici clade Romanum no- men affecerant. Non tamen Tiberio, ut graviori bel- lo cladem ulcisceretur, cura animum momordit. Cla- rum inde inter Germanos Frifium nomen : diffimulan- te Tiberio damna, ne cui bellum permitteret. Pacis Tibe-
units.tr: But as the best remedy for a private injury is forgetting, so for a public one it is often overlooking. The Frisii, rebelling over the unfairness of their tributes, had twice put the Roman army to flight and twice inflicted disaster on the Roman name. Yet this did not stir Tiberius to take vengeance with a heavier war. From then on the name of the Frisii became famous among the Germans, while Tiberius pretended not to notice the losses, so that he would not have to grant war to anyone. Tiberius' love of peace-

units.la: Tiberius ultra modum amator, belli gerendi avidita- tem non una de causa abjecerat. Prima est, quam hic tangit Cornelius : ne cui bellum permitteret. Belli inauspicata gestio principem vilipendio affectura erat; auspicata ducem gloria nominis coronatura. Id vero maximopere cavebat Tiberius, ne quis praeter ipsum in oculis & in ore, civium, militum, provinciarum magnus esset. Id sibi maxime formidulosum, privati hominis nomen supra principis attolli : frustra studia fori, & civilium artium decus in silentium acta, si militarem gloriam alius occuparet : & catera utcunque facilius dissimulari, ducis boni imperatoriam virtutem esse. uti de Domitiano, Tiberii admiratore, in Vita Julii Agricolae. Altera causa est molestiarum belli fuga, & quietis non lacessendae prudentia. Si qua clade affecti Frisii, vicinas Germaniae nationes, in subsidium commiseratione sui, aut formidine Romani exercitus, traxissent, bellum inexplicabile metueretur. Frisiis autem iterum atque iterum victoribus, Galli spe libertatis erecti, Germani praedandi cupidine, gravio-rem motum concitarent. Praestantior igitur ultione cladis dissimulatio judicabatur. 3. Infixum animo Tiberii consilium Augusti erat, coercendi intra terminos imperii, non extra priscos limites aviditate prose- rendi. Qua de causa ne Britanniam quidem, fructu Germaniae longe uberiorem, vel Augustus vel hic Tiberius lacessendam ducebat. Consilium id divus Augustus vocabat, Tiberius praecipue. in vita Agricolae. 4. Omnem agitationem rerum Tiberius metuebat, reputans animo publicum sibi odium, extremam aetatem, magisque fama quam vi stare res suas : ut de eo VI. Annalium Cornelius. Quo factum, ut Artabanus Parthorum imperator, senectutem Tiberii ut inermem despiciens, arma concessio limite proferret. d.l. 5. Si quid alicubi aegrum, si quid potentiae reformi- dandae, arte & occultis dolis, quam vi armata, negotium conficere magis imperatorium existimabat : destinata retinens, consiliis & aliis res externas moliri, arma procul habere. d. l. Sed quid patres, quid populus Romanus, languen-te inertia Tiberio? eámne ignominiam geminæ cla-dis in nomine Romano inolescere sinebant? provin-ciam Frifiorum à corpore imperii avelli, susque deque habebant? neque senatus in eo cura, animi imperii exter-na debonefterentur. Pavor interius occupaverat animos, cui remedium adulatione quaerebatur. Ter-rebat patres praepotens apud Tiberium Sejani gratia, ipsius Tiberii in optimum quenque simultas, aut oc-culta sævitia. De amplitudine imperii cogitare iis non vacat, qui domi libertate oppressa, carcerem, Donu-fam ac Gyarum intulas, carnificis denique manum ex-pavescunt.
units.tr: Tiberius, excessively fond of peace, had set aside his eagerness to wage war for more than one reason. The first is the one Cornelius touches on here: so that he would not grant war to anyone. A war begun without the auspices would bring the prince contempt; one begun under good auspices would crown the general with glory. Tiberius took the greatest care that no one but himself should be great in the eyes and on the lips of citizens, soldiers and provinces. This was especially alarming to him: that a private man's name should be raised above the prince's; that the efforts of the forum and the honour of civil arts would be consigned to silence if someone else seized military glory; and that other things could be overlooked more easily, while the imperial courage was the mark of a good general. So Cornelius says of Domitian, Tiberius' admirer, in the Life of Julius Agricola. The second reason was a desire to escape the troubles of war and a prudent wish not to disturb quiet. If the Frisii, having been struck by some disaster, had drawn the neighbouring German nations to their aid, out of pity for them or fear of the Roman army, a war that could not be disentangled would have been feared. And if the Frisii, victorious again and again, had roused the Gauls, lifted up by hope of freedom, and the Germans, eager for plunder, a more serious uprising would follow. Overlooking the disaster was therefore judged a better course than avenging it. 3. The plan fixed in Tiberius' mind was Augustus' plan: to keep the empire within its borders, not to extend it beyond the ancient limits out of greed. For this reason neither Augustus nor this Tiberius thought Britain, far richer than Germany, should be attacked. The divine Augustus called this a plan, and Tiberius especially so, in the Life of Agricola. 4. Tiberius feared every upheaval, reckoning that the public hated him, that his age was advanced, and that his position rested more on reputation than on force. So Cornelius says in Book VI of the Annals. As a result, Artabanus, king of the Parthians, looking down on Tiberius' old age as if it were defenceless, advanced with arms past the frontier. The same place. 5. If something was amiss somewhere, or if some power needed to be feared, Tiberius thought it more the mark of a commander to settle the matter by skill and secret tricks than by armed force: keeping his plans fixed, to pursue foreign affairs by counsel and other means, and to keep arms at a distance. The same place. But what were the senators and the Roman people doing while Tiberius lay in listless inactivity? Did they allow this disgrace of a twofold defeat to take root in the Roman name? Did they let the province of the Frisii be torn from the body of the empire, and treat it as a matter of no concern? Nor did the senate care that the empire's external affairs were being dishonoured. Fear had seized their minds inside the city, and they sought a remedy in flattery. The all-powerful favour of Sejanus with Tiberius frightened the senators, as did Tiberius' own hostility towards the best men and his hidden cruelty. Those who, with liberty crushed at home, dread prison, exile and the Gyarae, and finally the executioner's hand, have no leisure to think about the extent of the empire.

units.la: LXXXV.
units.tr: LXXXV.

units.la: Miseranda quam metus expressit adulatio.
units.tr: How wretched the flattery that fear has wrung out.

units.la: Foeda magis, quae levitate animi, aut animo lucran-di depromitur: sed illa, quam metus procreat, fervi-lior. Servientis enim reip. indicium est, nimiis inemi-nentes honorum acclamationibus defungi. Patres Romani, qui sæva Tiberii judicia formidabant, qui in-teriorem Sejani familiaritatem horrebant; aram cle-mentiæ, aram amicitiæ, effigiesque circum Cafaris aut Sejani censuere: crebrisque precibus efflagitabant, vi-fendi fui copiam facerent. Quazfitior erga Neronem adulatio: ut ferme priorem posterior supergreditur. Matre caesa, cum poena ipsi extimescenda foret, obvias tribus, festo cultu senatum, exstructos quà incederet spectaculorum gradus invenit. xiv. Annal. Mitto vo-ci divinæ sacrificatum, divinos honores passim decre-tos, & quorum pleni sunt Annales. Nostri mons ho-mines praeter metus necessitatem in adulationem, priscis Romanis ignoratam, sponte ruunt. Aliquo e proceribus nominato, capite aperto in genua procum-bunt: eo gestu poculum exhaurientes, nomen praefati celebrant, Qui eam adorandi magis quam adulandi speciem detrectant, in pedes erecti nudato vertice ad nomen alicujus dynastae poculum capacius evacuant. Quod festivitatis genus Gallia, regibus addictius serviens, ignorat. Jam titulorum, jam inscriptionum acervi, jam subscriptionum humilimorum mancipiorum, parum aut libertatis prisçæ, aut non adulatorii dedecoris sapiunt. Humanitas ea, & comitatis dexteritas vocatur: quam revivisçens aliquis è Romana vel è Germanica antiquitate, opprobrium temporum vocaret.
units.tr: Flattery that springs from lightness of mind or from a desire for gain is more disgraceful, but that which fear produces is more servile. For it is a sign of a servile commonwealth to hand out excessive and extraordinary acclamations of honour. The Roman senators, who dreaded Tiberius' savage judgments and shuddered at Sejanus' intimate friendship, voted an altar of clemency, an altar of friendship, and statues of Caesar and of Sejanus around the Caesar's, and with frequent entreaties they begged for the chance to see him. More refined was the flattery towards Nero, and the later outdid the earlier. When he had put his mother to death, though he had to fear punishment himself, the senators met him on the road with the tribes, in festive dress, and found tiers of seats set up where he would pass. Annals, Book XIV. I say nothing of the sacrifices offered to his voice, the divine honours decreed everywhere, which fill the Annals. Our people, beyond the necessity of fear, rush headlong into flattery, unknown to the ancient Romans. When some noble is named, they fall on their knees with bared heads, and as they drain the cup in that posture they toast the name of the man so named. Those who avoid this show of worship rather than flattery stand on their feet, bare their heads, and empty a larger cup to the name of some lord. Gaul, which serves kings more devotedly, does not know this kind of festivity. Now the heaps of titles and inscriptions, now the signatures of the most abject slaves, savour little of ancient liberty or of anything other than the shame of flattery. They call this courtesy and the skill of good manners. Anyone who brought back to life the Roman or German antiquity would call it the disgrace of the age.

units.la: LXXXVI.
units.tr: LXXXVI.

units.la: Crescit abjecta adulatione arrogan-tia.
units.tr: Arrogance grows out of abject flattery.

units.la: Sive quod leve hominum ingenium tantæ se magnitudinis esse putat, quanta sibi tribuitur; sive quod nimium abjectos, & dignitatis suæ oblitos, dignos calcari judicat. Cum reditus ad urbem desperabatur, in litus Campaniæ patres, & cum equitibus plebecula ruebat. Satis constabat auctum ei (Sejano) arrogan-tiam, fœdum illud in propatulo servitium spectanti. quodnam servitium? campo aut litore jacentes, nullo discrimine noctem ac diem, juxta gratiam aut fastum janitorum perpetiebantur. donec idque vetitum. & revenere in urbem trepidi, quos non sermone, non visu dignatus erat. Huc fastus equitis Volsinensis excreverat, ut janitoribus ejus innotescere senatori Romano magnificum haberetur. Huc cum provexit projecta servientium in omnibus assentatio.
units.tr: Either because the light human mind thinks itself as great as the greatness that is ascribed to it, or because it judges those who are too abject and have forgotten their own dignity to deserve being trampled on. When return to the city was despaired of, senators, knights and the common crowd rushed to the shore of Campania. It was well established that his (Sejanus') arrogance grew as men watched that foul servitude in plain view. What servitude? Lying on the plain or the shore, they endured night and day without distinction, according to the favour or the pride of his doorkeepers, until this was forbidden. And they returned to the city in alarm, those whom he had not deigned to speak to or to look at. From this, the pride of the Volsinian knight had grown so great that it was regarded as a distinction for a Roman senator to be known to his doorkeepers. To this point the abject flattery of all his servants had carried him.

units.la: Reges Orientis non innatus tantum animis tumor, sed servientium ingeniorum timor, & divini honoris exhibitio, ad tantum arrogantiæ fastigium evexit. Etiam constantioris animi viri, parata nimii obsequii copia, sui obliviscuntur. Alexandrum Macedonum regem, cultus divinos admittere, colentium Persarum consuetudo docuit. Julium Cæsarem supra morta-lem conditionem fastu ascendere, cumulantium insue-tos honores minime Romana adulatio commonefe-cit. Nec jure postea ob acceptatos honores in eum conspiraverunt, quem animi elatione nihil vulgare sa-pere decretorum excessu stimulaverunt.
units.tr: Not only an innate swelling of spirit but also the fear of servile minds and the offering of divine honour raised the kings of the East to such a height of arrogance. Even men of steadier spirit, when an abundant supply of excessive obsequiousness is at hand, forget themselves. The customs of the Persians, who worshipped their kings, taught Alexander of Macedon to accept divine worship. Roman flattery, which heaped up unaccustomed honours, did not warn Julius Caesar that he was rising by his pride above the condition of mortals. Nor did they rightly conspire against him afterwards because of the honours he accepted: they had goaded on, by an excess of decrees, a man whose elation of mind made him think nothing ordinary.

units.la: LXXXVII.
units.tr: LXXXVII.

units.la: Nemo praesenti gratiae potentioris ministri confidat.
units.tr: No one should trust in the present favour of a more powerful minister.

units.la: Non modò ob incertitudinem favoris, levi momento mutabilis; sed etiam quia ruente eo casus iis, qui fulcro innitebantur, extimescendus. quidam malè alacres, quibus infaustæ amicitiæ gravis exitus imminebat. Nuper in Gallia multis amicitia Richelii exitio, fuisset; nisi præter multorum exspectationem alterius purpurati, pro Gallo Siculi, potentia exsurrexisset.
units.tr: Not only because the favour is uncertain and can change in a moment, but also because when he falls, the fall is to be feared by those who lean on his support. Some men, too cheerful, faced a grave outcome from an ill-omened friendship. Recently in France many would have perished through their friendship with Richelieu, had not the power of another cardinal, a Sicilian in place of a Frenchman, risen up beyond the expectation of many.

units.la: QUINTUS ANNALIUM TACITI liber per Aphorismos explicatus.
units.tr: The Fifth Book of the Annals of Tacitus, explained by Aphorisms.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Suum cuique decus posteritas rependit.
units.tr: Posterity repays each man his due honour.

units.la: CREMUTII Cordi extrema verba sunt: IV. Annalium. Multorum oculos aut livor, aut potentiae admiratio perstrinxit: qui defunctorum bona vel mala, detracta externorum larva, acutius intuentur. Livia, quam Juliam Augustam adoptiva acclamatio appellat, post Tiberium Neronem Augusto imperatori nupta, sermones de se & candida hominum judicia coercuit. Post fata domum, exuta fortunae blandientis toga, sua dote apparuit. Sanctitate domus priscum ad morem, castis[?] ultra quam antiquum foeminis probatum, mater impotens, uxor facilis, & cum artibus mariti, simulatione filii bene composita. Non eam quicquam auri & gemmarum, non aulae potentia in sepulcrum sequitur: sequitur morum rectitudo; nec, si qua fuit, pravitas abscondITUR. Ab animo fortuna, non a fortuna hominis animus dignitatem foeneratur. Nemo priscorum regum, aut insequentium in populari statu ducum, ab opulentia posteritati commendatur. Romulum vigilantia, Numam Pompilium religio, Tullum Hostilium alacritas, Ancum vitæ integritas, Tarquinium Priscûm libe[?]tatis, Servium Tullium sollicitudo de Rep. supra nubes evexit. Nulla auri aut voluptatum mentione, Bruti liberatoris patriæ magnanimitas, Decii devotus pro salute civium animus, Fabricii continentia, Scipionis rerum gestarum magnitudo, Catonis gravitas, in ore omnium, ne omnes percenseam, feruntur. Adeo & de hominibus veri Dei cognitionem non adeptis, quodam verborum sensu, verum est: sua eos opera post fata comitari.
units.tr: The last words of Cremutius Cordus, in the fourth book of the Annals, are these: "The eyes of many are dazzled either by envy or by admiration of power, while those who look more keenly see the good or bad deeds of the dead once the mask of externals has been stripped away." Livia, whom the acclamation of adoption called Julia Augusta, was married to the emperor Augustus after Tiberius Nero. She restrained talk about herself and favourable judgments of men. After her death, the house having cast off the toga of flattering fortune, she showed what she had been. In the sanctity of her house she was approved beyond the ancient custom of chaste women: a mother overbearing, a wife compliant, and with her husband's arts and her son's pretence well arranged. No quantity of gold or gems, no power of the court, follows her to the tomb; her moral uprightness follows her, and whatever wickedness there was is not hidden. A soul gains its dignity from its character, not a man's character from his fortune. None of the early kings, nor of the leaders who followed in a popular state, is commended to posterity for wealth. Romulus was raised above the clouds by his vigilance, Numa Pompilius by his piety, Tullus Hostilius by his zeal, Ancus by his integrity of life, Tarquin the Elder by his love of liberty, and Servius Tullius by his concern for the commonwealth. With no mention of gold or pleasures, the magnanimity of Brutus, liberator of his country, the devoted spirit of Decius for the safety of the citizens, the self-restraint of Fabricius, the greatness of Scipio's deeds and the gravity of Cato are carried on everyone's lips, not to list them all. So, in a certain sense of the words, it is true even of men who have not attained the knowledge of the true God, that their works accompany them after death.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Nec cum principibus, nec de iis jocandum.
units.tr: Nor should one joke about princes, nor about those close to them.

units.la: Illud ex æqualitatis opinione tædium fui; istud ex acerbitate odium movet. Tiberii increpationem[?] fius consul meruit, dicax idem, & Tiberium acerbis facetiis irridere solitus, quarum apud prapotentes in longum memoria est. Scurræ quidem & moriones, qui jocando principum aures tenent, primam sæpe in aula paginam faciunt. Sed iis ex abjectione commendatio, & ex permissu principis. Quanquam ne sic quidem indignationem fatis effugiunt: quod Cleinens Marotta, Francifco I. Galliarum regi diu ob facetias & dicacitatem acceptus, ad extremum invisus; docuerit;
units.tr: The one arouses weariness through a belief in equality; the other stirs hatred through bitterness. Fius the consul earned Tiberius's rebuke. He was witty too, and used to mock Tiberius with bitter jests, which are remembered at length among the very powerful. Jesters and buffoons, who hold the ears of princes by joking, often take the first page in a court. But theirs is a recommendation won through abjection and by the prince's permission. Yet even so they do not fully escape indignation, as Clément Marot showed: long welcomed by Francis I, king of the French, for his jests and wit, he was at the end hated.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Gratia vero præpondetat:
units.tr: But favour prevails:

units.la: Moribus nimirum corruptis, & quibus nulla honestatis cura. Tiberius matris[?] vefecundia liberatus, in Agrippinam & Neronem crudelior, literis eos ad senatum quæsita asperitate perstrinxit. Magno senatus pavore ac silentio: donec pauci, quibus nulla ex bonesto spe, & publica mala singulis in occasione gratia trahun-tur, ut referretur postulmere. In cognitionibus, præmiis, in reip. cura, quid principi placeat; aut quid consulto expediat, feré spectatur. Ex hac fœdæ lacunæ scaturigine judicia contremiscunt, bene merita evanescunt, status imperii laborat. Miserum principem, pem[?], apud quem vera reticentur: miseriorem, cujus aures vero praeclusae sunt. Sic tamen vivitur in aula: pauci quae grata principi loquuntur; caeteri torrente abrepti, sententiae se illorum accommodant. alii a primoribus, maximeque a magistratibus trepidabatur, trepidabatur non veri expiscandi caligine, sed mentis Tiberii indagandi labyrintho. quippe Tiberius etsi infense invectus, catera ambigua reliquerat. Si clara voce sententiam, de trucidandis Agrippina & Nerone, reclusisset; boni illi patres ultimi supplicii reos pronun-ciassent. Ita jus & injuria non a natura, aut legum praescripto, sed praepotentis voluntate depromptum, totum patrum confessum in se convertit.
units.tr: Morals being corrupt, and with no care for honour. Tiberius, freed from respect for his mother, was crueller towards Agrippina and Nero, and in a letter to the senate he attacked them with carefully sought harshness. There was great fear and silence in the senate, until a few men, for whom there is no hope of honest gain and for whom public evils are an occasion for personal favour, were drawn into demanding that the matter be referred. In trials, in rewards, and in the care of the commonwealth, what pleases the prince, or what is deliberately expedient, is mostly what is looked to. From this foul spring judgments tremble, deserving men fade away, and the state of the empire suffers. Wretched is the prince before whom truths are kept silent; more wretched still the one whose ears are closed to the truth. Yet thus one lives at court: few say what is pleasing to the prince, and the rest, swept along by the torrent, adapt their opinions to theirs. Others trembled before the leading men, and especially before the magistrates, trembled not from the darkness of seeking out the truth but from the labyrinth of probing Tiberius's mind. Indeed, Tiberius, though he had attacked fiercely, had left the other matters ambiguous. If he had unlocked his opinion with a clear voice, on putting Agrippina and Nero to death, those good fathers would have pronounced the accused worthy of the final punishment. Thus right and wrong, drawn not from nature or the precept of laws but from the will of the all-powerful, turned the whole assembly of fathers against itself.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Nonnunquam veritas patrocinium, unde minus exspectes, contra potentiorum gratiam nanciscitur.
units.tr: Sometimes truth finds a defender from where you would least expect, against the favour of the more powerful.

units.la: Patribus metu in adulationem abreptis, & Agrippinae causa laborante, Junius Rusticus, componendis patrum actis dilectus a Caesare, fatali quodam motu, ut qui nullum ante constantiae specimen dederat, infe-rere se dubitantibus, ac monere consules, ne relationem inciperent: differebatque, brevibus momentis summa verti posse, dandumque interstitium poenitentiae senis. ita unus e senatorum numero, adulatorum unus ante creditus, voluntatem Caesaris, a senatu subscribendam, remorabatur. Quod hic Junius Rusticus, in Achaeo-rum consessu Cycliades quondam fuerat. Philippus Macedonum rex, cui Perseus regum ultimus successit, quaedam Achaeis odiosa, cuniculos ad eorum statum subvertendum ducentia, proposuit. Cycliades, qui inter assentatores regios ad eum diem habitus fuerat, liberè in senatu pronunciavit, non licere legibus Achaeorum de aliis rebus referre, quam propter quas convocati essent. Atque ita relationem inhibendo, regis astutiae resistens, confessum decernendi quae nollet necessi-tate liberavit. Verum enim vero Junius Rusticus, principi servire docendus, non parem Cycliadi libertatis decernendi eventum sortitus est. Nec populus, ef- figies Agrippina ac Neronis gerens, quicquam pensi ef- fecit, Siquidem Sejanus ira violentior, & criminandi segetem nactus, instabat: spretum dolorem principis, ab senatu defcivifle populum. Et Tiberius nihil hac mora mitigatus, probris etiam congerendis acerbior, apud patres conquerebatur, quòd frande unius fena- toris imperatoria majestas elusa publice foret. Frustrà à quoquam civium libertas linguæ, libertate exultatum ire jussa, acuitur. necidem est, Macedoni ab Achæo- rum populo, ac Romæ Tiberio, temporum rerumque domino, obstrepere.
units.tr: With the fathers swept into flattery through fear, and Agrippina's cause failing, Junius Rusticus, chosen by Caesar to draw up the minutes of the fathers, by a certain fateful impulse, having given no earlier proof of constancy, began to address the wavering and to warn the consuls not to begin the report. He said that the sum of affairs could be turned in brief moments, and that a breathing-space should be given for the old man's repentance. Thus one of the senators, one previously believed to be only a flatterer, delayed the will of Caesar which the senate was to subscribe. This Junius Rusticus had once been what Cycliades was in the assembly of the Achaeans. Philip, king of the Macedonians, whom Perseus, the last of the kings, succeeded, proposed certain measures odious to the Achaeans, which led to undermining their state. Cycliades, who until that day had been counted among the royal flatterers, declared freely in the senate that it was not lawful under the laws of the Achaeans to report on any matter other than those for which they had been convened. And so, by blocking the report, he resisted the king's cunning and freed the assembly from the necessity of decreeing what it did not wish. But Junius Rusticus, who had yet to be taught to serve the prince, did not win an outcome of deciding freely equal to Cycliades'. Nor did the people, bearing effigies of Agrippina and Nero, achieve anything of weight. For Sejanus, more violent in anger and having found a harvest for accusation, pressed on: the prince's scorned grief had been drawn away from the senate by the people. And Tiberius, not softened by this delay and sharper still in heaping up reproaches, complained before the fathers that the imperial majesty had been publicly mocked by the trick of one senator. The freedom of tongue of any citizen was sharpened, with orders to rejoice in freedom. Indeed it is the same thing: to clamour against Macedon at the people of Achaea, and at Rome against Tiberius, lord of the times and of affairs.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Exitus dominationis tentatæ, non ingressus, non via spectanda.
units.tr: The outcome of an attempted domination, not its beginning; the outcome is what should be considered.

units.la: Magnus est in historia Corneliana hiatus, multò lu- ctuofior de deprehenso & punito Sejano: qui ex hi- storia Dionis Cassii supplendus.
units.tr: There is a great gap in the Cornelian history, and a much more sorrowful account of Sejanus being caught and punished, which must be supplied from the history of Dio Cassius.

units.la: Novilunio quodam, magna salutantium in domo Sejani frequentia, lectus in aula, in qua salutantes ad- mittebantur, multitudine insidentium totus confra- &tus est. progrediente ipso è domo, felis per medios discurrit. quumque in capitolio facrificaffet, ac inde forum descenderet, fervi ejus stipatores, cum propter turbam eum sequi non possent, in viam quæ ad carce- rem ducit diverterunt, ac per scalas Gemoniás defcen- dentes, lapsi deciderunt. Augurium deinde captandi, nulla boni ominis avis apparuit; corvi autem circum- volitantes, obstrepentesque ei, confertim ad carcerem devolarunt, ac super eum consederunt. Hæc neque à Sejano, neque ab alio ullo prodigia in animum admif- fa sunt: nemo enim, ad præfentia respiciens, ne deo quidem tantam brevi futuram mutationem prædicen- ti credidisset. Itaque adulationis pleni omnes, ejus fortunam jurabant, collegamque eum Tiberio non jam in consulatu, sed in summa rerum administranda innuentes, destinabant.
units.tr: On a certain new-moon day, when there was a large crowd of callers at Sejanus's house, the couch in the hall where callers were admitted collapsed entirely under the weight of those sitting on it. As he came out of the house, a cat ran through the middle of the crowd. When he had offered sacrifice on the Capitol and was coming down from there into the Forum, his attendants could not follow him because of the crowd, so they turned into the road that leads to the prison, and while going down the Gemonian steps they slipped and fell. Then, when he tried to take the omens, no bird of good omen appeared; instead, ravens flying around him and screaming at him flew down together to the prison and settled on top of it. Neither Sejanus nor anyone else took these portents to heart. For no one, looking only at the present, would have believed that such a great change was about to come even for a god foretelling it in so short a time. And so all of them, full of flattery, swore by his fortune, and, pointing to him as Tiberius's colleague not now in the consulship but in the administration of the whole state, they marked him out for it.

units.la: bit Jofephus, Judaicarum rerum XVIII.
units.tr: So Josephus writes, Jewish Antiquities XVIII.

units.la: Aversus Tiberii animus.
units.tr: Tiberius's mind turned against him.

units.la: Quorum etsi nihil jam Tiberium latebat, id tamen agitabat, qua ratione eum e medio tolleret: ac non inveniens, quomodo id tuto posset manifesto peragere, mirabili usus est consilio erga illum & erga alios, ad consilia eorum introspicienda.
units.tr: Although Tiberius was by now not unaware of these things, he kept turning over how he might remove him from the way; and, not finding how he could safely do it openly, he used a remarkable plan both against Sejanus and against others, to look into their intentions.

units.la: Actus Tiberii in evertendo Sejano.
units.tr: Tiberius's actions in overthrowing Sejanus.

units.la: Assidue multa ac varia de se ad senatum ac Sejanum scribebat: modo se male affectum, ac tantum non animam agere; modo bona valetudine uti, venturumque Romam. Sejanum alias laudibus extollere, interdum deprimere; amicorum Sejani alios honore, alios ignominia propter eum afficere. Itaque Sejanus & superbiae & metus in medio, semper animi pendere. Neque metu adductus ad novas res consurgere; neque tur-sus ex confidentia quicquam conari, quia diminutio erat de ipsius potentia facta: reliqui itidem omnes, quum brevi temporis vicissitudine divertissimos nuncios acciperent, ac neque suspicere jam Sejanum, neque contemnere auderent, Tiberiique aut mortem aut adventum exspectarent: ancipites haerebant. &c. Edixit etiam ne cui hominis sacrificaretur, (atqui Sejano res sacra fieri solebat) neve in suum honorem quicquam decerneretur, (quippe multa Sejano decernebantur) quod jam ante interdictum, tum propter Sejanum repetebatur. Neque enim id concessurus alteri erat Tiberius, quod sibi ipsi non permisisset[?]. Haec effecerunt, ut contemptus Sejani adeo apud populum augeretur, ut jam non occulte ab eo se subtraherent; eumque deserebant[?]. Tiberius ubi haec cognovit, sum-pto animo, ut qui populo ac senatu auxiliari usurus foret, ad eum evertendum se accingebat. Rumore igitur sparso, quasi tribunitiam potestatem Sejano esset daturus, quo magis improviso hominem adoriretur: eum apud senatum per literas, per Naevium Sertorium Macronem perferendas, accusavit. Quum[?] jam ante occulte praetoriis cohortibus praefecerat, & quae agenda essent docuerat.
units.tr: He constantly wrote many and varied things about himself to the Senate and to Sejanus: at one time that he was in poor health and scarcely breathing; at another that he enjoyed good health and would come to Rome. At times he raised Sejanus with praises, at other times he cast him down; and on account of him he favoured some of Sejanus's friends with honours and others with disgrace. So Sejanus, caught between pride and fear, was always in suspense. Frightened, he did not rise to new undertakings, nor, on the other hand, did he dare to attempt anything out of confidence, since his power had been diminished. All the others likewise, when in a short space of time they received the most conflicting messages, and dared neither to look up to Sejanus nor to despise him, waited for either Tiberius's death or his arrival, and hung in doubt. Etc. He also issued an edict that no one should be sacrificed to (yet sacred rites were customarily performed for Sejanus), and that nothing should be decreed in his own honour (indeed many things were being decreed for Sejanus); this had already been forbidden before, but now it was renewed on account of Sejanus. For Tiberius was not going to allow another to have what he himself had not permitted himself. These measures had the effect that contempt for Sejanus grew so much among the people that they now no longer withdrew from him in secret but openly deserted him. When Tiberius learned of this, he took heart, as one who was about to use the help of the people and the Senate, and he prepared himself to overthrow him. Therefore, a rumour having been spread as though he were about to give Sejanus the tribunician power, so that he might attack the man more unexpectedly, he accused him before the Senate by letter, to be delivered through Naevius Sertorius Macro. He had already secretly placed Macro in command of the praetorian cohorts and had instructed him what was to be done.

units.la: Aggressio.
units.tr: The attack.

units.la: Is noctu, tanquam aliud ob negotium, Romam ve-nit: mandata cum Memmio Regulo tum consule (nam collega ejus Sejano favebat) & Gracino Lacone nocturnorum vigilum custode communicat. Sub au-toram in palatium ascendens, (senatus enim in Apol-linis indictus erat) in Sejanum nondum eo ingressum incidit, tristemque ob non datas ad fe à Tiberio literas conspicatus consolabatur; remotis arbitris dicens, ferre fe ei tribunitiam potestatem. Quo nomine gnalætitia perfusus, in curiam insiluit. At Macro militibus praetorianis, qui circa eum & senatum erant, in castra ablegatis, quum prius fe iis à Tiberio praefectum esse declaraffet, feque literas ferre ab eo, quibus praemia ipsis darentur: in eorum locum nocturnos custodes templo circumfudit. ipse tum ingressus, epi-stola consulibus exhibita, egrediebatur, antequam recitarentur. Custodia ejus loci Gracino mandata, ipse in castra nequid ibi novarum oriretur, contendit.
units.tr: Macro came to Rome by night, as though on some other business, and communicated his orders to the consul Memmius Regulus (for his colleague Sejanus was favouring him) and to Graecinus Laco, the guardian of the night watch. Going up to the palace at dawn (for the Senate had been summoned to the temple of Apollo), he met Sejanus, who had not yet entered it, and seeing him sad because no letters from Tiberius had been sent to him, he comforted him, saying, when the others had been dismissed, that he was bringing him the tribunician power. Overjoyed at this, Sejanus leapt into the senate house. But Macro sent the praetorian soldiers who were around him and the Senate away to their camp, having first declared that he had been set over them by Tiberius and that he was bringing letters from him by which rewards would be given to them; and in their place he surrounded the temple with the night watchmen. He himself then went in, and while the letter was being shown to the consuls, he went out again before it was read. He entrusted the guard of that place to Graecinus, and he himself hurried to the camp, to make sure nothing new arose there.

units.la: Epistola Tiberii.
units.tr: The letter of Tiberius.

units.la: Interim epistola recitatur bene longa. In quâ nihil confertim contra Sejanum continebatur: sed aliæ principio res, deinde brevis ejus insectatio, tum rursus aliud quiddam, iterumque aliud contra Sejanum. ex-trema pagina duos Senatores Sejani familiares plec-tendos, ipsum in custodia habendum mandabat. Neque enim palam eum necari Tiberius jubebat: ve-rebatur, enim nequis ex eo tumultus oriretur. Quin etiam alterum consulum ad fe vocabat, quasi ne tutò quidem iter facere posset. Hæc literarum summâ erat.
units.tr: Meanwhile the letter, which was quite long, was read out. In it nothing was said directly against Sejanus in a continuous way; rather, first there was one subject, then a brief attack on him, then something else again, and once more something else against Sejanus. On the last page he ordered that two senators who were friends of Sejanus be punished, and that Sejanus himself be kept in custody. For Tiberius did not order him to be killed openly, since he feared that some tumult might arise from it. Indeed, he even summoned the other consul to himself, as though he could not even travel safely. This was the substance of the letter.

units.la: Senatorum habitus.
units.tr: The senators' demeanour.

units.la: Antequam ea recitarentur, multa & varia auribus & oculis percipere erat. Laudare Sejanum senatus, ut tribunitiam potestatem acceptum: acclamatio-nibus spes quisque suas animo præcipere, animi in eum & favoris præsentiam ostentare. Postquam nihil eorum quæ fperarant, literarum argumento depre-henfum: ibi verò hæsitatio, & fecundum eam moesti-tia. tia coóriri. Et quidam eorum, qui Sejano assidebant, exsurgere. Quem enim paulo ante amicum habere magni duxerant, cum eo ne sedem quidem jam communem habere dignabantur. Jamque praetores ac tribuni circundare eum, ne prosiliens foras aliquid turbarum daret. Et dedisset haud dubie, si initio gravi aliqua oratione ictus fuisset. Nunc singula quae recitabantur, quasi sola & levia praetermittens, ac omnino vel nihil de se, aut certe non extrema perscripta esse sperans, loco suo commorabatur.
units.tr: Before those letters were read out, one could perceive many different things by ear and eye. The senate praised Sejanus as though he had received tribunician power; with acclamations each man anticipated in his mind the hopes he had of him, and displayed his goodwill and favour towards him. After none of the things they had hoped for were found in the letter's contents, then indeed hesitation arose, and sadness followed it. Some of those who had been sitting beside Sejanus stood up. Men whom they had lately thought it a great honour to count as friends, they now did not deign to share a seat with. And now the praetors and tribunes surrounded him, lest he leap up and cause some outbreak of violence. And he would undoubtedly have done so, had he been struck at the start by some grave speech. Now, passing over each of the things being read out as if they were trivial and unimportant, and hoping that nothing about himself, or at least nothing of the gravest kind, had been written, he remained in his place.

units.la: Comprehensio Sejani.
units.tr: The arrest of Sejanus.

units.la: Regulo eum ad se vocante, non audiens dicto fuit, neque id fastu (jam enim animo dejectus erat) sed cuiquam parere insolens. Iterum ac tertium inclamanti, porrecta manu, Sejane ades huc, id modo interrogavit, Mene vocas? Surgenti demum Laco ingressus astitit. Perlecta epistola, omnes uno ore clamore & maledictis eum incessere: pars injuriam ab eo passi, alii quibus terrorem obtulerat, alii amicitiam ejus obliterantes, quidam mutatione ejus fortunae laeti. At vero Regulus neque omnes sententiam interrogavit, neque capitis anquisivit, veritus ne suffragiis variantibus quicquam turbarum oriretur. Uno censere jusso, alteroque in vincula ducendum assentiente, aede eductus, comitantibus cum Lacone magistratibus, in carcerem trahitur.
units.tr: When Regulus summoned him to come to him, he did not obey. This was not out of arrogance (for he was already dejected in spirit), but because he was unaccustomed to obey anyone. When Regulus called to him a second and a third time, holding out his hand, Sejanus only asked, "Do you call me?" Only when he rose did the Laco come in and stand beside him. The letter having been read through, everyone shouted and abused him with one voice: some who had suffered wrong at his hands, others whom he had terrified, others who were forgetting his friendship, and some who were glad at the change in his fortune. But Regulus neither asked everyone's opinion nor inquired into the charge that carried the death penalty, fearing that with differing votes some disturbance might arise. When one man had been ordered to give his opinion, and another agreed that he should be led into chains, he was taken out of the temple, accompanied by the Laco and the magistrates, and dragged off to prison.

units.la: Supplicium Sejani.
units.tr: The execution of Sejanus.

units.la: Populus omnes statuas ejus dejecit, confregit, raptavit, &c. Capite mulctatus, in Gemonias projicitur, triduumque ludibrio vulgo habitus in Tiberim protruditur. Liberi ejus ex Senatusconsulto necantur.
units.tr: The people threw down, broke and dragged off all his statues, and so on. Condemned to death, he was thrown onto the Gemonian steps, and after being exposed to the mockery of the common people for three days, was thrown into the Tiber. His children were put to death by decree of the Senate.

units.la: Haec è Dionis libro LVIII.
units.tr: These things are from Dio's book 58.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Sexus & ætas tenera atrocitatem pœnæ mitiget.
units.tr: Sex and tender age should soften the severity of the punishment.

units.la: Calliditate Tiberii, furore Caligulæ, stoliditate Claudii, sævitia Neronis, integram per hominis ætatem sine modo supplicia cumulabantur. Sed nullum miseratione triftius exemplum, quam raptæ ad necessi[?] filiolæ Sejani. Auxit commiseratiónem nescia immi-nentium malorum, nescia culpæ paternæ simplicitas. puella adeò nescia, ut crebrò interrogaret, quod ob deli-ctum, & quò traheretur? neque factuam[?] ultrà, & posse fe puerili verbere moneri. Satis in Sejani fuppli-cio miseriarum fuerat, fatis inconstantiæ rerum huma- narum, & levitatis plebejæ, exempli. Quem maneut præstantiorem se universi ad curiam comitati fuerè, eodem die ut vilem homuncionem in carcerem tra-hebant. quem coronis ante dignati fuerant, ei tuni vincula injecerunt. quem tanquam dominum stipa-verant, eum ut fugitivum custodiâ cinxere; tegumen-to detrasto âlapas ingesserunt. quem anté præstexta purpura decoraverant, cui genua flexerant, cui ut Deo sacrificaverant, eum ad mortem duxerunt. Dio lib. 58. Eadem plebis Romanæ ira (nam non omnis culpa Ti-berii) supplicio Sejani, & tanta rerum conversione non lenita, ad liberos ejus, ad liberos ætatis & sexus tene-ritudine fragiles se effudit. Séd odii paterni gravitas, & ultionis timor, tantam acerbitatem exegerit. cur in pudicitiam virginculæ, cur in famam lævitum? Tra-dunt temporū ejus auctores, quia triumvirali supplicio affici virginem inauditum habebatur, à carnifice la-queum juxta compressam. Violenta legum & pudendâ interpretatio! Leges, non civiles magis quàm huma-næ, innocentem ætatem, castàm ætatem, ætatem cui ab omnibus favetur, etiam in culpa deprehensam, triumvirali supplicio eximunt. Hi ; callidi scilicet le-gumi nterpretes, flagitio scelus obtegentes, ob cul-pam alienam puniendam, in publico, idque impuri carnificis corpore, devirginant! Augetur invidia, cor-porum in loca infamia & præcipitia abjectione. exin oblíss saucibus, id ætatis corpora in Gemonias abjectæ. Ita omnimodo modum Romani, ut antea colendo Sejano, ita nunc vindicando excedunt. Nos, ab excessu utrobique abhorrentes, non impetus; nonirá in judi-cando, sed ratio quietos ducat;
units.tr: Through Tiberius's cunning, Caligula's madness, Claudius's stupidity and Nero's savagery, punishments were heaped up without limit throughout a man's whole life. But no example is sadder to pity than the little daughters of Sejanus, who were dragged off to execution. Their simplicity, ignorant of the evils hanging over them and ignorant of their father's guilt, increased the pity. The girl was so ignorant that she kept asking what the offence was and where she was being taken, and promised she would not do it again, and said she could be corrected with a childish beating. In Sejanus's punishment there had been enough of misery, and enough of an example of the inconstancy of human affairs and the fickleness of the common people. The man whom all had accompanied to the senate house as the most distinguished of men, on that same day they dragged to prison as a worthless little fellow.
