Whom they had lately honoured with garlands, on him they now put chains. Whom they had attended as their master, him they now hemmed in with guards as a fugitive; having stripped off his cloak, they struck him with blows. Whom they had lately adorned with the purple-bordered robe, before whom they had bent the knee, to whom they had sacrificed as to a god, him they led to death. Dio, book 58. The same anger of the Roman people (for not all the blame lies with Tiberius), not softened by the punishment of Sejanus or by so great a reversal of fortune, poured itself out upon his children, who were fragile by the tenderness of their age and sex. But the severity of their father's hatred and the fear of vengeance demanded such cruelty. Why against the modesty of a little virgin, why against the good name of a girl? Its authors hand down that, because it was unheard of for a virgin to be subjected to the punishment reserved for the triumvirs, the executioner first violated her and then put a noose about her. Oh, the violent and shameful interpretation of the laws! The laws, no less human than civil, release from the triumviral punishment an innocent age, a chaste age, an age favoured by all, even when caught in guilt. These clever interpreters of the law, covering shame with crime, in order to punish another's guilt, deflower her in public, and that by the body of an impure executioner! Resentment is increased by the infamy of the place where the bodies were put and by their being cast down so shamefully. Then the mangled bodies of such tender years were thrown onto the Gemonian steps. Thus the Romans exceeded every measure, just as before they had exceeded it in honouring Sejanus, so now in avenging him. Let us, shrinking from excess on both sides, be guided not by impulse, nor by anger in judging, but by reason, and let us remain calm.

units.la: VII. Credulus fingendis inanibus rumor.
units.tr: VII. Credulous rumour that invents empty things.

units.la: Ea rumoris credulitate sæpe factum est, ut homines ne in municipiis quidem nobiles, ad regni quandam delibationem pervenirent. Fingebat avida novitatis Græcia, Drusum Germanici filium apud Cyclades insulas, mox in continenti visum. at hic dolo Sejani, odio & metu Tiberii, in carcerem datus, morti asservabatur. Lapsum custodia, pergere ad paternos exercitus, Ægyptum aut Syriam invasurum fingebant simul, credebantque.
units.tr: By this credulity of rumour it often happened that men who were not even noble in their own towns came to a kind of foretaste of kingship. Greece, greedy for novelty, invented that Drusus, son of Germanicus, had been seen among the Cyclades islands, and soon afterwards on the mainland. But he, through the treachery of Sejanus and the hatred and fear of Tiberius, had been thrown into prison and was being kept for death. They invented and at the same time believed that, having escaped custody, he would make for his father's armies and would invade Egypt or Syria.

units.la: Quam multa hodie ad similitudinem ejus figmen-ti, quia fieri posse conjectura suggerit, ut facta aut su-tura, orbi credenda obtruduntur! Plura vel de famæ inanitate, vel de hominum aliena persona res novas molientium audacia, fecundo Annalium libro, circa Clementis actionem habes.
units.tr: How many things today, similar to that fiction, are thrust upon the world to be believed as done or about to be done, because conjecture suggests they could happen! More on either the emptiness of rumour, or the boldness of men who stir up revolution under another's name, you will find in the second book of the Annals, concerning the affair of Clemens.

units.la: VIII. Fœda magistratuum, pudenda collegarum altercatio.
units.tr: VIII. A shameful quarrel among magistrates, a disgraceful wrangling of colleagues.

units.la: Qui litibus civium componendis dilecti sunt, eos lite domestica compingi turpe est: & quos fraternus collegii nexus conjunxit, animorum disjunctione distrahi, dolendum.
units.tr: It is shameful that those who have been chosen to settle the disputes of citizens should be embroiled in a quarrel among themselves, and it is lamentable that colleagues joined by the brotherly bond of a college should be torn apart by a division of minds.

units.la: Attamen non raro collegas, & in magistratu quidem collegas, occulta simultate, quæ aliquando erumpat, fervere videas. diu acta discordia consulum[?] erupit. Ea ab animi levitate, & altercandi promptitudine, quieti suæ, quieti aliorum adversa, fermè oritur. nam Trio facilis capessendis inimicitiis, & foro exercitus. Forenses igitur homines, aut theatrali studio operas miscere solitos, venalesve rabularum linguas, ad magistratuum collegia non temere admoveri suaserim.
units.tr: Yet not infrequently you may see colleagues, and in magistracy colleagues especially, seething with a hidden rivalry that at some point breaks out. The long-standing discord of the consuls broke out. This almost always arises from a lightness of mind and a readiness to quarrel, which is hostile to one's own peace and to the peace of others. For Trio was quick to take up enmities, and practised in the forum. I would therefore advise that men of the forum, those accustomed to bring their efforts to theatrical pursuits, or hired tongues of hack advocates, not be rashly admitted to colleges of magistrates.

units.la: Qui homines, pabuli rixarum defectu, vel sua vitia collegis objicere non erubescunt. Trio ut segnem Regulum ad opprimendos Sejani ministros oblique perstrinxerat. qui meliori jure à Regulo, modestiae nisi lacesseretur retinente, ut noxius conjurationis ad dis-quisitionem trahebatur. Nam & Dioni(lib.58.) τὰ [?]Σηιανῦ [?]πφρονηκίνα, Sejano factioni adhaesisse dicitur. Memmio autem Regulo omnium primo Sertorius Macro opprimendi Sejani consilium communicavit, nec ille segnem in eo evertendo operam navavit. Huic vitilitigantium dedecori sapienter se patres in-terponebant, orantes, ponerent odia in perniciem itu-ra. Nam privatorum simultates intra privatum da-mnum subsistunt: publicam personam gerentium dissensio, nisi cohibeas, in publicum malorum sensum erum-pit.
units.tr: Men who, lacking material for quarrels, are not ashamed to throw their own faults in the face of their colleagues. Trio had obliquely censured the sluggish Regulus for failing to crush the ministers of Sejanus. Regulus, who had the better right, since he restrained himself out of modesty unless provoked, was drawn into the inquiry as a participant in the conspiracy. For Dio also says that Trio had clung to the faction of Sejanus. Sertorius Macro was the first to share with Memmius Regulus the plan for crushing Sejanus, and Regulus did not show a sluggish effort in overthrowing him. To this disgrace of quarrelling litigants the fathers wisely interposed themselves, pleading, let them lay aside hatreds that will issue in destruction. For private feuds remain within private harm; but the dissension of those who bear a public persona, unless you restrain it, bursts out into a public sense of evils.

units.la: SEXTUS
units.tr: SEXTUS

units.la: SEXTUS ANNALIUM TACITI liber per Aphorismos explicatus.
units.tr: SIXTH BOOK OF TACITUS' ANNALS, explained by aphorisms.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Non est ferenda in sene, in principe, in severo errorum humanorum vindi-ce, libido.
units.tr: Lust is not to be tolerated in an old man, in a prince, or in a severe punisher of human errors.

units.la: DE sene Cicero libro i. offic. Luxuria vero cum omni aetate turpis,tum senectuti foedissima est. Sin autem & libidinum intemperantia accesserit, du-plex malum est, quod & ipsa senectus concipit dedecus, & facit adolescen-tium impudentiorem intemperantiam. De principe Ovidius:
units.tr: Cicero, in book 1 of De Officiis, on old age: "Luxury is shameful at every age, but in old age it is most disgraceful. If intemperance in lusts is added, it is a double evil: old age itself takes on disgrace, and it makes the intemperance of the young more shameless." Ovid, on a prince:

units.la: Non bene conveniunt, nec in una sede morantur, Majestas & amor.
units.tr: "Majesty and love do not agree well, nor do they stay in the same seat."

units.la: De severo delictorum judice juvenalis:
units.tr: Juvenal, on the severe judge of crimes:

units.la: Quis tulerit Gracchos de seditione querentes ? Quis coelum terris non misceat, & mare coelo, Si fur displiceat Verri, homicida Miloni; Claudius accuset moechos, Catilina Cethegum ?
units.tr: "Who would endure the Gracchi complaining of sedition? Who would not mix heaven with earth and sea with heaven, if theft displeased Verres, or murder displeased Milo, if Claudius accused adulterers and Catiline accused Cethegus?"

units.la: Libro 1. v. 195.
units.tr: Book 1, verse 195.

units.la: Tiberius & septuagenarius, & Romani imperii, terra-rum splendidissimi, princeps, & levium etiam delicto-rum vindex acerrimus, Capreas libidinem caprinam explendi latibulum, relicta Romæ frequentia, selegit.
units.tr: Tiberius, both a septuagenarian and the most splendid prince of the Roman empire, and also the fiercest avenger even of slight crimes, chose Capri as a hiding place for his goatish lust, leaving behind the crowds of Rome.

units.la: Cumque aliquando in conspectum Romæ venisset, saxa rursum & solitudinem maris repetiit, pudore sceleris lerum & libidinum: quibus adeò indomitis exarserat, ut more regio pubem ingenuam stupri pollueret. Saxa occultare, solitudinem abscondere, mare eluere putabat; quæ cœlum aspexit, fama prodidit, animus infixa circumferebat. Hinc pudor cœtus hominum adeundi, & ad eadem saxa adhæsio.
units.tr: And when at some time he came into view of Rome, he went back again to the rocks and the solitude of the sea, out of shame at his crimes and lusts, by which he had burned so unrestrainedly that, in royal fashion, he defiled freeborn youths with debauchery. He thought he could hide things with rocks, conceal them in solitude, and wash them away in the sea. But fame, which had seen the sky, betrayed him, and his own mind carried its fixed thoughts about with him. Hence his shame at approaching gatherings of men, and his clinging to those same rocks.

units.la: Nimirum
units.tr: Indeed

units.la: Exemplo quodcunque malo committitur, ipsi Displicet autori: prima est hæc ultio, quod se Judice nemo nocens absolvitur, improba quamvis Gratia fallacis prætoris viceritur urnam.
units.tr: "Whatever wrong is committed by example displeases the author himself. This is the first punishment: no guilty man is acquitted by his own judgment, though shameless favour may overturn the urn of the deceitful praetor."

units.la: Juvenal. lib. 5. v. 1.
units.tr: Juvenal, book 5, verse 1.

units.la: Est tamen, quod in ipso Tiberii flagitio probes: quod solitudine occultavit, quod pudorem intra animum concepit, quod Romæ celebritatem stupris & adulteriis non implevit. Quàm multi regum palàm nequitiam ausi, aulam suam fornicem, aulicos lenones esse- cere. Tangit eam vitiorum inveteratam impuden- tiam, more regio, Cornelius. Nec reges tantùm Asia- tici, luxu & dominatione effrenes, libidine non occul- tata exarserunt. Romæ Nero stupris & raptibus com- pita implevit: Domitianus nondum princeps, jam stupris filium principis agebat. Heliogabalum, & ejus- modi generis humani propudia, prætereo. Sanctam etiam apud Germanorum gentem, regum libidinem non infamem fuisse. Tacitus undecimo libro Anna- lium, in Italo Cherufcorum rege, innuit. modò comi- tatem & temperantiam nulli invisam, sapius vinolen- tiam ac libidines, grata barbaris, surpans. Sed nec errantium multitudine Tiberius absolvitur; & quod celebritati loci subduxit, flagitiorum gravitate cumu- lavit. tuncque primùm ignota ante vocabula reperta sunt, sellariorum & spintriarum, ex seditate loci ac multiplici patientia. Sed senem caprini generis Saty- rum, indomitæ libidinis Tiberium, Capreiarum late- bris relinquimus.
units.tr: Yet there is something in Tiberius's shameful conduct that you may approve: that he hid it in solitude, that he kept his shame within his own mind, and that he did not fill Rome with the spectacle of his debaucheries and adulteries. How many kings have openly dared wickedness, making their court a brothel and their courtiers pimps! Cornelius touches on this long-established shamelessness of vices, which was royal in fashion. Nor were only Asian kings, unbridled in luxury and domination, inflamed by lust they did not conceal. At Rome Nero filled the crossroads with debauchery and rapes. Domitian, not yet emperor, was already playing the emperor's son in debauchery. I pass over Heliogabalus and such disgraces of the human race. Nor was the lust of kings infamous even among the German people, which is held in high regard. Tacitus, in book 11 of the Annals, hints at this in the case of the Italian king of the Cherusci, who, while not hated for courtesy and temperance, often pleased the barbarians with drunkenness and lusts. But Tiberius is not acquitted by the multitude of those who err. What he withdrew from the crowded life of the city, he heaped up with the gravity of his crimes. And then for the first time unknown words were invented, of sellarii and spintriae, from the solitude of the place and the manifold submission of its victims. But we leave the old man, a goatish satyr of unbridled lust, Tiberius, in the hiding places of Capri.

units.la: Adula-
units.tr: Adula-

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Adulatio, quæ nimia, ipsis autoribus derisui vel noxæ.
units.tr: Flattery, when excessive, is harmful or ridiculous even to its own authors.

units.la: Non displicent regnantibus ingenia Friderici Toletani in aula Philippi II. Hispaniarum regis; Curtii Rufi sub Claudio imperatore, qui Curtius adversus superio-res tristi adulatione, arrogans minoribus, inter pares difficilis. Sed nec minores arrogantia, pares morositate offendendi autor fuit; & principem offenderis, qui
units.tr: The talents of Frederick of Toledo at the court of Philip II, king of Spain, did not displease rulers; nor did those of Curtius Rufus under the emperor Claudius, who, as Curtius, was in dealings with superiors sadly flattering, arrogant toward inferiors, and difficult among equals. Yet neither was the author of offence by arrogance toward lesser men or by peevishness toward equals; and you offend a prince if

units.la: Cui male si palpere, recalcitret, undique tutus, ut Horatius loquitur.
units.tr: "If you stroke him badly, he kicks back, but he is safe on every side," as Horace puts it.

units.la: Ludibrio fuit Togonii Galli adulatio, senatores ad satellitium destinantis. Nam principem orabat diligere, senatores, ex quibus viginti forte ducti & ferro accincti, quoties curiam intrasset, salutem ejus defenderent.
units.tr: The flattery of Togonius Gallus became a laughingstock, since he proposed that senators be assigned as bodyguards. For he begged the prince to love the senators, from whom perhaps twenty, chosen and girded with steel, would defend his safety whenever he entered the senate house.

units.la: Quasi non aut Julius Cæsar a senatoribus in ipsa curia interemptus fuisset, aut Tiberius ulli hominum ordini, quam senatorio, salutem suam minus sideret. Unde tamen Togonio ea gratificandi Tiberio perfuasio? Crediderat nimirum epistola, subsidio sibi alterum ex consulibus poscentis, ut tutus a Capreis urbem peteret, de qua epistola Dio libro LVIII. At consulis tutelam non ferio Tiberius, sed ad augendam Sejani invidiam, poposcerat. Sententiam Togonii ludibrio habens imperator, epistolæ inserit: quam deinde speciem formentium in limine curia gladios? & e senatorum consessu palæstram, e patribus gladiatores facientium. neque sibi vitam tanti, si arma tegenda foret. hoc ad imitationem magnanimitatis Julianæ, veteratoria simulatione. nam & formidine ac solicitudine perpetua degebat: nec satellitium & prætorias cohortes unquam exarmabat.
units.tr: As if Julius Caesar had not been killed by senators in the senate house itself, or as if Tiberius trusted his safety to any order of men less than the senatorial! Yet what persuaded Togonius to gratify Tiberius in this way? He had certainly believed the letter in which Tiberius asked the consuls for help, so that he might safely reach the city from Capri, concerning which letter Dio writes in book 58. But Tiberius did not accept the protection of a consul; he had asked for it in order to increase the unpopularity of Sejanus. The emperor, treating Togonius' proposal as a joke, inserts into his letter: what kind of show is this, swords at the threshold of the senate house, and a wrestling ground in the assembly of senators, senators making gladiators of themselves! Nor would his life be worth so much, if arms had to be hidden. This was in imitation of Julian magnanimity, a crafty pretence. For he lived in constant fear and anxiety, and he never disarmed his bodyguard or the praetorian cohorts.

units.la: Ita Togonius irrisu dimissus.
units.tr: So Togonius was dismissed with mockery.

units.la: Junio Gallioni, qui censuerat, ut prætoriani auctis stipendiis, jus apiscerentur in quatuordecim ordinibus sedendi, noxæ fuit modum excedens adulatio. Gratiam enim captando, gravem offensam meruit. Tibe-[?] rius enim sic accepit, quasi prava militum ambitione regnum sibi, more Sejani, pararet. Intempestive adu-lantem violenter increpuit: velut coram rogitans, quid illi cum militibus, quos neque dicta imperatoris, neque pramia nisi ab imperatore accipere par effet, re-perire prorsus quod divus Augustus non providerit, an, potius discordiam & seditionem à satellite Sejani quaesitam? quà rudes animos, nomine honoris, ad corrumpendum militia morem propelleret. Ita nequiter illi, ut [?] Sofiæ Plautino, prima cessit parafitatio. Hoc pretium, Gallio meditata adulationis tulit, statim curia, deinde, Italia exactum.
units.tr: Junius Gallio, who had proposed that the praetorians, with increased pay, should obtain the right of sitting in the fourteen rows, was harmed by flattery that exceeded the proper measure. For in seeking favour he incurred a grave offence. Tiberius took it as if, through a corrupt ambition of the soldiers, he were preparing a kingdom for himself in the manner of Sejanus. He sharply rebuked the flatterer who had come at the wrong time, as if asking him in person: what business had he with soldiers, who ought to receive orders and rewards only from the emperor? Was there anything at all that the divine Augustus had failed to foresee? Or was it rather a discord and sedition, sought out by the henchman of Sejanus, by which he would drive rude minds, under the name of honour, to corrupt the custom of the soldiery? Thus, as in Plautus' Sophia, [?] his parasitic arts were wickedly the first to give way. This reward Gallio's contrived flattery obtained: he was at once driven from the senate and then from Italy.

units.la: Dulce venenum, dulcis proditio, in principatu & Republica adulatio Petro Gregorio vocatur. lib. 8. cap 7. Adulatio enim homines prorsum ex stultis in-sanos facit: ut loquitur apud Terentium Parmeno, Eun. Act.2. Sc.2.
units.tr: Sweet poison, sweet betrayal: in a principate and in a republic, flattery is called this by Peter Gregory, book 8, chapter 7. For flattery makes men from fools into utter madmen, as Parmeno says in Terence, Eunuchus, act 2, scene 2.

units.la: Adulatio, quibus irrepit, blandiendo nocet, ridendo, lædit, gratificando vulnerat, palpando interimit. Tribuendo alicui bonum, quod non habet; vel nimium extollendo bonum, quod habet; vel approbando malum, quod habet. Prius & medium parafitandi genus venialibus peccatis, postremum mortalibus annumerat. Non male: si sensum potius & vim verborum, quam verba ponderemus. Prior enim laudandi modus, rhetoricationi, & puerili vanitati tramissus, irrisu quàm pœna dignior habetur. Tertius nec excusationem admittit, & gravi oraculi divini fulmine prosternitur. Ef. 5. v. 20. Nullo non modo fre-quenter ab aulicis ministris peccatur: nec, nisi à contantis judicii principe, scorpii cauda interimentis blandimentum repellitur.
units.tr: Flattery, by whatever means it creeps in, harms by fawning, wounds by mockery, injures by gratifying, and kills by stroking: by attributing to someone a good he does not have; by extolling beyond measure a good he does have; or by approving a wrong he has. The first and middle kinds of parasitic speech he counts among venial sins, and the last among mortal ones. Not badly, provided we weigh the sense and force of the words rather than the words themselves. For the first mode of praise, which is indulged to rhetorical and childish vanity, is regarded as deserving mockery rather than punishment. The third admits no excuse and is struck down by the heavy thunderbolt of the divine oracle: Isa. 5. v. 20. In no other way is fault committed so often by court ministers; and unless a prince of unshaken judgment rejects the flattery that kills like a scorpion's tail, it is not repelled.

units.la: Quod genus hominum Constantinus Magnus, sui alias minimè detractor, tineas soricesque palatii ap-pellavit, qui ollam nimirum, quæ priscis aulæ vocaba-tur, non commune bonum sectantur. juxta prover-bium bium Græcanicum : ζῇ χύτρᾳ, ζῇ φιλία[?]: dum fervet olla, vivit amicitia.
units.tr: Constantine the Great, not otherwise a detractor of his own, called this kind of people the moths and mice of the palace, who pursue not the common good but the pot, as it was called in the old court. According to the Greek proverb: "He lives by the pot, he lives by friendship" [ζῇ χύτρᾳ, ζῇ φιλία]: while the pot boils, friendship lives.

units.la: Nec principes tantum, verùm populus universus, quem fui juris esse ferunt, adulatoribus aures damno suo præbet. Quid enim oratores Athenis, nisi adula-tores publici, vel Socratis judicio, fuerunt? Qui dum eam potentiam, eam virtutem sibi adesse persuaden-tur, quæ insulis, quæ regnis evertendis abundè suffi-ciat, in eluctabiles calamitates attraxerunt. Sapien-tiores Atticis Thessali, odio parasitationis civitatem Adulationem dictam, Melitensibus habitatam, solo ac-quarunt. Nobis adulatio duplici de causa suspecta esse debet: vel quod Thrasones ridendos propinat; vel quod Gnathonibus ipsis, non satis eruditis, in perni-ciem cedit, quod in aphorismo, adjectis è Tacito exemplis, expressimus.
units.tr: Not only princes but the whole people, which they say is of its own right, offers its ears to flatterers to its own harm. For what were the orators at Athens but public flatterers, according to Socrates' judgment? While they persuaded themselves that they possessed that power and that virtue which would amply suffice to overthrow islands and kingdoms, they dragged themselves into calamities from which there was no escape. Wiser than the Athenians were the Thessalians, who, from hatred of parasitic flattery, razed to the ground the city called Adulation, inhabited by the Melitians. For us, flattery ought to be suspect for two reasons: either because it serves up Thrasos to be laughed at, or because it turns to the ruin of Gnathos himself, who is not learned enough. We have expressed this in the aphorism, with examples added from Tacitus.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Alterum accusaturus crimine vaca-re ipse debet.
units.tr: Whoever is about to accuse another of a crime must himself be free of crime.

units.la: Ne paria nimirum, aut graviora, ab adversario cri-mina audiat. Ex hoc suspicionis fundamento Haterius Agrippa consules anni prioris invasit, cur mutua accusatione intenta, nunc silerent? metum prorsus & noxam conscientia profædere haberi. Consulares illi Trio & Regulus fuere: quorum ille Regulum ut fe-gnem ad opprimendos Sejani asseclas perstrinxerat, hic nisi lacesseretur moderationis retinens, non modo re-tuderat collegam, sed ut noxium conjurationis ad dis-quisitionem traxerat. Trio nova quæstione & con-scientia territus, æmulationem inter collegas, & si qua discordes jecissent, melius obliterari respondit. Trioni adversus Regulum & Haterium accidit, quod de hominum ingenio Cleon apud Thucydidem tradit: [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters] Alioqui natura comparatum est, ut colentes quisque contemnat, nihil cedentes admiretur. lib.3. In quem sensum & Hermocrates apud Syracusanos: [illegible, ~25 letters]
units.tr: Naturally, so that he does not hear from his opponent charges equal or graver than his own. On this ground of suspicion they attacked Haterius Agrippa, consul of the previous year, asking why, since mutual accusations had been brought, they now kept silent: fear and a guilty conscience, they said, were plainly the cause. The consulars in question were Trio and Regulus. Regulus, as a sluggard, had reproached Trio for failing to crush the followers of Sejanus; Trio, keeping a measure of restraint unless provoked, had not merely rebuked his colleague but had dragged him into the inquiry as an accomplice in the conspiracy. Trio, terrified by the new inquiry and by his conscience, replied that rivalry between colleagues, and whatever discords they had let slip, were better forgotten. What befell Trio against Regulus and Haterius is what Cleon in Thucydides reports about human nature: [illegible] [illegible]. Otherwise it is the natural way of things that each man despises those who yield to him and admires those who give way to nothing. Book 3. To the same effect Hermocrates speaks among the Syracusans: [illegible].

units.la: Homines natura cedentibus imperare, invadentes cave solent. lib. 4.
units.tr: Men by nature tend to lord it over those who yield and to be wary of those who attack. Book 4.

units.la: Alio quodam sensu contemptu quis tutus, clariori-bus viris impune insectando negotium facessit. Hæ-texius invifior fuit, quia somno aut libidinosis vigiliis marcidus, & ob segnitiam quamvis crudelem princi-pem non metuens, illufribus viris perniciem interga-neum ac stupra meditabatur. Principes enim potentiæ retinendæ anxii, hoc genus mortalium, ut factioni-bus cogendis minus idoneum, negligentia tramittunt.
units.tr: In another sense, one who is safe through contempt can cause trouble by attacking more distinguished men with impunity. Haterius was the more hated because, drowsy from sleep or from debauched wakefulness, and not fearing the prince on account of his sluggishness, however cruel, he plotted ruin and debauchery against illustrious men. Princes, anxious to keep their power, overlook this sort of man out of carelessness, as less fit for gathering factions.

units.la: Quod fit bonum viri officium, quem modo laudavi Thu-cydidem audiamus. ὃς αἰτίως τοῖς ἀρχαῖς ἢ ἔχει δὲ ... nam qui paribus qui-dem non cedunt, ergo superiores autem honestè se ge-runt, & ergo inferiores moderatè; iis res maximè pro-spere cedant. libro v. Quas gravissimi autoris fenten-tias, etsi de bellico conflictu prolatas, jure quodam meo ad togæ disceptationes detorsi.
units.tr: This is the good duty of a man; let us hear Thucydides, whom I have just praised. [ὃς αἰτίως τοῖς ἀρχαῖς ἢ ἔχει δὲ ...] For those who do not yield to their equals, but behave honourably towards their superiors and moderately towards their inferiors, affairs turn out most prosperously for them. Book 5. These sentences of a most weighty author, though spoken of warlike conflict, I have by a certain right of my own turned to the disputes of the gown.

units.la: IV. Compendiosa parando odio via, judicandi severitas.
units.tr: IV. The short way to prepare hatred: severity in judging.

units.la: Quæ nec fine multorum offensione fit, nec offen-fio fine animorum aversione. Cotta Meffalinus favi-fima cujusque sententia autor, eoque inveteratain vi-dia. Hos ob metum plerique simulato honore co-lunt, iis via decedunt, hos amicos habere, fficto magis quam fyncero voto, exoptant. Ast ubi primula lapsas eorum rima, ubi offensi domini suspicio, passim in eos insurgitur. ubi primùm facultas data, arguitur. sed properanter Meffalinus arguitur. objecta enim crimi-na nullum Tiberii odium, amicitiæ potiùs fiduciam, insimulant. C. Cafarem quasi incesta virilitatis, dixisse, quem & Tiberius oderat, nec nisi odio Romanorum & senatus fucceffurem voluerat. sacerdotales epulas novendialem cœnam dixisse arguebatur. qui fine no-candi studio jocus liberalior erat. Coci enim magis, quam
units.tr: This comes neither without the offence of many, nor offence without the alienation of minds. Cotta Messalinus, author of the most severe opinion on each man, was for that reason long envied. Many, out of fear, honour such men with feigned respect, yield to them, and wish them as friends with a pretended rather than a sincere wish. But when once a crack appears in them, when the suspicion of an offended master arises, they are attacked on every side; as soon as the opportunity is given, they are accused. Messalinus, however, was accused in haste, for the charges brought against him accused him not so much of Tiberius' hatred as of his confidence in friendship. They said he had called Gaius Caesar a man of incestuous virility, whom Tiberius also hated, and whom he had wished as successor only out of hatred of the Romans and the senate. He was accused of having called the priests' feast a "novendial dinner". This, being without any intent to harm, was rather a freer jest.

units.la: Scueri judi-ces. quam Augusti, sordes hac voce notabantur. Hic cocus nundinalis est: in nonum diem solet ire coctum: in Plauti Aulularia habetur. in rei pecuniariae disceptatiuncula forte jecerat: illos quidem senatus, me autem tuebitur Tiberiolus meus. Fidentis potius principi, quam metuentis oratio. Quare Tiberius, contra primorum civitatis exspectationem rescripsit: ne verba prave detorta, neu convivialium fabularum simplicitas, in crimen duceretur. Quam animi moderatio-nem si erga omnes Tiberius prompsisset, non se viven-tium odio, superstitum liberiori judicio objecisset. Sed nimirum saevitiae autoribus, contra quam civium plerique, favebat: favore praevio sermonibus illorum ignoscebat.
units.tr: For this word branded the meanness of cooks rather than of Augustus. [Scueri judices.] This cook is a market-day cook; he is accustomed to go off on the ninth day cooked; it occurs in Plautus' Aulularia. In a little dispute over money he had said by chance: "That senate will indeed protect them, but my little Tiberius will protect me." This was the speech of a man confident in the prince rather than afraid of him. Therefore Tiberius, contrary to the expectation of the leading men of the state, replied in writing that words should not be twisted wickedly, nor the simplicity of after-dinner talk be brought into a charge. Had Tiberius shown such moderation of mind towards everyone, he would not have exposed the living to hatred, nor the survivors to a freer judgment. But surely he favoured the authors of cruelty, contrary to the practice of most citizens: with favour given beforehand, he pardoned their talk.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Clamosa res malorum conscientia.
units.tr: A noisy thing is a guilty conscience.

units.la: Tiberius qui omnia praemebat, premere erumpen-tem conscientiae vocem non potuit. Quid scribam vobis P.C. aut quomodo scribam, aut quid omnino non scribam hoc tempore, dii me deaque pejus perdant, quam perire quotidie sentio, si scio. Non epulae illum, non libidines, non somni leniebant. Non aut tympanorum sonitus, aut forensium rerum strepitus, aut pereuntium reorum ejulatus, non denique mille negotiorum caterva compescere internum clamorem valebant. Adeo facinora atque flagitia sua ipsi quoque in supplicium verterant. Neque frustra praestantissimus sapientia firmare solitus est, si recludantur tyrannorum mentes, posse aspici laniatus & ictus; quando ut corpora verberibus, ita saevitia, libidine, malis consul-tis animus dilaceretur. quippe Tiberium non fortuna, non solitudines, protegebant, quin tormenta pectoris, suaque ipsa poenas fateretur.
units.tr: Tiberius, who suppressed everything, could not suppress the voice of conscience breaking out. What shall I write to you, conscript fathers, or how shall I write, or what shall I not write at all at this time? May the gods and goddesses destroy me worse than I feel myself perishing every day, if I know. Feasts did not soothe him, nor lusts, nor sleep. Neither the sound of drums, nor the din of public business, nor the wailing of the condemned as they perished, nor finally a whole crowd of affairs could hold back the inner clamour. So much had their crimes and shameful deeds turned against themselves as punishment. Nor in vain has the most excellent in wisdom been accustomed to affirm that if the minds of tyrants are laid open, lacerations and blows can be seen; for as bodies are torn by lashes, so the mind is torn by cruelty, lust, and evil counsels. Indeed, neither fortune nor solitude protected Tiberius from being compelled to confess the torments of his breast and his own punishments.

units.la: Breviùs hæc Cicero in Paradoxis complexus est: Te conscientiæ stimulant maleficiorum tuorum: te metus examinant judiciorum, atque legum: quocunque aspexisti, ut furiæ, sic tuæ tibi occurrunt injuriæ, quæ te respirare non sinunt. Asperius more suo venalis: cur tamen hos tu Evasisse putes, quos diri conscia facti Mens habet attonitos, & surdo verbere cædit, Occultum quatiente animo tortore flagellum?[?] &c. Nocte dieque suum gestant in pectore testem, &c. Hi sunt qui trepidant, & ad omnia fulgura pallent.
units.tr: Cicero summed these things up more briefly in the Paradoxes: "The stings of your misdeeds prick your conscience; the fear of trials and laws examines you; wherever you look, your injuries meet you like Furies, and they do not let you breathe." More bitterly, in his own manner: "Why do you think those have escaped whom a mind conscious of a dreadful deed holds stunned, and strikes with a deaf lash, while the hidden torturer shakes the secret whip? ... By night and by day they bear their witness in their breast ... These are the ones who tremble and turn pale at every flash of lightning."

units.la: Libro 5. v.192.
units.tr: Book 5, verse 192.

units.la: Quod ab Epicuro apud Senecam dictum est: potest nocenti contingere, ut lateat, latendi fides non potest: verè dictum est, si de hominum tantum scientia acci-pias; impiè, si de Dei, quem nihil fugit, notitia.
units.tr: What Epicurus says in Seneca is this: a guilty man may be able to remain hidden, but he cannot be trusted to stay hidden. This is true if one understands it of human knowledge alone, but impious if it is understood of God's knowledge, from whom nothing is hidden.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Sycophantæ & senatoris personæ non bene commiscentur.
units.tr: The roles of informer and senator do not mix well.

units.la: Sintne ferendæ in libera republica, aut in egregio principatu, delationes, alibi disputatum est. Ut ignö-minia res ea careat, ita dignitatem certè ægrè admittit. Quod non Tiberiano ævo observatum, cùm primores senatus infimas etiam delationes exercerent, alii propalàm, multi per occultum. Neque discerneres alie-nos à conjunctis, amicos ab ignotis, quid repens, aut vetustate obscurum: perinde in foro, in convivio, quæque de re locuti incusabantur: ut quis prævenire & reum destinare properat: pars ad subsidium sui, plures infesti quasi valetudine & contactu. O delatoria tempora! O sycophantarum lunatā conciliabula! O temporum Tiberianorum nævi! Oderant senatores delationem, & exercebant, accusatores deleri volebant, & accusabant. Excusatius illi, qui ne prævenirentur timebant. Minùs excusatè, qui nocendi studio, aut prava consuetudine, ceu pestifero moris afflatu, læ-debant.
units.tr: Whether informers should be tolerated in a free commonwealth, or under an excellent prince, has been discussed elsewhere. Although such an activity lacks infamy, it very rarely admits of dignity. This was not unnoticed in the age of Tiberius, when the leading men of the senate even carried out the lowest kinds of informing, some openly, many in secret. You could not tell strangers from kinsmen, friends from strangers, or what was recent from what was obscure by age. Equally, in the forum, at a dinner, or in any remark made on any subject, people were accused. Each man hurried to forestall the others and mark out a defendant: some for their own protection, most hostile as if by a contagion of sickness. O informing times! O conventicles of informers, moonstruck! O blemishes of the Tiberian age! The senators hated informing and yet practised it; they wished the accusers destroyed, and yet they accused. Those were more excusable who feared being forestalled. Less excusable were those who injured others from a zeal for harm or from a corrupt habit, as if breathed on by a pestilential custom.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Extremæ orationis constantia gloriæ aut saluti esse potest.
units.tr: Constancy in a final speech can bring either glory or safety.

units.la: Gloriae fuit Cremutio Cordo fui & librorum defensio. iv.Annal. Saluti fuit M.Terentio interrita in extremis facundia. Fatetur fc Sejano fuisse amicum, & ut esset expetivisse: quanquam id fortunae suae minus fortasse expediat. Quidni enim eum colar, quem princeps honoribus, affinitate, dignitate supra caeteros extollit; per quem ad honores omnibus aditus? per quem unum ad Caesaris amicitiam via reclusa? ut quisque Sejano intimus, ita ad Caesaris amicitiam validus. contra, quibus infensus esset, metu ac sordibus conflictabantur. Nulla igitur in colendo Sejano culpa. culpa fuisset in negligendo. sic enim, praeter negligentiae periculum, principis iudicium privato sperneretur. Non est nostrum aestimare, quem supra caeteros, & quibus de causis attollas. Tibi summum rerum iudicium dii dedere: nobis obsequii gloria relicta est. At vero non quid in propatulo gereretur, sed quid in occulto princeps foveret, spectandum erat. Quid si enim imperator odio in Sejanum concepto, qui factioni ejus adhaerent, aut qui fortunam magis quam aequitatem rerum sequantur, cognoscere voluit? Quid si, ut Agamemnon, qui fugam navium suadebat, per Ulyssem interea fugientes coercebat: ita Tiberius, quos propter Sejanum puniret, in Sejano ad praecipitia allexit? Aequitati id non esse consentaneum, ita Terentius concludit: abditos principis sensus, & si quod occultius parat, exquirere illicitum, anceps: nec ideo adsequare. Quis enim mentem ejus, verbis & actioni adversam, praeter Deum inspiciat? Caeterum haec Terentii ratiocinatio etiam, extra scopum orationis, ad locum communem, De non indagando principum secreto, adferri solet. Sane ut carbo in sinu vestium, ita secreti cognitio aegre in animo servatur. Servati etiam, sed aliunde emanantis, non absque discrimine est arcani custodia. Si enim per alium, quem minus suspectum princeps habet, secretum erupit; aut si rumor aliquis & conjectura hominum a mente principis non abludit; eum cui cogitationes patefecit, alienis oculis ut proditorem intuetur. Aut igitur non sunt indaganda principium atcana, aut praeter tacitürnitás: tem fortunæ etiam immolandum. Non fine causa, ut in illa superstitionum nebula, apud Persas silentii quos- que numen autore Marcellino, colebatur, Quanquam arcana regum mira fide; optimates pauci in concilium admissi, celabant; ita ut nec metu nec spe votem oc- culta proditurum eliceres. Ægyptios vero, naturæ ge- nio loquaces, lex coercebat, abscindi illi linguam ju- bens, qui arcana reip. detexisset, quod in Diodori Siculi antiquitatibus observes. Athenis, quanquam gatrule dicacibus, miro silentii involucro actiones Areopagi tegebantur. quæ rebus in proverbium abiit: Areopagita taciturnior. Romani vero, majestate ad principes re- lapsa, legis terrore silentium civibus primoribus ex- torquebant; consilii publici renunciatores, ut tranf- fugas, vivicremio aut furcae suspendio addicentes: fi qua in his rebus Pauli JC. autoritas: Mæcenas, beni- gno licet Augusto semper usus, annulo fignatorio; ra- nam Seriphiam, pérpetuo silentio mutatm; gerente, fe ad taciturnitatem excitabat. Sed mañtum de tabula. Pergit Terentius defensione fui? Quid ergo? indi- flinéta hæc defensio & promiscua dabitur? imò juftiterminis dividatur. Insidia in Remp: consilia cadit ad- versum imperatorem, puniantur: de amicitia & ossi- cii, idem finis & te Cafar & nos absolverit. Hæc ma- fculæ orationis summa: Conflantia orationis, & quia repertus erat, qui efferet quæ omnes animo agitabant; eo usque potuere, ut accusatores ejus, additis quæ ante deliquerant, exilio aut morte multarentur. Orationis constantia evasit, accusatoribus punitis, quem trepida modestia perdidisset: id quod in aphorismo expressis mus.
units.tr: Cremutius Cordus gained glory from his defence of himself and of his books (Annals, book 4). Marcus Terentius gained safety from his unbroken eloquence at the end. He confesses that he had been a friend of Sejanus and had sought to be one. Yet this perhaps was less helpful to his own fortune. For why should I not cultivate the man whom the prince raises above the rest with honours, marriage connection and rank, through whom there is access to all offices, through whom alone the way to Caesar's friendship is opened? As each man is close to Sejanus, so is he strong in Caesar's friendship. On the contrary, those against whom he was hostile were struggling with fear and disgrace. So there was no fault in cultivating Sejanus. The fault would have lain in neglecting him. For in that case, apart from the danger of neglect, the prince's judgement would have been scorned by a private citizen. It is not for us to judge whom he raises above the rest, and for what reasons. The gods have given the supreme judgement of affairs to you; to us is left the glory of obedience. But it was not what was done in the open, but what the prince was fostering in secret, that had to be considered. For what if the emperor, out of hatred conceived against Sejanus, wished to find out who adhered to his faction, or who followed fortune rather than justice? What if, as Agamemnon, who was urging flight of the ships, meanwhile restrained the fleeing men through Ulysses, so Tiberius drew into ruin, through Sejanus, those whom he would punish on account of Sejanus? That this is not consistent with justice Terentius concludes thus: To seek out the hidden feelings of the prince, and whatever he prepares more secretly, is unlawful and hazardous, and one does not thereby attain it. For who could look into his mind, which is opposed to his words and actions, except God? Moreover, this reasoning of Terentius, lying outside the scope of the speech, is commonly cited under the commonplace on not inquiring into the secrets of princes. Indeed, as a coal in the folds of a garment, so the knowledge of a secret is hardly kept in the mind. Even when a secret is kept, but has leaked from elsewhere, the guarding of it is not without danger. For if a secret has escaped through another person whom the prince holds less suspect, or if some rumour and conjecture of men does not differ from the prince's mind, he regards the one to whom he has revealed his thoughts as a traitor, with hostile eyes. Therefore either the secrets of princes are not to be inquired into, or, apart from silence, fortune must also be sacrificed to them. Not without reason, amid that mist of superstitions, the godhead of silence was also worshipped among the Persians, according to Marcellinus. Yet the kings kept their secrets with remarkable fidelity; the few nobles admitted to the council concealed them, so that you could not draw out from them by fear or hope any secret they would betray. The Egyptians, indeed, naturally talkative, were restrained by law, which ordered that the tongue be cut out of anyone who had disclosed the secrets of the state; this you may observe in the Antiquities of Diodorus Siculus. At Athens, though the men were very talkative, the proceedings of the Areopagus were covered by a remarkable veil of silence, whence the proverb arose: "more silent than an Areopagite." The Romans, however, once the majesty had slipped back to the princes, extorted silence from the leading citizens by the terror of the law, condemning those who reported public counsels, as deserters, to be burned alive or hanged on a gallows; in these matters the authority of Paulus the jurist is to be found. Maecenas, although he always enjoyed the kindly favour of Augustus, urged himself to taciturnity by a signet ring, as a frog, changed into a Seriphian, bearing perpetual silence. But enough of that tablet. Does Terentius go on with his defence of himself? What then? Will this defence be given without distinction and indiscriminately? Rather let it be divided by just limits. Plots against the commonwealth and counsels against the emperor are to be punished; in matters of friendship and duty, the same end, Caesar, will acquit both you and us. This is the chief point of the speech. The constancy of the speech, and because someone was found who would say what all were thinking in their minds, prevailed so far that his accusers, with added the offences they had committed earlier, were punished with exile or death. The constancy of the speech brought safety, with the accusers punished, to the man whom a trembling modesty would have destroyed. This is what we have expressed in the aphorism.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Extremum servitutis, affectus humani punitio. Et affectus quidem innoxii ac mollioris, ut lacry- marum: idque in imbecillo sexu aut ætate. Pendet in ambiguo vita clarorum genere aut virtute virorum: ut qui occupandæ Reip. consilia agitaverint, aut agitaturi viderentur. Damnatis affinitate, amicitia, similitudine vitæ connexum esse; probro dabatur. Sermo liberior, aut vultus erectior, crimen adversus dominantes erat. Si causa mortis decerat, sola inter teos receptio carnificis manum poscebat. Nondum satis miseriarum, nec dominanti sævitiæ. Ne fœmina quidem exsortes periculi, quā occupanda Reip. argui non poterant, ob lacrymas incusabantur. necataq; est anus Vitia Fufii Geminimater, quod filii necem flevisset. Et hæc quidem apud senatum, suspicioni principis gratificaturum: quid de ipso sperraveris? Qui ne quidem familiarium intimis, & in omni secessu individuis, pepercit. Sed ad fœminarum punitas lacrymas revertor. Undecim casus, ut vocant, in quibus mulieres Earum non postrema est, quod in delicto deprehensæ, parem pœnam non subeant. Hic vero, miti nimirum senatu & principe, nullum ob delictum, ob lacrymas, ob naturalem in filios amorem, ob suorum neces commiserationem, plectuntur. Domitiano imperante vultus ac gemitus, ad supplicia adstantium, in tabulas referebantur. Sed gemitus virorum, sed ultione metuendorum.
units.tr: The last extremity of slavery is the punishment of human feeling. Feelings that are harmless and gentler, such as tears, are also punished, especially in the weaker sex or at a young age. Life hangs in doubt on account of the distinguished family or the virtue of men, as when they have plotted, or seemed about to plot, the seizing of the commonwealth. It was counted a reproach to be connected with the condemned by kinship, friendship, or similarity of life. A freer speech, or a more upright countenance, was a crime against the rulers. If no cause of death was lacking, the mere reception of a fugitive by a friend called for the executioner's hand. Cruelty was not yet satisfied with miseries, nor with the ruler's savagery. Even women, who were not exempt from danger, who could not be accused of seeking to seize the commonwealth, were blamed for their tears. The old woman Vitia, mother of Fufius Geminus, was put to death because she had wept for her son's death. And these things were done before the senate, to gratify the suspicion of the prince. What might you hope from him yourself? He spared not even the closest of his household and his inseparable companions in every retreat. But I return to the punishment of women's tears. The eleven cases, as they are called, in which women are not in the lowest rank of... [sic] ... Yet those women who are caught in an offence do not undergo an equal penalty. Here, indeed, under a mild senate and prince, they are punished for no offence, for tears, for natural love of their sons, for pity at the deaths of their kin. Under Domitian's rule, the groans and cries of bystanders at the executions were written down in the registers. But the groans were of men, and men to be feared for their vengeance.

units.la: Quid bos, quid placida commeruisti oves? Quid placidum fœminarum genus, principi non exti-mescendum sola lacrymarum destillatione commeruit? ut illud in Fastis Ovidii, de bobus & ovillo genere, huc detorqueam.
units.tr: What did the ox, what did the gentle sheep deserve? What did the gentle race of women deserve, not to be feared by the prince, merely by the dropping of tears? So I may turn that line of Ovid's Fasti, about the oxen and the sheep, to this purpose.

units.la: IX. Sententia cum moderatione libera senatorem commendat.
units.tr: IX. A free opinion, tempered with moderation, commends a senator.

units.la: Anceps quidem est sævo sub principe libertas: sed nisi per adversa nitatur, splendorem virtus amittit. Quarto Annalium libro in M.Lepido, nunc in L.Pisonc, senatoris temperatè liberi exemplum proponitur. L. Piso Pontifex, rarum in tanta claritudine, fato obiit: nullius servilis sententia sponte autor, & quoties ne-
units.tr: Freedom under a savage prince is certainly precarious, but unless virtue strives against adversity, it loses its lustre. In the fourth book of the Annals, the example of a senator who was free yet moderate is set forth first in Marcus Lepidus and now in Lucius Piso: Lucius Piso, the Pontifex, a rare man in such high standing, died by fate; he was never the author of any servile opinion of his own accord, and whenever necessity pressed, he wisely moderated himself.

units.la: B b cessitas ingrueret, sapienter moderans. Servilis sententia[?] est, quæ ad placitum superiorum, non ad animi sen-sum, aut rei veritatem applicatur. Ea aut omnia rerum consilia uno decreto absolvit, aut particularia facta cum lege aut cum ratione convenire ostentat.
units.tr: A servile opinion is one that is framed to suit the will of superiors, not the feeling of the mind or the truth of the matter. Such an opinion either settles all public counsels by a single decree, or shows that particular acts agree with law or with reason.

units.la: Prioris exemplum est in Stratocle, qui regi Demetrio à consiliis erat. Hic regis voluntati in omnibus hæc sanctione subscripsit: Quicquid rex Demetrius jubet, id erga Deum sanctum est, & apud homines longè ju-stissimum. Quasi vero fas & nefas, jus & injuria, à regis voluntate penderet. Et tamen non pauci illud,
units.tr: An example of the former is Stratocles, who was among the counsellors of King Demetrius. He subscribed to every wish of the king with this formula: "Whatever King Demetrius commands is holy before God and by far the most just among men." As if right and wrong, justice and injustice, depended on the king's will. And yet not a few people accept that saying, "What has pleased the prince has the force of law."

units.la: Quod principi placuit, legis habet vigorem, ita acci-piunt. Posterioris exemplum est in adulatoria patrum sententia, incestum Claudii cum Agrippina senatus-consulto confirmantium. Hæc cum libertate decer-nendi, veritatis nutrice, non ad amussim[?] conveniunt;
units.tr: An example of the latter is the flattering opinion of the fathers, who confirmed by senatorial decree the incest of Claudius with Agrippina. These things do not agree with the freedom of decreeing, the nurse of truth, nor with strict exactness.

units.la: Aliquando gravior præsentis periculi metus vocem in[?] faucibus opprimit: ne in loquentis damnum erumpat; In quo minus est vitii, quàm in lingua ad adulandum mansuefacta. Cum Galliæ legati, principes civitatum, flentes de Ariovisti injuria quererentur, soli Sequani, gravissimam omnium[?] injuriam experti, vocem nul-lam mittebant. Id cum admiraretur Cæsar, Divitiaco docente comperit: hoc esse miseriorem graviorem q; fortunam Sequanorum, quàm reliquorum; quod soli nec in occulto quidem queri, nec auxilium implorare auderent: absentisque Ariovisti crudelitatem, velut si coram adesset, horrerent. Propterea quod reliquis tamen fugæ facultas daretur; Sequanis vero, qui in-tra fines suos Ariovistum recepissent, quorum oppida omnia in potestate ejus essent, omnes cruciatus essent perferendi. Cæsar lib.i. de Bello Gallico.
units.tr: Sometimes the greater fear of present danger chokes the voice in the throat, lest it burst out to the speaker's harm. This fault is smaller than a tongue tamed for flattery. When the envoys of Gaul, the chiefs of their states, complained in tears about the wrong done by Ariovistus, only the Sequani, who had suffered the gravest wrong of all, uttered no word at all. When Caesar wondered at this, he learned from Diviciacus that the fortune of the Sequani was more wretched and grievous than that of the others, because they alone did not dare to complain even in secret, nor to implore help; they dreaded the cruelty of Ariovistus, though he was absent, as if he were present. The others at least had the chance of flight, but the Sequani, who had received Ariovistus within their borders, whose towns were all in his power, had to endure every torment. Caesar, On the Gallic War, book 1.

units.la: Quod Sequanis, Ariovisti impotenti dominatione compressis, id sæpe senatoribus, curia quasi careret conclusis, contingit. quibus eloqui quod honestum, quod salutare, capitale est: nec silentii semper libertas conceditur. His cum Creonte Thebano extremum votorum est:
units.tr: What happens to the Sequani, crushed by the unbridled dominion of Ariovistus, often happens to senators, as if the Curia were shut up. For them, to speak what is honourable and wholesome is a capital offence, and freedom of silence is not always granted. For them, with Creon of Thebes, the final prayer is:

units.la: Tacere liceat: nulla libertas minor
units.tr: Let me be allowed to be silent; no freedom is less

units.la: A rege petitur. Nam ab Oedipo quodam responderetur:
units.tr: Sought from a king. For an Oedipus might answer thus:

units.la: Imperia solvit, qui tacet, jussus loqui.
units.tr: He who keeps silent, when ordered to speak, dissolves commands.

units.la: Ut est in Senecae Oedipo:
units.tr: As is in Seneca's Oedipus:

units.la: Act. 3.
units.tr: Act. 3.

units.la: Est & in stultro placendi studio, inter aequales & collegas, pars in dicenda sententia quaedam servitutis. Multi enim non quid e Rep. esse sentiant, sed unde vel paucorum gratia & autoritas vel plurium consensus trahant, loquuntur. Utrobique servilis adulatio aliquid turpitudinis adjunctum habet: quam tamen vel necessitate assentiendi, vel fronte minus ferrea velari posse arbitrantur. Sane libertatem ita laudavimus, ut moderationem ei adjungeremus. Nam nihil profutura linguae libertate perniciem accersere, vel in consulto clamore claris viris obstrepere, non est hominis in aulica & civili vita eruditi. Diogenem, contra turbam semper occursu nitentem, & coetus hominum sterqui-linia vocantem, necnon accenso lumine medio in foro homines quaerentem, quasi is solus hominem saperet a curiali sede removemus.
units.tr: There is also, in the eagerness to please, among equals and colleagues, a certain element of servitude in giving one's opinion. For many do not speak according to what they believe is for the good of the commonwealth, but according to where they may draw the favour and authority of a few or the agreement of the many. In either case servile flattery carries some added shamefulness, which they nevertheless think can be veiled by the necessity of assenting or by a face less than iron. Certainly we have praised freedom only on condition that we add moderation to it. For to bring ruin upon oneself by a freedom of tongue that will profit nothing, or to shout down distinguished men in a deliberative clamour, is not the mark of a man educated in court and civil life. We remove Diogenes, who always struggled against the crowd by running into it and calling people dung-heaps, and who looked for men with a lit lamp in the middle of the forum, from the curial seat, as if he alone were wise.

units.la: X. Vicaria regis potestas colenda.
units.tr: X. The vicarious power of the king is to be cultivated.

units.la: Qualis fuit Romae imperatorum nomine praefectus urbi: non enim omnes magistratus cum Arnisaeo, erudito alias viro, eo nomine accipimus. Praefectos urbi Tacitus commemorat, sub Romulo Dentrem Romulium, sub Tullo Hostilio Numam Marcium, sub Tarquinio Superbo Spurium Lucretium, sub Augusto Cilnium Maecenatem, Messallam Corvinum, Taurum Statilium, sub Tiberio L. Pisonem. Cui praecipua ex eo gloria, quod praefectus urbi recens, continuam potestatem, & insolentia parendi graviorem, mire temperavit. Originem, causam, vim potestatis ejus his verbis author exprimit: profectis domo regibus, nec mox magistratibus, ne urbs sine imperio foret, in tempus diligebatur qui jus redderet, ac subitis mederetur. Ergo non regum tantum & imperatorum, sed & libera rep. consulum, vicarii fuerunt. Plura de hos-
units.tr: Such was the prefect of the city at Rome in the name of the emperors; for we do not accept all magistrates in this sense, with Arnisaeus, otherwise a learned man. Tacitus mentions the prefects of the city: under Romulus, Denter Romulius; under Tullus Hostilius, Numa Marcius; under Tarquin the Proud, Spurius Lucretius; under Augustus, Cilnius Maecenas, Messalla Corvinus, Taurus Statilius; under Tiberius, Lucius Piso. His special glory is that, as a newly appointed prefect of the city, he wonderfully tempered a continuing power which was heavier because of the insolence of obedience. The author expresses the origin, cause and force of that power in these words: when the kings had left home, and no magistrates had been appointed soon after, so that the city should not be without authority, someone was chosen for the time being to administer justice and to remedy sudden crises. Therefore the vicars were not only of kings and emperors, but also of the free commonwealth's consuls. More on these matters...

units.la: Fatidicis libellis fides non temerè habenda.
units.tr: Prophetic booklets are not to be readily believed.

units.la: Multae enim vanorum hominum, decipientium aut deceptorum, impofturæ circumferuntur. Quod sentiens Tiberius, commonefecit: quia multa vana sub nomine celebri vulgabantur, sanxisse Augustum, quem intra diem ad praetorem urbanum deferrentur, neque habere privatim liceret. Multa ficto Sibyllae nomine vana circumferri arbitratur: ante omnia au-tem de ipsorum Sibyllae antiquae librorum auctoritate, confirmanda an abroganda, quaeri oportuit. ἐπιλαύπωρ@· πῶς πόλεις ἡ ζήτησις τῆς ἀληθείας, ᾧ ἐπί, τὰ ἑτοῖμα μᾶλλον ἀγάπης ἐρίζοντα. Ita segnis apud multos est veritatis veftigatio, ad ea fe potius quae in promptu sunt convertentes: inquit Thucydides libro primo. Quod nec Tiberium fefellit; qui Afinio Gallo censen-te, ut libri Sibyllini adirentur, renuit: libro 1. Annal.
units.tr: For many impostures are circulated by vain men, some deceiving and some deceived. Tiberius, aware of this, reminded the senate that, because many vain things were spread under a famous name, Augustus had decreed that such writings must be brought within a day to the urban praetor and could not lawfully be kept privately. Tiberius judged that many vain things were circulated under the false name of the Sibyl, and that above all the authority of the ancient Sibylline books themselves had to be examined, to see whether they should be confirmed or abrogated. "So slothful is the search for truth among most men, who turn rather to what lies ready to hand" [ὡς πόλεις ἡ ζήτησις τῆς ἀληθείας, ᾧ ἐπί, τὰ ἑτοῖμα μᾶλλον ἀγαπῶντες]: so Thucydides in book 1. This did not escape Tiberius, who, when Asinius Gallus proposed that the Sibylline books be consulted, refused: Annals, book 1.

units.la: Nec multum tantum vanitatis inest ejusmodi vatici-niis, verum etiam ad res gerendas, fidem semel nactis[?], impedimenti. Ariovisti à Cæsare victi hæc causa ad-fertur: Quod apud Germanos ea consuetudo effet, ut matres familias eorum fortibus & vaticinationibus declararent, utrum proelium committi ex usu effet, nécne: atque ea ita dicerent, Non esse fas Germanos superare, si ante novam Lunam proelio contendissent. Qua eorum superstitione comperta, Cæsar, territos suis eos in castris cecidit.
units.tr: Nor do such prophecies contain only a great deal of vanity; they also hinder the conduct of affairs once they have gained credence. The cause of Ariovistus's defeat by Caesar is given as follows. It was the custom among the Germans for their mothers of families, by lots and prophecies, to declare whether it was expedient to engage in battle or not; and they said that it was not right for the Germans to be victorious if they fought before the new moon. Caesar, having discovered this superstition, attacked them in their camp while they were terrified.

units.la: Annonâ servientis Romae catena.
units.tr: The chain of the grain supply, which enslaves Rome.

units.la: Quae ubi suppetiit, facile plebecula, imperii secura, quiescebat; ubi vero defecit, freno concusso tumul-tuabatur. Gravitate annonae juxta seditionem ventum: multaque & plures per dies, in theatro licentius efflagi-tata, quàm solitum adversum imperatorem. Reme-dium dium adversus ejusmodi seditiones, ab annonæ gravitate ortas, mollius vel duriusculum. Mollius vel annonæ subvectione, pretii levatione, sumptuum dimensione, vel blandiloquæ orationis delinitione. Durius a sententiæ exhauftione, ad operas coactione, castigante tumultum objurgatione. Ad hoc remedium Tiberius conversus, incusavit magistratus patresque, quòd non publica auctoritate populum coercuissent. Ex ea incusatione castiganda plebi factum fe-natusconsultum, prisca severitate. Nimis durum & humanitatis oblitum remedium est, ad quod se Hatto Moguntinus præsul convertit. quem a soricibus ob id confossum, monumentum Rheni infra Bingam testatur.
units.tr: When grain was available, the common crowd, secure in the empire, kept quiet; but when it failed, they rioted as if the bridle had been shaken off. Because of the scarcity of grain, sedition came close, and for many days far more was shouted in the theatre, and more freely, than was usual against the emperor. The remedy for such seditions, arising from the scarcity of grain, is either milder or somewhat harsher. The milder remedy is the bringing in of grain, the lowering of prices, the limiting of expenses, or the soothing of flattering speech. The harsher remedy is the exhaustion of opinion, the compelling of labour, and rebuke that punishes the tumult. Tiberius turned to this harsher remedy and blamed the magistrates and the senators for not having restrained the people by public authority. From that blame a senatus consultum was passed to punish the common people, in the old severity. Too harsh and forgetful of humanity is the remedy to which Hatto, bishop of Mainz, turned; he was pierced through by mice for this, as the monument in the Rhine below Bingen bears witness.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: USURA necessarium orbi luxurian-ti Malum.
units.tr: USURY, a necessary evil for a luxurious world.

units.la: Tria in hac dissertatione nobis, Cornelianum du-ctum sequtis, agenda. 1. Vitium usuræ è latebris protrahendum. 2. Necessitas pro temporum & locorum varietate excusanda. 3. Remedium necessitati hominum quærendum.
units.tr: In this dissertation, following Cornelius's lead, three things must be dealt with: (1) the vice of usury must be dragged out of its hiding places; (2) the necessity of usury must be excused according to the variety of times and places; (3) a remedy for men's necessity must be sought.

units.la: VITIUM Usuræ.
units.tr: THE VICE OF USURY.

units.la: His argumentis demonstratur:
units.tr: The following arguments demonstrate this:

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Quod fertilem accusandi materiem suppeditat, non est omni culpæ suspicione purgatum. Usura fertilem accusandi materiem suppeditat. Ergo. Assumptio-nem non obscure Cornelius pronunciat. Magna vis accusatorum in eos irrupit, qui pecunias fœnore aucti-tabant. aut igitur natura sua fœnus, aut hominum saltem persuasione malis accensebatur. Reprehen-sionem non in nuda querentium opinione agitari, facillime probatur. Qui enim rem suam alterius cum detrimento auget; qui nulli operationi, nulli negotio intentus, aliena diligentia pascitur; qui rem natura sterilem, & permutationi rerum duntaxat succeden-tem, fructum parere cogit: is viri boni officium explere minime videtur. atqui haec omnia in usurarium di-vitem, in foeneratorem omnia cadunt. à boni igitur viri officio longissimè foeneratur recedit.
units.tr: What supplies abundant matter for accusation is not purged of every suspicion of fault. Usury supplies abundant matter for accusation. Therefore it is not purged of suspicion. Cornelius clearly states the minor premise: A great force of accusers broke in upon those who increased their money by interest. Either by its nature interest is evil, or at least men are persuaded that it is. That the censure is not driven merely by the opinion of complainers is very easily proved. For the man who increases his own property to another's loss; who, intent on no work or business, is fed by another's diligence; who forces fruit from a thing barren by nature, which serves only the exchange of goods: such a man seems in no way to fulfil the duty of a good man. But all these things apply to the rich usurer, to the moneylender. Therefore the moneylender is very far removed from the duty of a good man.

units.la: Ipsorum etiam, qui foenora exercent, iudicio foenus in turpibus habetur. A se enim nomen cum odio de-linantes, in eos utrumque retorquent, qui immodica usura egenos exugunt, aut qui pignoribus in breve dierum spatium acceptis lapsui iunt tenuioribus. Quod genus hominum, Lombardiorum appellatione plebi exosum, sacris in Batavia & honorum aditu arcetur. Alio praeterea fuco quaerendi odium velatur; poenam morae, aut id quod interest, interesse barbare, in patrocinium vocando. Qui igitur nulla ex mora damno auctì, non mercaturae, non agro colendo, non opificio operam navantes; integra domesticarum facultatum forte, imo in maius aucta, splen-did in otio publico & privato victitant, quid ad eos aut poena morae aut id quod interest spectabit? Plena est Belgarum maritimorum regio, hoc otioso hominum negotio (Rententiers vocant ab annuo pe-cuniae locatae reditu) plena Liguria, plena Castilia & Lufitania; nec erubescenda apud eos victus quaerendi frequentatione. His nulli gratis pecuniam elocan-tibus, nulli occupationi vacantibus, nullum ex nomi-num cunctatione damnum oboriri queat. Specioso igitur vocabulo res apud multos odiosa, nova nomen-clatura res legibus & hominum iudiciis prohibita, ob-tingitur.
units.tr: The judgment of the moneylenders themselves also holds interest to be a dishonourable thing. For they, abandoning the name with hatred, turn it back upon those who drain the needy with excessive usury, or who take pledges for a short term and trip up the poorer sort. This kind of men, hated by the common people under the name of Lombards, is excluded from the sacred rites in Batavia and from access to honours. Besides, the hatred is veiled by another pretext: by calling in the penalty for delay, or what is called interesse, in barbarous fashion, as a defence. Therefore, those who suffer no loss from delay, who are not engaged in trade, in tilling the land or in craft, but who live splendidly in public and private leisure with their domestic resources perhaps intact or even increased: what will the penalty for delay or what is called interest concern them? The maritime region of the Belgians is full of this leisured business of men (they call them Rentiers, from the annual return on money lent); Liguria is full of it, and Castile and Lusitania. Nor is a living sought by such frequent dealing a thing to blush for among them. For these men lend their money to no one free, and are idle from any occupation, so no loss can arise for them from a delay in payment. Thus, under a specious word, a thing hateful to many is defended, and a thing prohibited by laws and human judgments is maintained under a new nomenclature.

units.la: Exceptio.
units.tr: Objection.

units.la: Sparsa à nobis primo in conflictu tela ista testudinis obiectae umbra declinari poterunt. 1. nullo accipientiū detrimento, sublevamento potius, pecuniam locari. & esse mutui dationem inter charitatis opera, etiam Dei praecipientis ore, pronunciatam. 2. Plus operae in reip. salutem, in civium communionem adferre, qui pecuniam rerum expedité gerendarum necessum, quam qui operam manuariam, aut nudum opere consilium, in medium conferat. Ea quae locantur, aut commodato praebentur, natura esse sterilia: & tamen pretium pro usu eorum, non reclamante consuetudine, nec aequitate repugnante, exigi. Minus esse malum, ideoque rationem boni inducere, usurariam pecuniae exactionem, quam inopum extremam negligentiam. [illegible, ~20 letters] inquit Philosophus, quinto Moralium. nullam pendenti usuram fieri injuriam, qui conventione ultro astrictus, pacto laesuro abstinere potuisset.
units.tr: The missiles we first hurled in the opening clash can be deflected by the shadow of this shield-wall. (1) Lending money does no harm to those who receive it; it is rather a relief. The lending of a loan is pronounced among the works of charity, even by the mouth of God commanding it. (2) He who provides money for the proper conduct of public affairs brings more service to the safety of the commonwealth and to the fellowship of citizens than he who brings manual labour or mere counsel into the common stock. Things that are lent out, or provided on loan, are barren by nature; yet a price is demanded for their use, custom not objecting and equity not opposing. The usurious exaction of money is a smaller evil, and so induces a semblance of good, than the extreme negligence of the poor. [...] says the Philosopher, in the fifth book of the Ethics. No injustice is done to one who pays interest, since he was bound by his own free agreement and could have abstained from a contract that would harm him.

units.la: Ad haec, & his convenientia, sermone in pauca contracto, respondemus.
units.tr: We shall reply to these and to what agrees with them, having contracted the discussion into a few words.

units.la: ad 1.
units.tr: To the first.

units.la: Mutui, quod gratuitum est, nec naturam nec appellationem usura induit. nec charitatis augustum nomen meretur, quod suo commodo juvandis aliis inservit. [?]ἡ ἀγάπη οὐ ζητεῖ τὰ ἑαυτῆς, Charitas quae sua sunt non quaerit: sacro Apostoli gentium ore pronunciatur. 1.Cor.13.v.5. Verum igitur beneficentiae nomen aucupantes, gratuitam operam elargiantur; non ut vaccis mulgendis pabulum, ut gregi mactandarum suum siliquas, lucrum captura manu suggerant. Si qui vero rebus ex ea pecunia auctis, redhostimentum ultro offerant; ut gratia relata capiatur; non ut punctum nomen a severissimo flagitatore exigatur.
units.tr: A loan, being gratuitous, takes on neither the nature nor the name of usury. Nor does what serves others at one's own advantage deserve the venerable name of charity: Charity seeks not her own [ἡ ἀγάπη οὐ ζητεῖ τὰ ἑαυτῆς], as is pronounced by the sacred mouth of the Apostle of the Gentiles, 1 Cor. 13.5. Therefore let those who catch at the name of beneficence lavish their service without payment; not like men who bring in profit with a grasping hand, as fodder for milking cows or as fattening for a flock to be slaughtered. But if some, when things have been increased by that money, offer a return of their own accord, so that gratitude is received, that is one thing; not that an exact debt be exacted by a most severe creditor.

units.la: ad 2.
units.tr: To the second.

units.la: Pecunia in medium conferatur, emendo, vendendo, opera locanda; quod plus est, largiendo. Sic antiquissimi mortalium, bene quam plurimis faciendo, nihil ab aliis exigendo, bonitatis admiratione benevolentiam civium, autoritatem apud omnes, regna denique & claritatem nominis acquisiverunt. Pelops ab ipso nominata in peninsula, Tarquinius priscus Romano in imperio, & recentiori memoria Cosmus Medicaeus Florentiae, non usuris acerbe cogendis, verum munificentia animis hominum alliciendis, ad supremum honorum fastigium citatis bigis asceenderunt. Quin & dubitandi ubertim materia succrescit, optandine sint regnis, aut rerump. æqualitati, cives opulentia præ cæ-teris multum eminentes. Nam & possessionum exæ-quata ratio magis naturæ convenit; & civium tran-quillitati, pari societatis commercio, magis consulitur; & libertati omnium minus periculi extimescendum.
units.tr: Money should be brought into the common stock by buying, selling, and letting out labour, and, what is more, by giving. Thus the most ancient of mortals, by doing good to very many and asking nothing from others, won through admiration of their goodness the goodwill of the citizens, authority among all, and finally kingdoms and fame of name. Pelops, in the peninsula named after him; Tarquin the Elder, in the Roman empire; and, in more recent memory, Cosimo de' Medici at Florence: they did not rise to the highest pinnacle of honours by harshly exacted usuries, but by munificence that drew men's minds to them, riding in chariots. Indeed, there arises abundant matter for doubt whether citizens who far surpass others in wealth are to be wished for in kingdoms, or in the equality of the commonwealth. For an equal distribution of possessions agrees more with nature; the tranquillity of citizens is better served by an equal exchange in society; and less danger to the liberty of all is to be feared.

units.la: ad 3.
units.tr: To the third.

units.la: Aliud est domum aut navim, aliud pecuniam uten-dam locare. Domus & navis usu fit deterior: pecu-nia valore eadem refunditur. Deinde pecunia ad re-rum permutationem, ut mensura divitiarum; cetera manu fabricata, in usum, non in mensuram, sunt in-venta. ita ut frustra istinc patrocinium pecuniario au-cupio quæratur.
units.tr: It is one thing to let out a house or a ship for use, and another to lend money for use. A house or ship becomes worse through use; money is repaid with the same value. Moreover, money was invented for the exchange of goods, as a measure of wealth, while other manufactured things were invented for use, not as a measure. So a defence of the moneylending trade is sought there in vain.

units.la: ad 4.
units.tr: To the fourth.

units.la: De exacta boni & mali ratione, non de gradu mali-tiæ, in nomen boni surrepturo, quæstio nobis hic ven-tilatur. Non enim aggressor, qui interimere poterat, exuviis detractis vita donata, plausum & præmium captabit.
units.tr: Our question here concerns the exact reckoning of good and evil, not the degree of wickedness, in the case of one who is about to usurp the name of good. For an attacker who could have killed, and who spares a life after stripping his victim of spoils, will not win applause and reward.

units.la: ad 5.
units.tr: To the fifth.

units.la: Similis est quinti effugii solutio. Nam qui se spon-sione interveniente à piratarum manu liberat, cupidi-tate quidem vitæ crimine conventionis purgatur. Pi-ratæ verò & latrones eo contractu aliquid ex necessi-tate coacti & inviti trahenti, facinoris nequitia non absolvuntur. Sua igitur natura mores & facta homi-num, non alieno metu aut indigentia, pendantur. His ita expeditis ad reliqua contra usuram argumenta ve-niamus.
units.tr: The answer to the fifth escape is similar. For one who frees himself from the hand of pirates by an agreement made under pressure is indeed cleared of the crime of the contract by his desire for life. But pirates and robbers, who by that contract drag something from a man forced by necessity and against his will, are not absolved of the wickedness of the deed. Therefore the morals and deeds of men are weighed by their own nature, not by another's fear or need. With these matters thus settled, let us come to the remaining arguments against usury.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Quod præstantissimis legum latoribus ignominia notatur, ejus erubescenda macula non temerè elui-tur. Usura præstantissimis legum latoribus ignomi-nia notatur. Ergo. De primo legum Juliarum autore Tacitus: pecunias fœnore auctitabant, adversum le-gem dictatoris Cæsaris, quâ de modo credendi possiden-dig intra Italiam cavetur. Acerrima Julii dictatoris mens, & in procurando civium bono solertia, quos se-[?]queretur antecessores, Lycurgum, Charondam, Za-leucum. leucum, magna legum latorum nomina, habuit.
units.tr: That which is marked with infamy by the most distinguished lawgivers is not lightly washed from its shameful stain. Usury is marked with infamy by the most distinguished lawgivers. Therefore. Concerning the first author of the Julian laws, Tacitus writes: they increased money by interest, contrary to the law of the dictator Caesar, by which provision is made within Italy concerning the manner of lending and holding property. The mind of the dictator Julius was very keen, and he was skilful in securing the good of the citizens. His predecessors, whom he followed, were Lycurgus, Charondas and Zaleucus, great names among lawgivers.

units.la: Si quid in capessenda rep. libertati adversum molitus est; si in illum jactari poterit Senecae discrimen, sacrilegia minuta puniuntur, magna in triumphis feruntur, (epist. 88.) vel temporum illorum necessitati, vel sublimi ejus ingenio, humiliorum non capaci, impingatur. Euripideo sane versu a regnandi cupiditate justitiae studium ipse exemit, ita Latine reddito: Nam si violandum est jus, regnandi gratia Violandum est, aliud rebus pietatem colas. Si contra hujus autoritatem legis excipias, eam in desuetudinem consensu civitatis abiisse: respondum a Cornelio habeas, non id factum consensu omnium, aut usu publico; sed quia privato usui bonum publicum postponitur, quod idem nostris moribus, contra inveteratam quarundam gentium consuetudinem, contra tolerantiam magistratuum, conniventiam regum, respondeas.
units.tr: If he undertook anything against liberty in seizing the commonwealth, and if the charge of Seneca can be cast against him, that petty sacrileges are punished, while great ones are carried in triumphs (ep. 88), let it be imputed either to the necessity of those times or to his lofty genius, which was not capable of humbler things. Indeed, by a verse of Euripides, rendered into Latin thus, he himself removed the pursuit of justice from the desire to rule: For if right must be violated, it must be violated for the sake of ruling; in other things cultivate piety. If against the authority of this law you should object that it has passed into disuse by the consent of the state, you may have the answer from Cornelius: this was not done by the consent of all, nor by public practice, but because the public good is postponed to private use. You may give the same answer for our own customs, against the long-standing custom of certain nations, against the tolerance of magistrates and the connivance of kings.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Quod autoritate clarissimorum eruditione & morum integritate virorum damnatur, non est in bono rum censu habendum. Ulfura autoritate clarissimorum &c. Tacitus inter eos, Cato Major, Cicero, Plutarchus, Aristoteles: omnes opulentia, praeter erudi-tionem, conspicui.
units.tr: That which is condemned by the authority of most famous men, distinguished for learning and integrity of life, is not to be counted among goods.
