Usury is condemned by the authority of most famous men, etc. Among them are Tacitus, Cato the Elder, Cicero, Plutarch and Aristotle, all of them conspicuous for wealth apart from their learning.

units.la: Tacito forum fœneratorium fœnebre malum significanter appellatur. Sane vetus urbi fœnebre malum. Cato de augenda re familiari quid esset fœnerari interrogatus, quid hominem occidere respondit. Cicero in Catone Majori, & in Officiorum libris, adversus fœnerandi crudelitatem copiosus est. Plutarchus in Moralibus in Nicia, in Crasso augendae fœnore pecuniae studium reprehendit. Aristoteles in sordidis quaestibus extremo loco fœneratoriam, ut homine ingenuo minime omnium dignam, reponit. [?] Ulfura autem, inquit, est nummi e nummo partus: adeo ut maxime praeter naturam sit habenda ista lucrandi ratio. (Politic. a.) Quid autem sibi Seneca voluerit, immensum divitiarum cumulum, exhauriendis fœnore regnis & urbibus, augendo, ipse viderit. Elegantiùs procul dubio de contemnenda paupertate scripsit, quam in vita civili egit cupiditatum lucri abstinentiùs. Forte eum, ut Stoicum, Zenonis aut Cleanthis paradoxon, Soli sapienti licere fœnerari, à recta semita abduxit. Quantò ad sapientiæ normam rectius, quod in epistola quadam scripsit: Primi mortalium, qui[?] ex his geniti, naturam incorrupti sequebantur, eandem habebant ducem & legem, commissi melioris arbitrio. (epist.9 l.[?]) Atqui primi mortalium sunt hi, qui integro naturæ primæ semine, ut luxus ostentationem, ita facultatum per fœnus accumulationem aut ignorabant, aut aspernabantur. Hi sunt primi mortalium, de quibus Lyricus poëta, sed altiùs philosophia morali quam poëtì imbutus, Horatius:
units.tr: Tacitus significantly calls the moneylenders' forum a deadly evil: Indeed, the forum of the city is an old deadly evil. Cato, asked what it meant to lend at interest in order to increase one's household property, replied that it meant to kill a man. Cicero, in his Cato the Elder and in the books On Duties, is copious against the cruelty of lending at interest. Plutarch, in his Moralia, in the lives of Nicias and Crassus, reproves the eagerness to increase money by interest. Aristotle, among sordid gains, puts moneylending last, as least of all worthy of a free man. Usury, he says, is money born of money, so that this way of making gain is to be held most of all contrary to nature (Politic. a.). What Seneca meant by heaping up an immense mass of riches, by draining kingdoms and cities with interest, he himself will have seen. He undoubtedly wrote more elegantly about despising poverty than he practised, in civil life, a more moderate restraint from the desire for gain. Perhaps, as a Stoic, he was led from the straight path by a paradox of Zeno or Cleanthes, that only the wise man may lend at interest. How much more correctly, by the rule of wisdom, he wrote in a certain letter: The first of mortals, who were born from these, followed uncorrupted nature, and had the same guide and law, the judgment of a better nature entrusted to them. (epist. 9.) Yet the first of mortals are those who, with the whole seed of primal nature, either did not know or spurned the accumulation of wealth through interest, just as they did the display of luxury. These are the first of mortals of whom the lyric poet Horace speaks, though he was imbued with moral philosophy more deeply than poets usually are:

units.la: Beatus ille, qui procul negotiis, Ut prisca gens mortalium, Paterna rura bobus exercet suis, Solutus omni fœnore. Epod. 2.
units.tr: Happy is he who, far from business, like the ancient race of mortals, works his ancestral fields with his own oxen, free from all interest. Epod. 2.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Quo publica civium concordia turbatur, à socie-tate hominum est ablegandum. Fœnore publica ci-vium concordia turbatur, Ergo fœnus à societate hominum est ablegandum. Sanè vetus urbi fœnebre malum, inquit Tacitus, & seditionum discordiarum creberrima causa. Non aliâ luculentior T. Livio post exactos Romana urbe reges, primâ inprimis decade, facundiæ materia. Trahi à creditoribus quifolvendo non erant, in nexum cives dari, feriles ad operas cogi, in tergum liberorum hominum animadverti. Inde obæratorum & plebis indignationes, inde adversum patres crebrò coortæ clamorum ac seditionum tempestates. Prima in montem Sacrum secessio, & civitatis à civitate avulsio, ob fœneratorum impotentiam. Ortum ejus calamitatis, & reipublicæ à seipsa distractionis, libro secundo Livius describit. Magno natu quidam in forum venit, &c. unde usuram evertendis hominum bonis, & opprimendæ ingenuorum liber-tati, tati, natam esse, facillime didiceris. Haec prima, haec media, haec ultima fax discordiarum civitatis Romanae. Haec eadem Britanniam quondam, haec Allobrogas, haec alias Europae nationes, Romano nomini ob foenoris magnitudinem infestas, ad bellum aut cupiditatem belli arrexit. Atheniensium enim, Carthaginiensium, & aliarum civitatum, ob aeris alieni molestiam concussiones producere non vacat.
units.tr: Whatever disturbs the public harmony of citizens must be banished from human society. Usury disturbs the public harmony of citizens; therefore usury must be banished from human society. Indeed, as Tacitus says, usury was an old and deadly evil for the city, and the most frequent cause of sedition and discord. Livy, after the kings were expelled from the Roman city, offered no richer material for his eloquence than in the first decade. Citizens who could not pay were dragged off by their creditors and given over as bondsmen, forced to serve as laborers, and had the lash laid on the backs of free men. From this came the indignation of debtors and the plebs, and from this against the fathers there arose again and again storms of outcry and sedition. The first secession to the Sacred Mount, and the tearing of the state from itself, came about because of the powerlessness of the moneylenders. Livy describes the beginning of this calamity, and of the state's self-division, in the second book: An old man came into the forum, etc. From this you will very easily learn that usury arose to overturn men's goods and to oppress the liberty of free-born men. This was the first, the middle and the last torch of discord in the Roman state. The same usury once roused Britain, the Allobroges, and other nations of Europe, hostile to the Roman name because of the size of the interest, to war or to a desire for war. For the Athenians, the Carthaginians and other states had no leisure to stir up upheavals on account of the burden of debt.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Quod priscis Romanorum moribus arcto legum lupato constrictum, frustra de eo retinendo laboratur, Usura &c. Propositionem tot eruditorum monumentis depraedicata veterum Romanorum sanctiras[?] fulcire poterit. Assumptionem Taciti verba stabiliunt: eo cohibebatur antiquis quoque & minus corruptis moribus. Haec generatim dicta, suis, ut speciebus rerum, exemplis aptantur, Nam primo duodecim tabulis sanctum, ne quis unciario foenore amplius exer-ceret, cum antea ex libidine agitaretur, ex unciarii foenoris exilitate, legum in re odiosa severitas perspicitur.
units.tr: That usury, held in check by the strict bridle of the laws under the old Roman customs, is labored over in vain when one tries to retain it. The proposition is supported by the sanctity of the ancient Romans, extolled in so many scholarly monuments. The assumption is established by the words of Tacitus: usury was restrained by this even among the ancients and the less corrupt morals. These general statements are fitted, as species to their kinds, with examples: for first, by the Twelve Tables it was enacted that no one should charge more than the unciary rate of interest, when before it had been practised at will. From the smallness of the unciary interest one sees the severity of the laws in a hateful matter.

units.la: Centesimae enim pars duodecima, quod antea sin-gulis mensibus, nunc anno pendebatur, dein rogatione tribunitia, ad semuncias redacta. ita ut fortis pars ducentesima, non invidenda locatoribus, annua usura persolveretur. Cum & hoc ipsum populo, qui majori ex parte plebejus & pauperculus, nimis iniquum videretur, postremo vetita versura: id est, foenus cum pulvisculo ablatum. Versuram enim a foenore ratione tantum diversam, re ipsa consentire, & foeneratori quidem eum qui dat foenori, versuram facere qui accipit, locupletissimi sunt latinitatis autores.
units.tr: For the twelfth part of a hundredth, which had been paid monthly before, was now paid yearly; then by a tribunician proposal it was reduced to semunciae, so that the annual interest paid was a fiftieth part, not to be grudged to the lenders. Since even this seemed too unfair to the people, who for the most part were plebeian and poor, finally versura was forbidden, that is, interest combined with principal was taken away. The most learned authors of Latin hold that versura differs from usury only in form but agrees with it in substance, and that the one who lends makes usury, while the one who borrows makes versura.

units.la: Quin & aliquando in favorem obaeratorum lex, te-ste Livio, perlata: Ut deducto eo de capite, quod ulu-ris pernumeratum effet, id quod superesset, triennio aequis portionibus persolveretur. Ut novas tabulas, nulli bono unquam probatas, nec justae legis viri habituras, nisi in poenam fortasse foeneratorum, praete-ream[?]. Ergo Romanis legibus usurae licentia primum[?] coarctata, deinde concisa, postremo funditus eversa. Gratia tamen potentium, & foeneratorum fraudes, tot plebiscita populi & tribunitias rogationes, tot leges & edicta, diu impune perfregerunt. quae fraudes toties repressa, miras per artes rursum oriebantur. ut fere fit, quod paucis factiosis compendio est, vim legum gratia, metu, muneribus perrumpat. Qui legum, donec vindicentur, contemptus jus nullum perfractoribus acquirit.
units.tr: Indeed, at times a law was also passed in favor of debtors, as Livy testifies: that, once the amount already paid as interest had been deducted from the capital, the remainder should be paid back in equal portions over three years. Such new account-books, never approved by any good man, and not to be held by men of a just law, except perhaps as a punishment for moneylenders, were a further matter. Thus under Roman law the license of usury was first restricted, then cut back, and finally utterly overthrown. Yet through the favor of the powerful and the frauds of the moneylenders, so many plebiscites, tribunician proposals, laws and edicts were for a long time broken with impunity. These frauds, though often repressed, rose again by wondrous arts. As usually happens, what is a profit to a few factious men, they force through the force of the laws by favor, fear and bribes. Contempt for laws, so long as they are not avenged, gives no right to those who break them.

units.la: Pene per oscitantiam omiseram, apud Romanos olim, vetita jam versura, furem dupli, foeneratorem quadrupli, ut furem manifestum & perfrictæ frontis, condemnatum. unde quadruplatorum nomen iis primo ortu adhaesit, qui foeneratores, pacto silentio delitescentes, è turba eruebant.
units.tr: I had almost overlooked, through carelessness, that among the Romans of old, when versura was already forbidden, a thief was condemned to pay double, and a moneylender four times as much, as a manifest thief and one of shameless brow. Hence the name "quadruplators" first clung to those who, hiding behind a tacit agreement, dragged moneylenders out of the crowd.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Nec Romani magis quam Graeci usuram (nam apud Indos, Scythas, & alias gentes loco & lingua barbaras, fere nomen cum re ignorabatur) publicè aver-fabantur. De Lycurgi, foenerationi adversi, legibus antea dictum. Cum deinde contagione Persica, & Lysandri intempestiva popularitate, opes & luxus in urbem influxissent, simul cum iis foenoris tabes irrupit. Nec diu tamen sancta in gente sedem fixit: nam Agis, Plutarcho commemorante, odio insolitae exactionis, omnes foeneratorum tabulas, igne suppositò, in luce fori concremavit. quo nullum clarius lumen se unquam vidisse Agesilaus, Xenophontea Principis idea, exclamavit. Quanto apud Athenienses odio foeneratores, quantæ aversationi fuerint, ex Aristophane, Atticæ antiquitatis claro scriptore Comico, tractatu De Republica ostendi. Ut à Graecis ad pro-pioraloca[?] abeam: lepidum est, quod nomine Socratis jactatur, quinque hominum genera à Republica omni dimovenda: Foeneratorem è foro, Judicem iniquum è consistorio, Sacerdotem avarum è templo, Adulatorem ab aula, Meretricem è proflibulo. Quod etsi antiquitatem Socraticam non sapit, non invenusti tamen scommatis videtur.
units.tr: The Romans were no less than the Greeks publicly averse to usury (for among the Indians, the Scythians and other nations barbarous in place and language, the thing was nearly unknown, and with it the name). Earlier we spoke of the laws of Lycurgus, who opposed lending at interest. Then, when wealth and luxury had flowed into the city through Persian contagion and the untimely popularity of Lysander, the canker of usury broke in along with them. Yet it did not fix its seat long in that holy nation: for Agis, as Plutarch recalls, out of hatred for the unaccustomed exaction, set fire to all the moneylenders' account-books and burned them in the light of the forum. Agesilaus, in Xenophon's ideal of a prince, cried out that he had never seen a clearer light. How much the Athenians hated moneylenders, and how great was their aversion to them, I have shown in my treatise On the Republic, from Aristophanes, the clear comic writer of Attic antiquity. To pass from the Greeks to more recent places: it is witty what is bandied about under the name of Socrates, that five kinds of men should be removed from every republic: the moneylender from the forum, the unjust judge from the court, the greedy priest from the temple, the flatterer from the court, and the harlot from the brothel. Although this does not smack of Socratic antiquity, it seems not an unpleasant jest.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Haec Romanorum, haec gentium de fœnore perfuasio. Quid Moses, quid David, quid prophetæ; vel potius quid Deus per illos pronunciaverit; quid Novo in Fœdere Christus, quid ejus legati sanxerint, ad quid universum orbem gentium interfitio sublato astrinxerint, deinceps perlustremus.
units.tr: Such was the conviction of the Romans and of the nations concerning usury. Let us next go through what Moses, what David, what the prophets said, or rather what God declared through them; what Christ in the New Covenant, and what his ambassadors, sanctioned; and to what they bound the whole world of nations once interest was removed.

units.la: Moses.
units.tr: Moses.

units.la: Primus legum inter gentes conditor, legum a Deo ipso pronunciatarum divinus promulgator, acerrimè fulminatis. contra usuram insurgit. Si, inquit, pecuniam mutuam dederis populo meo, pauperi qui est tecum, non eris ei sicut fœnerator, ne imponito ei usuram. Exod. xxii. v. 25. Iterum: Si attenuato fratre tuo apud te, vacillabit manus ejus, confirmabis illum: peregrinum etiam aut inquilinum, ut vivat tecum. Non accipies ab eo ullius generis usuram, sed timebis a Deo tuo, ut vivat frater tuus tecum. Pecuniam tuam ne dato ei in usuram, nec in reditus exactionem cibum tuum. Levitici xxv. v. 35.
units.tr: The first lawgiver among the nations, and the divine promulgator of laws pronounced by God himself, thundered most fiercely against usury. "If," he says, "you lend money to my people, to the poor man who is with you, you shall not be to him as a moneylender; do not impose interest on him." Exod. 22. v. 25. Again: "If your brother becomes poor beside you and his hand wavers, you shall support him; even the stranger or sojourner, that he may live with you. You shall take from him no kind of usury, but you shall fear your God, that your brother may live with you. Do not give him your money at interest, nor your food for profit." Lev. 25. v. 35.

units.la: Qui in voce Nefchech, quasi fœnoris excessu mordentis, latibulum quæruntur; altera voce Tharbith, quamvis multiplicationem designante, adjecta refutantur. Quam qui fœnoris nuncupatione in versione speciatim efferunt, suo sensu per me fruantur. Sed missa Critica, alium ad locum Mosaicæ auctoritatis contendimus. Ne dato in usuram fratri tuo, usuram pecuniæ, usuram cibi, usuram ullius rei, quæ in usuram datur. Deut. 23. v. 20. Quod autem proxime annectitur; Extraneo dabis in usuram: causam nostram non vulnerat.
units.tr: Those who seek a hiding place in the word Nefchech, as though it signified the biting excess of interest, are refuted by the addition of another word, Tharbith, which signifies increase. Those who in translation expressly render it by the name of interest may enjoy their own opinion for all I care. But, setting aside the critical questions, I press our case with another passage of Mosaic authority: "Do not lend upon usury to your brother: usury of money, usury of food, usury of anything that is lent upon usury." Deut. 23. v. 20. What is joined immediately after, "to a foreigner you may lend upon usury," does not harm our cause.

units.la: Nam i. Nocri, non quemvis extraneum, peregrinum nimirum aut inquilinum, hoc in loco significat. Hos enim loco ex Levitico supra laudato, Deus usuræ exactioni eximit. Sed extraneum fidei & cognitionis Dei, extraneum à fœdere Dei & gratia seclusum, extraneum tabernaculo sancto & nomini Jacobi palàm vel occultè adversantem. Nunc autem gentium interfes pto dirupto, nationibus (ne dicam civibus & urbis ejusdem incolis) fœderis communicatione nexis, communi fratrum appellatione sociatis, etiámne quis in extranei nomenclatura fubterfugium quæritet?
units.tr: For first, Nocri in this place does not signify any foreigner whatever, that is, a stranger or sojourner. Those, indeed, God exempts from usury in the passage from Leviticus quoted above. But he means a foreigner to the faith and knowledge of God, a foreigner excluded from the covenant and grace of God, one who openly or secretly opposes the holy tabernacle and the name of Jacob. Now, since the wall of partition between the nations has been broken down, and nations (not to say citizens and inhabitants of the same city) are bound together by fellowship in the covenant and joined by the common name of brothers, can anyone still seek a refuge in the name of "foreigner"?

units.la: 2. Deus, absolutus ut vitæ hominum ita fortunarum arbiter, poterat gentes vicinas fœnore imposito fa-cultatibus exugendas Judæis propinare. quo pacto Ægyptiorum bona, ex absoluta dominii potestate, fine furti suspicione iisdem in prædam concessit. imò petpœnam talionis hoc gentibus infligi poterat, ut quod ab aliis exigerent, reciproca exactione pateren-tur. Ut tacceam (3.) [illegible, ~12 letters] propter duritiem cordis, hunc nævum connivéntia paterna & tolerantia, quò facilius à fratrum spoliatione abstine-tent, ut quondam justi matrimonii divortium, pet-missum.
units.tr: 2. God, as absolute master of the lives and fortunes of men, could have handed over neighbouring nations, burdened with interest, to the Jews to be drained of their resources. In this way, by the absolute power of ownership, he gave the goods of the Egyptians to the same people as spoil without any suspicion of theft. Indeed, by way of the penalty of retaliation, this could have been inflicted on the nations, so that they might suffer the same exaction in return for what they exacted from others. Not to mention (3.) [illegible], this blemish was tolerated by paternal forbearance on account of the hardness of their hearts, so that they might more easily abstain from despoiling their brothers, just as a divorce was once permitted for the sake of a lawful marriage.

units.la: David.
units.tr: David.

units.la: Regum in gente Deo peculiari máximus, & spiritus divino oraculo vaticinantis entheum[?] receptaculum; inter purioris vitæ notas hanc non postremam posuit, Argentum suum non exposuit fœnori. Psalmo xv. v.5. Et passim in Psalmis maledictionem imprecantibus fœnerator, ut malè ominatæ vitæ cumulus, infaustis peccatoribus adjicitur.
units.tr: The greatest of kings in God's peculiar people, and a dwelling place of the divine Spirit prophesying by divine oracle, placed among the marks of a purer life this no small item: He has not put out his silver to usury. Ps. 15. v. 5. And throughout the Psalms the moneylender is set, like the sum of an ill-omened life, among the unhappy sinners who call down curses.

units.la: Si qui vero in Mose exceperint, temporariam eam fuisse, civilem, genti Hebraeæ proprie dicatam, dè non exercendo fœnore sanctionem: ea exceptio, etiam in lege Mosis frigida, in Psalmo locum planè nullum invenit. Altius enim Davidis meditationes porrigebantur; ut qui divino spiritu raptu novum fœdus prospiceret, filium suum & Dominum Messiam præ sacrificiis Mosaicis (Psal. 50.) animi visceribus gere-ret[?]; nationibus ad Deum convertendis normam vi-veridi[?] præscriberet. Nec satis apte fœnoris interdictio inter forenses exigui loci usus referetur; nisi eadem animi integritatem, justi & æqui operationem, veritatis eloquium; nisi obtrectationis fugam, mali facinoris aversationem, sinistri rumoris declinationem; nisi ammantium[?] Dei venerationem, iurisiurandi sanctam observationem, æquitatis in iudicio præ lucro desiderium, inter externos ritus quis reponat. Nec eam incrustationem, vitæ æternæ promissio, clausula principio Psalmi respondens, admiserit. Quod ad umbraculum in voce Nefchech captatum, illud in supra commemoratis diffiavimus. Et alioqui infirma est, quæ ab origine vocis deducitur, argumentatio.
units.tr: If anyone should object that the prohibition in Moses was temporary, civil, and peculiar to the Hebrew nation, and that the rule against practising usury was of that kind, then that exception, weak even in the law of Moses, finds no place at all in the Psalm. For the meditations of David reached higher: inspired by the divine Spirit, he foresaw the new covenant, bore in his inmost heart his Son and Lord the Messiah above the Mosaic sacrifices (Ps. 50.), and prescribed the rule of living for the conversion of the nations to God. Nor is it fitting to reckon the prohibition of usury among the petty customs of the courts; unless someone also places among the external rites the integrity of mind, the practice of what is just and fair, the speaking of truth, unless flight from slander, aversion to wicked deeds, avoidance of evil report, unless reverence for God, the holy keeping of an oath, and the desire for fairness in judgement rather than gain. Nor would the promise of eternal life, which answers to the opening clause of the Psalm, admit such a limitation. As for the shelter sought in the word Nefchech, we have already dispelled it among the matters mentioned above. Moreover, an argument drawn from the etymology of a word is in any case weak.

units.la: Salomo.
units.tr: Solomon.

units.la: 'A patre non degenerans filius, & omnium qui sunt, fuerunt, erunt, hominum sapientissimus a Deo judicatus, pondus præcepto a comminatione accersivit. Qui auget, inquit, substantiam suam usura & fœnore (ut ab interpretis verbis non abeam) gratiose largitu-ro tenuibus eam congregabit.
units.tr: A son not degenerate from his father, and judged by God the wisest of all men who are, were, or will be, added weight to the precept with a threat. "He who increases," he says, (not to depart from the interpreter's words) "his substance by usury and interest, will gather it for him who gives graciously to the poor."

units.la: Nec comminationi tantum, sed & pœnæ inflictioni, usuræ frequentatio subjacuit. a Nehemia enim locupletiores ob fœnus exercitum gravissima objurgantur increpatione, & ad restitutionem quæ præter sortem acceperant coguntur. Nehem.5.
units.tr: Not only the threat but also the infliction of punishment fell upon the frequent practice of usury. For through Nehemiah the richer men who practised usury are sharply rebuked with the gravest reproof, and are compelled to restore what they had taken beyond the principal. Neh. 5.

units.la: Propheta.
units.tr: The Prophet.

units.la: Ezechiel recensitis vitæ immaculatæ indiciis, pergit: In usuram non dederit, & fœnus non acceperit. cap.18. v.8. Mox inter facinorosos legis æternæ transgressores fœnorum sectatores commemorat. Qui in usuram dederit, qui fœnus acceperit, hiccine vivat? nequaquam. v.13. I nunc, divinæ autoritatis majestatem eleva, inter augusti temporis, angustioris loci sanctiones, aut consilia, æternum Dei decretum commenti audacia profana.
units.tr: Ezekiel, after listing the marks of an unblemished life, goes on: "He has not given upon usury, nor received interest." Ch. 18. v. 8. Soon afterwards, among the wicked transgressors of the eternal law, he mentions the pursuers of interest. "He who has given upon usury, and he who has received interest, shall he live? By no means." v. 13. Come now, exalt the majesty of divine authority, and with profane daring devise, out of the decrees of a short time and the regulations of a narrow place, an eternal decree of God.

units.la: CHRISTI contra fœnus autoritas.
units.tr: The authority of Christ against usury.

units.la: Christus non venit legem soluturus, Matth. 5. v.17: sed, cum redemptionis ministerio, exactiorem præ Pharisaica, & internam animi, præcepti observationem exacturus. v. 20. Non igitur divinæ legis autora-mentum, etiamsi nihil novi adjecisset, solvere voluit. Nihilominus quasdam sparsim vestigia, legi patris convenientia, mandatis evangelicis impressit. ex quibus
units.tr: Christ did not come to loosen the law (Matt. 5:17), but, while serving redemption, he came to require a stricter observance of the precept than the Pharisees', one that is inward in the mind (v. 20). So he did not wish to dissolve the authority of the divine law, even if he had added nothing new. Nevertheless, he left scattered traces that agree with the Father's law and impressed them on the evangelical commands. From these we shall gather what offers itself at first glance and without forcing.

units.la: prima fronte, & ultrò, oblata colligemus. 1. [illegible, ~30 letters] φῆς. Matth.5.v.42. Gratuitam donationem, aut mutui saltem collocationem, non fœnoratoriam erogationem, discipulis injungit. Nec adjectioni ne aver- ferit locus fuisset, fi aliqua ex mutui datione spes lucri affulfiffet. 2. [illegible, ~25 letters] Joh.13. v.34. Si novo mutui amoris ardore præcipiendo veterem legem Christus excessit; nequaquam priscam legem, prophetarum repetitione renovatam, abrogavit. 3. Avaritiam, fœnoris dilectam nutricem, multis modis explosit. Inprimis Lucæ xv. v.10, & deinceps, plena nervorum monita legeris. 4. [illegible, ~20 letters] Mutuum date, nihil inde sperantes, Luc.6.v.35. Vide quid hic exceptioni pateat, è verbis Christi etiam inimicis esse benefacendum; nec esse eis mutui dationem denegandam, etiam cum fortis amittendæ periculo. Quod nostram de fœnore sententiam adeò non infringit, ut stabiliat potiùs. Nam fi beneficii genus est mutui præstatio, utique non est rei familiaris acerbo quæstu augendæ captiuncula. Si de forte etiam & capite discrimen in- super habendum, dum homini cuicunque profuetis: non sunt in nervum obærati, ob non solutam usuram, abducendi. Sanè hic aliquid præcipi, quod superet vulgarem nationum honestatem, è versu Lucæ præcedenti liquebit. Christo adde Paulinam autoritatem. 1.Theff.4.v.6. Sequuntur objectiones, è sacro codice petitæ, & earum depulsiones.
units.tr: (1) …φῆς. Matt. 5:42. He enjoins his disciples to make a gratuitous gift, or at least to lend, not to make a usurious payment. Nor would there have been any place for the addition ne averferit ("do not turn away") if any hope of gain had shone from the giving of a loan. (2) …Joh. 13:34. If by commanding a new ardour of love in lending Christ went beyond the old law, he by no means abrogated the ancient law, which was renewed by repetition in the prophets. (3) He drove out avarice, the beloved nurse of usury, in many ways. Above all, read the sturdy warnings in Luke 15:10 and following. (4) …"Lend, expecting nothing thereby" (Luke 6:35). See what exception can be made here: from Christ's words, even enemies are to be done good to, and the lending of a loan is not to be refused to them, even when there is danger of losing the principal. This does not weaken our view on usury so much as strengthen it. For if lending is a kind of benefit, then surely it is no petty trick for increasing one's property by harsh gain. If one must even risk the principal, the sums lent to anyone at all are not to be sought back with interest, nor are debtors to be dragged into prison for unpaid usury. Indeed, that something is commanded here which surpasses the common honesty of the nations will be clear from the preceding verse of Luke. Add to Christ the authority of Paul: 1 Thess. 4:6. What follows are objections drawn from the sacred code, and their refutations.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Parabolam ab usurario mutuari Christum non pu- duit. Matth.25. Refp. nec ab iniquo œconomo, domini fui bona dilapidante & codicillos immutante, (Luc.16.) nec à fure nocturno similitudinem ductam, sibi & suis applicare, eum piguit. non ut fraudulentiam fervorum aut furtum comprobaret, sed ut futuri providentiam, ut ad patrisfamiliæ exemplum vigilantiam commendaret. Parabolæ ultra scopum loquentis extendendæ non sunt. Non exparabolis materiæ commen-
units.tr: Christ did not disdain to borrow a parable from a usurer (Matt. 25). Answer: nor was he ashamed to draw a comparison from the unjust steward who squandered his master's goods and altered the bonds (Luke 16), nor from the thief in the night, applying it to himself and his own. He did not do this to approve the fraud of servants or theft, but to commend vigilance in the manner of the householder, to teach foresight for the future. Parables are not to be extended beyond the purpose of the speaker.

units.la: ) [illegible, ~5 letters] commentamur, sed ex materiis parabolas interpretamur: inquit Tertullianus, libro De Pudicitia.
units.tr: Not "from parables do we invent matter, but from matter we interpret parables": so says Tertullian in his book On Modesty. (The rest of this citation is illegible.)

units.la: Non ut aliis relaxatio, vobis autem angustia. 1.Cor. 7. v. 13. Resp. Nullis ibi de fœnoris locatione apex. tributi voluntarii in pauperes conferendi exæquatio, ut largitionis fundus non exhauriatur, nihil cum fœnore habet commercii.
units.tr: "Not that others should be eased and you distressed" (2 Cor. 8:13). Answer: there the word does not concern the placing of a loan at interest. The equalising of a voluntary contribution for the poor has nothing to do with usury, so that the fund of generosity is not exhausted.

units.la: Locus jastatur inprimis, 1.Tim.5. v.8. Resp. Nullus hic de congerendo per rapinas aut per usuram lucro, omnis de non abjicienda suorum cura, de non oneranda iis alendis ecclesia, sermo. Nulla de acquirendarum facultatum alacritate aut modo, omnis de impendendarum promptitudine admonitio. Alias omnis vel genere vel excessu injustus quæstus hoc dicto palliari poterit.
units.tr: The passage that is brandished first of all is 1 Tim. 5:8. Answer: there is no talk here of heaping up gain by plunder or by usury; the whole concern is not to neglect one's own, and not to burden the church by having them supported. There is no mention of eagerness or method in acquiring wealth; the whole admonition concerns readiness in spending it. Otherwise any unjust gain, whether in kind or in excess, could be excused by this saying.

units.la: Omnia quæ vultis &c. Matth.7. v. 11. Resp. contra usuram hoc Christi dictum, Alexandro Severo tantopere adamatum, militat. Omnes enim gratuitum in re tenui mutuum, quam fœnus cum onere, acceptare malumus.
units.tr: "All things that you wish…" (Matt. 7:11). Answer: against usury this saying of Christ, which Alexander Severus so greatly loved, is on our side. For all of us would rather accept a free loan of a small thing than a usurious loan with its burden.

units.la: Sacrorum sensu vindicato, Doctorum ecclesiae, Hieronymi, Augustini, Ambrosii, nec non Concilio-rum, & Clementis Papæ autoritates supererant. Sed, ne fastidio lectorem obruamus, fontis integritate percepta, de rivulis non laboramus.
units.tr: With the sense of Scripture vindicated, there remain the authorities of the teachers of the Church, Jerome, Augustine and Ambrose, as well as those of the councils and of Pope Clement. But lest we overwhelm the reader with tedium, having grasped the integrity of the source, we do not labour over the streams.

units.la: Sic turmis a jure naturæ, Romano, gentium, divino, pontificio conscriptis, conferta acie usura oppugnatur.
units.tr: Thus, with troops drawn up from the law of nature, Roman law, the law of nations, divine law and papal law, usury is assailed with a massed battle line.

units.la: NECESSITAS
units.tr: NECESSITY

units.la: Usurae.
units.tr: Usury.

units.la: Morum humanorum infirmitas, a divina perfectione longissime recedens, vel inde deprehendi potest, quod agnito imbecillitatis vitio, cum non simus ferendis remediis, in eosdem quos incusavimus errores relabamur. Quod, inter alia, & hoc de usura tractatu patebit. Cum legibus, institutis, clamore gentium damnata est usura: tamen ad eam, vitæ necessitudiné; ut ad sacram in tempestate anchoram, recurrimus. Ita vitæ ducendæ necessitas, inter difficultatum scopulos enavigans, omni lege potentiór habetur.
units.tr: The weakness of human conduct, which falls very far short of divine perfection, can be seen from this: once we have recognised the fault of our weakness, we slide back into the very errors we have condemned, even though we are not willing to accept the remedies. This will be clear, among other things, from this treatment of usury. Usury has been condemned by laws, by institutions and by the outcry of nations; yet we return to it out of the necessity of life, as sailors in a storm return to the sacred anchor. So the necessity of living, steering between the rocks of difficulty, is held to be stronger than every law.

units.la: Necessitatem fœnoris parit vel accipientium fœ-nore vel collocantium utilitas.
units.tr: The necessity of interest arises either from the advantage of those who borrow at interest or from that of those who lend it.

units.la: Accipientium, vel privata in vita vel publica.
units.tr: The borrowers' necessity is either private, in their own lives, or public.

units.la: Privata. Quantus eorum numerus obverfat, qui rem familiarem vel agro colendo, vel taberna instito-ria vel officina aperienda, vel navigatione deniquè auctori, regina actionum pecunia destituti resiliunt. Qui opulentiorem aliquem, ut, cum periculo amit-tendæ fortis, gratis carere suo velit, nulla adigere ra-tione possunt. Hinc pactum inter eos de pretio an-nuo vel menstruo; quod usui pecuniæ succedat. Pa-ctio ea legibus olim adversa: hominis egeni, pauxilla pecunia sublevandi, desertio deterior.
units.tr: Private. How many people there are who, lacking money, the driving force of all activity, shrink back from keeping up their household by working the land, opening a shop or workshop, or finally from trade by sea. They cannot force any wealthier person to surrender his property to them for nothing, at the risk of losing his capital. Hence an agreement between them about an annual or monthly price, which stands in place of the use of money. Such a bargain was once contrary to the laws, but it is worse to abandon a needy man who wants a little money to help him.

units.la: Publica. Multa occurrunt vigilibus reipublicæ, vel mœnibus reficiendis; vel milite repente conscribendo, vel pace redimenda, quæ præsentem pecuniam, vacuo ærario, deposcant. Hic opem alicujus darda-narii implorare, quam tempus deferere, honestius. Frustra enim legum apices defendas, legum cum civi-tate evertendarum iniftante periculo: nec legibus ne-ceffitas, verum necessitate leges corrigendæ.
units.tr: Public. Many things fall to the guardians of the commonwealth: repairing the walls, enlisting soldiers at short notice, or buying peace, all of which demand ready money when the treasury is empty. Here it is more honourable to seek help from some lender than to abandon the moment. For you cannot defend the letter of the laws when the danger threatens that the state, and with it the laws, will be overthrown. Necessity does not bend to the laws; rather the laws must be corrected by necessity.

units.la: Communi cum publico singulorum. Conclusa pa-[?]corum opulentorum arcis, aut in ærario vel fisco stipata, renummaria; negotia conquiescunt, mercatura silet, agri squalore defetti mœrent. Ut puteorum quorundam venæ, hauriendo limpidiores & uberiores manant: ita currendo fœnore pecunia agitatio, fœ-renfes hominum actiones & tabernas aperit. Severitate legis exercendæ fœnoratores ad pœnam, impe-rante Tiberio, trahebantur; qui rationes familiares, repetito à debitoribus ære, componebant. hinc inopia rei nummariæ, commoto simul omnium ære alieno: & quia tot damnatis, bonisq; eorum divenditis, signatum argentum fisco vel ærario attinebatur. Præscriptum quidem Patrum auctoritas, ut duas quisque fœbonis[?] partes in agris per Italiam collocaret. Sed creditores insolidum appellabant, nec decorum appellatio minuere fidem. Igitur quod vulneri cataplasma parabatur, latius vulnus diduxit: & avaritia creditorum cohibita, tenuitatem indigentium non erexit. Ita primo concursatio, & preces: dein strepere pratorii tribunal. Qui modo sanguisugas fœneratores detestati, legum auxilia imploraverant; nunc animis ex inopia mutatis, usuram desiderant. & quod remedio litibus componendis quaerebatur, latiora litium semina spargebat.
units.tr: Common, that is, the public need of individuals. When the money of wealthy men is shut up in their coffers, or piled up in the treasury or the fisc, the coin is withdrawn from circulation; business comes to rest, trade falls silent, and the fields, worn down by neglect, mourn. As the veins of certain wells flow clearer and more abundantly the more they are drawn upon, so when money circulates through lending, it opens up the activities of men, the trades and the shops. When the law against usury was enforced under Tiberius, the usurers were dragged to punishment; they had settled their household accounts by calling in their debts. Hence came a shortage of coin, since at the same time everyone's debts were called in; and because so many were condemned and their goods sold off, the silver that had been struck was kept back in the fisc or the treasury. The authority of the Fathers did indeed prescribe that each man should invest two parts of his money in lands throughout Italy. But the creditors called in their debts in full, and that demand did not lessen their good faith. So what was prepared as a plaster for the wound spread the wound wider; and the greed of the creditors, though restrained, did not lift up the poverty of the needy. Thus at first there was running about and entreaties; then the praetor's tribunal began to ring with complaints. Those who had lately detested the usurers as bloodsuckers and begged for the help of the laws, now, their feelings changed by want, demand usury. And what was sought as a remedy for settling lawsuits sowed wider seeds of lawsuits.

units.la: Nautico Batavorum populo si quis fœnerationem interdicat, continuo quiescente mercatura, res cum privata publica sternetur. Privatae paucorum divitiae, in publicum emissae, rem Batavam, ne ad veteres casas, veterem ad solitudinem relabatur, a lapsu cohibent. Vita maritimorum Belgarum navibus, & mercatura navium alumna, volvitur. naves pecunia instruuntur: pecuniam usura expedit. Idem de Genuatibus, Liguriae saxeam solitudinem colentibus, dictum putes. Hi cives suos, hi vicinos reges, hi remotiores pecunia prænumeranda sustinent, & grato accipientibus fœnore simul rem suam auditant. Currentis pecuniae si fontem, fœnore prohibito, obstruas: nec rivuli negotiationum, nec inopum solatia sequentur.
units.tr: If anyone forbids lending at interest to the seafaring people of the Dutch, trade will at once come to rest, and the public and private fortunes alike will be laid low. The wealth of a few private persons, once put into public use, keeps the Dutch state from sliding back into its old huts and its old solitude. The life of the Belgian seafarers, and trade, the nurse of shipping, turn on the ships; ships are fitted out with money, and money is put to work by interest. You might think the same of the Genoese, who inhabit the rocky wastes of Liguria. They support their own citizens, their neighbouring kings and those further away with money paid in advance, and at the same time they increase their own wealth by the welcome interest paid by those who borrow. If you block the spring of running money by forbidding interest, neither the streams of business nor the comforts of the poor will follow.

units.la: Id vero gravius, quod rei nummariae inopiam non modo vitae commodè expediendae facilitas deserit; sed etiam eversis fortunis fama, extremum bonorum solatium, laborat. Copiam vendendi, inquit Tacitus, facta vilitate, quanto quis obaratior, agris distra-bebant. multiq; fortunis provolvebantur. eversio rei familiaris dignitatem ac famam præceps dabat.
units.tr: What is worse is that the lack of money deprives people not only of the ease of managing their lives comfortably, but also, once their fortunes are overturned, their reputation, the last comfort of goods, suffers too. Tacitus says: "When the price had fallen, the more heavily anyone was in debt, the more eagerly they sold their lands; and many were thrown into ruin. The overthrow of a household brought dignity and reputation headlong down."

units.la: Atque hæc pecuniam fœnore accipientium excusa-ta necessitas.
units.tr: And this is the excuse of necessity for those who take money at interest.

units.la: Collocantium alii indigentium desiderato usu pur-gantur, alii favore publico sublevantur.
units.tr: Of those who lend, some are cleansed by the desire of the needy for their service, others are supported by public favour.

units.la: Priori in classe vulgares divitiarum corrasores, quo-rum in numero Alphius Horatii, (Epod. 2.) locantur.
units.tr: In the first class are the common grabbers of riches, among whom Alphius in Horace (Epod. 2) is placed.

units.la: De M. Crasso Plutarchus: τῆς φιλίας ἰδίας ἀπό[?]
units.tr: Plutarch on Marcus Crassus: "of his own friendship ..." [τῆς φιλίας ἰδίας ἀπό[?]]

units.la: τῶν αὐτῶν ἀπήτει δ' ἀνδρῶν, τοῦ ... [illegible, ~40 letters]
units.tr: "He demanded these same things from men ..." [τῶν αὐτῶν ἀπήτει δ' ἀνδρῶν, τοῦ ... illegible, about forty letters]

units.la: i.e. amicis absque fœnore mutuabat : severé autem elapso mutuationis tempore exigebat. eratque usus gratuitus multis fœnoribus molestior. quod locum Taciti, quem manu terimus, non leviter illustrat.
units.tr: That is, he lent to his friends without interest, but when the time of the loan had strictly run out, he demanded repayment. And the free loan was more troublesome to many than interest. This does not slightly illuminate the passage of Tacitus that we are handling.

units.la: Publici in favoris tutela versantur
units.tr: Those who are under the protection of public favour.

units.la: 1. Pupilli : quibus publicè tutores, ad res curan- das, conceduntur. Hi, ne ad tenuitatem maturè dela- bantur, usura facultatum locatarum sustentantur.
units.tr: 1. Wards, for whom guardians are granted at public charge to manage their affairs. Lest these be quickly reduced to poverty, they are sustained by interest on their invested property.

units.la: 2. Collegia docentium : quorum ad subsidia cum annui reditus legantur, vix poterit ab iis usura remo- veri.
units.tr: 2. Colleges of teachers, for whose support annual revenues are bequeathed; it will hardly be possible to remove interest from these.

units.la: 3. Senatores : qui nec publico salario, nec judicandi sportulis juvantur. Senatorem ofnare divitias, dede- corare paupertatem, fi non ratione probatæ, saltem receptæ usu sententiæ est. Hinc Claudii oratione lau- dati, qui ob angustias familiares ordine senatorio fpontecederent, moti qui remanendo impudentiam paupertati adjicerent. xii. Annal. At fundum rei fa- miliaris quamvis locupletissimum citò exhaurias, fiefi aliunde deficientes venas expleas. Mercatura fena- toribus plerunque interdicta ; agricultura è dignitate esse in desuetudinem abiit ; opificium inter sordes nu- meratur ; nec quicquam generosum officina educare creditur. Unde igitur lapsuræ rei, nisi à fœnore quod nulli noceat, subsidium?
units.tr: 3. Senators, who are helped neither by a public salary nor by the fees of judging. It is an established practice, if not justified by reason at least accepted by custom, that a senator should increase his riches and dishonour his poverty. Hence the speech of Claudius, in which he praised those who, because of narrow family means, withdrew from the senatorial order, moved by the thought that by remaining they would add shamelessness to poverty. Annals, book 12. But however wealthy the estate of a household may be, you can drain it quickly, unless you fill the veins that fail from some other source. Trade has generally been forbidden to senators; agriculture, which was once thought to befit dignity, has fallen into disuse; manual craft is counted among the base things, and a workshop is not thought to bring up anything noble. From what source, then, will a falling fortune be helped, if not from interest, which harms no one?

units.la: Quod fi favore vel ætatis & imbecillitatis, vel etiam dignitatis, foveri fœnus poterit : cur aliis in hominum generibus pro scelere habendum? Nam quod purga- tæ rationi, quod legi divinæ repugnat ; nulla vel gratia hominum vel existimatione violari jure poterit. Aut igitur totum cum umbra fœnus est abrogandum ; aut nemini, qui jus quidem civitatis mobilcum habeat, ejus facultas præcidenda.
units.tr: But if interest can be favoured because of age and weakness, or even because of dignity, why should it be counted a crime in other classes of men? For what is opposed to purified reason and to the divine law cannot rightly be violated by any favour of men or by any esteem. Therefore either usury must be abolished entirely, root and branch, or its use must be cut off from everyone who nevertheless enjoys the rights of citizenship.

units.la: Necessitatem legi oppositam pro nostro captu con- templati fumus : nunc fi quod huic antidotum in promptu fit, ut sua legi constet majestas, inquira- mus.
units.tr: We have considered, according to our capacity, the necessity that is opposed to the law. Now let us inquire whether there is at hand some antidote to this, so that the majesty of the law may stand firm.

units.la: REMEDIA laborantí necessitate honestati.
units.tr: Remedies for honest men labouring under necessity.

units.la: Ea sunt vel depellendae foenoris necessitati, velne irrumpat avertendæ.
units.tr: These remedies are either for removing the need for interest, or for preventing it from breaking in.

units.la: Priori in genere Tiberius, pro sagacitate ingenii & populares adjuvandi studio, nec tamen si mensariorum exemplo, tulit opem Cafar, disposito per mensas millies fefertio, factaque mutuandi copia fine usuris per triennium, si debitor populo in duplum praediis cavisset. Sic refectafides [?], & paulatim privati quoque creditores reperti. Sed id Tiberio quidem facile fuit, aerario tot per annos alta in pace provinciarum tributis locu-pletato. Quid si vacuum aerarium? quid si pecunia foenore fumenda ipsum indigeat? quid si indigenti aeris praedia, quibus in duplum caveat, defecerint? Non omni igitur reipublicae, nec omni indigentiae ca-fui, haec norma adoptanda.
units.tr: For the first kind, Tiberius, out of his shrewd judgement and eagerness to help the common people, though not in the manner of the bankers, brought relief. Caesar set out a thousand sesterces on the tables and made money available to borrow without interest for three years, provided the debtor gave the people security in land to twice the amount. In this way credit was restored, and gradually private lenders too were found. But this was easy for Tiberius, since the treasury had been enriched by provincial tributes through many years of deep peace. What if the treasury were empty? What if the money itself had to be borrowed at interest? What if the lands by which a needy man could give security to twice the amount had run out? This rule, therefore, is not to be adopted for every state or against every kind of want.

units.la: Romani Pontifices, qui versuram omnem vetitam esse voluerunt, in ambiguo ad montes pietatis consu- gerunt. Eorum aliquem numerum Petrus Gregorius, capite 16. libri 13. de Republica, recensent. Sed si quis montium eorum verticem intentiori cura speculatus fuerit, parum ad nostrum Dionysium facere parvo negotio deprehendet. Nobis de antidoto prius quam de pharmaco, de morbi aversione quam in venas admissi depulsione, agendum.
units.tr: The Roman Pontiffs, who wished every kind of usury to be forbidden, took refuge, in their uncertainty, in the monti di pietà. Peter Gregory, in chapter 16 of book 13 of his De Republica, lists some of these mounts. But if anyone examines the summit of those mounts more closely, he will easily find that they do little to help our Dionysius. For us, the antidote must be treated before the drug, the averting of the disease before the expulsion of what has already entered the veins.

units.la: Ante omnia igitur cavendum, ne otiosorum turba rempublicam irrumpat. Sua quisque negotia, ut stationem militès, descripta habeat. Sic fiet, ut nec usura quisquam fere indigeat, & qui abundant opibus, ipsi potius mercaturae animum, aut agriculturae vel pastioni pecorum, adjiciant, quam otio per foenoris exactionem alendo indulgeant.
units.tr: Above all, then, we must take care that a crowd of idlers does not break into the commonwealth. Let each person have his own business laid out, as soldiers have their posts. In this way hardly anyone will need usury, and those who abound in wealth will apply their minds to trade, agriculture or the pasturing of flocks, rather than indulge in idleness by exacting interest.

units.la: Ne tamen à paucis opulentis vitae agendae facultas tenuioribus, coemptione agrorum aut sodalitatum monopoliis, praeripiatur: ista quidem omni è coetu tollantur; agris emendis modus, quem transfilire nefas, praescribatur.
units.tr: Yet, lest the means of living be snatched from the poorer by a few wealthy men through buying up lands or through monopolies of guilds, such practices should be removed from every assembly, and a limit to buying lands, which it is wrong to exceed, should be prescribed.

units.la: 3. Homines extremè pauperes civitate non temerè donandi: recepti in civitatem frugalitatis, parcimoniae, laborum admonendi.
units.tr: 3. Men who are extremely poor are not to be granted citizenship lightly; those received into the citizenship should be reminded of thrift, frugality and labour.

units.la: 4. Si qua prodigè viventibus pecunia locetur, fortem cum lucro amittendam esse lex praemoneat.
units.tr: 4. If any money is lent to those who live prodigally, the law should warn in advance that the principal, along with the profit, is to be lost.

units.la: 5. Vitiorum praecisa radice, facile fuerit usurae mederi, sed quia vitia cum hominibus nascuntur, cum hominibus intereunt: difficilior quam vis prudenti medico curatio. Saepius ex depravata hominum indole, quaedam rerum indigentia, partus usurae procreatur. Aviditas plura lucrandi utrumque, tam creditorem quam creditur, ad legis contemptum propellit. Aviditati spes inanis, & praesentium rerum fastidium, obstetricatur. Multos luxus, & indomitae inguinis aut gulae libidines, fundum avitum exhaurientes, cum versura praecipitant. Tolle corruptos mores: foeneratorem sustuleris.
units.tr: 5. Once the root of vices is cut away, usury could easily be cured; but because vices are born with men and die with men, the cure is more difficult than a prudent physician would find it. Often from the corrupt disposition of men there arises a certain need for goods, and usury is born of that need. Greed for gaining more drives both lender and borrower into contempt of the law. Empty hope and disgust with present circumstances act as midwives to greed. Many luxuries, and the unbridled lusts of belly and gullet, drain the ancestral estate, and men rush headlong into ruin through borrowing. Remove corrupt morals, and you will have removed the moneylender.

units.la: 6. Aut infamia foeneratores notandi, aut inter viles homines antiquo Graeciae more habendi, aut gravibus personis foenori saltem interdicendum. Ad exemplum Alexandri Severi; qui, Aelio Lampridio teste, Senatores si foeneraverint (id est, mutuo pecuniam dare) ... sumpta. Nam et Tertullianus loquitur, phrasi eo seculo non inusitata) usuras accipere primo vetuit, nisi aliquid muneris causa acciperent. Sic in vilipendium adducta foeneratione, paulatim qui sunt generosi animi ultro fe ea abdicabunt.
units.tr: 6. Moneylenders should either be marked with infamy, or be held among base men as in ancient Greece, or at least usury should be forbidden to men of standing. Take the example of Alexander Severus, who, according to Aelius Lampridius, forbade senators to lend money (that is, to give money on loan) ... to take it. For Tertullian also speaks (a phrase not unusual in that century) of how he first forbade them to receive interest, unless they received something as a gift. So, once usury has been brought into contempt, those of noble spirit will gradually renounce it of their own accord.

units.la: 7. Sed quando hac folertia nondum laboranti aliquo casu reipublicae succurritur; non puerili aetati, non profeffioris collegiis, non dignitati senatoriae subveniatur: aliam in curam rationum inveniendarum indu- stria nobis est dirigenda.
units.tr: 7. But since the state in some present trouble cannot yet be helped by this cleverness, we must not turn to the youth of wards, the colleges of the professions, or senatorial dignity for help. Instead, let our diligence be directed to another care: finding the means.

units.la: Principiò igitur cujusvis viri boni est, patriae sc & publico bono, non sibi tantum aut uni familiae, natum esse meminisse. Quas igitur in sinu reip. paravit facultates, pro ea[?] indigente sponte, quod commodiori tempore recipiat, profundat. Quod si vitam quoque debemus patriae, & in ea pro civibus prodigenda tot heroum exempla recordamur, prodigiúmne habebitur, paucas argenti laminas ex affluenti copia publicum in usum elargiri? Quod si amor mortalium, si patriae charitas refrixerit; leges, consensu sanciendae, cogendi ad officium potestatem habebunt. Sic, ne omnia cum sumptu & onere civium munia recensceam, Athenis Atticis opulentissimi quique triremem impendio suo ornare jubebantur. Sic in omni olim republica certos militiae annos, quod nummis conferendis gravius, implere omnes cogebantur; & ad debitum non respondere capitale erat. Ingrati sunt, & beneficii temporum suorum immemores, qui ad avertendum patriae, in quo & singulorum, incendium situlam gratis conferre dedignantur.
units.tr: First of all, then, every good man ought to remember that he was born for his country and the common good, not for himself alone or for one family. Therefore, the resources he has gathered in the bosom of the commonwealth, let him freely pour out for the public need, to be recovered at a more convenient time. If we owe our very lives to our country, and recall in it so many examples of heroes who spent themselves for their fellow citizens, will it be deemed a monstrous thing to give a few silver plates out of abundant wealth for public use? If the love of mortals and charity towards one's country has grown cold, then laws, sanctioned by common consent, will have the power to compel men to their duty. Thus, not to enumerate all the burdens and expenses borne by citizens, at Athens the wealthiest men were ordered to fit out a trireme at their own cost. Likewise, in every commonwealth of old, all were compelled to fill certain years of military service, which was more burdensome than contributing money; and to fail to answer a levy was a capital offence. They are ungrateful, and forgetful of the benefits of their own times, who disdain to contribute a bucket of water freely to quench the fire that threatens their country, in which the welfare of individuals too is at stake.

units.la: Superest pupillaris infirmitas, pia collegiorum natio, & senatoriae dignitatis gravitas.
units.tr: There remain the weakness of orphans, the pious foundation of the colleges, and the dignity and gravity of the senatorial order.

units.la: Quod ad favorem pupillorum: 1. Si ex antiquo more agris colendis, & assignatis unicuique haeredum libertis aut servitiis, viveretur, res esset expeditior. 2. Aut mercatura honesta, aliave occupatione parentes vixerunt, aut illaudato otio. Mercatura per familiares, cura & inspectione tutorum, dum ipsi adolescant, expediri poterit. Sordidum aut inhonestae vacuae culpam superstites liberi luant. 3. munere sacro aut civili defunctorum liberi publicam benevolentiam, & superiorum curam, prae aliis merebuntur. 4. Tot nationes usuram ignorantes, partus educare suos potuere. & nobis aliquid de luxu praecidendum; ad paupertatis & laborum patientiam tenera aetas assuefacienda. 5. Plures inopum aut mediocris fortunae, artificum, hortulanorum, aliorum foetus remanent: quos Deus & inductria nutrit. quidni igitur & divitum lautae familiae vitam sine usura instruant?
units.tr: As for favouring orphans: (1) If we lived by the ancient custom of cultivating the fields, each assigned to a freedman or slave of the heirs, the matter would be simpler. (2) Our parents lived either by honest trade or some other occupation, or by blameworthy idleness. Trade can be carried on through relatives, under the care and supervision of guardians, while the children grow up. The surviving children should bear the blame for any sordid or dishonourable idleness. (3) Children of the dead who have performed sacred or civil office will deserve public goodwill and the care of their superiors before others. (4) So many nations, ignorant of usury, have been able to bring up their offspring. We must also cut something from luxury, and accustom tender age to patience in poverty and labour. (5) Many children of the poor or of middling fortune remain: of craftsmen, gardeners and others. God and industry nourish them. Why, then, should not the luxurious households of the rich also provide for their children's lives without usury?

units.la: 6. Alia, & de novo agitanda, est quaestio; qua lege quáve rectorum sapientia, tenerae aetati profpicien-dum fit. Nunc divinae & gentium leges valeant: nec boni paucis finis causa bene inventa statuta solvantur. Gymnasiorum reditus multis in locis annuo agrorum cultu, fine pecuniae elocatione; aut liberali Principum erogatione fundantur. Et, ut joci aliquid admisceam, Soli sapienti, secundum Zenonis & Chrysippi decre-tum, licebit foenerari.
units.tr: (6) Another question, to be raised anew, is by what law or by what wisdom of rulers tender age is to be provided for. For now, let divine and national laws prevail; nor should good statutes, well devised for the sake of the common good, be dissolved for the benefit of a few. In many places the revenues of the gymnasia are founded on the annual cultivation of fields, without lending money at interest, or on the generous bounty of princes. And, to add a little jest, the wise man alone, according to the decree of Zeno and Chrysippus, will be permitted to lend at interest.

units.la: Senatores, ubi nullis fovetur è publico sumptibus, mercatura potius minus erubescenda, aut agro per operas colendo, paftione denique pecorum, salinis, metallifodinis, quam vetita legibus usura, dignitatem & vitam suffulcient. Si sordes Patres Conscriptos non decent; nec usurae decebunt. Satius fuerit, virum probum, sua fe virtute pauperi sub toga involventem, id quod naturahoneftum est fine dote sequi; quam peculatu, subjectis testamentis, expilatione aerarii, di-reptione sociorum, denique foenore iniquè exercen-do, locupletari.
units.tr: Where senators receive no support from public funds, they will rather sustain their dignity and livelihood by trade, which is not to be ashamed of, or by working the land, pasturing flocks, salt-works and metal mines, than by usury, which the laws forbid. If meanness does not become the Conscript Fathers, neither will usury become them. It will be better for an upright man, who wraps himself in his toga poor in wealth but rich in virtue, to pursue what is honourable by nature without a dowry, than to grow rich by peculation, by forged wills, by plundering the treasury, by defrauding partners, and finally by practising usury unjustly.

units.la: XIV. Imperium clementia temperan-dum.
units.tr: XIV. Empire must be tempered with clemency.

units.la: Quod praeceptum Tiberio, vergentibus imperii & vitae annis, neglectum; maturo eum odio expoluit.
units.tr: Tiberius neglected this precept as his years of life and rule waned, and with mature hatred he cast it off.

units.la: Causae saeviendi vel vulgares iis temporibus fuere, vel levitate ineptae, vel ab aviditate fiscum explendi, vel denique à truculentia animi, & puniendi confuetu-dine provocatae. Inter vulgares primum locum po-ftulatio majestatis tenuit; omnium tum accusatio-num complementum; & unicum crimen eorum, qui crimine carebant. Quod adeò fervebat, ut ab hilari-tate epularum, homines nullum judicium metuentes, abrepti, fine judicii mora trucidarentur. Confidius Proculus nullo pacto diem natalem celebrans, rapiuit in curiam paritergue damnatum interfectusque. nec à propinquis damnatorum abstinebatur: violentia contagionis judiciariae, veluti flammae, proxima quaeque
units.tr: The causes of cruelty in those times were either commonplace, or absurdly trivial, or prompted by greed to fill the treasury, or finally provoked by the savagery of his temper and his habit of punishing. Among the commonplace causes, the first place was held by the charge of treason (maiestas), the sum of all accusations then and the only crime of those who had no crime. This raged so fiercely that men who feared no trial were dragged from the merriment of feasts and put to death without any delay of judgment. Confidius Proculus, who in no way celebrated his birthday, was dragged into the senate, and was at once condemned and killed. Nor were the relatives of the condemned spared: the violence of judicial contagion, like a flame, consumed whatever lay nearest.

units.la: Sabiendi causa
units.tr: The case of Sabinus.

units.la: Majestas quæque prehendente. fororiejus Sancia aqua atque igni interdictum. Magnus ad hanc crudelitatem stimulus in accusatorum protervia: qui variis de causis, cum negotio ipsi carerent, negotium locupletissimo cuique facessebant. Quorum e grege Q. Pomponius, moribus inquies, hac & hujusmodi a se factitari, prætendebat, ut parta apud Principem gratia, periculis Pomponii Secundi fratris mederetur. Ergo præter lucri captati aviditatem, inquietudinem animi, truculentiam ingenii, etiam metus ne ab aliis prævenirentur, & venandi principis gratiæ ipse, ad accusandum levia ingenia propellebantur.
units.tr: Treason, seizing whoever came to hand. His sister Sancia was interdicted from water and fire. A great spur to this cruelty was the insolence of the accusers, who, for various reasons, though they had no business of their own, made business for the wealthiest men. From this flock Q. Pomponius, restless in character, pretended that these and similar things were done by him, so that, having won favour with the Prince, he might remedy the dangers of his brother Pomponius Secundus. Therefore, besides the greed for gain, the restlessness of mind, the savagery of temper, and the fear of being forestalled by others, the light-minded were driven, in their hunt for the prince's favour, to accuse on their own initiative.

units.la: Ridicula rebus in lacrymandis causa damnationis fuit, virum notitia illustrem, & clarorum hominum amicitia spectabilem, inter familiae imagines habere, nonnullis datum erat crimini, quod Theophanem Mi-tylenaum, proavum eorum, Gn. Magnus inter intimos habuisset: quodque defuncto Theophani, coelestes honores Graeca adulatio tribuerat. Quasi ob id, rerum statu mutato, Pompejanæ etiamnum factionis mansissent, Cæsareis adversatæ; aut ob divinos proavi honores, & ipsi nihil mortale saperent. Fœcunda ad aliorum criminationem leviorum hominum ingenia!
units.tr: It was a ridiculous ground for condemnation, in those tearful times, to keep among the family images a man famous for his acquaintance and distinguished by friendship with eminent men. Some were charged with the crime that Gnaeus Magnus had counted Theophanes of Mytilene, their great-grandfather, among his intimates, and that after Theophanes' death Greek flattery had granted him heavenly honours. As if, the state of affairs having changed, they had still remained of the Pompeian faction, hostile to the Caesarean party; or as if, because of their great-grandfather's divine honours, they themselves savoured of nothing mortal. How fertile are the minds of light men for accusing others!

units.la: Creberrima supplicio-rum, sub iniquiori principe, causa est; damnandorum opulentia, damnantis ava-ritia. Quæ Sex. Marium, Hispaniarum ditissimum, evertit. Sed hoc miserrimum, quod ne fama quidem ad posteros integra, ficto flagitio ut infestabiles, ut supplicii omnem atrocitatem meriti, trahuntur. defertur incestasse filiam, & saxo Tarpejo dejicitur, ut ne vulgari quidem aut famosorum crimine, aut morte genere interiret. ac ne dubium haberetur, magnitudinem pecuniae malo vertisse, auraria sq. ejus, quam publicarentur, sibimet Tiberius sepesuit.
units.tr: The most frequent cause of executions under a more unjust prince is the wealth of those to be condemned and the avarice of the condemner. This ruined Sextus Marius, the richest man in Spain. But this is most wretched: not even his fame survives intact for posterity, for he is dragged along as a dangerous man, charged with a fabricated disgrace and deserving every atrocity of punishment. He is charged with having committed incest with his daughter, and is thrown from the Tarpeian rock, so that he did not even perish by the ordinary death for crime or infamy. And lest there be any doubt that the magnitude of his wealth had turned to his harm, Tiberius appropriated for himself his gold mines, which were to be confiscated.

units.la: Avaritiam omnium malorum radicem esse, ut loquitur Paulus Apostolus, 1. Tim. 6. matrem, ut Pho-cyllides; scaturiginem, ut Philosophorum nonnemo: Tiberii & tyrannorum facinora loquuntur. Sed ut aphorismi Paulini veritas clarius patescat: per decem praeceptorum membra eam diducemus.
units.tr: That avarice is the root of all evils, as the Apostle Paul says (1 Tim. 6), the mother of them, as Phocylides says, and the fountain, as some philosopher says: the deeds of Tiberius and of tyrants bear witness to this. But that the truth of the Pauline aphorism may appear more clearly, we shall unfold it through the members of the ten precepts.

units.la: 1. Avaritia est plena à Deo defectio: subtracta à supremo numine in aurum fiduciâ.
units.tr: 1. Avarice is a complete defection from God: a withdrawal of trust from the supreme Deity into gold.

units.la: 2. Est idoli adoratio: quo sensu ab eodem Aposto-lo εἰδωλολατρεία [?] nominatur. Saltem hæc in primis adulterandæ religionis, & ad imagines se prosternen-dæ, causis.
units.tr: 2. It is the worship of idols, which is why the same Apostle calls it idolatry [εἰδωλολατρεία]. At least this is among the chief causes of adulterating religion and of prostrating oneself before images.

units.la: 3. Plurima ob lucri aviditatem perjuria, blasphemiæ; quotidianæ tabernariorum execrationes au-diuntur.
units.tr: 3. Many perjuries and blasphemies are committed for the sake of gain; the daily curses of tavern-keepers can be heard.

units.la: 4. Lucri cupiditas à Sabbathi celebratione plures, quam alia culpa, detinet; aut medio in sacrorum peragendorum coetu, cogitationes à verbi divini perce-ptu in forum, in sutrinam, in maecellum abstrahit.
units.tr: 4. The desire for gain keeps more people from the keeping of the Sabbath than any other fault; and even in the middle of the assembly for sacred duties, it draws the thoughts away from hearing the divine Word into the market, the cobbler's shop, and the meat market.

units.la: 5. Parentes, ob hæreditatis exspectationem, mul-torum voto morti, ut nimium vivaces, devoventur. Inventi quinimò, qui boli à principe captandi-spe, pa-rentum nomen aboleri flagitarunt. Nec defuere, qui parentes majestatis, aut alterius criminis, postula-rent.
units.tr: 5. Because of the expectation of inheritance, parents are cursed to death by many, as being too long-lived. Indeed, some have been found who, hoping to win the prince's favour by this bait, demanded that the name of parent be abolished. Nor were there lacking those who would accuse parents of treason or of some other crime.

units.la: 6. Avaritia multos ad latrocinia, ad piraticam, ad bella insontibus inferenda, ad supplicia divitibus accommodanda, ut hic Tiberium impellit.
units.tr: 6. Avarice drives many to robbery, to piracy, to waging war on the innocent, and to punishments suited to the rich, as it impels Tiberius here.

units.la: 7. Avaritia prostibula, pudicitia prostrata, forni-ces, lupanaria, meretriculis implet. Nec Jovi in aurum mutato aditus ad Danaën negatur. Eadem alios, & quidem summos ecclesiæ præsides, ut lupanaria in-cautorum adolescentium laqueos, aperiant, hortatur.
units.tr: 7. Avarice fills brothels, stews and bawdy-houses with prostitutes, and the way to Danaë is not denied to Jove transformed into gold. The same avarice urges others, and indeed the highest presidents of the Church, to open brothels as snares for unwary young men.

units.la: 8. Avaritia furtis, impofturis, adulterinis mercibus & nummis, orbem humanum complet.
units.tr: 8. Avarice fills the whole human world with thefts, frauds, and counterfeit wares and coins.

units.la: 9. Avaritia testamentorum suppositiones, iniquas eorum accusationes & judicum sententias, receptas causidicorum perfidia, extorquet.
units.tr: 9. Avarice extorts forged wills, unjust accusations and sentences from judges, and the treachery of lawyers as an accepted practice.

units.la: 10. Ab avaritia exempla cupiditatis humanæ, in alienam domum, servum, jumentum abducta, pe-tantur.
units.tr: 10. From avarice come the examples of human covetousness: another's house, slave, or beast of burden is carried off.

units.la: Denique per avaritiam homo ab amore Dei, à cha-ritate proximi, in perversum sui amorem avertitur. Apex tyrannicæ crudelitatis est, ex consuetudine sævire. Qua Tiberius non satiatus miserorum pœnis, potius irritatum supplicii, cunctos qui carcere attine-bantur accusati societatis cum Seiano[?], necari jubet. Ergo Tiberio ad damnationem accusatio, ad suppli-cium jubendum carcer suffecit. Jacuit immensa strages: omnis sexus, omnis ætas: illustres, ignobiles: dispersi, aut aggregati.
units.tr: Finally, through avarice a man is turned away from the love of God and from charity to his neighbour, into a perverse love of himself. The apex of tyrannical cruelty is to rage from habit. Tiberius, not sated with the punishments of the wretched, and rather irritated by the punishment, orders all who were held in prison, accused of association with Sejanus, to be put to death. So for Tiberius, accusation sufficed for condemnation, and prison for ordering execution. There lay an immense slaughter: every sex, every age, the illustrious and the lowly, scattered or heaped together.

units.la: Non potuit breviori facundia tanti mali tragœdia depingi. Sed neque hic leges ærumnarum flectit. neque propinquis aut amicis assistere inlacrymare, ne visere quidem diutius dabatur. Sed circumjecti custodes, & in mœrorem cujusque intenti, corpora putrefacta asse-ctabantur, dum in Tiberim traherentur. ubi fluitan-tia, aut ripis appulsa, non cremare quisquam, non con-tingere. Interciderat fortis humana commercium, vi metus: quantumque savitia glisceret, miseratio arce-batur.
units.tr: No tragedy of so great an evil could be depicted in fewer words. But not even here does he bend the laws of misery: they were not allowed to stand by their relatives or friends, to weep with them, nor even to visit them for long. Rather, guards stood around, intent on each one's grief, and dogged the putrefying bodies while they were dragged into the Tiber, where, floating or washed up on the banks, no one dared to burn them or touch them. Human fellowship had been cut off by the force of fear, and as cruelty grew, pity was held back.

units.la: Gratulare tibi Gallia, gratulare Germania, tan-torum fere sævitiæ exemplorum per omne ævum nescia. Tiberium vero, fortis humanæ oblitum, nun-quam intermoritura fama, sed fama sinisterior, per se-cula diffundat.
units.tr: Rejoice for yourself, Gaul; rejoice, Germany, which through all ages has been almost ignorant of examples of such savagery. As for Tiberius, who forgot human kind, may a fame that never dies, but a more sinister fame, spread him through the ages.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Periculosus à servitute ad dominationem transitus.
units.tr: A perilous transition from servitude to domination.

units.la: Illud Claudiani:
units.tr: That line of Claudian's:

units.la: Asperius nihil est humili cum surgit in altum:
units.tr: Nothing is harsher than a lowborn man when he rises high.

units.la: Non tantum de humilitate generis, sed de quavis fortunæ asperioris, aspero sub domino, jactatione servili, licet accipias. Cajus Cæsar, qui nomine Caligulæ innotuit, quàm superbè post Tiberium dominatus est, tam se submissè Tiberio imperante gessit. Unde mox scitum Passieni oratoris dictum percrebuit. Neque meliorem unquam servum, neque deteriorem dominum fuisse. Cui Passieni dicto illud Aristotelicum non refragatur: Οὐκ ἐπ᾽ ἀξίαις μὴ ἀρχ[?], Nunquam imperio bene prae-erit[?], qui non aliorum imperio paruit. De civili enim imperio, ubi per vices paretur ac impe- ratur, non de servili conditione & dominandi potes-tia, hæc accipias. Veruntamen ut lubricus, ita non semper infirmus, post servitutem in imperio grestus figitur. Trajani bonitatis, & in imperio lenitudinis, hanc causam Plinius indagat, quod sævo sub Domi-tiani dominatu trepidare didicerit. Quo sensu Galba ad Pisonem: Utilissimus quidem ac brevissimus bonarum malarumque rerum dilectus, cogitare quid autem noluerit sub alio principe aut voluerit. Hiftor. Animi imbecillitas est, non personæ vultus mutatus, quæ ad alteram subito fortunam delata, ferre secundum vitæ blandioris flatum nequit.
units.tr: This may be taken not only of humbleness of birth but of any fortune that was harsher, of a harsh master and servile harassment. Gaius Caesar, known by the name Caligula, ruled as haughtily after Tiberius as he had behaved submissively while Tiberius was in power. Whence the witty saying of the orator Passienus soon became common currency: that there had never been a better slave nor a worse master. Aristotle's statement does not contradict Passienus' saying: [οὐκ ἂν εὖ ἄρξειε μὴ ἀρχθείς], "he will never rule well who has not obeyed another's command." But you should take this of civil government, where obeying and commanding take turns, not of servile condition and the power of lording it over others. Yet, though slippery, he is not always weak: after servitude his steps are firmly fixed in power. Pliny traces to this cause the goodness of Trajan and the gentleness of his rule, namely that he had learned to tremble under the savage domination of Domitian. In this sense Galba says to Piso in the Histories: "Indeed the most useful and shortest way of distinguishing good things from bad is to consider what one would not wish, or would wish, under another prince." It is a weakness of spirit, not a change in the person's countenance, that cannot bear the breeze of a more pleasant life when it is suddenly carried into a different fortune.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Multum sibi in imperantes conjectura permittit.
units.tr: Conjecture takes a great deal of liberty concerning rulers.

units.la: Nec imperantes divinatione, & in se ac aliosinquisitione, omnes abstinent. Non omiserim præsagium Tiberii, de Ser. Galba tum consule: quem accitum, & diversis sermonibus pertentatum, postremo Græcis verbis in hanc sententiam allocutus: Et tu Galba quandoque degustabis imperium. Veram ac brevem potentiam significans. Quæ de Thrasullo, Tiberii in Chaldæorum scientia rectore, afferuntur: iis nec addam nec demam fidem. Quis arbiter eorum, cum præter crassum libertum nemo adesset, sermones excepit? Quis post eventum rerum non hæc à Thrasullo, aut artis ejusdem aliquo, confecta suspicetur? Aut, si de historia non dubitatur, quis adeo stupidum Thrasullum existimet, ut non è sermone Tiberii, gestu, solitudine præcipitis loci, truci liberti aspectu, sibi anceps discrimen instare provideret? Hæc suo gustui quisque applicabit: me diremptorem non interponam.
units.tr: Nor do all people refrain from divining about rulers and from inquiring into their own and others' fortunes. I will not omit the prophecy of Tiberius concerning Servius Galba, when Galba was consul. Tiberius summoned him, tested him with various conversations, and at last addressed him in Greek words to this effect: "And you too, Galba, will one day taste of empire." This signifies a true but brief power. As for what is reported about Thrasyllus, Tiberius's instructor in the science of the Chaldeans, I will neither add to nor take away from the credibility of those accounts. Who was the witness to their words, since no one was present except the coarse freedman? Who, after the event, does not suspect that these things were composed by Thrasyllus, or by someone practising his art? Or, if the account itself is not in doubt, who would think Thrasyllus so stupid as not to foresee, from Tiberius's speech, his gesture, the solitude of the steep place, and the grim look of the freedman, that a perilous crisis hung over himself? Each will apply these things to his own taste; I will not step in as arbiter.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Providentia res humanæ reguntur.
units.tr: Human affairs are governed by providence.

units.la: Multis ante Tacitum seculis quærebatur, & hodie anxie quæritur: Fatone res mortalium & necessitate immuimmutabili, an forte volvantur. Illa sententia ne-ceffitate rem liberrimam, voluntatem humanam, & eam consequentes actiones, illigat: haec mundum omni Dei providentia, Deum ipsum imperio, exolvit. Nec in hoc opinionum confli&tu, consensionem omnium facili negotio extorqueris. quippe sapientissimos ve-terum, quaeque sectam eorum aemulantur, diversos reperies. Hoc autem aevo, cum miseratione seculi, quae-ftionem non inter sapientes modo, verum inter titivi-litia hominum, magno clamore, jurgio, sacrorum interdictione, ferro tandem & igni, agitari videas. maxi-me ubi agitur de salutis aeternae principio. Sed hanc, ut Tacito ignoratam, nec disceptationibus Politicis temere involvendam, nondum attingo. De rerum humanarum regimine, insita multis, Epicurèam maxi-me sectam aemulatis, opinio fuit; non initia nostri, non finem, non denique homines diis cura. quae sententia non providentiam modo e rebus, sed ipsum Deum tol-lit.
