Qualem enim Deum fingemus, aut propter osci-tantiam res mortalium & coelestium non curantem, aut propter imbecillitatem praeffe universo non va-lentem? Est tamen perfuafionis hujus aliqua, vulgo plausibilis, ratiuncula: quia tristia in bonos, lata apud deteriores creberrima videant. Quomodo enim, fi mundus providentia regatur, indigna dignis, indignis digna tribuantur? aut hic in agonotheta iniquitas, aut in praemiorum caeca diversitate casus locum habebit. Quod argumenti Epicurae telum, quomodo infringi debeat, suo loco videbimus. Alii ab his multum diversi, fatum quidem congruere rebus putant. sed ne-que hi in principio necessitatis, in causa rerum moven-darum conveniunt. Mathematici, & quos Chaldaeos vocamus, a vagis stellis, & definito astrorum motu, omnia quae in mundo geruntur suspendunt. Stoici in fiderum cursu minus defixi, aeterna rerum ac altiora principia, & nexus naturalium causarum scrutantur. Horum perfuafu, aeterna constitutione, nexuque cau-farum latentium, & multo ante destinatarum, suum quaeque ordinem immutabili lege percurrunt. Hi insuperabili fati necessitate ipsum Jovem, (quæ crebtâ[?] est apud Homerum, Zenone multis ætatibus antiquorem, locutio) devinciunt. Ut minus jam mirandum videatur, quod Platonis etiam fectatores[?] pronunciant: Nec consilio prudenti, nec remedio sagaci, diuinæ providentiæ fatalis dispositio subverti vel reformari potest. Ac ne scelera quidem, & peccandi necessitatem, huic dispositioni excipiunt. Decantata Tragi-cis Oedipi fabula, fati ordinatione parricidio & matris incestu ante nativitatem miseri. Cujus filii, Eteocles & Polynices, regni aviditate ac civilium armorum crepitu scelesti, à Thebani belli scriptore Statio absol-vuntur.
units.tr: For many centuries before Tacitus this question was asked, and it is still asked anxiously today: whether the affairs of mortals are governed by fate and unchangeable necessity, or are turned by chance. The first view binds the free thing, the human will, and the actions that follow from it, by necessity. The second strips the world of all divine providence and takes from God himself his rule. Nor in this conflict of opinions will you easily extract agreement from everyone: for you will find the wisest of the ancients, and those who imitate their school, to be divided. In our own age, to our sorrow, you may see the question stirred up not only among the learned but among the common crowd of people, with great clamour, quarrelling, the forbidding of sacraments, and at last sword and fire, most of all where the question concerns the beginning of eternal salvation. But this question, unknown to Tacitus, and not to be rashly tangled up in political debates, I do not yet touch. Concerning the governing of human affairs there was an opinion, natural to many, who imitated chiefly the Epicurean school: that neither our beginnings nor our end, nor finally men at all, are a care to the gods. This view removes from things not only providence but God himself. For what kind of God shall we imagine, one who either does not care for the affairs of mortals and of heaven through sluggishness, or who is not strong enough to preside over the universe through weakness? Yet there is some little argument for this persuasion, commonly plausible: because they see that sad things most often happen to good men, and joyful things to the worse. For how, if the world were governed by providence, would unworthy things be given to the worthy, and worthy things to the unworthy? Either injustice will have its place in the judge of the games, or chance will have its place in the blind distribution of rewards. How this weapon of the Epicureans ought to be broken, we shall see in its proper place. Others, very different from these, think that fate indeed agrees with things. But neither do these agree about the source of necessity, about the cause that sets things in motion. The mathematicians, and those whom we call Chaldeans, make all that happens in the world depend on the wandering stars and the fixed motion of the heavenly bodies. The Stoics, less bound to the course of the stars, search out the eternal and higher principles of things, and the connection of natural causes. By their persuasion, all things run their own order by an unchangeable law, through the eternal arrangement, the connection of hidden causes, and causes appointed long before. These, by the inescapable necessity of fate, bind even Jove himself (an expression frequent in Homer, and older than Zeno by many ages). So it may seem less surprising that even the followers of Plato pronounce: that the fated arrangement of divine providence can be overturned or reformed neither by prudent counsel nor by shrewd remedy. Nor do they exempt from this arrangement even crimes and the necessity of sinning. The fable of Oedipus, sung by the tragedians, tells how by the ordering of fate the wretched man was guilty of parricide and incest before he was born. His sons, Eteocles and Polynices, wicked in their greed for the kingdom and in the clash of civil arms, are acquitted by Statius, the writer of the Theban war.

units.la: —— —— manet hac ab origine mundi
units.tr: From the origin of the world this day has remained fixed for war,

units.la: Fixa dies bello, populique in prælia nati.
units.tr: and for the peoples born for battle.

units.la: Horum judicio non Paris raptæ Helenæ, & propter eam eversæ Trojæ, sed fatum in culpa. De quo Lucanus, Romæ ruinam indignatus, queritur:
units.tr: By their judgment it was not Paris, who carried off Helen, nor the overthrow of Troy on her account, but fate that was to blame. Of this Lucan, indignant at the ruin of Rome, complains:

units.la: Invida fatorum series, summisque negatum
units.tr: The envious sequence of the fates, and the denial to the highest things

units.la: Stare diu, nimioque graves sub ponderā[?] lapsu,
units.tr: of standing long, and falling heavily under their own excessive weight.

units.la: Libro 1. v.70.
units.tr: Book 1, line 70.

units.la: Nec tamen is interiores belli scelesti causas diffitetur
units.tr: Yet he does not deny the inner causes of the wicked war:

units.la: Quemque sua rapiunt scelerata in prælia causa:
units.tr: Each man is swept into battle by his own wicked cause.

units.la: Hos polluta domus, legesque in pace timenda,
units.tr: These by a polluted house, and by laws to be feared in peace;

units.la: Hos ferro fugienda fames, mundique ruina,
units.tr: these by hunger to be shunned in war, and by the ruin of the world;

units.la: Permiscenda fides: nullum furor egit in armis.
units.tr: by faith to be confounded. Frenzy has driven no one to arms.
Book 2, line 251.

units.la: Fati prætextu & fe[?] Bruto ab armis dehortanti Cato, apud eundem, purgat:
units.tr: In the same poem Cato, dissuading Brutus from arms, excuses himself under the pretext of fate:

units.la: Summum Brute nefas civilia bella fatemur:
units.tr: Brutus, we admit that civil wars are the greatest wickedness;

units.la: Sed quo fata trahunt, virtus secura sequetur,
units.tr: but whither the fates draw us, virtue will follow without fear,

units.la: Crimen erit superis, & me fecisse nocentem.
units.tr: and it will be a charge against the gods that I, a guilty man, did it.
Line 285.

units.la: Sed hæc quidem innocentiæ jactantia, & criminis is[?] superos aversio, in cœlum procul dubio injuria est. Nec mitior illa apud Senecam culpæ solatio:
units.tr: But these are indeed the boasts of innocence and the shifting of guilt onto the gods, which is undoubtedly an injury to heaven. Nor is Seneca's consolation for guilt any milder:

units.la: Fati ista culpa est: nemo fit fato nocens.
units.tr: That is the fault of fate: no one is made guilty by fate.

units.la: Oedipo Act. 5. Sc. 2. Benigniorem interpretationem facilius ista in eodem dramate acceperint:
units.tr: Oedipus, Act 5, Scene 2. Those same words in the same drama may more easily be taken in a kinder sense:

units.la: Fatis agimur, cedite fatis. Non sollicita possunt cura Mutare rati stamina fusi. Quicquid patimur mortale genus, Quicquid facimus, venit ex alto.
units.tr: We are driven by the fates; yield to the fates. Anxious care cannot change the threads spun by the fixed spindle. Whatever mortal kind suffers, whatever it does, comes from on high.

units.la: Choro 5.
units.tr: Chorus 5.

units.la: Ista quae sequuntur, duriora: nec tamen Stoicae familiae insolita.
units.tr: What follows is harsher, yet not unfamiliar to the Stoic school:

units.la: Omnia certo tramite vadunt: Primusque dies dedit extremum. Non illa Deo vertisse licet, Quae nexa suis currunt causis.
units.tr: All things go on a certain course; and the first day gave the last. It is not permitted even to God to have turned aside those things which run bound to their own causes.

units.la: Plura de impia hac pietate, nam adsunt plura, conge-rere non libet. Nos non Deum fato, sed Deo fatum subjicimus. imo ne subjicimus quidem; si fatum nihil aliud est, quam aeternum Dei de mundi statu decretum; & nihil est in Deo, ex Theologorum sententia, quod a Deo ipso separetur.
units.tr: I do not wish to gather more about this impious piety, though there is more. We do not subject God to fate, but fate to God. Indeed we do not even subject it: if fate is nothing other than God's eternal decree concerning the state of the world, and if, according to the opinion of the theologians, there is nothing in God that is separated from God himself.

units.la: Inexplicabili fati textura filum actionum humanarum involvi, cum triste cogitatu videatur: quidam benigniores seriei fatalis interpretes electionem vitae nobis relinquunt: quam ubi elegeris, certum imminentium ordinem. Est hoc aliquod libertatis humanae solamen, non modo a coactione, verum etiam necessitate absoluta, & quoad originem inexplicabili, solutae: verum providentiae divinae, ab incerta hominum electione pendenti, cancelli & aeterna sapientia indigni nexus circumfunduntur. Sunt & qui voluntatem humanam, nullo mortalis vitae tempore impeditam, fati jugo excipiant. Sed haec sublimiori, quam sunt civilium rerum tractationes, pulpito mandamus.
units.tr: Some think that the will of man is caught in the inexplicable web of fate, which seems a sad thought. Some of the more kindly interpreters of the fated sequence leave us the choice of our life; once we have chosen it, the order of what is to come is fixed. This is some comfort to human freedom, which is freed not only from compulsion but from absolute necessity, and in its origin is inexplicably loosed. But the bonds and the fences of divine providence, which depend on the uncertain choice of men, and are unworthy of eternal wisdom, are thrown around it. There are also those who hand over the human will, untouched by any time of mortal life, to the yoke of fate. But we leave these matters to a loftier platform than the handling of civil affairs.

units.la: Illud ab instituto nostro non alienum: cur, si providentia mundus regatur, bona malis, mala bonis contingant? Respondetur a Stoicorum sententia: neque mala vel bona, quae vulgus putet: multos qui conflictari adversis videantur, beatos: at plerosque, quam magnas per opes, miserrimos: si illi grave[m] forunam[?] constanter tolerent, bi proferâ inconsulte ut tantur. Rotundè ante Zenonem Plato: [illegible, ~25 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] Nihil bono mali accidit ne vivo nec mortuo. in Socratis Apologia. Non sunt ex opinionis imbecillitate, sed ex Dei sapienti judicio, bona vel mala æstimanda. Ne putentur mala, dantur & bona: ne putentur magna & summa, dantur & mala: itemque auferuntur ista & bonis, ut probentur; & malis, ut crucientur. inquit in quadam epistola Augustinus. Atqui fame, dolore, frigore, æstu, nuditate affligi miserum est; pauper-tate & ignominia premi, acerbum. ne de voce malorum contendamus: ne in re feria puerili lusu jocemur. Sed unde tu te bonum, ideoque poena indignum, probaveris; nisi virtute, cujus in arduis, non in mollitie, commoratio, incedas? Dura & aspera viri probi, ut exercitationem, improbi ut poenam tolerant. Illi alacres, hi gementes: illi spe elutandi, hi emergendi deperatione. Plura è Senecæ de Providentia libro, & ex Arcanis nostris, pag. 648 solidiora è S. codice de spe æternæ gloriæ petenda.
units.tr: This is not foreign to our purpose: why, if the world is governed by providence, do good things happen to the wicked and bad things to the good? The Stoic view answers that the things which the crowd thinks good or bad are neither: many who seem to be struggling with adversity are happy, while most who abound in great wealth are most wretched; if the former bear a heavy fortune constantly, and the latter use prosperity unwisely. Plato said plainly before Zeno: [illegible]. Nothing bad happens to a good man, either living or dead, as in Socrates' Apology. Good and evil are to be judged not by the weakness of opinion, but by the wise judgment of God. Lest they be thought evil, good things are also given; lest great and highest things be thought to be these, evil things are also given: and likewise these things are taken away from good men, that they may be proved, and from bad men, that they may be tormented, as Augustine says in a certain letter. And yet to be afflicted with hunger, pain, cold, heat and nakedness is wretched; to be pressed by poverty and disgrace is bitter. Let us not quarrel about the word "evil," nor jest in a matter of childish play. But how will you prove yourself good, and therefore unworthy of punishment, unless by virtue, in whose hard places, not in softness, you dwell and advance? The good man endures hardships and roughness as exercise, the wicked as punishment: the one cheerfully, the other groaning; the one with hope of overcoming, the other in despair of rising again. More solid things are to be drawn from Seneca's book on Providence, and from our Arcana, p. 648, and from the holy codex, on seeking the hope of eternal glory.

units.la: XVIII. A fine vita, ut fabula, non à principio judicanda.
units.tr: XVIII. The end of a life, as of a play, is not to be judged from its beginning.

units.la: Multis ante Epicurum exortum sœculis David, rex Hebræorum pientissimus, bruti sæ animum induisse, & propè Dei providentiâ negata lapsum, florentibus malis; exitu tandem eorum infpectu, ad saniorem mentem rediisse, Psalmo 72. fatetur. Ne & nos præ-maturo judicio abrepti, quorundam vitam beatam præ-dicemus: cumulum illustrium personarum, inedia aut αβγ absumptorum, prodente memoriæ Taciti, consideremus.
units.tr: Many centuries before Epicurus arose, David, the most devout king of the Hebrews, confesses in Psalm 72 that he had taken on a brutish mind and had almost denied God's providence, because evils were flourishing; only when he saw their end did he return to a saner mind. Lest we too, carried away by premature judgment, call anyone's life happy, let us consider the long list of illustrious persons who were consumed by hunger or otherwise, as Tacitus's memory reports.

units.la: 1. Afinium Gallum, divitiis & luxu inter patres Romanos eminentem, adeò ut luxuriæ patronus contra Frontonem existeret, (2. Annal.) egestate cibi perem-ptum, haud dubium: sponte vel necessitate, incertum habebatur.
units.tr: 1. Afinius Gallus, eminent among the Roman senators for his wealth and luxury, so much so that he stood as a champion of luxury against Fronto (Annals, book 2), was destroyed by lack of food. There is no doubt of that; whether he did it voluntarily or from necessity was uncertain.

units.la: 2. Cru-
units.tr: 2. Cru-

units.la: 2.: Drufus, qui Germanico patre superbus, in fra-trem Neronem instinctu Sejani crudelis, in Tiberium imperatorem contumax, e civium favore suprema ex-spectaverat. Hic in carcere diu (ut & Afinius per tri-ennium) maceratus, tandem exstinguitur, cum se mi-serandi alimentis, mandendo e cubili tormento, nonnum ad diem detinuisset.
units.tr: 2.: Drusus, who, proud of his father Germanicus, was cruel to his brother Nero at the instigation of Sejanus, and defiant toward the emperor Tiberius, had looked for his last hour from the favour of the citizens. Here, long wasted in prison (as Asinius also was for three years), he was at last extinguished, when, miserably sustaining himself on food, by chewing the stuffing of his bed as a torment, he had delayed the end for some days.

units.la: 3. Agrippinam, ferocis animi mulierem, & vivente marito vix Tiberio concedentem, post diuturnam custodiam, fama est, voluntate exstincta. nisi si negatis alimentis, assimulatum esse finis, qui videretur sponte-sumptus. Fertur quidem quasi in laudem ejus, quod aqui impatiens, dominandi avida, virilibus curis faeminarum vitia exuerat. Sed non pudicitia foeminae servata majori laudi, quam quae virorum sunt, imperii tractatio & rerum bellicarum cura, affectata opprobrio.
units.tr: 3. Agrippina, a woman of fierce spirit, who while her husband lived scarcely yielded to Tiberius, after long confinement was, the report goes, put out of the way by will, unless by denial of food, a pretence of a death that seemed self-chosen. It is related, indeed, as if in her praise, that being impatient of equality and greedy for power, she had cast off the vices of women by manly cares. But a woman's chastity is not kept with greater praise than men's virtues; the management of empire and the concern for warlike affairs, when affected, turn to disgrace.

units.la: 4. Coccejus Nerva, divini humanique juris insigni scientia, grata familiaritate principis, ad culmen felicitatis humanae eductus, integro statu, corpore illaso, moriendi consilium cepit. Aqua cogitatione quanquam eum Tiberius precibus avocare nitebatur, aversatus sermonem Nervae, abstinentiam cibi conjunxit.
units.tr: 4. Cocceius Nerva, of remarkable learning in divine and human law, raised to the height of human happiness by the prince's pleasing intimacy, with his state intact and his body unharmed, formed a plan of dying. Although Tiberius tried by entreaties to turn him from that thought, having shunned Nerva's conversation, he joined abstinence from food.

units.la: 5. Plancina supplicio merito favore principis erepta, cum gratia deflagrante accusaretur, sua manu, fera magis, quàm immerita supplicia persolvit. Nemo igitur praesenti fortunae & scelerum cursui confidens, aeternam sibi felicitatem spondeat. Nemo aliorum praeter meritum florentem domum intuitus, vel aemulatione torreatur, vel de providentiae divinae nutu in dubium abeat.
units.tr: 5. Plancina, rescued from punishment by the prince's favour, when she was accused amid blazing hatred, paid the penalty by her own hand, a death more savage than undeserved. Let no one, therefore, trusting in present fortune and the course of crimes, promise himself eternal happiness. Let no one, looking upon a house flourishing beyond its merit, be consumed with envy, or fall into doubt about the will of divine providence.

units.la: XIX. Morte potentis adversarii non nimium laetandum.
units.tr: XIX. We should not rejoice too much at the death of a powerful adversary.

units.la: Nam & ruina quidam proterunt; & ut mortifera quaedam animalia, si non morsu, solo attactu lædunt. Agrippinae odio Plancina, potentiae ejus muliebri ardore aemula, Tiberio fovebatur. Mortua Agrippinâ,
units.tr: For some men also trample others down by their fall, and, like certain deadly animals, they wound even without biting, by touch alone. Plancina, rival to Agrippina in her womanly ardour for power, was favoured by Tiberius out of hatred for Agrippina. When Agrippina was dead,

units.la: potentia hujus crevisse videbatur. Contrà ômhiùm exspectationem Agrippinæ pernicies, quod vix credibile, Plancinam traxit. Quæ hic aulæ temeritas? aut quod imperii arcànum? ut odium & gratia deferen̄ jus valuit. Remota causa tollitur effectus: quifcho- lás Logicas triverunt; loquuntur. Veniæ delictorum causa, gratia Tiberii erat; gratiæ causa Odium, ut diæ Agrippinæ. Exftinto mortuæ, quæ morsura non erat, odio, gratia eviluit: gratia evanescente justitiæ locus dabatur.
units.tr: Plancina's power seemed to have grown. Contrary to everyone's expectation, Agrippina's ruin, which is hardly credible, dragged Plancina down with her. What recklessness is this at court? What secret of empire? How strongly the right to hate and to favour could prevail! When the cause is removed, the effect is removed; this is what the logic schools have worn threadbare, and they are right. The cause of the pardon of crimes was Tiberius' favour, and the cause of that favour was hatred, namely of Agrippina, as I have said. When the hatred was extinguished, since she who was dead could no longer bite, the favour faded away; and once favour faded, room was given to justice.

units.la: Quàm non sincerà fit de mortuis lætitiâ, eadem Plancinâ cum marito Pisone, Germanico rebus humanis strepto, docuerit, Nuncio mortis accepto, Piso cædit victimas, adit templa diis gratias actūrus. Plancinâ gaudio infolentior, luctum amissæ soroṙis tum primum læto cultu mutavit. 2. Annal. Atqui immodérati gaudii mox pœnas Piso daturus erat, quas vivo adversario fortasse non dedisset. Et Plancinæ, favoré Liviæ sublevatæ, dilata magis quàm ablata ultio est; Sexto Pompejo, qui Sicula classe Tyrrhenum mare infestabat, ab Antonio in Asia occiso, mirum in modum Antonius, Octavius, patres, plebesque Romana, Italia gaudebant. Atqui mox graviùs inter victores partium Juliarum bellum exarsit: Italiam non vaga pirata- rum excursione, sed armorum lato incendio rapturum: his fuga Cleopatræ, ignavia Antonii, celerem finem imponere potuisset. Antonius certè, qui oppresso Pompejo regnum quietum (peraverat), Octavii perni- citate, & fraude Cleopatræ, sua manu concidit. Draconem ingentis magnitudinis non nemo ferro conse- cisse memoratur. Victoriæ gaudio elatus, cum sublato in altum gladio triumphans exclamaret; guttæ quæ- dam pestiferæ saniei à lamina in lacertum delapsæ, vena nas & totum corpus infecere. Ita quem vivus non potuit, victus victorem serpens interemit.
units.tr: How far from sincere is joy at the death of an enemy is shown by the same Plancina together with her husband Piso, when Germanicus was taken from the living. On receiving the news of his death, Piso sacrificed victims and went to the temples to give thanks to the gods. Plancina, more insolent in her joy, then for the first time exchanged her mourning for her lost sister for festive dress. 2. Annals. Yet Piso was soon to pay the penalty for his immoderate joy, a penalty he might perhaps not have incurred had his adversary still been alive. And Plancina, raised up by the favour of Livia, was merely postponed in her punishment rather than spared it. Likewise, when Sextus Pompeius, who had been harrying the Tyrrhenian sea with a Sicilian fleet, was killed in Asia by Antony's men, Antony, Octavius, the senators and the Roman commons, and all Italy, rejoiced in a remarkable way. Yet soon afterwards a more serious war broke out among the victors of the Julian party, a war that was going to snatch Italy away not by the roving raids of pirates but by a wide conflagration of arms. Cleopatra's flight and Antony's cowardice could have put a swift end to this. Antony, at any rate, who had crushed Pompey and seemed to have a quiet kingdom, fell by his own hand, through the swiftness of Octavius and the treachery of Cleopatra. It is recorded that someone killed a dragon of huge size with a sword. Elated with joy at his victory, as he exclaimed in triumph with his sword raised high, a few drops of poisonous gore slid from the blade down his arm, and infected his veins and his whole body. So the serpent, once conquered, killed the victor whom it had not been able to overcome while alive.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Degeneres nuptiæ moerore populum afficiunt.
units.tr: Degenerate marriages fill the people with grief.

units.la: Ex Taciti sensu, aut ex opinione vulgi. Tot luctibus funesta civitate, pars mœroris fuit, quod Julia Drusi filia, quondam Neronis uxor, denupsit in domum Rubelli Blandi, cujus avum Triburtem equitem Romanum plerique meminerant. Quod nunc mœrori, olim gaudio fuerat, summos cum infimis connubio miscentes. Adeo fe populus ipse contemnit, ut quod antiqua Roma Genutio autore ægre tot digladiationibus obtinuit, nunc ultro oblatum in dolorem vertat? Dolor ille, fi quis fuit, intra paucas familias stetit: populo non nisi simulatus esse potuit. Tiberio vero cur generum eum præ aliis deligeret, ratio non defuit. Sic antea neptibus maritos, L. Cassium Callibus oppida-num, M. Vinicium plebeji generis virum, legerat. Ubi Status quam vocant ratio agitur, de dignitate domus prudentibus viris multum remittitur. Quæ ratio in eo versabatur, ne acui illustriori nuptæ, animo & opibus ad res novas stimularentur.
units.tr: This is from Tacitus' meaning, or from the opinion of the common people. The city was already bleak with so many mournings, and part of the grief was that Julia, daughter of Drusus and once wife of Nero, married into the house of Rubellius Blandus, whose grandfather Triburtes, a Roman knight, many people remembered. What was once a cause of joy has now become a cause of sorrow, as the highest mingle in marriage with the lowest. Does the people itself so despise itself that what ancient Rome with Genucius as its author scarcely obtained after so many struggles, it now turns into grief when it is offered freely? That grief, if there was any, stayed within a few families; among the people it could only have been feigned. Yet there was no lack of reason why Tiberius chose such a son-in-law over others. Thus earlier he had chosen husbands for his granddaughters: Lucius Cassius of Callibus, a townsman, and Marcus Vinicius, a man of plebeian stock. When what they call the reason of state is at work, prudent men concede a good deal of the dignity of the family. That reason lay in this: that more distinguished brides, with their spirit and wealth, should not be spurred on to revolution.

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Imago præfecturæ sapienti viro pro ludibrio.
units.tr: The image of a prefecture is a mockery for a wise man.

units.la: Sive enim dignitas est præfectura; in metuentium Munus & colentium veneratione consistit: five onus est; nulla non suscepti oneris laudatio: five emolumenti causa geritur; ridicula est, nullo fructu; fructus præscriptio. Ælius Lamius administranda Syria imagine tandem exolutus urbi præfuerat. Non quod imagina- riam Syriæ, sed quod veram urbis præfecturam gessit, autoritatem acquisivit. Verum huic nostræ assertioni obstrepit, quod non permissa provincia dignationem addiderat. Dignatio nimirum ex commiseratione, commiseratio populi & favor ex injuria oriebatur. Sic Labeoni, quod præturam intra stetit, commendatio ex injuria: Capitoni, quod consulatum adeptus est, odium ex invidia oriebatur. 3. Annal. Iterum nobis occurritur recitatis Cæsaris literis; & incusantibus, egregium quemque, & regendis exercitibus idoneum, abnuere id munus. Ut dem, multos tranquillitatem urbis oneri provinciali cum dignitate prætulisse: multum fi&i & simulati literas Tiberii prompsisse, Tacitus his verbis innuit; oblitus Arruntium, ne in Hispaniam pergeret, decimum jam annum attineri. Gratificari multis Tiberiis, rei gerendæ potestatem per-mittere paucis volebat.
units.tr: For if the prefecture is a dignity, it consists in the reverence and honour of those who fear and worship the holder. If it is a burden, every bearer of such a burden is praised. If it is undertaken for profit, it is ridiculous, since it yields no fruit, and the fruit is what is promised. Ælius Lamius, after being released from the administration of Syria in name only, at last governed the city. He won authority not because he held an imaginary governorship of Syria, but because he truly held the prefecture of the city. Yet this assertion of ours is challenged by the fact that the province, which was not entrusted to him, had nonetheless added to his dignity. Dignity, of course, arose from pity, and pity and popular favour arose from injustice. So Labeo's commendation arose from injustice, because he stopped short of the praetorship, while Capito's hatred arose from envy, because he obtained the consulship. (Tacitus, Annals 3.) Again we meet the letters of Caesar being read out, and many men, accusing each other, say that every outstanding man, fit for commanding armies, refuses that office. Granting this, that many men preferred the tranquillity of the city to a provincial office with its dignity, Tacitus hints at the fictitious and feigned letters of Tiberius that he produced: having forgotten that Arruntius was being kept, for now the tenth year, from going to Spain. Tiberius wished to oblige many men, and to grant the power of conducting affairs to only a few.

units.la: Qui secretarii regis Poloniæ, consiliarii regis Galliarum, Palatini Comitis Cæsareæ majestatis, episcopi Hierosolymorum, titulo fine re, superbiunt: quàm bene cum aphorismo nostro iis conveniat, pro sapien-tia sua viderint.
units.tr: Those who boast of the titles of secretary to the King of Poland, counsellor to the King of France, Count Palatine of Caesarean majesty, and Bishop of Jerusalem, while having the title without the reality: let them see for themselves how well this fits with our aphorism, according to their own wisdom.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Quæ tãta[?], admiratione homines in se convertunt.
units.tr: Those things which, by their wonder, draw men's attention to themselves.

units.la: Ut est inter pisces balæna, inter quadrupedes unicornis, inter aves Monocodiata, aut qui à Tacito hic recensetur Phœnix. Neque enim dentur ejusmodi animalia nécne, curatius explorare, politicæ disciplinæ est. Cornelii nos duētum secuti, avem hanc, raritate aut fabulæ audacia insignem, articulatè contempla-bimur.
units.tr: As the whale is among fishes, the unicorn among quadrupeds, the monocodiata among birds, or the phoenix which Tacitus here lists. For it is a matter for political learning to examine more carefully whether such animals exist or not. Following the guidance of the Cornelii, we shall examine this bird, remarkable for its rarity or for the boldness of its legend, point by point.

units.la: 1. A Loco Ægypto. Post longum seculorum am-bitum avis Phœnix in Ægyptum venit. Ægyptus est, quæ ut ingenia hominum varia ac mobilia, ita partus animalium portentosos gignit aut recipit. Hæc crocodilos, hæc hippopodamos, aquæ & terræ commora-tione ambiguos, hæc alia animantia, de quibus ad fa-stidium Diodorus Siculus; hæc cœli, terræ, aquarum miracula producit. Cœlum Ægypti ne in tenuem quidem pluviam, psecada[?] Græci appellant, nedum in largiorem imbrem, nisi prodigio, resolvitur. quod ac-cidisse prodigium, post debellatam cum Antonio Cleopatram, terra sub Romanorum jugum itura, Dio & ex eo Xiphilinus autores sunt aquâ fluminis annuo incremento terram oppressam irrigans, excipiendo frugum fœtui mollit. Sic ut Nilo exundante, & rur-sum se intra ripas colligente, nix ulla terra Ægypto ubertate contendat. hæc eadem Ægyptus phœnicem, si qua fides antiquis, orbi spectandum præbuit.
units.tr: 1. From its place, Egypt. After a long circuit of centuries the phoenix bird came into Egypt. Egypt is the land which, just as it produces men of varied and changeable wits, so it gives birth to or receives monstrous kinds of animals. This land produces crocodiles, hippopotami, creatures ambiguous between water and land, and other living things, about which Diodorus Siculus writes to the point of tedium; it produces wonders of sky, earth, and water. The sky of Egypt does not break into even a thin rain, which the Greeks call psecada, much less into heavier showers, except by a portent. That such a portent happened, after Cleopatra was defeated with Antony, when the land was about to come under the yoke of the Romans, Dio and Xiphilinus after him attest: the water of the river, irrigating the land weighed down by its yearly rising, softens it for receiving the fertility of the crops. So when the Nile overflows and then gathers itself again within its banks, no snow can compete with Egypt's fertility on earth. This same Egypt, if we may trust the ancients, offered the phoenix to the world to be seen.

units.la: 2. à SIDERE, Sole, cui consecratur. Sacrum Soli id animal. Ut inter metalla aurum, splendore cæteris præfulgens, ita inter aves quæ nitore ac raritate emi-net, soli sacratur.
units.tr: 2. From its star, the Sun, to which it is consecrated. The animal is sacred to the Sun. As among metals gold, shining above the rest in splendour, so among birds that which excels in brilliance and rarity is dedicated to the sun.

units.la: 3. à FORMÆ novitate. Areæ distinctu pinnarum à cateris avibus diversum. ita fere autor naturæ ordi-bem, & in eo contenta, dispositu; ut quæ pretio aut opere aut denique tempore rara sunt, etiam figuræ insolentia se commendarent.
units.tr: 3. From the novelty of its form. Different from other birds in the distinctive arrangement of its plumage's patches. So, in the same way, the author of nature arranged the order of the world, and in it the disposition of things, so that those things which are rare in price, or work, or indeed in time, commend themselves also by the unusualness of their shape.

units.la: 4. à TEMPORE, quingentis annis. Denumera annorum varia traduntur, maximè vulgatum, quin-gentorum spatium. alii excedendo, nongentos annos adjiciunt. Sive enim fabulosa est narratio: veritas tanto spatio deprehendi, mendacium redargui, ob ho-minum interitum, & annalium corruptionem, non potuit. Sive de veritate nihil dubitatur; miraculosa rerum momenta non crebro intervenire, naturæ con-sentaneum.
units.tr: 4. From its time, five hundred years. Various numbers of years are handed down; the most common is a span of five hundred years. Others, exceeding this, add nine hundred years. For whether the account is fabulous, the truth could not be ascertained over so long a span, nor the lie refuted, because of the death of men and the corruption of records. And if there is no doubt about the truth, it is consistent with nature that the miraculous moments of events do not occur frequently.

units.la: 5. à SEDE, Heliopoli, in civitatem, cui Heliopo-lis nomen, advolavisse. id vero mirum, avem soli sa-cratam, ad civitatem à sole nominatam potissimum se contulisse.
units.tr: 5. From its seat, Heliopolis. that it flew into the city whose name is Heliopolis. This indeed is remarkable: a bird consecrated to the sun chose above all to betake itself to a city named after the sun.

units.la: 6. à GREGE comitantium. multo caterarum volucrum comitatu, novam faciem mirantium. adeo, non homines tantum admiratio, & novitatis cognos-cendæ aviditas capit. etiam bruta animantia insolita alicujus rei facie, in admirationem rapta, perstrin-guntur.
units.tr: 6. From its flock of companions. with a great retinue of other birds, marvelling at the new sight. So much does wonder, and the eagerness to learn what is new, seize not only men. Even dumb animals, carried away into admiration by some unusual appearance, are struck with wonder.

units.la: 7. à NATIVITATE, Arabia. falsum hunc phœ-nicem, neque Arabum à terris credidere. Commoda gignendis aut fingendis insolitis animalium formis Arabia. Sive enim Felix Arabia: longiquitate loci Ro-manis & Græcis impenetrabilis: & felicitati conve-niens judicatur, cum auri & aromatum pretio, etiam avium pulcherrimam gignere. Sive deserta, aut pe-træa: illa ob siticulosum terræ incultæ squalorem; ista ob altiorem scopulorum asperitatem inaccessa, securitatem commorationi, aut figmento audaciam suggessit.
units.tr: 7. From its birthplace, Arabia. they did not believe this phoenix false, nor did they believe it came from Arabian lands. Arabia is a convenient place for begetting or inventing unusual forms of animals. For whether Arabia is Happy, being by the remoteness of its position impenetrable to Romans and Greeks, and being judged suited to its happiness since it produces, along with its gold and spices, the most beautiful birds as well; or whether it is desert or rocky: the former, because of the thirsty squalor of its uncultivated soil, the latter, because of the higher roughness of its cliffs, inaccessible, has offered security for dwelling, or boldness for a fiction.

units.la: 8. ab Obitu & regeneratione. Confectio quippe annorum numero, ubi mors propinquet, suis in terris struere nidum, eique vim genitalem affundere, ex qua foetum oriri, & primam adulto curam sepeliendi patris: neque id temere, sed sublato murrha pondere, tentatoque per longum iter, ubi par oneri, par meatui sit, subire patrium corpus, inque solis aram perferre, atque adolere. Miram avis unius [illegible, ~10 letters], & se-ipsam refoventis naturæ solertiam! Cujus ad secreta curiosos hominum oculos admissos, magis miran-dum. Sed hæc de obitu & ortu phœnicis fabulosis narrationibus aucta esse, ipse Cornelius agnoscit. Ita-que iis judicio recte æstimantium permissis, quod in-dagationis nostræ est, scrutabimur. Si sacrorum mysteriis applicare; pro-bro nobis non dabitur, imperio illuminando aliquid istinc pigmenti capere.
units.tr: 8. From its death and regeneration. For when the bird, worn out by the number of its years, senses death approaching, it builds a nest in its own land and breathes into it a generative power, from which the offspring arises, and the first care of the grown bird is to bury its father: and this is not done carelessly, but when the weight of myrrh has been lifted and the way has been tested over a long journey, so that it can bear the burden and sustain the journey, it carries the father's body and brings it to the altar of the sun and burns it. Wonderful the [illegible] of this one bird, and the skill of a nature that renews itself! Still more wonderful that curious human eyes have been admitted to its secrets. But Cornelius himself acknowledges that these accounts of the death and birth of the phoenix have been embellished by fabulous narratives. Therefore, leaving these matters to those who judge rightly, we shall examine what belongs to our inquiry. If we apply it to the mysteries of sacred things, we shall not be disgraced if we take from there some pigment for illuminating the empire.

units.la: Hieroglyphica interpretatione, quæ ab Ægyptio-rum more manavit, avem Ægyptiacam pro rege & re-gis imperio fumemus.
units.tr: By hieroglyphic interpretation, which arose from the custom of the Egyptians, we shall take the Egyptian bird as standing for the king and the king's rule.

units.la: 1. Regis & regni majestati Ægyptum, convenien-tissimum utrique locum, assignamus. Hæc ortum[?] regiæ potentiæ, hæc cultum insigniorem tribuit, De antiquitate regni Ægyptiaci multus est Diodorus Siculus: nec ei fides Græcis à scriptoribus derogatur. Consentientia Græcis Tacitus, 2. Annalium, com-memorat. Quanquam Scythas Ægyptiis controver-siam de antiquitate movisse, Pompeji Trogi com-pilator recenset. Sed multum gentis & regni ve-tustatem interesse, quis non videt? Dispersi enim primi mortales, dissipati, ac sine imperio vagi, aut ubi quis humanitatis cultus, patribus familias vici parebant. Moxin urbes & mœnia collecti, suum quæ-que civitas regem obsequio secuta est. Quod vel hi-storia Josuæ, angusto in terræ districtu triginta regum victoris, docebit. Ægyptus multis ante Josuæ ætatem sæculis uno sub rege collecta, exemplum gentibus quod sequerentur præbuit. Quanquam autem vena-tio populorum, & violentum imperium, primo Nimrodi[?] tribuitur; (Genef. 10) eique aliquot urbes, imperii sedes, assignantur: tamen primum in sacris Pharaonem regem, & regem quidem non injustum, nominari (Genef.12[?]) deprehendo.
units.tr: 1. We assign to the majesty of the king and kingdom Egypt, a place most suitable to both. It is this land that gave the origin of royal power and bestowed upon it a more distinguished honour. Diodorus Siculus says much about the antiquity of the Egyptian kingdom, nor is credit for him denied by Greek writers. Tacitus, in the second book of the Annals, mentions things agreeing with the Greeks. Although Pompeius Trogus's epitomiser records that the Scythians raised a dispute with the Egyptians about antiquity, who does not see how much the antiquity of a nation and kingdom matters? For the first mortals were scattered, dispersed, and wandered without rule, or, where some culture of humanity existed, villages obeyed their heads of families. Soon gathered into towns and walls, each city followed its own king in obedience. This the history of Joshua will teach, with the victory over thirty kings in the narrow district of the land. Egypt, gathered under one king many centuries before Joshua's time, offered an example for the nations to follow. Although the hunting of peoples and violent rule are attributed first to Nimrod (Gen. 10), and several cities, the seats of his rule, are assigned to him, yet I find that in Scripture the first king named is Pharaoh, and indeed a king not unjust (Gen. 12).

units.la: Quod ad cultum popularis obsequii, & regii fastidii eminentem majestatem, idem Genesios liber, Josephi in historia, ad animorum usque raptum, ideam depingit. Neque potuit Maro luculentius obsequii regii, quam ab Aegyptiis, monumentum petere.
units.tr: As to the worship of popular obedience and the eminent majesty of royal disdain, the same book of Genesis, and Josephus in his history, paint the image of it, even to the seizing of minds. Nor could Virgil seek a more splendid monument of royal obedience than that from the Egyptians.

units.la: Praeterea regem non sic Aegyptius, & ingens, Lydia, nec populi Parthorum[?], aut Medus Hydaspes Observant.
units.tr: Moreover, Egypt and mighty Lydia do not so observe the king, nor the peoples of the Parthians, nor the Median Hydaspes.

units.la: IV. Georg. v.211.
units.tr: Georg. IV, v. 211.

units.la: 2. SOL ut phoenix inter aves, ita rex & imperium inter mortales assimulari queat.
units.tr: 2. As the sun is to the phoenix among birds, so the king and empire may be likened among mortals.

units.la: Sol & coelestium corporum moderator & lunę subjectorum dicitur: ita rex celsa simul & submissa imperio unus regit.
units.tr: The sun is said to govern both the heavenly bodies and the moon, which is subject to it; so the king, exalted yet also humble, alone rules the empire.

units.la: Solis cursum bis in Aegypto mutatum, credula incolarum ejus loci antiquitas sibi persuasit. Bis regnum ibi immutatum, convenientius dicetur.
units.tr: Credulous antiquity of the inhabitants of that place persuaded itself that the course of the sun was changed twice in Egypt. It would be more fitting to say that the kingdom was changed twice there.

units.la: Solis deliquium homines formidant, quadrupedes expavescunt. Regii solii obortas tenebras propinquiores exhorrescunt, damnum remoti sentiunt.
units.tr: People fear an eclipse of the sun; quadrupeds dread it. The nearer subjects shudder at the darkness that gathers over the royal throne; those at a distance feel only the loss.

units.la: Sol quo non mole corporis, radiorum benigno sparsu penetrat. Rex quanquam palatio non discedens, curae solicitudine & ministerii vigilantia omnia obit.
units.tr: The sun penetrates with the kindly scattering of its rays, not by the bulk of its body. The king, though not leaving his palace, goes everywhere with the anxious care and watchful service of his ministry.

units.la: Solem gentes quàm plurimae adoraverunt: demissione animi & subjectione corporis adorant & reges. inde Americani populi juramentum fidelitatis regi & soli exigunt.
units.tr: Many peoples have worshipped the sun: they adore it with humbled spirits and bowed bodies, and kings too. Hence the American peoples demand an oath of loyalty to the king and to the sun.

units.la: Soli equos & currus antiquitus dicatos, & ei mili-tiam coeli subjectam, vanos apud autores legimus. Regem currus antiquo more, equi etiam recenti, arma denique & copiae, regni tutela, comitantur.
units.tr: We read in ancient authors of horses and chariots dedicated to the sun, and of the host of heaven made subject to it, but these are empty tales. Kings are attended by a chariot in the old fashion and by horses in the more recent one, and finally by arms and troops, the protection of the kingdom.

units.la: Solem miseria hominum affici, ideoque homine nondum labe peccati collapso, septuplo splendidiorem fuisse, sunt qui scripto consignaverunt. Regis est, civium miseriam suam ducere, & subditorum calamita- te tanquam sua affici. Prodigii loco scriptores recen- fent, quod Stephano Bathore Poloniæ rege Mofcoviæ regionem raptante, urente, vastante; Joannes Basi- lius Mofcoviæ moderator nuptiis & epulis folennibus vacavit. Et Neronem, urbe Roma incendio depasta, cantilavisse, populus Romanus indignabatur.
units.tr: Some have put it in writing that the sun is affected by the misery of men, and that before man had fallen into the stain of sin, the sun was seven times more splendid. It is the king's part to regard the misery of his citizens as his own and to be affected by the calamities of his subjects as if they were his own. Writers count it as a portent that when Stephen Báthory, king of Poland, was plundering, burning and laying waste the region of Muscovy, John Basil, ruler of Muscovy, devoted himself to weddings and solemn feasts. And the Roman people were indignant that Nero sang to the lyre while Rome was consumed by fire.

units.la: Soles multiplicati (quod nisi per phasma fieri non potest) divisionem imperii, aut gravem populi opprefi- onem, portendere creduntur. Reges in uno regno multiplicati, damni instantis nullo dubio, interpreta- tionem non defiderant.
units.tr: Multiple suns (which cannot come about except by an apparition) are believed to portend the division of an empire or a grievous oppression of the people. Kings multiplied within one kingdom need no interpretation, since the coming harm is beyond doubt.

units.la: Denique Solis præfentia hilaritatem, lucem, fœcun- ditatem ingerit; absentia moestitiam, caliginem, fte- rilitatem inducit. Ita regum præfentiâ labentes regni partes refoventur; absentia, aut, quæ est loco abfen- tiæ, imperandi inscitia, tristi casu aut mœrore membra imperii involvit.
units.tr: Finally, the presence of the sun brings cheerfulness, light and fertility; its absence brings sadness, darkness and barrenness. Thus the failing parts of a kingdom are revived by the presence of the king; his absence, or what amounts to absence, namely incompetence in ruling, involves the members of the empire in sad misfortune and grief.

units.la: 3. Regem imperii insignia, ut phœnicem diftin- &tus pinnarum, à cæteris mortalibus externa rerum facie distinguunt. Sæpè & forma corporis, vultus majestate verendus, incessus & statura corporis ere- &tior, præcellentiorem facit. Unde Græcorum adagi- um, ἐσθλὸν ἀξίαν τυραννίδος, forma imperio gerenda digna.
units.tr: 3. Kings are distinguished from other mortals by the insignia of empire, as the phoenix is set apart by the distinctness of its feathers, and by the outward appearance of things. Often the very form of the body, a face venerable in its majesty, a bearing and a stature more lofty, makes a man more eminent. Hence the Greek proverb: "a fine form is worthy of the rule of a tyrant" [ἐσθλὸν ἀξίαν τυραννίδος], meaning that beauty of form is fitting for one who is to wield power.

units.la: 4. Quingentis annis, fatali imperiorum periodo, insignes mutationes accidere, politicorum coryphæis perfuafiffimum est, quam sententiam in Arcanis Re- gnorum uberiùs examinavi.
units.tr: 4. That remarkable changes happen in the five-hundredth year, the fated cycle of empires, is most firmly held by the leaders of the political writers; I have examined this opinion more fully in the Secrets of Kingdoms.

units.la: 5. Certam regi imperii sedem, nec eam fortuitò oblatam, nec temerè mutandam, convenire, iisdem in arcanis docui.
units.tr: 5. I have shown in the same secrets that a king ought to have a fixed seat of empire, one that is neither chance-given nor rashly changed.

units.la: 6. Regem multitudo sequentium, & imperium admiratione virtutis ac majestatis accipientium, exor- nat. Admirationem inter subjectionis voluntariæ causas esse, & scriptor Apocalypfeos Johannes agno- vit. καὶ ἐθαύμασεν ὅλη ἡ γῆ ὀπίσω τοῦ θηρίου. totus orbis admirabundus feram sequebatur. cap.13.v.3.
units.tr: 6. The multitude of followers adorns a king, and empires receive him with admiration of his virtue and majesty. That admiration is among the causes of voluntary subjection is recognised even by John, the writer of the Apocalypse: "And the whole earth wondered after the beast" [καὶ ἐθαύμασεν ὅλη ἡ γῆ ὀπίσω τοῦ θηρίου]; the whole world, full of wonder, followed the beast. Rev. 13.3.

units.la: 7. Arabiam regum veneratione, opulentia, justitia admiadministratione conspiciendam fuisse, passim Romani & Græci autores. Nec tacet de regina Arabiæ sacer codex, 1.Reg.10.
units.tr: 7. That Arabia was to be conspicuous for the reverence paid to its kings, for their wealth and for justice in their administration, Roman and Greek authors say everywhere. Nor does the sacred book pass over the queen of Arabia, 1 Kings 10.

units.la: 8. Solium regni successione, obitum paternum non sentiente, fere reficitur. Diversos & eosdem quodam-modo imperatores, maxime ubi paternis institutis vestigio insistunt, vita humana agnoscit. Quin & alicubi terrarum (si vera de Catajæ regno spargun-tur) dissimulato regis defuncti obitu, & proximo semper sine strepitu à paucis familiarium suffecto, reges immortales creduntur.
units.tr: 8. The throne is almost restored by succession, when the death of the father is not felt. Human life knows different rulers who in a certain sense are the same, especially where they follow their fathers' institutions step by step. Indeed, in some parts of the world (if what is spread about the kingdom of Cathay is true), the death of the king is concealed, and a successor, always the nearest of the household, is set up quietly by a few, and the kings are believed to be immortal.

units.la: Hæc fabulosis, vel fabulosè auctis, narrationibus decerpta, illustrandum ad regnum accommodare volui. Quæ si cui præter mentem autoris torta videantur, dum fabulosè doceant, nihil honestis moribus allusione decedet.
units.tr: I have wished to draw these things from fabulous, or fabulously embellished, stories and apply them to the illustration of kingship. If anyone thinks them twisted beyond the author's intention, since they teach through fable, nothing of honest morals is lost by the allusion.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Αὐτοχειρία [?] Tiberiano ævo nimium frequentatæ.
units.tr: Suicide [αὐτοχειρία] far too frequent in the age of Tiberius.

units.la: Non modo ab iis, qui immiti principe inter reos recepti, veniæ impetrationem desperabant: verùm quos tædium suspensæ vitæ, & metus aliquando sæviturì domini, premebat. Causa, præter honesti exitus opi-nionem, facilior venis abruptis vitæ exitus, nam promp-tæ ejusmodi mortes, metus carnificis faciebant [?], plus enim terroris instrumenta mortis coràm vîsa, & vultus carnificis, idque publico in urbis aut sub urbani loco, incutiunt. Oculi enim omnium primi vincuntur. Altera causa à legum erga eos favore. quia damnati, publicatis bonis, sepultura prohibebantur: eorum qui de se statuebant, humabantur corpora, manebant testamenta, pretium festinandi. Non quod seipsos absol-vendo præmium hoc mererentur, sed quia non da-mnatorum nulla pœna judicabatur. Quadruplatorum tamen præmia, ex accusati bonis, manebant. ut supra demonstratum.
units.tr: This was not only among those who, received as accused persons under a savage prince, despaired of obtaining pardon, but also among those whom the weariness of a suspended life and the fear that their master would one day rage against them oppressed. The cause, besides the opinion that it was an honourable exit, was that the exit from life through severed veins was easier; for such deaths, being quick, made the executioner's fear less, since the instruments of death and the executioner's face, seen in front of them, and that in a public place in the city or in a place outside the city, strike more terror. For the eyes of all are overcome first. The second cause was the favour of the laws towards such men: because the condemned, with their goods confiscated, were forbidden burial; the bodies of those who decided on their own death were buried, their wills remained valid, a reward for haste. Not that by acquitting themselves they earned this reward, but because no punishment was adjudged against those not condemned. Nevertheless the rewards of the informers remained, drawn from the goods of the accused, as demonstrated above.

units.la: XXIV.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: Aperte vel irasci, quàm occulte odi[?] fe, virilius habetur.
units.tr: It is considered more manly to be openly angry than secretly to hate.

units.la: Hoc enim animi vel metuentis, vel subdolè occa-sionem nocendi exspectantis; illud nihil timentis est. Quo rationis fundo Tiberius missis ad senatum lite-ris, disserit, morem fuisse majoribus, quoties dirimerent amicitias, interdicere domo, eumque finem gratiæ po-nere. Plura vide ad 2. librum Annalium, ad eum lo-cum, componit epistolas, quis amicitiam et renuncia-bat.
units.tr: For the one belongs to a man who is fearful, or who subtly waits for an occasion to harm, while the other belongs to a man who fears nothing. On this ground Tiberius, in a letter sent to the senate, argues that it was the custom of our ancestors, whenever they broke off friendships, to forbid entry to the house and to set an end to favour. See more on the second book of the Annals, at the passage he composed letters, by which he renounced friendship.

units.la: Sed hic cautiones quædam, ne simplicis præcepti loco aphorismus accipiatur, observandæ sunt. 1. non omnem majorum consuetudinem esse pro regula ha-bendam. Multa duritie veterum meliùs & lætiùs mu-tata, Messalinus 3. Annalium disserit. 2. Multò tamen minùs probandum esse morem hujus ævi, quo ob ver-bi aliquam contumeliam amicitia abrumpitur, ferro stricto concurritur, perinde ac si oraculi vicem habe-ret illud à barbaro rege pronunciatum: contatio fer-vilis, statim exequi, regium videtur. 3. Ubi gravis a-micitiæ solvendæ causa apparet, intermissione potiùs usus levandam, quàm subita animi alieni denunciatio-ne abrumpendam. dissuendam potiùs, quàm diffe-candam: ut prisca circa hanc rem locutione utar.
units.tr: But certain cautions must be observed here, lest what is a simple precept be taken as an aphorism. 1. The custom of our ancestors is not to be held as a universal rule in every case. Messalinus, in the third book of the Annals, argues that many things were changed for the better and more pleasantly from the old harshness. 2. Yet much less is the custom of this age to be approved, by which friendship is broken off over some verbal insult, and men run at each other with drawn sword, as if a word pronounced by a barbarian king had the force of an oracle: to obey a servile order at once seems kingly. 3. Where there appears a serious cause for dissolving a friendship, it should be eased by letting it lapse gradually rather than broken off by a sudden declaration of hostility to another's face: it should be unstitched rather than torn, to use an old expression about this matter.

units.la: 4. Operam dandam, ne interdictus amicitiæ usus, & finis gratiæ positus, in hostilitatem, in inimicitias ex amicitia transeat. Id enim cùm turpe est, tum ob se-creta olim communicata periculosum. 5. Id tamen eam domus prohibitionem præ se ferre non enim tan-tùm gratiæ antiquæ modus ponitur; sed irruptura ódio januæ aperitur. 6. Similem familiaritatis re-ciationem potentioribus magis in tenuiores, quàm paribus in pares, aut quod ineptius, tenuioribus in va-lidiores convenire. 7. Ipsis magnatibus laudi dari, si aut non sentiant conceptam animo injuriam, aut u-rentem dissimulatione concoquant. Singulare est, quod de Julio Cæsare Dio scribit, injurias cum nunquam ultum fuisse, ac ne indoluisse quidem. id tan-tum in ultione necessaria spectasse, ne ipsi ad honores contendenti in posterum remora poneretur.
units.tr: 4. Care must be taken that a forbidden use of friendship, and an end set to favour, do not pass from friendship into hostility and enmity. For this is both shameful and, because secrets once shared may be used, dangerous. 5. Yet the closing of the house does not by itself display that such enmity exists; for it is not merely the limit of former favour that is set, but the door is opened to hatred about to break in. 6. A similar withdrawal of familiarity fits the more powerful against the humbler better than equals against equals, or, what is more absurd, the humbler against the more powerful. 7. Praise is given to the great themselves if they either do not feel the wrong conceived in their mind, or digest a burning one by dissembling. Dio writes something singular of Julius Caesar: that he never took revenge for injuries, nor even grieved over them; he looked only to what was necessary in vengeance, that a hindrance should not be placed in his own path as he sought honours in the future.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Magis hominum quàm morum in aula Tiberiana fit mutatio.
units.tr: There is more change of men than of morals in the court of Tiberius.

units.la: Aliquo ob avaritiam[?], superbiam, crudelitatem se-moto; qui succedit, etsi meliorem de se spem diffun-dit, occulte eadem exprometur. Mamercum Scaurum, judicio postulatum, non quidem amicitia Sejani, sed labefecit haud minus validum ad exitia Macronis odium, quia easdem artes occultius exercebat. Factioni minus & ambitus decurrui Macro studebat, recenti Sejani casu deterritus. animi tamen continentiam, & erga omnes aequitatem, fronte magis quam animo gerebat.
units.tr: When someone is removed on account of avarice, pride or cruelty, the successor, although he spreads a better hope of himself, secretly practises the same things. Mamercus Scaurus, brought to trial, was undone not by the friendship of Sejanus but no less by the hatred of Macro, which was strong enough for destruction, because Macro practised the same arts more covertly. Macro, deterred by the recent fall of Sejanus, was eager to avoid faction and ambition, yet he showed restraint of mind and fairness towards all more in his face than in his heart.

units.la: Principis igitur est, chamaeleontes aulicos non vultus demissione, non uno aut altero facto spectare, sed interiora animi penitius explorare. Quod si prima conjectura difficile est, tempore & mora, non sic diu claudente simulatione, fit facillimum. Inferioris autem conditionis homines, quibus cum aulico negotium, non statim ob semotionem prioris, exactione aut formidine ingerenda acerbi, laetitia exultantes gestiant; sed in speculam, & in custodiam sui intenti, magis homines quam vitam aulae immutatam suspicentur. Verum Macronem, & quas exitii aliis parandi artes exercuerit, spectemus. detuleratque argumentum tragoediâ a Scauro scriptâ, additis versibus qui in Tiberium flecterentur. ingenii luxuriantis lusus pro crimine, ubi nihil in vita criminis, torquentur. nec quicquam fere tam caute scribi potest, raptu praeser-tim poeticae altitudinis se effundente, quod non in aliquem culpa pollutum deflecti queat. Quod enim de Atreo aut Thyeste, quod de Medaea a poëta dictum; ob morum similitudinem in Tiberium commodabitur. O foecunda sycophantarum ingenia, & ad nocen-dum tantum erudita! Quibus nunquam immotuisse, quam necessitudine amicitiæ illigatum esse, ad vitæ securitatem est munitus. Multi enim ab amicis, aut amicitiam simulantibus, circumventi, gratia principis & dignitate exciderunt. Inter eos Cornelius Gallus, poëta non incelebris, quem Augustus Ægypto præfecerat, recensatur. Hic à Valerio Largo, secretorum & mensæ ob amicitiæ fiduciam participe, provinciæ superbè administratæ accusatus, dignitatem & vitæ solatium amisit. quam vitæ mutationem non ferens, manu sua ictus, miserandā morte concidit. Et Largus quidem rector pro Gallo Ægypti fuit, delationis procemio superbus. Hominum tamen in se audacia odia, & scommota violatæ amicitiæ, non effugit. Huic obviam factus Proculius, nares & os manu compressit: ne respirare quidem Largo præsente tutum esse, significans. Alius Largum accedens, Notúsne ci esset, percontatus: negante Largo, in tabulas adductis testibus, assignavit, quasi scilicet unus securitatis modus esset, sycophantis non innotescere, quæ apud Dionem libro 53 legas.
units.tr: It is therefore the mark of a prince to watch courtier chameleons not by the lowering of their countenance or by one deed or another, but to examine the inner depths of the mind more closely. If this is difficult at first conjecture, it becomes very easy with time and delay, since simulation does not keep its lid on for long. Men of inferior rank, however, who have business with a courtier, do not at once rejoice and exult because the previous man has been removed, expecting bitter exactions or fear to be inflicted on them. Instead, intent on watching and guarding themselves, they suspect that the men have changed rather than the life of the court. But let us look at Macro and the arts of destruction he practised on others. He brought forward a subject from a tragedy written by Scaurus, adding verses that could be bent against Tiberius. The playful excesses of a luxuriant talent were made into a crime, where nothing in his life was criminal, and they were tortured. Almost nothing can be written so cautiously, especially when poetic sublimity pours itself out in rapture, that it cannot be twisted to stain someone with blame. For what the poet said of Atreus or Thyestes, or of Medea, will be applied to Tiberius because of the similarity of character. O fruitful wits of sycophants, trained only for harm! For the security of life it is a better fortification never to have stirred them up than to have been bound to them by the ties of friendship. Many, surrounded by friends or by men feigning friendship, have fallen from the prince's favour and dignity. Among them is counted Cornelius Gallus, a poet not unknown, whom Augustus had set over Egypt. Accused by Valerius Largus, a sharer in his secrets and table through the confidence of friendship, of administering his province arrogantly, he lost his dignity and the consolation of life. Unable to bear this change of fortune, he struck himself with his own hand and died a pitiable death. Largus indeed became ruler of Egypt in place of Gallus, proud of his opening of the accusation. Yet he did not escape the boldness of men, nor the hatreds aimed at himself, nor the resentments stirred by violated friendship. Proculeius, meeting him, pressed his hand over Largus's nostrils and mouth, signifying that it was not even safe to breathe in Largus's presence. Another man, approaching Largus, asked whether he was known to him; when Largus denied it, the man produced witnesses in the records, as though the only way to safety were for sycophants not to become known. You may read this in Dio, book 53.

units.la: Ne tamen perpetuum sibi in gratia principis munimentum delatores promittant: audiant verba sententia. Ac tamen accusatores, si facultas incideret, pœnis afficiebantur. Non animus puniendi Tiberio, quorum malitia ad sævitiam abutebatur, deerat; sed facultas expectabatur. Alii ob remissionem, & antiqui rigoris teporem, ad pœnam trahuntur. Ut Ser-vilius Cornelius[?]que, perdito Scauro famosi, quia pecuniam & Vario Ligure omittenda delationis ceperant, in insulas, interdicto igni atque aqua, dimoti sunt, alii contra, nihil remissi aut languidi agentes, ob canini officii sedulitatem puniuntur. Abudius Rufo functus adilitate, dum Lentulo Getulico, sub quo legioni præfuerat, periculum facessit, quod in Sejani filium generum destinaverat, ultro damnatur, atque urbe exigitur. Adeò vitia etiam iis, qui ad præsidium iis uœuntur, exosa: ubi deposita utilitatis opinione, vero pretio æstimantur, pro gratia odium mercentur. Fidei enim violatæ [?]{lætæ} indicium fuit, benefactorem à necessario, ducem à legato suo, arrepta accusatione violari.
units.tr: Yet lest informers promise themselves a perpetual protection in the prince's favour, let them hear the words of a sentence: accusers too were punished whenever the opportunity arose. Tiberius lacked no will to punish those whose malice he abused for his cruelty; he was waiting for an opportunity. Others were dragged to punishment for remissness and for the lukewarmness of the old rigour. Thus Servilius Cornelius(?) and others, who after Scaurus had been destroyed were branded as infamous because they had taken money from Varius Ligur to drop the accusation, were banished to islands, forbidden fire and water. Others, on the contrary, who acted with no slackness or languor, were punished for the zeal of their dog-like service. Abudius Rufo, having held the aedileship, was condemned of his own accord and driven from the city, because while he was bringing danger upon Lentulus Getulicus, under whom he had commanded a legion, he had himself destined Getulicus for a son-in-law to Sejanus's son. So hateful are vices even to those who are sought out for protection: when the opinion of usefulness is laid aside, men are valued at their true price, and they earn hatred in place of favour. For it was a sign of violated faith that a benefactor should be attacked by one bound to him, and a leader by his own legate, the accusation having been seized upon.

units.la: XXVI. In extremis audacia pro munimento.
units.tr: XXVI. Boldness in extremity as a defence.

units.la: Mortem omnibus ex natura æqualem, oblivione apud posteros vel gloria distinguì. Ac si nocentem innocentemque idem exitus maneat, acrioris viri esse, merito perire: primo libro Historiarum Otho ad militem perorat. Atque hic quidem ficto propter Pisonem metu, ad arma sine cunctatione prorumpit. Lentulus Getulicus in vero meru positus, verborum prius quàm ferri audaciam expromit. Unus omnium Sejani affinium incolumis, non casui salutem, non principis oblivioni, sed animo audenter postulanti, debuit. Ausus ad Cæsarem mittere literas: Affinitatem sibi cum Sejano haud sponte, sed consilio Tiberii captam: perinde se quàm Tiberium falli potuisse. neque errorem eundem illi sine fraude; alius exitio habendum. sibi fidem integram, & si nullius insidiis peteretur, mansuram: successorem non aliter quàm indicium mortis accepturum. firmarent velut fœdus, quo princeps taterarum rerum potiretur, ipse provinciam retineret.
units.tr: Death comes equally to all by nature; what distinguishes men is oblivion or glory among posterity. And if the guilty and the innocent meet the same end, it is the mark of the braver man to die deservedly. In the first book of his Histories, Otho harangues the soldiers. Otho, moved by a feigned fear of Piso, rushes to arms without hesitation. Lentulus Getulicus, placed in real danger, first puts his boldness into words before he draws the sword. Alone of all Sejanus' relatives he remained unharmed, owing his safety not to chance or to the prince's forgetfulness, but to his bold manner of pleading. He dared to send a letter to Caesar: that his kinship with Sejanus had been entered into not willingly but by the design of Tiberius; he could have been deceived just as Tiberius was; nor was the same mistake without guilt for him, but for another it should be counted as a matter of destruction. For himself, his loyalty would remain intact, and would do so even if no one plotted against him; his successor would receive it as nothing other than a sign of death. Let them confirm, as it were a covenant, that the prince should hold the supreme power while he himself kept his province.

units.la: Hæc aut Getulicum scribere ausum, aut Tiberium concoquere potuisse, quem levicula etiam offendebant, mirum alicui videri queat. Sed præter ultimæ necessitatis in Getulico stimulum, amborum vitæ & favoris comparatio, ambigendi graviorem causam exemerit. Getulicus ea tempestate superioris Germaniæ legiones curabat. Tiberius curva senecta languidus, Caprearum fœdis in latebris, inter pueros adnatantes, delitescebat. Getulicus mirum amorem affectus erat, effusa clementia, modicum severitate. Tiberius nimia severitate, & majestatis lege crudeliter exercita, odium omnium ordinum meruerat. Getulicus proximo quoque exercitui per L. Apronium socerum non ingratus, trahere Germanicum exercitum, rapere Gallias ad prædam urbis poterat. Tiberio, in oblivionem militum aut odium adducto, longè imperatorium nomen, longè principatus inanis gloria fuit: [?] sed quod nec ipsum quidem latebat: reputantem a-nimo, publicum sibi odium extremum ætatem, magis-que fama, quàm vi, stare res suas.
units.tr: That Getulicus dared to write this, or that Tiberius could digest it, might seem strange to someone who knew how even trivial things offended him. But besides the goad of extreme necessity in Getulicus, a comparison of the lives and favour of the two men removed a graver cause for doubt. Getulicus at that time had charge of the legions of Upper Germany. Tiberius, weak with a bowed old age, lay hidden in the foul recesses of Capri, swimming among boys. Getulicus was greatly loved, with a lavish mercy and moderate severity. Tiberius, through excessive severity and the law of majesty cruelly applied, had earned the hatred of every order. Getulicus, through his father-in-law Lucius Apronius, was not unpopular with the nearest army too, and he could draw the German army across and seize the Gauls for the plunder of the city. For Tiberius, with the soldiers' goodwill fallen into oblivion or hatred, the imperial title was far off, and the empty glory of the principate was far off too. But this he did not even hide from himself, reflecting in his mind that public hatred stood against his last years, and that his affairs rested more on reputation than on force.

units.la: Qui ad reip. clavum rerum mortalium arbitri fe-dent, ac multò etiam magis qui infra clavum cursi-tant, Tiberii submissione, & imbecillitatis agnitione, monendi erant, ne omnia ad vivum resecando, se & rempublicam in discrimen conjiciant: nisi res ea longiùs à scopo me abducturà erat. Multi dum leviùs in-juriæ gravem opinionem persequuntur, in certiorem calamitatem, damnosiùs opprobrium tractantes, in-cidunt. Quàm qui sapienter agunt, sensu contumeliæ dissimulato, avertunt.
units.tr: Those who sit at the helm of the commonwealth as arbiters of mortal affairs, and even more those who scurry about below the helm, ought to be warned, by Tiberius's submission and by the recognition of his weakness, not to cut everything down to the quick and so put themselves and the commonwealth in peril. But that would lead me too far from my aim. Many, while they pursue a heavier resentment for a slighter injury, fall into a surer calamity, handling the disgrace to their own loss. Those who act wisely dissemble the sense of insult and turn it aside.

units.la: XXVII. Autoritas armis illatis efficacior.
units.tr: XXVII. Authority established by arms is more effective.

units.la: Sed cùm diversis è causis, diversorum animis au-toritas illabatur: non apud omnes vim eandem sempet obtinet. In rebus belli nulla major quàm ex victoriâ autoritas: cognita Gallorum infirmitate, quantum jam apud eos, hostes uno proelio auctoritatis effent consecuti. inquit iv. de Bello Gallico Cæsar. & apud eundem eodem libro de populo Romano Ubi: tantum esse nomen apud eos (extremòs Germanorum) atque opinionem exercitus Romani, Ariovisto pulso, & hoc novissimo proelio facto, etiam ad ultimas Germanorum nationes, uti opinione & amicitia populi Rom. tuti esse possint. quod nostrum, de auctoritatis efficacia, aphorismum mirum in modum confirmat. Autoritate & terrore nominis una hora nonnunquam efficitur; quod armis circumferendis toto vix anno obtineas. Porcius Cato, cum omnium Hispaniæ civitatum mœnia dejici, ut faciliores imperio accipiendo effent, cu-peret: brevi literarum significatione, quod alii ab ar-mis ægrè impetraffent, impetravit. Uniuscujusque civitatis binis obsidibus, domum remissis, singulas li-teras ad suos perferendas dedit. iis præcepit, ut omnes eodem die eas aperitas recitarent. Literarum summa haec erat: Diruite muros hodierno die. Cum igitur singulae civitates spatium deliberandi, & ad finitimas communicandi causa mittendi non haberent; cumq; singulae metuerent, ne caeteris morem gerentibus, si ipsae solae dicto audientes non essent, ut mancipia co-rona venderentur, imperata fecerunt. Atque ita omnes pariter Hispani uno die moenia ipsi sua destru-xerunt.
units.tr: But since authority glides into the minds of different men from different causes, it does not always hold the same force among everyone. In matters of war no authority is greater than that which comes from victory: having learned the weakness of the Gauls, how much authority the enemy had won among them by a single battle, says Caesar in the fourth book of the Gallic War. And in the same book, speaking of the Roman people: the name and reputation of the Roman army, with Ariovistus driven out and this last battle fought, was so great among the furthest Germans that even the remotest nations of the Germans could be safe through the reputation and friendship of the Roman people. This wonderfully confirms our maxim on the efficacy of authority. By authority and the terror of a name, something is sometimes accomplished in one hour which you could hardly obtain in a whole year by carrying arms about. Porcius Cato, wanting the walls of all the cities of Spain pulled down so that they might be more easily brought under the empire, by a brief written message obtained what others had with difficulty obtained by arms. He sent home two hostages from each city and gave them each a single letter to carry to their own people, instructing them that all should open and read their letters on the same day. The sum of the letter was: "Pull down your walls today." Since individual cities had no time to deliberate, nor to send to their neighbours to consult, and since each feared that if the others complied and it alone did not obey, it would be sold at auction like slaves, they did as they were commanded. And so all the Spaniards alike, on one day, destroyed their own walls with their own hands.

units.la: Quanquam est hic aliquid & stratagematis, non modo autoritatis Catonianae: iccirco & a Polyaeno, unde historiam hausimus, inter stratagemata libro octavo referitur. Hinc non inepte a Scipione Amirato dictum: Unam lanciam existimationis, plus aliquando valere, quam centum auri libras. Quod tamen in ipso conflictu, & in acie, nisi existimationi nominis vires respondeant, parum valebit. Nos hoc praeambulo in antecessum praemisso, quid ad sententiam hanc stabiliendam Tacitus momenti afferat, confide-remus. Vehementer pertinere ad bella adminiftran-da, quid hostes, quid socii de imperatoribus existi-ment: recte ab oratore Romano pronunciatum est. Ipsa enim potentis populi, aut boni ducis fama plerunque bella profligantur, exteri reges in officio con-tinentur. Artabanus summus Parthorum arbiter, metu Germanici fidus Romanis, aquabilis in suos. tan-tam vim esse existimationis, tantam verendi nominis lucem, ut non modo arma hostilia dissipet, verum & alienigenis, & externi imperii populis lucem salutis adferat! detracta autem magnae virtutis, potentiae, felicitatis opinione tenebris lucem, pacem bello per-misceat! mox superbiam in nos, saevitiam in populares sumpsit. unde ea rerum, unde animorum mutatio? non tantum a prospero rerum flatu, qui plerunque leviores animos extollit. fretus bellis, quae secunda ad-versum circumjectas nationes exercuerat. sed etiam a gravioris aetatis in imperatore Romano despectu. senectutem Tiberii ut inermem despiciens. Vergentes vitae annos auctoritati imperantis detrahere, quia in Arcanis regnorum docui, fastidio repetitione futurâ non repono. Id modò pro re præfenti moneo, in Ti- berio cur contemneretur, tantum causæ non fuisse. Pleraque in summa fortuna auspiciis & consiliis, quam telis & manibus geri: sapientibus viris persuasum est. Alieno enim ductu, suis auspiciis bella imperatorem gerere, nec novum, nec summæ fortunæ inconveniens est. Cui igitur imperatori cruda senectus, mens vivi-da, constans imperii ratio: eum cur ob ætatem ingra-vescentem spernas, rationis nihil est.
units.tr: Yet there is something of a stratagem here too, and not only of Cato's authority; for that reason Polyaenus, from whom we drew the story, also records it among the stratagems in book eight. Hence Scipio Amiratus said, not unfittingly: a single lance of reputation is sometimes worth more than a hundred pounds of gold. Yet in the actual clash and in the battle line this will count for little, unless the strength answers to the reputation of the name. Having set down this preface in advance, let us consider what weight Tacitus brings to establishing this opinion. A Roman orator rightly pronounced that what enemies and allies think of their commanders greatly matters to the conduct of wars. For the very reputation of a powerful people or of a good leader often brings wars to an end, and foreign kings are kept in their duty. Artabanus, the chief arbiter of the Parthians, was faithful to the Romans through fear of Germanicus and even-tempered towards his own people. Such great power has reputation, such a light of a revered name, that it not only scatters hostile arms but also brings the light of safety to foreigners and to peoples of an alien empire; but when the opinion of great virtue, power and good fortune is removed, it mingles darkness with light and war with peace! Soon he assumed arrogance towards us and cruelty towards his own subjects. Whence this change of affairs, whence this change of minds? Not only from the prosperous breath of fortune, which commonly lifts up lighter minds, relying on the wars which had gone well for him against the surrounding nations, but also from contempt for the older age of the Roman emperor, regarding Tiberius's old age as defenceless. That the declining years of his life detract from the authority of a ruler I have taught in my Secrets of Kingdoms, and out of distaste for repetition I do not restate it here. This only I note as bearing on the present matter: there was not so much cause for Tiberius to be despised. It is the settled view of wise men that most things in high fortune are done by auspices and counsels rather than by weapons and hands. For a commander to wage wars under another's leadership but by his own auspices is neither new nor unfitting for one of high fortune. Therefore, for whatever commander has a vigorous old age, a lively mind and a steady plan of rule, there is no reason to despise him because his years are advancing.

units.la: Triplici via autoritatem comparari: Forma impe-rii, Potentia, Moribus imperantis: à magnis indoctri-na civili viris præceptum est. In forma imperii tria re-quirunt: Severitatem, Constantiam, Adstrictionem. Potentiam quinque instrumentis dari afferunt: Opibus, Armis, Consiliis, Fœderibus, Fortuna. Mores in imperante duplices confiderant: Internos & Exter-nos. In illis Pietatem & Providentiam eminere volunt: in his Gestum oris ad Gravitatem, flexum ponunt. Quæ etiam omnia ad hostem in officio continendum non requiruntur; ad civem tranquille gubernandum spectantia: tamen Tiberio non defuisse, fa-cilè monstravero.
units.tr: Authority is gained in three ways: from the form of the empire, from power, and from the character of the ruler. This has been taught by great men learned in civil affairs. For the form of the empire they require three things: severity, constancy and tightness of rule. They say power is given by five instruments: wealth, arms, counsels, alliances and fortune.
