They distinguish two kinds of character in the ruler, internal and external. In the former they want piety and foresight to stand out; in the latter they place a bearing of the face and manner that tends towards gravity. All these things are not required for keeping an enemy in duty; they pertain to governing citizens in tranquillity. Yet I will easily show that none of them was lacking in Tiberius.

units.la: Severitatem in Tiberio adeò scriptores non deside-rant, ut sævitiam potiùs incusent. Quæ sævitia in la-fciviente opibus & luxu populo, nec non ad res novas ere&o, propemodum necessaria fuit. Potuitque non minus Tiberius, quam Cotys rex Thracum, increpan-ti furorem sæviendi respondere: ἀλλ' ἡ ἐμὴ μανία [?] τοὺς ἀρχομένους σώφρονας ποιεῖ [?]: At meus hic furor subditos sapere docet. Nihilominus, ne nimius rigor in nervum erumperet, clementiam aliquando & veniæ indulgentiam miscuit.
units.tr: Writers do not so much miss severity in Tiberius that they rather accuse him of cruelty. This cruelty, in a people wanton with wealth and luxury, and roused to revolution, was almost necessary. And Tiberius could no less than Cotys, king of the Thracians, have answered the man who rebuked his rage for cruelty: "ἀλλ' ἡ ἐμὴ μανία τοὺς ἀρχομένους σώφρονας ποιεῖ" [ἀλλ' ἡ ἐμὴ μανία τοὺς ἀρχομένους σώφρονας ποιεῖ]: "But my madness makes my subjects sensible." Nevertheless, lest excessive rigour break out into open harshness, he sometimes mingled clemency and the indulgence of pardon.

units.la: Quod ad Constantiam: non modò minimis quoque in rebus, ut loquitur Valerius, omnia antiquæ consuetudinis momenta servavit; aut callida interpretatione novitatem antiqui ritus formula incrusta-vit: verùm etiam ad decretis suis, à vitæ & imperandi consuetudine non temerè recessit. Prioris viæ ratio illi fuerit, quod sub Nerone postea pronunciatum: super omnibus negotiis melius atque restius olim provisum: & quae convertuntur, in deterius mutari. Posterioris: non convalescere plantam, quae saepius transfertur. quod a magno doctore Seneca prolatum.
units.tr: As to constancy: he not only, as Valerius says, kept all the weight of ancient custom even in the smallest matters, or by a clever interpretation covered over the novelty of a rite with the form of the old one; he also did not rashly depart from his decrees or from his custom of living and ruling. The reasoning behind the former course was what was later proclaimed under Nero: that concerning all affairs, things had formerly been provided for better and more firmly, and that what is changed is changed for the worse. The reasoning behind the latter is that a plant which is transplanted too often does not take root, a saying put forward by the great teacher Seneca.

units.la: Adeo vero imperii per se gubernandi astrictus fuit, quod tertium auctoritatis comparandae membrum, ut neminem unquam juxta se attolleret, aut surgere festinantem, & ad tribunitiae potestatis fastigium anhelantem, praecipiti lapsu detraxerit. Sejanus, uno momento a summa sede ad perniciem detrusus, docuerit.
units.tr: So bound was he to governing the empire by himself that, as the third element of acquiring authority, he never raised anyone up beside him. He cast down with headlong fall anyone who hurried to rise and panted for the summit of tribunician power. Sejanus, thrust in a single moment from the highest seat to destruction, shows this.

units.la: His addo reip. administrationem, auctoritati simul & benevolentiae parandae in servientem: quae IV. Annalium describitur. Mandabat honores, nobilitatem majorum, claritudinem militiae, illustres domi artes spectando: ut satis constaret, non alios potiores fuisse sua consulibus, sua praetoribus species. Minorum quoque magistratuum exercita potestas: legesque, si majestatis quaestio eximeretur, bono in usu. &c. Quorum etsi quaedam, crescente Sejani & mox everca potentia, mutata: pleraque tamen mansere.
units.tr: To these I add his administration of the state, which served at once to win authority and goodwill among those who served him. It is described in Annals IV. He conferred honours by regard for nobility of birth, distinction in military service, and skills distinguished at home, so that it was clear that the appearance of consuls and praetors was no more powerful than his own. The power of the lesser magistrates was also exercised, and the laws were in good use, provided the charge of treason was removed. And so on. Although some of these were changed as Sejanus's power grew and soon became excessive, most remained.

units.la: Potentiam, auctoritatis verae consiliatricem, non in amplo quamvis feracis terrae districtu, si caetera absint, reponimus. Nam si viri, si arma, si consilia defuerunt: praedam potius eam, quam firmam potentiam censemus. Igitur primo loco non spernimus; alendae paci & sustinendo bello; plenum aerarium. Quod principi non defuisse; tot annorum alta in pace paritas, parcimonia imperantis, & tot hostium damno erogationum exempla clarum fecerint. Secundo loco plusculum in armis, quae tamen facultate opum indigent, in pace praesertim, ubi nihil ex hoste deprædando speri ponimus. Quibus instructiorem prisco aevo Tiberium fuisse, IV. Annalium libro vidimus. Italia duabus classibus, Misenum apud & Ravennam, nec non rostratis apud Liguriam navibus; Antonio victo detractis, continebatur. Rhenus, Gallia contra Germanos propugnaculum, octo legionisbus custodiebatur. Hispaniam , recens perdomitárn, treslegiones insidebant. Numidia, Africa, Ægyptus, quatuor legionibus coércebatur. Totidem Syria , & quicquid terrarum Euphrati prætenditur. Panno-niam , Mœfiam , Dalmatiam , sex legiones vincie-bant., Urbem ipsam tres urbanæ , novem prætoriæ cohortes regebant. Auxiliarium cohortium, quæle-gionibus affundebantur, & sociarum apud provincias triremium, haud facilè quis numerum subduxerit,
units.tr: We do not place power, the counsellor of true authority, in a wide territory of however fertile land if other things are absent. For if men, arms and plans were lacking, we judge that territory to be plunder rather than firm power. So first, we do not despise the treasury, which is full and serves to feed peace and sustain war. That the prince did not lack this is clear from the long high level of prosperity over so many years of peace, the thrift of the ruler, and the examples of expenditure set against the loss of so many enemies. Second, a fair amount in arms, which nevertheless need resources, especially in peace, when we think nothing is to be hoped for from plundering the enemy. We saw in Annals book IV that Tiberius was better equipped with these in those earlier times. Italy was held by two fleets, at Misenum and at Ravenna, together with the beaked ships near Liguria, taken over after Antony was defeated. The Rhine, Gaul being the bulwark against the Germans, was guarded by eight legions. Spain, lately thoroughly subdued, was garrisoned by three legions. Numidia, Africa and Egypt were held in check by four legions, and as many were in Syria and all the lands stretching toward the Euphrates. Pannonia, Moesia and Dalmatia were bound by six legions. The city itself was governed by three urban and nine praetorian cohorts. As for the auxiliary cohorts, poured in beside the legions, and the allied triremes in the provinces, one could hardly reckon their number.

units.la: Quibus tamen non ita sidebat imperator, ut fœdera externorum populorum & regum sperneret. Mauri taniam Juba, donum populi Romani, acceperat: fir-mæ sociétatis æternùm vinculum. Hyberi, Albani, & accolæ Mæotidos paludis reges , nec non Thraciæ moderatores, in tutelam magnitudinis Romanæ con-ceferant. Quod apud Germanos validum, Hermun-duri & Suevi,tacito fœdere allciebantur. Catti,Che-rusci, & cæteri Romano nomini infesti , ad mutua pet dissensiones exitia occultè instigabantur. Quæ pars consiliorum, quibus plus etiam quam armis valuit, Tiberii fuerat. Unde feliciter illi imperium, tutum ab externo infultu, securum à domesticis turbis , flue-bat. Talem igitur principem , opibus & armis inftrus-&tum, fœdere potentium populorum subnixum, con-filio promendo validum , fortuna ipsa suffultum , ne-mo non barbari animi contempserit.
units.tr: Yet the emperor did not rely on these so far that he scorned the alliances of foreign peoples and kings. Juba of Mauretania had received as a gift from the Roman people, an eternal bond of firm alliance. The kings of the Iberians, the Albanians and those dwelling by the Maeotian marsh, as well as the rulers of Thrace, had taken refuge in the protection of Roman greatness. Among the Germans, who were strong, the Hermunduri and the Suevi were attracted by a tacit alliance. The Chatti, the Cherusci and the others hostile to the Roman name were secretly incited to destroy one another through mutual dissensions. This part of his plans, in which he was even more powerful than with arms, belonged to Tiberius. Whence his empire flowed on happily, safe from external assault and secure from domestic disturbance. Such a prince, equipped with resources and arms, supported by the alliance of powerful peoples, strong in promoting counsel and sustained by fortune itself, no one of barbarian spirit would have despised.

units.la: Qui mores animi, quæ virtutes ad conciliandam autoritatem faciant , & quàm earum etiam simulacra quædam Tiberium juverint, in Augusto explanando aperuimus.
units.tr: Which moral qualities and virtues make for winning authority, and how some images of them helped Tiberius, we made clear in explaining Augustus.

units.la: Quas hic, secuti Lipfium,produximus,Pietatem & Providentiam , illám pro captu gentilitiæ superstitio-nis ; istam eximiam ei fuisse reperio. Qua factum,ut non surgentes modò, sed surrectûros ahcubi motus; providerit ; & ne immensum serperent, consilio fa-gaci impediverit. Quod ad externos, in gravitate gestus,mores : ad horriditatem usque severus, & compositus ore spectabatur. Nisi quod in extrema fencta, præcgracilis & incurva procerit as , nudus capillo vertex, ulcerosa facies, ac plerunque medicami-nibus interstincta, pudori illi fuit. Quae ne autorita-tem minuerent, insularum latebris, & rara videndi sui copia, praevertit.
units.tr: These we have here brought forward following Lipsius: Piety and Providence. The former, according to the measure of gentile superstition, and the latter I find was outstanding in him. By this it came about that he foresaw not only the movements that were rising but also those about to arise elsewhere, and by a wise plan he prevented them from spreading far. As to his bearing towards foreigners, he was seen as grave in his gait and manners, severe even to harshness, with a composed face. Except that in extreme old age, when he was very thin and bent in stature, with a bald crown, an ulcerous face, and mostly smeared with medicines, this was a source of shame to him. So that these things would not diminish his authority, he kept himself away by hiding in the islands and by rarely allowing himself to be seen.

units.la: Non igitur Artabano spernendae Tiberii senectutis & Romano nomini per ferociam insultandi, causa superfuit. Cui non defuisse vires, non defuisse autoritatem, mox clade sua didicit. Solo enim nominis Romani terrore, & legionum ostentu, & consiliorum astuta ratione, Tiberius eum debellavit. Nomine tantum & autore opus, ut sponte Casaris, ut genus Arsacis, ripam apud Euphratis cerneretur.
units.tr: Therefore there was no cause for Artabanus to despise Tiberius's old age and to insult the Roman name through ferocity. He learned by his own defeat that the Romans lacked neither strength nor authority. For by the mere terror of the Roman name, by the display of legions and by the crafty reasoning of plans, Tiberius overcame him. The business needed only the name and the author, so that, as if by Caesar's own will, the line of Arsaces was seen on the bank of the Euphrates.

units.la: Ergo autoritas Romani nominis autoritas imperantis Tiberii, nondum judicio legatorum evilucrat. Quae non tantum Romanis munimento, sed validissimis nationibus terrori aut propugnaculo fuit. Quae tamen autoritas, ubi collapsis viribus nuda remanse-rit, non diu innitentes juverit.
units.tr: Therefore the authority of the Roman name, the authority of the ruling Tiberius, had not yet been lost through the judgment of the legates. This authority was a protection not only to the Romans but a terror to, or a bulwark against, the most powerful nations. Yet this authority, once its strength had collapsed and it remained bare, did not long avail those who leaned on it.

units.la: Quamvis Pontica pinus Sylvae filia nobilis, Jactis & genus, & nomen inutile: Nilpictus timidus navita puppibus Fidit.
units.tr: Although the Pontic pine, the noble daughter of the forest, has both lineage and name, they are useless when cast away; the timid sailor, painted on his stern, trusts not in it.

units.la: Campani magis nomen ad praesidium sociorum, quam vires afferente, ludibrio Samnitibus fuere.
units.tr: The Campanians, offering the name rather than the forces as protection to their allies, became a laughingstock to the Samnites.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Splendidum juris belli nomen publicae rapinae imponitur.
units.tr: The splendid name of the right of war is given to public robbery.

units.la: Alii satis juris in ipsis armis & victoria, non requisita belli causa, ponunt. Ad quorum sensum Ariovi-stus: Jus esse belli, ut qui vicissent, iis quos vicissent, quemadmodum vellent, imperarent. apud Caesarem libro primo De bello Gallico. Alii explendae aviditati, & proferendis imperii finibus, speciosum titulum quaerunt. Frequens apud priscos mortales fuit rerum repetundarum legatio. quam hic Artabanus imita-tur, missis qui gazam a Vonone relictam in Syria Ciliciaque reposcerent. perinde quasi profugi regno Venonis aut magna gazafuisset, aut ea ad Artabanum pertineret. Alii causas ex obsoleta antiquitate sin- gunt, quod ab eodem Artabano factitatum, veteres Persarum ac Macedonum terminos reposcente, seque inuasurum posse Cyro, & post Alexandro, per vaniloquentiam minante. ac si Cyrus aut Alexander pro Parthis, vilissimis tum servientium mancipiis, regnandi jura quæsivissent. ac tamen nonnullis hodie scriptoribus ea bellandi causa placet: non attendentibus vaniloquentiæ nomine eam causæ jactationem a Tacito venire. Hoc jure Romam sibi, & quicquid Romani imperii nomen præfert, Turcarum imperator, quasi Constantini successor, destinat. Hoc jure Franci reges, limites regni Gallorum ad Rheni ripam, & Alpium radices, voto extendunt. Hoc eodem jure mundi imperium, saltem quà Romanis parebat, imperatoris Romanorum esse, Alexiorum familiæ persuadebatur. Quibus si vetera, & memoria hominum labante obducta, spectare velint: iis ipsis, quæ diu possederunt, exeundum fuisset.
units.tr: Others find sufficient right in the arms themselves and in victory, with no cause of war required. Ariovistus agrees with this view: he says the right of war is that those who have conquered may command those whom they have conquered as they wish (in Caesar, book 1 of the Gallic War). Others seek a showy pretext for satisfying their greed and extending the bounds of their empire. Among the ancients it was common to send an embassy demanding the return of property, and Artabanus imitates this when he sends men who should demand back the treasure left by Vonones in Syria and Cilicia, as if the fugitive from Vonones' kingdom had either possessed a great treasure, or as if it belonged to Artabanus. Others invent causes from obsolete antiquity, as Artabanus himself did when, demanding the old boundaries of the Persians and Macedonians, he threatened that he would be able to attack Cyrus, and afterwards Alexander, by empty boasting. As if Cyrus or Alexander had sought rights to rule over the Parthians, then the most worthless of slaves! Yet some writers today approve this as a cause for war, not noticing that Tacitus calls such a boast empty talk. By this right the Turkish emperor, as successor of Constantine, claims Rome for himself and whatever bears the name of the Roman empire. By this right the kings of the Franks, by their wish, extend the limits of the kingdom of the Gauls to the bank of the Rhine and the foot of the Alps. By this same right it was maintained to the house of the Alexii that the empire of the world, at least wherever it obeyed the Romans, belonged to the emperor of the Romans. If they wish to look to old claims, obscured as human memory fades, then they would have to give up the very lands which they have long possessed.

units.la: Partho feraci Asia excedendum, & ad Scythiæ foli-tudines migrandum foret: Turcæ eadem Scythiæ vastitate claudendi: Francis ad veteres Germaniæ casas & sylvas revertendum. Sin hæc iniqua & dura videantur: quod quisque occupavit, aut hæreditate acceptit, eo se limite contineat.
units.tr: The Parthians would have to leave fertile Asia and migrate to the wastes of Scythia; the Turks would have to be shut in by the same Scythian desolation; the Franks would have to return to the old huts and forests of Germany. But if these demands seem unjust and harsh, then let each man keep within the limit of what he has seized or received by inheritance.

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: Pudenda eunuchorum & libertorum in regno potentia.
units.tr: The shameful power of eunuchs and freedmen in a kingdom.

units.la: In libero vero populo multo magis pudenda, Nam qui virilitatis indigent, viris; qui libertatis plenæ, in- genuis impetrare indecorum. Orientis reges eunu-chis gaudebant: vel quod fideliores cæteris, familiam suam respectantibus, ducebant: vel quod nihil ab iis, nulla animi altitudine, nec regni capacitate, metuendum. Non despectum id apud barbaros, ultroque potentiam habet. Romanorum imperatoribus sero id genus ministerii acceptum, aut ad honores etiam admisadmissum, De Eutropio sanè, consule facto, Claudianus:
units.tr: In a free people it is far more shameful still. For it is unseemly to ask men for those who lack manhood, and freeborn men for those who have full liberty. Eastern kings delighted in eunuchs, either because they thought them more faithful than others in attending to their household, or because nothing was to be feared from them, since they had no greatness of spirit nor capacity for rule. Among barbarians this is not despised, and indeed it holds power. Late did this kind of service come to the Roman emperors, or was it even admitted to honours. Certainly Claudian wrote of Eutropius, when he was made consul:

units.la: Heu terra cœliq; pudor! trabeata per urbesOstentatur anus, titulumq; effœminat anno.
units.tr: Alas, shame of land and sky! An old woman in consular robes is paraded through the cities, and disgraces the title of the year.

units.la: libro I. in Eutropium,
units.tr: Book 1 against Eutropius,

units.la: Non tamen puduit Romanos imperatores, jam inde a primis imperii temporibus, libertorum opera in summis reip. negotiis abuti. Claudium Narcissus, Calixtus, Pallas, quoquo vellent, circumegerunt. Neroni quanquam non infra servos ingenium, magnarum tamen rerum participes liberti alebantur. Ab eo imperante missus in Britanniam Polycletus, ad legatorum componenda dissidia, militibus quoque Romanis terribilis incessit. Sed hostibus irrisui fuit, apud quos flagrante etiam tum libertate, nondum cognita libertorum potentia erat, mirabanturque, quod dux & exercitum tanti belli confessor [?] servitiis obedirent.
units.tr: Yet the Roman emperors were not ashamed, from the very first times of the empire, to use the services of freedmen in the highest affairs of state. Narcissus, Calistus and Pallas drove Claudius about wherever they wished. Under Nero, although his mind was not inferior to that of slaves, freedmen were nourished as sharers in great affairs. Polycletus, sent by him into Britain to settle disputes among the legates, was feared even by the Roman soldiers. But he was a laughing-stock to the enemy, among whom, while liberty still burned and the power of freedmen was not yet known, they wondered that a leader and an army of so great a war obeyed slaves.

units.la: xiv. Annal.
units.tr: xiv. Annals.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: Male discrimini armorum committitur, quod astu expediri potest.
units.tr: A matter of great importance is entrusted to the hazard of arms, when it could be settled by craft.

units.la: Pugnaces aliis ad ravim [?] usque laudentur: Tiberia-num est, consiliis & astu res externas moliri, arma procul habere. Ne barbari quidem, quibus contatio servilis, statim exequi regium videtur, ita cupidine vindictæ inardescunt, ut non interdum usus, ità dissimulata, vincat.
units.tr: Some praise fighters to the point of folly. It is the Tiberian way: to contrive foreign affairs by plans and cunning, keeping arms far off. Even barbarians, to whom a servile trick seems at once a royal thing to carry out, burn so fiercely with desire for revenge that they do not always let the dissimulation that has been used win the day.

units.la: Nec tantum Tiberio lenta cum securitate consilia placuere: aliquando & apud priscos Romanos, armis & bello innutritos, locus iis dabatur. Unde illud apud Catonem de re rustica proverbium: Romanos sedendo vincit. quanquam id de obsidendis urbibus nonnemo interpretatur.
units.tr: Nor did Tiberius alone favour slow plans with calm security; at times the ancient Romans too, reared on arms and war, gave them room. Hence Cato's proverb on farming: He conquers the Romans by sitting still. Though some interpret this of besieging cities.

units.la: inquit Lucianus, i. c.
units.tr: says Lucian, in the same place.

units.la: Consilium lentum præstat veloce: citati Pœnitet, & calide suscipit acta dolor.
units.tr: A slow plan is better than a hasty one: the hurried man repents, and grief takes up what was done in heat.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Veneni genus inimica largitio.
units.tr: Poison is a hostile kind of largesse.

units.la: Quos ferro jugulare pudor aut metus prohibet, amicitiæ specie, aut venenatis epulis, aut donorum corruptione, sæpè magnates evertunt. Ultrumque teli genus Artabanus, ferro diffidens, adhibuit. Abdum specie amicitia vocatum ad epulas lento veneno in- teremit. Sinnacen dissimulatione ac donis moratus est, Creberrimum tollendi inimicos aut suspectos in aula genus, veneni propinatio. quod ne celeritate exitus autorem prodat, lentum sæpè ad simulandum fortuiti morbi languorem sumitur. à quo nec diligentissimi ac fidissimi ministri, nec rursus ipsi principes & eorum propinqui, satis cavere possunt. Burrhus, primus im- perii Neroniani autor, quod gravitatem oris princeps lascivus ferre nequiret, tantum beneficium venenato medicamine rependisse creditur. de quo Cornelius XIV. Annalium. Claudium imperatorem boleti esu ab uxore exstinctum, consentiens historicorum est per- suasio. nec Seneca in Apocolocynthosi sceleris con- scientiam celare potuit. Quin ipsum Augustum à Li- via uxore, ob reconciliatum Agrippam Posthumum, verita ne eo ab insula revocato Tiberius imperii spe excluderetur, veneno sublatum, aliqui suspicati sunt. Modum veneficii Dio Cassius libro 56. describit: quem ob novitatis insolentiam adducam. Ficus quasdam in arboribus adhuc pendentes, quas sua manu Augu- stus decerptas comedere consueviflet, veneno infecif- se, eique medicatas carpendas obtulisse, ipsa sanas edisse, memoratur. quod tamen Xiphilinus non veri- simile sibi fieri coarguit: & Dio ipse dubius judicii creditum vulgo scelus proponit. Occultior grassandi modus, & animo quàm corpori nocentior, est missis donis Corruptio. quæ si ad reconciliandos rebelles, aut à prava via abducendos veteres amicos, paretur: non admodum vituperanda. Quanquam nec eam quidem largitionem, quae ministros alienae aulae domino suo infidos, largitori fideliores reddat, aut quae spargendis muneribus, captata vulgi gratia factioni[?] studeat, politicinostri magnopere reprehenduntur.
units.tr: Those whom shame or fear keeps from cutting down with the sword, men of rank often overthrow by the show of friendship, by poisoned feasts, or by corruption with gifts. Artabanus, distrusting the sword, used both kinds of weapon. He invited Abdus to feasts under the show of friendship and killed him with slow poison. He delayed Sinnaces by dissimulation and gifts. The most common way of removing enemies or suspects at court is the administering of poison. So that the speed of the outcome may not betray the author, a slow poison is often chosen, feigning the lingering of an accidental illness. Against this neither the most diligent and faithful ministers, nor the princes themselves and their relatives, can be sufficiently on guard. Burrhus, the first architect of Nero's rule, because the wanton prince could not bear the seriousness of his face, is believed to have repaid so great a service with poisoned medicine; Cornelius writes of this in book 14 of the Annals. That the emperor Claudius was killed by his wife with a dish of mushrooms is the agreed view of historians. Nor could Seneca hide his awareness of the crime in the Apocolocyntosis. Indeed some suspected that Augustus himself was removed by poison from his wife Livia, who feared that, if Agrippa Postumus were reconciled and recalled from his island, Tiberius would be shut out of hope of the empire. Dio Cassius, in book 56, describes the method of the poisoning, which I shall adduce because of its novelty. Some figs still hanging on the trees, which Augustus was accustomed to pluck with his own hand and eat, are said to have been infected with poison, and offered to him to pick once they had been medicated; he himself ate them unharmed. Xiphilinus, however, argues that this is not likely to have happened, and Dio himself, doubtful in judgement, puts forward the crime that was commonly believed. A less obvious way of attacking, and more harmful to the mind than to the body, is corruption by sent gifts. If this is prepared to win back rebels, or to lead old friends away from a wrong path, it is not greatly to be blamed. Yet even that largesse which makes the servants of another's court faithless to their lord and more loyal to the giver, or which, by scattering gifts, seeks to win the favour of the crowd for a faction, is strongly reproved by our politicians.

units.la: Hi peperam[?] huc trahunt illud Ciceronis: Proprium hoc esse prudentiae, conciliare sibi animos hominum, & ad usus suos adjungere. Sed de utroque corruptionis genere, veneni & donorum, alibi liberalius.
units.tr: These men wrongly drag here that saying of Cicero: that it is the mark of prudence to win men's minds and bind them to one's own purposes. But of both kinds of corruption, poison and gifts, I will speak more freely elsewhere.

units.la: XXXII. Subita vitae mutatio vitae periculosa.
units.tr: XXXII. A sudden change of life is dangerous.

units.la: Praesertim si a leniori vivendi consuetudine, ad asperiorem victus rationem recedas. Phrahates apud Syriam, dum omisso cultu[?] Romano, cui per tot annos insueverat, instituta Parthorum sumit, patriis moribus impar, morbo absumptus est.
units.tr: This is especially so if you withdraw from a milder way of living to a harsher manner of life. Phraates, while in Syria he gave up the Roman way of life to which he had been accustomed for so many years and adopted the customs of the Parthians, unequal to his ancestral ways, was carried off by sickness.

units.la: Ventum aequabiliter urgentem minus nauticae rei periti timent, quam qui post intervalla quietis repentino impetu velis incumbit. Nec vela obliqua navigatione, pedem facientes, e latere in latus, nisi per aliquam in medio moram, transportant. Quid igitur Phraati consilii suppeditandum fuerat? num diversus a majorum institutis, raro venatu, segni equorum cura, lecticae gestamine, fastu erga patrias epulas, Vononem imitaretur? Hoc benevolentiae hominum con-ciliandae, & regno non conducebat. Ita natura, ita fortuna hominum beneficia sua & calamitates tem-peravit, ut sine nocumento commodum, quin illud cum isto arripias, aegerrime apprehendas.
units.tr: Sailors who know little of their craft fear a wind that blows steadily less than one that, after an interval of calm, rushes suddenly into the sails. Nor do ships moving obliquely, zigzagging from side to side, make progress except after some delay in the middle. What, then, should Phraates have done? Should he have departed from his ancestors' institutions and imitated Vonones: rarely hunting, careless of his horses, travelling in a litter, and proud toward his native feasts? That would not have helped him win men's goodwill or served his kingdom. So nature and fortune have tempered men's benefits and calamities alike, so that you cannot seize the advantage without the harm, and you grasp the one only with great difficulty.

units.la: XXXIII. Degener morum mutatio vitae & famae dedecora.
units.tr: XXXIII. A degenerate change of morals brings disgrace to life and reputation.

units.la: Quorum in adolescentia animus in nequitia peregrinatus, virili aetate masculum robur suscepit, tenerae aetatis imbecillitatem virtute obliterant. At qui a primae aetatis honesto cursu ad mollitiem, ad dedecus, ad turpitudinem declinant, famam & lucem secuturis vitiis magno ambitu quæsiverunt. Horum in numero Vitellius, regendis provinciis prisca virtute egit. Unde regressus, & formidine C. Cæsaris, familiaritate Clau-dii, turpe in servitium mutatus; exemplar apud poste-ros adulatorii dedecoris habetur. cesseruntque prima postremis, & bona juventa senestus flagitiosa oblitera-vit. Huic occini poterat, quod Herculi mulierum amoribus emollito uxor ogganniit:
units.tr: Those whose minds wandered into wickedness in youth take on manly strength in mature age, and they wipe out the weakness of tender years by virtue. But those who turn aside from an honourable course in early life to softness, disgrace and vileness seek fame and renown with great effort, only to have their vices follow them. Among these was Vitellius, who in his earlier years governed provinces with ancient virtue. Then, turning back, and out of fear of Caligula and through his intimacy with Claudius, he changed shamefully into a slave; he remains an example to posterity of servile disgrace. The first things gave way to the last, and his shameful old age blotted out his good youth. Of him could be said what Hercules' wife cried out when he had been softened by love for women:

units.la: Cœpisti melius, quàm desinis : ultima primis Cedunt.
units.tr: You began better than you end: the last things give way to the first.

units.la: Ovid. epist. Heroid.
units.tr: Ovid, Epistulae Heroidum.

units.la: imò & sapientissimo Hebræorum Salomoni in os in-geri potuerat, nisi eum resipuisse piè crederemus.
units.tr: Indeed, the same reproach could have been thrown in the face of Solomon, the wisest of the Hebrews, had we not believed that he repented.

units.la: XXXIV.
units.tr: XXXIV.

units.la: Mercenaria militia merentibus ignobilis, utentibus infida.
units.tr: Mercenary soldiering is ignoble for those who serve and faithless for those who employ them.

units.la: Priscis non ignorata ea militia, nec nationibus qui-bufdam indecora visa. Sarmatarum natio Sceptruchi utrimque donis acceptis, more gentico diversa induere. Qua vero æstimatione apud alios, militiam gloriâ æstimantes, non mercede vendentes, fuerit; Partho-rum oratio ostendit. Parthus imperium Orientis, claritudinem Arsacidarum; contraque ignobilem Hi-berum mercenario militte, differebat. Nec obscura tan-tum & servilis ea militia, verùm & mercenario popu-lo postremùm damnosa. Cares, Iberi, peregrina mili-tia victum quærentes; illi Persarum, hi Carthaginien-sium, apud quos merebant, jugum subibant. Quàm vero non tutò credatur alienigenis, auxilia aut stipen-diariam militiam pollicentibus, in Arcanis regnorum diduxi.
units.tr: Mercenary service was not unknown to the ancients, nor did some nations regard it as disgraceful. The Sarmatians, taking gifts from both sides, the Sceptuchi, dressed differently in the manner of their people. What esteem it held among others, who valued soldiering for glory and did not sell it for wages, the speech of the Parthians shows. The Parthian argued the empire of the East and the renown of the Arsacids, and against this he set the base Iberian who served for hire. This service is not only obscure and servile, but in the end also ruinous to a people who live by wages. The Carians and Iberians, seeking a living by foreign service, came under the yoke, the former of the Persians, the latter of the Carthaginians, in whose pay they served. How little one may safely trust foreigners who promise auxiliaries or mercenary troops, I have explained in the Arcana of kingdoms.

units.la: XXXV.
units.tr: XXXV.

units.la: Ornata auro acies hostem non ter-ritat.
units.tr: Ornata auro acies hostem non territat.

units.la: Ferro enim, non auro, vulnera ingeruntur. Aurum cupidinem magis, quàm metum, adversæ aciei acuit, Pharasmanes inter cætera pugnæ incitamenta horri-dam. dam suorum aciem, picta auro Medorum agmina: hinc viros, inde prædam ostendere.
units.tr: Wounds are inflicted by iron, not by gold. Gold rouses the greed of an opposing line more than its fear. Among other incitements to battle, Pharasmanes showed his own line, horrid and the troops of the Medes glittering with gold: on one side men, on the other plunder.

units.la: Nostra memoria Sueci, famelica domi natio & cultu miseranda, cultarum gentium & vestitu ac auro micantium, plerumque superiores evasere. Est tamen id quibusdam nationibus in more positum, ut in proelium ituri, ornamenta corporis, animi incitamentum, aut honestæ mortis solatium, assumant. Nitorem sane armorum, & moderatum vestium cultum, in milite non carpimus: dum ne industri[?]æ oblitus, oculos magis fulgore, quam corpora ferro perstringat. Hostium se spoliis induere, quam ipsitorum tabernis operam dare, magis ex horrida militia videtur. Mortem contemnere æquo animo qui poterit, quem corporis munditiæ capiunt?
units.tr: In our own memory the Swedes, a people starved at home and wretched in their way of life, have often prevailed over nations that were well dressed and glittering with gold. Still, among some nations it is the custom that men going into battle put on bodily ornaments, as an incitement to courage or a comfort for an honourable death. We do not, of course, find fault with a soldier's bright arms or a moderate concern for his dress, provided that, without neglecting diligence, he dazzles the eyes more with splendour than he pierces bodies with steel. It seems more fitting to a dreadful soldiery to clothe oneself in the spoils of enemies than to labour in one's own workshops. Who will be able to despise death with a calm mind if he is captivated by the niceties of his body?

units.la: XXXVI. Duci in agmine, duci in proelio parendum.
units.tr: XXXVI. In the march one must obey the leader; in battle one must obey the leader.

units.la: Hoc à ratione & solertia: ducum neglectus ab inconsiderata ferocia. Non placet illa Sarmatarum confusio: apud quos non una vox ducis: se quisque stimulant, quæ & hodie inter præcipuas cladium causas, cum ferociæ militaris non pœniteat, Polonis.
units.tr: This follows from reason and skill; neglect of commanders comes from thoughtless ferocity. That confusion of the Sarmatians does not please me, among whom there is not one voice of the leader, and each man spurs on himself. This is among the chief causes of defeats even today for the Poles, though they are not sorry for their martial ferocity.

units.la: Magis placet Cattorum Tacito laudata consuetudo: præponere electos, audire præpositos, nosse ordines, intel-ligere occasiones, differre impetus, dissimulare diem, vallare noctem, fortunam inter dubia, virtutem inter certa numerare: quodque rarissimum, nec nisi ratione disciplinæ concessum, plus reponere in duce quàm in exercitu. quæ omnia apud Polonos in contrarium abeuntia, multos eorum conatus infregerunt. Ut bene à Macedonici belli scriptore dictum fit, Militarem sine duce turbam, esse corpus sine spiritu. & à declamatore Fabio: Ut remiges sine gubernatore; ita milites sine imperatore, nihil valere.
units.tr: The custom of the Chatti, praised by Tacitus, pleases me more: to put forward the chosen, to obey those set over them, to know the ranks, to understand opportunities, to defer attacks, to conceal the day, to fortify the night, to count fortune among uncertain things and courage among certain ones; and, what is very rare and granted only by the discipline of reason, to place more trust in the leader than in the army. Among the Poles all these things turn out the opposite, and this has broken many of their enterprises. As the writer of the Macedonian war rightly said, a military crowd without a leader is a body without spirit; and the declaimer Fabius: as oarsmen without a helmsman, so soldiers without a commander are worth nothing.

units.la: XXXVII. Est & fugæ quædam peritia.
units.tr: XXXVII. There is also a certain skill in flight.

units.la: Aliain eo, ut in sequentium ordine distracto, rur- sum instes. cum Parthis sequi vel fugere pari arte. Suetus, distraheret turmas, [?] patium [?] itibus quaererent. Alia in eo, ut simulato trepido recessu, hostem in commodiori loco, aut in insidias abducas. Quod saepe à Græcis ducibus, nec raro à barbaris factitatum. Plus artis est in abducendis à muro hostili, aut ab iniquitate proelii & loci, copiis. de quo in Belgica militia, cum eam ingenti volumine scriberemus, multa exempla adduximus. Romani, ut caeterarum rerum graves, ita in pugna stabili omnia ponentes, postremo recedendi modo raro, rariùs primo & medio usi leguntur.
units.tr: There is one skill in drawing the enemy out of order, so that, when his line has been broken in pursuit, you press him again; and there is an equal art with the Parthians of pursuing or fleeing. Accustomed... they broke up their squadrons and sought ... [?] ... Another skill lies in feigning a fearful withdrawal, so as to lead the enemy into a more favourable place or into an ambush. This has often been practised by Greek commanders and not rarely by barbarians. It takes more skill to draw troops away from an enemy's wall, or away from the unfavourable nature of the battle and the ground. I brought forward many examples of this when I wrote at great length about Belgian warfare. The Romans, serious in other matters and placing everything in a stand-up fight, are read to have used a method of retreat rarely at the end, more rarely at the beginning and middle.

units.la: De Germanis antiqui aevi & moris Tacitus: Cedere loco, dummodo rursus infestes, consilii quàm formidinis arbitrantur, quod [?] dicerent. Illud de Germanis probrofius: Sine pudore flagitii, sine [?] cura ducum, abire, fugere: pavidos adversus [?] inter fe-cunda, non divini, non humani juris memores. quod tamen non Taciti, sed ducis hostium apud Tacitum judicium. Hodie aliter de Germanis, & in primis Helvetiis, ab exteris judicatur.
units.tr: Concerning the Germans of ancient times and their custom, Tacitus says: they think that giving up a position, provided they attack again, is a matter of plan rather than fear, since they said [?]. That remark about the Germans is more damning: without shame for the disgrace, without [?] regard for their leaders, they leave and flee, cowards before [?] among the fruitful..., not mindful of divine or human law. Yet this is not Tacitus' own judgement but the judgement of the enemy's leader, as reported by Tacitus. Today the Germans, and above all the Swiss, are judged differently by foreigners.

units.la: XXXVIII.
units.tr: XXXVIII.

units.la: Idem in bello falsus quod verus ru-mor sæpè potest.
units.tr: The same thing in war can often be false as well as a true rumour.

units.la: Nam subitis territæ, aut in falsum gaudium conje-ctantes [?], mentes colligendi sui, & veri indagandi spatium sibi non permittunt. Orodes rex Parthorum vulnere per galeam accepto, nec à Pharafmane occideretur, pernicitate equi, & obje&tu satellitum protegebatur. Fama tamen occisi falsò credita exterruit Parthos, vitioriamque concessere. Quare folertes aliquando duces occisum hostium du&torem, injiciendo metui & suis confirmandis, commenti sunt. Fervida inter Romanum & Numidam pugna, Jugurtha gladio, quem non in strenuè cæso milite tinxerat, elato, frustra pugnare Romanos, Marium manu sua occisum, clamavit. nec caruisset successu commentum, nisi re-pente Marius à persecutione fugientis alæ reversus, suis cognoscendum se obtulisset. Pari arte occisi ducis rumor suos & hostes celatur: ne illi moeroris consternatione pugnae alacritatem deferant; isti fiducia ad acriorem pugnam accendantur. Publius Valerius, Herdonium capitolio expulsurus, primo in limine occiditur. Volumnius corpore ejus tecto, tanquam du-cente consule ire pergit, hostem arce expellit. Hac de causa tristiorum rerum nuncii, ducum aliquando manu confodiuntur, ne veritas ad multorum notitiam pervagata, animos metu, vel novarum rerum cupidi-tate polluat. Fama enim, & hominum credulitate, non minus bella, quam armis, geruntur.
units.tr: For those who are terrified by sudden alarms, or who rush into false joy, do not allow themselves the time to collect their minds and to search out the truth. Orodes, king of the Parthians, having taken a wound through his helmet, was not killed by Pharasmanes but was protected by the speed of his horse and by his attendants throwing themselves in the way. Yet the false report of his death, believed, terrified the Parthians, and they yielded the victory. Therefore clever commanders have sometimes devised the feigned killing of the enemy's leader, to cast fear upon the enemy and to strengthen their own men. In a fierce battle between a Roman and a Numidian, Jugurtha, raising the sword with which he had stained it on a soldier not slain without vigour, shouted that the Romans were fighting in vain, since Marius had been killed by his own hand. The stratagem would not have lacked success, had not Marius suddenly returned from pursuing a fleeing wing and presented himself to be recognised by his men. By the same art the rumour of a slain commander is hidden from both his own men and the enemy: lest the one, struck with grief, should lose their eagerness for battle, and the other be fired to fiercer fighting by confidence. When Publius Valerius was about to drive Herdonius from the Capitol, he was killed at the very threshold. Volumnius, covering his body, went on as if the consul were leading, and drove the enemy from the citadel. For this reason the messengers of sadder news are sometimes slain by the hand of commanders, lest the truth, spread abroad among many, should infect minds with fear or with a desire for revolution. For war is waged no less by rumour and by men's credulity than by arms.

units.la: XXXIX.
units.tr: XXXIX.

units.la: Æquitate quam vi regnum tueri satius est.
units.tr: Justice is a safer defence of a kingdom than force.

units.la: Quos enim metu coercueris, excusso terrore, mutatis rebus animos extollunt. Quos benevolentia de-vinxeris, ii nec adverso rerum flatu, nisi depuduerunt, benefactorem deserunt. Sinnaces defectionem popularium ab Artabano molitur: affluentibus paulatim, qui metu magis quam benevolentia subjecti, repertis autoribus, sustulerant animum. Autore tantum opus est, & temporum opportunitate hi quos auxiliares tibi speraveras, inter primos rebellantium spectabis.
units.tr: Those whom you have held down by fear raise their spirits when the terror is shaken off and circumstances change. Those whom you have bound to you by goodwill do not desert their benefactor, even when the wind of fortune turns against him, unless they have lost all shame. Sinnaces engineers the defection of the people from Artabanus: the people gradually flowing over, who, subject more from fear than goodwill, once authors were found, had raised their spirits. Only an author is needed, and given the opportunity of the times, you will see among the first of the rebels those whom you had hoped would be your auxiliaries.

units.la: Nec satis certa peregrini satellitii fiducia. quos enim patria noverca ejecit, qui fidem impollutam re-gibus externis commodent? quis neque boni intelle-ctum, neque mali cura, sed mercede aluntur, ministri sceleribus. deficiente aere deficiens; aut majori ex di-verso mercede, transibunt. Nec externa auxilia, & regum affinitates respicias. Tutum fortassis exilium, rarissime subsidium impetrabis. Vidit prior aetas Artabanum ad Hyrcanos Carmanosque profugum; vidit & nostra aetas, reges a suis desertos aut detentos; vidit causam dicentes, supplicio affectos; vidit haere-des[?] regno ejectos, ignominia notatos. Verba multo-rum fortem commiseratorum audita, subsidia a pau-cis collata. Aliqua fortassis in animorum mobilitate spes: quo hic profugus Artabanus erexit, Atque in-terim posse Parthos absentium aquos, prasentibus mo-biles, ad poenitentiam mutari. Quae spes Artabanum non omnino fefellit: & sunt qui ipsi eadem hoc tem-pore aluntur. Neque ego iis omnem spem praecido. Certius tamen retinendi exaequitate regni, quam re-parandi ex animorum mobilitate fundamentum.
units.tr: Nor is confidence in a foreign bodyguard sufficiently secure. For whom has a stepmother country cast out, who would lend unstained faith to foreign kings? Men who know neither goodness nor care for what is right, but are fed by pay, ministers of crimes. When the money fails, they fail; or for greater pay from the other side, they will switch over. Nor should you look to foreign aid and royal marriage alliances. Exile is perhaps safe, but you will very rarely obtain help. An earlier age saw Artabanus fleeing to the Hyrcanians and Carmanians; our own age has seen kings deserted or detained by their own people; it has seen men pleading their cases and punished with death; it has seen heirs thrown out of the kingdom and branded with disgrace. Many words of pity were heard, and a few aids were brought together. Perhaps there is some hope in the fickleness of minds: with this hope the fugitive Artabanus raised himself, and meanwhile the Parthians, faithful to absent men but fickle toward present ones, could be turned to repentance. This hope did not wholly deceive Artabanus, and there are those who are being fed by the same hope even now. Nor do I cut off all hope for them. Yet a firmer foundation for keeping a kingdom lies in equity than in recovering it from the fickleness of minds.

units.la: XL.
units.tr: XL.

units.la: Imponere iræ veljustissimæ modum.
units.tr: To set a limit to anger, even the most just anger.

units.la: Infirmiores animos, quos ratio non mitigat, obli-vio injuriæ & fuga temporum, satisfactio & amico-rum deprecatio, vindicta & poenæ satietas, placave-rint. Non autem Tiberium, quæ cæteros mollire solent, tempus, preces, fatigas, mitigabant, quod accerbi ani-mi, & in ultionis cogitatione pervicacis indicium. At causa iræ & offensæ gravitas mitigationem saltem, & veniæ spem, incidit. Causa iræ Tiberianæ vel incerta, vel antiquata. quin incerta vel abolita prograviffimi & recentibus puniret, addo, vel inepta, vel iniqua. Inepta: quia amicitia civium, & captâ hominum po-tentiorum gratia, nemini esse noxæ debet. Iniqua: quia si amicitia Sejani poenam meretur, poenam lue-re ante omnes Tiberius debebat. Nam & amiciffi-mus diu Sejano fuit, & cæteris ad eum colendum fe-neftram aperuit. Aliqua tamen Sejani culti Tiberio, perfuafione saltem animi, causa. At successoris ejus Caji offensionem quis vitaverit? Ut justam poenæ infligendæ causam nactus diceretur, Antonii magis quam Augusti nepos videri volebat. Sic enim & immolando pro Augusti Actiaca victoria, & immolatio-nem omittendo, peccaturi erant.
units.tr: Milder minds, which reason does not soften, are placated by forgetting an injury and the passing of time, by satisfaction and the entreaties of friends, by revenge and the satiety of punishment. But Tiberius was not softened by the things that usually soften others: time, prayers and entreaties did not mollify him. This was a sign of a bitter spirit, stubborn in the thought of revenge. Yet the cause of anger and the gravity of an offence usually allow at least some mitigation and hope of pardon. The cause of Tiberius's anger was either uncertain or out of date. Indeed, I add, he punished most severely offences that were uncertain or abolished, or else foolish or unjust. Foolish: because the friendship of citizens, and winning the favour of powerful men, ought to be harmful to no one. Unjust: because if friendship with Sejanus deserves punishment, Tiberius himself should have paid the penalty before all others. For he was the most intimate friend of Sejanus for a long time, and he opened the window for all others to court him. Yet there was some cause for Tiberius's cultivation of Sejanus, at least in the persuasion of his mind. But who could avoid the offence of his successor Gaius? In order to seem to have found a just cause for inflicting punishment, he wished to appear the grandson of Antony rather than of Augustus. For they would sin both by sacrificing for Augustus's victory at Actium and by omitting the sacrifice.

units.tr: Of all enemies, ... [Ἁπάντων ἐχθρῶν, ...] [illegible]

units.la: τὰ τῶν ... [illegible, ~30 letters] quas enim ob causas Parthi regem suum expulerant, harum ille reus populi voce iuvebatur, odio ob invidiam, insidiis ob metum obnoxius. Verbà sunt Xiphelini in Caligula. Quid enim illis agas, qui Tyrannorum mores in se agnoscunt, Tyrannorumq; vitam & facta probant; nomen tyranni non admittunt?
units.tr: ... For by the same causes for which the Parthians had expelled their king, he, the accused, was aided by the voice of the people, exposed to hatred on account of envy and to plots on account of fear. These are the words of Xiphilinus on Caligula. For what can you do with those who recognise the manners of tyrants in themselves, approve the life and deeds of tyrants, yet do not admit the name of tyrant? [τὰ τῶν ...]

units.la: XLI. Veritatis magna in aula caritas.
units.tr: XLI. Truth is held in great esteem at court.

units.la: Cunctarum rerum vilis in palatio annona, praeter-quam veritatis, quae raro regibus aperitur. Agnovit eam pretiosae rei jacturam Ludovicus XI. Galliae rex sollertissimus. Veritatem, inquit, pater meus animum agere dicebat: ego vero mortuam, & quidem intestatam, puto. Nec in senatu quam in aula, eorum quae ad vitam regis pertinent, veritas apertior. Senatoriae adulationis plura, quam priscae gravitatis, monumenta sub principibus vera audire aeternis exstant.
units.tr: At court every commodity is cheap except truth, which is rarely opened up to kings. Louis XI, the most shrewd king of France, recognised the loss of this precious thing. "My father used to say that truth was alive," he said; "I, however, think it is dead, and indeed intestate." Truth about matters that concern the life of the king is no more open in the senate than in the court. Under the princes there survive, as eternal records, more monuments of senatorial flattery than of ancient dignity, and they show how truth was heard.

units.la: Morum dedecora, publicae imperii clades, horrenda scelerum prodigia in plausum, in gratulationem, in templorum consecrationem vertebantur. Nec, si quis apud Neronem Thrasea, apud Domitianum Helvidius, eorum voces prae assentantium strepitu audiebantur. Claudii cum Agrippina incestus, e rep. esse acclamabatur. postulanti ei decretum fit, quo justae inter patruos fratrumque filias nuptiae etiam in posterum statuerentur. XII. Annal. Matris caede a Nerone perata, cum hic dignum scelere exitum timeret; miro certamine procerum decernuntur supplicationes apud omnia pulvinaria, utque Quinquatrus, quibus apertae essent insidiae, ludis annuis celebrarentur. Aureum Minervae simulacrum in curia, & juxta principis imago statueretur. Dies natalis Agrippinae inter nefastos esset. XIV. Annal.
units.tr: The shameful conduct of princes, the public disasters of the empire and the monstrous crimes were turned into applause, congratulation and the consecration of temples. Even if anyone, like Thrasea under Nero or Helvidius under Domitian, spoke out, his voice could not be heard above the clamour of the flatterers. The incest of Claudius with Agrippina was acclaimed as being for the public good, and when he asked for a decree permitting marriages between uncles and their brothers' daughters for the future, it was granted. (Tacitus, Annals 12.) When Agrippina had been put to death by Nero, and he feared a fitting end for his crime, the nobles competed in decreeing thanksgivings at all the shrines, and that the Quinquatrus, on which the plot against her had been revealed, should be celebrated with annual games. A golden statue of Minerva was to be set up in the senate house, and an image of the prince beside it, and the day of Agrippina's birth was to be counted among the unlucky days. (Annals 14.)

units.la: Quo quidem adulantium patrum, aut adulationem admittentis Neronis, secordia deprehenditur. Non enim dies natalis Agrippinae inter damnatos haberi poterat; quin simul Neronis dies natalis damnaretur[?]; matre enim nunquam nata, filius in lucem prodire non poterat.
units.tr: By this very thing the folly of the fathers who flattered, and of Nero who allowed the flattery, is exposed. For the birthday of Agrippina could not be counted among the condemned days without at once condemning the birthday of Nero too; for a son could never have been born into the light if his mother had never been born.

units.la: Rursus Poppaea marito Othoni erepta, pellice primum deinde per duplex adulterium conjuge facta; Octavia ficto adulterii crimine in infulam Pandate-riam remota, tandem mori adacta: gratiae ob id actae, & dona templis decreta. Breviter, quoties fugas & caedes princeps iussit, toties gratiae diis actae: quaeque rerum secundarum olim, tum publicae cladis insignia fuere. eodem Annalium libro. Deinde filia ex infau-sto matrimonio nata, vota quae suscepta erant exsolu-ta, additae supplicationes, templumque Foecunditati, &c. Rursus, infante intra quartum mensem defuncta, exortae adulationes, censentium honorem divae, & pulvinar, aedemque & sacerdotem. xv. Annal.
units.tr: Again, Poppaea was snatched from her husband Otho, first made a concubine, then by a double adultery made a wife; Octavia, removed to the island of Pandateria on a false charge of adultery, was at last forced to die. Thanks were rendered to the gods for this, and gifts were decreed to the temples. In short, whenever the prince ordered flights and killings, thanks were rendered to the gods as often; and these things, once signs of prosperity, became then signs of public disaster (same book of the Annals). Then, when a daughter was born of the ill-omened marriage, the vows that had been made were paid, and more thanksgivings were added, and a temple was built to Fecundity, and so on. Again, when the infant died before the fourth month, flatteries arose: some proposed divine honours for her, a couch, a shrine and a priest (Annals 15).

units.la: Tanta foedarum erga unum principem (nec omnia recensui) adulationum seges! quid si ad aliorum scae-va & saeva facta, faustis acclamationibus insignita, me converterem? Plura saepe peccantur, dum demere-mur, quam dum offendimus. Quaedam imo virtutes odio sunt, severitas obstinata, invictus adversum gra-tiam animus. Inde initia magistratuum nostrorum meliora fermè, & finis inclinat: bene à Pæto Thrasea dictum est. Nam & Nero, & alii post eum principes, dum veritatis copia invidetur, dum flagitia plausu, scelera laudatione excipiuntur, indies corruptiores, & se & adulantes & rempublicam pessundederunt.
units.tr: Such a crop of disgraceful flatteries towards one prince (and I have not listed them all)! What if I turned to the savage and cruel deeds of others, marked with favourable acclamations? Men often sin more while they seek to please than while they give offence. Some virtues are even hateful: stubborn severity, and a mind unbending against favour. Hence the beginnings of our magistrates are generally better, and their endings decline; Thrasea rightly said this of Paetus. For Nero and the other princes after him, while the supply of truth was begrudged, while crimes were met with applause and wickedness with praise, grew daily more corrupt and ruined both themselves, and the flatterers, and the commonwealth.

units.la: Erumpit tamen aliquando veritas, & se auribus quamvis honesto obseratis ingerit. quod fit 1. per inimicos, qui plus interdum blandientibus amicis, apud quos vera offensura reticentur, prosunt. Ac pri-vatae quidem conditionis hominibus probra coram objiciuntur: principes per infames libellos, per codicillos & supremas tabulas, si proferantur, vera audiunt.
units.tr: Yet truth does at some point break out, and forces itself upon ears that are closed, however honourable they are. This happens (1) through enemies, who sometimes do more good than friendly flatterers, who keep silent about what would give offence. Private individuals are reproached with their disgraces openly to their face; princes hear the truth through infamous libels, through codicils and last wills, if these are produced.

units.la: Nam nisi moriendi quis certus, aut victo[?] ira animi do-lore, libertate linguae coram audiente principe non utitur. Fulcinius Trio supremis tabulis multa & atro-cia in Macronem, ac praecipuos libertorum Cafaris, compo[illegible, ~4 letters]fuit : ipsi fluxam senio mentem, & continuo ab-scessu, velut exsilium objectando. Tria iunt quæ tabu-lis Tiberio Fulcinius exprobravit. 1. Macrorus ac li-bertorum non cohibita sævienti ac rapiendi licentia. 2. senectute delirans principis animus. 3. spontaneum deserta patria exilium. Quæ ab hæredibus occultata, recitari Tiberius iussit : patientiam libertatis alienæ ostentans, & contemtor suæ infamiæ : anscelerum Sejani diu nescius, mox quoquo modo dicta vulgari male-bat, veritatisque cui adulatio officit, per probra saltem gnarum fieri. Miserum principem apud quem vera reticentur ! quique errorum suorum, nisi per expro-brationem inimicam, gnarus esse non potuit ! Sic veri audiendi copiam Drusus, Germanici liberorum natu minor, per diras & imprecationes, fecit : quæ supra ipso hoc libro describuntur. Sic Titius Sabinus moriturus veri copiam fecit : non imprudentem Tiberium tantam invidiam adiisse : quaesitum meditatumque, ne quid impedire credatur, quo minus novi magistratus, quo modo delubra & altaria, sic carerem reliquidant. IV. Annal. Sic veri copiam Agrippina atrox, & periculo propinquæ tum offensa, non invidit : Non ejusdem ait mactare divo Augusto victimas, & posteros ejus infestari. non in effigies mutas divinum spiritum transfusum : sed imaginem veram caelesti sanguine ortam, intelligere discrimen, suscipere sordes, fraustra[?] Pulchram praescribi, cui sola exitii causa sit, quod A-grippinam stulte prorsus ad cultum dilegerit, oblita Sofia ob eadem afflicta. ibidem. Sic verum non reticuit Clemens, Agrippæ Posthumi, minimè servili animo & lingua, servus. qui clauso ore tractus in palatium, percontanti Tiberio, Quomodo Agrippa factus esset, animose respondit, Quomodo tu Cæsar[?].2.Annal. Sic verum in extremis Neroni Flavius Tribunus aperuit : Oderam te, inquit, nec quisquam tibi fidelior militum fuit, dum amari meruisti. odisse coepi, postquam parricida matris & uxoris, auriga, histrio, & incendiarius extitisti. xv. Annal. Sic C. Petronius, mori a Nerone adactus, flagitia principis sub nomipibus[?] exoletorum fœminárûmque, & novitate cujusque stupri perscribit, atque obsignata misit Neroni. xvi. Annal.
units.tr: For unless someone is sure of dying, or, overcome by the pain of anger, speaks freely in the presence of the prince, he does not use his tongue in liberty. Fulcinius Trio, in his last will, made many fierce charges against Macro and the chief freedmen of Caesar: "his mind was fluid with age, and he was continually withdrawing, as if objecting to exile." There are three things which Fulcinius reproached Tiberius with in his will: (1) the unrestrained licence of Macro and the freedmen, raging and plundering; (2) the prince's mind, deranged by old age; (3) a voluntary exile from his deserted country. What the heirs had concealed, Tiberius ordered to be read out, showing a patience at others' liberty, and disregarding his own infamy; he had long been ignorant of the crimes of Sejanus, and soon he was angry that they were made public in any way, wishing the truth, which flattery hinders, to become known at least through reproaches. A wretched prince, before whom the truth is kept silent, who could not know his own errors except through hostile reproach! Thus Drusus, the younger child of Germanicus, gave the prince a hearing of the truth through curses and imprecations, which are described in this very book above. Thus Titius Sabinus, about to die, gave the truth a hearing: "that Tiberius, not unwittingly, had incurred such great hatred; it was sought and planned that nothing should seem to hinder the new magistrates from leaving, in the same way, the shrines and altars as they were." (Annals 4.) Thus fierce Agrippina, offended at the time by a danger to her kin, did not begrudge the truth: "It is not for the same man to sacrifice victims to the deified Augustus and to harass his descendants. The divine spirit was not poured into mute effigies; but a true image born of heavenly blood understands the danger, takes on the filth, [...] Beautiful, for whom the only cause of destruction is that he had foolishly chosen Agrippina for worship, having forgotten Sophia, who was afflicted for the same reasons." (Ibid.) Thus Clemens, the servant of Agrippa Postumus, not at all a slavish man in spirit or tongue, did not conceal the truth. Dragged into the palace with his mouth shut, when Tiberius asked him how Agrippa had been made, he answered spiritedly, "As you, Caesar, were made." (Annals 2.) Thus Flavius, a tribune, revealed the truth to Nero at the end: "I hated you," he said, "and none of the soldiers was more loyal to you while you deserved to be loved. I began to hate you after you became the murderer of your mother and wife, a charioteer, an actor and an incendiary." (Annals 15.) Thus Gaius Petronius, forced to die by Nero, described in detail the prince's disgraces under the names of his catamites and women, and the novelty of each debauchery, and sealed it and sent it to Nero. (Annals 16.)

units.la: 2. Vicinus veri audiendi modus est, qui fit per accusatores, qui studio cuncta proferendi occulta prin-cipum crimina, quasi à reo exagitata, deregunt. Quod non raro Tiberio, quamvis obstrepente nè audiret populo, ut quibus occulto rumore convitiis profcin-deretur perciperet, contigit.
units.tr: (2) Another way of hearing the truth is through accusers, who in their eagerness to bring out all the hidden crimes of princes, drag them out as if they had been wrung from the accused. This often happened to Tiberius, although the people were shouting so that he could not hear; he learned from a secret rumour what abuse was being hurled at him.

units.la: 3: Tremore aliquo injecto, in mentem scelerum memoria redit. Nero cùm Vestæ templum iniisset, repente cuncos per artus tremens, seu numine exterrente, seu facinorum recordatione hunquam timore vacuus, deseruit inceptum. xv. Annal. Eidem, matris recenti cæde tepenti, obversabatur mâris illius & litorum gravis aspectus: & erant qui crederent, sonitum tubæ collibus circum editis, plàn&usquè tumulo matris audiri. xiv. Annal. Theodoricus Gothorum rex non postremi commatis, occisis per cupiditatem iræ Symmacho & Boëthio, cùm nemo hominum factum id culpare auderet, piscis hiante ore cibum capturo siensæ appositus, terrorem illi & gravem iniquæ cædis memoriam, tepentis & exanimi commotione mortis pronubam, injecit. Sic multa sibi audire, multa vide-re timor, conscientiâ factinoré perturbatâ, fingit: ut fictus hominum plausus, aut veri patcus termo, synce-rum esse gaudium non sinant.
units.tr: (3) When some fear has been put into them, the memory of crimes returns to their minds. When Nero had entered the temple of Vesta, suddenly, trembling in every limb, whether terrified by a divine power or by the recollection of his deeds, never free from fear, he abandoned what he had begun. (Annals 15.) To the same man, while his mother's recent murder was still fresh, the grim sight of that man and the shore kept coming before him; and some believed that the sound of a trumpet was heard from the surrounding hills, and wailing from his mother's tomb. (Annals 14.) Theodoric, king of the Goths, no mean man, after he had killed Symmachus and Boethius through anger and greed, when no man dared to blame the deed, had a fish placed before him as he was about to take food with gaping mouth; it brought him terror and a heavy memory of the unjust killing, a bridesmaid of death, in the stirring of the lifeless and cooling body. So fear, with a conscience disturbed by deeds, imagines that it hears many things and sees many things; and so feigned applause of men, or the rare word of truth, do not allow joy to be sincere.

units.la: 4: Quædam morionés quasi per jocum, aut qui mente mota in aulis aluntur homunciones, casu aut instinctu, vera in medium proferunt. Uno hoc nomine non inutiles futuri: cæterarum rerum inutilia palatii pondera, cibariorum otiosi fortes, graviorum vitiorum offensione aut præcipiendo frucht calami-tas.
units.tr: (4) Some things are brought out into the open by chance or by impulse, as if in jest, by the jesters, or by the little men fed in courts whose minds are unsettled. They are of no use in any other respect: the useless burdens of the palace, idle eaters of food; but by giving offence in graver vices they serve to forewarn of calamity.

units.la: 5. Casus nonnunquam, & inter venandum aberra-tio, in casam aliquam delatis, ab ignorantibus quo præsente loquantur, veritatem recludit: Ibi à rurico-lis, pastoribus, hortulanis aut facinora sua & avari-tiam, aut errorem fallacibus aulæ ministris creden-tium, admirabundi audiunt: aut, quid in.ex subditos delisti, vel in imperantem infesti animi, latent percipiunt.
units.tr: (5) Sometimes chance, or a wrong turn while hunting, leads to some cottage, and the truth is unlocked when people speak in front of those who do not know who is present. There, from country folk, shepherds or gardeners, the courtiers hear with astonishment either their own greed and wrongdoing, or the errors of the deceitful court ministers, which the believers commit; or they perceive what hidden grudges the subjects bear against their ruler, or what hostile feelings they harbour against the one in command.

units.la: 6. Quo fine curiosiores nonnulli, dissimulata maiestate, vili habitu & fine comitatu, compita & diversoria pererrant: sermonem de rege & ejus aula ultro jaciunt. Quod inter veteres Antigono, inter recentiores Henrico Navarraeo Galliarum regi, impingunt. Hic prima aetate maternam religionis sectam secutus, cum ob securam Galliae possessionem ad plurium sensum se circumegisset: quid vel Hugonotae vel Catholici (factionum ea per Galliam nomina) de ea immutatione sentirent, scire cupidus; illorum execrationem perfidiae, horum syncerae transitionis in partes incredulam diffidentiam audivit.
units.tr: 6. For this reason some more curious people, laying aside their dignity, wander through crossroads and inns in shabby clothing and without an entourage, and freely start conversations about the king and his court. Among the ancients this was attributed to Antigonus, and among more recent figures to Henry of Navarre, king of France. In his early years he had followed his mother's religious party, but when he had turned to the side of the many, once possession of France was secure, he wished to know what the Huguenots or the Catholics (the names of the factions across France) thought of that change. He heard from the one side curses of treachery, and from the other a distrustful disbelief in his sincere change of allegiance.

units.la: 7. Aliquando publica civium querela, & se non continens vox hominum, pro veritatis indicio est. Quo Nero plebis Romanae de incensa Roma judici-um, culpam in eum autorem delata, cognovit. Non ope humana, non largitionibus principis, aut deum placamentis, decedebat infamia, quin jussum incendium crederetur. Ergo rumori abolendo Nero subdidit reos, & quaesitissimis pœnis affecit. &c. xv. Annalium. Ergo qui sunt ingenio insanabili, verum eos aliquando celari quam doceri, satius. Siquidem aut quae detecta sunt, novis sceleribus operiunt; aut pudore deposito, famae vilipendio in omnem nequitiam prorumpunt. Quibus autem aliqua bonae mentis scintilla superest, veritatis patefactione ad emendationem vitae utuntur.
units.tr: 7. Sometimes the public complaint of the citizens, and the voice of men that cannot be restrained, is a sign of the truth. By this means Nero learned, from the judgement of the Roman plebs about the burning of Rome, that the blame had been laid upon him as its author. Neither by human help, nor by the prince's largesse, nor by appeasing the gods, did the infamy depart; the belief persisted that the fire had been ordered. Therefore, to put an end to the rumour, Nero handed over culprits and punished them with the most exquisite torments. &c., Annals book 15. Therefore those whose natures are incurable are better kept in ignorance of the truth than taught it. For either they cover up what has been discovered with new crimes, or, having cast off shame, they rush into every wickedness with contempt for their reputation. Those who still retain some spark of a good mind use the disclosure of the truth to amend their lives.

units.la: 8. Sunt qui per exploratores, quid homines de se sentiant, inquirant. Sed hi nec profutura semper principi aperiunt: & saepe falsa veris aggerendo, crudelitatem magis accendunt. Alii aut per tribunos, aut per domesticos & necessarios, aut ipsa denique populi concione advocata, rumorem de se & de publica utilitate sensum expiscantur. Verum indicia ea non incorrupta esse, bene a Germanico olim judicabatur. Tribunos & centuriones lata sapius, quam comperta nuntiare: libertorum servilia ingenia, amicis inesse
units.tr: 8. There are those who inquire through spies what men think of them. But these never report what would be useful to the prince, and often by heaping falsehoods upon truths they inflame his cruelty all the more. Others, through tribunes, or through household servants and intimates, or finally by summoning an assembly of the people itself, fish out the rumour about themselves and the feeling concerning the public good. That such reports are not sound was judged long ago by Germanicus: tribunes and centurions report what is heard more often than what is established; the servile natures of freedmen are inclined to flattery towards friends.

units.la: [Catchword: none printed.] adulationem : si concio vocetur, illic quoque, quæ passi- ci[?] incipiant, reliquos adstrepere. 2. Annalium.
units.tr: [Catchword: none printed.] Flattery. If an assembly is called, there too, whatever begins to be said here and there, the rest raise a clamour in agreement. Annals, book 2.

units.la: 9. Defectum omnium aliquando prophetæ, Dei missu severa voce intonantes, compensant. Herodi nihil nisi blandum audienti Johannes baptista obstre- pit: Non licet tibi habere uxorem fratris tui. Achabo in delictis suaviter dormitanti Elias: Tu es qui Israë- lem conturbas. Davidi in veternum conjecto Nathan: Tuesillehomo. Qua parrhefia an pastores ecclesiæ imitari prophetas debeant, & an par illorum fit po- testas; rursus an coram populo increpatio fieri de- beat; non est huius loci inquirere.
units.tr: 9. Prophets, sent by God, sometimes make up for the failings of all men by thundering with a severe voice. When Herod heard nothing but flattery, John the Baptist rebuked him: "It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife." When Ahab was pleasantly sleeping in his sins, Elijah said to him: "Are you the one who troubles Israel?" When David had fallen into drowsiness, Nathan said: "You are the man." Whether the ministers of the Church ought to imitate the prophets in this frankness [parrhesia, παρρησία], and whether their authority is equal to theirs, and again whether rebuke ought to be given before the people, is not a question for this place.

units.la: 10. Veri tamen cupidis, nec admonitori asperis, non defuturi sunt fideles promenda veritate & hone- state suadenda ministri. Sic Augusto non defuit A- grippa, Mæcenas, Athenodorus, & postremus omnium Varus. quo mortuo, ingemuisse Augustus dicitur, quod jam à quo verum audiret, nemo luperstes esset. Neroni autem Burrhus quidem & Seneca monitores erant, sed in vitia præcipiti non omne quod conduce- ret aperientes. Quare & conjurationis in se patrum, equitum, militum, virorum & fœminarum, tam diu ignarus fuit, & conjuratione oppressa senatus ulti- mum decretum non effugit. Ita veritatis occultandæ, & ex eo perniciei, culpa præcipua penes reges est. Qui vero veritatem non aspernantur, qui sapientiam ferio studio inquirunt, ab ea apprehendenda non aber- rabunt. Ego amantes mei amb[?], & studiose quærentes me inveniunt me: inquit divina sapientia, & ejus ore veritas. Prov. Salomonis VIII. v.17.
units.tr: 10. Yet for those who desire the truth, and are not harsh in admonishing, faithful ministers who will bring the truth forward and urge honesty will not be lacking. Thus Augustus did not lack Agrippa, Maecenas, Athenodorus, and, last of all, Varus. When he died, Augustus is said to have groaned that there was no longer anyone left from whom he could hear the truth. Nero, however, had Burrhus and Seneca as advisers, but they did not lay out everything that would have been useful, for he was rushing headlong into vice. Hence he was for so long unaware of the conspiracy against himself among senators, knights, soldiers, men and women alike, and when the conspiracy had been crushed, the senate did not escape his final decree. So the chief blame for hiding the truth, and for the ruin that follows from it, lies with kings. But those who do not spurn the truth, who earnestly seek wisdom, will not go astray in laying hold of it. I love those who love me, and those who seek me early shall find me, says divine wisdom, and the truth from her mouth. Proverbs of Solomon 8:17.

units.la: XLII.
units.tr: XLII.

units.la: Gratia superiorum pro merito.
units.tr: The favour of superiors according to merit.

units.la: In honoribus nimirum adipiscendis, & parte Reip. administranda, Poppæus Sabinus pro teste adduca- tur: modicum originis, principum amicitia consulatus ac triumphale decus adeptus; maximisque provinciis per quatuor & viginti annos impositus, nullam obexi- miam[?] artem, nec generis eum splendor, nec merita in patriam, nec magnæ spes virtutis commendabat. Et tamen multos natalibus illustres, multos meritis in rempublicam insignes, plurimos ingenio excellentes, animique magnitudine superiores, ut gratia principis, ita honorum adeptione anteibat. Quæ depravatio sæculi nec cum Tiberio orta est, nec cum eo sepulta. Ac Tiberius tamen, in hoc homine præ cæteris extollendo, aliquid secutus creditur. Plerosque alios casus, aut cæcus amor regit. Quod Tiberium ad amplexandum Sabinum impulit, est quod par negotiis, neque suprà erat. neque enim eminentes virtutes se-stabatur[?] & rursum vitia oderat. ex optimis periculum sibi; à pessimis dedecus publicum metuebat. ut ipsum Cornelius primo Annalium explicat. Legatis uti paribus tantum oneri, non superioribus; aut successus eorum ægris oculis intueri, non Tiberiani tantum moris fuit. A Iulio Cæsare ideo Labienus discessisse perhibetur, quod se ob virtutis præstantiam animo alieniori apud eum esse suspicaretur. Ventidium, Parthicæ arrogantiæ ternâ victoriâ malleum, non dissimulata offensione, loco ac dignitate Antonius dimovit. Sex. Pompeji classem cum delere apud Siciliam, aut magna saltem clade afficere, posset Agrippa; in fugam compulisse satis ratus, plenam victoriam Augusto reservavit. Nota est è sacro volumine Ioabi, in expugnatione Rabbæ Ammonitarum ampliata, a-stutia. 2.Sam.12. Non igitur vel novum quid Tiberius, vel præter omnem rationem, in fovendo præ ex-cellentioribus ingeniis Poppæo Sabino, commisit. Dabuntque operam callidi aulæ aut militiæ ministri, ne gloria virtutum suprà principem velle ascendere videantur. Se & rempublicam juvari eorum opera principes volunt; obscurari factorum amplitudine erubescunt.
units.tr: In obtaining offices and in administering a part of the commonwealth, Poppaeus Sabinus may be cited as a witness: of humble origin, he obtained the consulship and triumphal honour through the friendship of princes, and was placed over the greatest provinces for twenty-four years. Yet no outstanding skill, nor the splendour of his family, nor his services to the fatherland, nor great hopes of virtue commended him. And yet, while many men illustrious by birth, many distinguished for their services to the state, very many excellent in talent and superior in greatness of spirit, were surpassed by him in the favour of the prince, so too in the attainment of office. This corruption of the age did not arise with Tiberius, nor was it buried with him. And yet Tiberius is believed to have followed some motive in raising this man above the rest. Blind love governs most other such cases. What moved Tiberius to embrace Sabinus was that he was equal to the business and not above it. For he dreaded eminent virtues, as a danger to himself, and hated vices in turn, while from the best men he feared danger and from the worst public disgrace; as Cornelius Tacitus explains at the beginning of the Annals. To use legates who were equal to the burden, not superior to it, or to look with sick eyes upon their successes, was not peculiar to Tiberius. Labienus is said to have departed from Julius Caesar because he suspected that, on account of his outstanding virtue, he stood in a less friendly mind towards him. Antony removed Ventidius, the hammer of Parthian arrogance after three victories, from his post and rank, without concealing his offence. When Agrippa could have destroyed the fleet of Sextus Pompeius near Sicily, or at least inflicted a great defeat upon it, he thought it enough to drive it into flight, and reserved full victory for Augustus. The cunning of Joab at the storming of Rabbah of the Ammonites, recorded in the sacred volume, is well known. 2 Samuel 12. Therefore Tiberius did nothing new or contrary to all reason in favouring Poppaeus Sabinus over more excellent talents. Clever ministers of the court or the army will also take care not to seem to wish to rise above the prince by their virtuous deeds. Princes want to be aided by their services, both themselves and the commonwealth; they blush to be overshadowed by the greatness of their deeds.

units.la: XLIII.
units.tr: XLIII.

units.la: Cruenta pax lento bello miserior.
units.tr: A bloody peace is more wretched than a slow war.

units.la: Hic tantum viles mercenariorum animæ, & id raro concursu illic illustriores quotidiana fori tabe pereunt.
units.tr: Here only the base lives of mercenaries perish, and that rarely in combat; there the more illustrious perish through the daily wasting of the forum.

units.la: Hic calido conflictu sensum mortis eximente; illiq; prævio terrore, & manu carnificis intercunt. Hic nulla mortis infamia, sæpe & gloria vitæ pro bona causa effusæ; illic ignominia defunctum & hæredes, cum publicatione bonorum, sequitur. Tædet funerum; judiciaria lue cumulatorum, toties exempla recenseri: Si quid tamen aut poenæ genere, aut mortis constantia insignitum, manu ducente Tacito non præteribo.
