Eo jam cruditate morum perventum erat, ut locus carnificinæ curia, sanctus ille patrum confessus; effeti Vibulenus Agrippa equés Romanus, cum peroraffent accusatores, in ipsa curia depromptum sinu venenum hausit: prolapfuque at moribundus, festinatis lictoris, rum manibus in carcerem raptus est, faucesque jam examinis laqueo vexata. Ne mori quidem suo arbitrio miseris concessum: & mors quæ laqueum & manus lictorum fugeret invidebatur. Quin & ad regum corpora accusatoria pestis, non exemptæ supplicio su-prema dignitate, pervasit. Ne Tigranes quidem Armenia quondam potitus, ac tunc reus, nomine regio supplicia civium effugit. Quod vero sequitur, C.Gal- bam consularem, & duos Blæfios voluntario exitu cecidisse: constantiæ monumenta, ex illorum temporum judicio, forent. Sed clariora constantiæ in exemplo tremis pignora, à Pifoniana in Neronem conjuratione accersita, referam.
units.tr: Here, in a hot clash, the sense of death is taken away, and men perish by the terror that goes before it and by the executioner's hand. Here no infamy attends death, and often a life poured out for a good cause brings glory; there the dead man is followed by disgrace, and his heirs too, with the confiscation of his goods. I am weary of funerals and of recounting so many examples from the judicial plague that heaped up victims. Still, if anything stands out either for the kind of punishment or for constancy in death, I will not pass it over, since Tacitus leads the way. Matters had reached such a pitch of cruelty that the place of execution was the senate house, that holy assembly of the Fathers. When the accusers had finished speaking, Vibulenus Agrippa, a Roman knight, drew poison from his bosom in the very senate house and drank it. He fell dying, and the lictors' hurried hands dragged him to prison, his throat already tormented by the noose. Not even to die by their own choice was this granted to wretched men, and death that escaped the noose and the lictors' hands was grudged them. Indeed the accusing plague spread even to the bodies of kings, whose supreme dignity was no protection from punishment. Not even Tigranes, once master of Armenia and then a defendant, escaped the punishments of citizens by the name of king. As for what follows, that the consular Gaius Galba and two Blaesii fell by a voluntary exit, these would be monuments of constancy by the judgement of those times. But I will cite the clearer pledges of constancy, three examples drawn from the Pisonian conspiracy against Nero.

units.la: Epicharis, quam libertini generis mulierem Tacitus, Polyænus scortum fuisse memorat, ad indicium extorquendum tormentis dilacerari jubebatur. At ille lam non verbera, non ignes, nec vira eo acriusa torquentium, ne a fœmina ferventur, pervicere quin objecta denegaret. xv. Annal. nam quæ de voluntaria morte sequuntur, pro constantia admiratione non adduco.
units.tr: Epicharis, whom Tacitus calls a freedwoman and Polyaenus says was a prostitute, was ordered to be torn apart with torments to extort information from her. But neither blows, nor fire, nor the fiercer efforts of the torturers could bring her to confess; she kept denying the charges. As for what follows about her voluntary death, I do not cite it as an example to be admired for constancy. Annals 15.

units.la: Post hanc Plautius Lateranus, raptus in locum fervi libus poenis sepultum, manu Statii tribuni trucidatur, plenus conflantia silentii, nec tribuno objiciens eandem conscientiam. Annæi Senecæ in ultimis, ad quæ fe diu hortulano secessu præparaverat, constantiam quid attinet referre? Illud præter scopum adjungo: non omniomnibus cum autoribus insontem criminis à Nerone insimulati obiisse. Polyaenus certe, libro VIII. strata-gem. in primo conjuratorum loco cum ponit. Πίσων [?] καὶ Σενέκας [?] ἐπιβουλὰς [?] συνεστήσαντο [?] πρὸς Νέρωνα [?]. i. e. Piso & Seneca insidias in Neronem struxerunt. Polyaeno Dio Cassius accedit, ὁ δὲ δὴ Σεῦνος [?] καὶ ὁ Ῥοῦφος [?] ἐπιβουλῆς [?] τινὲς [?] τῷ Νέρωνι [?]. Seneca autem & Rufus praefectus, & alii quidam illustrium virorum, insidias Neroni struxerunt. Sed ad institutum revertor. Paulinam, mortis nisi coercita fuisset sociam, ita maritus alloquitur: Vita delinimenta monstraveram tibi, tu mortis decus mavis. non invidebo exemplo. Sit hujus tam fortis exitus constantia penes utrosque par, claritudinis plus in tuo sine. Subrius deinde Flavius admonitus fortiter protendere cervicem: Utinam, ait, tu tam fortiter fe-rias. Proximum constantiae exemplum, Sulpicius Asper centurio praebuit. percontanti Neroni, cur in caedem suam conspiravisset? breviter respondens: Non aliter tot flagitiis ejus subveniri posse. Quod & XLI. aphorismo dictum inferas. Plura Nerone imperante constantis obitus exempla qui desiderat, è XVI. Annalium libro depromat.
units.tr: After her, Plautius Lateranus, dragged to the place reserved for the burial of slaves who suffered servile punishments, was put to death by the hand of the tribune Statius, full of constancy and silence, and did not implicate the tribune in the same guilt. What is the point of recounting the constancy of Annaeus Seneca at his end, for which he had long prepared himself by retiring to his garden? I add this beside my aim: not all authors agree that he died innocent of the crime with which Nero charged him. Polyaenus, at any rate, in Book 8 of his Stratagems, places him first among the conspirators: Piso and Seneca [Πίσων καὶ Σενέκας ἐπιβουλὰς συνεστήσαντο πρὸς Νέρωνα] formed plots against Nero. Dio Cassius agrees with Polyaenus: But Seneca and Rufus [ὁ δὲ δὴ Σεῦνος καὶ ὁ Ῥοῦφος ἐπιβουλῆς τινὲς τῷ Νέρωνι] , some of the conspirators against Nero. Seneca, he says, and Rufus the prefect, and certain other men of distinction, laid plots against Nero. But I return to my subject. Her husband addresses Paulina, who would have shared his death had she not been restrained: I had shown you the comforts of life, but you prefer the glory of death. I will not grudge you the example. Let the constancy of so brave an exit be equal in both of you; there is more renown in yours. Then Subrius Flavus, reminded to stretch out his neck bravely, said: Would that you struck so bravely. The nearest example of constancy was given by Sulpicius Asper, the centurion. When Nero asked him why he had conspired to kill him, he answered briefly: Not otherwise could so many of his crimes be remedied. You may infer this is also said in aphorism 41. Whoever desires more examples of constant deaths under Nero's rule should draw them from Book 16 of the Annals.

units.la: XLIV.
units.tr: XLIV.

units.la: Non quaevis natio publicae libertatis est patiens.
units.tr: Not every nation is capable of public liberty.

units.la: Publicam libertatem aut plenam capio, aut à supe-riori autoritate pendentem. Illa est, quae nescia alieni plena, imperii, suo se arbitrio, suis legibus gubernat. Ista quae libertate ab externo imperio delibata, in caeteris po-pulo[?] imperii summam, aut ἰσηγορίαν [?] permittit. Haec ut suo libramine subsistat, multo etiam magis quae ad plenam libertatem anhelat, potentiam & opum ac hominum armis ferendis aptorum multitudinem requirit: nec sunt spernenda civitatis aggesta munimenta, quae nihil sunt, nisi ingenium libertatis tuendae appetens, ut olim Graecanicae nationis, accedat. Quae omnia Seleucia, pro captu illius loci, retinuit. civitas potens, septa muris, neque in barbarum cœrru-pta, sed conditoris Seleuci retinens. Formam deinde rei-publicæ Seleucensis, politeiæ Aristotelicæ, ex Aristocratia & Democratia permixtæ, proximè accedentem Cornelius describit. Trecenti opibus aut sapientia dicti di-lecti, ut senatus: sua populo vis. ne consiliorum vulgatio, actionum confusio nasceretur; austrictiori numero rerum gubernaculum commiserat. ne liber-tas in dubium veniret, sua vis populo permansit. Senatum autem vel ab opibus legebant, ut imperio autoritas, ut otii facultas adesset; vel à sapientia, ne umbræ hominum, aut statuis Mercurialibus, respublica commutaretur. Sed hoc in populari statu, aut inter populum & optimates divisio, incommodi, quod ex æmulatione imperii gerendi facilè discordia obrepit; discordia latus nudatum potentiori vicino objicit. quo-ties concordes agunt, spernitur Parthus: ubi dissenserit, dum sibi quisque contra æmulos subsidium vocant, ac-citus in partem, adversus omnes valescit. Quod li-bertatis populi venenum nunquam nimis suspicitur, nunquam fatis cavetur. Cavendum in primis iis civitatibus, quæ in tutelam aliquo recepto, lubrico inter clientelam & servitutem, seu plenam subjectionem, gradu vacillant. Ad lites dirimendas patronus vocatus, paulatim ad jus dicendum, inde ad leges ferendas progreditur. Sed &, quod minùs crebrò, non minùs periculosè accidit, regis alicujus aut populi, nullum protectionis jus adepti, armata potentia in partem non vocanda. Periculum enim subest, ne aut incendio oleum subjiciat, aut parte altera oppressa, adversus omnes insurgat. Romani adversus Arvernos & Sequanos ab Æduis, Germani adversus Æduos à Sequanis, iterum Julius Cæsar adversus Ariovistum, in subsidium vocati, claris exemplis monitum nostrum illu-strent. Sed plena est Græcanica, plena Romana, plena barbara historia triftioribus invocati auxilii eventis. Concordiæ igitur, & publicæ tranquillitati, & imperantium parentiumque consensioni, vel libertatis tu-endæ causa, studendum. Sua senatui autoritas non adimenadimenda, nec imperantium superbia plebecula op-primenda. Denique quod publicum est, ad se pars al-tera ne rapiat. Quod si crasis diu subsistere nequive-rit, ut est difficilis mixturae imperii perpetuitas, quo-rum nam manu civitatis jura tradenda? paucorumne an multitudinis? de libertatis contra externam poten-tiam firma defensione loquor. Pro populo Tacitus, contra paucorum dominationem, decidit. Artabanus plebem primoribus tradidit ex suo usu. nam populi im-perium, juxta libertatem: paucorum dominatio, regia libidini propior est. Servire enim ditioribus plures condocefacti, nec regium imperium aspernabuntur. Et comiter unum externae nationis observare, dum li-bidinem dominandi in cives effundant, pauci non de-dignantur. Ea enim natura est mortalium, ut domina-ri quam ex aequo cum multis vivere, & unum observare, quam non multis praeesse malint. Quae causa est, cur tam pauca sint hodie, etiam in potentioribus nationibus, libertatis vestigia. Nec Tiridates, qui Artabano armorum jure successit, id ignoravit. Ut enim civitati potenti gratificaretur, ut se diversorum ab Artabano morum, nec libertatis publicae insidiatorem, ostenderet, rem Seleucensem populo permisit. Quod nisi gratum universo populo, nisi applausum in novo regno mereri praevidisset, nunquam id vel in gratiam Romanorum facturus fuisset.
units.tr: I understand public liberty either as full, or as dependent on a higher authority. The first is that which, ignorant of foreign rule, governs itself by its own judgement and its own laws. The second is that which, having tasted liberty while subject to a foreign empire, allows the people a share in sovereignty or equality of speech. So that this may stand on its own balance, a state that pants for full liberty requires power, and a multitude of men fit to bear arms; nor are the fortifications of a city to be despised, which are nothing unless the spirit of defending liberty, such as once belonged to the Greek nation, is present. Seleucia retained all these things according to the measure of that place: a powerful city, enclosed by walls, not fallen into barbarism, but keeping the character of its founder Seleucus. Cornelius then describes the form of the Seleucian commonwealth, which comes closest to Aristotle's polity, mixed from aristocracy and democracy: Three hundred were chosen for their wealth or wisdom, as the senate; the power remained with the people. So that the counsels would not be divulged and actions thrown into confusion, they had committed the helm of government to a smaller number; so that liberty would not be called into doubt, the power remained with the people. They chose the senators either from wealth, so that there would be authority in command and leisure for office, or from wisdom, so that the commonwealth would not be changed into the shadows of men or into statues of Mercury. But in a popular state, or in a division between the people and the nobles, there is this disadvantage: discord easily creeps in from rivalry over governing, and discord exposes the weakened flank to a stronger neighbour. When they act in harmony, the Parthian is despised; when they disagree, each calls in help against his rivals, and the one who is summoned into the quarrel grows strong against all. The poison of popular liberty is never suspected enough, and never guarded against enough. Especially to be guarded against are those states which, having received a protector, totter on the slippery step between clientage and slavery, or full subjection. A patron is called in to settle disputes, and gradually advances to pronouncing judgement, and from there to enacting laws. But there is also another danger, less frequent yet no less perilous: a people that has acquired no right of protection must not be drawn into a quarrel by the armed power of some king or people. For there is danger that he will pour oil on the fire, or, once one side is crushed, will rise against all. The Romans against the Arverni and Sequani, called in by the Aedui; the Germans against the Aedui, called in by the Sequani; and again Julius Caesar against Ariovistus, called in for help: these clear examples illustrate our warning. But Greek history is full, Roman history is full, and barbarian history is full of the sad outcomes of help that was invoked. Therefore we must strive for concord, for public tranquillity, and for the agreement of rulers and ruled, or for the defence of liberty. The senate's authority must not be taken away, nor the common people crushed by the arrogance of rulers. Finally, let neither part seize for itself what belongs to the public. But if such a mixture cannot last long, since a mixed government is hard to keep in perpetual balance, into whose hands are the rights of the state to be surrendered: those of a few or of the multitude? I speak of a firm defence of liberty against foreign power. Tacitus decides for the people, against the domination of a few. Artabanus handed the common people over to the nobles for his own advantage; for the rule of the people is close to liberty, but the rule of a few is closer to royal lust. For many who have been taught to serve the wealthier will not disdain a royal rule, and a few are not ashamed to serve courteously one foreign ruler, provided they can vent their lust for domination against their fellow citizens. For such is the nature of mortals: they would rather rule than live on equal terms with many, and rather serve one than be set over many. This is why, even among the more powerful nations today, there are so few traces of liberty. Nor was Tiridates, who succeeded Artabanus in arms, ignorant of this. In order to please the powerful city, and to show that he differed from Artabanus in his manners and was no enemy of public liberty, he left the affairs of Seleucia to the people. Unless he had foreseen that this would be pleasing to the whole people, and would win applause in his new kingdom, he would never have done it, not even to gratify the Romans.

units.la: XLV.
units.tr: XLV.

units.la: Et celeritate & procrastinatione peccatur.
units.tr: Both haste and procrastination are faults.

units.la: Celeritate: actiones nondum remotis impedimen-tis praecipitando. Procrastinatione: summa rerum o-missa, in levibus haerendo, aut dies ignavo otio teren-do. Tiriditates in regni adeptione & festinatione, & cunctatione, impegit. Nam contra Phrahatis & Hie-ronis, qui validissimas praefecturas obtinebant, brevis morae petitionem, Surena patrio more Tiridatem insigni regio evinxit. quod iis qui diademati imponendo non interfuerant metum, & ex eo res novandi cupiditacem injecit. Quod fi jam dubitationem praevenisset, viscera regni intrando: omnes in consensum traxisset. Assidendo castellum, in quod pecuniam & pellices, Arta-banus contulerat, dedit spatium exuendi pacta[?]. Castelli obsidio legato committi poterat, regem hic tempus extrahere, & regno novo inutile, & majestati indecorum fuit. De belli impetu, & victoriarum cursu, obsidione diuturno non hebetando, alibi commodius dicetur.
units.tr: By haste, when a man rushes into actions before the obstacles have been removed. By procrastination, when he neglects the chief matters, clings to trifles, or wastes his days in lazy idleness. Tiridates stumbled in gaining the kingdom through both haste and hesitation. For when Phrahates and Hieron, who held the most powerful commands, asked for a short delay, Surena, in the native manner, invested Tiridates with the royal insignia. This struck fear into those who had not been present at the placing of the diadem and from that fear aroused a desire for revolution. If he had forestalled their doubts by entering the heart of the kingdom at once, he would have drawn them all into agreement. By besieging the fortress into which Artabanus had moved his money and concubines, he gave him time to cast off the agreements [?]. The siege of the fortress could have been entrusted to a legate; for the king to prolong matters there was both useless for the new kingdom and unbecoming to his majesty. The impetus of war and the course of victories, which a lengthy siege would not blunt, will be discussed more fittingly elsewhere.

units.la: XLVI. Amoris frequentior quàm odii simulatio.
units.tr: XLVI. Feigned love is more frequent than feigned hatred.

units.la: In consiliis dandis, accipiendisve, in re aliqua impetranda vel nobis offerenda, spectandum, quo quis erga nos animo, quo erga alios affectu, vel qua rei postulatae indigentia, loquatur. Adversa Tiridati factio ad Artabanum, in Hyrcanis magna illuvie degentem, Parthorum non postremi reddendae dominationi venere. Fide non statim eorum sermoni Artabanus habita, qua repentina mutatio exquirit, nec enim eam legationem fine mutatione, nec mutationem rerum fine gravi animorum conversione, nec banc fine causa esse posse, vetus regnandi providit. Tum Hiero pueritiam regis increpat: neque penes Arsacidem imperium, sed inane nomen apud imbellem externa mollitia, vim in Abdagefis domo. Tres non levis momenti visae deserti regis causae. 1. infirma viribus & autoritate aetas. 2. mollis vitae apud Romanos actae cultus. 3. in Abdagefis regis moderatorem invidia. Postremam causam ut motu efficacissimam Artabanus arripiens, pro imperandi usu intellexit, falsos in amore, odia nonfingere. Plures amore quàm odio simulato, credentibus imponunt. Prioris membri illustrem nobis probationem Caesar, v. libro de bello Gallico, suppeditat. Ambiorix Eburonum regulus, cum hyberna Q. Titurii Sabini, & L. Aurunculeji Cottae, legatorum Caesaris, vi subita adortus, expugnare non potuit; ad fallacias, & ad verba Romanis danda, se convertit. Pro Caesaris in fe beneficiis, plurimum fe ei debere confitetur, neque fe aut judicio, aut sua voluntate, castra Romana oppugnavisse. ejusmodi sua esse imperia, ut non minus in fe haberet juris multitudo, quam ipse in multitudinem habeat. eam repentinae Gallorum conjurationi resistere nequivisse. omnibus hibernis Cæsaris oppugnandis hunc esse, Gallorum omnium consensu, dictum diem. Communi patriae quoniam pro pietate satisfeçerit: habere fe nunc rationem officii. pro beneficiis Cæsarem monere, orare Titium pro hospitio, ut suae ac militum saluti consulat. magnam manum Germanorum conductam Rhenum transiisse: hanc biduo affore. fi hinc abire tempestive velint, tutum fe iter per fines suos daturum. quod cum faciat; & civitati sese hibernis levatae consulere, & Cæsari pro ejus meritis gratiam referre. Hac fistula ad irritiendas Romanas aquilas, ab aucupe fallaciarum pleno, inflata; quam res levissima effet, autore hoste de summis rebus consilium capere; tamen sententia Sabini, qui profectionem suadebat, pervicit. Consilium igitur inimicissimi hominis, amica oratione fallentis, securi, insidiis in valle circumventi, ad unum fere omnes truci-dantur.
units.tr: In giving or receiving counsel, and in obtaining something or in what is offered to us, we must consider with what disposition someone speaks to us, with what feeling towards others, and from what need of the matter requested. The faction hostile to Tiridates came to Artabanus, who was living in the Hyrcanian wilds in great squalor, to offer him the rule of the Parthians, and they were no mean men. Artabanus, who from long experience of ruling foresaw that this embassy could not come without a change, nor a change without a serious shift of minds, nor this without a cause, did not at once give their words credence, which seeks a sudden change. Then Hiero rebukes the boyhood of the king: the empire is not in the hands of the Arsacid, but he is an empty name among an unwarlike people softened by foreign luxury, and the power lies in the house of Abdageses. Three causes of the king's desertion seemed of no slight weight: (1) an age weak in strength and authority; (2) the soft manner of life led among the Romans; (3) the envy of the king towards the governor of the house of Abdageses. Artabanus, seizing the last cause as the most effective to move, understood from the practice of ruling that feigned love and not feigned hatred is the way to deceive. More men are imposed upon by feigned love than by feigned hatred, when they are believing. Caesar, in the book on the Gallic War, supplies us with an illustrious proof of the former part. Ambiorix, the petty king of the Eburones, when he suddenly attacked the winter quarters of Q. Titurius Sabinus and L. Aurunculeius Cotta, legates of Caesar, could not take them by force; he turned to tricks and to words to give to the Romans. Pleading Caesar's benefits to himself, he confesses that he owes him very much, and that he did not attack the Roman camp by his own judgment or will. Such were his commands that the multitude had no less right over him than he has over the multitude. He could not resist the sudden conspiracy of the Gauls. The day for attacking all of Caesar's winter quarters was set, by the consent of all the Gauls. Since he had satisfied his duty to his common country through piety, he now has regard for his obligation: out of gratitude for Caesar's benefits, he warns him and begs Titurius, for the sake of hospitality, to consult the safety of himself and his soldiers. A great band of hired Germans, he says, had crossed the Rhine, and would be there within two days. If the Romans wish to leave in time, he will give them a safe route through his territory; by doing so he will both provide for his own state, relieved of the winter quarters, and repay Caesar with thanks for his merits. This pipe, blown by a fowler full of deceits to provoke the Roman eagles, though it was a very slight thing to take counsel on the highest matters from the word of an enemy, nevertheless prevailed by the opinion of Sabinus, who urged departure. Thus the counsel of the most hostile man, deceiving with friendly speech, was trusted, and they were surrounded in an ambush in a valley and slaughtered almost to a man.

units.la: Mirus amoris fingendi artifex Nero, qua no-cte matrem perditurus erat, fecundas parentum iracundias, & placandum animum spargit. Sermone hoc allectae, blandimento metum eximit: comiter exceptam, supra fe collocat. Suavi sermone tracto in longum convictu, prosequitur abeuntem, artius oculis & pectori haerens. xiv. Annalium. Idem Seneca blandissima oratione excepto, adjicit complexum & oscula, factus natura & consuetudine exercitus velare o-dium fallacibus blanditiis. eodem Annalium volumine.
units.tr: Nero, a wonderful artificer of feigned love, on the night he was about to destroy his mother, scatters flattering words about the anger of parents and soothes her spirit. Captivated by this speech, she is set at ease by his flatteries; he receives her kindly and places her above himself. After a long and pleasant conversation, he escorts her as she leaves, clinging to her more closely with his eyes and breast. Annals, book 14. The same Seneca, having received her with the most flattering speech, adds an embrace and kisses, made by nature and practice to veil hatred with deceitful flatteries. In the same volume of the Annals.

units.la: Sed quid in his, quae prope quaestionem non attingunt, vaga oratione feror? De subditorum in imperantes, & imperantium primos ministros, ficto amore agitur. Verum enim vero si facile a superioribus erga humiliores, ab hoste in hostem, amorem fingi demon-stratum est; in amoris & admirationis erga superiores[?] probanda simulatione non laborabitur. Si enim id quod minùs animo concipitur, verum fuerit; verum erit & illud, quod facilè animo persuadetur. In tanta igitur adulantium, adstrepentium, dicta & facta admi-rantium multitudine, ut in circumfusa probationum nebula, exemplis congerendis parco.
units.tr: But why do I wander in a rambling discourse over things that hardly touch the question? The matter concerns feigned love of subjects towards rulers, and of rulers towards their first ministers. Indeed, if it has been shown to be easy for superiors to feign love towards humbler men, and for enemy to feign it towards enemy, then there will be no labour in proving feigned love and admiration towards superiors. For if what is less readily conceived in the mind is true, then that also is true which is easily persuaded to the mind. Therefore, in so great a multitude of flatterers, of those applauding and admiring words and deeds, I spare the gathering of examples, as if in a cloud of proofs spread all around.

units.la: Secundum Artabani sententiæ membrum fuit, Odia non fingi: inferiorum nimirum erga superiores. Nam erga pares quorumquisque[?] levium hominum est, qui non in alterius gratiam odia nonnunquam fingat. Titium Sempronio odio esse quis odoratur: & se averso in Titium animo coram Sempronio fingit. Sed filo[?] orationis ultra debitum protracto, nolo in hac materia diducenda ultrà molestus esse.
units.tr: The second part of Artabanus's saying was that hatreds are not feigned, namely those of inferiors towards superiors. For towards equals it is the habit of light men to feign hatreds at times, to win another's favour. Someone sniffs out that Titius is hated by Sempronius, and in Sempronius's presence he pretends his mind is turned against Titius. But since the thread of my discourse has been drawn out beyond what is due, I do not wish to be any more tiresome in unfolding this matter.

units.la: XLVII Occasione fervidè utendum.
units.tr: XLVII. The opportunity must be seized eagerly.

units.la: Quæ si in diem prolatetur, non eadem se facie semper, non ansâ eâdem offeret. Artabanus cognita Parthorum in se inclinatione, & fluxa erga Tiridatem fide, non ultrà moratus, quàm dum Scytharum auxilia conciret, pergit properus, & prævenientes inimicorum astus, amicorum pœnitentiam. Duo sunt tempora, quibus celeritate adhibenda opus videtur: aut summa rei benè gerendæ occasione, aut re in extremum discrimen adducta. Utrumque temporum momentum oscitantiam, & diuturnam deliberationem, dedigna-tur. Prioris momenti exemplum verbis Cornelii deprompsimus. Posterioris Q.Cicero, in Nerviis ab Ambiorige castra assultante oppugnatus, & à Cæsare summo discrimine ereptus, præbebit. Cæsar unum communis salutis auxilium in celeritate ponebat, venit magnis itineribus in Nerviorum fines. &c. libro v. De bello Gallico.
units.tr: If the matter is put off until another day, it will not present itself with the same face or the same handle. Artabanus, having learned that the Parthians were leaning towards him and that Tiridates' loyalty was unreliable, did not delay beyond the time it took to call up the Scythian auxiliaries. He hastens on, forestalling the enemy's stratagems and the regret of his friends. There are two moments when speed seems to be required: either when the highest opportunity for successfully conducting an affair is at hand, or when the matter has been brought to the point of extreme peril. Each of these moments scorns idleness and long deliberation. I have taken an example of the first from the words of Cornelius. Q. Cicero, attacked in his camp by Ambiorix among the Nervii and rescued by Caesar from the greatest danger, will supply an example of the second. Caesar placed the one help for their common safety in speed; he came by forced marches into the territory of the Nervii, &c. Book v of the Gallic War.

units.la: Sed quid Cæsarem adduco, qui non ubique exspectata necessitate, summa belli confi-ciendi celeritate usus fuisse perhibetur. Nimirum illi, ad altissima quæque contendenti, nihil procrastinan-dum fuit.
units.tr: But why do I bring forward Caesar, who is reported to have used the greatest speed in finishing a war, not always waiting for the necessity to arrive? Clearly, for him, hastening towards every lofty goal, nothing was to be put off.

units.la: XLVIII.
units.tr: XLVIII.

units.la: Ars regia est, animorum expugnatio.
units.tr: The royal art is the conquest of minds.

units.la: Non enim armis, quod gladiatorium est, omnia committenda. Nec subditos armis conterere, regi futuro gloriosum. Artes, quibus Artabanus popu-lum rebellem reduxit sunt 1. mota sui commiseratio. 2. fraus. 3. preces. finis propinquior, dubiorum illectio, promptorum confirmatio: neque exuerat padorem, ut vulgum miseratione adverteret, non fraus, non preces: nihil omissum, quo ambiguos illiceret, prompti firmarentur. Irae leniendae commiseratio movetur: commiserationem ciet summae fortunae in imam praecipitatio. Quo argumento Athenienses, clade ad Syracusas comminuti, rerum conversionem sperabant. Regum vero extrema conditio quamvis hostiles animos in miserationem vertit. Nec tamen uni sit fulcro innitendum, ut non eo lapsuro de alio cogitetur. Fraus igitur vel illiciendis in dissensionem inimicis, vel quovis alio modo (infinita enim sunt fraudis genera) adhibetur. Nec precum reges, ab altera forte in meliorem transituros, pudeat. Non earum Davidem, generosum virum, & subditorum injuria regno depulsum puduit. 2. Sam. 19. Praeter has Artabani machinas, & aliae, expugnandis aliorum animis, torqueri queant. Ex his est trepidatio injecta: aut contra beneficentia, blandimentum, clementia. Clementia Julius Caesar, victarum sanguini parcendo, militum Pompejanorum, & civium ambiguorum animos expugnavit. Blandimentis Absalom, Hebraeis patri abstrahendis, pugnavit. 2. Sam. 15. v. 5. Beneficentia, annona nimirum curanda, & theatrorum effuso sumptu, Augustus in animos civium irrepsit. Beneficentia prisci Romani, nondum imperio ad unum delato, ad summos honores enisi sunt. Beneficentia Augustum secuti imperatores, nummis dubio militi divide ndis, regnum sibi firmarunt. Beneficentia Medicaeus, inopum miseria levanda, scholis & templis erigendis , imperium Florentiæ & universæ Hetruriæ quæsivit. Validissimum igitur domandis animis telum, ferro multò potentius, beneficentia. Contrà terrore verbis injecto, regum non infimi nutantem principio regni potentiam stabilierunt. De Saule 1. Sam. 11.v.7. De Jehu 2.Reg.10.v.3. Sed quia de blandioribus expugnandorum animorum tormentis hic agimus, ista non amplius urgemus.
units.tr: Not everything should be entrusted to arms, which is the business of gladiators. Nor is it glorious for a future king to crush his subjects by force. The arts by which Artabanus brought his rebellious people back were: (1) arousing pity for himself; (2) deceit; (3) entreaties. The nearer aim was to entice the wavering and strengthen the willing. He did not put off shame in order to win the crowd by pity, and he left out neither deceit nor entreaties: nothing was omitted by which he might entice the doubtful and confirm the ready. Pity is stirred to soften anger, and a fall from the highest fortune to the lowest arouses pity. By this argument the Athenians, broken at Syracuse, hoped for a change of fortune. Indeed, the extreme plight of kings turns even hostile minds to pity. Yet one should not lean on a single prop, but think of another in case the first gives way. So deceit is used, either to set enemies at odds or in any other way (for the kinds of deceit are endless). Nor should kings be ashamed to beg, in case they may one day pass to a better state. David, a noble man, was not ashamed of such entreaties when he was driven from his kingdom by the wrong done by his subjects (2 Sam. 19). Besides these devices of Artabanus, others may be turned to the conquest of men's minds. Among them is the striking of fear; or, on the contrary, kindness, flattery and clemency. By clemency Julius Caesar conquered the minds of Pompeian soldiers and of wavering citizens, by sparing the blood of the vanquished. By flattery Absalom fought to draw the Hebrews away from their father (2 Sam. 15:5). By kindness, namely by providing for the grain supply and by lavish spending on the theatres, Augustus crept into the minds of the citizens. The early Romans, before power had been handed to one man, strove for the highest honours by kindness. The emperors who followed Augustus strengthened their rule by distributing money to a soldiery whose loyalty was doubtful. By kindness the Medici, relieving the misery of the poor and building schools and churches, sought power in Florence and in all Tuscany. Kindness, then, is by far the most powerful weapon for taming minds, far stronger than iron. On the other hand, by inspiring terror with words, some of the greater kings made secure a power that was wavering at the start of their reign (of Saul, 1 Sam. 11:7; of Jehu, 2 Kings 10:3). But since we are here dealing with the gentler tortures for conquering minds, we will not press these matters further.

units.la: XLIX.
units.tr: XLIX.

units.la: Rex populi defertor proditionis crimine cives exsolvit.
units.tr: A king who deserts his people releases the citizens from the charge of treachery.

units.la: Non eni[m] [illegible, ~6 letters] ciente lupum pastore, gregi fugere, aut alium custodem circumspicere, illicitum. Artaba-no armis in regnum irrumpente, & fraude præter armorum terrorem, omnia permiscente, deliberabatur à Tiridate, impetu bellum an contatione[?] gereretur. Aliis conflictus & festinati casus placebant. Alii ob-jecto amne sociales copias exspectandas censebant, in prompto ad periculà Tiridate, sententia quæ vide-batur tutior electa. Sed quia fugæ speciem discessum, multi bellatorum domos dilabebantur, vel ad Artaba-num transfibant. donec Tiridates cum paucis in Syriam, revectus, pudore proditionis omnes exsolvit. non tantum eos, qui defecerant, culpæ pudore; sed & post fugam transituros culpa exemit. Arctiori[?] enim fide, quod ad defensionem mutuam, protectorem in tutelam receptis, quàm isti protectori, obligatur. Et regem, quidem pro subditis mortem oppetere, divini & humani juris est: subditos autem omnes pro rege ju-gulum secandum præbere, nullo jure mandatur. Hæc ita sunt, fuga Davidis perfidiæ culpa, qui Absalomem sequebantur, exsoluti sunt? non arbitramur exsolutos. non enim in eadem causa David, qua Tirida-tes, fuit: nec Hebræi cum Parthis pari erga regnan-tem innocentia. 1, David tot meritis in patriam, & populi à circumjectis hostibus multifaria liberatione, ut in extrema senectute deserĕretur[?], non meruerat, Tiridatis nullum dum benefactum erga patriam ex-stabat. stabat; & animi imbecillitas, regno tanto frenando inidonea, prima se fronte prodebat. 2. Davidem annis provectum, nec aliena sapientia nitentem, Israelitae; Tiridatem puerum Parthi, & ab eunuchi regimine pendentem, deserebant. 3. Absalomi ante excessum Davidis illi adhaerebant; hi, praeter alteram factionem, rebus jam desperatis recedebant. 4. David redeundi animum non abjiciebat, ducem exercitus & fidos palatii satellites, secum ducebat. quod caput est discriminis: non in alienam regionem, sed suae non ignobilem appendicem, se conferebat. Tiridates nec redeundi animo, nec fido comitatu, in Syriam provinciam Parthis hostilem, revehebatur. 5. Denique David manum conferre, & de regni possessione decertare, non cunctabatur: Tiridates, cum spe fiduciam, cum armis animum abjecit. Perfidi igitur Israelitae; excusanda Davidis fuga. quamvis melius, meo judicio, objicienda hosti Sionis porta, animis civium confirmandis, praetoria cohorte animanda, facturus videbatur. Davide graviori culpa purgato; erat quid de Casimiri Poloni secessu, quid de Polonorum quorundam, & post eos Borussorum, qui sociali aut clientelari fide regibus devincti sunt, defectione promerem: nisi temporum horum controversiis interponendum judicium subterfugerem.
units.tr: For it is not permitted for the flock, when the shepherd sees the wolf, to flee or to look round for another guardian [illegible, ~6 letters]. When Artabanus was breaking into the kingdom with arms, and with fraud, besides the terror of arms, throwing everything into confusion, Tiridates deliberated whether the war should be waged by attack or by delay. Some liked pitched battles and hasty encounters. Others thought that, with a river put between them, the allied forces should be awaited, Tiridates being ready for dangers; this opinion, which seemed the safer, was chosen. But because the withdrawal had the look of flight, many of the soldiers slipped away home or went over to Artabanus, until Tiridates, carried back into Syria with a few men, released them all from their oath by the shame of his treachery. He freed from the blame of guilt not only those who had already deserted, but also those who would go over after the flight. For subjects received under protection are bound by a closer faith, in mutual defence, to that protector. That the king should face death for his subjects is of divine and human law; but that all subjects should offer their throats to be cut for the king is commanded by no law. Since this is so, were those who followed Absalom released from the guilt of treachery by David's flight? We do not think they were released. For David was not in the same case as Tiridates, nor were the Hebrews, toward their reigning king, in the same innocence as the Parthians. (1) David had not deserved, by so many services to his country and by his many-fold liberation of the people from surrounding enemies, to be deserted in extreme old age; Tiridates had as yet no good deed to his country to show, and the weakness of his spirit, unfit to curb so great a kingdom, showed itself at first sight. (2) The Israelites deserted David, now advanced in years and relying on no foreign wisdom; the Parthians deserted Tiridates, a boy dependent on the rule of an eunuch. (3) The adherents of Absalom went over to him before David's departure; these men, apart from the other faction, were leaving when affairs were already despaired of. (4) David did not give up the intention of returning; he took with him the commander of the army and the faithful bodyguard of the palace. This is the chief point of difference: he betook himself not into a foreign region but into a not ignoble appendage of his own. Tiridates was carried back into Syria, a province hostile to the Parthians, with neither the intention of returning nor a faithful escort. (5) Lastly, David did not hesitate to join battle and contend for possession of the kingdom; Tiridates, with his hope gone, cast away his confidence, and with his arms, his spirit. The Israelites were therefore faithless, and David's flight is to be excused, although, in my judgment, he would have done better to close the gate of Zion against the enemy, to strengthen the minds of the citizens, and to animate them with his praetorian cohort. With David cleared of the graver fault, there was something to be said about the withdrawal of Casimir of Poland, and about the defection of certain Poles and, after them, of the Prussians, who are bound to their kings by an allied or clientage faith; but I would be shirking the judgment that these controversies of our times require.

units.la: L. Gratior non prodigi principis munificentia.
units.tr: L. The munificence of a prince who is not a spendthrift is more welcome.

units.la: Judicio enim, non animi morbo, largiri creditur. Deusta parte Circi cum montis Aventini aedificiis, Tiberius millies sestertium collocato, pretia domuum & insularum exsolvit. quod fecit tanto acceptius in vulgum, quanto modicus privatis aedificationibus. Neronis autem, qui Claudio successit, in publicum liberalitas, & cladis Lugdunensis solatium, minus volenti plebi fuit. Nam & congesto aere avidus, & prodigendo dissolutus, & aedificando im[?]odibus habe-[?]
units.tr: For it is believed to flow from judgement, not from a diseased mind. When part of the Circus was burned along with the buildings on the Aventine hill, Tiberius set aside a hundred million sesterces and paid the prices of the houses and blocks of flats. He did this all the more acceptably to the common people, in proportion as he was sparing in private building. But the liberality of Nero, who succeeded Claudius, towards the public, and his consolation for the disaster at Lyons, were less pleasing to the unwilling populace. For he was thought greedy in hoarding money, dissolute in squandering it, and extravagant in building.

units.la: batur. Non facto virtus : sed faciêntis animo , & omnium rectrice providentia, spectatur.
units.tr: Virtue is judged not by the deed but by the mind of the doer, and by the providence that governs all things.

units.la: LI. Ab occasu ortum prospicere, aulicæ folertiæ est.
units.tr: LI. To watch the rising from the setting is the mark of courtly shrewdness.

units.la: Ita præfentem rerum arbitrum colere, ut regnaturi post eum gratiam aucuperis, culpæ quidem non dat- tur. Sed datur culpæ, ita exorientem solem adorare, ut occidentem negligas. quod à Macrone factitatum: qui gratiam C. Cafaris nunquam sibi neglectum, acriùs indies fovebat. Qua de causa ei Tiberius,Occidentem ab eo deseri, orientem spectari exprobravit. Datur deinde culpæ, via morum detorta futurám gratiam venari. Ulti Macroni visum est, uxorem suam Enniam inmittendo amore juvenem illicere, pacloque matri- monii vincire. qui primum turpis quamvis magnæ rei mercatus est. deinde nullo pacto nefariorum ho- minum stabilis gratia paratur : Ipse Macronem Cajus, cujus dominationi fidem & honestatem posthabuit, inter regni primordia trucidavit. quod ex Dione Xi- philinus memorat. Gratia quidem hominum quo- rúmvis, & maximè imperio admovendorum, negli- genda non est. Verùm gratificatione scelerum eam captare,non est fyncerae indolis. Quanquam & Senè- ca cum Burrho, five firmandæ gratiæ, five satiétati li- bidinum accersendæ, adolescenti Neroni quædam vi- tiorum delinimenta indulsit. Quod Xiphilino,& ante eum Dioni, non probatum. ὅτι ψυχὴ νέα τε καὶ ...
units.tr: To court the present arbiter of affairs so as to win the favour of the one who will reign after him is indeed not open to blame. But it is blameworthy to worship the rising sun so as to neglect the setting one. This was practised by Macro, who, never neglecting the favour of Gaius Caesar, cherished it more keenly with each passing day. For this reason Tiberius reproached him: that the setting sun was abandoned by him, while the rising one was watched. Further, it is blameworthy to seek future favour by a crooked course of conduct. Macro thought fit to lure the young man by sending his own wife, Ennia, to inflame his love, and to bind him with a marriage pact. He first bought a great thing at a shameful price. Then, by no means is a lasting favour won from wicked men. Gaius himself slew Macro among the first acts of his reign, having set his loyalty and honour below his own mastery; so Dio, as Xiphilinus reports. Indeed the favour of men of any kind, and above all of those who are to be promoted to power, is not to be neglected. But to catch at it by the indulgence of crimes is not of a sincere disposition. Although Seneca, together with Burrhus, either to strengthen his favour or to provide fuel for the young Nero's lust once he was satiated, indulged him in certain soothings of his vices. This was not approved by Xiphilinus, nor earlier by Dio: [ὅτι ψυχὴ νέα τε καὶ ...] ("that a young soul ...").

units.la: Animus quippe juvenilis & arrogans luxuque & licentia immoderata innutritus, non modo non saturatur ; sed iis ipsis corrumpitur.
units.tr: For a youthful and arrogant mind, nourished by luxury and immoderate licence, is not only not satisfied by such things, but is actually corrupted by them.

units.la: LII. Simulatio viles etiam & nullius acu- minis animos intrat.
units.tr: LII. Simulation enters even base minds and those of no sharpness.

units.la: Quod certum indicium, non semper cum prudentia eam commorari. Cajus Caligula ersi commotus ingenio, simulationum tamen falsa in sinu avi perdi-dicerat. Successor Caji Claudius, hebes ingenio, & a-liorum suasu duƈtilis, ad vitæ suæ tutelam imperante Cajo plenæ stultitiæ simulationem induerat. Nero delirio quodam animi ad publicam aurigationem, lustam, citharæ in publico theatro cantum industus, mirus tamen simulandi artifex cluebat. Vitellius, fagina [?] corporis gravis, nec quicquam providum pingui animo concipiens, premere tamen res adversas, & integram sibi fortunam, integram mentem, victore Mutiano & Antonio, similare poterat. Sed est quædam insipida stulta dissimulatio: ut hæc ipsa Vitellii, dissimulatio ne cladis remedia malorum differentis. Ut in extremis positi Tiberii, morbi gravitatem accubatione, & epularum præter vires lautitia, tegentis.
units.tr: This is a sure sign that it does not always go together with prudence. Gaius Caligula, though unbalanced in temperament, had nonetheless learned false simulation in the bosom of his grandfather. Gaius's successor Claudius, dull in mind and pliable to the persuasion of others, while Gaius was emperor, had put on a simulation full of folly in order to protect his own life. Nero, through a certain madness of mind, was devoted to public chariot-driving, to the lyre, and to singing on the public stage, yet he was still thought a remarkable artist of dissimulation. Vitellius, heavy in body and conceiving nothing far-sighted in his fat mind, could nonetheless conceal adverse circumstances, and feign a whole fortune and a whole mind, even when Mutianus and Antonius had conquered. But there is a certain insipid and foolish dissimulation, such as this very dissimulation of Vitellius, which postpones the remedies for disaster. Like that of Tiberius, when at the point of death he concealed the gravity of his illness by lying down and by a luxury of feasting beyond his strength.

units.la: Stulta vero simul & impia, immo demens & sacrilega, illa simulatio, qua Cajus Caligula modo Jupiter fulmine armatus, modo Juno, Diana, Venus, & quid vis aliud quam homo videri volebat, qua cum luna coire, & a Victoria se coronari fingebat, qua imitatione Jovis, adulteria & cum sororibus incestum committebat. Perversa simulatio fuit, qua Nero, pellem ferinam indutus, alligatos cruci pueros & puellas inibat, ut abbreviator Dionis commemorat. Nec probanda syncerę pietati, quamvis politicorum vulgo magnam in admiratione nem adducta, Minois, Lycurgi, Numæ, Muhammedis, dementandæ religione plebi sicta cum diis & deabus conversatio. Temporibus magis excusata, quam laude cumulata, Græcorum & Romanorum sicta de cantu Neronis lætitia. Periculosa enim vitæ fuit aut a theatro absentia, aut intentioris curæ negligentia. Hæc enim promptissima Cossutiano arcessendi Thrafcam Pætum materia. Nunquam pro salute principis, aut cœlesti voci immolavifle. Huic uni incolumitatem Neronis esse sine arte, sine honore. Ejusdem animi esse, Poppæam divam non credere, cujus in actâ divi Augusti & divi Julii non jurare. Ut imperium evertat,libertatem praeferre: ubi everterit, ipsam aggredi; Frustra Cassium amotum, si aemuli Brutorum gliscant. xvi. Annal. Prudens igitur & moderata simu-latio, quae nec honorem Deo eripiat; nec ulli homini iniuria fit, ferenda; immoderata, stulta; impia honorifico prudentiae albo eradenda.
units.tr: Yet that simulation is both foolish and impious, indeed mad and sacrilegious, by which Gaius Caligula wished to appear now as Jupiter armed with the thunderbolt, now as Juno, Diana, Venus, or anything else rather than a man; by which he feigned to couple with the moon and to be crowned by Victory; and by which, in imitation of Jupiter, he committed adulteries and incest with his sisters. Perverse was that simulation by which Nero, clothed in the skin of a wild beast, lay with boys and girls bound to a cross, as the epitomiser of Dio records. Nor is it to be approved by sincere piety, although the conversation of Minos, Lycurgus, Numa and Muhammed with gods and goddesses, feigned to dull the religion of the common people, is greatly admired by the general run of political writers. The rejoicing of the Greeks and Romans over Nero's singing is more excused by the times than praised as a great merit; for it was dangerous to be absent from the theatre, or to neglect a more serious care. For this was the most ready material for Cossutianus to summon Thrasea Paetus. Never to have sacrificed for the safety of the prince, or for the heavenly voice. That the safety of Nero rested on this one man alone, without skill and without honour. That it is the mark of the same mind not to believe Poppaea a goddess, whose deeds of the deified Augustus and the deified Julius he did not swear by. To prefer liberty so as to overthrow the empire; and once he has overthrown it, to attack liberty itself; in vain has Cassius been removed, if the rivals of the Bruti flourish. Xvi. Annals. Therefore prudent and moderate simulation, which takes nothing of God's honour and does no wrong to any man, is to be tolerated; immoderate, foolish and impious simulation is to be erased from the honourable roll of prudence.

units.la: LIII.
units.tr: LIII.

units.la: Solicita imperii susceptio, laboriosa gestio, anxia depositio.
units.tr: The taking up of empire is anxious, its management laborious, its laying down full of worry.

units.la: De suscipiendo & gerendo imperio alibi a nobis actum: de tradendo superest differendi materia. In-ter vanitates vitae humanae molestissimas Ecclesiastes vel praecipuam commemorat, optima ratione confti-tuta[?] alteri, qui fortassis insipiens sit futurus; esse relin-quenda. Nec illum fefellit anxiae mentis praesagium: stulto Roboamo in sapientis patris locum subvecto; & bene ordinata imperii membra stultitia dissipante; Nec Tiberium inanis cura angebat, cui successor ante oculos versabatur C. Caligula, bipedum omnium stultissimus, simul ac nequissimus, quique per viginti tres annos a Tiberio collecta aerarii subsidia triennio dis-perfurus; acta Tiberii rescissurus; nepotem ejus obtruncaturus erat. eoque dubitavit de tradenda Rep. a reip. complexu, non minus quam a vita discedere miserum: miserius nescire cui tantam rerum molem committitas, cui eripias. Nepos Drusi genitus, sanguine & caritate propior, sed nondum pubertatem egref-sus. Haec erat ea temporum illorum fides, aut ea impe-rii alieni patientia, ut tutelae aetas pupilli & imperii li-brandi[?] cura tutò committeretur. quod caput est foli-citudinis: non alio, quam imperatorio in militibus, nomine autoritatem ceteris eminendi gerebant: ridiculum autem videbatur, & nomini Romano indecorum, puerum septuennem exercitui praeesse, arma quorum getendorum[?] capax non erat dirigere, signum militi-bus dare, turbidas belli metu provincias nutu suo refi-cere. Neronem, Tiberii nepote aetate non parum pro-vectiorem, servitii inveterati jam patiens multitudo [non?] ferebat: quemadmodum princeps vix septeinde-cim annos egressus, suscipere eam molem aut propulsare posset: quod subsidium in eo qui a foemina regeretur: num praelia quoque & oppugnationes urbium, & caeteră belli per magistros administrari possent, frequendo anquirebant. xiii. Annal. quid in impubere remp. capessituro futurum? qui fremitus, vel quae potius rerum mutatio non exspectanda? Illud aliud agens adverto, viderint maritimae nationes, quae se magnifico Reip. quae se splendido libertatis nomine commendant, utri Romanorum statui propius accedant: priscae populi majestati, quae magistratus annuos, annua imperia creabat; ad recentiori Tiberii principatui, ubi manente Reip. appellatione, manente Consulum & praetorum, manente patrum conscriptorum specie, Principis, & imperatorii militum ductus, nomine unus praecipua rerum gerebat. qui tamen eo audaciae nondum profectus erat, ut puerum, sanguine & caritate sibi proximum, cervicibus eorum imponeret, aut saltem patribus commendaret. Atqui Tiberius factionem Sejani, & alios cupiditatis altioris suspectos, crudeli modo e medio sustulit. Nimirum per senatum, & Majestatis lege: qua & Barbefeldiam factionem, nihil parcendo, aliquis perculit. In caeteris imperator submisse se gerebat: consuli via decedebat; in cornu tribunalis, ne praetorem curuli depelleret, sedebat. multa quae mixtam cum principatu libertatem arguebant, agebat. Haec non, quod mihi alteri utri factioni adjungam aut oppositam, ut qui utrique (non tamen ut factioni) faveam; sed commentandi libertate infero: rara temporum felicitate, ubi sentire quae velit, & quae sentias dicere licet. lib. i. Histor.
units.tr: I have treated the taking up and exercising of empire elsewhere; what remains is the matter of handing it on. Among the most troublesome vanities of human life, Ecclesiastes names one as chief, and rightly lays down that it must be left to another, who may perhaps turn out a fool. Nor did that anxious mind's foreboding deceive him: when the foolish Rehoboam was raised to the place of his wise father, his folly scattered the well-ordered members of the realm. Nor was Tiberius tormented by an empty care, though before his eyes his successor was Gaius Caligula, the most foolish of all bipeds and at the same time the most wicked, who was to squander in three years the treasury reserves gathered by Tiberius over twenty-three years, to rescind Tiberius's acts, and to put his grandson to death. Therefore he hesitated to hand on the state, for it was no less wretched to be parted from the embrace of the commonwealth than from life; more wretched still not to know to whom you may commit so great a mass of affairs, or from whom you may snatch it away. Drusus's son, the grandson, was born of closer blood and affection, but had not yet reached puberty. Such was the trust of those times, or such patience with another's rule, that the minority of a ward and the care of holding the empire in balance could be safely entrusted to him. This was the chief worry: they bore the authority of standing above the rest only through the imperial name over the soldiers. It seemed ridiculous, however, and unbecoming to the Roman name, for a boy of seven to command an army, to give the signal to soldiers, and by a nod to restore provinces disturbed by fear of war, when he was not capable of wielding the arms. The multitude, long accustomed to servitude, could not bear Nero, who was by no means much older than Tiberius's grandson; they kept asking, frequently, how a prince scarcely past seventeen could take up or ward off such a burden, what support lay in one who was ruled by a woman, and whether battles, sieges of cities and the rest of the business of war could be administered through agents. (Tacitus, Annals 13.) What uproar, or rather what change of affairs, was to be expected once a boy who had not reached puberty took hold of the state? I note this in passing: let the maritime nations see which of the Roman forms they more closely resemble, those that commend themselves by the grand name of the Republic, by the splendid name of liberty: the ancient majesty of the people, which created magistrates and commands for a year each, or the more recent principate of Tiberius, where, though the name of Republic remained, and that of Consuls and praetors, and the appearance of the Fathers of the conscript order, one man, the Prince, with the leadership of the imperial soldiers, administered the chief affairs by name. Yet he had not yet advanced so far in audacity as to set a boy, closest to himself in blood and affection, upon their necks, or at least to commend him to the Fathers. And yet Tiberius removed the faction of Sejanus, and others suspected of too high an ambition, by a cruel method: namely through the senate and by the law of treason, by which someone also struck down the faction of Barbefeldia, sparing no one. In other matters the emperor behaved humbly: he yielded the way to a consul, he sat at the corner of the tribunal so as not to push a praetor from his curule chair, and he did many things that argued a liberty mixed with the principate. I say this not because I attach myself to either faction, or set myself against it, since I favour both (though not as factions), but in the freedom of comment, in the rare felicity of the times, when one may think what one wishes and say what one thinks. (Tacitus, Histories 1.)

units.la: Si in Rep. potius, quam in domo, successore Tiberius quaesivisset, res expeditu facilior fuisset. Nunc ad se & Caesarem familiam oculis conversis, in lubrico & intricato senticeto haeret. Germanici filio robur juventa, vulgi studia, eaque apud avum odii causa. Proximus a nepote, ut sanguinis conjunctione, ita succedendi imperio spe, Caligula erat. sed duae res vote Tiberii obstabant. Popularis erga domum Germanici favor invidia eum torquebat: sinistri in gesturo impe-rium mores eum versabant. Erga Claudium, alterum Drusi majoris filium, propensiori animo ferebatur. Nam nec ullus populi in eum favor, nulla existimatio; aemulatione ipsum torrebat; & is morum honestate sincerior, composita atate bonarum artium cupiens erat. Sed, ne quid usquam intaminatum occurreret, imminuta mens ejus obstitit. erat enim & mente & sermone tardus, manu & capite tremulus. Sin extra domum successor quarereretur, ne memoria Casarum nomen in ludibria & contumelias verteret, metuebat. Quippe illi non perinde cura gratia praesen-tium, quam in posteros ambitio. Qua ambitione faces praeferente, nominis solennitatem in posteros voto extendebat. Quo voto excidisset, si ad alienam familiam successio pervenisset. Atqui poterat re-publica populo reddita, magnam gratiam a viventi-bus, gloriam apud posteritatem inire. Huic desiderio obstabat, quod, ut Galba ad Pisonem adoptandum dif-ferit, immensum imperii corpus stare ac librari sine re-ctore non poterat. Sed maxime his votis obstrepe-bat, timor, ne libertate populo potito; nulla autori gratia habita, nomen Casareum execratione foret, im-periumque Tiberii tyrannicae dominationis appella-tione traduceretur. Igitur incertus animi, fesso corpore re, consilium cui impar erat fato permisit. Cui fato nihil obsistere, nec humano consilio occurri posse, mul-tis antea rationibus ei persuasum fuit. Ita Tiberii providia ratio, Tiberii sagax ille animus, Tiberii folli-cita de successore cura, cogitationum conflictu delas-fata, fato cedebat. Obiiceris: ubi hic futurorum ex astris, quam in Tiberio scriptores celebrant, notitia? Qui sibi, qui Galbae imperium praedicere potuit, suc-cessorem suum videre, & ita frustra fato se macerando obluctari, non potuit? Vidit hanc difficultatem Taci-tus: ideoque eum & fato omnem rem permisisse, nec imminentium ignarum fuisse, subjungit: jaclis[?] tamen Vocibus, per quas intelligeretur providum futurorum, quam ei futurorum perspicientiam, me quidem judi-ce, non astra, non vaticinia; sed Caji audacia & domi-nandi libido, populi in eum favor, militum studium, & supra omnia Macronis praefens opera, suggere-bant.
units.tr: If Tiberius had sought a successor in the Republic rather than in his household, the matter would have been easier to settle. As it is, with his eyes turned upon his own family and the Caesars, he sticks in a slippery and tangled thicket. Germanicus's son had the strength of youth, the favour of the common people, and that was the cause of hatred in his grandfather. Next to the grandson, both by blood-relationship and by hope of succeeding to the empire, was Caligula. But two things stood in the way of Tiberius's wish. The popular favour toward Germanicus's house tormented him with envy; the sinister morals of the man who was to hold the empire troubled him. He was inclined rather toward Claudius, the other son of the elder Drusus. For Claudius had no favour of the people toward him, no esteem; Tiberius was tormented by rivalry toward him; and Claudius, purer in the honesty of his character and of an age well suited to the liberal arts, was eager for them. But, lest anything should appear anywhere unblemished, his mind was impaired, and stood in the way. For he was slow both in mind and in speech, and trembled in hand and head. If on the other hand a successor were sought outside the family, Tiberius feared that the memory of the Caesars would be turned into mockery and insult. For his concern was not so much for present favour as for the ambition toward posterity. Carrying that ambition as a torch before him, he extended in his wish the solemnity of the name to posterity; and that wish would have been lost had the succession passed to a foreign family. Yet he could have won great gratitude from the living and glory with posterity, by restoring the Republic to the people. What stood in the way of this desire was that, as Galba deferred adopting Piso, the immense body of the empire could not stand and be balanced without a ruler. But these wishes were chiefly drowned out by fear: that once liberty had been granted to the people, with no thanks given to its author, the Caesarean name would be cursed and the empire of Tiberius would be branded with the title of tyrannical domination. Therefore, uncertain in mind, with his body wearied, he left to fate the decision for which he was unequal. That nothing could resist fate, nor could human counsel meet it, had been persuaded to him long before by many arguments. Thus Tiberius's provident reasoning, his shrewd spirit, his anxious care about a successor, was broken in the conflict of his thoughts, and yielded to fate. You will object: where, then, was that knowledge of the future from the stars, which the writers celebrate in Tiberius? Could he not foresee his own successor, and foresee Galba's rule, and so strive in vain, wearing himself out against fate? Tacitus saw this difficulty; therefore he adds that Tiberius left the whole matter to fate and was not ignorant of what was impending, yet by the words he threw out, by which he might be understood to be wise about the future. As for that foresight of the future attributed to him, in my judgment it was suggested not by the stars or by oracles, but by Gaius's audacity and lust for domination, by the favour of the people toward him, by the zeal of the soldiers, and above all by the present work of Macro.

units.la: Dubium hoc loco moveri queat: Si Tiberius mor-ti vicinus de successore eligendo secum deliberat; an ea res meri imperantium arbitrii, exclusa legum aut populi potestate, fit habenda? Exemplum formandi imperii non esse a Romanis, postquam in dubiam li-bertatis & servitutis aleam sub Augusto concesserant, petendum, multa suadent. Aliud enim illis tempori-bus agebatur, aliud agi plebi persuadebatur. Princi-pem fe senatus, imperatorem militum, dominum fer-vorum, in caeteris unum senatorum, unum fe civium Tib. ferebat. Libertatis antiqua nomina audiebah-tur, dominationis recentia opera videbantur. Haec in imperio suscipiendo imperio, haec in gerendo, haec in tradendo aliis dominatio locum habebat. In suscipiendo: cum maxime imperium verbis & vultu Tiberius detrecta-ret, armis & excubiis in forum, in curiam fe comitan-tibus, dominum fe rerum gerebat. In gerendo impe-rio idem Tiberius: sed malo a Nerone specimen do-minationis, juris appellatione obtectae, petere. Thra-feam, senatus facile genere & opibus & animi virtute principem, sibi ob easdem artes invisum, interimere Nero decrevit. Senatus ornamentum, fenectu ob hoc decretum territo, per ipsum senatum evertere aggre-diebatur. Patribus convocatis, duae praetoriae cohor-tes armatae, templum genetricis Veneris insedere. Aditum senatus globus togatorum obsederat, non occultis gladiis, dispersique per fora ac basilicas cu-riei militares: inter quorum aspectus & minas ingressi curiam senatores. xvi. Annalium. Oratores deinde; Marcellus & alii dominorum palpatores, ad accufan-dum subornantur. A pavido senatu, & cum juri divino ac humano tum sibi metuente, faturae modo sententitiæ exiguntur. Thrafea interim, adjecto Sorano tuì[?] miseranda filia, venis incisis vita abit. Quam in sulci[?]-piendo, quam in gerendo imperio, pro jure voluntâ-tem, juris tamen inani larva personarum, expedivere; eam & in transferendo, non exspectato patrum, non populi aut legum suffragio, expromere potuerunt.
units.tr: Here a question may be raised: if Tiberius, close to death, deliberates with himself about choosing a successor, is that matter to be regarded as the sole will of the rulers, with the power of the laws or of the people excluded? Many considerations suggest that a model for forming an empire must not be sought among the Romans after they had, under Augustus, entrusted themselves to the doubtful hazard of liberty and servitude. For one thing was being done in those times, and another was being persuaded to the common people. Tiberius bore himself as Prince to the Senate, as commander to the soldiers, as master to the slaves, and in other matters as one senator among senators, one citizen among citizens. The ancient names of liberty were heard; the recent works of domination were seen. In taking up the empire, in managing it, and in handing it on to others, domination held its place. In taking it up: although Tiberius most of all refused the empire in words and expression, he was master of affairs, with arms and guards accompanying him into the forum and into the senate-house. In managing the empire, the same Tiberius, but Nero, under a bad example, sought to exhibit a display of domination veiled under the name of law. Nero decided to destroy Thrasea, a senator easily first in birth, wealth and strength of character, and hated by him for those same qualities. Thrasea, the ornament of the Senate, was alarmed by this decree and, through the senate itself, set about overturning it. When the Fathers had been summoned, two praetorian cohorts, armed, occupied the temple of the mother Venus. A crowd of men in togas, not concealing their swords, besieged the entrance to the senate, and soldiers were scattered through the forums and basilicas; among their looks and threats the senators went into the senate-house. (Tacitus, Annals 16.) Then speakers were suborned to accuse him, Marcellus and others who flattered the masters. The fearful Senate, fearing both divine and human law, but also fearing for itself, was compelled to give opinions as if at dictation. Meanwhile Thrasea, with the wretched daughter of Soranus added, cut his veins and departed this life. Just as they had dispatched the expression of will as law in taking up the empire and in managing it, though the form of law was an empty mask of persons, so they could also bring out their will in transferring it, without waiting for the vote of the Fathers, of the people, or of the laws.

units.la: LIV. Aliena vitia faciliùs quàm nostra nobis apparent.
units.tr: LIV. Other people's faults are more readily apparent to us than our own.

units.la: Id fit, quia amore nostri dementati, omnia nostra, étiam ipsos errores amamus; aut aliorum severi ju-dices, nobis ignoscimus. Perfrictioris[?] quidam frontis, victiorum suorum similitudinem in aliis non ferunt; quorum ad virtutes & ingenii altitudinem non aspirant. Quorum in numero C. Caligulam, sceleribus suis blandientem, aliena denudantem, cognoscimus. Cui Tiberius L. Sullam irridenti, omnia Sulla vitia; & nullam ejusdem virtutem babiturum pradixit.
units.tr: This happens because, driven mad by love of ourselves, we love everything that is ours, even our own errors, or else we are severe judges of others and pardon ourselves. Some men of brazen forehead cannot bear to see their own vices reflected in others, and they do not aspire to the virtues or the loftiness of mind of those others. Among such men we recognise Gaius Caligula, flattering his own crimes and laying bare those of others. When Caligula mocked Lucius Sulla, Tiberius told him that he would have all of Sulla's vices and none of his virtue.

units.la: Nec vanum hoc Tiberii augurium, rebus ipsis posteri-tati deprehensum, fuit. Sulla cupidus voluptatum, sed gloriæ cupidior: uti de eo Sallustius bello Jugurthino judicat. Cajus libidinum mancipium, & divinos honores invadens. Sulla otio luxurioso erat. Cajus per luxum opes publicas, Galliæ censum, & privato-rum emendicata aut rapta patrimonia exhausit. De Sullæ uxore potuit honestius consuli. Cajus inter uxo-rem & sorores, quod ad congrediendi usum, non di-scernebat. Sulla victoriæ successu immutatus, remp. crudeliter & avarè habuit, Cajus imperium adeptus, nullum trucidandi, territandi, rapiendi modum habuit.
units.tr: Nor was this augury of Tiberius vain; the facts themselves, as posterity has found, bore it out. Sulla was desirous of pleasures, but more desirous of glory, as Sallust judges him in the Jugurthine War. Gaius was the slave of his lusts, and seized divine honours. Sulla was given to luxurious idleness. Gaius, through extravagance, exhausted the public resources, the tribute of Gaul, and the private patrimonies either begged or seized. Sulla's wife might be spoken of more honourably. Gaius made no distinction between his wife and his sisters as regards the use of intercourse. Sulla, changed by the success of victory, governed the commonwealth cruelly and greedily; Gaius, once he had gained power, had no limit to killing, terrifying and plundering.

units.la: Sic vitiorum pondere lanci imposita, longè Cajus præponderat. Sed quæ Sullæ virtutes memorantur, ab eorum commercio Cajus longissimè recessit. la[?] literis Græcis atque Latinis, juxta atque doctissimè[?] eruditus. Cajus eruditos perosus, literas sacratiores vix primis labris libavit. Ingenti animo Sulla, rerum gestarum magnitudine domui suæ, quanquam nobilissimæ, præluxit. Cajus degeneri animo, & vitæ turpitudini næuos Germanico, Augusto, Romano nomini aspersit. Sullam ab negotio nunquam voluptas remorata est. Cajus nullam nisi in voluptate vitam duxit; nullum nisi in crudelitate exercenda negotium curavit. Sulla facundus, callidus, & amicitia facilis. Cajus leviter disertus, ingenio hebes, vel potius furiata mente lymphaticus, amicis atque inimicis juxta infestus. Sullæ ad simulanda negotia altitudo ingenii incredibilis. Cajus mente commotus, simulationum duntaxat quædam falsa in sinu avi didicerat. Sulla multarum rerum, ac maximè pecuniæ, ex animo liberali, largitor. Cajus, ex animi deficiente judicio, pecuniarum profundendarum vorago. Sullæ felicissimo omnium, ante civilem victoriam, nunquam super industriam fortuna fuit. Cajo inertissimo hominum nec fortuna unquam, nisi forte in spoliando cochleis oceano, aut trepida è Germaniis fuga, respondit. Imperium aliquando & dictaturam, rep. legibus firmata, Sulla deposuit. Cajus legum & honestatis eversor, dignum tyranno vitæ & imperii exitium invenit. Quem ei Tiberius vaticinatus prædixit. nam crebrò cum lacrymis minorem ex nepotibus complexus truci alterius vultu: occides hunc tu, inquit, & te alius.
units.tr: Thus, with the weight of vices placed in the scale, Gaius far outweighs Sulla. But as for the virtues recorded of Sulla, Gaius withdrew very far from any association with them. Sulla was learned in Greek and Latin literature, and most learnedly educated. Gaius, hating the learned, barely touched the more sacred letters with his lips. Sulla, with a great spirit, outshone his house by the greatness of his deeds, though it was already most noble. Gaius, with a degenerate spirit and a disgraceful life, cast stains upon Germanicus, Augustus and the Roman name. Pleasure never delayed Sulla from business; Gaius led no life but one of pleasure, and attended to no business but the exercise of cruelty. Sulla was eloquent, clever and easy in friendship. Gaius was slightly eloquent, dull of mind, or rather lymphatic with a maddened mind, hostile alike to friends and enemies. Sulla's depth of mind for feigning affairs was incredible; Gaius, disturbed in mind, had learned only certain false pretences in his grandfather's bosom. Sulla, generous of spirit, was a giver of many things, above all of money; Gaius, from a failing judgement of mind, was an abyss for squandering money. Sulla, the most fortunate of men before his civil victory, never had fortune outrun his industry; for the most inert of men, Gaius, fortune never answered, except perhaps in plundering shells from the ocean or in his frightened flight from Germany. Sulla at one time laid down power and the dictatorship, the commonwealth having been secured by laws. Gaius, the destroyer of laws and honour, found an end of life and power worthy of a tyrant. Tiberius foretold this to him: often, embracing the younger of his grandsons with tears, and with a grim look at the other, he said: "You will kill this one, and someone else will kill you."

units.la: LV.
units.tr: LV.

units.la: Infirma est firmitatis in morbo simulatio.
units.tr: A feigned firmness is weak in sickness.

units.la: Civilem Reip. morbum, virorum & armorum defectum, distractas per civitates & pagos dissensionum factiones, mollitiem dissolutæ disciplinæ, utiliter celare hostem queas. At hoste viscera corporis pervadente, fauces aut ilia morbo urente, non est diuturna fine nocumento aperto simulatio. Tiberio tamen, qui nihil non simulate egit, hic simulandi modus placuit. Gravescente valetudine, nihil & libidinibus omittebat. in patientia firmitudinem simulans, solitusque eludere medicorum artes, atque eos qui post tricesimum atatis[?] annum ad internoscenda corpori suo utilia vel noxia, alieni consilii indigerent. Multum sanè in vulgata me-dicinæ arte videtur esse vanitatis, multum contraria-rum opinionum,non parum in fundamento naturalis disciplinæ vacillationis. Sed quid ea libidinum non in-termiffum usum, valetudine ingravescente, juverint; non fatis perspicio. nisi aut intemperantem volupta-tum usum nihil obesse vigori censuerit; aut peculia-rem in corpore suo naturam deprehenderit. Sed hæc in transcursu; & ne locum istum omnino praeter-irem.
units.tr: You may usefully conceal from an enemy the civil disease of a state: the lack of men and arms, the factions of dissension scattered through its cities and villages, the softness of a dissolute discipline. But when the enemy pervades the vitals of the body, and disease burns the throat or the bowels, a pretence cannot last long without open harm. Yet to Tiberius, who did everything by pretence, this mode of dissembling pleased. As his health grew worse, he gave up none of his lusts; he feigned firmness in patience, and was accustomed to mock the arts of physicians and of those who, after their thirtieth year, needed another's counsel to learn what was useful or harmful to their body. Certainly much vanity seems to lie in the common art of medicine, much contrariety of opinions, and not a little wavering in the foundations of natural science. But how those uninterrupted indulgences of lust helped him as his sickness grew worse, I do not clearly see, unless he judged that immoderate use of pleasures did no harm to vigour, or discovered some peculiar nature in his own body. But these things in passing, lest I pass over that place altogether.

units.la: LVI.
units.tr: LVI.

units.la: Non eadem omnibus decóra.
units.tr: Not the same things are fitting for all.

units.la: Unum quidem est naturâ omnibus decorum:quod ab honestate profectum, neminem ab observatione fui absolvit. Sed praeter illud,peculiaris uniuscujusque natura,ætas praeterea,sexus genus vitæ,locus fortunæ personam cuique suam decori imposuit. De propria singulorum natura Tacitus, & apud eum Arruntius, accipiendus est. Sævo Tiberii mandatu multi vim sibi inferentes, venis manu sua incifis vita excessere. Domitius autem defensionem meditando, Marfus tanquam inedia obiturus, ultra Tiberii suprema pro-duxere vitam. Quæ res doctrinam suppeditatura erat, Nemini quamvis in extremis posito salutem de-sperandam, nec spei vacillatione vitam hanc esse ab-rumpendam. Sed quia, qui Tiberii sævitiam effuge-re,in acerbiorem Caji crudelitatem inciderunt, huic loco nunc non immorabor. Arruntio cum easdem moras, & exspectationem mortis Tiberii, amici sua-derent; Non eadem omnibus decora,respondit. Gra-vem enim personam, ludibria spei & metus non fe-rentem, Arruntio natura indiderat. Aliis procrastina-re destinata, & inter incertæ exspectationis aleam pendere licuit. Arruntio semel mori,quàm inter spem & metum jastari, decentius videbatur. Dispar magis exemplum inter Ulyssem & Ajacem, ætate & officio juncẗos, animo multum dissimiles, poetæ & oratores producunt. Ulysses dissimulando, perferendo, occa- Vlysses. sionem præstolando; Ajax nihil cunctando, omnia Ajax. perfringendo, nihil injuriarum ferendo; scenam vitæ egerunt. Quare ille & Calypsus ac Circes, mulierum infulanarum, imperia pertulit, & mendici habitu fallendo, convitia domi suæ, donec vindictæ compotem occasio se faceret, perrulit. Hic ob levem contumeliæ opinionem, adjudicatis Ulyssi armis Achilleis, furore correptus, vitam indignatione abrupit. scriptoribus Romanis, Ciceroni inprimis & Annæo Senecæ, Utis- censis Cato laudatur. Hic cum mutationem rerum, Cato. & unius imperium ferre nequiret, ferro in viscera adacto, & vulnere manibus distento, imminentem servitutem effugit. Cicero autem & Brutus, tempori Cicero. inservientes, vitam aliquandiu sub domino produxere. Alii præsentia veteribus, tuta periculosis præsentes, alii. cum orbe converso circumactum, faciei rerum acquieverunt. Magna Catonis, magna Scipionis & Jubæ, eandem mortis pro libertate violentiam sponte passorum, apud Romanos fama. Nobis laudare Catonem, temporum meorum festa, ut Justinianum lo- quentem imitemur, non permittit. Commodior in- Cæsarius cum ter eundem Catonem & Julium Cæsarem, quod ad Catone col- morum diversitatem, comparatio feretur. Cæsar be- latio. neficiis ac munificentia magnus habebatur: integritate vitæ Cato, ille mansuetudine & misericordia clarus factus: huic severitas dignitatem addiderat. Cæsar dando, sublevando, ignoscendo; Cato nihil largiundo gloriam adeptus est. in altero miseris perfugium: in altero malis perniciès. illius facilitas, hujus constantia laudabatur. Sall. B. Catil.
units.tr: There is indeed one kind of decorum that is by nature common to all, which springs from honesty and absolves no one from observing it. But besides that, each person's peculiar nature, and moreover age, sex, way of life, place and fortune, have imposed on each a decorum of its own. Concerning the proper nature of individuals, Tacitus, and Arruntius as he presents him, must be consulted. At Tiberius' savage command, many inflicted violence on themselves and died by cutting their veins with their own hand. Domitius, meditating a defence, and Marsus, as if about to die of starvation, prolonged their lives beyond Tiberius' last days. This matter would have supplied a lesson: that no one, however placed in extremity, should despair of safety, nor cut short this life through wavering hope. But since those who escaped Tiberius' savagery fell into the harsher cruelty of Caligula, I will not dwell on that point now. When friends urged Arruntius to the same delays and to waiting for Tiberius' death, he answered: "Not the same things are fitting for all."
