For nature had given Arruntius a serious character, which could not bear being the plaything of hope and fear. For others it was allowed to put things off and to hang in the lottery of uncertain expectation. For Arruntius it seemed more becoming to die once than to be tossed about between hope and fear. The poets and orators bring forward a different example in Ulysses and Ajax, joined in age and office, but very unlike in temper. Ulysses. Ulysses, by dissembling, enduring and awaiting his opportunity; Ajax. Ajax, by not delaying at all, breaking through everything, bearing no injury, played out the scene of life. Hence the former bore the commands of Calypso and Circe, the island women, and, by feigning the guise of a beggar and by deceit, endured abuse in his own house until opportunity made him master of his vengeance. The latter, over a slight opinion of insult, after the arms of Achilles had been adjudged to Ulysses, was seized by fury and broke off his life in indignation. Cato. Among Roman writers, above all Cicero and Seneca the Younger, Cato of Utica is praised. When he could not bear the change of affairs and the rule of one man, he drove a blade into his vitals and, with the wound pulled open by his hands, escaped the impending servitude. Cicero. But Cicero and Brutus, serving the times, prolonged their lives for a while under a master. Others. Others, content with present things, safe for the timid and present for the dangerous, went along with the turning of the world and acquiesced in the face of affairs. The fame among the Romans of great Cato, great Scipio and Juba, who of their own accord suffered the same violent death for liberty, is great. Our times do not permit us to praise Cato, as I would imitate Justinian's speaking. A more suitable comparison of Caesar with Cato can be made, as regards the diversity of their characters. Caesar was held great for his benefits and munificence; Cato became famous for the integrity of his life. To the one, mildness and mercy gave lustre; to the other, severity had added dignity. Caesar gained glory by giving, relieving and pardoning; Cato, by bestowing nothing. In the one there was a refuge for the wretched; in the other, ruin for the wicked. The former's easiness and the latter's constancy were praised.

units.la: In his, quæ in utraque partem laudabilia sunt, Doctrina quo quemque ingenii facilitas rapit, in eo maxime ei decori. elaborandum. Expendere itaque oportebit, quid Cic. 1. offic. quisque habeat sui, eaque moderari, nec velle experiri, quàm fe aliena deceant. id enim quemque decet,quod est cujusque suum maximè: Suum igitur quisque no-scat ingenium, acremque fe & vitiorum & bonorum suorum judicem praebeat; ne fcepici plus quàm nos videantur habere prudentiae. illi enim non optimas, sed sibi accommodatissimas fabulas eligunt. qui enim voce freti sunt, Epigonos, Medeamque; qui gestu, Menalippam, Clytemneftram: &c. ergo histrio hoc viderit in scena, quod non videbit sapiens in vita? Ad quas igitur res aptissimi erimus, in iis potissimum elaborabimus. Sin aliquando necessitas nos ad ea detru-ferit, quae nostri ingenii non erunt: omnis adhibenda erit cura, meditatio, diligentia, ut ea fi non decore, at quam minimum indecore facere possimus. nec tam est enitendum, ut bona, quae nobis data non sunt, fe-quamur, quam ut vitia fugiamus. Verba sunt Cicero-nis, lib.1.offic. Est & in aetate, est in sexu decori discri-men fervandum. Aliud ephebum ac adolescentem, aliud maturi judicii virum, aliud emensi vitae spatium gravem aetatem decet. quae ab iis, qui de officiis prae-cepta tradiderunt, petenda. In sexu, mulierem silentium & domus custodiam decere; virum sermonem & negotia forensia commendare pragmatici volunt. In vitae genere alia est persona & sermo dignitatem gerentis, alia privatae vitae cum multitudine adhaeren-tis, alia eruditi, alia illiterati, vivendi & loquendi ratio, alia docentis, alia docenti aurem praebentis gravitas, attentio, venustas. Interipsos etiam domesticae vitae affectus, quibus nulla reip. pars demandata, magna in fortunae favore aut aversatione, in claritate generis aut obscuritate, in rerum abundantia aut inopia, in li-bertate aut addicta dominis aetate, in incolatu aut peregrinitate, non parvum vitae in publico agendae discrimen. de quibus praecepta sigillatim tradere, in-gentioris esset voluminis. Nec ad eandem normam, nunquam cum tempore & rebus mutandam, praescri-pta omnibus quadrabunt. Pro sua quisque aut sa-pientiorum prudentia, quid cum deceat, aut dedeceat, cum quibus ipsi res agatur, quid ad utilitatem, & ea potiorem honestatem, ducat, sine praecepti regula videbit.
units.tr: Doctrine of decorum. In those things which are praiseworthy on either side, each person should labour most at whatever his natural facility of talent carries him towards. Therefore one must weigh what each has of his own, and moderate it, and not wish to try how far other people's qualities would suit him, for each person is suited to what is most his own. Let each therefore know his own nature, and show himself a keen judge of his own vices and virtues, lest they seem to have more prudence than we do. For they choose not the best plays but those most suited to themselves. Those who rely on voice choose the Epigoni and Medea; those who rely on gesture, Menalippe and Clytemnestra. Shall the actor therefore see on the stage what the wise man will not see in life? Therefore we shall labour chiefly at those things for which we are most fit. But if at some time necessity has driven us to things that are not of our nature, every care, thought and diligence must be applied so that we may do them, if not with decorum, at least with as little indecorum as possible. Nor should we strive so much to pursue the goods that have not been given to us, as to flee from our vices. These are the words of Cicero, book 1 of the Offices. There is also a distinction of decorum to be observed in age and in sex. Another thing befits a youth and a young man, another a man of mature judgement, and another a man who has traversed the span of life, the grave age. These things should be sought from those who have handed down precepts about duties. In sex, the teachers of practical wisdom want silence and the keeping of the house to befit a woman, and speech and public business to commend a man. In the kind of life, one person and one manner of speech befit one who holds dignity, another one who lives a private life among the crowd; another befits the learned, another the unlettered, in their manner of living and speaking; another befits the teacher, and another the gravity, attentiveness and charm of one who offers his ear to the teacher. Among the very emotions of domestic life, to which no part of the commonwealth is committed, there is no small difference in how one must conduct oneself in public: in great favour or disfavour of fortune, in the brilliance or obscurity of birth, in abundance or want of means, in liberty or in an age given over to masters, in residence or in foreign sojourn. Precepts about these things, handed down one by one, would fill too large a volume. Nor will the same rule, which must never be changed with time and circumstances, fit all prescriptions. Each person, by his own prudence or that of wiser men, will see without a rule of precept what is fitting or unfitting, with whom he has to deal, and what he deems to be useful, and, above that, honourable.

units.la: Illud postremo non dissimulandum, magnam esse temporum, magnam locorum vim & rationem, quoad decorum, observandam. Tempori non servientem importunitatem{h}, ἀκαιρίᾳ[?] cum Theophrasto; loca non convenientem actionem, ἀπρεπῆ[?], quae vox ab origine sua ad latiorem ambitum deflexit, dixeris. Tempore igitur ludus laetitiae gestio, festis gaudio diebus moeror non convenit. Quod non tantum a gentilibus temporum discrimen, sed ab ecclesia Chri-stiana observatum, a Deo autore mandatum. Certos jejunio & lamentationi dies, jugo tyrannorum pre-mente, olim ecclesia praefixit. Eadem a festis nativita-ti Christi, aut primis hebdomadae diebus, quos quia cultui divino consecrabantur dominicos appellabant, jejunii maceratione & in templo geniculationem sub poena separationis[?] removit. Sed certior decori autor Deus, vae illis & perniciem extremam minita-tur, qui tempore fletibus destinato boves & oves ma-stando, carnes inglutiendo, vinum e pateris haurien-do, fidibus & psalterio canendo, hilarem sine cladis publicae cura diem ducunt. Passim apud Isaiam, Jere-miam, Amosem, & alios prophetas. Idem populo a captivitate reducto, templo e ruderibus excitato, Ju-daeis ab Hamanis destinata saevitia liberatis, sublatis jejunii diebus festos dies & epulares instituí permisit. Esdras, Nehemias, Chaggaeus, Estheraे liber pro testimonio consulendus.
units.tr: Finally, it must not be overlooked that the weight and reason of times and places are great and must be observed where propriety is concerned. Importunity that does not serve the occasion, with Theophrastus, is unseasonableness [ἀκαιρία]; an action unsuited to a place you might call unbecoming [ἀπρεπές], a word which from its origin has been bent to a wider sense. So play and exuberant mirth do not suit the time, nor does grief suit festal days. This distinction of times was observed not only by the Gentiles but also by the Christian Church, and was commanded by God as its author. Long ago, while the yoke of tyrants pressed upon it, the Church appointed fixed days for fasting and lamentation. The same Church removed fasting, mortification, and kneeling in the temple, under penalty of separation, from the festivals of Christ's nativity and from the first days of the week, which they called Lord's days because they were consecrated to divine worship. But God, the surer author of propriety, threatens woe and utter destruction to those who, at a time set for weeping, slaughter oxen and sheep, devour flesh, drink wine from bowls, sing to the lyre and psaltery, and spend a cheerful day with no care for public calamity. This appears everywhere in Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos, and the other prophets. The same God, when the people had been brought back from captivity, the temple raised from its ruins, and the Jews freed from the cruelty Haman had planned, permitted the days of fasting to be abolished and festal and feasting days to be instituted. Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai, and the book of Esther are to be consulted as witnesses.

units.la: Nec mundi salvator, ceremoniis prisca legis obdu-stis, hanc temporum diversitatem quoad decorum sustulit. Non possunt, inquit, filii sponsi lugere, quamdiu sponsus iis adest. Venient autem dies, cum ablatus ab iis sponsus fuerit, tunc jejunabunt. Matth. 9. v. 15.
units.tr: Nor did the Saviour of the world, when the ceremonies of the old law were set aside, remove this difference of times as regards propriety. "The sons of the bridegroom cannot mourn," he says, "as long as the bridegroom is with them. But the days will come when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then they will fast." Matt. 9. v. 15.

units.la: Quod jejunii ob sponsum ab iis ablatum tempus, a passionis initio ad resurrectionem patefactam capi de-bere, Christo interpreti credamus. Joh.16. v.16,2a[?]. & gaudii redituri dies. v. 22. Ne quis enim cum vul- go interpretum: dies illos luctus pro toto absentiæ. Christi à terris tempore accipiat, dissuadent Christi eodem capite verba: Expedit vobis me abire. v. 7. obstrepunt tot Pauli ad lætitiam hortationes. Philip. 4. v. 4. 1. Theflal. 5. v. 16. obsistit fe non capiens apo- ftolorum gaudium. Act. 2. 3. 4. 5 &c. Rom. 8. v. 35. 38. Temporiqui fe convenientem geret, nec in loco di- fcernendo errabit. Non enim fi saltare non inhone- ftum, & in foro, in templo, in exequiis matris decebit. Nec fi ferix cogitationes, fi lectio, fi fcriptio laudatur; & inter nuptiales convivas locus iis occupationibus, honestè dabitur. Sed ne & nos immoderata copia a- nimos lædamus, currentem calamum, sufflamina- mus.
units.tr: That the time of fasting on account of the bridegroom taken from them ought to be understood as running from the beginning of the passion until the resurrection was made manifest, let us believe Christ as interpreter: John 16. v. 16, 2a [?], and the days of returning joy, v. 22. That the days of mourning should be taken, with the common run of interpreters, as the whole period of Christ's absence from the earth, is dissuaded by Christ's own words in the same chapter: "It is expedient for you that I go away," v. 7. The many exhortations of Paul to joy oppose it: Phil. 4. v. 4; 1 Thess. 5. v. 16. The joy of the apostles, which reason cannot grasp, resists it: Acts 2, 3, 4, 5, etc.; Rom. 8. v. 35, 38. One who conducts himself fittingly to the time will not err in discerning the place. For dancing is not unbecoming in itself, and it will be no more unbecoming in the forum, in the temple, or at a mother's funeral than it is anywhere else. Nor, if cheerful thoughts, reading, or writing are praised, will those occupations be honourably given a place among the guests at a wedding feast. But lest we too wound minds by an immoderate abundance, let us check the running pen.

units.la: LVII. Imperii diuturnitas deteriores im- perantes facit.
units.tr: LVII. The longer a rule lasts, the worse it makes those who rule.

units.la: Crescit enim cum licentia dominandi libido, cum hac privatæ fortis hominum fastidium. Tum domi- nationis columnis tempore firmatis, minùs de funda- mento imperii, benevolentia hominum concilianda, cogitatur. Præterea aut cura reip. ut quæ morâ tæ- dium fui moveat, abjicitur; aut suspicace fene&tutis, ætate subrepente, potentiores opibus, genere, virtute; ideoque imperio gerendo digniores, ad cædem defti- nantur. Tiberius post tantam rerum experientiam, vi dominationis convulsus, in omnem crudelitatem & lasciviam mutatus abiit. Ne dum à minus firmo ani- mo, & rerum usu non edocto, mutatio in deterius non fit extimescenda. Titum, Vespasiani filium, eo nomine felicem prædicant, quod in primis imperii & ætatis annis, nondum torrente dominationis abre- ptus, ad plures abiit. De quo, cum Augusti mutatio- ne in diversum comparato, festivum Romanorum di- &um jactabatur: neque illum unquam amatum iri, fi breviori tempore vixisset; neque hunc, fi diuturniori. ἕη ἔτ' ἂν σεμνῷ ἐφιλήθη ποτὲ, εἰ ἐλάττω χρόνον ἐξήκεις[?], ἔτ' ἂν ἔτος εἰ τοὺς ἐλάττονα. Xiphilinus in Tito. Solum, omnium ante se imperatorum, Vespasianum in melius mutatum fuisse, Cornelius alicubi commonefacit, quo raritatem morum imperio in melius commutandorum indicat. Verum huic Taciti sententiae hoc, quod de Augusto modo proferebamus, obstare videatur. Non obstat tamen, rem non obiter examinantibus, Vespasianus pravi moris homo, donec privatus vixit, si assiduitatem muneris & vigilantiam excipias, à multis habebatur. In Augusto jam tum adulescentulo, multa futurae magnitudinis, multa egregiarum virtutum indicia exstabant. Imperii autem acerbitas, & avara tributi exactio, nondum firmata regni sede, temporum necessitatibus, & seditionum tumultui compescendo adscribitur. ἐπαγγέλλεσθαι[?] τὰς πολιτείας, καὶ ἀλλὰ τὰς σωτηρίας ἡδονὰς ἀπὸ τῶν μεγάλων ἐπὶ τοῦ χρόνου λαμπρότητας[?] Xiphil. in Tito. Obstat de Vespasiano amarulenta pecuniae, etiam à benemeritis provinciis, etiam è re sordida, exactio. quam idem Xiphilinus reip. indigentia, & principis in eam cura, pecuniâ in publicum usum conversâ, excusat. Obstat Philosophorum Stoicae sectae in exilium ejectio; nonnullorum saeva animadversione trucidatio. Ita ut illa verba Taciti, expulsis insuper sapientia professoribus, atque omni bona arte in exilium acta, non de Domitiano, verum de Vespasiano intelligenda videantur. Verum cum immoderata arrogantis sectae obloquendi libertas alia via compesci nequiverit, & solutam obedientiam dissolutio imperii sequatur: damus hanc Flavio veniam, si remotis autoritatis tuendae obstaculis, non sibi magis quàm publicae tranquillitati consuluit. nisi forte Dio, Stoicae sectae nunquam satis aequus, hanc liberae factionis arrogantiam in majus extulit. Vitanda sane imperantibus inhumana crudelitas, sed & parendi necessitate astrictis nimia verborum in superioris licentia cavenda.
units.tr: For with long power the lust to dominate grows, and with it contempt for private citizens. Once the pillars of dominion have been fixed in time, less thought is given to the foundations of empire and to winning the goodwill of men. Moreover, concern for the commonwealth, which tends to stir disgust through its delay, is cast aside; or, as age creeps on, suspicion of the new grows, and those who are richer in resources, birth and virtue, and therefore more worthy to govern, are marked for slaughter. Tiberius, after such great experience of affairs, was overturned by the lust for power and went away changed into every kind of cruelty and wantonness. Nor is a change for the worse to be feared less in a man of weaker spirit and without experience of affairs. They praise Titus, the son of Vespasian, as fortunate on this account: that in the first years of his rule and of his life, not yet swept along by the rush of power, he passed on to more years. Concerning him, when the change was compared with that of Augustus, the witty Roman saying was bandied about: that he would never have been loved had he lived a shorter time, nor Augustus had he lived a longer one. [ἕη ἔτ' ἂν σεμνῷ ἐφιλήθη ποτὲ, εἰ ἐλάττω χρόνον ἐξήκεις[?], ἔτ' ἂν ἔτος εἰ τοὺς ἐλάττονα.] Xiphilinus in Titus. Cornelius reminds us somewhere that Vespasian alone, of all the emperors before him, was changed for the better, and by this he indicates how rare it is for rulers to change for the better. Yet what we have just said of Augustus seems to stand in the way of this opinion of Tacitus. It does not, however, stand in the way for those who examine the matter carefully: Vespasian, a man of bad habits while he lived as a private citizen, was held by many to be good, if you except his diligence and vigilance in office. In Augustus, even as a young man, there were already many signs of future greatness and of distinguished virtues. But the harshness of his rule and his greedy exaction of tribute are ascribed to the needs of the times, and to the need to suppress the uproar of sedition, before his seat of power was firmly established. [ἐπαγγέλλεσθαι[?] τὰς πολιτείας, καὶ ἀλλὰ τὰς σωτηρίας ἡδονὰς ἀπὸ τῶν μεγάλων ἐπὶ τοῦ χρόνου λαμπρότητας[?]] Xiphilinus in Titus. Against Vespasian stands the bitter exaction of money, even from provinces that had deserved well, and even by base means; yet the same Xiphilinus excuses this by the poverty of the commonwealth and the emperor's care for it, since the money was turned to public use. Against him stands also the expulsion of the Stoic philosophers and the cruel slaughter of some of them. So those words of Tacitus, expelled moreover the teachers of wisdom, and every good art driven into exile, seem to be understood not of Domitian but of Vespasian. But since the immoderate freedom of a proud sect to speak against the government could not be checked by any other means, and since dissolute disobedience is followed by the dissolution of empire, we grant this indulgence to Flavius, if, having removed the obstacles to upholding authority, he looked to his own safety no more than to public tranquillity. Unless perhaps Dio, never fair enough to the Stoic sect, magnified this arrogance of a free faction beyond its measure. Inhuman cruelty must certainly be avoided by those who rule; but those who are bound by the necessity of obeying must also guard against excessive license of speech against their superiors.

units.la: LVIII. Nec furioso gladius, nec puero sceptra committenda.
units.tr: LVIII. Neither the sword to a madman, nor the sceptre to a boy.

units.la: MǷ ἀρχὴ μηδέ, Graecorum recte monetur adagio. Regi enim, non regere aetas ea nata est. Cajus Caesar, & furiosus & adolescens, imperii habenas, non bene ominantibus prudentioribus, capessiturus erat. Eum vix finitâ pueritiâ, ignarum omnium, aut peßimis in-nutritum, meliora capessiturum Macrone duce, Arrun-tius providus futurorum negabat. Pravae ominationis causa in paucis verbis quadruplex, ab uno fermè filo omnes pendentes. 1. aetas imbecilla. 2. rerum ignoran-tia. 3. prava in dominatione patrui educatio. 4. scelera-ta ministrorum affuefactio. Primum ex fe argumen-tum sufficiens: negata & auctoritate pueris, & animi firmitate. Caeteraab hoc ita fluunt, ut tamen non o-mninò convertantur. Nam & stolidis aliquando feni-bus maculae eae adhaerescunt: pueris verò frequentius. A fene nobilis illa vox, non à puero, profecta : Ovidius ...
units.tr: "Let no one begin to rule" [μὴ ἀρχὴ μηδέ] is rightly warned against by a Greek proverb. That age is born to be ruled, not to rule. Caius Caesar, both mad and a youth, was about to take up the reins of empire, and the wiser men did not augur well of it. Arruntius, far-sighted about the future, said that he was scarcely out of boyhood, ignorant of everything, or reared among the worst men, and would take up better things under Macro as his guide. There are four reasons for this unfavourable prediction, all hanging almost from one thread: (1) an immature age; (2) ignorance of affairs; (3) an upbringing under an uncle's harsh rule; (4) being accustomed to the wicked deeds of his ministers. The first reason is sufficient by itself, since boys are denied both authority and firmness of mind. The others follow from this so closely that they are not wholly separate from it. For those stains sometimes cling to foolish old men too, but far more often to boys. That noble saying, "from an old man and not from a boy," came from an old man: Ovid ...

units.la: LIX. Pravae educationis damnum liberi, culpam parentes, dolorem utrique sentiunt.
units.tr: LIX. A bad upbringing harms the child, the parents bear the blame, and both feel the grief.

units.la: Senum igitur, & maxime parentum, sapientia in-euntis aetatis inscitia regenda est. Quae si a tenera radice plantae luxuriantis castigatio negligitur, in sylvescentem naturam excrescit. Quodque magis exhor-tescendum, se & a se pendentes ruina subita proster-net[?]. Sex. Papinius consulari familia, repentinum & informem exitum dilegit, jacto[?] in praeceps corpore, causa jactus a desperatione: desperatio a vitae & rei familiaris depravatione: depravatio a matris indulgentia. Causa ad matrem referebatur: quae pridem repudiata, assentationibus atque luxu perpulisset juvenem ad se, quorum effugium nonnisi morte invenire[t]. Ergo ut simiae foetum suum amplexu & ad pectus ap-pressu, ita haec filium luxu & assentatione interemit. Caveant igitur parentes, caveant nutritii ac paedagogi assentationes, nisi fidei suae commissorum interitus autores audire, & culpam depravati moris gerere certo cum damno velint. Igitur accusata in senatu, quanquam genua patrum advolveretur, lustumque[?] communem, & magis imbecillum tali super casu feminarum animum, aliaque in eundem dolorem maes-ta & miseranda diu ferret, urbe tamen in decem annos prohibita est, donec minor filius lubricum juventa exiret. Ergo cum dolore infamiam, cum damno culpam luens, non expectatum assentatione praemium mater tulit: & alteri filiorum melius, matre amota, consultum. Amplus hic excurrendi locus esset, nisi pervulgatus de educatione campus, inquirendi materiam praescinderet. Unum hoc moneo: arboretum amoenum fixuro, seminarium tenerorum virgul-torum, & primam crescentium plantarum radicem, aut primo fe effundentes surculos non esse hortulanó negligendos.
units.tr: The sense of elders, and above all of parents, must therefore govern the ignorance of a young person as it grows. If the pruning of a plant's tender root is neglected while it is still sprouting, the plant grows into a wild and untamed nature. What is more, one must warn that a sudden fall may lay low both those who hang themselves and those who depend on them. Sextus Papinius, of a consular family, chose a sudden and shapeless death, throwing his body headlong. The cause of the throw was despair; the cause of the despair was the ruin of his life and fortune; the cause of the ruin was his mother's indulgence. The blame was laid on his mother, who, though long since divorced, had by flatteries and luxury drawn the young man to herself, and he could find no escape from her except by death. So, as the ape crushes its offspring in its embrace and presses it to its breast, so she destroyed her son with luxury and flattery. Let parents therefore beware, and let nurses and tutors beware of flattery, unless they wish to hear themselves named as the authors of the ruin of those committed to their trust, and to bear the blame of a corrupted character with certain loss. Accordingly, when she was accused in the senate, although she threw herself at the knees of the senators, and although she endured for a long time her shared grief and her mind, weaker than a man's in such a calamity, and other sorrowful and pitiable tokens of the same pain, she was nonetheless banished from the city for ten years, until her younger son should leave the slippery years of youth. So the mother, paying for her infamy with grief and for her fault with loss, received not the reward that flattery had promised; and it was better for the other son that his mother was removed. Here there would be room for a long digression, were it not that the well-worn field of education cuts short the matter I have to investigate. I give only this one warning: for one who means to plant a pleasant orchard, a nursery of tender shoots, the first root of growing plants, or the young twigs that first put forth their leaves, the gardener must not be neglectful.

units.la: LX. Sola mors nulla simulatione aut mi-nis absterretur.
units.tr: LX. Only death is not turned aside by pretence or threats.

units.la: Quod apud Ariftophanem in Ranis Æfchylus: Μόνῳ θεῶν γὰρ ἢ Φυτάλῳ ἢ δώμων ἐχέ,
units.tr: What Aeschylus says in Aristophanes' Frogs: Μόνῳ θεῶν γὰρ ἢ Φυτάλῳ ἢ δώμων ἐχέ

units.la: Mors sola donis nescit oblatis capi: honnihil à nobis immutatum dici recte queat: Πλαξὶν μόνῳ γὰρ ἢ Φυτάλῳ ὅτι ἔχει λόγων,
units.tr: Death alone does not know how to be won by gifts offered. Nothing need be changed by us in rendering this rightly: Πλαξὶν μόνῳ γὰρ ἢ Φυτάλῳ ὅτι ἔχει λόγων

units.la: Mors sola verbis spernit argutis capi.
units.tr: Death alone scorns to be won by clever words.

units.la: Quanquam hæc ita sint, tamen Tiberius, uti per ô-minem vitam simulationum techniis confutus, itâ etiam contrá mortem irruentem se simulatione ar-mavit. Jam Tiberium corpus, jam vires, nondum dis-simulatio deserebat. Idem animi rigor, sermone ac vultu intentus, quasi interdum comitate, quamvis manifestam defectionem tegebat. Sed biduo inter-mortuus, non potuit obitum ullos mortales celare; nec vitam reducem sæva in morte simulare. Aliis in rebus diu simulatio etiam perspicacissimos fallit: Fu-cus cadaverosæ faciei illitus, pro formidanda faciem splendentem oculis deceptis objicit. Vulpinam no-cendi astutiam multi blandimentis, & simulata amici-tiæ fronte obducunt. Hilaritatem in luctu, aut contrá luctum in hilaritate multi fingunt. Quæ creberrima fallendi materies, plurimi vitiorum fasciculis in sinu abditis, proborum virorum externa larva vultum in-duunt. Etiam vires quis in defectione, visus acumen exacutientibus oculis assimulare conatus est. Solam in morte vitam, in dissolutione animæ præsentiam; nemo mortalium fingendo repræ-sentavit.
units.tr: Yet although this is so, Tiberius, who had been refuted by the arts of pretence throughout his whole life, armed himself with pretence even against death as it rushed upon him. Now his body, now his strength, but not yet his dissimulation, was failing him. The same stiffness of mind, intent on speech and expression, concealed at times, with a show of courtesy, a manifest collapse. But having lain senseless for two days, he could not hide his death from mortals, nor, in his cruel dying, feign a returned life. In other matters pretence has long deceived even the most perceptive; a cosmetic daubed on a corpse-like face presents a shining face to eyes that have been deceived, in place of a terrifying one. Many cover the fox-like cunning of harming with flattery and a feigned face of friendship. Many feign cheerfulness in grief, or, on the contrary, grief in cheerfulness. This is the most frequent material for deception: many, with bundles of vices hidden in their bosom, put on the face of upright men under an outward mask. Some have even tried to imitate strength while in weakness, and keen sight while their eyes were dim. Only life in death, and the presence of the soul in its dissolution, no mortal has ever represented by feigning.

units.la: LXI. Nullæ contra domesticas insidias excubiæ.
units.tr: LXI. No watch against domestic plots.

units.la: Tiberium circumstantes satellites, & objectæ foribus excubiæ, satis contra externos assultus munierant; munire contra nepotes, & quos fidissimos ministrorum habuerat, non poterant. Macro, cui suam ac regni salutem commiserat, in gratiam Caji opprimi senem objectu multa vestis jubet, discedique ab limine. Explicatius hæc Dio, & culpa in Cajum rejecta. [illegible, ~14 letters] ὡς καὶ [illegible, ~10 letters] καὶ [illegible, ~12 letters] καὶ [illegible, ~8 letters], ὡς καὶ [illegible, ~12 letters] [illegible, ~10 letters], ἐξ [illegible, ~10 letters] [illegible, ~14 letters], [illegible, ~12 letters] [illegible, ~6 letters] τῷ αὐτῷ καὶ τῷ Μακρῷ[?]. i. e. Cibum petenti negavit, quasi damnum ei laturum: injectisque multis ac densis vestimentis, tanquam calefactione egenti, suffocavit eum; nonnihil etiam Macronis auxilio u-sus. libro 58[?]. Simili suorum perfidia, simili mortis genere, Benhadadus Syrorum rex obiit. Chazael enim, quo in militiæ & aulæ ministerio summa cum fidei opinione usus erat, acceptam stragulam intingens in aquam super faciem illius extendit, atque ita is mortuus est. 2. Reg. 8. v. 15. ideo nimirum stragulam aquæ immersam madefecit, ut poris obstructis densatior, nullum respirationi meatum præberet. Quo in loco non prætereunda est interpretum vulgatorum oscitantia: qui Elisæum mendacii infimulan-tes, versu decimo vertunt: dic ei, omnino revalescés. Gallica versio mollienda interpretatione moderatior: vous pourriez vivre, naturali nimirum vivendi facul-tate, nullis insidiis oppressa.
units.tr: Tiberius's bodyguards and the guards posted at his doors had sufficiently protected him against outside attacks, but they could not protect him against his grandsons and those whom he had held as the most faithful of his ministers. Macro, to whom he had entrusted his own safety and that of the kingdom, ordered the old man to be smothered under a heap of clothing and the doorway cleared, in Caligula's favour. Dio explains this more fully and puts the blame on Caligula: [illegible Greek]. That is: he refused food to the old man when he asked for it, as though it would harm him; then, heaping many thick garments on him as if he were in need of warming, he suffocated him, partly with Macro's help. Book 58[?]. Benhadad, king of Syria, died by a similar treachery of his own people and a similar kind of death. Hazael, whom he had used in the army and at court with a high reputation for loyalty, took a cloth, dipped it in water and spread it over his face, and so he died (2 Kings 8:15). No doubt he soaked the cloth in water so that, its pores being blocked and the cloth thicker, it allowed no passage for breathing. Here the carelessness of the Vulgate translators must not be passed over: they accuse Elisha of lying and, in verse ten, render: "Say to him, you will certainly recover." The French version, more moderate, softens the sense: vous pourriez vivre, "you could live," that is, by the natural faculty of living, not overcome by any plots.

units.la: Huc illos procul dubio [illegible, ~3 letters] Keri in margine adscriptum [illegible, ~3 letters] pro לא[?], ei pro non, adduxit.
units.tr: To this, without doubt, the marginal note of the Keri led them, which has written in the margin [illegible] for לא, "to him" for "not."

units.la: Adduxit & responsio Chazaelis, quasi ex ore prophetæ, dixit mihi, Omnino vives. v. 14. Sed utri tandem aptius mendacium incudetur, aulicone mancipio, ad gratiam respondere edocto; an viro Dei, nihil gratiam aut odium regum curanti ? [?] aü-tem, & marginalis biblici textus annotatio ; ingeniosis hominum commentis, non ore Dei prodiit. Recte igitur recentior interpres: abi, dic; non omnino reva-lefces: nam ostendit mihi Jehova, eum omnino mo-riturum. Nec rarum est: Vau copulativum pro con-junctione causali accipi.
units.tr: The reply of Hazael also led them, as if from the mouth of the prophet: "He said to me, You will surely live" (v. 14). But which of the two is more fitting to be charged with a lie: a courtier servant taught to answer for favour, or the man of God, who cared nothing for the favour or hatred of kings? But the marginal annotation of the biblical text came from the clever inventions of men, not from the mouth of God. Rightly, therefore, the more recent translator renders: "Go, say, you will not surely recover, for the LORD has shown me that he will surely die." Nor is this rare: the copulative Vau is taken for a causal conjunction.

units.la: Sed hæc ὡς [illegible, ~5 letters]. Poterant infinita exempla regum, à domesticis aut à custodia sua occisorum, adduci: nisi materia multorum jam diligentiâ præce-pta, silendi legem nobis imponeret:
units.tr: But these [illegible Greek]. Countless examples could be adduced of kings killed by their own household or by their guards, were it not that the matter, already handled with great diligence by many, imposes on us the law of silence.

units.la: LXII.
units.tr: LXII.

units.la: Extremus vitæ actus ad plausum fo-lertissimus.
units.tr: The final act of life most skilful for applause

units.la: Morum illi tempus: egregium vita famaque, quoad privatus, vel in imperiis sub Augusto fuit.
units.tr: His time for manners: an outstanding life and reputation, so long as he was a private man, or held commands under Augustus.

units.la: Vitæ, ut diei; serenitas[?] non ab aurora ortu, sed à perpetuo Phœbi lucentis fluxu, judicanda. Nec po-test ullus vitæ tenor perpetuus esse, si ab externo filo pendeat: Fugax virtutis & evanidus color est, qui depulso constantiæ & conscientiæ fuco, solo metu aut pudore tingitur.
units.tr: The serenity of a life, as of a day, is to be judged not from the dawn's rising but from the constant flow of the shining Phoebus. Nor can any course of life be perpetual if it hangs on an external thread. The colour of virtue is fleeting and fading when, the dye of constancy and conscience being removed, it is tinted only by fear or shame.

units.la: Annum & arborem nostri à vernali flore, sed au-tumnali fructu æstimamus. Fabula etiamsi quovis actu steterit, nisi quinto probe peracto ad Plaudite venerit, coronam non meretur. Tiberius, contra scenicorum artificum morem, in prima vitæ scenâ Roscium imitatus, paulatim ad deteriora flexit. Ejus vitam & mores (nam fortunam, judicio non subje-ctam[?], non judico) per quinque dramatis actus, exa-mini appensos; tanquam brevi tabella collustrabi-mus.
units.tr: We judge a year and a tree not by their spring blossom but by their autumn fruit. Even if a play has held its ground in every act, it does not deserve the crown unless, the fifth act well performed, it comes to Plaudite. Tiberius, contrary to the custom of stage performers, imitated Roscius in the first scene of his life and gradually turned to worse things. His life and manners (for I do not judge his fortune, which is not subject to judgement) we will set out for examination over five acts of the drama, and survey them as in a brief table.

units.la: PRIMUS TIBERIANÆ vitæ Actus:
units.tr: FIRST ACT OF TIBERIUS' LIFE:

units.la: Tiberius ... Drama ... Keti. Aüimi tiñ- Bufa: Drama Ti- beriana vitæ.
units.tr: Tiberius ... Drama ... Keti. Aüimi tiñ- Bufa: Drama of Tiberius' life.

units.la: Secundus Actus.
units.tr: Second Act.

units.la: Occultum ac subdolum fingendis virtutibus, donec Germanicus [?]ac Drusus superfuere.
units.tr: Secretive and sly in feigning virtues, as long as Germanicus and Drusus survived.

units.la: Tertius Actus.
units.tr: Third Act.

units.la: Idem inter bona malaque mixtus, incolumi ma-tre.
units.tr: The same man, a mixture of good and bad, while his mother was alive.

units.la: Quartus Actus.
units.tr: Fourth Act.

units.la: Intestabilis saevitia, sed obtectis libidinibus, dum Se-janum dilexit, timuitve.
units.tr: Detestable cruelty, but with his lusts concealed, while he loved, or feared, Sejanus.

units.la: Quintus Actus.
units.tr: Fifth Act.

units.la: Postremo in scelera simul ac dedecora prorupit, post-quam remoto pudore & metu suo tantum ingenio ute-batur. Haec morum Tiberii, haec vitae catastrophe, a promisso boni ingenii flore percipiendis fructibus multum diversa. Nimirum quia solstitialis herba, vivo succo non radicata, quo luxuriavit caniculae calore emarcuit. Fixas nisi radices virtus egerit, quovis vel aestu vel aquae pluviae torrente decidet. Quae à fama & hominum opinione, id est fumo, dependet; fumo in auras dissipato, vel ante, evanescet. Tiberius ad famam omnia dirigens, fama virtutum simulationem metiens, ad famae aeternitatem non pervenit. Famae nimirum bonarum laudum buccinatricis: nam quamvis, etiam vitae non bene actae, famam sapiens nemo moratur. Plotina, Trajani imperatoris uxor, non parum Tiberio sapientior, cum palatium primum ingrederetur, ad scalas & ad multitudinem conversa: Talis, inquit, hic ingrediar, qualis & egredi volo: atque ita semper omne imperii tempus gessit, ut nullam culpae vituperationem sustineret. Dio in Trajano.
units.tr: Finally he broke out into crimes and disgrace at once, once he had put aside shame and fear and used only his own disposition. This was the outcome of Tiberius' character and life, very different from the promised flower of a good nature from which fruit was to be gathered. Indeed, like summer grass, not rooted in living sap, it withered in the heat of the dog-star under which it had flourished. Unless virtue puts down fixed roots, it will fall to any heat or torrent of rain. Virtue that depends on reputation and men's opinion, which is to say on smoke, will vanish once the smoke is dispersed into the air, or even before. Tiberius, directing everything toward his reputation and measuring the appearance of virtue by fame, did not attain the eternity of fame. Fame is indeed the trumpeter of good praise, for although even a life not well lived may have fame, no wise man sets store by it. Plotina, the wife of the emperor Trajan, not a little wiser than Tiberius, when she first entered the palace, turned toward the stairs and the crowd: "I will enter here," she said, "as I wish to leave." And so she conducted herself through her whole time of power, so as to bear no blame for any fault. Dio, in Trajan.

units.la: Dio in Trajano.
units.tr: Dio, in Trajan.

units.la: Ipse Trajanus diverso à Tiberio itinere, quod gloriae adipiscendae stadium ingressus est, à carceribus ad cal-cem decucurrit. Ea inprimis evitando, quorum causa recenti abominatione Domitianus, Tiberii in mul-
units.tr: Trajan himself, by a course different from Tiberius', entered the race-course of winning glory and ran from the starting gates down to the turning-post. Above all he avoided those things for whose sake Domitian, an imitator of Tiberius in many respects, had been hated with recent abhorrence.

units.la: tis imitator, fuerat. Primò omnium, quia illi illuftrea vires necando, & vastitatem senatus faciendo, regnum suum firmabant: hic primo imperii adeptu sua manu senatui scripsit, nulli viro bono mortem aut infamiam illaturum, quod jurejurando sacrarum, fide rerum praftabat.
units.tr: First of all, because the others strengthened their rule by killing illustrious men and laying waste the senate, Trajan, on attaining power, wrote with his own hand to the senate that he would bring death or infamy on no good man, and he guaranteed this by a sacred oath and his faithful word.

units.la: Illi diffidentia, dissimulatione, delationibus alendis fundamenta folio suo substernebant: hic neminem metuendo, delatores é rep. sustulit. Illi multorum hæreditatibus, multorum fifcoadjudicandis bonis in-hiabant: hic alienis facultatibus æquè ac cædibus abs ftinebat. Illi consortia hominum fugiebant, aut formidandi intererant: hic familiari consuetudine, ve- nationibus, conviviis, conventibus joca & feria misce- bat. Illi servos in dominum majestatis in quaestione torquebant: hic omnem ejusmodi torturam, & ipsam majestatis quaestionem abolebat. Illi fidiffimis fi- dem habere dubitabant: hic fidem neque maximè fùfpe&is denegabat. Suriæ enim, insidiarum apud fe delati, medico barbam tondendam, fiduciæ signum, præbuit. Illi rationem imperandi non aliter consta- re, quàm fi uni reddatur, arbitrabantur: hic imperio cum senatoribus, cum præfectis communicato, glà- dium contra fe stringendum, fi malè imperaverit, por- rexit. Militaribus in rebus illi ad exercitum ducem dum segnes, bonorum militari gloriæ invidebant: hic duxidem & autor bellorum, claros imperio Romano triumphos peperit. Jure igitur nomen Optimi, quod neminiantè contigerat, viventi delatum defun- &to adhæsit. Libidinum quidem maculis, αν και ενδεικνυμενος non purgabatur. Sed eas quæsitus, iis quas dixi artibus, civium amor & benevolentia tegebat. Portum jam subeunte na- vecolligenda sunt vela, & anchoram demissuri funes laxandi. Quid exoptandi habeat aula Tiberiana, quam ut exploratores trivimus, facundiffimi Romae- norum verbis, ut pondus existimationis ab autore fer- moni accedat, pandemus. Quis est, proh Deùm atque hominum fidem, qui velit, ut neque diligat quenquam, nec ipse ab ullo diligatur, circumfluere omnibus copiis, atque in omnium rerum abundantia vivere? Hæc enim est tyrannorum vita nimirum: in qua nulla fides, nulla caritas, nulla stabilis benevolentiæ potest esse fiducia: omnia semper suspecta, atque solicita: nullus locus est amicitiæ, quis enim aut eum diligat, quem metuit, aut eum, à quo se metui putat? Coluntur tamen simulatione amicitiæ duntaxat ad tempus. quod si forte, ut fit plerumque, ceciderint; tum intelligitur, quàm fuerint inopes amicorum. Cicero de Amicitia, Quam autem apud viros bonos existimationem fucati sermones, torta in contrarium sensum verba, & mendacio infectæ simulationes mereantur; pro me poëtarum Tragicorum aquila, Æschylus in Prometheo vincto, eloquatur.
units.tr: Those rulers laid the foundations of their throne on distrust, dissimulation and the nourishing of informers. This one, fearing no one, removed the informers from the commonwealth. Those rulers gaped after the inheritances of many and the confiscation of many men's goods to the treasury. This one kept his hands off other men's property no less than off their lives. Those rulers avoided the company of men, or joined it only out of fear. This one mixed jokes and festivities into his familiar company, hunting, banquets and social gatherings. Those rulers put slaves to torture in inquiries into treason against their master. This one abolished all such torture, and the very inquiry into treason. Those rulers hesitated to trust their most faithful men. This one denied trust neither to those most under suspicion. For when Suria was reported to him for plotting, he gave his barber the order to shave his beard, a sign of confidence. Those rulers thought that the exercise of power could not be secure unless it rested in one man. This one shared his power with the senators and the prefects, and offered his own sword to be drawn against himself if he ruled badly. In military affairs, those rulers were slack in leading their armies, and begrudged good soldiers their military glory. This one led the armies himself and, as author of the wars, won for the Roman empire triumphs that were renowned. Rightly, then, the name of Best, which had fallen to no one before, was attached after his death to the man who had been called it while living. Indeed, he was not cleansed of the stains of his lusts, although he was not ... But by the arts I have described he covered them with the love and goodwill of the citizens. Now, as the ship nears harbour, the sails must be gathered in and the ropes loosened for dropping anchor. What the Tiberian court desires, as we have sought out its spies, we shall set forth in the words of the most eloquent Romans, so that the weight of authority may attach to our discourse from its author. Who, in God's and men's good faith, would wish to swim in every resource and live in every abundance of goods, while loving no one and being loved by no one? For this is surely the life of tyrants, in which there can be no faith, no affection, no firm confidence in goodwill: everything is always suspected and anxious; there is no place for friendship, for who could love the man he fears, or love the man by whom he thinks himself feared? Yet such men are courted, for a time only, by a pretence of friendship; but if they fall, as often happens, then it is understood how destitute of friends they were. Cicero, On Friendship. But what esteem feigned speeches, words twisted to a contrary sense, and simulations tainted with lies deserve among good men, let the eagle of the tragic poets, Aeschylus in his Prometheus Bound, speak on my behalf.

units.la: — — — νόσημα γὰρ[?]
units.tr: ... for it is a disease [νόσημα γὰρ]

units.la: Αἴσχιστον εἶναί φημι σωφρόνων λόγων[?].
units.tr: "The most shameful thing, I say, is of sober words" [Αἴσχιστον εἶναί φημι σωφρόνων λόγων]

units.la: A qua nos morbi fœditate prohibeat, liberet, abluat; qui cum sit mens purissima, compositos dolos, fraudes, & omnes fallacias æterno odio aversatur.
units.tr: May He keep us from, free us from, and cleanse us of that foulness of disease; for since He is the purest mind, He abhors composed deceits, frauds and all treachery with eternal hatred.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END
